Remote Learning and In-Person Schooling: Effects on Students

The way students learn can shape more than their grades. It can influence their motivation, relationships, and sense of identity. Remote learning and in-person schooling offer different experiences, and neither is perfect for every student. Understanding their effects can help families and schools make better choices.

Remote learning can give students greater flexibility. Without a daily commute, they may have more time for sleep, family responsibilities, or independent study. Some students feel motivated by being able to work at their own pace. Recorded lessons can also be replayed when a topic is difficult. For students who feel anxious in a crowded classroom, learning from home may make it easier to participate.

However, remote learning also requires strong self-discipline. At home, students may face distractions such as phones, television, or household noise. Without a teacher nearby, it can be harder to stay focused and finish assignments. Long hours in front of a screen may also cause tiredness and reduce interest in schoolwork. When students receive less immediate feedback, they may feel unsure about their progress.

In-person schooling provides a more structured routine. Students attend classes at set times, and teachers can notice when someone is confused or losing focus. Classroom discussions and hands-on activities can make lessons feel more engaging. Seeing classmates work can also encourage students to keep trying. For many learners, the separation between school and home makes it easier to concentrate.

In-person school can support social development in important ways. Students practice listening, sharing ideas, working in groups, and resolving disagreements. Everyday conversations during breaks can help friendships grow naturally. These experiences teach students how to understand different points of view. On the other hand, busy school environments may feel stressful, especially for students who need quiet or more time to respond.

Remote learning changes the way students build relationships. Video calls and online chats allow classmates to stay connected, but they do not always create the same sense of closeness as meeting face to face. It may be harder to notice someone’s feelings through a screen. Students who are shy might find online communication more comfortable, while others may feel isolated. A lack of casual interaction can make it difficult to feel part of a school community.

School experiences can also shape identity. In person, students explore their interests through clubs, sports, performances, and conversations with peers. They may discover skills and values by taking part in shared activities. Teachers and classmates can recognize their strengths, helping them feel confident. Yet comparison, peer pressure, or exclusion can also affect how students see themselves.

Remote learning can give students more control over how they present themselves. They may feel safer speaking from a familiar place, and online tools can help them express their ideas in different ways. At the same time, limited contact may make it harder to develop a strong sense of belonging. Students may miss chances to try new roles and receive encouragement from others. Their identities can feel less connected to school life.

The effects of either learning style depend on a student’s personality, circumstances, and support. A student with reliable technology and a quiet study space may thrive remotely, while another may struggle without direct help. In-person schooling may provide structure and connection, but it may not meet every student’s needs equally. Teachers can support motivation by setting clear goals, giving useful feedback, and making lessons active. Schools can strengthen social development and identity by creating welcoming spaces where all students can participate.

Overall, remote learning and in-person schooling influence motivation, social development, and identity in different ways. Remote learning can encourage independence and flexibility, but it may also bring distraction and isolation. In-person schooling offers routine and face-to-face connection, while sometimes creating pressure or overstimulation. The best learning environment is one that helps students feel engaged, supported, and accepted. By combining the strengths of both approaches when possible, schools can give more students the chance to succeed.

The paper addresses an important problem: how to learn useful molecular representations from SMILES and use them for property prediction and molecular design. Its combination of sequence modeling, latent-space optimization, and property-guided generation is potentially valuable to both cheminformatics research and practical drug discovery. The topic is timely, and the focus on a shared representation for prediction and design could make the work broadly relevant.

A key strength is the paper’s clear motivation for learning representations directly from molecular strings rather than relying exclusively on hand-engineered descriptors. The proposed workflow appears to connect molecular encoding, property estimation, and candidate generation in a coherent way. If supported by adequate experiments, this integration could offer a useful alternative to pipelines that treat prediction and design as separate tasks. The paper also recognizes an important practical constraint: optimized outputs must correspond to chemically valid and meaningful molecules, not merely favorable points in a learned space.

The experimental evaluation should be strengthened by comparisons with strong and current baselines, including established fingerprint-based models and competitive pretrained molecular language models. Comparisons should use identical data splits, preprocessing, and evaluation protocols wherever possible. The authors should also clarify whether splitting is random, scaffold-based, or time-based, since random splits can overstate generalization to novel chemical structures. Performance should be reported across multiple seeds, with uncertainty estimates or statistical tests where appropriate.

For property prediction, the paper would benefit from a fuller account of data sources, dataset sizes, missing-value handling, and train-validation-test separation. It should explain how duplicate molecules, alternative SMILES for the same compound, and potential label leakage are handled. Results should include metrics suited to each task and, where relevant, calibration or uncertainty measures. An ablation study would help establish the contribution of the encoder, pretraining strategy, latent-space objective, and any chemical constraints.

The latent-space optimization section requires particular care. The authors should describe how optimization is performed, how candidate molecules are decoded, and how invalid or duplicate outputs are treated. They should report validity, uniqueness, novelty, and property improvement together rather than emphasizing target-property scores alone. Optimization should also be assessed for synthesizability, structural plausibility, and distance from the training distribution. Without these checks, apparent gains may reflect exploitation of model errors rather than meaningful molecular improvement.

The paper should discuss the limitations of SMILES representations, especially their dependence on string form and the possibility that equivalent molecules receive different encodings. It would be useful to report whether randomized SMILES or other augmentation improves robustness. The authors should also clarify how stereochemistry, charged states, and molecular sanitization are handled. These implementation details can materially affect both prediction accuracy and generation quality.

Overall, the work has a promising direction, but the strength of its conclusions depends on a more rigorous evaluation of generalization and generated candidates. I recommend clarifying the experimental protocol, adding stronger baselines and ablations, and broadening the assessment of chemical quality. With these revisions, the paper could make a useful contribution to molecular representation learning and property-guided design.

Using a phone while driving is a dangerous habit that can have serious consequences. A driver who looks at a screen takes their eyes off the road. Even a few seconds of distraction can be enough to miss a red light, a pedestrian, or a sudden change in traffic. Phone conversations can also take a driver’s attention away from making safe decisions. Texting is especially risky because it requires looking, reading, and typing. A distracted driver may drift into another lane or fail to stop in time. This can lead to crashes that injure or kill drivers, passengers, cyclists, and pedestrians. The consequences can affect victims and their families for many years. Drivers may also face fines, legal charges, or higher insurance costs. An accident can damage vehicles and make roads less safe for everyone. Using a phone behind the wheel is not worth the risk of missing a message or call. Drivers should silence their phones or put them out of reach before starting a trip. Staying focused on the road is a simple choice that can help save lives.

Conditions at Mauritania’s Mbera refugee camp are worsening as more people flee violence in neighboring Mali, stretching already limited services and supplies. The camp, in southeastern Mauritania near the Malian border, has hosted refugees for years. Recent arrivals have added pressure to a community where access to water, food, health care and shelter is already difficult.

Families arriving from Mali say insecurity and conflict have forced them to leave their homes. Many have traveled long distances with few belongings, and some arrive exhausted or in need of medical attention. Aid workers say the influx is making it harder to meet the needs of both new arrivals and long-term residents.

Water remains one of the camp’s most pressing challenges. Residents may have to wait for supplies or travel to collect them, while demand rises with each new group. Limited sanitation facilities also increase the risk of disease, particularly among children.

Food assistance is another concern, with households facing shortages and rising needs. Humanitarian organizations warn that funding constraints have limited their ability to provide consistent support. Some families are reportedly reducing meals or relying on help from neighbors.

Shelter conditions are difficult, especially for people arriving without tents or other protection from the harsh climate. Crowded living spaces offer little privacy and can leave families vulnerable to heat, cold and rain. Health facilities, meanwhile, face growing caseloads and shortages of staff and essential medicines.

Children make up a significant share of those affected. Aid agencies say interrupted schooling and limited access to safe spaces can leave young people at greater risk. Women and girls also face heightened protection concerns in crowded settings with inadequate sanitation.

Mauritanian authorities and humanitarian partners are working to assist refugees, but say resources are not keeping pace with needs. Agencies have appealed for additional funding and supplies to support emergency services and longer-term programs. They also stress the importance of strengthening assistance for host communities, which share scarce local resources.

The situation reflects the wider impact of conflict and displacement across the Sahel. Continued violence in Mali has driven repeated movements of people across the border, with no clear indication of when many will be able to return. For families in Mbera, immediate priorities remain safety, food, clean water and a place to live.

Humanitarian organizations say urgent support could help prevent conditions from deteriorating further. Without it, they warn, shortages may deepen and vulnerable residents could face worsening health and protection risks. For now, refugees and local aid workers are trying to cope with rising needs amid uncertainty over how long the crisis will last.

The paper addresses an important problem: estimating the value of a target policy from data collected under a different behavior policy. Its focus on importance resampling is timely, since the method is intuitive and can reuse existing logged data without requiring a new deployment. The discussion of applicability would be strongest if it clearly distinguishes ordinary importance sampling, self-normalized estimators, and resampling-based variants, as these methods have different bias and variance properties. In particular, the paper should state the assumptions required for valid evaluation, including adequate support of the behavior policy wherever the target policy acts. A central limitation is the potentially high variance of importance weights, especially over long horizons or when the policies differ substantially. The paper should quantify this issue through effective sample size or similar diagnostics, rather than relying only on qualitative discussion. Empirical comparisons with doubly robust, model-based, and direct-method estimators would also help establish when importance resampling is practically useful. The evaluation should include realistic settings, multiple behavior–target policy divergence levels, and uncertainty estimates across repeated trials. The proposed extension to policy optimization is promising, but optimizing an estimator can exploit its noise and produce policies whose apparent gains do not reflect true performance. The authors should explain how they control this selection bias and whether the resulting optimization procedure has convergence or finite-sample guarantees. It would also be helpful to clarify computational costs and how resampling choices affect reproducibility and stability. Overall, the topic is valuable, but stronger theoretical framing and more comprehensive empirical evidence are needed to support the paper’s claims.

In today’s world, technology helps us communicate quickly and easily. We can send messages, join video calls, and share ideas with people across the globe. However, face-to-face interaction still matters because it creates a stronger sense of connection. When people meet in person, they can notice facial expressions, gestures, and tone of voice. These cues help us understand one another more fully and avoid misunderstandings. In-person conversations also give people a chance to listen carefully without the distractions of notifications and screens. Spending time together can build trust, friendship, and a sense of belonging. Face-to-face interaction is especially important for children, who learn social skills by talking and playing with others. It can also help classmates and coworkers solve problems by encouraging direct discussion and teamwork. Technology remains useful, but relying on it too much may leave people feeling lonely or disconnected. A balanced life includes online communication as well as time spent together in person. We should make an effort to put our devices away during conversations and give others our full attention. In an increasingly technology-dependent world, face-to-face interaction reminds us that meaningful communication begins with being present.

This paper addresses an important challenge in molecular machine learning: learning reliable molecular representations from SMILES while supporting both property prediction and molecular design. The topic is timely, since SMILES-based models are scalable but can be sensitive to the choice of molecular string representation. The manuscript’s central premise—that robustness should be considered alongside predictive performance—is compelling. Its potential contribution would be strongest if it clearly distinguishes robustness to alternative SMILES enumerations from robustness to noise, distribution shift, and changes in dataset composition. The paper would also benefit from a precise definition of “robust” early in the introduction.

The evaluation should compare the proposed method with strong, well-tuned baselines, including established SMILES language models and relevant graph-based approaches. Comparisons should use consistent data splits, preprocessing, and hyperparameter budgets wherever possible. If the method relies on randomized SMILES, the authors should report how many enumerations are used during training and inference and assess sensitivity to that choice. It would also be useful to compare canonical and randomized SMILES directly. For property prediction, performance should be reported across multiple datasets and task types rather than relying on a single benchmark. Results should include appropriate uncertainty estimates, such as confidence intervals across seeds or repeated splits. The manuscript should specify whether its splits are random, scaffold-based, or time-based, since these settings measure different forms of generalization. Scaffold or temporal evaluation would make the robustness claims more convincing.

The molecular-design experiments require particularly careful validation. The authors should define the design objectives, constraints, and optimization procedure in enough detail to support reproducibility. Generated molecules should be assessed for validity, uniqueness, novelty, and similarity to training compounds. Property improvements should be verified with appropriate predictive uncertainty or, ideally, independent computational or experimental evaluation. The paper should clarify whether reported design gains reflect genuine molecular improvements or exploitation of weaknesses in the property predictor. An ablation study should isolate the effects of each architectural and training component. Further ablations could test the contribution of SMILES augmentation, representation aggregation, and any auxiliary objectives. The authors should also report computational costs, including training time and inference overhead, to establish practical value.

Several methodological details need careful exposition. The treatment of stereochemistry, salts, tautomers, and invalid SMILES could materially affect both representation learning and evaluation. The authors should explain how data leakage is prevented, especially when multiple SMILES strings or closely related compounds occur across splits. Any use of pretrained models should be described with enough detail to identify potential overlap between pretraining and evaluation data. The limits of the approach should be discussed, including dependence on tokenization and the fact that distinct SMILES strings can encode the same molecule. Error analysis across molecular scaffolds and property ranges would help identify where the method succeeds or fails. A concise account of failure cases would also make the design claims more balanced.

Overall, the paper tackles a meaningful problem and could offer a useful contribution to molecular machine learning. Its impact will depend on whether the experiments substantiate robustness beyond improvements on standard random splits. I recommend revision to strengthen the evaluation, clarify key methodological choices, and temper claims that are not directly supported by the results. With these changes, the work could provide a more reliable basis for assessing SMILES-based models in prediction and molecular design.

The Vatican says Catholics’ cremated remains should be kept together in a consecrated place, such as a cemetery or church columbarium, rather than scattered or divided among relatives. The guidance, reaffirmed by the Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith, responds to questions about storing ashes at home and making keepsakes from them.

Catholic teaching permits cremation, provided it is not chosen to deny the faith in the resurrection of the body. But the Church says cremated remains must be treated with respect and kept in a place set aside for the dead. Scattering ashes in the air, on land or at sea is not allowed under the rules.

The Vatican also rejects dividing ashes among family members or turning them into jewelry and other keepsakes. Officials say these practices can blur the distinction between human remains and personal mementos, and may encourage beliefs incompatible with Christian teaching.

In limited circumstances, a local bishop may authorize ashes to be kept in a private home, the guidance says. Such permission may be considered when there are serious and exceptional reasons, and the remains must still be handled respectfully.

The Vatican’s position builds on instructions issued in 2016, which said cremation does not affect the Church’s belief in bodily resurrection. The newer clarification was prompted by questions from a local bishop about whether ashes could be divided or preserved in a domestic setting.

The rules reflect the Church’s emphasis on communal remembrance and the dignity of the deceased. Catholics are encouraged to pray for the dead and to visit their graves or burial places. For families considering cremation, church officials say the remains should ultimately be placed in a recognized sacred site.

Schools should require students to participate in activities beyond regular classes, as long as they offer a range of choices and reasonable flexibility. These activities can help students grow in ways that academic lessons alone may not. Sports, clubs, music groups, volunteering, and other programs teach practical skills. Students can learn teamwork by working toward a shared goal. They can also practice leadership by organizing events or helping younger members. These experiences may make students more confident and independent.

Activities beyond class can also help students discover their interests. A student who joins a drama club might find a love of acting. Another might develop a talent for coding, art, or debate. Trying different activities gives students a chance to learn what they enjoy. It can also connect them with classmates who have similar interests. These friendships can make students feel more included at school.

Participation may support students’ well-being, too. Exercise can improve physical health and reduce stress. Creative activities give students a break from studying. Volunteering can help them understand their community and care about other people. When students feel connected to school, they may be more motivated to attend and learn.

However, schools should not require every student to join the same activity. Some students have jobs, family responsibilities, health concerns, or long commutes. Others may need extra time for homework or rest. A strict requirement could add pressure instead of creating a positive experience. Schools should listen to students’ needs and make participation manageable.

To make a requirement fair, schools should provide free or low-cost options. They should offer activities at different times and allow students to choose programs that suit them. A student might participate through a club, a sport, community service, or another approved activity. Schools should also make exceptions when a student has a serious reason they cannot take part. This approach gives students choices while ensuring that opportunities are available to everyone.

In conclusion, schools should encourage and generally require some participation beyond regular classes. Such activities build skills, help students explore interests, and strengthen connections with others. The requirement should be flexible and inclusive rather than a burden. With thoughtful choices and support, schools can help students benefit from learning outside the classroom.

Remote instruction can support students in several important ways. When used thoughtfully, it can make school more accessible and help students learn in a setting that works for them. It is not a perfect replacement for in-person classes, but it can be a valuable option.

One way remote instruction helps is by supporting attendance. Students who are sick, recovering from an injury, or temporarily unable to travel may still join lessons from home. Those who live far from school or depend on unreliable transportation can also avoid missing class because of travel problems. A student with a short-term family responsibility may be able to attend remotely rather than fall behind. Recorded lessons and digital course materials can help students review what they missed, though they should not replace regular participation. Flexible access can make it easier for students to maintain a steady connection to school.

Remote learning can also improve focus for some students. A quiet, familiar study space may feel less distracting than a busy classroom. Students can sometimes adjust their surroundings, such as choosing a comfortable seat or reducing background noise. Digital lessons may let learners pause and replay explanations when they need more time. This can be especially helpful for students who process information at different speeds. However, home environments can also include distractions, so students need routines and a suitable place to work. Teachers can support focus by providing clear instructions, short activities, and regular breaks.

Student well-being is another area where remote instruction may help. It can reduce the stress of commuting and give students more time for sleep, meals, or family responsibilities. Some students feel more comfortable asking questions through chat or private messages than speaking in front of a class. Remote options may also help students stay connected to school while managing a temporary health challenge. Teachers can check in with students and encourage them to share concerns when appropriate. At the same time, learning from home can feel lonely, so regular interaction with classmates and teachers remains important. Schools should make sure students know where to find academic and emotional support.

Remote instruction can encourage engagement when lessons are designed to involve students actively. Teachers can use polls, shared documents, discussion boards, and small online groups to invite participation. Students who are hesitant to speak aloud may contribute through writing or other digital tools. Collaborative projects can help classmates exchange ideas even when they are in different places. Clear goals and timely feedback can also help students understand their progress. Lessons that include choices, practical examples, and varied activities are more likely to hold students’ attention. Technology alone does not create engagement; thoughtful teaching does.

For remote instruction to work well, students need reliable internet access and appropriate devices. Schools can help by lending equipment, offering technical assistance, and providing alternatives when connections fail. Teachers should keep platforms organized so students can find assignments and resources without confusion. Families can support learning by helping establish schedules, while recognizing that every household has different needs. Schools should also consider accessibility, including captions, screen-reader compatibility, and flexible ways to participate. These steps make remote learning fairer and easier to use.

Remote instruction works best as part of a balanced approach. In-person learning provides social contact, hands-on activities, and immediate support that can be difficult to reproduce online. Remote options can complement those strengths by helping students stay involved when attending school physically is difficult. They can also give students more ways to review material and communicate with teachers. Schools should listen to students and families to understand what is working and what needs improvement. With careful planning, remote instruction can support attendance, focus, well-being, and engagement. It can help more students remain connected to learning and make progress toward their goals.

This paper explores an interesting direction by using image quality metrics as alternative energy functions to improve image generation with BEGANs. The topic is relevant because standard adversarial objectives can be difficult to optimize and may not align well with perceptual image quality. A key strength is the potential to connect established quality measures with the distinctive energy-based training framework of BEGAN. The paper should clearly explain how each metric is incorporated into the objective and whether it replaces or supplements the original loss. It should also justify the choice of metrics, since measures designed for comparing images may behave differently when used as training signals. The evaluation would be more convincing with comparisons against the standard BEGAN objective and appropriate baselines, using both quantitative metrics and human or perceptual assessment. Ablation studies could clarify which components drive any improvements and whether gains persist across datasets and training settings. The authors should also discuss possible trade-offs, such as reduced diversity, artifacts, or sensitivity to metric-specific biases. Overall, this is a promising approach, but stronger methodological detail and comprehensive evaluation are needed to establish its effectiveness.

Success is often imagined as a straight path from setting a goal to reaching it. In reality, most people face setbacks along the way. They may struggle in school, experience family problems, or encounter difficulties at work. Although these challenges can be discouraging, they can also teach important lessons. With support from education, family, and work, people can use setbacks as opportunities to grow and move closer to success.

Education can help people understand their strengths and improve their weaknesses. A student who earns a poor grade may feel disappointed at first. However, that grade can show which subjects or skills need more practice. A teacher can explain difficult material, recommend useful resources, or help the student make a better study plan. Classmates can also offer encouragement and share strategies. When students keep trying instead of giving up, they learn persistence. They also discover that mistakes are a normal part of learning. These lessons can help them handle challenges beyond the classroom.

Family support is another important part of overcoming setbacks. Family members can offer comfort when someone feels stressed or discouraged. They may remind a person of past achievements and encourage them to keep working toward future goals. Practical help can matter too, such as providing a quiet place to study or helping with daily responsibilities. Families do not always agree, and sometimes their expectations can create pressure. Honest conversations can help people explain what they need and find solutions together. Knowing that someone cares can make difficult tasks feel less overwhelming. This support can give people the confidence to try again after failure.

Work can also teach valuable lessons about success. Employees may face criticism, lose a job, or struggle with a demanding task. These experiences can be painful, but they can also reveal areas for improvement. A supportive manager or coworker may give helpful advice and model effective ways to solve problems. Work experience can build skills such as communication, patience, and responsibility. Even an unsuccessful project can teach a person how to prepare more carefully next time. Learning from workplace setbacks can open the door to new opportunities.

Success does not mean avoiding every problem. It often means responding to problems with effort, flexibility, and the willingness to seek help. Education provides knowledge and guidance, family offers encouragement and care, and work builds experience and practical skills. Each kind of support can help people recover from setbacks and make wiser choices. People may reach their goals at different times, and their paths may not look the same. What matters is continuing to learn and moving forward. Setbacks can become stepping stones when people combine determination with support.

Jeff Sessions’ confirmation as attorney general has renewed debate over his record on civil rights and his independence from President Donald Trump’s White House. The Senate approved the Alabama Republican for the nation’s top law-enforcement post in a 52–47 vote on Wednesday. The vote largely followed party lines, with one Republican joining Democrats in opposition.

Sessions’s supporters say his decades in public service and experience as a federal prosecutor qualify him for the job. They describe him as a firm advocate for law and order and point to his work as Alabama’s attorney general and a US senator. Opponents, however, argue that his record raises questions about how he would enforce civil-rights protections.

During his 1986 judicial nomination hearings, witnesses accused Sessions of making racially insensitive remarks and opposing efforts to protect Black voters. Sessions denied the allegations, but the Senate rejected his nomination to a federal judgeship. As a senator, he later opposed aspects of the Voting Rights Act and challenged federal oversight of some state election laws.

At his confirmation hearing last month, Sessions said he would enforce civil-rights laws and treat people fairly. He also rejected claims that he had shown racial bias, calling the accusations false. Civil-rights groups said his assurances did not resolve their concerns.

His relationship with Trump has added another layer to the debate. Sessions was an early and prominent supporter of Trump’s presidential campaign, and critics worry that political loyalty could compromise the Justice Department’s independence. The department is expected to investigate matters involving the administration as well as the public.

Sessions has pledged to follow the law and said no one is above it. He has also said he would recuse himself from investigations in which his prior campaign role creates a conflict. Senators from both parties pressed him on whether he could resist improper pressure from the White House.

The new attorney general will oversee the FBI, federal prosecutors and enforcement of civil-rights laws. His decisions could shape policy on voting rights, immigration and policing. Advocacy groups and lawmakers say they will closely monitor whether his actions match his promises.

The paper addresses an important need by examining how a bibliographic database could improve access to Chinese technical research. Its focus on scope, data quality, and potential applications gives the study a useful and coherent structure. A major strength is the recognition that Chinese-language technical literature is often underrepresented in international discovery tools. The database could support research assessment, systematic reviews, technology monitoring, and cross-language scholarship. The paper would be stronger if it clearly defined what counts as a technical paper and explained the subject areas and publication types included. It should also specify the sources used to build the database, the period covered, and the criteria for selecting records. Because coverage may vary across disciplines, regions, and publication venues, the authors should report these differences rather than relying only on an overall coverage estimate. The data-quality evaluation is central to the paper and should include transparent measures of completeness, accuracy, duplication, and consistency. A sample-based comparison with authoritative source records would help validate these measures. The authors should explain how names, affiliations, dates, and Chinese-English title variants are normalized, since errors in these fields can substantially affect retrieval and analysis. They should also describe how records are updated and how corrections or missing metadata can be reported. The discussion of applications is promising, but it would benefit from concrete examples that demonstrate what the database enables beyond existing resources. Comparisons with relevant Chinese and international databases would clarify its distinctive contribution and limitations. The paper should address licensing, access conditions, privacy considerations, and the sustainability of long-term maintenance. Overall, this is a worthwhile and potentially valuable project, but its contribution will depend on transparent methods and rigorous evidence that the database is both sufficiently comprehensive and reliable. I recommend revision, with particular attention to documenting coverage and strengthening the data-quality validation.

Letting students choose their own summer learning projects can make learning more exciting. Instead of completing the same assignment as everyone else, students can explore a topic they truly care about. One student might build a model, while another researches animals or writes a short story. Having choices can help students feel more responsible for their learning. When they select a project, they are more likely to stay motivated and work hard. They can also choose a project that matches their interests and strengths. At the same time, exploring a new subject may help them discover a talent they did not know they had. Summer projects can teach useful skills beyond the classroom. Students might practice planning, researching, problem-solving, and managing their time. They can learn to set small goals and keep working until they finish. These skills are helpful in school and in everyday life. Choosing a project also allows students to learn at their own pace. They can make their work simple or challenging depending on their experience. Families may enjoy taking part by offering ideas, materials, or encouragement. Teachers can still provide clear guidelines so projects are thoughtful and educational. Overall, letting students choose their summer learning projects helps them become curious, confident, and independent learners.

The paper investigates recurrent neural networks applied to multiple molecular string representations for molecular property prediction and structure optimization. The topic is timely, since molecular design requires models that can connect chemical structure with desired properties while supporting the generation of new compounds. Considering multiple string representations is a potentially valuable way to reduce dependence on any single serialization of a molecule. The work’s central premise is that recurrent models can learn useful structure–property relationships and guide optimization through these representations. The paper would benefit from stating its main research questions and contributions more explicitly near the outset. In particular, readers should be able to distinguish methodological novelty from an application of established sequence-learning techniques.

A major strength is the focus on representation choice, which is often treated as a minor implementation detail despite its potential effect on learning and generation. The authors should explain how each representation is constructed and whether all strings encode the same molecular graph without ambiguity. They should also clarify how stereochemistry, aromaticity, charges, and disconnected components are handled. A fair comparison requires controlling for tokenization, model capacity, training data, and optimization budgets across representations. The study should include suitable baselines, such as a conventional fingerprint-based predictor and a strong molecular graph model, where feasible. Comparisons with established molecular string models would further help establish the practical value of the proposed approach.

The evaluation would be stronger if data splitting procedures were described in enough detail to assess scaffold generalization and possible overlap between training and test molecules. Property prediction results should include uncertainty estimates or repeated runs, particularly when differences between representations are small. Performance should be reported with metrics appropriate to each property and accompanied by clear definitions of the evaluation protocol. For structure optimization, the paper should specify the objective functions, constraints, starting molecules, and stopping criteria. It is important to report not only the best optimized scores but also success rates, diversity, novelty, validity, and synthetic accessibility. The authors should assess whether optimization exploits predictor errors by validating generated candidates with independent models or experimental evidence when available.

Ablation studies could reveal whether gains arise from the recurrent architecture, the use of multiple representations, or the optimization procedure itself. The paper should also discuss how molecular strings are selected or combined during generation, since different serializations may impose different search biases. Reproducibility would improve with details on hyperparameters, random seeds, software versions, and access to code and data. The discussion should address the limitations of recurrent networks, including their sequential processing and potential difficulty modeling long-range structural dependencies. It should also consider whether improvements persist across datasets and property types rather than being specific to a single benchmark.

Overall, the topic is promising, and the emphasis on multiple molecular string representations could yield useful insights for molecular machine learning. However, the paper’s conclusions will depend on rigorous, transparent comparisons and a comprehensive evaluation of optimized structures. I recommend revision to strengthen the methodological description, benchmarking, and validation of optimization outcomes. With these improvements, the work could make a meaningful contribution to the study of molecular representation and sequence-based design.

A series of unusual crater chains on Mercury may be the scars left by comets that broke apart as they passed close to the Sun, according to a new study.

The finding offers a possible explanation for long, narrow rows of pits seen across the planet’s battered surface. Researchers say the chains could have formed when fragments of a comet struck Mercury one after another.

Comets are loosely bound mixtures of ice, dust and rock. A close approach to the Sun can expose them to intense heat and powerful tidal forces, which may pull them apart.

If a comet breaks up, its pieces can remain strung along a similar orbit. Should that trail intersect a planet, the fragments may hit in succession, leaving a line of craters.

Scientists have identified crater chains on Mercury that appear consistent with this process. Their arrangement differs from the more familiar isolated impact craters, though other explanations remain possible.

The planet’s surface is densely marked by impacts accumulated over billions of years. That makes it difficult to determine whether a particular row of craters formed in one event or through separate impacts over a long period.

Researchers compare the shapes, spacing and alignment of the pits to test the comet-fragment idea. A chain with regularly spaced craters along a common path could point to a group of related impacts.

Mercury’s proximity to the Sun makes it a compelling place to investigate how solar forces affect small bodies. Comets that pass through the inner solar system can experience both strong heating and gravitational stress.

The proposed explanation could also shed light on the history of comets that no longer exist as intact objects. Their fragments may have struck planets long after the original bodies broke apart.

Still, crater chains are not definitive evidence of cometary origins. Some can form when material ejected by a large impact lands in a line, while others may be linked to geological features beneath the surface.

Distinguishing among these possibilities requires detailed measurements of the craters and their surroundings. Images and topographic data from NASA’s MESSENGER spacecraft have provided much of the information available for Mercury’s surface.

Future observations could help clarify the chains’ ages and the materials from which they formed. Researchers may also compare them with crater patterns on the Moon and other worlds.

The European-Japanese BepiColombo mission is expected to add new measurements of Mercury after it enters orbit around the planet. Its observations could reveal surface details that help scientists assess how the chains formed.

If the comet explanation is confirmed, the crater rows would provide a rare record of objects disrupted by the Sun. They could help researchers reconstruct the movement of small bodies through the inner solar system.

For now, the chains remain clues rather than a settled case. But each aligned crater offers a possible glimpse of a comet’s final journey—and of the forces that can tear such a visitor apart.

This paper studies resampling-based corrections for off-policy value learning and compares their stability with importance sampling methods. The topic is important because distribution mismatch can make off-policy learning both biased and highly variable. The paper’s central contribution is to examine whether resampling can reduce this instability while preserving useful value estimates. Its focus is timely for reinforcement learning settings in which target-policy data are expensive or unavailable.

The paper is generally well motivated and presents a clear practical problem. The comparison with importance sampling is appropriate, since importance sampling provides a principled baseline but can suffer from extreme weights. The proposed resampling perspective is intuitive and may offer a useful alternative when weight variance is large. The discussion also highlights an important distinction between correcting the data distribution and controlling estimator variance.

The strongest aspect of the work is its attention to stability rather than predictive performance alone. This emphasis is valuable because unstable updates can undermine otherwise accurate estimators. The paper would benefit, however, from a more precise definition of stability. It should specify whether stability refers to bounded estimates, convergence of learning curves, reduced variance, robustness to random seeds, or some combination of these properties. Reporting these measures separately would make the claims easier to evaluate.

The methodological description should make the resampling procedure fully reproducible. In particular, the paper should state how samples are selected, whether sampling is with or without replacement, and how resampled frequencies affect the learning update. It should also explain how the method handles zero-probability or rarely observed actions. These cases are central to off-policy correction and can materially change the conclusions.

The comparison with importance sampling should be carefully controlled. The methods should use the same data, target policy, function approximator, optimization settings, and evaluation protocol wherever possible. The paper should report whether importance weights are clipped or normalized, since these choices can strongly influence both variance and bias. If several variants are included, their parameters and selection criteria should be stated clearly. A comparison against per-decision importance sampling and a doubly robust baseline would also strengthen the experimental picture.

The theoretical analysis is promising but appears to need more detail about its assumptions. The authors should clarify the coverage conditions required for the target policy and behavior policy. They should distinguish guarantees for tabular settings from claims that apply with function approximation. Any convergence or variance result should identify the relevant sampling assumptions and the role of finite data. A discussion of the bias introduced by resampling would be especially valuable, since lower variance does not by itself ensure better value estimates.

The empirical evaluation should cover a broader range of mismatch levels. Results under mild distribution shift alone would not establish robustness in the settings where correction methods are most needed. It would be useful to vary the behavior policy, effective sample size, reward scale, and trajectory length. The paper should include confidence intervals or uncertainty estimates across independent runs. Ablations could isolate the effects of resampling, weight normalization, clipping, and other implementation choices.

The results should also be interpreted with care. Improved stability may come at the cost of increased bias, slower adaptation, or loss of rare but important transitions. The authors should report value-estimation error alongside variance and learning-curve behavior. Where feasible, performance should be compared with the true value function or a high-quality reference estimate. Computational cost and memory use should also be discussed, particularly if resampling adds overhead.

Overall, the paper addresses a meaningful problem and offers a potentially useful approach to off-policy value learning. Its emphasis on stability is a strength, and the comparison with importance sampling has clear practical relevance. The main limitations are the need for sharper definitions, fuller methodological detail, and stronger evidence separating variance reduction from bias. I recommend revision before publication. With a more rigorous analysis and a broader, carefully controlled evaluation, the work could make a valuable contribution.

The paper addresses a timely and valuable problem: organizing Chinese scholarly publications into a knowledge graph that supports discovery and analysis. Its strongest contribution is the potential to connect publications, authors, institutions, venues, and research topics across a fragmented and linguistically diverse literature. The paper should clearly state its intended users and use cases, since these choices shape both the graph schema and its evaluation. The data sources, coverage period, inclusion criteria, and collection process need to be described in enough detail to assess representativeness and reproducibility. In particular, the authors should explain how they handle variant author names, institution aliases, Chinese segmentation, and multilingual metadata. The proposed ontology and entity-relation model should be justified against relevant existing academic knowledge graphs, with examples of how it represents complex scholarly relationships. The extraction and entity-linking pipeline is central to the work, so its methods, training data, and error-handling procedures require fuller documentation. Evaluation should report precision, recall, and F1 for key entity and relation types, using a clearly described annotated test set and, ideally, independent annotators. The paper would also benefit from comparisons with baseline systems or existing Chinese and international scholarly graphs. Beyond component-level accuracy, the authors should demonstrate practical utility through a concrete task, such as author disambiguation, literature search, or research trend analysis. Because metadata can be incomplete or biased toward particular disciplines, publishers, and institutions, the paper should discuss these limitations and their effect on downstream conclusions. A public release of the graph, schema, code, or representative samples would substantially improve reproducibility, subject to licensing and privacy constraints. Overall, the topic is promising, but stronger methodological transparency and a more comprehensive evaluation are needed to establish the graph’s reliability and broader value. I recommend revision before publication.

Autonomous vehicles are often presented as a way to make travel easier and safer. However, they may also create challenges for drivers and communities. One practical concern is that the technology can struggle in unusual conditions. Heavy rain, snow, faded road markings, or construction zones may confuse a vehicle’s sensors. When the system is uncertain, a human driver may need to take control quickly. Yet drivers who rely on automation can become distracted or lose the skills needed to respond. This creates a difficult question about who is responsible when a crash occurs. Responsibility might involve the driver, the vehicle’s manufacturer, or the company that designed its software. These disputes could make insurance claims and legal cases more complicated. Safety is another major concern because no system can predict every action a pedestrian or another driver might take. A vehicle may also have trouble recognizing people or objects in unfamiliar situations. Even a rare software error could affect many vehicles if they use the same system. Cyberattacks are another risk, since connected vehicles may be vulnerable to hacking. Communities could face challenges as well. Autonomous cars may change jobs for taxi, delivery, and truck drivers. Workers who lose these jobs may need support and opportunities to learn new skills. The vehicles could also make transportation less equal if they are expensive or unavailable in rural areas. Cities may need to redesign roads, traffic signals, parking areas, and public transit systems. If self-driving cars make travel more convenient, people might take more trips, increasing traffic rather than reducing it. Communities must also consider how vehicles collect and use location data. Protecting that information will be important for people’s privacy. Autonomous vehicles may bring real benefits, but those benefits are not automatic. Careful testing, clear laws, reliable safety standards, and public discussion will be needed before they become a routine part of everyday life.

Police in southeastern Nigeria have launched an investigation into an alleged infant sale after several people were arrested, according to local reports. Authorities have not released full details about the arrests or the circumstances surrounding the case. The incident has renewed concern over so-called “baby factories,” where women and children are allegedly exploited and infants sold or trafficked. Officials and child-protection advocates have urged the public to report suspected abuse and called for stronger action against trafficking networks.

Optimism and initiative are two qualities that can help people move toward their goals and create a better life. Optimism means believing that improvement is possible, even when circumstances are difficult. Taking initiative means acting without waiting for someone else to solve every problem. Together, these qualities help people turn hopes into plans and plans into progress.

For example, a student who struggles with a subject can believe that practice will help and then ask questions, make a study schedule, and keep working. The results may not come immediately, but each effort can build knowledge and confidence. Optimism helps the student see a setback as a challenge to learn from rather than proof of failure. Initiative makes that positive attitude useful by encouraging action. The same approach can help someone find a job, improve their health, or strengthen a friendship.

These qualities also make life better by helping people feel more responsible for their choices. Instead of waiting for perfect conditions, they look for small steps they can take now. They may also inspire others, because a person who works steadily and stays hopeful can encourage friends, family, or teammates. However, optimism does not mean ignoring real problems, and initiative does not mean trying to do everything alone. People still need to plan carefully, accept advice, and ask for help when necessary.

There will always be obstacles, and some goals may need to change along the way. A hopeful person can adjust without giving up on the possibility of a meaningful future. A proactive person can learn from mistakes and try a different method. In this way, optimism and initiative support one another: hope gives action a purpose, and action gives hope a foundation. By practicing both qualities, people can make steady progress toward their goals and build lives that are more fulfilling.

Teenagers should have a 10 p.m. curfew on school nights because it can support their safety, sleep, and success at school. At that age, many teens are still learning how to make responsible choices. A clear curfew gives families a simple way to set expectations. It can also help parents know where their children are in the evening. Being home earlier may reduce the chance of teens getting caught in unsafe situations late at night. For example, there may be fewer adults around to help if something goes wrong. A curfew can also encourage healthier sleep habits. Teenagers need plenty of sleep to grow and stay focused. However, staying out late can make it difficult to get enough rest before an early school day. Lack of sleep may affect mood, memory, and classroom performance. A 10 p.m. limit could help teens build a regular bedtime routine. Still, every family and teenager is different. Some teens may have evening jobs, sports, or other important activities. Parents should consider these responsibilities and make reasonable exceptions when needed. Overall, a 10 p.m. school-night curfew can be helpful when families discuss it fairly and allow room for trust and responsibility.

Astronomers at Aberystwyth University have recorded a rare flash as a meteorite struck the Moon, offering a fleeting glimpse of an impact that is usually too brief to see. The flash was detected during observations of the Moon’s unlit portion, where a sudden burst of light stood out against the dark surface. Researchers say such flashes happen when space rocks slam into the lunar ground at high speed. With no atmosphere to slow them down, even relatively small objects can hit the Moon directly. The impact’s brightness and duration may help astronomers estimate the size and speed of the incoming rock. Scientists can also use these observations to improve estimates of how often the Moon is struck. The event highlights how monitoring lunar impacts can contribute to understanding hazards in the space around Earth. Researchers are now examining the recorded data to learn more about the collision. Though the flash lasted only moments, it has provided a valuable record of a rare cosmic event.

Two bearded dragons abandoned in a cardboard box in Northumberland have been rescued and given veterinary care. The reptiles were found in poor conditions after being left without the warmth and shelter they need. They were taken to a local animal rescue, where staff arranged an examination by a vet. Both dragons are now receiving care and will be monitored as they recover. Rescuers said bearded dragons need specialist heating, lighting and diets to stay healthy. They urged anyone unable to care for a pet to contact an animal charity or rescue rather than abandon it. The circumstances of the abandonment have not been confirmed. The rescue hopes the dragons will be ready for suitable new homes once their condition has stabilised.

Seeking diverse perspectives and listening respectfully can make discussions more thoughtful and useful. Each person brings different experiences, knowledge, and ideas to a conversation. Hearing these differences can help us understand a topic more fully. It may also reveal solutions that we would not have considered on our own. When people listen carefully, they show that others’ contributions matter. This helps create a welcoming space where everyone feels more comfortable sharing. Respectful listening does not mean agreeing with every opinion. Instead, it means paying attention and responding without insults or interruptions. Asking sincere questions can help us understand why someone holds a particular view. We may discover that we share common concerns even when we disagree. Considering different ideas can also challenge our assumptions and help us learn. In school, this can lead to richer group projects and stronger class discussions. Outside school, it can help people solve problems and work together. By seeking diverse perspectives and listening respectfully, we can become more open-minded and make better decisions.

Good decisions rarely come from seeing a problem in only one way. When people gather varied perspectives, they can understand more of the facts, risks, and possible solutions. This is important because individuals often have blind spots. A person may focus on cost while overlooking safety, or value speed without considering long-term effects. Hearing from others can reveal what one person might miss.

Different perspectives are especially useful when a decision affects many people. For example, a school planning a new schedule should listen to students, teachers, families, and staff. Students may explain how early start times affect their sleep. Teachers may point out how class time shapes learning. Families can describe transportation or childcare challenges. Staff members may identify practical concerns about maintaining the building. Together, these views can help the school create a plan that works better for everyone.

Listening to different people can also prevent costly mistakes. Businesses, for instance, can lose money when leaders make plans without consulting the workers who understand daily operations. A manager might approve a new system that seems efficient but is difficult to use. Employees who handle the work can identify problems before the system is introduced. Fixing a weakness early is usually less expensive than repairing it after a failed launch.

Varied perspectives also help people challenge assumptions. If everyone in a group thinks alike, they may accept an idea simply because it feels familiar. Someone with a different background or experience may ask a question that changes the discussion. That question can lead the group to check its evidence, consider another possibility, or improve its plan. Respectful disagreement is not a sign that a decision is failing. It can be a sign that people are taking the decision seriously.

However, gathering opinions does not mean that every suggestion must be followed. Groups still need to evaluate information carefully and make a clear choice. They should consider who has relevant experience, what evidence supports each view, and what consequences may follow. It is also important to hear from people who are often left out, since their needs may otherwise be ignored. A fair process gives people a genuine chance to speak without allowing one person to dominate.

People can make this process more effective by asking open questions and listening without interrupting. They can summarize what they have heard to make sure they understand it correctly. Groups should also distinguish between facts, personal experiences, and guesses. When time is limited, they can invite input from people with different kinds of knowledge and focus on the most important risks. These steps help a group learn from differences instead of becoming distracted by them.

In the end, strong decisions are not always the ones everyone agrees with immediately. They are decisions made after careful thought, honest discussion, and attention to likely consequences. Gathering varied perspectives gives people a fuller picture of a problem. It can uncover better options and expose dangers before they become expensive failures. By listening to others and weighing their ideas fairly, individuals and groups can make wiser choices and avoid mistakes that could have been prevented.

A fabricated announcement that major banks were withdrawing financing from Whitehaven Coal briefly disrupted trading in the company’s shares and drew attention to opposition to a proposed mine. The false notice, circulated online, claimed lenders had pulled support for the Australian coal producer. Whitehaven shares were temporarily halted while the Australian Securities Exchange assessed the information and sought clarification. The company said the announcement was not genuine and that it had not received the reported funding withdrawal. Trading resumed after the clarification, though the episode prompted questions about how quickly unverified claims can affect markets. The notice also echoed campaigners’ concerns about financing new coal projects and their environmental impact. Opponents of Whitehaven’s proposed mine have argued that it would extend fossil-fuel production and threaten local ecosystems. The incident underscored the need for investors to verify market-sensitive claims through official company and exchange announcements.

Collaboration is an important skill that helps people succeed in school, work, and everyday life. In school, students can share ideas, explain difficult topics, and learn from one another. Working in groups also teaches them how to listen and respect different opinions. At work, collaboration allows people to combine their strengths and complete tasks more effectively. Coworkers can solve problems together and often find better ideas than they would on their own. Teamwork can also make a workplace more supportive and enjoyable. In everyday life, people collaborate when they plan events, care for family members, or help their neighbors. Sharing responsibilities can save time and make difficult tasks easier. Collaboration also helps build trust and stronger relationships. Although working with others may require patience and compromise, these skills are valuable. Overall, collaboration helps people achieve more together than they might achieve alone.

Students today can complete schoolwork online from home or attend classes in person. Both options have advantages, but I believe most students benefit more from learning in a classroom. In-person classes give students a regular schedule and a place set aside for learning. Seeing teachers face to face makes it easier to ask questions and get help right away. Students can also discuss ideas with classmates and learn from different points of view. These conversations can make lessons more interesting and memorable. Going to school also helps students practice cooperation and communication. However, online learning can be useful in many situations. It saves travel time and allows students to work in a comfortable setting. Some students may focus better at home or need a more flexible schedule. Online lessons can also help students who are sick or live far from school. Still, studying at home can bring distractions such as phones, television, or household noise. It may also feel lonely without daily contact with teachers and classmates. Not every student has a reliable internet connection or a quiet place to work. For these reasons, schools should consider each student’s needs. A mix of online and in-person learning could offer flexibility while preserving social interaction. Overall, attending classes in person is usually the stronger choice, while online learning works best as a helpful alternative.

Mid Staffordshire NHS Foundation Trust is facing health and safety charges over the deaths of patients at Stafford Hospital. The charges relate to alleged failings in patient care between 2005 and 2008. Prosecutors say the trust failed to provide safe treatment and adequate nursing care, exposing patients to avoidable risks. The case follows years of concern about standards at the hospital and investigations into its services. Reports highlighted problems including poor monitoring, delays in treatment and a shortage of staff. The trust has previously acknowledged serious failures in care and apologised to patients and families. The prosecution is being brought under health and safety law, rather than as a criminal case against individual clinicians. If convicted, the trust could face a substantial financial penalty. Families of patients who died have called for accountability and answers about how the failures were allowed to continue. The case is expected to examine the trust’s management and the systems it had in place to protect patients. It marks a significant step in efforts to address one of the most serious NHS care scandals in England.
