A Brazilian study has found that people who were breastfed for longer as infants tended to score higher on intelligence tests and achieve more education and income as adults. The research, published in The Lancet Global Health, followed nearly 3,500 people born in Pelotas, Brazil, in 1982. Researchers compared participants’ reported breastfeeding duration with cognitive test results and social outcomes measured decades later. Those breastfed for at least a year had, on average, higher IQ scores than those breastfed for less than a month. They also completed more years of schooling and earned higher incomes in adulthood. The researchers said the association remained after accounting for factors including family income, maternal education, and birth weight. Breast milk contains nutrients and other substances that may support early brain development, offering one possible explanation for the findings. But the study was observational, meaning it cannot establish that breastfeeding itself caused the later differences. Other influences, including family environment and unmeasured social factors, could have contributed. Experts have also noted that breastfeeding duration is difficult to separate from broader circumstances that shape a child’s development. The results add to a large body of research on breastfeeding, but they do not settle the question of its long-term effects on intelligence. Studies in other populations have produced mixed findings, in part because research designs and methods differ. Specialists say randomized trials of breastfeeding are not practical, so researchers must rely on observational evidence and careful comparisons. They also emphasize that infant feeding choices are shaped by health, work, and access to support. Breastfeeding is associated with established health benefits for infants and mothers, but the size and certainty of any long-term cognitive benefit remain debated. The authors said their findings support policies that make breastfeeding easier, while experts urged caution in interpreting the results.

The Electoral College has shaped American presidential elections since the country’s founding. Under this system, voters choose electors who formally cast ballots for president. Although the system has a long history, there are strong arguments for replacing it with a direct popular vote. A direct vote would make every person’s vote count equally, regardless of where they live. In the current system, candidates often focus on a small number of closely contested states. They may spend little time campaigning in states where one party is already dominant. This leaves many voters feeling that their voices do not matter. With a popular vote, candidates would have reason to seek support across the entire country. Another argument is that the Electoral College can produce a winner who received fewer votes nationwide than a rival. This has happened in several presidential elections. Such outcomes can weaken public confidence in the fairness of elections. The candidate who receives the most votes should, many argue, become president. A direct popular vote would also make the counting process easier to understand. Voters would not have to learn how state-by-state electoral totals determine the result. The current system gives some states more influence per voter than others because of how electoral votes are allocated. Equal voting power is an important principle in a democracy. Replacing the Electoral College could strengthen that principle. Critics worry that a national vote might encourage candidates to focus only on large cities. However, candidates would still need votes from many different communities to build a national majority. States could continue to manage elections, while using shared standards to help ensure accurate results. Changing the system would require a major constitutional amendment, so reform would be difficult. Even so, the question deserves serious public discussion. A direct popular vote would make the presidential election more closely reflect the choice of the country’s voters. For these reasons, replacing the Electoral College could make American democracy fairer and more representative.

Completing high school in four years can be more valuable than graduating early because education is about more than finishing classes as quickly as possible. Staying for all four years gives students time to learn, grow, and prepare for what comes next. An extra year or two can help students explore subjects they might not have considered before. They may discover an interest in science, art, technology, or another field. Taking a wider range of classes can also help them make more thoughtful plans for college or a career.

High school is also a place to build important academic skills. Students can improve their writing, research, and problem-solving by taking advanced courses and completing long-term projects. They have more opportunities to ask teachers for help when a subject is difficult. That support can make a real difference before they begin college or enter the workforce. A stronger foundation may help students feel more confident about challenging work later.

Completing four years can also provide time to take part in school life. Students might join clubs, play sports, perform in school productions, or help with community service. These experiences can teach cooperation, leadership, and responsibility. They can also help students form friendships and feel connected to their school. Such relationships may be an important source of encouragement during a challenging period of life.

Another advantage is having more time to mature. Students often learn to manage their schedules, communicate clearly, and make decisions through everyday experiences. These skills cannot always be developed by finishing academic requirements early. A little more time can help students understand their strengths and areas for improvement. It can also give them a chance to make mistakes and learn from them while support is nearby.

Graduating early can be the right choice for some students, especially if it meets their personal needs or goals. However, leaving school sooner may mean missing classes, activities, or friendships that would have been meaningful. Students should consider more than the number of credits they can earn. They should think about how each option could affect their learning, well-being, and future opportunities.

In the end, completing high school in four years can offer a fuller experience and a steadier path into adulthood. The additional time can support stronger academic preparation, personal growth, and lasting connections. Success is not measured only by how quickly someone reaches graduation. For many students, using all four years wisely is a more valuable way to prepare for the future.

Amnesty International has warned that redevelopment plans in Port Harcourt could displace thousands of people unless authorities put strong housing safeguards in place. The warning comes amid concerns about demolitions and the clearance of informal settlements in the Rivers State capital. Residents risk losing their homes and livelihoods if projects proceed without clear protections, the rights group said. Amnesty called on the Rivers State government to ensure that any redevelopment complies with national and international human rights standards.

The organization said people facing eviction should receive advance notice and be consulted meaningfully before decisions are made. It also urged officials to provide adequate alternative housing, rather than leave residents to find shelter on their own. Compensation, where applicable, should be fair and accessible, it said. Families should not be forced out while disputes over their homes or relocation remain unresolved.

Informal-settlement residents often rely on nearby markets, transport links and social networks for work and support. Relocation far from these services could deepen hardship, particularly for low-income households. Amnesty urged the government to publish detailed plans, including information about affected communities, timelines and relocation arrangements. It also called for independent monitoring and a process through which residents can challenge decisions.

Urban renewal can improve infrastructure and living conditions, the group acknowledged, but said development should not come at the cost of people’s rights. Authorities should assess the impact on vulnerable groups, including children, older people and people with disabilities. Community representatives should be included in planning, with information provided in languages residents can understand. The government should also ensure that any evictions are lawful, necessary and carried out with dignity.

Amnesty said it had raised concerns about the risk of forced evictions in Port Harcourt and urged officials to act before displacement occurs. Residents and civil society groups have called for greater transparency around redevelopment proposals. The Rivers State government’s response to the warning was not immediately available. The rights group said it would continue to monitor developments and press for safeguards that allow residents to remain housed as the city changes.

Adolescence is a time of change, discovery, and difficult choices. Teenagers begin to understand who they are while also trying to fit in with others. Friends can provide support, laughter, and a sense of belonging. However, the desire to be accepted can sometimes make it hard to make independent choices. This is when peer pressure can become a serious challenge.

Peer pressure does not always involve someone directly demanding that you do something. It can also be the quiet feeling that everyone else is acting, dressing, or thinking in a certain way. A teenager might join a trend simply because they fear being left out. They might hide their interests because they worry that others will make fun of them. These choices may seem small, but they can gradually make someone feel disconnected from their true self.

Staying true to yourself means understanding your values and making choices that reflect them. It does not mean refusing to change or ignoring advice from others. Adolescence is a time for learning, and listening to different viewpoints can help a person grow. The important thing is to think carefully before making a choice. Ask yourself whether it feels right, whether it could hurt you or someone else, and whether you would make the same choice without pressure.

One challenge teenagers face is the fear of rejection. It can be difficult to say no when friends are encouraging you to do something uncomfortable. Still, a clear and respectful response can show confidence. You might say, “That is not for me,” or suggest doing something else instead. A true friend should respect your decision, even if they do not share it. If someone repeatedly tries to control or embarrass you, it may be worth reconsidering that friendship.

Challenges also come from school, family expectations, social media, and personal doubts. Teenagers may compare their appearance or achievements with carefully selected images online. This can create the false impression that everyone else has a perfect life. Remembering that social media rarely shows the whole story can help protect self-confidence. It is also helpful to spend time with people who value you for more than your popularity, appearance, or success.

Being yourself does not mean handling every problem alone. Trusted friends, family members, teachers, and counselors can offer guidance when a situation feels overwhelming. Asking for help is not a sign of weakness. It shows that you care about making a thoughtful decision. Having supportive people nearby can make it easier to resist harmful pressure and recover from mistakes.

Mistakes are part of growing up, too. A poor choice does not have to define a person forever. Instead, it can be an opportunity to understand what happened and make a better decision next time. Taking responsibility builds maturity and self-respect. Every challenge can teach teenagers more about their boundaries, beliefs, and strengths.

Staying true to yourself may not always be easy, especially when others disagree. Yet genuine confidence grows when your actions match your values. You do not need to impress everyone to have worth. People who respect your individuality are more likely to become meaningful friends. In the end, adolescence is not about copying someone else’s life; it is about discovering your own. By thinking independently, seeking support, and treating yourself with patience, you can face peer pressure without losing sight of who you are.

Although Venus is scorching, cloud-covered, and difficult to explore, studying it could reveal how planets with similar beginnings to Earth can evolve so differently. Its uncertain history of oceans—and the possibility, not proof, of past or present microbial life—makes missions there especially valuable. By investigating Venus, scientists can better understand climate change, the limits of habitability, and Earth’s own future.

Schools should consider requiring students to complete community service because it can benefit both students and their communities. Volunteering gives students a chance to help people and organizations that need support. It can also teach responsibility, cooperation, and compassion. Students may discover new interests or learn useful skills through their service. However, a required program should offer a range of activities so students can choose something that suits their abilities and schedules. Schools should also make sure that students with jobs, family responsibilities, or disabilities have fair alternatives. Community service should not become a punishment or just another box to check. With thoughtful planning, a requirement can make volunteering meaningful rather than burdensome. Overall, schools should require community service while giving students flexibility in how they complete it.

Schools should consider adopting a four-day schedule with longer school days to conserve energy, but the change should be made carefully. Closing school buildings one extra day each week could reduce the use of lights, heating, and air conditioning. It might also lower transportation costs and give families more time for appointments and activities. However, longer days could be tiring for students, especially younger children. When students are exhausted, they may have trouble concentrating and remembering what they learn. Schools would need to make the extra hours useful rather than simply adding more time at desks. Lessons could include breaks, hands-on projects, and opportunities for physical activity. Teachers would also need enough planning time and support to prepare for the longer schedule. A four-day week could create problems for families who rely on school for meals or supervision. Some parents might not have flexible jobs or affordable childcare on the extra day off. Schools could help by offering meal programs, tutoring, or optional activities. Before making a permanent change, districts should ask students, families, teachers, and community members what they need. They should also compare energy savings with the cost of providing extra services. A trial period could show whether attendance, learning, and student well-being improve or suffer. If the schedule harms students or creates unfair burdens for families, it should be adjusted. Overall, a four-day schedule may conserve energy, but it should only be adopted when it supports learning and meets students’ needs.

The paper addresses an important problem: generating realistic face images while assessing their perceptual quality more meaningfully than with pixel-level measures. Its integration of energy-based generative modeling and perceptual assessment is potentially valuable, particularly for capturing complex image distributions. The topic is timely, and the focus on human-perceived fidelity could make the work relevant to both computer vision research and practical applications. However, the paper should explain more clearly how its energy function is defined and optimized, since these choices are central to reproducibility and model behavior. The training procedure also needs sufficient detail, including sampling strategy, computational cost, and measures taken to stabilize optimization. The perceptual assessment component requires a precise description of its criteria and validation, with evidence that it aligns with human judgments. If learned perceptual metrics are used, the authors should discuss possible biases and whether the metric favors particular facial attributes or image styles. The experimental evaluation should compare the proposed method with strong, recent generative baselines under consistent settings. Quantitative results would be more convincing when paired with a well-designed user study and confidence intervals or significance tests. The paper should also assess diversity and mode coverage, since high visual quality alone does not establish that a generator represents the data distribution well. Ablation studies could clarify the separate contributions of the energy-based model and the perceptual assessment framework. Results across different demographic groups and facial characteristics should be reported to identify potential disparities. The authors should address privacy and misuse risks associated with realistic face synthesis, as well as safeguards or intended-use limitations. Overall, the work has promising motivation, but its contribution will be difficult to assess without stronger methodological detail and broader validation. I recommend revision with particular attention to reproducibility, fair comparisons, and evidence that the proposed perceptual assessment reflects human perception.

Students should not need a high academic average to join extracurricular activities or sports. These programs can help students grow in ways that grades alone cannot measure. Team sports teach cooperation, discipline, and perseverance. Clubs encourage students to explore interests and build useful skills. Taking part in activities can also help students feel connected to their school and make new friends. A strict grade requirement could exclude students who would benefit most from that support. However, students still need to make time for their schoolwork. Schools can provide tutoring or study periods for students who are struggling. Coaches and club advisers can also check in with students about their progress. If a student’s grades fall, the school could make a plan to help before suspending participation. This approach encourages responsibility without treating activities as a privilege only for top students. Overall, students should be allowed to participate while receiving support to succeed both in school and outside the classroom.

A dispute has emerged in Tamworth over plans to remove a pig sculpture wearing a police helmet, a public artwork created in tribute to Sir Robert Peel. Peel, the Victorian statesman born near the town, is widely regarded as a founder of modern policing.

The sculpture has become a familiar local landmark, blending a nod to Peel’s legacy with the town’s affection for its distinctive public-art pigs. But its future is now uncertain, prompting debate among residents about whether it should remain on display.

Supporters of keeping the work say it is a playful, recognisable tribute that connects local history with Tamworth’s artistic identity. They argue that removing it would erase a much-loved feature and risk diminishing the town’s character.

Others question whether the sculpture is an appropriate way to commemorate Peel, whose legacy is more complex than a police helmet can suggest. Some residents also say public artworks should be reviewed when they no longer reflect the community’s values or priorities.

The controversy has sparked calls for the council to explain the reasons behind the proposed removal and clarify what might happen to the sculpture. Residents have also suggested alternatives, including relocating it, refurbishing it or inviting the public to vote on its future.

The discussion reflects a broader challenge facing towns with historic monuments and public art: how to balance heritage, changing attitudes and local attachment. Peel remains a significant figure in Tamworth, but opinions differ over how best to represent him.

Council representatives have not yet resolved the dispute, and the sculpture’s final fate remains unclear. For now, the helmeted pig has become more than a quirky landmark—it is at the centre of a conversation about history, identity and who gets to shape public spaces.

An explosion near the U.S. Embassy in Kabul injured civilians and American troops, according to initial reports. The Islamic State claimed responsibility for the bombing. Afghan emergency workers and security forces rushed to the scene as people nearby sought shelter. The injured were taken to hospitals, though officials had not immediately released a confirmed casualty count. The condition and number of U.S. service members hurt were also unclear. Authorities restricted access to the area while bomb-disposal teams examined the site. The attack heightened concerns about security around diplomatic facilities in the Afghan capital. U.S. officials said they were working to establish the full circumstances of the blast. No further details about the device or how it was detonated were immediately available. The bombing came amid ongoing threats from Islamic State militants in Afghanistan. Further information is expected as investigators assess the damage and speak with witnesses.

Exploring Venus is worthwhile, even though it is one of the most dangerous places in our solar system. Venus is similar to Earth in size and has a rocky surface, which makes it an important planet to study. However, its thick atmosphere traps heat, creating temperatures hot enough to melt lead. The atmospheric pressure at the surface is also crushing, and clouds of sulfuric acid make exploration even more difficult. These conditions mean that spacecraft sent to the surface usually survive only briefly. Despite these risks, studying Venus can help scientists understand how planets change over time. Earth and Venus may have started with some similar features, but their climates developed in very different ways. Learning why could help us better understand Earth’s climate and the future effects of climate change. Venus may also have had liquid water long ago, and some researchers have wondered whether simple life could exist in its clouds today. There is no confirmed evidence of life on Venus, so this possibility needs careful investigation. Robotic spacecraft and atmospheric probes can explore the planet without putting human lives at risk. Although Venus is a challenging world, its secrets could teach us a great deal about our planet and the possibility of life elsewhere.

An alternative high school program can help students succeed in school while meeting the needs of their everyday lives. Unlike a traditional schedule, it may offer flexible class times, smaller classes, or online lessons. This flexibility can make it easier for students to balance school with family responsibilities and part-time work. However, students still need to stay organized and complete their assignments on time.

One important benefit is that alternative programs can prepare students for college. Teachers and counselors can help students explore colleges, choose courses, and understand the application process. Students may also get support with writing essays, applying for financial aid, and preparing for entrance exams. Smaller classes can give students more chances to ask questions and receive personal guidance. These experiences can help them feel more confident about continuing their education.

A flexible school schedule can also give students more time with their families. Some students care for younger siblings, help with household tasks, or need to attend family appointments. Being able to study at different times can make these responsibilities easier to manage. Students can remain involved at home without giving up on their education. Families may also feel more connected to a student’s progress when they can support learning at home.

Alternative programs can create opportunities for students to work, too. A student might take a job to earn money, gain experience, or help support their family. Work can teach useful skills such as communication, responsibility, and time management. At the same time, students should make sure their work hours do not interfere with learning or rest. With guidance from teachers and family members, they can build a balanced schedule.

Overall, an alternative high school program can support college preparation, family time, and work opportunities. Its flexibility can help students pursue their goals while managing important responsibilities. When students use the available support and stay committed, they can prepare for a successful future.

A higher academic standard for sports participation can help students balance schoolwork and athletics. When students know they must maintain their grades to play, they may be more motivated to study and manage their time. Strong academic standards can also reinforce the idea that education should come before extracurricular activities. However, setting the standard too high may unfairly exclude students who are working hard but facing challenges outside school. Some students may need extra time or support to improve their grades, rather than losing access to sports. Athletics can build confidence, teamwork, and a sense of belonging, which may also help students succeed in class. Schools should set clear and reasonable expectations while offering tutoring and other academic support. This approach makes participation fairer and encourages students to grow both academically and athletically.

After-school academic support can help students succeed in school and enjoy more free time. It gives students a chance to ask questions and review lessons they found difficult. With a teacher or tutor nearby, they can understand confusing ideas before falling behind. Students can also get started on homework while support is available. This can make assignments easier to finish and reduce stress at home. Regular help may improve grades and build confidence. It can also teach students useful habits, such as planning their work and managing their time. When students finish more schoolwork after class, they may have fewer tasks to complete in the evening. That leaves more time for family, hobbies, exercise, and rest. Of course, students still need to balance study time with breaks. Overall, after-school academic support can help students learn more effectively and make better use of their free time.

The paper addresses an important problem: how to improve signal reconstruction and downstream task performance by incorporating wavelet-based representations into convolutional and recurrent neural networks. The topic is timely, given growing interest in models that combine learned features with structured signal-processing priors. The central idea is promising, particularly for signals with localized transients, multiple timescales, or nonstationary behavior. Wavelet decompositions can expose structure that may be difficult for standard networks to learn from raw inputs alone. The proposed combination of wavelet features with CNNs and RNNs could therefore offer both practical and conceptual value.

A major strength is the potential to connect multiscale analysis with end-to-end learning. CNNs can exploit local patterns in wavelet coefficients, while RNNs may model their temporal evolution. This division of labor is sensible for sequential reconstruction tasks. The approach may also improve conditioning by reducing scale disparities or separating signal components across frequency bands. If supported by rigorous evidence, these benefits would make the work relevant to applications such as biomedical sensing, audio processing, and communications.

The paper should make its main methodological contribution explicit. It is important to distinguish the proposed architecture from prior work using wavelet transforms as preprocessing, multiresolution CNNs, or learned filter banks. The authors should explain whether the wavelet transform is fixed, learnable, or partly learnable, and justify that design choice. They should also specify the wavelet family, decomposition depth, boundary handling, and coefficient normalization. These choices can substantially affect reconstruction quality and reproducibility.

The experimental evaluation should include strong and well-matched baselines. Comparisons should cover conventional CNN and RNN models, a model using raw inputs, and a wavelet-based model without the proposed network components. Ablation studies are needed to isolate the contributions of the wavelet representation, CNN layers, RNN layers, and any conditioning strategy. The paper should report performance across multiple signal types or datasets and describe the train, validation, and test splits clearly. Results should include appropriate reconstruction metrics, such as error measures and, where relevant, perceptual or task-specific scores. Variability across runs should be reported, especially if observed gains are modest.

The claim of improved conditioning needs a precise definition and direct evidence. The authors could examine optimization stability, gradient behavior, convergence speed, or sensitivity to initialization and noise. They should also report computational cost, since wavelet transforms and recurrent layers may add latency or memory requirements. A discussion of robustness to distribution shifts and changes in signal-to-noise ratio would strengthen the practical case. The paper should address limitations, including dependence on wavelet choice and possible loss of information at boundaries or through coefficient reduction.

Overall, this is a promising direction with a plausible rationale and potential practical impact. Its contribution will be convincing only if the experiments separate the effects of the representation from those of the network architecture. I recommend revision focused on methodological clarity, comprehensive ablations, and stronger evidence for the claimed conditioning benefits. With these improvements, the paper could make a useful contribution to signal reconstruction and learning.

A four-day school week may seem like a convenient way to give students more time off, but it can create serious problems for their learning and well-being. When schools remove one day from the week, they often make the other school days longer. These extended days can leave students tired and less able to concentrate in class. Younger children may find it especially difficult to stay focused for so many hours. A shorter week can also mean less time for teachers to explain difficult topics and answer questions. Even if schools add minutes to the remaining days, those minutes may not fully replace the learning lost. Students who miss lessons because of illness or appointments may have fewer chances to catch up. Long weekends can also interrupt routines and make it harder for students to remember what they learned. Some students may spend their extra day studying, but others may not have a quiet place or an adult who can help them. This can widen the gap between students from different backgrounds. The schedule may also create problems for families who need to arrange childcare on the day school is closed. Students whose parents work may be left unsupervised or may need to care for younger siblings. These responsibilities can cause stress and take time away from homework and rest. School is also an important place for students to receive meals, support, and social interaction. Spending one fewer day at school can reduce access to these resources. Although a four-day week may save money or appeal to some families, its effects deserve careful attention. Schools should protect students’ learning and well-being before changing the weekly schedule.

The United States should abolish the Electoral College because it can produce results that do not reflect the choice of most voters. In a presidential election, people cast ballots in their states, but the winner is officially chosen by electors. Most states award all their electoral votes to the candidate who wins the state, even if the margin is very small. As a result, millions of votes for the losing candidate do not affect the final outcome. This system can also allow a candidate to become president without winning the most votes nationwide. That has happened several times in U.S. history, including in 2000 and 2016. Many voters may feel that their voices matter less when the national popular-vote winner loses.

The Electoral College also gives more attention to a small number of closely contested states. Candidates often spend much of their time and money campaigning in those states. Meanwhile, voters in states that reliably support one party may receive fewer visits and less attention. This can make people feel that their political concerns are being ignored. A nationwide popular vote would give every vote equal weight, wherever the voter lives. Candidates would have reason to seek support across the whole country instead of focusing mainly on swing states. It could also encourage more people to vote, since ballots would count toward one national total.

Supporters of the Electoral College argue that it protects the role of states and prevents large cities from controlling elections. They also say that the system encourages candidates to build support across different regions. These concerns deserve consideration, but a popular vote would not make rural votes count less than urban votes. It would count each person equally, while candidates could still campaign in every kind of community. The country could also use safeguards, such as a nationwide recount rule for extremely close elections. Changing the system would require a constitutional amendment, so it would take broad agreement and careful planning. Even so, fairness in choosing the nation’s leader is worth that effort. The president represents all Americans, and each American’s vote should matter equally. Therefore, the United States should abolish the Electoral College and elect its president by the national popular vote.

US-backed Syrian forces advanced toward Manbij as they sought to retake the northern city from Islamic State militants, raising concerns about the safety of residents caught in the fighting. The operation brought together local fighters supported by a US-led coalition, which has provided air power and other assistance in the campaign against the extremist group.

Manbij is a strategic hub near the Turkish border and sits on routes linking Islamic State-held areas in Syria. Its capture would weaken the group’s control and disrupt the movement of fighters and supplies. But the city’s civilian population faces mounting danger as front lines move closer.

Residents have reported difficulty leaving, with roads blocked or unsafe and Islamic State militants restricting movement in some areas. Aid groups have warned that people remaining in the city could face shortages of food, water and medical care. Families fleeing the fighting may also encounter mines, booby traps and unexploded weapons.

The advancing forces have urged civilians to move away from combat zones where possible. However, safe passage has not been assured for everyone, and many residents may be unable or unwilling to leave their homes. The coalition has said it takes precautions to limit civilian harm, while acknowledging the risks inherent in urban combat.

Airstrikes and ground clashes could intensify as the fighters close in on Islamic State positions. The militants have previously used civilians as human shields and fortified buildings, complicating efforts to dislodge them. Any assault on densely populated neighborhoods could cause casualties and damage essential infrastructure.

The campaign is part of a broader effort to roll back Islamic State territory in Syria and Iraq. The group has lost significant ground but remains capable of mounting attacks and resisting advances. For civilians in Manbij, the immediate concern is whether they can find a safe route out before the fighting reaches their neighborhoods.

A well-planned school-year schedule can help students learn more effectively and prepare for the future. Regular school days give students steady routines and frequent opportunities to practice new skills. When lessons build on one another, students can remember information and understand challenging ideas more deeply. A balanced schedule also includes time for breaks, meals, exercise, and rest. These activities support students’ health and help them stay focused in class. Teachers can use the school year to check students’ progress and provide extra help when needed. Students also benefit from having enough time to complete projects, ask questions, and improve their work. A predictable calendar makes it easier for families to plan and support learning at home. Longer breaks can give students time to recharge, explore hobbies, or gain experience through camps and community activities. However, schools should help students review important skills so they do not lose confidence during breaks. Learning to manage assignments and meet deadlines teaches responsibility. These habits are valuable in college, training programs, and many careers. A thoughtful school-year schedule supports academic growth while helping students build the skills they need for future success.

Practical understanding and creative thinking are both important for achieving goals and building things. Practical understanding helps us know what materials, skills, and steps are needed. It also allows us to notice risks and solve everyday problems. Creative thinking helps us imagine new possibilities and find original solutions. Without creativity, we might keep using the same methods even when they do not work well. However, an imaginative idea may fail if we do not understand how to put it into practice. For example, building a useful invention requires both an inventive design and knowledge of tools and materials. The two abilities are most powerful when they support each other. Practical understanding makes ideas workable, while creative thinking helps us make them better.

An Isle of Wight hospital trust’s reliance on a flawed patient-tracking spreadsheet delayed care and contributed to a patient’s death, according to an investigation into the case.

The spreadsheet was used to monitor patients awaiting appointments and treatment. But errors in the system meant that a patient who needed follow-up care was not acted on in time.

The delay contributed to the patient’s death, the investigation found. It highlighted how a tool intended to help staff manage care had instead left important information at risk of being overlooked.

The case involved the Isle of Wight NHS Trust, which provides hospital and community services on the island. The findings have raised questions about the trust’s systems for tracking patients and ensuring that outstanding clinical actions are completed.

Spreadsheets can be useful for organising information, but they depend on accurate data entry and reliable checks. Without safeguards, records can be missed, changed incorrectly or left unreviewed.

The investigation’s findings point to the importance of clear responsibility for monitoring waiting lists and following up patients. They also underline the need for systems that alert staff when care is overdue.

The trust has faced scrutiny over how it manages patient information and clinical risk. The case is likely to prompt renewed attention to whether other patients may have been affected by similar weaknesses.

Health services are increasingly expected to use digital systems that provide a clear, auditable record of decisions and actions. A spreadsheet may not offer the protections or oversight required for high-risk clinical tracking.

The investigation did not make the loss any less severe for the patient’s family. It did, however, identify failures that could help prevent similar delays in future.

The trust’s response to the findings, including any changes to its tracking processes, will be central to rebuilding confidence. Families and patients will want assurance that no one is left waiting because a record has been overlooked.

The case is a stark reminder that administrative systems are part of patient safety. When those systems fail, the consequences can be measured not only in delays, but in lives.

Everyone faces setbacks at some point, whether in school, sports, or personal life. A setback can feel discouraging, especially when we have worked hard toward a goal. However, difficulties do not have to define us or stop us from moving forward. Perseverance helps us keep trying even when progress is slow. Resilience helps us recover, adapt, and learn after disappointment.

For example, a student who receives a poor grade might feel tempted to give up. Instead, they can review their mistakes, ask their teacher for help, and change their study habits. The next test may still be challenging, but each effort can build confidence and understanding. Over time, improvement becomes a greater achievement than the grade alone. The student has learned how to respond to a problem rather than avoid it.

Setbacks can also teach patience. Success often takes longer than we expect, and mistakes are a natural part of learning. When people stay determined, they become more willing to try new approaches. They may discover strengths they did not know they had. Support from family, friends, and teachers can make it easier to keep going, but the decision to persevere belongs to each person.

Resilience does not mean pretending that failure does not hurt. It means acknowledging disappointment and choosing to take another step. Every challenge can offer a lesson that prepares us for future goals. Through perseverance and resilience, setbacks can become opportunities for personal growth. In the end, achievement is not only reaching a goal, but also becoming stronger and wiser along the way.

Subject: Investing in Development for a Safer, More Stable World

Dear Members of Congress,

The attacks of September 11th showed how deeply events in one part of the world can affect people everywhere. They also renewed an urgent debate about how to build a safer and more peaceful international community. Military and security measures may address immediate threats, but lasting stability requires tackling the conditions that allow despair and conflict to grow. Poverty, hunger, preventable disease, and lack of opportunity can leave communities vulnerable to instability. International development aid is an important part of a comprehensive response.

I urge you to support increased, sustained funding for effective development programs. Aid should help expand access to education, health care, clean water, and reliable food supplies. It should also support local businesses, job creation, and infrastructure that connects people to opportunity. Programs that empower women and strengthen civil society can help communities become more resilient. When people have meaningful choices and a stake in their future, they are better positioned to resist violence and extremism.

Development assistance is not a substitute for diplomacy or security efforts. Rather, it complements them by addressing long-term sources of hardship and instability. Aid is most effective when it is carefully targeted, coordinated with local partners, and accountable for results. We should invest in transparent programs that respond to community priorities and measure their impact. We should also work with international institutions and partner governments to reduce waste and avoid duplication.

Increased aid is both a humanitarian responsibility and a practical investment in global stability. A world with fewer people living in extreme poverty is more likely to be a world where peace can take root. Please make development funding a priority in the next budget and support policies that help vulnerable communities build lasting prosperity. The lessons of September 11th call for resolve, compassion, and a commitment to address challenges before they become crises. Thank you for your consideration.

Sincerely,
[Your Name]

The paper addresses an important problem: reducing communication overhead in distributed deep learning while preserving convergence. Its Gaussian-based gradient compression approach is promising, particularly if it can represent gradient distributions accurately with low computational cost. The paper should clearly explain how the Gaussian model is estimated, updated, and applied across layers and training steps. It should also specify the compression ratio and account for the metadata required to encode and reconstruct gradients. The claim of maintaining convergence performance needs support from rigorous analysis or broad empirical evidence, ideally both. Experiments should compare the method with established compression baselines and uncompressed training under identical hardware, model, and data settings. Results across multiple architectures, datasets, and network conditions would help establish how general the approach is. In addition to final accuracy, the evaluation should report training time, communication volume, and convergence behavior over time. Ablation studies could clarify which parts of the Gaussian modeling contribute most to performance. The authors should discuss sensitivity to non-Gaussian or rapidly changing gradient distributions, as these may limit the method’s effectiveness. Overall, the topic is valuable, but stronger methodological detail and comprehensive comparisons are needed to substantiate the paper’s claims.

In 1976, NASA’s Viking 1 spacecraft photographed a strange landform on Mars that looked like a human face. The image quickly became known as the “Face on Mars,” and it captured the public’s imagination. Some people wondered whether the shape was a monument built by an ancient civilization. Others suggested that it might be evidence of life on Mars. Scientists, however, cautioned that one photograph was not enough to support those claims. The picture had been taken from a particular angle and showed a landscape with deep shadows. In 2001, NASA’s Mars Global Surveyor took clearer images of the region. These photographs showed that the “face” was a natural hill, shaped by ordinary geological processes. Its face-like appearance resulted from lighting, shadows, and the way people recognize familiar patterns. The discovery is a good example of how an exciting image can lead to questions that science later answers with better evidence. It also shows why scientists rely on repeated observations rather than a single photograph. Today, robotic spacecraft and rovers continue to explore Mars, studying its rocks, climate, and ancient water. Their findings help researchers investigate whether the planet once had conditions suitable for microbial life. In the future, humans may travel to Mars to conduct research that robots cannot do as easily. Such missions would require careful preparation, including reliable equipment, safe landing systems, and protection from radiation. Although the Martian face was not an artificial monument, it remains a memorable symbol of curiosity about the Red Planet. Its story reminds us that exploration begins with wonder and advances through evidence.

The proposed South Bristol Link Road is expected to improve journeys across the city and support economic growth, but campaigners warn it could increase pollution and traffic. The road would connect South Bristol with the A370 and the wider motorway network, offering an alternative to congested routes through residential areas. Supporters say the link could shorten travel times for commuters, buses and freight. They also argue that better access would help businesses, attract investment and make it easier to reach employment sites. The scheme is intended to improve connections to areas including South Bristol’s growing housing and enterprise developments. However, opponents question whether the predicted time savings will last once more drivers use the route. They say easier road travel could encourage people to drive rather than choose public transport, cycling or walking. That extra traffic, they warn, could worsen air pollution and add carbon emissions. Residents have also raised concerns about noise and the effect of new roads on nearby communities and green spaces. Project backers say the design can include measures to limit environmental impacts and that improved traffic flow may reduce congestion elsewhere. The debate reflects a wider challenge for Bristol: how to support growth and improve transport while meeting climate and air-quality goals. The road’s eventual impact will depend on how much traffic it attracts and whether it is delivered alongside reliable public transport and active-travel options.

Facial-expression recognition is increasingly being discussed as a way to support learning in classrooms. It uses cameras and software to estimate emotions from students’ facial movements. In theory, this technology could help teachers notice when students seem confused, frustrated, or engaged. A teacher might then explain a difficult idea again or offer help to a student who is struggling. It could also help schools evaluate whether lessons are holding students’ attention. These possibilities make the technology seem useful, especially in large classes. However, recognizing emotion from a face is not as simple as it may appear. The same expression can mean different things to different people. A quiet student may be concentrating rather than bored, while a frown may reflect tiredness or discomfort. Students also express emotions differently because of culture, personality, disability, or individual habits. As a result, recognition software can make inaccurate or unfair judgments. Privacy is another serious concern. Students may not want their faces constantly recorded and analyzed, particularly if they do not understand how the information will be used. Schools would need clear rules about consent, data storage, access, and deletion. The information should never be used to punish students, rank them, or make important decisions without careful human review. Teachers should treat any software result as a possible signal, not as proof of what a student feels. They should check in with students directly and consider the classroom context. In many cases, supportive conversations and observations may be more reliable than automated analysis. Schools should also test systems for accuracy across different groups before using them. Families, students, teachers, and privacy experts should have a voice in deciding whether the technology is appropriate. If a school cannot protect students’ data or explain the benefits clearly, it should not use the system. Facial-expression recognition may offer limited help, but it cannot replace trust and human understanding. The best learning support comes from teachers who listen, notice individual needs, and create a safe classroom. Used cautiously and transparently, technology might assist that work, but students’ rights and well-being must come first.

Thousands of protesters marched through Manchester on Sunday, opposing government austerity measures and proposed restrictions on trade unions as the Conservative Party conference opened in the city.

The demonstration brought together trade union members, campaigners and residents concerned about public spending cuts. It was organised by unions and allied groups, which said the policies risked weakening public services and workers’ rights.

Crowds gathered in the city centre before setting off along a route near the conference venue. Many carried union banners and placards calling for an end to austerity. Others urged the government to protect jobs, pay and local services.

The march took place as Conservative delegates arrived for the party’s annual conference. The timing put the protesters’ criticism in direct view of ministers and party officials attending the event.

Union leaders said proposed changes to industrial action rules could make it harder for workers to strike. They argued that the measures would limit collective bargaining and reduce the ability of unions to represent their members.

The government has said changes to strike laws are intended to protect the public from disruption and ensure essential services continue. Ministers have also defended spending restraint as necessary to manage public finances.

Protesters disputed that case, saying cuts had already placed pressure on hospitals, schools and local authorities. Several speakers called for greater investment in public services and improved wages.

The march included contingents from a range of unions, alongside community organisations and anti-poverty campaigners. Participants travelled to Manchester from across the country, organisers said.

Police officers monitored the demonstration and managed traffic along the route. The march proceeded peacefully, with no immediate reports of major disorder.

Speakers addressed the crowd at a rally after the march. They urged the government to abandon the proposed restrictions and reconsider its approach to public spending.

Some participants said they had joined because of concerns about the cost of living and the effect of cuts on their communities. Others said protecting the right to strike was central to maintaining fair working conditions.

The demonstration added to a series of protests planned around the conference. Organisers said they wanted to keep public attention focused on the policies being debated inside.

The Conservatives’ gathering is expected to include discussions on the economy, public services and labour relations. The government’s proposals are likely to remain a point of dispute between ministers and unions.

Union representatives said they would continue campaigning after the conference ends. They warned that further industrial action could follow if negotiations failed.

The scale of the march underscored the strength of opposition among campaigners, though it did not indicate how the wider public views the government’s plans. Ministers have maintained that their policies are needed to address economic challenges.

As the rally concluded, organisers thanked participants and called for continued coordination among unions and community groups. The conference continued nearby, with the demonstration’s message forming a visible backdrop to the party’s proceedings.

This paper addresses an important challenge in reinforcement learning: learning efficiently when rewards are sparse or change over time. Its focus on automated curriculum generation is timely, since manually designing task sequences can be costly and difficult to generalize. The paper would benefit from a clearer definition of what counts as a curriculum and how its generation differs from existing adaptive task-sampling methods. The authors should explain how the approach handles dynamic rewards, including whether changes are known in advance or detected online. Evaluation should include strong baselines, such as random task selection, fixed curricula, and established adaptive curriculum methods. Results across multiple environments and random seeds would help establish robustness, while reporting uncertainty would make comparisons more reliable. Ablation studies could clarify which components of the curriculum-generation method contribute most to performance. The paper should also discuss computational overhead and whether gains in learning efficiency persist when this cost is included. Finally, clearer descriptions of the reward setups and training protocol would improve reproducibility. Overall, the topic is promising, but the strength of the contribution depends on rigorous comparisons and a precise account of how the method adapts to changing reward conditions.

The paper addresses an important problem: automatically designing training curricula that help agents learn efficiently without sacrificing robustness. Its focus on reinforcement learning and cooperative goal-setting agents offers a promising alternative to fixed, hand-designed schedules. The central idea is timely, especially for tasks where learner progress and task difficulty change over time. The paper’s strongest contribution is its framing of curriculum generation as a collaborative decision-making problem. This framing could clarify how goals are selected, revised, and coordinated across agents. The authors also recognize that a useful curriculum must balance challenge, coverage, and learner readiness. However, the paper needs to define “balanced” more precisely and explain how balance is measured. It is unclear whether the objective prioritizes learning speed, final performance, transfer, fairness across skills, or some combination of these. The paper should specify the agents’ observations, actions, reward functions, and communication protocol in enough detail for readers to reproduce the method. In particular, the cooperation mechanism needs to be distinguished from shared rewards or centralized control. The experimental evaluation should compare the proposed approach with strong baselines, including fixed curricula, heuristic adaptive curricula, and relevant single-agent methods. Ablations would help establish whether cooperation, reinforcement learning, and goal-setting each contribute measurable benefits. The evaluation should also test multiple task domains and random seeds, and report uncertainty rather than only average results. Claims of improved learning efficiency should be supported by learning curves and clearly defined sample-efficiency measures. The authors should examine whether the generated curricula generalize to new learners, task variations, or different levels of initial ability. Potential failure cases deserve attention, such as agents repeatedly selecting easy goals or overlooking less frequently practiced skills. A discussion of computational cost and the scalability of coordination would strengthen the practical assessment. Overall, the topic is compelling and the approach has clear potential, but the paper requires sharper definitions and more rigorous empirical evidence to substantiate its claims. I recommend revision, with particular emphasis on reproducibility, baseline comparisons, and a principled evaluation of curriculum balance.

The proposals include a football ground alongside housing and other facilities, subject to planning approval. The project is intended to provide the club with a modern stadium and generate funding through the wider development. The plans will now be considered by Southend-on-Sea City Council, which may seek further information or revisions before making a decision. Local residents and other stakeholders are expected to have an opportunity to comment during the planning process. The club has described the development as important to its future, though construction would depend on securing the necessary approvals and finance.

Schools should help student-athletes succeed in class while giving them time to train and compete. Sports teach teamwork, discipline, and perseverance, but demanding schedules can make schoolwork difficult. A balanced program should treat academic success as just as important as athletic achievement. Coaches can support this goal by planning practices around class schedules and limiting unnecessary travel. Schools should also set reasonable limits on practice hours, especially during exam periods. Student-athletes need access to tutors, study halls, and teachers who can answer questions about missed work. These supports should help students learn rather than simply complete assignments. Athletes also have a responsibility to plan ahead, attend class, and communicate when they need help. Families, teachers, and coaches can work together to notice when a student is becoming overwhelmed. Schools should monitor both academic progress and students’ health, including stress and sleep. When workloads become too heavy, reducing practice or competition may be the best choice. By setting clear priorities and providing practical support, schools can help student-athletes grow both in the classroom and on the field.

The paper addresses an important and technically challenging problem: learning competitive bidding policies in contract bridge when players cannot observe one another’s cards. Its focus on self-play is well motivated, since bidding outcomes depend on how opponents respond as well as on the bidding policy itself. The topic could appeal to researchers in game-playing AI, imperfect-information learning, and computational bridge. A central strength is the use of a realistic domain with a rich convention system and consequential partnership decisions. The paper also highlights a practical challenge that is often overlooked: a bidding system must work with a partner that follows the same learned policy.

The evaluation would be more convincing if the paper clearly specified its bridge rules, auction representation, scoring method, and treatment of conventions. It should describe the self-play training procedure in enough detail for readers to reproduce it, including the policy architecture, training schedule, and stopping criteria. The authors should explain how private hands and public auction history are represented and how the model avoids relying on information unavailable to a bidder. Because self-play can produce policies that exploit their own conventions, evaluation against independent opponents is essential. Results should include comparisons with established bidding systems and relevant learning-based baselines. Where possible, these comparisons should use identical deals and seating arrangements to reduce variance.

The paper should report uncertainty, for example through confidence intervals across many deals or repeated training runs. It should also compare performance under more than one scoring scheme, since a policy that succeeds under duplicate scoring may behave differently under rubber bridge or other objectives. Ablations could reveal whether gains come from self-play, the policy representation, or particular training choices. A useful analysis would examine bidding accuracy, contract selection, and downstream trick-taking outcomes separately. The authors should discuss how the learned policy handles rare auctions and whether its performance is robust to distribution shifts in opponents’ bidding styles. Potential weaknesses of self-play, including cycling behavior and overfitting to a narrow opponent population, deserve explicit attention.

The paper’s claims should distinguish clearly between improved bidding decisions and improved overall match results. If the policy depends on a fixed partner model, the authors should state this limitation and avoid implying that it can communicate effectively with arbitrary partners. Human interpretability is another relevant concern, as opaque conventions may limit practical adoption even when the scores improve. The discussion would benefit from examples of representative auctions, including both successful decisions and instructive failures. Any use of simulated data should be described alongside the simulator’s assumptions and validation against real play. The authors should also clarify whether the learned system is intended as a benchmark, a competitive agent, or a tool for studying bidding behavior.

Overall, the subject is promising, and self-play offers a plausible approach to adapting bidding policies to strategic opponents. However, the strength of the paper depends on rigorous baselines, reproducible methods, and evaluation beyond the training population. I recommend revision if these elements are not already provided. With clearer experimental evidence and a more careful account of limitations, the work could make a useful contribution to research on learning in imperfect-information games.

The paper addresses an important problem: when can convolutional neural network representations preserve enough information to reconstruct uniformly or irregularly sampled time series, and how sensitive are those representations to perturbations? The topic is relevant to signal processing, machine learning, and applications in which observations arrive at nonuniform times. A unified treatment of invertibility and stability could offer useful guidance for designing architectures and interpreting their outputs. The paper’s focus on both sampling regimes is a strength, since many practical datasets do not follow a perfectly regular schedule. The work appears potentially valuable, but its contribution depends on making the assumptions and guarantees precise.

The paper should clearly distinguish exact invertibility from approximate reconstruction and stability. These are related properties, but one does not automatically imply the others. In particular, the authors should state whether invertibility is intended on the entire signal space, on a restricted class of signals, or only up to a prescribed error. The relevant signal spaces and norms should be specified early. The authors should also define the representation map, including its layers, nonlinearities, padding conventions, and treatment of boundary samples. Without these details, the scope of any theorem is difficult to assess.

For uniformly sampled data, the analysis should explain how stride, pooling, channel count, filter support, and downsampling affect information loss. If the guarantees rely on a frame condition, rank assumption, or injectivity property, those conditions should be stated explicitly and connected to familiar concepts where possible. The paper would benefit from examples showing when the conditions hold and when they fail. A simple counterexample involving an overly aggressive stride or a rank-deficient filter bank could clarify why the assumptions are necessary. The role of nonlinearities also deserves careful treatment, especially when they are not injective. If invertibility is obtained only through redundant channels or a specific architecture, that architectural dependence should be emphasized.

The irregular-sampling setting raises additional questions that merit a detailed discussion. The authors should define precisely what makes a sampling pattern admissible, including any bounds on gaps, clustering, or local sampling density. It would be useful to distinguish irregular observation times from missing values on an otherwise fixed grid. The paper should state whether the sampling locations are known to the network and whether they are supplied as input, encoded in the filters, or handled by a preprocessing step. Stability claims should account for perturbations in both observed values and sampling locations if either can vary. The analysis should also clarify what notion of distance is used between irregularly sampled signals. Comparisons based only on index-wise norms may be misleading when time intervals differ substantially.

The stability results should identify the constants in their bounds and explain how those constants depend on the architecture and sampling pattern. A qualitative statement that the representation is stable is less informative if the stability constant can become arbitrarily large. The authors should discuss whether the bounds remain useful as sequence length increases or as samples become highly clustered. Where exact constants are unavailable, numerical estimates or interpretable upper bounds would still help. The paper should also distinguish robustness to small measurement noise from robustness to structural changes in the sampling pattern. These perturbations have different implications for practical deployment.

The theoretical presentation would be stronger if every theorem were accompanied by a short explanation of its assumptions and practical meaning. The proof strategy should make clear which steps are standard and which constitute the paper’s main technical contribution. Any dependence on finite-dimensionality, compact support, bounded input amplitude, or bandlimitedness should be highlighted rather than left implicit. The authors should avoid presenting results for a restricted signal class as guarantees for arbitrary time series. A concise summary table comparing assumptions and conclusions for uniform and irregular sampling would improve accessibility.

The experimental section should test the theoretical claims rather than serve only as a general performance demonstration. Useful experiments would vary sampling density, gap size, noise level, filter-bank redundancy, and network depth. Reconstruction error and perturbation sensitivity should be reported alongside task-level accuracy. Comparisons with relevant alternatives, such as interpolation-based preprocessing and established reconstruction methods, would help establish the practical value of the proposed approach. Ablations should isolate the effects of sampling-aware components and architectural choices. The paper should include results on both synthetic signals with controlled properties and realistic datasets with genuinely irregular timestamps. Reporting variability across random seeds and sampling patterns would make the evidence more convincing.

The authors should also discuss computational and implementation costs. Sampling-aware convolution or reconstruction procedures may introduce overhead that matters in long sequences or streaming applications. It would be helpful to report runtime and memory use, particularly relative to standard convolutional models. The paper should clarify whether reconstruction requires solving an optimization problem or can be performed by a direct, learned inverse. If an iterative procedure is used, convergence behavior and stopping criteria should be described.

Overall, the subject is timely and the combination of invertibility, stability, and irregular sampling has clear potential. The paper’s strongest contribution would be a precise account of when CNN representations preserve information, together with practical conditions that can be checked or engineered. At present, the central claims should be evaluated in light of the definitions, assumptions, and evidence described above. I recommend revision focused on sharpening the formal setup, exposing the limits of the guarantees, and strengthening the empirical validation. If these points are addressed, the work could provide a useful contribution to theory and practice for convolutional models of sampled time series.

Whether the School Day Should Be Extended for All Students

Some people believe that students should spend more time at school each day. They argue that a longer school day could help students learn more and get extra support. However, extending the day for everyone may create problems, too. Schools should consider students’ needs before changing the schedule.

One possible benefit is having more time for lessons. Teachers could explain difficult topics without rushing through them. Students might also have more opportunities to ask questions and practice new skills. Extra time could be used for art, music, sports, or science projects. These activities can make learning more enjoyable and help students discover their interests.

A longer school day could also provide time for homework support. Students who need help might work with a teacher before going home. Those who do not have a quiet place to study could finish assignments at school. This could reduce stress for some families. It might also help students who need additional instruction catch up with their classmates.

Still, extending the school day for all students could have disadvantages. Students need time to rest, play, and spend time with their families. A very long day may leave them tired and less able to focus. Younger students, especially, may find it difficult to learn well after many hours in class. Teachers could also become exhausted if they have to work longer without enough breaks.

A longer schedule may create difficulties for families as well. Parents might need to change their work or transportation plans. Some students could have less time for sports, jobs, or other responsibilities. Schools would also need to pay for extra staffing, meals, and transportation.

Instead of extending the day for everyone, schools could offer optional programs after regular classes. Students who want extra help or activities could choose to stay. Schools could also improve lessons during the existing day so that time is used effectively. In conclusion, extending the school day may have benefits, but it should not be required for all students. A flexible approach would give students support while still allowing them time to rest and enjoy life outside school.
