My grandfather came to America with little more than a suitcase and hope. He left his home country because he wanted his family to have a safer, brighter future. Saying goodbye to the people and places he loved was one of the hardest things he had ever done. When he arrived, he struggled to understand English and find steady work. He took any job he could, even when the hours were long and the pay was low. Some days, he came home exhausted, but he still made time to encourage his children. He learned new customs while holding on to the traditions that mattered to him. He missed his relatives and often worried about those he had left behind. Money was tight, so he saved carefully and went without many things he wanted. He made sacrifices so his children could have warm clothes, good meals, and opportunities to study. Although life was difficult, he never stopped believing that his hard work would lead to something better. Over time, he learned English and gained confidence in his new community. His family slowly built a home and made friends in America. My grandfather also taught his children to be grateful, responsible, and proud of their heritage. His journey was not easy, but each challenge made him more determined. Because of his sacrifices, later generations had choices he never had. His story reminds me that building a better life often takes courage, patience, and love. I am proud of my grandfather and hope to honor his efforts through my own hard work.

Virtual learning offers students a level of flexibility that traditional in-person schooling often cannot match. Students can attend lessons from home and may be able to review recorded lectures at a convenient time. This can make it easier to balance school with family responsibilities, health needs, or extracurricular activities. Online classes may also provide digital tools, such as practice quizzes and links to additional explanations. These resources can help students review difficult subjects at their own pace. However, virtual learning does not always provide stronger academic support. Students may find it harder to ask questions or get immediate help from a teacher online. They can also feel isolated and miss the encouragement that comes from studying with classmates in person. Traditional schools provide face-to-face guidance, regular routines, and opportunities to learn through group activities. At the same time, in-person schedules can be less convenient for students who need more control over when and where they study. Overall, virtual learning offers greater flexibility, but its academic support depends on the quality of instruction and the student’s ability to stay engaged. A combination of online resources and in-person interaction may offer the best balance for many students.

A proposed outdoor trial of genetically modified wheat designed to repel aphids has renewed debate over how far agricultural research should go in the open air.

The trial would test wheat engineered to release a scent that discourages the crop’s common insect pests. Researchers say the plants could offer a way to reduce aphid damage and reliance on insecticides.

The wheat produces a blend of naturally occurring compounds associated with plant defenses. In laboratory and controlled-environment studies, the scent has been shown to repel aphids and attract some of their natural predators.

Supporters argue that testing the crop in a field is necessary to learn whether those effects hold under real farming conditions. They say carefully managed trials can provide evidence about the plant’s behavior, potential benefits and possible risks.

The proposal has drawn opposition from campaigners who object to releasing genetically modified crops outside contained facilities. Some have warned they may destroy the wheat if the trial proceeds.

Those threats have sharpened concerns about both the trial’s security and the broader dispute over public acceptance of biotechnology. Researchers say crop destruction would set back work intended to develop alternatives to chemical pest control.

Aphids can weaken wheat plants by feeding on their sap and can transmit viruses. Farmers commonly manage them with insecticides, although the effectiveness and environmental effects of those treatments vary.

The research team says the modified wheat is intended to repel aphids by emitting a volatile compound, rather than by producing an insect-killing toxin. The scent may also help draw in insects that prey on aphids, though that effect needs to be assessed outdoors.

Scientists caution that results from a field trial would not, by themselves, establish that the crop is safe or suitable for commercial use. The trial would be one step in a longer assessment process.

That process typically involves monitoring the plants, recording effects on nearby organisms and controlling what happens to harvested material. Regulators may also require measures to prevent the crop from spreading beyond the test area.

Opponents question whether those safeguards can address the possibility of pollen or seeds moving beyond the plot. They also raise concerns about effects on wildlife, farmers’ control over seed and the wider use of genetic engineering in agriculture.

Some campaigners say the trial risks normalizing a technology they believe could deepen dependence on industrial farming. They argue that non-GM approaches, including crop rotation and supporting natural predators, deserve greater investment.

Researchers counter that pest-management methods need to be judged by evidence rather than by the technique used to develop them. They say the goal is to determine whether the wheat could reduce pesticide use, not to replace one rigid farming model with another.

The possibility of deliberate damage has prompted calls for authorities to protect the site and investigate threats. Scientists have also said security must be balanced with transparency about the trial’s location, methods and results.

Keeping details secret could make it harder for local communities to assess the work, while disclosing them may increase the risk of interference. That tension has become a familiar challenge for controversial field research.

The trial’s organizers say they intend to engage with residents and explain how the experiment will be monitored. Critics, however, may see consultation as insufficient if they oppose the release itself.

The dispute reflects a broader question facing agriculture: how to produce food while reducing chemical use and limiting harm to ecosystems. New crop technologies may contribute, but their benefits and risks can be difficult to predict before testing.

A field experiment could reveal whether the wheat’s scent works amid changing weather, varied insect populations and the complexity of an actual farm environment. It could also identify unintended effects that laboratory studies cannot capture.

For now, the proposal remains caught between scientific scrutiny and public resistance. Whether the trial goes ahead may depend not only on regulatory approval, but also on how authorities respond to threats and whether opponents believe their concerns have been heard.

Schools should keep a longer summer vacation instead of switching to a year-round schedule. A long break gives students time to rest after months of studying. They can spend more time with family and friends, explore hobbies, or travel. Summer also offers opportunities to attend camps, get a job, or learn skills outside the classroom. These experiences can help students grow in ways that school lessons may not. Teachers benefit from a chance to recharge and prepare for the next school year, too. Some people argue that year-round schedules prevent students from forgetting what they learned. Shorter breaks may make it easier to remember schoolwork. However, students can review important subjects during the summer without attending school all year. Schools can also offer optional summer programs for students who need extra help. A year-round schedule may be difficult for families who depend on summer childcare or plan vacations together. It could also make it harder for students to join seasonal activities. A longer summer break gives families more flexibility. Schools should make sure students have support during the year, but they should still protect time for a meaningful summer vacation. For these reasons, keeping a longer summer break is the better choice.

Doctor Strange topped the UK box office rankings, holding on to first place as audiences continued to turn out for the Marvel adventure. Several new releases entered the chart, reshaping the lower positions over the weekend. The latest arrivals drew varied audiences, though none managed to overtake the superhero hit. Family animation and established franchises also helped sustain cinema attendance. The rankings reflected a mix of big-budget releases and smaller films finding their audience. Strong word of mouth appeared to benefit titles that had been in cinemas for several weeks. Newcomers, meanwhile, faced competition from films with proven staying power. Box office figures showed that audiences were still willing to choose a range of genres. The fresh entries added momentum to a chart led by a familiar title. Doctor Strange’s continued success underscored the appeal of spectacle-driven cinema. The coming weekend will show whether the new films can climb higher or if the leader remains firmly in place.

People often face decisions and problems that feel too difficult to handle alone. In these moments, seeking trusted guidance can help them see a situation more clearly. A trusted person might be a parent, teacher, coach, counselor, or close friend. Because these people care about our well-being, they can offer advice with our best interests in mind. They may also have experience that helps them recognize risks we have not noticed. For example, a student choosing classes could speak with a teacher who understands the student’s goals and strengths. That conversation might reveal choices the student had not considered. Guidance can also help people cope with personal problems. When someone is stressed or discouraged, talking honestly with a supportive person can make the burden feel smaller. A friend may listen without judging, while a counselor can suggest practical ways to manage difficult feelings. Sometimes, simply explaining a problem aloud helps us understand what is bothering us. However, seeking advice does not mean letting someone else make every decision. We should listen carefully, ask questions, and consider whether the advice fits our situation. Different people may offer different opinions, so it is important to think for ourselves as well. We should also choose advisers who are trustworthy, respectful, and willing to listen. Someone who pressures us or ignores our needs may not be the right person to guide us. Once we have considered helpful advice, we can make a choice that reflects our values and goals. This process builds confidence because we learn how to weigh options rather than act impulsively. It can also strengthen relationships by showing that we trust and value other people. No one has to face every challenge alone. By seeking guidance from people we trust and making thoughtful choices for ourselves, we can make better decisions and cope more effectively with problems.

Analysts caution that violence in Nigeria has multiple causes, including insurgency, criminal activity, local disputes and competition over land and resources. They say sanctions can limit access to international financial systems but are unlikely to end the violence on their own. After World War II, Europe faced a crisis that reached far beyond its ruined cities. Farms had been damaged, animals had been lost, and many families lacked food and the means to rebuild their lives. In response, volunteers helped transport livestock to communities that urgently needed it. Their work was practical, but it also carried a message of hope.

The volunteers’ journeys were often difficult adventures. They traveled through damaged roads, across borders, and into regions where railways and bridges had been destroyed. Transporting animals required patience, skill, and careful planning. Cattle, horses, sheep, and pigs needed food, water, ventilation, and regular attention along the way. A delay or breakdown could put both the animals and the mission at risk.

The volunteers also had to cope with shortages of fuel, equipment, and reliable information. They sometimes encountered unfamiliar languages and customs, so cooperation with local people was essential. Weather made the work harder, especially when roads were muddy or icy. Even under these conditions, volunteers worked to keep the animals safe and calm. Their journeys demanded courage, but also kindness and responsibility.

The humanitarian value of the work became clear when livestock arrived at farms. Animals could provide milk, meat, wool, and labor for plowing fields. A healthy cow might help feed a family, while a horse could make it possible to cultivate land again. In this way, a shipment of livestock supported not only immediate survival but also long-term recovery. The animals helped communities become more self-sufficient.

The volunteers’ work also built connections between people from different countries. Those who transported livestock often depended on local farmers, officials, and aid organizations. Each successful delivery showed that cooperation could cross national boundaries, even after years of conflict. For the recipients, the animals represented a chance to begin again. For the volunteers, every journey was a reminder that humanitarian service could take many forms.

Although the work was demanding, it was not always dramatic or celebrated. Much of it involved careful preparation, routine checks, and solving small problems before they became serious. Yet these ordinary efforts had lasting importance. By moving livestock where it was needed, volunteers helped restore farms and strengthen communities. Their adventures were more than stories of travel; they were acts of care during a difficult period in European history.

The paper presents a timely and potentially valuable toolkit for designing, training, and evaluating complex-valued neural networks across diverse tasks. Ablations and implementation details—especially initialization, normalization, and optimization—would help readers assess which choices drive performance. The authors should also discuss limitations, computational costs, and the extent to which the toolkit supports extensibility and long-term maintenance. Overall, the work has strong potential, but its impact will depend on clear evidence of usability, reproducibility, and advantages over existing alternatives.

Two women have accused the late Liberal Democrat politician Clement Freud of sexually abusing them when they were children, prompting an apology from his widow and condemnation from his former party.

The allegations were reported by the BBC, which said the women described abuse spanning several years. Both said Freud targeted them while they were underage. Their accounts have renewed scrutiny of the public image of a man who was once a prominent broadcaster and parliamentarian.

Freud died in 2009, aged 84. He had served as a Liberal MP and was known to audiences for his work on radio and television. He was also a familiar figure in British public life for decades.

One woman said Freud abused her when she was a child. The other described a separate pattern of alleged abuse. The BBC reported that the women had spoken to investigators about their experiences. Their allegations have not been tested in a criminal court.

Freud’s widow, Jill Freud, apologised to the women after the claims emerged. She said she was deeply sorry for what they had endured. Her apology was reported as an expression of sympathy and regret, rather than an admission that she had known about the alleged abuse.

The Liberal Democrats condemned the allegations and said the reported behaviour was abhorrent. The party expressed sympathy for the women and acknowledged the seriousness of their accounts. Freud had been a member of the party’s predecessor, the Liberal Party, and later became associated with the Liberal Democrats.

The accusations have led to renewed questions about what those around Freud knew during his lifetime. They also raise concerns about how allegations of abuse were handled in institutions and social circles where influential figures held sway.

The women’s accounts add to wider public discussion about historic child sexual abuse and the barriers faced by survivors seeking to be heard. Many people who report abuse years later say they were children at the time and did not feel able to speak out. Investigations into historic allegations can be difficult because witnesses may be unavailable and evidence can be limited.

The BBC said it had taken steps to assess the women’s accounts before reporting them. The allegations remain allegations, and Freud cannot respond because he is dead. No criminal proceedings can be brought against him.

The women’s decision to come forward has drawn attention to their experiences as well as to Freud’s legacy. His career included work as a broadcaster, writer and politician. He was widely recognised for his distinctive public persona.

The Liberal Democrats’ response reflects the party’s effort to distance itself from conduct described in the reports. Its condemnation does not establish the truth of the claims, but signals that it regards the allegations as serious. The party has also faced broader scrutiny over how it responds to historic misconduct linked to former members.

Jill Freud’s apology has been welcomed as an acknowledgement of the women’s distress, though it cannot undo the harm they say they experienced. The women’s accounts have prompted calls for them to be listened to with care and respect. Their allegations are now part of a wider reckoning with the histories of powerful figures.

The case underscores the importance of allowing survivors to speak without prejudging the facts. It also highlights the distinction between expressing support for complainants and reaching a legal finding. For the two women, the public response has brought renewed attention to events they say took place many years ago.

Freud’s death means the allegations cannot be examined in a criminal trial. The women’s accounts, however, have prompted an apology from his widow and a clear rebuke from his former political home.

The Electoral College is the system the United States uses to choose its president. Each state receives electoral votes based on its number of members in Congress, and most states award all their votes to the candidate who wins the state. Supporters say this system protects the role of smaller states and encourages candidates to build support across the country. However, it does not represent every voter equally. Because each state gets at least three electoral votes, voters in less populous states have more electoral influence per person than voters in larger states. In addition, a candidate can win the presidency without receiving the most votes nationwide. This has happened several times in U.S. history, including in 2000 and 2016. Such outcomes can make voters feel that their individual ballots matter less. The winner-take-all system also means candidates often focus on a few closely contested states. Voters in states that strongly favor one party may receive little attention during campaigns. A direct popular vote would give every vote equal weight, no matter where it was cast. Candidates would have a reason to seek support in every state and community. Critics argue that a national vote could lead candidates to focus mainly on large cities. Yet campaigning in many regions would still be important for winning votes across the country. Changing to a direct vote would require a major constitutional change or another legally secure plan. It would also be important to set clear rules for recounts and election disputes. Although the Electoral College has a long history, tradition alone is not a strong reason to keep an unfair system. The president should be chosen by the candidate who receives the most votes from the people.

The paper addresses an important challenge in recurrent neural networks: learning long-term dependencies without losing useful information over many time steps. Its focus on ReLU-based recurrent networks with identity connections is well motivated, since these connections can help preserve signal and gradient flow. The topic is relevant to sequence modeling and memory-intensive tasks, where conventional recurrent architectures may struggle with vanishing gradients or limited effective memory.

The paper’s central idea is clear and potentially valuable. Identity connections provide a direct route through which information can persist, while ReLU activations can support non-saturating dynamics under suitable conditions. Together, these design choices offer a plausible way to improve learning over long sequences. The work also has practical appeal because the architecture appears relatively simple compared with more elaborate gated models.

A key strength is the attention to both long-sequence learning and memory retention, rather than focusing only on performance on short benchmark sequences. The paper would be most convincing if it clearly distinguishes the contribution of the identity connections from that of the ReLU activation. Ablations that remove each component in turn are essential for establishing which design choices drive the reported gains. Comparisons with standard recurrent networks and established gated architectures would also help place the results in context.

The experimental section should provide enough detail for readers to assess whether the tasks genuinely require long-term memory. Sequence lengths, dependency distances, training procedures, and evaluation metrics should be reported explicitly. It would also be useful to include multiple random seeds, uncertainty estimates, and consistent hyperparameter-search budgets across methods. Without these controls, apparent gains may reflect tuning differences or variability rather than a robust architectural advantage.

The paper should discuss stability carefully. ReLU-based recurrent dynamics can produce growing activations, inactive units, or sensitivity to initialization, so readers need evidence that the proposed model remains well behaved during training. Reporting activation statistics, gradient norms, and the frequency of dead units would strengthen this analysis. The authors should also clarify whether gradient clipping, normalization, or other stabilization techniques are required.

The claims about memory capacity deserve precise support. Retaining information across time is not necessarily the same as retrieving it accurately when needed, and benchmark results alone may not establish the mechanism. Targeted synthetic tasks with controlled dependency lengths could help characterize the limits of the model. Evaluating performance as sequence length increases would reveal whether the gains persist or degrade gradually.

The paper would benefit from a clearer account of computational cost. Identity connections may be inexpensive, but the total training time, parameter count, and memory use should be compared with those of the baselines. Such measurements would help determine whether any accuracy gains justify practical trade-offs. The discussion should also distinguish improvements in optimization from increases in representational capacity.

Overall, the proposed direction is promising and addresses a consequential limitation of recurrent models. The main concerns are the need for stronger component-wise analysis, careful stability diagnostics, and sufficiently controlled comparisons. If these issues are addressed, the paper could make a useful contribution to research on long-sequence learning. I recommend revision, with particular emphasis on clarifying the evidence for long-term memory and strengthening experimental reproducibility.

The paper presents a GAN-based approach to audio synthesis that models both spectral magnitudes and instantaneous frequencies, evaluated on the NSynth dataset. The topic is relevant, and the use of phase-related information alongside magnitude is a promising way to address limitations of magnitude-only synthesis. The paper’s main contribution would be clearer if it explained precisely how the two representations are encoded, generated, and combined during waveform reconstruction. The evaluation should compare the method with strong NSynth baselines and include both objective audio metrics and listening tests. In particular, perceptual quality, timbral similarity, and artifact rates would help establish whether the proposed representation improves on existing approaches. Ablations separating the effects of magnitude modeling and instantaneous-frequency modeling are also important. The authors should report training details, model capacity, and computational costs so that the results are reproducible and the comparisons fair. Because NSynth contains structured instrument and pitch labels, it would be useful to clarify the data split and whether the model generalizes to unseen instruments or pitches. The discussion should address potential weaknesses, such as phase reconstruction errors and instability in instantaneous-frequency estimates. Overall, the approach is promising, but stronger methodological detail and more comprehensive evaluation are needed to substantiate its advantages.

The paper presents an interesting approach to audio synthesis by combining conditional generative adversarial networks, phase-based spectrogram representations, and progressive training. Its focus on phase is well motivated, since phase information can affect perceived realism and the quality of reconstructed audio. The use of conditioning also offers a flexible way to guide generation toward desired acoustic properties. Progressive training is a promising strategy for stabilizing learning and gradually introducing finer signal detail. Overall, the topic is relevant to current work in neural audio generation.

The paper would benefit from a clearer explanation of how the phase-based representation is constructed and converted back into waveforms. In particular, the authors should discuss phase unwrapping, consistency constraints, and any assumptions made by the synthesis procedure. The conditioning mechanism also needs to be specified in enough detail for readers to reproduce the model. Please clarify which components are trained progressively, how transitions between training stages are handled, and how training stability is assessed. The experimental section should compare the proposed method with strong, recent baselines under matched data and compute settings. Ablations are needed to isolate the contributions of phase representation, conditioning, and progressive training. Evaluation should include objective measures of audio quality as well as listening tests with adequate participant numbers and statistical analysis. The paper should also report training cost, inference speed, and performance across different signal lengths or audio domains. Examples of generated audio would help readers judge perceptual artifacts that numerical metrics may miss. Finally, the authors should discuss limitations, including possible failure cases and sensitivity to dataset size or distribution.

The approach appears promising, but the strength of the evidence depends on clearer methodological detail and more comprehensive evaluation. I recommend revision before acceptance.

After-school involvement can play an important role in a student’s life. Activities such as sports, clubs, music, volunteering, and part-time work give students meaningful ways to spend their time. They also help students discover interests that may not come up during regular classes. By trying something new, students can learn what they enjoy and what they want to improve.

Taking part in activities encourages personal growth. Students practice setting goals, managing their time, and following through on commitments. When they face a challenge, such as learning a difficult skill or preparing for a performance, they can build patience and confidence. Mistakes become chances to learn rather than reasons to give up. These experiences can help students become more independent and responsible.

After-school activities also help students form stronger relationships. Working toward a shared goal can bring classmates together, even if they might not usually spend time with one another. Students learn to listen, communicate, and cooperate with teammates and group members. They may also build trusting relationships with coaches, teachers, and mentors. Feeling connected to a group can help students feel supported and included.

Involvement can also create opportunities for the future. Students may develop skills in leadership, problem-solving, or public speaking that are useful in school and at work. Volunteering can introduce them to community needs, while clubs and sports can help them explore possible careers or long-term interests. These experiences may also strengthen applications for scholarships, programs, or jobs. Most importantly, students gain examples of what they can accomplish through effort.

Of course, students need to balance activities with schoolwork, rest, and family responsibilities. Choosing activities that genuinely interest them can make that balance easier. When students are involved in a healthy and manageable way, they grow as individuals, build meaningful relationships, and prepare for new possibilities. After-school involvement is therefore more than a way to fill free time; it can help students shape the people they hope to become.

The paper investigates frequency-based image smoothing as a defense against adversarial attacks on neural networks. It addresses an important problem: small input perturbations can cause models to make incorrect predictions. The central idea—that smoothing or suppressing selected frequency components may reduce sensitivity to adversarial noise—is plausible and relevant. The topic is of interest to researchers working on robust vision systems and input preprocessing.

A key strength is the paper’s focus on a defense that is conceptually simple and potentially easy to deploy. Frequency-domain analysis may also help explain why certain perturbations affect model predictions. If supported by careful experiments, the approach could offer useful insight into the relationship between image spectra and model vulnerability. The work may further encourage comparisons between spatial-domain and frequency-domain defenses.

However, the paper needs to define its method precisely. It should specify the transform used, the frequency components modified, the smoothing operation, and any parameters required at inference time. The authors should explain how these choices are made and whether they are fixed across datasets and models. Without this information, it is difficult to reproduce the results or determine which component of the method provides the benefit.

The evaluation should include a broad range of threat models. Results against only a particular attack or perturbation budget would not establish that the defense is robust. The authors should test strong, adaptive white-box attacks that account for the preprocessing step. They should also include transfer-based and black-box attacks where appropriate. If smoothing is non-differentiable, the evaluation should use suitable gradient-estimation or attack methods rather than treating non-differentiability as protection.

The paper should report clean accuracy alongside robust accuracy. A defense that reduces attack success by substantially degrading ordinary predictions may have limited practical value. Results should be presented across multiple datasets, architectures, and random seeds, with variability or confidence intervals where feasible. Comparisons should include relevant preprocessing defenses and adversarially trained models. The authors should also compare against simple baselines, such as Gaussian blur and standard low-pass filtering, to establish whether the proposed frequency-based design adds value.

Ablation studies would strengthen the paper. In particular, the authors should examine how performance changes with smoothing strength, frequency cutoff, and image resolution. They should test whether gains persist when attack budgets and preprocessing parameters are varied. An analysis of which frequency bands are most associated with improved robustness would help substantiate the proposed explanation. The paper should also discuss possible artifacts, including loss of fine detail and changes to high-frequency textures.

The security claims need careful qualification. Input smoothing is a preprocessing step, not a general guarantee of robustness, and an adaptive attacker can optimize against it. The authors should distinguish empirical resistance to tested attacks from formal robustness guarantees. They should also discuss whether the defense could be bypassed by perturbations concentrated in frequency bands that it preserves.

Overall, the paper addresses a worthwhile question and presents a promising direction, but its contribution depends on rigorous evaluation and clear methodological detail. The current case for effectiveness would be more convincing with adaptive attacks, stronger baselines, and a fuller analysis of accuracy trade-offs. I recommend revision before publication, with emphasis on reproducibility and threat-model coverage. If these concerns are addressed, the work could make a useful contribution to the study of frequency-aware defenses.

Biryani’s Many Histories Come Together in India’s Kitchens

Biryani is among India’s best-known celebratory dishes, yet there is no single version—or simple account of its origins. Its name is commonly traced to the Persian words birian, meaning fried or roasted, and birinj, meaning rice. The dish is often linked to Persian and Central Asian cooking traditions that reached the Indian subcontinent through trade, migration and conquest. Rice cooked with meat and fragrant spices had precedents across those regions, but the biryani familiar in India developed through local exchange and adaptation. Mughal-era kitchens helped make elaborate rice-and-meat dishes prominent, though historians caution against assigning biryani to one ruler or moment. Over centuries, cooks shaped it around local ingredients, tastes and techniques.

A defining feature of many biryanis is the combination of rice, meat or vegetables, spices and aromatics. Cooks commonly use long-grain basmati in northern styles, while regional recipes may call for other rice varieties. Meat choices include chicken, mutton, beef and fish, depending on local custom and availability; vegetarian versions use vegetables, paneer or legumes. Whole spices such as cardamom, cloves, cinnamon and bay leaf often scent the cooking fat. Ginger, garlic, chilies, herbs and browned onions provide further layers of flavor.

Two broad methods are often used, though recipes do not always fit neatly into either category. In the “pakki” method, the meat and rice are cooked separately before being layered and finished together. In the “kacchi” method, marinated raw meat is layered with partly cooked rice, then sealed and cooked slowly until both are done. The sealed-pot technique, often called dum cooking, traps steam and allows the ingredients to finish gently. Some cooks seal the lid with dough; others use a tight-fitting lid and weight. Saffron, rose water, kewra water, ghee or fried onions may be added, but their use varies by recipe.

Hyderabadi biryani is one of the country’s most widely recognized styles. Its kacchi form is known for layering marinated meat with rice and cooking the pot on dum. Kolkata biryani, shaped by the city’s own history and tastes, is commonly associated with a mild, aromatic profile and the addition of potato. Lucknowi, or Awadhi, biryani is often prepared through a more measured layering process, with emphasis on fragrance and carefully cooked rice. In coastal regions, cooks draw on seafood and local ingredients, producing versions distinct from those of the north. Malabar biryani, particularly associated with Kerala, often uses short-grain rice such as kaima or jeerakasala rather than basmati.

The dish also reflects communities and family traditions that do not always follow regional labels. Sindhi biryani is often noted for its bold seasoning and tangy elements, while Bohri cooks have their own distinctive preparations. In parts of western India, local spice blends and preferred meats give biryani yet another character. Even within one city, households may disagree over the right balance of rice, meat, heat and fragrance.

That variety is part of biryani’s enduring appeal. It is served at weddings, festivals and family gatherings, as well as in restaurants and street-side eateries. Preparing it well takes attention to timing: rice must remain distinct, meat must turn tender, and spices should perfume rather than overwhelm. The final pot is often rested before serving, then opened at the table to release its aroma. Biryani’s history remains layered, much like the dish itself—a shared culinary inheritance continually remade in India’s kitchens.

The paper addresses an important challenge in neural instrument synthesis: selecting audio representations that work well with convolutional generative models while preserving perceptual quality. Its focus on both synthesis and evaluation is a strength, since representation choices can affect not only what a model generates but also how its outputs are judged. The topic is timely and relevant to researchers in audio generation, music information retrieval, and digital sound design.

The paper would benefit from a clearer statement of its central research questions and hypotheses. In particular, it should explain why the selected representations are appropriate for convolutional architectures and what advantages they are expected to offer over waveform modeling or alternative time-frequency transforms. The methods should specify preprocessing parameters, including sample rate, window and hop sizes, frequency scaling, normalization, and any phase-handling procedure. These details are essential for reproducibility and for interpreting differences between representations.

The experimental design should ensure that model capacity, training data, optimization, and compute budgets are comparable across conditions. If representations have different dimensionalities or temporal resolutions, the paper should discuss how these differences affect model complexity and synthesis latency. Evaluation should combine objective measures with listening tests, because common signal-based metrics may not reliably reflect timbral similarity or musical usefulness. Listening-test procedures should report participant numbers, expertise, stimulus randomization, playback conditions, and statistical analysis. The paper should also distinguish fidelity to reference recordings from diversity, controllability, and artifact reduction.

Results would be easier to assess if uncertainty estimates and appropriate significance tests were reported alongside aggregate scores. Representative audio examples and spectrograms could help readers understand characteristic strengths and failure modes. Ablations would clarify which preprocessing choices contribute most to performance, while tests across instruments and recording conditions would establish how broadly the conclusions generalize. The discussion should acknowledge trade-offs such as temporal precision, frequency resolution, phase reconstruction, and computational cost. It should also avoid treating a single metric or listener preference score as a complete measure of synthesis quality.

Overall, this is a promising and practically valuable line of research, but the paper’s conclusions will depend on rigorous comparisons and transparent reporting. I recommend strengthening the methodological description, broadening the evaluation, and clarifying the relationship between representation design and model behavior. With these revisions, the work could provide useful guidance for building convolutional generative systems for instrument sound synthesis.

Tindle Newspapers plans to acquire the Isle of Man’s three weekly newspapers and a local news website, expanding its presence in the island’s media market. A nursery in Anglesey has temporarily closed after an outbreak of E. coli prompted testing and public health investigations. Health officials are working with the nursery and local authorities to identify the source of the infections and limit further spread. The closure is a precaution while cleaning and other safety measures are carried out. Testing is being arranged for children and staff who may have been exposed, in line with public health advice.

Families have been contacted and asked to watch for symptoms, which can include stomach cramps, diarrhoea and vomiting. Some E. coli infections can cause more serious illness, particularly in young children and other vulnerable people. Anyone who is unwell should seek medical advice and follow guidance on staying away from childcare settings. Officials have urged people not to prepare food for others while experiencing symptoms.

The nursery is expected to reopen once authorities are satisfied that it is safe to do so. No reopening date has been announced. Public health teams are tracing contacts and reviewing hygiene procedures at the site. They have also asked families to maintain careful handwashing, especially after using the toilet and before eating.

The number of confirmed cases and the precise source of the outbreak have not been publicly established. Officials say investigations are continuing, and further information will be shared with affected families. Parents have been advised to contact health services if they have concerns about a child’s symptoms.

Autonomous vehicles are often described as a major step toward safer and more convenient transportation. They use cameras, radar, software, and other sensors to understand the road and make driving decisions. Although the technology could improve people’s lives, it also raises important concerns about safety, cost, and liability. These concerns must be addressed before self-driving cars become common.

Safety is one of the most important issues. Human drivers can become tired, distracted, or impaired, and automated systems do not experience these problems in the same way. As a result, autonomous vehicles may reduce some crashes caused by human error. However, they can also make mistakes when road conditions are unusual. Heavy rain, snow, glare, or faded lane markings may confuse sensors and software. Construction zones can also be difficult because signs and traffic patterns may change quickly. A vehicle must recognize pedestrians, cyclists, emergency vehicles, and unexpected hazards in time to respond. Even a small software error could affect many vehicles if they use the same system. For this reason, manufacturers need to test vehicles in many different settings before selling them widely. They should also explain what a vehicle can and cannot do. Drivers may become overconfident and stop paying attention if they believe the car can handle every situation. Clear instructions and reliable warnings could help prevent this kind of misuse. Safety testing should continue after vehicles are released, because real-world problems may not appear during early trials.

Cost is another major concern. Developing autonomous vehicles requires expensive sensors, computer systems, software, and testing. Those expenses can make self-driving cars costly to buy and maintain. Some companies may eventually lower prices through mass production, but there is no guarantee that the technology will become affordable for everyone. Repairs may also be expensive if a camera or sensor is damaged. In addition, vehicles may need regular software updates and specialized service. Higher costs could mean that wealthier people gain access to safer transportation first, while lower-income communities are left behind. Companies and governments should consider ways to make the benefits available to more people. Public transportation could also use autonomous technology, but only if it is safe, reliable, and reasonably priced. The total cost should include not just the vehicle, but also the roads, communication systems, and training needed to support it.

Liability becomes complicated when an autonomous vehicle causes a crash. With an ordinary car, responsibility often falls on the driver, although other parties can sometimes be involved. In a self-driving vehicle, the cause might be a driver’s failure to intervene, a software defect, a sensor malfunction, or poor vehicle maintenance. The manufacturer, software developer, vehicle owner, or fleet operator could each have some responsibility. Investigators may need access to vehicle data to understand what happened. That data can help establish the facts, but it also raises concerns about privacy and how personal information is used. Laws must clearly explain who is responsible in different situations. Without clear rules, injured people may struggle to receive compensation, and companies may face uncertain legal risks. Governments should create standards for recording and protecting relevant data. They should also require companies to report serious crashes and safety problems.

Autonomous vehicles could eventually make roads safer and help people who cannot drive themselves. However, these possible benefits do not remove the need for careful planning. Safety systems must be thoroughly tested, costs should be considered fairly, and liability rules must protect the public. Companies, lawmakers, and communities all have a role in addressing these issues. The technology should be introduced gradually, with honest information about its limits. If society takes these concerns seriously, autonomous vehicles may become a useful part of transportation rather than a source of new and avoidable problems.

Schools should encourage students to take part in optional extracurricular activities. These activities give students a chance to explore interests beyond their regular classes. A student who enjoys music might join a band, while someone who likes science could take part in a club. Trying new activities can help students discover talents they did not know they had. Extracurriculars also help students stay active, especially sports and outdoor clubs. Regular movement can support both physical health and better moods. Clubs and teams give students a natural way to meet others with similar interests. They can also help students make friends outside their usual classroom groups. Working together teaches useful skills such as communication, responsibility, and cooperation. These activities can make school feel more welcoming and enjoyable. However, participation should remain optional because students have different interests and responsibilities. Schools should also make activities affordable and offer a variety of choices. By encouraging extracurriculars without requiring them, schools can help students grow while respecting their individual needs.

Anonymous accounts on X, formerly known as Twitter, are circulating unverified claims about people in Delhi’s political and media circles, renewing concerns about defamation and online accountability. The posts often mix allegations, speculation and insinuation, while offering little evidence that readers can independently check. Some have drawn wide engagement through reposts and screenshots before the claims could be assessed.

The accounts typically use pseudonyms and may not identify who runs them. That distance can make it harder for people targeted by a post to seek a correction or response. It can also leave readers unsure whether a claim comes from firsthand knowledge, political rivalry or deliberate fabrication.

The material ranges from alleged personal relationships and private disputes to claims of misconduct and influence. In many cases, the posts do not provide documents, named sources or a clear account of how the information was obtained. This article does not repeat the allegations because they remain unverified.

People familiar with Delhi’s public life say the posts can spread quickly in a close-knit environment where political, business and media networks overlap. A claim may be treated as credible simply because it is repeated by multiple accounts, even when those accounts trace back to the same original post. Screenshots can further detach a statement from its context and make later corrections difficult to locate.

The targets may face reputational damage before they have a chance to respond. Journalists and political figures can also come under pressure to address claims that would not otherwise merit public attention. Silence may be interpreted as an admission, while a denial can give the allegation fresh visibility.

Indian law provides remedies for defamation, but pursuing a case can be costly and time-consuming. Questions of jurisdiction and identity may complicate action when an account’s operator is unknown or appears to be outside the country. Legal experts say the circumstances of each post matter, including whether it asserts a fact, expresses opinion or forms part of a public-interest discussion.

Online platforms have procedures for reporting posts and may respond to valid legal requests. However, moderation decisions are not a substitute for independent fact-checking, and enforcement can be uneven. Users may also find that content remains accessible through reposts after an original post is removed.

The issue poses a challenge for news organisations, which can face pressure to cover viral claims without amplifying unsupported material. Editors say verification requires more than counting views or checking whether prominent accounts have shared a post. Reporting should seek documents, corroboration and responses from those named, while making clear what remains unknown.

Media researchers have warned that anonymous speech can serve a legitimate role, including protecting sources and enabling people to discuss sensitive issues. Anonymity alone does not establish that a claim is false or malicious. But repeated publication of serious allegations without substantiation can undermine trust and cause lasting harm.

Those affected by the posts have urged users to avoid forwarding claims as fact and to preserve evidence if they believe they have been targeted. They can also seek legal advice or use platform reporting channels, though neither route guarantees a quick resolution. A correction or retraction, when warranted, may not travel as far as the original claim.

The broader concern is how to balance free expression with protection against demonstrably false and damaging statements. Greater transparency about sourcing and clearer distinctions between reporting, opinion and rumour could help readers assess online claims. For now, the circulation of unverified gossip in Delhi’s political and media networks underscores the limits of accountability when the speaker’s identity is concealed and the audience is already listening.

Joining an overseas volunteer program can seem like a generous way to help, but it is worth considering whether that choice is right when important needs remain at home. Many communities face challenges such as poverty, loneliness, poor access to education, and environmental damage. These problems may be less visible than crises abroad, but they still affect people who need support. Volunteers can often make a meaningful difference by helping in their own neighborhoods. They may already understand the local language, culture, and concerns, which can make their efforts more useful. Staying home can also help people build lasting relationships rather than offering brief assistance and then leaving. Overseas programs sometimes require substantial travel and participation fees, and that money might support local charities more directly. In some cases, short-term volunteers lack the training needed for the tasks they are assigned. Their presence can unintentionally take work away from local professionals or create dependence on outside help. Good intentions alone do not guarantee that a project benefits the people it aims to serve. Before traveling, a volunteer should learn whether the organization is community-led and what results its work has achieved. They should also consider family responsibilities, studies, employment, and other commitments at home. Choosing to stay does not mean being selfish or indifferent to people in other countries. It can instead reflect a thoughtful decision to meet responsibilities and help where one is best prepared. People who still want to contribute internationally could donate, share reliable information, or support long-term partnerships. Ultimately, volunteering is most valuable when it responds to real needs and respects the people receiving help. By carefully weighing local duties against overseas opportunities, individuals can make a responsible choice about where their time and skills will do the most good.

Extending the school day may seem like a good way to help students learn more, but it could create serious problems. Students already spend many hours attending classes, completing assignments, and participating in activities. Adding more time at school could leave them feeling tired and overwhelmed. When students are exhausted, it can be harder for them to pay attention and remember what they have learned. A longer day might therefore reduce the quality of learning instead of improving it.

Students also need time outside school to rest and develop important interests. Many take part in sports, music, clubs, or community activities after classes. Others have family responsibilities or part-time jobs. Extending the school day could force students to give up some of these experiences. Free time also helps young people relax, spend time with family, and take care of their health. Without enough time to recharge, students may experience more stress and lose motivation.

Teachers could be negatively affected as well. They already spend time planning lessons, grading work, and communicating with families beyond their classroom hours. A longer school day could increase their workload and leave them with less time to prepare effective lessons. It might also make it harder for teachers to balance their jobs with their personal lives. Over time, exhaustion could contribute to burnout and cause more teachers to leave the profession. Schools could then struggle to find and keep experienced educators.

Extending the day would also require additional resources. School buildings would need to stay open longer, using more electricity, heating, and water. Districts might have to pay staff extra hours or hire additional workers. Bus schedules, meal services, and after-school programs could also become more expensive to operate. These costs could place pressure on school budgets that are already limited. Money spent keeping schools open longer might be better used for tutors, classroom materials, counselors, or smaller class sizes.

A longer schedule would not necessarily solve the reasons students struggle in school. Some students may need more support rather than more hours in a classroom. Schools could improve learning by offering focused tutoring, engaging lessons, and help for students who are falling behind. They could also protect time for rest and activities that support students’ overall development. For these reasons, extending the school day could harm students, increase pressure on teachers, and strain school resources. Schools should look for ways to improve learning without simply making the day longer.

Facial-expression technology can help teachers understand students’ reactions during lessons. By analyzing visible expressions, it may highlight confusion, interest, or frustration that a student does not express aloud. This information could help teachers adjust their explanations, identify topics that need review, and offer support sooner. It may also help researchers evaluate teaching methods and make learning activities more responsive. However, facial expressions do not reliably reveal a person’s true emotions. A student’s expression can be influenced by culture, disability, fatigue, personal habits, or factors unrelated to the lesson. The technology may therefore misinterpret students and lead teachers to make unfair assumptions. Collecting and analyzing students’ facial data also raises serious concerns about privacy, consent, and data security. Schools should not treat automated emotion estimates as facts or use them to punish or label students. Overall, this technology may offer limited insights, but it should be used cautiously and alongside respectful conversation and human judgment.

The Electoral College should be replaced with a nationwide popular vote for president. In a democracy, each citizen’s vote should count equally, no matter where that person lives. Under the current system, however, the importance of a vote can depend on the state where it is cast. Most states award all their electoral votes to the candidate who wins that state, even if the victory is narrow. As a result, a candidate can win the presidency without receiving the most votes nationwide. This has happened several times in American history, including in 2000 and 2016. Many voters may feel that their voices did not matter in those elections. A nationwide popular vote would make the candidate with the most votes the winner. Every vote would contribute directly to the same national total. Candidates would also have a reason to campaign in every state, not only in a handful of closely contested ones. Under the current system, candidates often focus their time and attention on battleground states. Voters in states considered safely won or lost may receive less attention from campaigns. A popular vote could encourage candidates to listen to a broader range of communities. It would also make the result easier for people to understand. Instead of counting electoral votes, the country would compare the candidates’ total votes nationwide. Some people argue that the Electoral College protects the influence of smaller states. However, a popular vote would not prevent people in those states from voting or having their concerns heard. Candidates could still seek support from rural and urban communities alike. Changing the system would require a constitutional amendment or another legally valid approach, so it would not be simple. Still, the challenge of reform should not stop Americans from considering whether the system is fair. A nationwide popular vote would better reflect the choice of the country’s voters. For these reasons, the United States should replace the Electoral College with a popular vote for president.

Autonomous vehicles could make roads safer by reducing crashes caused by distracted or tired drivers. However, their sensors and software can still fail, especially in bad weather or unusual traffic situations. These risks raise questions about who is responsible when a self-driving car causes an accident. The technology may also be expensive, making autonomous vehicles unaffordable for many people at first. Over time, they could lower costs by reducing collisions and making transportation more efficient, but those savings are not guaranteed. Personal freedom is another concern because some people may not want a computer making decisions about where and how they travel. The collection of location data could also threaten privacy if companies or governments misuse it. Society should encourage useful innovation while setting clear safety, cost, and privacy rules.

The paper examines whether complex-valued neural network operations improve performance on standard classification tasks. The topic is timely, as complex representations may capture phase and amplitude relationships that real-valued models do not express as naturally. The paper’s central contribution would be clearer if it stated precisely which operations are novel and how they differ from established complex-valued architectures. The experimental design should compare the proposed model with strong real-valued and complex-valued baselines under matched parameter counts and training budgets. Dataset selection and preprocessing also need justification, particularly if the tasks do not naturally contain complex-valued inputs. The authors should explain how real-valued data are mapped into complex representations and test whether conclusions depend on that choice. Results should include multiple random seeds, uncertainty estimates, and appropriate statistical comparisons. Ablations separating the effects of complex weights, activations, normalization, and loss functions would help identify what drives any gains. Computational cost, training stability, and sensitivity to initialization should be reported alongside accuracy. The paper would also benefit from error analysis and discussion of cases where complex-valued operations do not help. Claims of broad effectiveness should be tempered if improvements occur only on a narrow set of benchmarks. Overall, the work could make a useful contribution, but stronger methodological detail and evidence are needed to establish that the observed benefits are robust and attributable to complex-valued operations.

A meteor exploded over the Atlantic Ocean in June 2025, releasing energy comparable to roughly 20,000 tons of TNT, according to NASA. The blast occurred about 1,000 kilometers off the coast of Brazil, far from populated areas. NASA estimated the object was around 20 meters wide before it entered Earth’s atmosphere. It broke apart high above the ocean, producing a powerful flash and shock wave. The event was detected by sensors designed to monitor nuclear explosions, which also record energy released by meteors. NASA said it was the strongest such atmospheric explosion since the 2013 Chelyabinsk event in Russia. The Chelyabinsk meteor was larger and caused widespread damage, injuring more than 1,000 people when windows shattered. No injuries or damage were reported from the Atlantic blast. Scientists say oceanic explosions can go unnoticed because they occur far from observers and may leave few traces. The incident underscores the value of monitoring near-Earth objects, including those too small to be detected well in advance.

Personal growth and success do not usually happen all at once. They develop through the choices people make each day. Three important influences on this journey are perseverance, lifelong learning, and positive role models. Together, these qualities help people overcome challenges and work toward meaningful goals.

Perseverance is the ability to continue trying when progress is difficult or slow. Everyone faces setbacks, such as failing a test, losing an opportunity, or struggling to learn a new skill. It can be tempting to give up when an effort does not produce an immediate result. However, mistakes and disappointments can teach us what to change. A student who receives a low grade, for example, can review the material, ask for help, and prepare differently next time. This response turns a setback into a chance to improve. Perseverance also builds confidence because each challenge overcome shows us what we can do. It does not mean ignoring problems or refusing to change direction. Instead, it means staying committed while being willing to try a better approach.

Lifelong learning is another essential part of personal growth. Learning does not end when someone finishes school. People continue to gain knowledge through books, work, conversations, and new experiences. The world changes quickly, so learning helps people adapt to new ideas and situations. It can also reveal interests and abilities that a person did not know they had. Someone who learns a new language, for instance, may discover a passion for travel or communication. Lifelong learning encourages curiosity and helps people make thoughtful decisions. It also reminds us that no one knows everything. Being open to learning from others can strengthen both our skills and our understanding of the world.

Positive role models can also guide people toward success. A role model may be a family member, teacher, coach, friend, or public figure. Their actions can show us how to handle responsibility, treat others, and respond to difficult moments. A hardworking teacher, for example, can inspire students to approach their own responsibilities with care. Role models can offer encouragement when our confidence is low. They may also help us imagine goals that once seemed out of reach. Still, it is important not to copy someone blindly. We can learn from their strengths while making choices that fit our own values and circumstances.

These three influences work best together. Perseverance helps us keep going, learning helps us improve, and role models can offer guidance and inspiration. Imagine a student who hopes to become a doctor. The student may need perseverance to manage demanding classes, lifelong learning to build knowledge, and role models to understand the responsibilities of the profession. Progress may be gradual, but each effort can bring the goal closer. Even if the student eventually chooses a different path, the habits developed along the way will remain valuable.

In the end, success is not only about awards, money, or recognition. It can also mean becoming more capable, thoughtful, and fulfilled. Perseverance teaches us to face difficulty, lifelong learning keeps us growing, and positive role models help us see what is possible. These qualities do not guarantee an easy path, but they can help us meet challenges with purpose. By practicing them, we can make steady progress toward the lives we hope to build.

This paper addresses a promising area: using complex-valued neural networks (CVNNs) to represent phase as well as magnitude in image and audio recognition. Its central premise is well motivated, since phase can encode useful structure in signals that magnitude-only models may discard. The paper’s strongest contribution is its effort to connect this representational advantage to practical recognition tasks. The discussion of both image and audio applications also gives the work useful breadth. However, the claims would be more convincing if the paper defined its scope and contributions more precisely. In particular, it should distinguish native complex-valued operations from approaches that split real and imaginary components and process them with conventional layers. These designs may have different representational properties and computational costs.

The treatment of phase information needs greater technical detail. The authors should explain how phase is represented, normalized, and preserved through each layer, and how phase wrapping is handled. They should also clarify whether the reported gains arise from phase-sensitive modeling or simply from increased parameter counts. Appropriate ablations comparing magnitude-only, phase-only, and joint magnitude–phase inputs would help answer this question. For audio, results should be tied to the chosen transform and its properties; for images, the paper should explain how complex features are constructed and interpreted.

The activation-function discussion is relevant but currently needs stronger justification. Common real-valued activations do not transfer directly to the complex plane without choices that affect analyticity, stability, and information loss. The paper should compare its chosen functions with suitable alternatives, including component-wise and magnitude-based activations where appropriate. It should report how activation choice affects accuracy, convergence, and numerical stability rather than presenting it as a minor implementation detail. Clear definitions and equations would make this section reproducible.

Computational cost is a central concern and deserves a more complete evaluation. Complex multiplication generally requires more arithmetic than real multiplication, while memory use can also increase because both real and imaginary components must be stored. The paper should report parameter counts, peak memory, training time, and inference latency alongside recognition accuracy. Comparisons should use matched architectures and hardware, and should clarify whether the real-valued baselines have comparable capacity. An analysis of energy use or throughput would further support claims about practical deployment. The authors should also discuss whether any accuracy improvement justifies the additional cost for the intended applications.

Overall, the topic is timely and the paper has the potential to clarify when complex-valued models are useful. The experimental section would benefit from stronger baselines, repeated runs, uncertainty estimates, and tests on more than one dataset per modality. A concise limitations section should address sensitivity to preprocessing, noise, and domain shifts. I recommend revision, with priority given to isolating the contribution of phase, strengthening the activation-function analysis, and quantifying computational overhead. These changes would make the conclusions more rigorous and help readers judge whether CVNNs offer a practical advantage over well-tuned real-valued networks.

The restrictions may be adjusted as weather conditions change, authorities said. Heat-wave warnings remain in place across affected areas.
