Expressing opinions honestly is an important part of learning and communicating with others. At the same time, our words can affect how people feel. We should aim to be truthful without being unkind. This takes thought, patience, and practice.

Before sharing an opinion, it helps to understand what we really think and why. We can ask ourselves whether we have enough information. We should also consider whether the moment is right for the conversation. If someone is upset or busy, it may be better to wait. Choosing a calm time can make it easier for both people to listen.

The way we speak matters as much as what we say. We can use “I” statements, such as “I see it differently” or “I felt disappointed.” These phrases explain our perspective without blaming someone else. We should avoid insults, sarcasm, and words like “always” or “never.” Such language can make people feel attacked and stop them from listening.

Listening is also essential when opinions differ. We should give others a chance to explain their views. We can ask questions to understand what they mean instead of assuming the worst. Even if we disagree, we can acknowledge the parts of their opinion that make sense. This shows respect without requiring us to change our own beliefs.

Honesty does not mean saying every thought that comes to mind. We can be truthful while choosing words that are considerate. For example, instead of saying, “Your idea is terrible,” we could explain what concerns us and suggest an improvement. We should be specific and focus on the idea, not the person. If our words hurt someone, we should listen, apologize sincerely, and try to express ourselves better.

Respectful disagreement can strengthen relationships. It helps people learn from different experiences and consider new possibilities. We may even discover that we share some common ground. When we speak openly and listen carefully, conversations become more useful and fair. In the end, honesty and kindness work best together. We can stand by our opinions while still treating others with dignity.

Students should be allowed to use mobile devices at school when they are used responsibly. Phones and tablets can help students look up information, use learning apps, and organize assignments. They also make it easier to contact family in an emergency. However, devices can distract students from lessons and encourage cheating or cyberbullying. Schools should set clear rules, such as requiring phones to be silent and put away during instruction unless a teacher approves their use. Students who break these rules should face fair consequences. With sensible limits, mobile devices can support learning while keeping students focused and safe.

Student-Led Summer Assignments: Creativity, Personalized Learning, and Motivation

Summer assignments are often designed to help students remember what they learned during the school year. However, when every student receives the same task, the work may not feel relevant or inspiring. Student-led summer assignments offer a different approach. They allow students to choose a topic, set a goal, and decide how to show what they have learned. This freedom can support creativity, personalized learning, and motivation.

One important benefit is the chance to be creative. Students can explore a question that interests them and approach it in their own way. For example, one student might write a short story, while another creates a video or builds a model. These different formats let students use their strengths and experiment with new ideas. They can also make connections between school subjects and their hobbies. A student who enjoys cooking might investigate how measurements and chemistry affect a recipe. When students make choices, learning can feel less like completing a worksheet and more like making something meaningful.

Student-led assignments also make learning more personal. Students have different interests, skills, and goals, so one assignment may not work equally well for everyone. Choice allows each learner to select a suitable challenge. A student who needs more practice in mathematics could explore budgeting for a project. Another student could investigate local history or learn a new language. Students may work at a pace that fits their summer schedules, while still setting clear goals. They can also choose whether to work independently or with others. This flexibility can help students take responsibility for their progress.

A further benefit is increased motivation. People are more likely to put effort into work when they see its purpose and have a say in it. Choosing a topic can make students curious enough to keep exploring. Setting a personal goal can also give them a reason to continue when the work becomes difficult. Completing a project they selected can build confidence and a sense of accomplishment. Students may return to school eager to share what they discovered. Their enthusiasm can encourage classmates to ask questions and exchange ideas.

Of course, student-led assignments still need guidance. Teachers can offer a clear set of learning goals and examples of suitable projects. They can help students choose realistic plans and break large tasks into smaller steps. Families can support students by providing time, materials, or encouragement without taking over the work. Teachers should also consider that students have different access to technology and other resources. Offering several ways to complete a project can make participation fairer. Regular check-ins or reflection questions can help students stay on track.

In conclusion, student-led summer assignments can make learning more creative, personal, and motivating. They give students room to follow their interests while practicing important skills. With helpful guidance and flexible options, these assignments can be both enjoyable and educational. Instead of seeing summer learning as a chore, students may view it as an opportunity to explore. That experience can help them become more confident and independent learners throughout the year.

Setbacks are a natural part of life, and everyone experiences them at some point. A poor grade, a missed opportunity, or a difficult mistake can feel discouraging. However, challenges can also teach us important lessons. When something goes wrong, we have a chance to reflect on what happened and decide what to do next. This process helps us become more resilient.

Resilience is the ability to recover from difficulty and keep moving forward. It does not mean that we never feel disappointed or afraid. Instead, it means that we learn to face those feelings without giving up. For example, a student who receives a low test score can review their mistakes and try new study methods. Although improvement may take time, each effort can bring them closer to their goal.

Setbacks can also help us discover strengths we did not know we had. A challenging situation may require patience, creativity, or courage. As we practice these qualities, we become more confident in handling future problems. We may also learn to ask others for support, which is an important skill rather than a sign of weakness.

Personal achievement often requires persistence. Many successful people have faced failures before reaching their goals. Their setbacks did not guarantee success, but they provided opportunities to learn and adapt. When we use difficulties as lessons, we can make better choices and develop stronger habits.

Of course, a setback can be painful, and it is important to give ourselves time to recover. What matters is not avoiding every failure, but choosing how to respond to it. By reflecting, seeking help, and trying again, we can turn disappointment into progress. In this way, setbacks can build resilience and help us achieve goals that once seemed out of reach.

A constructive mindset helps people focus on solutions instead of giving up when problems arise. It does not mean pretending that everything is easy or perfect. Instead, it means learning from challenges and choosing helpful actions. This attitude can contribute to success at work, school, and home.

At work, a constructive mindset makes it easier to handle feedback. Rather than taking criticism personally, a worker can use it to improve. When a project becomes difficult, looking for practical solutions can help the whole team move forward. A positive, respectful attitude also strengthens relationships with coworkers. Over time, these habits can build trust and create more opportunities to learn and grow.

At school, students with constructive mindsets are more willing to keep trying after making mistakes. They understand that a low grade or confusing lesson does not define their abilities. Instead, they can ask questions, seek help, and adjust their study habits. This approach makes learning feel like a process rather than a test of natural talent. It can also help students work cooperatively and encourage their classmates.

At home, a constructive mindset supports healthier communication. Family members can listen to one another and look for fair ways to solve disagreements. Sharing responsibilities becomes easier when people focus on helping rather than blaming. This attitude can also help everyone stay patient during stressful times. As a result, home can feel more supportive and peaceful.

A constructive mindset cannot prevent every setback, but it can shape how people respond to one. It encourages patience, responsibility, and steady effort in many parts of life. By practicing it each day, people can make progress, strengthen relationships, and contribute to their communities.

The paper studies whether reinforcement learning converges to equilibrium in dominance-solvable games and how this result can guide reward design in multi-agent systems. The topic is timely, since learning dynamics and incentive design are central challenges in deploying interacting agents. A useful contribution would be to connect a formal convergence result with practical design principles rather than treating theory and application separately. The paper’s focus on dominance-solvable games offers a clear starting point, but the authors should define the class of games precisely and explain why it is relevant to their target applications. The assumptions on the agents’ information, action spaces, update rules, and exploration behavior need to be stated in a consolidated form. In particular, the paper should distinguish convergence of policies, value estimates, and realized play, since these are not interchangeable claims. The convergence argument should identify whether it is almost sure, in expectation, or in some weaker sense. It should also clarify whether convergence is to a unique equilibrium or merely to a set of outcomes consistent with iterated elimination of dominated strategies. The treatment of function approximation and non-stationarity deserves particular attention, because both can invalidate guarantees established for tabular or stationary settings. If the theoretical result relies on restrictive learning rates or exploration schedules, the paper should discuss whether these conditions are practical. The application to reward design is promising, but the current conceptual bridge between equilibrium convergence and desirable system-level behavior should be made explicit. Convergence alone does not ensure that the resulting equilibrium is socially efficient, safe, or aligned with the designer’s objectives. The authors should specify what properties a reward designer can control and what constraints are assumed to be known. A concrete worked example would help show how the theory changes the choice of rewards compared with standard heuristic design. The empirical section should compare against suitable baselines, including unshaped rewards and at least one established reward-shaping approach. Ablations could isolate the effects of the proposed design method, exploration, and the game structure. Reporting variance across random seeds and sensitivity to hyperparameters would strengthen the evidence. The experiments should also include cases near the boundary of the dominance-solvable setting, illustrating what happens when the assumptions fail. The paper would benefit from a clearer discussion of scalability as the number of agents and actions grows. I recommend revising the presentation to separate proven guarantees from conjectures and empirical observations. Overall, the work addresses an important problem and could make a valuable contribution if its assumptions, convergence claims, and practical implications are articulated more carefully. My recommendation is revise and resubmit, subject to a strengthened theoretical exposition and more rigorous empirical validation.

The paper addresses an important problem: reducing the cost of geometric correspondence estimation while preserving robustness to mismatches. Its combination of graph neural networks and SIFT feature matches is a plausible way to exploit local and global consistency among candidate correspondences. The topic is relevant to image matching, structure from motion, and related vision applications. The central contribution should be stated precisely, especially in relation to existing learned match filtering and correspondence-pruning methods. The paper would benefit from a clear explanation of how the correspondence graph is constructed and which geometric or feature attributes are supplied to the network. It should also specify the pruning objective, the decision threshold, and whether the method is trained jointly with or separately from the downstream estimator. A key concern is whether pruning removes valid but atypical correspondences, such as those arising from repeated patterns, low-texture regions, or large viewpoint changes. The experiments should therefore report not only the number of matches retained but also the recall of true correspondences. Evaluation on diverse datasets and challenging conditions would help establish the method’s generality. Comparisons should include strong classical robust estimators and recent learned filtering approaches, using consistent input matches and tuning protocols. In addition to final geometric accuracy, the paper should report runtime, memory use, and the cost of graph construction and network inference. Ablation studies are needed to isolate the effects of graph design, network architecture, training data, and pruning aggressiveness. The authors should clarify how ground-truth inliers are defined and how results are aggregated across scenes or sequences. Statistical variation across runs would make the reported improvements more convincing, particularly if the gains are small. A discussion of failure cases and sensitivity to thresholds would also improve the practical value of the work. Overall, the approach is promising, but its contribution and effectiveness will be convincing only with rigorous comparisons, transparent implementation details, and evidence that pruning improves efficiency without sacrificing geometric reliability.

The paper addresses an important problem in graph classification: how to build hierarchical representations that preserve useful structural information while reducing graph complexity. Its central idea—combining multiple convolution and pooling operations over successively pooled representations—is intuitive and potentially valuable. The approach may help capture patterns at different scales that a single pooling strategy could miss. The topic is relevant to applications in which graphs vary in size and structure.

A key strength is the explicit focus on learning from pooled representations rather than treating pooling as a one-time preprocessing step. This design could support progressively higher-level feature extraction. Combining several operations may also improve flexibility across graph types. The paper would be stronger, however, if it explained more clearly how the proposed hierarchy differs from existing hierarchical graph neural networks. A concise comparison with closely related convolution-and-pooling methods would help establish the contribution.

The technical description should specify the convolution and pooling operators, the order in which they are applied, and how information is passed between levels. It should also clarify whether pooling is learned, deterministic, or a combination of both. The authors should discuss how the method handles variable graph sizes, disconnected components, and graphs with very few nodes. If multiple pooled representations are combined, the paper should explain the fusion mechanism and its computational cost. A diagram showing the full forward pass would make the architecture easier to understand.

The experimental evaluation should include strong, recent baselines and use consistent data splits and tuning procedures. Ablation studies are especially important here: they should isolate the effects of each convolution, pooling operation, and hierarchy level. Comparisons against simpler architectures would show whether the added complexity is justified. Results should be reported across multiple random seeds, with uncertainty or statistical testing where appropriate. The paper should also provide runtime and memory measurements, since repeated operations over pooled graphs may be expensive.

Further analysis of sensitivity to the number of pooling stages and the choice of pooling ratios would improve the evaluation. The authors should examine whether performance gains hold across datasets with different graph sizes and structural characteristics. Interpretability would also be valuable: visualizations or case studies could show what information each hierarchy level retains. Limitations, including possible loss of fine-grained structure during pooling, should be acknowledged. Overall, the approach appears promising, but the paper needs clearer positioning, fuller methodological detail, and more comprehensive experiments to support its claims. I recommend revision before publication.

This paper addresses an important problem: predicting how objects interact over time in 2D games. Its object-centered perspective is a promising alternative to modeling each frame as an undifferentiated image. The topic is relevant to visual prediction, game-playing agents, and model-based planning. The paper’s central premise is that representing entities and their dynamics explicitly can improve prediction and support downstream decisions. This premise is compelling and, if supported by strong evidence, could make the work useful to researchers across several areas.

The paper’s clearest potential strength is its focus on interactions rather than appearance alone. In games, collisions, movement, and changes in object state often determine what happens next. An object-centered model may therefore offer a more interpretable account of game dynamics than a purely pixel-based predictor. The approach could also make predictions more robust to changes in object position or scene layout. These advantages are especially relevant in settings where visual observations are complex but the underlying mechanics are relatively structured.

The presentation would benefit from a more precise definition of the proposed representation. The paper should specify how objects are detected, tracked, and associated across frames. It should explain whether object identity is maintained through occlusion, rapid movement, or changes in appearance. The authors should also clarify which properties are represented for each object, such as position, velocity, shape, or discrete state. Without these details, it is difficult to determine which part of the system is responsible for any observed gains.

The dynamics model also requires a clearer description. The paper should distinguish between learned object motion, explicit interaction rules, and any game-specific assumptions. It should explain how interactions are inferred and how the model handles events involving multiple objects. If the method predicts future states autoregressively, the paper should discuss how prediction errors accumulate over longer horizons. A comparison between one-step and multi-step predictions would help reveal whether the model captures stable dynamics rather than only local visual continuity.

The experimental evaluation should be designed to test the paper’s main claims directly. The authors should include strong pixel-based and object-based baselines, as well as ablations that isolate the effects of object detection, interaction modeling, and temporal history. Evaluation across multiple game types is important because a method that succeeds in one title may rely on its specific visual style or mechanics. The paper should report results across several prediction horizons, since short-term accuracy alone may not establish usefulness for planning. It would also be helpful to evaluate performance on unfamiliar levels or layouts to measure generalization.

The choice of metrics deserves careful justification. Pixel similarity can reward visually plausible frames even when important interactions are wrong. Conversely, small rendering differences may lower pixel scores despite accurate object-level predictions. The paper should therefore include measures of object localization, state prediction, collision or interaction prediction, and event timing where appropriate. Qualitative examples should show both successful and failed predictions, particularly around collisions and other abrupt state changes. Reporting uncertainty would further clarify whether the model recognizes situations in which its predictions are unreliable.

The paper should discuss the limits of its approach more explicitly. Object-centered modeling may struggle when objects are small, visually similar, partially occluded, or animated in ways that complicate tracking. It may also depend on a reliable object detector, whose errors could propagate into the dynamics model. The authors should quantify computational cost and compare it with relevant baselines, especially if the intended use involves real-time control. A discussion of how the method handles stochastic game mechanics would also be valuable.

Overall, the topic is worthwhile, and the object-centered framing offers a credible path toward more structured visual prediction. The paper’s potential contribution depends on demonstrating that explicit object and interaction modeling improves prediction beyond existing alternatives, rather than merely producing more interpretable representations. Stronger methodological detail, broader evaluation, and targeted ablations would make its claims easier to assess. I recommend revision focused on clarifying the model, strengthening the experimental comparisons, and addressing generalization and failure cases. With these improvements, the work could provide a useful contribution to visual dynamics modeling for 2D games.

This paper addresses an important problem: learning hierarchical representations from graphs while preserving information across multiple views. Combining multi-view graph neural networks with graph pooling is a promising direction, particularly for tasks where nodes or edges have complementary features or relationships. The topic is relevant to graph classification, molecular modeling, and other settings that require graph-level representations.

The paper’s main strength is its emphasis on integrating information from multiple views rather than treating each view in isolation. A hierarchical design could also help capture both local structure and broader graph organization. The proposed approach would be especially compelling if it explains how view-specific representations are aligned or combined at each pooling stage. Clear diagrams and a concise description of the architecture would help readers understand this interaction.

The evaluation should compare the method with strong single-view and multi-view baselines, as well as established graph pooling approaches. Comparisons should use consistent data splits, tuning budgets, and evaluation metrics. Ablation studies are important for determining whether gains come from multi-view fusion, the pooling strategy, or their combination. The authors should also report variability across multiple runs and test whether improvements are statistically meaningful. Results on graphs of different sizes and densities would help establish how broadly the method applies.

Several methodological details need careful attention. The paper should define what constitutes a view and explain how the method handles views with missing, noisy, or conflicting information. It should justify the pooling criterion and show whether information discarded during pooling can be recovered or is otherwise accounted for. Complexity and memory costs should be reported, since processing multiple views and multiple hierarchy levels may limit scalability. A sensitivity analysis of key hyperparameters, including the number of pooling stages and retained nodes, would strengthen the empirical claims.

The discussion should acknowledge potential limitations, such as dependence on the quality of the views or reduced performance when one view dominates. Interpretability would also be a useful consideration: visualizations or analyses could show which views and nodes influence the learned graph representation. Overall, the topic is promising and the proposed combination has clear potential. I recommend revision to strengthen the methodological explanation and provide more comprehensive evidence for the method’s effectiveness and scalability.

Creativity and personal dreams play an important role in shaping our goals and everyday lives. Creativity helps us imagine new possibilities instead of accepting things as they are. A dream can begin as a simple idea, such as learning an instrument or helping a community. Over time, that idea may grow into a goal that gives our efforts direction. When we have something meaningful to work toward, ordinary tasks can feel more purposeful. For example, a student who dreams of becoming a doctor may study science with greater focus. Someone who hopes to be an artist might make time to sketch each day. Creativity also helps us find different ways to overcome obstacles. If one plan does not work, we can adjust it or think of a new approach. Dreams do not always come true exactly as we imagine, and that is part of growing. Sometimes our interests change as we learn more about ourselves and the world. Changing a goal does not mean we have failed; it can mean we are choosing a path that suits us better. Personal dreams can also encourage us to take small, steady steps. These steps may include practicing a skill, asking for advice, or managing our time carefully. The people around us can inspire our dreams, but we should choose goals that feel meaningful to us. It is also important to balance ambition with rest and responsibility. Creativity can make even everyday routines more enjoyable by adding curiosity and fresh ideas. In the end, our dreams and creativity help us build a life that reflects who we are and what we value.

This paper presents a timely benchmark for evaluating whether language models can generate plausible explanations for observations from incomplete evidence. Its focus on abductive reasoning addresses an important gap in evaluations that emphasize deduction, prediction, or surface-level question answering. The human-created nature of the benchmark is a potential strength, particularly if the examples reflect realistic ambiguity and varied explanatory contexts. The paper would benefit from a clearer definition of what counts as a successful abductive explanation. In particular, plausibility, explanatory coverage, consistency with the evidence, and originality may need to be assessed separately. Please describe how the examples were collected, screened, and annotated, including the expertise and number of annotators. Inter-annotator agreement and the procedure for resolving disagreements are essential for judging the reliability of the labels. The authors should also explain whether the benchmark includes multiple valid explanations for each observation, since abduction often permits more than one reasonable account. A useful analysis would distinguish errors caused by faulty reasoning from errors caused by missing background knowledge or ambiguity in the prompt. The evaluation should compare a diverse range of language models and include relevant human performance as a reference point. Baselines using simple heuristics or retrieval would help establish whether the task requires substantive reasoning. The paper should report results across categories and difficulty levels rather than relying only on an aggregate score. It should also test for data leakage, especially if examples or close paraphrases could have appeared in model training data. Potential biases in the benchmark’s topics, cultural assumptions, and writing style deserve explicit discussion. Releasing the data, annotation guidelines, and evaluation code would substantially improve reproducibility and enable future comparisons. Overall, this work could make a valuable contribution, but its impact depends on careful validation of the benchmark and a nuanced interpretation of model scores. I recommend revision with a stronger account of annotation quality, evaluation design, and limitations.

The paper studies extensions of DiffPool for hierarchical graph classification and compares them empirically with competing methods. The topic is relevant, since learning graph representations at multiple scales remains an important challenge. A key strength is the focus on both architectural design and experimental evaluation rather than proposing a model in isolation. The multi-scale perspective is well motivated, and the comparison with established approaches could make the results useful to researchers and practitioners. However, the paper should state its specific contributions more precisely and distinguish them from prior DiffPool variants and other hierarchical pooling methods. The motivation for each extension would be clearer if linked to an explicit limitation of the original DiffPool approach. The method section should provide enough detail to reproduce the model, including pooling assignments, scale interactions, and training objectives. It should also explain how graph-level representations from different scales are combined and whether the design introduces substantial additional parameters. The empirical evaluation would be stronger with a clear account of dataset selection, preprocessing, train-validation-test splits, and evaluation metrics. Because graph classification benchmarks can be small and variable, results should be reported across multiple random seeds with uncertainty estimates or statistical tests. Baselines should use comparable tuning budgets and, where possible, implementations and settings consistent with their original papers. Ablations are particularly important: they should isolate the contribution of each proposed extension and test whether improvements come from multi-scale structure rather than model capacity. The paper should also report computational costs, including runtime and memory use, since dense DiffPool assignments can be expensive on larger graphs. Discussion of failure cases, sensitivity to pooling ratios, and performance across graphs of different sizes would add useful context. Claims of superiority should be calibrated to the datasets and metrics actually evaluated, especially if gains are small or inconsistent. Overall, the work addresses a worthwhile problem and may offer a useful contribution, but its impact depends on sharper positioning, reproducible experimental detail, and rigorous evidence that the extensions improve performance beyond strong, fairly tuned baselines.

The paper addresses an important problem: improving image classifiers’ resilience to adversarial examples while detecting inputs that may be unreliable. Its focus on generative latent-variable models offers a promising alternative to methods based solely on discriminative confidence scores. The topic is timely, and the combination of robustness and detection could be valuable in safety-sensitive applications. However, the paper’s claims need to be assessed against a carefully specified threat model and strong, current baselines. As presented by the topic alone, the central contribution is not yet clear enough to judge its novelty or practical significance.

The paper should define precisely what it means by a generative latent-variable model. It should identify the latent prior, the observation model, and the inference procedure used at training and test time. If the classifier uses a latent representation, the paper should explain how class predictions are derived from that representation. The authors should also distinguish robustness provided by the model from robustness obtained through preprocessing, rejection, or additional adversarial training. This distinction matters because detection and classification can improve through different mechanisms.

A rigorous threat model is essential. The paper should state the perturbation norms, budgets, and image constraints considered, as well as whether attacks are targeted or untargeted. It should clarify whether the adversary knows the model, detector, and decision thresholds. In particular, evaluations should include adaptive attacks that optimize against the complete system, including any latent-space score or rejection rule. Attacks crafted only against the classifier could overstate robustness if the detector is not included in the attack objective. The authors should also report how the system behaves when an input is rejected, rather than treating detection as a substitute for correct classification without qualification.

The evaluation should cover more than one dataset and architecture, or explain convincingly why its chosen setting is representative. Results should be compared with standard adversarial training, established detection methods, and relevant generative-model baselines. Comparisons should use consistent threat models, data splits, and computational budgets. The paper should report clean accuracy alongside robust accuracy and detection performance, since improvements in one metric may come at the expense of another. For detection, metrics should include threshold-independent measures such as area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, as well as performance at operationally meaningful false-positive rates. Confidence intervals or repeated runs would help establish whether the reported differences are reliable.

The authors should investigate whether latent variables capture semantic structure that helps distinguish adversarial inputs, rather than merely measuring reconstruction error or input atypicality. Useful ablations would remove the latent prior, change the inference method, or replace the generative score with a simpler baseline. A study of sensitivity to model capacity, latent dimension, and training data would further clarify which components drive the results. It would also be helpful to test corruption and distribution-shift benchmarks, since a detector that flags ordinary unfamiliar images may have limited practical value. The paper should discuss the possibility that benign out-of-distribution inputs and adversarial examples are not reliably separable.

Efficiency and calibration deserve attention as well. If inference requires iterative latent optimization or repeated sampling, the added latency may be substantial. The paper should report runtime, memory use, and any dependence on the number of optimization steps or samples. Threshold selection should be described transparently, including whether thresholds are chosen using held-out adversarial examples. The authors should avoid implying that a single threshold transfers automatically across datasets, attack strengths, or deployment environments. Any proposed deployment strategy should explain how false alarms and missed detections would be handled.

The paper would also benefit from clearer limitations. Generative models may assign high likelihood to some out-of-distribution inputs, and likelihood alone is not a reliable guarantee of adversarial detection. Latent representations can introduce inference error, and this error may vary across classes or image regions. The authors should discuss these risks and avoid equating a favorable benchmark result with a general robustness guarantee. Releasing code, model configurations, attack implementations, and evaluation scripts would make the findings easier to verify.

Overall, the topic is compelling, and latent-variable modeling could offer useful tools for understanding uncertainty and detecting suspicious inputs. The paper’s potential contribution depends on demonstrating gains under adaptive attacks and fair comparisons, not merely on favorable results from non-adaptive evaluations. I recommend that the authors sharpen the novelty claim, specify the threat model, and expand the empirical analysis before making strong claims about robustness. With these revisions, the work could provide a clearer and more useful assessment of generative models for adversarial defense and detection.

Technology has become an important part of everyday life. Children and teenagers use phones, computers, tablets, and televisions for school, communication, and entertainment. These devices can be useful, but using them too much may cause problems. Excessive technology use can affect young people’s health, learning, and relationships.

One harmful effect is reduced physical activity. When children spend many hours sitting in front of screens, they may have less time to exercise or play outside. A lack of movement can contribute to poor fitness and other health concerns. Screen use late at night can also make it harder to fall asleep. Poor sleep may leave students tired and less focused during the day.

Too much screen time can interfere with learning as well. Notifications, games, and videos may distract students from homework and classroom tasks. Some young people find it difficult to concentrate on reading or studying without checking a device. Heavy technology use may also limit opportunities to develop patience and problem-solving skills through real-world activities. On social media, teenagers can feel pressure to compare their appearance, popularity, or lifestyle with others. This can harm their confidence and contribute to stress or sadness.

Families may also be affected by excessive device use. Family members who focus on their screens may have fewer face-to-face conversations. As a result, they might miss chances to share concerns, listen to one another, and build close relationships. Arguments can arise when parents set limits or when children feel that their devices are being taken away. Excessive technology use can even disrupt family meals and other shared activities.

Technology itself is not the enemy, and it provides many valuable opportunities. The key is to use it in a balanced way. Families can set screen-free times, such as during meals and before bed. Children and teenagers should also make time for exercise, hobbies, schoolwork, and in-person friendships. Parents can support healthy habits by setting clear limits and following them themselves. With thoughtful boundaries, young people can enjoy technology while protecting their health, learning, and relationships.

Technology is an important part of everyday life. We use it to communicate, learn, work, and relax. Smartphones make it easy to contact family and friends, even when they live far away. The internet also gives students quick access to information and educational resources. At work, digital tools can help people finish tasks more efficiently. Technology can also make daily activities, such as shopping and paying bills, more convenient.

However, technology has some drawbacks. Spending too much time on screens can affect sleep and reduce physical activity. Social media may make people feel anxious or compare themselves unfairly with others. Online information is not always accurate, so it is important to check reliable sources. Technology can also distract students from their studies and make it harder to focus. In addition, sharing personal information online can create privacy risks. Some people may feel lonely if they rely on digital communication instead of meeting others in person. Overall, technology is most helpful when people use it thoughtfully and balance it with offline activities.

Extending the school day can affect students’ homework, sleep, and academic success in both helpful and harmful ways. With more time at school, students may finish some assignments before going home. They can also ask teachers for help while they are still in class. However, a longer school day may leave students with less time for homework, hobbies, and family. If students get home late, they may rush through assignments or feel too tired to concentrate. Their sleep may suffer if they stay up late trying to finish their work. Getting enough sleep is important because it helps students focus, remember information, and manage stress. A longer day could improve academic success if the extra time is used for tutoring, practice, or engaging lessons. On the other hand, simply adding hours may not help if students become exhausted or lose motivation. Schools should balance learning time with breaks and opportunities for rest. Overall, an extended school day can benefit students only when it supports learning without taking too much time away from sleep and life outside school.

Disputes over shared water resources have long added to tensions between Israelis and Palestinians, highlighting the need for cooperation as scarcity grows. Water is essential not only for drinking and sanitation but also for farming, industry, and public health. In a region facing high temperatures, irregular rainfall, and recurring drought, dependable supplies are increasingly important. Yet access to water is shaped by political arrangements, infrastructure, and the realities of occupation and conflict. These overlapping pressures have made water management a sensitive and persistent issue.

Israelis and Palestinians draw on interconnected sources, including the Mountain Aquifer beneath the West Bank and the Jordan River basin. The aquifer is replenished by rainfall, but its water moves across administrative boundaries and is difficult to manage without coordination. Palestinians say that restrictions on drilling, building, and maintaining water infrastructure have limited their ability to develop supplies. Israeli officials point to existing agreements and security concerns, while arguing that cooperation mechanisms remain in place. The result is a system that both sides describe differently and that many residents experience as unequal and unreliable.

The 1995 Oslo II agreement established a Joint Water Committee to coordinate certain water projects in the West Bank. It also set temporary allocations and recognized Palestinian water rights, while leaving key issues for later negotiations. Nearly three decades later, a final agreement on water has not been reached. Critics say the temporary arrangements have endured far longer than intended. They also note that approval processes can delay or prevent projects, including wells, pipelines, and treatment facilities.

In some Palestinian communities, households depend on costly trucked water when networks fail or do not reach them. The expense can take a substantial share of family income, particularly in remote areas. In other places, aging pipes leak large quantities before water reaches homes. Intermittent service means residents often store water in tanks, creating added costs and public-health concerns. Farmers also face uncertainty over access to irrigation, which can affect harvests and livelihoods.

Israeli communities, too, face the effects of regional water stress, though Israel has expanded desalination and wastewater reuse. Desalination plants provide a major share of Israel’s household water, and treated wastewater is widely used in agriculture. These technologies have helped reduce dependence on rainfall. However, they require significant investment, energy, and infrastructure. Palestinians have not had comparable access to large-scale systems, and extending such capacity would require funding, permits, and reliable electricity.

Environmental damage compounds the challenge. Untreated sewage and agricultural runoff can pollute shared groundwater and waterways. Over-pumping can lower aquifer levels and increase the risk of salinity. Climate change is expected to intensify heat and drought across the eastern Mediterranean, putting added pressure on already strained supplies. Experts warn that isolated solutions may shift the burden rather than secure water for the region as a whole.

Cooperation could offer practical gains even when broader political negotiations stall. Joint monitoring could improve information about groundwater levels, contamination, and consumption. Shared investment in wastewater treatment and repairs could reduce pollution and losses. Transparent procedures for approving infrastructure could help communities plan for reliable service. International donors and technical agencies have supported projects, but sustained progress depends on access, funding, and agreement among the parties.

Any durable approach will need to address both immediate needs and long-term rights. Palestinians seek greater control over water resources and the ability to build infrastructure without prolonged delays. Israelis seek secure supplies and protection for shared sources from contamination and overuse. Analysts say those concerns are not mutually exclusive, but resolving them requires trust and enforceable arrangements. Clear targets for equitable access, conservation, and pollution control could provide a starting point.

Local initiatives show that cooperation is possible in specific settings. Engineers and municipal officials have worked together on water networks and treatment projects, sometimes with support from outside partners. Such efforts can improve daily life, even if they do not settle questions of sovereignty or allocation. Their success often depends on consistent coordination and the ability to maintain facilities. Conflict and movement restrictions can quickly disrupt that work.

The stakes extend beyond household taps. Water insecurity can undermine agriculture, deepen economic hardship, and heighten public frustration. It can also increase the risk of disputes when communities compete for limited supplies. Reliable access is therefore both a humanitarian concern and a matter of regional stability. Experts say planning for drought, reducing waste, and protecting aquifers should be shared priorities.

As climate pressures intensify, the cost of inaction is likely to rise. New desalination, reuse, and conservation projects could help, but technology alone cannot resolve unequal access or political disputes. Agreements will need to account for changing demand and include transparent oversight. They must also ensure that infrastructure can be built, repaired, and operated safely. Without such provisions, even well-designed projects may fail to deliver lasting benefits.

Water does not follow political boundaries, and its management cannot be separated from the realities of daily life. Israeli and Palestinian communities depend on many of the same fragile systems. A sustainable path will require cooperation alongside meaningful attention to rights and fairness. For residents facing shortages today, the consequences are immediate. For the region, resolving the dispute is an essential part of building a more secure future.

Polish prosecutors have challenged claims that explosive materials were found on wreckage from the 2010 Smolensk air disaster, reopening a bitter dispute over the investigation. The dispute comes as renewed scrutiny of victims’ misidentified remains has intensified criticism of how Polish authorities handled the aftermath.

The crash killed all 96 people aboard, including President Lech Kaczyński and senior government and military officials. Their plane went down near Smolensk in western Russia while approaching an airfield in thick fog.

Some investigators and commentators have argued that traces detected on aircraft debris point to an explosion. Prosecutors say the tests cited in support of those claims are not conclusive evidence that explosives were present. They have cautioned that substances used in everyday materials can produce similar readings and that laboratory results must be assessed in context.

The competing interpretations have long fueled political conflict in Poland. Kaczyński’s twin brother, Jarosław Kaczyński, and allies have repeatedly questioned the official account of the crash, while other investigators have attributed it to pilot error and difficult weather conditions.

The latest controversy is compounded by revelations that some victims’ remains were wrongly identified and placed in the wrong graves. The errors came to light after bodies were returned to Poland and buried, prompting exhumations and renewed anguish for families.

Prosecutors have acknowledged serious failures in the handling and identification of the remains. The mistakes have also raised questions about the quality of post-crash procedures and the trustworthiness of other findings.

Officials have not said that the identification errors establish anything about the cause of the crash. But relatives and political figures say the failures make a transparent, credible account essential.

Poland’s investigation has shifted over the years as governments changed, with successive authorities reviewing evidence and challenging earlier conclusions. Disagreements over access to wreckage in Russia have further complicated efforts to settle the case.

Prosecutors say their assessment of explosive-residue claims is based on expert analysis, not political pressure. Critics, however, argue that conflicting reports and past mistakes have left the public uncertain about what evidence can be trusted.

For families, the debate is not only about the cause of the disaster but also about whether the dead were treated with dignity. The latest dispute is likely to keep the Smolensk tragedy at the center of Poland’s political and public life.

The paper addresses an important question: whether gradient-sign methods can be justified theoretically and remain effective in practical deep learning. Its combination of convergence analysis and empirical evaluation is a strength, since results in either area alone would provide an incomplete picture. The theoretical contribution should clearly state the assumptions on the objective, gradients, step sizes, and model smoothness. In particular, the authors should distinguish guarantees for convex or smooth settings from claims about nonconvex neural-network objectives. The paper would be stronger if it explained precisely what notion of convergence is established, such as convergence to a stationary point or a bound on gradient norm. The analysis should also clarify whether sign-based updates converge to the same solutions as standard gradient descent or merely provide a weaker stationarity guarantee. Any dependence of the convergence rate on dimension, gradient noise, or step-size choice deserves explicit discussion. On the empirical side, the experiments should cover diverse architectures, datasets, and optimization settings to support broad conclusions. Comparisons with standard gradient descent and adaptive optimizers should use carefully matched tuning budgets and computational resources. Reporting several random seeds, variability, and confidence intervals would make the results more reliable. The paper should also specify how learning rates and other hyperparameters were selected. Because gradient-sign methods discard magnitude information, an ablation examining sensitivity to gradient scaling and normalization would be particularly informative. It would help to report both optimization outcomes and practical measures such as wall-clock time, memory use, and final test performance. The authors should discuss cases where the method performs poorly, rather than focusing only on favorable examples. A limitation is that theoretical assumptions may not reflect the nonsmooth, stochastic, and nonstationary behavior encountered in modern training. The presentation would benefit from a concise statement connecting each theoretical result to the experiments designed to test it. Overall, the topic is relevant and the combined approach is promising, but the paper needs sharper qualification of its guarantees and more rigorous experimental reporting before its conclusions can be fully assessed.

Summer assignments can help learners keep their minds active during the long break. However, students do not always benefit from receiving the same tasks. I believe learners should have a strong role in choosing and creating their summer assignments. Having a choice can make schoolwork feel more interesting. Students are more likely to complete tasks that connect with their goals and hobbies. For example, someone who loves animals might research wildlife conservation. A student interested in cooking could write a recipe collection and practice useful math skills. Another learner might create a short film or build a small science project. These assignments can help students learn in ways that suit them. Creating their own tasks also encourages responsibility. Learners must decide what they want to study and make a plan to finish it. They can practice setting goals and managing their time. These skills are useful both in school and in everyday life. Students may also feel proud when they complete something they designed themselves. Still, learners should not have complete freedom without any guidance. Some students may choose tasks that are too easy or unrelated to learning. Others might feel unsure about what to do. Teachers can prevent these problems by offering clear expectations and helpful suggestions. They might provide a list of project ideas or ask students to include reading, writing, and problem-solving. Teachers should also make sure the workload is reasonable. Summer is a time for rest, family, and personal interests, so assignments should not take up every day. Parents can support students by helping them gather materials and organize their plans. They should guide rather than take over the work. A balanced choice of assignments can keep learning enjoyable without making the break feel like another school term. It can also help students discover new interests and strengths. For these reasons, learners should help choose and create their summer assignments, with teachers providing suitable guidance.

This paper studies object-centric prediction models that combine scene segmentation, motion detection, and learned dynamics to forecast events in physical environments. The topic is timely and important for robotics, autonomous systems, and embodied AI. Its central premise—that separating objects and their interactions can improve prediction—is well motivated. The paper also addresses a useful gap between pixel-level forecasting and models that explicitly represent physical entities.

A major strength is the integration of perception and prediction within a common framework. Combining segmentation with motion cues may help distinguish persistent objects from transient visual changes. Learned dynamics offer flexibility in settings where hand-designed physical models are incomplete. The approach could therefore support prediction across a broad range of environments and object types.

The paper would benefit from a more precise definition of its object-centric representation. It is unclear how the system handles occlusion, object entry and exit, or uncertain object boundaries. The authors should explain how segmentation errors propagate into motion estimates and downstream predictions. They should also clarify whether object identities are maintained consistently across frames or inferred independently at each time step.

The treatment of motion detection requires further detail. The paper should specify how camera motion is separated from object motion, particularly in moving-camera scenes. It would also be useful to distinguish detected motion from inferred physical interaction. For example, two objects may move together without directly causing one another’s motion.

The learned dynamics component needs a clearer account of its assumptions and training procedure. The authors should state which physical properties are represented, which are learned, and whether the model respects basic constraints such as object persistence or non-penetration. If these constraints are not enforced, the paper should discuss the kinds of implausible predictions that may result. Details about training data, prediction horizons, and computational cost are also needed for reproducibility.

The experimental evaluation should include strong and relevant baselines. These should cover both object-centric approaches and competitive video-prediction or physics-informed models. Ablations are essential to establish the contribution of segmentation, motion detection, and learned dynamics individually. Results should also be reported across varied scenes, object counts, camera conditions, and interaction types.

Quantitative metrics alone may not show whether predicted events are physically meaningful. I recommend adding qualitative examples and measures of object identity consistency, interaction accuracy, and physical plausibility. The paper should report uncertainty or failure cases, especially when visual evidence is ambiguous. A discussion of generalization to unseen objects and environments would further clarify the method’s practical scope.

Overall, the topic is promising, and the proposed combination of components has clear potential. However, the current presentation needs stronger methodological detail and a more comprehensive evaluation to support its claims. I recommend revision, with emphasis on clarifying the representation, addressing perception errors, and demonstrating the value of each component experimentally.

The paper presents a benchmark for evaluating program-synthesis systems on grid-world tasks using a novel domain-specific language. The topic is timely, and the combination of structured environments and executable programs offers a promising way to study generalization and compositional reasoning. A key strength is the potential for the benchmark to test more than task completion, including whether a system can produce concise, interpretable programs. The paper would be stronger if it clearly specified how tasks were generated and how difficulty, diversity, and train–test separation were controlled. It should also explain the language’s syntax and semantics in enough detail for independent implementations and comparisons. The evaluation would benefit from baselines spanning both program-synthesis methods and general-purpose language models, with consistent access to demonstrations and other task information. Please report multiple runs and uncertainty estimates, and include ablations that isolate the effects of the language design and task structure. Since grid-world benchmarks can reward memorized patterns, the authors should assess robustness to new layouts, rule combinations, and task sizes. The paper should also discuss limitations, including whether performance on this benchmark transfers to realistic programming tasks. Releasing the benchmark, reference interpreter, evaluation code, and baseline implementations would substantially improve reproducibility. Overall, this is a promising contribution, but the paper needs clearer benchmark construction details and a broader, more rigorous evaluation to establish its value.

Online learning has become an important option for students who must balance education with work and family responsibilities. Traditional classes often require students to travel to campus at specific times. For people with busy schedules, those requirements can make college difficult to manage. Online courses offer more flexibility and can help students make progress toward their goals.

One major benefit of online learning is the ability to study at convenient times. Students may watch lectures or complete assignments after work, during a lunch break, or when their children are asleep. This flexibility makes it easier to fit education into an already full day. It can also reduce the need to choose between attending class and meeting family or work obligations.

Online learning can save time and money as well. Students do not have to commute to campus, which may lower transportation costs and leave more time for studying or family. Some online programs also provide digital materials, reducing the need to buy certain textbooks. These savings can be especially helpful for students supporting themselves or others.

Another advantage is that online courses can help students develop useful skills. Learners often need to organize their schedules, meet deadlines, and work independently. These habits can benefit them in both school and the workplace. Online classes may also improve confidence with digital tools that are common in many careers.

However, flexibility does not mean that online learning is effortless. Students still need to manage their time and ask for help when they need it. A quiet place to study and reliable internet access can make a major difference. Support from instructors, classmates, and family members can also help students stay motivated.

Overall, online learning can make education more accessible to people with demanding lives. It gives working students and caregivers more control over when and where they study. With planning and support, they can continue their education while meeting important responsibilities. For many students, this flexible path creates new opportunities for personal growth and career advancement.

Making informed decisions is an important skill that helps us solve problems and reach our goals. We make choices every day, from deciding how to spend our time to choosing what subjects to study. Some decisions are simple, while others can affect our future. In difficult situations, it is helpful to listen to advice from different people.

Each person may see a problem from a different point of view. Parents can share lessons from their experience, while teachers may offer knowledge and guidance. Friends might understand our feelings and explain how a choice could affect our relationships. Experts can provide reliable information about topics they know well.

Listening to several opinions can help us notice details we might have missed. It can also show us the possible benefits and risks of each option. However, we should not follow every piece of advice without thinking carefully. People may have different values, experiences, or reasons for recommending something.

Before making a decision, we should consider who is giving the advice and whether the information is trustworthy. We can ask questions to understand the reasons behind each opinion. It is also useful to compare advice with facts and consider what matters most to us. In the end, we are responsible for our own choices.

For example, a student choosing an extracurricular activity might ask family, friends, and a teacher for suggestions. Each person could point out something different, such as the time commitment, the enjoyment, or the skills to be learned. The student can weigh these ideas and choose an activity that fits their interests and schedule.

Considering advice from different people does not mean letting others decide for us. It means gathering information before choosing a path. By listening respectfully and thinking independently, we can make wiser decisions. This habit can help us become more confident, responsible, and prepared for the future.

The paper studies unsupervised multi-image matching with graph neural networks, using cycle consistency and geometric constraints to improve correspondence quality across multiple views. The problem is important because many matching methods focus on image pairs and can produce mutually inconsistent results when extended to larger image collections. A graph-based formulation is a natural fit for representing images, candidate correspondences, and relationships among them. The combination of learned matching with geometric verification is also well motivated. A major strength is the focus on global consistency rather than treating each image pair independently. Cycle constraints can help suppress ambiguous or spurious matches by requiring correspondences to agree across paths in the image graph. Geometric constraints provide a complementary signal that ties matching decisions to plausible scene structure. The unsupervised setting is practically valuable, particularly where annotated correspondences are scarce or expensive to obtain. The paper would benefit, however, from a clearer formal definition of the graph and its nodes, edges, and message-passing operations. It should also explain precisely how candidate matches are generated and how the model represents uncertainty in those candidates. The cycle-consistency objective needs a detailed mathematical description, including which cycles are considered and how their contribution is normalized. Similarly, the geometric loss should specify the assumed camera or scene model and the procedure used to estimate geometric transformations. These assumptions can materially affect performance, especially in scenes with nonrigid motion, occlusion, or large viewpoint changes. The authors should clarify how the method handles incomplete image graphs and pairs with few reliable keypoints. The interaction between cycle and geometric constraints is central to the contribution, so an ablation study should isolate each constraint and their combination. Comparisons should include strong contemporary pairwise and multi-view matching baselines under the same feature extraction and evaluation conditions. The evaluation would be more convincing with multiple datasets that vary in scene type, image count, viewpoint, and correspondence density. It should report standard matching metrics and explain how thresholds and ground-truth correspondences are established. Runtime, memory use, and scaling with the number of images also deserve attention, since cycle enumeration and graph processing may become expensive. The paper should state whether all images are processed jointly or in batches, and how the method behaves when the collection grows. Since the approach is unsupervised, it is important to distinguish any training-time supervision, pretrained components, or external data from the method’s own learning signal. Sensitivity analyses for loss weights, graph connectivity, and cycle length would help establish robustness. Failure cases should be included, particularly for repetitive textures and scenes with weak geometric structure. The presentation would improve if the authors gave a concise algorithm overview and a worked example of how a correspondence is supported by multiple cycles. Claims about generalization should be supported by experiments on data not used for tuning. Overall, the proposed direction is promising and addresses a meaningful limitation of independent pairwise matching. The conceptual contribution appears strongest in the integration of global cycle consistency with geometric reasoning, but its novelty relative to prior multi-view graph methods should be stated more precisely. I recommend revision with expanded methodological detail and stronger empirical validation before the work is accepted.

The paper addresses an important problem in differentiable neural architecture search: architecture parameters can receive biased or noisy gradient estimates, causing optimization to favor designs that perform poorly after full training. The topic is timely and relevant to researchers working on efficient model selection. The proposed focus on correcting gradient estimates is promising because it targets a central weakness of continuous relaxation methods. Overall, the paper presents a potentially useful direction, but its claims would benefit from stronger theoretical clarification and more comprehensive empirical validation.

The introduction explains why architecture-search failures matter in practice. It appropriately connects optimization behavior during search with the quality of the final discrete architecture. However, the paper should distinguish more carefully between gradient-estimation error, optimization instability, and generalization failure. These phenomena can lead to similar outcomes but require different evidence and remedies. A clearer problem statement would help readers understand exactly which failure mode the proposed method addresses.

The method’s central idea is intuitive and appears technically plausible. Correcting the estimated gradient may reduce the influence of misleading updates and improve the search trajectory. The paper should define the uncorrected estimator, the correction term, and the resulting estimator with consistent notation. It should also explain the assumptions under which the correction is valid. In particular, readers need to know whether the correction is unbiased, approximately unbiased, or simply empirically beneficial. If the method introduces additional estimates or samples, the resulting variance should be discussed alongside bias. A brief derivation would make the rationale easier to assess.

The relationship between the proposed correction and existing approaches should also be strengthened. The paper should compare its method with established techniques for variance reduction, bilevel optimization, architecture-parameter regularization, and search-space pruning. It is important to explain whether the method is novel in its estimator, its implementation, or its application to architecture search. A more precise account would help distinguish the contribution from prior work that also modifies architecture gradients. The authors should avoid implying that all poor architectures arise from gradient bias alone.

The experimental section is central to the paper’s claims. The selected benchmarks appear relevant, but the study should cover a broader range of search spaces and task types if the method is intended to be generally useful. Comparisons should use identical search budgets, data splits, and computational resources wherever possible. The paper should report how many independent runs were conducted and provide variability measures, not only best-run results. Since architecture search can be highly stochastic, confidence intervals or statistical tests would make the conclusions more convincing. The authors should also report search cost, including wall-clock time and memory use, because gradient correction may add overhead.

The ablation study should isolate the contribution of each component. In particular, it should compare the correction against the original estimator, a simplified correction, and relevant variance-reduction alternatives. Such comparisons would reveal whether improvements come from correcting bias, reducing variance, changing the effective learning rate, or adding implicit regularization. Sensitivity analyses for key hyperparameters are also needed. The paper should show whether performance remains stable under reasonable changes to the correction strength and architecture-optimizer settings. It would be useful to test how results change with different search durations and random seeds.

The evaluation should distinguish search performance from final model performance. Any reported search-time validation metric should be supplemented with results after retraining the selected discrete architecture from scratch. The retraining protocol must be described in sufficient detail to ensure fair comparison. If the proposed method selects architectures that are better only under a particular training schedule, that limitation should be made explicit. The paper should also report whether the selected designs are consistently strong across independent retraining runs.

The discussion of limitations is currently too brief. Gradient correction may depend on assumptions that do not hold equally across all search spaces or optimization regimes. The method might also interact with weight sharing, which can distort architecture comparisons independently of gradient-estimation error. The authors should discuss whether the correction is compatible with common search algorithms and whether it requires access to information unavailable in standard implementations. Potential failure cases would provide a more balanced account of the method’s scope.

The presentation is generally understandable, but several passages would benefit from tighter organization. The paper should introduce its notation before the derivation and use the same symbols throughout. Algorithm details should be sufficient for an independent implementation, including update order, sampling choices, and any stabilization procedures. Reporting exact hyperparameters and computational settings would further improve reproducibility. The code and search configurations should be made publicly available if possible.

The results are encouraging if they hold across the settings tested, and the paper addresses a consequential source of failure in differentiable architecture search. Its strongest contribution is the attempt to connect estimator quality with the selection of better discrete designs. At present, however, the evidence should more directly establish that the proposed correction, rather than an incidental change to optimization dynamics, causes the reported gains. A stronger theoretical account, carefully controlled ablations, and broader multi-seed experiments would substantially improve the work. I recommend revision before acceptance, with priority given to clarifying the estimator’s properties and strengthening the empirical comparisons.

People often form an opinion of someone within moments of meeting them. This first impression can be influenced by a person’s appearance, voice, behavior, and choice of words. Although it may seem difficult to change how others see us, I believe it is possible.

A person can make a positive impression by being polite, friendly, and attentive. For example, making eye contact and listening carefully can show respect and confidence. Dressing appropriately for the situation may also help others feel comfortable. However, people should not pretend to be someone they are not just to gain approval.

First impressions are not always accurate. Someone who seems shy at first may become more open once they feel comfortable. Similarly, a person who appears confident might later show kindness and humility. As people spend more time together, their opinions can change based on what they learn about each other.

If someone makes a poor first impression, they can improve it through consistent actions. Apologizing for a mistake and treating others with consideration can show personal growth. It may take time for others to change their minds, but patience and honesty can help. Therefore, people cannot control every first impression, but they can influence how it develops. In the end, a person’s actions over time matter more than a single meeting.
