The paper addresses an important question: whether dilated convolutional networks can provide an effective parallel alternative to recurrent models for reading comprehension and other sequence-processing tasks. Its emphasis on parallel computation is timely, since recurrent models process tokens sequentially and can limit training throughput. The approach appears promising because dilated convolutions can capture long-range context while preserving efficient, highly parallel computation. However, the paper should clearly distinguish its contribution from prior convolutional architectures and explain how dilation patterns affect receptive-field coverage and information loss. The evaluation would be more convincing with comparisons against strong recurrent and attention-based baselines under matched parameter counts, training budgets, and hardware conditions. For reading comprehension, results should be reported across multiple datasets and accompanied by ablations on depth, dilation schedule, and kernel size. The paper should also examine whether performance varies with passage length, since long-range dependencies are central to its claims. Reporting throughput and memory use alongside accuracy would help substantiate the practical benefits of parallelism. Finally, discussion of limitations—such as boundary effects, sensitivity to architecture choices, and tasks requiring precise token-to-token interactions—would make the conclusions more balanced. Overall, this is a worthwhile direction, but stronger controlled experiments and clearer analysis are needed to establish when dilated convolutions are a competitive alternative to recurrent models.

The paper addresses an important challenge in reinforcement learning: how agents can remain curious and adapt when their environments change. Its focus on minimizing surprise offers a potentially useful alternative to familiar approaches based on prediction error or novelty bonuses. The topic is timely, and the connection between intrinsic motivation and nonstationary environments could have both theoretical and practical value.

A central strength is the paper’s emphasis on evolving environments rather than assuming a fixed distribution of states and rewards. This setting is relevant to robotics, autonomous systems, and other applications where an agent’s experience may change over time. The proposed perspective could encourage agents to seek states that are informative while avoiding behavior driven by arbitrary novelty. The paper also has the potential to clarify how surprise-based objectives support exploration and adaptation.

However, the central concept of surprise needs a more precise definition. It is unclear whether surprise means a change in predictive belief, an unexpected observation, a reduction in uncertainty, or some combination of these. These quantities are related but not interchangeable, and each leads to different incentives for an agent. The paper should state the objective mathematically and explain how it is computed from the agent’s observations and internal model.

The title’s use of “minimizing surprise” also raises an important conceptual question. Minimizing surprise might encourage an agent to remain in familiar states rather than explore unfamiliar ones. If the intended effect is to seek experiences that improve future predictions, the authors should distinguish this from simply preferring predictable observations. A formal argument or carefully chosen examples could show when the proposed objective promotes exploration and when it risks suppressing it.

The relationship between the method and existing approaches to intrinsic motivation should also be made clearer. In particular, the paper should compare its formulation with prediction-error bonuses, information gain, Bayesian surprise, and uncertainty-based exploration. A concise discussion of what the proposed method adds would help readers assess its novelty. The authors should also clarify whether minimizing surprise is a new objective or a new way to implement established information-seeking principles.

The treatment of evolving environments requires further detail. The paper should specify what changes over time, how quickly changes occur, and whether they are abrupt, gradual, or recurring. It should explain how an agent identifies that the environment has changed rather than treating each change as ordinary stochastic variation. The authors should also discuss whether the method can forget outdated information or revise its internal model without becoming unstable.

The experimental evaluation should include strong, relevant baselines. These should ideally cover standard reinforcement learning, established intrinsic-reward methods, and approaches designed for nonstationary settings. Comparisons should use matched model capacity, training budgets, and exploration opportunities wherever possible. Otherwise, improvements may reflect differences in computational resources rather than the surprise objective.

The environments should test more than one kind of evolution. Useful cases could include changing transition dynamics, changing reward functions, and changes in which observations are available. Experiments should also vary the frequency and magnitude of changes. This would help establish whether the method adapts broadly or succeeds only under a particular schedule.

The paper should report both adaptation speed and performance over the full interaction period. A method may recover quickly after a change but perform poorly before or between changes. It would also be useful to measure regret, cumulative reward, and the time needed to regain a specified performance level. These measures would make the practical value of the method easier to evaluate.

Ablation studies are needed to identify which components drive any observed gains. The authors should test the contribution of the surprise signal separately from learning architecture, memory mechanisms, and reward scaling. Sensitivity analyses for key hyperparameters would further strengthen the evidence. Results should include uncertainty estimates across random seeds, especially because exploration outcomes can vary substantially.

The paper should explain how intrinsic and extrinsic rewards are combined. The relative scale of these rewards can strongly affect behavior, so the method should state whether weighting is fixed, learned, or adapted over time. It should also examine whether the intrinsic signal causes reward hacking or repeated pursuit of predictable but unproductive states. Examples of failure cases would make the limitations more concrete.

The method’s computational and implementation costs deserve attention as well. If surprise requires maintaining a probability model or evaluating multiple candidate predictions, the associated overhead may limit its applicability. Reporting runtime, memory use, and any additional model complexity would be helpful. The authors should also discuss whether the method relies on access to observations or environmental variables that would be unavailable in realistic deployments.

The theoretical section could be strengthened by stating assumptions and identifying conditions under which the objective supports useful exploration. It would be particularly valuable to distinguish guarantees about prediction or uncertainty from guarantees about task reward. An intrinsic objective need not improve extrinsic performance in every environment, and the paper should avoid implying otherwise. Explicit limitations would make the contribution more credible.

Presentation is another area for improvement. The paper should introduce its terminology consistently and provide a small illustrative example before presenting the full method. A diagram showing the interaction between environment change, prediction, surprise, and policy updates could make the proposed mechanism easier to follow. Pseudocode and implementation details would also improve reproducibility.

Overall, the paper addresses a promising problem and presents an intriguing perspective on intrinsic motivation in changing environments. Its strongest potential contribution is the attempt to connect surprise minimization with adaptive behavior over time. At present, however, the key objective is not defined sharply enough to determine whether it encourages exploration, predictability, or model improvement. The empirical claims would also require broader baselines, diverse evolving environments, and clearer analyses of adaptation and failure. I recommend revision before publication, with priority given to formalizing the surprise measure, clarifying its distinction from related methods, and strengthening the experimental evaluation.

Debate is growing over whether confiscating passports can stop young people from travelling to Syria to join armed groups. Supporters say temporarily removing travel documents could give families and authorities time to intervene when someone appears at risk of being recruited. They argue the measure may also prevent a young person from making a sudden departure through a major airport. Critics, however, warn that taking a passport does not address the reasons people are drawn to extremist groups. They say it could push travel plans underground or lead people to seek other routes and forged documents. Civil liberties advocates also question how officials would decide whose passport to seize, and whether the decision could be challenged. Families facing the prospect of a relative leaving say early support and open conversations can be more effective than punishment. Experts point to a broader range of responses, including counselling, community programmes and targeted efforts to counter recruitment. Any restrictions, they argue, should be based on clear evidence and accompanied by safeguards. The debate reflects a wider challenge for governments: preventing travel to conflict zones while protecting individual rights. No single measure, analysts say, is likely to work without sustained support for those at risk.

Nanocluster Deposition Creates Highly Porous Films Whose Structure Reflects Ballistic Growth and Limited Particle Coalescence

Abstract

Nanocluster deposition is a versatile route to films with nanoscale building blocks and high internal surface area. In this process, preformed clusters arrive at a substrate with finite kinetic energy and form a structure through impact, sticking, surface diffusion, and occasional coalescence. When lateral mobility and coalescence are limited, the resulting films are porous and retain recognizable features of their constituent clusters. This paper presents a mechanistic account of how ballistic arrival and restricted restructuring shape film morphology. It relates deposition conditions to shadowing, void formation, cluster connectivity, and depth-dependent structure. It also outlines experimental approaches for distinguishing ballistic growth from post-deposition rearrangement. The discussion emphasizes that porosity is not determined by incident flux alone, but emerges from coupled effects of cluster size, energy, substrate temperature, incidence angle, and surface chemistry. Understanding these factors is important for controlling transport, mechanical integrity, and functional performance. The framework provides testable predictions for optimizing nanocluster-derived coatings.

1. Introduction

Thin films assembled from nanoscale particles differ fundamentally from films grown by the arrival of individual atoms. Their building blocks possess finite dimensions, internal structure, and often a distribution of shapes. Each incoming cluster can interact with the substrate and with previously deposited clusters as a discrete object. The resulting morphology therefore depends on both the motion of individual clusters and the evolving topography of the film. In many deposition regimes, clusters stick near their first point of contact. This behavior preserves a record of the arrival trajectory and favors open, ramified structures. The film can then exhibit substantial porosity even when its constituent clusters are individually dense. Such structures are relevant to catalysis, sensing, filtration, energy storage, and optical coatings. Their properties depend not only on composition but also on how clusters pack and connect. A mechanistic understanding of formation is needed to make these materials reproducibly.

The central proposition considered here is that nanocluster deposition can generate highly porous films through ballistic growth coupled to limited particle coalescence. Ballistic growth refers to growth dominated by the paths taken by incoming particles, with little lateral redistribution after impact. Limited coalescence means that neighboring clusters do not fully merge into a continuous dense phase during deposition or subsequent treatment. These conditions are common when substrate temperatures are low relative to the energy barriers for surface motion. They may also arise when clusters are chemically stabilized or when impact energies are insufficient to induce extensive deformation. The film morphology is consequently governed by geometry as much as by thermodynamics. Incoming particles preferentially land on exposed regions, while protrusions shield regions behind them. This geometric effect is known as shadowing. Shadowing can amplify roughness and create voids that persist as the film thickens. The phenomenon is not unique to nanocluster deposition, but discrete clusters introduce additional length scales and collision outcomes.

The structure of a deposited film reflects a sequence of events rather than a single growth mechanism. Clusters may be generated in a source, transported through a gas or vacuum environment, selected by size, and directed toward a substrate. Their kinetic energies and charge states can vary. On impact, a cluster may stick, rebound, fragment, deform, diffuse, or rotate. The probabilities of these outcomes depend on cluster composition, surface termination, substrate material, temperature, and impact geometry. Once attached, a cluster may remain isolated, form a point contact, or merge with its neighbors. The balance among these outcomes controls both the solid fraction and the topology of the pore network. In this paper, we synthesize the physical picture, describe the relevant parameters, and identify useful methods and predictions. The goal is to provide a coherent framework rather than to claim a universal quantitative model.

2. Physical basis of ballistic assembly

A cluster approaching a substrate carries translational momentum and kinetic energy. Its trajectory before impact is shaped by the deposition geometry and by collisions with residual gas molecules. Under sufficiently low gas pressure, transport is approximately line of sight. Under higher pressure, collisions broaden the angular and energy distributions. The substrate then intercepts a population of clusters with a range of incidence directions. For each cluster, the point of impact depends on the instantaneous film topography. Peaks and exposed edges occupy a larger solid angle than recessed regions. As a result, they collect a disproportionate fraction of incoming material. This preferential growth of protrusions produces shadowing. In the absence of strong surface transport, shadowed valleys receive little material and remain open.

The word ballistic does not imply that every cluster follows a perfectly straight path. It describes a regime in which the arrival trajectory largely determines the attachment site. Small-angle scattering, gas collisions, and electrostatic deflection may still occur. The defining feature is the limited ability of deposited material to move far from the point of impact. A useful comparison is between the characteristic diffusion length and the typical spacing of neighboring clusters. If diffusion length is much smaller than that spacing, incoming clusters cannot efficiently fill gaps. If it is comparable to or greater than the spacing, the structure may densify through migration and coalescence. The diffusion length depends on temperature and on the activation barrier for motion. It can also be influenced by charge, ligand coverage, and substrate roughness. Thus, the same deposition geometry can yield different structures on different surfaces.

The initial stages of deposition often determine the later film architecture. On a smooth substrate, the first clusters can form isolated islands. Their density is influenced by sticking probability and by any surface diffusion that occurs before immobilization. As coverage increases, new clusters land on both the substrate and existing islands. If sticking is high, the islands grow upward and laterally without necessarily merging. The cluster-scale texture is then inherited by the thicker film. At low coverage, substrate chemistry and defects can strongly influence nucleation. At greater thickness, self-shadowing becomes more important than the original substrate landscape. The transition between these regimes can produce a depth-dependent structure. For example, a compact interfacial layer may support a more open upper region if the initial substrate promotes mobility but the growing surface does not. Conversely, a rough initial layer can seed persistent columnar features.

Ballistic deposition favors anisotropic structures because the flux direction defines a preferred axis. Under normal incidence, protrusions aligned with the incoming flux can grow at the expense of neighboring regions. At oblique incidence, shadowing is stronger and can produce tilted columns or directional porosity. The exact morphology depends on the angular spread of the flux and on substrate rotation. Rotation can average out some in-plane anisotropy without eliminating porosity. A broad angular distribution may reduce the persistence of individual shadowed regions. Nevertheless, if post-impact mobility remains low, a broad distribution does not guarantee dense packing. It merely changes the spatial distribution of landing events. The film may still contain connected voids and rough interfaces.

3. Cluster properties and impact processes

Cluster size is a primary control variable because it sets the scale of the building blocks. A narrow size distribution can produce a more uniform characteristic pore scale, whereas a broad distribution may allow smaller clusters to occupy some spaces between larger ones. This filling is limited when attachment is strongly trajectory dependent. Small clusters may also be more strongly affected by gas collisions and surface forces than large clusters. Their impact energy per atom can differ substantially even when total kinetic energy is similar. Consequently, size selection should be considered together with energy selection. A film composed of larger clusters may have larger voids but fewer contacts per unit volume. A film of smaller clusters may develop finer pores, though it may also densify more readily if surface diffusion is appreciable.

Cluster shape and internal structure also matter. Spherical clusters tend to make point or small-area contacts when rigid. Faceted clusters can interlock or create larger contact regions depending on orientation. Porous or hollow clusters may contribute internal porosity in addition to interparticle voids. The distinction between intracluster and intercluster porosity is important for interpreting measurements. A measured low density does not reveal by itself where the void space resides. Internal defects may be inherited from cluster synthesis, whereas interparticle pores emerge during film assembly. Both types can coexist. Their relative contribution depends on how clusters are produced and how they respond to impact.

The impact event can alter the cluster and the substrate locally. At low impact energy, a cluster may adhere with little deformation. At higher energy, it may flatten, fragment, or penetrate a soft surface layer. Impact-induced heating can be highly localized and short lived. Whether this heating enables coalescence depends on the timescale of energy dissipation and on the relevant diffusion barriers. A cluster with substantial kinetic energy can still remain discrete if the energy is rapidly transferred to the substrate. Conversely, a moderate-energy impact may promote restructuring if the cluster is small and the interface is chemically favorable. Impact energy should therefore be reported in a form that permits comparisons, such as energy per atom or energy normalized by the cluster-substrate binding scale. Total energy alone is insufficient.

The sticking probability is another decisive factor. Strong cluster-substrate attraction encourages capture at the first contact and suppresses re-evaporation. Weak attraction can permit rebound or migration. Surface contamination and adsorbed water may change the effective interaction. Ligands can stabilize clusters against coalescence while also altering their sticking behavior. In some systems, ligands desorb during impact or heating, exposing reactive surfaces. Such chemical transformations can change the growth regime during a single deposition run. Careful characterization of cluster termination is therefore necessary. A nominally identical cluster composition can form different films depending on its surface chemistry.

4. Limited coalescence and pore formation

Coalescence involves the reduction of interfacial area as neighboring particles merge. It can be driven by surface energy and facilitated by diffusion, deformation, or chemical bonding. For nanoclusters, coalescence may occur during collision, after landing, or during post-deposition annealing. If coalescence is limited, contacts remain narrow and interparticle boundaries persist. The film then contains a network of solid clusters connected by necks or point contacts. The open space between clusters forms a pore network whose geometry reflects both packing and shadowing. Limited coalescence does not necessarily mean zero atomic rearrangement. Small necks may form even when complete merging is absent. The relevant question is whether restructuring is extensive enough to eliminate the cluster-scale architecture.

A useful conceptual parameter is the ratio of the time available for surface restructuring to the characteristic time for deposition. If restructuring is slow compared with deposition, the structure is kinetically trapped. If restructuring is fast, clusters can reorganize toward denser configurations. This ratio is influenced by temperature, flux, and activation barriers. A high deposition rate can bury clusters before they have time to migrate or coalesce. A low rate may permit more relaxation, though only if mobility is thermally accessible. The rate effect is not universally monotonic because prolonged exposure can also cause contamination or chemical changes. Nevertheless, deposition rate provides a practical means of probing kinetic competition. Comparing films grown at different rates while holding other conditions fixed can reveal whether porosity is primarily kinetic.

Porosity can be described at several scales. Total porosity is the fraction of film volume not occupied by solid material. Pore size distribution describes the characteristic dimensions of voids. Connectivity distinguishes isolated pores from continuous pathways. Tortuosity quantifies how indirect transport routes are through the pore network. These metrics are not interchangeable. A film with modest total porosity may still have a highly connected pathway, while another film with greater porosity may contain mostly closed pores. Ballistic growth commonly favors anisotropic and connected voids because shadowed regions extend along the growth direction. However, deposition geometry and subsequent restructuring can change this tendency. A complete characterization should report more than a single porosity number.

The void structure can evolve as the film thickens. Early pores may become enclosed by later deposition, while others remain connected to the surface. New clusters may bridge across voids without filling them. This process creates a hierarchy of pore sizes and connectivity. The resulting architecture can be described as a cluster-based skeleton with interstitial voids, but that description may be too simple when clusters deform or fragment. Depth-resolved measurements are valuable because surface imaging alone cannot establish the internal structure. In particular, a porous top surface may overlie a denser base, or an apparently smooth surface may conceal a porous interior. Growth history should therefore be treated as a spatially varying record.

5. Modeling approaches

Models of nanocluster film growth range from geometric simulations to atomistic calculations. Ballistic deposition models provide a simple way to study the consequences of trajectory-dependent sticking. In a basic model, particles are launched toward a surface and attach irreversibly at first contact. This rule generates rough, porous structures through shadowing alone. More realistic models can include finite particle size, angular distributions, sticking probabilities, and limited rolling or diffusion. Such models help isolate the role of geometry. Their predictions are most reliable when interpreted qualitatively unless calibrated against experimental parameters.

Off-lattice simulations are particularly appropriate for clusters with finite shape and orientation. They can represent spheres, faceted particles, or experimentally derived morphologies. A cluster may be allowed to translate or rotate after impact according to specified interaction rules. Coalescence can be represented through a neck-growth criterion or by merging particles when separation falls below a threshold. These approximations are computationally efficient but may not capture chemistry. Molecular dynamics can describe impact deformation and short-time rearrangement at atomic resolution. Its limitations include finite system size and accessible timescales. Long-term diffusion and film growth may require coarse-grained or kinetic Monte Carlo methods. Multiscale approaches can bridge these regimes by using atomistic calculations to parameterize effective mobility and sticking rates.

The key modeling challenge is distinguishing geometric effects from material-specific interactions. A purely ballistic model may reproduce roughness but fail to predict the correct pore dimensions or mechanical strength. A model with excessive diffusion may eliminate the observed cluster-scale texture. Sensitivity analysis is therefore essential. Simulations should vary impact energy, cluster size, surface mobility, and angular distribution independently where possible. They should also report how porosity is calculated and whether pores are treated as accessible or merely geometric voids. Direct comparison with three-dimensional experimental reconstructions provides a stronger test than matching only the projected surface appearance. Model validation should include multiple observables, such as density, roughness, pore connectivity, and contact morphology.

6. Experimental characterization

Scanning electron microscopy can reveal surface texture and cross-sectional morphology. It is useful for identifying columns, exposed clusters, and large voids. However, a two-dimensional image cannot reliably quantify three-dimensional connectivity. Transmission electron microscopy can resolve particle contacts and local neck formation in thin or sectioned samples. Electron tomography can reconstruct the internal pore network, although specimen thickness and reconstruction artifacts must be considered. Focused ion beam sectioning can provide cross sections but may modify delicate porous structures. A combination of methods is preferable to reliance on a single image.

X-ray reflectivity and ellipsometry can provide average density and thickness estimates. X-ray reflectivity is especially useful for layered films with sufficiently smooth interfaces, but rough porous films can complicate interpretation. Grazing-incidence small-angle X-ray scattering can probe characteristic length scales and structural correlations. Neutron scattering may offer complementary contrast, especially when isotopic or compositional contrast is available. Gas adsorption measurements can estimate accessible surface area and pore size, but they do not necessarily detect closed pores. The interpretation depends on the adsorbate, temperature, and pore accessibility. Gravimetric or quartz-crystal measurements can help determine deposited mass and, when combined with thickness, estimate apparent density.

Surface-sensitive techniques should be paired with bulk-sensitive measurements. Atomic force microscopy provides topographic roughness over a defined scan range, but roughness is not equivalent to porosity. Profilometry can measure thickness and large-scale uniformity, though it cannot resolve nanoscale voids. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy can identify surface chemistry and ligand residues. Infrared or Raman spectroscopy may detect chemical transformations during deposition or annealing. Mechanical tests can reveal how pore architecture affects adhesion and stiffness. Electrical and thermal measurements can provide indirect evidence of contact networks and transport pathways. Since porous films may be fragile, measurement-induced damage should be assessed.

A robust characterization protocol should distinguish mass density, geometric porosity, and accessible porosity. Mass density can be estimated from deposited mass and volume, but thickness uncertainty can dominate the result. Geometric porosity requires a structural model or direct three-dimensional imaging. Accessible porosity depends on probe size and surface chemistry. Reporting the method and uncertainty is essential. Measurements should also be made across multiple locations and samples because ballistic growth can produce lateral heterogeneity. Statistical treatment is especially important for broad pore distributions. Reproducibility requires documenting source conditions, substrate preparation, deposition angle, flux, and post-treatment history.

7. Process variables and structure control

Substrate temperature is often the most direct control over surface mobility. Increasing temperature can promote diffusion, neck growth, and densification. The response may be abrupt if a mobility threshold is crossed. In some systems, temperature also changes ligand coverage or induces chemical reactions. Thus, a temperature series should be accompanied by compositional analysis. Excessive heating can cause sintering, stress, or loss of desired porosity. The optimum temperature depends on the balance between mechanical stability and accessible surface area.

Impact energy can be adjusted through source settings, acceleration fields, or transport conditions. Low-energy deposition tends to preserve cluster identity but may produce weak contacts. Moderate energies may improve adhesion and form necks without eliminating porosity. High energies can cause fragmentation, implantation, or local densification. The useful range is material dependent. Energy-resolved measurements can help separate these regimes. If the energy distribution is broad, a single nominal value may be misleading.

Deposition angle controls shadowing and anisotropy. Normal incidence generally reduces directional column tilt but does not eliminate pore formation. Oblique incidence can increase open structure by enhancing geometric screening. Substrate rotation can average directional effects and improve macroscopic uniformity. Yet rotation does not necessarily increase packing density because each cluster may still be immobilized after impact. Combining oblique incidence with rotation offers a way to tune anisotropy separately from overall porosity. These effects should be evaluated with three-dimensional imaging rather than surface appearance alone.

Flux and deposition rate influence the time available for relaxation between impacts. High flux can trap structures before they reorganize. Lower flux can allow surface processes to act, provided the substrate temperature and chemistry permit mobility. Flux also affects local heating and the likelihood of overlapping impacts. A systematic rate series can therefore clarify kinetic competition. The total film thickness should be controlled when comparing rates because thickening itself changes shadowing and pore evolution. Cluster size and size distribution should likewise be held constant or explicitly varied.

Substrate roughness and chemistry determine the initial nucleation landscape. A rough substrate may promote anchoring and generate a nonuniform interfacial layer. A chemically attractive surface can increase sticking and suppress lateral migration. A weakly interacting surface may encourage diffusion or rebound. Surface functionalization offers a route to control these effects, but it can introduce additional complexity through chemical reactions. The substrate should be cleaned and characterized immediately before deposition. Even small amounts of contamination can alter contact angles, adhesion, and film continuity.

8. Functional implications

High porosity can increase accessible surface area and facilitate transport of molecules through a film. This is advantageous in catalytic and sensing applications. However, high surface area alone does not guarantee high activity. Pore accessibility, active-site chemistry, and transport limitations also matter. Narrow contacts can impede electronic or thermal conduction. A highly porous film may therefore be chemically active but electrically resistive. The design objective is often a connected solid skeleton with an accessible pore network, not maximum void fraction.

In optical applications, porosity changes the effective refractive index and can reduce reflectance. A controlled gradient in density may provide an index-matching layer. Ballistic deposition can naturally produce depth-dependent density, but uncontrolled gradients may also cause scattering and inhomogeneity. The cluster size relative to the wavelength determines whether the film behaves as an effective medium or exhibits significant scattering. Optical characterization should therefore include both spectral response and structural information. Surface roughness and pore connectivity can influence optical losses.

Mechanical properties are strongly affected by the contact network. Films with point contacts may have low stiffness and poor wear resistance. Neck growth can improve cohesion while retaining some porosity. Adhesion to the substrate is another concern because the porous interface may concentrate stress. Residual stress can arise from impact, thermal mismatch, or shrinkage during annealing. A post-treatment that strengthens contacts may also reduce pore volume. Mechanical optimization is thus a tradeoff among strength, density, and functional accessibility.

For electrochemical applications, interconnected pores can improve electrolyte penetration and shorten diffusion distances. At the same time, poor particle connectivity can limit charge transport. A conductive scaffold or selective necking may help address this conflict. In filtration, pore size and connectivity determine selectivity and pressure drop. A broad distribution can create bypass pathways that reduce performance. In thermal coatings, porosity can suppress heat transport but may compromise durability. These examples underscore that the desired architecture is application specific. The deposition process should be tuned to the functional metric rather than to porosity alone.

9. Limitations and open questions

The phrase ballistic growth can describe a broad range of conditions. It is therefore necessary to specify the degree of trajectory control, the angular distribution, and the extent of post-impact motion. Similarly, limited coalescence is relative rather than absolute. Some systems retain clusters visibly, whereas others form substantial necks without becoming fully dense. Quantitative descriptors are needed to compare studies. Candidate measures include contact-area fraction, coordination number, neck-to-particle diameter ratio, and accessible pore connectivity. These quantities should be linked to material performance.

A major unresolved issue is the role of transient impact dynamics. Many experimental measurements characterize the final film but cannot observe the first moments after collision. Molecular simulations offer insight, yet they may not capture realistic cluster sizes or timescales. Time-resolved in situ methods could clarify whether clusters deform, rebound, or migrate. Another challenge is separating the effects of ligands from those of kinetic energy and temperature. Ligands can both inhibit coalescence and alter adhesion. Controlled ligand-removal experiments would help isolate these contributions.

The origin of depth-dependent porosity also warrants further study. Some changes arise from evolving shadowing, while others reflect altered substrate interactions or accumulated stress. A film can become denser or more porous with thickness depending on the competition among these mechanisms. Depth-resolved density measurements and tomography could reveal the growth trajectory. In situ monitoring of mass, thickness, and roughness would complement ex situ analysis. Such measurements are particularly important for films intended for scalable manufacturing.

Scale-up poses practical challenges. Large-area deposition can produce nonuniform flux and angle distributions. Source stability and cluster-size drift may affect reproducibility. Substrate motion can average some variations but may also alter the deposition history. Porous films can be sensitive to handling and environmental exposure. Standardized reporting of process conditions is therefore essential. Interlaboratory comparisons would benefit from common reference materials and shared analysis protocols.

10. Conclusions

Nanocluster deposition can produce highly porous films when incoming clusters attach with limited post-impact rearrangement. Ballistic trajectories and geometric shadowing favor growth on exposed features and leave recessed regions underfilled. Restricted diffusion and limited coalescence preserve cluster-scale texture and maintain interparticle voids. The final architecture is controlled by coupled variables, including cluster size, shape, impact energy, surface chemistry, substrate temperature, incidence angle, and deposition rate. No single variable determines porosity independently. The same nominal cluster material can form dense or open films under different kinetic conditions.

A complete account of film structure requires distinguishing intracluster defects from intercluster voids. It also requires separating total porosity from accessible porosity and pore connectivity. Surface imaging should be complemented by bulk-sensitive and three-dimensional methods. Modeling is most useful when it links measurable process parameters to multiple structural observables. Functional optimization should consider transport, contact strength, and stability in addition to surface area. Future work combining controlled deposition, in situ observation, tomography, and multiscale modeling can establish more predictive design rules. Such advances will enable nanocluster films to be tailored for applications in which a precisely controlled porous architecture is essential.

Replacing traditional schooling with remote learning is one of the biggest educational changes of recent years. Online classes allow students to learn from home and connect with teachers through digital tools. This approach can be convenient, especially for students who live far from school or need flexible schedules. However, replacing the classroom entirely creates serious challenges. One major difficulty is unequal access to technology. Some students do not have a reliable computer, fast internet, or a quiet place to study. As a result, they may miss lessons or struggle to complete assignments. These problems can make existing educational inequalities even worse.

Remote learning also requires students to manage their time independently. In a classroom, teachers can set routines and notice when someone is having trouble. At home, students may face distractions from family members, household chores, or entertainment. Younger students, in particular, may need more guidance than an online format can easily provide. Staying motivated can also be difficult when lessons take place on a screen every day. Long hours of screen use may cause tiredness, headaches, or difficulty concentrating. Some students learn better through hands-on activities that are hard to recreate online.

Communication is another challenge. In person, students can ask quick questions and receive immediate feedback. Online, technical problems or unclear instructions may interrupt this exchange. Teachers may also find it harder to recognize confusion when they cannot see the whole class. This can delay help for students who are falling behind. Remote learning can affect social development as well. Schools give students daily opportunities to make friends, work in teams, and practice resolving disagreements. Without these interactions, some students may feel isolated or lonely. Group projects and discussions can still happen online, but they often feel less natural.

Teachers face difficulties too. They must learn new platforms, redesign lessons, and support students with different needs. Preparing effective online activities can take considerable time. Schools also need to protect students’ privacy and make sure that learning platforms are secure. Despite these challenges, remote learning can be useful when it is planned carefully. Schools can lend devices, provide internet access, and offer printed materials when needed. Regular check-ins and clear routines can help students stay engaged. A mix of online and in-person instruction may provide flexibility while preserving social contact. Overall, remote learning offers valuable opportunities, but it cannot simply replace traditional schooling without careful support. The best approach is one that considers each student’s access, well-being, and way of learning.

The rise of trending topics has changed how news is discovered, reported, and discussed. Before social platforms became central to public life, editors and broadcasters largely decided which stories deserved immediate attention. Newsrooms relied on reporters, wire services, audience tips, and scheduled ratings to gauge public interest. Real-time social media analysis added a new, constantly updating signal: what people were talking about online. Platforms began displaying popular hashtags and subjects, turning scattered posts into visible lists of shared attention. These lists made “trending” a familiar feature of the digital news experience. They also encouraged journalists to treat online conversation as a possible early warning system. A breaking event can now surface through eyewitness posts before a newsroom receives an official briefing. Videos, photographs, and location details shared by users may provide the first clues about what has happened. Reporters can monitor those posts, contact witnesses, and use digital tools to verify material. This has helped news organizations respond more quickly to sudden events. During elections, natural disasters, protests, and emergencies, social activity can offer a fast picture of what people are seeing and asking. It can also reveal questions that official sources have not yet addressed. But a trend is not the same as a verified news story. A topic may rise because of coordinated promotion, celebrity attention, jokes, or a sudden burst of misleading claims. Algorithms shape what users see, while platform rules and user demographics influence which voices become prominent. As a result, a trending list is an imperfect measure of public opinion. Journalists must investigate the people, events, and incentives behind a surge in posts before presenting it as meaningful. Verification has become a central part of social-media reporting. Newsrooms check dates, locations, original sources, and the context of images and videos. They may compare posts with public records, satellite imagery, or information from people on the ground. This work takes time, even when online discussion moves at great speed. The pressure to publish first can create risks, including amplifying false information or misidentifying individuals. Some news organizations now assign staff to monitor social platforms and explain how online claims are being checked. Others use software to flag unusual activity, though automated systems cannot replace editorial judgment. Trending topics have also reshaped the relationship between journalists and audiences. Readers can challenge coverage, offer firsthand accounts, and draw attention to overlooked communities. Their participation can broaden reporting, but it can also expose reporters and sources to harassment. The same platforms that help stories spread can reward outrage and simplify complex issues into slogans. Newsrooms therefore face a choice between following online attention and providing context that may not generate immediate engagement. Editors increasingly have to distinguish what is popular from what is important. That distinction matters because trends can fade within hours, while the effects of the events they describe may last for years. Real-time analysis has made journalism faster and more responsive, but not automatically more accurate or representative. Its lasting value depends on careful verification, transparent methods, and a willingness to correct mistakes. Trending topics are now part of the modern news cycle, not a substitute for reporting. They show where attention is gathering; journalists still have to establish what is true and why it matters.

Density-Functional Analysis of Technetium Atom and Dimer Trapping in Calcium Aluminate Nanopores

Abstract

Technetium is a long-lived fission product whose mobility in cementitious and ceramic waste forms is strongly influenced by its oxidation state and local coordination environment. Calcium aluminates are promising components of engineered waste forms because they combine chemical durability with structural diversity and can form nanoscale pores and interfaces. This paper presents a computational framework for examining the trapping of isolated technetium atoms and technetium dimers in calcium aluminate nanopores. The study is formulated as a density-functional theory investigation, with explicit attention to spin polarization, relativistic effects, pore geometry, and competing adsorption configurations. Because no new calculations are reported here, numerical energies and structures are not asserted as results. Instead, the paper defines the models, observables, and validation steps required for a reproducible assessment. It explains how binding energies, charge transfer, spin states, vibrational stability, and thermodynamic corrections can distinguish genuine trapping from artifacts of finite models. The analysis emphasizes that technetium atom and dimer trapping need not follow the same mechanism. An isolated atom may form localized bonds to oxygen or aluminum, whereas a dimer may retain a metal–metal bond or dissociate upon adsorption. Pore termination, water, hydroxyl groups, and charge compensation can alter both outcomes. The proposed framework therefore treats these factors as variables rather than assuming a single idealized surface. The resulting predictions can guide experimental characterization and the design of calcium aluminate materials for technetium immobilization, while clearly identifying the calculations needed before quantitative conclusions can be drawn.

Introduction

Technetium-99 is a radioactive fission product of concern in the long-term management of nuclear waste. Its half-life is approximately 2.1 × 10^5 years, making its chemical retention relevant over geological timescales. Under oxidizing conditions, technetium commonly occurs as pertechnetate, TcO4−, a highly soluble and weakly sorbing anion. Under more reducing conditions, lower-valent technetium species can be less soluble and may form oxides, clusters, or metal-rich phases. Waste-form performance therefore depends not only on the bulk composition but also on local redox conditions and the availability of coordination sites. Cementitious materials and calcium aluminate ceramics are of interest because they can provide alkaline environments and chemically diverse mineral phases. Their pore surfaces may offer sites that are absent from an ideal bulk crystal. At the nanoscale, defects, under-coordinated ions, and hydroxylated terminations can substantially change adsorption energetics. A useful atomistic description must consequently distinguish bulk incorporation from surface adsorption and pore confinement.

Calcium aluminate is not a single structure but a family of compounds with different calcium-to-aluminum ratios and crystal arrangements. Phases such as CaAl2O4, CaAl4O7, and Ca3Al2O6 differ in their coordination networks and potential pore surfaces. Their hydration products also differ from the anhydrous phases and can create layered or gel-like environments. The present work focuses on a generic calcium aluminate nanopore as a model environment, while recognizing that any quantitative prediction must specify the phase and termination. The term nanopore here refers to a finite void bounded by calcium aluminate walls, rather than a macroscopic open channel. Such a pore may be constructed computationally by removing atoms from a periodic supercell and relaxing the resulting surface. Alternatively, a slab model with a vacuum gap can represent an exposed pore wall. These representations are not interchangeable, because curvature, periodic images, and surface reconstruction differ. A robust study should compare at least two geometries or demonstrate that the selected model captures the relevant coordination motifs.

The central question is whether a technetium atom or a technetium dimer can be stabilized within such a pore. The atom and dimer provide distinct probes of the local chemical environment. An isolated technetium atom has several possible spin states and can interact with multiple surface atoms. A dimer introduces a Tc–Tc bond whose retention or disruption provides an additional energetic scale. Confinement can favor adsorption by increasing the number of contacts, but it can also impose strain or restrict favorable coordination. The balance depends on the pore size, surface stoichiometry, charge state, and electronic structure treatment. This paper develops a computational protocol for evaluating that balance without presenting unperformed calculations as established findings. It provides testable hypotheses, energy definitions, and criteria for interpreting candidate structures. It also identifies the limits of semilocal density-functional theory for transition-metal systems.

Background and chemical context

Technetium has the electronic configuration [Kr]4d5 5s2 in its neutral atomic ground-state description. The distribution of electrons among 4d and 5s-derived states can change upon bonding and oxidation. Consequently, a single nominal oxidation state may not adequately describe technetium adsorbed at a heterogeneous interface. A density-functional calculation should examine the projected electronic density of states and spin density alongside formal oxidation-state assignments. Formal charges are useful bookkeeping devices, but they are not direct observables. Bader, Hirshfeld, or other population analyses can provide comparative charge trends, although their numerical values depend on the partitioning scheme. Agreement between multiple indicators is more persuasive than reliance on one charge metric. Local coordination numbers and bond-length distributions also help distinguish metallic, ionic, and covalent interactions.

The dimer deserves separate treatment because gas-phase Tc2 bonding is not captured by simply doubling the atomic energy. A dimer’s stability depends on its spin multiplicity, bond length, and occupation of bonding and antibonding orbitals. When placed in a pore, the molecule may remain intact, elongate, rotate, or dissociate into two surface-bound atoms. A calculation that begins from only one geometry could miss the lowest-energy outcome. Several initial orientations and separations should therefore be sampled. The relevant comparison includes the energy of an intact adsorbed dimer, the energy of two independently adsorbed atoms, and the energy of the bare pore plus a gas-phase dimer. The resulting quantities answer different questions and should not be conflated. A favorable adsorption energy does not by itself prove that a dimer will remain molecular.

The chemical state of the pore wall is equally important. An ideal anhydrous surface may expose under-coordinated Ca or Al atoms and reactive oxygen atoms. In a hydrated material, surface hydroxyls and adsorbed water can passivate these sites or provide hydrogen-bonding and proton-transfer pathways. A pore may also contain vacancies, substitutions, and trapped counterions. Technetium species can respond strongly to these local variations. For instance, oxygen-rich terminations may stabilize oxidized species, whereas reduced or defect-rich regions could favor more metal-like coordination. The computational model should therefore state its oxygen chemical potential, protonation pattern, and total charge. In charged periodic calculations, a compensating background may be introduced by the code, but this can create finite-size artifacts. Neutral defect complexes or explicit counterions are preferable when chemically meaningful.

Methods

The proposed calculations use spin-polarized density-functional theory with periodic boundary conditions. A plane-wave basis and projector augmented-wave potentials or an equivalent all-electron approach are suitable. The exchange-correlation functional should be selected and documented explicitly. A generalized-gradient approximation such as PBE can provide a practical baseline, but its treatment of localized 4d states and adsorption energies should be checked. A dispersion correction may be included when water, hydroxylated surfaces, or weakly bound configurations are relevant. The correction should be applied consistently to the pore, adsorbate, and reference calculations. A hybrid functional or a carefully benchmarked DFT+U treatment can serve as a sensitivity test if localized states are found. The value of any Hubbard parameter must be justified rather than chosen solely to obtain a desired oxidation state.

Scalar relativistic effects are important for technetium and should be represented in the pseudopotential or basis. Spin–orbit coupling may affect electronic levels and fine energetic differences. It should be evaluated at least for the most competitive structures if the computational approach permits. For a neutral atom, the reference spin state must be treated consistently with the selected relativistic approximation. The same applies to the isolated dimer, whose possible spin states should be optimized separately. Convergence tests should include plane-wave cutoff, k-point sampling, and supercell size. A large pore supercell may require only the gamma point, but that assumption must be demonstrated. The vacuum thickness in slab models should be sufficient to prevent spurious interactions between periodic images.

A structural model should begin with a specified calcium aluminate phase and crystallographic orientation. The bulk lattice constants should first be optimized using the same functional and pseudopotentials planned for the adsorption calculations. A pore can then be generated by removing a region of atoms from a supercell or by constructing opposing surfaces around a confined void. The resulting structure should be relaxed with selected inner atoms fixed only when needed to represent bulk-like material. The pore dimensions should be reported using both geometric diameter and local coordination descriptors. Several pore sizes are desirable because confinement can change the preferred adsorption geometry. Surface terminations should preserve a chemically reasonable stoichiometry or include an explicit account of compensating defects. The model should avoid arbitrary net charge unless a well-defined charged-state calculation is intended.

For each pore structure, the bare host should be fully relaxed before adding technetium. Candidate adsorption sites include oxygen-rich corners, calcium-associated regions, aluminum-associated regions, and pore centers. Initial configurations should place the atom at multiple distances and orientations relative to these sites. For the dimer, initial structures should sample different Tc–Tc separations, orientations, and positions relative to the pore wall. Both intact and deliberately dissociated starting geometries should be included. The electronic optimization should explore multiple initial magnetic moments to reduce the risk of trapping in an unintended spin solution. The final structures should be checked for residual forces and for convergence of the electronic state. A structure with large imaginary vibrational modes may represent a saddle point rather than a stable trapping configuration.

The binding energy of a technetium atom to a neutral pore can be defined as Ebind(atom) = E(pore + Tc) − E(pore) − E(Tc), with all terms evaluated using compatible numerical settings. Under this convention, a negative value indicates exothermic binding relative to the chosen separated references. For a dimer, the corresponding molecular adsorption energy is Ebind(dimer) = E(pore + Tc2) − E(pore) − E(Tc2). The dimer dissociation energy in the pore can be evaluated by comparing the relaxed intact structure with a configuration containing two separated, adsorbed atoms. A separate energy difference should compare adsorbed Tc2 with two gas-phase atoms plus the pore. These quantities must be reported with clear sign conventions. Zero-point and finite-temperature corrections can alter close energetic rankings and should be estimated where differences are small. For charged species, the reference states and charge-compensation procedure must be stated explicitly.

Thermodynamic interpretation requires care because a binding energy is not a kinetic barrier. A strongly bound state may be inaccessible if diffusion into the pore or dissociation of a precursor is slow. Minimum-energy paths can be investigated with a nudged elastic band method for migration, entry, or dimer dissociation. The free-energy change for adsorption depends on the gas-phase entropy of the incoming species and on the temperature and pressure. In a liquid or hydrated environment, chemical potentials of water, oxygen, and protons may be more relevant than vacuum references. A grand-canonical treatment or an explicitly solvated model can be needed to compare redox states under realistic conditions. The present framework therefore treats adsorption energies as mechanistic descriptors rather than direct predictions of macroscopic retention.

Electronic and structural analysis

Relaxed structures should be characterized by Tc–O, Tc–Ca, Tc–Al, and Tc–Tc distances. Coordination numbers can be determined using a consistent distance criterion or a bond-order analysis. The criterion should not be adjusted separately for each configuration. A radial distribution function can provide a less arbitrary view of coordination in larger models. Bonding analysis may use projected density of states, crystal orbital Hamilton population, or related methods, provided the chosen implementation is described. These quantities can help distinguish direct Tc–Tc bonding from two independent surface bonds. They can also reveal whether technetium-derived states lie within the host band gap or hybridize with the valence and conduction manifolds.

Charge and spin analyses are essential because adsorption may change the electronic state substantially. Spin-density isosurfaces can identify whether an unpaired electron remains localized on technetium or becomes distributed over neighboring oxygen atoms. Local magnetic moments should be compared across the atom, dimer, and adsorbed configurations. Population analysis should be interpreted as a trend, not as an exact oxidation-state measurement. If distinct spin solutions lie close in energy, both should be retained in the reported results. A state that is lower in energy by less than the numerical uncertainty should not be presented as uniquely preferred. The uncertainty should include convergence sensitivity and functional dependence, not merely the final self-consistent-field tolerance.

Vibrational analysis can test local stability and estimate zero-point energy corrections. Full phonon calculations for large pore models may be expensive, but finite-displacement calculations around the adsorbate and its immediate environment can provide a useful first check. Translational and rotational modes of an isolated molecule require special treatment when comparing gas and adsorbed states. For a dimer, the Tc–Tc stretching frequency is a particularly informative observable. A substantial change relative to the isolated molecule would indicate altered bond strength, although frequency comparisons depend on the functional and mass treatment. Simulated infrared or Raman signatures may assist interpretation of future measurements. Such predictions should be reported with appropriate scaling and uncertainty.

Results and interpretation framework

No optimized structures or numerical energies are claimed in this paper. The following interpretation framework states the outcomes that the proposed calculations can discriminate. A stable atom-trapping configuration would be indicated by a reproducible local minimum with favorable binding relative to the defined reference and no relevant unstable vibrational modes. If the atom forms multiple short Tc–O contacts, the interaction may have substantial covalent or ionic character. If it instead coordinates primarily to calcium or aluminum, the electronic structure would need to establish whether those contacts are bonding or merely geometric. A large relaxation of nearby pore atoms would indicate that trapping is coupled to host reconstruction. Such reconstruction can be energetically favorable but may carry a kinetic cost.

An intact dimer-trapping configuration would require both a favorable adsorption energy and a persistent Tc–Tc bond after relaxation. The bond may be lengthened or weakened without being fully broken. Evidence for retention should combine geometry, bond-order measures, and a vibrational mode associated with Tc–Tc stretching. If the dimer dissociates spontaneously during optimization from several distinct starting geometries, dissociative trapping is a plausible outcome within the model. However, this conclusion would remain conditional on the functional, spin state, pore termination, and cell size. The possibility of a metastable intact state should be assessed with constrained scans or transition-state calculations. A single relaxation cannot determine whether an experimentally introduced dimer remains intact on relevant timescales.

The comparison between atom and dimer trapping has several possible regimes. The pore may bind an isolated atom strongly while destabilizing the dimer, favoring dissociation into separate sites. It may instead stabilize the dimer through cooperative contacts with the wall while preserving metal–metal bonding. A third possibility is weak interaction with the pore, in which confinement changes geometry but not electronic structure appreciably. The energetic ranking can differ between dry and hydroxylated pores. Water may block direct coordination sites, but it can also facilitate proton transfer and stabilize charged intermediates. The predicted ranking should therefore be presented as a matrix over relevant surface conditions, not as a single universal number.

A meaningful comparison should include at least three reference processes. The first is adsorption of Tc relative to an isolated gas-phase atom. The second is adsorption of Tc2 relative to a gas-phase dimer. The third is conversion of an adsorbed dimer into two adsorbed atoms. These reference processes answer different questions about capture and molecular integrity. The first two quantify thermodynamic attachment under a specified reference convention. The third assesses whether the pore favors an intact cluster or dissociated atoms. If the dimer is formed from atoms in the material rather than introduced as a gas-phase molecule, an additional chemical-potential framework is needed. The computational paper should avoid using the word “trapping” as if it implied both favorable binding and slow release.

Finite-size and methodological uncertainty may be substantial. Pore models can contain artificial under-coordinated atoms at their boundaries. Periodic images of technetium may interact if the cell is too small. A charged adsorbate may interact with its compensating background and alter the apparent binding energy. Dispersion corrections can influence weakly bound configurations, while self-interaction error may affect electron localization. Functional sensitivity should be assessed for the main structural conclusions, even if only a subset of structures can be recalculated with a more expensive method. Where results depend on a small energy difference, the conclusion should be described as unresolved. Reporting uncertainty is more informative than selecting a single functional result without qualification.

Relevance to experiments

The proposed calculations can guide experiments by identifying structural signatures associated with candidate technetium environments. X-ray absorption spectroscopy can probe local coordination and oxidation-state trends. Tc–O distances and coordination numbers predicted for a pore-bound atom could be compared with extended X-ray absorption fine structure measurements. A retained dimer may exhibit a Tc–Tc scattering path, although detecting it in a disordered material may be challenging. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy can provide complementary chemical-state information, subject to radiation and charging effects. Electron paramagnetic resonance may be informative for paramagnetic states, but the signal can be broadened or absent in concentrated or strongly coupled systems. The predicted spin density and magnetic moments can help determine which techniques are most diagnostic.

Raman and infrared spectra can test for molecular or oxide-like species. A Tc–Tc vibrational mode would support an intact dimer assignment if it is sufficiently intense and spectrally distinguishable. Calculated frequencies should account for anharmonicity and the surrounding matrix before direct quantitative comparison. In hydrated calcium aluminate, water and hydroxyl bands may overlap with technetium-related features. Isotopic substitution is not generally practical for technetium because it is monoisotopic in stable form, but host isotopic substitutions may help identify matrix-coupled vibrations. Spectroscopy should be interpreted jointly with structural and thermodynamic evidence.

Leaching experiments remain the direct measure of macroscopic immobilization. A favorable atomistic binding energy does not guarantee low release because diffusion through the bulk and dissolution of the host can dominate. Conversely, modest local binding may still contribute to retention if the pore network is inaccessible or if the technetium species is kinetically trapped. Calculated migration barriers and defect formation energies can complement adsorption studies. The most useful computational predictions will therefore connect local coordination to plausible transport pathways. Comparisons among phases and hydration states can help explain why nominally similar calcium aluminate materials exhibit different retention behavior.

Limitations

The framework described here is an idealized atomistic treatment. Real waste forms contain compositional variation, impurities, grain boundaries, radiation damage, and evolving hydration products. A single nanopore model cannot represent the full distribution of environments. The use of a periodic cell also imposes artificial order and may suppress long-wavelength relaxation. Explicit solvent models are computationally demanding, while implicit solvation models may not capture specific proton-transfer chemistry. The choice of technetium reference state is especially important because isolated atoms and dimers may not be the species introduced in an aqueous waste stream. Pertechnetate and lower-valent oxyanions should be studied in follow-up work if the goal is to model realistic aqueous uptake.

Density-functional theory itself has limitations. Semilocal functionals can over-delocalize electrons and may misrepresent redox energetics. Hybrid functionals can improve localization but increase computational cost and may not consistently improve all energy differences. DFT+U introduces a parameter that can affect spin and oxidation-state assignments. Relativistic and spin–orbit effects can alter state ordering, especially for technetium-derived states. These effects should be included when they are comparable to the energetic differences under discussion. Benchmarking against molecular calculations or higher-level electronic-structure methods for small clusters can help establish the reliability of the chosen approach.

The model also does not directly determine kinetic trapping. Adsorption energies describe endpoint thermodynamics, whereas diffusion and reaction barriers govern rates. A dimer may be thermodynamically unstable but kinetically persistent. An atom may bind strongly at the pore entrance yet fail to penetrate the interior. Ab initio molecular dynamics or transition-state searches can address selected pathways, but their accessible timescales remain limited. Multiscale modeling may be required to connect atomistic barriers with long-term retention. Any claim about geological stability must therefore combine electronic-structure results with transport, dissolution, and radiation-damage considerations.

Conclusions

This paper establishes a density-functional framework for analyzing technetium atom and dimer trapping in calcium aluminate nanopores. It emphasizes that the relevant material is a family of phases and surface environments rather than one universal pore structure. It defines adsorption and dissociation energies that separate attachment from molecular integrity. It also specifies structural, electronic, magnetic, vibrational, and thermodynamic diagnostics for evaluating candidate states. No numerical trapping energies or optimized structures are presented because no calculations are reported here. The principal hypothesis is that atomic and dimeric technetium can respond differently to confinement because their coordination requirements and internal bonding differ. The direction and magnitude of that difference must be established by calculations that sample pore size, surface termination, hydration, charge, and spin state.

A reliable study should use converged periodic models, multiple initial geometries, and consistent reference energies. It should test functional sensitivity and include relativistic effects appropriate to technetium. It should distinguish favorable adsorption from kinetic immobilization and should not infer a unique oxidation state from one charge-partitioning method. It should also compare dry and hydrated environments when the intended application involves cementitious materials. These precautions are necessary because small energetic differences can be comparable to methodological uncertainty. The proposed workflow provides a basis for reproducible calculations and experimentally testable predictions. Its eventual results could help identify which calcium aluminate environments most effectively retain technetium and whether retention proceeds through isolated atoms, intact dimers, or more oxidized species.

The paper presents a graph neural representation designed to improve theoretical expressivity and evaluates it on minimum vertex cover optimization. The combination of formal analysis and a concrete combinatorial task is promising and relevant to graph learning. The authors should state their main contributions more precisely and clarify which assumptions underlie the expressivity claims. In particular, it would help to distinguish the proposed representation’s capabilities from those of established higher-order or positional graph neural methods. The evaluation should include strong, well-tuned baselines and report performance across multiple graph sizes, densities, and graph families. Since minimum vertex cover is NP-hard, the paper should explain how solution quality is measured and whether runtime and scalability are assessed alongside it. Ablations could reveal which components drive any gains and whether the theoretical improvements translate into practical benefits. The results would be more convincing with repeated runs, uncertainty estimates, and details sufficient for reproduction. The authors should also discuss cases where the method offers little advantage or incurs substantial computational overhead. Overall, the work appears potentially valuable, but clearer positioning and more comprehensive empirical evidence are needed to support its claims.

A person’s ability to inspire others is shaped not only by what they achieve but also by how they communicate, behave, and pursue their goals. Inspiration happens when people feel encouraged to believe in themselves and take positive action. A powerful speech can motivate someone, but lasting inspiration usually comes from a combination of words and actions. Communication is important because it helps people understand ideas, feel included, and recognize what is possible. A good communicator listens as carefully as they speak. Listening shows respect and helps a person respond to what others truly need. Clear and honest words can build trust. When people trust someone, they are more likely to consider that person’s ideas and follow their example. A hopeful message can also help people see opportunities during difficult times. However, words have little influence when they are not supported by behavior.

A person’s behavior shows what they value. Treating others with kindness and fairness can inspire people to act the same way. Keeping promises demonstrates reliability. Admitting mistakes shows courage and humility. These actions remind others that being a leader does not mean being perfect. It means taking responsibility and learning from experience. People often remember how someone treated them more than what that person said. A person who stays calm during a challenge can encourage others not to give up. In contrast, someone who speaks about respect but behaves selfishly may lose the trust of others. Consistent behavior makes a person’s message believable.

Drive is another important part of inspiring others. Drive is the willingness to work toward a goal, even when progress is slow. People who show determination can help others believe that difficult goals are worth pursuing. Their effort demonstrates that success often requires patience and practice. A person with drive does not have to be famous or naturally gifted. They can inspire others simply by continuing after a setback. At the same time, healthy drive includes knowing when to rest and ask for help. Working toward a goal with purpose can give other people a reason to care about it too. When determination is combined with humility, it becomes an example rather than a demand.

Communication, behavior, and drive are strongest when they work together. Clear communication explains a goal, respectful behavior earns trust, and drive shows commitment to making the goal real. For example, a student who encourages classmates, includes them in a group project, and works steadily can motivate the whole group. Each quality supports the others. Without communication, people may not understand the purpose. Without good behavior, they may not trust the person leading them. Without drive, inspiring words may not lead to action. The most inspiring people make others feel capable, valued, and hopeful. They do not simply ask people to follow them; they help people find their own reasons to move forward. In the end, inspiration grows when a person’s words, choices, and efforts reflect the same positive purpose.

Northern Ireland is preparing to welcome Syrian refugees as local authorities and community groups make arrangements for their arrival. The resettlement effort is expected to provide families fleeing conflict with housing, schooling and access to health services. Supporters say the program reflects a humanitarian duty and offers people a chance to rebuild their lives in safety. Volunteers and charities are working to organize practical help, including language support and household supplies. However, the plans have also drawn opposition from some residents and political voices concerned about resources and the pace of resettlement. Officials have urged the public to avoid misinformation and assess the arrangements on the basis of verified information. They say the number of arrivals will be coordinated with local capacity and existing support services. Community leaders hope that direct contact between residents and new arrivals will ease concerns and build understanding. The debate highlights the challenge of balancing public concerns with the urgent needs of people displaced by war.
