A Gaussian Graphical Framework for Representing Interference and Non-Interference and Identifying Causal Effects

Abstract

Causal inference often assumes that one unit’s treatment does not affect another unit’s outcome. This assumption, commonly called no interference, is convenient but may be unrealistic in networks, households, classrooms, markets, and infectious-disease settings. We develop a Gaussian graphical framework for expressing both interference and non-interference, and for determining when causal effects can be identified from a causal model. The framework represents variables as nodes in a directed acyclic graph, or DAG, and causal dependencies as directed edges. For Gaussian structural equation models, each variable is a linear function of its parents plus an independent error term. Interference is represented by directed paths from one unit’s treatment to another unit’s outcome, while non-interference is represented by the absence of such paths under a specified unit and exposure mapping. We distinguish graph-based absence of causal influence from statistical independence, and we clarify how latent variables, treatment assignment, and conditioning can complicate this distinction. We define direct, spillover, total, and policy effects using potential outcomes and relate these estimands to interventions in a structural causal model. We show that causal effects are identified when the graph and available variables imply an appropriate adjustment, mediation, front-door, or instrumental-variable strategy, subject to explicit assumptions. A linear-Gaussian example illustrates how interference changes regression coefficients and how the graph reveals which effects are recoverable. We also describe limitations, including model misspecification, hidden confounding, feedback, and the fact that Gaussianity alone does not identify causal direction. The framework provides a transparent language for representing cross-unit influence and for separating estimable causal effects from associations.

1. Introduction

Causal questions frequently concern more than the effect of a treatment on the person or object receiving it. A vaccination may alter the infection risk of a contact. A student’s tutoring may influence classmates. A firm’s pricing may affect competitors. A household member’s employment may change another member’s labor supply. Such situations involve interference, meaning that one unit’s treatment can affect another unit’s outcome.

A common starting point in experimental and observational research is the stable unit treatment value assumption. One part of this assumption says that each unit’s outcome depends only on that unit’s treatment. This condition is often referred to as no interference. When it fails, a conventional treatment-versus-control contrast can combine own-treatment effects with spillovers, and its interpretation can become unclear.

The challenge is not merely to acknowledge that units may interact. Researchers need a precise representation of which treatments can affect which outcomes, which pathways carry those effects, and which causal quantities are identified by the observed data. A graphical model offers a compact way to organize these relationships. In particular, a directed acyclic graph encodes proposed causal ordering and conditional independence implications, while a structural equation model gives a parametric representation of the variables.

This paper develops a Gaussian graphical framework for these tasks. The framework is intended as a modeling and identification aid, not as a claim that all causal systems are Gaussian or acyclic. Gaussianity supplies a tractable likelihood and linear conditional expectations. The graph supplies substantive causal structure. Neither feature, by itself, guarantees that causal conclusions are correct.

We focus on interference between units indexed by i and j. Let A_i denote the treatment assigned to unit i, and let Y_i denote its outcome. Under interference, Y_i may depend on A_j for one or more j other than i. A graph makes these dependencies visible by including edges from A_j to Y_i, directly or through intermediate variables. Conversely, a graph can express a restricted form of non-interference by excluding such cross-unit causal paths.

The paper has five objectives. First, it defines a multivariate Gaussian structural equation model suitable for representing cross-unit effects. Second, it formalizes graph-based interference and non-interference. Third, it distinguishes causal effects from regression coefficients and observational associations. Fourth, it presents identification conditions for several common causal effects. Fifth, it illustrates the framework with a small example and discusses practical limitations.

The central message is that interference is best treated as a property of a specified causal system and estimand. It is not a universal binary label attached to a dataset. A system may exhibit interference for one outcome, exposure definition, or time horizon and no interference for another. Likewise, identifying a causal effect requires more than detecting a cross-unit edge: it requires assumptions about treatment assignment, confounding, measurement, and the mapping from assignments to exposure.

2. Related concepts and notation

Let there be n units. We write A = (A_1, ..., A_n) for the vector of treatments and Y = (Y_1, ..., Y_n) for the vector of outcomes. Let X denote measured pre-treatment covariates, and let U denote unmeasured variables. Each unit may also have a set of neighbors, denoted N_i, defined by a network, spatial relation, household membership, or other substantive structure.

In the classical no-interference formulation, the potential outcome for unit i under the treatment vector a is written Y_i(a_i). The outcome depends only on i’s own assignment. Under general interference, the potential outcome is Y_i(a), which can depend on the entire treatment vector. This notation is conceptually broad but often too high dimensional for estimation. Researchers therefore define an exposure mapping, such as the number or proportion of treated neighbors.

Let g_i(a) be a specified summary of assignments relevant to unit i. A restricted interference model writes the potential outcome as Y_i(a_i, g_i(a)). This representation assumes that assignments affect Y_i only through own treatment and the chosen summary. The assumption is substantive. If two treatment configurations have the same value of g_i but different effects on Y_i, then the mapping is inadequate.

We use a directed acyclic graph G = (V, E). Each node in V represents a random variable, and each directed edge in E represents a direct causal relation under the model. A directed path from one variable to another represents a possible mediated causal influence. A missing edge is a claim about the absence of a direct effect, not necessarily the absence of an indirect effect.

For a variable V_k, let pa(V_k) denote its parents in the graph. A linear Gaussian structural equation model has the form V_k = β_k0 + sum over l in pa(V_k) of β_kl V_l + ε_k, where the errors are mutually independent Gaussian variables with mean zero and positive variances. In vector form, V = B V + ε, where B is strictly triangular after a topological ordering. Thus V = (I − B)^{-1} ε, and V is multivariate Gaussian.

The independence of structural errors is a modeling assumption. It can be relaxed by allowing correlated errors, but correlated errors may represent unmeasured common causes and can obscure causal interpretation. In graphical notation, latent common causes can instead be represented explicitly as unobserved nodes. We will make the distinction clear when it matters.

We use do(A_i = a) to denote an intervention that sets A_i to a, replacing the structural equation for A_i with a constant. A joint intervention do(A = a) sets the full assignment vector. The causal effect of such an intervention is defined by comparing the distributions of outcomes under the corresponding interventions, rather than by comparing observed groups alone.

3. Graphical representation of interference

3.1 Unit-indexed graphs

A basic representation creates separate nodes A_i and Y_i for each unit i. An edge A_i → Y_i represents a direct own-treatment effect. An edge A_j → Y_i, where i is not equal to j, represents a direct cross-unit effect. More generally, a directed path from A_j to Y_i represents a causal route by which unit j’s treatment can affect unit i’s outcome.

For example, A_j → M_i → Y_i represents a spillover mediated by a variable M_i, such as a change in unit i’s information, behavior, or local environment. The effect is cross-unit even though the final edge into Y_i comes from M_i rather than directly from A_j. A definition based only on direct edges would therefore miss mediated interference.

We say that the graph exhibits interference for outcome Y_i under assignment A_j if there is a directed path from A_j to Y_i, for at least one j not equal to i, and if the path is not rendered causally irrelevant by a zero parameter or a prohibited intervention. This definition concerns the modeled causal system. It is stronger than observing a statistical association between A_j and Y_i.

We say that the graph satisfies unit-level non-interference for Y_i if no directed path exists from any A_j with j not equal to i to Y_i. This condition is relative to the included variables, the modeled time interval, and the treatment definition. It does not assert that units are unrelated in every respect. Their outcomes may share causes, and their treatments may be correlated, without one unit’s treatment causing another unit’s outcome.

For the entire population, a strict no-interference graph has no directed path from A_j to Y_i for every pair i not equal to j. A weaker graph may allow interference only within specified clusters. If units are partitioned into groups, one may permit cross-unit paths within each group while excluding paths between groups.

3.2 Direct effects and paths

A direct effect corresponds to a causal influence not mediated by the other variables represented in the graph. In a structural equation, it is often associated with a nonzero coefficient on a parent treatment. An indirect effect is transmitted through one or more mediators. The total effect includes all directed paths from the treatment to the outcome.

In a linear structural equation model, the total effect of V_j on V_i is the sum of the products of edge coefficients over all directed paths from V_j to V_i. This follows from the expansion of (I − B)^{-1}. If no directed path exists, the total effect is zero under the model. If paths exist, their effects may nevertheless cancel, so a zero total effect does not prove that the graph has no interference.

This distinction matters for empirical testing. A graph with a path can imply a nonzero effect only when the relevant path coefficients and their combined contributions do not cancel. Conversely, a nonzero observational association does not establish a causal path because common causes may generate the association.

The graph is therefore a structural hypothesis. Data can assess whether its statistical implications are compatible with observations, but observational fit alone generally cannot establish the causal orientation of edges. In a Gaussian distribution, conditional independence patterns can sometimes identify a Markov equivalence class, but multiple DAGs may entail the same conditional independences.

3.3 Exposure mappings and graph reduction

A unit-indexed graph can become large when n is large. An exposure mapping reduces the assignment vector to a smaller set of variables. For example, define G_i as the number of treated neighbors of unit i. A graph may then include edges from A_i and G_i to Y_i. This compressed graph is useful when the scientific question concerns own treatment and aggregate neighborhood exposure.

The reduction is valid only if G_i captures all assignment features relevant to Y_i under the intended model. If neighbor identity matters, a count may be insufficient. If effects depend on treatment saturation, timing, or network position, a scalar summary may also be insufficient. A more detailed mapping may include weighted exposure, distance-specific treatment, or distinct categories of neighbors.

The exposure-mapping approach changes the estimand. An effect comparing G_i = 1 with G_i = 0 is not necessarily the effect of treating a particular neighbor. It is an effect of changing the defined exposure while holding the rest of the intervention specification fixed. Researchers should state the mapping before interpreting a spillover estimate.

A graph may represent a mapping node G_i as a deterministic function of assignments. Deterministic nodes do not introduce new randomness, but they can simplify notation. If the mapping is imperfect, the graph’s implied conditional independences and effect interpretations may not correspond to the actual system.

3.4 Interference and dependence

Interference and statistical dependence are related but distinct. Interference is a causal property: an intervention on one unit’s treatment changes another unit’s outcome distribution. Dependence is a distributional property: two variables are not independent. Common causes can produce dependence without interference. Interference can also occur in a way that yields no marginal dependence under a particular assignment distribution, for example through cancellation or lack of treatment variation.

In a Gaussian model, zero partial correlation is equivalent to conditional independence for the variables being considered, provided the relevant covariance matrix is nonsingular. This result concerns statistical distributions, not causal effects. A conditional independence can arise because of parameter values, conditioning choices, or lack of variation. It does not by itself establish the absence of a causal pathway.

For this reason, we do not define non-interference as a zero correlation between A_j and Y_i. Nor do we infer interference solely from a nonzero correlation. Instead, the graph encodes the causal restriction, and identification assumptions connect that graph to estimable contrasts.

4. Structural model

4.1 General linear Gaussian system

Let V collect all treatment, covariate, mediator, and outcome variables. The structural equations are V = B V + ε, where B has zeros for prohibited edges and ε follows a multivariate normal distribution with mean zero and covariance matrix Ω. In the standard recursive model, Ω is diagonal. We initially adopt this diagonal-error formulation.

Because the graph is acyclic, a topological ordering makes B strictly lower triangular. The reduced-form distribution is Gaussian with mean (I − B)^{-1} μ_ε and covariance (I − B)^{-1} Ω (I − B)^{-T}. This gives a direct link between the causal graph and the observed covariance structure.

A structural coefficient β_ij represents the direct effect of V_j on V_i under the linear model. It does not generally equal the total causal effect. The total effect is the sum over directed paths, as described above. In the presence of nonlinearities or interactions, this simple coefficient interpretation no longer suffices.

For binary or categorical treatments, the Gaussian equation for the treatment assignment is often not a realistic structural model. The outcome and mediator equations may still be approximated as Gaussian conditional on treatment, or the Gaussian model may be used as a working model. More generally, the graph can be retained while the node-specific conditional distributions are changed.

4.2 Treatment assignment

Treatment assignment may be randomized, observational, or partially randomized. In a randomized design, A can be generated independently of pre-treatment potential outcomes, perhaps conditional on strata or clusters. In an observational study, treatment may depend on measured covariates and unmeasured factors.

A Gaussian equation for a continuous treatment can represent assignment as a linear function of covariates. For a binary treatment, one can use a probit model or a latent Gaussian variable thresholded into treatment categories. The causal graph is unchanged by this choice, but the likelihood and identification calculations differ.

With interference, assignments may be jointly dependent. Cluster randomization creates dependence within clusters by design. Network interventions may impose constraints on the number of treated units. Assignment dependence does not itself imply outcome interference. The assignment mechanism and the outcome mechanism should be represented separately.

In a randomized design, the assignment mechanism is known or controlled, which can support identification of direct and spillover effects. However, the treatment contrast must still correspond to a well-defined intervention, and the design must generate enough variation in the relevant exposure categories.

4.3 Latent causes and correlated errors

If two variables share an unmeasured cause, a graph may include a latent node U with arrows to both variables. Alternatively, a model may represent their structural errors as correlated. The latent-node representation is generally more transparent for causal interpretation because it makes the common-cause hypothesis explicit.

Correlated errors can reproduce covariance patterns that resemble causal effects. If the covariance is treated as merely residual correlation, regression coefficients may not have causal interpretations. Identification therefore depends on whether the model includes sufficient confounders or makes additional assumptions, such as valid instruments or front-door conditions.

The standard Gaussian DAG assumes independent errors conditional on the represented parents. This is not an innocuous statistical convenience. It rules out unrepresented common causes. When that assumption is implausible, the graph should be expanded or the identification claim weakened.

5. Causal estimands under interference

5.1 Potential outcomes

For a fixed assignment vector a, let Y_i(a) denote the potential outcome for unit i. The observed outcome is Y_i = Y_i(A), under consistency. Consistency means that the observed outcome equals the potential outcome corresponding to the assignment actually received, with treatment versions defined adequately.

The total effect of changing the full assignment from a to a′ for unit i is E[Y_i(a′) − Y_i(a)]. This effect can be difficult to interpret when the assignment vectors differ in many components. It is often more useful to define a contrast that changes a focal treatment or a specified exposure while holding the remaining intervention features fixed.

The direct effect for unit i compares two own-treatment states at a fixed exposure to others. For example, it may be defined as E[Y_i(1, g) − Y_i(0, g)]. The spillover effect compares two exposure levels while holding own treatment fixed, such as E[Y_i(a_i, g_1) − Y_i(a_i, g_0)].

A total effect can combine direct and spillover pathways. If a focal intervention changes A_i and also changes neighbors’ exposures, the resulting effect on Y_i may include both. The exact decomposition depends on the intervention and the exposure mapping.

5.2 Population and policy effects

An average direct effect averages unit-specific direct effects over a target population. An average spillover effect averages the response to a change in exposure to treated neighbors. A policy effect compares outcome distributions under two assignment policies, such as independent treatment with probability p versus cluster-based treatment at a specified saturation.

Policy effects are often more realistic than effects of a single treatment in a network. A policy changes many assignments simultaneously, and its outcome consequences may depend on the pattern of coverage. The policy must be described sufficiently precisely to define the intervention distribution.

In a Gaussian structural model, a policy intervention can be evaluated by replacing the treatment assignment mechanism and propagating the resulting means and covariances through the structural equations. For linear outcomes, expected policy effects can often be computed from the reduced-form coefficients. Variance effects may also be relevant when the policy changes the distribution of exposure.

5.3 Controlled and natural effects

A controlled direct effect fixes a mediator or exposure at a specified value while changing treatment. A natural direct effect compares treatment states while setting the mediator to the value it would naturally take under a reference treatment. Natural effects require stronger cross-world assumptions and can be difficult to identify.

Under interference, mediator definitions may be unit-specific and jointly dependent. A mediator for one person can be affected by several units’ treatments, and that mediator can affect several outcomes. This makes conventional mediation decompositions more demanding. Graphical paths remain useful, but the estimand must specify which treatments and mediators are intervened upon.

We focus on effects identifiable from the observed distribution under standard graphical assumptions. We do not claim that every path-specific effect is identified. In particular, recanting-witness structures, exposure-induced mediator-outcome confounding, and latent confounding can prevent path-specific identification.

6. Identification principles

6.1 Identification and the causal graph

An estimand is identified if it is uniquely determined by the observed data distribution together with the stated causal assumptions. A model can be statistically estimable yet causally unidentified. For example, a regression coefficient can be estimated precisely while still combining a treatment effect with confounding.

A DAG helps identify adjustment sets, mediator structures, and instruments. The graph does not validate itself. Its causal interpretation relies on substantive knowledge, design information, and assumptions that cannot generally be tested from observational data alone.

We use the do-calculus and the back-door criterion as conceptual tools. In a Gaussian linear model, identified effects often reduce to linear combinations of regression coefficients or covariance terms. The graphical conditions remain important because a numerical formula is causal only under the assumptions that justify it.

6.2 Back-door adjustment

Suppose X is a set of pre-treatment covariates that blocks every back-door path from A_i to Y_i and contains no descendant of A_i. Then the effect of A_i on Y_i may be identified by standardizing over X. Under no interference, this is the familiar adjustment formula.

Under interference, the exposure vector or mapping must be included in the treatment definition. Let T_i denote a joint exposure such as (A_i, G_i). If a covariate set blocks all noncausal paths from T_i to Y_i, then conditional outcome comparisons can identify effects of T_i, provided positivity and consistency hold. The adjustment set may need to include covariates of neighbors or network structure.

A common difficulty is that treatment of one unit can affect covariates or mediators of another unit. Adjusting for such post-treatment variables can block part of the effect or induce bias. The graph should distinguish pre-treatment confounders from post-treatment variables and specify which causal effect is sought.

Positivity requires that each relevant exposure level occur with positive probability within covariate strata. In network settings, structural constraints may make some exposure combinations impossible. If a neighbor configuration never occurs, the corresponding causal contrast cannot be recovered without extrapolation or stronger modeling assumptions.

6.3 Randomized assignment

When treatment is randomized independently of potential outcomes according to a known design, the assignment can remove confounding for contrasts supported by that design. Under interference, randomization may identify average outcomes under assignment strategies, including spillover effects, if the design provides variation in both own treatment and peer exposure.

Cluster randomization can identify effects of cluster-level policies but may not identify individual spillovers within clusters if all members receive the same assignment. Two-stage randomization, in which clusters are assigned treatment saturation and units are then assigned within clusters, can provide variation useful for separating direct and spillover effects.

Randomization does not eliminate the need to define the estimand. The effect of assigning a unit to treatment at a fixed saturation level differs from the effect of increasing the overall saturation. Nor does randomization repair an exposure mapping that omits relevant features of the assignment vector.

6.4 Mediation and front-door identification

If treatment affects an outcome through a mediator, the total effect includes that pathway. Adjusting for the mediator generally does not estimate the total effect. It can instead estimate a controlled direct effect under appropriate conditions, or a direct effect under stronger mediation assumptions.

A front-door strategy can identify a total effect when the mediator captures all directed causal paths from treatment to outcome, there is no unblocked confounding of treatment and mediator, and mediator-outcome confounding is controlled in the required way. In an interference setting, these conditions must be stated for the relevant cross-unit treatment and outcome relations.

Gaussianity can simplify estimation once the front-door conditions hold. It cannot create the conditions. A mediator that is affected by unmeasured treatment-outcome confounding, or that fails to carry all causal pathways, does not support front-door identification simply because the data are jointly normal.

6.5 Instrumental variables

An instrumental variable Z can identify a causal effect of treatment when it affects treatment, is independent of relevant unmeasured causes, affects the outcome only through treatment, and satisfies an appropriate relevance condition. Additional assumptions may be needed for a local average treatment effect with heterogeneous effects.

With interference, an instrument for A_i may affect neighbors’ treatments or outcomes. The exclusion restriction must account for these pathways. A randomized encouragement can be invalid for an individual treatment effect if it changes peer exposure directly, though it may still identify a policy effect of the encouragement.

In linear Gaussian models, instrumental-variable estimators can be expressed through covariances. Their causal validity still rests on the instrument assumptions. A strong first stage and a Gaussian likelihood do not establish exclusion or independence.

6.6 Identifying total effects from a fully specified model

If the structural graph is correct, all relevant confounders are represented, and the parameters are identified from the observed distribution or design, then total effects can be calculated as sums of path products. For a treatment A_j and outcome Y_i, the total effect is the corresponding entry of (I − B)^{-1}, under the linear model and intervention semantics.

This calculation is not a substitute for identification analysis. Some edge coefficients may not be separately identified from observational data, even when the covariance matrix is known. Distinct causal models can generate the same Gaussian distribution but imply different intervention effects.

Acyclicity and independent errors can impose strong restrictions, but they do not always choose a unique causal orientation. If the causal order is not known, additional assumptions, experiments, temporal information, or domain knowledge may be required.

7. A worked example

7.1 Three-unit system

Consider three units arranged in a line, with unit 2 between units 1 and 3. Each unit receives a treatment A_i, and each has an outcome Y_i. Suppose treatments are randomized independently, and treatment of a unit can affect its own outcome and the outcomes of adjacent units.

A simple structural model is Y_1 = τ A_1 + γ A_2 + ε_1, Y_2 = τ A_2 + γ A_1 + γ A_3 + ε_2, and Y_3 = τ A_3 + γ A_2 + ε_3. Here τ is the direct effect, and γ is the direct spillover effect along each adjacent link. The graph contains A_i → Y_i edges and cross-unit edges from each treatment to neighboring outcomes.

If γ equals zero, the outcome equations have no cross-unit treatment effects, and the model satisfies non-interference for these outcomes. If γ is nonzero, interference occurs between adjacent units. There is no modeled effect between units 1 and 3 because no path from A_1 to Y_3 or from A_3 to Y_1 is included.

Under this model, the total effect of A_2 on Y_1 is γ, and the total effect on Y_2 is τ. The total effect of A_1 on Y_2 is γ. These effects are identified by randomized variation in assignments, assuming treatment compliance and outcome measurement are adequate.

If treatment assignments are independent Bernoulli variables with probability p, then A_2 is independent of the error terms and of A_1. A regression of Y_1 on A_2 identifies γ under the model. A regression of Y_1 on A_1 alone identifies τ for the own-treatment component, since A_1 is randomized and independent of A_2. However, if the assignment design correlates A_1 and A_2, omitting A_2 can contaminate the coefficient on A_1.

7.2 Adding a common cause

Now suppose an unmeasured neighborhood characteristic U affects both A_2 and Y_1. The graph includes U → A_2 and U → Y_1. Even if there is no causal edge A_2 → Y_1, A_2 and Y_1 may be associated through U. A naive regression could report an apparent spillover effect.

If U is measured, adjusting for it may block the back-door path. If U is unmeasured, randomization of A_2 can eliminate this confounding, but observational data alone may not identify γ without additional assumptions. The example shows why statistical dependence is not sufficient evidence of interference.

7.3 Mediation

Suppose treatment A_2 changes a shared information variable M_1, which then affects Y_1. The equations may be M_1 = α A_2 + η_1 and Y_1 = τ A_1 + δ M_1 + ε_1. The spillover total effect of A_2 on Y_1 is αδ, while the direct effect is zero in this specification.

A regression of Y_1 on A_2 without conditioning on M_1 can identify the total spillover effect under randomized assignment. A regression that conditions on M_1 does not estimate the same total effect. Under the model and suitable assumptions, it may help estimate a controlled direct effect, which is zero here.

If M_1 and Y_1 share an unmeasured cause, the mediator-outcome relation is confounded. The total effect may remain identifiable through randomized treatment, but the mediation decomposition may not be. This distinction illustrates that identifying a total effect does not imply identifying each pathway-specific component.

7.4 Gaussian covariance illustration

Let A_1, A_2, and A_3 be independent, mean-zero Gaussian variables with unit variance, used here as continuous treatments for algebraic convenience. Let the outcome errors be mutually independent Gaussian variables, also independent of the treatments. Under the three-unit model, Cov(A_2, Y_1) equals γ, and Cov(A_1, Y_1) equals τ.

These equalities make the causal parameters recoverable from simple covariances because the treatments are randomized and independent. If A_1 and A_2 are correlated, then Cov(A_1, Y_1) equals τ Var(A_1) plus γ Cov(A_1, A_2). The marginal association no longer isolates the direct effect.

If the treatment variables are observed with error, even randomized assignment may not make the measured treatment independent of the outcome error in the required way. Measurement error can attenuate estimates and complicate the graph. The causal model should distinguish assignment, receipt, and exposure where these differ.

8. Estimation

8.1 Likelihood-based estimation

For a specified Gaussian structural model, parameters can be estimated by maximum likelihood. If the graph is fixed and errors are independent, each equation can often be estimated as a regression on its parents. This factorization reflects the recursive structure.

When the graph is known, the model can impose useful restrictions and improve precision relative to an unrestricted covariance model. These gains depend on the graph being correctly specified. A missing cross-unit edge can bias estimates when the true system contains interference, while an unnecessary edge can increase variance and obscure interpretation.

Likelihood methods can accommodate missing data under appropriate missingness assumptions. In network settings, missing outcomes or missing ties may induce more complicated selection processes. If missingness depends on unobserved outcomes or treatment, a standard Gaussian likelihood may be inadequate.

8.2 Bayesian estimation

A Bayesian analysis can place priors on edge coefficients, error variances, and graph structures. Priors may regularize high-dimensional network effects and incorporate substantive knowledge about plausible spillover range. Posterior uncertainty can then reflect uncertainty about parameters and, in some formulations, graph structure.

A posterior probability for an edge is not equivalent to proof of a causal effect. It is conditional on the likelihood, prior, model space, and causal assumptions. If hidden confounding is excluded by construction, posterior precision cannot account for it unless the model explicitly represents it.

Bayesian model averaging can summarize uncertainty across candidate graphs. Yet observationally equivalent graphs may imply different intervention effects. Additional design information or substantive restrictions may be required to distinguish them.

8.3 High-dimensional interference

When n is large, the number of possible cross-unit edges grows quadratically. Sparsity assumptions, known network structures, spatial kernels, or low-dimensional exposure mappings can reduce complexity. The choice among these methods changes the substantive model.

A sparse graph assumption may be plausible when influence is local. A distance-decay model may be appropriate when effects weaken with separation. A community-level model may be more realistic when interactions occur through shared institutions rather than direct ties.

Regularization can stabilize estimation, but it does not by itself solve causal confounding. Variable selection based on predictive performance may omit weak but causally important paths or retain proxies that are predictive but not causally interpretable.

9. Model checking and sensitivity analysis

9.1 Statistical implications

A Gaussian DAG implies conditional independence restrictions. These restrictions can be examined using residual correlations, likelihood-ratio tests, or other model diagnostics. Violations may indicate omitted edges, latent common causes, non-Gaussian features, or incorrect functional forms.

Failure to reject an implied independence does not establish that a causal edge is absent. The study may lack power, the relevant treatment may have little variation, or path effects may cancel. Conversely, a detected dependence may reflect confounding rather than a causal path.

Residual diagnostics should examine linearity, homoscedasticity, influential observations, and error distributions. Network data may also exhibit clustering or dependence not captured by the assumed independent errors. Robust or hierarchical models may be needed.

9.2 Sensitivity to unmeasured confounding

Because causal graphs are not fully testable, sensitivity analysis is essential. Researchers can vary the strength of a hypothetical unmeasured common cause and examine how effect estimates change. For Gaussian models, sensitivity parameters can be expressed through residual correlations or coefficients linking a latent variable to treatment and outcome.

A sensitivity analysis should target the specific cross-unit relation of interest. Confounding of A_j and Y_i may differ from confounding of A_i and Y_i. Shared environmental variables, homophily, and network formation can create distinctive biases in spillover estimates.

The analysis should also consider confounding induced by conditioning. In network settings, conditioning on a common effect or a post-treatment network variable can open noncausal paths. The graphical model can help identify such risks before estimation.

9.3 Sensitivity to exposure mapping

Researchers should assess whether alternative exposure mappings lead to materially different conclusions. A count of treated neighbors, a proportion treated, and a distance-weighted exposure may represent different causal interventions. If results change substantially, the estimand is mapping-dependent.

One strategy is to compare nested mappings, beginning with own treatment and a simple neighbor summary, then adding distance, neighbor type, or treatment timing. Such comparisons should be guided by scientific knowledge rather than unrestricted searches for statistical significance.

Cross-validation can assess prediction under alternative mappings, but predictive fit alone does not establish causal validity. A mapping that predicts outcomes well may fail to capture the intervention relevant to the policy question.

10. Interpretation of non-interference

Non-interference should not be treated as a generic statement that units are independent. Outcomes can be correlated because of shared shocks even when treatments do not spill over. Likewise, treatments can be correlated by design while outcomes remain causally unaffected by other units’ treatment.

A useful formulation is conditional and scope-specific. For example, one may state that, within a particular follow-up period and under a specified network definition, unit j’s assignment has no causal effect on unit i’s outcome when i and j are in different clusters. This is testable only to a limited degree, but it is clear about the claim.

The no-interference assumption may be plausible when interactions are physically or institutionally blocked, when the outcome is measured before spillovers can occur, or when units are sufficiently separated. It may be less plausible in dense social, biological, or economic systems.

An approximation can be useful even when exact non-interference is false. If spillovers are weak relative to direct effects, a no-interference analysis may provide a rough answer, but its target and potential bias should be reported. A partial-interference model, in which interference is allowed within clusters but not between them, is often a more defensible compromise.

11. Extensions

11.1 Nonlinear structural models

The Gaussian linear framework is transparent but restrictive. Nonlinear structural equations can represent thresholds, saturation, interactions, and heterogeneous effects. The graph-based definitions of interference and identification remain applicable, although path coefficients no longer generally sum to a total effect.

A generalized linear model may use a non-Gaussian outcome distribution while retaining a DAG. For binary outcomes, causal effects may be reported as risk differences, risk ratios, or odds ratios. These scales are not interchangeable, and conditional and marginal effects can differ.

In nonlinear models, a coefficient is usually not itself a marginal causal effect. Interventions must be propagated through the full model, often by g-computation or simulation. The structural graph still clarifies which variables are intervened upon and which pathways contribute.

11.2 Dynamic interference

Interference may unfold over time. A treatment at one time can change another unit’s later behavior, which can alter subsequent exposures and outcomes. A longitudinal DAG can represent time-indexed treatments, mediators, and outcomes, with edges constrained to move forward in time.

Feedback across units is possible in a dynamic system without creating a directed cycle in the time-indexed graph. For example, A_1 at time 1 may affect Y_2 at time 2, which affects A_1 at time 3. The expanded temporal graph remains acyclic when time is represented explicitly.

Identification in longitudinal interference settings often requires sequential exchangeability, consistency, and positivity conditions for treatment histories and exposure histories. Standard regression adjustment can fail when time-varying confounders are affected by prior treatment. G-methods may be required.

11.3 Partial interference and clusters

Partial interference assumes that units may affect one another within known clusters but not across clusters. It can substantially reduce the dimensionality of the treatment mapping. Under this assumption, potential outcomes for a unit depend only on assignments within its cluster.

The assumption is credible when clusters are physically isolated or institutionally defined, but cluster boundaries may not align with actual social or economic interactions. A sensitivity analysis can allow weak cross-cluster effects or use alternative cluster definitions.

Cluster-level randomization identifies cluster policy effects under the randomization scheme. Estimating within-cluster spillovers may require individual-level treatment variation in addition to cluster-level variation. The design should be matched to the intended estimands.

11.4 Network formation

Networks are often endogenous. Units select friends, firms form partnerships, and locations develop through economic and social processes. If network ties are affected by treatment or share causes with outcomes, conditioning on the observed network can introduce bias or change the estimand.

A graph may include network formation variables and their causes. If the network is measured before treatment and is not affected by treatment, it may serve as a covariate or define the exposure mapping. If it is post-treatment, it may be a mediator or collider.

Causal effects of network position or spillovers require assumptions about both assignment and network formation. A treatment-randomized design with a pre-existing network is often more informative than observational data with jointly determined treatments, ties, and outcomes.

12. Practical workflow

A practical analysis begins by defining the target population, treatment, outcome, time horizon, and intervention. Under interference, the researcher should specify whether the target is an individual effect, a neighbor spillover, or a policy effect.

The next step is to define the unit of analysis and the relevant interaction structure. The network or grouping should be justified substantively and measured before or during the relevant causal period. Researchers should distinguish observed ties from possible channels of influence.

The exposure mapping should then be specified. It should be detailed enough to preserve scientifically relevant differences while remaining estimable. Alternative plausible mappings should be considered before results are examined whenever possible.

A causal graph can be drawn with unit-indexed treatment, mediator, confounder, and outcome nodes, or with a compressed exposure representation. The graph should mark latent variables and distinguish pre-treatment from post-treatment quantities. Every edge should have a substantive interpretation.

Researchers should state which paths are allowed and which are excluded. In particular, a non-interference claim should identify the units or clusters across which effects are assumed absent. The claim should not be left implicit in a standard error choice or regression specification.

Identification should be assessed before fitting the model. The researcher should identify the adjustment set, randomized contrasts, instrumental assumptions, or other strategy that supports the target effect. If no strategy is available, the analysis should report associations rather than causal effects.

The model should be fit using methods appropriate to the outcome and treatment distributions. Gaussian likelihoods are useful when their assumptions are reasonable or when they serve as approximations. Standard errors should account for the design and dependence structure, but dependence-robust uncertainty estimation does not correct confounding.

Finally, results should be reported in terms of the defined intervention and estimand. Direct and spillover effects should not be conflated. The paper should disclose assumptions, positivity limitations, uncertainty about the exposure mapping, and sensitivity to unmeasured causes.

13. Limitations

The framework depends on a causal graph that may be uncertain. Graphical clarity does not eliminate the possibility of omitted variables, incorrect directionality, or misspecified interference channels. A graph is a disciplined representation of assumptions, not a guarantee of truth.

The linear Gaussian model may be inappropriate for bounded, binary, count, or highly skewed outcomes. It may also fail when effects are heterogeneous or when treatment effects interact with network position. Extensions are available, but they require additional modeling choices.

A DAG excludes contemporaneous feedback. Many real systems involve reciprocal interactions. Time indexing can represent some feedback, but the relevant time scale must be observed or credibly specified. If feedback occurs within the measurement interval, a static DAG may be misleading.

Gaussian observational distributions can be compatible with multiple causal graphs. Even when a graph is statistically identifiable up to a Markov equivalence class, causal effects may differ across members of that class. Interventions or external scientific information can be necessary.

The framework also assumes that treatments and outcomes are well defined. In practice, treatment versions may differ, exposure may be measured with error, and outcomes may be affected by noncompliance. These issues need to be represented explicitly or addressed through design-based estimands.

Network data often violate simple sampling assumptions. The observed network may be incomplete, boundary units may have unobserved neighbors, and units may enter or leave the study. Such problems can bias estimates of both exposure and spillover effects.

Finally, identification does not ensure useful precision. Strong interference can create highly correlated exposures, and limited variation can make spillover estimates unstable. A design may identify an effect in principle but provide little information in a finite sample.

14. Conclusion

We have presented a Gaussian graphical framework for representing interference and non-interference and for organizing causal identification. Unit-indexed DAGs represent cross-unit influence through directed edges and paths. A strict no-interference condition is expressed as the absence of directed paths from another unit’s treatment to a focal outcome, relative to a specified model and scope.

The framework separates causal influence from statistical dependence. Common causes can induce association without interference, while causal paths can be difficult to detect in observational distributions. Graphs make assumptions explicit, but they do not establish those assumptions from data.

Potential outcomes clarify the estimands. Direct effects, spillover effects, total effects, and policy effects answer different questions. Exposure mappings can make these quantities tractable, but they are substantive restrictions that should be defined and assessed carefully.

Identification follows from the design and the causal structure, not from Gaussianity alone. Back-door adjustment, randomization, mediation, and instrumental-variable strategies can identify effects under their respective assumptions. In a linear Gaussian structural model, identified effects can often be calculated from path coefficients, but observational equivalence and hidden confounding remain important limitations.

The proposed approach is most useful when researchers need a transparent account of who can affect whom, through which variables, and under what assumptions a causal contrast is estimable. It encourages explicit treatment of cross-unit pathways rather than relying on an implicit no-interference assumption. By combining graphical structure, potential-outcome estimands, and identification analysis, the framework supports more precise and credible causal reasoning in systems where units are connected.

Japan’s imperial couple visited communities devastated by the 2011 earthquake and tsunami as workers continued efforts to stabilize the damaged Fukushima Daiichi nuclear plant.

Emperor Naruhito and Empress Masako met residents during a visit to Iwate Prefecture, one of the regions hardest hit by the disaster. The March 11, 2011, earthquake and tsunami killed nearly 20,000 people and triggered meltdowns at the Fukushima plant.

The couple spoke with survivors and local officials, listening to accounts of recovery and the challenges that remain. Their visit was intended to honor those who died and recognize communities still rebuilding more than a decade after the catastrophe.

In coastal towns, reconstruction has brought new seawalls, roads and public facilities. Yet some residents have not returned, while others continue to cope with grief, disrupted livelihoods and the loss of familiar neighborhoods.

The imperial couple’s appearance drew people who gathered along their route and at community events. Residents welcomed the visit as a sign that the disaster and its aftermath remain in the nation’s memory.

Meanwhile, crews at Fukushima Daiichi are carrying out work to reduce risks at the wrecked facility. The plant suffered three reactor meltdowns after tsunami waves knocked out power and cooling systems.

Operators are managing large volumes of water used to cool melted fuel and are monitoring radiation levels across the site. The water is treated to remove most radioactive material before being diluted and released into the sea under a government-approved plan.

The discharge has drawn objections from fishing communities and criticism from some neighboring countries. Japanese authorities and the plant’s operator, Tokyo Electric Power Company, say the releases are monitored and meet safety standards.

The most difficult task remains removing melted fuel debris from the reactors. The material is highly radioactive, and attempts to retrieve small samples have proceeded cautiously.

Decommissioning the plant is expected to take decades. Officials say the work must balance safety, technical limits and the concerns of residents whose lives were changed by the disaster.

The visit connected the continuing recovery of affected communities with the unresolved challenges at the plant. For many residents, rebuilding has advanced, but the consequences of the disaster remain part of daily life.

The paper addresses an important design question in session-based recommendation: how loss functions and negative-sampling strategies affect recommendation quality. Its focus is timely, since session data are often sparse and implicit, making both target construction and optimization choices consequential. The review would benefit from a clearer statement of the paper’s main research questions and hypotheses. Please specify which session-based recommendation architectures are evaluated and why they are representative. The loss functions should be defined precisely, including any weighting, temperature, or regularization terms. Similarly, the negative-sampling procedures need enough detail to be reproducible, such as the sampling distribution, number of negatives, and whether samples are drawn per session or per batch. A particularly valuable contribution would be a controlled comparison in which the model, data split, and training budget remain fixed while only the loss or sampling strategy changes. The experimental section should include strong baselines and explain how hyperparameters were tuned consistently across methods. Please also report results on multiple datasets with different levels of sparsity and session-length distributions. Accuracy metrics such as Recall and NDCG are appropriate, but their cutoffs and computation procedures should be stated. Since sampling can alter the apparent ranking task, evaluation should use a clearly defined candidate set and, where feasible, include full-catalog ranking. Statistical significance tests or confidence intervals would help establish whether observed differences are reliable. An ablation study could separate the effects of the loss function, the sampling distribution, and their interaction. The paper should also examine training time and memory use, because some strategies may improve accuracy at substantially higher computational cost. Potential sampling biases deserve discussion, especially if frequently occurring items are more likely to be selected as negatives. The conclusions should distinguish empirical findings from general claims and avoid implying that one strategy is universally best. Overall, the topic has practical value, but the paper’s impact will depend on careful experimental control, transparent reporting, and a nuanced interpretation of trade-offs.

People often say that being yourself is the best way to live, but it is not always easy. The way we act can change depending on who is around us. At school, someone may be confident with friends but quiet around a teacher. At home, a person might speak more freely because they feel safe. These changes do not always mean that someone is being fake. Sometimes they show that people are trying to be respectful, fit in, or avoid conflict.

First impressions play a big part in how we behave. When meeting someone new, we may choose our words carefully or try to appear confident. We might worry that a small mistake will shape the other person’s opinion of us. People can also make quick judgments based on clothing, facial expressions, or the way someone speaks. Because of this, a first impression may not show a person’s full character. Someone who seems distant might simply be nervous.

Being authentic does not mean acting exactly the same in every situation. It means staying honest about our values and not pretending to be someone we are not. We can adjust our behavior while still being true to ourselves. For example, being polite in a formal setting does not make a person less genuine. However, changing ourselves constantly just to gain approval can become exhausting. It may also make it hard to know what we truly think and feel.

A good balance is to consider others without losing sight of who we are. We can be open-minded, respectful, and willing to adapt while still keeping our own beliefs. We should also give people time before deciding what they are like. First impressions can be useful, but they are not always accurate. When we allow others to feel comfortable, they may show more of their true selves. In the end, authenticity grows when people feel accepted rather than judged.

This paper investigates whether neural machine translation (NMT) models can support interpretable word alignment by measuring how deleting a source word changes the probability of a target word. The question is relevant to machine translation interpretability and to the broader challenge of understanding what information a model uses to produce its outputs. The proposed approach is intuitively appealing: if removing a source word reduces the probability of a target word, that word may contribute to the target prediction. The paper’s focus on a measurable intervention gives the method a clearer interpretation than attention weights alone. Overall, the work has promise, but its claims would benefit from a more careful treatment of what deletion effects establish and how reliably they correspond to alignment.

A central strength is the use of model behavior rather than internal attention distributions as the basis for alignment. This may avoid treating attention as a direct explanation when it does not necessarily reflect causal influence. The deletion procedure is also straightforward to describe and potentially easy to reproduce. It could be useful in settings where conventional alignments are unavailable or expensive to obtain. The paper would be stronger, however, if it clearly distinguished causal influence on a model’s probability from linguistic alignment between source and target words. A source word can affect a target prediction through context, agreement, or sentence structure without being its translation.

The method’s validity depends substantially on how source-word deletion is implemented. Removing a token may create ungrammatical or distributionally unusual inputs, so the measured probability change may reflect the disruption rather than the word’s specific contribution. The authors should report whether they delete surface words, subword units, or both, and explain how tokenization affects the intervention. They should also discuss what happens when a word is split into multiple subword tokens. Comparisons with alternative interventions, such as replacing a word with a mask or a neutral placeholder, would help determine whether results are specific to deletion. A sensitivity analysis across intervention types would be particularly informative.

The probability measurement requires further clarification. The paper should specify whether it evaluates the probability of a fixed reference target sequence, the model’s generated output, or individual target tokens under teacher forcing. These choices answer different questions and can produce different alignments. If probabilities are conditioned on a reference translation, the method may depend on translation quality and on the choice of reference. If they are taken from generated output, decoding decisions may complicate comparisons across interventions. The authors should also explain how they handle target tokens whose probabilities are very small and whether effects are measured as absolute differences, relative changes, or log-probability differences.

The experimental evaluation should provide stronger evidence that the resulting alignments are useful. Comparisons with standard alignment systems and appropriate NMT-based baselines are essential. Evaluation on established gold alignment datasets would make the results easier to interpret and compare. The paper should report more than aggregate alignment scores where possible, including precision, recall, and performance across language pairs or linguistic phenomena. Qualitative examples could reveal whether the method handles multiword expressions, function words, and reordered translations sensibly. An error analysis would also help identify cases where deletion effects are misleading.

The paper should address computational cost, since testing each source word may require many additional model evaluations. Runtime and memory comparisons with competing approaches would clarify whether the method is practical. It would also be useful to assess stability across model checkpoints, random seeds, and decoding settings. If small changes in model configuration produce substantially different alignments, that limitation should be made explicit. The authors should discuss how the approach behaves when one source word influences several target words or when several source words jointly support one target word.

The interpretation of interaction effects deserves particular attention. Deleting words one at a time cannot fully capture cases in which a target word depends on a combination of source words. The authors should acknowledge that independent deletion scores may overstate or understate individual contributions when source words are redundant or complementary. Testing selected word pairs or using a simple interaction analysis could help substantiate this point. The paper should also explain how it converts probability changes into discrete links, including any threshold selection procedure. Thresholds should be selected without using test-set gold alignments, or the potential for evaluation leakage should be discussed.

The presentation is generally accessible, but several methodological details should be consolidated to make reproduction straightforward. A precise algorithm or pseudocode would clarify the intervention, scoring, and link-extraction steps. The authors should release, or provide enough information to reconstruct, the model settings and evaluation scripts. It would also help to separate evidence for the method’s empirical performance from claims about interpretability. A successful alignment score does not by itself prove that the reported links faithfully explain the model’s internal computation.

In summary, the paper presents a simple and potentially valuable approach to interpreting NMT predictions through source-word interventions. Its strongest contribution is framing alignment in terms of measurable changes in target-word probability rather than relying solely on attention. The main concerns are the confounding effects of deletion, the dependence on probability-scoring choices, and the need for broader validation and stability analysis. Addressing these issues would make the method’s scope and limitations much clearer. I recommend revision, with priority given to intervention controls, stronger baseline comparisons, and a more precise account of what the resulting links represent.

Encouragement and constructive feedback both play important roles in student learning. Encouragement helps students feel confident enough to try challenging tasks and keep going when they make mistakes. A kind word from a teacher can remind students that effort and improvement matter. However, praise is most useful when it is sincere and connected to something specific, such as persistence or a thoughtful idea. Students also need constructive feedback to understand what they can improve. Clear, respectful suggestions help them recognize mistakes without feeling discouraged. For example, a teacher might praise a strong argument and suggest adding evidence to support it. The balance matters because too much criticism can weaken confidence, while praise without guidance may limit progress. Students should also learn to view feedback as a tool rather than a judgment of their ability. When teachers combine encouragement with practical advice, students are more willing to learn from challenges. This balance helps students build both confidence and the skills needed to succeed.

Tributes poured in Sunday after acclaimed actor Philip Seymour Hoffman was found dead at age 46 in his Manhattan apartment, in what authorities described as an apparent drug overdose.

Hoffman was discovered in the bathroom of his apartment in the West Village, according to police. A syringe and several envelopes believed to contain heroin were reportedly found nearby. The precise cause of death had not yet been confirmed, and officials said an autopsy would be conducted.

The Oscar-winning performer was celebrated for bringing unusual depth and humanity to characters across film, television and theater. His death stunned colleagues and audiences who had followed a career marked by fearless performances and a commitment to his craft.

Hoffman won the Academy Award for best actor for his portrayal of writer Truman Capote in the 2005 film Capote. He received three additional Oscar nominations, including for Charlie Wilson’s War, Doubt and The Master.

His many other screen roles ranged from the volatile assistant director in Boogie Nights to a weary family patriarch in The Savages. He also appeared in The Big Lebowski, Almost Famous and the Hunger Games films.

Director Paul Thomas Anderson, a frequent collaborator, praised Hoffman’s singular talent and said he would be missed by everyone who knew him. Actors and filmmakers shared similar expressions of grief, remembering not only his performances but his generosity and humor.

Meryl Streep, his co-star in Doubt, called him a great actor and a great man. The film’s director, John Patrick Shanley, said Hoffman had brought uncommon intelligence and compassion to his work.

Theater colleagues also paid tribute to an artist whose career began onstage. Hoffman was a respected director as well as an actor, and served as co-artistic director of the LAByrinth Theater Company in New York.

He directed productions including Our Lady of 121st Street and The Long Red Road, while continuing to perform in plays. His stage work earned him three Tony Award nominations.

Hoffman had spoken publicly about his history of substance abuse. He had said he became sober in his early 20s after struggling with drugs and alcohol, and that he later entered treatment after a relapse.

The news renewed attention to the challenges of addiction, even for people who appear successful and supported. Friends and admirers urged compassion, while cautioning against speculation before investigators established the facts.

Hoffman is survived by his longtime partner, costume designer Mimi O’Donnell, and their three children. He had largely kept his family life out of the public eye.

Born in Fairport, New York, Hoffman studied drama at New York University before beginning his professional career. His early film roles led to a reputation as one of the most versatile actors of his generation.

In recent years, he had continued to work across genres, appearing in independent dramas and major studio productions. His final completed performances included roles in The Hunger Games: Mockingjay films.

For many viewers, Hoffman’s appeal lay in his ability to make even difficult or deeply flawed characters feel recognizable. He often transformed supporting roles into vivid portraits that lingered long after the credits.

As condolences continued to arrive, theaters and film organizations reflected on the loss of a performer whose range seemed almost limitless. His death at 46 cut short a career that had already left a lasting mark on American film and theater.
