This paper studies a rank-promoting regularizer intended to improve the representations learned by reinforcement-learning agents and, in turn, their Atari performance. The central idea is to encourage a desired distribution of singular values in learned representations, rather than allowing a small number of directions to dominate. This is a promising angle on representation learning, and the link between representation geometry and downstream control is important. The paper is generally well motivated and addresses a practical problem in deep reinforcement learning. Its focus on Atari provides a familiar benchmark that makes comparisons with prior work possible.

The proposed regularizer appears conceptually simple and potentially easy to incorporate into existing training pipelines. That simplicity is a strength, particularly if the method adds little computational overhead. The paper would benefit from a clearer explanation of the regularizer’s mathematical form and the intuition for the specific rank-promoting objective selected. In particular, the authors should distinguish explicitly between encouraging high rank, flattening the singular-value spectrum, and preventing representation collapse, since these are related but not identical goals. It would also help to explain how the regularizer interacts with the agent’s existing objectives and which representation layers receive it.

The experimental evaluation should establish whether gains are robust across random seeds, games, and training budgets. Atari scores can have substantial variance, so reporting means alone is insufficient; confidence intervals or appropriate significance tests would strengthen the claims. The paper should specify the number of seeds and provide enough implementation detail to reproduce the regularizer and its coefficient selection. A comparison against relevant representation-learning baselines would clarify whether the benefit comes from rank promotion specifically or from adding an auxiliary constraint in general. Useful controls would include alternative spectral penalties, a parameter-matched baseline, and a version of the method with the regularization coefficient set to zero.

The analysis would be stronger if it measured representation properties directly, alongside game scores. For example, the authors could report singular-value spectra, effective rank, or feature diversity over training. Such measurements would test whether the method changes representations in the intended way and whether those changes correlate with performance. Ablations across regularization strengths and application layers are also important, since a penalty that helps one part of the network may harm another. The authors should discuss the computational cost of computing the relevant spectral quantities, especially if this cost grows with feature dimension.

Some claims may currently be broader than the experimental evidence warrants. If results are limited to particular agents, architectures, or Atari settings, the conclusions should be scoped accordingly. It would also be useful to report per-game results and explain how aggregate scores are calculated, since averages can obscure regressions on individual games. The paper should state whether hyperparameters were tuned using the same evaluation games and how evaluation checkpoints were selected. Clear separation of training and evaluation procedures would make the results easier to interpret.

Overall, the work presents a plausible and potentially useful regularization strategy for improving reinforcement-learning representations. Its main strengths are the relevance of the problem, the straightforward intervention, and the possibility of connecting representation structure to control performance. The key issue is whether the reported improvements are consistent and can be attributed specifically to the proposed rank-promoting mechanism. More direct representation diagnostics, stronger baselines, and fuller reporting of uncertainty would substantially improve the paper. Subject to these clarifications and additional analyses, I view the approach as worthy of further consideration.

The paper addresses an important problem: reducing neural network storage and inference costs while limiting accuracy loss. Its layer-wise approach, combining distortion-aware codebook optimization with knowledge distillation, is promising and potentially useful in practice. A key strength is the focus on adapting quantization to differences in layer sensitivity rather than applying a uniform strategy. The use of codebooks may also capture weight distributions more efficiently than simple fixed-step quantization. Knowledge distillation offers a complementary way to preserve predictive behavior after compression. However, the paper should define its distortion objective precisely and explain how it relates to downstream task performance. It should also clarify how codebooks are initialized, optimized, and selected for each layer, including the relevant computational overhead. The experimental section should compare against strong, recent quantization and distillation baselines under consistent bit-widths and evaluation settings. Results should include multiple architectures and datasets, as well as accuracy, model size, latency, and energy or memory measurements where feasible. Ablations are needed to isolate the contributions of distortion-aware optimization, layer-wise allocation, and distillation. The authors should report variance across runs and discuss sensitivity to hyperparameters and calibration data. It would also be helpful to assess performance under very low bit-widths and on hardware that can efficiently use the proposed codebooks. Overall, the method appears well motivated, but clearer methodological details and broader, more rigorous experiments are needed to establish its advantages and practical value.

This paper addresses a practical challenge in table-based question answering: beam search can retain plausible candidates that ultimately require costly or invalid execution. Using learned cost predictions to rerank candidates is a promising approach, and the topic is relevant to improving both inference efficiency and answer quality. The paper should clearly define its cost metric, explain how predictions are trained, and describe how reranking interacts with the original beam-search score. Evaluation should compare against strong search and reranking baselines, report both accuracy and computational cost, and include ablations that isolate the contribution of the learned predictor. It would also strengthen the work to test across datasets and analyze cases where predicted and actual costs differ substantially. Overall, the approach appears worthwhile, but its impact depends on rigorous evidence that reranking improves the efficiency–accuracy trade-off without introducing unacceptable bias.

How Solvent Composition and Ion Solvation Shape Forces Between Charged Surfaces in Mixed Liquids

Abstract

Forces between charged surfaces in liquids govern colloidal stability, membrane interactions, electrochemical interfaces, and many processes in materials science. In mixed solvents, these forces cannot generally be predicted by replacing the dielectric constant of a pure liquid with a bulk average. Solvent composition varies near surfaces and ions, while ion solvation, preferential adsorption, and molecular-scale structure alter both the effective charge and the range of interactions. This paper reviews the physical principles that connect solvent composition and ion solvation to forces between charged surfaces. It discusses continuum electrostatics, preferential solvation, dielectric decrement, ion-specific adsorption, charge regulation, solvent-mediated forces, and the limits of mean-field theories. Particular attention is given to how composition-dependent local environments modify screening and generate nonmonotonic force profiles. The discussion emphasizes experimental strategies for separating electrostatic, dispersion, hydration, and structural contributions. A unified interpretation requires treating solvent composition, ion distributions, and surface chemistry as coupled variables. Such a framework is essential for understanding and predicting interfacial forces in aqueous-organic mixtures, ionic liquids, and other multicomponent liquids.

1. Introduction

Charged surfaces immersed in a liquid interact through electric fields and through the molecular organization of the surrounding fluid. In a simple electrolyte, these interactions are often introduced using the Poisson-Boltzmann equation. That framework describes electrostatic screening by mobile ions and is useful when the solvent can be treated as a uniform dielectric continuum. Mixed liquids challenge this simplifying assumption. Their components may have different polarities, molecular sizes, hydrogen-bonding abilities, and affinities for surfaces or ions. Consequently, the composition near an interface can differ substantially from the bulk composition. Ions also reorganize their solvation shells as they approach surfaces or enter compositionally distinct regions. These changes can alter both the strength and the range of the interaction between surfaces. The resulting forces may be attractive or repulsive, monotonic or oscillatory, and sensitive to small changes in composition.

The phrase “mixed liquids” encompasses many systems. Examples include water-alcohol mixtures, water-acetonitrile mixtures, aqueous solutions of polyols, organic electrolytes, and mixtures containing ionic liquids. Some systems are fully miscible at all compositions, whereas others lie near a demixing transition. Even in a macroscopically homogeneous liquid, local composition fluctuations can be substantial. The properties of the interfacial region may therefore not be inferred from bulk composition alone. This is particularly important when the surfaces are separated by only a few molecular diameters. At such distances, solvent layering and discrete ion positions become prominent, and a continuum description may fail.

The central objective of this paper is to explain how solvent composition and ion solvation shape forces between charged surfaces. The discussion focuses on conceptual mechanisms rather than on a single material system. It first establishes the classical electrostatic baseline. It then considers local composition, ion solvation, and surface chemistry as coupled effects. Finally, it reviews experimental and computational approaches for identifying these contributions and outlines open questions.

2. Classical electrostatic baseline

In a uniform dielectric medium, the electrostatic potential ψ satisfies Poisson’s equation,

∇·(ε∇ψ) = −ρ,

where ε is the permittivity and ρ is the local charge density. In an electrolyte containing point-like ions at thermal equilibrium, the ion concentration depends on the local potential through Boltzmann factors. Combining this relation with Poisson’s equation yields the Poisson-Boltzmann equation. For a symmetric electrolyte at low potential, the equation can be linearized to give the Debye-Hückel description. The potential then decays approximately exponentially with distance from a planar charged surface. The characteristic decay length is the Debye length, which decreases as the ionic strength increases.

For two charged planar surfaces, the electrostatic interaction depends on their separation, surface charge or potential, electrolyte concentration, and boundary conditions. At sufficiently large separation, overlapping diffuse layers commonly generate repulsion between like-charged surfaces. The precise force depends on whether the surface charge is fixed, the surface potential is fixed, or the surface chemistry allows charge regulation. These boundary conditions are not interchangeable. Real surfaces often regulate their charge through protonation, deprotonation, ion binding, or adsorption of charged species.

The classical model assumes that the solvent is spatially uniform and that its dielectric response is adequately represented by a single scalar permittivity. It also often assumes that ions are point particles with no specific affinity for the surface. These assumptions can be useful when the surface separation is large compared with molecular dimensions and when the mixture is far from a phase transition. They become inadequate when solvent composition varies locally, ion sizes matter, or ion solvation energies differ significantly between environments.

In mixed liquids, the bulk permittivity itself depends on composition. A first approximation is to insert the measured bulk permittivity into the Debye length. This approach can capture broad trends but ignores interfacial enrichment or depletion of solvent components. It also overlooks composition-dependent ion activities and local dielectric response. Two mixtures with similar bulk permittivities may therefore produce different intersurface forces.

3. Solvent composition near charged surfaces

A mixed solvent is not necessarily compositionally uniform at a surface. One component may preferentially adsorb because of hydrogen bonding, dispersion interactions, surface polarity, or geometric packing. Another component may be depleted from the interfacial region. This surface-induced fractionation changes the local dielectric environment and the free energy of ion solvation. It can also alter surface wetting and the effective boundary condition for electrostatics.

The local composition is determined by a balance among bulk chemical potentials, intermolecular interactions, surface affinities, and electrostatic contributions. In a binary mixture, the local mole fraction of one component may vary with distance from the surface. If the mixture is close to a demixing critical point, the composition profile can extend over a relatively large distance. Away from criticality, the profile is generally shorter ranged, though molecular layering may remain important at nanometer scales.

A composition gradient can modify the electric field in several ways. If the permittivity varies spatially, Gauss’s law becomes a variable-coefficient equation. Field lines can be redirected toward regions of higher or lower permittivity, depending on geometry and boundary conditions. The electrostatic energy is then coupled to the composition field. In a thermodynamic description, the dielectric response contributes to the free energy, and the electric field can drive further composition rearrangement. This feedback means that solvent composition and electrostatics should not always be solved independently.

Preferential adsorption also changes the chemical environment of the surface. A surface enriched in water may support stronger hydration and different protonation equilibria than a surface enriched in an organic cosolvent. This can modify the density of ionizable surface groups and thereby change the surface charge. In this way, composition affects the force not only through dielectric screening but also through surface chemistry.

4. Ion solvation in mixed liquids

An ion in solution is surrounded by solvent molecules whose arrangement depends on the ion’s charge, size, and chemical identity. This solvation shell is often compositionally distinct from the bulk. In a mixed solvent, one component may preferentially occupy the first solvation shell even when it is a minority species in the bulk. Such preferential solvation can be driven by ion-dipole interactions, hydrogen bonding, polarizability, and packing constraints.

The free energy of transferring an ion between environments depends on the local solvent composition. An ion may be stabilized in a water-rich region but destabilized in an organic-rich one, or the opposite may occur for particular ions. This transfer free energy influences the ion’s spatial distribution near surfaces and across composition gradients. The resulting distribution cannot always be described by a simple Boltzmann factor involving only the electrostatic potential. It may also include a composition-dependent solvation term.

For an ion species i, a generalized equilibrium distribution can be written schematically as a concentration proportional to the exponential of the negative electrochemical potential. The electrochemical potential contains an electrostatic contribution, a chemical activity term, and a local solvation free energy. If the latter depends on composition, then gradients in solvent composition exert an effective force on the ion. This effect is sometimes called solvation-induced migration or preferential-solvation-driven partitioning.

Ion solvation also modifies effective ion size and correlations. A strongly hydrated ion may carry a relatively persistent shell, while a weakly solvated or highly polarizable ion may approach a surface more closely. The effective distance of closest approach influences the structure of the electrical double layer. In concentrated electrolytes, ion-ion correlations, finite-size effects, and solvent-mediated association may further alter the force profile.

The role of ion identity is especially clear in specific-ion effects. Ions of the same valence can interact differently with interfaces because their hydration free energies, polarizabilities, and surface affinities differ. A simple valence-based screening model cannot capture these distinctions. In mixed solvents, such specific-ion effects may become stronger or reverse direction as the solvent composition changes.

5. Coupling of composition, solvation, and electrostatics

The local composition, ionic distributions, and electric potential are coupled fields. A solvent component can enrich near a surface, changing the local permittivity and solvation energies. The altered electrostatic environment then changes the distributions of ions. Those ions, in turn, influence the local composition through preferential solvation and electrostatic forces. A complete equilibrium theory must account for this feedback.

One practical approach is to construct a free-energy functional containing mixing free energy, gradient penalties, electrostatic energy, ion chemical potentials, and surface contributions. The composition field can be represented by a local volume fraction. A mixing free energy describes the tendency of the components to mix or demix. A gradient term penalizes sharp composition changes. The electrostatic term depends on the spatially varying permittivity and charge density. Ion solvation terms encode the preference of each ion for local solvent environments. Surface terms describe adsorption and charge regulation.

Minimizing this free energy yields coupled equations for the composition, potential, and ion concentrations. The resulting equations are generally nonlinear. Their solutions can exhibit composition enrichment, depletion, and nonmonotonic ion profiles. Near a critical point, composition fluctuations can become long ranged and can mediate an additional force between surfaces. This force is distinct from ordinary electrostatic screening, though the two can interact.

The free-energy framework also clarifies why bulk dielectric constant alone is insufficient. The permittivity is one constitutive property of the local environment, but the solvent’s mixing thermodynamics and ion-specific solvation energies are independent inputs. Two mixtures with equal permittivity can have different composition susceptibilities and different interfacial adsorption behavior. They can therefore produce different forces despite similar bulk dielectric properties.

6. Interfacial force components

The net force between charged surfaces in a mixed liquid can contain several contributions. The electrostatic double-layer force is often the most familiar. It arises from the overlap of ionic atmospheres and electric fields. Its sign and magnitude depend on surface charge, electrolyte composition, and the charge-regulation response of the surfaces.

A second contribution is the osmotic pressure of the ions and solvent components confined between the surfaces. If ion concentrations are higher in the gap than in the bulk, the osmotic contribution can be repulsive. If ions are depleted, the pressure contribution may be reduced, potentially allowing other attractive interactions to dominate. Composition gradients can also generate an osmotic stress because the chemical potentials of the solvent components differ across the gap.

A third contribution comes from solvent-mediated structural forces. Molecules near a surface may form layers, chains, or hydrogen-bond networks. When two surfaces approach, these structures can be compressed or reorganized. The resulting force can oscillate with separation on the scale of molecular dimensions. Such oscillations are particularly important at short range and cannot be captured by a smooth continuum dielectric model.

Dispersion forces, including van der Waals interactions, are also present. Their magnitude depends on the optical and dielectric properties of the surfaces and liquid. In mixtures, the relevant dielectric response is frequency dependent, and composition can change the balance of dispersion forces. The electrostatic and dispersion contributions are not always simply additive because the same solvent structure influences both.

Hydration forces may arise when strongly bound water layers resist compression or removal. In aqueous-organic mixtures, the availability and organization of water at the interface can vary sharply with composition. A surface that retains a water-rich layer may experience a different short-range repulsion than a surface preferentially wetted by the organic component.

Finally, solvent composition fluctuations can mediate an effective force. If both surfaces favor the same component, overlap of their composition profiles can lower free energy and produce attraction. If they favor different components, overlap can instead be unfavorable. Near a critical point, the range of this composition-mediated force can become large. Its sign and magnitude depend on surface preferences and the thermodynamic state of the mixture.

7. Dielectric decrement and local dielectric response

Adding ions to a liquid often reduces the measured dielectric permittivity, an effect commonly referred to as dielectric decrement. In mixed solvents, the decrement can depend on both ion concentration and composition. Ions may orient nearby solvent molecules, restrict their rotational response, or alter hydrogen-bond networks. The dielectric response in the vicinity of an ion can therefore differ substantially from the bulk value.

A spatially varying dielectric constant changes the relationship between charge density and electric field. It also affects the electrostatic self-energy of ions. If the local permittivity is lower around an ion, the ion’s solvation free energy may increase, depending on the surrounding geometry and boundary conditions. This can influence ion partitioning and adsorption.

However, assigning a single local dielectric constant to a molecular-scale region is not always meaningful. Dielectric response is nonlocal at short length scales, and molecular polarization is anisotropic near interfaces. Continuum models can still be useful if their limitations are recognized and their parameters are calibrated against molecular simulation or experiment. The key question is not whether a local dielectric constant exists in an absolute sense, but whether a chosen coarse-grained description predicts observables accurately.

The dielectric decrement also complicates simple screening arguments. Increasing salt concentration typically shortens the Debye length through the rise in ionic strength. At the same time, a decrease in permittivity changes the electrostatic coupling strength. These effects can oppose or reinforce one another. In a mixed solvent, composition-dependent ion association can further reduce the number of free charge carriers. The resulting force cannot be inferred from nominal salt concentration alone.

8. Charge regulation and surface chemistry

Many surfaces do not maintain a fixed charge as the solution composition changes. Surface groups can protonate or deprotonate, bind ions, or exchange ligands with the liquid. The equilibrium state depends on local pH, ion activities, dielectric environment, and solvent-specific acid-base behavior. In a mixed liquid, standard aqueous pH concepts may not directly represent proton chemical potential, especially when the solvent composition is substantially nonaqueous.

Charge regulation can create feedback between the two surfaces. As the surfaces approach, their electrostatic potentials and local ion concentrations change. Surface groups may then adjust their degree of ionization. This adjustment modifies the force in turn. The interaction may consequently differ from fixed-charge or fixed-potential predictions.

Solvent composition affects charge regulation in several ways. It changes the dielectric response and thus the electrostatic cost of charging. It can alter the acidity or basicity of surface groups. It may also change the activity coefficients of ions and the availability of coordinating solvent molecules. Specific adsorption of counterions can reduce the effective surface charge or even reverse its sign under some conditions.

In experimental systems, charge regulation is often a major source of apparent disagreement between measurements and idealized theories. Two studies using nominally similar surfaces may obtain different forces because of variations in surface preparation, contamination, ion binding, or solvent composition. Reliable interpretation requires characterization of surface chemistry under the actual liquid conditions.

9. Predictions from continuum theories

A generalized continuum theory can incorporate composition-dependent permittivity, solvation free energies, and charge regulation. Such a theory can make several qualitative predictions. First, the force may vary nonmonotonically with bulk composition because the different contributions need not change in the same direction. Second, ions may accumulate in regions that are electrostatically unfavorable if their solvation preference is sufficiently strong. Third, the effective screening length may differ from that estimated using bulk dielectric data and nominal ionic strength. Fourth, composition-mediated interactions can add a force with a range controlled by the mixture’s correlation length.

Near a demixing transition, the composition correlation length increases. If the surfaces favor the same component, their overlapping adsorption layers can produce a long-ranged attraction. If they favor different components, the interaction can be repulsive or more complex. Electrostatic fields may shift the local composition and alter the effective distance to criticality. Thus, the force can become unusually sensitive to temperature, salt concentration, and solvent ratio.

Continuum theories are most reliable when the separation is large compared with molecular sizes and when the composition varies smoothly. They are less reliable at very short distances, where solvent layering and discrete ion positions dominate. A useful modeling strategy is to combine continuum descriptions at long range with molecularly informed corrections at short range. Such multiscale approaches can retain physical interpretability without discarding important molecular effects.

10. Molecular-scale mechanisms

At molecular separations, forces depend on the organization of individual solvent molecules and ions. A charged surface may induce orientational ordering of dipolar molecules. The resulting interfacial polarization can be anisotropic. In a mixture, different components may compete for adsorption sites or form distinct layers.

The first solvent layer can have a composition that differs sharply from the next layer. For example, one component may bind directly to the surface while another occupies the outer interfacial region. When two surfaces approach, these layers can merge, displace one another, or reorganize. The free-energy cost of this rearrangement can generate oscillatory or strongly asymmetric force profiles.

Ion solvation shells may also become distorted or partially lost near a surface. The cost of shell deformation can create an additional barrier to adsorption. Conversely, a surface that provides favorable coordination sites may stabilize a partially desolvated ion. This competition determines whether an ion remains in solution, adsorbs, or bridges between surfaces.

Ion bridging is a possible source of attraction between oppositely charged regions or between surfaces with specific binding sites. In a mixed solvent, the likelihood of bridging depends on whether the solvent stabilizes the ion in the gap and whether the surface coordination environment is favorable. This mechanism is distinct from the mean-field attraction predicted for opposite charges and can be highly ion specific.

Molecular simulations have revealed that local dielectric response, ion pairing, and solvent structuring can vary substantially with distance from charged interfaces. These observations caution against interpreting measured force curves solely through continuum screening parameters. At the same time, molecular simulations must be carefully validated because force predictions can depend on the quality of interaction potentials and polarization models.

11. Experimental approaches

Surface force measurements provide direct information about the interaction as a function of separation. Surface force apparatus methods and colloidal probe atomic force microscopy are commonly used for this purpose. In these experiments, one can vary solvent composition, salt concentration, temperature, and surface chemistry. The measured force must be interpreted with care because roughness, surface heterogeneity, and contamination can influence the result.

Electrokinetic measurements, such as electrophoretic mobility and zeta potential, provide indirect information about interfacial charge and double-layer structure. They are useful for tracking changes with composition but do not directly measure the force between two surfaces. The zeta potential corresponds to an electrokinetic shear-plane potential and should not be equated automatically with the surface potential.

Spectroscopic methods can probe local composition and solvation. Infrared and Raman spectroscopy can report on hydrogen bonding and solvent orientation. Nuclear magnetic resonance can reveal ion coordination and molecular mobility. X-ray and neutron scattering can provide structural information near interfaces, especially when contrast variation is available. Surface-sensitive techniques can help distinguish adsorption from bulk composition changes.

Calorimetry and ion partitioning measurements can constrain solvation free energies. Measuring activity coefficients and conductivity helps assess ion association and the concentration of free charge carriers. Dielectric spectroscopy can characterize bulk response across frequency, while interfacial dielectric properties remain more difficult to measure directly.

A robust experimental study should combine force measurements with independent characterization of surface charge, solvent composition, and ion speciation. It should also report the method used to control and define composition, since volume fraction, mole fraction, and mass fraction are not interchangeable. Temperature and water content should be carefully controlled, particularly in nominally nonaqueous systems where trace water can strongly alter ion solvation.

12. Computational approaches

Molecular dynamics simulations can provide detailed information about solvent and ion distributions near surfaces. Classical force fields are computationally efficient, but their predictions depend on parametrization and may fail for strongly polarizable or reactive systems. Polarizable force fields can better represent dielectric response and ion-specific interactions, though they are more expensive.

Ab initio molecular dynamics can capture electronic effects and chemical bonding more directly. Its computational cost generally limits accessible system sizes and timescales. It is therefore often used to validate local coordination structures or interfacial interactions rather than to simulate large-scale force profiles.

Enhanced-sampling techniques are valuable when ion adsorption, solvent exchange, or surface restructuring occurs on slow timescales. Potential of mean force calculations can quantify the free energy of moving an ion toward a surface. Simulations of two surfaces at varying separation can directly estimate the mean force, but finite-size effects and long-range electrostatics require careful treatment.

Coarse-grained simulations can explore larger length and time scales. Their reliability depends on whether they retain the relevant composition fluctuations, ion solvation preferences, and surface interactions. Parameterization against both bulk properties and interfacial observables is preferable to fitting only one class of data.

A productive multiscale workflow begins with molecular simulations or experiments that characterize local solvation and adsorption. These results can inform a continuum free-energy model. The continuum model can then predict long-range force trends over parameter ranges that are inaccessible to atomistic simulation. Disagreement between levels can reveal missing physics, such as charge regulation, ion association, or nonlocal dielectric response.

13. Representative system classes

Aqueous alcohol mixtures provide a useful example because their components differ in hydrogen bonding and polarity while remaining miscible over broad composition ranges. Alcohol molecules may adsorb preferentially at some surfaces, while ions can remain strongly hydrated in water-rich regions. The resulting composition and ion profiles depend on the alcohol identity, salt type, and surface chemistry. The force can therefore change nonlinearly with alcohol fraction.

Water-acetonitrile mixtures illustrate a different balance of polarity, hydrogen bonding, and ion coordination. Acetonitrile can solvate some ions effectively, while water may dominate the solvation of others. Salt dissociation and ion pairing can vary strongly with composition. Changes in the number of mobile ions can alter the force range even if the nominal salt concentration is fixed.

Polyol-water mixtures may exhibit strong hydrogen-bond networks and pronounced viscosity changes. The increased viscosity does not directly determine equilibrium forces, but it affects the timescale over which composition and ion profiles equilibrate. Polyols can also alter water activity and hydration forces. These systems are relevant to biological and soft-matter interfaces.

Ionic liquids and deep eutectic solvents present additional challenges. They may contain ions at concentrations so high that the dilute Poisson-Boltzmann framework is inapplicable. Their structure includes strong ion correlations, finite-size effects, and layering. When mixed with molecular solvents, the composition and degree of dissociation can vary near surfaces. The resulting forces can be oscillatory, long ranged, or strongly dependent on electrode potential.

Polymer-containing mixtures add another layer of complexity. Polymers may adsorb, deplete, or form bridging structures. Their presence can modify solvent composition and ion partitioning. Although polymer forces are not the primary focus here, they illustrate the general point that interfacial interactions in mixed liquids arise from coupled molecular components rather than from electrostatics alone.

14. Nonmonotonic composition dependence

A common but incorrect expectation is that increasing the fraction of a high-permittivity solvent must always increase electrostatic screening and weaken interactions. This expectation neglects changes in ion solvation, dissociation, surface charge, and local composition. A high-permittivity component may preferentially adsorb at the surface, producing a local environment unlike the bulk. It may also stabilize separated ions, increasing the free-ion concentration, or alter the surface’s degree of ionization.

Conversely, adding a lower-permittivity cosolvent can strengthen Coulomb interactions but may also promote ion pairing. If the number of free ions falls, the effective screening length can increase despite stronger pairwise electrostatic coupling. Surface adsorption may further complicate the trend. The measured force can therefore pass through a maximum or minimum as composition changes.

Nonmonotonic behavior is not merely an experimental nuisance. It is evidence that multiple mechanisms are competing. By measuring both the force and independent properties such as conductivity, dielectric response, and surface charge, one can identify which mechanism dominates in different composition regimes.

The composition dependence may also be asymmetric with respect to the two surfaces. If the surfaces have different chemical affinities, one component may enrich at one surface and deplete at the other. The gap then contains a composition profile that cannot be represented by a single average composition. Such asymmetry can produce forces that depend on surface orientation or preparation history.

15. Critical and near-critical mixtures

When a binary mixture approaches a liquid-liquid critical point, composition fluctuations become large and long ranged. Surfaces couple to these fluctuations through preferential adsorption. The overlap of fluctuation profiles can produce critical Casimir forces. These forces are distinct from electrostatic forces but can coexist with them.

Charged surfaces can influence critical fluctuations through electric-field-induced composition changes. Ions may also couple directly to the composition field through preferential solvation. The critical temperature and local susceptibility can then depend on salt concentration and surface charge. This coupling can shift or round the apparent critical behavior.

The sign of the fluctuation-mediated force depends on the surface boundary conditions for the composition field. Two surfaces that both prefer the same component often generate an attractive interaction under appropriate conditions. Surfaces that prefer opposite components can generate a repulsive interaction. Electrostatic interactions may either reinforce or oppose this contribution.

Near-critical mixtures therefore offer a sensitive test of coupled theories. Force measurements can reveal long-range composition-mediated contributions, while scattering experiments can characterize the correlation length. Care is needed to distinguish critical forces from residual electrostatic forces, especially because both can be long ranged.

16. Implications for colloids and soft materials

Colloidal stability depends on the balance of electrostatic repulsion, van der Waals attraction, and steric or hydration forces. In mixed liquids, solvent composition can alter all of these contributions. A cosolvent may change the surface charge, the ion cloud, and the solvent-mediated attraction at the same time. As a result, a colloidal dispersion may remain stable in one composition range but aggregate in another.

The familiar picture of a fixed electrostatic barrier can become unreliable when ion solvation changes with composition. Aggregation may occur even when the nominal ionic strength is low if the surface charge is reduced or if specific ion binding occurs. Conversely, a composition-induced increase in surface charge or hydration repulsion can stabilize particles.

These effects are relevant to formulation science, including paints, inks, food systems, pharmaceutical suspensions, and energy-storage materials. In each case, the relevant solvent mixture may contain multiple additives, polymers, and salts. Predictive models must therefore account for chemical specificity rather than relying on a single effective dielectric constant.

Charged membranes and biological interfaces provide another important context. Membrane surfaces contain chemically heterogeneous groups and are exposed to mixed aqueous environments. Ion-specific effects and local solvent composition can influence membrane adhesion, protein binding, and intermembrane forces. Even modest changes in hydration or ion partitioning may produce significant functional consequences.

17. Implications for electrochemical systems

Electrochemical interfaces are often studied in mixed solvents to expand the electrochemical window, adjust transport properties, or improve solubility. The double layer in such systems can differ substantially from that in water. Solvent molecules may orient and segregate near an electrode, while ions desolvate or adsorb specifically.

The force between two charged or polarized electrodes can influence capacitance, wetting, and nanoscale gap structure. Composition-dependent solvation affects the potential of zero charge and the voltage-dependent adsorption of ions. In concentrated electrolytes, the spatial arrangement of ions may be governed by correlations and crowding rather than dilute-solution screening.

Understanding these effects is important for batteries, supercapacitors, electrocatalysis, and ionic-liquid devices. In confined geometries, the solvent may be selectively retained or expelled. This can alter local composition and transport, as well as the mechanical force between electrode surfaces.

Electrochemical measurements should therefore be interpreted alongside structural and force measurements where possible. Capacitance alone does not uniquely determine the microscopic ion distribution. Combined measurements can better distinguish dielectric effects, adsorption, ion pairing, and solvent layering.

18. Limitations and sources of uncertainty

A major limitation in current understanding is the difficulty of measuring local solvent composition and dielectric response at nanometer scales. Many commonly available measurements provide bulk averages or indirect interfacial indicators. This limitation complicates the validation of coupled theories.

Surface heterogeneity is another source of uncertainty. Real surfaces contain defects, roughness, chemical patches, and contamination. These features can create local variations in charge and solvent affinity. The measured force is then an average over a distribution of interfacial environments.

Uncertainty in ion parameters can be substantial. Hydration free energies, polarizabilities, and ion-pairing constants depend on the solvent model and experimental conditions. In mixed liquids, standard reference data may be sparse. Predictions based on nominal ion concentration may therefore be misleading.

The definition of solvent composition also requires care. A quoted volume fraction can differ from the composition experienced by molecules after mixing because volumes may not be additive. Water content can vary through absorption from the atmosphere. Small amounts of water can have a disproportionate effect on the solvation of salts in organic-rich mixtures.

The separation between electrostatic and nonelectrostatic forces is not always unique. Solvent structure affects the dielectric response and dispersion interactions, while ion solvation contributes to both chemical and electrostatic free energies. Any decomposition depends to some extent on the theoretical framework used. It is more reliable to compare total forces and predicted observables than to overinterpret an arbitrary partition into components.

19. A unified conceptual framework

A useful conceptual framework treats the interface as a coupled thermodynamic system with four principal ingredients: solvent composition, ionic charge density, surface chemistry, and spatial structure. The bulk mixture establishes chemical potentials and susceptibilities. The surface modifies local composition through adsorption preferences. Ions respond to both electric fields and composition-dependent solvation. Surface groups adjust their charge in response to the local chemical and electrostatic environment.

The force is obtained from the change in free energy with surface separation. This definition remains valid regardless of whether a particular contribution is labeled electrostatic, osmotic, hydration, or structural. For practical modeling, the free energy should include all important degrees of freedom at the chosen scale. The corresponding force can then be compared directly with experiment.

At long range, a continuum description can be appropriate if it includes composition fields and ion-specific solvation. At molecular distances, atomistic structure and discrete adsorption events become essential. The two descriptions should be connected through consistent parameters and shared observables. This approach avoids treating molecular details as ad hoc corrections disconnected from thermodynamics.

A central prediction of the framework is that force laws are not universal functions of surface charge and ionic strength alone. They depend on the solvent mixture’s thermodynamic state, ion-specific transfer free energies, surface preference, and the distance scale of observation. Once these quantities are measured or calculated, the framework can nevertheless yield systematic predictions.

20. Research priorities

Future studies should map force profiles across controlled composition ranges while independently measuring ion activities, conductivity, and surface charge. Such datasets would help separate screening changes from charge regulation and ion association. Measurements should include both short and long separations to identify molecular layering and continuum behavior.

Improved interfacial spectroscopy is needed to quantify local composition and ion coordination. Combining surface-sensitive spectroscopy with force measurements would provide direct links between molecular structure and mechanical response. Neutron and X-ray methods with contrast variation are particularly promising for separating components in multicomponent mixtures.

Theoretical work should develop free-energy models that incorporate nonlocal dielectric response and composition-dependent ion solvation without excessive parameterization. These models should be tested against molecular simulations and experimental force curves. Explicit treatment of polarizability and charge regulation will be important for strongly heterogeneous interfaces.

Simulation studies should report uncertainty and test sensitivity to force-field choices. Comparisons among fixed-charge, polarizable, and quantum-informed models can clarify which molecular features control a given force. Larger-scale simulations near criticality and in ionic-liquid mixtures will require efficient coarse-graining.

Finally, standardized reporting is needed. Studies should specify surface preparation, roughness, salt identity, solvent composition basis, water content, temperature, and the method used to infer charge. Better reporting will make it possible to compare results across laboratories and build reliable quantitative models.

21. Conclusion

Forces between charged surfaces in mixed liquids arise from coupled electrostatic, chemical, and structural effects. The bulk dielectric constant and nominal ionic strength provide only a partial description. Local solvent composition can differ from the bulk, and ions can be preferentially solvated or partitioned according to their chemical identity. These processes alter screening, surface charge, ion adsorption, and solvent-mediated interactions.

The most important conceptual shift is to treat solvent composition and ion solvation as active interfacial variables rather than background properties. A composition gradient can reshape the electric field. Ion solvation can drive migration even in the absence of an electrostatic potential gradient. Surface chemistry can respond to both effects through charge regulation. Molecular layering and composition fluctuations can add forces that are not captured by conventional mean-field theories.

No single model is suitable for every separation scale or liquid composition. Continuum theories can describe long-range trends when extended to include composition and solvation fields. Molecular simulations and spectroscopy are needed to resolve short-range structure and ion coordination. Combining these approaches offers the most reliable route to prediction.

A deeper understanding of these forces has practical importance across colloid science, electrochemistry, membrane biophysics, and materials engineering. It can guide the design of stable dispersions, electrolyte formulations, and responsive interfaces. It can also explain why small changes in solvent ratio or salt identity sometimes produce unexpectedly large changes in adhesion or repulsion. Ultimately, quantitative prediction will depend on measuring and modeling the local environment between surfaces, not merely the bulk properties of the liquid.

The paper studies whether regularizing state representations can improve reinforcement-learning performance on Atari games, an important problem given the instability and sample demands of deep RL. Its central idea is promising: shaping the learned representation may help an agent retain useful information while avoiding features that are brittle or irrelevant to the task. The work is also well motivated by the gap between strong benchmark scores and robust, efficient learning.

A key strength is the focus on representations rather than relying solely on changes to the policy or value-learning algorithm. The evaluation across multiple games offers a useful test of whether the approach generalizes beyond a single environment. The paper would be stronger, however, if it stated its main contributions and hypotheses more explicitly near the beginning. It should also give enough implementation detail for readers to reproduce the regularizer, including its coefficient, scheduling, and interaction with the rest of the training objective.

The experimental section should compare against well-tuned baselines using the same network, training budget, and preprocessing. Results should be reported across multiple random seeds, with uncertainty estimates, since Atari performance can vary substantially between runs. Per-game results are important alongside aggregate scores, because averages can hide regressions on particular games. Ablations are needed to establish which component of the regularization produces any observed gains and whether those gains persist across coefficient values. The authors should also report learning curves and sample efficiency, not just final scores, and clarify whether evaluation uses the same protocol as the baselines.

The paper would benefit from a more direct analysis of what changes in the learned representations, such as their stability, diversity, or alignment with task-relevant information. It should discuss possible costs, including added computation and sensitivity to hyperparameter choices. Any claims of improved robustness should be supported by tests under changed observations or dynamics rather than inferred from average benchmark scores alone. Overall, this is a worthwhile direction with potential practical value, but the evidence and methodological detail need to be sufficiently comprehensive to support the paper’s claims. I recommend revision, with priority given to reproducible comparisons, statistical reporting, and targeted ablations.

A storm sank a tourist vessel in Brazil’s Pantanal wetlands, leaving several passengers and crew members missing, authorities said. The accident happened as severe weather swept across the region, known for its rivers and seasonal flooding. Officials have described the incident as deadly, though the number of confirmed fatalities was not immediately available. Rescue teams are searching nearby waterways and flooded areas for survivors. Strong winds and poor visibility are complicating the operation, local authorities said. The vessel was carrying tourists on a trip through the wetlands when the storm struck. Investigators are working to establish how many people were on board and whether the boat had adequate safety equipment. Authorities have not yet released the identities or nationalities of those missing. Emergency services urged other boat operators to avoid the area while dangerous conditions continue. The search is expected to continue as weather and river conditions allow.

Students should use phones at school only when they are needed for learning or emergencies. Teachers can allow phones for research, educational apps, or classroom activities. During lessons and tests, students should put their phones away so they can focus. Using phones responsibly helps students learn while avoiding distractions.

Rising antibiotic use in England is adding to concerns that bacteria are becoming harder to treat, prompting health officials and medical experts to call for more careful prescribing.

Antibiotics are essential medicines, but their overuse can encourage resistant bacteria to survive and spread. As resistance grows, infections that were once straightforward to treat may require stronger drugs or longer hospital stays.

Health services have warned that antibiotics are still being prescribed when they are unlikely to help, including for many coughs, colds and sore throats. These illnesses are usually caused by viruses, which antibiotics do not treat.

The increase has renewed calls for clinicians to prescribe antibiotics only when there is a clear medical need. Experts also say patients should be given better advice about when symptoms can be managed without the drugs.

Antibiotic use varies across the country and between healthcare settings. Prescribing can rise during winter, when respiratory illnesses place additional pressure on GP surgeries and hospitals.

Doctors face a difficult balance: treating serious bacterial infections promptly while avoiding unnecessary prescriptions. Delays can be dangerous for patients who need antibiotics, but prescribing them without good reason can undermine their effectiveness over time.

Medical leaders say decisions should be based on a patient’s symptoms, medical history and, where appropriate, test results. They encourage clinicians to explain why an antibiotic is not suitable and what signs should prompt a patient to seek further care.

The issue extends beyond individual prescriptions. Antibiotics used in hospitals and other settings can also contribute to resistance, making infection prevention and careful monitoring important parts of the response.

Public health specialists say patients can help by not requesting antibiotics for illnesses that are likely to be viral. They also advise people to take prescribed courses exactly as directed and not to share leftover medicines.

However, experts caution against blaming patients alone. Busy services, uncertainty about a diagnosis and limited access to timely testing can all influence prescribing decisions.

Calls for action include clearer prescribing guidance, better access to diagnostic tests and regular review of local prescribing patterns. Education for both clinicians and the public is also seen as essential.

The government and health services have previously set out plans to tackle antimicrobial resistance, including improving prevention and developing new treatments. Specialists say sustained effort is needed because resistance can spread across communities and borders.

They stress that antibiotics should remain available when they are genuinely needed. The goal, they say, is not to restrict lifesaving treatment but to protect its effectiveness.

With demand for care rising, clinicians are being urged to make every prescription count. More cautious use now could help ensure antibiotics continue to work for patients in the future.

A forgotten training device at Old Trafford triggered a false alarm that forced the stadium to be evacuated and delayed Manchester United’s match against Bournemouth. Supporters were asked to leave the ground before kick-off after a security alert prompted checks of the stadium. The device was later identified as a training item accidentally left behind after an exercise, rather than a genuine threat.

Police and security staff examined the object and confirmed there was no danger. The precautionary response nevertheless disrupted plans for thousands of fans and postponed the fixture. Manchester United and Bournemouth players had been preparing for the match when officials ordered the evacuation.

The delay created uncertainty outside the stadium as supporters waited for updates. Club staff worked with emergency services to assess the situation and determine whether it was safe to reopen the ground. Once the all-clear was given, officials began arranging a revised schedule for the game.

The incident underscored the need to treat suspicious objects seriously, even when they ultimately prove harmless. Authorities did not report any injuries. The clubs were expected to share further information about the rescheduled kick-off with supporters.

Old Trafford has hosted major fixtures for decades, and security procedures are routinely reviewed for match days. The false alarm showed how an otherwise minor oversight can have significant consequences at a crowded venue. Supporters were advised to follow official club and police updates for details about entry arrangements and tickets.

Technology is now part of everyday life, and it helps people learn, communicate, and enjoy entertainment. However, using it too much can affect how children interact with others. When children spend most of their free time on phones, computers, or tablets, they may have fewer face-to-face conversations. As a result, they might find it harder to read facial expressions, listen carefully, or express their feelings. Online communication can be useful, but it does not fully replace spending time together in person.

Excessive technology use can also change the activities children choose. Instead of playing outside, reading, or joining group activities, they may spend hours watching videos or playing games. Too much screen time can reduce physical activity and make it harder to develop hobbies. Children may also miss opportunities to cooperate, solve problems, and use their imagination through play. A balanced routine gives them time for both technology and other important activities.

Technology use may affect children’s behavior as well. Some children become impatient when they are used to fast-moving games and constant entertainment. They may feel upset when asked to stop using a device or have trouble concentrating on slower tasks. Using screens late at night can also interfere with sleep, which may lead to tiredness and irritability. These effects are not the same for every child, but they are worth paying attention to.

Technology itself is not harmful when used thoughtfully. Parents and children can set reasonable screen-time limits and choose age-appropriate content. Families can also make time for meals, outdoor activities, and conversations without devices. With a healthy balance, children can benefit from technology while continuing to build strong relationships, active habits, and positive behavior.

Desmidium swartzii is a freshwater green alga in the desmid group, a family of mostly microscopic organisms known for their distinctive cell shapes. It commonly grows attached to submerged plants or other surfaces in ponds and slow-moving water. Its cells join end to end to form long, threadlike colonies. Each cell is roughly three-sided in cross-section, so the filament can appear twisted when viewed under a microscope. This arrangement gives the colony a characteristic spiral or corkscrew-like appearance. The cells are held together by their walls and by mucilage, a slippery substance that can help the filament cling to surfaces.

Like other desmids, each cell has two similar halves, called semicells, joined at a narrow central region. A cell wall surrounds the cell and may show fine markings that are easiest to see with magnification. The cell contains chloroplasts, which capture light energy for photosynthesis, and a nucleus that directs cell activities. Its green color comes from chlorophyll, the pigment used to make sugars from light, water, and carbon dioxide.

Desmidium swartzii reproduces mainly by cell division. During division, the cell separates into two daughter cells, each receiving one original semicell and building a new one. Repeated divisions lengthen the filament and maintain its distinctive shape. Under suitable conditions, desmids can also reproduce sexually through conjugation, in which cell contents from two cells unite to form a resistant zygospore. The spiral colonies are therefore both a useful identifying feature and an example of how cell shape and attachment can organize microscopic life in freshwater habitats.

This paper addresses an important problem in learned image compression: how to reduce bitrate while preserving perceptual and structural quality. It focuses on combining learned transforms with hyperpriors to improve entropy modeling. The topic is timely, given the growing interest in neural codecs and the limitations of conventional hand-designed pipelines. The paper’s central premise is that a learned analysis and synthesis transform can produce a representation suited to the target distortion measure. A hyperprior can then provide side information that helps predict the distribution of latent codes. Together, these components offer a principled way to reduce coding cost. The subject is appropriate for a research audience in image processing and machine learning.

The paper is potentially valuable because it treats compression as an end-to-end optimization problem. It also recognizes that transform quality alone does not determine coding efficiency. Accurate probability models are essential because they control the expected number of bits used to represent quantized latents. The use of a hyperprior is therefore well motivated. The work could provide useful evidence about the interaction between representation learning and entropy modeling. Its relevance would be strengthened by a clear comparison with established learned codecs and strong conventional baselines. Overall, the research question is meaningful and technically interesting.

The main contribution should be stated more precisely. The paper should distinguish its proposed method from prior learned-transform codecs and hyperprior models. It should identify which components are novel, which are adopted from previous work, and which are modified. If the contribution is primarily an implementation or empirical comparison, that should be stated directly. If a new architecture or objective is proposed, the specific innovation should be isolated. A concise list of contributions would help readers assess the paper’s scope. The current framing should avoid implying novelty for established elements.

The method section should explain the full compression pipeline in reproducible detail. It should specify the analysis transform, synthesis transform, hyper-analysis transform, and hyper-synthesis transform. The paper should state the number of layers, kernel sizes, channel widths, nonlinearities, and any downsampling operations. It should explain how the main latent representation and hyperlatent are quantized. The treatment of quantization during training should also be described. For example, the authors should clarify whether additive uniform noise, a straight-through estimator, or another approximation is used. These details are necessary to interpret and reproduce the reported results.

The entropy model requires particular attention. The paper should define the conditional distribution used to model the main latents. It should clarify whether the model predicts scale, mean, or other distribution parameters. The authors should explain how the hyperprior conditions these predictions and whether spatial context is also used. Any factorization assumptions should be explicit. The paper should describe how probabilities are converted into arithmetic-coding or range-coding symbols. It should state whether the reported bitrate includes hyperprior side information. Without this information, the claimed coding gains are difficult to verify.

The rate-distortion objective should be presented mathematically and explained in plain language. The paper should define the distortion term and the rate estimate. It should identify the Lagrange multiplier or equivalent control parameter used to select the rate-quality tradeoff. The authors should explain how they train models at different operating points. If a single model supports multiple rates, the mechanism for controlling rate should be described. The paper should also clarify whether the entropy loss is estimated from predicted probabilities or measured from actual coded bitstreams. Reporting both estimated and realized rates would be especially useful.

The experimental design should be expanded or clarified. The training and test datasets should be named, and their sizes and image characteristics should be reported. The authors should state how training, validation, and test partitions are formed. Any image resizing, cropping, color conversion, or augmentation should be described. The test set should not overlap with training data. The paper should explain whether results are evaluated on full-resolution images or patches. This information is important because dataset selection can substantially affect compression results.

The baselines should be sufficiently strong and fairly configured. The study should compare against relevant learned codecs, including methods with comparable transforms and entropy models. It should also include conventional codecs where appropriate. All methods should be evaluated on the same images and with consistent color-space and metric conventions. If published results are used instead of reproduced runs, the paper should explain the resulting limitations. The authors should report the codec settings and implementation versions. A fair comparison is essential to support claims of improvement.

The evaluation should not rely on a single quality metric. Peak signal-to-noise ratio is useful for pixelwise fidelity but does not fully capture perceptual similarity. The paper should report structural measures such as SSIM or multiscale SSIM, if relevant to its stated objective. A perceptual metric may also be appropriate, provided its limitations are acknowledged. Rate-distortion curves should be shown across a meaningful range of bitrates. The paper should report aggregate results as well as variation across images. Confidence intervals or paired statistical tests would help establish whether small gains are reliable.

The bitrate calculation should be made transparent. The paper should distinguish bits per pixel from total file size. It should include the cost of coding the hyperlatent and any headers, padding, or metadata. If the reported rate is only an entropy estimate, that should be stated clearly. The authors should compare estimated rate with the actual output of an entropy coder. Small discrepancies can accumulate and may affect conclusions. Accurate accounting is especially important when claimed gains are modest.

Ablation studies are needed to show which components drive performance. The authors should compare the proposed model with an otherwise identical model that lacks the hyperprior. They should test alternative entropy models, such as a factorized prior or a simpler conditional model. They should also examine the effect of transform depth and latent channel capacity. If spatial context is included, its contribution should be separated from that of the hyperprior. An ablation on the rate-distortion weight would clarify how operating points affect quality and bitrate. These experiments would make the causal claims more persuasive.

The paper should investigate computational cost alongside compression efficiency. Learned codecs can incur substantial encoding and decoding time. The authors should report parameter count, peak memory use, and inference latency. Encoding and decoding times should be measured separately on specified hardware. If the entropy model requires sequential processing, that limitation should be discussed. The paper should compare complexity against relevant baselines where possible. Practical deployment depends not only on rate and distortion but also on speed and resource use.

The results section should support its claims with clear tables and plots. Tables should give exact rates and distortion values for each operating point. Rate-distortion curves should use consistent axes and identify all methods legibly. The paper should avoid drawing broad conclusions from a small number of examples. Visual comparisons should use the same crop, scale, and display conditions. It would be helpful to include crops showing texture, edges, and smooth regions. Such examples can reveal strengths and artifacts that aggregate metrics conceal.

The discussion should address likely failure cases. Learned codecs may perform differently on images outside their training distribution. The paper should examine whether performance changes on high-texture, low-light, or highly structured content. It should discuss potential artifacts, including blurring, ringing, block-like patterns, and loss of fine detail. If the model was trained on natural images, the authors should avoid assuming that the same results apply to medical, satellite, or document imagery. The scope of the conclusions should match the scope of the experiments. A thoughtful limitations section would improve the paper’s credibility.

The authors should also consider robustness and generalization. It would be useful to test the model on datasets not used during training. The paper should clarify whether test images differ in resolution or domain from training images. It should report performance for both familiar and shifted data, if feasible. The hyperprior may capture useful latent statistics, but its behavior under distribution shift is not self-evident. The authors should discuss whether retraining is required for new domains. These points matter for real-world use.

The presentation would benefit from clearer notation and terminology. Each latent variable should be introduced before it appears in equations. The paper should distinguish the learned transform from the probability model. It should define the role of the hyperlatent without assuming specialist knowledge. Acronyms should be expanded on first use. Equations should be accompanied by brief explanations of their practical meaning. These changes would make the work more accessible without reducing technical rigor.

The paper should ensure that its claims are calibrated to the evidence. If the method improves rate-distortion performance only at certain bitrates, that qualification should be explicit. If gains are limited to one metric or dataset, the conclusion should say so. The authors should avoid describing a statistically insignificant difference as a clear improvement. Any tradeoff between quality, bitrate, and complexity should be reported rather than obscured. This would give readers a more balanced account of the method’s value.

Reproducibility is another important concern. The authors should provide training details, including optimizer, learning-rate schedule, batch size, number of iterations, and initialization. They should state the random seeds or describe how repeated runs are handled. If code and pretrained models can be released, that would substantially strengthen the work. The paper should identify any external libraries or entropy-coding implementations that affect results. A compact reproducibility checklist would be useful. These measures would make independent verification more feasible.

The strongest aspect of the paper is its focus on entropy modeling as a central part of learned compression rather than as a minor post-processing step. The combination of a learned transform and a hyperprior is conceptually well motivated. The approach aligns representation learning with the statistical structure needed for efficient coding. The work also has potential practical relevance because coding efficiency directly affects storage and transmission costs. However, these strengths depend on rigorous evaluation and transparent implementation details. The paper should make that evidence central to its argument.

My overall assessment is that the topic is strong and the proposed direction is plausible, but the paper needs a more complete methodological and experimental account to support its claims. The most important revisions are to clarify novelty, specify the entropy model and rate accounting, and strengthen the baseline comparisons. A carefully designed ablation suite would establish the value of the hyperprior and each architectural choice. Broader evaluation metrics and complexity measurements would make the results more useful to practitioners. The authors should also improve reproducibility and narrow conclusions where evidence is limited. If these issues are addressed, the work could make a useful contribution to research on learned image compression. I recommend major revision before the paper is considered further.

However, the paper should define more precisely what “embedding” entails and distinguish its approach from learned heuristics, algorithm selection, and prediction-assisted algorithms. Robustness deserves further attention, particularly under distribution shifts and on inputs unlike those encountered during training. The authors should also explain how the conventional algorithm behaves when predictions are inaccurate and whether correctness or worst-case guarantees are retained. Overall, the direction is promising, but stronger experimental evidence and clearer analysis of reliability and cost are needed to support the paper’s claims.
