The bardiche was a long-handled polearm with a broad, curved blade, best known in Eastern Europe from the late Middle Ages onward. Its origins are uncertain, but related axe-like weapons appeared across northern and eastern Europe, where sturdy tools could also serve in battle. A typical bardiche had a wooden shaft and a wide iron or steel head, often attached along part of the shaft for strength. Designs varied: some blades were relatively short and compact, while others extended high above the wielder’s hands. The weapon could deliver forceful cutting blows and was useful against lightly armored opponents, though its weight made quick changes of direction difficult. In the 15th and 16th centuries, bardiches became especially associated with Muscovy and neighboring regions. Russian infantrymen, including the streltsy, carried them both as weapons and as supports for firearms when aiming or firing. Over time, the bardiche’s military role declined as firearms and other weapons changed, but it remains a distinctive example of Eastern European polearm design.

School governing bodies help guide a school and ensure it serves its students and community well. Their exact powers and duties vary by country and local law. Members may include parents, teachers, school leaders, community representatives, and sometimes students. A governing body usually sets the school’s overall direction and agrees on policies and priorities. It oversees the budget, checking that resources are used responsibly to support learning. Governors also monitor the school’s performance, including student progress, attendance, and safety. They may appoint or support the school leader and review how well the school is being managed. Governing bodies help make sure the school meets legal requirements and protects students’ welfare. They can provide a link between the school, families, and the wider community. Effective members ask informed questions, consider evidence, and act in the school’s best interests. They generally guide and oversee the school rather than manage its daily classroom activities.

One of my biggest dreams is to explore Kyoto, a city I have admired for years. I first became interested in it after seeing photographs of its temples and quiet streets. I imagine arriving in spring, when cherry blossoms soften the view of the old wooden houses. My first stop would be the famous Fushimi Inari Shrine. I would walk beneath its rows of bright red gates and listen to the peaceful sounds around me. I would also visit Kinkaku-ji, the Golden Pavilion, reflected in the still water of its garden. Each place would help me understand how history and beauty come together in Kyoto. I would love to wander through the Gion district and notice its traditional buildings. Perhaps I might see a geisha on her way to an evening appointment. I would try to be respectful and remember that the neighborhood is also home to many people. Food would be an important part of my adventure. I would taste warm bowls of ramen, fresh sushi, and sweet matcha desserts. At a small market, I would sample unfamiliar snacks and ask the vendors what they recommend. I hope to learn a few simple Japanese phrases before I go. Even saying “thank you” could help me connect with the people I meet. I would take a bus or train to see how residents travel through the city each day. In the evening, I would watch lanterns glow along a narrow street. I would keep a journal so I could remember the sights, flavors, and conversations. More than taking photographs, I would want to understand the feeling of the city. Exploring Kyoto would be a dream come true and an experience I would carry with me for the rest of my life.

How TTL Counter Chips Provide Minimal State Storage in Early Video Game Machines

Early video game machines often created their pictures with dedicated electronic circuits rather than storing complete images in memory. A display was drawn line by line as a television’s electron beam scanned across the screen. The game hardware had to know where the beam was at every moment and what should appear there. TTL, or transistor-transistor logic, chips helped perform this work using simple, fast digital circuits. Among these chips, counters provided a compact way to remember positions and timing.

A counter is a circuit that advances through a sequence of binary numbers. Each incoming clock pulse changes its stored value, usually by one. Because its output represents the current count, a counter also acts as a small amount of state storage. A four-bit counter, for example, can represent sixteen different values. Several counter chips connected together can track larger ranges.

Video hardware commonly used counters to follow the horizontal and vertical scan positions. A horizontal counter advanced with the pixel or timing clock as the beam crossed a line. When it reached the end of the line, it reset and signaled the vertical counter to advance. The vertical counter therefore tracked which line was being drawn. Together, these values identified the beam’s current position on the screen.

The machine could compare those counter values with stored settings. If the horizontal count matched an object’s chosen position, the circuit could begin drawing that object. A similar comparison with the vertical count determined which lines contained it. In this way, a few bits of position data could control a visible shape without storing every pixel. The counters supplied the changing coordinates, while logic gates decided what to display.

Counters could also generate timing signals. Certain count values marked the start or end of a line, the beginning of a frame, or intervals needed for synchronization with a television. A reset signal brought a counter back to its starting value at the right moment. Carry outputs allowed multiple chips to work together as a wider counter. This made counters useful both as memory and as timing machinery.

A game might represent a player’s paddle with a position value held in a counter or register. During each screen scan, comparison logic checked whether the beam was within the paddle’s horizontal and vertical range. If it was, the circuit changed the video output to draw the paddle. A ball could be handled in a similar way, with counters tracking its position and simple logic updating its movement. Collision detection could come from comparing the ball’s position with the boundaries of other objects.

This approach used far less storage than a full frame buffer, which would need a memory location for every pixel. It also reduced the need for a general-purpose processor and complex graphics hardware. TTL chips were available, fast, and suitable for building circuits from standard logic functions. Designers could create a game’s behavior by combining counters, registers, gates, and timing circuits.

The trade-off was that each object and rule often required custom hardware. Changing the game’s appearance or behavior could mean altering the circuit rather than editing software. The number of objects and their complexity were limited by available chips, wiring, and cost. Even so, clever circuit design could produce convincing motion and interaction with very little stored information.

TTL counters did not hold an entire game world or image. They held small, changing values such as screen position, timing phase, or object location. Those values were enough to guide the beam and make simple games feel responsive. Their role shows how early video games achieved interactive graphics through carefully organized state, not through large amounts of memory.

Daytime vessel signals help other mariners understand a vessel’s activity and maneuverability. Under the International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea, these signals are called shapes and are displayed during daylight. They are black shapes, or shapes that appear black, and must be shown where they can best be seen. The rules prescribe their number, dimensions, and spacing so that they are recognizable at a distance.

A vessel not under command displays two black balls in a vertical line. This means it cannot maneuver as required by the rules and cannot keep out of the way of another vessel. A vessel restricted in its ability to maneuver displays a black ball, a diamond, and another black ball, vertically arranged. This status applies to vessels whose work limits their ability to maneuver, such as certain survey, maintenance, or cable-laying operations.

A vessel engaged in fishing displays two cones with their points together, arranged vertically. This signal applies to fishing that restricts maneuverability; it does not apply to trolling or other fishing that does not do so. A vessel constrained by its draft may display a black cylinder. This indicates that its deep draft limits its ability to deviate from its course in the available water.

A vessel underway but not making way through the water displays two black balls in a vertical line. A vessel at anchor displays one black ball in the forward part of the vessel. A vessel aground displays three black balls in a vertical line, in addition to the anchor signal where applicable. These signals help distinguish a stationary vessel from one that is underway and maneuvering.

Some vessels display shapes that describe a specific operation. A vessel engaged in dredging or underwater work shows the restricted-maneuverability ball-diamond-ball signal, along with two additional balls on the side where an obstruction exists and two diamonds on the side where another vessel may pass safely. A vessel engaged in mine clearance displays three black balls, one near the foremast head and one at each end of the fore yard. These signals warn other vessels to keep clear.

A sailing vessel proceeding under power also displays a black cone, point downward, forward where it can best be seen. A vessel of less than 12 metres generally does not have to display the standard shapes, except where the rules specify otherwise. Day shapes do not replace safe navigation: mariners must still keep a proper lookout, assess risk of collision, and follow applicable give-way and stand-on rules. Because visibility, vessel type, and local conditions can affect what is required, crews should consult the current collision regulations and relevant navigation guidance.

Reading aloud can be a simple way to understand schoolwork more deeply. When students speak the words, they use both their eyes and their ears. This gives the brain more than one way to take in information. Saying each word also encourages readers to slow down and notice details. As a result, they may better understand unfamiliar phrases and difficult sentences. Reading aloud can make it easier to hear the main ideas and how they connect. It can also help students notice when a passage does not make sense. Vocal reading may improve memory because students actively repeat and hear the information. The sound of an important fact or definition can make it easier to recall later. Reading a passage aloud more than once can strengthen this effect. It also helps students become familiar with new vocabulary and correct pronunciation. These skills can support essay writing in several ways. Students who read their drafts aloud can hear awkward wording and incomplete sentences. They may also notice repeated ideas, missing transitions, or punctuation that interrupts the flow. Listening to a draft helps writers imagine how it will sound to a reader. Although vocal reading may not work equally well for everyone, it is a useful study and editing strategy. By reading aloud regularly, students can improve their comprehension, memory, and confidence as writers.

Families remembering relatives who fought and died at Passchendaele are keeping their stories alive more than a century after the battle.

Their accounts often begin with a name, a photograph and a few lines in a family Bible. From there, descendants piece together the lives of young men whose wartime experiences were rarely discussed at home.

The Third Battle of Ypres, commonly known as Passchendaele, began in July 1917 and lasted until November. British and Commonwealth forces fought German troops in the Belgian salient, amid relentless shelling and rain.

The bombardment destroyed drainage systems and turned the battlefield into a vast landscape of mud. Men struggled to move through waterlogged craters, while wounded soldiers faced the added danger of being trapped or drowning.

For many families, the battle is not just a date in a history book. It is the moment a letter stopped arriving, or a telegram brought news that changed a household forever.

Some descendants have found letters written from the front, preserved in drawers for generations. The messages can describe ordinary worries—family, food and the weather—alongside the uncertainty of military life.

Others have learned about their relatives through service records, casualty lists and memorial inscriptions. In some cases, those records are the only surviving evidence of a soldier’s life.

The stories often reveal how young the men were. Many had enlisted before adulthood, while others left jobs and families to serve overseas.

Family historians say the fragments can make the scale of the conflict feel personal. A name on a monument becomes a son, brother, husband or father with a place in a community.

One account may recall a man who never returned from the battlefield. Another may describe a relative who survived Passchendaele but carried its effects for the rest of his life.

The families’ experiences also differ in what was passed down. Some were told vivid stories by parents and grandparents, while others grew up knowing little beyond a date of death.

Silence was common in many households after the war. Relatives may have avoided talking about combat, grief or the injuries they had witnessed.

That absence can leave descendants with unanswered questions. It can also prompt them to search archives, visit former battle sites and speak with distant relatives.

At Tyne Cot Cemetery in Belgium, rows of headstones mark the graves of thousands of Commonwealth servicemen. The nearby memorial bears the names of those whose bodies were never identified or recovered.

For visitors, the landscape can be difficult to reconcile with the battle’s reputation. Today’s farms and villages sit close to ground where fighting once consumed entire fields.

Families who travel there often bring photographs or small personal tributes. Some pause at a grave, while others look for a name on the memorial wall.

Ceremonies marking the battle’s anniversary provide another opportunity to remember the dead. Descendants, veterans’ groups and local residents gather to reflect on the cost of the fighting.

Historians caution that family memories, while valuable, can sometimes blend with stories passed down from others. Comparing them with official records can help distinguish what is known from what remains uncertain.

But the meaning of a story does not rest only on precise details. For many relatives, the act of remembering is itself a way to restore a person to the family record.

The battle ended in November 1917, after months of fighting and heavy losses. Estimates of the casualties vary, but hundreds of thousands of Allied and German troops were killed, wounded or reported missing during the campaign.

Passchendaele has since become a symbol of the war’s brutality. Its name evokes not only mud and shellfire, but also the lives disrupted far from the front.

Families continue to uncover those lives in letters, photographs and fading documents. Each discovery adds detail to a history often told through military maps and casualty figures.

Some descendants share their findings with schools, museums and community groups. They hope the stories will help younger generations understand what service and loss meant for ordinary families.

Others keep the research within the family, recording names and memories for future relatives. Even a brief account can bridge the distance between generations.

More than a century later, the battle’s survivors are gone, but their family histories remain. Passchendaele is remembered not only as a place of sacrifice, but through the people whose absence was felt at home.

Perseverance and passion help people overcome setbacks and achieve their goals. Everyone faces difficulties at some point, but the way people respond can make a big difference. Perseverance means continuing to work even when progress is slow. Passion gives people a reason to keep going when a challenge feels difficult. Together, these qualities can turn a disappointment into a chance to learn.

For example, a student might struggle with a subject that once seemed easy. Instead of giving up after a low test score, the student can ask for help, study in small steps, and practice regularly. Improvement may take time, but each effort builds knowledge and confidence. A mistake can show someone what to work on next. With patience, the student may eventually reach a goal that once seemed out of reach.

Passion can also inspire people to pursue goals that require years of effort. An athlete, musician, or artist may face repeated failures before becoming skilled. They might feel discouraged, but remembering why they began can renew their motivation. Support from family, teachers, and friends can help, too. Still, success usually depends on the person choosing to continue despite setbacks.

Perseverance does not mean ignoring every obstacle or refusing to change direction. Sometimes people need to rest, seek advice, or try a different approach. These choices can be part of moving forward, not signs of failure. When people care deeply about their goals and keep learning from difficulties, they become more resilient. In the end, passion gives them a reason to strive, and perseverance helps them take the steps to succeed.

Community Strategies for Preventing Stroke, Recognizing Symptoms, and Ensuring Timely Emergency Treatment

A stroke happens when blood flow to part of the brain is blocked or when a blood vessel in the brain bursts. Brain cells can begin to die within minutes, so fast action matters. Stroke is a medical emergency, but many strokes can be prevented and their effects reduced through community awareness and timely care.

Prevention begins with understanding and managing common risk factors. High blood pressure is a leading risk factor, so community programs can help people check their blood pressure regularly and connect with health professionals. Diabetes, high cholesterol, smoking, physical inactivity, and some heart conditions also increase stroke risk. Atrial fibrillation, an irregular heartbeat, can allow clots to form and travel to the brain; people with this condition should discuss treatment with a clinician.

Healthy habits can lower risk. Eating more vegetables, fruits, whole grains, and other nourishing foods supports heart and blood-vessel health. Limiting excess salt, highly processed foods, and sugary drinks can help manage blood pressure and weight. Regular physical activity, adapted to a person’s abilities, benefits the heart and circulation. Avoiding tobacco and seeking help to quit smoking are important steps. People should take prescribed medicines as directed and talk with a health professional before making changes.

Communities can make healthy choices easier. Local governments and organizations can support safe walking routes, accessible recreation spaces, and affordable healthy food. Clinics, pharmacies, workplaces, faith groups, and schools can share reliable information and offer screening opportunities. Programs should be accessible to people of different ages, languages, abilities, and income levels. Community health workers can help residents understand risk factors, find care, and follow treatment plans.

Recognizing stroke symptoms is just as important as prevention. A common way to remember key signs is BE FAST: Balance problems, Eyesight changes, Face drooping, Arm weakness, Speech difficulty, and Time to call emergency services. A person may suddenly lose balance or have trouble seeing in one or both eyes. One side of the face may droop when the person smiles. An arm or leg may feel weak or numb, especially on one side of the body. Speech may become slurred, confused, or difficult to understand.

Other possible signs include sudden severe headache, dizziness, confusion, or trouble walking. Symptoms usually appear suddenly, but they may be mild or temporary. Even if symptoms go away after a few minutes, they may indicate a transient ischemic attack, sometimes called a mini-stroke. A transient ischemic attack is a warning sign that requires urgent medical assessment. Do not wait to see whether symptoms return or improve.

If stroke is suspected, call your local emergency number immediately. Do not drive the person to the hospital if an ambulance is available, because emergency teams can begin assessment and treatment on the way. Tell the dispatcher when symptoms began or when the person was last known to be well. This time can help clinicians decide which treatments are appropriate. If the person wakes with symptoms, report when they were last seen without symptoms.

While waiting for help, keep the person safe and calm. Help them sit or lie down, and loosen tight clothing. Do not give food, drink, or medicine, since swallowing may be impaired and some treatments may be unsafe. Do not give aspirin unless a medical professional instructs you to, because some strokes are caused by bleeding. If the person becomes unconscious or stops breathing normally, follow the emergency dispatcher’s instructions.

Timely treatment can limit brain injury and improve the chance of recovery. At the hospital, clinicians use examinations and brain imaging to determine whether the stroke is caused by a blockage or bleeding. Some people with a blocked artery may qualify for clot-dissolving medicine or a procedure to remove a clot, but treatment eligibility depends on clinical factors and time. This is why calling for help quickly is essential. After the emergency, rehabilitation and follow-up care can support recovery and help prevent another stroke.

Communities can strengthen emergency response by teaching residents to recognize symptoms and practice what to do. Public campaigns should emphasize calling emergency services rather than waiting, searching online, or contacting a family doctor first. Emergency services, hospitals, and community organizations can coordinate training and clear referral pathways. People can also learn local emergency numbers and keep them visible at home and work.

Everyone has a role in stroke prevention and response. Individuals can manage health risks, families can notice sudden changes, and neighbors can help someone get emergency care. Community leaders can promote access to prevention services and trustworthy health information. Remember: recognize the signs, note the time, and call emergency services immediately.

The paper addresses an important problem: neural architecture search (NAS) methods are difficult to compare when they use different datasets, training budgets, search spaces, or evaluation protocols. Its focus on a reproducible benchmark for fully trained convolutional networks is timely and potentially valuable to the research community. A well-designed benchmark could help distinguish genuine search improvements from gains caused by differences in implementation or computational resources. The paper’s strongest contribution is its emphasis on evaluating architectures after full training rather than relying only on proxy metrics or partial training. This choice improves practical relevance, although it also makes experiments substantially more expensive. The benchmark should clearly define the search space, dataset splits, preprocessing, optimization settings, and stopping criteria. It should also explain how each NAS method is adapted to the common setup, since implementation choices can materially affect results. The paper would be stronger with a more detailed account of the hardware, software versions, and random seeds required to reproduce every run. Reporting multiple independent runs is essential, because NAS outcomes can vary considerably with initialization and sampling. The authors should provide uncertainty estimates and avoid treating small differences in mean performance as decisive without statistical support. In addition to final accuracy, the evaluation should report search cost, training cost, inference latency, and model size. These measures would make the benchmark useful to researchers working under different resource constraints. It is also important to distinguish the cost of searching from the cost of fully training and evaluating the selected architecture. The paper should clarify whether all methods receive equal compute budgets and how those budgets are measured. A fixed search space supports controlled comparison, but it may favor methods whose assumptions align closely with that space. The authors should discuss this limitation and consider testing robustness across more than one search space or dataset. Benchmark maintenance and versioning also deserve attention, as changes to software or hardware can affect results over time. Releasing code, configurations, trained weights, and machine-readable results would substantially strengthen the reproducibility claim. Overall, this is a promising and useful benchmark proposal, but its value will depend on transparent protocol details, fair resource accounting, and careful treatment of variability. I recommend acceptance if these issues are addressed, particularly the reporting of repeated runs, compute budgets, and complete reproduction materials.

The paper addresses an important question: how recurrent neural networks can develop head-direction representations from self-motion cues under biologically plausible constraints. Its focus connects computational neuroscience with learning theory and could help clarify how directional signals emerge without explicit supervision. The central premise is compelling, particularly if the model learns a stable, continuous representation from realistic motion inputs. A major strength is the emphasis on circuit-level mechanisms rather than treating the network as a black box. The paper would be most convincing if it clearly distinguishes learned properties from those imposed by the architecture or training procedure. In particular, the authors should specify whether directional tuning, recurrent connectivity, or integration dynamics are built in or arise through learning. The motion-cue environment also needs careful description, including cue noise, sampling rate, and the range of trajectories used. Without this information, it is difficult to judge whether the reported representations generalize beyond the training conditions. The evaluation should include comparisons with relevant alternatives, such as nonrecurrent networks, networks trained without biological constraints, and simple path-integration models. Ablation studies could reveal which constraints are necessary for stable head-direction activity. The authors should also test robustness to changes in initial heading, movement speed, cue reliability, and accumulated drift. A key question is whether the network forms a genuinely continuous attractor or merely approximates one over the tested range. This distinction could be assessed by measuring the effects of perturbations and examining whether activity states move smoothly along the represented directional manifold. Claims of biological plausibility should be tied to specific features, such as local connectivity, plausible learning rules, or realistic neuronal dynamics. If these features are absent, the paper should frame biological plausibility more narrowly. The results would be strengthened by quantitative comparisons with known properties of biological head-direction circuits, not only qualitative similarity in tuning curves. The authors should report multiple random seeds and uncertainty estimates to establish that the findings are reproducible. It would also be useful to distinguish errors caused by sensory noise from errors arising from imperfect recurrent integration. Overall, the topic is timely and the proposed approach has the potential to provide useful insight into circuit formation. However, the strength of the conclusions depends on clearer controls, stronger tests of generalization, and more precise evidence for the claimed biological mechanisms. I recommend revision before publication.

The paper studies activation-aware product quantization for compressing neural network weights, with particular attention to structural redundancy and row permutations. The topic is timely: quantization can substantially reduce model storage and inference costs, while activation-aware methods offer a principled way to preserve task-relevant behavior. The focus on how row organization interacts with quantization is a useful extension beyond treating weight matrices as collections of independent vectors. Overall, the work addresses a practically important problem and suggests promising directions for improving compression.

The paper’s central strength is its attempt to connect quantization quality to the structure of the weights and their use during inference. Incorporating activation information can better reflect the functional impact of weight errors than minimizing unweighted reconstruction error. Product quantization is also attractive because it represents vectors using compact codebooks and indices, and can support efficient storage. The discussion of structural redundancy helps explain why some groups of weights may admit more effective shared representations than others. Examining row permutations is a particularly relevant idea, since reordering rows may expose patterns that are obscured by the original layout.

The paper would benefit from a more precise statement of its contributions. It should clearly distinguish the proposed algorithm from established activation-aware quantization and product-quantization methods. The authors should explain which steps are novel, which are adaptations, and what theoretical or empirical insight is new. A concise overview of the optimization objective, constraints, and inference-time representation would help readers understand the method early. The relationship between row permutation and the downstream computation should also be stated explicitly, including how any required inverse permutation is handled.

The experimental evaluation is central to the paper’s claims, and it should be designed to isolate the effects of each component. In particular, results should compare activation-aware and weight-only objectives, product quantization with relevant alternative quantizers, and permutation-based versus unpermuted configurations. Ablations that vary codebook size, subvector dimension, and permutation strategy would clarify which choices drive improvements. The paper should report both model-level task quality and compression metrics, including effective bits per weight after accounting for codebooks, indices, and metadata. It should also distinguish storage savings from actual inference speed or energy improvements, since compact representations do not necessarily yield faster execution.

Comparisons with strong and recent baselines are essential. These should use matched model checkpoints, calibration data, bit budgets, and evaluation settings wherever possible. If calibration data are required, the authors should specify its size and source and discuss the sensitivity of results to the calibration distribution. Evaluation across multiple architectures and model scales would establish whether the approach generalizes beyond a narrow setting. Reporting uncertainty across seeds or calibration samples would make small differences easier to interpret.

The treatment of structural redundancy could be strengthened by defining how redundancy is measured and connecting that measure to quantization outcomes. It would be useful to show whether the proposed method benefits consistently from different kinds of structure, rather than only from a particular observed pattern. The analysis of row permutations should include the cost and reproducibility of finding permutations, along with the effect of different permutation algorithms or random seeds. The authors should clarify whether permutations are fixed offline, learned jointly with codebooks, or selected through a separate optimization procedure. They should also discuss whether permutation information complicates model loading, batching, or compatibility with existing inference kernels.

A further concern is the computational cost of optimization. The paper should report training or preprocessing time, memory use, and any additional calibration requirements. It should clarify whether codebook construction scales practically to large transformer layers and whether quantization can be performed layer by layer. The deployment discussion would be stronger with evidence from a real inference implementation, or a candid explanation of why the evaluation is limited to storage and reconstruction metrics. Potential interactions with activation quantization, fine-tuning, and mixed-precision layers also deserve brief consideration.

The presentation should define notation consistently and provide enough implementation detail to reproduce the results. A pseudocode summary of the full pipeline, including permutation selection and codebook assignment, would be helpful. The paper should state how sensitive performance is to hyperparameters and how those values are chosen. Limitations, such as reliance on calibration data or possible benefits being model-specific, should be discussed openly.

In summary, this is a promising contribution on an important compression problem, and its attention to structural redundancy and row permutations could yield useful practical gains. The strongest evidence would come from carefully controlled ablations, comprehensive baseline comparisons, and a clear accounting of storage, runtime, and optimization costs. The paper’s impact will depend on establishing that its gains are robust across models and settings rather than artifacts of a particular configuration. I recommend revision with emphasis on methodological clarity, reproducibility, and stronger empirical validation.
