How electric–magnetic duality shapes entanglement growth from local excitations in four-dimensional Maxwell theory

Abstract

We study how electric–magnetic duality influences the growth of entanglement after a local excitation in four-dimensional free Maxwell theory. The theory admits a continuous rotation between electric and magnetic fields in the absence of charges and monopoles. Local operators can be chosen to transform nontrivially under this rotation, while the stress tensor and the equations of motion remain invariant. We focus on the vacuum-subtracted von Neumann entropy of spatial regions after insertion of a localized, gauge-invariant excitation. We distinguish universal conclusions from results that depend on the definition of the local operator, the ultraviolet regulator, or the treatment of gauge constraints at an entangling surface. The duality angle controls how electric and magnetic components are distributed, but it does not by itself change the propagation speed or the causal support of the excitation. In a free theory, the leading entanglement signal can be understood through the spread of the excitation’s one-particle wave packet and the algebra of observables accessible to each region. We explain why duality-related states have identical entanglement for appropriately duality-covariant regions and operator algebras, and why apparent differences can arise when electric and magnetic boundary data are treated asymmetrically. We also describe the role of edge degrees of freedom, the distinction between local and global sectors, and the limitations of particle-based interpretations. The resulting picture is that duality constrains entanglement growth strongly, but does not supply a universal numerical growth law independent of operator and regulator choices.

1. Introduction

Entanglement provides a sensitive probe of how quantum information is distributed in space. In relativistic quantum field theory, local excitations offer a controlled way to study this distribution. One can prepare an excited state by acting on the vacuum with a local operator and then compare the entanglement of a spatial region before and after the excitation. The resulting excess entropy depends on the field content, the operator, the geometry, and the time elapsed since preparation. Gauge theories add a further complication because the physical Hilbert space does not factorize naively across spatial boundaries. Maxwell theory is a particularly useful setting for addressing these issues. It is free, relativistic, and conformally invariant in four spacetime dimensions. It also possesses electric–magnetic duality, a symmetry that exchanges the field strength with its Hodge dual. This duality gives a precise way to ask whether entanglement growth tracks electric and magnetic character or only the underlying propagation of degrees of freedom.

In this paper, we examine that question for local excitations in four-dimensional Maxwell theory. Our aim is not to assert a single universal formula for entanglement at all times. Rather, we identify the symmetry statements that hold independently of detailed regulator choices, and we make explicit where further choices enter. The main conclusion is that duality rotates the electric and magnetic content of an excitation without changing its causal propagation. When the state, observable algebra, and regulator are all transformed consistently, duality-related preparations have the same entanglement. If only the state is rotated while the regional algebra is held fixed in a way that distinguishes electric from magnetic flux, the entropy can appear to change. Such a difference reflects the chosen algebraic or boundary prescription rather than a violation of the bulk duality equations.

The discussion is organized as follows. Section 2 introduces the Maxwell theory and its duality transformation. Section 3 describes local excitations and the notion of excess entanglement. Section 4 addresses the Hilbert-space and algebraic subtleties of gauge fields. Section 5 analyzes entanglement growth and its symmetry constraints. Section 6 discusses the particle and wave-packet pictures. Section 7 considers conformal symmetry, global sectors, and duality anomalies. Section 8 outlines a practical calculation strategy. Section 9 summarizes limitations and possible extensions.

2. Maxwell theory and electric–magnetic duality

We work in four-dimensional Minkowski spacetime with metric signature convention chosen so that the Maxwell action is
S = -1/(4g^2) ∫ d^4x Fμν Fμν,
with the appropriate metric contractions understood. Here Aμ is the gauge potential, Fμν = ∂μAν - ∂νAμ is the field strength, and g is the gauge coupling. In the absence of electric currents, the equations of motion are ∂μFμν = 0. The Bianchi identity is ∂μ(*F)μν = 0, where *F denotes the Hodge dual. These two equations have the same form. This observation underlies electric–magnetic duality.

In terms of electric and magnetic fields, the source-free equations are ∇·E = 0, ∇·B = 0, ∂tB = -∇×E, and ∂tE = ∇×B, up to conventional factors associated with the definition of g. A continuous duality rotation acts as Eθ = E cos θ + B sin θ and Bθ = B cos θ - E sin θ. Equivalently, Fθ = F cos θ + *F sin θ, with a sign that depends on the convention for the Hodge star. The energy density, momentum density, and stress tensor are invariant under this rotation. The equations of motion are also invariant in the source-free theory. The coupling does not enter the classical equations after a suitable normalization, though it matters in the canonical normalization of fields and in the quantization of charged sectors.

A local gauge-invariant operator that transforms under duality can be constructed from the field strength. For example, a complex self-dual combination F+ = F + i*F transforms by a phase under duality. Its Hermitian components correspond to electric- and magnetic-type operators. A real smeared operator may be written as Oθ(x) = cos θ OE(x) + sin θ OM(x), where OE and OM denote appropriately chosen electric and magnetic field-strength components or derivatives thereof. The exact form must be specified to define a physical state. A field-strength insertion at a point is an operator-valued distribution, so a finite-energy state generally requires smearing in spacetime or space.

The duality transformation is simplest in the topologically trivial, source-free sector of the theory. Electric charges obstruct the naive conservation of magnetic flux in the same way that magnetic monopoles obstruct the naive conservation of electric flux. In the presence of both kinds of charges, duality acts on the charge lattice and may be reduced from a continuous symmetry to a discrete subgroup. The present analysis primarily concerns the free photon sector without charged matter or monopoles. This restriction is appropriate for isolating the effect of duality on entanglement generated by local photon excitations. It should not be confused with a statement that all global sectors of Maxwell theory are duality invariant in an identical manner.

3. Local excitations and excess entropy

Let |0⟩ denote the vacuum, and let O be a local gauge-invariant operator smeared around a spatial point or a compact spacetime region. A normalized excited state can be prepared as |Ψ⟩ = N O|0⟩, where N is a normalization constant. For a spatial region A at time t, we denote the reduced state by ρA(t). The vacuum-subtracted entropy is ΔSA(t) = SA(t) - SA,0, where SA,0 is the vacuum entropy of A. This subtraction removes state-independent ultraviolet divergences when the same regulator and algebra are used for both states. It does not automatically remove every divergence associated with gauge constraints or operator singularities. A well-defined calculation therefore requires a specified smearing procedure and a specified definition of the regional degrees of freedom.

A local operator does not create a perfectly localized particle. It creates a superposition of momentum modes, with a spatial profile set by the smearing function and the operator’s spectral content. At early times, the excitation is localized near its preparation region. At later times, its wave packet propagates outward at the speed of light in the free theory. For a region whose boundary is crossed by the wave packet, the reduced state changes as degrees of freedom become accessible on both sides. The resulting entanglement growth is sometimes described using a quasiparticle picture. That language can be useful, but it must be applied cautiously to a gauge field, since the photon’s polarization and the Gauss constraints affect the regional decomposition.

For a local operator with definite duality charge, the relation between electric and magnetic preparations is particularly transparent. If O+ transforms as O+ → exp(iθ)O+, then acting with O+ on the vacuum changes the state only by an overall phase when the vacuum is duality invariant. Such a phase has no effect on entanglement. This statement applies when the transformation is represented as a symmetry on the relevant Hilbert space and when the operator is an eigenoperator of that symmetry. In practice, a real electric operator is generally a sum of operators with opposite duality charges. Rotating it can then change the relative phases of components, even though the full duality transformation remains a symmetry. The entanglement of the rotated state is nonetheless unchanged if the regional algebra and state are both transformed by the same unitary symmetry.

It is useful to separate three questions. The first is whether two preparations are related by a duality transformation. The second is whether the regional observable algebra is invariant under that transformation. The third is whether the regulator and boundary prescription respect it. If all three answers are yes, the entropies agree. If any answer is no, a difference can occur without contradicting duality of the local field equations. This separation will guide the rest of the paper.

4. Gauge constraints and regional algebras

In an ordinary tensor-product quantum system, one writes the Hilbert space as HA ⊗ HĀ and defines ρA by tracing over the complement. Gauge theories do not generally admit this factorization in terms of gauge-invariant physical degrees of freedom. Gauss’s law relates the electric flux through the boundary of A to the charge inside A. In pure Maxwell theory, the corresponding constraint is that the divergence of the electric field vanishes in the bulk. The magnetic field obeys an analogous constraint through the Bianchi identity. These relations couple data on opposite sides of the boundary.

One common approach is to define a local algebra of gauge-invariant observables supported in A. This algebra may be chosen to include or exclude operators measuring flux through the boundary. Different choices can have different centers, meaning sets of operators that commute with every element of the algebra. Another approach is to enlarge the Hilbert space by adding boundary or edge degrees of freedom, so that a tensor-product decomposition becomes available before imposing the physical constraints. These approaches can lead to different entropy assignments, especially in their boundary contributions. They are not simply interchangeable numerical conventions, because they encode different choices about which observables are regarded as belonging to the region.

For Maxwell theory, an electric-center prescription treats normal electric flux at the boundary as central data. A magnetic-center prescription instead emphasizes magnetic flux. Duality exchanges these two descriptions. Consequently, a calculation that privileges electric flux need not display manifest invariance under a duality rotation that exchanges electric and magnetic variables. A duality-covariant prescription must transform the regional algebra together with the fields, or otherwise include the boundary data symmetrically. In that setting, the entropy relation follows from unitary equivalence.

The universal short-distance terms in entanglement entropy can also be delicate. For a spherical region in a conformal field theory, the logarithmic term is related to the conformal anomaly. In four-dimensional Maxwell theory, the precise accounting of this term has historically depended on how gauge degrees of freedom at the entangling surface are represented. A consistent treatment of the anomaly, edge modes, and the chosen algebra is essential when comparing duality-related states. State-dependent differences may be finite while state-independent boundary contributions are not, but this separation should be verified within a common regulator rather than presumed.

The local bulk equations alone do not determine a unique entropy for a subregion. They determine correlation functions and dynamics once a state is specified, but a regional entropy additionally requires an algebra or factorization prescription. Therefore, a claim that electric and magnetic excitations produce different entanglement must specify what is being held fixed at the boundary. Conversely, a claim of exact equality must state whether the duality transformation acts on the boundary variables and on the regulator.

5. Duality constraints on entanglement growth

Suppose a duality transformation Uθ is represented unitarily on the physical Hilbert space. Let |Ψθ⟩ = Uθ|Ψ⟩. For any region A with algebra AA, define the transformed algebra as UθAAUθ−1. The restriction of |Ψθ⟩ to that transformed algebra has the same entropy as the restriction of |Ψ⟩ to AA. This follows because unitary conjugation preserves the spectrum of the reduced state, or, in algebraic language, preserves the state–algebra pair up to isomorphism. The equality is exact under the assumed implementation.

If instead one compares the states |Ψ⟩ and Uθ|Ψ⟩ using the same fixed algebra AA, the entropy equality follows only when Uθ maps AA to itself. A duality rotation of the local field strengths may map an electric-centered algebra to a magnetic-centered one rather than leaving it unchanged. In that case, equality is not guaranteed for the fixed algebra. The difference is an algebraic effect, not evidence that the two states propagate differently. This distinction is especially important when discussing edge modes or flux sectors.

For a duality-covariant setup, the time evolution commutes with the duality symmetry. The Hamiltonian and stress tensor are duality invariant in the source-free theory. Thus, if the initial state and the regional algebra are transformed consistently, the full time-dependent entanglement curves agree. In particular, the onset time for entanglement production is unchanged, because the causal propagation of the wave packet is unchanged. The location of any entropy peak and the subsequent decay or saturation are also mapped to corresponding locations by the same symmetry. The detailed shape of the curve depends on the operator’s smearing and on the region’s geometry, but not on the duality angle when the comparison is fully covariant.

This statement does not mean that every electric operator and every magnetic operator have identical entanglement in every fixed operational setup. A detector designed to couple only to electric fields defines a different measurement context from one designed to couple only to magnetic fields. Likewise, an algebra that records electric flux but not magnetic flux is not invariant under the exchange. Such setups can distinguish duality-rotated preparations. The distinction is physically meaningful if the apparatus or boundary condition genuinely breaks the symmetry. It is not a universal property of the source-free Maxwell vacuum.

The growth of excess entropy can be characterized by its temporal regimes. Immediately after a sharply localized insertion, the state differs from the vacuum only near the insertion, subject to the nonzero tails introduced by smearing. If the excitation begins inside A, the region initially contains most of its localized profile. As the wave packet approaches the boundary, correlations between the inside and outside portions increase. Once the packet is largely outside, the excess entropy may decrease, although the exact behavior depends on whether the operator creates one wave packet, several correlated components, or a broad continuum of modes. The duality angle does not alter these kinematic stages in a symmetric setup.

A simple schematic description represents the excitation as a pair of correlated outgoing wave packets. If one member lies in A and the other in its complement, the entropy of A is elevated. As both members enter the same side, that contribution can diminish. In a local field theory, the operator generally creates a continuum rather than a literal pair of sharply defined particles. The pair picture is therefore an approximation whose quality depends on energy resolution and the operator’s spectral profile. Duality rotates the polarization content of each photon but leaves this spatial correlation structure unchanged.

The leading state-dependent contribution can often be related to changes in two-point functions or to a modular-energy expectation value. For sufficiently small perturbations of the vacuum, the first variation of entropy obeys the entanglement first law, δSA = δ⟨KA⟩, where KA is the vacuum modular Hamiltonian for the region. For a ball in a conformal field theory, the modular Hamiltonian is a local integral of the energy density with a known position-dependent weight. Since the Maxwell stress tensor is duality invariant, the first-order entropy variation is duality invariant for duality-related perturbations and a duality-covariant region. At higher orders, entropy depends on more detailed correlation data, but unitary symmetry still enforces equality when the full state–algebra pair is mapped.

The first-law result is useful but limited. Local operator insertions can produce nonperturbative states whose entropy change is not small. Moreover, pointlike insertions may yield singular energy and entropy profiles. A finite smearing scale provides a controlled perturbation only when its normalization and amplitude are chosen appropriately. It is therefore unsafe to infer the full time-dependent entropy from the stress tensor alone. Stress-energy invariance constrains the energy distribution, but entropy also depends on quantum correlations and on the regional algebra.

6. Photon modes and the wave-packet picture

In four dimensions, the free Maxwell field has two physical photon polarizations. In a helicity basis, duality rotations act as opposite phases on the two helicities. This makes the symmetry action on one-particle states particularly simple. A duality eigenstate can be chosen to have definite helicity, and a local field-strength operator can create a superposition of such states. The duality angle changes the relative coefficients of helicity components for a generic real operator. It does not change their dispersion relation, since both polarizations have energy ω = |k|.

The entanglement of a one-photon wave packet across a spatial partition is not determined solely by its helicity. It depends on the wave function in momentum space, including its polarization and spatial profile. If the duality transformation acts as a momentum-independent phase within each helicity sector, then the reduced state of a suitably defined spatial algebra is unitarily related to the original one. This gives a mode-based version of the symmetry argument. However, localization of photons is subtle, and the decomposition into sharply localized photon modes is not unique. A field-algebra calculation is often more robust than assigning particles to points.

There is a further distinction between a local gauge-invariant excitation and a charged excitation. A local insertion of Fμν creates photons without introducing an electric charge. A charged operator requires a nonlocal dressing, such as a Wilson line or a Coulombic field extending to infinity. Such dressings carry long-range fields and can alter entanglement across a boundary in ways that are not captured by the local wave-packet picture. Electric and magnetic charged dressings are exchanged by duality, but their boundary conditions and allowed charge sectors must be transformed as well. The present results should not be applied to charged states without including these contributions.

A pointlike field-strength insertion also contains ultraviolet components of arbitrarily high energy. The apparent sharpness of its causal front is accompanied by singular local observables. Smearing the operator over a spatial width ℓ regularizes these features and introduces a timescale of order ℓ. At times much larger than ℓ, a coarse-grained propagation picture may be appropriate. At times comparable to ℓ, the entropy curve is sensitive to the precise smearing. Duality continues to constrain the result if the smearing is applied equally to electric and magnetic components.

The number of polarization degrees of freedom and the absence of a longitudinal propagating photon in the physical spectrum are both relevant to entanglement. Gauge fixing can introduce unphysical components in intermediate calculations. These components must cancel from gauge-invariant observables or be accounted for through constraints and ghosts in a covariant quantization. A calculation that assigns entanglement independently to gauge-dependent field components can therefore produce spurious polarization dependence. Duality comparisons should be performed using physical states and gauge-invariant regional observables.

7. Conformal symmetry, topology, and quantum duality

Four-dimensional source-free Maxwell theory is classically conformally invariant. Conformal transformations can map certain region geometries and causal domains into one another. For example, the vacuum reduced state of a ball has a modular flow related to a conformal transformation. This structure can simplify perturbative entropy calculations for spherical regions. It does not eliminate the need to specify the gauge-theory algebra, but it gives a controlled framework for studying the local response of the vacuum.

The classical duality rotation is not always a symmetry of the full quantum theory in the strongest possible sense. Global flux sectors, charge quantization, and the periodicity of the gauge field can restrict the allowed rotations. In a compact gauge theory with quantized electric and magnetic charges, the duality group often becomes discrete. In curved backgrounds, the duality current can also exhibit an anomaly associated with gravitational topology. These facts are not typically relevant to a local, flat-space calculation in the trivial photon sector, but they matter when making global statements about exact quantum invariance.

Even when a continuous rotation is not a symmetry of the full theory, discrete duality transformations may relate selected sectors. Entanglement comparisons must then be performed between states in the sectors that are actually mapped into one another. A local perturbative calculation in the vacuum can still exhibit the classical rotation of the photon field, while nonperturbative global data break the continuous symmetry. The distinction between perturbative local dynamics and global quantum structure should be maintained.

The entangling surface itself can carry data associated with electric or magnetic flux. On a manifold with nontrivial topology, there may be harmonic modes or discrete flux sectors that are not represented by local photon oscillators. These modes can contribute to the entropy, and their transformation under duality can be nontrivial. For simply connected regions in flat space and states in the trivial sector, such contributions may be absent or reducible to boundary terms. More general topologies require separate treatment.

A duality-covariant entropy prescription is most naturally formulated by transforming the full operator algebra, including its center and any edge variables. If the duality transformation has an anomaly or fails to act within the chosen sector, exact equality can be modified. Such modifications are expected to be tied to global or boundary data rather than to a change in local photon propagation. Identifying that distinction is crucial for interpreting any measured duality dependence.

8. A practical calculation framework

A concrete calculation begins by specifying the spacetime dimension, metric convention, and normalization of the Maxwell action. One then chooses a gauge-invariant operator O and a smearing function f. The normalized state is |Ψ⟩ = N O[f]|0⟩. The region A, its time evolution, and the algebra associated with it must be fixed. A regulator should be selected that treats the state and vacuum consistently. If the goal is to test duality, the regulator and algebra should be duality covariant or their noncovariance should be documented.

In a free theory, the state can often be characterized through correlation functions. For a Gaussian state, the reduced density matrix is determined by the restricted two-point functions of the canonical variables. A local operator acting linearly on the field creates a state that may be non-Gaussian in a strict sense, depending on the operator and normalization. For quadratic observables or coherent displacements, Gaussian methods can nevertheless be useful. One should not assume Gaussianity for an arbitrary field-strength insertion without checking it.

Canonical quantization in a spatial slice can express the theory in terms of transverse electric and magnetic modes. Gauss’s law imposes ∇·E = 0, and the Bianchi identity imposes ∇·B = 0. The duality transformation mixes these transverse variables. To compute a regional entropy, one can use a lattice regulator, a continuum algebraic method, or an extended Hilbert-space construction. Each method makes different boundary choices explicit. Comparisons across methods are meaningful only after matching these choices.

A lattice calculation offers direct numerical access but can obscure continuum duality if the discretization treats electric and magnetic variables differently. A compact lattice gauge theory has discrete flux sectors and may realize duality only at special couplings or through a transformation between distinct formulations. A continuum calculation can preserve the local symmetry more transparently but must control distributional operator insertions and boundary terms. Both approaches can be informative when their limitations are stated.

One useful diagnostic is to compute the excess entropy for a family of angles θ and test whether it is constant under a duality-covariant prescription. A second diagnostic is to transform the algebra along with the state and compare the two reduced spectra. A third is to repeat the calculation with electric- and magnetic-center choices. If the results differ only by boundary contributions or by center-dependent terms, that pattern supports the interpretation that the discrepancy is tied to regional data rather than bulk dynamics.

The entanglement first law provides an independent check for small perturbations. One can calculate the change in the expectation value of the vacuum modular Hamiltonian and compare it with the linear entropy variation. For a ball, the modular Hamiltonian is determined by the stress tensor. Since the stress tensor is duality invariant, the linear response should be independent of θ under a consistent comparison. A failure of this test can signal an inconsistent normalization, a gauge-dependent operator, an untransformed boundary prescription, or a regulator artifact.

To study growth in time, one should evaluate the state on a sequence of spatial slices and track the same algebraic prescription at each time. A finite smearing width makes the initial condition well defined. The region can be chosen as a ball, half-space, or another geometry with known causal structure. The evolution of the wave packet can then be compared with the change in entropy. Numerical and analytic results should distinguish the onset of growth, the peak, and late-time behavior, rather than compressing the entire history into a single rate.

No single rate of entanglement growth is expected for all choices of operator and region. The local excitation may contain a narrow or broad frequency distribution. The region may intercept a small or large fraction of the wave packet. The operator may create one dominant helicity or a balanced helicity superposition. These details determine the numerical curve. Duality constrains how the curve changes under a consistent rotation, but it does not fix the curve from symmetry alone.

9. Interpretation and limitations

The phrase “electric excitation” can refer to several distinct constructions. It may mean a field-strength component such as F0i, an operator that couples to an electric detector, a state with electric flux at a boundary, or a charged state carrying electric charge. These constructions need not have the same entanglement properties. Their magnetic counterparts are likewise distinct. Any quantitative claim should identify which meaning is intended.

For a local photon excitation in the source-free theory, electric and magnetic components are not independent species. They are related through the equations of motion and the duality rotation. A polarization-based interpretation is often more appropriate than treating them as separate kinds of particles. The entanglement growth is then governed by how the photon’s spatial and polarization correlations are divided by the region. Duality changes the polarization basis while preserving the underlying free propagation.

This conclusion does not make electric–magnetic distinctions unobservable. Boundaries, material media, charges, monopoles, and detector couplings can break or reduce duality. A conducting boundary, for example, imposes boundary conditions that privilege particular components of the electromagnetic field. In such a system, duality-related excitations need not have identical regional entropies. The difference is then a consequence of the symmetry-breaking environment and should be included in the physical model.

Similarly, a thermal state or a state with a background flux may not be invariant under the same duality transformation as the vacuum. The entanglement response can then depend on the orientation of the excitation relative to the background. The vacuum result should not be extrapolated automatically to these cases. A systematic extension would classify the state, the operator, the algebra, and the boundary conditions under the residual duality group.

The results also depend on working in four dimensions. The role of duality, conformal invariance, and the number of propagating polarizations varies with spacetime dimension. In other dimensions, the Hodge dual of a two-form has different rank, and the dual theory may involve a gauge potential of another degree. The general symmetry argument still applies when an exact unitary duality exists, but the detailed local algebra and edge structure can change substantially.

A further limitation is that the von Neumann entropy is only one measure of quantum correlations. Relative entropy, mutual information, and Rényi entropies can be more robust under changes in ultraviolet regulator or can isolate correlations between separated regions. Duality should constrain these quantities through the same state–algebra mapping, although their sensitivity to boundary sectors may differ. Mutual information between disjoint regions is often finite and may offer a cleaner observable for testing duality in numerical studies.

Relative entropy is particularly useful because it is well defined for a pair of states on a fixed algebra and obeys strong positivity properties. A duality transformation maps the relative entropy of one state pair to that of the transformed pair when the algebra is transformed as well. This provides a regulator-independent formulation of the symmetry constraint in many settings. It does not remove the need to choose the algebra, but it can reduce dependence on additive entropy counterterms.

10. Conclusion

We have examined the role of electric–magnetic duality in entanglement growth after local excitations of four-dimensional Maxwell theory. In the source-free photon sector, duality rotates electric and magnetic field strengths while preserving the equations of motion, the stress tensor, and the photon dispersion relation. It therefore does not alter the causal propagation of a local wave packet. For a duality-covariant definition of the regional algebra and regulator, duality-related states have identical entanglement at every time. This follows from the unitary equivalence of the complete state–algebra pair.

The qualification concerning the regional algebra is essential. Gauge constraints prevent a unique naive factorization of the physical Hilbert space. Choices involving electric flux, magnetic flux, centers, or edge modes can treat the two sides of the duality differently. If the state is rotated but the boundary prescription is not, an apparent change in entropy can occur. Such a difference is not, by itself, a contradiction of bulk duality. It indicates that the comparison has retained a duality-breaking feature of the observable algebra, regulator, boundary, or global sector.

The time dependence of excess entropy is controlled by the spatial profile of the excitation, its smearing, the geometry of the region, and the correlations created by the operator. A quasiparticle picture can provide intuition but is not exact for generic local insertions in a gauge field. The entanglement first law supplies a useful perturbative check, since the Maxwell stress tensor is duality invariant. Beyond linear response, the full correlation structure matters, while the exact symmetry statement continues to hold whenever its assumptions are satisfied.

Several directions merit further study. Explicit calculations with duality-covariant edge-mode prescriptions would clarify the finite boundary contributions. Lattice simulations could test the symmetry constraints while tracking how discretization affects electric and magnetic variables. Relative entropy and mutual information may provide particularly clean diagnostics. Extensions to compact gauge theories, charged matter, monopoles, curved backgrounds, and nontrivial topologies would reveal how global sectors and anomalies modify the local vacuum result.

The central lesson is that electric–magnetic duality shapes entanglement growth primarily by constraining comparisons, not by imposing a universal growth curve. It identifies which electric and magnetic preparations are physically equivalent when the complete setup respects the symmetry. It also pinpoints the circumstances in which a measured difference is meaningful: the environment, algebra, boundary prescription, or global sector must distinguish the duality partners. With these qualifications, entanglement provides a precise way to separate the symmetry of Maxwell dynamics from the choices required to define spatial quantum information.
