At 3:17 in the morning, every screen on Earth went black.

Phones lost their bars, radios fell silent, and satellites stopped answering. In the city of Marrow Bay, Dr. Lena Voss watched the lights blink out across the harbor. The darkness was so complete that people began shouting just to prove they were still there.

Then the bells in the old cathedral rang once. They had no power, and no one had touched them.

Lena ran to the observatory, where her grandfather’s notebooks lay in a locked cabinet. He had spent his life studying a prediction carved into a stone tablet beneath the cathedral. Its oldest line read, “When the world loses its voice, the buried sun will open its eye.”

For years, Lena had called it a metaphor. Now the ground beneath her feet began to tremble.

Across the harbor, the sea pulled away from the shore. Boats settled onto the mud as if an invisible hand had drained the bay. Beyond them, a black ridge rose from the ocean, shedding water in glittering sheets.

People gathered on the beach, staring. At the ridge’s center, a red light appeared and slowly widened. Lena understood then that the “buried sun” was no sun at all. It was an enormous machine, sealed beneath the seabed before human history began.

Her grandfather’s final note named it the Listener. It had been built to hear every voice on Earth, and the blackout was its first breath. Lena found a second line carved into the tablet’s rubbing: “It wakes to silence, and answers with the end.”

The red light brightened. A low tone rolled over the water, too deep to hear and too powerful to ignore. Windows shattered throughout the city, though no one heard them break.

Lena climbed the cathedral steps and pulled the great bell’s rope. The bell rang again, then again. Around her, people began shouting names, songs, prayers, anything that could make a sound. The Listener’s light flickered.

Lena understood the last part of her grandfather’s note. The machine could hear every human voice, but it could not understand a single voice alone. It was searching for a world speaking as one.

So she began a simple rhythm: three knocks, a pause, three knocks. The crowd copied her, pounding doors, walls, and the stones beneath their feet. Soon the whole city was beating out the same uneven pulse.

Across the bay, the red light shuddered. The ridge sank inch by inch beneath the waves. One by one, the cathedral bells joined the rhythm, though no hands pulled their ropes.

At 3:42, the lights returned. Phones rang, radios crackled, and satellites began to answer. The sea rushed back over the harbor mud.

People cheered, then fell quiet. On every screen, across every network, the same words appeared: “WE HEARD YOU.”

Lena looked toward the dark water. Far below, something answered with three slow knocks.

Learning can be fun when we explore new ideas through music, science experiments, and theater. Songs help us remember facts, practice new languages, and share feelings. In science, simple experiments let us see how things work with our own eyes. We can mix safe ingredients, grow plants, or test which objects float. Theater gives us a chance to act out stories and understand different people. Working together on a play also builds confidence and teamwork. These activities make learning exciting and help us remember what we discover.

The government is facing accusations of secrecy after blocking the publication of a risk register linked to its NHS reforms.

The document is understood to outline potential problems that could arise as changes to the health service are introduced. Campaigners and opposition politicians say the public should be able to examine those risks.

Ministers have declined to release the register, arguing that disclosure could undermine the policy process. The government has said officials need space to assess possible outcomes frankly while reforms are being developed.

Critics say that explanation does not justify keeping information about a major public service from patients and taxpayers. They argue that the public has a right to know how changes might affect care, staffing and access to services.

The dispute has intensified scrutiny of the government’s plans for the NHS. Reform proposals can involve changes to how services are organised, funded and delivered, making their possible consequences a matter of widespread concern.

Opposition figures have called for the register to be published in full. Some have also urged ministers to release a version with genuinely sensitive material removed.

Health campaigners say withholding the document risks weakening confidence in the reforms. They argue that early disclosure could help identify problems before they affect patients.

Ministers, however, say the reforms are intended to improve the health service and that the decision on publication should not be taken as evidence of hidden failings. They maintain that the risk register is part of internal planning rather than a final assessment of the policy.

The government’s position has revived a broader debate about transparency in public decision-making. Officials often produce risk assessments to weigh potential benefits against possible harms, but such documents are not always made public.

Critics say the distinction between internal advice and information of public interest is especially important when decisions affect essential services. They have questioned whether keeping the register confidential serves the public or simply limits scrutiny.

The row may also complicate efforts to build support for the reforms. Without access to the underlying assessment, opponents say, it is harder for Parliament and the public to judge whether safeguards are adequate.

The government has not indicated whether it will reconsider its decision. The dispute is likely to continue as ministers press ahead with the NHS changes and campaigners demand greater openness.

The paper presents a neural machine translation approach that combines dependency-parse structure with recurrent sequence representations of the source sentence. Its central idea—encoding source words in a graph informed by syntactic dependencies—could help the model capture long-distance relationships that standard sequence encoders may overlook. The topic is relevant, and the proposed integration of structural and sequential information is potentially valuable. The paper would be stronger if it clearly distinguished its contribution from prior syntax-aware translation methods and explained how dependency information enters the encoder and decoder. It should also report the datasets, language pairs, preprocessing choices, and parsing tools in sufficient detail for reproducibility. Evaluation should include strong contemporary baselines, ablation studies isolating the effects of graph encoding and recurrent representations, and appropriate significance testing. Translation quality metrics are useful, but targeted analysis of syntactic phenomena and representative translation examples would better demonstrate the method’s specific benefits. The authors should discuss how parsing errors affect performance and whether the approach generalizes across languages with different syntactic properties. Overall, the work addresses an important problem and offers a promising direction, but its claims should be supported by clearer methodological detail and more comprehensive evaluation. I recommend revision before acceptance.

Nokia has challenged a small startup’s use of the name “HERE,” arguing that it could confuse customers about who provides its services. The dispute centers on the startup’s branding and Nokia’s rights in the HERE name, which is associated with mapping and location technology.

In a formal objection, Nokia reportedly said the startup’s use of the term risks creating an impression of a connection between the two businesses. The company has not publicly detailed every point in its case, and the startup’s response was not immediately available.

Trademark disputes often turn on how similar names are used, the products or services involved, and whether consumers are likely to mistake one company for another. The word “here” is also an ordinary term, which can make the scope of any trademark claim a key issue.

Nokia’s challenge does not by itself establish that the startup has infringed a trademark. The matter could be resolved through negotiations, a change to the startup’s branding, or a decision by the relevant trademark authority or court.

The startup’s size may shape the practical stakes, but it does not determine the legal outcome. Smaller companies can face significant costs in defending a name, while established firms often argue that they must act to protect their trademarks.

The case also highlights the difficulty of choosing distinctive names in crowded technology markets. Businesses increasingly use short, familiar words for apps and digital services, raising the possibility of overlap across industries.

Neither company has disclosed whether talks are underway. For now, the dispute leaves the startup’s future use of “HERE” uncertain and could offer a further test of how trademark rights apply to common words.

Digital devices have become a regular part of everyday life. Phones, tablets, computers, and televisions help people communicate, learn, and relax. However, relying on them too much can create problems at home and at school. When screens take up most of a person’s attention, important relationships and experiences may suffer.

One way excessive device use weakens family bonds is by reducing face-to-face conversation. Family members may sit together at dinner while each person looks at a separate screen. They can share a room without sharing their thoughts or feelings. Over time, small conversations that once helped people feel close may happen less often. Parents may miss chances to learn about their children’s worries, interests, and achievements. Children, in turn, may feel that their parents are not fully listening to them. Devices can also interrupt family activities, such as games, walks, and celebrations. These moments are valuable because they help families build memories and trust.

Digital devices can affect friendships and other relationships as well. Text messages and social media make it easy to stay in touch, but they do not always provide the warmth of an in-person conversation. Online communication can lead to misunderstandings because people cannot always see tone or facial expressions. Constant notifications may also interrupt conversations with friends. When someone repeatedly checks a phone while another person is speaking, the speaker may feel ignored. Social media can make people compare their lives with carefully selected images of others. This comparison may cause jealousy, loneliness, or pressure to appear perfect. Healthy relationships need attention, honesty, and time, not just frequent online contact.

Students’ focus can also be weakened by excessive screen use. Notifications encourage students to switch between homework, games, videos, and messages. Each interruption can make it harder to return to a task. As a result, assignments may take longer and include more mistakes. Students may also remember less when they try to study while watching videos or checking messages. Late-night screen use can interfere with sleep, leaving students tired in class. Without enough rest, it becomes more difficult to concentrate, learn new ideas, and manage emotions. Technology is useful for schoolwork, but students need to use it with purpose.

Another cost of constant device use is the loss of meaningful experiences. A person who records every moment may spend less time enjoying it. Children and adults can miss the sights, sounds, and feelings of the world around them. Outdoor play, hobbies, reading, and quiet reflection may be replaced by scrolling. These activities can help people discover their interests and develop patience and creativity. Real experiences also teach skills that screens cannot fully provide, such as cooperating, solving problems, and noticing others’ feelings.

The answer is not to reject technology completely. Digital devices can help families communicate across distances and give students access to useful information. The goal is to create a healthier balance. Families can set aside screen-free time during meals or before bed. Students can silence notifications while studying and take regular breaks. Friends can agree to put their phones away when spending time together. These simple choices can make room for more listening, attention, and shared activity. When people use devices thoughtfully, technology can support their lives instead of taking them over.

Scotland’s suicide rates are closely linked to deprivation, prompting renewed calls to tackle inequality and improve support for people at risk.

Public health experts say people living in the most deprived areas face a substantially higher risk of suicide than those in the least deprived communities. The pattern has been highlighted in calls for a stronger response that addresses both immediate mental health needs and the wider conditions shaping people’s lives.

Deprivation can involve low income, insecure work, poor housing and limited access to services. These pressures may compound one another, increasing distress while making it harder to find timely help. Campaigners say the relationship is complex and does not mean that poverty alone determines an individual’s risk.

They are urging the Scottish Government and local authorities to strengthen services and reduce the social inequalities that can contribute to poor mental health. Priorities include easier access to counselling, crisis support and treatment, particularly in communities where services are under pressure.

Supporters also want more help available through schools, workplaces, housing services and community organisations. They say frontline staff should be equipped to recognise signs of distress and guide people towards specialist care. Services, they add, need to be accessible without long waits or complicated referral processes.

People with lived experience should help shape those services, advocates say. They argue that support is more likely to work when it reflects the realities facing individuals and families. That includes recognising the effects of debt, unemployment, discrimination and isolation.

Health professionals stress that suicide is rarely caused by a single factor. Mental illness, relationship breakdown, bereavement and physical health problems can all play a part, alongside economic hardship. They caution against treating deprivation as a simple predictor of an individual’s circumstances.

The calls come amid broader concern about pressure on mental health services and the uneven impact of the cost of living. Charities say people in crisis need rapid, compassionate responses, while longer-term prevention requires investment in secure housing, decent jobs and accessible care.

Officials have said suicide prevention requires action across government and society, not solely within health services. They point to national strategies and local initiatives, though campaigners say progress should be measured against clear outcomes and the experiences of those seeking help.

They are also calling for better data to identify gaps in support and understand which interventions make a difference. Such information could help direct resources to communities facing the greatest need, while protecting privacy and avoiding stigma.

Advocates say no one should have to reach crisis point before receiving help. They want sustained funding for community-based support, alongside efforts to reduce poverty and improve access to essential services.

Anyone worried about their own safety or someone else’s should contact emergency services if there is immediate danger. In Scotland, people can also call NHS 24 on 111 for urgent health advice, or Samaritans free on 116 123, at any time.

King Arven ruled a kingdom built around a silver river.  
Its people believed the river had been poured into the world by the Maker Above.  
They believed the Maker had shaped every mountain, seed, and storm.  
Arven believed it too, until the river began to run backward.  
First the fish vanished.  
Then wells filled with salt.  
Then the moon appeared at noon, pale as a cracked egg.  
The priests said the Maker was testing his people.  
Arven asked them what lesson could be learned from dead wells.  
They answered that doubt was a lesson in itself.  
Arven summoned them to the palace court.  
He placed a clay bowl before them and filled it with water.  
“Did the Maker make this bowl?” he asked.  
“Of course,” said the high priest.  
“Then why does it leak?” asked Arven.  
The priests frowned.  
“Because the potter shaped it poorly,” one said.  
Arven nodded toward the sky.  
“And if the world leaks, who shaped it poorly?”  
Before the priests could answer, thunder split the clouds.  
A voice rolled down from above.  
“I made the world perfect,” it boomed.  
“Then why is the river running backward?” Arven called.  
“Why are the wells salty?”  
“Why does the moon wander where it does not belong?”  
The voice went silent.  
Arven climbed the palace tower and shouted again.  
“Did you forget the laws you gave the stars?”  
A seam opened in the heavens.  
Rain poured through it in shining sheets.  
The people fled to the hills, but the hills began to sink.  
Arven ordered every shipwright to build one enormous vessel.  
He asked no priest for permission.  
He asked every family to bring tools, seeds, and animals.  
They worked through the dark beneath a sky that had split like cloth.  
The Maker watched, but offered no plan.  
Arven called up to the clouds.  
“Can you not mend your own roof?”  
The thunder answered with a groan.  
Water swallowed the fields.  
Water climbed the towers.  
The great vessel rose from its cradle and turned toward the eastern mountains.  
Arven stood at its prow, guiding it by the stars that still held their places.  
For forty days, the world vanished beneath the flood.  
The Maker’s voice returned only once.  
“Why did you not trust me?” it asked.  
Arven gripped the rail as waves struck the hull.  
“Why did you not build a world that could endure?” he replied.  
No answer came.  
At last, the rain stopped.  
The vessel settled against a mountain peak.  
When the water withdrew, Arven led the survivors down to the mud.  
They found the river running forward again.  
They found the wells sweet beneath the stones.  
The people asked whether the Maker had saved them.  
Arven looked at the patched vessel and the hands that had built it.  
“The world was saved by those who noticed its flaws,” he said.  
Then they planted seeds, and the first green shoots rose from the ruin.

William Shakespeare is one of the most quoted writers in the English language.
His plays and poems have given readers memorable lines about love, ambition, grief, time, and human nature.
These quotations often appear in everyday conversation, though their original contexts may be more complex than their familiar uses suggest.
Reading them in context can reveal how Shakespeare’s characters think, argue, and change.
Shakespeare wrote for the theater, so many of his most famous lines are spoken aloud by characters.
His language blends striking imagery, wordplay, rhythm, and emotional intensity.
He also wrote 154 sonnets, many of which explore love, beauty, desire, and the passage of time.
The quotations below offer an introduction to this rich literary legacy.

“Shall I compare thee to a summer’s day?” opens Sonnet 18.
The speaker asks whether the beloved should be compared with a summer day.
Summer can be beautiful, but it is brief and sometimes harsh.
The speaker argues that the beloved’s beauty will endure in the poem’s lines.
The sonnet is a meditation on art’s power to preserve what time would otherwise diminish.
Its promise of immortality is poetic rather than literal.
The line is famous partly because it begins with a direct, memorable question.

“Let me not to the marriage of true minds admit impediment” begins Sonnet 116.
Here, marriage suggests a steadfast union of minds and spirits.
The speaker says that genuine love does not change when circumstances change.
The poem compares love to a fixed star that guides ships through uncertain seas.
This image makes love seem constant, even when people cannot measure its full worth.
The sonnet is often read at weddings, although its claims are idealized.
It presents love as a commitment that withstands time and difficulty.

“Love looks not with the eyes, but with the mind” appears in A Midsummer Night’s Dream.
Helena speaks the line while reflecting on love and attraction.
Her words suggest that affection can shape how a person sees another.
The play complicates this idea through its magical changes and romantic confusions.
Characters fall in and out of love under the influence of a potion.
The comedy shows how desire may be irrational, shifting, and difficult to control.
The quotation therefore expresses an insight while also inviting playful skepticism.

“If music be the food of love, play on” begins Twelfth Night.
Duke Orsino speaks these words as he dwells on his love for Olivia.
He asks for music, hoping that it will satisfy or perhaps exhaust his desire.
The metaphor compares love to an appetite that can be fed.
Yet Orsino’s language can sound theatrical, revealing his enjoyment of his own feelings.
The play contrasts his romantic speeches with the practical wit of other characters.
The line captures both the intensity and the self-dramatizing side of love.

“All the world’s a stage, and all the men and women merely players” comes from As You Like It.
The melancholy Jaques delivers the speech in which this line appears.
He compares human life to a play with entrances, exits, and changing roles.
The speech describes seven stages, from infancy through old age.
Its theatrical metaphor encourages readers to consider how identity changes over time.
It also suggests that people perform roles shaped by family and society.
The passage is memorable for turning an ordinary theater image into a philosophy of life.

“Some are born great, some achieve greatness, and some have greatness thrust upon ’em” is spoken in Twelfth Night.
The sentence appears in a letter designed to deceive the character Malvolio.
Its grand tone persuades him that Olivia secretly admires him.
The quotation is often repeated as sincere advice, but its comic context matters.
Malvolio takes the message seriously and behaves in increasingly foolish ways.
Shakespeare uses the episode to make ambition, vanity, and self-deception comic.
The line shows how words can inspire someone while also manipulating them.

“Now is the winter of our discontent” opens Richard III.
Richard speaks the line as he reflects on the political change that has followed the end of conflict.
The image of winter suggests hardship, while the approaching summer suggests relief.
Richard soon reveals that peace does not satisfy him.
He plans to pursue power through deception and violence.
The speech establishes his intelligence and ambition, as well as his bitter view of the world.
The quotation is frequently shortened, but the full thought depends on its contrast between winter and summer.

“Uneasy lies the head that wears a crown” comes from Henry IV, Part 2.
King Henry speaks it while thinking about the burdens of rule.
A crown may represent authority, but it also brings anxiety and responsibility.
The king contrasts his sleeplessness with the rest enjoyed by ordinary workers.
The line gives a personal dimension to political power.
It suggests that status can bring worries rather than comfort.
Shakespeare often portrays rulers as vulnerable people, not merely symbols of government.

“The better part of Valour, is Discretion” is a line from Henry IV, Part 1.
Falstaff says it after finding a reason to avoid danger in battle.
The saying means that good judgment may be wiser than reckless courage.
Falstaff’s comic cowardice makes the line amusing.
At the same time, it expresses a sensible idea about survival.
Shakespeare often lets foolish or comic characters speak truths that more serious characters overlook.
The quotation’s humor comes from the gap between Falstaff’s grand phrasing and his self-interest.

“Beware the Ides of March” is spoken in Julius Caesar.
A soothsayer warns Caesar about the date associated with his assassination.
Caesar dismisses the warning, helping to establish his confidence and pride.
The phrase became a lasting expression of foreboding.
In the play, however, the warning is only one sign among many that Caesar’s power is threatened.
The tragedy explores ambition, political loyalty, public persuasion, and the consequences of violence.
Its famous line invites audiences to notice how characters interpret warnings differently.

“Et tu, Brute?” is traditionally associated with Caesar’s final moments in Julius Caesar.
The Latin phrase means “And you, Brutus?”
It expresses shock at being betrayed by someone Caesar regards as close.
The precise wording varies among editions and performances of the play.
The phrase has become a cultural shorthand for personal betrayal.
Its force depends on the relationship between Caesar and Brutus, not just the words themselves.
The scene asks whether Brutus’s actions are motivated by public duty, personal rivalry, or both.

“To be, or not to be: that is the question” begins a soliloquy in Hamlet.
Hamlet considers whether it is better to endure suffering or resist it.
His reflections turn toward death, uncertainty, and the fear of what may follow.
The speech is not a simple statement of a wish to die.
It is a careful exploration of thought, hesitation, and the limits of human knowledge.
Hamlet’s ability to analyze every possibility also helps prevent him from acting.
The quotation remains powerful because it gives a universal shape to a deeply personal crisis.

“There is nothing either good or bad, but thinking makes it so” is another line from Hamlet.
Hamlet says it while speaking with Rosencrantz and Guildenstern.
The words suggest that experience is shaped by a person’s judgment and perspective.
They do not mean that every action is morally equivalent.
Instead, the line points to the complexity of interpreting events.
Hamlet’s own thoughts often make his world feel more painful and uncertain.
The quotation invites readers to ask how much of their experience comes from circumstances and how much from interpretation.

“What a piece of work is a man!” appears in Hamlet.
Hamlet begins by praising human beings as remarkable in reason, ability, and form.
He then confesses that humanity no longer delights him.
The speech moves from admiration toward despair.
That contrast shows how a person’s emotional state can change the meaning of the same facts.
The passage is often quoted as a celebration of human potential.
Its full context, however, includes Hamlet’s deep disappointment with the world.

“Out, damned spot! out, I say!” is spoken by Lady Macbeth in Macbeth.
She imagines that blood remains on her hands long after Duncan’s murder.
The spot represents guilt that cannot be washed away.
Earlier in the play, Lady Macbeth dismisses the idea that guilt will overwhelm her.
Her sleepwalking scene reveals how badly that confidence has failed.
The quotation turns an invisible moral burden into a vivid physical image.
It is one of the play’s strongest portrayals of guilt and psychological collapse.

“Fair is foul, and foul is fair” is a chant spoken by the witches in Macbeth.
The paradox blurs the boundary between what appears good and what is evil.
It prepares the audience for a world of deception and moral confusion.
Macbeth’s rise to power depends on appearances that conceal violent intentions.
The line also shows how language in the play can unsettle ordinary certainty.
Its balanced rhythm makes the paradox especially memorable.
Readers can use it as a guide to the play’s recurring theme of misleading appearances.

“Brevity is the soul of wit” comes from Hamlet.
Polonius says it while giving a speech that is notably long and indirect.
The mismatch between his words and his behavior creates comedy.
The line has since become advice to express ideas concisely.
Its original setting makes the advice more complicated than a simple rule.
Shakespeare often creates humor by letting characters reveal themselves through the way they speak.
This quotation is both a memorable maxim and a joke about its speaker.

“Parting is such sweet sorrow” appears in Romeo and Juliet.
Juliet says it as she and Romeo reluctantly say good night.
The phrase combines opposing emotions: sadness at separation and sweetness in love.
Its oxymoron reflects the play’s intense emotional language.
The young lovers experience joy and fear in quick succession.
The line is often quoted to describe any affectionate farewell.
In the play, it also foreshadows how love and sorrow will become inseparable.

“Romeo, Romeo, wherefore art thou Romeo?” is Juliet’s famous question in Romeo and Juliet.
The word “wherefore” means “why,” not “where.”
Juliet is asking why Romeo must belong to the family that her family treats as an enemy.
Her speech focuses on names and whether a name can define a person.
She wonders if Romeo could be separated from his family identity.
The scene is about social division as much as romantic longing.
Knowing the meaning of “wherefore” makes the quotation’s emotional point clearer.

“For never was a story of more woe than this of Juliet and her Romeo” closes Romeo and Juliet.
The Prince speaks these words after the lovers have died.
The line frames their private tragedy as a public lesson for Verona.
The feud between their families has helped bring about the deaths.
The closing speech emphasizes the cost of hatred and delayed reconciliation.
Its formal rhythm gives the play a solemn ending.
The quotation also reminds readers that the lovers’ story belongs to the whole community.

“Cowards die many times before their deaths; the valiant never taste of death but once” comes from Julius Caesar.
Caesar speaks these words while dismissing fears about danger.
The sentence expresses his belief that living in fear can resemble repeated death.
It also reveals his confidence, which may shade into overconfidence.
The play tests whether bravery is wisdom or simply pride.
The line’s balanced structure makes it sound like a proverb.
Its dramatic context encourages readers to question the certainty behind the maxim.

“Give every man thy ear, but few thy voice” is advice from Polonius in Hamlet.
He tells his son Laertes to listen widely and speak selectively.
The advice recommends attentiveness and restraint.
Polonius’s other behavior, however, can be intrusive and meddlesome.
That contrast makes it useful to distinguish a character’s good advice from the character himself.
The line is often applied to conversation and judgment.
It also reflects Shakespeare’s interest in how people gather information before acting.

“The course of true love never did run smooth” is spoken in A Midsummer Night’s Dream.
Lysander says it while discussing the obstacles faced by lovers.
The play includes parental opposition, mistaken identities, and magical interference.
Its comic plot eventually resolves many of these difficulties in marriage.
The line acknowledges that love may encounter obstacles without claiming that every obstacle is tragic.
Its relaxed, conversational phrasing makes it easy to remember.
It remains one of Shakespeare’s most familiar observations about romance.

Shakespeare’s quotations endure because they combine memorable language with questions that remain relevant.
They can sound like complete sayings, yet their meaning often deepens when read in the full scene or poem.
A quotation may reveal a character’s wisdom, vanity, fear, or misunderstanding.
The speaker’s circumstances are therefore part of the quotation’s meaning.
Readers can also notice how Shakespeare uses contrasts, such as love and sorrow or appearance and reality.
His metaphors make abstract ideas visible through images of stars, seasons, stages, and blood.
His wordplay can shift a line from serious reflection to comedy.
The same passage may support different interpretations in different performances.
Actors bring changes of tone, pace, and emphasis to the printed words.
That flexibility is one reason the plays continue to be performed around the world.
When studying a quotation, identify its speaker and the situation in which it is spoken.
Then consider the surrounding lines and the character’s motives.
Finally, ask how the language shapes the audience’s response.
This approach turns familiar sayings into invitations to read more closely.
Shakespeare’s literary quotations are not just ornaments of English.
They are small entrances into the dramatic worlds and human questions his writing continues to explore.

The paper addresses an important question: whether perceptual sensitivity measured from neural-network features can predict human image-quality judgments and guide image generation. Its strongest potential contribution is connecting a measurable model property to both evaluation and practical generation outcomes. The work would benefit from a clearer definition of “perceptual sensitivity” and a stronger rationale for the selected neural-network features. The authors should explain how human judgments were collected, how agreement was quantified, and whether the evaluation set represents varied image content and distortions. Comparisons with established perceptual metrics and relevant neural-network baselines are essential to show that the proposed measure adds value. The analysis should also distinguish correlation with human ratings from causal usefulness in improving generated images. For the generation experiments, details of the optimization procedure and suitable controls would help rule out gains caused by prompt, sampling, or compute differences. Reporting uncertainty, effect sizes, and results across multiple datasets would make the conclusions more robust. Limitations—such as dependence on the tested model, image domain, or participant population—should be discussed explicitly. Overall, the topic is promising, but the paper’s claims will be convincing only if its methods, comparisons, and evidence for practical utility are sufficiently rigorous.

The Pinault family has returned two bronze animal heads from Beijing’s Old Summer Palace to China, decades after their removal amid foreign looting. The sculptures, depicting a rat and a rabbit, once formed part of a fountain clock commissioned for the imperial gardens in the 18th century. British and French troops looted the palace in 1860 during the Second Opium War, scattering its artworks around the world.

The heads resurfaced at auction in Paris in 2009, where their sale sparked anger in China and renewed calls for their return. Chinese officials and cultural groups argued that the objects had been taken unlawfully and should not be treated as ordinary market commodities. The auction’s planned buyer, French fashion executive François-Henri Pinault, later acquired the works through his family’s company.

In 2013, the Pinault family announced that it would donate the sculptures to China. They were subsequently handed over to the National Museum of China in Beijing, where they became part of the country’s efforts to recover and display cultural heritage taken abroad. The return was widely welcomed by Chinese officials, though it did not resolve broader disputes over artworks removed during colonial-era conflicts.

The rat and rabbit are two of the 12 zodiac animal heads created for the palace fountain. Several other heads have also returned to China through purchases and donations, while some remain missing. The episode continues to illustrate how high-profile auctions can bring contested objects—and questions of ownership and restitution—back into public debate.

Teaching English functional writing skills helps learners communicate effectively in everyday and professional situations. These skills include writing emails, forms, messages, instructions, letters, and short reports. Begin by identifying learners’ needs, language levels, and the situations in which they will use English. Set a clear lesson objective, such as writing a polite request email or completing a form accurately. Teach the purpose, audience, and typical structure of the chosen text before asking learners to write. Present a model text and guide students to notice useful phrases, tone, and layout. Explain key language features, including verb forms, sentence patterns, punctuation, and formal or informal expressions. Break the lesson into manageable stages: introduce the task, explore the model, practise language, plan, draft, and review. Provide sentence starters, word banks, checklists, and graphic organizers to support learners who need them. Encourage students to use these resources as scaffolds, gradually reducing support as their confidence grows. Include short, focused practice activities, such as arranging sentences, completing a message, or correcting a sample text. Give learners a realistic writing task with a clear purpose and audience. Adapt the task by offering different levels of support, alternative topics, or extension challenges. Pair and group activities can help students discuss ideas and give one another constructive feedback. Teach learners to review their writing for meaning, organization, grammar, spelling, and tone. Use simple rubrics that explain what successful writing looks like and make assessment criteria clear. Digital tools and printable classroom materials can be adapted to different ages, contexts, and access needs. With structured teaching and flexible resources, learners can build practical writing skills they can use beyond the classroom.

Starting seeds indoors gives you more control over a plant’s early growth and can extend your growing season. Transplanting carefully helps seedlings adjust to outdoor conditions and continue growing without a setback. Success starts with choosing plants suited to your climate and the space available in your garden. Check seed packets for days to maturity, preferred temperatures, and whether a crop is best sown indoors or directly outdoors. Some plants, such as carrots and radishes, usually do better when sown directly because their roots dislike disturbance. Tomatoes, peppers, and many flowers are often good candidates for starting indoors.

Use clean containers with drainage holes, such as seed trays, pots, or recycled containers that have been thoroughly washed. Fill them with a fresh, fine-textured seed-starting mix rather than heavy garden soil. Moisten the mix before sowing so it is evenly damp but not waterlogged. Follow the seed packet for planting depth, since some seeds need light while others should be covered. If the packet gives no guidance, a common rule is to sow a seed about twice as deep as its width. Place one or two seeds in each cell, then label each variety with its name and sowing date.

Keep the mix consistently moist while seeds germinate, using a gentle spray or bottom-watering to avoid washing them away. A clear cover can hold in moisture, but remove it once seedlings emerge to improve airflow. Many seeds germinate best with warmth, though the ideal temperature varies by plant. After emergence, provide strong light for about 12 to 16 hours daily using a bright window or grow lights. Keep lights close enough to prevent stretched, weak stems, while following the fixture’s safety instructions. Rotate containers near a window so seedlings receive light evenly. Water when the surface begins to dry, and empty any standing water from trays.

Once seedlings develop their first true leaves, thin crowded cells by snipping weaker sprouts at soil level. Handle seedlings gently, and avoid pulling them if that might disturb neighboring roots. Begin feeding only when needed, using a diluted, balanced fertilizer according to its label. Before planting outdoors, harden seedlings off so they can adapt to sun, wind, and cooler temperatures. Start about seven to ten days before transplanting by placing them outdoors in a sheltered, shaded spot for a short period. Gradually increase their time outside and exposure to direct sunlight each day. Bring them indoors during harsh weather, and do not let them dry out during this adjustment.

Transplant when seedlings are sturdy, the soil is workable, and outdoor temperatures suit the crop. Check local frost dates, but also follow the plant’s temperature needs; warm-season crops can be harmed by cold nights even after the last frost. Choose a cloudy day or work in the late afternoon to reduce stress from heat and sun. Water seedlings well before removing them from their containers. Prepare the garden bed by loosening the soil and removing weeds, then dig holes wide enough for the roots. Space plants according to the seed packet or plant label so they have room for air, light, and mature growth.

Ease each seedling out by supporting its leaves or root ball, not by squeezing or pulling its stem. Set it at the depth it grew in the container, except for tomatoes, which can often be planted deeper along their stems. Firm soil gently around the roots and water thoroughly to settle the soil and remove large air pockets. Add a light layer of mulch, keeping it away from stems, to help conserve moisture and limit weeds. Shade newly transplanted seedlings temporarily if the weather is bright or hot. Check soil moisture frequently during the first week and water when the root zone begins to dry. Watch for wilting, pests, and signs of disease, and respond promptly without overwatering. With thoughtful preparation, gradual hardening, and steady aftercare, seedlings can establish strong roots and thrive in the garden.

At first, people blamed the observatories when the nearest stars began to vanish. One by one, familiar points dimmed from the night sky, though no telescope could find a cause. The Sun remained, steady and warm, and life went on beneath it. Children learned constellations from old books, tracing stars that no longer shone. Cities switched off their brightest lights, hoping darkness might coax the missing ones back. It did not, but people discovered that the Milky Way looked grander without the glow of distant towns. Farmers planted by moonlight and the habits of the seasons, no longer checking star charts. Sailors trusted compasses, then satellites, then the coastlines they could see. The news grew quieter as each disappearance became less surprising than the last. At night, neighbors gathered on rooftops to share tea and point out what was still there. They gave the empty patches names, as if the stars had moved into another country. Some mourned; others felt a strange relief at having fewer immensities to worry about. Years passed, and children stopped asking when the stars would return. Humanity did not solve the mystery; it simply learned to make a home under a smaller sky.

Mara found the notebook beneath a loose floorboard in the rented room. Its black cover was warm, though the house had been empty for years. On the first page, someone had written, “Write a name, and the heart will stop.” Mara laughed at the melodrama and wrote her own name.

A sharp pain tightened her chest. She fell beside the bed, clawing at the floorboards. Then the room went dark.

Mara woke on the same boards, gasping, with the notebook open beside her. Her name had vanished from the page. A new line had appeared beneath it: “One life restored.”

She should have thrown the notebook into the river. Instead, she tested it on a dead moth, then on a mouse caught in a trap. The moth twitched back to life. The mouse sprang from her palm and vanished under the dresser.

That evening, a stranger knocked on her door. He was thin, pale, and smiling as if they had already shared a joke. “You found it,” he said, glancing at the notebook. “I’ve been looking for you.”

Mara asked who he was. “Elias,” he replied. “I wrote the first name.”

Before she could shut the door, he stepped inside. He told her the notebook was a bridge between dying and returning, but it needed practice. “People are more reliable than mice,” he said.

Mara gripped the notebook against her chest. Elias’s smile widened. “You’ve already proved it works on yourself. Now let’s see what it can do for someone else.”

He reached for her. She snatched up a pen and wrote his name. Elias crumpled without a sound, his smile still fixed on his face. For a moment, Mara could hear only the rain.

Then the notebook’s pages began to turn by themselves. A line appeared: “One life ended. One life owed.”

Elias’s body jerked. He drew a ragged breath and sat up, delighted. “There,” he whispered. “That’s the part I love.”

Mara stumbled toward the door, but Elias stood first. He looked at her with bright, hungry eyes. “Again?” he asked.

She tore the page from the notebook. Elias seized her wrist, and the pen skittered across the floor. The ripped paper smoked between them, letters fading into ash.

For the first time, his expression faltered. Then he laughed softly and reached for the pen. Mara realized he was not afraid of dying. He was eager to find out how many times he could come back.

Outside, someone hurried up the steps. Elias turned toward the knock, still smiling. Mara grabbed the notebook and opened to a blank page.

This time, she wrote no name. She wrote: “Let the dead stay dead.” The house shuddered, and every light went out.

When the darkness lifted, Elias was gone. The notebook lay cold in Mara’s hands, its pages blank. From somewhere beneath the floor came a patient tapping, as if someone were waiting to be written back.

Assessing a child’s readiness to stay home alone involves more than checking their age. Laws and recommendations vary by location, so first learn the rules where you live. Consider your child’s maturity, judgment, confidence, and ability to follow instructions. A child who is responsible in familiar situations may still feel frightened or overwhelmed when alone. Readiness is individual, and siblings of the same age may differ.

Talk with your child openly about staying home alone before making a decision. Ask how they feel about it and listen without pressuring them to say yes. Discuss possible situations, such as a phone call, a power outage, or someone knocking at the door. Notice whether your child can explain safe choices and ask for help when needed. Children should know that they can contact you or another trusted adult at any time.

Assess practical self-care skills as well as emotional readiness. Your child should be able to use the phone, communicate their address, and reach emergency services if necessary. They should know how to lock and unlock doors safely and understand not to let strangers inside. Teach them not to share online or in person that they are home alone. They should also know which adults are approved to visit or pick them up.

Review household hazards together. Explain how to avoid fire, medicines, cleaning products, weapons, and other dangerous items. Make sure these items are secured and that your child knows not to use appliances or equipment you have not approved. Teach basic fire safety, including how to leave the home and where to meet outside. Discuss what to do if they smell smoke, see a fire, or hear a smoke alarm.

Create a clear plan for ordinary needs and unexpected events. Write down your contact information, emergency numbers, a nearby trusted adult, and the home address. Agree on check-in times and how your child should contact you if plans change. Set simple rules about food, visitors, outdoor activities, and caring for younger siblings. Keep the instructions easy to find, and review them together.

Build independence gradually rather than starting with a long absence. Begin with a brief period while you remain nearby, then discuss what went well and what felt difficult. Increase the time only when your child is comfortable and consistently follows the plan. Avoid leaving a child alone overnight or for longer than they can manage safely. Reassess readiness after changes in routine, health, or family circumstances.

Preparation should include practicing self-care tasks your child may need to handle. These might include preparing a simple snack, managing personal hygiene, and keeping the home secure. Practice using the phone and responding to realistic scenarios through role-play. Make sure your child knows they can choose not to stay alone and can tell you if they feel unsafe. A successful plan balances growing independence with dependable adult support.

Amputation, according to the most overconfident physicians of the imaginary School of Cutting Things Off, is the universal remedy for any complaint that can be attached to a limb. A sore finger? Remove the hand; a blistered toe? The foot has clearly outlived its usefulness. Its chief advantage is that the original symptom can no longer bother the patient in quite the same way. Unfortunately, this treatment may introduce larger problems, including permanent disability, infection, and the need to explain why a paper cut required a surgeon. Modern medicine sensibly rejects amputation as a cure for minor ailments and favors treatments suited to the actual problem. The entry is satire, not medical advice: consult a qualified health professional rather than anyone carrying a saw.

Cirrhosis in children is a long-term condition in which healthy liver tissue is replaced by scar tissue.
As scarring builds up, the liver can become stiff and have trouble doing its many jobs.
The liver helps digest food, process medicines, store energy, and remove waste from the blood.
Cirrhosis usually develops gradually, although the underlying liver problem may begin early in life.
It is not contagious and cannot spread from one child to another.

Many different conditions can cause cirrhosis in children.
Some children are born with inherited disorders that affect how the liver handles substances such as copper, iron, or certain proteins.
Biliary atresia, a condition in which bile ducts are absent or blocked, is an important cause in infants.
Other bile-duct disorders can also damage the liver over time.
Long-term hepatitis B or C infection may cause cirrhosis, though vaccination and modern treatments have reduced some of these risks.
Autoimmune hepatitis occurs when the immune system mistakenly attacks the liver.
Some metabolic diseases, cystic fibrosis, and certain heart conditions can also lead to liver scarring.
In some cases, medicines or toxins cause lasting liver injury.
Sometimes doctors cannot identify a clear cause.

Symptoms vary depending on the cause and how much the liver is affected.
Early cirrhosis may cause few or no noticeable symptoms.
A child may feel tired, weak, or less interested in food.
Nausea, poor appetite, or discomfort in the upper right part of the abdomen may occur.
Some children grow more slowly or gain weight poorly.
Jaundice, which makes the skin or whites of the eyes look yellow, can develop.
Dark urine, pale stools, and itching may occur when bile flow is affected.
Fluid may collect in the abdomen, causing it to look swollen.
The spleen can enlarge, and small blood vessels may become visible under the skin.
Easy bruising or bleeding can happen if the liver makes fewer proteins needed for blood clotting.
Some children develop swelling in their legs or ankles.
In advanced disease, toxins may affect the brain, causing confusion, sleepiness, or changes in behavior.
Vomiting blood or passing black, tar-like stools can signal dangerous bleeding and requires emergency care.

Cirrhosis can affect nearly every part of a child’s health.
A damaged liver may not remove waste or process nutrients and medicines properly.
Poor nutrition and impaired growth can make it harder for children to develop as expected.
High pressure in blood vessels around the liver can cause enlarged veins that may bleed.
Fluid buildup and infections are other possible complications.
Severe liver damage can lead to liver failure, which may be life-threatening.
Cirrhosis may also affect school, energy, mood, and everyday activities.
The effects differ from child to child, and treatment depends on the cause and severity.
Doctors may use blood tests, imaging, and sometimes a liver biopsy to assess the condition.
Treatment may include medicines, nutrition support, or procedures to manage complications.
Some causes can be treated directly, but established scar tissue may not fully reverse.
Children with advanced liver failure may need a liver transplant.
Early diagnosis and regular care by a pediatric liver specialist can help protect health and plan treatment.

I was born beneath a thatched roof, in the first village beside the river. We counted the seasons by floods and feared the dark beyond our cooking fires. When I was old enough to walk, my people learned to bake clay into bricks. By my hundredth year, the village had become a walled city, crowded with markets and noisy carts. I watched our first scribes press stories into wet clay, hoping the river would not wash them away. Generations later, their descendants built towers that scraped the clouds. They harnessed lightning, then sent messages through the air faster than any horse could run. I had outlived my friends, my children, and even the names of the streets where we had played. Still, the world kept changing. Silver ships rose from the plains, carrying our people beyond the blue sky. Their first landing on the Moon was broadcast to every home, and I wept at the sound of their voices. Soon, bright stations circled Earth, and travelers returned with tales of red deserts and distant stars. On my five-hundredth birthday, a young pilot asked what the village had been like. I told her about the river, the fires, and the first brick. Then I watched her ship lift into the night, carrying our oldest curiosity farther than I had ever dreamed.

Linux gives each process its own virtual address space, so a program uses addresses that are separate from the addresses used by other programs. The processor’s memory-management unit translates these virtual addresses into physical RAM addresses. Linux sets up page tables that record which physical memory pages a process may access and what operations are allowed, such as reading, writing, or executing. The processor checks these permissions during memory access, helping prevent one process from reading or changing another process’s memory. Many pages are also shared safely, for example when processes use the same read-only program code or shared memory. If a process accesses a page that is not currently mapped, or violates its permissions, the processor raises a page fault. Linux examines the fault and may load the needed page from storage, create a new page, or update the mapping. Some faults are expected and handled transparently, such as when a page has not yet been loaded into RAM. If the access is invalid, Linux typically sends the process a signal, often causing it to terminate. Page tables and fault handling therefore let Linux manage memory efficiently while enforcing boundaries between processes. They are a core part of process isolation, though security also depends on correct kernel behavior and hardware protections.

Spatial variability in soil biological indicators refers to differences in living organisms and biological activity across a field. These indicators include soil microbes, earthworms, enzyme activity, respiration, and the breakdown of organic matter. They help show how well soil supports crops and performs essential ecosystem functions. Unlike some chemical properties, biological indicators can change quickly in response to weather and management.

Biological activity often varies over short distances. Soil texture, moisture, temperature, and organic matter can differ between patches, creating distinct habitats for organisms. Crop rows, wheel tracks, fertilizer bands, and residue piles can also produce localized patterns. Differences in drainage, slope, and past land use may add further variation.

This patchiness matters when soil quality is assessed. A sample taken from one spot may not represent the whole field, and a field-wide average can hide important hotspots or depleted areas. Results may therefore depend on where, when, and how samples are collected. Seasonal changes can make comparisons especially difficult.

A sound sampling plan should match the purpose of the assessment. For a general field estimate, collect multiple samples from across the area and combine them, while keeping clearly different zones separate when their conditions or management histories vary. Repeated sampling at the same locations can help track changes over time. Sampling should also be done at consistent depths and, where possible, under similar seasonal conditions.

Using several complementary biological indicators gives a more reliable picture than relying on one measurement. For example, microbial activity can indicate active nutrient cycling, while earthworm counts can reflect habitat conditions and soil structure. Biological results should be interpreted alongside soil properties, crop performance, and management records. This broader view helps distinguish natural variability from signs of degradation.

Recognizing spatial variability can improve farm decisions. Targeted management may direct organic amendments, cover crops, or reduced traffic to areas that need them most. Mapping indicator results can reveal patterns and guide follow-up testing. Ultimately, accounting for biological variation makes soil-quality assessments more representative and useful for sustainable agriculture.
