Polytrichum piliferum, commonly called bristly haircap moss, is a small, upright moss found in many cool regions of the world. It belongs to the Polytrichaceae family and is especially adapted to dry, exposed places. Its plants usually grow in dense, low cushions or patches, often only a few centimeters tall. The leaves are narrow, stiff, and crowded around the stem. Each leaf typically ends in a long, colorless hair point, which gives the species its bristly appearance. The hair points may look silvery or pale against the darker leaves. When dry, the leaves often curl or press close to the stem; when damp, they spread outward. The stems are usually dark reddish-brown near their bases, while younger growth may appear greener.

Like other mosses, Polytrichum piliferum reproduces by spores rather than flowers or seeds. Its spore capsules are borne on slender stalks and are often angled or nodding. A hairy covering called a calyptra protects the developing capsule and contributes to the species’ common name. The capsules mature from green to brown, and their spores are released when conditions are suitable.

This moss commonly grows on dry, acidic, sandy or gravelly soil. It is often found on open ground, dunes, heathland, rocky slopes, roadsides, and recently disturbed sites. It tolerates strong sunlight and limited moisture better than many mosses. Look for it in patches where competing vegetation is sparse, particularly on bare mineral soil.

To identify Polytrichum piliferum, examine the whole plant as well as its leaf tips and habitat. The distinctive long, pale hair points are a useful clue, but check that the leaves are narrow and arranged densely along upright stems. The cushion-forming growth and preference for dry, exposed soil also support identification. Similar haircap mosses can be difficult to distinguish, so capsule features and a regional moss guide may be helpful. For a confident identification, use a hand lens and compare several features rather than relying on color alone.

European Security Agencies Prepare for Possible Return of Islamic State Fighters

European governments are reviewing security plans as the Islamic State group loses territory in Iraq and Syria, raising concern that some of its foreign fighters could try to return home. Officials say the military defeat of the group’s self-declared caliphate has not eliminated the threat. European security services are assessing who may be on the move, how they could travel and what risks they might pose.

Thousands of people from Europe are believed to have travelled to the region to join Islamic State, also known as ISIS or ISIL. Some have been killed, while others are thought to remain in conflict zones, detention facilities or displaced-person camps. The number and whereabouts of those still alive are uncertain.

Authorities are updating watch lists and sharing information among national agencies and international partners. Police and border officials are being alerted to possible changes in travel routes, including the use of forged documents or journeys through third countries. Governments are also examining how to track people who return without being detected at the border.

Officials distinguish between the risks posed by trained fighters and the broader challenge of managing returnees. Some may have taken part in combat or received instruction in weapons and explosives. Others may have provided support roles, been coerced into joining, or travelled as children. Security agencies say each case requires individual assessment.

Several European countries have increased monitoring of people suspected of links to the group. Measures can include surveillance, travel restrictions and prosecution under laws against terrorism or participation in a foreign armed group. Authorities must balance those steps with legal protections and the need for evidence that can stand up in court.

Collecting reliable evidence from Iraq and Syria remains difficult. Investigators may have limited access to conflict sites, witnesses and records, while evidence gathered in unstable conditions can be hard to verify. European prosecutors are working with international partners to improve the collection and preservation of material.

The prospect of returnees has also renewed debate over citizenship and repatriation. Some governments have argued that citizens who joined the group should face trial where they are held. Others have raised concerns about the conditions and legal safeguards in detention facilities in the region. Families and rights groups have called for clearer procedures, particularly for children.

Security analysts warn that the loss of territory could prompt the group to shift from governing land to clandestine operations. Islamic State has retained networks and supporters despite setbacks on the battlefield. Its leaders have urged followers abroad to act, though authorities say it is difficult to determine how many people might respond.

European police forces are also watching for online activity that could encourage attacks or help recruits connect with extremist networks. Officials say propaganda and encrypted communications can complicate investigations. They stress that online interest alone does not establish a person’s intent to commit violence.

Governments are expanding cooperation through intelligence-sharing arrangements and joint investigations. But differences in national laws and surveillance rules can slow coordination. Officials say timely information-sharing is especially important when a suspected fighter moves across borders.

Experts say prevention and rehabilitation will be necessary alongside policing. Some returnees may require close supervision, while children and people who were exploited may need psychological and social support. Local authorities are preparing to involve social workers, schools and community organizations in selected cases.

The scale of the challenge remains unclear. Not every person who travelled to join the group will return, and not every returnee will pose a security threat. European officials say their immediate priority is to identify individuals, assess credible risks and prevent attacks while respecting due process.

As Islamic State’s territorial control contracts, European security agencies are preparing for a threat that may be less visible but harder to measure. The group’s defeat on the battlefield has changed the security landscape rather than ended the conflict. Governments are now trying to ensure that the movement of fighters, families and supporters does not create new dangers at home.

A powerful earthquake struck central Myanmar, killing residents, injuring others and damaging buildings, while raising fears of further tremors. The quake shook communities across the region and sent people rushing into the streets. Residents described strong shaking that lasted long enough to topple household items and crack walls. Some buildings suffered serious structural damage, and parts of the affected area were left strewn with debris. Emergency workers began searching damaged structures and helping people who needed medical care. Hospitals faced an influx of injured residents, though the full number of casualties was not immediately clear. Officials warned that the toll could rise as teams reached more remote communities. Rescue efforts were complicated by damaged roads and concerns about the stability of weakened buildings. Authorities urged residents to stay away from structures showing cracks or other signs of damage. Many people spent the night outdoors, reluctant to return to homes that might not be safe. The earthquake also disrupted daily life, with some businesses and public services temporarily shut. Engineers and local officials began assessing damage to buildings and infrastructure. The initial quake was followed by additional tremors, prompting renewed alarm among residents. Seismologists say aftershocks can follow a major earthquake, sometimes for days or longer. They urged people to remain cautious and follow safety instructions from local authorities. Emergency agencies worked to coordinate rescue operations and distribute essential supplies. Community members also joined efforts to clear debris and assist neighbors. The disaster has renewed concerns about the resilience of buildings in earthquake-prone parts of Myanmar. Officials said assessments would be needed to identify unsafe structures and determine where support was most urgent. Families searched for relatives and tried to establish whether loved ones were safe. Authorities appealed for calm while warning that conditions could change as aftershocks continued. The scale of the damage and the needs of affected communities were still being assessed. For residents across central Myanmar, the immediate priority remained finding shelter, medical help and reassurance amid the continuing uncertainty.

People often learn by facing challenges themselves, but they can also grow by watching what happens to others. A friend’s experience, a family member’s advice, or a story about someone overcoming hardship can offer useful lessons. Observing others helps us see choices and consequences more clearly. It can also remind us that difficulties are a normal part of life. This understanding makes challenges feel less isolating.

For example, a student who watches a classmate prepare steadily for an exam may notice how small study sessions add up. Instead of waiting until the last minute, the student can try the same approach. If the classmate struggles despite working hard, that experience can also show the importance of asking questions or changing study methods. In this way, observation teaches both what may work and what may need improvement. It gives people ideas they can adapt to their own situations.

Other people’s experiences can help us respond calmly when problems arise. Seeing someone handle a disagreement with patience may demonstrate that listening is more useful than reacting angrily. Watching a person recover from a mistake can show that failure does not have to define the future. Their example may encourage us to take responsibility, make a new plan, and try again. These lessons can build confidence before we face a similar situation ourselves.

Stories and examples can also develop empathy. When we learn about another person’s struggles, we may better understand why they act or feel a certain way. This can help us offer support instead of judging them quickly. Empathy strengthens relationships and makes it easier for people to ask each other for help. A supportive community can make difficult moments more manageable.

However, observing others does not mean copying every choice they make. People have different goals, resources, and personalities. A strategy that works well for one person may not suit someone else. We should think carefully about what we observe and decide which lessons fit our circumstances. It is also important to learn from negative examples without repeating the same mistakes.

Ultimately, other people’s experiences can act like guides, but they cannot make every decision for us. By paying attention to their choices, successes, and setbacks, we gain knowledge without having to learn every lesson the hard way. We can combine that knowledge with our own judgment and experience. This helps us approach challenges with greater preparation and resilience. Learning from others reminds us that growth is possible, even when life is difficult.

Discovering and nurturing our personal abilities and interests is an important part of growing up. Each person has a unique combination of talents, preferences, and strengths. Some people find it easy to draw or play music, while others enjoy solving problems, helping people, or organizing activities. We may not recognize our abilities right away, so it is useful to try different things. Joining a club, taking a class, or volunteering can introduce us to interests we have never explored. Reading about unfamiliar subjects can also help us find what captures our attention. We should notice which activities make us feel curious and energized. It is equally helpful to pay attention to tasks that we learn quickly or enjoy practicing. Asking trusted friends, teachers, and family members what they think we do well can offer a new perspective. Their opinions can guide us, but they should not decide our future for us.

Once we discover an interest, we can nurture it through regular practice. Improvement usually comes from patience and effort rather than instant success. Setting small, clear goals can make progress easier to see. For example, someone learning an instrument might practice for twenty minutes each day. A student interested in science could complete simple experiments or visit a science museum. Keeping a journal of our activities and progress can help us understand what we enjoy most. We should also learn from mistakes instead of treating them as proof that we lack ability. Feedback from knowledgeable people can show us what to work on next. At the same time, taking breaks is important because rest helps us stay motivated. We can nurture more than one interest, even if we cannot give every activity equal time.

It is important not to compare our progress too closely with other people’s. Everyone develops at a different pace, and some skills take years to build. We should remain open to changing our minds as we learn more about ourselves. An interest that once seemed exciting may become less important, and a new one may take its place. Exploring different paths is not a waste of time; it helps us make thoughtful choices. Parents and teachers can support young people by providing encouragement and opportunities without forcing them into particular activities. Schools can help by offering a variety of subjects, clubs, and creative projects. Communities can also make it easier to explore through sports teams, libraries, workshops, and volunteer programs. Not everyone has access to these opportunities, so people can also begin with simple activities at home or free resources online.

Discovering our abilities is not only about choosing a career. It can help us build confidence, make meaningful friendships, and contribute to our communities. When we use our strengths to help others, our talents gain purpose. Nurturing an interest also teaches us discipline, resilience, and curiosity. These qualities can benefit us in many parts of life. In the end, learning about ourselves is an ongoing journey. We can begin by trying new things, noticing what matters to us, and practicing with care. With time, support, and effort, we can develop our abilities and make room for the interests that bring meaning to our lives.

Sterling’s post-Brexit weakness could push up the cost of living, but the impact is unlikely to be felt equally across British households. A cheaper pound makes goods and services priced abroad more expensive in the UK. That can feed through to food, fuel, clothing and household equipment, as well as to the costs businesses face.

The exchange rate is not the only influence on prices. Energy markets, wages, taxes and supply-chain disruptions also matter, and retailers may absorb some currency-related costs rather than pass them on immediately. Even so, a sustained fall in sterling can add to inflationary pressure, particularly for products that Britain imports in large quantities.

Brexit has contributed to uncertainty about the UK’s trade arrangements and economic outlook, factors that can weigh on the pound. But sterling moves for many reasons, including interest-rate expectations, global investor sentiment and changes in the currencies of the UK’s trading partners. It is therefore difficult to attribute any particular decline solely to Brexit.

For households, the effect often arrives gradually. Importers may pay more for goods when contracts are renewed, and manufacturers can face higher bills for components and raw materials. Those costs may then be reflected in shop prices, although the timing and size of increases vary by sector.

Food is one area where currency movements can matter. The UK imports a substantial share of the food it consumes, along with ingredients and packaging used by domestic producers. A weaker pound can raise the cost of those imports, though harvests, transport costs and global commodity prices can be just as important.

Fuel and energy bills can also be exposed to international prices, which are commonly traded in US dollars. A fall in sterling means more pounds are needed to buy the same amount of fuel at an unchanged dollar price. The final cost to consumers depends on wholesale markets, taxes, regulation and suppliers’ pricing arrangements.

The burden is likely to be heavier for lower-income households. They typically spend a greater proportion of their budgets on essentials such as food, heating and transport, leaving less room to absorb price rises. Wealthier households may face higher costs too, but are generally better able to adjust their spending or draw on savings.

Pensioners and people on fixed incomes may be particularly vulnerable if benefits or pensions do not keep pace with prices. Renters could also feel pressure if higher costs for landlords and businesses feed into rents or other charges, although the link is neither automatic nor immediate. Families with children may face added strain from rising food, clothing and school-related expenses.

Some households may benefit from a weaker pound. British holidaymakers travelling abroad usually find their money buys less, while exporters can earn more in sterling from overseas sales. Firms that compete with imports may also become more competitive, potentially supporting jobs and wages in some sectors.

However, the gains are uneven and do not necessarily offset higher prices for imported goods. Export businesses often rely on imported components, and any boost to overseas sales depends on demand and their ability to expand production. The exchange-rate effect can therefore create winners and losers even within the same industry.

Whether sterling weakness leads to lasting inflation depends partly on how businesses and workers respond. If companies pass on higher costs and workers seek wage increases to maintain purchasing power, price pressures can persist. If demand is weak, businesses may instead accept lower profit margins, limiting the rise in consumer prices.

The Bank of England monitors exchange rates alongside other indicators when setting interest rates. It may respond to persistent inflation, but raising rates can also increase mortgage costs and borrowing expenses for households and businesses. Policymakers must weigh the risk of entrenched price rises against the harm that tighter financial conditions can cause.

For households, the practical impact will depend on the mix of purchases they make, where they live and how their incomes change. Tracking spending, checking energy and insurance deals, and seeking available benefits or debt advice can help, though such steps cannot remove economy-wide pressures. The broader question is how quickly wages and support payments adjust when essential costs rise.

A weaker pound is not a guarantee of an inflation surge, nor does every household experience it in the same way. But if sterling remains low while import costs stay elevated, families with limited financial buffers are likely to feel the squeeze first. The path of prices will ultimately depend on currency movements, global markets and domestic policy working together.

Officials in Afghanistan’s southern Helmand province have warned that Taliban advances could overwhelm government forces already struggling with shortages and inadequate support. The warning comes as fighting intensifies across several districts, putting pressure on security units and raising fears for civilians.

Provincial officials said troops lacked sufficient ammunition, food, medical supplies and reliable reinforcements. Some units had been deployed for extended periods, while damaged equipment and limited air support hampered operations. Officials urged the central government to provide urgent assistance and strengthen coordination among security forces.

Taliban fighters have increased attacks on government positions and reportedly seized or contested territory in parts of the province. The group’s gains have threatened supply routes and made it harder for government forces to move between bases. Local authorities said the situation remained fluid, and independent verification of battlefield claims was difficult.

Residents described growing insecurity and concern that further fighting could disrupt daily life. Families in affected areas have faced displacement, while access to health care and other services has become more difficult. Humanitarian organizations have warned that continued clashes could deepen the needs of civilians already affected by years of conflict.

Government representatives have said they are monitoring the situation and working to support forces in Helmand. They have also emphasized that security operations are continuing, though they have not publicly detailed the scale or timing of additional assistance. The gap between those assurances and provincial officials’ appeals has fueled concern about the government’s ability to hold its positions.

Helmand has long been a strategic battleground because of its size, location and key transport routes. Analysts say shortages and weak coordination can leave forces vulnerable even when they retain numerical or technical advantages. They caution that the situation could shift quickly as both sides seek to control key districts.

Provincial officials appealed for immediate supplies and reinforcements, warning that delays could lead to further losses. They said government forces were determined to defend their positions but could not do so indefinitely without adequate support. The coming days are expected to test whether Kabul can stabilize the front and prevent the Taliban from expanding its gains.

The paper addresses a timely topic by examining how deep learning can support clustering and by combining a taxonomy, a proposed method, and comparative experiments. This scope could make the work useful to researchers seeking an overview as well as a practical comparison of methods. The taxonomy is potentially valuable, but its organizing principles should be stated explicitly and applied consistently. In particular, the paper should clarify how it distinguishes deep clustering from methods that use learned representations followed by conventional clustering. The proposed approach needs a more precise description of its motivation, architecture, objective function, and training procedure. The authors should explain which components are novel and how the method differs from the closest existing approaches. The experimental section is central to the paper, so datasets, preprocessing, hyperparameter selection, and evaluation protocols should be reported in enough detail to ensure reproducibility. Comparisons should include strong and recent baselines, with comparable tuning budgets and appropriate clustering metrics. Because clustering results can vary with initialization, the authors should report results over multiple runs and provide measures of variability or statistical significance. Ablation studies would help establish which parts of the proposed method contribute to its performance. The paper should also discuss sensitivity to key hyperparameters, computational cost, and scalability to larger datasets. If labels are used for evaluation or model selection, the authors should clarify how they avoid introducing information leakage. The discussion would benefit from a more balanced account of limitations, including cases where the method performs poorly or offers little advantage. Overall, the topic and combined scope are promising, but the paper’s contribution and empirical claims need clearer justification and stronger reproducibility evidence. I recommend revision before acceptance, with particular attention to the taxonomy’s rigor and the fairness and completeness of the experimental evaluation.

The paper presents an RL-guided operations research framework for improving solutions to the capacitated vehicle routing problem (CVRP), with a particular focus on diversifying the search states explored by an optimization algorithm. The combination of reinforcement learning and established routing heuristics is promising, especially if the learned policy guides search without sacrificing feasibility or solution quality. A key strength is the emphasis on state diversification, which may help reduce premature convergence and expose regions of the solution space that conventional local search overlooks. The paper would benefit from a clearer explanation of the framework’s components, including the state representation, available actions, reward design, and how the RL policy interacts with the OR solver. The authors should specify how capacity constraints and other feasibility requirements are enforced throughout the search. The experimental evaluation should compare the method against strong, recent CVRP baselines using consistent computational budgets and multiple problem sizes. It would also be useful to report solution quality, runtime, and variability across repeated runs, rather than presenting only best-case outcomes. An ablation study should isolate the contribution of RL guidance and state diversification from that of the underlying optimization operators. The paper should clarify whether training and test instances are separated and discuss how well the policy generalizes to unseen distributions and larger instances. Statistical testing would strengthen claims that observed improvements are reliable. Practical considerations, such as training cost and inference overhead, should be included to assess whether the approach offers a net computational benefit. Overall, the work has potential, but clearer methodological detail and a more comprehensive, reproducible evaluation are needed to support its claims.

At 9:07 p.m., the Belligerent Goose was three deep at the bar and two drinks short of legally becoming a ferry.

It was the night of the annual Purge, and owner Marty had put up a sign that read, “NO PURGING IN THE RESTROOMS.”

Nobody knew whether the sign was legally binding.

Marty said it was because he had printed it in bold.

The Goose’s regulars had gathered for their usual Thursday special: half-price wings and full-price denial.

There was Darlene, who could win an argument with a weather report.

There was Pete, who claimed he had once punched a vending machine so hard it apologized.

There was Lenny, who had been banned from three bowling alleys and one church raffle.

And there was Joy, who kept the gang’s unofficial minutes in a notebook labeled “WITNESSES.”

They had not formed a gang.

They had simply met at the same bar for eleven years and started wearing matching jackets to make the parking lot easier.

The jackets said GOOSE CREW in crooked yellow letters.

Darlene had sewn them herself.

She had also sewn one pocket upside down, but nobody mentioned it.

At 9:10, the television announced that the Purge would begin in fifty minutes.

Marty turned it down.

“I don’t need the news telling my customers what time it is,” he said.

Pete raised his glass.

“I know what time it is,” he said.

“What time?” asked Joy.

“Almost free wings.”

The Purge siren sounded at ten.

Everyone in the Goose paused.

A man near the dartboard dropped a peanut.

The peanut hit the floor with the weight of a verdict.

Outside, the streetlights went dark.

Inside, the bar’s emergency bulbs clicked on, giving everyone the complexion of suspicious mushrooms.

Marty locked the front door.

He locked the back door.

He locked the door to the alley, which had been stuck open since April.

The door to the alley remained open.

“Security,” Marty said, “is mostly a state of mind.”

Then the power went out completely.

The jukebox stopped in the middle of a song about loving somebody forever.

The song had not convinced anyone.

In the darkness, someone shouted, “Is this part of the Purge?”

“Everything is part of something,” Darlene replied.

The emergency lights returned.

Marty found the breaker panel under a framed photograph of a younger Marty holding a bass.

The photograph had been taken before he gave up music and bought the bar.

It had also been taken before his hair surrendered.

While Marty studied the breaker, a crash came from the front of the Goose.

The gang scattered.

Darlene ducked behind a barrel of pretzels.

Pete climbed under the bar, knocking his own hat off.

Lenny stood perfectly still because he had mistaken fear for strategy.

Joy opened her notebook and wrote, “Crash, probably dramatic.”

A man in a motorcycle helmet stumbled through the open alley door.

He carried a leaf blower in one hand and a garden gnome in the other.

The gnome wore a tiny helmet.

The man shouted, “Everybody down!”

Everyone went down, except Lenny, who sat down more slowly than usual.

The man stared at the room.

“Why is there a bartender?” he asked.

“Why is there a gnome?” Marty replied.

The man glanced at the gnome.

“Long story.”

“Is it a Purge story?” asked Joy.

“It’s a yard story,” he said.

He introduced himself as Crank.

He had been trying to rob a house two blocks away.

The house’s owner had mistaken him for a landscaper.

Crank had mistaken the owner’s security system for a microwave.

The leaf blower had been part of his escape plan.

The gnome was collateral.

Marty pointed toward the front door.

“You need to leave.”

Crank shook his head.

“There are people outside.”

A second crash came from the street.

This one sounded like a dumpster getting promoted to a weapon.

The Goose’s customers crowded away from the windows.

Pete peeked between two slats.

Three figures were running down the block.

They carried baseball bats, a traffic cone, and what looked like a folding patio table.

“They’re armed,” Pete whispered.

“With what?” asked Darlene.

“A patio table.”

“That’s not a weapon,” she said.

A loud bang echoed outside.

The patio table folded shut.

Everyone flinched.

“Okay,” Darlene said. “It has potential.”

Marty dragged a heavy table across the front door.

Pete helped him.

Then Pete asked if the table was the bar’s new security system.

“It’s our old dining furniture,” Marty said.

“Same thing,” Pete replied.

Crank sat on a barstool and set the gnome beside him.

Joy stared at the garden ornament.

“Does the gnome have a name?”

“Not anymore,” Crank said.

A siren wailed somewhere nearby.

Then another answered it.

The Goose’s regulars listened as the city transformed into a distant argument involving engines, yelling, and very poor decisions.

Marty poured himself a drink.

He poured one for Darlene.

He poured one for Pete.

He poured one for Joy.

He poured one for Lenny, who had not asked but looked like he was going to need it.

Crank received a glass of water.

“I’m trying to be a better person,” Crank said.

“You broke into a house,” Marty replied.

“I’m at the beginning of the process.”

A crash sounded in the alley.

The stuck door swung wider.

A shopping cart rolled into the bar.

It carried two bags of ice, a single shoe, and a sleepy orange cat.

The cat hopped out and climbed onto the bar.

Marty looked at it.

“Are you paying?”

The cat closed its eyes.

“Apparently not,” Marty said.

Joy wrote down “unlicensed feline.”

The gang considered whether to barricade the alley door with chairs.

They had only five chairs that did not wobble.

They put the sturdy ones against the door.

The sixth chair, which did wobble, was assigned to Lenny.

Lenny said he felt singled out.

“You are,” Darlene said.

The lights flickered.

Marty peered at the breaker panel again.

He flipped a switch.

Nothing happened.

He flipped it back.

The jukebox sprang to life at full volume.

It resumed the love song where it had left off.

The singer declared that he would cross every ocean for his beloved.

From somewhere outside, someone yelled, “Don’t!”

The jukebox stopped again.

At 10:23, a knock came at the front door.

Nobody moved.

The knock came again.

It was polite, which made it worse.

“Who is it?” Marty called.

“Delivery,” said a voice.

“What delivery?”

“Chicken.”

Marty looked at the wings on the counter.

“We have chicken.”

“Not this chicken,” said the voice.

Darlene leaned toward the window.

A delivery driver stood on the sidewalk holding a paper bag.

Behind him, a person in a silver mask was trying to open a parked car with a banana.

The driver noticed the gang watching.

“Can I come in?” he asked.

“Are you armed?” Marty called.

“With chicken.”

“Come in.”

They moved the table just enough to let the driver squeeze through.

His name was Sal.

He had been delivering food because his boss believed tips were worth more than survival.

Sal set the bag on the counter.

The receipt said, “ONE LARGE PIZZA, EXTRA CHEESE.”

“This is not chicken,” Joy said.

Sal checked the bag.

“I know.”

“Then why did you say chicken?”

“I panicked.”

Crank nodded sympathetically.

They shared the pizza.

The gang had never trusted a stranger so quickly.

The silver-masked person outside gave up on the car.

They picked up the banana and vanished down the street.

At 10:41, the front door shook.

The table scraped backward an inch.

Marty grabbed a baseball bat from behind the bar.

Pete grabbed a pool cue.

Darlene grabbed the gnome.

Crank grabbed his leaf blower.

Lenny grabbed his drink.

“Excellent,” Darlene said. “We have a plan.”

“What’s the plan?” asked Joy.

“We’ll know when it starts.”

The door shook again.

The table moved another inch.

A voice outside shouted, “Open up!”

Marty raised the bat.

Darlene tightened her grip on the gnome.

Pete lifted the pool cue like a knight holding a very long breadstick.

Joy crouched behind the pretzel barrel.

Crank aimed the leaf blower at the door.

The door swung open.

A woman in a glittery crown stumbled inside.

She held a plastic shopping bag and looked exhausted.

Behind her, someone ran past carrying a lamp.

The woman raised both hands.

“I’m not here to hurt anyone,” she said.

“Are you in a gang?” Marty asked.

“I’m in a choir.”

“Same thing,” said Darlene.

The woman introduced herself as Maribel.

She had been walking home from a costume party when the Purge began.

Her crown was made of cardboard.

Her gown was a bedsheet with holes for her arms.

She had lost one shoe and found someone else’s.

The shoe was the one in the shopping cart.

The cat had followed her from the street.

“That’s my shoe,” Maribel said.

The cat yawned.

“Good for the cat,” said Pete.

Maribel asked to use the phone.

Marty handed her the bar’s old landline.

It had not worked in six months, but he wanted to be supportive.

Maribel dialed.

The phone rang.

Everyone looked at it.

A voice answered on the other end.

“Emergency services. What is your emergency?”

Maribel whispered, “I’m in a bar.”

The dispatcher replied, “That is not an emergency.”

“It might become one.”

The dispatcher sighed.

“Bars usually do.”

Maribel hung up and returned the phone.

“Any luck?” asked Joy.

“No, but someone understood me.”

Outside, the sirens grew louder.

A group of masked figures hurried down the sidewalk.

They wore matching red scarves.

The gang watched them pass.

“They’re organized,” Pete said.

“Not very,” Darlene replied.

One of the figures tripped over a curb.

The others stopped to help.

For a moment, the whole group looked like a company picnic that had taken a wrong turn.

Then they disappeared around the corner.

At 11:06, Marty decided the Goose needed a mascot.

He proposed the cat.

The cat remained asleep on the bar.

Pete proposed the gnome.

Crank objected.

The gnome, he said, had been through enough.

Joy suggested the chicken pizza.

Nobody disagreed.

Marty put the gnome on the counter anyway.

He set the cat beside it.

“Welcome to the Goose family,” he said.

The cat opened one eye.

The gnome looked unchanged.

At 11:17, someone pounded on the back door.

The chairs rattled.

Lenny sprang up from his wobbling seat.

The seat collapsed.

He landed on the floor with a sound like a dropped lasagna.

“Are you all right?” Joy asked.

“I think so,” Lenny said.

“Can you stand?”

“I’ve been reconsidering that.”

The pounding stopped.

A quiet voice called through the alley.

“Please help.”

Marty hesitated.

Everyone looked at him.

The Goose had rules against trouble.

It had more rules against letting trouble freeze outside.

They shifted the chairs.

Crank stood ready with the leaf blower.

Darlene held the gnome.

Marty opened the door two inches.

A teenager stood outside, clutching a bicycle helmet.

He looked frightened and embarrassed.

“My bike chain came off,” he said.

“That’s the emergency?” Marty asked.

“I’m sorry.”

The gang pulled him inside.

Pete fixed the chain with a butter knife.

The teenager thanked him and asked if anyone had seen his sister.

No one had.

Joy wrote down his name and number.

The boy stared at her notebook.

“Are those witnesses?”

“Only if something interesting happens,” she said.

He sat with the group until the sirens faded in the distance.

At midnight, the city’s warning system announced that the Purge was over.

The voice sounded cheerful, as though it had been waiting all evening to share a coupon.

Marty unlocked the front door.

Nobody rushed outside.

They waited for someone else to go first.

The cat went first.

It stepped into the alley, sniffed the air, and returned to the bar.

“That’s the word,” Darlene said.

The street was scattered with paper, broken glass, and several items that had clearly been stolen from places with better lighting.

A plastic crown lay in the gutter.

Maribel picked it up and placed it on her head.

The gang cleaned the bar together.

Pete swept the floor.

Joy recorded the damages.

Lenny inspected the chairs and declared the broken one a victim.

Crank gave Marty the garden gnome as payment for the water.

Marty accepted it as collateral.

Sal delivered the wrong pizza to the right bar.

He promised to tell his boss the truth.

Everyone wished him luck.

They were not sure whether that meant he should or should not.

At 12:38, Darlene found the shopping cart.

It had rolled back outside by itself.

The single shoe was gone.

The cat was still in the bar.

Marty found a cardboard box and made it a bed.

The cat climbed into it.

“You can’t stay,” he told it.

The cat fell asleep.

Marty sighed and wrote “temporary employee” on the box.

The Goose Crew gathered beneath their crooked sign.

Their jackets were dusty, their drinks were warm, and one sleeve had been singed by the emergency light.

They took a group photograph beside the gnome.

The cat refused to look at the camera.

“Next year,” Pete said, “we should go somewhere safe.”

“Where?” asked Joy.

“Somewhere without a bar.”

Nobody answered.

Marty turned off the lights.

The cat opened its eyes.

The gnome did not.

And somewhere outside, a delivery driver was still searching for the chicken.

The bridge was meant to sing.

Elias Vale had spent twelve years designing a suspension bridge whose cables would hum softly in the wind. He believed cities needed beauty as much as roads. On the morning the first span opened, he stood beneath it with his daughter, Mara, and listened.

Then a construction crane failed.

The boom struck the unfinished tower, and steel screamed above them. Elias dragged Mara toward the riverbank. A falling beam caught his leg, and the bridge shuddered as workers ran for cover.

Mara did not make it out.

The investigation cleared Elias of blame, but no report could quiet the sound he carried home. He stopped visiting the site. He stopped sketching. When the firm offered him a desk job, he accepted without reading the title.

His wife, June, tried to help. She left drawing paper on his table and opened the curtains each morning. Elias thanked her, then covered the paper with old newspapers.

Months passed, then a year. Friends learned not to ask about the bridge. Elias learned to answer questions with facts: the span was stable, the failure had been unforeseeable, the city had reopened the road.

At night, he dreamed the cables were calling his name.

One winter evening, he drove to the unfinished overlook above the river. He had brought a folded note and a bottle of water. The cold pressed through his coat as he watched the dark current.

He thought of stepping beyond the railing, and the thought frightened him less than it should have. For a long time, he stood very still.

Then his phone rang.

June had not asked where he was. She had only said she could not find him, and that frightened her. Elias looked at the note in his hand and felt shame rise like heat.

“I’m at the river,” he said. “I’m not safe alone.”

June stayed on the line while she called for help. Elias moved away from the railing and sat on the gravel. He counted each passing car until a patrol officer arrived.

The next morning, he told June everything. He told her about the note, the dreams, and how the engineer he had been seemed like someone who had died with Mara.

June did not argue. She took his hand and said, “You don’t have to be that man today.”

He began seeing a counselor. At first he spoke only about measurements and load limits. Slowly, he learned to name the things those numbers could not hold.

He visited the bridge with June on a bright spring afternoon. The span was complete, its cables quiet in the mild air. Elias felt grief, but he also felt the ground beneath his shoes.

A maintenance worker had planted wildflowers near the path. Elias knelt to straighten a bent stake, surprised that his hands still knew how to make something steadier.

He did not draw a new bridge that day. He went home, opened the curtains, and sat beside June at the table.

For the first time in a long while, the blank page did not look like a verdict.

Disney films dominated the 2016 box office, leading ticket sales in both North America and worldwide. In North America, Finding Dory finished the year as the top-grossing release, earning about $486 million. Rogue One: A Star Wars Story followed with roughly $424 million, despite opening in December. Captain America: Civil War and The Jungle Book also ranked among the year’s biggest domestic hits. Worldwide, Captain America: Civil War led the pack with about $1.15 billion in ticket sales. Finding Dory brought in roughly $1.03 billion globally, while Zootopia earned about $1.02 billion. The Jungle Book and Rogue One each added more than $900 million worldwide. The results reflected Disney’s strength across animation, live-action remakes, and the Star Wars and Marvel franchises. Altogether, the studio’s slate made 2016 a landmark year at the box office.

FDA food-transport safety requirements in the United States are governed mainly by the Sanitary Transportation of Human and Animal Food rule under the Food Safety Modernization Act (FSMA). The rule is intended to prevent food from becoming unsafe during transportation, rather than to address every aspect of food safety. It applies to shippers, loaders, carriers, and receivers involved in transporting food by motor or rail vehicle, and to certain activities connected with those shipments. Coverage depends on the parties’ roles and the food involved, so companies should assess each part of their supply chain.

The rule covers food for people and animals, including food ingredients, but it includes exemptions and modified requirements. For example, it generally does not apply to transportation of food completely enclosed by a container, unless the food requires temperature control for safety. It also excludes certain transportation activities, such as transportation by ship or air, and some shipments conducted by farms. Other exemptions apply to particular products or parties. Businesses should consult the rule’s definitions and exemptions rather than assume that a shipment is covered or exempt.

A shipper must establish written procedures addressing sanitary transportation when the rule applies. These procedures may cover temperature controls, prevention of cross-contamination, protection from non-food cargo, and the condition of vehicles and equipment. The shipper must communicate relevant requirements to the carrier and, where applicable, to the loader. Agreements can assign responsibilities, but a contract does not automatically remove a party’s legal duties.

Carriers must provide vehicles and equipment that are suitable for the food being transported and maintain them in sanitary condition. When temperature control is required, carriers must demonstrate that the vehicle can maintain the necessary conditions. Carriers must also provide information about temperature conditions when required by the shipper or receiver. Written agreements may specify which party performs particular tasks, such as checking equipment or monitoring temperatures.

Loaders must ensure that food is loaded under conditions that prevent contamination and, where required, verify that temperature-controlled shipments are at the specified temperature. They should check that vehicles are clean and suitable for the load. Receivers should assess whether transportation conditions may have made food unsafe and take appropriate action if problems are identified. These responsibilities should be clearly documented across the supply chain.

The rule requires relevant personnel to be trained in sanitary transportation practices. Training should be appropriate to each person’s job, including handling, inspection, cleaning, and temperature-control duties. Companies should retain records of procedures, agreements, training, and other required activities. Records generally need to be kept for at least 12 months after the relevant activity, though some records have different retention periods.

Railroads have specific obligations when they act as carriers under the rule. A railroad transporting covered food must comply with applicable carrier requirements, including providing suitable equipment and maintaining it in sanitary condition. Rail carriers should coordinate with shippers and other supply-chain partners about food safety conditions, temperature controls, cleaning expectations, and records. A railroad that only transports sealed, non-temperature-controlled food may fall within an exemption, but the details of the shipment matter.

FDA food-transport requirements are separate from railroad safety rules administered by the Federal Railroad Administration. Railroads may also need to comply with Department of Transportation hazardous-materials requirements, equipment rules, and other federal or state requirements. Those obligations depend on the cargo, equipment, route, and the railroad’s role. Compliance programs should therefore consider both food-safety and rail-safety regulations.

Implementation dates for the FDA rule depended on company size and category. Large businesses were generally required to comply beginning April 6, 2017. Small businesses, defined under the rule by employee count and other criteria, generally had a compliance date of April 6, 2018. Certain businesses transporting food without a direct contractual relationship with the shipper had a later date of April 6, 2020. These dates have passed, so covered businesses should treat compliance as an ongoing obligation, not a future project.

Implementation typically begins with mapping shipments, identifying each party’s role, and determining which foods and activities are covered. Next, companies should review contracts, procedures, equipment, and recordkeeping practices for gaps. They can then assign responsibility for cleaning, inspections, temperature monitoring, training, and corrective actions. Periodic audits help confirm that written procedures match actual operations.

Costs vary considerably by fleet size, route network, food types, existing equipment, and the maturity of a company’s safety program. A small operator with suitable vehicles and established procedures may face relatively modest costs for staff time, training, documentation, and occasional inspections. A larger railroad or carrier may need substantial investment in equipment upgrades, cleaning systems, temperature monitoring, information technology, and supplier oversight. FDA does not prescribe a fixed compliance fee or a single required technology.

Typical cost categories include employee training, legal or regulatory review, procedure development, contract updates, and recordkeeping systems. Equipment-related costs may include vehicle repairs, insulation, refrigeration, sensors, calibration, and cleaning supplies or services. Rail operations may also incur costs for inspecting railcars, coordinating equipment availability, and documenting cleaning and temperature conditions. These expenses should be distinguished from costs required by separate transportation or environmental rules.

Companies can control costs by using risk-based procedures and existing quality-management systems where they meet FDA requirements. They should avoid buying monitoring technology before determining whether it is necessary for the foods and routes involved. Reliable records, clear agreements, and effective communication can reduce duplicated work and help prevent costly product losses. When requirements are uncertain, businesses should consult FDA guidance, qualified food-safety professionals, and legal counsel.

This overview is educational and is not legal advice. The exact obligations depend on the shipment, the parties’ roles, and applicable exemptions. Companies should review the current text of 21 CFR Part 1, Subpart O, along with FDA guidance and any relevant railroad regulations.

Mara and Eli slipped away from the village dance, laughing as they ran toward the moonlit river. They had planned to spend one quiet night together before Mara’s father sent her to the city. At the old ferry dock, Eli took her hands and promised they would make a life of their own. Then a gunshot cracked across the water. Mara’s father emerged from the trees, his hunting rifle raised and his face pale with fury. “Come home,” he shouted, “or I’ll make sure neither of you leaves.” Eli pulled Mara behind the ferry shed as a second shot splintered the wood above them. Their romantic escape became a desperate scramble through reeds and mud. They reached the riverbank, but the ferry was chained to its post. Mara spotted a narrow rowboat half-hidden beneath the dock. As her father’s footsteps drew closer, Eli cut the rope with his pocketknife. They shoved off just as the rifle flashed again, sending a spray of water over their shoulders. At dawn, they reached the far shore together, shaken but free, and watched the sun rise on a future they would choose themselves.

This paper studies ways to improve adversarial imitation learning through sigmoid-based f-divergence objectives and extensions to learning from observations. The topic is timely and relevant to researchers working on imitation learning and reinforcement learning. The paper’s central idea is to connect the choice of adversarial objective to the divergence being optimized, rather than treating the discriminator loss as a minor implementation detail. This perspective is potentially valuable because objective choice can affect both optimization stability and the quality of learned policies. The extension to learning from observations also addresses an important practical setting in which expert actions are unavailable.

The manuscript’s strongest feature is its attempt to provide a unified account of these objectives. The relationship between discriminator formulations and f-divergences can help clarify why different adversarial imitation methods behave differently. The sigmoid-based parameterization appears to offer a principled alternative to familiar classification losses. If the derivation is correct and its assumptions are made explicit, it could help practitioners select objectives with greater understanding. The paper also appears to connect theoretical formulation with empirical evaluation, which is appropriate for this topic.

The observation-only setting is a meaningful extension rather than a simple change in terminology. In many applications, demonstrations consist of trajectories or state observations without recorded actions. A method that can use such data would broaden the practical reach of adversarial imitation learning. The paper should clearly explain how the learning signal is obtained in this setting and what assumptions are required about the expert data. In particular, it should distinguish learning from state observations from settings that still rely on known dynamics, privileged information, or action labels.

The main concern is whether the paper establishes that its proposed objectives offer a reliable improvement over strong alternatives. Empirical comparisons should include representative adversarial imitation baselines and, where feasible, non-adversarial imitation methods. The baselines should be implemented with comparable architectures, data budgets, and tuning effort. It would also be useful to report results across several random seeds, with uncertainty intervals rather than only point estimates. Without this information, apparent gains may reflect variance or differences in implementation rather than the objective itself.

The experiments should isolate the contribution of the sigmoid-based divergence formulation. Ablations comparing the proposed objective with standard discriminator losses would help establish that this design choice drives any observed gains. The paper should also report sensitivity to important hyperparameters, such as learning rates, regularization, and discriminator update frequency. If the method introduces additional parameters or computational costs, these should be reported and compared with those of the baselines. Such analysis would make the practical value of the method easier to assess.

The theoretical discussion needs particular care. The paper should state the conditions under which the proposed discriminator objective corresponds to the claimed f-divergence. It should clarify whether the result holds for optimal discriminators, for finite-capacity function classes, or under a particular parameterization. Any assumptions about support overlap, sampling distributions, or realizability should be stated explicitly. The discussion should also distinguish properties of the divergence itself from properties of the resulting policy optimization procedure. A divergence that is well behaved in isolation does not automatically guarantee stable or effective policy learning.

For the learning-from-observations extension, identifiability deserves a more detailed treatment. Observations alone may not uniquely determine expert actions or a policy, especially when the same state can be associated with multiple actions. The authors should explain what information is sufficient for their approach and whether temporal structure is essential. If transition data or environment interactions are required, this should be stated prominently. A clear account of these requirements would prevent readers from interpreting the method as requiring less information than it actually does.

The paper would benefit from stronger diagnostic analysis. Learning curves could show whether improvements arise from faster learning, better final performance, or reduced instability. Measures of discriminator saturation or gradient behavior might help explain why the sigmoid-based objective works. For observation-only experiments, the authors should discuss whether the learned policy matches expert occupancy measures and whether evaluation depends on aspects of the environment not present in the demonstrations. Qualitative examples may also help illustrate failure cases and the conditions under which the method is most effective.

Reproducibility is another important consideration. The paper should provide sufficient implementation details, including network architectures, preprocessing, reward or score transformations, and optimization schedules. The exact form of each objective should be given in a way that allows independent implementation. Public code and evaluation scripts would substantially strengthen the work, although the manuscript should remain understandable without them. The authors should also specify how model selection and hyperparameter tuning were performed to avoid accidental test-set bias.

The presentation is generally strongest when it links mathematical definitions to practical consequences. However, the manuscript should avoid implying that one divergence is universally preferable. The choice may depend on the data regime, function approximation, environment, and optimization procedure. A more nuanced discussion of these trade-offs would make the conclusions more credible. The authors should also define terminology consistently, especially when distinguishing demonstrations, observations, trajectories, and expert occupancy distributions.

Overall, this is a promising study of an important design choice in adversarial imitation learning. Its combination of divergence-based objectives and observation-only learning has the potential to be useful to both theorists and practitioners. The key issue is whether the paper’s claims are supported by sufficiently controlled experiments and clearly stated theoretical assumptions. I recommend revision focused on stronger baseline comparisons, ablations, uncertainty reporting, and a more precise account of the observation-only setting. With these changes, the paper could make a meaningful contribution to the understanding and application of adversarial imitation objectives.

A milestone is a marker that shows how far someone has traveled or how much progress has been made. The word has a practical meaning and a figurative one. In its original sense, a milestone was a stone placed beside a road to show the distance to a destination or from a starting point. Travelers could use these markers to judge how far they had come and how much farther they needed to go. Some historic roads still have old milestones that reveal how journeys were measured in the past. Today, signs and digital maps usually provide distance information, but the idea of a milestone remains familiar.

Milestone also describes an important event or achievement in a longer process. Learning to read, finishing a school year, or completing a first work project can each be a milestone. In science, a major discovery or successful experiment may mark a turning point. In a community, opening a new library or reaching an important anniversary can be celebrated as a milestone. These events matter because they show that meaningful progress has occurred.

Milestones help people divide large goals into smaller stages. A student writing a research paper might set milestones for choosing a topic, finding sources, drafting, and revising. Each completed stage offers evidence of progress and helps make the final goal feel more manageable. Milestones can also help teams coordinate work by making expectations and deadlines clearer. When progress slows, reviewing earlier milestones can reveal what is working and what needs to change.

Not every milestone has to be dramatic or public. A small personal achievement may be important because it reflects effort, growth, or persistence. Reaching a milestone does not mean the entire journey is over; it often points toward the next stage. People may mark milestones with celebrations, certificates, photographs, or quiet reflection. These traditions help them remember what they accomplished and recognize the support they received.

Milestones can be useful, but they should not become the only measure of success. People develop at different rates, and some valuable progress is difficult to count. Comparing personal milestones with someone else’s can create unnecessary pressure. It is better to choose markers that fit a person’s own goals and circumstances. Looking back at milestones can build confidence, while looking ahead can provide direction. In both their literal and figurative meanings, milestones help us understand distance, recognize achievement, and see how far a journey has taken us.
