The first person Mara brought back was her brother.

Jonah had been dead for eleven years, buried beneath the old apple tree where they used to hide from storms. The resurrection engine stood in the town hall, built from copper coils and a bell that rang whenever it found a soul. Mara had saved for years to use it. She told herself she only wanted to hear Jonah laugh again. She did not tell herself she was afraid of forgetting the sound.

At dawn, she placed his cracked pocket watch on the engine’s brass plate. It had stopped at 4:17, the moment the river took him. The machine began to hum. Every window in the hall clouded with frost. Then the bell rang once.

Jonah opened his eyes on the table.

He looked exactly seventeen, with wet hair and a river pebble pressed into his palm. For a moment, Mara saw the boy who had taught her to skip stones. Then he turned his face toward her, and his smile faltered.

“Mara,” he whispered. “You’re old.”

She laughed, because she had rehearsed laughing. Then she reached for him.

He flinched.

The room went quiet except for the engine’s ticking. Jonah stared at her hands, marked by time and work, and asked how long he had been gone. Mara told him. He tried to sit up, but his body trembled as if it had forgotten the weight of itself. The machine had returned his breath, not his strength.

For three days, Jonah stayed in Mara’s cottage. He asked about everyone he remembered. Their mother was dead. His friends had children. The town had paved the road by the river. The orchard had been cut down to make room for houses.

Mara answered each question gently, leaving out the funerals when she could. Jonah listened with the polite patience of a guest. At night, he slept in the room where their mother used to sing them lullabies. Mara sat in the hall, afraid that if she slept, he might vanish.

On the fourth morning, Jonah found the pocket watch on the table. He wound it, though it could not keep time. “You brought me back because you missed me,” he said.

“I did,” Mara replied.

“Did you ask if I wanted to come?”

She had no answer that did not sound selfish.

Jonah looked out at the new houses. “I remember the river,” he said. “I remember being scared. Then I remember being somewhere quiet.”

Mara gripped the edge of the table. “I thought you deserved another chance.”

“Maybe I did.” He turned to her. “But you decided what that chance was.”

That afternoon, Jonah walked to the river with her. The water was narrow now, held between concrete banks. They stood where the old bridge had been. Mara remembered shouting his name until her voice broke. Jonah remembered the cold, the dark, and a strange feeling of release.

He did not blame her. That made it worse.

When they returned, the resurrection engine was waiting in the town hall. Its maker had left instructions for a second passage. No one knew what it would do. Some said it would send a returned person back to death. Others said it would only erase what remained of them.

Jonah asked Mara to take him there.

She refused at first. She had already lost him once. The thought of choosing his death felt like committing it herself. Jonah held her hands, careful not to startle her.

“You gave me a choice once,” he said. “You just didn’t know you were taking it away.”

At sunset, they stood before the engine. Its coils glowed a dull red. Jonah placed the pocket watch on the brass plate. The bell stayed silent.

Mara began to cry. She told him she was sorry for the years she had spent trying to make grief into a problem with a solution. She told him she missed his laugh, his terrible singing, the way he stole the last piece of bread and blamed the dog. She told him she did not know how to let him go.

Jonah hugged her. His arms were thin, but his embrace was familiar. “You already did,” he whispered. “You just came looking for me.”

Mara rested her forehead against his shoulder. For a moment, she could almost believe they were children again, hiding from thunder beneath the kitchen table. Then the engine began to hum.

Jonah stepped onto the table without fear. He took Mara’s hand and guided it to the switch. She felt the tremor in her fingers. He covered them with his own.

“Don’t remember me as a lesson,” he said. “Remember me as your brother.”

Mara pressed the switch.

The bell rang once, clear and low. Jonah’s hand grew warm, then light. His face settled into the peaceful expression she remembered from the last photograph their mother had taken. He looked at Mara and smiled.

Then he was gone.

The engine stopped. The room smelled of rain and apple blossoms, though the orchard had been gone for years. Mara stayed beside the table until morning. She did not ask the machine to bring him back.

After that, she visited the river every year on the day Jonah died. She brought the pocket watch and sat beneath a young apple tree she had planted by the bank. The watch never moved, but she carried it anyway.

Sometimes she laughed at his jokes, even the ones he had told a hundred times. Sometimes she cried. She learned that love did not have to keep a body breathing to remain alive.

When the town asked whether she regretted the resurrection, Mara said she regretted the choice she had made for him. She said she was grateful for the chance to hear his voice once more. Both things were true.

In time, people stopped coming to her for instructions about the engine. Some wanted their spouses back. Some wanted their children. Mara never told them what to choose.

She only asked them to imagine the person they loved standing before them, free to say no. Then she listened while they decided what love meant.

At the river, the apple tree grew crooked, leaning toward the water. Each spring it opened white blossoms along its branches. Mara watched them fall onto the current and drift away.

She no longer mistook letting go for forgetting. She no longer believed that grief was a door she had to force open. And when she remembered Jonah, she let him stay where he had chosen to rest.

The collider began its final run at midnight. Beneath the mountains, magnets hummed around a ring of steel and concrete. Dr. Mara Venn watched the particle beams race toward their meeting point. She had spent twelve years preparing for this moment. The control room smelled of coffee and warm electronics. Her team counted down in quiet voices. At zero, two streams of particles struck each other. The monitors flashed white. Then every instrument went dark. For three seconds, the mountain held its breath. A small black circle appeared above the collision chamber. It was no bigger than a grain of sand. Yet the air bent toward it, and the floor groaned. “Shut it down,” Mara said. The power died, but the circle remained. It drifted upward through the chamber roof without tearing it. Security doors sealed across the facility. The black circle pulsed once, like a heart. Then it stopped moving. Mara felt the hairs on her arms rise. The circle was not growing. It was listening. A voice crackled through the emergency speakers. “Containment is failing,” said the control engineer. “No,” Mara replied. “Containment was never the question.” She approached the observation glass. The circle reflected nothing—not the lights, not her face, not even the glass itself. Around its edge, stars appeared. They were not reflections. They hung in a deep blue darkness beyond the tiny horizon. Mara pressed her palm to the glass. The stars shifted, forming unfamiliar patterns. A young technician named Ilyan stared over her shoulder. “Those are moving,” he whispered. The black circle widened to the size of a coin. The chamber trembled, but its walls did not crack. Instead, the room seemed to stretch away from it. Alarms sounded in the corridors. Mara ordered everyone to retreat. Nobody moved. The stars brightened, and a pale cloud turned slowly around them. She recognized the shape from no map or telescope. It was a galaxy, newly born. The circle opened like an eye. Beyond it, space spread without end. Mara understood then that the collider had not made a hole in their universe. It had made a doorway for something smaller. A universe had begun on the other side, expanding into its own vastness. Its first light spilled into the chamber. The instruments came alive, recording numbers that climbed beyond their limits. Ilyan laughed, then covered his mouth. “We made a cosmos,” he said. “We gave it a beginning,” Mara answered. She wondered whether anyone inside that young universe would look up one day. Perhaps they would study their sky and find a faint, impossible warmth. Perhaps they would name it the first dawn. The black circle began to shrink. Its stars drew together, though the new galaxy continued to shine. Mara hurried to the console and copied the final readings. The screen filled with patterns too complex for any code she knew. Then the circle vanished. Silence settled over the chamber. The walls stood whole, and the air smelled of dust. For a long moment, nobody spoke. Outside, dawn touched the mountains. The team emerged beneath a pale morning sky. Mara looked up, imagining another sky far beyond it. Somewhere, she thought, a first sun was rising. Somewhere, the first oceans were cooling beneath it. And somewhere, life might already be learning how to wonder. Her hand still tingled from the glass. She closed her fingers around the sensation. The universe had grown larger, though no one on Earth could see it. The collider’s final run had ended. Its smallest collision had begun forever.

The invitation arrived on a rainy Tuesday, written in blue ink on thick cream paper. Elias Venn recognized the handwriting before he read the name. Mara Vale had once written to him every week, back when he was famous and her sister still believed in him. The letter said she wanted to discuss a book. It gave an address on the edge of town and asked him to bring a pen he loved. Elias nearly threw it away. He had spent the last year avoiding anyone who remembered his old life. His novels had vanished from shop windows after the scandal. Critics called him a fraud, and readers called him worse. But the phrase “a book” tugged at the part of him that had survived. He chose his favorite fountain pen, a black one with a silver nib. Then he took the train to the address.

The house stood beside a narrow river, its windows dark against the afternoon. Mara opened the door before he could knock. She was older than he remembered, though only by a few years. Her face was calm in a way that made him uneasy. “You came,” she said. “You asked me to,” he replied. She stepped aside and let him enter. The hall smelled of dust, tea, and something faintly medicinal. On the table lay a stack of notebooks tied with green ribbon. Elias saw the name on the top one and stopped. “Lena,” he said. Mara nodded. “My sister’s journals.” He had not spoken Lena’s name aloud since the trial. For a moment, the rain on the windows was the only sound.

Mara poured tea and sat across from him. “You used to say every life held a story,” she said. “I did.” “You also said a story belonged to whoever could tell it best.” Elias looked down at the cup in his hands. “I was wrong about many things.” “You were wrong about Lena.” He flinched. Lena Vale had been his assistant, his friend, and, for a brief season, the person he loved. When his first novel became a sensation, he had claimed the pages as his own. Lena’s notes and drafts had formed its heart. She had trusted him with them. He had turned that trust into a career. When she confronted him, he had called her unstable. The public believed the celebrated author. Lena did not survive the winter that followed. “I know what I did,” he said. “Do you?” Mara asked. “I have read the papers.” “I mean, do you know what you did to her?” He could not answer.

Mara untied the ribbon and opened the first notebook. Lena’s handwriting leaned forward across the page, neat and impatient. “She kept writing,” Mara said. “Even after you told everyone she had invented the accusation.” Elias looked at the lines. He remembered that handwriting in the margins of his drafts. He remembered dismissing it, then stealing from it. “Why invite me here?” he asked. “Because you still love writing.” “I don’t know if I do.” “You brought the pen.” She reached across the table and placed a blank sheet between them. “I want you to write Lena’s story.” He stared at her. “That isn’t mine to write.” “At last, you understand.” Mara closed the notebook. “You’ll write it with me. Every fact checked. Every page read by the people you hurt.” “And if I refuse?” “Then I publish her journals.” “You have the right to.” “I do.” Her voice stayed level. “But I want the truth in the hands of the man who spent years burying it.” Elias felt anger rise, then falter. “This is revenge.” “Yes.” The answer came without hesitation.

Mara pushed the blank sheet closer. “You’ll write about the theft, the lies, and the years Lena lost to your fame.” “You want me to confess in public.” “I want you to make the confession impossible to polish.” He glanced at the pen. “You know how I write.” “I know how you hide.” She slid a small recorder onto the table. “Everything you say will be saved.” Elias looked from the recorder to the notebooks. He could leave, but the door behind him seemed farther away than it had before. “Why not expose me yourself?” he asked. “I will, if I have to.” Mara’s eyes shone, though no tears fell. “But I promised Lena I’d give you one chance to tell the truth before it was taken from your hands.” Elias had no answer for that either. He uncapped his pen.

The first sentence came slowly. “Lena Vale wrote the book that made me famous.” Mara did not praise him. She did not look satisfied. “Write what you did next,” she said. He continued. He wrote about the contracts he had hidden, the pages he had claimed, and the interview where he called Lena jealous. He wrote about the letter she sent him after the interview. He had kept it in a drawer for years, unread after the first line. Mara took the letter from her coat pocket and placed it beside his hand. “I found it in her room,” she said. Elias recognized the fold and the pale stain where rain had touched it. “You can read it later.” “I should have read it then.” “Yes.” He started another paragraph.

They worked until dusk. Mara corrected dates and names. Elias crossed out every sentence that tried to make him sound wounded. When he described Lena’s last winter, his hand began to shake. Mara watched without speaking. “She kept asking you to admit the truth,” she said. “I thought if I ignored her, people would forget.” “They did.” “I didn’t.” “You forgot enough to keep living comfortably.” He lowered his eyes. The words hurt because they were fair. He wrote until the room turned blue with evening. At the end of the first chapter, he set down his pen. “This is only the beginning,” Mara said. “I know.” “No, you don’t. You still think a good ending can balance the page.” “Can’t it?” “Not for Lena.” Mara gathered the pages and stacked them beside the notebooks. “There is no ending that gives her back.”

Elias returned the next morning. He brought the same pen and a second notebook. Mara had left the front door unlocked. They worked through Lena’s childhood, her first stories, and the years she spent helping him. He learned how much he had never asked her. The knowledge made him feel smaller than the disgrace had. Some days he wrote well. Other days he filled page after page with excuses, and Mara made him start again. “You keep turning guilt into the main character,” she told him. “Lena deserves the page.” He learned to leave himself out. When the first draft was complete, Mara sent it to a lawyer, a fact-checker, and two people who had known Lena. They returned it covered in notes. Elias revised every line. He removed the clever phrases he had once used to make cruelty sound like regret. At last, the manuscript carried a title: What Lena Wrote. Mara read it alone before anyone else. She came back with swollen eyes and a red pencil. “This is closer,” she said. “Is it enough?” “No.” He waited. “But it is true.”

The book was published six months later, with Lena’s name on the cover and Elias’s confession printed in full. He surrendered the royalties to a fund Mara created for young writers. The public wanted to know whether he felt forgiven. He said he did not. They wanted to know if the book had healed him. He said it was not written for that purpose. Some readers praised his honesty. Others called the confession another performance. Elias did not argue. Mara attended the first reading, sitting in the back row. When he reached the page about Lena’s final letter, he stopped and unfolded the original. He read her words aloud, stumbling over the last line. “You know how to make people listen,” Lena had written. “Please use it for something true.” No one applauded when he finished. The silence felt right. Afterward, Mara waited by the door. “You did what she asked,” he said. “You wrote what she asked.” She tucked the red pencil into her coat pocket. “That’s not the same as being forgiven.” “I know.” “Good.” She walked into the rain without looking back. Elias watched her go, then returned to the empty hall. On the table lay his pen, its silver nib dark with ink. He opened Lena’s notebook to a page he had never seen. At the top, she had written a sentence about a man who mistook a stolen story for a life. Elias read it twice. Then, for the first time, he left the words exactly as she had written them.

The play began with a wedding, a bright room, and two actors smiling beneath paper lanterns.
From the balcony, Mira watched as the bride lifted her glass.
A whisper moved through the audience: “She’s lying.”
No one onstage had said a word to suggest it.
Mira glanced around, but every face was turned toward the actors.
The groom made a clumsy joke, and laughter rippled through the seats.
Then came a second whisper: “He’s laughing at her.”
The bride’s smile seemed to shrink, though it had not changed.
Mira gripped her program and tried to focus on the painted backdrop.
In the next scene, a brother entered carrying a suitcase.
The audience murmured before he spoke, certain he had come to steal the family fortune.
Onstage, he only asked for a place to sleep.
A woman beside Mira shook her head, as if she had caught him in a lie.
Mira began to understand: someone was rearranging the story, but only inside their minds.
The actors continued, unaware of the suspicion gathering around them.
Every pause became guilt, every kindness a trick.
At the final curtain, the cast bowed to a silence heavier than applause.
Mira turned toward the empty seat beside her.
On its cushion lay a black glove, still warm.
From somewhere behind the walls came a soft, satisfied laugh.

The invitation arrived in a black envelope.

Elias Vane found it wedged beneath his apartment door, though he lived on the seventh floor.

Inside was a card stamped with a silver knife.

It read: “The Gloaming Society welcomes applicants who understand the art of disappearance.”

Elias smiled.

At last, someone had noticed his potential.

For months, he had practiced looking mysterious in shop windows.

He had also kept a notebook labeled FUTURE VICTIMS.

The notebook was mostly empty.

A few names had been crossed out, though, because Elias had decided they were “too obvious.”

He put on his best coat and followed the address to an old hotel.

The lobby smelled of dust and lemon polish.

A woman in a red suit sat behind a desk.

“Your appointment?” she asked.

“An audition,” Elias said.

She handed him a brass key and pointed toward the ballroom.

The room was lit by candles.

Around a long table sat seven people in dark clothes.

Elias recognized none of them, which he took as a sign of their professionalism.

A broad man at the head of the table introduced himself as Mr. Vale.

“Tell us why you wish to join,” he said.

Elias clasped his hands.

“I have always admired the discipline of your craft.”

One of the applicants coughed.

Elias continued.

“I’m ready to take the next step.”

Mr. Vale studied him.

“What experience do you bring?”

Elias had rehearsed this answer in the mirror.

“I’m good at making people disappear.”

The woman beside Mr. Vale raised an eyebrow.

“Can you give us an example?”

“Certainly,” Elias said.

He described the neighbor who had vanished from his building last winter.

He explained how he had carried a rolled carpet down the stairs at two in the morning.

He described the red stain on the elevator floor.

The room grew very quiet.

“Interesting,” said Mr. Vale.

Elias beamed.

“I knew you’d appreciate the details.”

“Where is the neighbor now?” asked the woman.

“Probably in the river,” Elias said.

He leaned forward, eager to impress them.

“Though I can’t be certain. I never checked.”

Mr. Vale glanced at the others.

Elias mistook their silence for admiration.

“I’ve improved since then,” he added.

He told them about the landlord, who had stopped answering his calls.

He told them about the butcher’s missing dog.

He mentioned the two strangers he had followed through the train station.

“They all came back,” he said, disappointed.

“Some people are harder to get rid of than they look.”

The woman in red entered without knocking.

She whispered to Mr. Vale, but Elias could hear every word.

“The police are downstairs.”

He felt a thrill.

“They’re here for me, aren’t they?”

No one answered.

Elias stood, smoothing his coat.

“I suppose this is part of the test.”

Mr. Vale held up a hand.

“Sit down, Mr. Vane.”

Elias laughed.

“Very clever.”

The ballroom doors opened.

Two uniformed officers stepped inside.

Behind them was Elias’s neighbor, alive and wearing a neck brace.

The landlord followed, carrying a small terrier.

Elias stared at them.

“But I—”

“You reported yourself,” said the woman in red.

She explained that the Gloaming Society was a police sting, created to catch people who bragged about violent fantasies.

Elias looked at the silver knife on the invitation.

It was only a printed emblem.

His knees weakened.

The officers asked about the carpet, the stains, and the river.

Elias tried to explain that he had wanted to be impressive.

He said he had only dragged the neighbor’s old rug downstairs.

He said the red stain was tomato sauce.

He said he had never harmed anyone.

The neighbor nodded.

“That part is true,” he said.

Elias was led away for questioning.

As he passed the table, Mr. Vale gave him a small, tired smile.

“Perhaps,” Elias said, “I’m not ready for the guild.”

“There is no guild,” Mr. Vale replied.

Outside, rain blurred the hotel windows.

Elias noticed his reflection in the glass and tried to look mysterious.

For the first time, he looked merely frightened.

The paper addresses a timely topic by organizing neural-network approaches to clustering and comparing their strengths and limitations. Its taxonomy could be valuable to researchers, particularly if it clearly distinguishes methods by architecture, learning objective, and use of external or pretrained representations. The comparative assessment is potentially useful, but the paper should explain how the selected methods and datasets were chosen to avoid a biased comparison. For each method, please report consistent metrics and clarify whether results are drawn from original studies or reproduced under a shared experimental setup. Differences in preprocessing, hyperparameter tuning, computational budgets, and random-seed handling can substantially affect clustering results and should be discussed. The hybrid method is an interesting contribution, but its design rationale and precise relationship to the component techniques need to be made explicit. Ablation studies would help establish which components drive any improvements, while comparisons against strong non-neural and neural baselines would clarify the method’s value. The paper should also address sensitivity to the number of clusters, initialization, and dataset characteristics, as well as scalability and computational cost. Claims about superiority should be calibrated to the evidence, especially if evaluations cover only a limited set of datasets. Overall, the work has promise, but clearer methodological detail and stronger, reproducible comparisons are needed to support its conclusions.

When Daniel was eight, his father handed him a wooden box. “These belonged to your grandpa,” he said. Inside lay a pocketknife, a brass compass, and a stack of faded photographs. Daniel’s grandfather had died before Daniel was born. So the objects felt like messages from someone he had never met.

His father, Michael, picked up the compass. “Dad carried this on every camping trip,” he said. “He said a compass was only useful if you were willing to choose a direction.” Michael smiled, then told Daniel how his own father had once led their family out of a stormy forest. Daniel listened, watching his father’s face grow younger with every detail.

The pocketknife had a chipped wooden handle. Michael showed Daniel the careful way his father had taught him to whittle. “He made me a bird from a stick during a long train ride,” Michael said. “I kept it on my desk for years.” Daniel asked whether they could try making one together. Michael hesitated, then nodded.

They sat on the porch with a fallen branch and a bar of soap. Michael’s first cuts were clumsy. “I haven’t done this since I was a boy,” he admitted. Daniel laughed when the bird’s beak came out crooked. Michael laughed too, and for a moment, the porch seemed crowded with three generations.

As Daniel grew, the box stayed on a high shelf. He took the compass to school for a history project. He used the photographs to make a family tree. Each time, Michael added another story. He told Daniel about his father’s terrible singing and his habit of saving every birthday card.

Years passed, and Daniel left for college. Michael gave him the compass, wrapped in a handkerchief. “Keep it close,” he said. Daniel promised he would. But the compass stayed in a drawer, untouched, while new roads carried Daniel far from home.

Then Daniel became a father himself. One rainy afternoon, his daughter Lily found the compass in his desk. She turned it over in her small hands and asked what it was for. Daniel looked at the needle, trembling toward north. At last, he remembered his father’s words.

He took Lily outside after the rain stopped. Together they followed the compass down a path behind their house. Daniel told her about Michael, and about the grandfather whose stories had traveled farther than he ever could. Lily carried the compass carefully, as if it were a tiny lantern.

At the end of the path, she found a fallen branch. “Can we make a bird?” she asked. Daniel fetched the pocketknife and showed her how to carve safely, guiding her hands with his own. The bird emerged crooked, its beak pointing somewhere between north and home.

That evening, Daniel called his father. He told him about the walk, the branch, and Lily’s bird. Michael was quiet for a moment, then began to laugh. Daniel heard the familiar warmth in his voice and felt the old stories opening again.

The wooden box no longer seemed like a place where memories were stored. It had become a beginning. In Lily’s hands, the compass pointed forward, while the carved bird carried her toward a past she could now call her own.

Cilla Black has reflected on a career that took her from Liverpool’s Cavern Club to the centre of British television, ahead of receiving a Bafta special award.

The singer and presenter is being honoured for her contribution to entertainment across several decades. The award recognises work that has reached audiences through both music and television. Black said she felt proud to be acknowledged by Bafta. She described the honour as a chance to look back on the people and opportunities that shaped her career.

Born Priscilla White in Liverpool in 1943, she grew up surrounded by the city’s lively music scene. As a teenager, she went to the Cavern Club, where local groups were beginning to attract attention. She became part of the circle that included the Beatles. Her early connection with the group would prove important to her future.

Black began singing at the Cavern while working in a typing pool. At first, performing was something she fitted around her day job. The club gave her the chance to develop in front of a live audience. It also helped bring her to the attention of people who could open doors in the music business.

The Beatles encouraged her and helped introduce her to their manager, Brian Epstein. Epstein became her manager and guided the start of her recording career. She adopted the stage name Cilla Black. Her debut single, “Love of the Loved”, was written by Lennon and McCartney. It reached the charts in 1963 and established her as a promising new singer.

Her follow-up records brought wider success. “Anyone Who Had a Heart” became a major hit in 1964. The song showcased her powerful, distinctive voice. “You’re My World” followed and became another signature recording. Both songs helped make her one of Britain’s best-known female singers of the period.

Black’s early success came during a remarkable era for British popular music. Liverpool was at the heart of the so-called Merseybeat movement. Her career, however, developed along its own path. She combined a strong pop voice with an approachable public image. That combination helped her connect with listeners beyond the clubs where she first performed.

She continued to record throughout the 1960s and appeared regularly on television. Her visibility on screen helped make her familiar to audiences who might not have followed the music charts. She was also a guest on popular variety programmes. In time, television would become the defining part of her working life.

Black said that the move into presenting was not something she had planned from the beginning. She had initially thought of herself as a singer. But television gave her another way to entertain people. She found that conversation and humour came naturally to her. The camera, she said, became a place where she could be herself.

Her first major television opportunity came with the variety show “Cilla”, which began in 1968. The programme featured music, comedy and celebrity guests. It also gave her the chance to perform her hit song “Step Inside Love”. The song, written by Paul McCartney, became closely associated with the show. The series ran until 1976 and established Black as a leading television personality.

During its run, “Cilla” attracted a wide range of performers. The programme reflected the variety format that was popular with British viewers at the time. Black’s warmth helped her guide the different segments. She was able to move between singing, interviewing and comedy. That versatility became a central feature of her television style.

Black later turned to game shows, where she found an even larger audience. She presented “Blind Date” from 1985 to 2003. The programme paired single contestants and asked them to choose a date without seeing one another. Its format created moments of suspense, awkwardness and humour. Black’s lively reactions became part of the show’s appeal.

“Blind Date” made her one of the most recognisable presenters in Britain. Her catchphrases entered everyday conversation. She developed an easy rapport with contestants, treating their stories with interest and good humour. The show’s success helped make Saturday-night television a regular home for her. It also marked a shift from her earlier identity as a pop singer.

In 2003, Black began presenting “The Weakest Link”, taking over from Anne Robinson. The quiz show required a different tone from “Blind Date”. Its contestants faced a more formal competition, while Black brought her own brisk, engaging manner to the role. She remained at the centre of the programme as its questions and eliminations unfolded. The series added another long-running format to her television career.

Across both shows, Black built a reputation for being direct but personable. She could tease contestants without losing their trust. She was also known for her enthusiasm and quick responses. Those qualities made her distinctive among British presenters. Viewers often felt that her personality was as important to a programme as its format.

The Bafta special award recognises that broad contribution. It celebrates not only a successful run of programmes, but also the way Black helped shape popular entertainment. Her career has crossed generations of viewers. Many first knew her through her records, while others discovered her through television. For some, she has been a familiar presence throughout their lives.

Black has said she is grateful to the audiences who stayed with her. She has also credited the teams behind her programmes. Producers, writers, musicians and studio crews all played a part in the work. She has recalled the importance of being surrounded by people who understood how to make entertainment feel effortless. The apparent ease on screen, she noted, depended on a great deal of work behind the scenes.

Her connection to Liverpool remained important throughout her career. She often spoke of the city with affection. The Cavern Club, where she had started out, became part of the story she told about her beginnings. The Beatles’ encouragement was another lasting influence. She remembered them not only as global stars, but as friends who helped a young singer find her way.

Black’s career also reflected changing roles for women in entertainment. She moved from being a performer in a male-dominated music industry to becoming the central figure in popular television programmes. She maintained a public career over decades, adapting as audiences and formats changed. Her success was built on both talent and a willingness to take on new challenges. The Bafta honour places that achievement in the context of British television history.

The award is a moment of recognition, but Black’s response has been to look back with characteristic warmth. She has described the journey as extraordinary. From singing in a Liverpool club to hosting programmes watched by millions, each stage brought a different kind of opportunity. She said she never expected the career to last as long as it did. The affection of viewers, she suggested, made the work especially rewarding.

For Bafta, the special award acknowledges a career that cannot be captured by a single role. Black was a chart-topping singer, a variety-show host and a game-show presenter. She helped bring music and celebrity guests into living rooms, then became a familiar guide through the rituals of Saturday-night entertainment. Her achievement lies in the way she made each role feel personal. The award celebrates a performer whose appeal endured well beyond her first hit records.

The six-year mission began with a simple question: What would it take for people to explore the solar system safely? A crew of four astronauts launched from Earth aboard the fictional spacecraft Wayfinder. Their journey would reveal both the beauty of distant worlds and the dangers that make space travel difficult.

First, Wayfinder passed the Moon, where ancient craters preserve a record of impacts. The astronauts practiced landing and learned how dust can damage equipment and spacesuits. Earth soon looked like a bright blue dot, reminding them how precious its air and water are.

At Venus, thick clouds hid the surface, while crushing pressure and scorching heat made a landing impossible. The crew studied the planet from orbit and learned how a powerful greenhouse effect can transform a world. Mars offered a very different challenge: cold deserts, thin air, and planet-wide dust storms.

Robotic vehicles explored Mars ahead of the astronauts, searching for signs that ancient water might once have supported life. Beyond Mars, Wayfinder threaded a safe route through the asteroid belt, where small rocky bodies travel at tremendous speeds. The crew then visited Jupiter, a giant planet whose immense storms include the long-lasting Great Red Spot.

Jupiter’s moon Europa fascinated the explorers because a hidden ocean may lie beneath its icy crust. Saturn’s rings looked delicate from a distance, but they consist of countless pieces of ice and rock moving in orbit. At Titan, a moon of Saturn, the crew observed rivers and lakes of liquid methane beneath a hazy atmosphere.

Farther out, Uranus and Neptune appeared as cold blue worlds, with powerful winds and little sunlight. Past Neptune, Wayfinder studied icy objects in the distant Kuiper Belt, where the dwarf planet Pluto follows a long, unusual orbit. The spacecraft also detected no living beings, but its instruments gathered clues about how planets and moons form.

After six years, the crew returned with samples, measurements, and new questions. Their discoveries showed that each destination has its own hazards, from radiation and extreme temperatures to thin air and treacherous terrain. They also showed why careful exploration matters: the solar system is both a dangerous frontier and a remarkable classroom.

Teacher encouragement can make a big difference in how students feel about learning. When teachers notice students’ effort and progress, students are more likely to believe in themselves. Kind words can help students feel comfortable asking questions and trying new things. Encouragement also teaches students that mistakes are part of learning, not a reason to give up. With support from their teachers, students may work harder and set goals for themselves. As their confidence grows, they are more willing to take on challenges and improve their skills. Teacher encouragement helps students feel valued and gives them a stronger chance to succeed in school.

Online learning offers important benefits for students who are balancing education, work, and family responsibilities. Its flexibility allows students to study at times that fit around shifts, childcare, and other daily tasks. Instead of commuting to campus, they can use that time for coursework, rest, or family. Many online classes also let students review recorded lessons whenever they need to. This can be especially helpful for learners who miss a lesson because of work or a family emergency. Online learning may also make education more accessible to people who live far from colleges. Students can often choose from programs that would otherwise be difficult to attend in person. Learning online can help students develop useful skills, such as time management and independent problem-solving. Digital assignments and discussion boards also give them practice using technology that is common in many workplaces. In some cases, online study can reduce costs related to travel, meals, or campus housing. However, students still need a quiet place to study and a reliable internet connection. They also benefit from setting a schedule and asking family members or employers for support. With planning and support, online learning can help busy students make progress toward their goals while meeting their responsibilities.

Microsoft products and software can provide a useful foundation for a career in engineering. Engineers rely on technology to design, analyze, communicate, and solve problems. Experience with Microsoft tools can help students build skills for these responsibilities. However, using software alone does not make someone an engineer. It is most valuable when combined with strong technical knowledge, curiosity, and practice.

Microsoft Excel is one of the most practical tools for engineering work. Students can use it to organize measurements, calculate results, and create charts. Formulas help automate repetitive calculations and reduce manual errors. Engineers may also use spreadsheets to compare design options or track project costs. Learning how to check formulas carefully is just as important as knowing how to enter them.

Microsoft Word can support clear technical communication. Students can use it to prepare reports, explain procedures, and document results. A well-organized report helps other people understand how a conclusion was reached. Features such as tables, captions, and references can make technical information easier to follow. Clear writing is important because engineers often share their work with clients, teammates, and the public.

Microsoft PowerPoint can help students present engineering ideas. A student might use it to explain a prototype, describe a research project, or summarize test results. Effective presentations use visuals to support the message rather than distract from it. Practicing presentations also helps students answer questions and explain complex ideas in plain language. These communication skills are useful in nearly every engineering workplace.

Other Microsoft products can provide experience with collaboration and organization. Teams allows people to communicate, hold meetings, and share files. OneNote can help students collect class notes and project observations. SharePoint and OneDrive support file storage and collaboration, although users must pay attention to access permissions and data security. Learning to manage shared work responsibly is part of being a dependable team member.

Some Microsoft tools connect more directly to technical tasks. Power BI can help users explore data and create visual reports. Visio can be used to make diagrams and process maps. Depending on their courses and projects, students may also encounter programming tools such as Visual Studio. These tools can introduce useful concepts, but engineers should choose software based on the problem they need to solve.

To qualify for engineering roles, students need more than product familiarity. They should study mathematics, science, and engineering principles. They also need to develop skills in areas such as design, testing, programming, and safety. Employers often look for evidence that applicants can apply what they have learned to real problems. A class project, internship, or personal design project can provide that evidence.

Students can show their software experience through a portfolio. For example, they might include a spreadsheet that analyzes experimental data, a report describing a design, and a presentation explaining the results. They should describe their own contributions honestly and explain the methods they used. Certificates can demonstrate training, but they do not replace practical experience. The strongest examples show both technical judgment and careful use of tools.

Responsible software use matters in engineering. Students should protect private information, respect licenses, and check the accuracy of calculations and data. They should also be willing to learn new programs, since engineering tools change over time. Microsoft experience can help students begin this process, but flexibility is equally valuable. A successful engineer keeps learning throughout their career.

Overall, Microsoft products can strengthen a student’s preparation for engineering. They help with analysis, documentation, presentations, and teamwork. When students use these tools to complete meaningful projects, they gain experience they can discuss with employers. Still, software skills are only one part of professional readiness. Combined with engineering knowledge, problem-solving ability, and clear communication, they can help students take an important step toward an engineering career.

A missing elderly man has been found dead at a country park in Cumbernauld, days after his wife’s death. Police said the man had been reported missing and was discovered during a search of the area. His death is not being treated as suspicious, according to reports. The circumstances surrounding his wife’s death have not been confirmed. Police have asked anyone with relevant information to contact them.

An optimistic outlook can make everyday life feel more hopeful and manageable. Optimism does not mean pretending that problems do not exist. Instead, it means believing that challenges can be faced and that things may improve. This attitude can support happiness, stronger relationships, and personal success.

Optimistic people often notice small things to appreciate, such as a kind conversation or a sunny morning. Gratitude can help them focus less on what is missing and more on what they already have. When something goes wrong, they may be more willing to look for a lesson or a next step. This does not remove disappointment, but it can make it easier to recover from it. Over time, hopeful thinking can encourage people to keep trying rather than give up.

Optimism can also improve relationships. People who expect that others can understand them are more likely to communicate openly. They may listen with patience and assume good intentions instead of quickly judging someone. When disagreements happen, an optimistic person can believe that the relationship is worth repairing. Encouragement and kindness can also help friends and family feel valued. These habits create trust and make it easier to work through difficult moments together.

A hopeful attitude can support success at school, work, and in personal goals. People who believe effort can make a difference are more likely to practice and learn from mistakes. They may see failure as feedback rather than proof that they are incapable. This mindset can help them stay motivated when progress is slow. Optimism also makes it easier to notice opportunities and ask for help when needed. Still, success usually requires realistic planning and consistent effort, not positive thoughts alone.

It is important to balance optimism with honesty. Ignoring serious problems can prevent someone from finding a useful solution. A healthy outlook recognizes difficulties while also looking for ways forward. In everyday life, this balance can help people feel happier, treat others well, and pursue their goals with confidence.

The paper studies how implicit bias in optimization, margin-based generalization, and explicit regularization interact in two-layer ReLU networks. This is a timely topic, since understanding when gradient-based training generalizes remains a central challenge in modern learning theory. The paper’s main strength is its effort to connect optimization guarantees with statistically meaningful margin bounds rather than treating training dynamics and generalization as separate questions. Its focus on regularized networks also makes the results potentially relevant to practical training procedures. The theoretical framing is promising and could help clarify which properties of learned solutions drive performance.

The manuscript should state its contributions more sharply at the outset. In particular, it should distinguish its results from prior work on implicit bias in homogeneous models, margin-based bounds, and optimization of shallow neural networks. A concise comparison table or a clearly organized related-work discussion would help readers identify what is genuinely new. The assumptions on the data, initialization, activation, and regularizer should be collected in one place and motivated. It should also be clear whether the guarantees hold for arbitrary data distributions or only under separability or other structural conditions.

The treatment of implicit bias needs especially careful explanation. The paper should specify the optimization algorithm, step-size conditions, and any assumptions needed for convergence or direction selection. For ReLU networks, parameter rescaling and neuron permutation can produce equivalent predictors, so the authors should explain how the stated bias is defined despite these symmetries. If the conclusions depend on a particular parameterization, that dependence should be made explicit. The relationship between the implicit bias induced by optimization and the explicit regularization term should also be separated conceptually. As written, it may be difficult to tell which component is responsible for each guarantee.

The margin-based generalization analysis is potentially valuable, but the paper should clarify the precise margin notion used and how it relates to the network’s parameter norm and output scale. Readers would benefit from seeing the resulting bound alongside standard norm-based or margin-based bounds, with a discussion of when it is tighter. The dependence on width, depth, sample size, and confidence level should be highlighted rather than left implicit in notation. If the bound is distribution-free, the manuscript should say so; if it relies on realizability or a positive margin, those requirements should be emphasized. It would also help to explain whether the bound applies to the final iterate, an averaged predictor, or all iterates satisfying the stated conditions.

The optimization section should make the scope of its guarantees equally precise. The authors should distinguish global convergence, convergence to a stationary point, and convergence to a solution with a particular margin, since these are materially different claims. Any dependence on network width or initialization scale should be stated in the main theorem discussion. The proof strategy appears to require substantial technical work, but the paper would be more accessible with an intuitive overview before the formal arguments. A diagram of the logical dependencies among the assumptions, optimization result, and generalization theorem could be useful.

The empirical component, if intended to support the theory, should include experiments that directly test its predictions. In particular, comparisons across regularization strengths and initialization scales could reveal whether the predicted margin and implicit-bias effects are observable. Baselines should include an unregularized counterpart and, where feasible, alternative norm or margin controls. The authors should report variability across random seeds and explain how hyperparameters were selected. These experiments would not prove the theorems, but they could show whether the proposed mechanism is relevant beyond the assumptions of the analysis.

Overall, the paper addresses an important question and offers a potentially useful synthesis of optimization and generalization theory for two-layer ReLU networks. Its strongest contribution is the attempt to connect training dynamics, regularization, and margin guarantees within a common framework. However, the novelty relative to existing results, the role of each assumption, and the precise scope of the guarantees need to be clearer. I recommend revision before publication, with priority given to sharpening the contribution statement, improving the interpretation of the implicit-bias claims, and making the margin bound and optimization conditions more transparent.

A longtime Star Wars collector has sold a prized collection of vintage toys to help pay for a new home. The collector, who spent decades tracking down figures and vehicles, said parting with the items was difficult but necessary. The collection included toys from the original 1970s and 1980s releases, many still in their original packaging. Some pieces had become especially valuable because of their rarity and condition. The sale attracted interest from collectors eager to own a piece of the franchise’s early history. Rather than selling everything at once, the owner worked with specialists to assess the items and find buyers. The proceeds will go toward the purchase of a house, turning years of collecting into a practical investment. The collector said the toys had brought years of enjoyment and connected them with fellow fans around the world. Many were acquired through auctions, conventions and trades with other enthusiasts. The sale also reflects a wider market for nostalgia-driven collectibles, where scarce vintage items can command high prices. Still, the owner said the decision was about more than money. A stable place to live and a fresh start mattered more than keeping the collection intact. The collector plans to hold on to a few sentimental pieces and continue following the Star Wars universe.

Russia imposed economic restrictions on Turkey after Turkish forces shot down a Russian military jet near the Syrian border, deepening a diplomatic crisis between the two countries. The measures, announced by the Kremlin, target several sectors of Turkey’s economy and include limits on imports, services and business activity.

Russian President Vladimir Putin signed a decree ordering the restrictions, which Moscow described as a response to what it called an unfriendly act. The jet was downed after Turkey said it had violated Turkish airspace despite repeated warnings. Ankara said the aircraft had crossed the border from Syria, while Moscow maintained that it had remained in Syrian airspace.

The incident killed one of the Russian pilots, and a Russian serviceman involved in a search-and-rescue operation also died. The Russian government said the restrictions would take effect in stages, with details to be set out by officials. Among the measures are a ban on some Turkish food imports and restrictions on Turkish companies operating in Russia.

Moscow also ordered a halt to charter flights between the countries and advised Russian tour operators to stop selling trips to Turkey. The government said it would tighten controls on Turkish nationals working in Russia and review existing agreements on trade and cooperation. Russian officials argued that the steps were necessary to protect national security and Russian citizens.

The restrictions could affect Turkey’s tourism industry, which relies heavily on visitors from Russia, as well as exporters of agricultural goods. Turkish businesses with operations in Russia may also face uncertainty as the measures are implemented. Analysts said the economic impact would depend on how broadly the restrictions were enforced and how long they remained in place.

Turkey condemned Russia’s response and urged Moscow to avoid escalating the dispute. Turkish officials said their forces had acted according to established rules of engagement and defended the country’s airspace. They also called for dialogue and proposed a meeting between the two countries’ leaders.

Putin, however, said the downing of the aircraft had dealt a serious blow to relations and accused Turkey of supporting groups hostile to Russia. Moscow rejected Ankara’s account of the jet’s flight path, and the two governments offered sharply different versions of the events. The disagreement added to tensions over their opposing positions in the Syrian conflict.

International leaders called for restraint and urged both countries to use diplomatic channels. NATO, of which Turkey is a member, expressed solidarity with Ankara while also stressing the need to prevent further incidents. The United Nations said it was concerned about the consequences of a confrontation between regional powers.

Before the crisis, Russia and Turkey had maintained substantial trade and energy ties despite political differences. The new restrictions threaten to disrupt those connections and could affect planned projects and commercial agreements. Both sides face pressure to limit the fallout while standing by their positions on the aircraft incident.

No immediate timetable was announced for lifting the measures. Russian officials said the restrictions could be adjusted depending on developments, while Turkish officials called for a peaceful resolution. The crisis now places relations between Moscow and Ankara at their lowest point in years.

Optimism is the belief that, even when life is difficult, better possibilities remain. It does not mean pretending that problems do not exist. Instead, it means facing challenges with hope and looking for ways to move forward. This attitude can make a meaningful difference in everyday life by fostering perseverance, compassion, and success.

Optimistic people are often more willing to keep trying after a setback. For example, a student who receives a low grade can treat it as a chance to learn rather than proof of failure. They might ask their teacher for advice, make a study plan, and try again. This response takes effort, but it is more useful than giving up. Optimism helps people see that progress can happen gradually. It can also make difficult tasks feel less overwhelming because each small step seems worthwhile. When people believe that their actions matter, they are more likely to persist.

Optimism can also strengthen compassion. People who hope for improvement may be more patient with others who are struggling. They can remember that mistakes do not define a person and that someone having a hard day may need understanding. A hopeful attitude encourages us to offer support instead of quick judgment. For instance, a person might help a classmate who is falling behind rather than assuming that the classmate is lazy. This kindness can build trust and make communities feel more welcoming. Compassion also benefits the person who gives it, because helpful actions can create a sense of connection.

In addition, optimism can contribute to success. Success does not always mean winning or achieving a major goal; it can also mean improving, learning, or completing an ordinary responsibility. Optimistic people are more likely to notice opportunities and take practical steps toward their goals. If a plan does not work, they can adjust it rather than deciding that success is impossible. Their confidence may also help them communicate clearly and cooperate with others. Still, optimism works best when it is balanced with honest thinking and consistent effort. Hope alone cannot replace preparation, but it can encourage people to prepare and keep going.

In everyday life, optimism helps people respond to difficulties with courage and care. It supports perseverance by making setbacks seem manageable, compassion by encouraging understanding, and success by motivating useful action. Everyone faces moments of disappointment, but a hopeful outlook can help turn those moments into chances to learn. By practicing optimism, we can make life better for ourselves and for the people around us.
