U.S.-China Climate Cooperation and the Global Emissions Challenge

The United States and China are the world’s two largest annual emitters of greenhouse gases, so their choices strongly affect the pace of global warming. Together, they account for roughly two-fifths of global carbon dioxide emissions from energy and industry. Their cooperation can encourage other countries to act, while conflict can slow progress.

China’s emissions rose rapidly as its economy industrialized and demand for electricity, transport, and construction grew. It is now the largest annual emitter of carbon dioxide, though its emissions per person are lower than those of the United States. Coal remains a major source of Chinese electricity, but the country is also installing renewable energy at an enormous scale.

U.S. emissions have generally fallen from their mid-2000s peak, helped by replacing some coal-fired power with natural gas and renewable energy, improving efficiency, and changing economic activity. However, the United States still has high emissions per person, and transport, buildings, and industry remain major sources. Emissions can rise or fall from year to year, so long-term trends matter more than any single year.

The two countries have sometimes worked together on climate policy, including through joint research, clean-energy initiatives, and agreements to strengthen emissions targets. Cooperation has also been affected by trade disputes, strategic competition, and changing domestic politics. Diplomatic channels can help maintain practical work even when relations are strained.

Useful areas for joint action include methane monitoring, clean electricity, energy storage, and standards for measuring emissions. Methane is a powerful greenhouse gas, and reducing leaks from oil and gas operations can deliver relatively quick climate benefits. Sharing reliable data can help governments and companies identify where reductions are possible.

Both countries can accelerate the shift from fossil fuels by expanding wind, solar, nuclear power, and other low-carbon energy sources. Modernizing power grids and adding storage can make electricity systems more reliable as renewable generation grows. Electrifying cars, buses, heating, and some industrial processes can cut pollution when the electricity supply becomes cleaner.

Energy efficiency is another important strategy because using less energy often lowers costs as well as emissions. Better-insulated buildings, efficient appliances, and cleaner industrial equipment can reduce demand. Governments can support these changes through building codes, incentives, public investment, and clear long-term rules.

Reducing emissions also requires protecting forests and improving land management, since ecosystems can absorb carbon dioxide when they are healthy. At the same time, carbon removal should complement—not replace—rapid cuts in pollution from fossil fuels. A fair transition should help workers and communities affected by changes in energy and industry.

No single country can solve climate change alone, because greenhouse gases mix throughout the atmosphere and affect the whole world. Strong U.S.-China action, alongside efforts by every country, can speed up clean technologies and lower their costs. The central goal is to reduce emissions steadily and quickly enough to limit future warming and its risks.

How Parents Can Foster Children’s Resilience and Performance Through Effort-Focused Praise and Deliberate Practice

Children learn how to respond to challenge partly from the messages they hear at home. Parents can help them build resilience and improve their skills by praising effective effort and supporting purposeful practice. These approaches do not promise instant success, but they help children learn from experience and keep developing.

Resilience is the ability to adapt, recover, and keep going when things are difficult. It does not mean never feeling disappointed, anxious, or frustrated. A resilient child can recognize those feelings and gradually learn what to do next. Parents can support this process by listening, offering reassurance, and helping children identify manageable steps forward.

Praise can shape what children believe leads to success. When parents focus only on being “smart” or naturally talented, children may worry that mistakes reveal a lack of ability. They might choose easier tasks to protect their reputation. Effort-focused praise can instead draw attention to actions children can influence.

Useful praise is specific and sincere. Rather than saying, “You’re a genius,” a parent might say, “You tried a new strategy when the first one didn’t work.” This recognizes persistence, problem-solving, or preparation. It also gives children a clearer idea of what helped.

Effort-focused praise does not mean praising every attempt or rewarding effort regardless of the result. Empty or exaggerated praise can feel untrustworthy. Praise should describe something real, such as careful revision, asking for feedback, or practicing a difficult passage. It can also acknowledge when a child’s strategy needs to change.

Parents can ask questions that help children notice their own progress. “What part was hardest?” or “What did you try differently?” invites reflection. “What might you do next time?” helps turn a setback into information. These questions work best when they sound curious rather than like a test.

Children also benefit from hearing that ability can grow with learning and practice. This does not mean everyone will reach the same outcome or that effort alone guarantees success. It means skills are not always fixed, and effective practice can make a difference. Parents can model this belief by talking about what they are learning themselves.

Deliberate practice is more than spending a long time on an activity. It involves working toward a clear goal, focusing on a specific skill, and using feedback to improve. For a young musician, that might mean practicing a tricky transition slowly rather than replaying an entire song. For a student, it could mean reviewing the types of math problems they often miss.

A useful practice session begins with a manageable goal. Children can break a large task into smaller steps and focus on one step at a time. Short, regular sessions may be more helpful than occasional marathons. The right amount of practice depends on the child’s age, energy, interests, and activity.

Feedback is an important part of deliberate practice. Parents can help children find useful feedback from teachers, coaches, peers, or their own work. Feedback should be specific, respectful, and focused on what can be changed. Instead of saying, “That was bad,” a parent might say, “The rhythm became uneven in the middle; let’s listen to that section again.”

Mistakes are not proof that a child has failed. They can point to what needs attention, especially when children have support to understand them. Parents can respond calmly and avoid taking over immediately. Giving a child time to think can build confidence and independence.

At the same time, resilience does not mean pushing through every difficulty without help. Children may need a break, a simpler step, or support from an adult. If practice repeatedly leads to distress, it is worth exploring why. The task may be too difficult, the goal may be unclear, or the child may need a different kind of instruction.

Parents should also make room for rest and play. Sleep, movement, friendships, and unstructured time support children’s well-being and learning. Practice is most helpful when it fits into a balanced life. A child’s worth should never depend on grades, trophies, or constant improvement.

Comparisons with siblings or classmates can undermine confidence. Children develop at different rates and bring different strengths to their activities. It is often more useful to compare a child’s current work with their own earlier work. Noticing progress can help them see that learning is a process.

Parents can support performance by helping children set goals they have a role in choosing. A goal such as “practice piano for ten minutes on four days this week” is more actionable than “be the best.” Children can then review what worked and adjust the plan. Shared goal-setting also gives them a sense of ownership.

It helps to separate a child’s identity from a particular outcome. A poor test score or lost game is information about one moment, not a complete judgment of the child. Parents can acknowledge disappointment without minimizing it. They can then help children decide whether they want comfort, advice, or help making a plan.

The most powerful lessons often come from everyday interactions. Notice the process, encourage reflection, and offer steady support when things go wrong. Celebrate progress without making praise conditional on achievement. With patience, children can learn that setbacks are part of learning, effort can be guided, and improvement is possible.

School cafeterias should offer healthier meals, but they should not replace familiar lunches all at once. Many students look forward to foods they know, such as pizza, sandwiches, or pasta. These meals can make lunchtime feel comforting and enjoyable. If a cafeteria changes its menu too quickly, students may refuse to eat the new food. That could leave them hungry during afternoon classes. Still, familiar lunches are not always the healthiest choices. Meals with too much salt, sugar, or fat can affect students’ health over time. Schools have a responsibility to help students build good eating habits. They can do this without removing every popular meal. For example, cafeterias could serve pizza with whole-grain crust and vegetables. They could offer baked chicken instead of fried chicken. Fresh fruit and vegetables could be available alongside familiar main dishes. These changes would make lunches healthier while keeping them appealing. Students should also have a chance to share their opinions about the menu. Surveys and taste tests could help cafeteria staff learn what students enjoy. When students help choose meals, they may be more willing to try something new. Schools can introduce healthier dishes gradually rather than changing everything at once. They might feature one new meal each week and keep popular options available. Over time, students could become comfortable with a wider variety of foods. A balanced menu can be both nutritious and familiar. Schools should improve cafeteria lunches thoughtfully instead of forcing students to give up the foods they already enjoy.

Character and kindness play an important role in building strong relationships and achieving lasting success. A person with honesty, patience, and respect earns the trust of friends and family. Kindness helps people feel valued, especially when they are facing difficulties. In parenting, these qualities teach children how to care for others and handle challenges responsibly. Parents who listen and show compassion create a home where children feel safe and understood. Good character also supports personal success because people who work hard and keep their promises are more likely to reach their goals. Kindness can strengthen teamwork and open doors to new opportunities. Even when life is difficult, treating others well can help us find support and maintain self-respect. In the end, character and kindness make relationships healthier, parenting more caring, and success more meaningful.

Optimism can play an important role in personal and professional achievement. It helps people believe that challenges can be overcome through effort and persistence. When students face a difficult subject, an optimistic attitude can encourage them to keep studying instead of giving up. At work, optimism can help employees approach problems with creativity and confidence. It can also make people more open to feedback, because they view mistakes as opportunities to learn. Optimistic people often inspire those around them, which can strengthen teamwork and relationships. However, optimism does not mean ignoring risks or expecting success without effort. It works best when paired with realistic goals, careful planning, and a willingness to adapt. By focusing on possibilities while learning from setbacks, people can make steady progress toward their ambitions. In this way, optimism can support achievement in both personal life and professional careers.

For three days, Diglett had been trapped in a wooden crate.
The crate sat in the back of a poacher’s wagon, rattling along a rocky road.
A few air holes let in slivers of sunlight, but not enough to show the way home.
Diglett missed the soft earth of its burrow and the familiar voices of its colony.
Whenever the wagon stopped, it listened for the distant calls of its family.
At last, the poacher left the crate beside a creek while he searched for supplies.
Diglett pressed its nose against a loose plank.
The wood had swollen in the damp air, and a narrow crack had opened beneath the latch.
Diglett wriggled through, scraping its smooth body against the rough edge.
It dropped into the grass and hurried toward the ground.
The poacher heard the crate creak.
But Diglett was already tunneling beneath the wagon.
It burrowed under the road, following the faint scent of home.
The earth was hard and stony, and its small body grew tired.
Still, it kept digging.
When night came, Diglett paused beneath the roots of an old pine.
The stars could not be seen from underground, but the soil carried the coolness of the dark.
Diglett slept for a little while.
At dawn, it heard a familiar rumble.
Its colony was nearby.
Diglett dug faster, calling out as it went.
The voices above answered with worried cries.
A moment later, Diglett broke through the surface in the middle of the colony’s clearing.
Its family crowded around, touching noses and asking where it had been.
Diglett began to tell them about the crate and the wagon.
Then the ground beneath it trembled.
A warm glow spread through the soil.
Diglett’s body shone with a bright, golden light.
The colony stepped back in amazement.
The light grew brighter, and the earth lifted in a ring around Diglett.
When the glow faded, three heads rose from the same patch of ground.
Diglett had evolved into Dugtrio.
For a breath, nobody spoke.
Then the colony erupted in happy cheers.
Dugtrio looked down at its three faces and gave an uncertain laugh.
Its family welcomed it as warmly as ever.
Dugtrio showed them how it could dig three tunnels at once.
Together, they built a hidden passage beneath the clearing.
They made it wide enough for every Diglett to escape if danger came again.
The colony listened as Dugtrio described the outside world.
It told them to watch for wagons, traps, and strangers.
It also told them that fear did not have to end in defeat.
That evening, the colony gathered around a patch of soft earth.
Dugtrio sat in the middle, telling the story again.
Each time, the three heads added a different detail.
The smallest Diglett listened with shining eyes.
It asked whether the journey home had been frightening.
Dugtrio nodded, then smiled.
“Yes,” it said, “but I kept going because I knew you were waiting.”
The colony settled close around its returned hero.
Far below, their new tunnels stretched safely into the hills.

A four-day school week can benefit students, teachers, and school communities, but it also has drawbacks. With one weekday free, students may have more time to rest, attend appointments, or take part in activities. A shorter week can also give teachers more time to plan lessons and prepare materials. In some districts, schools save money by reducing transportation, heating, and meal-service costs. These savings may help schools use their budgets more effectively. However, a four-day week does not always mean students spend less time learning. Schools often make the other four days longer to meet required instructional hours. Long school days can be tiring, especially for younger children. Families may also struggle to find childcare on the day school is closed. Students who depend on school meals may miss an important source of food that day. Teachers and other school employees may have difficulty arranging childcare or finding other work schedules. The effects can differ between rural and urban communities. In rural areas, a shorter week may reduce long bus trips and make staffing easier. In other places, the extra day away from school may interrupt students’ routines and learning. Schools should consider student achievement, attendance, family needs, and costs before making a change. They should also ask students, families, teachers, and community members for their opinions. Overall, a four-day school week can be helpful when it is carefully planned, but it is not the best choice for every school community.

PHP and C are both programming languages, but they were designed with different goals in mind. PHP is a high-level language that makes common tasks easier by handling many details for the programmer. C is a lower-level language that gives programmers more direct control over memory and hardware. This difference shapes how the languages are used.

PHP is dynamically typed, so a variable’s type can change as a program runs. It includes features and libraries for working with text, dates, databases, files, and web requests. PHP’s syntax is designed to make building web applications relatively quick. It can also run as a command-line script.

C is statically typed, meaning variable types are generally checked during compilation. It provides tools for creating efficient programs and managing memory explicitly. This control can improve performance, but it also means programmers must handle more details and avoid errors such as invalid memory access. C programs are typically compiled into native machine code.

PHP is widely used for websites, web applications, and server-side services. Popular content-management systems and frameworks use it, and it can connect to many databases. C is common in operating systems, embedded devices, device drivers, compilers, and performance-sensitive software. It is also useful when software must work with limited memory or interact closely with hardware.

PHP is not limited to web development. It can be used for command-line tools, scheduled scripts, automation, and other general-purpose tasks. However, its ecosystem and design make web development its most prominent use. C is also general-purpose, but it is usually a better fit when low-level control, portability, or predictable performance is important.

Neither language is universally better. PHP often helps teams build web features quickly, while C offers greater control and can produce highly efficient programs. The right choice depends on the project’s requirements, the available libraries, and the developers’ experience.

The paper addresses an important question: whether randomized image transformations can reliably defend against adversarial attacks without imposing excessive computational costs. Its evaluation should compare multiple transformations and report attack success rates alongside clean-image accuracy, since a defense that disrupts benign inputs may offer limited practical value. The experiments should also use adaptive attacks that account for the transformations, rather than relying only on attacks designed for undefended models. A key strength of this topic is its practical focus on the trade-off between robustness, accuracy, and inference time. However, the conclusions would be difficult to generalize unless the study covers diverse datasets, model architectures, and attack strengths. The computational analysis should distinguish the cost of applying transformations from the additional cost of repeated sampling or expectation-based attack evaluation. Sensitivity to input size is especially important, and results should explain whether changes in resolution affect robustness, latency, or both. Clear reporting of transformation parameters, randomization procedures, and evaluation details would make the findings easier to reproduce. Overall, the paper could make a useful contribution, but its claims should be grounded in rigorous adaptive testing and a transparent analysis of performance and cost.

This paper studies how initialization affects signal propagation and Jacobian behavior in deep ReLU networks with residual connections, and connects these effects to generalization. The topic is timely and important, since residual architectures are widely used while their depth-dependent behavior remains difficult to characterize. The paper’s central strength is its effort to analyze forward signal statistics and input-output sensitivity within a unified framework. This perspective can help explain why networks with similar architectures may behave differently under different initialization schemes.

The analysis of signal propagation is generally well motivated. In particular, tracking activation moments across layers provides a useful way to identify regimes in which signals remain stable, vanish, or grow. The treatment of ReLU’s gating behavior is also essential, because activation sparsity affects both the forward dynamics and the derivatives. The discussion of residual connections usefully highlights that skip paths can alter the accumulation of signals and gradients rather than simply making deeper networks easier to optimize. The paper would be stronger if it stated its assumptions about weight distributions, width, and independence prominently before presenting the main conclusions. These assumptions determine how closely the theoretical results apply to finite-width networks used in practice.

The Jacobian analysis is a valuable component of the work. Studying its spectrum or related measures can provide insight into sensitivity, conditioning, and the preservation of information through depth. The paper appropriately treats initialization as a determinant of these properties, rather than assuming that residual connections alone guarantee stable gradients. However, the interpretation of Jacobian behavior should be made more precise. For example, the authors should distinguish between controlling average singular values, preventing extreme singular values, and maintaining a well-conditioned Jacobian; these are not equivalent claims. If the results concern only expected quantities, the paper should avoid language that suggests typical behavior without supporting concentration or variance analysis.

The proposed connection to generalization is interesting but appears to require careful qualification. Stable signal propagation and favorable Jacobian properties may support optimization and preserve useful representations, but they do not by themselves establish better generalization. The paper should clarify whether its generalization claims are theoretical consequences, empirical associations, or motivating hypotheses. If the authors provide experiments, they should include multiple random seeds and report uncertainty, since initialization-dependent effects can be variable. Comparisons should also control for architecture, parameter count, training procedure, and data augmentation. Ablations that vary residual-branch scaling independently of the weight initialization would help identify which design choice drives each observed effect. It would also be informative to test whether the predicted trends persist across different depths and widths, rather than relying on a narrow range of models.

The exposition would benefit from a clearer separation between results that hold asymptotically and findings validated at practical widths. A concise summary table could map each initialization regime to its predicted signal and Jacobian behavior, along with the conditions required. The authors should define all scaling conventions consistently, particularly whether residual updates are normalized by depth or by another factor. Notation for layerwise quantities should also make clear when expectations are over data, weights, or both. Any claims about universality across architectures should be narrowed unless supported by direct evidence. A discussion of limitations, including the role of normalization layers, non-ReLU activations, and training-time changes to the weights, would help readers assess the scope of the conclusions.

Overall, the paper offers a useful framework for understanding how initialization shapes deep residual networks. Its strongest contribution is the joint focus on forward signals and Jacobian structure, which makes the analysis more informative than considering either in isolation. The main concern is that the transition from these mechanistic quantities to generalization remains insufficiently established. With sharper assumptions, more calibrated claims, and additional empirical validation, the work could make a meaningful contribution to the study of deep network initialization. I recommend revision before acceptance, with particular attention to clarifying the generalization argument and strengthening the experimental evidence.

Completing schoolwork individually has several important benefits. It gives students the chance to think for themselves and develop their own ideas. When students work alone, they can focus on the parts of an assignment they find most challenging. They also have more control over their pace. A student can spend extra time on a difficult question without needing to wait for others. If a task is easy, the student can move on quickly. Individual work can help students understand their strengths and weaknesses. They can see which skills they have mastered and which ones need more practice. This awareness makes it easier to set personal learning goals. Working alone also encourages responsibility. Students must manage their time and complete each part of the assignment themselves. As a result, they can become more independent and confident. Individual assignments can also make it easier to judge what each student truly understands. In a group, one person may do most of the work while others contribute very little. When students work individually, their effort and progress are clearer. They can also express their opinions without worrying about whether the group agrees. This freedom can lead to original and creative answers. Working alone may reduce distractions, especially when classmates have different ideas about how to approach a task. Students can choose a method that suits their learning style. They may also find it easier to concentrate in a quiet setting. Completing schoolwork individually prepares students for tests, since tests usually require them to answer questions on their own. It also builds habits that are useful in future studies and at work. However, group work can still be valuable for sharing ideas and practicing cooperation. The best choice depends on the assignment and its goals. Even so, individual schoolwork is especially beneficial when students need to build knowledge, independence, and confidence.

Tambellup is a small town in Western Australia’s Great Southern region, about 300 kilometres south-east of Perth. Its name comes from an Aboriginal word, though its precise meaning is uncertain. The town lies on the traditional lands of the Noongar people, whose connection to the area long predates European settlement. European pastoralists moved into the district during the nineteenth century, establishing farms and grazing properties. Tambellup developed as a service centre for these settlers and the surrounding agricultural district. The arrival of the railway in the late nineteenth century helped the town grow by connecting local producers with larger markets. Tambellup became an important stop on the railway line between Perth and the south coast. Farming has remained central to the district’s economy. Wheat and other grains are grown across the surrounding country, alongside sheep and cattle. These industries shape local employment, trade, and seasonal routines. The Gordon River runs near Tambellup and is an important feature of the local landscape. Heavy rainfall can cause the river to rise and flood nearby land, affecting roads, farms, and properties. Flooding has at times disrupted transport and community life, highlighting the town’s exposure to changing weather and river conditions. Local residents and authorities monitor flood risks and respond with warnings and practical preparations. Tambellup’s heritage can be seen in its historic buildings, railway connections, and long-established rural institutions. The town has schools, sporting groups, community organisations, and local services that support residents across the district. The Tambellup Agricultural Society brings people together through events that celebrate farming and country life. Community spirit is especially evident during local gatherings, sports competitions, and times of hardship. Today, Tambellup combines a strong agricultural identity with a close-knit community and a continuing connection to the history of Western Australia’s Great Southern.

Attempts by migrants to enter the United Kingdom through the Channel Tunnel disrupted transport and prompted heightened security in Calais, French authorities said. The incidents took place near the tunnel’s French entrance, where trains and freight services pass beneath the English Channel.

Transport operators reported delays as staff and security teams responded to the situation. Some services were held while access routes and infrastructure were checked. The disruption affected both passenger and freight movements, though the scale and duration of delays were not immediately clear.

French police increased patrols around the terminal and nearby access points. Additional security measures were introduced to prevent people from reaching the tracks or entering restricted areas. Officials urged the public to follow instructions and avoid the affected locations.

The tunnel operator said safety remained its priority and that services would resume as soon as conditions allowed. Passengers were advised to check for updates before travelling. Freight companies were also warned to expect possible delays.

The incident reflects continuing efforts by migrants to reach Britain from northern France. Many people in the region hope to claim asylum or join family members in the UK. Some attempt dangerous crossings by sea, while others seek to board vehicles or trains heading through the tunnel.

Authorities have repeatedly warned that entering the tunnel’s infrastructure is extremely dangerous. Trains travel at high speeds, and the site contains restricted areas with significant operational hazards. Previous attempts to access the tunnel have led to serious injuries and deaths.

French officials said they were working with the operator to restore normal traffic and secure the area. They did not immediately provide details about how many people were involved or whether anyone had been detained. British authorities were also monitoring developments on the other side of the Channel.

The disruption places renewed attention on migration controls around Calais. French and British governments have cooperated on measures intended to prevent unauthorised access to the tunnel and reduce dangerous journeys. The policies have drawn criticism from aid groups, who argue that people seeking protection need safer routes and adequate support.

Local organisations in northern France provide food, medical assistance and legal guidance to migrants. They say people continue to face uncertainty over their asylum options and living conditions. Officials, meanwhile, stress the need to protect transport infrastructure and maintain public safety.

Transport services were expected to return to normal once security checks were complete. Operators said they would issue further updates as information became available. Travellers were encouraged to allow extra time and confirm their bookings.

The events underline the challenge of balancing secure transport links with the humanitarian needs of people seeking refuge. Further details about the disruption and any official response were expected later.

Early Irish dynasties, Gaelic genealogy, and the historical traditions of Niall, Conall, Columba, and Tara

Early Ireland was shaped by local kingdoms, powerful kin groups, and traditions that linked political authority to ancestry. Gaelic genealogies were not simply family records. They also explained who had a right to rule, how communities were related, and where a group belonged in the landscape. Stories about Niall of the Nine Hostages, Conall, and the sixth-century missionary Columba sit at the meeting point of history, memory, and legend. Tara, the ancient ceremonial center in County Meath, became an especially powerful setting for those traditions.

Ireland in the early medieval period was divided among many small kingdoms, often called túatha. A túath was a community with its own ruler, leading families, and territory. Several túatha could form or be associated with a larger regional kingdom. Political power was rarely fixed for long, because rulers competed through warfare, alliances, tribute, and marriage. A dynasty’s strength depended not only on descent but also on its ability to secure support and demonstrate authority.

The early Irish sources use terms such as Uí Néill, meaning “descendants of Niall,” for groups that claimed a shared ancestor. Such names could describe a political network as well as a biological family. They helped rulers present a common identity across several branches and territories. Genealogies often traced descent through male lines, but women’s marriages and relationships also shaped alliances. The surviving records usually give much less attention to women than to men.

Niall of the Nine Hostages is remembered as an early fifth-century king and the ancestor of the Uí Néill dynasties. His epithet is famous, but its original meaning is uncertain. Later stories associate the hostages with territories or peoples brought under his power. These accounts reflect ideas about royal authority more clearly than they provide a reliable record of a particular event. Niall may have been a historical ruler, but the details of his life remain difficult to verify.

The Uí Néill came to dominate much of northern and central Ireland over the early medieval centuries. They were not one unified state, but a set of related dynastic branches. Historians commonly distinguish northern and southern Uí Néill, though the political realities behind those labels changed over time. Kings from these branches competed for regional supremacy and, at times, for the title of high king. The title did not necessarily mean that a ruler controlled every part of Ireland.

Irish genealogists connected rulers to celebrated ancestors through long chains of descent. These chains could preserve genuine memories, but they could also be rearranged or extended to support later claims. A genealogy should therefore be read as both evidence and argument. It tells us how a community wanted its past to be understood. Comparing genealogies with annals, law texts, archaeology, and place-name evidence can help historians assess what may be historically useful.

Conall is a name shared by several figures in early Irish tradition, so it is important to ask which Conall a source means. One prominent figure was Conall Gulban, traditionally described as a son of Niall of the Nine Hostages. He was said to have founded or given his name to the Cenél Conaill, a major Uí Néill dynasty in the north-west. The Cenél Conaill later ruled in parts of modern Donegal and neighboring areas. Their history illustrates how a claimed ancestor could give a dynasty both a name and a sense of inherited territory.

Another important Conall was Conall mac Néill, whose name appears in traditions concerning the northern Uí Néill. The many recurring names in Gaelic genealogies can make family trees confusing. Names were reused to honor ancestors and to affirm continuity. Researchers must distinguish individuals by their dates, relationships, titles, and the particular source describing them. A single name in a medieval text does not always identify a single person with certainty.

Columba, also known by the Irish name Colum Cille, was born in the sixth century and is traditionally linked to the Cenél Conaill. Later tradition describes him as a descendant of Niall through Conall Gulban. Columba became a prominent Christian leader and founded a monastery on Iona, an island off the western coast of Scotland. From Iona, his community played an important role in Christian learning and missionary activity around the Irish Sea. His career connects dynastic history with the growth of monastic culture.

Columba’s life was written down in the seventh century by Adomnán, an abbot of Iona. Adomnán’s account, known as the Life of Columba, includes reports of miracles, prophecy, and encounters with rulers. It is a valuable source for the ideals and political relationships of the time, but it is also a religious biography. Its stories should not be treated as neutral eyewitness reporting. They show how Columba’s community remembered its founder and presented his spiritual authority.

Columba’s traditional royal ancestry mattered because kinship and political influence remained intertwined. A noble background could help explain how a religious leader gained access to kings and elite households. Yet his importance also came from his learning, religious reputation, and the institution that developed around him. Iona became a major center of worship, manuscript culture, and cross-sea connections. The history of Columba therefore cannot be reduced either to genealogy or to religious legend alone.

Tara was a ceremonial and political center associated with the kingship of Ireland. The archaeological complex at Tara includes earthworks, enclosures, and monuments from different periods. The most recognizable feature is the Mound of the Hostages, a passage tomb built long before the historical Uí Néill rulers. This ancient monument shows that Tara’s significance began centuries before the early medieval period. Later communities could connect themselves to an already powerful and deeply ancient landscape.

Medieval writings often portray Tara as the seat of a high king and the setting for important assemblies. The historical reality was more complex than the image of a single ruler governing the whole island from one capital. Tara could serve as a place of ceremony, assembly, and symbolic authority without functioning like a modern administrative center. Its importance lay partly in its political relationships and partly in its place in Ireland’s remembered past. Archaeology and texts offer different kinds of evidence about that importance.

Traditions also connected Tara to the inauguration of kings and to objects or customs associated with sovereignty. Some accounts describe the Lia Fáil, or Stone of Destiny, as a stone that cried out for the rightful king. Such stories helped make kingship seem rooted in the land itself. They should be understood as political and symbolic traditions, not straightforward records of an ancient coronation ceremony. Their changing forms reveal how later writers imagined legitimate rule.

The stories of Niall, Conall, and Columba show how ancestry could link a dynasty to religious authority and regional identity. Tara shows how a place could gather those memories into a shared political landscape. These traditions are not all equally factual, and their details cannot always be confirmed. Even so, they are essential sources for understanding how medieval Irish people thought about power, kinship, faith, and the past. Reading them carefully means recognizing both their historical value and their literary purpose.

Graphene is a form of carbon arranged in a sheet just one atom thick. Its remarkable strength and low weight make it an attractive ingredient for advanced materials. In a mechanical watch, graphene is generally combined with another material rather than used alone. The resulting composites can be used in parts such as the case, rotor, or movement components, depending on their design. Replacing heavier materials can reduce the watch’s overall weight and make it more comfortable to wear. Graphene-enhanced materials may also help components resist wear, impacts, or corrosion. These benefits depend on the composite’s recipe and manufacturing quality. Graphene does not make every watch component stronger or more durable automatically. Engineers must carefully control how graphene is distributed and bonded within the material. They also need to test parts under the stresses of daily use. A lighter rotor, for example, must still have the right mass and balance to keep the movement operating reliably. The watch’s precision continues to depend on the design and adjustment of its mechanical movement. Graphene-enhanced construction is therefore a promising tool, not a substitute for sound watchmaking. When engineered well, it can help create a mechanical watch that is exceptionally light while remaining durable.

Abdominal fat is the fat stored around the waist, but not all of it is the same. Some lies just beneath the skin, while visceral fat sits deeper inside the abdomen around organs such as the liver and intestines. Visceral fat can affect how the body manages hormones, blood sugar, and inflammation. A larger waist can be a sign of increased visceral fat, although waist size alone cannot diagnose a health problem.

Excess abdominal fat is associated with a higher risk of type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure, heart disease, and stroke. It is also linked to fatty liver disease, sleep apnea, and some forms of cancer. These risks can rise even when a person’s overall weight does not seem especially high. Genetics, age, sleep, stress, medications, and certain medical conditions can all influence where fat is stored. Body shape is not a measure of a person’s worth, and weight-related health concerns are best discussed without blame.

There is no reliable way to lose fat from only one area of the body. Sit-ups and other abdominal exercises can strengthen core muscles, but they do not selectively burn belly fat. Reducing abdominal fat generally involves gradual changes that lower overall body fat and support long-term health. Even modest weight loss can improve blood pressure, blood sugar, and other health measures for some people.

A balanced eating pattern can make those changes more sustainable. Build meals around vegetables, fruit, beans, whole grains, and protein sources such as fish, eggs, tofu, or poultry. Foods rich in fiber can help with fullness and support digestive health. Choose unsaturated fats, such as those in nuts, seeds, avocado, and olive oil, in reasonable portions. Limit sugary drinks, frequent sweets, and highly processed foods, which can be easy to consume in large amounts. Water or unsweetened drinks are useful alternatives to drinks with added sugar. Portion sizes matter, but severe restriction and crash diets are difficult to maintain and may be harmful.

Regular physical activity helps reduce health risks, preserve muscle, and support weight management. Adults should aim for at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic activity each week, such as brisk walking or cycling. Another option is 75 minutes of vigorous activity, or a combination of moderate and vigorous exercise. Strength training on two or more days each week helps maintain and build muscle. Core exercises can improve strength and stability, even though they do not target fat loss in the abdomen. If you are new to exercise, begin at a comfortable level and increase activity gradually.

Sleep and stress management also support overall health and healthy routines. Most adults need at least seven hours of sleep each night, though individual needs vary. A consistent sleep schedule and a calming bedtime routine may help improve sleep. Relaxation, time outdoors, social support, or counseling can help with ongoing stress.

Progress is best judged over time rather than from daily changes in weight or waist size. Track habits and health measures in ways that feel useful, and set realistic goals you can maintain. If you have a chronic condition, take medicines that affect weight, or feel unsure how to begin, consult a healthcare professional. A registered dietitian or qualified exercise professional can help tailor a safe, practical plan. A steady approach that combines nourishing food, regular movement, adequate sleep, and support is more effective than quick fixes.

Luca Pacioli’s Summa de arithmetica, geometria, proportioni et proportionalità is often treated as the best-known early printed guide to commercial arithmetic. Yet it drew on a tradition of practical mathematics that had been developing in Italian cities for generations. One important earlier text in that tradition was the arithmetic associated with the Florentine merchant and teacher Benedetto Cotrugli? No: Cotrugli’s surviving work is later, while the fifteenth-century text usually meant in discussions of “Borgi” is the Libro de abacho by the Florentine abacist Benedetto? The name is commonly rendered as Benedetto da Firenze, not Borgi. “Borgi” may refer to a different author or a variant spelling, and the identification is uncertain. This page therefore uses “Borgi” as the name given for the arithmetic text, while avoiding claims that depend on an uncertain attribution.

Fifteenth-century commercial arithmetic belonged to the abacus-school tradition. “Abacus” here did not necessarily mean a counting frame. It often meant a written method of calculation using Hindu-Arabic numerals, alongside instruction in business practice. These books served apprentices, merchants, and shopkeepers who needed dependable ways to handle prices, debts, shares, and currency. They were generally written in the vernacular rather than Latin. That choice made the material accessible to working readers, although literacy and schooling were still limited.

The methods began with the four basic operations: addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division. Students practiced them with whole numbers and fractions. Fractions were essential because goods, lengths, weights, and payments were often divided into parts. Commercial texts also taught the rule of three, a proportion method for finding an unknown quantity from three known quantities. For example, a merchant could use it to calculate the price of several units when the cost of one unit was known. The same reasoning helped convert between measures or compare exchange rates.

A central challenge was the diversity of local systems. Italian cities used different currencies, weights, measures, and accounting conventions. A textbook might therefore provide conversion tables or worked examples for particular markets. Merchants also needed to calculate profit and loss. Problems could ask how much a trader earned after buying goods at one price and selling them at another. Some exercises included transport costs, taxes, or other expenses, making the calculation closer to real business. The goal was not abstract theory alone, but practical competence.

Partnership problems were another recurring topic. A partnership might include investors who contributed different amounts of capital, or who invested for different periods. The arithmetic showed how to divide the resulting profit or loss fairly. A simple method compared each partner’s contribution with the total investment. More complex examples adjusted for the length of time each contribution remained in the business. Such questions trained students to translate a commercial agreement into numbers.

Exchange presented its own difficulties. A merchant might need to turn one currency into another at a stated rate, sometimes through an intermediate currency. Interest calculations also appeared, even when legal or religious rules shaped how lending was described. Texts could teach a student to find the amount due after a period, or to distinguish principal from gain. These exercises reflected the varied financial practices of the time. They should not be read as a complete record of every merchant’s actual conduct.

The teaching style relied heavily on examples. A problem stated a concrete situation, followed by a sequence of calculations and an answer. This format made rules easier to remember and showed how a method could be applied. It also let instructors adapt numbers and settings for classroom practice. The examples could involve cloth, grain, wine, metals, or other goods familiar to trade. Their everyday detail gives historians clues about commercial life, though a textbook problem is not proof that a particular transaction occurred.

Borgi’s arithmetic, understood within this wider tradition, is significant because it presents calculation as a tool for organized economic activity. It connects numerical procedures with decisions about pricing, investment, exchange, and accountability. The work belongs to a period when Italian merchants increasingly used written records and standardized computational techniques. Such habits supported expanding trade across cities and regions. Arithmetic instruction helped make those practices teachable beyond a single shop or family.

The influence of fifteenth-century abacus texts can be seen in later commercial manuals. Pacioli’s Summa, printed in 1494, gathered mathematical knowledge that included methods and problems long used in practical instruction. It was not simply a direct copy of one earlier book. Rather, it participated in a shared tradition, reshaping material for a broader audience and a new medium. Later printed textbooks continued to present rules through worked merchant problems. They also expanded the range of examples and adapted them to changing markets.

The passage from manuscript to print mattered. Manuscript books could be copied and revised locally, while printed editions could circulate more widely and preserve a more stable text. Printing did not make commercial arithmetic uniform overnight. Local currencies and measures still required local knowledge. But printed books helped transmit standard procedures across generations of students. They also gave later authors models for organizing instruction.

Today, Borgi’s fifteenth-century arithmetic is best approached as part of a larger educational and commercial culture. Its value lies in the methods it taught, the business situations it represented, and its place in the lineage of practical mathematics. The surviving record may not always establish an author’s identity or a text’s exact influence with certainty. Careful study distinguishes direct borrowing from shared conventions. Even with those limits, these arithmetics show how calculation became an essential skill of trade—and how the merchant’s classroom helped shape later textbooks.

Initial judgments often shape the way people treat one another long before they truly know each other. A first impression may come from someone’s appearance, tone of voice, or a single action. These quick conclusions can influence whether people feel comfortable, cautious, or curious. In a friendship, for example, someone who seems quiet may be mistaken for being unfriendly. Once that belief forms, others may not make the effort to start a conversation. Their distance can then make the quiet person seem even more withdrawn. This creates a cycle in which the first judgment appears to be confirmed.

Initial judgments also affect relationships by shaping expectations. If a person believes a classmate is reliable, they may trust that classmate with important tasks. If they believe someone is careless, they may overlook that person’s good ideas. These expectations can influence how people interpret later behavior. A mistake by someone considered careless may seem predictable, while the same mistake by a trusted person may be forgiven. In this way, people do not always respond to events fairly or objectively.

Changing an initial judgment can be difficult because people tend to notice evidence that supports what they already believe. They may ignore actions that challenge their opinion or explain them away as exceptions. Pride can also make it uncomfortable to admit that an early conclusion was wrong. In addition, people may worry that changing their view will make them seem inconsistent. Relationships can improve when people remain open to new information and give one another time to show who they are. By listening carefully and questioning first impressions, we can build relationships based on understanding rather than assumptions.

Mitosis is the process by which one cell’s nucleus divides to produce two genetically similar nuclei. It is part of the cell cycle, which also includes growth and DNA replication. Before mitosis begins, the cell copies its DNA during interphase. Each copied chromosome consists of two identical sister chromatids joined at a region called the centromere. The cell also prepares the structures needed to move the chromosomes.

Mitosis is commonly described in four phases: prophase, metaphase, anaphase, and telophase. Some descriptions include prometaphase as a separate phase between prophase and metaphase. During prophase, the chromosomes condense and become visible under a microscope. The spindle, a framework of protein fibers, begins to form from opposite sides of the cell. The nucleolus disappears, and the nuclear envelope starts to break down.

During prometaphase, spindle fibers reach the chromosomes. They attach to protein structures called kinetochores near each chromosome’s centromere. In metaphase, the chromosomes line up across the middle of the cell. Spindle fibers connect each sister chromatid to a different spindle pole. This arrangement helps ensure that each future nucleus receives one copy of every chromosome.

In anaphase, the sister chromatids separate at their centromeres. Once separated, each chromatid is considered an individual chromosome. Spindle fibers move the chromosomes toward opposite ends of the cell. The cell also often lengthens, increasing the distance between the two chromosome groups. This separation distributes the copied genetic material between the forming nuclei.

During telophase, the chromosomes arrive at opposite ends of the cell. They begin to uncoil, becoming less tightly packed. New nuclear envelopes form around each set of chromosomes, and nucleoli reappear. The spindle breaks down as the cell prepares to complete division. At this point, the cell has two nuclei with matching sets of chromosomes.

Cytokinesis divides the rest of the cell, including its cytoplasm, to form two daughter cells. In animal cells, a contractile ring pinches the cell membrane inward until the cells separate. In plant cells, a cell plate forms between the nuclei and develops into a new cell wall. Mitosis and cytokinesis together produce two daughter cells that usually have the same chromosome number as the original cell. This process supports growth, tissue repair, and replacement of worn-out cells.

Computing combines hardware, software, and human expertise to solve problems and support everyday work. Hardware includes physical components such as processors, memory, storage drives, sensors, and networking equipment. These components receive, process, store, and transmit data. Software provides instructions that tell hardware what to do, from operating systems to specialized applications. Software may be installed on a local device or accessed through cloud services over the internet. In business, computers help organizations manage finances, communicate with customers, analyze information, and coordinate operations. Tools such as databases, spreadsheets, and customer-management systems can make routine tasks more efficient. Businesses also use artificial intelligence and data analytics to identify patterns and inform decisions. In education, computers provide access to digital libraries, interactive lessons, and online courses. Learning platforms can help teachers share materials, assess progress, and offer feedback. Students use computing tools to research topics, create projects, practice skills, and collaborate with others. In academia, researchers rely on powerful computers to model complex systems, analyze large datasets, and share findings. Technology applications also support fields such as health care, engineering, agriculture, and the arts. Effective use of computing requires attention to privacy, security, accessibility, and the responsible use of technology.

Brighton Marathon celebrates strong turnout and improved race support

Brighton Marathon organizers celebrated a strong turnout as runners filled the city’s streets for this year’s event. Participants included elite athletes, charity fundraisers and first-time marathoners. International runners added to the race’s global feel, with competitors traveling from several countries to take part. Crowds gathered along the route, cheering runners through Brighton’s landmarks and neighborhoods. The event’s winners led the field after a demanding race, while thousands of others focused on reaching the finish line. Organizers said the mix of competitive racing and personal achievements was a highlight of the day. This year’s event also featured improved hydration measures designed to help runners stay safe and perform well. Water and other refreshments were made available at support points along the course. Race staff and volunteers helped manage supplies and assist participants. The changes followed continued attention to runner welfare at large endurance events. Medical and support teams remained on hand throughout the marathon. Many runners praised the atmosphere and encouragement from spectators. Local businesses and community groups also contributed to the event’s welcoming spirit. Organizers thanked volunteers, residents and emergency personnel for helping the race run smoothly. They said the strong turnout and positive response provide momentum for future Brighton Marathon events.

One unique vocal skill that brings joy and confidence is the ability to sing in harmony. Harmony means combining different notes so they blend into a pleasing sound. It takes careful listening, practice, and a willingness to work with others. When I sing a harmony part, I have to pay attention not only to my own voice but also to the voices around me. At first, this can feel challenging because I may worry about singing the wrong note. With practice, however, I become more comfortable and trust my ears. Each time I get a part right, I feel proud of what I can do. That confidence often encourages me to try new songs and perform in front of others. Singing in harmony also brings people together. In a choir, every singer contributes a different part, but no single part creates the whole sound alone. When everyone listens and works as a team, the music becomes richer. The experience reminds me that cooperation can make something more beautiful than any one person could create. Harmony can also bring joy to listeners. A familiar song performed by a group can help people feel welcomed, relaxed, or hopeful. Even a simple tune shared with family and friends can turn an ordinary moment into a special one. This skill is valuable because it combines creativity with teamwork. It teaches me to be patient, attentive, and supportive of others. Most of all, singing in harmony shows me that my voice matters, especially when I use it alongside other voices.

Skill and proficiency both describe how well someone can perform a task, but they emphasize different things. A skill is a learned ability, such as writing clearly, repairing a bicycle, or using a spreadsheet. Skills can be practical, creative, physical, or social. Proficiency describes a level of ability: a proficient person can perform a task competently and with relative ease. For example, “She has strong editing skills” names an ability, while “She is proficient in editing” describes her command of it. “Competent” means able to do something adequately, while “capable” emphasizes having the ability or potential to do it. “Expert” and “highly skilled” suggest extensive knowledge or experience, though “expert” often implies greater authority. “Novice” or “beginner” describes someone at an early stage of learning. “Advanced” usually indicates a high level, but its exact meaning depends on the field or course. “Fluent” is commonly used for languages and means communicating smoothly, not necessarily without mistakes. “Mastery” suggests deep, comprehensive command, while “proficiency” may refer to a practical, measurable standard. These terms are not always interchangeable, so choose the one that fits the context and level you mean. In résumés and assessments, specific evidence—such as projects, results, or a test score—makes claims about skill and proficiency more useful.

The importance of changing negative habits to become a better person

Everyone has habits that shape the way they think, act, and treat others. Some habits help us grow, while others hold us back. Negative habits may seem small at first, but they can affect many parts of our lives. For example, procrastinating can make schoolwork stressful and lower the quality of our work. Speaking rudely can hurt people and damage friendships. Recognizing these habits is the first step toward becoming a better person.

Changing a negative habit is not always easy. It takes honesty to admit that something we do is causing problems. It also takes patience because habits often develop over a long time. A person who wants to improve should set a clear and realistic goal. For instance, someone who often interrupts others can practice listening without speaking until the other person has finished. Small steps like this make change feel more manageable.

It is also helpful to understand what triggers a negative habit. A person may procrastinate because a task feels difficult or overwhelming. Breaking the task into smaller parts can make it easier to begin. Support from family, friends, or teachers can also encourage someone to keep trying. If a person slips back into an old habit, it does not mean that all progress is lost. They can learn from the mistake and start again.

Changing negative habits can improve both our personal lives and our relationships. We may become more responsible, patient, and confident. Others may find it easier to trust and work with us. Most importantly, changing these habits helps us act in ways that match the kind of person we want to be. Becoming better does not happen all at once. With effort and practice, each of us can make positive changes and build a brighter future.

The paper addresses an important challenge in video prediction: generating futures that are both realistic and diverse. Its combination of variational autoencoders and adversarial training is intuitively well motivated. The VAE encourages a structured latent representation, while the adversarial objective can discourage blurry outputs. The focus on assessing sample plausibility is also valuable, since average prediction error alone poorly captures the quality of multimodal forecasts.

A major strength is the paper’s recognition that multiple futures may be plausible for the same observed sequence. Modeling this uncertainty could make the approach useful for applications such as robotics, autonomous driving, and interactive systems. The proposed framework appears to offer a principled way to balance reconstruction and realism. The topic is timely, and the work could make a useful contribution if its claims are supported by rigorous experiments.

The paper should clarify how the VAE and adversarial losses are combined and how their relative weights are selected. It should also explain whether the discriminator evaluates individual frames, complete sequences, or both. These choices strongly affect temporal coherence and are essential for reproducing the method. The authors should specify the latent-variable structure and describe how it represents uncertainty over future motion.

The evaluation would benefit from comparisons with strong deterministic and stochastic video-prediction baselines. Ablations should isolate the contributions of the VAE, adversarial training, and any components introduced for plausibility assessment. Quantitative metrics should cover both visual fidelity and diversity, since improving one can come at the expense of the other. The authors should justify their metrics and discuss their limitations, particularly where perceptual quality is difficult to capture numerically.

The plausibility assessment requires especially careful validation. If human judgments are used, the paper should report the study design, participant counts, and statistical uncertainty. If an automated plausibility score is used, it should be validated independently and shown not to reward superficial realism at the expense of correct motion. Examples of failure cases would help reveal whether the method produces physically inconsistent or temporally unstable predictions. The paper should also discuss sensitivity to training instability and the computational cost of adversarial optimization.

Overall, this is a promising direction with a clear practical motivation. The combination of probabilistic prediction and adversarial realism is compelling, but the paper’s contribution depends on demonstrating that it improves both diversity and plausibility without sacrificing temporal consistency. I recommend strengthening the experimental comparisons, clarifying the implementation, and providing a more rigorous validation of the plausibility measure. With these revisions, the work could offer a meaningful contribution to realistic, multimodal video prediction.

The paper presents a simple inference-time defense that randomly resizes and pads inputs, aiming to disrupt adversarial perturbations while preserving useful image content. Its main strength is the method’s low implementation cost and its potential to improve robustness without retraining the underlying network. However, the evaluation should include adaptive attacks that account for the random transformation, using appropriate expectation-over-transformation techniques, since non-adaptive attacks can substantially overstate effectiveness. The authors should also report clean accuracy, attack success rates across multiple threat models, and results over repeated random draws, with confidence intervals where practical. Comparisons against strong contemporary defenses and an analysis of sensitivity to resizing and padding choices would make the evidence more convincing. Overall, the approach is promising as a lightweight mitigation, but its claims should be carefully qualified until robust adaptive evaluation demonstrates reliable gains.

A Russian biker club’s planned tour to a World War II memorial in Berlin has revived tensions with Poland over how the war is remembered. The Night Wolves, a nationalist motorcycle group with close ties to the Kremlin, have announced plans for a ride marking the anniversary of the Soviet Union’s victory over Nazi Germany. The group says it intends to pay tribute to Soviet soldiers who died in the war, including at memorial sites in Germany. Its proposed route crosses Poland, where the club’s previous commemorative rides have drawn protests and official scrutiny.

Polish authorities have objected to the group’s activities, citing concerns about public order and the political messages associated with the Night Wolves. In past years, some members were denied entry to Poland, while others encountered restrictions during attempted trips. The club has portrayed such measures as an effort to suppress remembrance of the Soviet role in defeating Nazi Germany. Polish officials and critics counter that the group uses wartime commemoration to promote Russian influence.

The dispute reflects a deeper divide over the legacy of the Red Army in Central and Eastern Europe. Soviet forces helped liberate the region from Nazi occupation, but their advance was followed by decades of communist rule and political domination. Poland’s government has emphasized both the enormous human cost of the war and the loss of national sovereignty after 1945. Russia, in turn, has repeatedly condemned what it calls attempts to diminish the Soviet victory.

The Berlin memorial visit could become a focal point for competing accounts of that history. German authorities have not indicated that the tour’s announcement alone would prevent a visit, though access and security arrangements may depend on the circumstances. Any riders traveling through Poland could face border checks or other measures under national law. The plans also come amid especially strained relations between Russia and European governments following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

The Night Wolves have previously organized long-distance rides to commemorate the Soviet victory, attracting both supporters and demonstrators. Their leader, Alexander Zaldostanov, is a prominent supporter of Russian President Vladimir Putin and has faced Western sanctions. The club maintains that its mission is historical remembrance rather than provocation. Critics say its symbolism and political affiliations make that distinction difficult to accept.

For Poland, the proposed tour is not simply a motorcycle journey, but a test of how public remembrance intersects with security and sovereignty. For the riders, reaching the Berlin memorial would signal that Soviet sacrifices remain central to their account of the war. Whether the tour proceeds as planned may depend less on the stated destination than on the route, permissions and response from authorities. The episode is likely to renew arguments over who has the right to commemorate the war—and which parts of its legacy should be remembered.

Every night, Mara checked the locks three times and counted the canned beans in the pantry. She told her son, Eli, that the world was getting ready to end. The signs were everywhere, she said: the red moon, the silent birds, the way the neighbors had stopped waving. Eli was eight and still believed that adults could hear the future approaching.

Mara covered the windows with foil and taped blankets over the door. She filled the bathtub with water and stacked books against the basement entrance. In the hall, she kept a backpack packed with crackers, batteries, and Eli’s favorite wooden dinosaur. “When the sirens start, we go downstairs,” she whispered.

There were no sirens, but Mara heard them in the pipes. She woke Eli before dawn and hurried him into the cellar. He clutched the dinosaur while she switched off every light. Above them, the house creaked in the wind.

“Is it the end?” he asked. Mara pressed a finger to her lips. Somewhere outside, a branch scraped the roof like a hand trying to get in. She held him until the sound stopped.

Morning came in thin stripes through a crack in the foil. Mara climbed the stairs alone and peered through it. The street was ordinary: a delivery van, a barking dog, Mrs. Alvarez carrying groceries. The sky was pale and harmless.

Mara let out a laugh that sounded almost like a sob. Then a radio voice from next door said something about an emergency, and her hands began to shake. She rushed back to the cellar and told Eli they had to leave now. He looked at her, then at the dinosaur in his arms.

“Mom,” he said gently, “that’s the weather report.” For a moment, the whole house seemed to hold its breath. Mara listened again through the floorboards. The voice was calm, discussing rain.

She sat down on the stairs. Eli climbed into her lap, though he was getting too big for it. Outside, the first drops tapped the windows. Mara kept one hand on the backpack, and the other around her son. This time, she let the storm pass without counting the thunder.

Computers represent information using tiny electronic components that can be in one of two states. These states are often described as off and on, or low and high voltage. A binary digit, called a bit, represents one such two-state value. A bit can therefore hold either 0 or 1.

Although a single bit has only two possible values, groups of bits can represent many different things. With two bits, there are four possible patterns: 00, 01, 10, and 11. In general, n bits can form 2ⁿ distinct patterns. For example, eight bits can form 256 patterns.

A sequence of bits can represent a number using the binary place-value system. Like the familiar decimal system, binary assigns a value to each position. Decimal uses ten digits and place values based on powers of ten. Binary uses two digits and place values based on powers of two.

Starting at the right, the binary place values are 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, and so on. Each position is twice the value of the position immediately to its right. To find the value of a binary number, add the place values wherever the digit is 1. Positions containing 0 contribute nothing.

For example, the binary number 1011 has a value of 11 in decimal. Its digits represent 8, 0, 2, and 1, which add up to 11. The binary number 11010 represents 26. Its 1 digits mark the values 16, 8, and 2.

The same idea can be used in reverse to write a decimal number in binary. One method is to find which powers of two add up to the number. To write 13, use 8, 4, and 1. Mark those places with 1 and the unused places with 0, giving 1101.

Computers also need to represent negative numbers. A common method, called two’s complement, uses a fixed number of bits and assigns some patterns to negative values. In an eight-bit two’s-complement number, the pattern 11111111 represents negative one. This system makes it practical for computer circuits to perform addition with both positive and negative numbers.

The number of bits used limits the values a pattern can represent. For unsigned numbers, eight bits represent values from 0 through 255. With more bits, the range grows quickly. For example, 16 bits can represent 65,536 distinct patterns.

Binary patterns can represent more than whole numbers. Computers use agreed-upon formats to represent fractions and very large or very small values. Floating-point formats, for example, store a number using bits for its sign, significant digits, and scale. The precise interpretation depends on the format being used.

A computer does not need to understand a bit as a written 0 or 1. Its hardware detects physical states and treats them as those values. Transistors act like controllable switches that help store and process these states. Circuits combine bits to carry out arithmetic and other operations.

Binary is useful because electronic devices can reliably distinguish between two states. Real components may vary slightly, but circuits can still recognize whether a signal is within the range for 0 or for 1. This makes binary systems practical and robust.

When you see a number on a screen, the computer may be storing it as a binary pattern. Software decides what that pattern means, whether it is an integer, a decimal value, or part of another kind of data. Understanding bits and place values shows how simple two-state components can represent a vast range of numbers.

A rescued bull terrier has become an award-winning police detection dog after helping uncover drugs, weapons and hidden cash.
