The paper addresses a relevant challenge in semantic segmentation: reducing domain shift while preserving spatially detailed predictions. Its patch-level adversarial adaptation strategy is promising because local alignment can capture appearance differences that global alignment may overlook. The use of clustered label structures also offers a potentially effective way to incorporate semantic relationships into adaptation. However, the paper should explain more clearly how clusters are constructed, updated, and used during training. It should also justify the chosen patch size and assess how sensitive performance is to that choice. A key concern is whether adversarial alignment could match patches with different semantic content, thereby encouraging negative transfer. The authors should describe what safeguards, if any, prevent this failure mode. The evaluation would be more convincing with comparisons against strong global and local adaptation baselines under the same training and data conditions. Ablations should isolate the contributions of patch-level alignment, label clustering, and their interaction. Results should include per-class metrics, since aggregate scores can conceal gains or regressions on less frequent categories. Reporting variability across multiple runs would help establish whether the improvements are robust. The paper should also clarify computational cost, including training time and memory use, relative to competing methods. Qualitative visualizations of aligned patches and typical segmentation errors could make the proposed mechanism easier to assess. Any assumptions about access to target-domain images or labels should be stated explicitly, along with limitations on generalization to unseen domains. Overall, the approach is plausible and potentially useful, but clearer methodological details and stronger ablation and robustness analyses are needed to support the claims.

Success is not achieved by working every moment of the day. It comes from balancing purposeful effort with enough rest to stay healthy and focused. When students manage their time wisely, they can make steady progress without feeling overwhelmed. Planning ahead helps them decide which tasks are most important. Breaking a large assignment into smaller steps can make it easier to begin. It also prevents last-minute stress and rushed work. Purposeful effort means giving full attention to a task instead of merely spending many hours on it. A focused study session can be more useful than a long session filled with distractions. However, constant work can lead to tiredness and poor concentration. Rest gives the mind and body a chance to recover. Sleep, exercise, and enjoyable activities can help students return to their work with greater energy. Taking breaks does not mean giving up on a goal. Instead, it can make continued effort more effective. Wise time management also leaves room for family, friends, and personal interests. These parts of life support well-being and can make achievement feel more meaningful. Students who balance work and rest are more likely to build habits they can maintain. By planning carefully, working with purpose, and making time to recharge, they can move toward success in a healthy and lasting way.

Balancing online and in-person learning can help students succeed in school while also managing work and personal well-being. Each format offers advantages, but neither is ideal for every lesson or situation. By combining them thoughtfully, schools can create a more flexible and supportive learning experience.

Online learning gives students greater control over when and where they study. Recorded lessons allow them to review difficult ideas at their own pace. Flexible schedules can also help students who have jobs, family responsibilities, or long commutes. Digital resources make it easier to access readings, assignments, and feedback in one place. However, studying online requires reliable internet, suitable devices, and a quiet place to work. Not every student has access to these resources at home. Long hours in front of a screen can also cause tiredness and make it difficult to concentrate. Without regular interaction, some students may feel isolated or lose motivation.

In-person learning offers important benefits that technology cannot fully replace. Students can ask questions immediately and receive clearer explanations from teachers. Class discussions help them consider different opinions and develop communication skills. Working face to face with classmates can make group projects more engaging. Schools also provide routines and spaces that help students focus. For students who need extra support, teachers can notice confusion or distress more easily in person. At the same time, attending school every day may be difficult for students with health concerns, long travel times, or busy schedules. A classroom-only approach can leave too little room for individual needs.

A balanced approach should use each format for the tasks it handles best. Teachers might introduce new concepts in class and provide online materials for review. Students could complete some readings or quizzes remotely, then use classroom time for discussion and practical activities. Clear weekly schedules would help everyone understand when they need to attend and when they can study independently. Schools should also teach students how to plan their time, set goals, and avoid distractions. Access to devices, internet connections, and technical support must be available to all students. Teachers can check in regularly to identify learners who are falling behind or feeling overwhelmed.

Well-being should remain a central part of any learning plan. Students need breaks, enough sleep, physical activity, and time to connect with others. Schools can reduce unnecessary screen time by choosing digital activities carefully. They can also offer counseling and encourage students to speak up when they need help. Families, teachers, and students should communicate about workloads and responsibilities. A flexible plan may need to change as a student’s circumstances change.

The best balance will not look exactly the same for every learner. Schools should listen to students and use their feedback to improve lessons. When online and in-person learning are combined with care, students can gain flexibility without losing human connection. This approach can support academic progress, work responsibilities, and a healthier daily life.

When the mail carrier waved at me, I waved back with the caution of a man greeting a sniper. “Why did you do that?” Mara asked.

“He knows I know,” I whispered. She looked at the mail carrier, who was now trying to fit a catalog into our neighbor’s mailbox.

At the grocery store, a child dropped a banana near my cart. I sidestepped it, certain it was a test of my reflexes.

“Whose reflexes?” Mara asked. “The people who watch the produce aisle,” I said.

She suggested we take a walk, perhaps to clear my head. Outside, a pigeon landed on a lamppost and stared at me.

I stared back until Mara tugged my sleeve. “It’s just a pigeon,” she said.

“Exactly what a pigeon would want you to think.” At the crosswalk, a man in a yellow jacket smiled.

I pretended to check my phone while memorizing the jacket’s shade. Mara began walking a few steps ahead of me, which I interpreted as an attempt to make me easier to identify.

At the café, the barista asked whether I wanted room for milk. I told her I preferred not to discuss room dimensions with strangers.

Mara ordered for both of us. The barista gave her a muffin, and I inspected it for hidden messages.

There was a blueberry on top shaped like a tiny question mark. “Do you see it?” I asked.

“I see a blueberry,” Mara said, though her voice sounded rehearsed. At home, I found a note on the doormat.

It read, “Package delivered.” I photographed it from three angles, then called Mara in to witness the evidence.

She sat beside me and held my hand. “I’m worried about you,” she said.

I told her that was precisely the sort of sentence a concerned partner would say to conceal a larger operation. She didn’t laugh.

That frightened me more than the note. I spent the evening checking the curtains, the kettle, and the family calendar for signs of coordination.

At midnight, the smoke alarm blinked once. I woke Mara and announced that the ceiling had sent a signal.

She sat up, rubbed her eyes, and said the battery was low. We replaced it together, and the blinking stopped.

For a moment, the room felt ordinary. Then the new battery came in a little plastic wrapper.

I held it up to the light. “This is how they get you,” I whispered.

Mara sighed and hugged me anyway. I decided not to tell her that the wrapper had been listening.

India’s Supreme Court has ordered a federal investigation into alleged exam rigging in Madhya Pradesh, escalating scrutiny of a scandal linked to a series of suspicious deaths. The court directed the Central Bureau of Investigation to examine the allegations and determine whether the deaths are connected to the case. The order follows petitions seeking an independent inquiry into claims that candidates paid intermediaries to secure admission to professional colleges and government jobs. Investigators have been asked to review evidence gathered by state authorities and pursue any leads involving influential figures. The scandal, often referred to as the Vyapam case, has raised questions about the integrity of recruitment and entrance examinations in the state. Several witnesses and people associated with the probe have died, prompting public concern and demands for answers. Authorities have not established that all the deaths were linked to the alleged fraud. The court’s intervention comes amid criticism that the state-level investigation may not be sufficiently independent. Madhya Pradesh officials have said they will cooperate with the federal agency. The CBI is expected to examine records, interview witnesses and assess whether earlier investigations missed evidence. Opposition parties have called for accountability, while government representatives have urged the public not to prejudge the findings. Legal experts say the inquiry could take considerable time given the number of cases and people involved. The court’s order places the investigation under national attention as families and the public await clearer answers.

The first person disappeared on a foggy Tuesday, a boy who liked to ride his bicycle along the old logging road. By Friday, a woman walking her dog had vanished from the same stretch of woods. The police taped off the trail and told us to stay away.

I stayed away until I heard the helicopters circling overhead. From my kitchen window, I watched officers carry something wrapped in a gray tarp to the road. That night, I dreamed it was the boy’s bicycle, still spinning its front wheel.

The next morning, a deputy knocked on my door and asked when I had last seen the woodshed behind my house. I told him it had been there since I moved in. He glanced past me, toward the dark tree line, and wrote something in his notebook.

I began locking my doors before sunset. Still, each night, I heard three slow knocks from beneath the floorboards. On the fourth night, I answered with one knock of my own.

The woods went silent. At dawn, investigators returned with shovels and a warrant. They dug beneath my shed and found a rusted hatch, hidden under the roots of an oak.

Inside were dozens of name tags, scraps of clothing, and a row of small, carefully arranged shoes. Then one officer lifted a cracked photograph from the dirt. It showed the woodshed, newly built, with a little boy standing beside it.

The boy was me. I backed toward the house as the deputy called my name. Beneath the floorboards, something knocked three times.

The paper addresses an important question: whether natural-language explanations can help people perform tasks more effectively, particularly when training data, tools, or expert support are limited. The topic is timely and relevant to both human-computer interaction and applied machine learning. Its focus on low-resource settings is a notable strength, since systems designed for well-resourced environments may not transfer reliably to settings with different languages, infrastructure, or user needs. The central premise—that explanations can support action rather than merely justify a system’s output—is promising. The paper is generally clear about its motivation and makes a useful case for studying task performance as an outcome. However, the contribution would be stronger if the authors defined “low-resource” more precisely. The term can refer to limited labeled data, scarce computational resources, underrepresented languages, or constrained access to expertise, and these conditions have distinct implications. The paper should also distinguish explanations from instructions, recommendations, and feedback, since these forms of language may affect performance through different mechanisms. A clearer account of the proposed mechanism would help readers understand why the explanations are expected to improve performance. For example, do they reduce cognitive load, support error detection, or help users build transferable knowledge? The related-work section is useful but would benefit from a more systematic comparison with research on explainable AI and instructional support. In particular, the authors should clarify what their approach contributes beyond presenting a system’s reasoning in natural language. The experimental design is a strong starting point, and the task-based evaluation is more informative than relying only on user satisfaction. Still, the paper should provide enough detail about participant recruitment, language proficiency, and relevant prior experience to assess the sample. These characteristics may substantially influence how participants interpret explanations. The authors should explain how the explanation texts were generated and whether they were reviewed for accuracy, readability, and cultural appropriateness. If explanations were generated automatically, the paper should report how errors or unsupported claims were handled. It is also important to establish that the comparison conditions are fair. For instance, explanations should not provide additional task information unavailable to the control group unless that information difference is the intended intervention. The outcome measures should cover both immediate performance and, where feasible, retention or transfer to new tasks. Completion time, accuracy, and error recovery may reveal different effects, so reporting them separately would be valuable. The analysis should include uncertainty estimates and effect sizes, not just statistical significance. Given the likely variability in low-resource settings, the authors should also examine whether benefits differ across participant groups or task types. Such analyses should be interpreted cautiously if the study is not powered for subgroup comparisons. The paper would benefit from a discussion of cases in which explanations may hinder performance, such as when they are too long, ambiguous, or overly confident. The authors should also address whether users can verify the explanations against available evidence. This matters especially where expert review or external reference materials are scarce. I encourage the authors to temper broad generalizations if the study covers only one language, region, or task domain. A short account of deployment constraints, including connectivity, device limitations, and maintenance costs, would make the practical implications more credible. The paper’s strongest potential contribution is its emphasis on usable explanations under realistic constraints. With clearer definitions, stronger methodological reporting, and a more nuanced treatment of explanation quality, the work could make a valuable contribution to the field. I recommend revision before publication.

The paper addresses an important problem: high-variance gradient estimates can make second-order optimization unreliable, especially in meta-learning and reinforcement learning. Its focus on comparing variance-reduction methods across both settings could offer useful guidance to researchers and practitioners. The paper should clearly define the estimators being compared, state the assumptions behind them, and explain how each affects bias, computational cost, and memory use. A strong evaluation would include well-tuned baselines, multiple random seeds, uncertainty estimates, and ablations that isolate the contribution of each method. The authors should also distinguish improvements in gradient variance from improvements in final task performance, since the two do not always align. For the meta-learning experiments, details about task distributions and inner-loop updates are essential for reproducibility. For reinforcement learning, the paper should report environment, policy, and rollout settings, and discuss sensitivity to reward scale and stochasticity. I recommend adding practical guidance on when each method is most effective, along with limitations such as overhead or dependence on problem structure. Overall, this is a promising and relevant study, but its conclusions will be convincing only if the comparisons are rigorous and the experimental details are sufficiently transparent.

For a billion years, the universe had been forgetting how to shine.

Stars guttered out one by one, leaving vast countries of darkness between them.
On the last inhabited world, people gathered beneath a sky with only three faint sparks.
They had no machines left to mend the heavens and no prayers they believed would be heard.
Still, each night, they told one another stories.
They spoke of morning, though morning had vanished.
They remembered the warmth of hands, the taste of rain, and the faces of those they had lost.
Their memories passed from voice to voice, growing brighter with every telling.
And somewhere in the silence between galaxies, something began to listen.
It listened to a child describing the blue sea her grandmother had never seen.
It listened to an old man singing the lullaby his mother had sung before the first star died.
It listened to lovers promising to stay, though they knew the world would not.
Every hope, every grief, every small act of kindness gathered in the dark.
The people did not know they were making anything.
They only knew that remembering together made the night less cold.
Then the darkness trembled.
From the gathered thoughts rose a figure vast as a nebula, shaped from countless human faces.
Its eyes held the first dawn anyone could recall.
Its hair streamed into space like rivers of gold.
The people fell silent as the figure knelt before their dying planet.
“I am what you have kept alive,” it said.
Its voice sounded like every loved one they had ever missed.
The figure opened its hands.
A single spark appeared between its palms.
It was small, but it carried the memory of every sunrise.
The spark drifted upward, and the black sky blushed with color.
Across the universe, dead stars stirred in their ashes.
Worlds frozen for ages felt warmth beneath their crusts.
Oceans broke through ice and lifted silver waves toward the light.
In empty valleys, seeds remembered how to split their shells.
The cosmic creator turned its gaze toward the people.
Where that gaze fell, wounds closed and weary hearts began to beat with wonder.
Yet it did not command the universe to live.
It offered each world a choice.
Light returned, but it could not erase sorrow.
The people still remembered the empty places at their tables.
They remembered the friends who had not lived to see the dawn.
The creator gathered their grief as gently as it had gathered their hope.
Together, they shaped the grief into deep blue shadows, beautiful against the morning.
Then the figure scattered its own body across the heavens.
Its hands became moons, its breath became wind, and its laughter became birds.
Its heart became a second sun, warm enough to travel between distant galaxies.
The people watched the sky fill with stars.
For the first time in generations, they looked outward without fear.
They built gardens beneath the new light.
They sent ships through space to find worlds waking from their long sleep.
Wherever they arrived, they brought stories before they brought tools.
They shared songs, names, and the memory of how darkness had once felt.
In return, the new worlds taught them strange flowers and unfamiliar constellations.
Life multiplied in a universe that had nearly forgotten its own name.
Love traveled faster than any ship.
It crossed oceans, deserts, and the gulfs between stars.
And wherever two beings listened to each other, the creator stirred.
It was no longer a giant in the heavens.
It was the light passed from one hand to another.
The people understood then that the universe had not been saved by a god alone.
It had been saved by what they had chosen to become together.
So they kept telling stories.
And every story gave the stars another reason to shine.

Everyone has a unique talent, whether it is singing, painting, solving problems, or helping others. Sharing that talent with the world can inspire people to explore their own abilities. For example, a student who performs music may encourage classmates to practice and express themselves. Sharing our skills can also create opportunities, such as joining a team, earning an award, or finding a future career. Recognition is rewarding, but it is not the only reason to share what we can do. Our talents can bring joy and help build stronger communities. When we share them with confidence and kindness, we may inspire others while discovering new opportunities ourselves.

Choosing a future career is an important decision, but students do not need to make it all at once. They can begin by learning more about themselves. Thinking about interests, strengths, and values can help students identify possible directions. For example, someone who enjoys solving problems might explore science, technology, or engineering. A student who likes helping people might consider teaching, health care, or social work. It is also useful to notice which school subjects feel engaging and why. However, students should not assume that one favorite subject determines their entire future. Many careers combine skills from several different areas.

Students can explore careers by reading reliable websites, books, and articles. Career guides can explain typical duties, education requirements, and working conditions. Speaking with professionals is another helpful way to learn what a job is really like. Students can ask about both the rewarding and challenging parts of someone’s work. Job shadowing, where available, lets them observe a workplace for a short time. Volunteering, internships, and part-time jobs can provide valuable practical experience. These activities also help students develop communication, teamwork, and responsibility.

Teachers, school counselors, and family members can offer advice and connect students with useful resources. Still, students should remember that advice is only one part of the decision. They should compare different options and consider the time, cost, and training each path requires. It is wise to keep an open mind because interests and opportunities can change. Students can set short-term goals, such as taking a relevant course or learning a new skill. They can then review their experiences and adjust their plans. A suitable future path is one that fits a student’s abilities, interests, and personal priorities. With curiosity, effort, and thoughtful exploration, students can make informed choices and feel more confident about the future.

Danny Boyle is planning a modestly budgeted sequel to Trainspotting, bringing back the original film’s cast for another look at the lives of its central characters.

The project would reunite Boyle with actors including Ewan McGregor, Ewen Bremner, Jonny Lee Miller and Robert Carlyle, who starred in the 1996 film. The original, adapted from Irvine Welsh’s novel, became a landmark of British cinema and helped establish its young cast internationally.

Boyle has indicated that the follow-up would not try to recreate the first film’s scale or energy simply for nostalgia. Instead, the smaller budget is expected to give the filmmakers room to focus on character and the passage of time.

The sequel is understood to draw on Welsh’s later novel, Porno, which revisits the characters years after the events of Trainspotting. That story follows them as they navigate middle age, old rivalries and new schemes.

The return of the original cast is central to the project’s appeal, though details of the plot and production schedule have not been fully confirmed. Reuniting the actors would also allow the film to explore how their characters have changed since audiences first met them.

Trainspotting made a lasting impression with its sharp humor, restless style and unflinching portrayal of addiction and working-class life in Edinburgh. Its soundtrack and memorable scenes helped turn it into a cultural touchstone beyond the United Kingdom.

A more restrained production could distinguish the sequel from the original’s fast-paced approach. Boyle has suggested that the story’s age and experience call for a different perspective rather than a straightforward repeat.

The project also faces the challenge of meeting expectations attached to a film that remains beloved decades after its release. Fans will be watching to see whether the sequel can retain the original’s irreverence while giving its characters a convincing next chapter.

For Boyle and the cast, the film would mark a return to one of the defining works of their careers. Any further announcements are expected to clarify the production’s timing and how closely it will follow Welsh’s source material.

The paper addresses an important challenge in continual learning: adapting to distribution shifts while retaining knowledge from earlier tasks. Its combination of memory guidance, variational inference, and adaptive posterior updates is potentially valuable. The topic is timely, and the proposed approach could be relevant to applications where data distributions change over time. However, the paper needs to make its contributions and assumptions clearer before its claims can be evaluated confidently.

The introduction should distinguish the method more precisely from existing variational continual learning and memory-based approaches. It would help to state the paper’s main contributions as specific, testable claims. The authors should explain what kinds of distribution shifts they target, such as covariate, label, or concept shift. These cases may require different responses, so treating them as a single setting could obscure the method’s scope. The paper should also define what it means for posterior updates to be adaptive and identify the signals that control this adaptation.

The method section needs a clearer account of how memory is constructed, updated, and queried. The authors should specify whether memory contains raw examples, features, summaries, or posterior statistics. If examples are stored, the paper should report the memory budget and discuss privacy and storage implications. It should also explain how the method selects information for retention and whether this selection depends on uncertainty, task boundaries, or observed shift. The variational objective should be written explicitly, with each loss term and its role explained. In particular, the relationship between the memory-based term and the posterior regularizer should be justified. The paper should clarify whether posterior updates are performed online or in batches and how computational costs scale with the number of tasks. Any approximations to the posterior should be identified, along with their likely effects on performance.

The experimental evaluation should be broadened and made more rigorous. The authors should compare against strong continual-learning baselines, including relevant replay, regularization, and variational methods. Comparisons should use matched model architectures, training budgets, and memory constraints wherever possible. The benchmark suite should include controlled distribution shifts as well as established continual-learning settings. It should also include shifts that occur gradually and shifts that occur abruptly, since these present different adaptation challenges. Results should report both average performance and forgetting, rather than relying on a single aggregate score. Performance immediately after a shift and after subsequent adaptation should be reported separately. The authors should include multiple random seeds and provide measures of variability. Statistical testing or confidence intervals would help establish whether reported differences are reliable. Ablation studies should isolate the effects of memory guidance, adaptive updates, and the variational objective. Additional analyses should examine sensitivity to memory size, learning rates, and the strength of posterior regularization. The paper should also report runtime and memory overhead, since these costs may limit practical use. Calibration and predictive uncertainty should be evaluated, given that the method explicitly models posterior uncertainty. A useful analysis would test whether uncertainty rises appropriately under unfamiliar or shifted inputs. The authors should describe all data preprocessing and shift-generation procedures so that the experiments can be reproduced. Hyperparameter selection should be explained, including whether the same tuning effort was allocated to each baseline. Code, configuration files, and evaluation protocols should be made available if possible.

The discussion should address situations in which memory guidance may fail, such as when stored examples are unrepresentative of the current distribution. The authors should consider whether adaptive updates could overreact to noisy or temporary shifts. They should also discuss the possibility that preserving earlier knowledge may conflict with learning a genuinely changed target concept. A clear statement of limitations would make the paper’s claims more credible. The conclusion should avoid implying general robustness unless supported by evidence across diverse shift types and benchmarks. Overall, the proposed direction is promising, but the paper currently needs stronger methodological exposition and more comprehensive empirical validation. I recommend revision before acceptance, with particular emphasis on clarifying the shift assumptions, detailing the adaptive posterior mechanism, and testing the method against carefully matched baselines.

Important life decisions are shaped by both personal choice and the guidance of others. Listening to family, teachers, and friends can help us see options and consequences we may have missed. However, their advice should not replace our own judgment, because we are the ones who must live with the results. By considering different viewpoints and reflecting on our values and goals, we can make thoughtful decisions. In the end, good guidance supports us, but the final choice should be our own.

When the storm clouds gathered over the academy, Professor Vale hurried her students into the practice hall. “Today we’ll learn the Shielding Charm,” she announced, raising her wand. “Keep your movements steady, and never cast without one.”

Milo leaned back in his chair, perfectly calm. He had always been confident, though his classmates mistook it for showing off. As the others practiced, their shields flickered like soap bubbles. Milo watched quietly, his hands resting on the desk.

Then a crash shook the windows. A lightning bolt struck the courtyard, and a heavy stone gargoyle broke loose from the roof. It hurtled through the open doorway toward the class.

Professor Vale shouted the shielding incantation, but her spell struck the gargoyle only a moment before it reached them. Milo stood. He lifted one empty hand and spoke a single, clear word.

A bright silver barrier burst into existence around the students. The gargoyle slammed against it with a thunderous boom and crumbled into harmless chunks of stone. The shield remained, glowing steadily as dust drifted through the air.

Professor Vale lowered her wand, staring at Milo. “You cast that without a wand?”

Milo shrugged, though his cheeks reddened. “I wanted to know if I could.”

For once, no one laughed at his confidence. Professor Vale studied the fading light, then smiled. “Next lesson,” she said, “we’ll learn when not to try something new.”

Brexit has reopened difficult questions about the border between Northern Ireland and the Republic of Ireland, raising concerns over trade, travel and political stability. The border was largely invisible after the 1998 Good Friday Agreement helped end decades of conflict, and both countries’ membership of the EU made cross-border movement easier. The UK’s departure from the EU created a challenge: Northern Ireland shares a land border with an EU member, while the rest of the UK does not. Checks on goods entering Northern Ireland from Great Britain were introduced under post-Brexit arrangements to avoid routine controls along the land border. Those arrangements have been revised, most recently through the UK-EU Windsor Framework, which eased some checks while keeping safeguards for the EU single market. The framework has reduced some friction, but disputes over its implementation continue to shape UK-EU relations. Unionist parties have objected to rules that they say create barriers within the United Kingdom and weaken Northern Ireland’s place in it. Nationalists and many businesses, meanwhile, have stressed the value of avoiding a hard border and maintaining access to both UK and EU markets. Political disagreement over the arrangements has at times disrupted power-sharing at Stormont, though the devolved government is now operating. The UK and Irish governments have sought to manage tensions through talks and cooperation, while differing on aspects of Brexit and its consequences. Any return to extensive checks at the land border could damage local trade and revive concerns about the peace settlement. For now, the border remains open for everyday movement, but the rules governing goods remain politically sensitive. Future relations will depend on whether London, Dublin and Brussels can sustain practical cooperation while addressing competing economic and constitutional concerns.

This paper addresses an important challenge in semantic segmentation: adapting models to a new visual domain without target-domain labels. Its focus on patch-level representation disentanglement is timely, since global alignment can overlook local variations in appearance and context. The proposed approach appears to offer a useful way to separate domain-specific information from semantic content. This could help preserve class structure while reducing sensitivity to changes in lighting, weather, or imaging conditions.

The paper’s main strength is its attention to local representations. Patch-level processing may capture fine-grained differences that image-level adaptation misses, and the motivation is clear. The method would be especially compelling if it explains precisely what is disentangled, how the components are learned, and how semantic information is protected during alignment. Clear notation and a step-by-step account of the training objective would help readers assess these design choices.

The experimental evaluation should include comparisons with strong, recent unsupervised domain adaptation methods, as well as relevant ablations. In particular, ablations should isolate the contributions of patch partitioning, the disentanglement objective, and any auxiliary losses. Results across multiple source–target pairs would help establish whether the method generalizes beyond a single benchmark. Reporting variation across random seeds, or confidence intervals where feasible, would also strengthen the evidence.

The paper should provide enough implementation detail for reproduction, including patch size, sampling strategy, loss weights, and training schedule. It would also be useful to explain how the method handles objects that span multiple patches, since local processing may disrupt broader scene context. The authors should discuss computational cost and memory use relative to the baseline. Qualitative examples of successful and failed adaptations could clarify what the method learns and where it remains limited.

The analysis would benefit from examining class-wise performance, especially for small, rare, or visually ambiguous categories. It should also distinguish improvements due to better domain invariance from those due to regularization or increased model capacity. If the method relies on assumptions about the relationship between source and target label distributions, those assumptions should be stated and discussed. Potential failure cases, such as large semantic shifts or substantial changes in object composition, deserve attention.

Overall, the topic is relevant and the patch-level perspective is promising. The paper could make a meaningful contribution if its methodological details and empirical evidence support the claimed benefits. My assessment would depend particularly on the strength of the baseline comparisons, the completeness of the ablations, and the clarity of the disentanglement mechanism. I recommend revision to address these points and improve reproducibility.

GAMT deficiency is a rare inherited disorder that affects the body’s ability to make creatine.
Creatine helps supply energy to cells, especially in the brain and muscles.
The condition is caused by changes in both copies of the GAMT gene.
These changes reduce the activity of an enzyme called guanidinoacetate methyltransferase.
As a result, the body makes too little creatine and may build up a substance called guanidinoacetate.
High guanidinoacetate levels can be harmful to the brain.
GAMT deficiency is usually inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern.
This means a person typically inherits one altered GAMT gene from each parent.
Parents who each carry one altered copy usually do not have symptoms.
The condition can affect people in different ways and to different degrees.
Signs often begin in infancy or early childhood, though the age of recognition varies.
Development may be delayed, including sitting, walking, or learning new skills.
Speech and language difficulties are common.
Some people have intellectual disability or need ongoing learning support.
Seizures may occur and can vary in type and severity.
Behavioral differences can include hyperactivity, impulsivity, or autistic features.
Movement difficulties may include poor coordination, tremor, or involuntary movements.
Low muscle tone or muscle stiffness may also occur.
Not everyone with GAMT deficiency has all of these features.
A clinician may suspect the condition when developmental difficulties occur with seizures or movement problems.
Diagnosis can involve measuring creatine and guanidinoacetate in urine, blood, or brain fluid.
Brain magnetic resonance spectroscopy can help identify low creatine in the brain.
Genetic testing can confirm changes in the GAMT gene.
Early diagnosis matters because treatment may reduce guanidinoacetate and improve creatine availability.
Treatment often includes creatine supplements and medicines that limit guanidinoacetate production.
A low-arginine diet may also be recommended by a specialist.
Treatment plans need careful medical supervision and regular monitoring.
Speech, physical, occupational, and educational support can help address individual needs.
Families may benefit from genetic counseling and connection with clinicians experienced in metabolic disorders.

Between 1750 and 1850, ships carried goods, people, ideas, and disease across oceans on a scale that helped connect distant regions. These maritime networks did not create globalization from nothing, but they intensified older connections and made them more regular and far-reaching. Their growth was shaped by European empires, Asian trading states, Indigenous societies, merchants, sailors, and enslaved people. The result was an increasingly interdependent world, built through both cooperation and coercion.

The Atlantic system linked Europe, Africa, and the Americas. European ships carried manufactured goods to African ports, where merchants exchanged them for captives, many of whom were forced across the Atlantic to labor in the Americas. This transatlantic slave trade expanded plantation production of sugar, coffee, and tobacco. Ships then carried these commodities to European and North American markets. Although Britain outlawed its participation in the slave trade in 1807 and slavery was abolished at different times across the Americas, illegal trafficking and forced labor continued.

The Indian Ocean had long connected East Africa, Arabia, India, Southeast Asia, and China. During this period, monsoon winds still guided seasonal voyages, while ports such as Bombay, Calcutta, and Singapore became major commercial centers. Ships carried cotton textiles, spices, tea, opium, and other goods between these regions. European companies increasingly influenced trade, but Asian merchants and producers remained essential to its operation. In 1757, the British East India Company’s victory at Plassey helped it expand political control in Bengal, tying colonial rule more closely to commerce.

In the Pacific, voyages linked the Americas with East Asia and island communities. Spanish ships had carried American silver across the Pacific to Manila since the sixteenth century, and this trade continued into the early nineteenth century. Chinese demand for silver helped connect mines in the Americas to markets in Asia. Later, British and American merchants expanded trade in furs, sandalwood, and other goods. These exchanges brought new opportunities, but they also disrupted Indigenous economies and exposed communities to disease and dispossession.

New technologies and institutions made ocean trade more efficient, though change was gradual. Better charts, navigational instruments, and ship design reduced some risks at sea. Insurance, credit, joint-stock companies, and commercial ports helped merchants finance voyages and spread losses. Steamships began to supplement sailing vessels, especially on coastal and river routes, but wind-powered ships remained central throughout much of the period. The opening of the Suez Canal in 1869 came after this era, so it did not drive maritime trade between 1750 and 1850.

Growing trade changed everyday life around the world. Europeans increasingly consumed tea, sugar, coffee, and cotton goods, while factories relied on raw materials produced far from home. In India, British policies reshaped textile production and encouraged the export of raw cotton and other commodities. In the Americas, plantation wealth depended heavily on enslaved labor and the seizure of Indigenous lands. Ports grew into crowded centers where languages, religions, and customs met.

Maritime globalization also spread knowledge and political ideas. Sailors, migrants, merchants, and missionaries carried news, books, scientific observations, and religious beliefs between continents. The same routes transmitted epidemics and enabled imperial armies to move quickly. The Haitian Revolution, which began in 1791, showed how ideas of liberty circulated across the Atlantic while challenging the slave system that sustained it. Yet access to these networks and their benefits was deeply unequal.

By 1850, maritime trade had woven distant economies more tightly together, but it had not made the world equal or peaceful. Industrial growth, colonial expansion, slavery, and competition for resources all shaped the expanding networks. These routes helped lay foundations for modern globalization by accelerating the movement of commodities, labor, capital, and information. They also left enduring legacies of exploitation and economic dependence that continued long after the ships had reached port.

The first snow fell on the morning Mara died.
It dusted the windowsill where she had kept her blue glass birds.
Elias watched it gather while the doctor folded his hands.
“She was peaceful,” the doctor said.
Elias nodded, though peace seemed a word made for the living.
He had heard it spoken over too many beds.
Mara’s hand lay beneath the quilt.
It was still warm when he took it.
He waited for the warmth to leave.
By dusk, the snow had covered the garden path.
By midnight, it had hidden the world.

Elias buried her beneath the pear tree.
She had planted it during their first spring together.
“You’ll eat the fruit before I do,” she had joked.
He had promised that he would.
The promise had sounded harmless then.
Now he stood beside the fresh earth, unable to imagine a harvest.
He had outlived every person he had ever loved.
He had outlived kings, countries, and the names of his own childhood.
His face remained young, but his eyes had grown old.
For two hundred years, he had called that a curse.
For two hundred years, he had secretly called it a gift.
After Mara, he could no longer pretend either word fit.

He went to the river where the old ferryman lived.
The ferryman had no boat.
He sat on the bank, mending a net that had never caught a fish.
“I want to die,” Elias said.
The old man looked up.
“So do many people,” he replied.
“I have tried.”
“I know.”
The ferryman tied a knot in the net.
“Then you know you cannot.”
Elias knelt in the wet grass.
“Tell me how.”
The old man’s eyes were the color of river stones.
“Prove you are ready.”

Elias asked what proof could satisfy a creature who had watched him fail.
The ferryman pointed across the water.
“Take the road east,” he said.
“At the end, you will find a house with a red door.”
“Who lives there?”
“Someone who needs you.”
Elias almost laughed.
He had spent a lifetime helping people.
He had carried wounded soldiers from fields.
He had fed strangers through winters.
He had held hands at bedsides until his own hands stopped shaking.
“I have done enough,” he said.
“Perhaps,” said the ferryman.
“Go anyway.”

The road east crossed a country Elias had not seen before.
He passed villages with unfamiliar names.
He slept in barns and under bridges.
He ate when people offered food and kept walking when they did not.
On the seventh day, he found the house with the red door.
It stood alone beneath a hill.
A girl sat on the front step.
She was about ten years old.
A wooden crutch rested beside her.
“You’re late,” she said.
“I didn’t know I was expected.”
“Everyone says that.”

Her name was Nessa.
Her mother had died in the spring.
Her father had gone to find work and never returned.
The village had promised to care for her.
The village had then forgotten.
Nessa asked Elias if he knew how to mend a roof.
He did.
She asked if he could cook.
He could.
She asked if he could make a wooden leg.
He said he could try.
“That’s what people say before they leave,” she replied.
Elias looked at the red door.
It needed paint.
“I won’t leave today,” he said.

He stayed through the winter.
He patched the roof and filled the stove.
He carved Nessa a leg from pear wood.
She learned to walk with it, slowly and angrily.
Elias learned to listen without offering solutions.
At night, she told him stories about her mother.
He told her stories about Mara.
They did not compare the dead.
They let each person keep her own shape.

In spring, Nessa asked why Elias never grew older.
He said he had once been given a life without an end.
“By whom?” she asked.
“I don’t know.”
“Do you want an end?”
“Yes.”
“Then why are you still here?”
He looked at her crutch by the hearth.
“Because you need help.”
“Everyone needs help,” she said.
“That can’t be the whole answer.”
Elias had no answer to that.

The ferryman came to the red door in early summer.
He carried no net this time.
Nessa greeted him as if she had been expecting him.
“You can go now,” she told Elias.
He felt the old grief rise, familiar as a tide.
“I can stay,” he said.
“You can,” said Nessa.
“But you don’t have to.”
The ferryman waited by the gate.
Elias looked at the house, the mended roof, and the pearwood leg.
He looked at the path where Nessa had learned to walk.
He realized he had mistaken being needed for being alive.
He had stayed because leaving frightened him.
He had loved Mara, but he had also asked her to make forever bearable.
He had loved Nessa, but he had almost asked her to do the same.

Nessa took his hand.
“You should go see the world,” she said.
“I have seen it.”
“Not this world.”
She was right.
The world kept changing, even when he wished it would stop.
Elias bent and kissed her forehead.
“Will you be all right?”
“I’ll be sad,” she said.
“That isn’t the same thing.”
“No,” he agreed.
She smiled, and for a moment he saw the girl she might become.
He left before he could ask her to promise anything.

At the river, the ferryman offered him a small boat.
Elias stepped inside.
The current carried him toward a bank hidden in mist.
“Am I ready?” he asked.
“That is not for me to decide,” said the ferryman.
“What happens when we reach the other side?”
“You will find out.”
Elias sat with his hands folded.
For the first time, he did not bargain with the dark.
He did not count the years he had lost.
He did not ask the river to turn back.
He remembered Mara beneath the pear tree.
He remembered Nessa standing on her wooden leg.
He felt grief beside him, no longer a chain, but a companion.
The mist opened.
On the far bank stood a woman holding blue glass birds.
Mara smiled.
Elias stepped from the boat.
The ferryman pushed away.
Behind him, the river went on flowing.

The paper addresses an important problem: estimating second-order gradients in stochastic computation graphs can be substantially more expensive and noisy than estimating ordinary gradients. Its focus on control variates is well motivated, since variance can make curvature estimates unreliable and hinder optimization. The topic is relevant to researchers working on stochastic optimization, probabilistic modeling, and higher-order automatic differentiation. The paper’s central contribution appears to be a framework for reducing variance in second-order gradient estimators. A clear explanation of how the proposed control variates are constructed would help readers assess the contribution. In particular, the authors should state which assumptions about the graph, distributions, and differentiability are required. The relationship between the estimator and established score-function and pathwise-gradient methods also deserves careful discussion. A derivation that identifies each source of variance and shows how the control variates address it would strengthen the presentation. The paper should establish that the resulting estimator remains unbiased, or precisely characterize any bias introduced by approximations. If the method relies on learned or estimated control-variate coefficients, their estimation procedure and its effect on the guarantees should be explained. The computational cost of constructing and applying the control variates should be compared with the cost of the unmodified estimator. Empirical results should include a range of graph structures and stochastic distributions, rather than relying on a single favorable example. Comparisons with relevant baseline estimators are essential, using consistent compute budgets and tuning procedures. Reporting variance reduction alongside wall-clock time would clarify whether lower variance translates into practical gains. The experiments should also examine sensitivity to sample size, dimensionality, and control-variate quality. Confidence intervals or repeated-run statistics would make the reported improvements easier to judge. Ablations separating the effects of individual control variates would clarify which components drive performance. The exposition would benefit from a compact worked example that illustrates the estimator on a simple stochastic graph. Notation should be standardized, especially where first- and second-order derivatives appear together. The authors should discuss limitations, including cases where the control variates may be difficult to compute or provide little benefit. Overall, the topic is valuable and the proposed direction is promising, but the paper’s strength depends on rigorous derivations and convincing, reproducible comparisons. With clearer guarantees, stronger empirical evaluation, and improved presentation, the work could make a useful contribution to variance reduction for higher-order stochastic gradients.

This paper addresses an important question: whether biologically inspired neural networks can predict video sequences in ways that relate to visual familiarity and macaque neural responses. The integration of computational modeling, behavioral concepts, and neural data could offer a valuable framework for studying visual processing. A key strength is the potential to compare model predictions with responses in a biological visual system rather than evaluating performance only through machine-learning benchmarks. The paper would benefit from stating its central hypotheses and contributions more explicitly at the outset. In particular, it should clarify how “visual familiarity” is defined and how familiarity is distinguished from repetition, predictability, or exposure. The methods should describe the network architecture, training data, objective functions, and video-prediction procedure in enough detail to support replication. The authors should also explain how macaque responses were recorded, preprocessed, and aligned with model outputs. Because neural comparisons can depend strongly on stimulus selection and analysis choices, these decisions should be justified and, where possible, tested for robustness. The results would be clearer if prediction accuracy, familiarity-related effects, and neural correspondence were reported as separate outcomes before their relationships are interpreted. Appropriate baselines are essential, including conventional predictive models and biologically motivated models without the relevant familiarity mechanism. Statistical analyses should account for variation across animals, neurons, and stimuli, rather than treating all observations as independent. The discussion should distinguish evidence of correlation between model activity and macaque responses from evidence that the model captures underlying biological mechanisms. It should also consider alternative explanations, such as low-level visual features or unequal stimulus exposure. If the results support stronger predictions for familiar stimuli, the authors should specify which neural or computational measures show this effect and how large it is. Overall, the topic is promising, but clearer operational definitions, stronger controls, and more transparent analysis would make the conclusions substantially more persuasive. I recommend revision, with particular attention to reproducibility and the link between the model’s predictions and the macaque data.

Ulster Bank is reducing Saturday opening hours at 11 branches as it pursues voluntary job cuts, prompting concern from unions about the impact on staff and customers. The changes are part of a wider effort to reshape the bank’s branch network and operations. Affected branches will offer shorter Saturday services, though the precise hours may vary by location. The bank has not announced compulsory redundancies as part of the voluntary reduction programme. Union representatives have warned that fewer staff and shorter opening times could make it harder for customers to access in-person banking. They have also raised questions about the effect of the changes on employees’ workloads and job security. Ulster Bank says customers can continue to use its digital services and other available banking channels. However, unions argue that online options are not suitable for everyone, particularly those who rely on branch support. The changes come as banks across the sector respond to shifting customer habits and pressure to reduce costs. Customers are advised to check their local branch’s opening hours before visiting.

Perseverance and optimism can help people move forward when life becomes difficult. Everyone faces setbacks, whether at school, at work, or in personal life. A setback can make someone feel discouraged or uncertain. However, it does not have to determine what happens next. Perseverance means continuing to try even when progress is slow. Optimism means believing that improvement is possible. Together, these qualities can help people face challenges with courage.

For example, a student might fail an important test despite studying hard. Instead of giving up, the student can review mistakes, ask the teacher for help, and try new study methods. The next test may still be challenging, but each effort can build knowledge and confidence. Athletes also show perseverance when they practice after losing a competition. They learn from their mistakes and work toward performing better next time. Optimism helps them imagine success, while perseverance helps them prepare for it.

These qualities are useful beyond school and sports. Someone looking for a job may receive several rejections before finding the right opportunity. Staying hopeful can prevent disappointment from turning into defeat. Continuing to improve skills and apply for suitable positions can eventually lead to success. Still, optimism does not mean pretending that problems do not exist. It means recognizing difficulties while believing that useful steps can be taken.

Setbacks can teach people patience, resilience, and self-understanding. Progress may take longer than expected, and some goals may need to change. Even so, a positive attitude and steady effort can make challenges easier to manage. Perseverance and optimism do not guarantee that everything will go as planned. They do help people learn, adapt, and keep moving toward what matters. By practicing both qualities, people can turn many setbacks into opportunities for growth.

Maintaining healthy sleep routines for children during summer and throughout the year helps support their growth, learning, mood, and overall health. Children need more sleep than adults, and the amount they need depends on their age. Most preschoolers need about 10 to 13 hours of sleep in 24 hours, including naps. School-age children generally need 9 to 12 hours, while teenagers usually need 8 to 10 hours. These ranges are guidelines, and individual needs can vary.

A steady sleep schedule helps the body know when it is time to rest. Try to keep bedtime and wake-up time similar each day, including weekends and school breaks. During summer, later sunsets, vacations, and changing activities can make routines less predictable. Keep a familiar bedtime routine even when the family is away from home. If your child’s schedule has shifted, move bedtime earlier gradually, by about 15 minutes at a time.

A calming routine can help children transition from busy activities to sleep. It might include a bath, putting on pajamas, brushing teeth, and reading together. Keep the routine pleasant and predictable, and choose activities that help your child feel relaxed. Avoid making bedtime a time for arguments, rushed tasks, or exciting games. Offer age-appropriate choices, such as which pajamas to wear or which story to read.

Create a sleep environment that is quiet, comfortable, and as dark as practical. Use curtains or a sleep mask if early summer daylight makes it hard to settle. Keep the room at a comfortable temperature and reduce noise where possible. A night-light may help a child who is afraid of the dark. Make sure the sleep space is safe and appropriate for your child’s age.

Screens can make it harder for children to wind down, especially when they are used close to bedtime. Set a family rule to turn off phones, tablets, computers, and television at least 30 to 60 minutes before sleep. Keep devices out of the bedroom overnight when possible. Choose quieter activities instead, such as drawing, reading, or listening to a calm story. Adults can support the habit by following similar screen limits.

Daytime habits also affect nighttime sleep. Regular physical activity and time outdoors can help children feel ready for bed. Try to schedule vigorous play earlier in the day rather than immediately before bedtime. Keep meals and snacks on a regular schedule, and avoid large meals just before sleep. If your child still naps, consider whether the timing or length of the nap is making bedtime difficult.

If your child resists bedtime, respond calmly and consistently. Give clear reminders before the routine begins and praise cooperation. Comfort children who feel worried, while helping them practice settling back to sleep. Avoid using sleep as a punishment or promising rewards that are difficult to maintain. Small, steady changes are often more effective than changing several habits at once.

Some sleep difficulties may need professional advice. Talk with a pediatrician if your child regularly struggles to fall asleep, snores loudly, has pauses in breathing, or is unusually sleepy during the day. Seek guidance if sleep problems affect behavior, school, or family life. A clinician can help identify possible causes and suggest age-appropriate steps.

Healthy sleep routines do not need to be perfect to be useful. Occasional late nights during holidays or special events are normal. Return to familiar habits afterward, and keep expectations realistic as children grow and their needs change. With consistency, patience, and a supportive sleep environment, families can protect children’s sleep in summer and throughout the year.

The manuscript presents a hierarchical neural network for video prediction that combines recurrent feedback with sparse convolutions and relates its design to predictive suppression in visual neuroscience. The topic is timely and potentially valuable to both computational vision and systems neuroscience. Its central premise—that predictive processing can improve video representations while offering testable links to neural response suppression—is compelling. The paper is generally well organized, and the proposed architecture is described in a way that makes its main components understandable. The integration of temporal prediction and hierarchical feature processing is a notable strength. The use of recurrent feedback also provides a plausible mechanism for incorporating top-down context over time. Sparse convolutions may offer computational benefits and encourage localized, structured representations. However, several issues should be addressed before the claims are fully supported.

The paper should state more precisely what is novel relative to existing predictive coding networks, recurrent video models, and sparse convolutional architectures. A concise comparison table would help readers distinguish the proposed method from these related approaches. The authors should also clarify whether feedback is implemented between every pair of adjacent levels or only at selected levels. The timing of recurrent updates, including the number of iterations per video frame, needs to be specified. It is important to explain how recurrent state is initialized and whether it is reset between sequences. The training objective should be described in full, including all loss terms, their weights, and the prediction horizon. The authors should clarify whether predictions are made in pixel space, feature space, or both. If multiple prediction targets are used, their relative contributions should be reported.

The experimental section would benefit from stronger and more carefully matched baselines. In particular, comparisons should include models with feedback removed and models with sparse convolutions replaced by dense convolutions. These ablations are essential for determining which architectural components account for any observed gains. The paper should report performance across multiple random seeds and provide measures of variability. It should also evaluate the model on more than one dataset, or explain why the selected dataset is sufficient to support the broader conclusions. Dataset splits and preprocessing procedures should be documented clearly to rule out temporal leakage. The authors should report both short-term and longer-horizon prediction results, since recurrent feedback may affect these regimes differently. In addition to pixel-level metrics, perceptual or feature-based measures would help characterize prediction quality. Qualitative examples are useful, but they should be selected systematically rather than only showing favorable cases. Runtime, memory use, and the practical cost of recurrent iterations should also be reported.

The neuroscience discussion is intriguing, but some claims currently risk overstating the correspondence between model behavior and biological predictive suppression. The authors should define exactly which model quantity is treated as the analogue of neural suppression. For example, suppression could refer to reduced activity, reduced prediction error, or a change in response to expected versus unexpected input; these are not interchangeable. The paper should distinguish computational analogy from direct evidence of biological mechanism. It would strengthen the argument to compare model responses under matched expected and unexpected stimuli. The authors should also consider whether reduced activity could arise from saturation, normalization, or other mechanisms unrelated to prediction. Relevant neural predictions should be stated in a form that can be tested experimentally. If the model predicts effects of stimulus predictability, temporal context, or hierarchical level, these predictions should be made explicit. A discussion of limitations in mapping artificial network units onto neural populations would further improve the paper.

The treatment of sparsity also needs clarification. The authors should specify whether sparsity is imposed through fixed connectivity, learned masks, regularization, or another procedure. They should report the resulting connection density and assess sensitivity to the sparsity level. It would be useful to determine whether performance gains persist when parameter count and compute are controlled across dense and sparse models. The paper should explain how sparse operations are implemented, since theoretical sparsity does not always translate into lower computation in practice. Finally, the authors should discuss how robust the model is to distribution shifts, such as changes in motion statistics or object appearance.

Overall, this is a promising and potentially significant study. Its strongest contribution is the attempt to connect a concrete video-prediction architecture with a specific neuroscience hypothesis. The empirical claims would be more convincing with targeted ablations, broader evaluation, and clearer reporting of computational costs. The neuroscience interpretation should be tightened so that predicted activity suppression is not conflated with prediction error reduction. I recommend revision, with particular emphasis on establishing the contribution of feedback and sparsity separately and grounding the biological claims in explicit, testable comparisons.

An 18-year-old refugee from Dunkirk has died after falling beneath a truck while trying to reach family in Britain. The young man was reportedly attempting to board the vehicle as it travelled toward the Channel crossing. He was struck and killed, according to local reports. Emergency services attended, but he could not be saved.

The death has renewed concern over the dangerous journeys people make to cross from northern France to the UK. Refugees and migrants in the Dunkirk area often face uncertainty about their safety and future. Some try to travel in lorries or other vehicles, despite the risk of serious injury or death. Authorities have not publicly released the young man’s identity.

It was not immediately clear when his family in Britain had last heard from him. Local officials and support workers are expected to provide assistance to people affected by the incident. The circumstances surrounding the death are being examined. The tragedy highlights the dangers faced by people seeking to reunite with relatives across the Channel.
