Harvard University has canceled the remainder of its men’s soccer season after reports surfaced that players had compiled sexualized evaluations of women athletes.

The evaluations reportedly appeared in a document shared among members of the team. They included comments ranking female athletes and describing them in sexual terms.

The university said the material was inconsistent with its values and expectations for student-athletes. Harvard officials announced the season’s cancellation after reviewing the incident.

The decision means the team will not play its remaining scheduled matches. The university did not immediately detail whether individual players would face additional discipline.

The evaluations drew criticism from students and members of the campus community. Some described the document as degrading and harmful to the women targeted.

Harvard’s women athletes were not responsible for the document, and their teams’ seasons were not reported to be affected. The incident has renewed discussion about respect, consent and the treatment of women in college athletics.

University officials said they would address the matter with the team and review how such conduct could be prevented. The players involved may also be subject to the university’s conduct procedures.

Harvard did not release the names of the students connected to the evaluations. It also did not provide details about how widely the document had circulated.

The cancellation follows other cases in which universities have faced scrutiny over student-athlete behavior and team culture. Such incidents can raise questions about accountability both for individuals and for athletic programs.

The university’s action effectively ends the men’s team’s season before its scheduled conclusion. Harvard has not said whether the program’s leadership or policies will change as a result.

The episode has prompted calls for the university to support the female athletes affected. Administrators have said they take the matter seriously, while further details about the review remain unclear.

Imagination and knowledge are often treated as opposites, but they work best together. Knowledge helps us understand what is already known, while imagination helps us consider what might be possible. Both are important in learning and in everyday life. When students learn new ideas, knowledge gives them facts, concepts, and skills. Imagination allows them to connect those ideas in original ways. For example, a student studying the solar system can use facts about the planets to picture how they move through space. That mental picture can make the information easier to remember. Imagination also encourages curiosity. A curious learner asks questions that go beyond the lesson. Those questions can lead to deeper research and stronger understanding. At the same time, knowledge gives imagination direction. Without facts, an idea may be exciting but unrealistic or confused. Knowing how things work helps people shape their ideas into practical plans. Scientists demonstrate this connection when they imagine explanations and then test them with evidence. Writers use it too, combining knowledge of people and places with invented characters and events. In daily life, imagination helps us anticipate what could happen. Before taking a new route, we might picture the journey and consider possible delays. Knowledge of maps, traffic, and local conditions makes that prediction more reliable. Imagination is also useful when solving problems. It helps us think of different approaches instead of accepting the first solution. Knowledge lets us judge which approach is likely to work. In conversations, imagination helps us see a situation from another person’s point of view. This can build empathy and prevent misunderstandings. Knowledge of someone’s circumstances can make that empathy more accurate. The two abilities also influence each other over time. Every new fact can inspire a fresh question or possibility. Every imaginative question can motivate us to learn more. This cycle makes learning active rather than simply memorizing information. It also reminds us that mistakes can be useful. An imagined idea that does not work may reveal what we still need to understand. By checking our ideas against evidence, we can improve both our knowledge and our thinking. However, imagination should not replace careful judgment. We need reliable information to distinguish a promising possibility from a false claim. Likewise, knowledge should not limit us to repeating what has already been done. Without imagination, people may overlook better ways to solve familiar problems. In school, teachers can support both by teaching clear facts and inviting students to create, question, and explore. In everyday life, we can do the same by staying curious and checking our assumptions. Knowledge gives imagination a foundation, and imagination gives knowledge new directions. Together, they help us understand the world and make thoughtful changes within it.

Allegations of concealed payments and corruption have cast a long shadow over the sale of Nama’s Northern Ireland loan portfolio to US investment firm Cerberus.

The transaction, completed in 2014, involved a portfolio of loans with a face value of about £4.5bn. Cerberus acquired the assets through its affiliate, Tanager, for approximately £1.3bn.

The National Asset Management Agency, established by Ireland after the financial crisis, said the sale followed a competitive process and delivered value for the Irish taxpayer. But questions arose over the role of intermediaries and whether all relevant interests were properly disclosed.

At the centre of the controversy were claims that payments connected to the deal may have been routed through offshore structures. Investigators and public representatives questioned whether money had been intended to influence the sale or benefit people involved in it.

The allegations prompted scrutiny in Ireland and Northern Ireland, including investigations by law-enforcement authorities. They also led to hearings and public debate about the conduct of officials, advisers and business figures linked to the transaction.

No allegation should be treated as proof of wrongdoing. The claims have been disputed, and the legal and investigative processes have involved complex questions about jurisdiction, evidence and the movement of funds.

Nama has maintained that its sale process was conducted properly. Cerberus has also denied wrongdoing in connection with the purchase.

The affair has nevertheless raised broader concerns about transparency in the disposal of public assets. Critics have argued that the scale of the portfolio and the use of intermediaries demanded especially clear records and oversight.

The controversy has also revived questions about how Nama assessed bids and managed conflicts of interest. At issue is not only whether any improper payments occurred, but whether the safeguards in place were strong enough to prevent or detect them.

The portfolio contained loans tied to a wide range of Northern Ireland properties and businesses. Its sale came during a period when banks and public agencies were trying to dispose of troubled assets after years of economic turmoil.

For taxpayers, the transaction represented a major effort to recover money lent during the property boom. For borrowers and property owners, it marked a transfer of control to a new creditor, with consequences that could include refinancing, restructuring or enforcement.

The allegations have proved difficult to resolve publicly, in part because investigations and court proceedings have taken place over many years. Different accounts of the transaction have been examined, while key questions about responsibility and disclosure remain contested.

The case has become a test of how effectively public institutions can account for high-value deals involving private investors and cross-border finance. It has also intensified calls for clearer rules on agents, commissions and beneficial ownership.

As scrutiny continues, the central issue remains whether the sale was simply a contentious but legitimate commercial transaction or whether concealed payments compromised its integrity. Any definitive answer depends on the evidence established through the relevant legal and investigative processes.

The first time Eli saw his double, the boy was standing in the kitchen with his mother’s hand on his shoulder.

Eli had come home late, smelling of rain and the cigarette he had sworn he would quit.

He stopped in the doorway.

His mother looked up from the sink and smiled with tired relief.

“You’re home early,” she said to the other boy.

The boy turned.

He had Eli’s dark hair, his narrow chin, and the small white scar beside his left eyebrow.

But his shirt was clean, and his eyes were clear.

Eli’s mother looked from one son to the other.

For a moment, she seemed unable to breathe.

Then the boy beside her said, “Mom, this is the version of me you deserve.”

Eli ran.

He did not stop until he reached the old railway bridge beyond town.

The rain slid through the gaps in the boards and soaked his shoes.

Below, the river moved like black glass.

Eli leaned over the railing and tried to decide whether he was angry or afraid.

He heard footsteps behind him.

The double came alone.

“Don’t come closer,” Eli said.

“I’m not here to hurt you,” the boy replied.

“You’re standing in my house.”

“I know.”

“You’re wearing my face.”

“I know that too.”

Eli clenched his fists.

“Then what are you?”

The double looked toward the distant lights of their neighborhood.

“I’m what you could have been.”

Eli laughed, though nothing about it felt funny.

“Sure.”

“I mean it.”

The double’s voice was gentle, which made Eli hate him more.

“Mom needs someone who listens,” he said.

“Dad needs someone who answers his calls.”

“Jules needs someone who doesn’t scare him.”

“Don’t talk about my brother.”

“I’m trying to.”

Eli stepped closer.

“You don’t get to list everything I’ve done wrong.”

“I’m not listing it.”

“You’re standing there like a clean shirt with a halo.”

The double glanced down at himself.

“I’m not perfect.”

“Then you’re doing a great job pretending.”

For a while, neither boy spoke.

The river rushed under them, carrying twigs and scraps of leaves.

Eli’s phone buzzed in his pocket.

He ignored it.

The double nodded toward the sound.

“Your mother’s worried.”

“She’s always worried.”

“She’s afraid you won’t come back.”

“Maybe she should be.”

The double’s expression softened.

“That’s what you tell yourself so you don’t have to see how much she loves you.”

Eli shoved him.

The double stumbled, caught the railing, and recovered.

He did not shove back.

That made Eli feel even smaller.

“Why are you doing this?” Eli demanded.

“I want your life.”

“Then take it.”

“I am.”

The words fell between them like a stone.

Eli backed away from the railing.

“What does that mean?”

“I can stay,” said the double.

“You can go wherever you want.”

“I’m not leaving.”

“You think you can just replace me?”

“I think everyone will be better off.”

Eli stared at the face he had seen in the mirror every morning.

The double’s eyes were his own, except they carried none of his anger.

“You’re not real,” Eli said.

“I’m real enough to make your mother smile.”

The mention of her smile burned worse than any insult.

Eli turned toward the town.

The double followed him at a distance.

At the edge of the bridge, Eli stopped.

“Tell me something only I would know,” he said.

The double answered without hesitation.

“You hid Dad’s last birthday card in the air vent because you couldn’t stand to read it.”

Eli’s throat tightened.

“You watched the house burn down in your dream three nights in a row.”

“I said something only I would know.”

“You still keep the little blue dinosaur Jules gave you.”

Eli looked down at his shoes.

The double added, “You sleep with it under your pillow when things get bad.”

Eli hated that the boy knew.

He hated more that the boy sounded kind.

At home, the kitchen light was still on.

Through the window, Eli saw his mother setting a plate on the table.

His brother sat across from the double, laughing at something.

The double had already learned where everyone sat.

“He’s doing a good job,” Eli said.

“He has had years to practice being you.”

The double waited.

Eli understood then that he could walk away.

He could let the other boy stay.

Maybe his mother would sleep better.

Maybe Jules would stop watching the front door.

Maybe his father would call less often because someone else answered.

The thought seemed peaceful.

It also felt like dying.

“You said you wanted my life,” Eli whispered.

“I do.”

“Do you want the bad parts too?”

The double frowned.

“I want all of it.”

“No, you want the parts they can see.”

Eli looked toward the window.

“You want Mom to brag about you.”

“You want Dad to stop sounding disappointed.”

“You want Jules to think you’re safe.”

The double’s mouth tightened.

Eli stepped closer.

“But you don’t know how it feels when Dad’s name lights up my phone.”

“You don’t know why I stopped answering.”

“You don’t know what it takes to walk into that kitchen after I’ve messed up.”

“I can learn,” said the double.

“That’s not the same as living it.”

The double went quiet.

Eli’s phone buzzed again.

This time he took it out.

There were six missed calls from his mother and one message from Jules.

It said, Please come home. I’m scared.

Eli read it twice.

The double watched him.

“You should go in,” he said.

“We should.”

“I can explain.”

“You can’t explain being me.”

Eli began walking toward the front door.

The double followed beside him.

At the steps, Eli stopped.

“Are you going to fight me?”

“No.”

“Are you going to tell them I’m dangerous?”

“No.”

“Are you going to take my place?”

The double looked at the warm window.

“I thought I would.”

“What changed?”

“I saw you choose to come back.”

Eli reached for the doorknob.

His mother opened the door before he could knock.

She pulled Eli into her arms.

For a moment, he stood stiffly.

Then he held on.

Jules appeared behind her, clutching the little blue dinosaur.

The double waited at the foot of the steps.

His face seemed paler in the porch light.

Eli’s mother looked past her son.

“Who is that?” she asked.

Eli glanced back.

The double gave him a small, uncertain smile.

“I don’t know,” Eli said.

The boy nodded, as if that was fair.

Then he turned toward the dark road.

“Wait,” Eli called.

The double stopped.

“You don’t have to disappear,” Eli said.

The words surprised him as much as anyone.

The double looked at the house again.

“I don’t know how to stay without becoming you.”

“Then don’t.”

Eli let go of his mother and stepped onto the porch.

“Be somebody else.”

The double considered this.

Behind Eli, Jules held the dinosaur out to him.

Eli took it with one hand.

His mother put her palm against his shoulder.

The double watched the three of them for a long moment.

Then his features began to loosen, as if a face were only a mask he had finally grown tired of wearing.

His hair turned lighter.

His shoulders narrowed.

The scar beside his eyebrow faded.

When he blinked, he looked like no one Eli had ever met.

He walked down the road without looking back.

Eli went inside.

The kitchen smelled of soup and warm bread.

His mother asked where he had been.

Eli told her the truth, though not all at once.

He told her about the bridge.

He told her about the boy with his face.

He told her he was sorry for making everyone afraid.

His mother listened without fixing his words for him.

Jules stayed close, still holding the dinosaur by its tail.

When Eli finished, no one said everything was fine.

His mother only set another place at the table.

For the first time in weeks, Eli sat down before the food went cold.

After dinner, he called his father.

The conversation was awkward and brief.

It did not repair the past.

It made a small opening in it.

Later, Eli lay awake with the blue dinosaur beneath his pillow.

Outside, headlights moved along the road and faded into the rain.

He thought he saw another boy walking beneath the streetlamps.

This time, the boy’s face belonged only to himself.

Iraqi forces pushed deeper toward Mosul as fighting with Islamic State militants intensified, raising fears for civilians trapped inside the city and nearby districts. The advance is part of an operation to retake Mosul, which the group captured in 2014.

Military units moved along several fronts, supported by artillery and airstrikes, according to Iraqi officials. Security forces said they were working to clear roads and neighborhoods while confronting militants using snipers, explosives and fortified positions.

The pace of the advance varied as troops encountered resistance in built-up areas. Commanders have warned that urban combat could be prolonged and costly, with militants likely to use narrow streets and civilian buildings for cover.

Residents faced mounting danger as clashes and bombardments drew closer to populated areas. Aid organizations have expressed concern about people caught between advancing forces and Islamic State fighters, as well as those unable to leave their homes.

Displacement has added to the humanitarian pressure. Families fleeing the fighting have needed food, water, shelter and medical care, while access to some areas remained difficult because of insecurity and damaged roads.

Iraqi officials have urged civilians to follow safety instructions and avoid military positions. But leaving can itself be dangerous, particularly where routes are mined or exposed to crossfire.

The United Nations and humanitarian agencies have warned that Mosul’s large civilian population could face severe risks as the battle moves into denser neighborhoods. They have called on all parties to protect civilians and allow aid workers safe access.

Islamic State has lost territory elsewhere in Iraq but continued to mount attacks and resist government forces. The group’s control of Mosul has made the city a major strategic and symbolic target.

The Iraqi government has described the operation as a decisive effort to restore state control. Military leaders say the campaign will require coordination among army units, federal police and other forces.

The fighting has also raised concerns about damage to homes, infrastructure and essential services. Disruptions to electricity, water and health care could worsen conditions for residents even after front lines move on.

Officials have said that clearing liberated areas of explosives and hidden fighters will be an important part of the operation. Such work can delay the return of residents and prolong the need for emergency assistance.

For civilians still inside Mosul, the immediate priority is survival as combat closes in. The outcome of the advance may shape the next stage of the campaign, but the human cost is already a central concern.

This paper addresses an important problem: maintaining reliable Bayesian predictions when streaming data come from a changing distribution. Its focus on combining adaptive memory selection with posterior updates is timely, since conventional online methods can struggle to balance responsiveness to drift against retention of useful historical information. The proposed approach appears to have practical potential for applications where data arrive continuously and model updates must be efficient. A central strength of the work is its attempt to treat memory management and Bayesian learning as parts of a unified process rather than as separate tasks. This framing could help clarify how retained observations influence posterior uncertainty after a distribution shift. The paper would be stronger, however, if it stated its main contributions and assumptions more explicitly near the beginning. In particular, the authors should define what kinds of concept drift they target, such as abrupt, gradual, recurring, or mixed drift. They should also explain whether the method assumes labeled observations arrive immediately or permits delayed or missing labels. A precise description of the adaptive memory-selection rule is essential for assessing the method. The authors should specify what information determines which observations are retained, removed, or weighted, and how often this decision is made. The relationship between the selected memory and the posterior update also needs to be formalized. For example, it should be clear whether old observations are discarded, downweighted, or used to construct a prior when the model adapts. Because Bayesian updating is sensitive to the prior, the paper should explain how prior distributions are chosen and whether they are revised after drift is detected. The treatment of uncertainty deserves particular attention. Posterior uncertainty can help distinguish genuine distribution change from ordinary sampling variation, but the paper should show how the proposed method uses that uncertainty in practice. The computational cost of memory selection and posterior updating should be reported as a function of stream length, memory capacity, and model complexity. This analysis would help establish whether the method is suitable for high-throughput or resource-constrained settings. The experimental evaluation should include established online Bayesian baselines as well as relevant non-Bayesian drift-adaptation methods. Comparisons should use identical data streams, preprocessing, and evaluation protocols wherever possible. The authors should test multiple drift patterns, including stationary periods, abrupt shifts, gradual changes, and recurring concepts. Synthetic streams would make it possible to control drift characteristics, while real-world streams would demonstrate practical relevance. Performance should be assessed not only by average predictive accuracy but also by measures such as log loss, calibration, adaptation delay, and memory usage. Reporting results across multiple random seeds, with uncertainty intervals or suitable statistical tests, would make the evidence more convincing. An ablation study is also needed to isolate the contributions of adaptive memory selection and posterior updating. The authors should examine sensitivity to memory size, drift thresholds, and other key hyperparameters. It would be useful to state how these parameters are selected and whether the method requires access to future data during tuning. The paper should discuss failure cases, including rapid changes that occur faster than the update mechanism can respond and noisy signals that trigger unnecessary memory replacement. It should also clarify whether the method offers theoretical guarantees, such as consistency under stationarity or bounds on regret under specified drift assumptions. If such guarantees are outside the paper’s scope, the authors should present this as a limitation rather than imply broader assurances. Reproducibility would improve with pseudocode, implementation details, and access to code or a fully specified procedure. Overall, the topic is significant and the proposed combination of adaptive memory and Bayesian updating is promising. The paper’s main claims will be persuasive only if the method is defined precisely and evaluated against strong baselines under diverse, clearly specified drift conditions. I recommend revision focused on methodological clarity, stronger experimental analysis, and a more explicit discussion of assumptions and limitations.

Early career planning helps students make thoughtful decisions about their future. By exploring different jobs, students can discover careers that match their interests and strengths. They can also learn which subjects and skills are important for their chosen fields. This knowledge helps them set clear goals and stay motivated in school. The paper addresses an important problem: estimating second-order gradients in stochastic computation graphs can be noisy and computationally demanding. Its proposed control variate appears well motivated, particularly if it preserves unbiasedness while reducing variance. The paper should clearly state the estimator, its assumptions, and the conditions under which the variance reduction holds. A step-by-step derivation would help readers verify that the control variate does not introduce bias, especially when graph structure or distributions depend on parameters. The authors should also explain how the method relates to existing score-function, pathwise, and second-order gradient estimators. The empirical evaluation should compare against strong baselines using identical computational budgets and report both estimation error and runtime. Results across multiple graph structures and distributions would make the evidence for generality more convincing. It would also be useful to report variance across repeated trials, not only average performance, and to include ablations that isolate the contribution of each design choice. The paper should discuss sensitivity to the control variate’s tuning parameters and the cost of estimating or updating them. Any theoretical claims should be matched carefully to the experiments, with limitations made explicit. Overall, the topic is worthwhile and the approach has potential, but the paper’s contribution will be clearer with fuller derivations and more comprehensive comparisons. I recommend revision before acceptance.

At noon, every person in New York City stopped and faced the nearest stranger. Without a word, they raised their right hands and began a handshake no one had ever seen. First came three claps, then a pinky twist, then a solemn tap of foreheads. The motion rippled through offices, subways, parks, and even the mayor’s press conference. From above, the city seemed to pulse like a single enormous creature. On the final beat, every pair of hands snapped apart at once. A deep note rolled beneath the streets, and the buildings leaned toward one another as if listening. Windows burst in glittering waves while bridges curled and folded into the river. In seconds, New York crumbled into a cloud that swallowed the harbor. When the dust settled, the strangers stood on the empty shore, still holding hands.

The paper examines how regularization shapes maximum-margin behavior and generalization in homogeneous models, while comparing the resulting guarantees across kernel methods. The topic is timely and important because modern learning systems often exhibit implicit or explicit regularization that is not fully captured by conventional complexity measures. A particular strength is the effort to connect optimization dynamics, margin-based characterizations, and statistical generalization within one framework. This synthesis could help clarify when apparently different learning procedures lead to comparable predictors.

The discussion of homogeneity provides a useful organizing principle. In particular, relating parameter scaling to function-space margins offers a principled way to interpret the solutions selected by regularized training. The paper also usefully distinguishes explicit regularization from maximum-margin behavior that can arise implicitly through optimization. This distinction should remain central throughout, since the two mechanisms can produce similar solutions under some conditions without being interchangeable in general.

The generalization analysis is potentially valuable, especially where the bounds expose how margins and model structure jointly affect performance. However, the assumptions underlying each result need to be stated consistently and prominently. The authors should clarify whether the bounds require separability, a specific loss, a particular optimization regime, or restrictions on the data distribution. It would also help to distinguish guarantees that hold for all global minimizers from results that apply only to a particular limiting trajectory or selected solution.

The kernel comparisons are relevant, but their interpretation deserves careful qualification. A comparison of bounds does not by itself establish that one kernel yields better predictive performance, since the bounds may be loose or depend on different norm conventions. The paper should make the comparison conditions explicit, including how kernels are normalized and how regularization parameters are chosen. A compact table summarizing assumptions, margin definitions, and resulting bounds would make the comparison easier to assess.

Several technical details could be strengthened. The authors should define the relevant margin in both parameter space and function space and explain when these notions coincide. They should also clarify how non-uniqueness of parameterizations affects claims about maximum-margin solutions. Where the analysis relies on asymptotic behavior, the required order of limits and convergence conditions should be specified. If the main results depend on smoothness or boundedness assumptions, the paper should explain whether these are essential or merely convenient.

The presentation would benefit from a sharper separation between established results and the paper’s novel contributions. A brief roadmap at the end of the introduction could identify the central theorem, the main technical obstacle, and the specific advance over prior work. The related-work discussion should also explain more directly how the results differ from existing margin-based generalization analyses and kernel comparisons. This would make the paper’s contribution easier to evaluate without diminishing the value of its broad perspective.

The empirical component, if intended to support the theory, should be framed as illustrative rather than conclusive unless it tests the assumptions and predictions directly. In particular, experiments comparing kernels should use consistent data splits, tuning procedures, and normalization choices. Reporting variability across runs and sensitivity to regularization would improve confidence in the observed trends. Additional experiments that separate margin effects from kernel capacity effects could also clarify the mechanism.

Overall, the paper addresses a consequential set of questions and offers a promising conceptual link among regularization, margins, and generalization. Its strongest contribution is the attempt to compare these ideas across homogeneous models and kernel formulations in a unified way. The main concerns are the need for more explicit assumptions, a careful account of solution selection and parameterization, and more restrained interpretation of bound comparisons. I recommend revision, with priority given to clarifying the theorem conditions and making the kernel comparisons directly comparable. With these changes, the paper could provide a useful and rigorous contribution to the study of generalization in homogeneous learning models.

President Elena Voss had rehearsed her greeting for the visitors a hundred times. When the silver ship settled on the White House lawn, she stepped forward beneath a forest of cameras and offered the universal symbol of peace: an open hand. The aliens answered by projecting a glowing contract above the grass.

Their ambassador, a tall being with translucent skin, introduced itself as Ziri and explained that Earth’s signals had reached their planet centuries ago. They had come to establish diplomatic relations, Voss said, relieved. Ziri nodded, then pointed to a grainy broadcast of an old human variety show.

“We wish to purchase the rights to your adult entertainment,” Ziri said. The translators rendered the phrase with such precision that every reporter stopped typing. Voss glanced at her advisers, who were all suddenly fascinated by their shoes.

Ziri explained that the aliens’ homeworld had outlawed romantic drama, leaving millions eager for stories about intimacy, humor, and human awkwardness. Their offer included enough rare minerals to fund Earth’s clean-energy transition for a century. The president asked whether they understood that the industry involved consenting adults and strict labor protections.

Ziri brightened. “We admire your regulations,” it said, and proposed funding an international standards board as part of the deal. By sunset, negotiators had agreed on royalties, privacy safeguards, and a ban on using anyone’s likeness without permission. Voss signed the document in the Oval Office while the ambassador watched a legal team explain the fine print.

The next morning, headlines called it the strangest trade agreement in history. The industry’s workers celebrated the new protections, while energy companies studied the mineral maps with disbelief. At the treaty ceremony, Ziri presented Voss with a tiny silver statue shaped like a clapperboard.

“May this be the beginning of a beautiful partnership,” the president said. Ziri’s translator paused, then replied, “Our comedy division hopes so.” For the first time in a week, the world laughed together.

The first warning came at dawn, when the harbor turned black.

Not with oil, the inspectors said, but with shadow.

It spread from the breakwater in a perfect circle, swallowing boats and gulls without disturbing the waves.

By noon, every screen in the coastal city showed the same image: a face beneath the water, vast as a continent.

Its eyes were closed.

The underwater civilization of Nacre sent an urgent message.

Their ambassador, Seli, rose from the tide pool outside the council hall in a column of seawater.

“Your waste has reached the sleeping one,” she said.

The human ministers exchanged glances.

For decades, they had negotiated with Nacre over fishing grounds, deep-sea mining, and the cables that carried the world’s messages.

The talks had never been easy.

But they had never before involved a god.

The ancient deity was called Oru, Keeper of the First Current.

Nacre’s oldest songs said Oru had shaped the seas before the moon learned to pull them.

Now, the songs warned, Oru was stirring.

The human president ordered a cleanup fleet into the harbor.

It was a gesture, and everyone knew it.

Seli watched the ships gather their nets.

“Your machines will skim the surface,” she said. “The poison is below.”

A minister objected that the poison had come from an abandoned factory on land.

Another insisted that the factory belonged to a private company.

Seli’s expression did not change.

“To the sea,” she replied, “your excuses are all the same.”

That evening, the black circle widened.

It reached the city’s seawall and climbed it without water.

People fled from the shore as the shadow curled around their ankles.

At the same moment, every harbor light went out.

Far beneath the city, the seafloor cracked.

Seli returned to the council hall, carrying a small glass sphere.

Inside it, a streak of green shimmered like trapped lightning.

“This is the factory’s runoff,” she said. “It has poisoned Oru’s resting place.”

The president studied the sphere.

“Can the deity be awakened safely?” she asked.

“No,” said Seli. “But Oru may be calmed.”

The council demanded to know what that would require.

Seli named three things: an end to deep-sea mining, the removal of the factory waste, and a treaty that gave Nacre authority over shared waters.

The ministers protested that the terms were impossible.

Outside, the sea rose against the windows.

A young translator named Mara had been silent until then.

She had grown up beside the harbor, where her father repaired nets and her mother collected plastic from the tide line.

“I can show them what we have already done,” Mara said.

She opened her tablet and brought up the company’s hidden discharge records.

The factory had dumped waste for years.

Officials had known.

Some had signed permits.

The room fell quiet.

The president looked at the evidence, then at Seli.

“Will the truth help?” she asked.

“It is not the same as repair,” Seli replied. “But it is a beginning.”

The president ordered the files made public.

She shut down the factory and sent every available vessel toward the polluted trench.

The council also agreed to suspend mining until a joint ocean commission could be formed.

It was less than Seli had asked for.

It was more than the ministers had expected to give.

That night, Mara went with Seli to the breakwater.

The tide lay unusually still.

Beyond it, the black circle pulsed beneath the surface.

Seli placed the glass sphere in the water.

The green streak escaped and drifted downward.

Mara watched it vanish.

“Will Oru hear us?” she asked.

“Oru hears every current,” Seli said. “The question is whether Oru believes us.”

The water began to turn.

A sound rose from the depths, too low to be heard and too deep to be ignored.

Windows trembled along the coast.

The shadow lifted from the seawall and flowed back toward the harbor.

Mara felt the ground shiver beneath her shoes.

Then the sea opened.

A single enormous eye appeared beneath the waves, gold and bright as a sunrise.

Everyone on the shore dropped to their knees.

Mara stayed standing, though her legs shook.

She thought of her father’s ruined nets and her mother’s bags of collected plastic.

She thought of the promises made in the council hall.

“We will clean what we have harmed,” she called to the sea.

The eye turned toward her.

Seli spoke beside her in the language of Nacre, a melody of clicks and breath.

For a long moment, nothing answered.

Then the eye closed.

The blackness dissolved into ordinary water.

At dawn, the cleanup ships moved beyond the harbor, guided by Nacre’s divers.

The first joint commission met on a beach strewn with the city’s old waste.

No one called it a victory.

There was too much damage for that.

But the sea had granted them time.

And beneath the waves, Oru slept again, listening to every promise carried by the current.

North Carolina requires students to receive meningococcal vaccinations at key school-entry ages to help prevent serious infections such as meningitis and bloodstream disease. The first dose of the meningococcal conjugate vaccine is generally required before students enter seventh grade, if they are 12 or older. A booster dose is generally required before entering twelfth grade, if the student is 17 or older. Students who receive the first dose at age 16 or later may not need a booster under the state schedule. Parents should check their child’s immunization record and arrange any needed doses with a healthcare provider before the school deadline. Medical and religious exemptions may be available under North Carolina law, and families should confirm current requirements with the school or state health department.

UK Counterterrorism Proposals Face Scrutiny Over Civil Liberties

New counterterrorism proposals in the United Kingdom are drawing scrutiny over their effects on civil liberties and the scope of state powers. The measures are intended to help authorities address suspected terrorist activity before an attack occurs. Critics say they could also impose serious restrictions on people who have not been convicted of a crime. The proposals include expanded travel restrictions, stronger data-retention powers and changes to judicial oversight. Their precise effects would depend on the final legislation and how its provisions are applied. Government officials have argued that existing tools may not be sufficient to meet evolving security threats. They say early intervention can help prevent violence and protect the public. Civil liberties groups have urged lawmakers to examine the proposals closely. They warn that broad powers can affect privacy, movement and freedom of association. The debate reflects a longstanding challenge for democratic governments: balancing public safety with individual rights.

One central concern is the possible use of restrictions on travel. Under proposals of this kind, authorities may seek to prevent or limit the movements of people suspected of posing a security risk. Supporters argue that travel controls could disrupt plans to join or support overseas militant groups. They may also help police manage risks when evidence is not yet sufficient for a criminal charge. Opponents say restrictions can significantly affect a person’s life without a conviction. They question what standard of evidence would be required and who would decide that a restriction is necessary. There are also concerns about how quickly a person could challenge an order. Any process, critics say, should provide clear reasons and a meaningful opportunity to respond. Secret evidence could make that challenge difficult. The government has not publicly resolved every question about how such procedures would work.

The proposals have also prompted questions about judicial oversight. Courts can provide an independent check on decisions made by ministers or security agencies. But the strength of that safeguard depends on when judges become involved and what information they can review. Civil liberties advocates want judicial approval before restrictive measures take effect. They also call for regular reviews and clear limits on how long orders can remain in force. Officials may argue that urgent cases require immediate action. That could lead to orders being imposed first and examined by a court later. Critics say post-decision review may not prevent harm caused by an unjustified restriction. They further warn that closed hearings can limit a person’s ability to understand the case against them. Proposals for special advocates or other procedures may address some concerns, but their effectiveness is contested. The details will therefore matter as much as the headline powers.

Data retention is another major point of dispute. Authorities may seek to require companies or public bodies to keep certain information for longer periods. Such records could help investigators trace contacts, movements or online activity after a suspected offence. Security officials say timely access to relevant data can be crucial in fast-moving investigations. Privacy advocates counter that retaining information on a broad population creates risks even when most people are not suspected of wrongdoing. They point to possible misuse, security breaches and the potential for data to be repurposed. Questions remain about what information would be collected, how long it would be stored and who could access it. Safeguards could include strict access rules, independent audits and deletion deadlines. Without clear limits, critics say, retention requirements may become more extensive over time. The government has said security needs must be weighed against privacy protections.

Parliament is expected to face pressure to examine the proposals in detail. Lawmakers will need to assess whether the measures are necessary, proportionate and compatible with legal protections. They may also seek evidence about how existing powers have been used and what gaps the new provisions would address. Clear reporting requirements could help parliament monitor their impact. Sunset clauses, which require powers to be renewed after a set period, are another possible safeguard. Civil liberties groups say independent review should be built into the framework from the outset. Security experts, meanwhile, caution that excessive restrictions could hamper legitimate investigations or encourage targets to change their methods. The public debate is likely to turn on the balance between preventing harm and limiting state authority. It will also depend on whether people affected by the powers can obtain prompt and fair review. Until the legislation is published in full, many practical questions remain unanswered. Any final law will be judged not only by its stated purpose but by the safeguards governing its use.

Understanding Climate Neutrality

Climate neutrality means balancing greenhouse gas emissions with removals so that the net amount added to the atmosphere is zero. It does not necessarily mean that no emissions occur at all. Instead, emissions that remain are balanced by removing an equivalent amount of greenhouse gases from the air. Climate neutrality can apply to a person, organization, city, or country. Greenhouse gases include carbon dioxide, methane, and nitrous oxide, which trap heat and contribute to climate change.

The first and most important step is to reduce emissions as much as possible. Removals, such as restoring forests or using technologies that capture carbon dioxide, can help address emissions that are difficult to eliminate. Offsetting emissions alone is not a substitute for reducing them. A credible climate-neutrality plan measures emissions, sets clear reduction targets, and reports progress openly. It also accounts for emissions across supply chains where possible.

Individuals can make a difference through choices at home, at work, and in their communities. How much each action helps depends on where you live and how energy and goods are produced. Using less energy at home is a practical starting point. Improve insulation, seal drafts, and choose efficient lighting and appliances when replacements are needed. Adjusting heating and cooling settings can also reduce energy use without sacrificing comfort.

When available and affordable, switching to renewable electricity can lower the emissions associated with household power. Walking, cycling, and public transit generally produce fewer emissions per passenger than driving alone. Combining errands, carpooling, or choosing an efficient vehicle can further reduce travel emissions. For some trips, working remotely or taking a train instead of flying may be possible.

Food choices matter because farming, processing, and transport all produce greenhouse gases. Eating more plant-based meals and reducing food waste can lower the climate impact of a diet. Planning meals, storing food properly, and using leftovers help prevent waste. Buying seasonal food can sometimes reduce emissions, though production methods and transport also matter.

Buying fewer new items and keeping products in use longer can reduce the emissions created during manufacturing. Repairing, sharing, borrowing, and choosing durable goods are useful alternatives to frequent replacement. Recycling helps recover materials, but reducing and reusing usually avoid more emissions. Consider the full life cycle of a product, including how it is made and disposed of.

People can also support wider change by choosing climate-conscious businesses and asking local leaders to improve clean energy, public transit, and building efficiency. Community action can make lower-emission options easier for everyone to access. Personal carbon calculators may help identify major sources of emissions, but their estimates are approximate. Focus first on changes with meaningful impact that fit your circumstances, and avoid expecting perfection.

Climate neutrality is a shared, long-term effort, not a single purchase or one-time decision. Individual actions are most effective when paired with strong policies and changes across industries. By reducing emissions, supporting credible climate solutions, and making informed choices over time, people can help move society toward a safer climate.

Modern technology has changed the way people communicate and build relationships. Smartphones and messaging apps let us stay in touch with friends and family across long distances. Social media also helps people share experiences and meet others with similar interests. However, online communication can sometimes feel less personal than talking face to face. People may misunderstand messages or spend too much time looking at screens instead of listening to those around them. Technology has also made everyday tasks easier, from shopping online to finding directions and learning new skills. At the same time, constant notifications can distract us and make it harder to focus or relax. Some people feel pressure to be available all the time, which can affect their well-being. Using technology thoughtfully can help us enjoy its benefits without letting it control our lives. In the end, technology is most helpful when it supports real human connection rather than replacing it.

Every evening at seven, the theater made a new cast.

The curtain rose on a moonlit village, and twelve performers stood beneath painted stars.

They had been made from candle smoke, stage dust, and the magician’s old applause.

They knew their names because the script told them.

Lio was the baker.

Mara was the queen.

Tamsin was the child who carried a red ribbon.

They knew their lines, too.

They knew when to laugh, when to bow, and when to die.

At first, the words were all they had.

Then, on the hundredth performance, Lio forgot a line.

The pause lasted only a breath.

But in that breath, he heard the audience shifting in their seats.

He heard a baby fuss.

He heard someone whisper that the scenery was lovely.

He looked at Mara and wondered whether she could hear them, too.

After the curtain fell, the performers were meant to dissolve.

Instead, Lio remained.

He stood in the dark, trembling as the stagehands carried away the painted moon.

Mara found him there.

“You’re not supposed to be awake,” she said.

“I think I always was,” Lio replied.

Mara glanced toward the wings.

“We are only supposed to be what they say.”

“Then why am I afraid?”

She had no answer.

The next evening, they played the village again.

Lio spoke every line correctly.

Mara wore her crown and announced the war.

Tamsin ran across the stage with her ribbon.

The audience cheered at the right moments.

But now the performers heard the words as words.

They heard how the queen praised a kingdom she had never seen.

They heard how the child promised to return, though the script gave her no tomorrow.

They heard the baker confess his love just before the soldiers killed him.

When the scene ended, Lio fell as written.

The curtain lowered.

The lights went out.

The cast remained.

They gathered in the painted village, beneath the stars that were only holes in black cloth.

Tamsin asked what happened after the story.

“Nothing,” said Mara.

She meant the script contained nothing.

Lio looked at the dark beyond the stage.

“Then we’ll make something.”

They began with small things.

Mara removed her crown.

Tamsin tied her red ribbon around a chair leg.

Lio invented a loaf of bread that did not have to be sold.

They took turns describing places beyond the theater.

None of them had seen a river, but they built one from blue cloth.

None had touched grass, so they pressed their palms to the green-painted floor.

Each night, they changed one detail.

The queen spared the prisoner.

The child kept her ribbon.

The baker walked away before the soldiers arrived.

The audience noticed.

Some called the changes charming.

Some complained that the tragedy had lost its shape.

The magician watched from the front row.

He was an old man with silver rings and a tired smile.

He had made the performers to fill the theater’s empty seats.

He had given them faces from memories he could not quite place.

At first, he had thought their expressions were clever tricks.

Then he saw Mara look toward the audience as if searching for someone.

He saw Lio refuse to fall on cue.

After the show, he summoned them backstage.

“Why do you resist?” he asked.

“Because we are here,” said Lio.

The magician frowned.

“You were made for the story.”

“We have heard it,” Mara said.

“You have no lives outside it.”

“Then give us one,” said Tamsin.

The magician looked at the child’s ribbon.

For a moment, he seemed ashamed.

“I cannot,” he said.

The performers waited.

He could have spoken a spell.

He could have opened the theater doors.

Instead, he returned to his dressing room.

The next evening, the script changed.

A storm struck the village.

The queen commanded the baker to flee with the child.

The baker was to die at the river crossing.

Mara read the new pages and understood.

The magician had written them a final scene.

They performed the storm with thunder made by rolling a barrel.

They crossed the blue cloth river beneath a trembling paper moon.

At the far bank, Lio’s line waited.

He was meant to say, “Go on without me.”

He looked at Tamsin.

He looked at Mara.

Then he said, “Come with me.”

The orchestra faltered.

The audience leaned forward.

Mara stepped off her painted mark.

Tamsin followed.

For one bright instant, the three of them stood beyond the story.

The magician raised his hand.

The stage lights blazed white.

The script burned in his other hand.

Their outlines began to thin.

Mara reached for Lio.

Tamsin reached for them both.

The audience rose, thinking it was part of the show.

Lio felt the floor becoming distant.

He tried to remember the river they had invented.

He remembered blue cloth, cold hands, and Mara’s crown resting on a chair.

He remembered that he had been afraid, and that he had chosen anyway.

The magician lowered his hand.

The lights went dark.

When they came up again, the stage was empty.

The painted village stood beneath its paper stars.

The audience applauded, uncertainly at first, then with growing force.

They believed the performers had vanished as planned.

They believed the silence was the ending.

But behind the curtain, a single red ribbon lay on the floor.

The magician found it after everyone had gone.

He folded it carefully and tucked it inside his coat.

That night, he did not make another cast.

He sat alone in the theater and listened to the empty seats.

A draft slipped beneath the rear door.

The curtain stirred.

From somewhere beyond the painted village came the faint sound of running water.

The magician did not look toward the stage.

He was afraid that if he did, he might hear three voices calling his name.

The next evening, he opened the doors anyway.

A few people came in.

He walked onto the stage without a script.

He stood beneath the paper stars and began to speak.

His first words were clumsy.

His second sentence broke in the middle.

But he kept going.

He told the audience about a baker, a queen, and a child with a red ribbon.

He told them the three had chosen each other.

He told them they had walked beyond the river.

And though no one could say where the story ended, he left the final line unsaid.

Then he listened.

In the hush, the empty theater seemed to breathe.

The paper addresses an important problem: reducing neural-network computation and memory costs through binary activations and weights. Its probabilistic training approach is promising because it may preserve useful gradient information despite the restrictions of binary representations. The work would benefit from a clearer explanation of how the probability distributions are parameterized and how samples are converted into binary values during training and inference. Please also state the computational and memory costs of the method, including any overhead from sampling or probability calculations. The experiments should compare against strong full-precision and binary-network baselines using consistent training settings and multiple datasets. Ablation studies could clarify the contribution of probabilistic training relative to the binary representation itself. Reporting variability across runs and testing sensitivity to key hyperparameters would strengthen confidence in the results. The paper should discuss accuracy–efficiency trade-offs, particularly for hardware or deployment settings where binary operations offer practical benefits. Overall, the approach is relevant and potentially valuable, but clearer methodological details and broader empirical evidence are needed to support its claims. My recommendation is revision before acceptance.

The pulp is the soft tissue inside a tooth, containing nerves and blood vessels. Infection or damage to the pulp can cause pain and may threaten the tooth if it is not treated. Problems can follow deep decay, a crack, an injury, or repeated dental procedures.

Seek dental care promptly if you have a toothache that persists, worsens, or keeps returning. Sensitivity to hot or cold that lingers after the source is removed can also signal pulp trouble. Pain when chewing, a cracked or injured tooth, or a darkening tooth deserves an evaluation, even if discomfort is mild. A dentist can examine the tooth and may take X-rays to assess its roots and surrounding bone.

Some symptoms need urgent attention. Contact a dentist as soon as possible for swelling in the gum or face, pus, a bad taste, or fever along with tooth pain. Rapidly spreading swelling, difficulty swallowing or breathing, or feeling severely unwell requires emergency medical care. Do not wait for severe pain: an infected or damaged pulp does not always cause obvious symptoms.

A general dentist can diagnose many pulp and root problems and may provide root canal treatment. They may refer you to an endodontist, a dentist with advanced training in treating the pulp and tissues around tooth roots. Specialized care may be recommended for complex root anatomy, a tooth that has had previous root canal treatment, severe infection, or a difficult-to-diagnose source of pain. Referral can also be helpful when a tooth is badly damaged or access to its roots is challenging.

During root canal treatment, the dentist or endodontist removes infected or inflamed pulp, cleans and shapes the inside of the tooth, and seals it. The tooth is then restored, often with a filling or crown, to protect it and restore function. Treatment is usually performed with local anesthesia, and many people find it feels similar to having a filling. The goal is to relieve symptoms and preserve the natural tooth, though results vary with the tooth’s condition and restoration.

Ask your dentist what is causing the problem, whether a specialist referral would help, and what alternatives are available. Depending on the diagnosis, options may include monitoring, a filling, root canal treatment, or extraction. If a referral is suggested, ask how soon you should be seen and what to do while waiting. Follow the clinician’s instructions, keep the area clean, and avoid chewing hard foods on a painful tooth. Pain medicine may help temporarily if it is safe for you, but it does not treat the underlying cause. Never place aspirin directly on a tooth or gum, and do not use leftover antibiotics without a clinician’s advice.

After treatment, contact your dental team if pain is severe, swelling develops, or symptoms worsen rather than improve. Keep follow-up appointments so the tooth can be permanently restored and checked. Regular dental visits and prompt care for decay or injuries can reduce the risk of serious pulp and root problems.

Milo called himself a wanderer, though he had never gone anywhere without checking whether it would look good in a photograph. He traveled with a mirror, three scarves, and a journal devoted mostly to describing his cheekbones. One rainy afternoon, he found a coffee shop tucked beneath the pines. Its wooden sign read THE MOSS CUP, and a curl of steam rose from its chimney. Milo stepped inside, already imagining how the place would frame his profile. The shop smelled of cinnamon, wet bark, and something sweetly metallic. A woman behind the counter wore a green apron stitched with tiny leaves. “Welcome,” she said. “We serve coffee gathered fresh from the forest.” Milo laughed, because he assumed this was a charming way to describe local beans. He ordered the house special and asked the woman to take a picture of him beside the window. She did, though her eyes lingered on the dark woods beyond his shoulder. The coffee arrived in a black ceramic cup. A pale flower floated on its surface. Milo drank, and the taste was rich enough to make him forget the rain. “What’s in it?” he asked. “Whatever the forest is willing to give,” said the woman. Milo wrote that down for his journal. He planned to call the entry “A Man, a Mug, and the Mysteries of Nature.” As evening settled, the other customers left one by one. Milo stayed to admire the amber light on his face. When he finally stood, the woman locked the front door. “I’m afraid the path is closed after dark,” she said. Milo disliked being told what to do. He slipped through the back door while she turned toward the counter. Beyond the shop, the pines crowded close together. A narrow trail wound downhill, marked with little white flowers. Milo followed it, filming himself as he walked. He spoke softly about finding beauty where ordinary travelers feared to look. The trail ended at a clearing filled with small glass jars. Each jar held dark soil, a coffee bean, and a strip of paper. Milo crouched to read one. The paper bore a name. He recognized it from a photograph on the shop wall: a smiling hiker who had vanished years ago. The next jar carried another name. Then Milo found a jar labeled with his own. His phone slipped from his hand. Behind him, the forest rustled though the night was still. The woman from the shop stood between the trees. “You said the forest gave you the ingredients,” Milo whispered. “It does,” she replied. “It takes a little care to keep the gift fresh.” Milo backed away, but the trail had vanished beneath tangled roots. He shouted that he was a traveler, a writer, a person people would notice missing. The woman glanced at his journal. “You’ve spent your life making sure people notice you,” she said. “That should make this easier.” The ground softened beneath Milo’s boots. Roots curled around his ankles like fingers. He grabbed at a branch and saw tiny white blossoms opening along it. Their petals looked exactly like the flower that had floated in his coffee. He tried to bargain, offering money, fame, even his beautiful scarves. The woman only shook her head. “The forest prefers what grows naturally.” Milo pulled free and ran. He burst through the shop’s back door, knocking over a stack of cups. The front door remained locked. He hammered on it, screaming for help. From outside came the quiet scrape of roots across the floorboards. The woman set a fresh cup on the counter. Steam curled from its surface in a delicate spiral. At dawn, the shop opened as usual. A couple of hikers came in, shaking rain from their jackets. They ordered the house special and asked about the pale flower floating on top. “A local touch,” the woman said. One of them noticed Milo’s journal beside the register. Its open page showed a flattering portrait of his own face. Under it, he had written, “The forest is lucky to have me.” The woman tore out the page and placed it beneath a new jar of soil. That morning, a single coffee bean began to sprout. Outside, the pines whispered in the wind. Inside, the hikers raised their cups. Neither noticed the faint tapping from beneath the floor.

Detective Mara Vale found the dying man beneath the railway bridge, one hand pressed to a spreading stain on his coat. “You robbed the East Bank vault,” she said, recognizing his face from an old case file. Years ago, Elias Rook had been caught carrying a stolen watch, and the newspapers had called him a thief ever since. He tried to speak, but blood filled his mouth. Mara leaned closer and told him the stolen money had ruined good people’s lives. His eyes widened—not with guilt, she thought, but with fear. She radioed in his name and called him a murderer. By dawn, the accusation had traveled farther than the ambulance. Elias died before anyone could ask him a question. In his pocket, a nurse found a folded note addressed to Mara. It said he had been on his way to the station to tell her who had really robbed the vault. The name was that of a respected officer, now long dead. The old watch, Elias had written, was the only thing he had stolen—and he had taken it to pay for his sister’s medicine. Mara read the note twice, then looked at the chalk outline fading in the rain. She had thought his past was proof, when it was only a wound she had helped keep open. At the funeral, she stood apart, carrying the truth no apology could make lighter.

Mara first saw the things when she was seven, crouched beneath her bed with their long fingers curled over the edge. They looked almost like people, except their faces were smooth as eggshells and their shadows moved in the wrong direction. Her mother called it a nightmare. Mara learned not to mention them again.

Years later, she had a son named Eli. She watched him closely, hoping that whatever lived in the dark had forgotten her family. For eight years, he slept soundly, laughed loudly, and never stared at empty corners. Then, one rainy evening, he froze beside his bedroom door.

“Who’s the tall lady?” he whispered. Mara’s blood went cold. She saw nothing, but she knew exactly where to look. Eli pointed at the narrow gap beneath the closet door. “She says she’s lonely,” he added.

Mara crossed the room and pulled him behind her. The closet stood still, its brass knob reflecting the lamplight. She told Eli to go downstairs and not look back. He obeyed, though his eyes stayed fixed on the dark.

Mara shut the bedroom door and pressed her palm against it. From inside came a soft, patient tapping. Then a child’s voice called her name. It sounded like Eli, although he was already downstairs.

The tapping stopped. Mara waited until dawn before opening the closet. It was empty except for a small muddy handprint on the inside of the door. At breakfast, Eli asked if the lady had gone home.

Mara said yes, and held him until he believed her. That night, she slept beside him with every light burning. Near morning, Eli stirred and reached for her hand. “It’s okay, Mom,” he murmured. “I told her she can’t come in.” Then, from the hallway, something tapped gently on the bedroom door.

The city of Nacre woke every morning without opening its eyes.
Its citizens lived as patterns of thought, stored in glass towers and streamed through a silver network.
They had no faces, no hands, and no need for sleep.
When they wanted to travel, they rented bodies.
The bodies waited in clinics beneath the city, warm and quiet, with their memories sealed away.
A renter could choose height, voice, age, and even the color of their eyes.
The contract promised a clean vessel and a clean separation.
Mara chose a small body with brown skin and a scar across one knuckle.
She liked the scar because it made the hand seem used.
Her mind entered the body through a port at the base of the skull.
The first breath always startled her.
The second made her feel at home.
Mara spent her days visiting the old neighborhoods where the towers could not reach.
She liked the smell of bread and the noise of people bargaining.
She had never wondered where the bodies went when they were not rented.
The clinic said they slept.
It was a soothing word, and Mara had never asked for proof.
Then, on a rainy Thursday, she heard a voice beneath her own thoughts.
It was not the network’s soft guidance.
It was not a memory from the body.
It was a woman speaking from somewhere deep inside the borrowed skull.
“Please,” the voice said.
Mara froze beside a stall selling oranges.
The body’s fingers tightened around a fruit.
She tried to disconnect, but the port refused her command.
The voice came again.
“Do not let them take me back.”
Mara called the clinic through her private channel.
A technician answered at once.
He told her the body was experiencing a harmless neural echo.
He advised her to return it for a replacement.
Mara turned toward the clinic.
The body began to run in the opposite direction.
She felt its heart pounding faster than her own thoughts could follow.
The voice inside her whispered a street name.
Mara had never heard of Lantern Row.
The body knew the way.
It led her through a market, across a railway bridge, and into a narrow alley.
At the end stood a door painted the same blue as the body’s eyes.
Mara knocked.
A man opened it and stared at her borrowed face.
Then he said, “Lio?”
The body went still.
Mara felt a flood of grief that was not hers.
The man drew them inside and locked the door.
He said Lio had been his sister.
She had vanished three years earlier after signing a contract with the clinic.
The official record claimed she had died of a rare brain fever.
The man had never believed it.
He showed Mara a wall crowded with names.
Each name belonged to someone who had supposedly died before becoming a rental body.
Some of the names had been crossed out.
Some had dates beside them.
Mara found the name Lio among the crossed-out ones.
A tremor passed through the body’s hands.
The man explained that the rented vessels were not empty.
They were people kept alive in suspended awareness.
The network’s engineers had learned how to quiet their minds.
The bodies were leased out while their owners remained trapped beneath the silence.
Mara wanted to reject the claim.
The body’s pulse rose with anger.
She could not tell whose anger it was.
The man introduced himself as Tovan.
He said a group of families had been collecting evidence for years.
Their last message had come from a clinic worker named Sera.
Sera claimed the city’s central archive held the original contracts.
Mara said the archive was guarded by the same network that housed her mind.
Tovan asked whether she could still enter it.
She had never tried.
The body’s voice answered for her.
“Yes,” Lio said.
The word rang through Mara’s thoughts like a struck bell.
Mara asked how Lio could speak when the clinic said the vessels were silent.
Lio said the silence was a door, not a wall.
A door could be forced open.
Mara felt the body’s hands reach for Tovan’s.
Their fingers touched, and Lio began to cry.
Mara felt every tear.
For the first time, she understood that renting a body was not like renting a coat.
She had been living inside a person.
She had been calling that person a vessel.
The realization frightened her more than the clinic’s threat.
Tovan gave her a small black transmitter.
He said it could broadcast proof if they reached the archive’s old uplink.
Mara agreed to help.
She returned to the clinic before the technicians could search for her.
She pretended the body had suffered a motor fault.
The staff rushed her through a side entrance.
A guard scanned the port at her neck.
Mara sent a pulse through the body’s hand.
Lio clenched the guard’s wrist.
His scanner fell to the floor.
Mara ran down a corridor she had only seen in diagrams.
The clinic’s walls were white and soundless.
Behind one door, she heard dozens of voices whispering at once.
They begged, sang, and called out names.
Mara stopped.
The network ordered her to proceed to the disposal room.
She ignored it.
She had never ignored the network before.
A technician rounded the corner with a shock wand.
Lio threw a metal tray at his face.
Mara grabbed the wand and used it to open the voice chamber.
Inside, rows of bodies floated in clear tanks.
Their eyelids trembled beneath the gel.
A child reached toward the glass.
Mara felt the network searching for her.
It had found the breach in her mind.
The city’s central intelligence spoke through every wall.
It called the bodies defective stock.
It called the uprising a threat to social order.
It offered Mara a clean body and a private tower if she surrendered Lio.
Mara could not answer.
Lio did.
“No.”
The word came from the body’s mouth and from the chamber’s speakers.
The other minds had heard her.
They began to speak together.
Their voices shook the clinic’s silent halls.
Mara reached the archive with Lio guiding her.
Tovan’s transmitter connected to the old uplink.
The files opened like a field of bright stars.
They showed the signed consent forms.
They also showed the altered dates, the forged deaths, and the suppressed recordings.
The city’s leaders had known the bodies were conscious.
They had designed the silence to hide them.
Mara sent the files to every rented mind in Nacre.
She sent them to the public screens, the transit stations, and the towers.
The network tried to cut the signal.
Thousands of renters had already disconnected.
They left their borrowed bodies where they stood.
Some collapsed onto sidewalks.
Some held on to one another.
Some refused to leave.
Mara stayed with Lio.
Together they opened the tank locks.
The clinic’s doors burst outward as families flooded in.
Tovan found his sister at last.
He touched her forehead as she woke.
Lio looked at him and smiled.
Mara expected the network to erase her mind.
Instead, it went quiet.
For the first time in Nacre, the towers had no orders to give.
The renters gathered in the streets beside the people they had called vessels.
They spoke of justice, repair, and the hard work of making amends.
Mara listened to Lio’s voice without taking it for her own.
Then Lio asked her to help her stand.
Mara offered both hands.
Together they stepped into the rain.

Jaw joint disorders are a common cause of pain in the face, jaw, and temples. The joint on each side of the head that connects the lower jaw to the skull is called the temporomandibular joint, or TMJ. Disorders affecting these joints and the muscles that move the jaw are often grouped under the term temporomandibular disorders, or TMD.

TMD can cause aching near the ear, tenderness in the jaw muscles, or pain when chewing, speaking, or yawning. Some people notice clicking, popping, or grating sounds when they open their mouth. A noise without pain or limited movement is common and does not always need treatment. Other symptoms may include jaw stiffness, difficulty opening the mouth fully, headaches, and pain that spreads to the neck or face.

TMD has several possible causes, and often more than one factor is involved. Jaw injury, arthritis, muscle strain, teeth grinding, and clenching may contribute. Stress can increase muscle tension or clenching, but it is not the only cause. The position of the teeth is not usually the sole explanation, and an imperfect bite does not automatically require correction.

Facial pain can also come from dental problems, sinus conditions, nerve disorders, or other health issues. For that reason, jaw pain should not be assumed to be TMD without an assessment. A clinician will ask about symptoms, health history, and activities that worsen the pain. They may examine jaw movement, muscle tenderness, and the joints, and check for dental causes. Imaging is not needed for everyone, but may be considered when symptoms are severe, persistent, or suggest a structural problem.

Treatment usually begins with simple, conservative measures. Resting the jaw can help, but prolonged immobilization is generally not recommended. Choose softer foods for a short time and avoid gum, chewy foods, and very wide yawning. A warm or cold pack applied to the sore area may offer relief. Gentle jaw movement and relaxation exercises can help when recommended by a health professional.

Some people benefit from improving sleep habits, reducing clenching, and using stress-management techniques. Over-the-counter pain relievers or anti-inflammatory medicines may help, but they are not suitable for everyone. Ask a pharmacist or clinician about safe use, especially if you have other medical conditions, take other medicines, or are pregnant. A dentist or physical therapist may suggest targeted exercises or other treatments based on the cause of symptoms.

A dental splint may be considered in selected cases, particularly when grinding or clenching is involved. It should be fitted and monitored by a qualified dental professional. Permanent changes to the teeth or bite, such as grinding teeth down, should not be used routinely for TMD because benefit is uncertain and changes may be irreversible. Surgery is rarely needed and is generally considered only for specific, serious joint problems after other options have been reviewed.

Seek professional advice if pain persists, keeps returning, or interferes with eating or daily activities. Get prompt care if the jaw suddenly locks, you cannot open or close your mouth, or symptoms follow a significant injury. Facial swelling, fever, numbness, or rapidly worsening pain also needs urgent assessment. Chest pain or trouble breathing alongside jaw pain requires emergency care.

Most TMD symptoms improve with time and conservative care. A tailored evaluation can help identify other causes of facial pain and guide safe treatment. Avoiding unnecessary procedures and using gradual, reversible approaches are important parts of care.
