California’s cap-and-trade program is designed to limit greenhouse gas emissions while giving businesses flexibility in how they meet that limit. The state sets a declining cap on emissions from covered industries and fuel suppliers. Companies must hold permits, called allowances, for the emissions they produce. They can reduce emissions directly or buy allowances from other participants. The system also allows companies to use a limited number of carbon offsets.

An offset credit represents a claimed reduction or removal of greenhouse gases outside the capped facilities. For example, a project might prevent forest loss, capture methane, or improve forest management. Companies can use eligible credits instead of cutting an equivalent amount of their own emissions. Supporters say offsets can lower compliance costs and direct money to climate projects. They may also encourage reductions in places not covered by the cap.

The central concern is whether an offset represents a real, additional, and lasting climate benefit. A project is additional if it would not have happened without the credit revenue. If a forest would have remained intact anyway, issuing credits for protecting it does not create a new reduction. Estimating what would have happened otherwise requires assumptions about future behavior and risks. Those assumptions can be difficult to verify.

Offsets can also face problems of permanence. A forest credited for storing carbon may later burn, be logged, or suffer from drought. In that case, some of the stored carbon returns to the atmosphere. Programs may set aside reserve credits or use other safeguards to address this risk, but those protections may not fully cover future losses. Monitoring over many years is essential.

Another concern is leakage. Protecting one area from logging may shift logging to another area rather than prevent it. The credited project could then appear to reduce emissions more than it does overall. Measuring leakage across regions is challenging. These uncertainties matter because each offset allows a company to emit more under the program than it otherwise could.

When offsets overstate their climate benefit, they can weaken the cap’s effect. The paper limit on emissions may remain unchanged, but actual emissions could be higher than the system’s accounting suggests. This can delay direct pollution cuts at factories, power plants, and fuel suppliers. It can also make progress toward state climate targets less reliable. Strong offset rules and independent verification are therefore important.

Offsets may also affect investment choices. If buying credits is cheaper than upgrading equipment, a company may postpone investments in electrification, energy efficiency, or cleaner industrial processes. Those upgrades can reduce emissions for many years and help develop new technologies. Delays may lock in high-emitting infrastructure. The concern is not that every offset prevents clean investment, but that generous or low-quality credits can change incentives.

At the same time, well-designed offsets may finance useful projects and offer flexibility during a transition. Some emissions are difficult to eliminate immediately, especially in sectors with limited alternatives. The key question is whether offsets complement direct reductions or substitute for them. A program should prioritize verified cuts at the source while allowing only a carefully limited role for credits.

Policymakers can improve offset integrity by requiring conservative baselines, clear evidence of additionality, long-term monitoring, and transparent accounting. They can strengthen protections against wildfire and leakage, and make project data accessible to the public. Regular independent reviews can identify credits that do not deliver their promised benefits. Limits on offset use can also reduce the risk that companies rely on them instead of making direct cuts.

Evaluating California’s program requires examining both reported compliance and real-world emissions outcomes. Useful questions include how many credits companies use, what kinds of projects generate them, and whether those projects would have happened anyway. It is also important to track whether covered businesses are investing in cleaner equipment and reducing emissions over time. Offset quality is not the only factor affecting those trends, but it is an important one.

In short, cap-and-trade offsets can support climate projects, but uncertain or overstated credits may undermine emissions reductions. They may also weaken incentives to invest in clean energy and industrial improvements. The outcome depends on the quality of the credits, the strength of oversight, and the limits placed on their use. A credible climate policy must ensure that claimed reductions are real and that offsets do not replace the direct cuts needed to meet long-term goals.

Two men were convicted over the grooming, abduction, rape and murder of teenager Kayleigh Haywood in Leicestershire.

The case centred on the 15-year-old, whose disappearance prompted an urgent search in November 2015. Kayleigh had been groomed online by a man who was later convicted of her murder. Investigators said he posed as a teenage boy and built her trust before arranging to meet her. He abducted her from outside her home in Loughborough.

Kayleigh was taken to a house in Leicester, where she was sexually assaulted. Her body was later found in a garden, bringing a devastating end to the search. The discovery led to a major investigation by Leicestershire Police.

The main defendant, 28-year-old Arshid Hussain, was found guilty of murder, rape and sexual offences against Kayleigh. He was also convicted of offences relating to the grooming and abduction that preceded her death. His co-defendant, 28-year-old Imran Khan, was convicted of rape and other sexual offences against her. The verdicts followed a trial at Leicester Crown Court.

The court heard how online contact had been used to lure Kayleigh into danger. Prosecutors described a calculated process that exploited her vulnerability and trust. The jury considered evidence about the defendants’ actions before and after the teenager disappeared. It also heard evidence about the assault and the circumstances in which her body was found.

The convictions brought a measure of justice to Kayleigh’s family, but could not undo the loss. Her relatives had endured years of grief while the case made its way through the courts. In a statement after the verdicts, they described the impact of her death on those who loved her. They remembered Kayleigh as a much-loved daughter and friend whose life had been cut short.

The case also renewed concern about the risks children face through online grooming. Police said offenders can use false identities to gain a young person’s confidence and arrange meetings. They urged parents and carers to talk openly with children about online contact. Young people were encouraged to tell a trusted adult if someone’s messages made them feel uneasy.

Officers credited the investigation to evidence gathered from witnesses, forensic work and digital enquiries. Detectives traced the events leading up to Kayleigh’s disappearance and identified those responsible. The case required close coordination between specialist teams and local officers. Prosecutors said the evidence presented at trial established the defendants’ roles in the crimes.

The court was expected to hear further proceedings on sentencing following the convictions. Murder carries a mandatory life sentence in England and Wales, with the judge setting a minimum term before parole can be considered. The sentences for the other offences would also be determined by the court. The convictions marked the conclusion of the trial, but the consequences of the crime remain with Kayleigh’s family and community.

Police continued to encourage anyone concerned about a child’s online safety to seek advice or report suspicious behaviour. They stressed that grooming can happen gradually and may not be immediately apparent to families. The case stands as a stark reminder of how online deception can lead to serious harm. Kayleigh’s name remains associated with efforts to raise awareness and protect young people.

The House of Commons has changed its rules to keep the identities of MPs arrested by police private in most cases. Under the new approach, an MP’s arrest will not be publicly identified by Parliament unless the case relates to their parliamentary duties or a constitutional matter. The change is intended to protect members’ privacy while investigations are under way.

Previously, arrests could be disclosed through parliamentary channels, prompting concern that unproven allegations might cause lasting reputational damage. Supporters of the revised rules say an arrest alone does not establish wrongdoing and should not automatically trigger public identification. They argue that the exception preserves transparency when an investigation bears directly on Parliament’s work or the constitutional order.

The policy does not prevent police or other authorities from releasing information under their own procedures. Nor does it limit the media’s ability to report details that are lawfully made public. Critics may question whether the exemptions are sufficiently clear and how decisions about them will be made.

The Commons will need to apply the rules consistently, particularly in cases where an MP’s public role overlaps with the alleged conduct. The change comes amid wider debate over how institutions should balance accountability with the rights of people under investigation. MPs have not been granted immunity from arrest or prosecution.

A water main rupture disrupted traffic in south London as Thames Water crews worked to repair the damage and restore normal service. The leak sent water across nearby roads, prompting disruption for motorists and possible delays to local bus routes. Thames Water said its teams were on site to assess the rupture and carry out repairs. Drivers were advised to use alternative routes while work continued. The incident may also have affected water pressure or supply to nearby properties, though the extent was not immediately clear. Residents were asked to report any continuing loss of water or pressure to the utility. Thames Water said it would provide updates as the repair progressed. Traffic and water services are expected to return to normal once the work is complete.

Polar Bears: Adaptations, Diet, Life Cycle, and Role in Creation

Polar bears are powerful Arctic mammals specially adapted to life on sea ice and along cold northern coasts. Their thick fur and layer of body fat help keep them warm in freezing conditions. Although their fur looks white, the hairs are transparent and reflect light, helping the bears blend into snowy surroundings. Beneath their fur, polar bears have black skin that absorbs warmth from sunlight. Their broad paws spread their weight across thin ice and act like paddles when they swim. Small bumps on their paw pads provide grip on slippery surfaces.

Polar bears are carnivores, and seals are their main prey. They often wait near breathing holes in sea ice or stalk seals resting on the ice. Their strong sense of smell helps them locate prey, even beneath snow. Polar bears may also eat birds, eggs, or other available food, especially when seals are scarce. Because sea ice is essential for hunting, the loss of ice can make finding food more difficult.

Most polar bears live alone, except when mothers are raising cubs or when bears gather near abundant food. Mating usually takes place in spring, but a pregnant female delays the development of the embryo until conditions are favorable. In autumn, she digs a den in snow, where she gives birth, commonly to one or two cubs. The cubs are tiny and helpless at birth, and their mother keeps them warm and feeds them with rich milk. They leave the den with her after a few months and learn to travel and hunt. Cubs may stay with their mother for more than two years before becoming independent.

In ecosystems, polar bears are top predators that help shape the populations and behavior of their prey. They also provide food for scavengers when their remains are available. Many faith traditions describe the natural world, including polar bears, as part of creation and a source of wonder and responsibility. From a scientific perspective, polar bears evolved through adaptations that help them survive in the Arctic. Caring for their habitat supports polar bears and the many other species that depend on healthy Arctic ecosystems.

Health savings accounts (HSAs), health flexible spending arrangements (FSAs), and health reimbursement arrangements (HRAs) all help people pay medical costs with tax advantages, but they follow different rules. An HSA is a personal account available to someone enrolled in an eligible high-deductible health plan and with no disqualifying other coverage. Contributions are generally deductible or excluded from income, investment growth is tax-free, and withdrawals are tax-free when used for qualified medical expenses. Money left in an HSA rolls over from year to year, and the account stays with its owner when they change jobs. Nonmedical withdrawals before age 65 generally incur income tax and an additional 20% tax; after 65, the additional tax no longer applies, though ordinary income tax does. Annual contribution limits and the minimum deductible and maximum out-of-pocket amounts for eligible plans are adjusted periodically, so people should check current IRS guidance.

An FSA is usually offered through an employer, and employee contributions are generally made before federal income tax. FSAs commonly have a “use it or lose it” rule, although an employer may allow a limited carryover or a grace period, not both. An HRA is funded solely by an employer, which sets the reimbursement terms within federal rules; unused funds generally are not portable to a new employer. Some employers offer arrangements that reimburse individual health insurance premiums, but these have separate requirements.

Congress can change these plans through legislation, while the IRS and other agencies issue regulations and guidance explaining how statutes apply. Political changes can therefore affect contribution limits, eligible expenses, plan designs, and which insurance arrangements qualify. For example, federal laws enacted in 2025 expanded HSA eligibility for certain people enrolled in bronze or catastrophic plans through the ACA marketplace, subject to statutory conditions. The same legislation also made certain direct primary care arrangements compatible with HSA eligibility and allowed HSA funds to cover specified related fees, within limits. These changes generally take effect in 2026, so people should verify the effective date and details before relying on them. Rules may also change through later legislation, agency action, court decisions, or annual inflation adjustments.

A tax-free HSA or FSA withdrawal must meet the IRS definition of a qualified medical expense, and the account holder should keep receipts and other records. The same expense cannot be reimbursed tax-free by more than one plan or deducted again on a tax return. Before choosing coverage, compare premiums, deductibles, employer contributions, expected care, and the tax value of contributions. Since eligibility and tax consequences depend on individual circumstances, consult current IRS publications, plan documents, or a qualified tax professional.

Mobile phones have become a common part of everyday life. Many students bring them to school, and some use them throughout the day. Although phones can be useful in certain situations, they should be prohibited during school hours. They distract students, make cheating easier, and weaken students’ ability to use dictionaries. Schools are places for learning, concentration, and developing useful skills. Phone notifications can interrupt a lesson at any moment. Even when a phone is silent, students may be tempted to check it. Messages and social media can take their attention away from the teacher. A student who is distracted may miss important instructions or explanations. It can also be difficult for that student to catch up afterward. Phones may distract nearby classmates as well. When students focus on screens, they have fewer opportunities to participate in discussions. They may also complete assignments less carefully. Keeping phones out of reach can help students concentrate on their work.

Phones can also make cheating easier. Students might use them to search for answers during a test. Some may photograph questions or share answers with others. Messaging apps can allow students to communicate secretly during an assessment. These actions are unfair to students who complete their work honestly. They also make it harder for teachers to know what students truly understand. A phone ban during lessons and tests would reduce these opportunities. Teachers could then assess students’ knowledge more fairly. Students would also have a stronger reason to prepare on their own.

Another concern is the effect phones can have on dictionary skills. In the past, students often learned to look up unfamiliar words in printed dictionaries. This practice taught them how to use guide words, alphabetical order, and pronunciation information. Phone translation and search apps can provide quick answers without teaching these skills. Students may become too dependent on automatic tools. As a result, they might struggle to find meanings or check spelling independently. Using a dictionary also encourages students to notice related words and different definitions. These details can improve vocabulary and reading comprehension. Schools should give students regular opportunities to practise these skills.

A school phone ban does not mean that phones are never useful. Students may need to contact their families in an emergency. Schools can arrange safe ways to make those calls. Teachers can also allow phones for specific learning activities when there is a clear purpose. However, such exceptions should be controlled. During ordinary lessons, phones should remain switched off and stored away. This rule would create a more focused classroom for everyone. It would also encourage students to communicate face to face. Most importantly, students could give their attention to learning instead of their screens. For these reasons, prohibiting mobile phones in schools is a sensible choice.

Technology can support communication, learning, and independence for autistic people. The right tools vary from person to person, so no single device or app works for everyone. Some people use technology every day, while others prefer occasional support or no technology at all. Autistic people should be involved in choosing tools that affect their lives. Their preferences, goals, sensory needs, and privacy matter.

Communication tools can offer ways to express needs, ideas, feelings, and choices. Augmentative and alternative communication, often called AAC, includes methods that supplement or replace speech. AAC can be unaided, such as gestures and signs, or aided, such as picture boards and electronic devices. A low-tech communication board may use pictures, words, or symbols arranged on a page. A person can point to a symbol to make a request or share information. Boards can be tailored for home, school, work, or community settings.

Speech-generating devices produce spoken output when a person selects words, symbols, or letters. Some are dedicated devices, while others are apps on tablets or phones. AAC apps may offer picture-based layouts, keyboards, phrase buttons, or a combination of these. A communication partner can help organize vocabulary around the person’s daily routines and interests. Vocabulary should include more than immediate requests, such as “I want a drink.” People also need words for conversation, opinions, humor, questions, and refusal. Access methods may include touch, switches, eye gaze, or scanning, depending on a person’s motor needs.

Text-to-speech tools can read typed words aloud. Speech-to-text tools can turn spoken language into written words. These features may help with conversations, writing, or communicating in noisy environments. Some people find it easier to communicate through text than speech. Messaging and email can give a person more time to think before responding. Video calls may help maintain contact, though they can also be tiring or difficult for some users. Communication partners should allow enough time for responses and avoid assuming that limited speech means limited understanding.

Visual supports can make information easier to understand and routines easier to follow. A visual schedule shows activities in order, using words, pictures, or both. Schedules can be printed or displayed on a phone, tablet, or computer. Timers and countdowns can show how much time remains before a transition. First-then boards clarify what is happening now and what comes next. Checklists can break a task into manageable steps. These tools can be useful at home, in classrooms, at work, and while traveling.

Learning technology ranges from accessible books to interactive educational programs. E-books can offer adjustable text size, audio narration, and built-in dictionaries. Captions can make videos easier to follow and can support learning new words. Recorded lessons allow learners to pause, replay, or review information at their own pace. Educational apps may teach literacy, numeracy, communication, or daily living skills. Their value depends on whether they match the learner’s goals and abilities. Clear instructions, predictable layouts, and limited distractions can make digital learning more accessible.

Some autistic learners benefit from tools that support organization and executive functioning. Calendar apps can show appointments, deadlines, and reminders. Task-management apps can divide a larger project into smaller actions. Alarms can prompt medication, breaks, or transitions, when appropriate. Notes apps can store instructions, ideas, or lists. A shared calendar may help coordinate plans with family members or support staff. These tools should be introduced gradually, with settings adapted to avoid overwhelming notifications.

Technology can also support sensory regulation. Noise-reducing headphones may make crowded or loud environments more manageable. Music or calming audio may help some people focus or relax. Screen filters and adjustable brightness can reduce visual discomfort. Sensory apps may provide predictable sounds, images, or breathing prompts. Such tools do not work for everyone, and personal preferences should guide their use. They should not be used to force someone to tolerate distressing situations.

Independence tools can help with daily activities and community participation. Step-by-step videos or photo instructions can guide tasks such as preparing food or getting ready to leave home. Navigation apps can help plan routes and identify stops. Maps and transit apps may show schedules, directions, and service updates. Location-sharing features can be useful when the person agrees and understands how the information is used. Smart-home devices can control lights, locks, thermostats, or reminders through voice or touch. Accessibility features on phones and computers, including voice control and screen readers, can also reduce barriers.

Choosing technology starts with identifying a specific goal. Ask what the person wants to do more easily, and what currently makes that task difficult. Whenever possible, let the person try several options before choosing one. Consider cost, ease of use, durability, language, and access to technical support. Check whether the tool works with the person’s existing devices and communication systems. A tool should fit into real routines rather than add unnecessary work. It is also important to plan what happens if a device is lost, broken, or out of battery.

Support from family members, educators, clinicians, and technology specialists can help with setup and practice. Training should focus on meaningful activities, not just the device’s features. Communication partners should model use of AAC by selecting words on the system while speaking, without demanding that the person copy them. The person should have access to their communication system throughout the day, including during challenging moments. AAC should not be withheld as a reward or removed as punishment. Progress should be judged by whether the tool helps the person communicate or participate, not by how often they use it.

Privacy and safety deserve attention. Review app permissions, account settings, and data-sharing policies before using a tool. Teach online safety in a respectful, practical way that matches the person’s age and support needs. Use strong passwords and discuss how to handle unwanted messages or requests for personal information. Avoid sharing a person’s private details without their permission when possible. Respect their choices about photographs, recordings, and location data.

Technology is most effective when it supports a person’s own goals and choices. It should complement human relationships and accessible environments, not replace them. Regularly check whether a tool remains useful as needs and routines change. Ask the autistic person what is helping and what is frustrating. Small adjustments to layout, alerts, vocabulary, or instructions can make a substantial difference. With thoughtful selection and respectful support, technology can open more ways to communicate, learn, and take part in everyday life.

The brothers met beneath the ruined bell tower, where the rain fell upward into a sky without stars. Malphas arrived first, dragging one scorched wing behind him. His brother, Oren, emerged from the fog with a chain wound around his throat. Neither offered a greeting. They had not spoken since the night their village burned. “You opened the gate,” Malphas said. “You told me the ritual would save them,” Oren replied. “I believed it.” “Belief doesn’t bury the dead.” Oren’s chain tightened as he spoke, each link glowing with the names of their family. Malphas looked away, ashamed of how familiar the names had become. For centuries, their curse had kept them alive, feeding on every grief they refused to share. They had blamed one another through wars, kingdoms, and the slow collapse of their own memories. “I thought you left me there,” Malphas whispered. “I thought you chose the gate over us.” Oren’s face softened, though the horns above it remained sharp as knives. “I was holding it shut,” he said. “You were already on the other side.” The rain paused in the air between them. Malphas remembered a hand gripping his wrist, then fire, then the terrible certainty that he had been abandoned. “I heard you calling,” he said. “I couldn’t reach you.” Oren lowered his eyes. “I know that now.” Beneath the tower, a black fissure opened, breathing cold wind. It was the source of their curse, the wound they had fed with blame. The old bargain said only one of them could enter and be freed. But the words had been carved by the same demon who taught them to distrust each other. Malphas stepped toward the fissure. Oren caught his arm. “Not alone,” he said. Together, they crossed the cracked stones and faced the darkness below. It reached for them with familiar voices, promising that one brother could survive if the other stayed behind. Neither answered. They clasped hands, and for the first time in centuries, the chain between their hearts grew warm. Then they jumped. The fissure closed above them, and the bell tower rang once, though no bell remained. At dawn, the rain fell downward over the empty ruins. No shadows rose to claim the brothers. Somewhere beneath the earth, two voices were finally quiet.

Security flaws in the way some media players process subtitles could allow attackers to compromise users’ devices, researchers warn. The vulnerabilities may be triggered when a player opens a malicious subtitle file alongside a video. In some cases, the file could exploit weaknesses in how subtitle text, formatting or embedded data is handled. A successful attack might let an intruder run code with the affected user’s permissions.

The risk can extend beyond files downloaded from unfamiliar websites. Subtitle files may be bundled with videos or fetched automatically from online services, sometimes without users checking their contents. Researchers say attackers could also use deceptive filenames or tamper with files shared through otherwise legitimate platforms. The precise impact depends on the player, its configuration and the operating system.

Potential consequences include installing malware, stealing data or gaining access to other files on a device. Security experts note that simply displaying subtitles should not require a player to trust arbitrary input. However, flaws in parsing and rendering can turn seemingly harmless text into an entry point. Older or less frequently maintained players may be especially exposed if fixes are unavailable.

Users should install the latest updates for their media players and operating systems. They should avoid opening subtitle files from unknown sources and be cautious when a player prompts them to download captions automatically. Disabling automatic subtitle downloads can reduce exposure, though it may not address every risk. Users should also obtain players from official sources and remove software they no longer use.

Developers are being urged to validate subtitle files carefully and limit the privileges of media applications. Security researchers say the issue highlights how overlooked file formats can become part of the attack surface. No single warning applies to every player or subtitle service, and users should check advisories from the software makers they rely on. Prompt patching remains the most effective defense when a fix is available.

This paper addresses an important question: whether a biologically inspired predictive-coding network can account for both video prediction and neural activity in primate visual cortex. The combination of computational modeling and neural comparison is potentially valuable. It could help connect theories of cortical computation with measurable responses to dynamic visual input. The topic is timely, and the paper appears to have the potential to interest researchers in computational neuroscience and machine learning. However, the strength of its conclusions depends on the clarity of the model, the rigor of the neural comparison, and the care with which competing explanations are considered.

The manuscript should provide a precise description of the network architecture and its biological motivation. It should distinguish features that are directly supported by evidence from choices made for computational convenience. In particular, the authors should explain how prediction errors and predictions are represented, transmitted, and updated across the network. The temporal update rules need to be stated clearly, including the role of feedback, feedforward connections, and any recurrent processing. A schematic of information flow would make the proposed mechanism easier to assess. The paper should also specify the objective function and explain how its terms relate to the proposed biological interpretation. If the network is trained end to end, that fact should be discussed alongside any claims about biologically plausible learning. The authors should clarify whether the model predicts future frames, reconstructs current frames, or performs both tasks, since these objectives can lead to different interpretations. Details about input preprocessing, temporal context, training data, optimization, and model selection should be sufficiently complete for replication.

The evaluation of video prediction should extend beyond illustrative examples. Quantitative results should be reported on held-out data using appropriate measures, with limitations of each measure acknowledged. Pixel-based scores alone may not reflect perceptual quality or the preservation of meaningful motion. Comparisons with suitable baselines are essential, including models without predictive-coding structure and models with comparable capacity and training data. The authors should report model size, computational requirements, and relevant training details to make these comparisons fair. Ablation studies could establish which architectural components are necessary for the reported performance. For example, removing feedback or changing the prediction-error pathway could reveal whether the biological motivation contributes to predictive accuracy. The manuscript should also test robustness to changes in scene content and motion, rather than relying on a narrow set of videos. If predictions become blurry or unstable over longer horizons, this behavior should be quantified and discussed. A clear separation between training, validation, and test data is necessary to rule out leakage.

The comparison with primate visual-cortex activity is the paper’s most distinctive contribution and requires especially careful treatment. The authors should describe the neural dataset, recording methods, stimulus conditions, and preprocessing in enough detail for readers to understand the analysis. They should explain how model units are matched or compared with neural populations, and whether this mapping is chosen before examining the results. Any selection of layers, time points, or neural regions should be justified and, where possible, tested on independent data. The analysis should account for differences in spatial and temporal sampling between the model and the recordings. It should also control for stimulus features that could drive both model and neural responses without reflecting predictive coding specifically. Comparisons with alternative models would help determine whether the proposed network explains neural activity better than generic convolutional or recurrent representations. Statistical procedures should account for the number of units, stimuli, and model variants tested. The authors should report uncertainty, not only aggregate correlations or averages. If neural responses vary substantially across animals or sessions, this variability should be visible in the results. Claims about cortical mechanisms should be calibrated to the evidence, especially if the data are correlational.

The paper would benefit from a more explicit discussion of what the results do and do not establish. Strong video-prediction performance would show that the architecture can perform the task, but would not by itself demonstrate that primate cortex uses the same computation. Likewise, a close match to measured neural activity would be suggestive rather than definitive evidence for predictive coding. The authors should discuss alternative interpretations, including the possibility that the observed similarity follows from shared sensitivity to image structure or motion. They should state whether the model makes predictions that could distinguish it from competing accounts. Such predictions might concern responses to unexpected events, temporal occlusion, or changes in stimulus predictability. If the current experiments do not test these cases, they should be identified as priorities for future work. The discussion should also address limitations arising from the scale of the videos, the behavioral context, and the neural measurements. This would make the paper’s contribution more precise and prevent readers from interpreting model fit as direct validation of a biological theory.

Overall, the study has a promising premise and may offer a useful bridge between predictive computation and visual neuroscience. Its potential impact will depend on whether the methods and comparisons are sufficiently transparent and whether the neural evidence is evaluated against strong alternatives. I recommend substantial revision focused on reproducibility, fair baselines, statistical rigor, and appropriately bounded biological claims. If these issues are addressed, the paper could make a meaningful contribution to research on predictive models of vision and their relationship to cortical processing.

Mara kept a notebook beside her bed, though most mornings it held only grocery lists and half-remembered dreams. She wanted to write a novel, but every sentence seemed clumsy once it reached the page. One rainy Tuesday, she showed a paragraph to her brother. “It’s not very good,” she said before he could read it. “Then you’ve written a paragraph,” he replied. “That’s better than the perfect one you haven’t written.” Mara scowled, but she kept the notebook open. Each day, she added a little more, even when the words felt stiff and the plot wandered into strange places. To feed her imagination, she began reading books unlike the ones she already loved. She read old mysteries, travel journals, poems, and stories from countries she had never visited. In each, she found a new way to notice the world. Still, writing was often uncomfortable. She wrote a scene she adored, then realized it made no sense. She cut it, saved the best line, and started again. Some evenings, the blank page seemed to accuse her of wasting her time. On those nights, she wrote one sentence just to prove she could. Weeks passed, then months. Her first draft ended with a twist she had guessed halfway through. Her second draft was shorter, stranger, and far more honest. When she sent it to a contest, the judges rejected it. Mara cried, then made tea and read a novel while the kettle cooled. The next morning, she opened her manuscript again. She could see its flaws more clearly now, which meant she knew where to begin. She revised a chapter, then another, learning that persistence was less like a grand leap and more like returning to a chair. At last, a small magazine accepted one of her stories. The editor suggested changes, and Mara felt the old sting of imperfection. She took a walk, came back, and made the story better. Her brother read the published copy and smiled. “So, are you a writer now?” he asked. Mara looked at the notebook, already filling with a new beginning. “I think I was when I kept going,” she said. Then she read a few pages from a book she had never tried before. She closed it, sharpened her pencil, and wrote the next imperfect sentence.

The paper addresses an important problem: reconstructing sequential signals while maintaining generalization across varied conditions. Its combination of deep recurrent networks and adaptive reweighting is potentially valuable, particularly when signal segments differ in difficulty or reliability. The topic is relevant to applications where temporal dependencies and nonuniform noise complicate reconstruction. However, the paper should state its central contribution more precisely and distinguish it from existing recurrent reconstruction and adaptive weighting methods. The motivation for the proposed reweighting strategy needs a clearer explanation, including how weights are computed, updated, and constrained during training. The authors should also justify the choice of recurrent architecture and discuss its computational cost relative to simpler or more recent sequence models. The experimental design would be stronger with comparisons against well-tuned baselines, including models without adaptive reweighting and established signal reconstruction methods. Ablation studies are needed to determine whether gains come from network depth, reweighting, or their interaction. The generalization analysis should specify the training and test distributions and evaluate performance under meaningful shifts, rather than relying only on random train-test splits. Reporting uncertainty across multiple runs and using appropriate statistical tests would make the results more convincing. The paper should provide sufficient implementation details, such as preprocessing, hyperparameters, stopping criteria, and the procedure for selecting model settings. Results would also benefit from metrics that reflect both reconstruction fidelity and temporal structure, alongside qualitative examples of successes and failures. Overall, the approach appears promising, but stronger methodological detail and more rigorous comparative and generalization experiments are needed to support the claims. I recommend revision before publication.

This paper investigates randomized input defenses as a means of reducing adversarial attacks on image classification models. The topic is important because adversarial examples remain a significant obstacle to deploying reliable computer vision systems. The paper’s central idea—to introduce randomness into preprocessing or input transformation—is intuitive and potentially useful. Its emphasis on evaluating defenses against adaptive attacks is particularly valuable, since non-adaptive evaluations can overstate robustness. The manuscript is generally clear about the threat it aims to address. However, it should define the threat model more precisely, including the attacker’s knowledge, query budget, and access to randomness. It should also distinguish robustness to specific attack algorithms from robustness under a well-specified worst-case threat model. Randomization can make gradients less reliable without removing adversarial vulnerabilities, so this distinction deserves careful treatment. The authors should explain how they avoid gradient obfuscation and whether attacks use expectation over transformation or another adaptive strategy. The evaluation would be stronger with a broader set of attacks, including both gradient-based and query-based methods where applicable. Results should be reported across multiple datasets and model architectures to establish whether the findings generalize. The paper should include clean accuracy alongside robust accuracy, since input transformations may reduce standard classification performance. It should also report confidence intervals or variation across independent random seeds. A direct comparison with non-randomized preprocessing and established adversarial training baselines would help contextualize the contribution. The computational cost of sampling and evaluating randomized inputs should be quantified. The authors should clarify whether randomness is sampled once per input, per model call, or at another stage, as this affects both reproducibility and attack design. Ablation studies could isolate the contribution of each transformation and identify which settings offer the best robustness–utility trade-off. The discussion should address potential failure cases, such as transformations that remove important image details or fail on perturbations tailored to the defense. Overall, the paper presents a relevant approach, but its claims should be calibrated to the strength and scope of its evaluation. With a more explicit threat model and rigorous adaptive testing, the work could make a useful contribution to research on adversarial robustness.

The paper addresses a relevant challenge by examining how binary neural networks can reduce computational and memory costs while maintaining useful accuracy. Its comparison of model accuracy, training time, and scalability offers a practical framework for evaluating efficiency across datasets. The study would be stronger if it clearly specified its hardware, software, preprocessing, and hyperparameter settings so that results can be reproduced. It should also compare against well-tuned full-precision and other efficient models, using consistent training budgets and multiple runs to account for variability. The scalability claims would benefit from experiments across datasets of substantially different sizes, with memory use and throughput reported alongside elapsed training time. The authors should discuss accuracy trade-offs and limitations, including whether binary operations are efficiently supported by the tested hardware. Overall, the topic is valuable, but clearer methodology and broader, statistically robust comparisons are needed to substantiate the paper’s conclusions.

The Florida black bear is a subspecies of the American black bear found only in Florida and parts of southern Georgia. Despite its name, its fur can range from black to brown or cinnamon, and some bears have a pale patch on the chest. Adults generally weigh about 100 to 400 pounds, with males usually larger than females. They have strong legs, curved claws, and a keen sense of smell that helps them find food. Florida black bears are omnivores, eating mostly plants, fruits, nuts, insects, and other small animals. Acorns, berries, palmetto fruit, and honey are among their seasonal foods.

These bears use a variety of habitats, including pine forests, hardwood hammocks, swamps, and scrub. They need large areas with food, water, cover, and safe places to rest or raise cubs. Important bear populations occur in several parts of the state, including the Ocala, Osceola, and Apalachicola regions. Florida’s bear population is estimated at roughly 4,000 animals, though estimates can change as survey methods improve. Bears are generally solitary, except for mothers with cubs and brief periods when adults gather around abundant food. Females usually give birth to one to four cubs in winter dens, and the cubs stay with their mother for about a year and a half.

Habitat loss and fragmentation are major threats because roads and development divide bear range into smaller, less connected areas. Vehicle collisions kill many bears, especially where roads cross their habitat. Bears may also be killed after searching for food in unsecured garbage, pet food, or other human sources. Feeding bears can make them lose their natural wariness and increase the risk of conflict. Climate shifts, disease, and limited movement between populations may add further pressures.

The Florida black bear was listed as threatened by Florida in 1974, and hunting was prohibited. After conservation efforts helped its numbers recover, the state removed it from the threatened list in 2012. It is not currently listed as threatened under the federal Endangered Species Act, but it remains protected by Florida law. Conservation work includes protecting and connecting habitat, reducing road deaths, monitoring populations, and educating residents. People can help by securing garbage and pet food, never feeding bears, and reporting bear activity to wildlife officials. These actions help bears remain part of Florida’s natural ecosystems.

At 6:12 a.m., Mara woke beneath the airport departure board with rainwater in her shoes. She had been on Flight 208 eleven times, though the ticket in her hand said this was her first. Each time, the plane took off at 8:05 and vanished into a storm over the coast. Each time, Mara woke again at the airport, at 6:12, with the same ticket and the same ache behind her eyes. She had tried warning the crew, the police, and the airline. No one believed her. On her eleventh loop, she spotted Theo by the coffee stand. He was her oldest friend, though they had not spoken in two years. He looked up and smiled as if nothing had happened between them. “You’re alive,” Mara said. Theo blinked. “That’s generally how I start the day.” She grabbed his sleeve and pulled him toward the windows. Beyond the glass, the sky was a smooth gray sheet. “Flight 208,” she said. “It goes into a storm and never comes out.” Theo’s smile faded. “How do you know?” “Because I’ve watched it happen ten times.” He studied her face, searching for a joke. “And you wake up here?” “Every time.” A burst of thunder rolled over the terminal, though the radar screens showed clear skies. Theo glanced at them. “That’s not right.” Mara felt hope flicker, small and dangerous. In the previous loops, he had always laughed at her. This time, he believed enough to be afraid. They found the flight’s captain near Gate 19, checking a tablet. Mara told him the storm would form over the coast. He shook his head and said the forecast was clear. Theo stepped forward. “I’m a meteorology student,” he said, though he had dropped out last spring. “Can you show me the route?” The captain hesitated, then turned the tablet around. Theo studied the map, frowning. “There’s a pressure pocket forming offshore,” he said. “The airport feed may be delayed.” Mara stared at him. “You can see it?” “Not enough to prove a storm,” he said. “But enough to ask for a delay.” The captain called dispatch. They waited while the clock crept toward eight. At 7:42, the storm alert finally appeared, warning of sudden violent winds along the flight path. The captain canceled takeoff clearance and ordered the passengers to disembark. A groan rose through the gate, followed by applause from a few people who had been watching the windows. Mara sank into a chair, trembling. The plane remained at the gate as rain hammered the roof. Theo sat beside her and offered his untouched coffee. “So,” he said, “do we have to do this again?” The clock changed to 8:05. Nothing reset. No flash, no lurch, no sudden return to the beginning. Mara laughed, and the sound broke into a sob. Theo put an arm around her shoulders. By noon, the storm had swallowed the coast, tearing roofs from houses and flooding the airport road. Flight 208 was still safe on the tarmac. When the rain eased, Mara and Theo stepped outside beneath a sky washed clean. “You saved them,” Theo said. “We saved them,” Mara corrected. He nodded, then asked if she wanted to get breakfast. For the first time in eleven mornings, Mara looked at the time without fear. The day was still uncertain. That was how she knew it was finally hers.

The paper addresses an important challenge in binary neural networks: how to represent and evaluate uncertainty when activations and weights are restricted to binary values. Its central idea, combining stochastic normalization, pooling, and weight sampling, is promising and potentially useful for both training and inference. The topic is relevant to researchers seeking efficient models that retain some benefits of probabilistic computation. The manuscript would benefit from a clearer statement of its main contributions near the beginning. In particular, it should distinguish the proposed method from prior stochastic binary networks and probabilistic normalization techniques. The motivation for treating normalization, pooling, and weight sampling within one framework is plausible, but the paper should explain their interactions more explicitly. A concise mathematical overview would help readers understand how probabilities are represented and propagated through each operation. The assumptions underlying the stochastic representations should also be stated and justified. For example, it is important to clarify whether variables are assumed independent and what errors that assumption may introduce. The training procedure appears to be a key contribution, so its steps should be described in enough detail to permit reproduction. The authors should specify how gradients are estimated through binary sampling and whether straight-through estimators or alternative approximations are used. If randomness is introduced during training, the manuscript should report how many samples are used and how sensitive results are to that choice. The evaluation would be stronger with a broader set of baselines, including deterministic binary networks and relevant probabilistic alternatives. Comparisons should use matched architectures, optimization settings, and computational budgets wherever possible. The paper should report variability across multiple random seeds rather than relying on single-run results. Ablation studies are particularly important here, since they can establish the individual and combined effects of stochastic normalization, pooling, and weight sampling. The authors should also examine whether improvements persist across datasets and model sizes. Accuracy alone may not capture the value of probabilistic predictions, so calibration and uncertainty-quality metrics would be informative. If efficiency is a claimed benefit, measurements of latency, memory use, and energy or operation counts should support that claim. The inference procedure needs a clear account of its sampling cost and whether deterministic approximations are available. Results should include uncertainty intervals or appropriate statistical tests where feasible. The manuscript should discuss limitations, especially possible variance, sensitivity to sampling choices, and performance on distribution shifts. Some terminology and notation may need tightening to avoid confusing stochasticity in the model with uncertainty in its predictions. Figures showing the training and inference pipelines would make the proposed framework easier to follow. Overall, the approach is promising, but the strength of the evidence depends on clearer methodological details and more comprehensive comparisons. I recommend revision, with priority given to reproducibility, ablations, and evaluation of predictive uncertainty and computational cost.

Delhi’s dengue crisis is putting hospitals under severe pressure as officials step up efforts to control mosquito breeding and warn that the disease is spreading worldwide.

Hospitals across the capital are treating a growing number of patients with high fever, severe body aches and other symptoms associated with dengue. Some facilities have reported crowded emergency departments and a heavier demand for beds and diagnostic tests. Doctors say most patients recover with supportive care, but severe cases can deteriorate quickly and require close monitoring. Dengue is a viral infection transmitted mainly by Aedes mosquitoes, which often breed in small collections of standing water. There is no specific antiviral treatment for the illness, making early medical assessment and careful management especially important.

Health authorities have urged residents with persistent fever, unusual bleeding, severe abdominal pain or repeated vomiting to seek medical care. They have also cautioned against self-medicating, particularly with medicines that can increase the risk of bleeding. Doctors advise patients to stay hydrated and follow clinical guidance rather than relying on unverified remedies. Officials have not provided a single, independently verified figure for the total number of people affected across the city. The scale of the strain is instead reflected in reports from hospitals and the stepped-up public response.

Municipal teams are inspecting homes, construction sites and public spaces for containers where mosquitoes can lay eggs. Workers are draining stagnant water, applying larvicide where appropriate and issuing notices when breeding sites are found. Authorities have asked residents to empty and scrub water coolers, flowerpot trays and other containers at least once a week. Covered water storage and the prompt disposal of tyres, cans and plastic waste can also reduce breeding opportunities. Officials say fogging may help control adult mosquitoes in targeted areas, but it cannot replace the removal of breeding sites.

The response is complicated by the number of places where water can collect, including rooftops, drains and unfinished buildings. Rainfall and warm weather can create favorable conditions for mosquitoes, while crowded neighborhoods make inspections more difficult. Local agencies are coordinating with health departments, schools and community groups to share warnings and organize clean-up efforts. Residents have been encouraged to report stagnant water and cooperate with inspection teams. Public health workers are also emphasizing that prevention requires action by households as well as government bodies.

The pressure on Delhi’s hospitals comes amid wider concern about dengue’s global reach. The World Health Organization has warned in recent years that dengue is expanding into new areas and affecting more people, with climate change, urbanization and increased movement among factors that may contribute. Aedes mosquitoes are now established in many regions where they were once less common. In 2024, WHO reported an unprecedented global burden, with more than 14 million cases reported worldwide during the year. The agency has said surveillance gaps mean the true number of infections may be higher.

Global trends do not mean every city faces the same level of risk, and local case counts need to be interpreted carefully. Still, public health experts say outbreaks can place sudden demands on clinics, laboratories and blood supplies. They stress that rapid diagnosis and clear advice can help prevent complications and ease unnecessary pressure on emergency services. Researchers are also tracking how changing temperatures and rainfall affect mosquito populations and the length of transmission seasons. Vaccines are available in some countries, but their use depends on national recommendations and individual circumstances.

For now, Delhi officials say reducing mosquito breeding remains the most immediate defense. They have urged residents to protect themselves from bites by using repellents, wearing clothing that covers the skin and keeping screens in good repair. People should seek prompt medical advice if symptoms worsen or warning signs appear. Hospitals are being asked to monitor supplies and coordinate referrals as demand rises. The coming weeks will test whether sustained neighborhood action can slow transmission and prevent the city’s health services from becoming more heavily overwhelmed.

The paper presents a learned iterative recurrent network for video reconstruction, combining adaptive reweighted sparsity regularization with an analysis of generalization. The topic is timely, and the integration of model-based structure with learned updates is potentially valuable for improving reconstruction quality and interpretability. The recurrent formulation is a natural fit for exploiting temporal information across video frames. The adaptive reweighting strategy may also offer a useful way to promote sparsity without relying on a fixed penalty throughout reconstruction. A major strength is the paper’s attempt to connect empirical performance with theoretical generalization behavior. However, the contribution needs to be distinguished more clearly from existing unrolled optimization networks, recurrent reconstruction methods, and reweighted sparsity approaches. The paper should state precisely which components are novel and explain how they differ from the closest prior work. The derivation of the network updates and the role of the adaptive weights should be described in enough detail for readers to reproduce the method. In particular, the authors should clarify how weights are initialized, updated, and stabilized, and whether the update rule is learned or prescribed. The generalization analysis is promising, but its assumptions and scope should be made explicit. The authors should explain which aspects of the architecture and training distribution the bounds cover, and how the theoretical quantities relate to practical performance. Experimental comparisons should include strong, recent baselines under matched data, measurement, and training conditions. Ablations are needed to isolate the effects of recurrence, adaptive reweighting, sparsity regularization, and any other architectural choices. Results across multiple sampling rates, noise levels, and video types would help establish robustness beyond the chosen test setting. The paper should report computational cost, memory use, and inference latency, since recurrent unrolling may involve substantial overhead. Statistical variation across runs or test sequences should also be provided where feasible. Visual examples are useful, but quantitative metrics and failure cases should receive equal attention. Overall, the approach appears promising, but stronger positioning, reproducibility details, and more comprehensive validation are needed before its advantages and generalization claims can be assessed with confidence.

Early voting in the 2016 presidential race drew intense attention as Donald Trump and Hillary Clinton battled for support across a sharply divided electorate. Millions of Americans cast ballots before Election Day, using in-person early voting and mail ballots. The scale and timing of those votes offered clues about turnout, but they did not provide a clear forecast of the final result.

Early voting patterns varied widely by state because election laws and voting schedules differed. Florida, North Carolina, and Nevada became closely watched battlegrounds, with both parties tracking turnout by party registration and demographic group. In states that reported such figures, Democrats often led Republicans in early ballots, though analysts cautioned that party registration did not reveal how each voter had voted. Republicans, meanwhile, pointed to strong participation among their supporters in several states.

The campaigns treated early voting as a central part of their turnout strategies. Clinton’s operation urged supporters to vote early, arguing that doing so would reduce the risk of last-minute disruptions and help the campaign organize its resources. Trump’s campaign also encouraged early participation, while his public comments about the process sometimes raised concerns among election officials and voting-rights advocates. Both campaigns deployed staff and volunteers to contact voters, provide information about polling locations, and encourage supporters to return mail ballots.

The candidates’ efforts reflected different priorities and coalitions. Clinton sought to mobilize Black and Latino voters, women, young people, and college-educated suburban voters. Trump emphasized turnout among white voters without college degrees, as well as voters who felt overlooked by political and economic change. Each campaign also worked to persuade independents and voters who remained dissatisfied with both nominees.

Polling provided another measure of the contest, but surveys showed a race that could shift from week to week. National polls generally gave Clinton an advantage through much of the fall, although the size of that lead varied among pollsters. State surveys suggested close contests in several battlegrounds, including Florida, North Carolina, Ohio, and Pennsylvania. Small differences between polls often fell within their margins of error.

The candidates’ standing changed after a series of major campaign events. In late October, the FBI announced it was reviewing additional emails potentially related to its investigation of Clinton’s use of a private email server. The announcement dominated news coverage and prompted renewed attention to the issue. Trump argued that it showed Clinton could not be trusted, while Clinton’s campaign called for the bureau to release the facts quickly. On November 6, FBI Director James Comey said the review had not changed the agency’s earlier conclusion that charges were not warranted.

The episode unsettled some voters and renewed debate about how much late-breaking news could affect the race. Polls taken during the final days varied in how they captured the announcement and the subsequent clarification. Analysts also warned that national polling could not determine the outcome on its own. The Electoral College meant that the result would depend on state-by-state contests, especially in a handful of closely fought states.

Campaigns on both sides sought to turn polling and early-vote data into practical decisions. They shifted advertising, arranged candidate visits, and concentrated volunteer efforts where the contest appeared tight. Clinton made a final push in states that offered favorable paths to an Electoral College majority. Trump focused on states where he believed his message on trade, immigration, and political change could draw additional voters.

Early ballots complicated the task of interpreting the final stretch. A high number of votes cast before Election Day could indicate strong engagement, but it did not necessarily show which candidate had gained an advantage. Changes in turnout compared with 2012 also required care: population growth, demographic shifts, and changes in voting rules could all affect the totals. Election officials urged voters not to treat preliminary turnout figures as unofficial results.

The broader campaign unfolded amid concerns about election administration and public confidence. Officials prepared for heavy turnout, monitored polling places, and responded to reports of confusion over registration and voting procedures. Voting-rights groups warned that differences in state rules could create barriers for some voters. Campaigns and outside organizations also urged supporters to report problems and seek help through voter hotlines.

On Election Day, early voting would be only one part of a much larger count. Polls offered a snapshot of voter intentions, while campaign activity aimed to convert those intentions into ballots. Neither could settle the contest before votes were tallied. With the candidates making final appeals and turnout still uncertain, the race remained a test of organization, persuasion, and the ability to bring supporters to the polls.

The closure has disrupted plans for several couples who had placed orders for receptions and other celebrations. Some say they have been unable to contact the business or recover money paid in advance.

With wedding dates approaching, the sudden loss of a caterer has left customers scrambling to find alternatives. The extent of the losses and the number of affected orders are not yet clear.

In response, businesses in the community have offered practical support. Some are helping couples source replacement food, while others have offered advice and assistance with last-minute arrangements.

The offers have brought relief to customers facing a difficult and costly situation. For couples, however, finding a new supplier at short notice may still mean changing menus or paying more.

Local residents have also shared information about available services and encouraged affected customers to seek help. The response reflects a wider effort to ensure celebrations can still go ahead.

Customers are being urged to keep copies of contracts, invoices and payment records. Those who paid by card may wish to ask their bank or card provider whether a refund or chargeback is possible.

People who believe they have lost money can also seek guidance from consumer advice organisations. The options available may depend on how they paid and the terms of their agreement.

The closure serves as a reminder to check a supplier’s references and cancellation policies before paying a large deposit. Couples may also want to confirm key arrangements in writing as their event approaches.

For now, affected customers are focused on salvaging their plans. Community businesses say they will continue to help where they can, as couples work to replace orders and limit further losses.

Dance is more than a series of steps set to music. It is a way for people to express feelings and ideas through movement. When words are difficult to find, a dancer can use gestures, rhythm, and facial expressions to communicate. Different styles of dance allow people to show different parts of their personalities. For example, hip-hop can feel energetic and bold, while ballet can be graceful and precise. Dance also supports physical fitness in many ways. It gets the heart pumping and helps build strength and stamina. Regular practice can improve balance, flexibility, and coordination. Because dancing is enjoyable, people may be more motivated to stay active. It can also help reduce stress by giving the mind a break from daily worries. Learning a dance routine takes focus and patience. Each small improvement can make a dancer feel proud. Performing in front of others may seem scary at first, but practice can help build confidence. Dancers learn to trust their bodies and accept that mistakes are part of learning. Over time, they may become more comfortable taking on new challenges. Dance also brings people together. In a class, dancers encourage one another and work toward shared goals. Group dances require people to listen, cooperate, and stay aware of those around them. Social dances can help strangers meet and enjoy an activity together. Dancing with family and friends can create happy memories. It can also help people appreciate cultures and traditions different from their own. Whether someone dances alone or with a group, the experience can be meaningful. Dance supports self-expression, fitness, confidence, and connection in a joyful and active way.
