Confidence helps us recognize our abilities and take responsibility for using them well. Humility reminds us that our abilities are not the whole story: we learn from others, depend on support, and sometimes make mistakes. These qualities are strongest when they work together. Confidence without humility can become arrogance, while humility without confidence can keep us from contributing. Service offers a practical way to balance both. When we serve, we bring our skills forward while paying attention to what other people actually need. We do not assume that we know best; we listen, ask questions, and remain willing to learn. At the same time, we do not dismiss what we can offer. Awareness of our place in a larger community helps put personal success in perspective. Our choices affect families, colleagues, neighbors, and people we may never meet. Communities also shape us through shared knowledge, care, and opportunity. Recognizing this interdependence can make gratitude more natural and entitlement less tempting. It can also encourage us to use influence responsibly and share credit fairly. A useful practice is to reflect on both our strengths and our limits. We might ask, “What can I contribute?” and “Whose perspective have I not considered?” Feedback from others can help answer both questions. So can small acts of service, such as mentoring, volunteering, or helping a teammate. These actions build confidence grounded in experience rather than praise alone. They also cultivate humility by showing how much we can learn from those we serve. Balancing confidence and humility is an ongoing practice, not a fixed achievement. Through service and awareness, we can contribute with courage while staying open, respectful, and connected.

Students today can learn either online from home or in person at school. Both choices have benefits, but they also have challenges. I believe students should attend classes in person whenever possible. Being at school gives students a regular daily routine. They can ask teachers questions and receive help right away. Teachers can also notice when a student is confused. In-person classes make it easier to take part in discussions. Students can share ideas, work in groups, and learn from one another. School is also a place to make friends and build social skills. These experiences can help students feel connected to their community. In addition, classrooms provide supplies and technology that some students may not have at home. However, online learning can be useful in certain situations. It allows students to study when they are sick or unable to travel. It can also save time for students who live far from school. Some students feel more comfortable learning in a quiet place at home. Online lessons may offer flexible schedules and helpful digital resources. Still, studying at home can bring distractions. Students may find it hard to stay focused without a teacher nearby. They might also miss spending time with classmates. Internet problems can make online lessons difficult. For these reasons, in-person learning is generally the better choice for most students. Schools provide structure, support, and opportunities to learn together. Online classes should remain available as an option when attending school is not possible. Overall, a mix of both methods can help meet different students’ needs.

Social pressure and role models can strongly influence who we become and the choices we make. From childhood, we learn about ourselves through our relationships with family, friends, teachers, and the wider community. These people can encourage us to explore our interests, but they can also make us feel that we must fit a certain image. As a result, personal identity is shaped by both our own values and the expectations around us.

Social pressure is not always negative. Friends may motivate one another to study harder, join a team, or try something new. A supportive group can help someone feel accepted and confident. However, pressure can also lead people to hide their true interests or make choices they do not believe in. Someone might change the way they dress, speak, or behave simply to avoid being left out. Over time, these small decisions can make it harder to understand what they genuinely want.

Role models also play an important part in shaping identity. They may be parents, older siblings, teachers, athletes, artists, or public figures. By watching how role models handle challenges, we can learn about patience, courage, responsibility, and kindness. A good role model does not have to be perfect; their effort and honesty can be more inspiring than their success. Role models can also show us possibilities we had not considered, helping us imagine different paths for our future.

At the same time, we should not copy a role model without thinking carefully. A person may admire someone’s achievements while disagreeing with their choices or behavior. It is important to decide which qualities fit our own beliefs. This ability to choose what we learn from others helps us build an identity that feels authentic.

Social pressure and role models often work together. A group may admire certain people and encourage everyone to follow their example. This can create a positive environment when the examples promote respect and effort. It can be harmful when popularity or success is treated as more important than honesty and well-being. Learning to question these expectations allows us to make thoughtful choices.

Ultimately, identity is not formed in isolation, but it is not completely decided by other people either. We can listen to advice, appreciate encouragement, and learn from role models while still reflecting on what matters to us. Saying no to pressure can be difficult, especially when acceptance feels important. Yet making a choice that matches our values can build self-respect and confidence. By choosing our influences carefully and thinking for ourselves, we can grow into people who are both connected to others and true to who we are.

Career exploration and planning help students make thoughtful choices about their future work. Instead of choosing a career based only on its salary or popularity, students can learn what different jobs are really like. They can consider their interests, strengths, values, and goals. This helps them find careers that fit who they are. A good fit can make work feel more meaningful and satisfying.

Exploring careers can begin with simple activities at school. Students might take interest surveys, research occupations, or talk with teachers and family members. They can also interview people who work in fields that interest them. Job shadowing, volunteering, and internships provide a closer look at daily tasks. These experiences can reveal whether a career matches a student’s expectations.

Planning turns career ideas into achievable steps. Students can learn which subjects, qualifications, and skills are needed for a particular job. They can choose courses that prepare them for future study or training. A plan may include attending college, learning a trade, or gaining work experience. Students can also set short-term goals, such as improving communication or learning to manage their time.

Career planning is not a promise to follow one path forever. People’s interests and circumstances can change, and new careers may emerge. Students who understand how to explore options can adjust their plans with confidence. They also become better at making decisions and solving problems. These skills are useful in school, work, and everyday life.

Preparing for a fulfilling job means thinking about more than a job title. Students can ask whether a career supports their values, lifestyle, and desire to help others. They can consider how work might contribute to their community. Careful exploration helps them recognize both the benefits and challenges of different occupations. It can also prevent disappointment caused by unrealistic expectations.

Ultimately, career exploration gives students information, while planning gives them direction. Together, these processes help students make informed choices and prepare for opportunities ahead. They encourage students to take responsibility for their futures. With curiosity, flexibility, and effort, students can build careers that provide purpose as well as success.

The invitation arrived as a beam of blue light in the middle of Dr. Light’s workshop.
It unfolded into a floating silver card covered in stars.
“Mega Man,” it announced, “you are invited to represent your world in the Cosmic Champions Tournament.”
Rush barked at the card.
Roll leaned closer to read the tiny letters at the bottom.
“They’re holding it beyond the moon,” she said.
Dr. Light adjusted his glasses and studied the glowing seal.
“Many worlds will be watching,” he warned.
Mega Man looked at the card and thought of the people who counted on him.
“What happens if I lose?” he asked.
The card shimmered.
“Then your world’s champion will fall,” it replied.
Mega Man tightened his blue gloves.
“Then I’ll have to win.”
A doorway of light opened in the workshop.
Mega Man stepped through, with Rush’s howl ringing behind him.
He emerged on a platform suspended above a planet of purple clouds.
Rings of seats circled a vast arena.
Robots, aliens, and strange creatures filled every row.
A tall announcer with four golden faces welcomed the crowd.
“Champions of the cosmos,” it boomed, “let the tournament begin!”
Mega Man’s first opponent was a stone giant named Graviton.
The giant raised one hand, and the arena’s floor tilted toward a black pit.
Mega Man fired a charged shot into the ground.
The blast broke the stone beneath Graviton’s feet.
The giant stumbled, and Mega Man leaped clear.
“Victory to the blue champion!” cried the announcer.
The next match paired Mega Man with a swift fighter made of living sparks.
She darted around him, striking before he could aim.
Mega Man remembered Dr. Light’s lesson: watch the pattern, not the speed.
He counted her flashes and fired between them.
His shot grazed her shoulder, and she bowed in surrender.
The crowd cheered louder than before.
In the final round, a masked champion called Null stepped into the arena.
Null carried a blade that swallowed every blast.
Mega Man fired once, then twice, but the shots vanished.
Null advanced without a word.
Mega Man glanced at the stars beyond the arena’s glass dome.
He realized the blade could absorb energy, but it could not absorb a choice.
Instead of firing, he rushed forward and kicked the weapon from Null’s hand.
The blade spun away and clattered across the floor.
Null raised both arms, signaling defeat.
For a moment, the arena was silent.
Then every world in the stands erupted in applause.
The announcer placed a glowing medal around Mega Man’s neck.
“Your world has a worthy champion,” it declared.
Mega Man smiled, though his arms ached.
The silver invitation appeared again, now bearing a message of thanks.
A doorway opened to the familiar workshop.
Mega Man stepped through as Roll and Dr. Light hurried to greet him.
Rush bounded around his legs, barking proudly.
“Did you win?” Roll asked.
Mega Man held up the medal.
“I think we all did,” he said.
That night, the medal shone softly beside his helmet.
Far away, another invitation began to glow.

Proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) are medicines that reduce stomach acid and are commonly used for acid reflux, ulcers, and related conditions. Examples include omeprazole, esomeprazole, and lansoprazole. They are effective for many people, and most users do not develop cardiovascular problems from taking them. However, research has raised questions about possible links between long-term PPI use and heart or blood-vessel conditions. Some observational studies have reported associations with heart attack, stroke, or cardiovascular death, but these studies cannot prove that PPIs caused the outcomes. People prescribed PPIs may already have health problems that increase their cardiovascular risk, which can complicate comparisons. A proposed explanation is that certain PPIs may affect blood-vessel function or reduce nitric oxide availability, but the evidence is not conclusive. PPIs can also rarely contribute to low magnesium levels, especially with prolonged use, which may cause abnormal heart rhythms in severe cases. Risk may be higher for people taking medicines that also lower magnesium, such as some diuretics. Studies of PPIs and cardiovascular outcomes have produced mixed results, and findings may differ by drug, dose, duration, and patient group. Current evidence does not establish that PPIs generally cause heart attacks or strokes. Do not stop a prescribed PPI suddenly without speaking with a healthcare professional, since the underlying condition may worsen. Ask your clinician or pharmacist whether you still need the medicine and whether the lowest effective dose is appropriate. Tell them about heart disease, kidney problems, low magnesium, or other medicines you take. Seek urgent care for symptoms such as chest pressure, sudden weakness on one side, or trouble speaking, regardless of PPI use. The benefits and potential risks should be reviewed individually, particularly when treatment is prolonged.

The paper addresses an important problem: conclusions about news summarization depend heavily on how datasets are collected and how baselines are evaluated. Its discussion of large-scale dataset construction is useful, particularly if it distinguishes article selection, summary provenance, and preprocessing choices. However, the review should more clearly assess whether summaries are genuinely abstractive or largely copied from article leads, since this can make extractive systems appear stronger than they are. It should also examine duplication, source and topic imbalance, temporal leakage, and the effects of filtering on dataset representativeness. The critique of extractive baselines would be stronger with a consistent comparison protocol covering sentence selection, length constraints, and tuning data. Reporting only ROUGE is insufficient; complementary measures and human judgments would better capture factuality, coherence, and usefulness. The paper should also distinguish weaknesses in the datasets from weaknesses in the metrics, rather than treating them as a single evaluation problem. Where possible, claims about bias or benchmark difficulty should be supported by quantitative analyses or reproducible examples. A clearer account of limitations and practical recommendations would help researchers apply the critique when creating new resources. Overall, the topic is timely, but the paper’s contribution will depend on turning its observations into a systematic, evidence-backed framework for dataset and baseline assessment.

Perseverance is the ability to keep working toward a goal when progress is difficult. In science and education, it often turns setbacks into opportunities to learn and improve. Many important discoveries began with questions that did not have easy answers. Scientists may repeat experiments many times before getting reliable results. When an experiment fails, they can study what went wrong and revise their methods. Each attempt provides information that brings them closer to a solution. This process shows that failure is not always the opposite of success. Sometimes it is an important step on the way.

Students also face setbacks, such as confusing lessons, disappointing grades, or challenging exams. It can be tempting to believe that one poor result means they cannot succeed. However, perseverance helps students treat difficulties as temporary rather than permanent. They can ask teachers for help, try new study strategies, and practice skills they have not yet mastered. Over time, these choices can build both knowledge and confidence. Progress may be slow, but consistent effort can make a meaningful difference.

Perseverance does not mean working without rest or refusing to change direction. It means staying committed while learning from experience and making sensible adjustments. In a laboratory, that might involve improving an experiment after unexpected results. In a classroom, it might mean changing a study routine after discovering that it is not effective. Both examples require patience, curiosity, and a willingness to try again.

Communities also play a role in helping people persevere. Encouragement from teachers, classmates, family members, and colleagues can make difficult goals feel possible. At the same time, people must learn to recognize and celebrate small steps forward. These moments can provide motivation when the final achievement still seems far away. By continuing despite setbacks, students and scientists can develop resilience as well as expertise. Perseverance helps transform mistakes into lessons and challenges into progress. Ultimately, achievement is often not a result of never failing, but of continuing to learn after failure.

The paper addresses a relevant challenge in continuous control by combining prioritized experience replay with parameter-noise exploration for deep deterministic policy gradients. Its central contribution is promising, but the paper should more clearly distinguish the effects of each technique from the gains achieved by their combination. The evaluation would be stronger with comparisons against well-tuned baselines across multiple tasks and random seeds, along with reporting variability and computational cost. Mara lay beside the window, where the afternoon light made a pale square on her blanket. Her illness had kept her in bed for months, but her thoughts still wandered through the house. Most often, they went to her son, Eli, and his grandmother, Ruth.

Ruth had raised Eli after Mara’s husband died. Now Ruth was old, and Eli was supposed to help her with meals, medicine, and the little walks she loved. Mara worried he had not done enough. The soup on Ruth’s tray had gone cold twice that week, and her pills had remained untouched beside the teacup.

When Mara asked Eli about it, he looked down at his shoes. “I’m trying,” he said. “I know,” Mara replied, though her voice held more sadness than certainty.

That evening, she heard Ruth call from the next room. Eli did not answer at once. Mara’s fingers tightened around the blanket, and she imagined Ruth waiting alone in the dimness.

Then she heard a chair scrape, followed by Eli’s gentle voice. “I’m here, Grandma. Let me help you.” Mara let out a breath she had been holding.

The next morning, Eli brought Ruth breakfast and sat with her while she ate. He read aloud from the newspaper, stumbling over the long words until Ruth laughed. Mara listened from her room and felt the tightness in her chest ease a little.

Later, Eli came to her bedside. His eyes were tired, and his hair fell across his forehead. “I should have been more patient,” he said. “I thought doing the chores was enough.”

Mara reached for his hand. “Care is more than a list of tasks,” she said. “But you can learn, and you have begun.” Eli squeezed her fingers, careful not to hurt them.

That night, Mara’s breathing grew shallow. Ruth came to sit beside her, and Eli stood on the other side of the bed. For a while, the three of them listened to the rain tapping the window.

“I’m sorry I worried about how you cared for her,” Mara whispered to Eli. “I wanted you both to be safe, and I was afraid.” Eli bowed his head, and tears fell onto their joined hands.

“You gave me enough love to learn how to give it back,” he said. Mara smiled at him, then turned toward Ruth. “Keep telling him your stories,” she murmured. Ruth promised she would.

Mara looked once more at her son, her face calm in the lamplight. “Be kind to yourself, Eli,” she said. “And be kind to each other.” He leaned close as she closed her eyes.

Her last breath left as softly as a sigh. Eli held her hand, while Ruth rested a hand on his shoulder. Outside, the rain stopped, and the first stars appeared.

The paper addresses an important challenge in video prediction: generating futures that are both realistic and diverse, rather than merely reproducing an average outcome. Its combination of adversarial learning and variational inference is well motivated, since these objectives can encourage visual fidelity while representing uncertainty over possible futures. The topic is relevant to applications where a single deterministic forecast is inadequate. The central contribution would be strongest if the paper clearly distinguishes its method from prior stochastic video prediction and adversarial generation approaches. In particular, the authors should state precisely how the two learning objectives interact and what each contributes.

A major strength is the emphasis on evaluating multiple plausible futures rather than judging only one predicted sequence. However, the paper should define “diverse” and “realistic” operationally and show that improvements in one do not come at the expense of the other. Adversarial losses can produce sharper frames, but they may also introduce temporal flicker or visually convincing yet inconsistent motion. The evaluation should therefore include measures of temporal coherence alongside image quality. It would also help to report results across multiple prediction horizons, since errors and uncertainty typically grow over time.

The experimental section should compare against strong deterministic and stochastic baselines under identical data, preprocessing, and evaluation conditions. Ablation studies are needed to isolate the effects of the adversarial objective, variational objective, and any components that connect them. The authors should explain how latent variables are sampled at inference and whether different samples produce meaningfully distinct outcomes. Diversity metrics should be interpreted carefully, because a model can achieve high diversity by generating implausible or irrelevant futures. Qualitative examples are useful, but they should be selected systematically and accompanied by examples of failures.

The paper would benefit from more detail about training stability, including sensitivity to loss weights, initialization, and adversarial optimization choices. If the approach requires substantial computation, training and inference costs should be reported so readers can assess practical usefulness. The authors should also clarify how the method handles scene changes, camera motion, and objects entering or leaving the frame. Any limitations in dataset scale or domain coverage should be discussed, especially if the method is intended to generalize beyond the training distribution. Statistical variation across runs would make the reported gains more convincing.

Overall, the paper presents a promising direction and tackles a meaningful problem. Its key claim is plausible, but the strength of the evidence depends on rigorous comparisons and a clear account of how realism, diversity, and temporal consistency are measured. I recommend strengthening the ablations, evaluation protocol, and discussion of failure cases before publication. With these revisions, the work could make a useful contribution to probabilistic video prediction.

This paper explores a promising combination of prioritized experience replay and parameter noise to improve deep deterministic policy gradients on continuous-control tasks. The motivation is clear: replay prioritization may make learning more sample-efficient, while parameter noise can encourage structured exploration. The evaluation would be stronger if it compared the combined method not only with standard DDPG, but also with each technique applied separately and with relevant contemporary baselines. Please report results across multiple random seeds, with measures of variability and consistent training budgets, since continuous-control performance can be sensitive to these choices. The paper should also clarify how replay priorities and parameter-noise scales are defined and tuned, and include ablations that isolate their contributions. Discussion of computational overhead, sensitivity to hyperparameters, and performance across different task types would help establish the method’s practical value. Overall, the approach is well motivated, but stronger experimental controls and clearer implementation details are needed to support the claimed improvements.

Mara had never believed in Heaven. She believed in warm bread, honest work, and leaving the world a little kinder than she found it.

So when she woke beneath a sky full of golden light, her first thought was that she must be dreaming. Her second was that someone nearby needed help.

A small man sat beside a river, looking sadly at the empty basket in his lap. Mara asked what was wrong, and he said he had lost the courage to cross. She took his hand and walked with him through the shining water.

On the other side, the man smiled and vanished into the light. A woman in a silver robe appeared where he had been. “You are in Heaven,” she said, “because of all the kindness you gave without expecting a reward.”

Mara stared at her. “But I never believed in any of this.” The woman nodded. “Kindness was your belief, whether you called it one or not.”

Mara looked across the wide, radiant fields. They were beautiful, but silence stretched through them, and she felt suddenly alone. “Is there anyone here who might like company?” she asked.

The woman smiled and pointed toward a garden beyond the hills. Mara followed a path lined with flowers, stopping to greet every soul she passed. At the garden gate, she found a boy trying to teach a stubborn bird to sing.

Mara sat beside him and listened as he told her about the people he missed. She told him about the little acts of kindness that had filled her life. Soon, the bird found its song, and the boy laughed.

Other souls gathered around them, drawn by the music and the stories. Mara realized that Heaven was not only a place she had been given. It was also a place she could help make warmer, one welcome at a time.

A geography fair is a chance to help others discover what makes a country distinctive. Start by choosing a country that interests you, or draw one at random if your class is exploring the whole world. Think about what you already know and what questions you would like to investigate. A focused question, such as “How does the climate shape daily life in Peru?” can guide your research.

Use reliable sources, including books, atlases, museum and government websites, and educational organizations. Compare information from more than one source, especially when facts differ. Record where each fact comes from so you can give credit and find it again. Avoid copying whole paragraphs; take notes in your own words and explain what the information means.

Begin with the country’s location and physical geography. Find it on a world map, name the neighboring countries, and identify nearby oceans or seas. Explore its landforms, such as mountains, plains, deserts, forests, rivers, and islands. Look at climate maps and learn how seasons, rainfall, or temperature vary across the country. Consider how these features affect farming, travel, housing, or access to water.

Next, investigate people and everyday life. Learn which languages are spoken and which religions and cultural traditions are important. Research foods, music, clothing, sports, holidays, or art, while remembering that no single example represents everyone. Find out how people live in cities and rural areas, and notice differences between regions. Use respectful, specific language rather than stereotypes.

You can also explore history, government, and the economy. Choose a few important historical events and explain how they shaped the country today. Find out how the government is organized, using age-appropriate sources. Research major jobs, products, or industries, and consider how geography influences them. If you discuss current issues, include more than one perspective and rely on recent, trustworthy reporting.

Turn your research into a clear story rather than a long list of facts. Choose a central idea, such as how rivers connect communities or how mountains shape travel. Select a small number of strong facts that support that idea. Include maps, photographs, diagrams, or objects that help visitors understand what you learned. Label visuals clearly, and make sure you have permission to use images or materials.

A display board can be organized into sections with short headings. Put the country’s name and a map where visitors can see them easily. Use readable lettering, brief captions, and enough space so the display does not feel crowded. A model, tasting activity, music sample, or simple game can make your presentation interactive, if it is safe and appropriate. Explain cultural items accurately, and avoid presenting sacred or private traditions as entertainment.

Practice speaking about your project in your own words. Prepare a short introduction, a few main points, and a closing thought. Make eye contact when comfortable, speak clearly, and pause to let visitors ask questions. If you do not know an answer, say so and explain how you would find out. Invite visitors to locate the country on a map or share what surprised them.

Before the fair, check your spelling, facts, labels, and source list. Ask a classmate or teacher to review your display and suggest improvements. Make sure your presentation can be understood by people who have not studied the country. Most importantly, stay curious: a good geography project does more than share facts; it helps everyone see how places, people, and environments are connected.

People often form quick opinions based on first impressions, but those judgments can change as they learn more. Someone who seems unfriendly at first may simply be shy or nervous. Spending time with that person can reveal kindness and make the original impression seem unfair. The same can happen with things, such as a book that seems boring until its story becomes exciting. Later experiences teach us to look beyond first impressions and judge people and things more carefully.

Conwy council’s newly elected leader has proposed forming an inclusive administration after a closely contested election left no party in control. The leader said the council should work across political lines to address residents’ priorities. No group secured enough seats to govern alone, making cooperation essential to passing decisions. Talks are expected with councillors from across the chamber about how the administration could operate. The proposal follows a campaign in which local services, housing and council finances featured prominently. Opposition members have yet to indicate whether they will support the arrangement. Any agreement is likely to depend on commitments over policy and how decisions will be shared. The council’s next steps will determine whether the proposed approach can provide stable leadership.

Poa ensiformis, commonly known as sword tussock-grass, is a perennial grass native to Australia. It belongs to the genus Poa, a group that includes many cool-season grasses. The species grows in dense, tufted clumps, with narrow leaves that can form a stiff, upright mass. Its leaf blades are generally firm and sword-shaped, which is reflected in the name ensiformis, meaning “sword-shaped.” Like other tussock grasses, it produces flowering stems that rise above the foliage. Its small flowers are grouped in open, branched clusters called panicles. The individual florets are modest in size and wind-pollinated.

Poa ensiformis occurs in a range of open habitats, including grassland, woodland, and grassy forest. It is often found in relatively moist sites, such as slopes, gullies, and areas near streams, but local conditions vary. The grass can grow on different soil types and is associated with regions that receive reliable seasonal rainfall. Its tussocks provide ground cover and can help shelter small animals and invertebrates. As a native perennial, it can persist through more than one growing season.

Flowering generally takes place in spring and summer, although the timing can vary with climate, elevation, and local rainfall. Plants may flower earlier in warmer areas or after favorable seasonal conditions. The species is recorded in eastern and southeastern Australia, including parts of Queensland, New South Wales, Victoria, and Tasmania. Its distribution is patchy rather than continuous, reflecting differences in habitat and climate. For precise local records, consult state flora databases or herbarium maps, since the accepted range and identification can vary among sources.

The paper addresses an important problem in reinforcement learning: estimating second-order gradients accurately enough to support curvature-based optimization. Its focus on variance reduction through control variates and action-dependent baselines is well motivated. Second-order information can improve optimization, but its estimation is often substantially noisier and more computationally demanding than first-order gradients. The paper’s central contribution appears to be a framework for reducing that noise while preserving the desired gradient or Hessian expectation. This is a promising direction with potential relevance to policy optimization and other stochastic control methods. The manuscript is strongest when it makes the connection between score-function estimators, baseline design, and second-order derivatives explicit. That connection is important because variance-reduction techniques that work for first-order gradients do not necessarily transfer directly to Hessian estimators. The paper also targets a practical weakness of likelihood-ratio methods, whose variance can grow rapidly with trajectory length and reward variability. A principled treatment of action-dependent baselines could therefore be valuable to both researchers and practitioners.

The main technical question is whether the proposed estimator is unbiased under the stated assumptions. The paper should provide a complete derivation showing which terms arise when differentiating the policy score and the baseline. In particular, the authors should clarify whether the baseline depends on the sampled action, the policy parameters, or both. An action-dependent baseline can reduce variance, but its dependence on the action means that the usual state-only baseline argument does not apply without additional correction terms or constraints. The manuscript should identify the exact condition under which the baseline contribution has zero expectation. If the estimator is unbiased only for a restricted baseline class, that restriction should be stated prominently. Likewise, the treatment of parameter-dependent control variates deserves careful explanation. Differentiating a control variate that depends on the policy parameters can introduce extra terms that are easy to omit. A derivation that separates the objective, score, baseline, and control-variate derivatives would make the result easier to verify.

The paper would benefit from a more precise statement of its assumptions. These should cover differentiability of the policy and reward model, interchange of differentiation and expectation, and any moment conditions needed for finite variance. The authors should also specify whether the results concern a finite-horizon problem, a discounted infinite-horizon problem, or both. If trajectories are truncated in practice, the relationship between truncation and estimator bias should be discussed. The notation for gradients, Hessians, and mixed derivatives should remain consistent throughout. A compact proposition summarizing the estimator’s expectation and variance properties would help readers understand the formal contribution. The proof should make clear whether the Hessian is the full Hessian, a directional second derivative, or a particular approximation. If symmetry of the estimated Hessian is not guaranteed sample by sample, the authors should explain how this is handled in optimization. It would also be useful to distinguish variance reduction from changes in curvature caused by approximation or regularization.

The empirical evaluation is central to assessing the contribution. The paper should compare the proposed method against standard likelihood-ratio Hessian estimators and relevant first-order or quasi-second-order baselines. Comparisons should use matched computational budgets, not only matched numbers of sampled trajectories. Reporting wall-clock time and memory use would clarify whether the variance reduction justifies the additional computation. The experimental section should include multiple random seeds and uncertainty intervals for all primary results. Variance should be measured directly, rather than inferred only from final returns or convergence speed. The authors should report how estimator variance changes with trajectory length, reward scale, and policy entropy. These factors are especially relevant because they can substantially affect score-function estimators. An ablation study should isolate the effects of the control variate and the action-dependent baseline. It should also examine sensitivity to baseline architecture and optimization. If a learned baseline is used, the training procedure and data separation strategy should be described to avoid unintended dependence between baseline fitting and gradient estimation. The paper should explain whether baseline fitting introduces bias, and if so, quantify or control it.

The empirical claims would be more persuasive if they included both small controlled tasks and at least one more challenging benchmark. Synthetic examples with known gradients or Hessians could validate the derivation and implementation. For larger tasks, the authors should state the policy class, optimizer, learning-rate schedule, and evaluation protocol in enough detail for reproduction. Results should include failure cases, not just settings in which the proposed estimator performs well. In particular, the method may be sensitive to poorly conditioned curvature estimates, so its behavior under noisy or indefinite Hessians should be examined. The paper should clarify whether damping, clipping, or other stabilization is required. If such techniques are necessary, their influence should be separated from the effect of variance reduction itself. A discussion of computational scaling with action dimension and trajectory horizon would also improve the practical value of the work. The authors should report whether the approach remains beneficial when the action space is large or continuous. These details will help readers judge where the method is likely to be useful.

The presentation is generally focused, but some additional intuition would improve accessibility. A simple example could show how an action-dependent baseline changes the second-order estimator and why it reduces variance. The paper should explain the distinction between minimizing estimator variance and minimizing error in a downstream Newton-style update. Those are related goals, but they are not identical. It would be helpful to discuss whether the proposed baseline is optimal within a defined class or merely a practical choice. If an optimal baseline is derived, the assumptions and computational cost of computing it should be stated. If it is approximated, the approximation should be described and evaluated. The related-work section should make clear how the method differs from existing variance-reduced policy-gradient estimators and stochastic Hessian estimators. It should also discuss whether established control-variate methods can be adapted to the same setting. This comparison would help establish the novelty and scope of the contribution. Terminology should be used consistently, especially when referring to Hessian estimators, second-order gradients, and curvature information.

Overall, the topic is significant, and the proposed combination of control variates with action-dependent baselines could offer a useful contribution. The paper’s strongest potential lies in a rigorous derivation paired with convincing evidence that variance reduction improves practical second-order optimization. At present, the key issues are the need for a fully transparent unbiasedness argument, clearer assumptions, and stronger empirical isolation of the method’s benefits. I recommend that the authors revise the manuscript to address these points before its claims are considered fully established. In particular, they should state precisely when the estimator is unbiased and provide tests that verify this property. They should also quantify variance reduction independently of downstream learning performance. With these revisions, the work could become a valuable addition to research on stochastic optimization for reinforcement learning.

Everyone makes mistakes, even people who try hard to do the right thing. A mistake can feel embarrassing or disappointing when it happens. Sometimes we wish we could go back and choose differently. However, mistakes can teach us lessons that success alone may not reveal. Learning from them can help us grow and make wiser choices in the future.

One way mistakes help us grow is by showing us what we need to improve. For example, a student who waits until the night before a test to study may earn a lower grade than expected. Instead of deciding that they are simply bad at the subject, the student can think about how they prepared. They may realize that studying a little each day would help them remember more. This understanding can lead to a better routine and stronger results.

Mistakes can also teach people to take responsibility. It may be tempting to blame a problem on someone else or pretend it did not happen. Yet accepting our part in a mistake gives us a chance to make things right. If someone accidentally hurts a friend’s feelings, they can apologize and listen to how the friend feels. A sincere apology can repair trust and help both people understand each other better.

Another important lesson is that choices have consequences. A person who spends all their free time on a phone may notice that they have less time for sleep, schoolwork, or family. Recognizing this result can help them set limits and make room for what matters. In this way, a mistake can encourage someone to pause before making a similar choice again. Over time, this habit can lead to more thoughtful decisions.

Learning from mistakes can also build patience and resilience. People do not always improve right away, and one mistake may be followed by another. Instead of giving up, they can consider what went wrong and try a different approach. For instance, someone who struggles to speak in front of a class might practice with a friend before the next presentation. Each attempt can make the task feel less frightening.

It is important to remember that making a mistake does not define a person. A poor decision is something someone did, not everything they are. Feeling guilty for a short time can help a person recognize that their actions mattered. But staying ashamed forever does not help them move forward. They can learn from the experience, make amends when possible, and choose to do better.

People can make learning from mistakes easier by thinking honestly about what happened. They can ask themselves what they were trying to do, what went wrong, and what they might change next time. Talking with a trusted adult or friend can offer a helpful point of view. Writing down a lesson can also make it easier to remember. The goal is not to criticize ourselves endlessly, but to understand our choices.

Of course, not every mistake has an easy solution, and some consequences may last a long time. Even then, people can look for a responsible next step. They might seek help, correct inaccurate information, or work to rebuild trust. Taking action cannot always erase the past, but it can improve what happens next. That effort shows maturity and care for others.

Mistakes are a normal part of learning at school, at home, and in friendships. When people reflect on them, they can discover better ways to study, communicate, and solve problems. They may also become more patient with others who are still learning. This does not mean that mistakes should be ignored or celebrated. It means that they can be useful when people respond with honesty and effort.

In the end, personal mistakes can become valuable teachers. They show us where our choices led and what we might do differently. By accepting responsibility, making amends, and trying again, we can grow stronger and wiser. The next choice is an opportunity to use what we have learned. That is how a mistake can help someone build a better future.

I hid beneath the yellow road and listened for the girl’s silver shoes. In this Oz, the road was a strip of bone laid across a land that had forgotten the sun. Dorothy came along with a dog, a scarecrow, and a tin man, all three carrying more courage than sense. I meant to lure her into the poppy fields, where every dream ends with a closed grave. So I whispered her name through the roots, sweet as her mother’s voice. She stopped, but Toto barked at the earth and scratched up my speaking skull. The scarecrow stuffed it with straw, which muffled my lies but not my rage. I sent wolves after them, stitched from shadows and the skins of lost travelers. The tin man chopped their paws away, while Dorothy stared at me through the dark. “You sound lonely,” she said, and that was worse than any curse. I tried to make the road collapse, but the girl’s shoes glowed and held it fast. Then the Witch’s black towers crumbled, exposing my hiding place beneath them. Dorothy spared me, which I found far crueler than death. Now I wait under the road, plotting again, while her footsteps fade toward home.

This paper addresses an important problem: explanation methods can produce plausible-looking attributions while differing substantially in what they measure. Its comparison of methods through attribution equivalence, sensitivity, and layer-wise relevance propagation (LRP) properties offers a useful framework for clarifying these differences. A key strength is the focus on formal properties rather than relying solely on visual inspection or application-specific examples. The paper would be stronger if it defined each property precisely and explained how the chosen tests relate to the practical reliability of explanations. In particular, the assumptions behind attribution equivalence and sensitivity should be made explicit, since conclusions may depend on the model architecture, input representation, and baseline or reference choice. The LRP discussion would also benefit from distinguishing properties that follow from the propagation rules from those established empirically. Please provide enough implementation detail and experimental coverage for readers to reproduce the comparisons, including the models, datasets, and parameter settings. A clearer account of limitations would help prevent readers from interpreting satisfaction of a formal property as proof that an explanation is faithful or useful. Overall, this is a promising and relevant comparison, and addressing these points would make its conclusions more precise and actionable.

Early experiences can shape how people see themselves and the world around them. A kind word from a teacher may help a student feel confident, while being excluded by classmates can make someone worry about fitting in. These feelings may last into adulthood and influence how people approach new relationships and challenges. Although early experiences matter, people can reflect on them and build new, healthier ways of thinking.

A former care worker and church teacher has been jailed for sexually abusing girls in Leeds and Bradford decades ago. The offences came to light after victims reported what had happened to them. The man was convicted of abusing girls who were in his care or under his influence. The court heard that he used positions of trust to exploit the victims. The abuse took place many years ago, but the victims’ accounts enabled the case to be brought forward. The judge described the offences as serious breaches of trust and imposed a lengthy prison sentence. The defendant will remain in custody for decades, according to the sentence handed down. Police said they hoped the outcome would reassure other survivors that they would be listened to. They urged anyone affected by abuse to seek support and report it. Officials also thanked the victims for their courage in coming forward.

Graduation requirements and elective courses both play important roles in a high school education, but they serve different purposes. Graduation requirements are the classes students must complete to earn a diploma. They usually include subjects such as English, mathematics, science, social studies, and physical education. Schools set these requirements to ensure that every graduate develops essential knowledge and skills. Students may also need to complete a certain number of credits or pass specific exams. Because these courses are compulsory, students have limited choice about whether to take them.

Elective courses, in contrast, are classes students choose from options offered by their school. Examples might include art, music, computer programming, journalism, or a foreign language. These classes allow students to explore personal interests and discover new abilities. Electives can also help students prepare for a future career or college program. For instance, someone interested in design might take photography or graphic design. Although electives are chosen by students, they may still need to complete a minimum number of elective credits to graduate.

The main distinction is that requirements provide a common educational foundation, while electives offer flexibility and personal direction. Both types of courses can contribute to a student’s growth. Required classes help students build broad skills they will use in many areas of life. Electives can make school more engaging and give students a chance to focus on subjects they enjoy. A balanced schedule includes both, helping students meet graduation standards while shaping an education that reflects their goals.

Calls for more research into whether repeated heading in football raises former players’ risk of dementia and other brain injuries are growing, as scientists and campaigners seek clearer answers.

The concern centres on the repeated impacts players experience when heading the ball, as well as accidental collisions during matches and training. Researchers say it remains difficult to separate the effects of heading from other factors, including age, playing position and previous head injuries.

Several studies have reported higher rates of neurodegenerative disease among some groups of former professional footballers than in the general population. But those findings do not, on their own, show that heading caused the increased risk.

Experts say long-term studies are needed to track players’ exposure to heading and monitor their health over time. Such research could help establish whether the number, force or timing of impacts makes a difference.

It could also clarify whether risks vary between professional, amateur and youth players. Researchers want better records of training and match exposure, since reliable data on how often players head the ball are limited.

The question has taken on added urgency as more former players and their families describe dementia diagnoses and other neurological problems. Some families have called for recognition of a possible link and for more support for those affected.

Medical specialists caution that dementia has multiple causes and can develop through different disease processes. A history of football participation cannot establish the cause of an individual’s illness.

Repeated head impacts may be relevant even when they do not cause an immediate concussion, researchers say. However, the extent to which routine heading contributes to lasting brain damage is still uncertain.

Concussion is a separate but related concern. Medical guidance generally recommends that players with suspected concussion stop playing and receive appropriate assessment before returning.

Football authorities in several countries have introduced measures intended to reduce head impacts, particularly for children. These include restrictions on heading in some youth training sessions and guidance on safe technique.

Critics argue that such steps should be based on stronger evidence and applied consistently. Others say precautionary limits are justified while research continues, especially for young players whose brains are still developing.

Researchers face practical challenges in investigating the issue. Dementia may emerge decades after a playing career, and memories of past exposure can be incomplete.

Studies also need to account for differences in career length, position, playing era and access to medical care. Former players may have experienced different rules, equipment and training practices from those in the game today.

Scientists have called for cooperation between football organisations, health services and independent research teams. Access to medical records and participation by former players could make future studies more informative.

Some researchers are also examining brain scans, biological markers and donated brain tissue. These approaches may help identify patterns of injury, but none can yet provide a simple test that predicts who will develop dementia.

Campaigners say research should be accompanied by practical support for players with symptoms and their families. They also want clear advice about warning signs and how to seek medical help.

The findings could eventually shape guidance on heading, concussion management and player welfare. For now, experts say the evidence supports continued investigation, but not a definitive claim that heading alone causes dementia.

A clearer answer may take years to emerge. Researchers say sustained studies are essential to establish the risks and help football make decisions grounded in evidence.

A four-day school week may sound appealing because students would get an extra day off. However, making each school day longer could create new problems. Students need enough time to learn, rest, and manage their responsibilities. Longer days may make it harder to balance all three.

One concern is that students could become tired before the school day ends. Sitting in class for more hours can make it difficult to concentrate. When students are exhausted, they may remember less of what they learn. They might also feel more stressed or frustrated.

Longer school days can affect students’ health, too. Children and teenagers need adequate sleep, exercise, and time to relax. If school ends later, students may have less time for sports, hobbies, or family activities. They may also get home later and have to rush through dinner and homework.

An extra day off does not necessarily solve these problems. Some students may use the day to catch up on assignments or attend appointments. Others may need to care for younger siblings or help their families. These responsibilities can make the day feel less like a break.

The schedule could also create difficulties for parents and caregivers. Families may need to find childcare for the additional day off. This can be especially challenging for adults who work five days a week. Students might also miss access to school meals or other support services.

A four-day week could affect learning in different ways. Longer lessons may be harder for younger students to handle. Students who need extra help could have fewer chances to meet with teachers. If they fall behind, the longer days may not give them the support they need.

Schools should consider students’ needs before changing their schedules. They could ask students, families, and teachers to share their concerns. If a four-day week is introduced, schools should provide support for childcare, meals, and academic help. In the end, a schedule should protect students’ well-being and responsibilities, not simply shorten the school week.

The paper addresses an important problem: attribution methods can produce markedly different explanations, and researchers need principled ways to evaluate them. Its unified analysis is a useful contribution, especially if it clarifies the assumptions and failure modes shared across methods. The proposed measure for evaluating feature relevance explanations could also improve comparisons, but the paper should explain precisely what properties it captures and why they matter. A key concern is whether the measure relies on assumptions—such as feature independence, a particular model architecture, or access to ground-truth relevance—that limit its practical use. The evaluation would be more convincing if it included diverse datasets, model types, and attribution methods, alongside established evaluation metrics. Ablation studies and sensitivity analyses could show which design choices drive the measure’s results. The authors should also discuss whether the measure rewards explanations that are faithful to the model, understandable to people, or both, since these goals are not always aligned. Clear definitions, reproducible implementation details, and examples of cases where the measure succeeds or fails would strengthen the paper. Overall, the work is promising, but its central claims depend on validating the proposed measure beyond the settings used in the initial experiments. I recommend revision with particular attention to the measure’s assumptions, empirical coverage, and interpretation.

An Afghan-born pilot has launched a global flight to encourage girls and women to pursue careers in aviation and science, technology, engineering and mathematics. The journey is intended to show that ambitious goals are within reach, even in fields where women remain underrepresented.

The pilot, who grew up in Afghanistan, hopes her flight will inspire young people to imagine a future beyond the barriers they face. She plans to share her experiences along the way, highlighting both the challenges of flying long distances and the opportunities that aviation can offer.

Her mission combines a demanding travel schedule with a message about education, confidence and persistence. For many girls, she says, seeing a woman take on a complex technical challenge can make a difference. The flight also aims to draw attention to the need for more access to STEM learning and aviation training.

Women remain a minority in many aviation roles, including commercial piloting and aircraft maintenance. Advocates say early encouragement, mentorship and practical training can help widen participation. They also point to the importance of visible role models who can make these careers feel attainable.

The pilot’s Afghan background gives the journey an added personal dimension. Her story reflects the determination required to pursue education and professional ambitions across cultural and practical barriers. She hopes young women will see that their origins need not define the limits of their futures.

The route will take her across multiple regions, with stops offering opportunities to meet students and community groups. At each stage, she intends to discuss flight, navigation and the skills needed to work in technical fields. Organizers say these conversations can help turn inspiration into concrete next steps.

Aviation requires careful preparation, sound judgment and teamwork, all skills that apply across many STEM careers. The pilot’s journey is also a reminder that progress in these industries depends on making training and opportunity more inclusive.

For aspiring pilots, the path can be costly and difficult to navigate. Scholarships, flight clubs and mentorship programs can provide crucial support, particularly for students without established connections to the industry.

The global flight is designed not only as a personal achievement but as a public call to action. Its message is that girls and women should be welcomed in cockpits, engineering labs and classrooms alike. As the journey continues, the pilot hopes each conversation will encourage another young person to take the first step toward a career in aviation or STEM.

Civilians in western Mosul are facing mounting danger as Iraqi forces step up their campaign to retake the city from Islamic State fighters. The push has brought heavier fighting into densely populated neighborhoods, where families have few safe routes out. Residents and aid workers have reported intense clashes, airstrikes and shelling, though conditions vary across the front lines. Iraqi forces have urged civilians to leave areas of combat, but many people are unable to flee because of insecurity, damaged roads or shortages of transport. Others fear being caught in crossfire or targeted while trying to escape.

The United Nations has warned that hundreds of thousands of people could be at risk as the operation advances. Aid agencies say that those who reach displacement camps may find limited shelter, clean water and medical care. Inside the city, food, fuel and essential medicines are increasingly difficult to obtain. Hospitals and emergency services are also under strain as casualties rise and access becomes more difficult.

Islamic State fighters have used explosives, sniper fire and other tactics to slow the advance, increasing the risks for civilians caught nearby. Iraqi authorities say their forces are working to protect residents, but the scale and complexity of urban combat make that difficult. Humanitarian organizations are calling for safe passage, protection of civilian infrastructure and access for relief workers. They also warn that people who remain trapped may need urgent assistance. As the battle continues, the fate of western Mosul’s residents is becoming an increasingly pressing concern.

The paper addresses an interesting intersection of quantum algorithms, statistical learning, and speech processing, but its contribution should be evaluated against strong classical expectation-maximization baselines. The authors should clearly specify the quantum subroutines, data-loading assumptions, and end-to-end complexity, since these factors can substantially affect whether the claimed speedup is practical. The evaluation on speech data would be more convincing with details on dataset size and preprocessing, repeated runs, uncertainty estimates, and comparisons of clustering quality as well as runtime. It would also help to discuss sensitivity to initialization and the number of mixture components, along with the effects of sampling and hardware noise if applicable. Overall, the topic is promising, but claims of quantum advantage should be carefully qualified and supported by reproducible experiments.

The hero arrived at the burning village just as the sun set. He wore a weathered cloak, carried a sword, and had no idea why everyone kept calling him Kael. “Because that’s what the author named you,” said a voice from the clouds. Kael looked up. The sky had a paragraph-shaped tear in it. “And why am I running toward danger?” he shouted. “It’s what heroes do,” the author replied. “I’m beginning to notice,” said Kael. A woman stumbled from a cottage, clutching a child. Kael raised his sword and charged toward the nearest bandit. Then he stopped. “Wait. Why is there only one bandit?” The bandit lowered his mask. “Budget constraints,” he said. Kael set down his sword. “I refuse to fight a villain who has no motive.” The bandit sighed. “I was promised a tragic backstory, but the author forgot.” “We’ll fix that,” Kael said. He turned to the clouds and demanded a new page. The sky rustled like paper. A backstory fell into the village square. The bandit read it aloud and discovered he had once been a baker. “I miss making cinnamon rolls,” he said. “Then stop burning villages,” Kael replied. The author’s voice boomed, “This is not how the climax is supposed to go!” “What is supposed to happen?” Kael asked. “You defeat him, save the child, and learn that the mysterious woman is your lost sister.” The woman blinked. “I’m not his sister.” “Exactly,” Kael said. “We’re not doing that.” He handed the child to her and offered the bandit a job at a bakery. The flames vanished, though nobody could explain why. The village gathered around, waiting for a speech about courage. Kael felt one forming in his mouth. He swallowed it. “Anyone know where the road leads?” he asked. “To the final battle,” the author said, hurriedly. “No,” Kael replied. “To the coast.” The world shuddered as he stepped off the marked path. The clouds tried to funnel him toward a mountain. Kael kept walking. Behind him, the woman and the former bandit followed, arguing about pastry recipes. Ahead, the blank horizon opened like a fresh page. For the first time, Kael chose what happened next.

The paper presents an unfolded reweighted ℓ1–ℓ1 recurrent neural network for video tasks and combines architectural development with theoretical and empirical analysis. Its central idea—unfolding an iterative reweighted optimization procedure into a recurrent network—is well motivated by the need to model temporal structure while retaining a degree of interpretability. The use of both ℓ1 terms appears promising for encouraging sparse representations and robust temporal modeling. The paper’s emphasis on generalization theory is a valuable complement to the experimental evaluation. Overall, the topic is relevant, and the proposed approach could be of interest to researchers in video learning and model-based deep networks.

The manuscript would benefit from a clearer explanation of the optimization problem from which the network is derived. In particular, the roles of the two ℓ1 penalties, their associated weights, and the reweighting scheme should be defined precisely. The authors should explain how each iteration maps to a recurrent layer and whether the resulting parameters are shared across iterations or learned independently. It would also help to state explicitly which parts of the architecture are derived from the optimization procedure and which are introduced as engineering choices. A diagram or pseudocode showing the complete forward pass would improve reproducibility.

The theoretical generalization analysis is potentially significant, but its assumptions and scope need to be made especially clear. The paper should define the hypothesis class, data assumptions, and complexity measures used in the bound. The authors should explain whether the result applies to the finite-depth unfolded network, the recurrent formulation, or both. Any dependence on depth, sequence length, parameter norms, or reweighting constants should be discussed and interpreted. The analysis would be more useful if the authors connected the bound to practical design choices and identified conditions under which it is non-vacuous. The paper should also distinguish clearly between a formal guarantee and empirical evidence that the bound predicts performance.

The experiments should provide enough detail to assess the strength and fairness of the comparisons. Please specify the datasets, train-validation-test protocols, input preprocessing, sequence lengths, and evaluation metrics. The baselines should include both competitive contemporary video models and relevant optimization-inspired or unfolded methods. All methods should receive comparable tuning effort and, where feasible, comparable computational budgets. Reporting results across multiple random seeds with variability estimates would make the comparisons more reliable. Ablations should isolate the contributions of reweighting, each ℓ1 term, recurrence, and unfolding depth. It would also be useful to report parameter counts, runtime, and memory use, since these affect the practical value of the proposed architecture. If the method is intended to generalize across video tasks, the authors should clarify which tasks are evaluated and avoid implying broader coverage than the experiments support.

The presentation could be improved by defining notation consistently and separating the algorithmic description from the theoretical development. Claims of superiority should be qualified when differences are small or lack statistical support. The authors should also discuss limitations, including sensitivity to hyperparameters and the cost of recurrent inference. Subject to these clarifications and stronger experimental reporting, the paper offers a promising approach with a potentially useful combination of structured modeling and learned representation. My recommendation is major revision, primarily to strengthen reproducibility, clarify the theoretical contribution, and establish the empirical advantages more convincingly.

Adolescents should not have to commit to a career path before starting high school. At that age, many students are still discovering their interests and strengths. Requiring them to choose a career too early could create unnecessary pressure. It might also lead them to ignore subjects and activities that could inspire them later. High school is a valuable time to explore different classes, clubs, and experiences. This exploration can help students make more thoughtful decisions about their future. However, it is useful for young people to learn about different careers and consider what they might enjoy. Parents and teachers can support them by offering guidance without making the decision for them. As students grow, their goals and interests may change. They should have the freedom to choose a career path when they are ready.
