Students should be allowed to use mobile devices at school, but only under clear rules. Phones and tablets can help students look up information and understand difficult topics. They also give students quick access to educational apps, digital textbooks, and classroom assignments. In an emergency, a student may need to contact family or call for help. However, mobile devices can distract students from lessons and make it harder to concentrate. They can also be used for cheating or for sharing hurtful messages. Schools should therefore require students to keep devices away during lessons unless a teacher gives permission. Teachers can allow devices for research, learning activities, or other useful tasks. Schools should also teach students how to use technology responsibly and respectfully. With fair rules, mobile devices can support learning without disrupting the classroom.

Northern Ireland’s police service is facing criticism after acknowledging that tissue from deceased victims had been retained without families being informed. The practice has prompted apologies and an effort to contact relatives affected by the handling of the remains.

The issue concerns tissue samples taken during post-mortem examinations in investigations into deaths. Police say some material was kept for evidential purposes, but families were not always told that it had been retained. The disclosure has raised questions about consent, communication and the treatment of bereaved relatives.

The Police Service of Northern Ireland has apologised to families for the distress caused. It said it recognised that relatives should have received clear information about what was retained and why. The force has begun outreach to identify and contact those who may have been affected.

Officials are reviewing records to establish how many cases are involved and whether tissue remains in storage. The review is also intended to clarify the circumstances in which samples were retained and the procedures followed at the time. Police have not yet provided a complete account of the scale of the issue.

The force’s response comes amid wider scrutiny of how institutions handle human tissue after death. In Northern Ireland, as elsewhere in the UK, the retention of samples for medical or investigative purposes is subject to legal and professional requirements. Families’ rights to information and the need to preserve evidence can sometimes intersect, but authorities are expected to explain decisions sensitively.

Relatives who were not informed may now be left questioning what happened to their loved ones’ remains. For families already coping with a sudden or traumatic death, the discovery can reopen painful memories. Advocacy groups have stressed that timely, honest communication is essential in such cases.

Police have said they will provide affected families with information and support as the review proceeds. The outreach is expected to include explanations of why tissue was retained and what has since happened to it. Where appropriate, officials will discuss arrangements for the return or disposal of material.

The force has also indicated that it is examining its policies and the way information is recorded and shared. Any changes could include clearer guidance for investigators and improved processes for notifying next of kin. Independent oversight may be sought to ensure that the review is thorough and credible.

The controversy has prompted calls for transparency about the decisions made in individual cases. Critics say an apology is important, but families also need a full explanation and assurance that the practice will not recur. They have urged police to avoid leaving relatives to discover the issue through media reports.

The PSNI has said it is committed to engaging with families and learning from the failures identified. It has not suggested that tissue was retained in every case for the same reason, and the circumstances may vary. Further details are expected as records are checked and relatives are contacted.

For now, the review remains ongoing, with the number of affected families still unclear. The police service’s challenge will be to provide answers while treating each family’s circumstances with care. For those affected, the apology marks a first step, but trust will depend on what the investigation uncovers and how the force responds.

Palmyra Atoll is a remote cluster of islands in the central Pacific Ocean. It lies about 1,000 miles south of Hawaii and is surrounded by a protected marine environment. The atoll is home to seabirds, crabs, fish, and many other forms of life. It also offers a striking example of how one invasive species can affect another.

For decades, black rats lived on Palmyra’s islands. They arrived with people and ships, rather than evolving there. Rats ate seeds, plants, eggs, and young animals. Their feeding changed the atoll’s forests and affected native wildlife.

Rats also helped create conditions that suited Asian tiger mosquitoes. These mosquitoes, Aedes albopictus, are native to parts of Asia but have spread around the world. They are recognizable by their black-and-white markings. Unlike many mosquitoes, they can breed in small pockets of water, including water collected in tree holes and discarded containers.

On Palmyra, rats gnawed into coconuts and other fruits. Rainwater could collect in the damaged fruit, creating small pools where mosquito larvae developed. The rats therefore provided breeding sites, even though they were not the mosquitoes’ only source of habitat. Their feeding also altered the forest, potentially changing how much shade and moisture were available.

Asian tiger mosquitoes bite people and other animals during the day. Their bites can be irritating, and the species can transmit diseases in some parts of the world. Its presence on Palmyra was a concern for people working and visiting there, as well as a possible threat to the atoll’s natural environment.

In 2011, conservation teams carried out a project to eradicate rats from Palmyra. They used carefully planned applications of rodenticide across the islands. The work required detailed preparation to reduce risks to native wildlife and other animals. Monitoring continued after the treatment to determine whether any rats had survived.

The eradication succeeded: the invasive rats were removed from the atoll. Researchers then watched for changes in the ecosystem. One surprising change involved the Asian tiger mosquito. After the rats disappeared, the mosquitoes also became difficult to find and were eventually no longer detected.

The likely explanation was a chain of ecological effects. Without rats chewing into coconuts and fruit, fewer water-filled breeding sites were available. Rat removal also allowed the forest to recover and changed the local habitat. Together, these changes may have made the atoll less suitable for the mosquitoes.

This result illustrates an indirect effect of conservation. The project targeted rats, not mosquitoes. Yet removing one invasive species changed the resources and conditions that another species depended on. Ecologists call this kind of relationship an indirect interaction.

The story does not mean that rats are always essential to mosquito populations. Mosquitoes can use many types of standing water, and their abundance depends on rainfall, temperature, vegetation, and other factors. On Palmyra, the connection between rats and breeding habitat appears to have been especially important. The sequence of events supports the explanation, but it is difficult to isolate every cause in a complex ecosystem.

It is also important not to conclude that removing rats will make mosquitoes disappear everywhere. Different islands have different habitats, species, and sources of standing water. In some places, mosquitoes may persist or even increase after rats are removed. Conservation plans must be based on local evidence and careful monitoring.

Palmyra’s experience shows why ecological restoration can have effects beyond its original goal. Removing invasive predators can help native plants and animals, while also changing the habitat used by insects. These changes can benefit some species and disadvantage others. An ecosystem is a network of connections, not a collection of isolated organisms.

The case also highlights the value of long-term observation. Without monitoring after eradication, the mosquito decline might have gone unnoticed. Scientists and conservationists can use such observations to form hypotheses, test them, and improve future projects. Unexpected outcomes are often among the most useful lessons in ecology.

Palmyra Atoll’s rat eradication became a notable conservation achievement. Its apparent effect on Asian tiger mosquitoes revealed a surprising link between a mammal, a fruit, and an insect. The central lesson is simple: changing one part of an ecosystem can reshape conditions for many others.

Camera-based remote air traffic control could help airports reduce costs and improve operations by allowing controllers to manage aircraft from facilities away from the airfield. The approach, known as remote or digital tower technology, uses high-resolution cameras and sensors to provide a live view of runways and taxiways.

Images are sent to a control room, where screens can display wide-angle views, zoomed details and visual information such as aircraft positions. Some systems also use infrared cameras and automated alerts to help staff monitor conditions in poor visibility or at night. Supporters say the technology could make it less expensive to provide tower services at smaller airports, where building and staffing a conventional tower may be difficult to justify.

A remote center could also serve several airports, with controllers switching between sites as traffic demands change. That flexibility may help airports extend operating hours or maintain service when a local tower is closed. Digital tools could further support coordination by highlighting potential conflicts or changes in runway conditions.

However, remote towers are not a simple substitute for existing facilities. Airports and regulators must ensure that camera coverage is reliable, communications are secure and controllers can respond quickly to equipment failures. Staff also need training to work with screen-based views, which can differ from looking directly out of a tower window.

Unions and safety experts have stressed that any efficiency gains must not come at the expense of staffing or oversight. Each installation must be tested and approved under the applicable aviation rules. As more airports assess the technology, its long-term value will depend on whether it delivers dependable service as well as lower costs.

The paper examines whether CLOTH is a genuinely challenging benchmark for reading comprehension and whether its baselines and error analysis support reliable conclusions. This is a worthwhile question, since benchmark difficulty can be overstated when performance is compared only with weak or poorly matched systems. The paper’s main strength is its focus on both aggregate results and the evidence needed to interpret them. Its discussion of CLOTH’s cloze format also helps clarify what kinds of reasoning the benchmark may reward. However, the evaluation would be more convincing if it separated difficulty arising from passage understanding from difficulty arising from answer-option selection. The baseline comparisons should include strong, reproducible models appropriate to the benchmark’s current state, as well as simple lexical and frequency-based controls. The paper should report relevant training details, tuning procedures, and computational settings so readers can assess fairness and reproduce the results. Because CLOTH questions are drawn from educational materials, the authors should also address possible overlap with model pretraining data and the effects of passage or question leakage. Aggregate accuracy alone is insufficient to establish that the benchmark is challenging. Results should be broken down by grade level, question type, passage length, and other meaningful item characteristics. Where feasible, uncertainty estimates or significance tests would help distinguish real differences from sampling variation. The error analysis is promising, but its categories need clear definitions and a transparent coding procedure. If errors are classified manually, the paper should report annotator agreement and explain how disagreements were resolved. Examples should illustrate not only model failures but also ambiguous, underspecified, or potentially flawed questions. The authors should test whether incorrect answers reflect failures of comprehension rather than artifacts such as implausible distractors or answer-position biases. A comparison with human performance, including the conditions under which people were tested, would provide a useful reference point. The conclusions should be calibrated to the tested models and methods rather than presented as definitive judgments about CLOTH’s overall difficulty. Overall, the paper addresses an important issue, but stronger baselines, more granular analyses, and a more systematic error study are needed to substantiate its central claims.

An Australian wedge-tailed eagle has damaged a farmer’s drone in an encounter that highlights growing tensions between wildlife and aerial technology. The incident occurred while the farmer was using the aircraft to survey farmland, according to reports. The eagle swooped at the drone, striking it and leaving it damaged. It was not clear whether the bird was injured. Wedge-tailed eagles are Australia’s largest birds of prey and are known for defending their territory. Drones can be mistaken for intruders, particularly when they fly near nesting or hunting areas. Farmers increasingly use the devices to monitor livestock, inspect fences and assess crops. The technology can save time and reduce the need to travel across large properties. But encounters with wildlife can result in costly repairs and may put animals at risk. Experts advise drone operators to keep a safe distance from birds and avoid flying near nests. They also recommend landing promptly if an animal begins to show defensive behaviour. The incident is a reminder that using drones responsibly means sharing the air with wildlife.

Success rarely comes without challenges. Many people face setbacks while working toward their goals. These difficulties can feel discouraging, especially when progress seems slow. However, perseverance can help people move forward despite obstacles. Perseverance means continuing to try even when something is difficult. It does not mean ignoring mistakes or pretending everything is easy. Instead, it means learning from setbacks and using that knowledge to improve.

For example, a student might receive a low grade on an important test. At first, the result may cause disappointment. The student could decide that the subject is too difficult and give up. But the student could also review the test, ask the teacher for help, and practice more regularly. The next test may still be challenging, but each effort can build stronger skills. Over time, the student may achieve a much better result.

Setbacks can also teach lessons that success alone cannot provide. A failed attempt can show someone which strategies do not work. It can encourage patience, problem-solving, and confidence. When people overcome difficulties, they often discover that they are more capable than they believed. This confidence can help them face future challenges.

Perseverance is useful in many areas of life. Athletes may lose games before they learn how to work as a team. Artists may create many imperfect pieces before developing their own style. People starting a business may encounter problems before finding a way to serve customers successfully. In each case, progress comes from effort, reflection, and a willingness to try again.

Still, perseverance does not mean repeating the same actions without thinking. People may need to change their plans or ask others for advice. Taking a break can also help someone return with renewed energy. The important thing is to keep learning and not let one setback define the future.

Ultimately, setbacks are a normal part of pursuing meaningful goals. They can slow progress, but they do not have to stop it. By staying patient, adapting, and continuing to work, people can turn difficulties into opportunities to grow. Perseverance does not guarantee that every goal will be reached, but it makes success more possible. It also helps people become stronger and wiser along the way.

When the soldiers dragged Ilyan into the palace, he thought they wanted a ransom.
Instead, they showed him the cracked mosaic in the throne room.
Its tiles pictured a moonlit garden, with silver rivers and black roses.
A jagged gap split the garden from the palace gate.
“Repair it before dawn,” said the queen.
“I am a potter, not a mosaicist,” Ilyan replied.
The queen pointed to his hands, stained blue from his craft.
“Those hands will do.”
He saw the iron collar around the queen’s neck and wondered who had put it there.
Then he noticed the mosaic’s tiny figures turning their heads.
The palace was alive, or the queen wanted him to believe it was.
Ilyan asked for colored glass, gold leaf, and a day’s rest.
The queen gave him the glass and denied him the rest.
At midnight, he began to work.
Each tile he set hummed beneath his fingertips.
The silver river flowed uphill.
A black rose unfolded its petals.
From the crack came a whisper, thin as a thread.
“Leave the gate broken,” it said.
Ilyan stopped.
The queen watched from her throne, pale and sleepless.
“What happens if I finish?” he asked.
“Your work will save us,” she said.
“From what?”
The queen looked toward the mosaic.
“From what I once called through it.”
She had opened the painted gate to bargain for eternal life.
Something had answered, and the palace had been closing around it ever since.
The crack was not damage, Ilyan understood.
It was the only thing keeping the door shut.
He put down his tools.
The queen’s guards seized him.
She offered him freedom if he completed the work.
He asked for the collar to be removed from her neck.
The queen laughed, then saw that he was serious.
“I cannot,” she said.
“The bargain binds me.”
Ilyan studied the garden and found a small figure kneeling beside the gate.
It wore the same blue-stained hands as he did.
He placed a bright shard in the figure’s palm.
The mosaic shuddered.
The whisper became a roar.
The queen ordered him to finish, and the guards dragged him forward.
Ilyan braced his left leg against the floor and reached for the final tile.
A blade fell.
His leg was taken below the knee, and pain swallowed the room.
Yet his hand closed around the shard.
He pressed it into the painted figure’s palm.
The gate in the mosaic swung shut.
The palace groaned as the silver river turned to stone.
The queen’s collar broke apart and fell at her feet.
At dawn, the guards carried Ilyan beyond the palace walls.
The queen followed, bearing his tools and a wooden crutch.
She asked him to teach her how to make tiles.
He looked back once at the silent palace.
Then he showed her how to shape a piece of blue glass.

The paper presents a timely investigation of how deep neural networks develop spatial and relational representations, and its focus on emergence offers a useful bridge between mechanistic analysis and observed behavior. The claims would be stronger with clearer operational definitions of “emergent” representations, comparisons across architectures and training conditions, and evidence that the representations support robust generalization rather than task-specific performance. Overall, the work has promise, but the authors should sharpen the causal analysis and discuss the limitations of inferring internal representations from behavioral results.

Figs are warm-season fruit trees valued for their sweet, edible fruits and adaptability to home gardens. Most varieties grow best in full sun, well-drained soil, and a sheltered spot with protection from harsh winter winds. Choose a variety suited to your climate, because cold tolerance, ripening time, and fruit quality differ considerably.

‘Brown Turkey’ is a popular choice for beginners because it is productive and tolerates some cold. ‘Celeste’ produces small, sweet fruits and is also relatively cold-hardy. ‘Chicago Hardy’ can survive colder winters than many figs, especially if its roots are protected. In mild climates, ‘Black Mission’ is prized for dark, richly flavored fruit, while ‘Kadota’ bears green-skinned figs with mild, sweet flesh. ‘Desert King’ is useful in cooler coastal regions, where its main crop can ripen reliably.

Figs may produce a breba crop on last year’s growth and a main crop on the current season’s growth. Some varieties produce both crops, while others provide a dependable harvest mainly from one. Check local recommendations, since a variety that ripens well in one region may not finish its crop in a shorter or cooler growing season.

The simplest way to propagate most figs is by taking dormant hardwood cuttings. In late winter, select healthy, pencil-thick stems and cut sections about 15 to 20 centimeters long, each with several buds. Keep track of which end is the base, since cuttings must be planted upright. Remove the lower buds, leaving a few near the top, and place the base in a moist, well-draining rooting mix.

Keep the mix evenly moist but not waterlogged, and place the cutting somewhere warm with bright, indirect light. New leaves can indicate growth, but they do not by themselves prove that roots have formed. Once a cutting has rooted and established several new leaves, gradually acclimate it to outdoor conditions before planting it in the garden.

Figs can also be propagated by layering a low branch, covering part of it with soil, and separating it from the parent plant after roots develop. This method keeps the new plant attached to its source of water and nutrients while it roots. Nurseries offer another reliable option when you want a named variety or need to avoid the uncertainty of rooting cuttings.

Plant a fig during a mild part of the growing season, after severe frost risk has passed. Dig a hole as deep as the root ball and wider than it, then backfill with the original soil. Water thoroughly after planting, and spread a layer of mulch over the root zone while keeping it a few centimeters away from the trunk.

Water young trees regularly during their first growing season to help them establish. Mature figs tolerate some drought, but consistent moisture while fruits develop helps prevent small or prematurely dropped fruit. Avoid overwatering, especially in heavy soil, because waterlogged roots can decline.

Figs often grow well without rich soil or frequent feeding. If growth is weak or a soil test indicates a need, apply a balanced fertilizer in spring according to its label. Excess nitrogen encourages leafy growth at the expense of fruit and may make the tree more vulnerable to cold damage.

Prune lightly, removing dead, damaged, crossing, or crowded branches. Heavy pruning can reduce the next crop, particularly on varieties that bear fruit on older wood. To keep a tree compact, shorten selected branches gradually rather than cutting back the entire canopy at once.

In cold regions, grow figs in large containers that can be moved into a protected, cool place for winter. In-ground trees may need their roots mulched and their branches wrapped or sheltered, depending on local conditions. Follow regional guidance, since the right winter protection depends on both the variety and the severity of local freezes.

Harvest figs when they are fully colored, softening, and beginning to hang downward; they do not ripen well after picking. Handle them gently because ripe fruits bruise easily and keep for only a short time. Pick fruit frequently during the season, and remove fallen or damaged figs to discourage pests and disease.

Check leaves and branches regularly for signs of scale, mites, or other pests, and use the least disruptive suitable control. Good spacing and airflow help reduce fungal problems, while clean pruning tools lower the risk of spreading disease. With a climate-appropriate variety, careful watering, and modest pruning, a fig tree can provide reliable harvests for many years.

Recognition can have a powerful effect on students in the classroom. When teachers notice a student’s effort, progress, or kindness, they show that the student’s work matters. This encouragement can inspire students to keep trying, even when a subject feels difficult. A student who receives praise for careful preparation may be motivated to study more consistently. Recognition also helps students understand which habits lead to success. Instead of focusing only on grades, teachers can celebrate perseverance, curiosity, and improvement. This reminds students that excellence is built through practice rather than achieved all at once. As students work toward their goals, they develop stronger learning habits. Recognition can also build confidence. A student who doubts their abilities may begin to believe in themselves after a teacher points out their strengths. That confidence can make it easier to ask questions, share ideas, and take on new challenges. Recognition from classmates can be meaningful too. A supportive classroom helps students feel that their contributions are valued. However, recognition should be sincere and fair. Teachers should acknowledge different kinds of progress so that every student has a chance to feel encouraged. They can offer specific feedback, such as praising a thoughtful answer or a noticeable improvement. When students feel seen and supported, they are more likely to participate and keep learning. In this way, recognition inspires students to pursue excellence while helping them become more confident learners.

Life can bring challenges that feel too difficult to handle alone. When problems arise, many people try to solve everything by themselves. They may believe that asking for help is a sign of weakness. In reality, seeking guidance can be a wise and courageous choice. A trusted person can offer a fresh perspective. This may help us notice solutions we could not see on our own. Guidance can also prevent small problems from becoming larger ones. For example, a student who is struggling with a subject can ask a teacher for extra help. The teacher may explain the material in a clearer way or suggest a useful study plan. Friends and family can also provide encouragement during stressful times. Simply talking about a problem can make it feel less overwhelming. Others may have faced similar challenges and can share what they learned. Their advice can help us avoid mistakes and make informed decisions. Of course, we should think carefully before following someone else’s advice. Different people may have different opinions, and not every suggestion will suit our situation. We can listen, ask questions, and decide what is best for us. Seeking guidance does not mean giving up our independence. Instead, it helps us build the skills and confidence to face future problems. People who support us can remind us of our strengths when we feel discouraged. They can also help us stay focused on our goals. Although we may still need to do the hard work ourselves, we do not have to do it alone. By reaching out for guidance, we can find clearer paths through life’s challenges.

Jonah Vale collected tobacco the way other men collected clocks. His shelves held clay pipes, brass tins, and pouches stitched from fox and deer hide. He knew the names of leaves grown in Virginia, Sumatra, and the hills of Peru. Yet he had never found a snuff that truly surprised him.

One rainy evening, a stranger entered his shop. The man was old, though his back was straight and his silver hair neatly combed. He wore a dark green coat that smelled faintly of cedar. “I’m looking for a little tobacco,” he said.

Jonah showed him the finest tins in the shop. The stranger looked at each one without interest. Then he placed a small, blackened tin on the counter. Its lid bore no label, only a crescent scratched into the metal.

“I’d like to know what this is,” Jonah said. “You may smell it,” the stranger replied, “but you mustn’t keep it.”

Jonah lifted the lid. Inside lay a fine brown powder, warm in color and strangely bright beneath the lamplight. Its scent reached him at once: smoke, orange peel, damp earth, and something like a summer garden after rain. It was the most intoxicating fragrance he had ever encountered.

He drew in a cautious pinch. The shop vanished.

Jonah stood on a hillside beneath a pale moon. A woman in a red scarf was laughing beside a little boy, and somewhere nearby, a fiddle played. He could feel cold grass beneath his shoes and smoke curling from a distant chimney. Then the vision broke, and he was back at the counter, gripping its edge.

“What was that?” he whispered. The stranger closed the tin. “A memory,” he said, “and not yours.”

Jonah begged to buy it. The old man refused, but after a long silence, he agreed to tell its story. He said he had once been a young apothecary in a village at the edge of the Carpathian Mountains. There he had fallen in love with a woman named Mara, who made snuff from tobacco, herbs, and dried orange peel.

Mara claimed the mixture could carry a person back to whatever moment they most feared losing. The young apothecary laughed at her, until she let him try it. He saw the day his mother had taught him to read, down to the blue thread in her sleeve. After that, he believed.

The couple filled a small tin and promised to share it only when their memories began to fade. But war came before they could grow old together. The young apothecary was sent away, and Mara stayed behind with their little son.

He returned years later to find the village burned and empty. In the ruins, he found the tin beneath the stones of their old hearth. He had carried it ever since, afraid to open it and afraid to forget them. “That powder is all I have left,” he said.

Jonah felt ashamed of his hunger to own it. “Then why show it to me?” he asked. The stranger looked toward the rain-blurred window. “Because I am forgetting the sound of her laugh.”

He opened the tin once more, and Jonah watched him take a pinch. The old man shut his eyes, smiling faintly as the fiddle seemed to rise between the shelves. Jonah did not ask what he saw. When the man opened his eyes, there were tears on his cheeks.

He placed the tin in Jonah’s hands. “Keep it for tonight,” he said. “But don’t sell it, and don’t use it to chase what you’ve already lost.”

Jonah agreed. The stranger stepped out into the rain, leaving no name and no address. For a long while, Jonah stood alone with the tin.

At last, he put it in a locked drawer. He did not open it again. But sometimes, on rainy evenings, the shop filled with the scent of orange peel and summer grass, and Jonah would hear a woman laughing somewhere far away.

Planned increases to probate fees for larger estates are drawing criticism, even as a proposed exemption would spare most smaller estates. The changes would raise the amount paid to obtain a grant of probate, a court document that allows an executor to administer a deceased person’s assets.

Under the plan, estates below a specified value would pay no fee, while charges would rise for estates above the threshold. Supporters say the exemption would reduce costs and paperwork for families dealing with modest estates. They argue that higher fees on larger estates could help fund the court system without burdening most people.

Critics, however, say the proposals could place a steep cost on families at an already difficult time. They warn that an estate’s headline value may not reflect the cash available to pay a fee, particularly when wealth is tied up in a home or other property. Executors might have to use personal funds or delay distributing assets while arranging payment.

Some advisers also question whether the fee bands are fair, saying estates just above a threshold could face a disproportionately large increase. They urge policymakers to consider gradual rates and clear rules for valuing assets. Others say the planned charges risk turning probate into a revenue-raising measure rather than a service fee.

The proposal has renewed calls for a review of how probate costs are calculated. Legal and financial professionals say families need time to understand any changes before they take effect. They also recommend checking whether the exemption applies automatically or requires an application.

The government has yet to settle the details, including the final thresholds and timetable. Until then, executors are being advised to seek guidance before making decisions based on the proposed rates. The debate highlights a broader question: how to protect families with limited means while ensuring larger estates contribute fairly to the cost of administering probate.

Cities and suburbs are home to a surprising variety of wildlife, from songbirds and bats to foxes, insects, and frogs. Parks, gardens, street trees, ponds, and even building ledges can provide food, shelter, and places to raise young. Native plants are especially valuable because they support local insects, which in turn feed many birds and other animals. You can help by planting a range of native flowers, shrubs, and trees, and by leaving some fallen leaves or stems for insects to shelter in. Keep cats indoors or supervised, and make windows safer for birds with screens, external shades, or visible decals. Avoid pesticides and herbicides, which can harm wildlife and reduce its food supply. Provide clean water in a shallow dish or pond, and keep it fresh to prevent disease and mosquitoes. Small, thoughtful changes across many properties can create connected habitats that help urban wildlife thrive.

Allowing students to attend classes from home has several advantages and disadvantages. Students can save time and money because they do not need to travel to school. They may also feel more comfortable and have greater flexibility in their schedules. However, learning from home can make it harder to focus and interact with teachers and classmates. Overall, home learning is useful for some students, but it cannot replace the benefits of attending school in person for everyone.

EasyJet is expanding its winter schedule from Belfast International Airport with new routes to Lyon and Lanzarote. The services will give Northern Ireland travellers more options for winter city breaks and warmer-weather escapes. The additions form part of the airline’s wider effort to broaden its seasonal flight offerings from Belfast.

Elias woke to the pale buzz of his alarm and the numb weight of both arms. He blinked at the ceiling, unsure whether he’d been asleep for minutes or years. When he tried to move, his hands answered with a prickling fizz. “Right,” he mumbled, remembering he’d fallen asleep across his desk. He rolled onto his back and flexed his fingers. Slowly, warmth returned, first as pins and needles, then as a dull ache. While he waited, he listened to rain ticking against the window. His half-finished notes lay scattered beside a cold mug of tea. At last, he sat up and swung his feet to the floor. The room tilted, then steadied. He stretched his shoulders and shook out his hands. The alarm stopped buzzing when he reached over and silenced it. Elias pushed the notes into a neater pile and carried the mug to the sink. A fresh cup of coffee steamed beside his keyboard. He settled into his chair, tested each finger on the keys, and opened the document. This time, he promised himself, he would stay awake long enough to finish the story.

The city had forgotten Mara Venn, and Mara had forgotten almost everything else.

She lived beneath an abandoned station, where the clocks had stopped at different hours.

Each night, she heard the names of people she had killed whispered from the walls.

Once, she had been an assassin for the Crown of Ash.

Her gift was stranger than a blade: she could remove a person from memory.

Not kill them, exactly, but make the world forget they had ever existed.

Then a team of supernatural agents found her.

They wore silver masks and carried lanterns filled with blue fire.

Their leader called himself Saint Orison.

He said Mara was a danger to every living mind.

The agents had tracked her by following the holes she left in history.

Mara tried to run, but the station doors sealed with frost.

Orison raised his lantern, and the dead names in the walls went silent.

“You will come with us,” he said.

Mara looked at the agents and felt the old power stir.

She reached for the youngest one first.

His name was Elias, though she had not yet heard it.

With a thought, she erased him.

His mask clattered to the floor, empty.

The others stared at the space where their teammate had stood.

Then their faces changed, because they could no longer remember why they were afraid.

Mara moved through them like a shadow through candlelight.

One by one, she removed their names, their histories, their reasons for being there.

Their weapons dropped as their hands forgot how to hold them.

Orison alone resisted, his lantern burning brighter with every stolen memory.

He spoke Mara’s true name, the one she had buried years ago.

For a moment, she remembered her childhood, her sister, and the man who had taught her to kill.

Then she erased the lantern.

Blue fire vanished, and Orison became only a frightened stranger.

When dawn came, the station was empty.

Mara stood on the platform, unable to remember why she had come there.

A single silver mask rested at her feet.

From somewhere in the walls, a forgotten voice whispered her name.

Whether teens should graduate at an older age to gain maturity and independence is a question worth considering. Many students finish high school at around eighteen, an age when they are still learning how to make important decisions. Staying in school longer could give teenagers more time to develop confidence and responsibility. It might also help them become better prepared for work, college, and adult life.

An extra year could offer students more chances to explore subjects and career paths. They could take practical classes about budgeting, communication, and problem-solving. With more time, students who are struggling might strengthen their skills before graduating. Teens who need emotional or academic support could also benefit from a less rushed schedule.

However, graduating later would not be the best choice for every student. Many teenagers are already mature and ready to move on at eighteen. Keeping them in high school could delay their college plans or entry into the workforce. It could also make school feel repetitive if students are not offered new challenges. Families and communities might face added costs as well.

Instead of requiring everyone to graduate at an older age, schools should provide flexible options. Students could choose extra programs, internships, or life-skills courses if they need more preparation. Others could graduate on the usual schedule and continue learning in college, training, or a job. This approach would respect the different needs and abilities of teenagers. Overall, an older graduation age might help some students gain maturity and independence, but it should not be forced on everyone.

Online education offers flexibility because students can learn from home and often choose when to study. It can also save time and money by eliminating the daily commute. However, learning online may make it harder to stay focused and ask teachers questions. Students can also miss the friendships and teamwork that develop in a classroom. Both options have benefits, so the best choice depends on a student’s needs and learning style.

Online learning at home can help students feel comfortable and do their best work. They can study in a familiar place with their favorite supplies nearby. Students may also choose a quiet spot where they can focus without distractions. Learning at home can make it easier to take short breaks when needed. These breaks help students rest and return to their work with more energy. Online lessons may also let students review recorded explanations at their own pace. This can help them understand difficult ideas more clearly. With fewer worries about traveling to school, students may have more time for sleep and homework. Better rest and stronger focus can improve school performance. However, students still need a routine and a suitable place to learn. When they use online learning responsibly, studying at home can support their comfort, well-being, and success.

Difficulties are a natural part of life, and they can teach us more than easy successes do. When something goes wrong, we may feel frustrated, worried, or disappointed. Those feelings are understandable, but they do not have to define what happens next. A challenge can become an opportunity to understand ourselves better. It can show us what we value and what we are willing to work for. For example, a student who struggles with a difficult subject may discover a new level of patience. At first, the student might believe that success comes easily to everyone else. That belief can make the problem feel even larger. However, asking questions and practicing regularly can change the situation. Each small improvement becomes evidence that effort matters. Over time, the student may grow more confident and independent.

Difficulties can also help us set meaningful goals. When we face a problem, we have a reason to think about what we want to change. A broad wish, such as “I want to do better,” can be turned into a specific plan. We might decide to study for thirty minutes each evening or ask a teacher for help once a week. Clear goals make progress easier to see. They also help us focus on actions we can control. Sometimes a goal needs to be adjusted as we learn more about the challenge. Changing a plan does not mean giving up. It can mean choosing a wiser path forward. Achieving a small goal can provide motivation to keep going.

Mistakes are another important part of personal growth. It is easy to feel embarrassed when we make one, especially when others notice. Yet a mistake can reveal what we misunderstood or what we need to practice. Instead of hiding it, we can examine what happened. We can ask ourselves what choices led to the result and what we might try next time. This does not mean blaming ourselves for everything. It means taking responsibility for the parts we can improve. For instance, a missed deadline might teach us to begin assignments earlier. A disagreement with a friend might remind us to listen before responding. Learning from these experiences can make our future decisions more thoughtful.

Of course, difficulties do not always lead to immediate success. Some problems take time, support, and several attempts to overcome. It is important to ask trusted people for guidance when we need it. Resting and taking care of our well-being can also help us continue. Growth is not a straight line, and setbacks do not erase the progress we have made. What matters is our willingness to reflect, adapt, and try again. Through challenges, we can become more patient, responsible, and resilient. We can set goals that give our efforts direction and learn from mistakes without letting them define us. Difficulties may be painful, but they can help us become wiser and better prepared for the future.

When timid transfer student Kai entered Moonblade Academy, the principal handed him a mysterious lunchbox and whispered, “Your destiny begins at noon.”

At noon, the lunchbox opened by itself, revealing the legendary Spoon of Infinite Power.

Before Kai could ask whether it came with a fork, his rival, Shadow-Riku, burst through the cafeteria wall.

“Prepare to face my ultimate technique: Slightly Improved Punch!” Riku shouted.

Kai raised the spoon, and a beam of golden light split the clouds, the cafeteria, and one perfectly innocent pudding cup.

Everyone gasped, including the pudding cup.

“This is only the beginning,” Riku said, unveiling his own artifact: the Fork of Infinite Power.

Their first clash shook the school, then the city, then a nearby planet whose inhabitants had been watching the wrong anime.

Just as Kai gained the upper hand, Riku revealed the Fork’s hidden form, the Fork of Infinite Power: Extra Spiky Edition.

Kai collapsed to one knee, his childhood memories flashing before him—especially the time he dropped a sandwich.

“Don’t give up!” cried his best friend Mina, who had arrived dramatically despite living three time zones away.

Her tears landed on the spoon, awakening its secret ability: Infinite Power, Now With Sauce.

Kai and Riku collided again, creating a shockwave that knocked the moon into a slightly different orbit.

Then the headmaster descended from the sky, holding the legendary Napkin of Absolute Destiny.

He declared that the battle was forbidden, unless it became more intense.

So Kai, Riku, and the headmaster joined forces against the true enemy: a vending machine that had swallowed their change.

The machine transformed into the Mega-Vendinator, powered by every coin ever lost beneath a couch.

Kai lifted his spoon, Riku raised his fork, and the headmaster snapped the napkin open.

Together they shouted, “Cafeteria Combo—Final Lunch Break!”

A blinding explosion filled the universe, and when the smoke cleared, the vending machine had dispensed one warm soda.

Kai took a sip—then froze as a mysterious voice whispered, “Next time, the soda fights back.”

Cannabidiol, commonly called CBD, is a compound found in the cannabis plant. Unlike tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), it is not intoxicating in the same way and does not produce the familiar cannabis “high.” Researchers are investigating whether CBD might help people with opioid use disorder, a medical condition involving harmful or difficult-to-control opioid use. This research is promising in some respects, but CBD is not an established treatment for opioid addiction or withdrawal.

Opioids include prescription pain medicines and drugs such as heroin and fentanyl. Opioid use disorder can affect health, relationships, and daily life, and it can be fatal, particularly because of overdose. Effective treatments already exist, including medications such as buprenorphine, methadone, and extended-release naltrexone. Counseling, recovery support, and care for related health conditions can also be important. CBD should not replace these evidence-based treatments.

Interest in CBD partly comes from studies of the brain and nervous system. Opioids act on receptors involved in pain, reward, and stress, while CBD interacts with several biological systems. Researchers have proposed that CBD could influence anxiety, stress responses, cravings, or the rewarding effects associated with drug cues. These possibilities are hypotheses, not proof that CBD reduces opioid use or prevents relapse.

Early research has included laboratory studies, animal experiments, and small studies involving people. Some human research has reported reduced cravings or anxiety in response to opioid-related cues after CBD exposure. Such findings can help guide further investigation, but they do not establish that CBD is safe and effective for treating opioid use disorder. Studies may involve few participants, brief follow-up, or outcomes that do not show whether people stop using opioids or remain in treatment.

Withdrawal is another area of interest. Opioid withdrawal can cause symptoms such as muscle aches, nausea, diarrhea, sweating, anxiety, and insomnia. Symptoms can be intensely uncomfortable and may increase the risk of returning to opioid use. Researchers are asking whether CBD could ease some symptoms, but current evidence is not strong enough to recommend it as a withdrawal treatment. Medically supported care can relieve withdrawal and help people begin ongoing treatment.

Rigorous clinical trials are needed to answer the key questions. Trials should enroll enough participants to detect meaningful effects and compare CBD with a placebo or established care. They should use consistent, well-characterized CBD products and clearly report dose, timing, and treatment duration. Researchers also need to follow participants long enough to assess opioid use, cravings, retention in care, relapse, and quality of life. Measuring withdrawal symptoms alone would not show whether CBD improves recovery or reduces overdose risk.

Good trials must also examine safety and interactions. CBD can cause side effects, including sleepiness, diarrhea, and changes in appetite. It can affect how the body processes some medicines, potentially changing their effects or risks. This matters for people taking medications for opioid use disorder, as well as medicines for other health conditions. Product quality is another concern because over-the-counter CBD products may vary in strength, purity, and labeling accuracy.

People considering CBD should discuss it with a qualified health professional, especially if they take other medicines or are receiving treatment for opioid use disorder. They should not stop methadone, buprenorphine, naltrexone, or other prescribed treatment without medical guidance. Anyone at risk of overdose should seek urgent help; naloxone can reverse an opioid overdose, and emergency services should be contacted. In the United States, the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline and local treatment services can help connect people with support.

The central message is cautious optimism: CBD offers questions worth studying, not a proven solution. Well-designed, independently conducted clinical trials are essential before clinicians can recommend it for opioid addiction or withdrawal. Until stronger evidence is available, people should rely on established treatments and work with healthcare professionals to make informed decisions.

This paper studies phase-aware speech enhancement using deep complex-valued neural networks, bounded complex masks, and an SDR-inspired training objective. The topic is important, as magnitude-only approaches can discard useful phase information and limit reconstruction quality. The combination of complex-domain modeling and a bounded mask is a plausible way to improve enhancement while controlling unstable predictions. The proposed objective also appears well motivated because it aligns training more closely with signal-level quality than a conventional magnitude loss.

A key strength is the paper’s coherent focus on interacting design choices rather than treating network architecture, mask parameterization, and loss function as unrelated components. The bounded-mask formulation deserves particular attention, since its practical benefit depends on how the bounds are chosen and whether they constrain useful corrections. The authors should explain the parameterization and bounds precisely, including how they affect gradients and complex-valued outputs. They should also clarify the SDR-inspired objective, its relationship to standard SDR or SI-SDR, and any safeguards against numerical instability or silent reference segments.

The experimental evaluation should include strong, clearly specified baselines, including magnitude-domain systems and complex-domain systems trained with conventional objectives. Ablations that vary one component at a time would help establish whether gains come from complex-valued layers, bounded masks, the objective, or their combination. Results should be reported across multiple noise types and signal-to-noise ratios, with consistent data splits and enough training detail for reproduction. Objective metrics are useful, but subjective listening tests or carefully designed perceptual evaluations would strengthen claims about audible improvement. The paper should report uncertainty or variation across random seeds where feasible, rather than relying on a single run.

The authors should also discuss computational cost and inference latency, since complex-valued operations may affect deployment on real-time devices. It would be helpful to analyze failure cases, especially on unseen noise, reverberant speech, and low-energy regions. Claims about generalization should be kept proportional to the diversity of the training and test data. Finally, the paper would benefit from clearer notation and a concise explanation of how complex convolutions and mask application are implemented.

Overall, this is a promising and relevant approach with a sound motivation. Its contribution will be most convincing if the paper provides rigorous ablations, transparent implementation details, and evidence that improvements are robust and perceptually meaningful.

Exploring career options during high school can help students make thoughtful choices about their futures. Many teenagers know they have interests but are unsure how those interests might become careers. Learning about different jobs can turn vague ideas into realistic possibilities. Students can explore careers by taking classes, joining clubs, volunteering, or talking with people in different fields. These experiences help them discover what kinds of tasks they enjoy. They may also learn which activities or work environments do not suit them. This knowledge is valuable because choosing a career often involves years of education and training. Early exploration can help students select courses that support their goals. For example, someone interested in engineering might choose more classes in math and science. A student curious about health care could volunteer at a community clinic or interview a nurse. Exploring careers also helps students understand the skills employers value. They may realize that communication, teamwork, and problem-solving matter in many professions. Meeting professionals can provide useful advice and show students what a typical workday looks like. However, career exploration does not mean that students must decide on one permanent path. Interests can change as people gain new experiences and learn more about themselves. The goal is to make informed choices, not to have every detail planned before graduation. Schools and families can support students by providing career fairs, job-shadowing opportunities, and honest conversations. Ultimately, exploring career options in high school helps students feel more prepared, confident, and open-minded as they plan their next steps.

Mara sat at her kitchen table with a blank job application glowing on her laptop. The form asked her to list three strengths. She stared at the question until the words began to blur. “I’m not especially good at anything,” she murmured. Her cat blinked from the windowsill, unimpressed. Mara thought of the years she had spent helping at the neighborhood library. She had never been paid much, and the work rarely felt important. Then she remembered how she had reorganized the crowded shelves so visitors could find books faster. She remembered calming a frustrated parent whose child had lost a favorite storybook. She remembered teaching herself the library’s new computer system when everyone else was too busy. Each memory seemed small on its own. Together, they formed a picture she hadn’t expected. Mara was patient, she realized. She was organized, too. And when something needed doing, she learned how to do it. Still, doubt tugged at her as she typed the words into the application. What if the hiring manager thought they sounded ordinary? She nearly deleted them. Then she pictured the little boy clutching his recovered book and grinning. The work had mattered to him, even if no one had given her an award for it. Mara added a short example beside each strength. The blank form no longer looked like a test she was bound to fail. It looked like a chance to tell the truth. When she clicked Submit, her hands were still trembling. But beneath the fear, she felt the first quiet spark of confidence.

At midnight, Mara noticed that her reflection was still smiling.

She had stopped smiling several seconds earlier.

The bathroom was quiet except for the radiator ticking in the wall.

Mara leaned closer to the mirror, and the girl inside leaned closer too.

Then the girl’s smile faded, though Mara’s mouth had not moved.

Mara stepped back.

Her reflection stayed where it was.

For one impossible moment, the glass held a room without her.

Mara ran into the hall and called her brother.

When they returned, the mirror showed only the two of them, pale and breathless.

Her brother laughed, embarrassed for her, and went to bed.

Mara remained in the bathroom until dawn.

The next night, she covered the mirror with a towel.

At 3:17, a soft knock came from beneath it.

She tore the towel away.

Her reflection stood with one hand raised against the glass.

Mara lifted hers in answer.

The girl’s palm met the place where Mara’s palm should have been.

Their fingers did not quite line up.

“Who are you?” Mara whispered.

The reflection opened its mouth.

No sound crossed the glass.

Still, Mara understood: I am what you leave behind.

After that, she watched herself whenever she could.

She began to notice that the reflection blinked a fraction late.

Or perhaps Mara was the one who had learned to wait.

She wondered if identity was only a habit shared by two faces.

One face moved; the other agreed.

One remembered; the other borrowed the memory.

On the seventh night, Mara stood before the mirror and did nothing.

The reflection did nothing too.

Minutes passed, then hours, and the bathroom grew cold.

At last, the girl in the glass turned toward the empty doorway.

Mara stayed perfectly still.

The reflection walked out of sight.

Mara heard no footsteps beyond the mirror.

In the morning, the glass showed the bathroom, the towel, and a pale woman staring back.

Mara raised her hand.

The woman did not.

Mara smiled, because she could think of nothing else to do.

Across the glass, the woman’s eyes filled with wonder.

William Ruto’s rise to power has been shaped by political reinvention, shifting alliances and a long-running dispute over Kenya’s response to the violence that followed the 2007 election.

Ruto, born in 1966 in Kenya’s Rift Valley region, entered national politics as a youth organizer for the opposition movement that helped bring Daniel arap Moi’s rule to an end.

He won a parliamentary seat in 1997 and later held several cabinet positions, including ministerial roles under President Mwai Kibaki.

For years, Ruto was associated with the political establishment that governed Kenya after the return of multiparty politics.

His fortunes changed after the disputed December 2007 presidential election, which triggered widespread violence and left more than 1,000 people dead.

Ruto became a prominent figure in the opposition Orange Democratic Movement, or ODM, led by Raila Odinga.

The two politicians campaigned together against Kibaki, whose declared victory was challenged by Odinga and his supporters.

The election crisis ended in a power-sharing agreement, with Kibaki remaining president and Odinga becoming prime minister.

Ruto served as agriculture minister in the coalition government, but his relationship with Odinga deteriorated.

The split reflected broader rivalries over political influence, regional support and the direction of the next election campaign.

In 2010, Kenya’s constitutional referendum and the proposed new charter became another point of division.

Ruto campaigned against the constitution, while Odinga supported it.

The new constitution was approved by voters and later introduced sweeping changes to the country’s political and administrative system.

Meanwhile, the International Criminal Court began investigating alleged crimes against humanity linked to the 2007–08 violence.

The prosecutor alleged that senior political figures had helped organize attacks against civilians.

Ruto was among those charged, alongside broadcaster Joshua arap Sang.

Ruto denied the allegations and said he was innocent.

He maintained that the charges were politically motivated and rejected claims that he had orchestrated violence.

In 2011, the ICC confirmed charges against Ruto and Sang, sending the case toward trial.

The proceedings drew intense attention in Kenya, where the accused remained influential political figures.

Ruto’s legal case unfolded as he sought to build a new political coalition ahead of the 2013 election.

He joined forces with Uhuru Kenyatta, the son of Kenya’s founding president and a former rival.

Kenyatta also faced ICC charges arising from the post-election violence.

Their alliance brought together politicians from communities that had previously been on opposing sides of the conflict.

They presented themselves as partners seeking national unity and reconciliation.

Critics, however, argued that the alliance was designed in part to protect their political interests and rally voters against the ICC cases.

The two men campaigned under the Jubilee Alliance banner.

Kenyatta ran for president, with Ruto as his running mate.

They won the 2013 election, narrowly defeating Odinga in a contest that was challenged in court but ultimately upheld.

Ruto became deputy president, marking a dramatic rise from opposition organizer to one of the country’s most powerful officials.

The election victory also placed two ICC indictees at the center of Kenya’s government.

The ICC cases proceeded amid disputes over witness cooperation and the availability of evidence.

Prosecutors said intimidation and interference had made it harder to secure testimony.

Ruto and his legal team denied wrongdoing and challenged the prosecution’s evidence.

In 2014, judges terminated the case against Ruto and Sang without entering a verdict on whether they were guilty or innocent.

The court said the prosecution’s case had been undermined by the loss or recanting of witnesses and other problems.

The charges against Kenyatta were withdrawn later that year after prosecutors said they lacked sufficient evidence to proceed.

The ICC’s handling of the cases became a major issue in Kenyan politics and in debates over international justice.

Ruto and his allies said the proceedings had unfairly targeted African leaders.

Human rights groups and other observers emphasized the need for accountability for victims of the violence.

Kenya’s post-election crisis had left deep social divisions, and many survivors continued to seek justice and compensation.

As deputy president, Ruto remained a central player in national politics, even as his relationship with Kenyatta grew increasingly strained.

The Jubilee partnership that had brought them to power began to fracture during Kenyatta’s second term.

Kenyatta later reached a political rapprochement with Odinga, further isolating Ruto within the governing coalition.

Ruto responded by building a campaign around ordinary citizens, describing his movement as a “hustler” cause.

The message contrasted people struggling to earn a living with what he called a privileged political establishment.

His supporters saw the approach as an effective appeal to economic frustrations and political exclusion.

Opponents said it simplified complex problems and obscured the influence of powerful political networks.

In 2022, Ruto ran for president with Rigathi Gachagua as his running mate.

He faced Odinga, who was backed by Kenyatta after their rapprochement, and several other candidates.

The campaign centered on the cost of living, employment, corruption and the distribution of economic opportunity.

Ruto was declared the winner with about 50.5 percent of the vote.

Odinga challenged the result, but Kenya’s Supreme Court unanimously upheld it.

Ruto was sworn in as president on September 13, 2022.

His victory completed a political journey from youth organizer and opposition politician to the country’s highest office.

It also underscored how quickly Kenya’s alliances can shift as leaders pursue new constituencies and electoral strategies.

Ruto’s history with the ICC remains a defining part of that journey, though the court never ruled on the truth of the charges against him.

The cases left unresolved questions about individual responsibility for the 2007–08 violence.

They also highlighted the difficulties of prosecuting alleged crimes when witnesses are vulnerable and political pressure is intense.

As president, Ruto has spoken of unity and national renewal, while facing the challenge of addressing economic hardship and public demands for accountability.

For many Kenyans, the legacy of the 2007 election violence remains a test of whether political reconciliation can be matched by justice for victims.

A witness told a court that she saw India Chipchase drinking with a man in Northampton hours before the 20-year-old was murdered.

Chipchase, a student from Oxford, was found dead at a house in the town in January 2016. The witness said she encountered her in the early hours of the morning and believed she was intoxicated.

She described Chipchase as being with a man and said the pair appeared to be together. The account was presented during the trial of the man accused of her murder.

Prosecutors said Chipchase had been out in Northampton before going to the defendant’s home. The court heard that she was later killed there.

The witness’s evidence formed part of the prosecution’s account of Chipchase’s final hours. Jurors were asked to consider it alongside other testimony and evidence about the events leading up to her death.

The trial heard that Chipchase had been drinking before she left the town centre. The witness said she appeared unsteady and affected by alcohol.

Details of the encounter were examined as the court sought to establish how Chipchase came to be at the house. The prosecution also presented evidence about the defendant’s movements and contacts that night.

The defendant denied murdering Chipchase. The case was heard at Northampton Crown Court.

The jury was told to assess the witness’s recollection carefully, including the timing and circumstances of what she saw. The court proceedings continued with further evidence about the investigation and the discovery of Chipchase’s body.

Technology improves daily life by making many everyday tasks faster and easier. People can use smartphones to pay bills, plan routes, and stay in touch with family. Online shopping and delivery services also save time, especially for people with busy schedules. Technology supports learning by giving students access to videos, digital books, and lessons from around the world. Educational apps can help students practise skills at their own pace and get quick feedback.
