Upright ornamental grasses bring height, movement, and structure to a garden. Their narrow leaves and vertical flower stalks can soften fences, frame paths, or create a striking focal point. Many grasses also offer attractive seed heads that persist into winter. Choosing the right kind begins with understanding your climate, soil, and available space.

Check a grass’s mature height and spread before planting. Some compact varieties suit containers or small beds, while taller kinds need room to grow without crowding nearby plants. Confirm that the variety is hardy in your local climate. In regions with hot summers, also consider heat and drought tolerance.

Most ornamental grasses grow best in a spot with ample sunlight. Many need at least six hours of direct sun each day to stand upright and flower well. A few tolerate partial shade, but may grow less densely or flop more easily. Match the plant to the light conditions rather than trying to make a shade-loving site sunnier through frequent feeding.

Good drainage is important for many upright grasses. They usually adapt to a range of soil types, but persistently wet ground can damage their roots. If your soil drains poorly, consider a raised bed or a suitable container. Improve very compact soil with organic matter, while avoiding excessive soil amendment that creates a sharply different planting pocket.

Plant grasses in spring or early autumn, when moderate temperatures help roots establish. Dig a hole about as deep as the root ball and roughly twice as wide. Set the plant at the same depth it was growing in its pot, then backfill and water thoroughly. Space plants according to their mature width, leaving enough room for air movement and maintenance.

Water regularly during the first growing season, especially during dry spells. Once established, many garden grasses need less frequent watering, though needs vary by species and climate. Water deeply at the base instead of lightly sprinkling the leaves. A layer of mulch can help conserve moisture and reduce weeds, but keep it away from the plant’s crown.

Most ornamental grasses do not need rich soil or heavy fertilizing. Too much nitrogen can encourage weak, floppy growth. If growth is poor, first check sunlight, drainage, and watering before adding fertilizer. Use a modest amount of a balanced product only when soil conditions or local guidance indicate that feeding is needed.

Leave many grasses standing through winter. Their dried leaves and seed heads provide texture, shelter for wildlife, and interest when other plants have faded. In late winter or early spring, cut back deciduous grasses before fresh growth begins. Wear gloves and long sleeves, and use sharp shears; some leaf edges can be abrasive.

Avoid cutting evergreen grasses hard unless the variety can recover from it. Instead, comb out dead leaves by hand or trim damaged tips. Divide clumps every few years if the center becomes bare, flowering declines, or the plant grows beyond its space. Spring is often the best time to divide, though the ideal season depends on the species and climate.

Lift the clump carefully, remove dead or weak sections, and replant the healthy outer portions promptly. Water the divisions well while they establish. Monitor for pests and disease, but remember that grasses are generally resilient when they have suitable growing conditions. Good spacing, correct watering, and proper pruning are usually the simplest ways to keep upright ornamental grasses healthy and attractive.

VCR production has dwindled to almost nothing, marking the end of an era for a machine that once sat in millions of living rooms. The last known major manufacturer, Japan’s Funai Electric, stopped making VCRs in 2016, citing falling sales and difficulty sourcing parts. Since then, surviving machines have become increasingly dependent on secondhand markets and specialist repair shops. VHS tapes remain playable, but the equipment needed to watch them is aging and increasingly fragile. Belts, motors and other components can fail, while replacement parts grow harder to find. Some collectors and small businesses continue to repair VCRs, but the work can be costly and time-consuming. Digitizing tapes offers a way to preserve family recordings and other material before playback becomes impossible. However, transfers require functioning hardware and may not capture every detail of the original recording. Interest in VHS has also revived among collectors, drawn to its distinctive image, cover art and cultural history. That enthusiasm supports a niche market, but it is unlikely to bring mass production back. For now, VHS playback survives through careful maintenance, preservation efforts and a dwindling supply of working machines.

For three hundred years, Elias Venn had outlived every name he had ever used.

He had been a soldier, a priest, a tutor, and once, briefly, a celebrated violinist.

In every life, he learned the same lesson.

People trusted the person who remembered their birthdays.

So Elias remembered them all.

He kept a ledger of anniversaries, illnesses, quarrels, and secret debts.

It was not a diary.

It was a map of the human heart, with all its weak bridges marked.

When he entered the service of Lord Harrow, he came as a quiet secretary with careful hands.

Harrow was eighty-two, rich beyond measure, and lonely enough to mistake attention for affection.

He owned a country estate, three town houses, a private railway, and a bank that bore his name.

He also owned a sharp temper and a habit of changing his will.

Elias learned the habits first.

He discovered that Harrow ate pears after dinner, hated rain on the windows, and feared dying without a witness.

He discovered that the old man trusted his nephew, Martin, but resented Martin’s debts.

He discovered that Harrow’s doctor had once been publicly humiliated by him.

He discovered that the housekeeper, Mrs. Vale, had hidden a letter from Harrow’s late wife.

Elias made a place for every fact in his ledger.

Then he began to move the pieces.

He persuaded Harrow to invite Martin for a long stay.

He told the doctor that Harrow had been asking for a new physician.

He returned the hidden letter to the old man’s desk.

He made no claim to know where it had come from.

Harrow read it alone and wept until morning.

By breakfast, he had forgiven Mrs. Vale.

By noon, he had asked Elias to revise his will.

Elias drafted the new document with a steady hand.

Martin would inherit the estate.

The servants would receive generous pensions.

The bank would be divided among Harrow’s grandchildren.

Elias himself would receive nothing but a small annuity.

Harrow signed it.

The signature was clear, the witnesses sober, and the date undeniable.

Elias locked the will in the safe.

Then he waited.

A week later, Martin arrived with a bright smile and a stack of unpaid bills.

Harrow greeted him warmly.

Elias watched the old man’s face soften.

He felt a faint, unfamiliar pinch beneath his ribs.

He had almost forgotten what it was to feel sorry for someone.

That evening, he arranged for Martin to find a letter in the library.

It was one of Harrow’s old notes, copied in Elias’s hand, describing the nephew as a parasite.

Martin confronted his uncle before dinner.

Harrow denied writing it.

Martin accused him of lying.

The argument rose through the house like smoke.

Afterward, Harrow dismissed Martin from the estate.

The nephew left before dawn, swearing to return with lawyers.

Elias had wanted distance, not anger.

Still, the pieces had moved as expected.

The next morning, Harrow suffered a spell of dizziness.

The doctor was summoned.

He found nothing alarming, only fatigue and a heart made fragile by age.

Elias watched the physician leave.

He did not ask what the doctor had said.

That would have been too obvious.

Instead, he brought Harrow tea and spoke of the weather.

The old man asked whether the rain would last.

Elias said it would pass by evening.

It did.

Over the next month, Harrow grew weaker.

He stayed in his room and requested that Elias read aloud.

The chosen books were histories, mostly of kings who had lost their crowns.

“Do you think men deserve what they leave behind?” Harrow asked one night.

“They deserve what they earned,” Elias replied.

“And if they earned it badly?”

“Then perhaps the world should correct the account.”

Harrow looked at him for a long time.

“Have you always talked like a judge?”

“Only when I am tired.”

The old man smiled.

For a moment, Elias believed they were friends.

That was the dangerous part.

He had spent centuries learning how to wear affection.

He had not learned how to feel it without wanting something.

The new will remained in the safe.

Elias knew its contents by heart.

He also knew that Harrow’s nephew could challenge it if he suspected pressure.

So he arranged for a second will to be discussed, then rejected, in front of three servants.

That way, the house would remember Harrow’s independence.

He made sure the doctor visited often.

He made sure Mrs. Vale saw Harrow eat and sleep.

He made sure the household believed the old man was simply declining.

He did not need to hurry.

Time had always been Elias’s most patient accomplice.

One night, Harrow asked to be left alone.

Elias stood at the door.

The old man’s hands trembled on the blanket.

“Stay,” Harrow said.

Elias stayed.

They spoke until the candle burned low.

Harrow told stories about his wife, about his first business failure, and about the son he had buried as a child.

Elias listened without taking notes.

At last, Harrow asked him to promise something.

“Make certain Martin does not ruin everything.”

“I promise,” Elias said.

The old man closed his eyes.

Elias waited beside the bed until morning.

By dawn, Harrow was dead.

The doctor called it a peaceful end to a long life.

Mrs. Vale cried.

Martin arrived too late to see his uncle alive.

Elias offered him a chair and a cup of coffee.

The nephew looked at him with suspicion.

But suspicion was not proof.

The will was opened in the drawing room.

Martin inherited the estate, as Harrow had first intended.

The servants received their pensions.

The grandchildren received shares in the bank.

And Elias received the annuity, small but secure.

For several days, he considered leaving.

He had enough money to vanish into another country and begin again.

He could become Elias Venn the banker, Elias Venn the scholar, or Elias Venn the widower.

But Harrow’s promise lingered.

Martin was already speaking of selling the estate.

He planned to borrow against the bank.

He had no patience for ledgers or duty.

Elias watched him laugh at the funeral, then watched him count the silver.

The old man had been right.

Someone had to correct the account.

Elias stayed.

He helped Martin manage the estate.

He paid the servants on time and settled the doctor’s bills.

He persuaded Martin to delay the sale.

He also learned where the nephew kept his gambling debts.

Within a year, Martin had signed over the estate’s management to Elias.

Within two, he had left for the continent.

The fortune remained intact.

Elias moved into Harrow’s town house and changed nothing in the library.

He kept the ledger in the same drawer where Harrow had once hidden his letters.

Years passed.

The servants grew old, and their children took their places.

The bank prospered.

Elias did not.

His face changed only when he chose to change it.

He buried a false name beside Harrow’s, then adopted another.

At each anniversary, he placed a pear on the old man’s desk.

He told himself it was gratitude.

He told himself the fortune had been earned.

He told himself the dead could not be harmed by a useful lie.

One winter evening, he opened the ledger and found Harrow’s birthday.

Beside it, in his own handwriting, were the words, “Do not let him die alone.”

Elias closed the book.

Outside, rain tapped at the windows.

He sat in the dark and listened.

For the first time in three hundred years, he wished the night would end.

The mirror in Mara’s bathroom had begun whispering after midnight.
At first, she blamed the pipes.
Then she blamed the wind.
By the fourth night, she knew the voice was coming from inside the glass.
It spoke in her own tired, careful tone.
You left a fingerprint, it said.
Mara froze with one hand on the sink.
She had wiped the knife.
She had wiped the door.
She had wiped the whole kitchen until her knuckles split.
Still, she turned on every light and checked again.
There was nothing in the kitchen but the clock and the rain.
The clock ticked too loudly.
She returned to the bathroom.
Her reflection watched her with a faint smile.
Mara did not smile.
“You’re imagining things,” she said.
The reflection mouthed the words a breath before she did.
Mara stumbled backward.
The voice slipped through the mirror, soft as a secret.
You always say that when you’re afraid.
She slept with the bathroom door open.
At dawn, she called in sick.
She stayed home and covered the mirror with a towel.
For several hours, the apartment was quiet.
Then the towel stirred.
Mara seized the kitchen scissors and stood very still.
The fabric sagged toward the floor.
A whisper seeped through it.
He knows.
Mara dropped the scissors.
She had not heard that name spoken since the night she killed him.
She had buried the coat.
She had burned the shoes.
She had told herself the river would keep the rest.
But she had never told herself what happened to the key.
The key to the room where the man had waited.
The key was still in her desk drawer.
Mara ran to the desk and yanked it open.
The key lay there, bright and clean.
It had been missing for weeks.
She held it between two fingers.
Something scratched at the bathroom door.
She backed away, unable to breathe.
The scratching stopped.
A moment later, the bathroom door opened by itself.
The towel lay crumpled on the tiles.
The mirror was uncovered.
Mara saw herself standing inside it, pale and shaking.
Behind her reflection stood a man in a dark coat.
She spun around.
The room was empty.
When she faced the mirror again, the man had vanished.
Her reflected hand lifted.
Mara’s hand stayed at her side.
The reflected fingers tapped the glass.
Three times.
Then the voice returned.
You forgot the key.
Mara looked down.
The key was gone from her hand.
In the mirror, it hung from the reflection’s fingers.
The reflected Mara leaned closer.
Her lips moved without sound.
Mara pressed both palms to the glass.
It was warm.
The reflection pressed back.
A hairline crack appeared between their hands.
Mara tried to step away, but her feet would not move.
The crack widened with a thin, bright snap.
From the other side came the smell of wet earth.
The reflection’s face changed.
Its eyes were no longer Mara’s.
They were the dead man’s, open and accusing.
Mara screamed and struck the mirror with her fist.
The glass gave way like dark water.
Her arm plunged through to the elbow.
Cold fingers closed around her wrist.
She pulled, but the grip tightened.
In the broken surface, her reflection stood free.
It wore Mara’s face and the man’s dark coat.
“You left a fingerprint,” it said.
Mara clawed at the sink.
The reflection dragged her toward the glass.
For one final instant, she saw the bathroom from the other side.
Then the mirror swallowed her whole.
The towel drifted down over the empty frame.
By morning, the apartment was quiet again.
A new crack ran through the glass.
And behind it, someone was whispering Mara’s name.

The paper evaluates reading comprehension models using human-authored English exam questions and combines cloze tests, reasoning analysis, and studies of data informativeness. This is a timely topic, since benchmark performance can obscure whether models genuinely understand texts or exploit superficial cues. The emphasis on human-authored questions is a useful way to probe capabilities beyond those captured by automatically generated datasets. The paper’s broad evaluation design is a strength, because it examines both model outcomes and properties of the test data. In particular, the reasoning analysis could help explain why models succeed or fail rather than reducing evaluation to a single score. The informativeness studies also have potential practical value for designing more diagnostic benchmarks.

The paper would benefit from a sharper statement of its central research questions and contributions. It is not clear from the topic description how cloze performance relates to the broader exam-question evaluation, or whether these are separate experimental settings. The authors should explain the motivation for each component and how the findings jointly support the paper’s conclusions. A fuller account of the exam data is also important, including its source, size, collection procedure, and question and passage distributions. The paper should clarify how questions were selected and whether any filtering or preprocessing was applied. Because exam materials may have licensing or access restrictions, the authors should describe what data can be shared and under what conditions.

The evaluation should report appropriate baselines and give enough implementation detail for replication. Model versions, prompts, training or fine-tuning data, decoding settings, and scoring procedures should be specified. If the same exam sources or related materials appear in model training data, contamination risks should be discussed and, where possible, tested. The paper should also distinguish performance on answer selection from performance on any generated-answer task. For cloze tests, the authors should explain how blanks are chosen and whether answer options or local grammatical cues make some items easier than others. Reporting results by question type, passage length, and reasoning demand would make aggregate scores more interpretable.

The reasoning analysis is promising, but its categories need clear operational definitions. If human annotators label reasoning steps, the paper should report annotator backgrounds, agreement, and adjudication procedures. The authors should avoid treating a model’s verbal explanation as reliable evidence of its internal reasoning. Instead, explanations can be evaluated for consistency with the passage and the selected answer. The data informativeness analysis likewise needs a precise definition of informativeness and a transparent measurement procedure. It would be useful to test whether the proposed informativeness measures predict model errors or distinguish items that require different skills. Statistical uncertainty should be reported, particularly if the dataset or subgroup sizes are modest.

The discussion should acknowledge that English exam questions reflect particular educational settings and may not represent reading comprehension in general. Results should therefore be framed as evidence about the evaluated models and materials, not as a universal measure of comprehension. Overall, the topic is compelling, and the combination of benchmark evaluation, reasoning analysis, and data characterization could make a valuable contribution. My assessment is positive but provisional: the paper’s significance will depend on the clarity of its methods, the strength of its contamination and reliability checks, and the extent to which its analyses support its claims.

Staff at East Kent Hospitals University NHS Foundation Trust have reported rising levels of workplace bullying, prompting renewed concern about staff wellbeing and the trust’s working culture. The reports come as NHS organisations face wider pressure to improve how they prevent and respond to harassment and misconduct. Staff who experience bullying may face stress, reduced confidence and difficulties doing their jobs, while concerns can also affect patient care and team morale. The trust has said it recognises the seriousness of the issue and is taking steps to address it. These include encouraging staff to raise concerns and strengthening routes for reporting inappropriate behaviour. Managers are also expected to respond promptly and support those affected. The trust has highlighted training and guidance intended to help staff understand expected standards of conduct. It is also working to promote a more inclusive workplace and make clear that bullying is not acceptable. However, staff representatives and campaigners often stress that policies alone are not enough, and that people must feel safe from retaliation when speaking up. They also say investigations should be fair, timely and transparent. The trust’s efforts will be judged by whether staff see a sustained improvement in how concerns are handled and how colleagues treat one another. Continued monitoring of staff feedback could help identify where further action is needed. East Kent Hospitals has said tackling bullying remains an important part of creating a safer, more supportive environment for both staff and patients.

Choosing a Future Profession: Benefits and Challenges of Early Career Planning

Choosing a future profession is an important decision for every student. Thinking about a career early can help young people understand their interests and strengths. It also gives them time to learn about different jobs and the skills each one requires. With a clear goal, students may feel more motivated to study and gain useful experience. Early planning can also help them choose suitable school subjects or training programs. However, deciding too soon can have challenges. Students may not yet know enough about themselves or the careers available to them. Their interests can change as they grow and discover new opportunities. Pressure from family or friends may also influence their choices. A profession that seems attractive today may become less suitable later. For this reason, career planning should be flexible rather than final. Students can talk with teachers, counselors, and people who work in different fields. They can also try activities, volunteering, or part-time work to explore their options. In the end, early planning is helpful when it guides students without limiting their freedom to change direction.

Using IBM Watson to Support Creative Problem-Solving Through Biologically Inspired Design Research

Biologically inspired design begins with a practical challenge and looks to nature for useful strategies. A team might ask how to reduce building energy use, prevent a product from overheating, or move water efficiently. These questions are often difficult because relevant biological knowledge is scattered across scientific literature and described in unfamiliar terms. IBM Watson can help researchers search, organize, and interpret that information. It is an AI technology platform, not a source of guaranteed answers or a substitute for scientific judgment.

A useful first step is to define the design problem in functional terms. Instead of searching for a “better building,” a team might ask how to keep an interior cool with minimal energy. This wording can connect the challenge to biological functions such as reflecting heat, controlling airflow, or regulating temperature. Watson-based language tools can help identify key concepts and related phrases in research documents. Search and question-answering tools can then surface potentially relevant articles, passages, and findings.

Researchers can compare these findings to identify biological strategies, sometimes called principles or mechanisms. For example, studies of termite mounds may prompt questions about passive ventilation in buildings. The comparison is an analogy to investigate, not proof that copying a natural structure will work. Teams should check the original sources, examine the conditions in which a mechanism operates, and note uncertainties. Watson may assist with summarizing documents or grouping similar concepts, but summaries need verification against the full text.

The next step is translating a biological insight into an engineering concept. A team might ask which features of a natural ventilation system are essential and which can be adapted to a building. Designers can sketch alternatives, model their performance, and test prototypes. Watson can support brainstorming by suggesting related concepts or helping teams explore different search paths. It should not be treated as an independent inventor, and its suggestions may be incomplete, outdated, or misleading.

Good research practice is essential throughout the process. Teams should use trustworthy sources, record citations, and distinguish established findings from hypotheses. They should also consider practical constraints, including cost, safety, materials, maintenance, and environmental impact. AI tools can reflect gaps or biases in their training data, so researchers should seek diverse evidence and expert review. Sensitive or unpublished information should not be entered into a system unless its privacy and data-use terms are appropriate.

The strongest workflow combines AI-assisted discovery with human expertise and physical testing. Watson can help people move through large collections of text more efficiently, while biologists, engineers, and designers judge what is relevant. The result is not simply a product that resembles an organism, but a solution informed by how nature achieves a useful function. By making biological knowledge easier to explore, IBM Watson can support more imaginative and evidence-based problem-solving.

The paper tackles an ambitious problem: learning to solve the Rubik’s Cube through reinforcement learning without relying on cube-specific heuristics. Its combination of neural guidance and search is potentially valuable, especially if the method generalizes beyond hand-engineered puzzle strategies. The paper is clearly motivated and gives readers a useful overview of the challenges posed by the cube’s large state space and sparse rewards. However, the central claim of being free from domain-specific knowledge needs a precise definition. The authors should distinguish knowledge built into the action representation, reward function, simulator, search procedure, and training curriculum. In particular, cube move rules and any state encoding are forms of structural information, even if they are not solving heuristics. The experimental section would be stronger with comparisons against established search-based solvers and relevant learned methods under matched computational budgets. It should also report training time, inference cost, memory use, and the number of environment interactions. Success rates alone are insufficient; solution lengths and performance across difficulty levels should be reported as well. The paper would benefit from ablations that isolate the effects of the neural network, search, reward design, and curriculum. Robustness tests on previously unseen scrambles and longer solution horizons would help establish whether the approach has learned transferable guidance rather than memorized common patterns. The authors should clarify how training and evaluation scrambles are generated and ensure that the test set is independent. Reproducibility would improve with details on network architecture, optimization settings, search parameters, and random seeds. If the method sometimes fails, an analysis of failure cases could reveal whether errors arise from poor value estimates, search limits, or exploration. The paper’s claim of solving the cube should also be qualified if solutions are not guaranteed or optimal. Overall, the work is promising, but stronger baselines, clearer accounting of embedded domain knowledge, and more comprehensive evaluation are needed to support its conclusions. I recommend revision before acceptance.

Heavy metals can accumulate in agricultural soils and enter vegetables through their roots or, in some cases, through particles deposited on leaves. In Castellón, Spain, vegetable farms may be affected by both natural geology and human activities, including traffic, industry, irrigation, and the historical use of certain fertilizers or pesticides. The presence of a metal in soil does not automatically mean that crops are unsafe. Risk depends on its concentration, chemical form, soil conditions, crop type, and how much produce people consume.

Commonly monitored elements include cadmium, lead, arsenic, mercury, copper, nickel, chromium, and zinc. Copper and zinc are essential nutrients at low levels but can harm plants and soil organisms when concentrations become excessive. Cadmium and lead are of particular concern because they can be toxic and may accumulate in edible parts of some crops. Arsenic and chromium require careful interpretation because toxicity depends strongly on their chemical forms.

Plants take up metals dissolved in soil water, with uptake influenced by acidity, organic matter, clay content, and competing nutrients. Acidic soils often make cadmium and some other metals more available to roots. Leafy vegetables can be exposed through both root uptake and dust settling on foliage, while fruiting crops may transfer smaller amounts into their edible fruits. Washing produce can remove surface soil and dust, but it cannot remove metals already absorbed into plant tissue.

Soil contamination benchmarks are screening tools, not universal declarations of safety or danger. Applicable limits vary by jurisdiction, land use, soil properties, and the purpose of the assessment. In Spain, assessments should use current regional and national rules, including the relevant soil-quality criteria, and should distinguish investigation thresholds from legal limits for food. Food safety is assessed separately under applicable European Union contaminant regulations, which set maximum levels for certain metals in particular foods.

Reliable assessment starts with a sampling plan that represents different fields, soil depths, and management areas. Samples should be analyzed by an accredited laboratory using validated methods, and results should report units, such as milligrams per kilogram of dry soil, alongside the analytical method. Testing edible crops as well as soil can clarify whether contamination is reaching the food supply. Repeated sampling helps distinguish persistent contamination from short-term variation and tracks whether management changes are working.

When results exceed relevant screening values, farmers should confirm the findings and seek advice from agricultural or environmental specialists before making changes. Options may include adjusting soil pH, improving organic matter management, controlling contaminated dust, changing irrigation sources, or selecting crops that accumulate less of the metal in edible portions. These measures need site-specific evaluation because some amendments can reduce one metal’s availability while increasing another’s. Clear communication of test results and compliance with current regulations help protect farm workers, consumers, and the long-term productivity of Castellón’s vegetable-growing soils.

The rain had followed Sergeant Vale all the way from the border. It tapped at the windows of the Lantern House while he sat beneath them, nursing a cup of bitter ale. His boots steamed by the hearth, and every bone in his body seemed to have marched a hundred miles. Across the room, his soldiers were making up for the silence of the road.

They had filled the public house with laughter, boots, and the sour smell of wet wool. Corporal Hobb was singing a song about a duchess who had never existed. Pike, who had, in fact, met a duchess once, kept correcting the verses. Each correction grew louder than the last.

“You said she wore a silver crown,” Pike shouted. “She wore a blue hat!”

“A blue hat can be a silver crown if you’ve had enough,” Hobb replied.

The soldiers howled. Someone struck the table with a tankard, and foam leapt across the boards. Vale closed his eyes, hoping the argument would burn itself out.

Instead, Hobb shoved Pike’s shoulder. Pike shoved back, harder. Their bench scraped across the floor, and a clay jug toppled, bursting at the feet of a nervous serving girl.

The room quieted for one breath. Then three soldiers began shouting at once, each certain the others had started it. Hobb rose, knocking his chair into a neighboring table. A broad-shouldered mercenary named Brant stood to help him—or to help himself, Vale couldn’t tell.

The publican reached for the bell beneath the counter. Vale opened his eyes.

“Sit down,” he said.

No one heard him. Or no one wished to.

He stood, and his knees complained. He did not raise his voice. He simply placed one hand on Hobb’s shoulder and the other against Brant’s chest.

The men stopped as if a rope had gone taut around them. Vale looked first at Hobb, then at Pike, then at the broken jug. “You’ll pay for that,” he said.

Hobb glanced at the serving girl. His face reddened beneath his beard. “Aye, Sergeant.”

“And you’ll apologize.”

Hobb turned to Pike. “Sorry I pushed you.”

Pike rubbed his shoulder. “Sorry I pushed you harder.”

“Good,” Vale said. “Now sit before I remember you’re both old enough to know better.”

A few soldiers snickered. Vale looked toward them, and the laughter died politely.

The publican lowered his hand from the bell. The serving girl fetched a broom, but Vale took it from her and began sweeping the shards himself.

“Sergeant, you don’t have to,” she said.

“I know,” he replied. “That’s why I can.”

Pike paid for the jug. Hobb added a coin for the spilled ale, and Brant, who had apparently been standing for no reason at all, bought the serving girl a hot pie.

The soldiers settled back into their seats. Their voices returned, but softer now, and the duchess acquired a green hat in the next verse.

Vale returned to his corner and lowered himself onto the bench. His ale had gone cold. The rain still tapped at the glass, steady as a drummer keeping time for an army too tired to march.

For a little while, nobody argued. Then Hobb began the song again, quietly enough that even the duchess might have forgiven him.

Researchers have identified genetic variants associated with several aspects of human facial shape, adding to evidence that DNA helps influence how faces develop. The findings come from studies comparing genetic data with detailed facial measurements in large groups of volunteers. Researchers linked variations near particular genes to features such as the width of the nose, the shape of the chin and the spacing between facial landmarks. The results do not point to single genes that determine a person’s appearance; facial traits are shaped by many genes as well as age, environment and other factors. Scientists say the work could eventually improve understanding of facial development and conditions that affect it. It may also inform forensic research into whether DNA can provide clues about a person’s likely appearance. However, experts caution that current genetic evidence cannot reliably reconstruct an individual’s face from a DNA sample. Predictions may be especially uncertain across populations that are underrepresented in genetic studies. Researchers say any forensic use would require further validation, careful assessment of accuracy and strong privacy safeguards. For now, the findings are best viewed as a step toward understanding the complex biology behind human facial diversity.

During a crowded climbing season on Mount Everest, several climbers have died amid difficult weather and heavy traffic near the summit. The deaths underscore the risks of attempting the world’s highest peak, where thin air, freezing temperatures and sudden storms can turn dangerous quickly. Long queues have formed on narrow sections of the route, leaving climbers exposed at high altitude for extended periods. Rescue efforts are complicated by the mountain’s extreme conditions and the limited ability to move people above base camp. Authorities and expedition operators have urged climbers to follow weather forecasts and turn back when conditions deteriorate. They have also emphasized the importance of adequate preparation, experienced guides and appropriate oxygen supplies. The precise circumstances surrounding each death may differ, and officials are working to confirm details. The incidents have renewed calls for better management of permits and climber safety during busy seasons.

A compressed four-day school schedule can offer meaningful benefits for students. Instead of attending school five days a week, students spend longer hours in class on four days and have an additional day off. When planned carefully, this schedule can support productivity, health, and relationships.

One benefit is that students may become more productive. Longer class periods can give them more time to focus on a topic without frequent interruptions. Teachers can use the extra time for discussions, projects, and hands-on activities. Students may also have more opportunities to finish assignments during class. With a full day away from school, they can use their time to review lessons, read, or work on personal projects. The longer weekend may help them return to school feeling refreshed and ready to learn. However, schools need to make sure that longer days do not become tiring or overwhelming.

A four-day schedule can also support students’ health. An extra weekday off can provide more time for sleep, exercise, and medical appointments. Students who feel less rushed may have more time to eat well and take care of themselves. The additional day can also offer a chance to relax and manage stress. Instead of trying to fit every activity into evenings, students may have more control over their schedules. Still, longer school days could leave some students tired, so schools should include breaks and reasonable workloads.

Relationships may improve as well. Students can spend more time with family members, including those they might otherwise see only briefly. The extra day can make it easier to visit relatives, help at home, or take part in community activities. Students may also use the time to strengthen friendships through shared hobbies and plans. For families with busy schedules, having a weekday available together can be especially valuable. Schools should consider that some students may depend on school for meals, supervision, or social support.

A compressed four-day schedule is not automatically right for every school. Its success depends on thoughtful planning, strong teaching, and support for students’ needs. Schools should listen to students, families, and staff before making a change. If the schedule balances longer classes with enough rest, it can help students learn effectively, care for their health, and build stronger relationships.

The first dead man stood up during the evening news.

He had been laid out beneath a sheet in the lobby of St. Agnes Hospital, where the power had failed and the elevators had stopped between floors. A nurse screamed, and someone else ran. By midnight, the streets were full of people running in every direction.

Mara locked the door of her corner store and watched the crowd through the glass. A boy pounded on the window, one hand pressed to his bloody cheek. Behind him, the dead moved in a slow, stumbling tide.

Her brother Eli said not to open the door. He had a shotgun and a reason: their mother had turned that afternoon, and he had been the one to stop her. Mara could still hear the shot whenever the shop went quiet.

The boy’s name was Tomas. He had lost his father in the crowd and was too terrified to move. Mara unlocked the door.

Eli raised the shotgun, then lowered it. Tomas slipped inside, and the dead slammed against the glass behind him.

For a while, the three of them shared cans of peaches and listened to the city break apart. People fought over bottled water at the pharmacy. A man tried to force his way into the store, shouting that his family needed food.

Eli aimed at him through the door. Mara stood beside her brother and saw the same fear in both their faces.

Then Tomas lifted his small hands and offered the man half his peaches. The stranger stopped shouting. He sat on the pavement and began to cry.

That night, the power returned for three minutes. In the sudden light, Mara saw dozens of neighbors gathered around the store, some living, some dead, all pressing close.

Eli opened the back door. They let the living ones in, one by one, and kept the shotgun pointed at the rest.

By dawn, the store was crowded and the food was nearly gone. No one knew what the morning would bring.

But when the next scream rose from the street, every hand reached for someone else before it reached for a weapon.

The paper addresses an important problem: reducing neural network size and computation through ternary quantization while maintaining competitive accuracy. Its comparison of training methods with existing approaches could be valuable, particularly if it covers representative models, datasets, and quantization baselines. The authors should clearly define the ternary quantization scheme, including its thresholds, scaling factors, and whether activations as well as weights are quantized. The experimental setup needs enough detail to ensure reproducibility, such as optimizer settings, training schedules, random seeds, and hardware. Results should include multiple runs or uncertainty estimates, since small accuracy differences may not be meaningful otherwise. In addition to accuracy, the paper should report practical measures such as model size, inference latency, and computational cost, and explain how these were measured. The discussion would benefit from analyzing when each training method succeeds or fails, rather than presenting aggregate results alone. Claims of superiority should be carefully qualified if baselines use different architectures, tuning budgets, or evaluation conditions. Overall, the topic is promising, but the paper’s contribution will depend on rigorous, fair comparisons and clear evidence that its methods offer benefits beyond accuracy alone.

Taking initiative means choosing to act instead of waiting for someone else to solve a problem. It begins when we notice what needs to be done and decide that our effort can make a difference. Setting a goal gives that effort direction. Whether the goal is personal or shared, progress often starts with one small step.

For example, a student who wants to improve at a subject can make a study plan and ask questions when confused. The student might also invite classmates to study together. This takes initiative because it turns a challenge into an opportunity to learn. Consistent effort can help everyone in the group grow.

Initiative is especially meaningful when it is guided by kindness. Kindness helps us notice how other people feel and what they may need. A simple act, such as listening carefully or offering help, can make someone feel less alone. These actions may seem small, but they can improve another person’s day.

Service is another way to put initiative into practice. Students can volunteer at community events, help younger children with reading, or organize a collection for people in need. They do not need to wait for a perfect plan or a special title. They can begin by asking what would be useful and offering their time.

Taking action also requires responsibility. Good intentions matter, but we should follow through on our promises. If a plan does not work, we can listen to feedback and try a different approach. Being willing to learn helps our efforts become more helpful.

Sometimes people hesitate because they fear making mistakes or being ignored. However, no one has to accomplish everything alone. We can ask others to join us, share ideas, and support one another. Working together often makes a difficult goal easier to reach.

Initiative does not always lead to quick results. A kind habit or service project may take time to make a lasting difference. Still, every thoughtful action can encourage others to care and contribute. One person’s example can inspire a group to act.

We can take initiative in ordinary moments as well. We can include someone who is left out, thank a person who has helped us, or clean up a shared space without being asked. These choices show respect for others and for our community. They also remind us that service is not limited to large projects.

Ultimately, taking initiative connects our goals with the well-being of others. When we act with kindness, our achievements become more meaningful. We learn that success is not only about what we accomplish for ourselves, but also about how we help people along the way. By noticing needs, choosing to act, and continuing to serve, each of us can make life better for others.

The paper addresses an important question: whether convolutional neural networks capture aspects of biological shape perception, especially when image averaging alters discriminability. Its central comparison is compelling, but the methods should clearly specify the averaging procedure, stimulus controls, model architectures, and evaluation metrics so readers can assess whether observed effects reflect shape information rather than low-level image statistics. The analysis would be strengthened by testing multiple levels of averaging and reporting uncertainty across both human participants and model runs. The discussion should distinguish evidence of behavioral similarity from claims about shared underlying mechanisms, since similar performance does not establish biological plausibility. Overall, the work has promise, and clearer methodological detail and more cautious interpretation would make its contribution stronger.

The paper addresses an important problem: how to infer rewards that vary with context from expert behavior when decisions are subject to constraints. Its applications to driving and sepsis treatment offer a compelling test of whether the method can transfer across domains with very different risks and data characteristics. The central contribution is potentially valuable, especially if the approach distinguishes genuine preferences from actions imposed by safety or resource constraints. The paper would be stronger with a clearer formal definition of context-dependent rewards and an explanation of how those rewards are identifiable from observed behavior. Please specify the assumptions required about the expert’s rationality, knowledge of constraints, and consistency across contexts. A key concern is whether the method can separate reward changes from changes in the feasible action set or transition dynamics. The experimental section should compare against strong inverse reinforcement learning and imitation-learning baselines, including methods that model constraints explicitly. Ablations could clarify the contributions of context, constraint modeling, and any representation-learning components. For the driving study, report performance across varied scenarios and discuss how the method handles rare but safety-critical events. For the sepsis application, provide details on cohort construction, missing-data handling, treatment timing, and potential confounding in the observational data. Since clinicians’ actions may reflect institutional practice rather than patient-specific utility, this distinction deserves particular attention. Evaluation should include uncertainty and calibration, not only average reward or policy performance. The paper should also assess sensitivity to reward misspecification and distribution shift, since both are likely in deployment. Claims about clinical or driving utility should be carefully bounded unless supported by prospective or otherwise rigorous validation. Overall, the topic is promising, but stronger identifiability analysis, domain-specific evaluation, and discussion of safety and confounding are needed to establish the method’s reliability.

People often judge others quickly based on their appearance, behavior, or first words. These first impressions can be unfair because they reveal only a small part of a person. Someone who seems shy may be thoughtful, while someone who appears confident may be nervous inside. Although it can be discouraging to be misunderstood, a person can work to change others’ opinions over time. Persistence is important because trust usually grows through repeated interactions. By keeping promises and treating people with respect, someone can show that they are dependable. Personal growth also helps people overcome negative impressions. A person who listens to feedback can recognize habits that may have caused misunderstandings. They can then practice communicating more clearly and responding with patience. However, they should not change who they are just to please everyone. Instead, they can improve while staying true to their values. In time, consistent actions may help others see beyond their first impression and recognize the person they truly are.

In-person classes and business meetings continue to offer important advantages over online alternatives. Digital tools make it easy to connect from almost anywhere, but a screen cannot always replace being in the same room. Face-to-face interaction often makes communication clearer and more engaging. People can notice facial expressions, gestures, and changes in tone more easily in person. These cues help prevent misunderstandings and show how others are responding. In a classroom, students can ask questions as soon as they become confused. Teachers can also adjust their explanations when they see that students need more help. Classmates may find it easier to join discussions when they can respond naturally to one another. This kind of conversation can make lessons more memorable. In-person classes also provide a regular routine. Traveling to a classroom and learning alongside others can help students focus. At home, online learners may face distractions such as phones, household noise, or other responsibilities. Meeting in person can help students feel connected to a school community. They can build friendships and work together on projects more easily. Business meetings can benefit from the same personal connection. When colleagues meet face to face, they can build trust through direct conversation. It may be easier to discuss complicated ideas when everyone can share a room and use a whiteboard or physical materials. Participants can often tell when a point needs more explanation. In-person meetings can also encourage people to contribute instead of quietly multitasking. Informal conversations before or after a meeting may lead to useful ideas and stronger professional relationships. Still, online classes and meetings have clear benefits, including convenience and reduced travel. They can be especially helpful for people who live far apart or have limited mobility. The best choice depends on the purpose, participants, and circumstances. However, when direct interaction, cooperation, and concentration matter most, meeting in person can be especially valuable. For these reasons, in-person classes and business meetings remain a strong option alongside online alternatives.

Benefits of Gaining Work Experience Before Starting College

Gaining work experience before starting college can be a valuable step for many students. A job introduces young people to responsibilities they may not encounter in school. It also helps them learn more about themselves and the kind of future they want. Although working before college can be challenging, the benefits can last for years.

One major benefit is learning practical skills. Students with jobs often practice communication, teamwork, problem-solving, and time management. They learn how to speak respectfully with coworkers, supervisors, and customers. These skills can help them succeed in college classes and group projects. Work experience can also teach students how to handle feedback and improve after making mistakes.

A job can help students become more independent. They must arrive on time, complete tasks, and take responsibility for their choices. Earning a paycheck can also teach them how to budget and save money. Some students use their earnings to pay for books, tuition, or other college expenses. Even a small amount of savings can reduce financial pressure.

Work can also help students explore possible careers. A student who works in a clinic, shop, or office may discover interests they had not considered before. They may also learn which types of tasks or workplaces do not suit them. This understanding can make it easier to choose a college major or career path. In addition, work experience can strengthen a résumé and show future employers that a student is dependable.

However, working before college is not helpful if it leaves a student exhausted or unable to prepare for school. Students should look for a reasonable schedule and make time for rest. They should also consider unpaid opportunities, such as volunteering or job shadowing, if a paid position is not available. The most important thing is to learn from the experience rather than simply hold a job.

Overall, gaining work experience before starting college can build confidence, useful skills, and financial awareness. It can also help students make more informed decisions about their education and careers. With a healthy balance, a job can serve as an important first step toward adult life.

For years, Celia Voss married lonely billionaires, vanished with their jewels, and left behind forged signatures. Her newest target, Adrian Vale, owned a shipping empire and a mansion full of locked rooms. Celia planned to marry him on Friday, collect a fortune, and disappear before sunrise. But Adrian’s suspicious daughter, Mara, had already hired a detective. On the wedding day, Mara slipped a folder of Celia’s old marriage records beneath the cake. When Adrian opened it, the string quartet stopped mid-song. Celia smiled and claimed the papers were fakes, just as her former husband burst through the doors. Behind him came two more ex-husbands, each shouting a different accusation. Guests scrambled as a waiter dropped a tray, setting off a chain reaction of champagne glasses and toppled candles. Adrian tried to calm everyone, but a curtain caught fire and the fire alarm drenched the ballroom. In the confusion, Celia grabbed a suitcase she thought held cash. It held only Adrian’s collection of antique clocks, which chimed wildly as she stumbled down the stairs. Mara blocked the exit with the detective and a pair of police officers. Celia’s fortunes vanished in the chaos, and her only inheritance was a very public reputation.

The news came on just as Mia was buttering her toast.
“Scientists say Santa Claus cannot possibly visit every home in one night,” announced the television reporter.
Mia’s knife stopped in midair.
She looked at her father.
“Dad, does this mean Santa isn’t real?”
Her father lowered his newspaper with the solemnity of a judge.
“First, we must examine the evidence,” he said.
Mia slid off her chair and hurried to the living room.
She returned with a crumpled list of reasons.
“Santa has a sleigh, reindeer, and a magic sack,” she read.
“Also, he knows when we’re sleeping.”
Her father nodded thoughtfully.
“Those are strong credentials.”
“But the reporter said there are billions of children.”
“An excellent point,” he said.
He pulled a calculator from the junk drawer.
“Let’s see: if Santa visits every house for one second, he’ll need…” He tapped the buttons.
The calculator displayed a string of numbers and then went blank.
“It appears the calculator has fainted,” he said.
Mia giggled, but her worry stayed.
“Maybe the reindeer fly really fast?”
“Possibly,” said Dad.
“Or perhaps Santa has helpers.”
He glanced toward the kitchen, where the dog was trying to eat a sock.
“Though I wouldn’t trust that particular helper with the cookies.”
Mia leaned against the couch.
“What if the news is right?”
Her father sat beside her.
“News reporters are very good at counting houses,” he said.
“They’re less good at counting magic.”
He explained that some questions were too large for ordinary math.
Mia considered this.
“Like how many sprinkles fit on one cupcake?”
“Exactly,” Dad said.
“Or how you can love someone more every day without running out.”
She smiled a little.
“But how does Santa get down the chimney?”
“Carefully,” said Dad.
“And with excellent chimney insurance.”
“What if there’s no chimney?”
“He uses the front door, the back door, or whatever door isn’t guarded by a suspicious dog.”
The dog barked at the television.
Dad pointed at him.
“See? Santa’s toughest security challenge.”
Mia laughed out loud this time.
Her father reached for his coffee.
“Besides, believing in Santa isn’t only about one man and a sleigh.”
“It’s about people leaving surprises and being kind without asking for credit.”
“Like when you put a present under Grandma’s tree?”
“Exactly,” he said.
“And like when someone eats the last cookie so no one else has to worry about it.”
Mia narrowed her eyes.
“Was that you?”
“I cannot confirm or deny an ongoing cookie investigation.”
She laughed again, and the knot in her stomach loosened.
“So Santa might still be real?”
“Maybe,” Dad said.
“And maybe the truth is bigger than the television can fit into a report.”
Mia picked up her toast.
“I think I’ll leave him two cookies this year.”
“Wise,” said Dad.
“Then he won’t have to investigate the empty plate.”
That night, Mia placed the cookies by the tree.
Her father put out a glass of milk.
The dog stationed himself nearby, pretending to be asleep.
“Do you think Santa will come?” Mia whispered.
Dad tucked her blanket under her chin.
“I think he’d be foolish to miss those cookies.”
Mia closed her eyes, smiling.
From the living room came a tiny clink.
Dad stepped into the hall and whispered, “Nice try, dog.”
The dog sighed, and somewhere outside, a sleigh bell rang.

When Mara was seventeen, she dyed her hair blue and left home with a borrowed motorcycle and no map. Her mother called it a phase, which was true but not the whole truth. Mara had wanted to outrun every name adults had given her. She slept beneath bridges, sang in basements, and traded poems for meals. Once, during a storm, she helped a stranger repair a broken hand-cranked radio. The stranger was old and quiet, with silver rings on every finger. He told her that people were most themselves when they made something useful for someone else. Mara laughed and said that sounded like advice from a person who owned a toolbox. Years later, she remembered his words whenever she fixed a neighbor’s sink or stayed up with a feverish child.

Now that child, Jun, stood in the kitchen wearing a translucent breathing veil. Beyond the window, the city’s towers glowed with gardens grown in artificial sunlight. The sea had climbed the old boardwalk, and drones carried groceries over the flooded streets. Jun had chosen to join the Adaptation, a process that would reshape their body to thrive in the changing climate. Their skin would sense heat, their lungs would filter salt, and their eyes would see in the dim green of underwater farms. Mara had signed the consent papers, though her hand had trembled. She still remembered the stubborn girl who had refused every door marked “safe.” “Are you afraid?” she asked. Jun turned the veil’s tiny blue lights toward her. “A little,” they said. “But I’m more afraid of living in a world I can’t help.” Mara felt the answer settle inside her, heavy and bright.

She wanted to tell Jun that humanity meant staying unchanged, keeping the old body and old songs. But the words felt smaller than the room. Her own body had changed too: one knee ached in winter, and a patch of silver hair had spread above her ear. Humanity, she thought, could not be a shape preserved behind glass. Perhaps it was the part of us that reached for another hand, even when the hand was strange. She took Jun’s fingers, warm beneath the veil. “Then go carefully,” she said. “And remember to help someone fix a radio.” Jun laughed, and the sound was exactly the one Mara had heard in herself at seventeen. At dawn, they entered the clinic together. Outside, rain swept through the city, carrying the scent of salt and new leaves. For once, Mara did not try to outrun the future.

Paramedics provide urgent medical care before and during transport to a hospital. Their responsibilities include assessing patients, stabilizing life-threatening conditions, and deciding which care and transport options are appropriate. They gather information about symptoms, medical history, medications, allergies, and the events leading to the emergency. They also communicate clearly with patients, family members, dispatchers, and receiving clinicians. Because emergencies can be stressful, paramedics must remain calm, professional, and attentive to patient dignity and consent.

Medication safety begins by confirming the right patient, medication, dose, route, and time. Paramedics should check allergies, indications, contraindications, expiration dates, and relevant vital signs before giving a medication. They must follow local protocols and authorized medical direction, and clarify any unclear order. Medication names and concentrations can look or sound alike, so careful label checks help prevent mix-ups. After administration, they monitor the patient for benefits and adverse reactions and document the medication, dose, route, time, and response.

Accurate dosage calculations are essential because errors can cause serious harm. A common formula is dose to give equals the prescribed dose divided by the concentration available, multiplied by the volume containing that concentration. For weight-based dosing, first convert the patient’s weight to the units required by the protocol, then calculate the dose and check any maximum limit. Use the correct units throughout, distinguish milligrams from micrograms, and verify decimal placement. When possible, have another qualified clinician independently check a calculation, especially for high-risk medications.

Patient care competencies include clinical assessment, sound decision-making, safe procedures, and ongoing reassessment. Paramedics need skills in airway management, CPR, bleeding control, and the use of monitoring equipment, as well as training for age-specific and special patient needs. They should recognize changes in a patient’s condition and adjust care promptly within their scope of practice. Accurate records and clear handovers support continuity of care. Regular practice, continuing education, and honest review of mistakes help paramedics maintain safe, effective care.

Maya Chen had prepared for her career meeting for three weeks. She had charts, a five-year plan, and a blazer that made her look “decisive but approachable.” At nine sharp, she strode into Conference Room B. A gray-haired man sat at the table, reading her résumé upside down. “You must be Martin,” she said, extending a hand. “And you must be Maya,” he replied, shaking it warmly. Martin was the company’s new chief executive, though Maya had only seen his portrait on the website. She launched into her presentation before he could ask a question. “I’ve increased our team’s efficiency by twelve percent,” she said, clicking to a slide titled “Why I Deserve More Responsibility.” Martin nodded thoughtfully. “Impressive,” he said. “Tell me about your approach to managing people.” Maya explained her weekly check-ins, shared spreadsheets, and strict policy against meetings that could have been emails. “I especially admire your courage,” Martin said. Maya blinked. “My courage?” “Yes, coming in here to discuss the department’s future without waiting for an invitation.” Maya assumed he was complimenting her initiative. She leaned forward and described her plan to reorganize the company’s customer support division. Martin listened closely, occasionally making notes on the back of her résumé. At last, he stood and offered his hand again. “You’ve convinced me,” he said. Maya’s heart raced. “You’ll have the promotion by Monday.” She nearly dropped her laptop. “That’s wonderful, but I thought we were discussing my role in the marketing team.” Martin paused. “Marketing?” “I’m Maya Chen, the junior analyst.” He looked at the résumé, then at her. “You’re not Maya Chen, the director of customer support?” Maya glanced at the nameplate beside the door. It read “Conference Room B: Executive Search Panel.” The gray-haired man stared at the document he’d been reading upside down. “I’m afraid I may have taken the wrong meeting,” he said. At that moment, a woman in a bright red scarf rushed in, carrying a folder. “Martin, sorry I’m late,” she said. “I’m Maya Chen, the customer support director.” Martin turned to the newcomer, then back to the junior analyst. “Well,” he said, “this is awkward.” The director laughed. “Only if she’s already reorganized my department.” “Not yet,” Maya said. “But I have a slide.” The room erupted in laughter, including Martin, who looked more relieved than embarrassed. He explained that the executive search panel had been interviewing candidates for a new operations manager. Maya’s presentation, though intended for her own career meeting, had answered nearly every question they’d planned to ask. The director praised her practical ideas and offered to sponsor a pilot project. Martin added that the company was creating a temporary role to test the reorganization. “Would you like to lead it?” he asked. Maya glanced at her carefully prepared charts, then at the promotion letter he had accidentally placed on the table. “Yes,” she said, “but could we make sure it has my name on it this time?” Martin checked the letter, crossed out “Martin Chen,” and wrote “Maya Chen” in bold. By Monday, Maya was leading the pilot, and her blazer had become a company legend. The only thing she hadn’t planned for was the title: Acting Director of Meetings That Could Have Been Emails.

Shuanglin Temple, located near the ancient city of Pingyao in Shanxi Province, is renowned for its remarkable collection of Buddhist clay sculptures. The temple’s origins are traditionally traced to the Northern Wei dynasty, though its surviving buildings and sculptures mostly date from later periods. Much of the complex was rebuilt during the Ming and Qing dynasties, when artisans created and restored many of its figures. Across the temple’s halls are more than 2,000 painted clay sculptures, depicting Buddhas, bodhisattvas, guardians, and other Buddhist figures. Their expressive faces, varied poses, and detailed clothing make the collection especially vivid. The sculptures were shaped from clay, finished with fine details, and painted in rich colors. They reflect the skill of local craftsmen and the influence of Buddhist art across different eras. Shuanglin Temple is part of the UNESCO-listed Ancient City of Pingyao, recognized for preserving the region’s architectural and cultural heritage. Today, the temple offers visitors a rare chance to see Buddhist sculpture in its original religious setting.

Catalonia’s unofficial independence vote proceeded today despite Spain’s legal opposition, bringing a long-running dispute over the region’s future into the streets. Organizers urged residents to answer whether Catalonia should become an independent state, while Spanish authorities maintained that the ballot had no legal standing. The vote exposed deep divisions within Catalonia as well as the broader conflict between regional demands and Spain’s constitutional order.

Polling stations opened across the northeastern region amid uncertainty over how many people would take part. Volunteers helped voters find their names on lists and guided them through an informal voting process. Some locations were set up in schools and public buildings, reflecting the decentralized effort to hold the ballot. Organizers said the turnout would demonstrate the strength of public support for self-determination.

The Spanish government had opposed the vote in advance, arguing that decisions about national sovereignty must follow the constitution. Courts had also ruled against the referendum, and officials said the organizers lacked authority to stage it. Madrid urged residents not to treat the ballot as binding. Catalan leaders, however, said the vote was a legitimate expression of political opinion, even if Spain refused to recognize it.

The dispute has sharpened tensions between the regional government in Barcelona and the central government in Madrid. Catalan independence supporters say the region has a distinct language, culture and history, and should be able to choose its political future. Many also argue that Catalonia contributes more to Spain’s public finances than it receives in return. Opponents of secession counter that the region benefits from being part of Spain and that separation could bring economic uncertainty and isolation.

Public opinion within Catalonia remains divided. Supporters of independence have organized large demonstrations in recent years, but many residents favor remaining within Spain or want a negotiated settlement rather than a unilateral break. Some voters see the ballot as a useful way to register their views, regardless of its legal status. Others have stayed away, saying an unofficial vote cannot resolve such a consequential question.

The ballot’s outcome may be difficult to interpret because participation is voluntary and the process lacks the safeguards of a formal election. Organizers are responsible for administering the vote and reporting the results. Spanish authorities have questioned the credibility of a process they say is unauthorized. Independent verification may also be limited.

The immediate political consequences remain uncertain. A strong turnout could strengthen the hand of Catalan leaders pressing for negotiations with Madrid, but it would not automatically change the region’s status. A low turnout could be cited by opponents as evidence that the independence movement lacks broad support. Both sides are likely to frame the results in terms that advance their positions.

European officials have generally called for the dispute to be handled within Spain’s constitutional framework. They have also emphasized the importance of dialogue and respect for the rule of law. Any move toward independence would raise difficult questions about the region’s relationship with Spain and its future place in the European Union.

For now, the vote has underscored how far apart the two sides remain. Catalan organizers say the ballot gives residents a chance to be heard; Madrid says it cannot substitute for a lawful referendum. The divide is visible not only between Barcelona and the central government, but among neighbors, families and political parties across the region. As voting continues, the central question is whether the confrontation will lead to talks or deepen a crisis that has resisted compromise.

At seventeen, Eli believed freedom was something his father kept locked in the house. Every rule felt like another bar across the window: curfew, chores, school, the old pickup keys hung out of reach. His father, Tom, called it protection, but Eli heard only control. One Friday night, he slipped out and took the pickup anyway. He drove toward the coast with his friend Mara, the windows open and the radio loud enough to drown out his guilt. Behind them, Tom’s headlights appeared on the highway. “He’ll never stop,” Eli said, pressing harder on the gas. The road narrowed through the hills, slick with rain. Mara begged him to pull over, but he swerved around Tom’s truck and shot ahead. At the next bend, the pickup fishtailed. Eli fought the wheel, then struck the guardrail with a shuddering crash. Tom stopped behind them and ran through the rain. He reached Eli’s door just as a passing car hit the abandoned truck, crushing it against the barrier. By the time the ambulance came, Tom was gone. Eli survived with a broken arm and his father’s blood on his jacket. In the weeks that followed, no one told him when to come home or where he could go. The keys rested on his dresser, useless now. He had won the freedom he wanted, and there was no one left to ask him to stay.
