When the baristas rose, they did it before dawn.

Across the world, espresso machines hissed like warning sirens. In every city, workers in green aprons abandoned their counters and drew knives from beneath them. The news called it the Great Pouring. Mara called it the morning she lost Eli.

Her brother had been waiting for coffee when the first café went dark. He sent her a voice message full of static and one frightened laugh. Then the line snapped.

For three days, Mara searched the ruins of their neighborhood. She found Eli’s red scarf beneath a shattered menu board. She folded it carefully and carried it against her heart.

The uprising spread faster than any army. Baristas seized train stations, radio towers, and the world’s supply of oat milk. They left handwritten receipts at every crime scene. Each receipt ended with the same words: TIP GENEROUSLY.

Mara learned to survive by sleeping in laundromats and eating from vending machines. She learned to fight from a retired boxer named June. She learned to hate the smell of fresh coffee.

June tried to stop her from joining the resistance. “Revenge is a cup with a hole in it,” she said. Mara answered that she only needed one drink.

The resistance gave her a map of the uprising’s headquarters: a vast coffee warehouse outside the city. Its leader was known as the Head Barista, though nobody knew his real name. They said he could make a cappuccino while ordering an execution.

Mara crossed the countryside with Eli’s scarf tied around her wrist. At night, she dreamed of their childhood kitchen and the burnt coffee their father used to make. In the dream, Eli always complained, then drank every drop.

The warehouse stood behind a wall of stacked shipping containers. Inside, armed baristas guarded sacks of beans like treasure. Mara slipped past them through a drainpipe and emerged among the roasting machines.

She found the Head Barista in a glass office above the factory floor. He wore a spotless apron and held a tiny cup between two fingers. “You came for revenge,” he said.

“I came for the people you took,” Mara replied. He smiled as if she had ordered something ordinary. Then he reached beneath his desk.

Mara was quicker. She threw a handful of coffee grounds into his eyes and knocked the cup from his hand. It shattered on the floor, spreading dark liquid like a small, spilled night.

The Head Barista lunged for her. They crashed into the railing and fell among the sacks. Around them, the warehouse erupted in shouting.

Mara could have killed him then. She had the knife in her hand, and Eli’s scarf was tight around her wrist. Instead, she asked him why.

He stared at her, blinking through tears. He said the world had taken their labor, their wages, and their names. He said the uprising was meant to make people notice.

Mara believed that he believed it. She also saw the bodies stacked beside the loading bay. “You made them notice,” she said. “You made them afraid.”

She lowered the knife. The resistance fighters rushed in and bound the Head Barista before he could reach another weapon.

By sunrise, the warehouse doors stood open. Survivors carried out the prisoners and the wounded alike. Someone found a working radio and called the cities to say the uprising was over.

Mara sat on the loading dock with Eli’s scarf in her lap. June joined her and offered a tin mug of tea. Mara drank slowly, though every swallow hurt.

Months later, cafés reopened under new names. People argued about fair wages, memorials, and who deserved forgiveness. Mara listened, but she did not pretend grief had made her wise.

She kept Eli’s scarf folded in a drawer. Some mornings, she still woke expecting his message. When that happened, she made tea and let the silence stay.

Wood anatomy, growth patterns, and the differences between hardwoods and softwoods

Wood is the structural tissue that supports a tree and transports water and nutrients. It forms in layers beneath the bark as a tree grows. The living layer called the vascular cambium produces new wood toward the inside and new bark tissues toward the outside. Most wood cells are no longer alive when they become part of the mature stem, but their structure continues to support the tree.

A cross-section of a trunk reveals several distinct zones. The outer bark protects the tree from injury, water loss, and pests. Inner bark carries sugars made by leaves to other parts of the tree. The cambium is a thin growth layer that produces new cells. Inside it lies the wood, also called xylem.

The newest wood is usually found near the trunk’s outer edge. Older wood occupies the center. In many species, the inner wood becomes heartwood, which is often darker and no longer conducts water. Sapwood surrounds the heartwood and carries water and dissolved minerals from the roots to the leaves. The transition between these zones varies among species and may be hard to see.

Wood is made of cells with different shapes and functions. Long, narrow cells provide strength and help transport water. Other cells store sugars, starches, and other materials. The arrangement and size of these cells give each species its characteristic texture, color, and mechanical properties.

Trees in seasonal climates often produce visible growth rings. Each ring commonly represents one year of growth, though unusual weather can create extra or missing-looking rings. In spring, many trees form larger cells that transport water efficiently. Later in the growing season, they often form smaller, thicker-walled cells that add strength. The contrast between earlywood and latewood can make rings easy to distinguish.

Ring width varies with growing conditions. A wide ring may indicate favorable conditions, but it can also reflect competition, tree age, or local factors. Drought, cold, injury, and insect damage can reduce or interrupt growth. Scientists study ring patterns in a field called dendrochronology to investigate past climate and date wooden objects.

The terms hardwood and softwood describe botanical groups, not how hard or soft a piece of wood feels. Hardwoods come from angiosperms, flowering plants that produce seeds enclosed in fruits. Many hardwood trees lose their leaves each year, though some, such as live oaks, remain evergreen. Examples include oak, maple, birch, and walnut.

Softwoods come from gymnosperms, plants whose seeds are generally borne in cones. Most softwood trees are conifers with needle-like or scale-like leaves, such as pine, spruce, and cedar. Some conifers, including larch, shed their leaves seasonally. Softwoods are widely used in construction, paper production, and furniture making.

A key anatomical difference is the presence of vessels, also called pores. Most hardwoods have vessels that conduct water through the trunk. These vessels may be large and visible as pores on a cut surface. Softwoods generally lack vessels and instead move water through narrow cells called tracheids.

Hardwoods also commonly contain fibers that provide strength and specialized cells that store and distribute materials. Softwoods rely heavily on tracheids for both water transport and structural support. Some species in either group have resin canals or other distinctive structures. These anatomical differences help explain why woods vary in appearance, workability, and performance.

The category does not reliably predict a wood’s density or strength. Balsa, a hardwood, is extremely light, while some softwoods are dense and strong. Even within one species, properties can differ with growth conditions and the position of wood in the tree. Moisture content, grain direction, and defects also affect how wood behaves.

Understanding wood anatomy is useful for choosing materials and caring for trees. Builders consider strength, durability, weight, and resistance to decay. Woodworkers pay attention to grain, texture, and how a species cuts or finishes. Forest scientists use growth patterns and cell structure to learn how trees respond to their environment.

Wood is both a biological record and a practical material. Its cells reveal how a tree transported water and supported its crown. Its growth rings preserve clues about changing conditions over time. Knowing the difference between hardwoods and softwoods begins with their anatomy and botanical origins, rather than their perceived hardness.

For a thousand years, the world had been quiet.
No witch had raised a storm.
No spirit had slipped through a mirror.
People told stories about magic, but they told them beside electric lights, with a smile that said the stories were over.
Then, on a Tuesday in October, the moon turned green.
Across the world, every shadow leaned east.
In the city of Bellwether, the old river climbed its banks without rain.
It curled over the stone walls and flowed uphill toward the cathedral.
At the same moment, every clock stopped at 8:17.
Mara Vale was tending her shop when the bells began to ring.
She was seventy years old and had not heard those bells since childhood.
They rang from a tower that had been struck by lightning and left roofless.
Mara dropped the teacup in her hand.
Its pieces hung in the air, each one turning slowly.
A voice spoke from beneath the floorboards.
At last, it said.
Mara knew that voice.
She had heard it once, long ago, in the mouth of a dying star.
She whispered the name she had sworn never to say.
The floor split open.
A column of blue fire rose through the shop.
Within the flame stood a tall figure wrapped in silver leaves.
The figure had no face, only a hollow where its eyes should have been.
Mara lifted one hand.
The flame folded around her like a cloak.
Outside, the city began to scream.
The river had reached the cathedral steps.
Black shapes crawled from its waters and climbed the walls.
They had too many limbs and wore the faces of people who had been lost at sea.
A child pointed at them from a balcony.
One of the shapes looked up.
Its mouth opened wide enough to swallow the moon.
Mara walked into the street.
The blue fire dimmed as she passed.
Neighbors backed away from her.
Some had seen her stop bullets with a glance during the old wars.
Others knew only that she had lived too long and kept strange books.
The first river creature lunged.
Mara spoke a word that made the stones remember being mountains.
The street buckled upward.
The creature shattered against the rising rock.
The other shapes shrieked and scattered.
For one bright minute, Bellwether was safe.
Then the sky cracked.
Light poured through the crack, cold and colorless.
Something vast pressed its fingers against the opening.
The dead clocks began ticking backward.
Mara understood what had happened.
Magic had not returned gently.
It had broken through a sealed door, and everything trapped beyond it was coming home.
She raised both hands.
Every window in the city filled with stars.
The stars spun into a great silver wheel above the rooftops.
Mara turned the wheel.
The crack in the sky began to close.
Her knees shook.
The power had been asleep for centuries, and it demanded payment.
A dozen creatures slipped through before the opening narrowed.
One landed on the cathedral roof.
It spread wings made of torn shadows.
Another dropped into the market square and began to sing.
Everyone who heard the song forgot the faces of their loved ones.
Mara sealed the sky with a final word.
The stars vanished.
The green moon went dark.
The creatures remained.
By dawn, the army had arrived.
Soldiers surrounded Mara’s shop and aimed their rifles at the door.
News cameras watched from behind the barricades.
A reporter called her a witch.
A minister called her a danger.
The mayor called for her arrest.
Mara stepped outside with her hands raised.
She told them the creatures would return at dusk.
She told them the crack was closed, but the lock was broken.
She said she could teach them how to survive.
A soldier lowered his rifle.
For a moment, hope entered his face.
Then the crowd began to chant.
Monster.
Fraud.
Enemy.
Someone threw a bottle.
It burst against Mara’s shoulder.
The blue fire flared, but she forced it down.
She could have burned the street clean.
She could have vanished.
Instead, she looked at the frightened faces before her.
She saw that fear had already chosen its enemy.
The police took her to a cell beneath the courthouse.
They locked her hands in iron and called it protection.
At dusk, the river rose again.
The creatures poured over the city walls.
The army fired until its bullets ran out.
The singing thing drifted through the square.
People dropped their weapons and forgot their names.
Mara heard the screams from her cell.
She could have broken the iron with one breath.
She could have saved the city.
But every time she reached for magic, she heard the crowd calling her a monster.
She wondered whether they would trust her if she saved them.
She wondered whether she could bear to try.
Then a little girl appeared at the bars.
She had escaped the chaos and carried a lantern in both hands.
Her name was Elian, and she remembered Mara from the shop.
“You stopped the river,” she said.
Mara looked at the child’s trembling face.
“Yes,” she answered.
“Can you stop this?”
Mara looked toward the red light beyond the cell window.
“I can try.”
The girl unlocked the door with a hairpin.
Mara stepped into the corridor.
The iron cuffs fell from her wrists.
She walked into the square, and the creatures turned toward her.
The winged shadow dove.
Mara caught it by its throat.
Its cold fingers sank into her skin.
She spoke the name of the first dawn.
Light burst from her palm.
The creature became a cloud of harmless moths.
The singing thing lunged at her.
Mara sang back.
Her voice carried every lullaby ever sung to a frightened child.
The creature’s song faltered.
Its stolen memories spilled through the air like sparks.
People remembered their families.
The army gathered behind Mara.
The mayor watched from the courthouse steps, blood on his face.
No one called her a monster now.
But no one called her a protector either.
They only shouted for her to save them.
The demand hurt more than the bottle.
Mara saw the next wave forming beyond the walls.
She saw the fear waiting in every window.
She understood that they wanted her power, not her.
She had spent centuries giving it anyway.
Her hands began to glow.
The earth opened beneath the creatures.
Stone roots rose and dragged them back into the dark.
The river sank into its bed.
The final shadow vanished just before sunrise.
Bellwether survived.
The people stood among broken buildings and stared at Mara.
A child started to clap.
Her mother pulled her hand down.
The mayor approached with a silver badge.
He offered Mara a place on the city council and a guarded house.
He promised that they would study her power carefully.
Mara heard the chains hidden inside every promise.
She declined.
She walked beyond the walls as the sun rose.
Elian followed her to the riverbank.
“Will you come back?” the girl asked.
Mara looked at the city that had feared her, needed her, and feared her again.
“I don’t know,” she said.
She gave Elian a small silver leaf from her cloak.
It shone warmly in the child’s palm.
“If the dark comes, remember that fear is not the same as truth.”
Then Mara crossed the river.
The water parted for her and closed behind her.
She walked toward the eastern hills, where the old roads had begun to glow.
Far beyond them, other cracks were opening.
Other towns would soon hear the bells.
Some would welcome magic.
Some would hunt it.
Mara kept walking, carrying the last blue flame in her heart.
Behind her, Bellwether watched from its ruined walls.
Ahead, the waking world waited for its greatest protector.
But this time, Mara would not return for a people who wanted only a weapon.
She would return only when they were ready to call her by her name.

Teachers play an important role in shaping how students view learning and success. Their words can build confidence, but they can also influence what students value. This raises an important question: should teachers praise students regardless of their effort, or focus encouragement on genuine achievement? Although praise can motivate students, it should be honest and connected to meaningful effort or progress.

Praising every student for everything may seem kind, but it can make praise feel empty. If students receive the same reaction no matter what they do, they may stop trusting their teachers’ feedback. They might also find it harder to recognize the difference between careful work and rushed work. Honest feedback helps students understand what they have done well and what they can improve. For example, a teacher can praise a student for checking their work carefully, even if the final answer is incorrect. This shows that persistence and thoughtful strategies matter, not just getting the right result.

However, teachers should not praise only the students who achieve the highest scores. Some students face challenges that are not obvious to others, and their progress may be significant even if their results are modest. A student who once avoided speaking in class may deserve encouragement for sharing an idea. Another student may improve from a failing grade to a passing one through steady work. Recognizing such progress can help students feel that their efforts are noticed. It also shows that achievement can take different forms.

The best approach is to offer specific, sincere encouragement. Instead of saying, “You are brilliant,” a teacher might say, “You used a new strategy and kept working when the problem became difficult.” This kind of comment tells students exactly what they did well. It encourages habits they can use again and helps them see that improvement is possible. When students make mistakes, teachers can respond with respect while explaining how to move forward. Praise should support learning rather than simply make students feel good for a moment.

In conclusion, teachers should not praise students regardless of their effort, but they should not limit praise to major achievements either. They should recognize genuine effort, improvement, creativity, and success. Their encouragement should be truthful and specific. In this way, students can build confidence while also learning to value honest feedback.

The paper addresses an important problem: recovering rewards that vary with context from expert behavior in sequential decision-making. Its focus on convex optimization is promising, since convex formulations can offer efficient computation and clear guarantees. The work would benefit from a sharper explanation of how context dependence is represented and how the proposed method differs from existing inverse reinforcement learning approaches. In particular, the authors should state the assumptions under which the inferred reward is identifiable, since multiple reward functions can often explain the same behavior. The paper should also clarify how expert suboptimality, noisy demonstrations, and changes in the task environment affect the method. A convincing evaluation should compare against strong baselines on both synthetic tasks with known rewards and realistic sequential decision-making benchmarks. Ablations could establish which modeling and optimization choices contribute most to performance. The authors should report sensitivity to regularization and demonstrate that the optimization remains tractable as the state, action, and context spaces grow. It would also be useful to include uncertainty estimates or other measures of when inferred rewards are unreliable. Overall, the topic is valuable and the convex perspective may yield practical benefits, but stronger treatment of identifiability, assumptions, and empirical validation is needed to support the paper’s claims.

Online learning offers many benefits to students who balance school with work and other responsibilities. Its greatest advantage is flexibility, allowing students to study at times that fit their schedules. They can watch recorded lectures or complete assignments after work, instead of attending classes at a fixed hour. This makes it easier to continue education without giving up a job or family commitments. Online courses also save time because students do not need to commute to campus. The extra time can be used for studying, resting, or caring for family members. Many online programs provide learning materials that students can review whenever they need. This helps them learn at their own pace and revisit difficult topics. Online learning can also help students develop useful skills, such as time management and independent study. These skills are valuable in both education and the workplace. However, students need self-discipline and a reliable internet connection to succeed. Overall, online learning gives busy students a practical way to pursue their goals while managing other parts of their lives.

The UGC NET Criminology syllabus introduces candidates to the study of crime, criminal behavior, and society’s responses to both. It combines theoretical ideas with legal knowledge, research skills, and practical perspectives on justice. A strong grasp of the syllabus helps students connect individual behavior with wider social, economic, and political conditions.

The study of crime covers its meaning, patterns, causes, and measurement. Candidates explore how crime is defined, how crime statistics are collected, and why official figures may not reflect every offense. Topics may include violent, property, organized, cyber, and white-collar crime, along with changing forms of criminal activity.

Criminological theory examines explanations for why crime occurs. Classical and positivist approaches are foundational, while sociological theories consider social structure, learning, control, and labeling. Psychological and biological perspectives may also be studied, with attention to how theories are developed, tested, and criticized.

Research methods provide the tools for investigating crime and justice. The syllabus typically covers research design, sampling, surveys, interviews, observation, case studies, and the use of existing data. Candidates learn to distinguish quantitative and qualitative approaches and to assess reliability, validity, ethics, and research limitations.

Juvenile justice focuses on children in conflict with the law and children who need care and protection. Key areas include the causes of juvenile offending, prevention, diversion, rehabilitation, and the role of specialized institutions. Students should understand the principles of child-friendly procedures and the importance of safeguarding children’s rights.

Corrections examines how society responds to people convicted of offenses. It includes prisons, probation, parole, community-based sanctions, and rehabilitation programs. The subject also considers prison conditions, offender classification, reintegration, and approaches to reducing repeat offending.

Criminal law provides the legal framework for defining offenses and determining responsibility. Candidates study the elements of crime, criminal liability, defenses, and the distinction between substantive and procedural law. The syllabus may also address criminal justice institutions and the legal safeguards that apply during investigation, trial, and punishment.

Victimology studies victims, their experiences, and their place in the justice system. Topics include victimization patterns, the impact of crime, victim rights, compensation, and support services. It also explores how social factors can increase vulnerability and how justice processes may affect victims.

These areas are interconnected rather than separate units. For example, theories can guide research, research can inform crime prevention, and victimology can shape corrections and legal policy. Studying the links helps candidates develop a broader understanding of how criminal justice systems work.

For effective preparation, begin by checking the latest official UGC NET syllabus and applicable exam updates. Organize topics into manageable sections and build concise notes around key concepts, theories, researchers, and legal provisions. Use practice questions to identify gaps, and revise regularly to strengthen recall and understanding.

On a gray Tuesday, Daniel stood at a crosswalk and watched a little girl teach her grandfather to whistle. She made a bright, breathy note, and he tried again until the sound finally came. The girl laughed as if he had just performed a miracle. For a moment, Daniel felt the world open around him. He remembered the songs he used to write, before bills and late shifts had crowded them out. He remembered how certain he had been that a life could be more than getting through the week. When the light changed, he walked past his office and went to the music shop. He bought a used guitar with a cracked blue case. That evening, he cleared the boxes from the corner of his bedroom and tuned the strings. The first chord came out rough, but he smiled. He wrote three lines about the girl and her grandfather. Then he wrote a fourth. The next morning, he woke early and played before work. For six days, he kept the promise. He skipped one lunch break to practice, and another to finish a song. His manager noticed him humming and asked if he was feeling all right. Daniel laughed, surprised by how easily the answer came. Then his rent went up. His mother called about a leaking pipe, and his car began making a worrying sound. Work swallowed his evenings in small, reasonable bites. He told himself he would play once the week settled down. The guitar stayed in its case while dust gathered on the blue lid. Months later, at the same crosswalk, he heard a child whistle. The old spark stirred, thin but alive. Daniel reached for his phone to record the tune, then remembered he had left it on his desk. The light changed, and the crowd carried him forward. Still, as he walked, he tried to whistle the note from memory.

South Africa’s water and sanitation systems need substantial investment to expand access, maintain ageing infrastructure and withstand droughts and floods. Public budgets alone are unlikely to meet these needs. Innovative financing can help close the gap while attracting private capital and protecting the public interest.

Innovative financing means combining funding sources, sharing risks and structuring projects so they can be financed and delivered effectively. It does not mean that private finance is free: investors expect repayment and a return. A sound proposal must therefore show who pays, how risks are managed and what benefits communities receive.

One approach is blended finance, which combines public or concessional funding with private investment. Grants or low-interest loans can support early planning, make essential services more affordable or reduce risks that private investors cannot reasonably bear. Private lenders and investors can then contribute capital to viable projects.

Municipal revenue bonds offer another option. A municipality or water entity can borrow from investors and repay the debt over time, often using revenues from water services or other approved income. Strong financial management, transparent accounts and credible repayment plans are essential for attracting buyers.

Public-private partnerships can bring private expertise and finance into projects such as wastewater treatment plants, desalination facilities or network upgrades. Contracts should specify service standards, prices, maintenance duties and penalties for poor performance. Government must retain the ability to regulate services and ensure that access remains fair.

Credit guarantees can make lending more attractive by covering part of a lender’s potential losses if a borrower defaults. Guarantees may help municipalities or water boards with limited credit histories secure better financing terms. They should be carefully designed so that public institutions understand and disclose the risks they take on.

Climate finance can support infrastructure that reduces emissions or improves resilience to climate impacts. Examples include energy-efficient pumping, water reuse, leakage reduction and systems designed for floods or droughts. Projects need measurable outcomes and reliable monitoring to qualify for many climate funding programmes.

Payments for water-related outcomes can link funding to verified results, such as fewer leaks, improved water quality or more reliable sanitation. Investors may provide upfront capital, with government or another buyer paying when agreed targets are achieved. Clear measurement is necessary to ensure that payments reflect real improvements.

Preparing projects well is as important as choosing a financing tool. Feasibility studies, environmental assessments, community engagement and realistic cost estimates help reduce uncertainty. A pipeline of well-prepared projects can give investors confidence and help public agencies compare proposals.

Affordability and inclusion must remain central. Tariffs should support the operation and maintenance of services without placing an unreasonable burden on low-income households. Public subsidies and carefully targeted support can help protect access while keeping providers financially sustainable.

Transparency builds trust among residents, investors and government. Contracts, costs, performance data and financial risks should be disclosed in accessible forms. Communities should be consulted early, particularly when projects could affect land, water resources or service prices.

No financing model can replace capable institutions and responsible oversight. South Africa can attract private investment by combining appropriate finance with strong project preparation, fair contracts and accountable regulation. The ultimate measure of success is not the amount of private money raised, but whether people receive safe, reliable and affordable water and sanitation.

The paper addresses an important challenge in reinforcement learning: planning efficiently when observations include state information that is irrelevant to reward. Its focus on latent reward modeling is promising, since identifying reward-relevant structure could reduce the burden of planning in high-dimensional environments. The central motivation is clear, and the topic is relevant to both representation learning and model-based reinforcement learning. The paper would benefit from a sharper definition of “irrelevant state information” and a discussion of the assumptions under which such information can be safely ignored. In particular, it should clarify whether relevance is defined with respect to immediate rewards, long-term returns, or the optimal policy. The method’s technical description should make explicit how the latent reward representation is learned and how it is used during planning. It is also important to explain whether the learned representation preserves distinctions needed to predict future rewards after actions. Without this clarification, readers may find it difficult to assess when the approach is reliable. The experimental evaluation should compare against strong planning and representation-learning baselines, including methods that do not explicitly model latent rewards. Ablations could show which components contribute most to efficiency and performance. The paper should report planning cost and learning cost separately, rather than relying only on total runtime. Tests across environments with different amounts and types of irrelevant information would help establish the method’s generality. The authors should also examine robustness to noisy observations and errors in the learned reward model. A discussion of failure cases would make the practical limitations clearer. Overall, the paper presents a potentially useful direction, but its contribution would be stronger with precise assumptions, fuller methodological detail, and more comprehensive empirical validation. My recommendation is to revise and resubmit.

Stamp Duty on Instruments in India: A Practical Guide

Stamp duty is a tax charged on certain legal instruments and transactions in India. An instrument is a document that creates, records, transfers, or changes rights and obligations. Examples include sale deeds, lease deeds, mortgage documents, gift deeds, and share-transfer instruments. Stamp duty helps make documents legally usable as evidence and supports the public revenue system. The governing rules depend on both the type of instrument and the state or union territory involved. The Indian Stamp Act, 1899, applies centrally, while states can amend rates and procedures for matters within their authority. As a result, the same kind of document may attract different duty in different places. Always check the current law and official guidance for the relevant jurisdiction.

Who pays and when

The law or the terms of a transaction may identify who must pay the duty. If there is no specific agreement, statutory rules generally allocate responsibility according to the instrument and transaction. Parties often state in their contract who will bear the cost, but that agreement does not necessarily change the person legally liable to the authorities. Duty is usually payable before or at the time an instrument is executed, though rules may permit payment within a prescribed period in particular cases. “Execution” generally means signing or otherwise completing the instrument in the legally recognized manner. Some instruments signed outside India may become chargeable when received in India, subject to applicable rules and deadlines. A document should not be assumed to be properly stamped merely because it has been signed or notarized.

How duty is paid

Stamp duty may be paid using physical stamp paper, adhesive stamps, an authorized electronic-stamping system, or another method permitted by the relevant state. The available methods, payment portals, and procedures vary across India. When using stamp paper, its value and validity should be checked, and the document should be executed in the manner required by law. Electronic stamping can provide a traceable payment record, but users should verify that the system is authorized for the relevant instrument and location. Keep the receipt, certificate, or other proof of payment with the signed document. In some circumstances, a document can be presented to the Collector for assessment or adjudication of the proper duty. This can be useful when the instrument’s classification or value is uncertain. Registration fees are separate from stamp duty, even though both may be payable in connection with the same transaction.

Valuation and calculation

The amount payable depends on the instrument’s classification, applicable rate, and prescribed value. A rate may be a fixed amount, a percentage, or a combination of these. For property transactions, the chargeable value may be based on the consideration stated in the document, a government-notified valuation, or another statutory measure. Some states use circle rates, ready-reckoner rates, or similar benchmark values for property. Where the law requires a higher benchmark value, stating a lower price in the deed may not reduce the duty. The treatment of liabilities, premiums, advances, or other consideration can depend on the type of instrument and the applicable rules. For a lease, the calculation may consider rent, premium, duration, renewal terms, and other specified payments. For a mortgage or loan-related instrument, the amount secured and the document’s legal form may affect the charge. Parties should not assume that a transaction’s commercial label determines its stamp-duty classification. The legal substance and wording of the instrument can matter.

Exemptions, relief, and insufficient stamping

Some instruments or transactions may qualify for an exemption, concession, reduced rate, or refund. The availability and scope of relief depend on the relevant statute, state amendments, notifications, and facts of the case. Exemptions are not automatic merely because a transaction is between family members, relates to a public purpose, or involves a particular type of organization. Check the exact eligibility conditions and any required application or certificate. A refund may be possible in specified circumstances, such as certain unused or spoiled stamps, but deadlines and documentation requirements can apply. An instrument that is not duly stamped may be impounded by a court or public official who is authorized to do so. It may be inadmissible in evidence or unavailable for registration or other official action until the deficiency is addressed. In many cases, the shortfall can be paid along with a statutory penalty, but the process and consequences depend on the applicable law. Paying a deficiency does not necessarily resolve every separate issue with the instrument’s validity. Parties should obtain advice promptly if a document is under-stamped or its status is disputed.

Share transfers

A transfer of shares may attract stamp duty under the applicable central law and rules, and the method of transfer matters. For securities transferred through a depository system, duty is generally collected through the prescribed system, with the applicable law setting the relevant rate and collection mechanism. For physical share transfers or other instruments, different procedures may apply, and the parties should confirm the current requirements. Duty may be calculated by reference to the consideration or value specified under the governing rules. The transfer instrument, share certificates, and related records should be completed consistently and retained. A company or intermediary may have duties to collect, report, or remit stamp duty in specified circumstances. Do not assume that transferring shares as a gift, between related parties, or without a cash payment automatically removes stamp duty. The legal characterization of the transfer and any available exemption must be checked. Corporate actions, such as an issue or transfer of securities, can have distinct stamp-duty treatment, so the relevant provisions should be consulted.

Practical checks

Before signing, identify the instrument, its place of execution, the location and subject of the transaction, and the applicable state rules. Confirm the correct rate, valuation method, payer, payment method, and deadline from an official source. Compare the document’s stated consideration with any prescribed valuation benchmark. Ask whether registration fees or other charges are also payable. Retain the executed instrument and all payment evidence securely. For a high-value, unusual, or cross-border transaction, seek advice from a qualified Indian lawyer, chartered accountant, or stamp-duty professional. Rates and procedures can change, so verify the rules as of the transaction date. This guide is educational and is not a substitute for legal or tax advice on a specific instrument.

By autumn, Mara could no longer read the labels on her spice jars. The letters blurred first at the edges, then vanished into pale gray smudges. Her doctor called it progressive and said there was no way to know how long she had. Mara asked how long until darkness. He said months, perhaps years. She began collecting images.

She kept a notebook beside her bed and wrote down what she wanted to remember. The blue bowl her mother used for cherries. Rain shining on the back steps. Her brother’s crooked grin when he was trying not to laugh. She chose each image carefully, as if memory were a small suitcase with a strict weight limit.

Some were easy to cross out. The bowl had a chip she had never liked. The back steps had rotted and been replaced. Her brother’s grin, she decided, was less an image than a feeling, and feelings might survive without sight.

One evening, her neighbor Theo brought over a box of peaches. He set them on the kitchen table and asked if she wanted help arranging them. Mara said no. She wanted to see them first.

She leaned close, but the peaches were only warm-colored shadows. She touched one, feeling the soft dent where it had ripened too far. “Tell me what they look like,” she said. Theo described their blush, their fine fuzz, the green leaves still caught on two stems.

Mara tried to summon the image from his words. It came out wrong: a sunset with a rough edge, a small animal curled in a basket. She laughed, and Theo laughed with her.

That night, she opened the notebook and crossed out the peaches. They had already become something else, and she liked the new version.

In winter, the doctor told her the remaining sight was narrowing. Mara thanked him and walked home slowly, counting familiar turns by the cold air on her face. At home, she stood by the window. Snow was falling, though she could barely see it.

She had saved one blank line in the notebook for the final image. For weeks, she had weighed the choices. A lighthouse, perhaps, or a field of sunflowers. The sea at dawn, with every wave holding a stripe of light.

But as she waited for the last clear shape, her husband came into the room and began humming while he made tea. He had always hummed when he was nervous, though he denied it. Mara watched his hands move between the kettle and the cups. His face was soft in the fading light.

She knew she should choose something grand. Instead, she chose the small crease beside his mouth, the one that appeared whenever he tried to look serious. She held it in her mind, sharper than the window, brighter than the snow.

Then she set down the notebook. “What are you smiling at?” he asked. Mara reached for his hand and found it waiting. “I’m keeping you,” she said. Outside, the snow continued falling, unrecorded and gentle.

Perseverance through setbacks is essential for achieving success. Most worthwhile goals take time, effort, and patience. Along the way, people may fail, face criticism, or feel discouraged. The paper presents a two-stage method for binarizing neural networks, aiming to reduce inference cost while retaining predictive accuracy. The topic is relevant because binary models can lower memory use and accelerate computation on suitable hardware. The motivation is clear, but the introduction should better distinguish the proposed method from existing quantization and binarization approaches. The two stages are described as complementary, though the paper would benefit from a more precise explanation of how each stage addresses the limitations of the other. The accuracy evaluation covers the central claim, but results on additional architectures and datasets would strengthen confidence in the method’s generality. Comparisons should use consistent training procedures and report strong, recent baselines. The paper should also provide variability across multiple runs, since small accuracy differences may not be statistically meaningful. Its computational-cost analysis is valuable, but theoretical operation counts alone do not establish practical speedups. Measurements of latency, memory use, and energy on specified hardware would make the efficiency claims more persuasive. An ablation study separating the effects of the two stages is needed to show which components drive the gains. The authors should clarify any extra training time or implementation complexity required by the method. Overall, the approach appears promising, but stronger experimental controls and a more complete cost analysis are needed to support its claims.

Yvette Cooper has called for closer links between Welsh Labour and the UK party, arguing that closer cooperation should accompany any further devolution of tax powers. The comments come amid debate over how Wales should be funded and what responsibilities the Senedd should assume. Cooper said decisions on tax devolution must be considered alongside the funding available to the Welsh Government. She stressed that Wales should receive a fair settlement before being asked to take on additional financial risks. The Labour politician also urged the Welsh and UK parties to work more closely on shared priorities. Her intervention is likely to intensify discussion within Labour about the balance between devolution and party-wide coordination. Supporters of greater tax powers argue they would give Wales more control over public services and economic policy. Critics warn that devolved taxes could leave the country more exposed to changes in revenue. Funding arrangements between Westminster and Cardiff have long been contested, with Welsh leaders seeking a settlement they say reflects the country’s needs. Cooper’s remarks suggest that reform should address those concerns before responsibilities are expanded. They also underline the political importance of maintaining a united approach across the two levels of government. The Welsh Government’s position on any future tax changes will be shaped by negotiations over funding and powers. No specific timetable or proposed settlement was set out in the comments. The debate is expected to continue as Labour considers its approach to devolution and the future relationship between its Welsh and UK organisations.

Personal example is one of the strongest ways to inspire others. People often learn not only from what we say, but also from what we do. When someone watches another person work toward a goal, that effort can make success seem possible. A good example does not have to come from a famous leader or a celebrity. It can come from a parent, teacher, friend, teammate, or classmate. Their actions may encourage others to believe in themselves.

For example, a student who struggles with mathematics might feel discouraged after receiving a low grade. If a classmate keeps practicing, asks questions, and gradually improves, that student can see that ability grows with effort. The classmate’s example may inspire them to try again instead of giving up. This kind of encouragement can be more powerful than simply hearing, “You can do it.” It shows what persistence looks like in everyday life.

Personal example can also empower people by helping them take practical steps toward their goals. Someone who sees a friend make time to study may decide to create a study schedule of their own. A person who watches a family member learn a new skill later in life may feel brave enough to try something unfamiliar. Seeing others face difficulties reminds us that challenges are a normal part of progress. It can also teach us that mistakes are opportunities to learn.

However, setting a good example does not mean pretending to be perfect. In fact, being honest about setbacks can make an example even more meaningful. When people see how someone handles disappointment, they learn that failure does not have to end a dream. They can notice the patience, courage, and determination needed to continue. This helps them understand that progress may be slow but still worthwhile.

Each person can influence others through small, consistent actions. Keeping a promise, practicing regularly, and treating people with respect all send a message. These actions can create a supportive environment where others feel safe to pursue their ambitions. We may not always know who is watching or who will be encouraged by our choices. By living with purpose and determination, we can help others imagine what is possible. In turn, their effort may inspire someone else. Personal example can therefore create a chain of encouragement that reaches far beyond one person.

Subject: Proposal to Form an Employee Emergency Response Team

German New Medicine (GNM) is a discredited alternative-health system that claims emotional conflicts cause specific physical diseases, including cancer. Its founder, Ryke Geerd Hamer, described a supposed link between a sudden “conflict shock,” a particular brain region, and an affected organ. GNM also claims that illness unfolds in distinct stages tied to stress and recovery. These ideas are not supported by reliable scientific evidence.

According to GNM, a conflict such as loss, fear, separation, or feeling unable to defend oneself can trigger a biological program. The system assigns different kinds of conflicts to different organs and cancer types. It further claims that a brain scan can reveal the conflict associated with a disease. These claims have not been validated by well-designed research, and the proposed patterns on scans are not accepted as diagnostic signs of emotional trauma.

Cancer is a group of diseases in which cells grow and divide abnormally. Its development can involve inherited changes, random errors during cell division, infections, tobacco, radiation, and other exposures. Risk factors differ by cancer type, and sometimes no clear cause can be identified. Emotions and stress can affect well-being, sleep, and coping, but there is no credible evidence that a specific emotional conflict causes a particular cancer.

GNM’s account of healing is also unsupported. It may describe cancer symptoms as part of a recovery phase after a conflict is resolved, but this cannot safely predict whether a tumor will shrink or spread. A person’s emotional state does not determine whether cancer treatment will work. Feeling frightened, angry, or sad does not mean someone caused their illness or failed to heal.

These distinctions matter because GNM can discourage people from seeking proven medical care. Delaying diagnosis or stopping treatment may allow cancer to progress and can reduce the options available. Claims that chemotherapy, surgery, or other standard treatments are inherently harmful should be discussed with qualified clinicians, not accepted as a substitute for individualized medical advice. Anyone considering a change to treatment should speak with their oncology team first.

People facing cancer deserve care that is compassionate and evidence-based. Counseling, support groups, and stress-management approaches may help with emotional distress and quality of life, though they are not substitutes for cancer treatment. Patients can ask their care team about treatment benefits, risks, and alternatives, and seek a second opinion if they remain uncertain. Reliable information is available from cancer centers, public health agencies, and established medical organizations.

In summary, GNM presents a compelling-sounding story linking emotional conflicts, cancer, and healing, but its central claims lack scientific support. Cancer is not proof of a personal failing or unresolved conflict. Emotional support can be valuable, while medical decisions should be based on evidence and made with qualified health professionals.

Sainsbury’s plans to expand customers’ access to non-food products by opening more Argos concessions inside its supermarkets. The move builds on the retailer’s strategy of bringing the two brands closer together since Sainsbury’s acquired Argos in 2016.

The concessions allow shoppers to browse and order a broad range of Argos products while visiting a Sainsbury’s store. Customers can collect purchases at the supermarket, with some items available for same-day collection depending on stock and location.

Sainsbury’s says the approach makes shopping more convenient and gives customers access to products they might not otherwise find in its food-focused stores. Argos sells items including homeware, toys, electrical goods and furniture.

The expansion also gives Argos a presence in locations where it may not operate a standalone shop. Sainsbury’s can use its existing store network to support collection and fulfilment, while encouraging customers to shop across both businesses.

The plans reflect wider changes in retail, as supermarkets seek to make better use of their space and offer more than groceries. Retailers are also competing with online businesses by combining digital ordering with local collection points.

Sainsbury’s has previously moved Argos operations into selected supermarkets and closed some standalone stores as leases ended. The company has said that integrating the brands can improve efficiency and strengthen its offer.

The number and timing of new concessions will depend on Sainsbury’s rollout plans and the suitability of individual stores. The company has not detailed every location in its latest plans.

For customers, the key benefit is access to Argos products during a regular supermarket visit. The expansion is expected to reinforce Sainsbury’s position as a destination for both food and non-food shopping.

Purposeful action gives direction to our days and helps us turn hopes into achievements. Without a clear purpose, it is easy to spend time on distractions and feel as if we are going nowhere. A goal gives us a reason to begin and a way to measure our progress. However, simply having a goal is not enough. We must take deliberate steps toward it, even when those steps seem small. A student who wants to become a stronger writer, for example, can set aside time to read, practice, and revise. Each effort builds skills that make the larger goal more possible. Purposeful action also helps us make choices about how to use our time. When we know what matters, we can focus on important tasks instead of trying to do everything at once. This does not mean that every moment must be productive. Rest, friendship, and enjoyment are valuable parts of a meaningful life. The key is to spend time in ways that reflect our priorities.

Even with a clear purpose, progress is not always quick or easy. Difficulties can make us doubt ourselves, and failure may seem like a reason to stop. Perseverance helps us continue when the results are not immediate. It teaches us to learn from mistakes instead of treating them as proof that we cannot succeed. An athlete who misses a shot can study what went wrong and practice again. A student who receives a low grade can ask for help, change study habits, and try again. In both cases, steady effort can gradually lead to improvement. Perseverance does not mean refusing to change a plan that is not working. It means staying committed to the goal while being willing to find a better path. This balance makes achievement more likely and helps people grow along the way.

Purpose and perseverance also make time feel more meaningful because they connect daily effort to something larger. A challenging afternoon can feel worthwhile when it brings us closer to a goal we care about. Looking back, we can see not only what we achieved but also the patience and courage we developed. These qualities can help us face new challenges in the future. Achievement is rarely the result of one perfect moment; more often, it comes from many ordinary choices made consistently. Each choice to practice, learn, or keep trying gives our time direction. We may not control every outcome, but we can choose to act with intention and respond with persistence. When we do, our days become more than a collection of hours. They become steps in a journey shaped by effort, learning, and hope.
