Orthodontic appliances can help align teeth, improve a bite, and support long-term oral health. Braces, clear aligners, retainers, expanders, and other devices all need regular care. Good daily habits help prevent cavities, gum irritation, bad breath, and damage to appliances. They also make orthodontic treatment more comfortable and predictable. Your orthodontist and dentist can tailor advice to your needs. Follow their instructions even when they differ from general guidance.

Brush carefully at least twice a day, and ideally after meals when you have braces. Use a soft-bristled toothbrush or an orthodontic brush. Angle the bristles toward the gumline, then brush above and below each bracket. Clean the chewing surfaces and the inside surfaces of your teeth as well. Brush slowly enough to reach around wires and brackets. An electric toothbrush can be helpful if it is comfortable and used gently. Replace a worn toothbrush or brush head promptly. A small travel toothbrush can make cleaning easier away from home. If you cannot brush after eating, rinse well with water and brush when you can.

Flossing remains important, even when braces make it more difficult. Use floss threaders, orthodontic floss, or another tool recommended by your dental team. Guide the floss gently beneath the wire and between the teeth. Avoid snapping floss into the gums. Clean both sides of each tooth, including near the gumline. Water flossers can help flush food and debris from around appliances. They do not always replace flossing, so ask your dentist how to use them as part of your routine. Interdental brushes may clean between brackets and under wires. Choose a size that fits without forcing it. Your dental team can show you the safest technique.

Brush your tongue gently to reduce odor-causing bacteria. Clean removable appliances each day according to their instructions. Rinse an appliance after removing it, unless your clinician has advised otherwise. Use a separate soft brush for retainers or aligners. Avoid hot water, which can warp many plastic appliances. Do not clean an appliance with abrasive toothpaste unless your orthodontist says it is appropriate. Store removable appliances in a ventilated case when they are not in your mouth. Keep the case clean and dry between uses. Never wrap an appliance in a napkin, where it may be lost or thrown away. Keep appliances away from pets, who may chew them.

Fluoride helps strengthen tooth enamel and prevent decay. Use fluoride toothpaste unless your dental professional has recommended a different product. Spit out toothpaste after brushing rather than rinsing extensively with water. This leaves more fluoride on the teeth. Your dentist may recommend a fluoride rinse, gel, or varnish if your risk of cavities is high. Follow the product directions and do not swallow mouth rinse. Children should use oral care products appropriate for their age and ability to spit. Ask your dentist whether additional fluoride is suitable for your child. Keep all dental products out of reach of young children.

Food choices affect both your teeth and your appliances. With braces, avoid hard foods that can bend wires or break brackets. Common examples include hard candy, ice, popcorn kernels, and very hard nuts. Sticky foods such as caramel and chewing gum can cling to brackets and wires. Cut firm foods, such as apples and raw carrots, into small pieces. Chew carefully and use your back teeth when appropriate. Avoid biting directly into foods that could pull on a bracket. Choose a balanced diet with vegetables, fruits, whole grains, and sources of protein. Limit sugary snacks and drinks, especially between meals. Frequent exposure to sugar gives cavity-causing bacteria more opportunities to produce acid.

Soda, sports drinks, energy drinks, and some fruit drinks can be acidic as well as sugary. Frequent sipping can increase the risk of enamel erosion and cavities. Water is usually the best drink between meals. If you have a sweet or acidic drink, avoid swishing it around your teeth. Rinse with water afterward. Wait about 30 minutes before brushing after an acidic drink or food, because enamel may temporarily be softened. Do not use a straw as a reason to drink sugary beverages often. Ask your dental team for advice if you have a dry mouth or take medication that affects saliva. Saliva helps protect teeth by washing away food and neutralizing acids.

Braces can trap food, so check your teeth after meals. A mirror and good lighting can help you spot debris. Spend extra time cleaning around the brackets and along the gumline. Puffy or bleeding gums may be a sign that plaque is not being removed thoroughly. Gentle, consistent cleaning usually helps mild gum inflammation improve. Do not stop brushing because your gums bleed. Contact your dentist if bleeding persists or worsens despite careful cleaning. Red, swollen gums can also have causes that need professional attention. Keep regular dental cleanings during orthodontic treatment. Orthodontic visits do not replace routine dental checkups.

A bracket may loosen, or a wire may shift during treatment. Call your orthodontist for guidance if a bracket is loose or a wire is broken. Do not pull off a bracket or cut a wire unless the clinic specifically instructs you to do so. If a wire is rubbing your cheek, cover the sharp area with orthodontic wax. Dry the area first so the wax sticks. Replace the wax as needed, especially after eating or brushing. Warm salt-water rinses may soothe minor irritation. Mix about half a teaspoon of salt into a cup of warm water, then rinse and spit it out. Do not swallow the rinse. If a wire is causing significant pain, injury, or trouble eating, contact the orthodontist promptly.

Mouth sores can occur as the cheeks and lips adjust to braces. Orthodontic wax can reduce rubbing against the appliance. Keep the sore area clean with gentle brushing. A mild salt-water rinse may offer temporary comfort. Avoid applying aspirin directly to a sore, because it can irritate tissue. Ask a pharmacist, dentist, or orthodontist before using numbing gels or other oral medicines. Seek advice if sores are severe, keep returning, or do not begin to heal. Fever, spreading swelling, or difficulty swallowing needs urgent medical attention. Do not try to reshape brackets or wires at home.

Discomfort is common for a short time after braces are placed or adjusted. Teeth may feel tender when biting. Choose soft foods such as yogurt, eggs, soup, or cooked vegetables for a day or two if needed. Take pain medicine only if it is safe for you and follow the label or a clinician’s directions. Do not place medicine directly on the gums or teeth. A cold drink or a cool compress on the face may provide comfort. Contact your orthodontist if pain is severe, unusual, or not improving. Pain that is accompanied by swelling or fever should be assessed promptly.

Clear aligners need consistent wear to work as planned. Wear them for the number of hours your orthodontist has prescribed. Remove them for meals and for drinks other than plain water, unless your clinician gives different instructions. Put them in their case whenever they are out of your mouth. Clean your teeth before putting aligners back in when possible. Trapped food or sugary liquid can increase the risk of tooth decay. Rinse aligners with cool or lukewarm water after removing them. Do not chew on aligners or use them as a substitute for a mouthguard. If an aligner cracks, gets lost, or no longer fits, contact your orthodontist for instructions. Do not skip ahead to another set unless your orthodontist tells you to.

Retainers help keep teeth from shifting after active treatment. Wear your retainer according to your orthodontist’s schedule. Some people need nightly wear long term, but the right plan varies. Put a removable retainer in its case whenever you take it out. Clean it regularly using the method your orthodontist recommends. Avoid hot water and harsh cleaners that may damage it. If a retainer feels unusually tight, do not force it into place. Contact your orthodontist to find out what to do. A retainer that is cracked, bent, or painful may need repair or replacement. Bring it to appointments so the orthodontist can check its fit and condition.

Fixed retainers are bonded behind some teeth and need careful cleaning. Floss threaders or interdental brushes can help clean around the wire. Brush along the gumline and around each bonding point. Avoid biting hard objects with the teeth attached to a fixed retainer. Tell your dentist or orthodontist if the wire feels loose or a bond has come off. Do not try to glue it back yourself. A loose wire may need prompt attention to prevent discomfort or unwanted tooth movement. Keep routine dental appointments so the retainer and surrounding teeth can be checked.

Other appliances, such as expanders or functional devices, may need special cleaning and use instructions. Follow the exact schedule provided by your orthodontist. Do not adjust or activate an appliance more often than directed. Ask for a demonstration if you are unsure how to turn an expander or fit a device. Clean around fixed parts carefully so food does not collect. Report persistent soreness, unusual pressure, a poor fit, or a damaged part. Do not stop wearing a prescribed appliance without speaking with the orthodontist. Keep small removable components away from children and pets.

Athletes with braces or other appliances should ask about a properly fitted mouthguard. A standard mouthguard may not fit well over braces. An orthodontic mouthguard can help protect the teeth, lips, and cheeks during sports. Check its fit as teeth move and treatment progresses. Replace a worn or damaged mouthguard. Remove removable appliances during contact sports if your orthodontist advises you to do so. Store removed appliances safely in a case. Follow any activity-specific instructions from your orthodontist or dentist.

People who play musical instruments may need time to adjust to an appliance. Practice gradually and ask your orthodontist about comfort strategies. Do not bend wires or trim appliances to make playing easier. Smokeless tobacco and smoking can harm oral tissues and stain teeth or appliances. Avoid tobacco and ask a health professional for help quitting if needed. Alcohol-containing mouth rinses may irritate some people’s mouths. Choose an appropriate rinse with guidance from your dental team. If you have allergies, sensitivities, or a condition that affects healing, tell your orthodontist before treatment or appliance adjustments.

Children and teens may need help building a reliable care routine. Caregivers can check that brushing reaches around every bracket. A visual checklist can make daily tasks easier to remember. Encourage children to carry a case for removable appliances. Do not scold a child for a lost or damaged appliance; contact the orthodontist and focus on the next step. Adults with braces benefit from the same careful cleaning and follow-up. Pregnancy, diabetes, immune conditions, and some medications can affect gum health or healing. Tell your dental and orthodontic teams about relevant health changes. They can adjust guidance or coordinate care when needed.

Call your orthodontist when an appliance breaks, becomes loose, or stops fitting as expected. Ask the clinic how quickly the problem needs attention. If the clinic is closed, use its emergency instructions or contact an appropriate urgent dental service. Seek urgent care for facial injury, uncontrolled bleeding, severe swelling, or trouble breathing or swallowing. Do not wait for a routine appointment if a serious symptom is worsening. For a swallowed or inhaled appliance part, get medical advice promptly, especially if breathing is affected. Never attempt to retrieve an object that is lodged in the throat.

Regular appointments help your orthodontist monitor tooth movement and appliance condition. Keep appointments even when treatment seems to be progressing well. Tell the orthodontist about pain, sores, breakages, or difficulty wearing an appliance. Bring questions and mention any changes in your health or medicines. Maintain dental checkups and cleanings throughout orthodontic treatment. Your dentist can identify cavities and gum problems that may not be obvious at home. Follow any treatment plan for cavities or gum disease promptly. Good communication helps your care team address small problems before they become larger ones.

A simple daily routine can make appliance care manageable. Brush thoroughly in the morning and before bed. Clean between your teeth at least once each day. Rinse after meals when brushing is not possible. Clean removable appliances as directed and store them safely. Choose foods and drinks that protect your teeth and appliances. Wear aligners or retainers for the prescribed amount of time. Attend orthodontic and dental appointments, and speak up when something feels wrong. Consistent care supports healthier teeth and gums during treatment. It also helps protect the results after treatment is complete.

Gold prices are shaped by several economic forces that influence how attractive the metal is to buyers and how much is available to sell. Understanding these forces can help explain why gold sometimes rises during uncertainty and sometimes falls even when headlines seem troubling. Gold is traded around the world, so its price reflects expectations and events across many countries. The price quoted in markets usually refers to a standard unit, such as a troy ounce. Because gold is also a commodity and a financial asset, its price responds to both physical supply and investor behavior. No single factor determines the price at all times. Instead, several forces interact, and their influence can change from one period to another.

Investment demand is one of the most important influences on gold prices. Investors may buy gold to diversify portfolios, protect wealth, or respond to uncertainty. When demand for gold investments rises faster than the amount available for sale, prices may increase. When investors sell holdings, the extra supply can put downward pressure on prices. Gold can be held as bars, coins, jewelry, exchange-traded products, or other financial instruments. These forms of ownership make it easier for different kinds of buyers to enter or leave the market.

Gold is often described as a safe-haven asset. This means that some investors turn to it when they worry about financial stress, conflict, or instability. During periods of fear, demand may rise because investors expect gold to retain value when other assets are falling. However, this pattern is not guaranteed. In a sharp market crisis, investors may sell gold to raise cash or cover losses elsewhere. The price may therefore fall temporarily even when uncertainty is high. How gold behaves depends on the cause of the crisis and on investors’ immediate needs.

Interest rates also affect investment demand. Gold does not pay interest or dividends, unlike many bonds and shares. When interest rates are high, investors may prefer assets that provide a stronger income. This can make gold less attractive, especially if other investments offer reliable returns. When interest rates fall, the opportunity cost of holding gold may decline. Investors may then be more willing to own gold, although other factors still matter. Expectations about future interest rates can influence prices before rates actually change.

Inflation is another major force shaping gold prices. Inflation refers to a general rise in the prices of goods and services over time. Some investors buy gold because they believe it can help preserve purchasing power when money loses value. This belief is one reason gold is often called an inflation hedge. Yet gold does not rise automatically whenever inflation increases. If inflation is high but interest rates rise even faster, gold may face pressure. The relationship depends partly on how investors expect inflation and monetary policy to develop.

Currency values matter because gold is commonly priced in U.S. dollars on global markets. When the dollar weakens, gold becomes less expensive for buyers using other currencies, all else being equal. This can encourage international demand and support the dollar price of gold. When the dollar strengthens, gold may become more expensive for overseas buyers. That can reduce demand and weigh on prices. The effect is not mechanical, because local economic conditions and investor preferences also influence purchases.

Gold prices are affected by the relationship between currencies and confidence. If investors lose trust in a currency, they may seek assets they view as more dependable. Gold can benefit from this shift, particularly when concerns involve the currency used to quote its global price. Exchange rates can also affect the income and costs of gold producers operating in different countries. A weaker local currency may lower some mining costs when measured in dollars. These cost changes can influence mining decisions and, over time, the amount of gold supplied.

Supply comes from several sources. Newly mined gold is a major source, but gold already held by households, investors, and institutions can also return to the market. Recycling is especially important when prices rise, because owners may decide to sell old jewelry or other gold items. Higher prices can encourage more recycling and help limit further price increases. At lower prices, owners may be less willing to sell. This makes recycled supply responsive to market conditions.

Mining supply changes more slowly than investment demand. Finding and developing a mine can take many years. Companies must explore deposits, obtain permits, secure financing, and build facilities before production begins. Once a mine is operating, output may be influenced by ore quality, equipment, labor, energy costs, and local rules. New discoveries do not immediately add large amounts of gold to the market. Because of these delays, a sudden increase in demand can move prices before mining supply has time to respond.

The cost of producing gold can affect the decisions of mining companies. When prices are high relative to costs, mines may expand production or reopen operations that were previously uneconomic. When prices fall below the cost of operating certain mines, companies may cut output or suspend production. These responses can eventually affect supply, though they are rarely immediate. Mining costs include labor, fuel, equipment, transportation, and environmental management. Costs can rise even when production stays the same, influencing how much gold companies are willing to produce.

Central banks are another important part of the gold market. Some central banks hold gold as part of their foreign reserves. They may buy or sell gold to diversify reserves, manage risk, or respond to changes in policy. Large purchases can strengthen demand, while significant sales can add supply. Central-bank activity can also influence expectations because it may signal a shift in confidence or reserve strategy. These decisions are usually based on long-term considerations rather than short-term price movements.

Jewelry demand connects gold prices to culture, income, and seasonal buying patterns. In some countries, households purchase gold jewelry as a store of wealth as well as an ornament. Rising incomes can support jewelry purchases, while economic weakness may reduce them. High prices can also discourage buyers or lead them to choose lighter designs. Jewelry demand therefore may respond differently from financial investment demand. A price rise might attract investors while making jewelry less affordable.

Technology and industry use gold in electronics, medical equipment, and other applications. Industrial demand is generally smaller than investment and jewelry demand, but it still contributes to the overall market. Manufacturers may change the amount of gold they use when prices move or when alternative materials become practical. These adjustments can take time because products must meet performance and safety requirements. Changes in technology can gradually alter industrial demand. This source of demand is usually less sensitive to daily market news.

Economic growth can influence several parts of the gold market at once. Strong growth may increase incomes and jewelry purchases. It may also raise interest rates if policymakers seek to prevent the economy from overheating. Higher rates can reduce investment demand for gold. During weak growth, investors may seek protection, but households may have less money for jewelry. The overall effect depends on which channels are strongest.

Government policy can affect gold prices through interest rates, currency management, and regulations. Central banks influence borrowing costs and monetary conditions. Governments can also change taxes, import rules, or mining requirements. Such changes may affect the cost and availability of gold in particular markets. Policies that create uncertainty can influence investor demand. Policy effects often take time to appear in production or trade data.

Geopolitical events may alter expectations about risk, trade, and currencies. Conflict or political instability can encourage some investors to seek assets they consider safer. Disruptions to mining regions or shipping routes can also affect supply. Even when physical production is unchanged, uncertainty can increase market volatility. Prices may move as investors revise their views of future events. The response can fade if the disruption proves temporary.

Gold is traded in both physical and financial markets. Futures contracts allow buyers and sellers to agree on a price for delivery at a later date. These contracts can influence expectations and price movements even when little physical gold changes hands. Exchange-traded funds may make gold exposure easier for investors. Their buying or selling can affect demand for the gold held on their behalf. The market price therefore reflects both physical transactions and financial positioning.

Market expectations are important because prices reflect what participants think may happen, not just what has already happened. If investors expect inflation to rise, they may buy gold before official inflation data confirms the trend. If they expect interest rates to increase, they may reduce gold holdings in advance. New information can quickly change those expectations. This is why gold prices can move sharply after economic reports or policy announcements. A price change does not always mean that current supply or demand has immediately changed.

The relationship among these forces is often more important than any one force alone. For example, rising inflation may support gold if investors fear loss of purchasing power. At the same time, a strong dollar or rapidly rising interest rates may limit that support. Increased investment demand can lift prices, while growing recycling supply may soften the rise. A disruption to mine production could add upward pressure if demand is already strong. Different forces can push in opposite directions at the same time.

It is also useful to distinguish short-term movements from long-term trends. Daily prices can be affected by trading flows, news, and changes in investor sentiment. Longer-term prices may reflect persistent shifts in inflation expectations, currency confidence, production costs, or central-bank behavior. A temporary surge in demand does not necessarily create a lasting increase in price. Likewise, a period of weak prices does not prove that gold has lost its role in portfolios. Time horizon matters when interpreting market changes.

Gold prices are difficult to predict with certainty. Economic relationships can change as policies, technologies, and investor preferences evolve. Historical patterns offer context, but they do not guarantee future results. Investors and students should consider several indicators together, including interest rates, inflation, exchange rates, mine output, recycling, and investment flows. A balanced explanation asks which forces are changing and how they interact. This approach is more reliable than attributing every price move to a single headline.

In summary, investment demand can rise or fall with risk appetite and expectations. Inflation may support gold when people seek to protect purchasing power, but the effect depends partly on interest rates. Currency movements, especially changes in the U.S. dollar, alter gold’s cost for international buyers. Supply responds through mining, recycling, and sales from existing holders, though mining adjusts slowly. Central banks, jewelry buyers, technology users, and financial markets add further influences. Together, these forces shape gold prices in a dynamic and interconnected way.

This paper studies how to learn reward functions that adapt to observed contexts, combining theoretical analysis with empirical evaluation of scalable algorithms. The problem is important for settings in which a single fixed reward cannot capture changing user preferences, task requirements, or environmental conditions. The paper’s central contribution is a framework for conditioning reward estimates on context and using those estimates in downstream decision-making. Its focus on scalability is valuable, since context-rich learning methods can become computationally impractical as data and feature dimensions grow. The theoretical results help clarify when context-dependent rewards can be identified and under what assumptions learning is reliable. The experiments further suggest that adapting rewards to context can improve performance over fixed-reward baselines.

The manuscript is generally well motivated, and the connection between its theoretical and empirical contributions is a strength. The presentation would be clearer if the authors stated the main novelty relative to existing contextual reward-learning and preference-learning methods earlier. In particular, the paper should distinguish more carefully between learning a reward that varies with context and learning a policy that varies with context. These are related but not equivalent objectives. The assumptions behind the theory also deserve a more intuitive explanation. The authors should discuss whether the assumed context coverage is realistic and how performance may change when some contexts are rare or absent during training. It would also help to clarify which parts of the proposed algorithm are essential to the guarantees and which are practical design choices.

The empirical section is promising, but the evaluation could be made more convincing. The baselines should include the strongest relevant methods, with enough implementation detail to support a fair comparison. Ablations would help identify whether improvements come from context conditioning, the scalable optimization procedure, or other components. The paper should report variability across random seeds and, where appropriate, confidence intervals or statistical tests. Runtime, memory use, and scaling behavior should be measured directly rather than inferred from algorithmic complexity alone. The authors should also explain how hyperparameters were selected and whether the same tuning budget was used across methods. Evaluation on more varied tasks or datasets would strengthen claims about generality. A discussion of failure cases would be useful, especially when contexts are noisy, ambiguous, or shift substantially at deployment.

The paper would benefit from a clearer account of how reward quality is measured independently of downstream policy performance. Strong task performance does not by itself establish that the learned reward is accurate or interpretable. If human judgments or preference labels are used, the data collection process and any potential annotator bias should be described in detail. The authors should also address whether context features could encode sensitive attributes and what safeguards would be appropriate in applications involving people. Overall, this is a relevant and potentially impactful contribution, with a useful combination of theory and scalable algorithms. I recommend revision to improve the positioning, strengthen the empirical comparisons, and clarify the assumptions and limitations. With these changes, the paper would provide a more complete and persuasive account of context-adaptive reward learning.

When the last star began to dim, Mara was summoned to the edge of the universe.
There, the old Keeper waited beside a door made of night.
“I have carried the future of humanity for ten thousand years,” he said.
“Now it is yours.”
He placed a small, warm sphere in her hands.
Inside it flickered every human life, past and yet to come.
Mara felt the weight of countless choices pressing against her palms.
“What am I supposed to do?” she asked.
“Choose which road humanity takes,” said the Keeper.
He opened the door, and three futures appeared.
In the first, people had conquered the stars but forgotten one another.
In the second, they lived gently on a single green world, never daring to leave.
In the third, their cities had vanished, yet small communities endured among the ruins.
Each future glowed with hope, and each hid a sorrow.
Mara searched the sphere for a sign.
She saw a child sharing bread with a stranger.
She saw a scientist turn away from a weapon.
She saw a crowd gather beneath a sky no one had charted.
None of these moments promised what would come next.
The old Keeper watched her in silence.
“Can you tell which future is best?” Mara asked.
“No,” he replied.
“Then how can I choose?”
“You cannot choose without doubt.”
Mara looked again at the three roads.
She realized each began with a choice people would make together, not a fate she could impose alone.
So she opened her hands and let the sphere drift toward the stars.
Its light scattered into a billion sparks, one for every human life.
The three futures folded into one vast, unwritten sky.
The old Keeper’s cloak turned to dust.
Mara remained, listening as humanity began to choose.

Digital integrated circuit design is the process of creating chips that represent and manipulate information using binary values, usually zeros and ones. These circuits are found in phones, computers, cars, medical devices, and many other technologies. Learning how they are designed helps students understand both the hardware behind digital systems and the methods used to build reliable products.

A digital chip begins with a specification describing what it should do, how fast it must operate, and how much power or area it can use. Designers translate that specification into a hardware description using languages such as Verilog or VHDL. The description defines logic and behavior rather than drawing every transistor by hand. Simulation tools help check whether the design behaves as intended before it is built.

The design is commonly organized into modules, such as counters, memory blocks, and communication interfaces. At the logic level, these modules are built from elements including gates, multiplexers, and registers. Combinational circuits produce outputs from current inputs, while sequential circuits also depend on stored state. Clock signals coordinate changes in many sequential circuits.

After verification, synthesis tools convert the hardware description into a network of logic cells. These cells are then arranged and connected during physical design, which includes placement, routing, and timing analysis. Engineers must consider electrical effects, manufacturing constraints, and power consumption. The final layout is prepared for fabrication at a semiconductor foundry.

Education in digital integrated circuit design combines theory with practical work. Students learn Boolean algebra, logic design, computer architecture, and basic semiconductor concepts. Programming skills are also useful because design and verification rely on scripts and specialized tools. Courses may introduce hardware description languages early so students can test concepts through small projects.

Hands-on exercises make abstract ideas easier to understand. A learner might build a simple arithmetic unit, a traffic-light controller, or a small processor. Designs can be tested on field-programmable gate arrays, or FPGAs, which allow hardware behavior to be explored without manufacturing a custom chip. Students can compare their expected results with simulation and board measurements.

Verification is a major part of professional practice. Test benches apply many input patterns and check that outputs meet the specification. Formal methods can prove selected properties across a broad range of possible conditions. Careful testing is important because a chip may contain millions or billions of interacting components.

Modern design also involves teamwork among specialists in architecture, logic, verification, physical implementation, and manufacturing. Education can prepare students for this collaboration through group projects, design reviews, and clear technical documentation. Open-source tools and educational chip programs can make some design experiences more accessible. However, advanced fabrication equipment remains costly and is often available through universities or industry partnerships.

As technology advances, designers face challenges such as increasing complexity, heat, security risks, and limits on energy efficiency. Emerging fields, including artificial intelligence hardware and chiplet-based systems, create new opportunities and learning needs. A strong educational foundation helps students adapt as tools and technologies change. By connecting digital logic, programming, physics, and problem-solving, digital circuit design education prepares learners to understand and create the hardware that supports modern life.

The paper addresses an interesting question by linking arousal-related global gain modulation to visual performance in convolutional neural networks, a connection with potential relevance to both neuroscience and machine learning. Its central claim would be more convincing if the authors clearly defined how arousal and gain are operationalized and explained why the proposed modulation is biologically plausible. The evaluation should include strong baselines, tests across varied visual tasks and noise levels, and ablation analyses that isolate global gain from other architectural or training effects. The paper should also report variability and statistical uncertainty, and clarify whether gains in task performance come at the cost of robustness or calibration. Overall, the topic is promising, but the conclusions should be calibrated to the breadth and rigor of the experimental evidence.

A Dundee man has been cleared of a charge of banging on his girlfriend’s door after she told a court she felt no fear or alarm. The allegation centred on an incident in which he was said to have struck the door. The court heard that his girlfriend did not consider his actions threatening or distressing. He was found not guilty of the charge.

Neonatal hepatic abscess is a rare but serious infection in a newborn’s liver that can progress quickly and requires urgent medical care. It may arise when bacteria spread through the bloodstream, enter through an infected umbilical catheter or portal vein, or reach the liver from a nearby infection; common organisms include Staphylococcus aureus, Escherichia coli, and other Gram-negative bacteria. Risk factors include prematurity, low birth weight, bloodstream infection, umbilical venous catheter use, and abdominal surgery. Signs are often nonspecific and may include fever or low temperature, poor feeding, lethargy, breathing difficulty, jaundice, an enlarged abdomen, or signs of sepsis. Some infants have few obvious symptoms, so clinicians may suspect an abscess when infection persists despite treatment. Diagnosis typically combines blood tests and cultures with abdominal ultrasound, with CT or MRI used when further detail is needed. Treatment usually involves intravenous antibiotics tailored to culture results, often for several weeks. A large, accessible abscess, or one that does not respond to antibiotics, may need image-guided needle drainage or catheter placement; surgery is uncommon but may be necessary in selected cases. Prompt recognition and follow-up imaging help limit complications, and suspected neonatal infection should be assessed urgently by a medical team.

By dawn, Elias had run out of excuses.

The bottle on the table was empty, and the little white pills beside it were gone.
His hands trembled as he watched rain stitch the window with silver threads.
Then a voice spoke from the dark corner.

“History is written by those who survive,” said Winston Churchill.
Elias turned sharply.
The corner held only his coat.

He had been hearing famous dead men for weeks.
Churchill arrived when he felt cornered.
Napoleon came when he wanted to conquer the day.
Lincoln appeared whenever he thought of his brother.

“You promised you’d visit him,” Lincoln said.
Elias pressed his palms against his ears.
The voice continued, gentle and unbearable.

His brother Daniel had died two years earlier.
They had argued over money, then over nothing, then over everything.
Elias had meant to call the next morning.

Instead, he had found a bottle and let the days fold over one another.
Now Daniel’s empty chair seemed to face him from across the room.
“I’m sorry,” Elias whispered.

Napoleon laughed from the hallway.
“Regret is a poor general,” he said.
Elias stood, nearly falling.

He wanted to shout that none of this was real.
But the voices had his memories, and memories were harder to dismiss.
He opened the front door.

Cold air reached him.
Across the street, the pharmacy sign glowed blue.
He imagined Churchill beside him, hat tipped against the rain.

“Courage,” the statesman said.
Elias took one step toward the curb.
A bus roared past, and the voice vanished beneath its brakes.

For a moment, the world was only wet pavement and breath.
Then Lincoln sat on the low brick wall nearby.
“You can’t bring him back,” Lincoln said.

“I know,” Elias replied.
“Knowing isn’t the same as living.”
Elias looked down at his shaking hands.

He had thought the drugs would quiet the voices.
At first they had softened every edge.
Then the edges returned with teeth.

Now even silence seemed to be speaking.
He crossed the street and entered the pharmacy.
The clerk looked up, wary but kind.

“I need help,” Elias said.
The words felt smaller than the truth, but they were true.
The clerk called an emergency number.

While they waited, Elias sat beneath a poster about recovery.
Napoleon paced behind the counter, muttering about defeat.
Elias let him pace.

A counselor arrived with a rain-darkened coat and a calm voice.
She asked what he had taken and when.
He answered as honestly as he could.

She asked whether he might hurt himself.
He thought of Daniel’s chair, and the answer frightened him.
“I don’t want to,” he said, “but I’m not sure I can stay safe alone.”

The counselor nodded and stayed beside him.
The voices grew faint as the ambulance doors closed.
Churchill offered no final speech.

At the clinic, a nurse took his coat and checked his pulse.
Elias expected judgment, but received a blanket.
The kindness hurt more than suspicion would have.

He told the doctor about the pills, the bottle, and the visitors.
The doctor listened without agreeing that the dead were speaking.
She said sleep, withdrawal, and illness could tangle perception.

“We’ll help you through tonight,” she said.
Elias held the blanket around his shoulders.
For once, he did not ask the voices what came next.

At sunrise, the rain stopped.
Daniel’s chair was still empty in Elias’s mind.
But beside it, he pictured a phone, a meeting, and another morning.

He had lost years to the promise that tomorrow would fix everything.
This time, tomorrow would need help.
He closed his eyes, and let someone sit beside him.

Mara had been told not to bring her phone on the spacewalk. She brought it anyway, tucked inside a pocket of her suit. It was mostly for taking pictures, she told herself. It was also for Pokémon Go.

The little green radar on her screen showed something nearby. Mara drifted past the station’s solar panels, trying to keep one hand on the safety rail. She should have been checking the antenna she’d come to repair. Instead, she was wondering whether a rare Pokémon could spawn in orbit.

A bright speck moved beyond the panel. Mara glanced up, expecting a loose bolt. The speck grew into a smooth silver craft, no bigger than a shuttle bus. It stopped a few meters away.

Mara froze. Her mission controller started speaking in her helmet, but she was too distracted to hear the words. The craft opened like a flower. Three tiny beings floated out, each wearing a glowing belt and a helmet shaped like a berry.

One of them waved. Mara waved back, then checked her phone. The radar showed a Pokémon right behind the visitors. She gasped and reached for a Poké Ball.

The aliens gasped too. One pulled a glowing sphere from its belt. The two spheres flew toward each other and bounced off with a soft, harmless ping. The aliens looked delighted.

Mara’s screen flashed. A message appeared: “New friend nearby!” She tapped it. The aliens tapped their own devices in perfect time.

They were playing Pokémon Go. Mara’s laugh came out as a burst of static. The smallest alien pointed at her screen and made a hopeful chirp. Mara showed it how to throw a curveball.

The alien watched closely, then flicked its wrist. Its ball spun through the air and landed neatly on a tiny floating creature that had appeared near the craft. The creature vanished in a sparkle. A triumphant jingle played from both phones.

Mara forgot about the antenna. She forgot about the station, the mission, and the fact that she was floating thousands of kilometers above Earth. She and the aliens compared teams.

The tallest one wore a blue badge. The smallest one wore yellow. The third had a red badge and an expression of fierce pride. They showed Mara a map of their home planet.

It was covered in PokéStops. Their capital city had a Gym on every corner. They had even built a special station on a moon, where rare Pokémon appeared during eclipses.

Mara showed them pictures of Earth. The aliens leaned close to the screen. When she zoomed in on her hometown, the smallest one chirped and tapped a spot near the river.

A rare Pokémon was hiding there. Mara felt a pang of homesickness. Then the station controller cut in again, louder this time.

“Commander, status report.” Mara looked at the broken antenna beside her. She had drifted several meters from it. The aliens followed her gaze.

The tallest one pressed a button on its belt. A beam of light reached out and steadied the antenna. Mara grabbed the rail and repaired the loose connection.

Her controller asked what had happened. “Unexpected visitors,” she said. “They’re helping.” The three aliens gave a coordinated wave.

Before leaving, they exchanged trainer codes with Mara. The smallest one sent her a gift: a postcard from a PokéStop on a blue-green world. The picture showed a stone arch beneath two moons.

Mara sent back a postcard of Earth, with a note that read, “Come visit. Bring extra Poké Balls.” The silver craft folded shut and glided into the darkness.

Mara returned to the station with her work done and a new friend in another solar system. The next morning, she found a message from the aliens. They had spotted a legendary Pokémon near Earth’s moon.

Mara smiled, checked the schedule, and asked mission control for permission to take a short walk.

After the battle, Mara returned to the mountain village alone. Her shield was split, and her brother’s name was carved into its rim. Everyone called her brave, but she could barely sleep. Each night, she heard the final clang of his sword as he fell. She tried to drown the sound with training, striking the practice post until her hands bled. The village healer asked her to sit beside the river instead. Mara refused, certain that resting would make her weak. One morning, she found a small wooden bird in her pack, carved by her brother when they were children. The sight of it loosened something inside her. She carried it to the river and let herself remember their games, their arguments, and his laughter. Then she remembered the battle, too, and wept until her shoulders shook. The healer sat nearby without asking her to stop. When the tears passed, Mara felt tired, but not hollow. She understood that grief was not a wound she could defeat with a sword. It was love with nowhere to go, asking to be heard. In the days that followed, she spoke of her brother at supper. The villagers shared their own losses, and the silence between them grew gentler. Mara still woke some nights to the memory of the battle. But now she let the memory come, and let it go. When she lifted her shield again, she carried his name not as a burden, but as a reminder of how deeply she could love.

MacKeeper’s maker has responded to a security breach that exposed customer account information, saying it has taken steps to address the incident. The company said the affected data included details linked to customer accounts. It has not publicly confirmed how many people were affected or precisely which fields were exposed. The breach was reported after security researchers identified information accessible online. The company said it secured the exposed data and began investigating how it became available. It also said it is reviewing its systems to prevent a similar incident. Customers may be notified directly if the investigation finds their information was involved. The company urged users to remain alert for suspicious emails or messages that appear to reference their MacKeeper accounts. Security experts recommend changing account passwords, especially if they have been reused on other services. They also advise enabling multifactor authentication where available. The incident raises fresh questions about how software providers protect customer records and disclose security problems. Further details are expected as the company’s investigation continues.

The portal opened in the middle of a ruined subway station.
Three figures stumbled through, blinking beneath the flicker of emergency lights.
A knight in silver armor raised her shield.
A red-haired mage clutched a staff crowned with blue flame.
Behind them came a halfling carrying a bow and a sack of apples.
“This is not the dragon’s lair,” the knight said.
Above them, a train hung crookedly from the tracks.
Its windows were dark, and vines crawled over its metal sides.
The halfling sniffed the air.
“Then why does it smell like burned dragons?”
A sudden clatter echoed from the tunnel.
The three adventurers took their places, ready for battle.
Instead, a boy in a yellow raincoat ran toward them.
“Please,” he gasped, “you have to help us.”
The knight lowered her shield.
“How many are you?”
“Twenty-seven,” he said, “and we’re trapped in the library.”
He led them through streets split by weeds and broken glass.
Tall buildings leaned against one another like tired giants.
Strange wagons sat abandoned along the road, their wheels melted.
The mage studied a red sign hanging over a shop.
“What kingdom uses letters like these?”
“No kingdom,” the boy replied.
“This was our world, before the sky turned white.”
At the library, survivors crowded behind a barricaded door.
A woman with a bandaged arm greeted them.
“Our water is running out,” she said.
“And something has been circling the building every night.”
The halfling spotted deep claw marks across the stone steps.
The knight recognized the scars from a beast she had fought in her own realm.
“It followed us through the portal,” the mage whispered.
A crash shook the front doors.
The survivors dragged tables into place as shadows gathered outside.
The knight planted her feet and lifted her shield.
The mage drew a ring of fire across the floor.
The halfling climbed onto a bookshelf to see through a shattered window.
A horned creature prowled in the street, its hide shining like black glass.
It charged.
The knight met it at the doorway, and the whole library trembled.
The mage’s flame wrapped around its horns, forcing it back.
From above, the halfling loosed an arrow into its open eye.
The creature roared and fled beneath the ruined buildings.
For a moment, no one spoke.
Then the survivors began to cheer.
The woman asked whether the adventurers could lead them to safety.
The mage looked toward the distant hills, where green shoots glimmered through the gray.
“We can,” she said, “if you’ll help us find our way home.”
The knight offered her hand to the woman.
Together, they stepped into the broken morning.

Michigan’s second confirmed measles case is a reminder that this highly contagious disease can spread wherever people are not protected. Health officials confirm cases through testing and investigate where an infected person may have exposed others. Anyone who may have been exposed should follow guidance from local public health officials.

Measles spreads through the air when an infected person breathes, coughs, or sneezes. The virus can remain in the air or on surfaces for up to two hours after that person leaves. Symptoms usually begin about 7 to 14 days after exposure, though they can take up to 21 days to appear.

Early symptoms often include a high fever, cough, runny nose, and red, watery eyes. A rash usually develops several days later, beginning on the face and spreading downward across the body. Measles can cause serious complications, including pneumonia, brain swelling, and, rarely, death. Infants, pregnant people, and people with weakened immune systems are especially at risk.

The measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine is the best protection against measles. Two doses are about 97 percent effective at preventing measles, while one dose is about 93 percent effective. The vaccine is routinely recommended for children, and adults should check whether they are fully vaccinated or otherwise have evidence of immunity. People born before 1957 are generally considered likely to have acquired natural immunity, but they should ask a health care provider if they are unsure.

If you think you may have measles, call a health care provider before visiting a clinic or emergency department. Calling ahead helps staff take precautions and reduces the chance of exposing others. Avoid public places while ill, and follow instructions from health officials about testing, isolation, and contacts.

People who have been exposed should contact a health care provider or local health department promptly, even if they feel well. Depending on their vaccination and immunity status, they may be advised to receive a vaccine or other preventive care. Checking vaccination records and getting recommended MMR doses helps protect individuals and the wider community.

Mosquito bites are usually minor, but they can cause itching, redness, and swelling. Mosquitoes pierce the skin with a slender mouthpart and feed on a small amount of blood. Their saliva can trigger a reaction from the body’s immune system. This reaction is what causes most of the familiar itching and swelling. Some people react more strongly than others. Children may develop larger areas of swelling than adults. Scratching can damage the skin and raise the risk of infection. A few simple steps can reduce bites and make discomfort easier to manage. Natural remedies may soothe symptoms, but they do not all have strong scientific evidence. They also do not replace medical care when warning signs appear.

Preventing bites is usually easier than treating them. Mosquitoes can bite at any time, though many species are most active around dawn and dusk. Some species, including those that spread certain illnesses, may bite during the day. Use an insect repellent registered with the relevant public health authority. In the United States, the Environmental Protection Agency registers repellents for use on skin or clothing. Common effective ingredients include DEET, picaridin, IR3535, and oil of lemon eucalyptus. Follow the product label for where, when, and how to apply it. Do not apply repellent to cuts, irritated skin, eyes, or the mouth. Adults should apply repellent to a child’s hands only if the label allows it, and should keep it away from the child’s eyes and mouth. Do not let young children handle repellent themselves. Apply sunscreen first, let it dry, and then apply repellent. Choose a product suited to the person’s age and situation. Oil of lemon eucalyptus and its active ingredient, PMD, should not be used on children under three years old. Do not use pure essential oil as a substitute for an approved repellent. Natural origin does not automatically mean a product is safe or effective.

Wear long sleeves, long pants, socks, and closed shoes when mosquitoes are active. Loose-fitting clothing can make it harder for mosquitoes to reach the skin. Clothing treated with permethrin can provide extra protection. Permethrin is for clothing and gear, not for direct application to skin. Follow the label and let treated items dry before wearing them. Do not apply permethrin to clothing while it is being worn. Use window and door screens, and repair holes promptly. Air conditioning can help keep mosquitoes out of indoor spaces. Use a mosquito net over a bed or stroller when needed. Make sure the net is securely tucked in and does not rest directly against the skin. Keep nets away from candles, heaters, and other sources of flame. Empty, scrub, or cover items that hold standing water at least once a week. Check flowerpots, buckets, toys, gutters, birdbaths, and outdoor containers. Replace water in pet bowls and vases regularly. Store water containers tightly covered. Keep grass and shrubs trimmed near places where people gather. These measures can reduce mosquito breeding sites around a home.

If you are bitten, try not to scratch. Wash the area gently with soap and water. A cool, damp cloth or wrapped cold pack can help reduce itching and swelling. Apply the cold pack for short periods, and place fabric between it and the skin. Do not put ice directly on the skin. A warm compress may also relieve itching for some people, though responses vary. Avoid heat that could burn the skin. A paste made from baking soda and water is sometimes used as a home remedy. Evidence that it works is limited, and it can irritate sensitive skin. If you try it, use a small amount on a small area and wash it off if irritation develops. Aloe vera gel may feel cooling, but evidence for treating mosquito bites is limited. Use a plain product and stop if it causes redness or stinging. A clean, cool tea bag is another traditional remedy, but reliable evidence of benefit is limited. Do not place dirty or used materials on broken skin. Avoid applying vinegar, bleach, toothpaste, or household cleaners to a bite. These products can irritate or injure skin. Essential oils such as tea tree, lavender, or peppermint can also cause irritation or allergic reactions. Do not apply essential oils undiluted, and do not swallow them. Keep all oils away from children’s faces and hands.

For troublesome itching, a pharmacist or clinician can advise whether an over-the-counter treatment is suitable. Calamine lotion may soothe some bites. A low-strength hydrocortisone cream may help with itching and inflammation when used according to its label. Do not use it on broken skin or for longer than directed. Ask a health professional before using it on a young child. An oral antihistamine may help with itching, but some types cause drowsiness. Check the label for age limits, cautions, and interactions with other medicines. Do not combine products with the same active ingredient unless a clinician says to do so. For pain, an appropriate over-the-counter pain reliever may help when used according to its label. Ask a health professional about medicines for infants, pregnancy, or ongoing medical conditions. A pharmacist can also help identify a suitable option if you take other medicines.

Most mosquito bites improve within a few days. Some swelling can last longer, especially after a strong local reaction. Seek medical advice if redness or warmth keeps spreading, pain worsens, pus appears, or you develop a fever. These signs may indicate an infection or another problem. Get urgent medical help for trouble breathing, swelling of the face or throat, dizziness, fainting, or widespread hives after a bite or sting. These symptoms can signal a severe allergic reaction. If possible, use an epinephrine auto-injector prescribed for the person and call emergency services. Do not wait to see whether severe symptoms improve on their own.

Mosquitoes can spread illnesses in some parts of the world. Fever, severe headache, rash, joint or muscle pain, confusion, or other unusual symptoms after mosquito exposure warrant medical advice, especially after travel. Mention where and when the exposure occurred. A clinician can advise whether testing or monitoring is needed. Preventing bites is especially important for infants, older adults, pregnant people, and people with weakened immune systems. Ask a health professional or travel clinic about local risks before visiting an area where mosquito-borne diseases occur. Follow current public health advice for vaccines, medicines, and other precautions where applicable. Repellents reduce risk but cannot prevent every bite. Combining repellent, protective clothing, screens, and removal of standing water offers stronger protection than relying on a single measure. For a bite that is already itchy, cooling the skin and avoiding scratching are simple first steps. Choose remedies carefully, because “natural” products can still cause harm. When symptoms are severe, unusual, or worsening, seek professional care.

Lifelong learning is important because the world is always changing. New ideas, technologies, and problems appear throughout our lives. By continuing to learn, we can adapt and make thoughtful choices. Learning does not have to happen only in a classroom. We can learn from books, conversations, work, travel, and everyday experiences. Each new skill can open doors to opportunities we may not have expected. Learning also helps us understand people whose experiences differ from our own. It encourages curiosity and keeps our minds active.

Embracing new challenges is another important part of personal growth. A difficult task may feel uncomfortable at first, but it can teach us patience and determination. When we make mistakes, we can use them to discover what to improve. Over time, facing challenges can build confidence. It also helps us become more flexible when plans change. Even small challenges, such as trying a new activity or speaking in front of a group, can help us grow.

Sharing knowledge makes learning more valuable. When we explain an idea to someone else, we often understand it better ourselves. We can also help others avoid mistakes and reach their goals. Sharing does not always mean giving a formal lesson; it can be as simple as offering advice or recommending a useful book. Everyone has experiences and skills worth sharing. By learning, taking on challenges, and helping one another, we can build a more thoughtful and supportive community.

Glaucoma: Causes, Risk Factors, Detection, and Treatment

Glaucoma is a group of eye diseases that damage the optic nerve, which carries visual information from the eye to the brain. The damage often develops gradually and can lead to permanent vision loss. Glaucoma is one of the leading causes of irreversible blindness worldwide. It may affect one or both eyes, and many people do not notice a problem until the disease is advanced.

The eye continually produces a clear fluid that nourishes its internal structures. This fluid normally drains through channels near the front of the eye. If it drains too slowly, pressure inside the eye may rise. Elevated eye pressure can damage the optic nerve, but glaucoma can also occur when pressure is within the usual range. This is why pressure alone cannot determine whether someone has glaucoma.

The most common form is primary open-angle glaucoma. In this type, drainage becomes less effective over time, and vision loss usually begins at the edges of the visual field. Another form, angle-closure glaucoma, occurs when the drainage angle becomes blocked. It can develop suddenly and requires urgent medical attention. Other forms may result from eye injuries, inflammation, certain medicines, or other health conditions.

Anyone can develop glaucoma, but some factors increase the likelihood. Risk rises with age, especially after 60. A close family member with glaucoma also increases a person’s risk. People of African, Hispanic, or Asian ancestry may have a higher risk of particular types of glaucoma. Other risk factors include high eye pressure, a thin cornea, severe nearsightedness, and previous eye injury. Diabetes and long-term use of steroid medicines may also be associated with increased risk.

Open-angle glaucoma often causes no pain or noticeable symptoms at first. As it progresses, a person may gradually lose peripheral, or side, vision. In later stages, the remaining field of vision may become very narrow. Central vision can be affected as the disease advances. Because this loss is usually permanent, waiting for symptoms before seeking an eye examination is unsafe.

Sudden angle-closure glaucoma can cause severe eye pain, a red eye, blurred vision, or halos around lights. A person may also experience headache, nausea, or vomiting. These symptoms need immediate emergency eye care. Prompt treatment can reduce the chance of severe, lasting damage.

A comprehensive eye examination is the best way to detect glaucoma. An eye-care professional may measure pressure inside the eye. They may examine the optic nerve and take images to look for changes. A visual-field test checks for areas of reduced sight. Additional tests can assess the drainage angle, corneal thickness, and nerve-fiber layer. No single test usually provides the whole picture, so clinicians consider results together and may repeat tests over time.

Routine eye examinations are important because early glaucoma may not affect everyday vision. How often someone needs screening depends on age, personal risk, and examination findings. People with higher risk or known glaucoma may need more frequent follow-up. An eye-care professional can recommend an appropriate schedule.

Glaucoma damage cannot usually be reversed, but treatment can often slow or prevent further loss. The main goal is to lower eye pressure to a level that helps protect the optic nerve. Treatment does not restore vision that has already been lost. However, starting care early can preserve useful vision for many years.

Prescription eye drops are a common first treatment. They lower pressure by reducing fluid production or improving fluid drainage. Using them exactly as directed is important, even when the eyes feel normal. Laser procedures can improve drainage or reduce fluid production, depending on the type of glaucoma. Surgery may be considered when drops or laser treatment do not control pressure well enough.

Treatment plans are tailored to the person and may change over time. Regular follow-up helps the clinician check pressure, optic-nerve health, and visual fields. Patients should tell their eye-care professional about side effects, difficulties using drops, or changes in vision. They should not stop prescribed treatment without medical advice. Managing other health conditions and protecting the eyes from injury can also support overall eye health.

Early diagnosis is crucial because glaucoma often causes no warning signs until damage has occurred. Once optic-nerve fibers are lost, they cannot be restored with current treatments. Detecting the disease before noticeable vision loss allows treatment to begin sooner. Consistent care can reduce the risk of severe impairment and help people maintain independence. If you have risk factors, a family history of glaucoma, or have not had an eye examination in some time, arrange a comprehensive checkup. For sudden eye pain, redness, blurred vision, halos, or nausea, seek emergency care immediately.

The paper addresses an important challenge in imitation learning: matching expert state-action distributions when policy changes also alter the states the learner visits. Its combination of likelihood-based action imitation and gradient estimation for policy-induced state distributions is promising and may offer a principled alternative to methods that focus only on matching actions at fixed states. The paper should clarify its assumptions, especially the availability and quality of expert data, the treatment of distribution shift, and the conditions under which the gradient estimates are unbiased or stable. A stronger comparison with established imitation-learning baselines, including evaluation across multiple environments and random seeds, would help establish the method’s practical value. The authors should also report computational costs and conduct ablations that isolate the contributions of likelihood matching and state-distribution gradient estimation. Overall, the approach appears potentially valuable, but its claims will be more convincing with clearer theoretical guarantees and broader empirical validation.

The trial of a mother and her partner accused of murdering a toddler and causing or allowing her death is under way. The pair deny the charges, and the case is being heard by a jury. Prosecutors allege the child suffered serious injuries while in the adults’ care. They say the toddler’s death followed a period of abuse and neglect. The prosecution is expected to present medical evidence and testimony about the child’s condition. Jurors will also hear evidence about the adults’ actions and the circumstances leading up to the death. The mother faces allegations that she either took part in the killing or failed to protect her child. Her partner is accused of murder and related offenses. Both defendants are entitled to the presumption of innocence unless and until they are found guilty. The court has warned jurors to consider only evidence presented during the proceedings. The defense is expected to challenge the prosecution’s account and examine the reliability of the evidence. Witnesses, including investigators and medical experts, are expected to give evidence. The trial is likely to examine the care the toddler received and when the injuries may have occurred. Proceedings are continuing, and no verdict has been reached. The court has not yet announced when the jury is expected to begin deliberations.

Sarah Payne’s brothers have spoken about the lasting trauma of their sister’s abduction and murder, describing how the loss shaped their lives long after the case ended.

Eight-year-old Sarah was abducted in July 2000 while playing near her grandparents’ home in West Sussex. Her body was found two weeks later. Roy Whiting, a convicted sex offender, was later found guilty of her murder and sentenced to life imprisonment.

In accounts of the family’s experience, Sarah’s brothers have recalled the shock of her disappearance and the painful uncertainty that followed. They were children themselves, yet had to face an intense police investigation, widespread media attention and the sudden absence of their sister.

The brothers have described how grief did not simply fade with time. Memories of Sarah remain part of everyday life, alongside the difficulty of growing up in the shadow of a crime that drew national attention. The case also left the family confronting questions about safety, trust and how to carry on after an unimaginable loss.

Sarah’s father, Michael Payne, became a prominent campaigner for changes to the system for monitoring sex offenders. The family’s tragedy helped intensify public debate over child protection and the handling of convicted offenders.

For Sarah’s brothers, however, the story is not only a matter of public policy or a notorious criminal case. It is the story of a sister they lost, and of the lasting effects on those who loved her. Their recollections underline that the consequences of abduction and murder continue for families long after a trial and sentence have concluded.

The paper addresses an important challenge in model-based reinforcement learning: learning useful latent dynamics without requiring the model to reconstruct observations. Its central idea is to let reward prediction and control-relevant objectives shape the representation, rather than relying on pixel-level reconstruction losses. This direction is well motivated, since accurate observation reconstruction may consume capacity on details that do not help decision-making. The topic is timely and relevant to both representation learning and sample-efficient control.

The strongest aspect of the work is its clear focus on task-relevant prediction. A latent model trained around rewards and future consequences could support more efficient planning than a model optimized for visual fidelity alone. The approach also has the potential to simplify training objectives and reduce computational costs. The paper’s conceptual framing is compelling and should interest researchers working on visual control and latent world models.

However, the paper should clarify precisely what is predicted in latent space and how those predictions are connected to rewards and actions. In particular, it is important to distinguish reward prediction from learning dynamics that remain useful over long planning horizons. The authors should explain how the representation avoids collapsing to features that predict immediate rewards but discard information needed for future decisions. If the method uses auxiliary objectives or regularization to address this issue, their roles should be described and tested explicitly.

The experimental section should establish whether gains come from the proposed learning principle rather than differences in model size, training budget, or hyperparameter tuning. Comparisons with reconstruction-based latent models and strong contemporary model-based baselines are essential. Results should include multiple random seeds, uncertainty estimates, and a clear account of environment and training-budget choices. The evaluation would be more convincing if it included tasks with delayed rewards, sparse feedback, and changes in reward structure, since these settings probe the limitations of reward-driven representations. Ablations should isolate the contribution of reward supervision, latent-dynamics prediction, and any planning or policy-learning components.

The paper should also discuss how the method behaves when rewards are noisy, incomplete, or changed after representation learning. These cases are important because a reward-specialized latent space may not transfer readily to new objectives. Reporting planning performance as horizon and model uncertainty increase would help assess the reliability of the learned dynamics. An analysis of computational cost, sample efficiency, and sensitivity to key design choices would further strengthen the practical case.

Overall, this is a promising and well-motivated research direction, with a potentially useful alternative to observation reconstruction for learning world models. The paper’s main claims would be stronger with sharper explanations of representation sufficiency and more comprehensive empirical controls. I recommend revision, with particular attention to long-horizon task performance, reward changes, and rigorous baseline comparisons.

This paper investigates whether reward-only latent dynamics models can support effective planning in model-based reinforcement learning for continuous-control tasks. The question is timely and relevant, especially because learning compact predictive models without direct state reconstruction could reduce modeling complexity. The comparison with state-based baselines is a useful way to assess whether reward-focused representations preserve information needed for control. A major strength is the clear emphasis on evaluating planning performance rather than representation quality alone. The paper would be more compelling if it stated its main hypotheses and contributions explicitly at the outset. It should also define precisely what “reward-only” means, including which observations, rewards, and action histories are available to the model. The experimental section should provide enough implementation detail to make the models and planning procedures reproducible. In particular, the planning horizon, search or optimization method, model-training schedule, and computational budget should be reported. Comparisons with state-based baselines need to use matched data, model capacity, and tuning effort wherever possible. The results should include multiple random seeds, uncertainty estimates, and appropriate statistical comparisons. Evaluation across diverse tasks would help establish whether the approach generalizes beyond environments where rewards are especially informative. It would also be useful to report sample efficiency, wall-clock cost, and sensitivity to reward sparsity or noise. Ablations could clarify how much performance comes from the latent dynamics model versus the planner and reward-prediction component. The discussion should address failure modes, particularly cases in which distinct states have similar rewards but require different actions. Overall, this is a promising direction, but stronger methodological detail and broader, carefully controlled experiments are needed to support the central claims.

Two Shih Tzu dogs died in an accidental house fire in Dungiven while their owners tried to rescue them. The fire broke out at the home, prompting the owners to make a desperate attempt to reach the pets. The dogs could not be saved, and the incident is understood to have been accidental. Further details about the fire were not immediately available.

When Mara was twelve, she asked her father if he believed in love.

“Love is a story people tell themselves,” he said, tightening the lid on a jar of screws.

She frowned. “Then why did you marry Mom?”

“Because we were young and foolish.”

He said it with a laugh, but the laugh ended too quickly.

After supper, Mara found him alone in the shed.

He was holding a faded blue scarf, its fringe unraveling between his fingers.

“Whose is that?” she asked.

“An old rag,” he said, and tucked it into a drawer.

Years passed, and Mara grew used to his answers.

Love was a trick.

Love was habit.

Love was two people agreeing not to leave.

When her mother died, he did not cry at the funeral.

He stood beside the grave with his hands clasped behind his back.

Only when everyone had gone did he kneel and brush dirt from the headstone.

At home, he kept the house exactly as it had been.

Her mother’s cup stayed on the shelf.

Her coat remained on its hook.

The blue scarf disappeared from the shed, but Mara never asked where it went.

One winter, her father slipped on the stairs and broke his hip.

Mara moved back to care for him.

She found him quieter than before, his sharp remarks worn thin by pain.

One evening, she brought him tea in the old cup.

He held it carefully, as if it might vanish.

“She used to make it too strong,” he said.

“Mom?”

He nodded.

“She said tea should wake the dead.”

Mara smiled. “Did you love her?”

His eyes went to the dark window.

“No,” he said.

Then he looked down at the cup and traced its chipped rim.

“I loved how she sang when she was angry,” he murmured.

“I loved that she never remembered where she put her glasses.”

“I loved the way she turned toward me in her sleep.”

His voice broke on the last word.

Mara sat beside him without speaking.

He reached for her hand, then stopped, as though affection were a language he had forgotten.

She took his hand first.

He held on.

In the morning, he asked her to find the blue scarf.

It was folded beneath his pillow, soft from years of secret keeping.

He draped it over his shoulders and looked toward the empty chair across the room.

“Love isn’t real,” he said.

But his fingers curled around the scarf as if someone were still holding the other end.

The knock came at dusk, three sharp blows against the cottage door. Mara froze with a spoon in her hand. Her father looked up from the hearth, and her mother quietly drew the curtains. Outside, a voice called, “By order of the district, open the door.” No one had told them what Mara was accused of. Only that she was to be taken away and held indefinitely. Her father had asked for a reason at the town office, but the clerk had turned his papers facedown. Now boots crunched across the gravel. “Stay behind us,” her mother whispered. Mara was eighteen, old enough to understand the fear in their faces. The door shuddered beneath another blow. Her father lifted the old hunting rifle from above the mantel. “Don’t,” Mara said. He glanced back at her, eyes wet, then lowered the barrel toward the floor. Her mother moved to the door and slid the bolt into place. The officers struck again, and the wood split near the latch. Her father fired once into the ceiling. Dust fell, and the men outside stopped. “We won’t let you take her without telling us why,” he shouted. A moment later, a stone shattered the kitchen window. Her mother pulled Mara down as glass scattered across the table. In the confusion, her father opened the back door. They ran into the orchard, carrying no coats and taking no time to look back. Behind them, the officers entered the cottage. Ahead, the road disappeared into a dark stretch of pines. Mara’s mother held her hand so tightly it hurt. Her father walked behind them, rifle lowered, listening for pursuit. At dawn, they reached a shepherd’s hut and found a radio beneath a blanket. The news called them dangerous fugitives, but still offered no charge against Mara. She listened, then asked her parents what they would do next. Her father set the rifle aside. “We’ll find the truth,” he said, “and we’ll make them say it aloud.”
