The paper addresses an important challenge in reinforcement learning: learning effective behavior when rewards are sparse and difficult to discover through random exploration. Its central idea—training first at states close to the goal and progressively increasing the distance—offers a clear way to combine goal-directed search with policy learning. The approach is intuitive and may reduce the time needed to discover useful trajectories compared with training from arbitrary initial states. The paper’s strongest contribution is its focus on how training-state selection can shape exploration, rather than relying only on changes to the reward function or learning algorithm. The method would be easier to assess if the authors specified how they choose the next training distance and when they decide the policy is ready to advance. They should also clarify how search is used, including its computational cost and whether it is available at training time, evaluation time, or both. A thorough experimental comparison with standard reinforcement learning baselines and established curriculum-learning or goal-conditioned methods is essential. Results should include multiple random seeds and report both success rates and sample efficiency, with uncertainty estimates. Ablations could determine whether the gains come from progressive distances, search itself, or their interaction. The evaluation would be stronger if it included tasks with varied dynamics, goal locations, and obstacle layouts. The authors should discuss sensitivity to curriculum parameters and the possibility that failures at a new distance prevent progress or cause forgetting. It would also help to report wall-clock time and search overhead, since fewer environment interactions may not translate into lower total cost. Overall, the topic is promising and the proposed strategy is intuitively motivated, but the paper needs clearer methodological detail and stronger comparative evidence to establish its effectiveness and generality.

A soldier injured in a training accident was moved out of a hospital’s public waiting area after his uniform raised concerns among other patients, officials said. The incident occurred at a regional medical center after the soldier was brought in for treatment. He had reportedly sustained non-life-threatening injuries during a routine exercise. While waiting to be assessed, the soldier remained in his military uniform, which included visible equipment associated with his unit. Some people in the waiting room became uneasy, prompting hospital staff to review the situation. The soldier was then taken to a more private area of the facility. Hospital representatives said the move was made to maintain a calm environment and protect the patient’s privacy. They emphasized that he continued to receive medical care without interruption. The decision was not described as disciplinary, and there was no indication that the soldier posed a threat. Military officials said they were reviewing the circumstances surrounding the training accident. They did not immediately release details about the exercise or the soldier’s identity. The hospital declined to identify the patients who raised concerns. Staff members said they followed standard procedures for managing sensitive situations in shared spaces. The episode has prompted discussion about how hospitals should balance public reassurance with the dignity and privacy of patients in uniform. Further information is expected as the military review proceeds.

Mara Venn kept the office keys on a chain around her wrist.
She said it was because people misplaced things.
Everyone knew she liked hearing them jingle when she walked past.
She managed the accounts department at Bellweather Supplies.
Her desk stood at the center of the room like a small, gray fortress.
From there, she could see every printer, doorway, and suspiciously generous gesture.
“Nothing is free,” she often said.
She said it when someone brought pastries.
She said it when the company offered flexible hours.
She said it when the sun came out.

On Monday morning, Theo from payroll arrived with a box of oranges.
He set it beside the kettle and smiled at everyone.
“Help yourselves,” he said.
Mara looked up from a spreadsheet.
“Why?”
Theo blinked.
“Because they’re oranges.”
“That doesn’t answer the question.”
He laughed, as if she had made a joke.
Mara wrote his name in the margin of her notebook.

By noon, three people had taken oranges.
By two, the box was empty.
Mara found Theo refilling it from a second box under his desk.
“Planning to make us all owe you?”
“Not at all,” he said.
“Then why keep doing it?”
“Because I bought too many.”
Mara studied him for a long moment.
She decided he was either foolish or unusually patient.
Both possibilities irritated her.

The next week, a storm flooded the street outside the office.
Rain rattled the windows, and the buses stopped running.
Mara stayed at her desk, waiting for the water to recede.
Theo appeared with a stack of spare umbrellas.
He handed one to the receptionist and another to a new intern.
Then he offered one to Mara.
“I have my own,” she said.
“You left it at home.”
Mara looked toward the umbrella stand.
Her empty hook seemed to mock her.
“I’ll manage.”
Theo placed an umbrella beside her chair anyway.
She watched him walk away, certain the umbrella would later be mentioned in some favor ledger.

It never was.
The umbrella sat by her desk for three days.
On Thursday, Mara carried it to Theo’s cubicle.
“You forgot this.”
“It’s yours now,” he said.
“I don’t accept gifts.”
“Then call it a loan.”
“I don’t borrow from coworkers.”
Theo shrugged.
“Then leave it by the door for the next person.”
Mara set it down with more force than necessary.
That afternoon, she saw the intern leave with it.

In spring, the company announced its annual staff awards.
Mara chaired the small committee because no one else wanted to.
The categories were punctuality, teamwork, and exceptional service.
The awards came with a certificate and a modest gift card.
Mara preferred awards that could be measured.
She believed praise made people lazy.
Still, the committee had to choose someone for teamwork.
Theo’s name appeared on every nomination slip.
He had helped the warehouse team reorganize their records.
He had stayed late to explain a new payroll system.
He had covered reception while the receptionist took her daughter to the dentist.
“He’s collecting admirers,” Mara said.
Her assistant, Leena, raised an eyebrow.
“Or he’s helping people.”
“That is how schemes begin.”

Mara reviewed the nominations again.
Every note mentioned a different favor.
None asked for anything in return.
She checked the dates and spoke to the people who had written them.
Their stories matched.
She searched Theo’s personnel file for a pattern of complaints.
There were none.
She inspected his expense reports.
They were tidy.
She asked the receptionist whether Theo had been angling for a promotion.
“He hasn’t even applied for one,” the receptionist said.
Mara frowned.
That seemed like a particularly elaborate way to hide ambition.

At the awards meeting, the committee waited for Mara’s decision.
She had prepared a list of reasons not to choose Theo.
He was too popular.
His good deeds were impossible to quantify.
The award might encourage others to expect attention.
Yet the other nominees had fewer votes.
The rules required a winner.
Mara tapped her pen against the table.
“Fine,” she said.
“Give it to Theo.”
Leena smiled.
“Are you going to tell him?”
“I suppose the certificate won’t walk over by itself.”

The ceremony took place in the break room.
People gathered around a plate of supermarket biscuits.
Mara stood beside a paper banner that sagged in the middle.
Theo looked surprised when she called his name.
He came forward, wiping his hands on his trousers.
Mara handed him the certificate and gift card.
“Your colleagues say you’ve been helpful,” she said.
The room went quiet.
Theo glanced at the certificate.
“Thank you, Mara.”
“Don’t thank me.”
“I’m thanking the committee.”
“The committee didn’t carry boxes upstairs.”
A few people laughed.
Mara felt heat creep into her cheeks.
She had not meant to say that.

Theo held the certificate carefully.
“I didn’t do those things for a prize,” he said.
“People always say that.”
“Maybe people sometimes mean it.”
Mara waited for the request that would follow.
Theo only smiled.
Then he offered the gift card to the interns, saying they should use it for the team lunch.
Mara’s suspicion flared at once.
“There,” she said.
“There what?”
“You’re turning an award into another favor.”
Theo looked down at the card.
“I thought lunch would be nice.”
“Nothing is free.”
“No,” he said gently.
“But sometimes someone pays because they want to.”

The room emptied slowly.
Mara stayed behind, stacking the paper cups.
Theo stayed too, gathering the crumbs.
She watched him work without announcing it.
When the break room was clean, he picked up his coat.
“Have a good evening,” he said.
Mara almost asked what he wanted.
Instead, she nodded.
At her desk, the umbrella still stood in the corner.
She had kept it there after all.
The following morning, the forecast promised more rain.
Mara carried the umbrella to the reception stand.
Beside it, she placed a small box of oranges.
Then she returned to her gray fortress.
When Theo noticed, he smiled but said nothing.
Mara waited for the scheme to reveal itself.
The office hummed around her.
For once, she did not write anyone’s name in her notebook.

The paper addresses an important problem: mapping neural network computation graphs onto distributed hardware while balancing communication, memory, and computation costs. Its focus on learning-based partitioning and device placement is timely, given the growing scale and heterogeneity of modern training systems. The work’s central motivation is clear, and the proposed approach appears relevant to practitioners seeking better performance than hand-designed heuristics can provide. A major strength is the joint treatment of graph partitioning and device assignment, which can avoid decisions that are locally attractive but globally inefficient. The paper would benefit from a more precise description of its optimization objective and the assumptions made about device capabilities, network topology, and workload characteristics. In particular, it should clarify whether communication costs are measured, modeled, or learned, and how the method handles variability in these costs. The learning formulation also needs sufficient detail for readers to reproduce it, including the state representation, action space, reward, training procedure, and stopping criteria. If the method uses a graph neural network or another architecture tailored to graph structure, the paper should explain why that choice is appropriate and compare it with simpler alternatives. The evaluation should include strong heuristic and optimization-based baselines, not only naive placement strategies. Comparisons should use identical hardware, workload, and tuning budgets wherever possible. Results across multiple graph sizes, model architectures, device counts, and network configurations would help establish how broadly the method generalizes. The authors should report both end-to-end execution time and relevant intermediate measures, such as communication volume, memory utilization, and load imbalance. Repeated runs and variation across random seeds are important because learning-based methods can be unstable. The paper should also provide uncertainty estimates or statistical tests for its main performance claims. An ablation study would help identify the contributions of the learning algorithm, graph representation, and cost model. Practical constraints deserve more attention, especially placement feasibility under device-memory limits and the handling of operator-specific hardware requirements. It would be useful to discuss whether the method supports dynamic workloads or requires retraining when the model or cluster changes. The authors should quantify the offline cost of training and tuning, as well as the runtime overhead of producing a placement. Some additional analysis of failure cases would make the limitations more transparent and help readers understand when conventional methods may be preferable. Overall, the topic is compelling and the approach has the potential to make distributed execution more efficient. With clearer methodological detail, broader and more rigorous evaluation, and a candid discussion of limitations, the paper could make a valuable contribution to systems for distributed neural network computation.

The European Union and the United States are seeking to restore a legal framework for transferring personal data across the Atlantic, after a court ruling disrupted the previous arrangement. The proposed EU-US Privacy Shield is intended to give companies a clearer basis for moving information between the two regions. It would also set out commitments on how US authorities and businesses handle data belonging to Europeans.

The effort follows a 2015 decision by the European Union’s top court, which invalidated the earlier Safe Harbor agreement. The court found that the arrangement did not adequately protect Europeans’ personal information from US government surveillance. Its ruling left many businesses uncertain about the legality of routine data transfers.

EU and US officials say the new framework offers stronger safeguards and more effective oversight. Companies joining the Privacy Shield would have to publish privacy policies and respond to complaints. European data protection authorities could refer unresolved cases to a new dispute-resolution process.

The agreement also provides for an independent ombudsperson to address concerns about access to data by US intelligence agencies. US officials have said surveillance would be subject to limits and oversight. They argue the framework gives Europeans meaningful avenues to raise complaints.

But privacy advocates and some European officials remain unconvinced. They question whether the promised limits on surveillance are sufficiently binding and enforceable. Critics also say the ombudsperson may lack the independence and authority needed to provide an effective remedy.

The underlying legal issue is whether Europeans can challenge government access to their data in a US court. Under European law, personal information transferred abroad must receive protections essentially equivalent to those at home. Skeptics warn that assurances and administrative procedures may not meet that standard.

Businesses, meanwhile, are eager for a stable system. Cross-border data flows support services ranging from online commerce to cloud computing and customer support. Without a dependable legal basis, companies may face added costs, uncertainty or restrictions on how they operate.

The European Commission has presented the Privacy Shield as a substantial improvement over Safe Harbor. Its future, however, depends on whether European privacy regulators and courts consider the protections sufficient. A legal challenge could again put transatlantic transfers at risk.

For companies, approval would not necessarily end compliance obligations. They would still need to follow European data protection rules and meet the framework’s requirements. Regulators could investigate complaints and suspend transfers in cases of noncompliance.

The debate reflects a broader tension between international business and fundamental rights. European institutions are under pressure to ensure personal data does not lose protection when it crosses borders. US authorities, in turn, have defended access to information as necessary for national security.

The Privacy Shield is therefore more than a commercial arrangement. It is a test of whether the two sides can reconcile differing legal systems and expectations about privacy. Its credibility will depend not only on written promises, but on whether people can obtain effective remedies in practice.

Every Friday at dawn, Sergeant Elias Vale became impossible to kill. Bullets passed through him, fire curled around him, and falling walls seemed to part at his shoulders. The gift lasted until midnight, then vanished without warning. Elias had learned to treat Fridays like borrowed holidays. He smiled more, worried less, and promised his squad he would always be there.

That Friday, the squad was ordered to escort a supply truck through a narrow market street. Mina walked beside him, humming softly beneath the engine’s growl. Corporal Reyes checked the rooftops, while young Tom kept glancing at the houses. Elias told them not to worry. “It’s Friday,” he said, tapping his chest. “Nothing can touch me.”

Halfway through the market, a child darted into the road after a red ball. Mina ran to pull him clear. Reyes shouted for the driver to stop. Then Elias saw a bundle beneath the truck, wired to a timer. He lunged toward it, certain his gift made him the safest person there.

The blast erased the street in a white flash. Elias woke on his knees, unharmed, with dust drifting down like gray snow. The truck had become twisted metal. Mina lay motionless near the curb, one hand still curled around the child’s coat. Reyes was buried beneath a fallen awning, and Tom was nowhere in sight.

Elias shouted their names until his throat tore. The child sobbed beside him, alive but alone. He dug at the rubble with bare hands, though his fingers could not reach the people trapped beneath it. For the first time, his invulnerability felt less like a gift than a locked door.

At sunset, medics carried the survivors away. Elias sat in the ruined street, watching the day slip toward midnight. He had made it through Friday, just as he always had. When the clock struck twelve, nothing changed in him. Yet he understood that surviving the blast had never meant he could save anyone else.

As the financier lay dying, he kept the circle’s names sealed behind his lips. For decades, their hidden accounts had made him rich—and kept every crime beyond the reach of discovery. His partners urged him to confess and buy himself peace, but he knew the truth would bind them all. He smiled at the silence he had guarded so faithfully. When his heart stopped, the circle was free to vanish.

EU leaders have rejected Britain’s hopes of keeping the benefits of the single market while restricting immigration after Brexit, insisting that access to the bloc’s economic system comes with shared rules. The position leaves the UK facing a choice between accepting the free movement of people and pursuing a more distant relationship with the European Union.

European officials have repeatedly said that the four freedoms—movement of goods, services, capital and people—are inseparable. British campaigners for Brexit, however, have argued that the country should retain access to European markets while gaining greater control over immigration.

The disagreement is expected to shape negotiations over Britain’s future trade and political ties with the EU. Leaders from several member states have warned that allowing Britain to select only the advantages it wants could encourage other countries to demand similar arrangements.

A senior EU position is that participation in the single market requires compliance with its rules, including free movement and contributions to the EU budget. Alternative agreements could preserve some trade links, but would not offer the same level of access without conditions.

The issue is particularly sensitive for sectors that rely on cross-border trade and workers, including finance, manufacturing and agriculture. Businesses have urged both sides to provide clarity, warning that prolonged uncertainty could delay investment and disrupt supply chains.

The British government has faced pressure to deliver on promises to reduce immigration while limiting economic damage from leaving the EU. Critics say those goals may be difficult to reconcile, especially if negotiations produce new barriers to trade.

EU leaders have also emphasized that the terms of any future relationship would depend on the choices Britain makes during the withdrawal process. They have declined to discuss a bespoke deal that would grant single-market benefits while exempting the UK from core obligations.

Negotiations are likely to involve competing priorities on trade, migration, regulation and financial contributions. For now, the EU’s message is clear: Britain may seek a close economic relationship, but it cannot expect the benefits of membership without accepting the rules that underpin them.

The paper presents a hybrid variational autoencoder–autoregressive model for image generation, but its central contribution needs to be distinguished more clearly from prior combinations of latent-variable and autoregressive methods. The authors should explain which component drives the reported gains and support this claim with ablations that remove or replace each component. Performance comparisons are useful, but they should include strong, current baselines evaluated on the same datasets, compute budgets, and sampling settings. In addition to aggregate quality metrics, the evaluation would benefit from measures of diversity, perceptual quality, and computational cost. The choice of loss weights appears important, yet the paper should justify how they were selected and report sensitivity analyses to show whether performance is robust to reasonable changes. It would also help to discuss trade-offs among reconstruction fidelity, prior matching, and generation quality, since improving one objective may weaken another. Overall, the approach is promising, but clearer attribution, more rigorous comparisons, and transparent loss-weight analysis are needed to establish its contribution.

Mara reached the city at sunset, limping beneath a sky the color of ash. Weeds split the highway, and young trees grew through the roofs of stalled cars. She had not seen another person in eleven days. Her water was almost gone, and the storm clouds promised a freezing night. At the edge of the city, she found a glass tower wrapped in ivy. Its doors hung open, swaying gently though there was no wind. Inside, roots snaked across the lobby tiles. A family of foxes watched her from beneath the reception desk, then slipped into the dark. Mara climbed to the fourth floor and chose a room with a working lock. She wedged a chair beneath the handle and spread her damp coat on the floor. Before sleeping, she listened to the city settle around her. Somewhere below, a metal door clanged shut. She told herself it was the wind. In the middle of the night, she woke to the sound of slow footsteps in the hallway. They stopped outside her room. Mara held her breath and gripped the knife at her belt. The handle turned once, carefully, then went still. She saw no shadow beneath the door. A faint scratching began on the wall behind her bed. It traveled upward, inch by inch, toward the ceiling. Mara backed away as dust drifted from the cracks. Something heavy crawled across the floor above her. The steps returned, circling the room, though the hallway remained silent. Then came a soft knock from inside the locked wardrobe. She ran for the window and climbed onto the ivy-covered ledge. The city below was empty, but every dark window seemed to be watching. At dawn, Mara found fresh claw marks on the outside of the glass.

Death had been awake for three hundred years, and his bones ached beneath their black coat. He was hoping for one quiet night when he saw the school bus drifting across the center line. The driver’s chin had sunk to his chest, and the road ahead curled toward a steep ravine. Death sighed and reached for the silver ledger tucked inside his sleeve. A bus full of children was not how he wanted to spend the evening. He stepped into the road and raised one pale hand. The driver’s eyes stayed shut. The bus rolled on, tires humming over the yellow paint. Death tried the old tricks: a sudden chill, a flicker of moonlight, a whisper in the driver’s ear. Nothing stirred him. The children slept beneath coats and backpacks, unaware of the danger. Death hurried alongside the bus, his cloak snapping in the wind. He could not touch the wheel, and he could not wake the driver by force. Then he spotted a small girl in the front seat, still awake, watching him. He tapped the window with one long finger. The girl blinked, then followed his gaze to the driver. She unbuckled herself and shouted, “Wake up!” The driver jerked upright, startled, and swerved hard. The bus skidded, struck a guardrail, and stopped with its front wheels hanging over the ravine. For a moment, everyone was silent. Then the children began to cry, and the driver stumbled out to call for help. Death leaned against a roadside post, breathing though he had no need to. The girl looked back and saw him standing in the moonlight. “Are you here for us?” she asked. Death closed his ledger. “Not tonight,” he said. Then, at last, he walked home beneath the quiet stars.

For centuries, Heaven had enjoyed a monopoly on the afterlife. Its gates were pearl, its streets were gold, and its advertisements promised eternal peace in a tasteful serif font. Then the alternatives arrived.

The first was Nirvana Now, a minimalist destination where residents could dissolve themselves immediately, no waiting, no paperwork. Its slogan was “Be less, sooner.” The second was Valhalla Plus, which offered unlimited feasting, complimentary axes, and a loyalty program that rewarded guests for dying heroically. A third competitor, The Elysian Fields, promised “nature, but with better weather.”

Heaven’s management held an emergency meeting in the Cloud Boardroom. “We have the best product,” said Archangel Gabriel, polishing a halo that had gone slightly gray. “We offer eternal bliss.” “Yes,” said the marketing director, “but we’ve been offering the same bliss since the beginning of time.” The room fell silent, which was awkward because silence was one of their premium features.

They hired a consultant from Earth named Martin, who had once rebranded a bank as “a feelings company.” Martin surveyed the pearly gates and frowned. “Your customer journey has too many judgment points.” “They’re important,” said Saint Peter. “People should know where they’re going.” Martin nodded sympathetically. “Of course. But could they know after they’ve downloaded the app?”

He proposed Heaven Lite, with a shorter intake interview and a cloud-based waiting room. The angels objected that judgment could not be streamlined. Martin called this “a legacy mindset.” He also suggested replacing the trumpet fanfare with a personalized welcome playlist. Gabriel asked whether the playlist could include hymns. Martin said that was precisely the kind of assumption driving people elsewhere.

The first customer survey arrived a week later. Heaven scored highly for cleanliness and low for spontaneity. Many respondents described eternity as “beautiful, but a little managed.” One wrote, “I miss having the option to make a mistake.” Another complained that every harp solo sounded like an announcement that a committee had approved something.

Meanwhile, Valhalla’s advertisements appeared across the clouds. A laughing warrior raised a golden mug beneath the words, “No regrets, just raids.” Elysium launched a wellness retreat featuring ambrosia smoothies and optional reincarnation. Nirvana Now quietly bought the rights to Heaven’s old slogan, “Peace everlasting,” and used it to advertise its exit policy.

Heaven responded with a grand campaign called Forever Starts Here. It featured children playing beneath a rainbow and a caption assuring viewers that all clouds were responsibly sourced. The campaign won an award from the Celestial Association of Eternal Brands. It did not win many new souls.

The trouble was that Heaven had mistaken its reputation for a relationship. It had assumed people wanted perfection, when many wanted a place that would let them remain a little unfinished. The angels tried adding a comedy club, but the jokes had all been approved by the Office of Moral Clarity. They tried a garden of mystery, but someone labeled every plant.

At last Saint Peter proposed a modest change. “What if,” he said, “we let people choose what peace means to them?” Gabriel stared at him. “That sounds complicated.” “So does eternity,” Peter replied, “when you spend all of it explaining why there’s only one correct way to enjoy it.”

The board voted, after three subcommittees and one prophetic dream. Heaven opened its gates to a new district called The Unfinished Garden. There, residents could wander without a map, ask questions without being graded, and take the occasional afternoon off from bliss. A small sign at the entrance read, “You may change your mind.”

The first visitors were cautious. Some stayed for an hour, then wandered back to the familiar streets. Others settled beneath the trees and discovered that silence felt different when nobody had scheduled it. Even the harps sounded better when the musicians were allowed to improvise.

Heaven’s numbers improved, though not enough to satisfy its quarterly forecasts. Martin left to advise Valhalla on customer retention. Gabriel let his halo grow a little crooked. Saint Peter kept the gate open.

And somewhere beyond the clouds, the afterlife became less like a verdict and more like a choice.

For nine centuries, Mara had watched humanity repeat its worst mistakes. The last war had ended with her exile from Earth, though she could no longer remember what crime had sent her away. She crossed the dark between stars in a ship assembled from abandoned satellites and stubborn hope. On every world she visited, she searched for signs of life. She found oceans beneath ice, forests of crystal, and winds that sang across empty plains. At last, on a blue moon circling a distant gas giant, her instruments detected a steady pulse beneath the soil. Mara dug until her hands bled, then found a silver seed, warm as a living heart. It unfolded in her palm and projected a map of underground chambers. Inside, she discovered tiny creatures arranged in a circle around a pool of light. They were not dead, but waiting. Mara spoke to them in every language she knew, including the one she had invented for lonely nights. The creatures answered with a rhythm that made the walls glow. They showed her visions of their vanished makers: a civilization that had destroyed itself through fear and greed. Mara nearly turned away. She had seen that story before, written across the ruins of Earth. Instead, she offered the creatures a choice. They could wake slowly, learn from the old world’s failures, and shape a new one together. For the first time in centuries, Mara felt that immortality might mean more than endless survival. The creatures accepted, and the pool of light rose like a small sun. They began by building homes that shared warmth and food. They made no throne, and gave no single voice the power to command them all. Mara stayed to teach them, but never called herself their ruler. When they asked why she had come so far, she said she wanted to find life that might do better than humanity. Their answer came as a chorus: “Then help us become better than you.” Outside, the stars shone without promise or judgment. Mara smiled, and for once, the future did not feel like a sentence.

The paper addresses a practical challenge in CNN transfer learning: deciding which feature channels to retain or regularize when adapting a pretrained model to a new task. Its focus on channel-wise mechanisms is well motivated, since channels can vary substantially in relevance across datasets and tasks. The proposed approach appears promising, but the paper should define its regularization and selection procedures precisely enough for readers to reproduce them. The authors should also clarify how the method differs from related channel pruning, attention, and feature-selection approaches. A thorough evaluation across multiple datasets, architectures, and transfer-learning settings would help establish the method’s generality. Comparisons should include strong fine-tuning and channel-selection baselines, with consistent training budgets and hyperparameter tuning. Ablation studies are needed to isolate the effects of regularization, channel selection, and any interaction between them. Reporting variability across multiple runs, along with computational cost and accuracy trade-offs, would strengthen the empirical claims. The paper should discuss sensitivity to the selection threshold or other key hyperparameters and explain how these are chosen in practice. Overall, the topic is relevant and the approach has potential, but stronger methodological detail and broader experimental validation are needed to support its contribution.

The paper studies neural networks that emulate iterative algorithms, focusing on how they represent numbers and whether their learned procedures generalize beyond the training distribution. This is a timely topic at the intersection of algorithmic reasoning, representation learning, and generalization. The central question—whether a network learns an algorithm or merely a collection of input-output associations—is important and clearly motivated. The emphasis on out-of-distribution (OOD) performance makes the work especially relevant to claims about neural reasoning.

A major strength is the paper’s attempt to connect behavioral generalization with the internal representation of numerical quantities. This perspective can help explain why models succeed or fail when tested on larger values, longer sequences, or unfamiliar input formats. The focus on iterative computation also provides a useful setting for studying how representations evolve across steps. If the experiments support the claims, they could offer insights beyond the specific tasks considered.

The paper would benefit from a sharper operational definition of “mimicking an iterative algorithm.” It should specify what evidence distinguishes algorithm-like computation from a function that happens to match the algorithm on tested examples. Similarly, the authors should define OOD generalization precisely and separate extrapolation to larger numbers from shifts in sequence length, operand distribution, or task format. These forms of distribution shift may place substantially different demands on a model.

The analysis of learned number representations is promising, but the conclusions should be tied to clearly stated measurements. Probes can reveal information available to a classifier without showing that the network uses that information during computation. The paper should therefore complement probing with causal interventions, such as perturbing selected activations or replacing representations while measuring the effect on outputs. It should also report how robust the findings are to probe capacity, training data, and layer selection.

The experimental design should include strong comparisons with simpler alternatives, including lookup-like models, standard multilayer networks, and architectures with explicit recurrence or algorithmic structure. Training and test splits should be described carefully to rule out leakage through value ranges, templates, or correlated examples. Results should be reported across multiple random seeds, with uncertainty estimates and enough implementation detail for reproduction. Where feasible, the authors should test substantially larger inputs than those used in training, rather than relying only on modest shifts.

The paper should also discuss limitations of the chosen tasks. Success on a narrow family of arithmetic or iterative problems does not establish general algorithmic reasoning, and failures may reflect optimization or data coverage rather than representational impossibility. A clearer account of these alternatives would make the interpretation more balanced. The authors should avoid broad claims unless they are supported by experiments across task families and model configurations.

Overall, this work addresses a significant question and has the potential to clarify the relationship between learned number representations and OOD algorithmic behavior. Its strongest contribution is the effort to connect internal representations with systematic generalization rather than treating accuracy as sufficient evidence. I recommend revision, with priority given to clarifying the claims, strengthening causal evidence, and broadening the evaluation. With these changes, the paper could provide a more convincing account of when neural networks genuinely reproduce iterative procedures and when their apparent competence depends on the training distribution.

Mara had spent years waiting for happiness to arrive like a letter with her name on it. When it didn’t, she began searching for it in small, desperate ways. She bought bright yellow curtains, learned to bake bread, and took long walks beside the river. For a few days, each thing helped. Then the comfort faded, and she felt more hollow than before.

One rainy evening, Mara found a stray kitten under the steps of her apartment building. She brought it inside and named it Lantern. The kitten slept beside her pillow, and for the first time in months, Mara laughed without forcing herself. That night, her neighbor’s lights went out during a storm. Mara decided Lantern’s happiness had stolen the electricity from him.

The idea seemed absurd in the morning, but it stayed. Whenever Mara felt a moment of joy, something bad happened nearby: a dropped glass, a slammed door, a siren in the distance. She began to believe happiness was a force that had to come from somewhere, and that it was taking something from other people. If she felt better, someone else must be suffering.

Mara tried to give her happiness away. She left bread outside her neighbor’s door and slipped coins into a stranger’s coat pocket. Still, whenever she smiled, she imagined someone paying for it. She stopped playing with Lantern and hid the yellow curtains in a closet. She even stopped eating the bread she baked.

Her neighbor, Mr. Bell, noticed the change and knocked one afternoon. Mara opened the door only a crack. He asked if she was all right, but she heard accusation in his gentle voice. She told him she knew what her happiness had done to him. Mr. Bell frowned and said nothing had happened to him. His lights had failed because of the storm.

Mara thought he was trying to protect her. That night, she gathered her savings and walked to the river, convinced she could return every bit of happiness she had taken. She climbed onto the wet stone ledge and leaned over the dark water. Lantern’s small, frightened cry followed her from the path.

Mr. Bell came running with a flashlight. He reached for Mara, but she stepped back, certain that his fear was another price she had caused him to pay. The stone shifted beneath her shoe, and the river surged below. Lantern cried again, and Mara hesitated.

Mr. Bell caught her wrist. For a long moment, neither of them spoke. Then Mara began to shake, and the belief that had seemed so solid cracked with the sound of the rain. She let him guide her down from the ledge. In the morning, she called a doctor, and Lantern curled in her lap while the yellow curtains waited in the closet.

The paper investigates adaptive channel-skipping methods for accelerating transfer-learned deep networks while maintaining predictive accuracy, an important goal for resource-constrained deployment. Its focus is timely, and evaluating the methods specifically after transfer learning could offer useful guidance beyond studies of models trained from scratch. The paper would benefit from a clearer statement of its main contribution and how its skipping strategy differs from existing pruning and dynamic-inference approaches. The experimental design should cover multiple architectures, datasets, and transfer-learning settings to establish that the results generalize. Comparisons should include strong, consistently tuned baselines, such as unmodified models, static channel pruning, and other adaptive methods. Please report not only theoretical operation counts but also measured latency, memory use, and energy where feasible, since channel skipping does not always translate into real hardware speedups. Accuracy results should include variability across runs and tests for statistically meaningful differences, particularly when the reported losses are small. The method’s skipping criteria, computational overhead, and behavior at inference time need enough detail to support reproduction. Ablations examining skip thresholds, skipped-channel proportions, and fine-tuning choices would clarify which design decisions drive the results. The paper should also discuss limitations, including sensitivity to distribution shift and whether skipped channels can disproportionately affect particular classes or input types. Overall, the work addresses a promising problem, but stronger baselines, broader evaluation, and more transparent reporting are needed to substantiate its claims.

Explore Sekhmet, the ancient Egyptian goddess associated with the sun, protection, medicine, and fierce power. This self-paced course introduces her mythology, including stories that portray her as both a force of destruction and a guardian of life. You’ll consider how these contrasting qualities can illuminate change, courage, and the need for balance. Short readings and reflection prompts invite you to connect the myths with your own experiences. Gentle practices, such as journaling and mindful breathing, offer ways to notice emotions without judgment. You’ll also explore how symbolic rituals can mark intentions for healing and personal growth. The course is educational and reflective, not a substitute for mental health care or medical advice. Move at your own pace and choose the practices that feel appropriate for you.

A hacktivist group has claimed responsibility for briefly disrupting access to BBC websites, describing the incident as a test of its cyberattack capabilities.

The group said it launched a distributed denial-of-service attack, which floods online services with traffic in an effort to make them unavailable. The BBC’s websites experienced access problems for a short period, according to the group’s account.

The claim has not been independently verified. The BBC had not publicly confirmed the group’s account or provided details about the cause of any disruption at the time of publication.

A successful denial-of-service attack can slow a website or prevent users from reaching it, but it does not necessarily mean that data has been accessed or stolen. There was no immediate evidence that the incident involved a breach of BBC systems or the exposure of personal information.

The group framed the action as a capability test, though it did not provide technical evidence to support its description. Such claims can be difficult to assess without information from the affected organization or independent cybersecurity researchers.

The episode comes amid continued concern about politically motivated attacks against public institutions and major media organizations. Hacktivist groups often use denial-of-service campaigns to draw attention to their causes or demonstrate their ability to disrupt online services.

Cybersecurity specialists say that even short outages can inconvenience audiences and put pressure on organizations’ response teams. They also caution that a group’s public claims may exaggerate the scale or impact of an incident.

Organizations commonly rely on traffic filtering, content delivery networks and other defensive measures to absorb or limit malicious requests. The effectiveness of those protections can vary depending on the size and design of an attack.

The BBC operates a broad range of digital services, including news pages, streaming platforms and regional websites. A disruption to one service does not necessarily mean that all of its online operations have been affected.

The duration and scope of the reported interruption were not clear. It was also unknown whether the disruption was linked to a wider campaign or was an isolated event.

The group did not say whether it planned further actions. The BBC had not announced any changes to its services or described an investigation.

Security analysts typically recommend that organizations preserve network records and coordinate with service providers after suspected denial-of-service activity. Those steps can help determine what happened and whether defenses need to be strengthened.

For users, brief access problems may result from an attack, routine technical faults or unusually high demand. Without confirmation from the organization or independent evidence, the precise cause of this incident remains uncertain.

The event will add a Scottish celebration to the annual fundraising campaign, which raises money for projects supporting children facing difficult circumstances.

Barrowman, an actor and entertainer, and Bird, a broadcaster, will guide the audience through the evening’s performances. The concert is expected to feature a mix of music and entertainment, though further details about the line-up and programme have not been announced.

Organisers say the Glasgow event will offer audiences a chance to enjoy live performances while contributing to a national cause. Funds raised by Children in Need help charities and community groups provide practical support, safe spaces and opportunities for young people.

Heart health is shaped by everyday habits as well as age, family history, and medical conditions. Cardiovascular disease includes problems such as heart attacks, strokes, and heart failure. Lifestyle changes cannot remove every risk, but they can lower the chances of disease and support overall well-being.

Choose a pattern of eating that emphasizes vegetables, fruits, whole grains, beans, nuts, and other minimally processed foods. Include fish and lean sources of protein, and use unsaturated oils in place of butter or other sources of saturated fat when practical. Limit processed meats, highly processed snacks, sugary drinks, and foods high in salt. Too much sodium can raise blood pressure, so compare nutrition labels and flavor meals with herbs, spices, citrus, or vinegar. A healthy eating pattern is more important than any single “superfood.”

Regular physical activity strengthens the heart and can improve blood pressure, cholesterol, blood sugar, mood, and sleep. A useful goal for many adults is at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic activity each week, such as brisk walking or cycling. Another option is 75 minutes of vigorous activity, or a combination of moderate and vigorous exercise. Add muscle-strengthening activities on two or more days each week. If you are inactive, start with short, comfortable sessions and increase gradually. Even brief movement breaks can help reduce long periods of sitting.

Avoid tobacco in all forms, including cigarettes, cigars, and smokeless products. Smoking damages blood vessels and increases the risk of heart attack and stroke. Quitting can benefit heart health at any age, and counseling, quitlines, and approved medicines can improve the chance of success. Avoid exposure to secondhand smoke when possible.

If you drink alcohol, keep in mind that less is generally better for health, and no one should start drinking for heart benefits. Alcohol can raise blood pressure and contribute to other health problems. Ask a health professional whether alcohol is safe for you, especially if you take medicines or have a medical condition.

Sleep and stress management also matter. Most adults need at least seven hours of sleep each night, though individual needs vary. Keep a regular sleep schedule and seek advice if persistent snoring, pauses in breathing, or daytime sleepiness may signal a sleep disorder. Relaxation practices, time outdoors, supportive relationships, and enjoyable activities can help manage stress. Consider professional support if stress, anxiety, or depression is difficult to manage.

Know your blood pressure, cholesterol, and blood sugar numbers, and discuss them with a health professional. Routine checkups can identify risks before symptoms appear. Take prescribed medicines as directed, and ask questions before changing or stopping them. A clinician can help tailor lifestyle goals to your health, abilities, and preferences.

Small, sustainable steps often work better than drastic changes. Choose one or two habits to focus on, track your progress, and ask friends or family for support. If you have heart disease, significant symptoms, or a long-term health condition, get guidance before beginning a strenuous exercise plan. Seek emergency care for possible heart attack or stroke symptoms, such as severe chest discomfort, sudden weakness on one side, or trouble speaking.

The melody began in the pipes beneath Mara’s apartment. At first, she mistook it for a kettle whistling two floors down. It came each night at 2:17, a thin tune of five notes, rising and falling like someone trying to remember a name. She asked the neighbors, but no one had heard it. On the fourth night, Mara recorded the sound. In the morning, the playback held only the hum of the refrigerator. Still, she could hum the five notes perfectly. She hummed them at work, on the train, and while brushing her teeth. Each time, the last note seemed to linger a little longer. Soon she began waking before 2:17, already listening. The melody always arrived on time. It sounded closer now, not in the pipes but just behind the walls. Mara pressed her ear to the plaster and heard a faint answer to her own breathing. She called a plumber, who found nothing but dry, rusted pipes. He laughed when she asked whether the pipes could carry music from somewhere far away. That night, the tune changed. A sixth note slipped between the third and fourth, soft as a finger laid on a piano key. Mara sat upright in bed, terrified—and relieved that she wasn’t imagining it. She sang the new version into her phone. The recording played back her voice, then a second voice beneath it, singing the same notes in a language she almost knew. After that, the melody followed her into daylight. It threaded through the squeal of bus brakes and the hiss of coffee machines. She stopped speaking because every sentence seemed to bend toward the tune. Her friends asked if she was ill, but their words arrived muffled, as though heard through a closed door. Mara answered by singing the five notes. One friend began to cry. The next night, the pipes fell silent. For the first time in weeks, Mara slept until sunrise. Then she found a new message on her phone: a recording made at 2:17. It began with five clear notes, followed by her voice whispering, “I’m here.” Behind the whisper came a sound like a door opening underwater. Mara replayed it once, then again, until she heard something breathing on the other side. She smiled, placed the phone to her ear, and waited for the melody to finish.

The paper addresses an important challenge in deep reinforcement learning by combining multi-task learning, high-dimensional Q-value representations, and heuristic guidance. Its approach could improve knowledge transfer and exploration, but the paper should more clearly explain how the representation scales with task complexity and how heuristic guidance affects learning bias and robustness. The evaluation would be stronger with comparisons against well-tuned single-task and multi-task baselines, ablations of each proposed component, and tests across tasks with varying degrees of similarity. Please also report computational costs and provide sufficient implementation details to support reproducibility. Overall, the work is promising, but stronger empirical evidence and clearer analysis are needed to substantiate its claims.

Nageswaraswamy Temple is an ancient Hindu temple in Kumbakonam, Tamil Nadu, dedicated to Shiva, worshipped here as Nageswarar. It is often called Nageswaran Temple and is among the town’s best-known Shaivite shrines. The temple stands in the historic center of Kumbakonam, a city renowned for its sacred sites and festivals. Its origins are traditionally associated with the early medieval Chola period, though the complex was altered and expanded over many centuries. Inscriptions and architectural features point to the importance of royal and local patronage in its development. The temple is especially valued for its early Chola stonework and its place in the region’s religious history.

According to legend, the serpent king Adisesha worshipped Shiva here and was relieved of a curse. This story explains the name Nageswarar, meaning “Lord of the Serpents.” Another tradition links the shrine to the cosmic churning of the ocean and the appearance of sacred nectar. Kumbakonam’s local legends often connect its temples with the pot of nectar that is said to have fallen here. Nageswaraswamy is also one of the Paadal Petra Sthalams, temples praised in the devotional hymns of the Tamil Shaiva saints known as the Nayanmars. Such recognition made the temple an important destination for generations of pilgrims.

The temple is celebrated for a striking shrine to Surya, the Sun god, whose sunlight is said to enter the sanctum at a particular time of year. The event is commonly associated with the Tamil month of Chithirai, though the precise dates and visibility can vary. The main complex features a granite structure, sculpted pillars, and carefully arranged courtyards. Its architectural style reflects the transition from early Chola forms to later additions made under subsequent rulers. The principal sanctum houses the Shiva lingam, while nearby shrines honor Parvati, Ganesha, Murugan, and other deities. The goddess is worshipped as Periyanayaki, and the temple also has a shrine associated with Rahu.

Worship follows traditional Shaivite rituals, with offerings, lamps, chanting, and periodic ceremonies performed by temple priests. Daily pujas take place at set times, but schedules may change during festivals or special observances. The annual Mahamaham festival brings large crowds to Kumbakonam, and the temple takes part in the city’s wider religious celebrations. Other important occasions include Maha Shivaratri and observances connected with the Tamil calendar. Visitors should dress modestly, remove footwear before entering designated areas, and follow posted instructions. Photography may be restricted inside the temple, so it is best to check before taking pictures.

The temple is located in central Kumbakonam and can be reached by local transport, taxi, or auto-rickshaw. Kumbakonam is connected by rail and road to major cities in Tamil Nadu, including Chennai and Thanjavur. Opening hours can vary, so visitors should confirm current timings locally before traveling. Allow time to explore the temple calmly and to appreciate its carvings and sacred spaces. The site remains an active place of worship, and respectful behavior helps preserve its spiritual atmosphere. Nageswaraswamy Temple offers visitors a meaningful encounter with Tamil devotion, Chola-era heritage, and the legends that continue to shape Kumbakonam.

The paper addresses an important systems problem: assigning neural network computations to available hardware devices to reduce inference latency. Its focus is timely as modern deployments increasingly combine heterogeneous processors, accelerators, and memory resources. A learning-based approach could help navigate the complex trade-offs among device speed, communication overhead, and execution constraints. The topic is relevant to both machine learning systems researchers and practitioners.

A key strength is the paper’s emphasis on inference performance rather than relying solely on theoretical device utilization. The proposed assignment strategy appears to recognize that the fastest device for an individual operation may not yield the fastest end-to-end execution. Modeling interactions between computation placement and data movement is therefore essential. The paper would be more compelling if it clearly distinguished its contribution from existing graph-partitioning, operator-placement, and hardware scheduling methods. A concise comparison of the assumptions and capabilities of these approaches would help establish the novelty.

The evaluation should report end-to-end latency across a diverse set of models and hardware configurations. It should also include strong, carefully tuned baselines, such as static placement heuristics and established scheduling methods. Results should be presented with repeated measurements and variability estimates, since inference timing can be sensitive to device load and runtime conditions. In addition to average latency, tail latency and throughput may matter for deployment settings. The paper should specify whether measurements include data transfers, synchronization, compilation, and warm-up costs.

The learning method needs a clear description of its inputs, training procedure, and optimization objective. In particular, it would help to explain how the method obtains training data and whether it requires profiling each model or hardware configuration. The authors should discuss generalization to unseen models, batch sizes, and devices. An ablation study could identify which features and components contribute most to performance. It would also be valuable to compare the learned policy with an oracle or exhaustive search on small instances, providing an estimate of the remaining optimization gap.

The paper should address practical constraints such as memory capacity, unsupported operations, and device-specific execution rules. Robust handling of these constraints is important for a system intended for real deployments. The authors should also clarify how the method behaves when hardware availability or workload characteristics change at runtime. If adaptation requires retraining or extensive profiling, its overhead should be measured and discussed. Reproducibility would be strengthened by releasing implementation details, benchmark configurations, and, where possible, code.

Overall, this is a promising direction with the potential to improve neural network inference on heterogeneous hardware. The central idea is worthwhile, but the paper’s impact depends on demonstrating reliable gains over strong baselines and clarifying how broadly the learned assignments generalize. I recommend revision focused on stronger experimental validation, a more precise account of the method’s novelty, and a fuller discussion of deployment overheads. With these additions, the work could make a useful contribution to efficient inference systems.

When the first child lifted a stone without touching it, Mara was standing in line for bread.

The stone rose a finger’s width, trembled, and fell into the dust.

The child stared at her hands.

So did everyone else.

Mara felt the old scar beneath her ribs grow warm.

She had been born again as a girl named Mara, in a city that had forgotten the sky.

No one remembered the stars, though people still dreamed of them.

No one remembered flight, though children sometimes woke with their arms spread wide.

For nine hundred years, Mara had kept her secret.

She had lived as a shepherd, a sailor, a widow, and once as a king’s fool.

Each life ended, and each time she returned with the same memory: a world on fire, and her hands raised to stop it.

The powers were returning now.

By nightfall, the child’s stone floated again.

A baker bent a spoon with a glance.

An old woman called the rain from a cloudless sky.

Fear traveled faster than wonder.

The city council summoned Mara because she had served as its oldest archivist.

They asked her what the signs meant.

She told them the truth.

Long ago, every human being had been born with a spark of power.

Some could heal, some could shape stone, and some could bend distance like cloth.

Together, they had built towers above the clouds and ships that sailed between worlds.

Then their greatest gift had become their greatest weapon.

The empire of Veyr tried to command the sun.

Its leaders meant to end every war with one shining threat.

Instead, they tore open a wound in the heavens.

Through it came a darkness that devoured memory, matter, and time.

Humanity’s strongest could not close it.

Mara had been one of them.

She had learned that the wound would seal only if every living spark surrendered itself.

The sacrifice would erase humanity’s powers, but save the world.

Mara had persuaded the others to agree.

She had carried their joined strength into the wound.

The darkness closed.

The powers vanished.

Mara died beneath a sky that had gone silent.

Or so she thought.

The council listened without speaking.

At last, its youngest member asked why she had not told them sooner.

Mara said she had spent centuries hoping the choice would become easier to defend.

It had not.

The council feared the powers would bring back the old disaster.

The children with gifts feared being caged.

The city split into factions before the next sunrise.

Some called Mara a savior.

Others called her a thief who had stolen what belonged to every child yet unborn.

Mara could answer neither charge.

She went to the hill beyond the city, where the first child waited.

The girl was named Tavi, and she was trying to lift a fallen branch.

It rose slowly, shedding bits of bark.

“Can you teach me?” Tavi asked.

Mara looked at the branch and remembered the burning sky.

“I can teach you how to listen,” she said.

They practiced until the stars appeared.

Tavi learned to raise pebbles, then leaves, then a cup of water.

She laughed each time, and the sound made Mara ache.

More children came the next day.

They arrived with gifts they could barely control.

One made flowers bloom through stone.

One heard the thoughts of birds.

One stepped from one side of the hill to the other without crossing the space between.

Mara taught them to breathe before they reached for power.

She taught them that strength was not proof of wisdom.

She taught them the story of Veyr, including the parts that made her look foolish.

The council sent guards to bring the children back.

The guards found themselves surrounded by blossoms, birds, and floating stones.

No one was hurt.

That restraint mattered more than any victory.

For the first time, Mara wondered whether the sacrifice had not ended humanity’s story, but merely paused it.

Yet the old wound in the heavens still waited beyond memory.

She could feel its coldness whenever the children’s powers grew bright.

One evening, Tavi asked whether they should give their gifts up again if the darkness returned.

Mara wanted to answer at once.

Instead, she watched the children share bread beneath the stars.

They argued over crumbs, apologized, and laughed.

They were not the people who had built Veyr’s empire.

They were not free of pride or fear, but they were learning.

“I don’t know,” Mara said.

Tavi frowned. “You saved us once.”

“I chose for everyone once,” Mara replied. “I may have been right, but that does not make it harmless.”

The girl studied her for a long time.

“Then next time, we choose together.”

Mara felt the scar beneath her ribs cool.

The old sacrifice had bought humanity centuries without power.

It had not bought wisdom, nor could it buy the future.

That would belong to the living.

The next morning, Mara stood before the council with Tavi beside her.

She asked them to stop hunting the gifted children.

Then she asked the children to promise they would never use their powers without listening first.

Neither side trusted the other.

They agreed anyway.

It was a small beginning, fragile as a candle in wind.

Mara watched the children raise the fallen stones and set them gently in a circle.

The circle was not a weapon.

It was not a wall.

It was a place where everyone could sit and speak.

Above them, the clouds opened.

For the first time in nine hundred years, Mara saw the stars clearly.

She did not know whether her ancient sacrifice had been justified.

But she knew what it had made possible.

A second chance, not for power, but for choice.

Electric rays are flattened marine fish named for their ability to produce electric shocks. They live in seas around the world, often resting on sandy or muddy seafloors. Special organs on either side of the head contain stacks of cells that work like tiny batteries. When the ray activates these organs, the cells produce an electrical discharge. Depending on the species, the shock can stun prey or discourage a predator. Electric rays eat animals such as fish, crabs, and worms, often catching them on or near the seafloor. Some species can also use their electricity to help detect nearby prey. Their eyes are usually small, so they rely on other senses to navigate and find food. Although their shocks can be painful, electric rays generally do not pose a serious threat to people who leave them alone. Giving a ray plenty of space and avoiding contact helps protect both the animal and the observer.

A Welsh family is raising funds to bring a loved one home from the Caribbean after a serious injury cut short a birthday celebration. The celebrant, whose name has not been made public, is receiving medical care overseas. Relatives say an air ambulance is needed to make the journey safely and provide medical support in transit. The cost of the specialist flight is beyond what the family can afford alone. They have launched a fundraiser and are appealing to the public for help. Donations will go toward the flight and other urgent arrangements. The family said the situation has been frightening, but they are focused on getting their loved one back to Wales. They are also working with medical staff and travel specialists to understand what can be arranged. Supporters have shared the appeal online, helping it reach people beyond the family’s local community. The family has thanked everyone who has donated or sent messages of support. They hope the funds can be raised quickly so the injured celebrant can continue recovery closer to home.

This paper studies the combination of latent-variable generative models and autoregressive image decoders for image modeling and synthesis. The topic is timely, since it brings together two approaches with complementary strengths. Latent variables can capture global structure and support controllable generation, while autoregressive decoders can model detailed dependencies among pixels or image tokens. The central idea is promising and potentially useful for both synthesis quality and representation learning.

The paper’s main contribution is its integrated modeling framework. It provides a clear motivation for using a latent representation to summarize high-level image properties, while leaving the decoder to refine local detail. This division of labor is intuitive and offers a plausible path to more coherent samples than either component might produce alone. The discussion of how the latent prior and autoregressive likelihood interact is especially relevant to the paper’s claims.

The experimental evaluation is a strength insofar as it considers both image quality and modeling performance. Including quantitative metrics alongside generated examples helps readers assess the method from more than one perspective. The results suggest that the combined model can produce visually convincing images and capture meaningful structure. The paper would be stronger, however, if the comparison baselines were described and matched more carefully. Differences in parameter count, training compute, data preprocessing, or decoding time can make apparent gains difficult to interpret.

A more systematic ablation study is needed to establish which parts of the framework drive the reported improvements. In particular, the authors should isolate the effect of the latent variables, the autoregressive decoder, and any mechanisms used to connect them. It would also be useful to vary latent dimensionality and decoder capacity, since these choices may determine whether the model benefits from both components or relies primarily on one. The paper should report training and inference costs, including the number of sequential decoding steps. Autoregressive generation can be expensive, and this tradeoff is important for practical use.

The methodological description should be expanded to make the work reproducible. The authors should specify the objective, optimization procedure, architecture details, and any approximations used to train the latent-variable model. If posterior collapse or weak use of the latent code is a concern, the paper should report diagnostics such as latent utilization or mutual-information estimates. Generated samples alone cannot establish that the latent variables carry useful information. Reconstruction quality and latent traversal or interpolation results would help clarify what the representation captures.

The claims about generalization also warrant more evidence. Evaluation on additional datasets, resolutions, or image domains would show whether the approach is robust beyond the main benchmark. If the model is intended to support controllable synthesis, the authors should demonstrate that changing latent variables produces predictable, meaningful changes in generated images. A discussion of failure cases would also improve the paper by showing where the approach struggles, such as with fine textures, rare objects, or long-range spatial consistency.

Overall, this is a promising study of a well-motivated combination of generative modeling techniques. Its strongest aspect is the clear conceptual complementarity between global latent structure and local autoregressive modeling. The current evidence, however, does not fully separate the contribution of the proposed integration from increases in model capacity or computation. I recommend revision focused on stronger ablations, fairer baseline comparisons, reproducibility details, and a more explicit analysis of computational cost. With these additions, the paper could make a useful contribution to image generation research.

Britain’s political leaders clashed over whether remaining in the European Union or leaving it would better protect the country’s security, sovereignty and prosperity, as the debate over the UK’s future in Europe intensified. Advocates on both sides argued that their approach would give Britain more control over its destiny. The dispute has reached beyond trade and regulation to encompass defence, intelligence, migration and the country’s place in the world. Supporters of EU membership say cooperation with European partners strengthens Britain’s security. They point to shared work on counterterrorism, policing and cross-border crime. Intelligence-sharing, they argue, helps authorities identify threats that do not stop at national borders. A close relationship with European governments also gives Britain a voice in shaping the continent’s response to international crises. Pro-Europe leaders say withdrawal could weaken those networks and make coordination slower. They warn that formal agreements could not fully replace the trust built through regular cooperation. On defence, they stress that Britain’s NATO membership would continue outside the EU. But they say EU institutions provide additional tools for coordinating policy, missions and sanctions. They also argue that membership increases Britain’s influence over decisions made by its nearest neighbours. Opponents of membership reject the idea that EU participation is essential to national security. They say NATO, bilateral partnerships and intelligence alliances are more important than EU structures. Britain, they argue, could maintain practical cooperation with European states after leaving. Some advocates of withdrawal say the EU’s political direction could limit Britain’s freedom to respond to future threats. They claim national governments should retain final authority over security policy. The disagreement also centres on sovereignty. Pro-membership politicians argue that Britain already pools some powers with other countries to address shared challenges. In their view, participating in EU decision-making is a way to exercise influence, not surrender it. They say Britain can help shape common rules while remaining a powerful member state. Leaving, they warn, could mean having to follow European standards without a vote on how they are made. Withdrawal supporters counter that membership places limits on decisions made by elected British governments. They argue that the UK should be able to set its own laws and negotiate international agreements independently. Some say that restoring authority to Parliament would strengthen democratic accountability. Others contend that cooperation between sovereign states does not require shared institutions. The economic consequences have proved just as contentious. Pro-Europe leaders say access to the EU’s single market supports British businesses, jobs and investment. They warn that new barriers to trade could raise costs for exporters and disrupt supply chains. Companies that operate across Europe, they say, benefit from common standards and predictable rules. Membership also helps Britain attract investment from firms seeking access to the wider market, supporters argue. Withdrawal advocates say Britain could thrive by pursuing trade with countries beyond Europe. They believe the UK could tailor regulations to domestic needs and negotiate deals suited to its economy. They also argue that leaving could reduce financial contributions to EU institutions. Critics respond that any savings might be offset by weaker growth or the cost of replacing existing arrangements. Business groups have called for clarity, saying uncertainty can delay investment decisions. Economists have differed over the scale and timing of the potential effects. Both camps accuse the other of overstating the risks and understating the costs. Security concerns have sharpened the argument as leaders consider the consequences of a changing international environment. Pro-membership politicians say Europe faces common pressures, including hostile state activity, cyberattacks and regional instability. They argue that coordination can make responses faster and more effective. Withdrawal supporters say Britain can act decisively without needing approval from EU partners. They also stress that the country has global diplomatic and military capabilities of its own. Neither side disputes that cooperation with European governments would remain important. The question is how much of that cooperation should be organised through EU institutions. Leaders have also disagreed over migration, which has become a defining issue for many voters. Critics of membership say EU rules restrict Britain’s ability to control movement from other member states. Supporters argue that migration contributes to the economy and that shared policies can help manage cross-border pressures. They say withdrawal would not automatically resolve broader challenges such as labour shortages or asylum claims. The competing arguments have left voters weighing political control against the benefits of collective action. Opinion polls have shown that views can shift depending on which issue is emphasised. Campaigns are expected to focus on concrete examples of how membership or withdrawal would affect daily life. Political analysts say the debate is likely to test the credibility of leaders as much as their policies. They note that claims about security and prosperity are difficult to measure in advance. Each side must persuade voters that its promises are realistic and its risks manageable. The dispute has exposed a broader question about Britain’s role in Europe. Some leaders see influence as strongest when exercised from within shared institutions. Others believe independence gives the country greater freedom to shape its future. The decision, they say, will affect not only trade and law but also Britain’s partnerships and global standing. As the argument continues, political leaders face pressure to explain what practical arrangements would follow either choice. Voters are seeking answers on intelligence cooperation, market access and the authority of Parliament. They are also weighing whether the benefits of shared rules outweigh the constraints they impose. For now, neither camp has settled the central dispute. Britain’s leaders remain divided over whether security, sovereignty and prosperity are best protected through EU membership or withdrawal.

Japanese pickled ginger, called gari, is commonly served alongside sushi. It is made from thin slices of young ginger pickled in a sweet, tangy mixture of vinegar, sugar, and salt. Its pale pink color may occur naturally in young ginger, though some versions are colored. Gari is typically eaten between different kinds of sushi, rather than placed on top of each piece. Its sharp, refreshing taste helps clear lingering flavors from the palate. This makes it easier to appreciate the distinct flavors of the next sushi bite. Ginger also adds a pleasant contrast to sushi’s savory fish, seasoned rice, and other ingredients. A small slice is usually enough, since its flavor can be quite strong. Gari is different from beni shoga, another Japanese pickled ginger that is often brighter red and more sour. Although gari is often called a palate cleanser, it is also enjoyed as a flavorful accompaniment. Traditionally, diners can use chopsticks or their fingers to pick up a piece between bites.

Employers have not publicly agreed to the union’s demands, and some bargaining details remain undisclosed. The strike could disrupt refinery operations if workers are not replaced or facilities cannot maintain normal staffing. Refiners may draw on inventories or adjust production to limit the immediate impact. Any prolonged shutdown could tighten fuel supplies and put upward pressure on gasoline and diesel prices. The effect on consumers will depend on the duration of the walkout and how many facilities are affected. Union officials said members were prepared to remain on strike until meaningful progress was made. Company representatives urged workers to return to negotiations and said they were assessing operational plans. Federal labor officials may help facilitate talks if both sides request assistance. Safety concerns are a central point of dispute, with workers seeking clearer procedures and greater accountability for hazards. Neither side announced a date for the next bargaining session.
