This paper studies how to learn classifiers when labeled positives are available but negative examples are drawn through a selective, potentially biased process. The problem is important because many practical datasets contain verified positives while the remaining population is unlabeled or only partially screened. The paper’s focus on limited supervision is timely and relevant to weak supervision, positive-unlabeled learning, and selective-label settings. Overall, the work addresses a meaningful methodological challenge, but the strength of its contribution depends on assumptions about how negative examples are selected. Those assumptions need to be made especially explicit.

The manuscript is strongest when it distinguishes the observed negative sample from the true negative population. This distinction is central, since treating selectively collected negatives as representative can produce systematically distorted decision boundaries. The authors should state clearly whether selection depends only on observed features, on the class label, or on unobserved variables as well. These cases imply different levels of identifiability and require different remedies. A concise formal description of the data-generating process would improve the paper substantially.

The paper would benefit from a sharper statement of its main contribution. It should clarify whether the novelty lies in the learning objective, the treatment of selection bias, the limited-supervision regime, or the theoretical analysis. A direct comparison with positive-unlabeled learning and learning from biased samples would help readers understand what is new. The related-work section should also distinguish the proposed setting from standard case-control sampling and from covariate-shift correction. Without this positioning, it is difficult to assess the scope of the advance.

The assumptions behind the proposed method require careful scrutiny. If the method assumes that selection probabilities are known or estimable, the paper should explain how they are obtained in realistic applications. If it instead assumes that selected negatives satisfy a particular coverage or overlap condition, that condition should be stated in operational terms. The authors should discuss what happens when some regions of the negative population have little or no chance of being selected. In such regions, reliable correction may be impossible without additional information.

The theoretical results are potentially valuable, but their practical implications should be clearer. The paper should identify which assumptions are needed for each result and whether those assumptions can be checked from the observed data. Any guarantees should specify whether they concern classification error, ranking quality, calibration, or another target. It would also help to explain how the rates depend on the number of labeled positives and selected negatives. If the theory does not cover model misspecification, this limitation should be acknowledged.

The experimental evaluation should include baselines that reflect the main alternatives available to practitioners. These should include a method that treats the sampled negatives as representative, a positive-unlabeled method, and a selection-bias correction method where applicable. Comparisons should use the same training information and computational budget. The paper should also report uncertainty across repeated runs rather than relying on a single split or seed. Confidence intervals or standard deviations would make the empirical conclusions more credible.

A key experimental question is whether the method remains effective across different forms and strengths of selection bias. The authors should vary the selection mechanism systematically, including feature-dependent and class-dependent selection when these are relevant. They should also test settings in which selection is weak, severe, and close to violating the method’s assumptions. Such experiments would reveal when the proposed approach provides meaningful gains and when it becomes unstable. Synthetic data can be useful here, provided the generation process is described transparently.

The real-data evaluation needs a careful account of how ground truth is established. If the full negative population is not labeled, the authors should avoid interpreting observed performance as unbiased population performance. Where complete labels are unavailable, the paper should state what can and cannot be concluded from the evaluation. A sensitivity analysis over plausible selection rates could strengthen the evidence. The authors should also explain whether hyperparameters were tuned using labels that would be available in the intended deployment setting.

The choice of metrics deserves further justification. Accuracy can be misleading when positives are rare or the negative sample is selectively collected. Precision, recall, area under the precision-recall curve, and calibration may provide complementary information, depending on the intended use. If threshold selection is part of the method, the thresholding procedure should be described and evaluated separately. Reporting results at multiple operating points would help establish whether improvements are practically useful.

The paper should include ablation studies that isolate the contribution of each component. In particular, it would be useful to compare the full method against versions without selection correction and without any limited-supervision adjustment. These comparisons would show whether gains arise from the central idea or from tuning and model capacity. An analysis of sensitivity to the estimated selection probabilities would also be informative. This is especially important if those probabilities are learned from sparse data.

There are several practical details that should be reported more fully. The authors should specify how missing or uncertain labels are handled, how class imbalance is addressed, and how the model is regularized. Computational complexity and runtime should be compared with those of the baselines. Reproducibility would be improved by releasing code, data-processing details, and the exact evaluation protocol. If release is not possible, the manuscript should provide enough pseudocode and parameter settings for an independent implementation.

The discussion should address limitations and possible failure modes directly. In particular, the method may not recover population-level behavior when the selection mechanism is unobserved or when important regions lack sampled negatives. It may also be sensitive to distribution shift between the data used to estimate selection and the deployment population. These limitations do not invalidate the contribution, but they should inform the claims. The authors should avoid implying that selective sampling can be corrected universally.

The presentation is generally organized around a consequential problem, but several concepts would benefit from precise definitions early in the manuscript. Terms such as “selectively biased,” “limited supervision,” and “negative example” can admit multiple interpretations. A notation table or a simple diagram of the sampling process would help readers follow the setup. The paper should also separate assumptions from empirical choices more clearly. This would make the method easier to reproduce and evaluate.

My overall assessment is that the topic is significant and the proposed direction has potential. The manuscript’s main strength is its attention to the mismatch between sampled negatives and the target population. Its main weakness is that the validity and generality of the conclusions depend heavily on the selection assumptions. The current presentation should make the identification limits and evaluation protocol more transparent. The empirical section would be more persuasive with stronger baselines, systematic bias experiments, and uncertainty estimates.

I recommend revision before acceptance. The authors should sharpen the contribution claim, formalize the data-generation assumptions, and expand the evaluation to test robustness under varied selection mechanisms. They should also clarify which performance claims are supported when population labels are unavailable. If these issues are addressed, the paper could make a useful contribution to learning under selective negative supervision.

Mara woke beneath a flickering light, her wrists tied to a chair.
The last thing she remembered was a white van and a hand over her mouth.
Now she was in a concrete room that smelled of rust and rain.
A narrow window showed only darkness.
Her captors had left a bottle of water and a sandwich on the floor.
Mara didn’t touch either.
She listened instead.
Somewhere beyond the wall, metal clanged.
Then came a heavy, uneven thud.
The sound came again, closer.
One of the men outside swore.
A second voice answered, suddenly afraid.
Mara tugged at the ropes until her wrists burned.
A crash shook dust from the ceiling.
The lights went out.
She heard running feet, then a roar so deep it seemed to come through the floor.
The door bent inward.
Mara pressed herself against the chair.
A claw punched through the metal.
The door tore open, and moonlight spilled into the room.
A huge head filled the doorway.
Its yellow eyes fixed on Mara.
It had short arms, ridged scales, and a scar that crossed its snout.
The tyrannosaurus sniffed the air.
Mara held her breath.
A tiny speaker clicked on somewhere near its neck.
“Do not be afraid,” said a calm, crackling voice.
The dinosaur blinked.
“My name is Atlas,” the speaker continued.
“I was made in a laboratory.”
Mara stared at the device strapped below its jaw.
“Can you untie me?” she whispered.
Atlas tilted his head.
One careful claw sliced through the ropes.
Mara stumbled free and nearly fell.
Atlas lowered his shoulder so she could climb onto a padded harness.
The men returned with flashlights and rifles.
Atlas turned between them and Mara.
He roared once.
The men dropped their weapons and fled down the corridor.
Mara climbed onto the harness.
“Hold tight,” Atlas said through the speaker.
He charged through the ruined doorway.
They burst into a courtyard filled with shipping crates.
Rain slicked the ground, and floodlights swept the walls.
A guard shouted from a watchtower.
Atlas ducked behind a stack of containers.
Mara clung to the harness as bullets sparked against steel.
“Can you run?” she asked.
“I can run very fast,” Atlas replied.
“That wasn’t what I meant.”
“I understand.”
Atlas sprang from cover.
He raced across the yard, dodging crates and puddles.
Mara laughed despite herself.
The gate ahead was locked.
Atlas lowered his head and struck it with his shoulder.
The gate flew open.
Beyond it stretched a forest, black with pines.
They plunged beneath the trees.
Branches whipped past Mara’s face.
Behind them, alarms wailed.
Atlas slowed near a stream and let her slide down.
Mara’s knees trembled.
“Are you hurt?” Atlas asked.
“No,” she said. “Just frightened.”
“I was frightened when they first switched me on,” Atlas said.
Mara looked at him.
“You remember the laboratory?”
“I remember bright lights, cold floors, and people arguing about what I was for.”
The stream burbled between them.
“They made you to scare people,” Mara guessed.
“They made me to obey,” Atlas said.
“Then why did you save me?”
A pause crackled through the speaker.
“You asked me to.”
Mara reached out and touched the scar on his snout.
Atlas did not move.
From the road came the distant growl of engines.
The kidnappers were searching for them.
Mara spotted a ranger station on a hill across the stream.
“If we reach that place, someone can help us.”
Atlas waded through the water, carrying her above the current.
They climbed the hill as dawn paled the sky.
At the station, Mara found a radio and called for help.
Atlas stood guard outside, watching the trees.
When helicopters arrived, their lights swept over the valley.
Mara told the rescuers everything.
She asked them not to cage Atlas.
The scientists who had built him were arrested before noon.
Atlas was taken to a protected reserve, where no one would command him.
Mara visited every weekend.
They explored trails, splashed through creeks, and watched storms roll over the mountains.
People called their story a grisly ordeal turned adventure.
Mara called it the beginning of a friendship.
Atlas called it a good reason to keep running.

Pebbles in conglomerates can preserve clues to the deformation experienced by the rocks that contain them. A conglomerate is a sedimentary rock made chiefly of gravel-sized clasts, including pebbles, cobbles, or larger fragments. After deposition and burial, a conglomerate may be compacted, folded, faulted, or otherwise deformed. Clasts can be flattened, stretched, rotated, fractured, or rearranged during these processes. Measuring their shapes and orientations can therefore help geologists estimate strain. Strain describes the change in shape or size of a material relative to its original state. It is not the same as stress, which is the force applied per unit area. Pebble-based estimates are useful because clasts are often easy to see and measure in outcrop. However, the original shapes and arrangements of the pebbles are usually not known exactly. This uncertainty is central to interpreting the results.

Before measuring deformation, geologists first describe the conglomerate and its setting. They identify the rock layers, sedimentary structures, clast types, matrix, and any visible fabrics. They also note folds, faults, cleavage, veins, and other features that may record deformation. The distinction between clasts and matrix matters because the two may respond differently to stress. A strong pebble may remain relatively intact while the surrounding finer material flows or compacts. A weak or fractured clast may deform more readily. Geologists commonly measure clasts on exposed surfaces, in oriented rock slabs, or in thin sections. An oriented sample preserves the direction of geographic north and the orientation of the rock layers. Without orientation information, measurements can describe shape but may not show how clast fabrics relate to regional deformation. Reliable work therefore begins with careful field records and representative sampling.

One basic method is to measure the long, intermediate, and short axes of individual pebbles. These axes are often written as a, b, and c, with a being the longest and c the shortest. A pebble’s axial ratios, such as a divided by b and b divided by c, summarize its three-dimensional shape. A population of measurements can be compared with expectations for clasts that have undergone deformation. If pebbles were initially similar in shape and were deformed together, their changes in shape may provide an estimate of bulk strain. In practice, geologists often measure apparent axes on a two-dimensional surface. A cross-section may cut a pebble away from its true longest or shortest dimensions. This can make a three-dimensional clast appear rounder or more elongated than it really is. Measurements from several differently oriented sections, or from three-dimensional imaging, can reduce this problem. The section orientation must be recorded because the measured shape depends on it.

Shape-fabric analysis examines the preferred orientation and elongation of many clasts. Geologists may record the direction of each pebble’s long axis and plot the results on a rose diagram or stereographic projection. A strong alignment can indicate that clasts were rotated or stretched into a common orientation. The average shape and alignment of clasts can be summarized using statistical tools such as eigenvectors and eigenvalues. These tools identify the principal directions along which the population varies most and least. In a deformed rock, these directions may approximate the principal axes of finite strain. Finite strain is the accumulated change in shape from the initial state to the present. The clasts’ orientations can also reveal sedimentary processes, however. Flowing water may align pebbles during deposition, and clasts may acquire a preferred orientation as they settle or roll. A measured fabric is therefore not automatically a tectonic strain fabric. Geologists compare it with bedding, sedimentary structures, and regional deformation to assess its origin.

The Rf–φ method is a classic approach for estimating strain from populations of elliptical objects. In this method, Rf represents the observed axial ratio of a clast, and φ represents the angle between its long axis and a reference direction. Measurements from many clasts are analyzed together rather than interpreted one at a time. The method tests how a population of initially varied ellipses might have been transformed by a common strain. It can estimate the magnitude and orientation of two-dimensional strain under specified assumptions. Those assumptions include a suitable initial shape distribution, a consistent deformation history, and clasts that behaved as passive markers. If the initial pebble shapes are poorly constrained, different strain values may explain the same measurements. The method is also sensitive to the number of clasts, measurement error, and the range of original shapes. It works best when the sampled pebbles are numerous, clearly outlined, and drawn from a reasonably consistent population. Results should be reported with the assumptions and uncertainty, not just as a single strain ratio.

Another approach compares clast shapes with an assumed or independently inferred original shape. For example, a population of originally near-spherical pebbles that is now strongly flattened may indicate substantial shortening perpendicular to the flattening plane. This interpretation is more convincing when the clasts are known to have been rounded before burial and when the deformation is consistent across the exposure. Some studies use undeformed conglomerates from the same source or depositional system as a reference population. Others compare clasts in less-deformed parts of the same region with those in more-deformed areas. Such comparisons can help separate inherited shape variation from tectonic modification. Yet source rocks and transport processes may produce pebbles with different shapes in different locations. A reference population may therefore not represent the true starting shapes of the measured clasts. The assumption of spherical starting clasts is especially risky because natural pebbles are rarely perfect spheres. Shape comparisons are strongest when supported by multiple independent lines of evidence.

Clast orientation can also be used to examine the direction of deformation. Pebbles may rotate toward the stretching direction in some deformation regimes, while their long axes may lie differently in others. The pattern depends on rock strength, matrix behavior, strain rate, and the geometry of the deformation. A cluster of long-axis directions can reflect tectonic stretching, but it can also reflect currents, gravity, or imbrication during deposition. Imbrication occurs when flat or elongated clasts tilt in a consistent direction, often in response to flowing water. Sedimentary orientation should be evaluated using structures such as cross-bedding, channel forms, and graded layers. If clast alignment cuts across bedding or varies systematically around a fold, tectonic processes may be more likely. Even then, orientation alone does not measure the amount of strain. It needs to be combined with shape measurements or other structural evidence. The relationship between clast axes and the regional strain directions should be tested rather than assumed.

Two-dimensional measurements are common, but deformation is three-dimensional. A pebble may be elongated in one direction, flattened in another, and little changed along a third. Measurements from a single face can miss one or more of these dimensions. Geologists can collect oriented serial sections, where successive slices reveal how the clast changes through the sample. Computed tomography can provide three-dimensional images without cutting the rock, when the clasts and matrix have enough contrast. Three-dimensional measurements allow a more complete estimate of clast geometry and fabric. They can also help identify internal fractures or complex shapes that are difficult to recognize on a surface. These methods require suitable samples, equipment, and careful image processing. The digital boundary between a pebble and its matrix may be ambiguous, especially when their compositions are similar. Three-dimensional data improve geometry, but they do not remove uncertainty about the original shapes or the history of deformation.

Pebbles may deform by several mechanisms, and each affects strain estimates differently. Some clasts change shape internally through crystal-scale processes or distributed microfracturing. Others rotate as rigid particles within a deforming matrix. Brittle clasts may crack, while ductile clasts may flatten or stretch without breaking. The matrix can compact around clasts, causing apparent flattening even if the clasts themselves remain nearly rigid. Pressure solution may dissolve material at stressed contacts and transfer it elsewhere. This process can shorten the rock while leaving some pebble interiors largely unchanged. Strong clasts can also shield nearby matrix from deformation and create local strain patterns. A conglomerate is therefore not always a uniform material with one simple strain. Strain may vary from pebble to pebble and from one part of the outcrop to another. Geologists examine clast boundaries, fractures, mineral textures, and matrix fabrics to determine which mechanisms were active.

Compaction is a major source of deformation in sedimentary rocks. As overlying sediment accumulates, the weight of burial can reduce pore space and flatten soft sediment or weak clasts. This burial-related compaction may occur before later tectonic folding or faulting. If it is not distinguished from tectonic strain, the estimated tectonic deformation may be too large or may have the wrong orientation. Clasts can record compaction perpendicular to bedding, especially when the matrix was poorly consolidated. Early cementation may preserve a more open framework and limit later flattening. The timing of cementation can therefore affect how pebbles respond. Geologists look for cement textures, compaction features, and relationships between sedimentary layers to assess the sequence of events. They may also compare vertical and horizontal strain indicators. Separating burial compaction from tectonic strain is difficult when both occurred in similar directions.

The original pebble population is another important limitation. Clasts may enter a basin with a wide range of shapes, and transport can round, abrade, or break them. Different rock types may have different initial shapes and mechanical strengths. A flat slate pebble and a nearly spherical quartz pebble do not make equivalent strain markers. Longer transport may preferentially remove fragile or angular clasts, changing the population before deposition. Sorting can also favor certain sizes and shapes. When the rock is deformed, the clasts that remain visible may be a biased subset of the original population. A robust study records lithology and size as well as shape. Analyses can be conducted separately for clast types that are mechanically and compositionally similar. Results from separate groups can then be compared. If the groups give very different strain estimates, the difference may reveal material effects or problems with the assumptions.

Sampling design affects the reliability of any pebble-based estimate. A small sample may not capture the natural variation in clast shapes and orientations. Measurements should be taken from multiple locations and, where possible, from several beds or structural positions. The chosen outcrop should be large enough to represent the rock while avoiding repeated measurement of the same clasts. Geologists should record how clasts were selected and whether any were excluded. For example, a clast may be excluded if its boundary is obscured or if it is broken by weathering. Such decisions can introduce bias if they are not documented. A consistent measurement protocol helps different observers obtain comparable results. Digital photographs with scales can preserve the data for later checking. Statistical summaries should include the number of measured clasts and the spread of the results. Reporting only an average can conceal important variability.

Geological strain estimates are often improved by combining pebble measurements with other evidence. Fold geometry can constrain shortening and rotation at the outcrop scale. Fault offsets can indicate displacement, although converting displacement into strain requires additional geometric information. Cleavage and mineral lineations may record deformation directions. Veins, pressure shadows, and deformed fossils can provide independent markers. Regional mapping helps determine whether local clast fabrics fit a broader pattern. Comparing results from multiple indicators can reveal whether deformation was homogeneous or occurred in stages. If pebble strain disagrees with other evidence, the disagreement should be investigated rather than averaged away. It may indicate that the pebbles preserve an older sedimentary fabric, that the conglomerate deformed differently from surrounding rocks, or that one method’s assumptions failed. Agreement among independent methods increases confidence but does not prove that every assumption is correct. The strongest interpretations explain both the agreement and the discrepancies.

Uncertainty should be treated as part of the result. Measurement error arises from irregular clast boundaries, limited exposure, image resolution, and differences among observers. Geological uncertainty arises from unknown initial shapes, changing deformation conditions, and incomplete knowledge of the rock’s history. Statistical uncertainty can be estimated by resampling or other methods that test how results vary with the selected clasts. Sensitivity tests can show how estimates change if unusual clasts are removed or if different starting-shape assumptions are used. A range of plausible strain values is often more honest than a single precise number. Precision in a calculation does not guarantee accuracy in the geological interpretation. Geologists should state which parts of the estimate are directly measured and which depend on assumptions. Clear uncertainty reporting allows readers to judge how strongly the data support the conclusion. It also helps future studies compare results from different sites.

Pebbles in conglomerates are valuable strain markers because they are abundant, visible, and often record deformation at several scales. Shape ratios, orientation fabrics, Rf–φ analysis, three-dimensional imaging, and comparisons with reference populations provide complementary ways to study them. Each method has strengths, but none can recover deformation automatically from present-day shapes alone. The interpretation depends on the initial clast population, depositional fabric, burial history, mechanical contrasts, and later tectonic events. Careful field context is therefore as important as measurement technique. The most reliable studies use representative sampling, separate appropriate clast groups, document orientation, and compare results with independent structural evidence. They also distinguish observed geometry from inferred geological history. Pebble-based estimates should be viewed as constrained interpretations, not direct recordings of a single strain value. Used with these cautions, conglomerate clasts can help reconstruct how rocks were shortened, stretched, and rotated through geological time.

This paper addresses the important problem of recognizing novel categories when only a few positive examples are available and negative examples may be unavailable or unreliable. Its focus on meta-learning one-class classifiers is well motivated, since conventional supervised classifiers often assume access to representative examples from both classes. The topic is relevant to open-set recognition, anomaly detection, and applications where new categories emerge over time.

A key strength is the attempt to learn a reusable classification strategy across tasks rather than fitting an isolated detector for each category. This framing could improve data efficiency and make deployment more practical. The paper would benefit from a precise definition of the learning setting, including how training tasks are sampled and how closely they resemble the novel categories encountered at test time. It should also clarify whether “positive examples” are labeled instances of the target category and what information, if any, is available about the surrounding data distribution.

The evaluation should compare the proposed method with strong one-class and few-shot baselines, including methods tuned with the same amount of validation data. Ablations would help establish which components of the meta-learning procedure contribute to performance. In particular, it would be useful to separate gains from the learned representation, the one-class objective, and the task-level adaptation mechanism. Results should be reported across multiple random seeds, with uncertainty estimates and appropriate statistical comparisons.

The paper should test sensitivity to the number of positive examples, the diversity of training tasks, and shifts between meta-training and test distributions. It should also examine cases where the target category is multimodal or overlaps substantially with other categories. Since one-class methods can trade recall against false positives, reporting only aggregate accuracy would be insufficient; precision-recall curves, area under the precision-recall curve, and operating-point results would give a fuller picture. The choice of threshold is especially important and should be explained, including whether it uses held-out negatives or other information unavailable in the intended deployment setting.

The authors should discuss computational and memory costs, as well as the practical requirements for collecting meta-training tasks. A failure analysis could reveal when a detector confidently accepts out-of-distribution examples and when a small positive set is too unrepresentative for reliable learning. The paper would also benefit from clearer guidance on reproducibility, including dataset splits, preprocessing, hyperparameter selection, and implementation details.

Overall, this is a promising direction with a potentially useful contribution, but the strength of the evidence depends on a carefully specified evaluation and direct comparisons with competitive alternatives. I recommend revision to address the methodological and reporting questions above. With these additions, the work could offer a clearer assessment of when meta-learning improves one-class detection and where its limitations remain.

The Great Wall of China is one of the world’s most recognizable historical landmarks. It is not a single wall built at one time, but a vast network of walls, fortifications, passes, and watchtowers created over many centuries. Its sections cross mountains, deserts, grasslands, and plains across northern China. Together, they reflect changing political needs, military strategies, and building techniques.

The earliest walls were constructed by separate states during China’s period of political division, before the country was unified. These states raised earthen barriers to defend their territories and mark boundaries. In the third century BCE, Qin Shi Huang unified much of China and ordered existing defensive walls to be connected and extended. His goal was to strengthen the northern frontier against raids by nomadic groups.

The Qin walls were made largely from packed earth, a method in which layers of soil were compressed to form sturdy barriers. Later dynasties repaired, expanded, or abandoned sections according to their circumstances. The Han dynasty extended defenses westward to protect trade routes and frontier settlements. In subsequent centuries, the wall system changed as kingdoms rose and fell.

Many of the most famous surviving sections were built or rebuilt during the Ming dynasty, from the fourteenth to the seventeenth century. Ming rulers faced repeated threats from northern forces and invested in stronger defenses. Builders used bricks and stone in many areas, making the walls more durable than earlier earthen structures. Watchtowers and beacon towers allowed soldiers to observe the landscape and relay warnings.

The wall’s purpose was broader than simply stopping an invading army. It helped control movement across the frontier and supported the defense of towns, farms, and strategic routes. Fortified gates could regulate trade and travel, while garrisons stationed along the wall could patrol vulnerable areas. In practice, the barrier was not always an impenetrable line, and its success depended on troops, supplies, diplomacy, and local conditions.

The Great Wall also shows how geography shaped military planning. Builders followed ridgelines where possible, using steep terrain as a natural defense. They placed towers at intervals so sentries could keep watch and communicate across long distances. Fires, smoke, drums, and other signals could carry messages from one post to another.

Over time, the wall gained meaning beyond its military role. It came to symbolize the strength, unity, and authority of the Chinese state. It also represents the labor of countless people, including soldiers, craftspeople, and workers recruited to build and maintain it. Their effort came at great human cost, and stories about the wall often preserve memories of hardship and sacrifice.

The wall’s cultural meaning is complex. For some, it stands as a source of national pride and a powerful emblem of China’s long history. For others, it prompts reflection on the burdens placed on ordinary people by rulers and large-scale projects. It also reminds us that borders can protect communities while separating people and cultures.

The Great Wall is not visible from the Moon with the unaided eye, despite a popular claim. Its narrow shape and the colors of its materials make it difficult to distinguish from the surrounding landscape even from much closer distances. This myth illustrates how the wall’s fame has inspired both wonder and exaggeration.

Today, many sections are protected as historic sites, while others have eroded or disappeared. Tourism brings visitors to restored stretches, but heavy foot traffic and development can damage fragile areas. Preservation requires careful maintenance, research, and cooperation with nearby communities. UNESCO recognized the Great Wall as a World Heritage Site in 1987.

The Great Wall’s enduring legacy lies in both its physical remains and the ideas attached to them. It tells a story of changing states, frontier encounters, engineering, and human labor. Its varied sections show that history is rarely the work of a single ruler or generation. As a monument, it continues to invite questions about defense, power, identity, and the ways societies remember their past.

The rain had begun before dawn and had not stopped. Elias Venn watched it crawl down the windows of the bus station. He had come to the town to disappear. For years, he had been good at that.

He chose a seat near the door and kept his back to the wall. A boy sat across from him, turning a paper cup in his hands. The child was perhaps eight, with a too-large coat and a bruise fading yellow beneath one eye.

Elias tried not to stare. He knew what it was to notice a target and pretend it was only a shape. The boy glanced up and saw him looking.

“Are you a soldier?” he asked. “Not anymore,” Elias said. The boy nodded as if that answer made sense.

A gray-haired man entered, shaking rain from his hat. “There you are, Milo,” he said. The boy’s shoulders tightened. The man took his wrist, not quite hard enough to cause a scene.

“Come along,” the man said. “We’re going home.” Milo looked at Elias once before following him out. Elias stayed seated, telling himself it was none of his business.

Then he saw the boy’s cup on the floor. Beneath it lay a folded note, damp at the edges. Elias picked it up.

The writing was uneven: Please don’t make me go back. The bus station seemed to grow very quiet. Elias stood.

Outside, the man was forcing Milo into a truck. Elias called out that the boy had dropped something. The man turned, annoyed.

Milo seized the pause and stepped away. “He’s my grandson,” the man said. “He’s coming with me.”

Elias looked at the boy’s face, then at the grip on his arm. He had spent years obeying men who spoke with certainty. He had seen what happened when nobody interrupted them.

“Let him go,” Elias said. The man gave a short laugh. “And who are you?” “Someone who should have spoken sooner.”

The man released Milo, but only to shove him toward the truck. Elias moved between them. He did not raise his voice or his hands.

A station attendant hurried outside and asked what was happening. The grandfather began explaining, smooth and practiced. Milo stood behind Elias, trembling.

“Show her your arm,” Elias said gently. Milo rolled up his sleeve. Finger-shaped bruises darkened his skin.

The attendant’s expression changed. She called the police and kept the truck from leaving. The grandfather complained, threatened, and demanded to know who would believe a child.

Milo said nothing. Elias knelt so they were eye to eye. “You don’t have to tell me anything,” he said. “Just stay where it’s safe.”

The boy grabbed his coat sleeve. Elias felt the small hand shake. For once, he did not pull away.

At the clinic, a nurse examined Milo while a social worker asked careful questions. The bruises were not the only evidence. There were old marks, a split lip, and fear whenever footsteps approached.

Milo’s grandfather was taken away for questioning. No one promised what would happen next. The social worker explained that Milo would stay with a foster family while the case was investigated.

Elias waited in the hallway, unable to sit still. On the wall hung a child’s drawing of a house beneath a bright orange sun. He thought of the people he had failed to protect.

When Milo came out, he held a blanket around his shoulders. “Are you leaving?” he asked. Elias swallowed.

“I was,” he said. “But I can wait until they find you a safe place.” Milo considered this, then nodded.

The rain eased by afternoon. A social worker drove Milo away, and he pressed his palm to the window as the car pulled out. Elias raised his hand in reply.

He had once believed remorse was a sentence with no end. Perhaps it was. But that day, it had given him one small instruction: when someone asked for help, do not look away.

The paper addresses an important problem: anomaly detection when training data are dominated by normal examples and anomalous data are scarce or unavailable. Its focus on meta-learning is timely, since the ability to adapt from limited examples could make anomaly detection more practical across domains. The inclusion of both image and time-series tasks also promises a useful assessment of generality. However, the paper needs to define “one-class data imbalance” more precisely and distinguish it from ordinary class imbalance and open-set recognition. The central research question and the specific gap in prior work should be stated more clearly. The authors should explain what is meta-learned, what constitutes a task or episode, and how adaptation occurs at test time. These choices determine whether the method is genuinely learning to adapt or simply applying a fixed representation with a tuned threshold. The paper should provide a complete algorithm description, including loss functions, sampling procedures, and inference steps. It is essential to report how normal and anomalous examples are used during meta-training, because this affects both the method’s assumptions and its applicability. If anomalous examples are used, their number, source, and relationship to test anomalies should be made explicit. The evaluation should include strong, current baselines for one-class and few-shot anomaly detection, as well as non-meta-learning methods with comparable backbones. Comparisons should use consistent data splits, preprocessing, model capacity, and tuning budgets. The authors should clarify whether test sets contain novel anomaly types and whether any information from those types is available during training or validation. Results should be reported separately for image and time-series benchmarks before any aggregate summary is presented. For images, the paper should describe the datasets, contamination levels, and any domain shifts between normal training data and test data. For time series, it should specify windowing, temporal dependence handling, and how anomalies are labeled and evaluated. AUROC alone is insufficient, particularly under severe imbalance, so the paper should also report metrics such as average precision and an operational measure at a fixed false-alarm rate. Confidence intervals or repeated-seed results are needed to establish whether observed gains are reliable. An ablation study should isolate the effects of the meta-learning objective, episode construction, adaptation steps, and any auxiliary losses. The paper should also examine sensitivity to the number of normal examples and the degree of training contamination. Computational cost and inference latency matter for practical deployment and should be compared with those of the baselines. The discussion would benefit from failure cases, especially where meta-learning harms performance or fails to transfer across modalities. Claims of generalization should be limited to the domains and settings actually tested. Reproducibility would be strengthened by releasing code, configurations, data-split details, and random seeds. Overall, the topic is significant and the proposed direction could be valuable, but the paper’s contribution cannot be fully assessed without clearer methodological assumptions and a more rigorous evaluation. I recommend revision focused on experimental transparency, appropriate imbalance-aware metrics, and evidence that the gains arise from meta-learning rather than confounding differences in data or tuning.

Residential wind turbines can generate electricity at home, but they are suitable only under the right conditions. The most important factor is the wind resource at the proposed site. Average wind speed, how often strong winds occur, and seasonal patterns all affect energy output. A turbine usually needs steady, unobstructed wind rather than occasional gusts.

The location and height of the turbine matter because buildings, trees, and hills can disrupt airflow. Mounting a turbine on a tall, properly engineered tower can provide stronger, smoother winds than placing it on a roof. Roof-mounted turbines often produce less power than expected because nearby surfaces create turbulence and vibration. A professional site assessment can help estimate realistic output.

The turbine’s size and rated capacity should match the household’s energy needs and local wind conditions. Rated capacity describes output under specific wind conditions, not the amount of electricity the turbine will produce every day. Small turbines may offset some household use, but they rarely supply all needs at sites with weak or inconsistent winds. A battery or connection to the electricity grid can help manage periods when the turbine produces little power.

Costs also affect suitability. The purchase price, tower, installation, maintenance, insurance, and replacement parts should be compared with expected savings over the system’s lifetime. Local electricity prices, available incentives, and the cost of other renewable options can change the financial case. Turbines have moving parts, so regular inspections and repairs may be needed.

Before installation, check local planning rules, building codes, noise limits, and setback requirements. Neighbors may be concerned about noise, visual impact, or shadow flicker, so consultation can be useful. The turbine and tower must also be designed for local weather extremes and installed safely. Overall, a residential wind turbine is most suitable where winds are strong and consistent, the site is open, regulations allow installation, and the expected benefits justify the costs.

At dawn, General Mara Venn climbed the hill above the ruined city. Her knees complained, and the old wound in her side burned in the cold. Below, the Legion gathered beneath black banners, its soldiers filling the valley like a dark tide. Mara had faced them forty years ago, when her hair was dark and her sword arm steady. Now that arm trembled when she lifted the blade.

Her remaining soldiers waited behind the city walls. Most were young enough to be her grandchildren. They had heard the stories of her victories, but they had never seen her lose. Mara wondered if they were afraid of the legend, or of the woman carrying it.

She returned to the command tent and unrolled a map across the table. The city’s western gate was broken, and the river bridge would not hold an army. There was only one path the Legion could take: the narrow street between the old bell tower and the market ruins. “We’ll make them come through here,” she said.

Captain Ilyan studied the map. “And if they bring their engines?” “Then we make sure they can’t use them,” Mara replied. She sent runners to the rooftops with jars of oil and bundles of rope. The youngest soldiers were placed behind the barricades, where they could fight without being exposed.

When the orders were given, Mara sat alone and polished her sword. Its edge had been repaired so many times that little of the original steel remained. She remembered the friends who had carried it beside her, and the ones who had not come home. For a moment, she wished she could join them.

Then the bell tower rang once. The Legion had begun its advance. Mara buckled on her armor and stepped into the street. The soldiers made a path for her, though she told them not to.

At the barricade, she turned to face them. “You don’t owe the world a glorious death,” she said. “You owe each other the chance to see tomorrow.” Their fear did not vanish, but it changed shape. Hands tightened around spears, and shields rose together.

The first Legion engines rolled into the narrow street. From the rooftops came fire, and the lead machine burst into flames. The soldiers cheered, but Mara kept her eyes on the advancing ranks. At their head rode a commander wearing the same black helmet she had seen in the old war.

Mara stepped beyond the barricade. Her legs shook, but they carried her forward. The commander lowered his spear and charged. She waited until the last instant, then turned aside and struck his horse’s reins. He crashed into the broken stones, and his soldiers faltered.

That heartbeat was enough. Ilyan shouted, and the defenders surged from cover. The Legion’s ranks broke against the barricades, then scattered through the smoke. Mara stood in the street until the last black banner fell.

When silence returned, she leaned on her sword. The young soldiers gathered around her, alive and astonished. “Is this the end?” Ilyan asked. Mara looked toward the brightening sky. “No,” she said. “It’s a beginning you’ll have to guard yourselves.”

A Scottish court has held a care employer responsible after a worker was injured in icy conditions while travelling between visits. The case concerned a care worker who slipped during a work-related journey on a winter day. She had been visiting clients as part of her duties when she fell on an icy path and suffered an injury. The court found that her employer had failed to take reasonable steps to protect her from the risk.

The ruling focused on the employer’s responsibility to assess hazards faced by staff working outdoors. That responsibility applied even though the worker was moving between clients rather than carrying out care inside a building. The court considered whether the employer had provided suitable guidance and precautions for icy weather. It concluded that the measures in place were not adequate.

The decision highlights the risks faced by care staff who travel on foot as part of their jobs. Ice can be difficult to see, particularly on paths and other untreated surfaces. Employers are expected to consider such foreseeable hazards and take practical steps to reduce them. Those steps may include weather-related procedures, warnings, suitable footwear, or changes to working arrangements.

The case also underlines that employers’ health and safety duties extend beyond their premises. Staff working in the community may face hazards on routes between appointments. A lack of control over public paths does not necessarily remove an employer’s duty to assess and manage risks. The court’s findings will be of interest to organisations employing mobile care workers.

The ruling does not mean employers can prevent every accident in winter weather. It does, however, reinforce the need for a clear plan when icy conditions are forecast or reported. Care providers may review their risk assessments and make sure workers know how to report unsafe routes. The case serves as a reminder that protecting staff is an essential part of delivering care safely.

Construction of the new Highland bridges is moving ahead, although strong winds have delayed crane work. Crews are progressing with bridge foundations and other tasks that can continue safely in unsettled conditions. The gusts have forced operators to pause lifts, since suspended loads can become hazardous in high winds. Project teams are monitoring forecasts and will resume crane operations when conditions meet safety limits. The pauses may affect the schedule, but officials have not announced a revised completion date. Workers are using the downtime to carry out ground-level work and prepare materials for upcoming lifts. The bridges are expected to improve connections across the Highland area once complete. Further updates are likely as construction advances and weather conditions change.

The hall, in West Bridgford, is currently used for weddings and other events, but the council is considering options for its long-term operation. Feedback gathered from residents highlighted the venue’s character and its importance as a local setting for celebrations. Officials are expected to consider public views alongside the costs of maintaining and running the hall. Further details are due as the council’s plans develop.

The paper addresses an important problem: reducing the cost of graph signal classification while preserving the useful structure captured by graph scattering transforms. Its central idea, spectrally guided pruning, is promising because it uses graph spectral information to identify transform components that may be redundant or uninformative. The topic is relevant to applications where graph size and computational constraints limit the use of deep or multiscale signal representations. A key strength is the attempt to evaluate efficiency alongside predictive performance rather than treating accuracy as the sole objective. The analysis of robustness is also valuable, particularly if it examines perturbations to graph structure, signal values, and spectral estimates.

The paper would benefit from a more precise description of the pruning criterion and how its thresholds or hyperparameters are selected. It should clarify whether pruning is performed once for a dataset or separately for each graph, and whether this requires access to test-time information. The authors should also explain how the method behaves when eigenvalues are repeated, closely spaced, or estimated inaccurately. Comparisons with unpruned scattering transforms and relevant lightweight baselines are essential, and should use consistent preprocessing, tuning budgets, and hardware. Runtime and memory results should include the cost of spectral decomposition and pruning, not only the cost of the final classifier. Reporting accuracy across multiple runs, with variability or confidence intervals, would make the performance claims more convincing. The robustness experiments should specify perturbation models and magnitudes, and distinguish robustness to signal noise from robustness to changes in graph topology. It would also be useful to include ablations that isolate the contribution of spectral guidance from the effect of simply reducing the number of transform coefficients. If the method relies on particular graph families or spectral assumptions, these should be stated and supported by experiments beyond the primary setting. Overall, the approach appears potentially useful, but its contribution will be clearer with stronger methodological detail and more comprehensive efficiency and robustness comparisons. I recommend revision before acceptance.

Arnold Henry Guyot was a Swiss-American geographer, geologist, and educator whose work helped shape the study of geography in the United States. He was born on September 28, 1807, in Boudevilliers, in what is now Switzerland. As a young man, he studied at the University of Neuchâtel and later pursued theology and science in Berlin. There he met the philosopher and educator Alexander von Humboldt, whose ideas encouraged Guyot’s interest in the natural world. Guyot also studied under the geographer Carl Ritter, who emphasized the connections between physical environments and human societies. After returning to Switzerland, Guyot taught and became involved in scientific research. In 1838, he visited the glaciers of the Swiss Alps with Louis Agassiz and other researchers. His observations of glaciers and their movement contributed to the emerging science of glaciology. Guyot later presented lectures on physical geography that helped make the subject more accessible to students and the public. Political changes in Switzerland disrupted his career, and in 1848 he moved to the United States. He settled in Cambridge, Massachusetts, where he taught geography and history at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology’s predecessor, the Lawrence Scientific School at Harvard. He also became a professor at Princeton, then known as the College of New Jersey, in 1854. Guyot taught there for nearly three decades and helped establish geography as a serious subject in American higher education. His teaching joined physical geography with the study of people, societies, and history. He believed that geography should explain relationships among landforms, climate, plants, animals, and human life. Guyot wrote textbooks and educational materials that introduced generations of American students to these ideas. His books included works on physical geography and the Earth’s history. He also helped organize and develop the American Geographical Society, which was founded in 1851. Through his research and teaching, he encouraged systematic observation and the use of maps and scientific evidence. Guyot studied mountains, rivers, climate, and the forms of the Earth’s surface. His name is especially familiar in oceanography because a flat-topped underwater mountain is called a “guyot.” The term was introduced by geologist Harry Hess in the twentieth century, in recognition of Guyot’s name and Princeton connection. Guyot’s work also influenced the development of geography education in schools and colleges. He helped bring European traditions of scientific geography into American classrooms while adapting them to the needs of a growing nation. Arnold Guyot died in Princeton, New Jersey, on February 8, 1884. His legacy lives on in American geographic education and in the enduring scientific term that bears his name.

At midnight, the Reaper drew seven names from a silver lottery drum.
Each belonged to a soul who had died under the dictator’s rule.
They gathered on the bridge between worlds, carrying no weapons, only their memories.
The dictator arrived in a velvet coat, still expecting a motorcade.
“Which of you is my escort?” he demanded.
The Reaper pointed to the smallest figure: a girl with a paper crown.
She had vanished from a village when his soldiers came.
Beside her stood a farmer, a nurse, a nameless clerk, and three others.
The dictator laughed, but the bridge did not echo.
They began walking, and every step brought back a voice he had silenced.
He ordered them to stop; they kept their pace.
At the far end, a gate opened onto a darkness without banners or thrones.
The girl held out her hand—not to forgive him, but to make sure he could not turn back.
The Reaper closed the lottery drum, and for once, no one asked who had won.

The paper addresses an important problem: learning classifiers when positive examples are labeled, many examples are unlabeled, and the available negative examples may be selected through a biased process. Its focus is timely because standard supervised methods can perform poorly when the labeled negatives do not represent the full negative population. The paper’s strongest contribution is its effort to distinguish the effects of unlabeled data and negative-sampling bias rather than treating all observed labels as equally reliable. The comparison of classification methods is potentially useful to researchers working with incomplete or selectively collected data. However, the paper should state its assumptions about how positives, unlabeled examples, and biased negatives are generated more explicitly. In particular, readers need to know whether selection probabilities are assumed to be known, estimable, or independent of the features after conditioning on specified variables. The evaluation would be more convincing if it included a broader range of bias mechanisms and class-imbalance levels. It should also compare against simple baselines, such as a standard supervised classifier and a positive-unlabeled method that ignores the biased negatives. Reporting uncertainty across repeated runs and using appropriate metrics for imbalanced classification would help establish the reliability of the results. The paper should clarify how its methods behave when the negative-sample bias is severe or the assumptions used for correction are violated. A more detailed discussion of computational cost and practical data requirements would improve its value for practitioners. The presentation would benefit from a concise summary of each method’s assumptions, strengths, and limitations. Overall, this is a relevant and promising study, but clearer assumptions and stronger, more systematic experiments are needed to support its conclusions. Subject to these revisions, I believe the work could make a useful contribution to research on learning from imperfectly labeled data.

At dawn, Prince Solan watched the first light spill over the eastern hills. His twin brother, Noctis, stood beside him, still wearing the silver cloak of the night watch. The brothers had been born during an eclipse, one beneath the sun and the other beneath the moon. Their people believed this meant they were destined to rule together.

Yet the old kingdom had always divided power between day and night. Solan governed the bustling hours, hearing petitions and guiding harvests. Noctis kept the streets safe after sunset, listening for danger and guarding the borders. Each brother thought his duty was harder than the other’s.

One winter, a storm swept through the valley and shattered the great river bridge. By morning, merchants were stranded on one bank and families on the other. Solan ordered repairs, but the river ran too high for workers to cross. Noctis proposed sending lantern boats through the darkness, yet his crews lacked enough timber.

The brothers argued until they saw a child carrying a small wooden toy between them. It had been carved by a father on one bank and painted by a mother on the other. The toy had crossed the river in a fisher’s boat, bringing comfort to both sides.

Solan and Noctis fell silent. Then they joined their plans, using daylight crews to gather stone and nighttime crews to guide the boats. Together, they built a new bridge strong enough to survive the flood.

Afterward, the twins changed the laws of the kingdom. Every major decision would be reviewed by both the council of day and the council of night. Guards would share reports at sunrise and sunset, so no warning was lost between shifts. Farmers, travelers, and city folk were invited to speak at either hour.

Some feared the arrangement would slow the kingdom. Instead, it made the rulers wiser and the people safer. Solan learned that quiet listening could be as powerful as swift action. Noctis learned that hope, like sunlight, could guide even the darkest watch.

When the twins grew old, they placed two crowns on the throne: one gold, one silver. They left their heirs a kingdom ruled not by competing halves, but by a shared promise. From then on, dawn and dusk became times of meeting, when every keeper of light greeted every keeper of shadow. And the bridge they built remained the kingdom’s proudest legacy.

Scotland’s 2014 independence referendum anniversary has revived debate over whether the country should hold a second vote and what its political future should look like. The vote took place on September 18, 2014, after a campaign that transformed Scottish politics. Voters rejected independence by 55.3% to 44.7%. The result was presented by both sides as decisive, but not necessarily permanent. More than a decade later, arguments over the question have returned amid changing political and economic conditions.

Supporters of independence say the referendum settled the issue only for the circumstances of 2014. They point to the United Kingdom’s departure from the European Union, which Scotland opposed in the 2016 Brexit referendum. They also argue that Scotland should be able to make its own decisions on taxation, public services and international relations. For many, the anniversary is a reminder that the constitutional debate remains unresolved.

Opponents counter that the 2014 result should be respected and that another referendum would deepen political uncertainty. They say Scotland’s economic prospects are closely tied to the wider UK, including through shared trade, public spending and currency arrangements. Some also argue that the Scottish Government should focus on issues such as healthcare, education and the cost of living. The dispute is not only about whether a vote should happen, but also about who has the authority to call one.

That question became more pressing after the UK Supreme Court ruled in 2022 that the Scottish Parliament could not legislate for a referendum without the consent of the UK Parliament. The ruling narrowed the immediate options available to independence campaigners. The UK Government has continued to reject calls for another legally authorised vote, while the Scottish Government has maintained that the issue should be decided democratically. The disagreement has left both sides seeking new ways to advance their case.

Political support for independence has fluctuated since 2014. Opinion polls have at times shown the country divided, with results varying according to the question wording and the political climate. Polling is not a substitute for an election or referendum, but it has shaped claims about public consent. The anniversary has again prompted parties to cite evidence that supports their positions.

The Scottish National Party, long the leading force behind independence, has faced pressure to make the case more clearly and to address practical questions about a transition. These include the future currency, public finances, borders and Scotland’s relationship with the European Union. Critics say the movement has not offered sufficiently detailed answers. Independence supporters respond that these questions can be resolved through negotiation and democratic mandate.

The wider party landscape has also changed. The SNP’s dominance has weakened amid political disputes, leadership changes and scrutiny of its finances. Labour has made gains in Scotland, presenting itself as an alternative focused on public services and a change of government in Westminster. The Conservatives and other parties continue to oppose independence, though their electoral fortunes have shifted. The result is a less predictable political environment than the one that followed the 2014 vote.

For some voters, the constitutional question remains central to Scotland’s future. Others say it has been allowed to overshadow immediate concerns, including housing, wages and pressure on public services. The debate therefore cuts across questions of national identity and everyday policy. Parties seeking support must show how their constitutional positions would affect people’s lives.

The anniversary has also brought renewed attention to the campaign’s legacy. The 2014 referendum saw high turnout and widespread public engagement, with communities debating the country’s future in workplaces, schools and homes. It established a model of a peaceful, democratic process that both sides continue to invoke. Yet the expectations created by the campaign have not been fully reconciled with the political limits that followed.

Whether a second referendum will take place remains uncertain. Any route to one would require a major political shift, including a change in the UK Government’s position or a new constitutional settlement. Independence supporters may instead seek to build public backing through elections and campaigning. Opponents will argue that those elections should be treated as contests over government, not as substitutes for a referendum.

For now, Scotland’s political future is being debated without an agreed mechanism for deciding its constitutional status. The 2014 anniversary has not resolved that impasse. It has, however, highlighted how Brexit, party change and public expectations have altered the debate since voters last went to the polls. The central question remains whether the result of 2014 should stand as a lasting answer or be reconsidered under today’s circumstances.

South Korea’s investigation into the 2014 Sewol ferry disaster exposed a chain of regulatory failures and negligence that helped turn an emergency into a national tragedy. The ferry capsized off the country’s southwestern coast on April 16, killing 304 people, most of them students on a school trip. Investigators found that the vessel had been illegally modified to carry more cargo and had inadequate stability. It was also overloaded and poorly secured cargo shifted as the ship made a sharp turn. The crew delayed evacuation and gave passengers instructions to remain in their cabins as the vessel listed. The captain and several crew members escaped, while many passengers remained aboard. Investigations also scrutinized the Coast Guard’s response, including delays and failures to coordinate rescue efforts. Regulators were faulted for weak oversight of ferry safety and for relying too heavily on industry self-inspection. The disaster prompted public anger over ties between regulators and ferry operators, and over the government’s handling of the emergency. Legal proceedings brought criminal cases against crew members and officials, though charges and outcomes varied. The captain was convicted of murder and sentenced to life in prison, while other crew members received prison terms for their roles. Some government officials and safety regulators also faced prosecution or disciplinary action related to oversight and the rescue response. The proceedings revealed how responsibility was spread across the ship’s operator, inspection bodies and public agencies. Families of the victims have continued to seek accountability and fuller disclosure about the disaster. The sinking led to changes in maritime safety rules, inspections and emergency-response procedures. Yet survivors and relatives have argued that reforms cannot undo the loss or guarantee that such failures will not recur. More than a decade later, the Sewol remains a stark test of whether South Korea can enforce safety standards and hold institutions accountable.

The paper addresses an important challenge in game-playing agents: integrating visual observations with textual instructions in a way that supports grounded decision-making. Its use of bidirectional feature modulation is a promising design choice, since information can flow both from language to visual representations and from visual context back to language features. The paper would be stronger if it clearly explained how this modulation differs from standard cross-attention or other multimodal fusion methods. Evaluation should cover diverse games, instruction styles, and visual conditions, with comparisons against strong unimodal and multimodal baselines. Ablation studies are also needed to establish whether bidirectional modulation itself drives any performance gains. The authors should report variability across runs and include examples of successes and failures to make the model’s behavior easier to assess. If the model is intended to generalize beyond its training settings, tests on unseen environments or paraphrased instructions would be especially valuable. Overall, the approach is promising, but clearer methodological justification and more comprehensive evaluation are needed to support the paper’s claims.

The paper addresses an important problem: unlabeled data in semi-supervised learning often contains hidden positives, making conventional negative-example assumptions unreliable. Its central idea—using deliberately biased negative examples within a positive-unlabeled learning framework—is potentially useful and merits investigation. The work is clearly motivated, and the connection between negative-example selection and PU classification could offer a practical alternative to methods that require unbiased labeled negatives. A key strength is the focus on a realistic source of bias rather than treating the unlabeled pool as a clean set of negatives. However, the paper needs to define precisely what “biased” means and specify the assumptions under which the proposed method can recover useful decision boundaries. In particular, it should explain how the selection mechanism for negative examples relates to the distribution of positive and unlabeled instances. The method’s identifiability and sensitivity to violations of these assumptions should also be discussed. The experimental section should compare against strong PU-learning and semi-supervised baselines, with hyperparameter tuning and data splits held consistently across methods. Ablations would help establish whether gains come from the biased-negative strategy itself or from other components of the learning pipeline. Results should include multiple datasets and report variation across random seeds, rather than relying only on average performance. Metrics appropriate to class imbalance, such as precision-recall AUC and class-specific recall, would complement accuracy. The paper should also test robustness to different positive prevalence rates and degrees of negative-selection bias. If the method requires prior knowledge of these quantities, the authors should state how they obtain it and evaluate the impact of estimation error. A clearer description of computational cost and practical requirements would help readers judge applicability. Overall, the topic is promising, but the strength of the conclusions depends on more precise assumptions and broader empirical validation. I recommend revision, with particular emphasis on establishing when the method works and how it compares with existing PU-learning approaches.
