Northern Ireland’s newspapers have ranged across veterans’ concerns, debates over the Troubles’ legacy, school funding, royal celebrations and lighter local news. Together, the stories reflect a region balancing unresolved questions of the past with the practical demands of everyday life.

Veterans’ grievances have featured prominently, with former service personnel raising concerns about how legacy investigations are conducted. Some veterans say they fear being treated unfairly, while families affected by Troubles-era killings continue to seek answers and accountability. The debate has renewed calls for a process that can address victims’ needs while ensuring fair treatment for those under investigation.

Coverage of the Troubles’ legacy has also focused on disagreement over how history should be remembered and examined. Political parties, campaigners and bereaved families remain divided on proposals for dealing with cases linked to the conflict. The arguments underline the difficulty of creating a system that commands confidence across communities.

Education funding has emerged as another pressing issue. School leaders and representatives have warned that financial pressures are affecting staffing, classroom resources and support for pupils. Parents and teachers have voiced concern that persistent uncertainty could widen gaps between schools and limit opportunities for children.

Alongside these serious topics, newspapers have reported on celebrations marking royal occasions. Local events have brought residents together for gatherings, displays and community activities, offering a more festive tone to the day’s coverage. Such occasions have also prompted reflection on the changing role of the monarchy and its place in Northern Ireland’s diverse society.

The region’s lighter stories have provided a contrast to political and social disputes. Reports have included community achievements, unusual local happenings and moments of humour that have drawn attention beyond the headlines. They offer a reminder of the everyday connections and shared interests that shape life across towns and villages.

Taken together, the coverage presents a varied picture of Northern Ireland. Long-running questions about justice and memory sit alongside concerns about public services and stories of celebration. The mix shows how local news can track both the pressures facing communities and the events that bring them together.

Every morning, the children of Europe crowded into Room 27, where the desks were old and the roof leaked whenever the clouds looked threatening. Germany sat at the front with a sharpened pencil and a ledger, insisting that everyone show their homework. Greece sat near the window, where the sun was warm, and explained that some assignments had been lost in a tragic series of school trips. France proposed forming a committee to discuss whether homework was, in principle, a social construct. Italy arrived late with a beautiful poster, several unpaid lunch bills, and no clear account of where the glue had gone. Spain and Portugal compared their grades and discovered that the teacher had been using different rulers to measure their mistakes. The headmaster, known as the Market, tapped his watch and announced that confidence was slipping. At once, Germany offered to lend everyone pencils, provided they signed a promise never to lose one again. Greece asked whether the promise could include a new pencil case. The class laughed, though nobody was sure who had paid for the joke. Across the hall, Britain kept its coat on and said it might join the group project after reviewing the terms. It had already moved its desk closer to the door. Meanwhile, the United States sent a note saying it would help, but only if the class continued buying its expensive notebooks. China offered a large box of notebooks on credit, along with a map showing where the desks might someday be rearranged. Russia stood by the radiator, selling warmth to anyone who would listen and reminding the class that the building had more than one entrance. The teacher tried to restore order by drawing a circle on the board and calling it a union. Everyone agreed the circle looked impressive. Then they argued over who should sit in the middle and who should pay for the chalk. When the bell rang, the class had produced three declarations, two emergency loans, and no finished assignment. Germany collected the pledges, Greece collected the erasers, and France asked for another meeting. Outside, the weather changed, and every child blamed a different cloud. Still, the next morning they returned to the same room, because the school had only one classroom large enough for all their ambitions.

At noon, Mara entered the café carrying a tuna sandwich and the confidence of someone who had found an empty table. The table was not empty. A man in a green suit sat there, staring at a bowl of soup as if it had disappointed him personally.

“Is this seat taken?” Mara asked.

“Only by my lunch,” he said. “It has strong opinions.”

Mara sat anyway, mostly because the other tables were full and partly because she wanted to know what soup could do wrong.

The man introduced himself as Detective Vale. He was not a detective, he explained, but his name was Vale and he had once solved a crossword.

Mara said she was a museum curator. This was true, although the museum was a small room above a dentist’s office.

They ate in silence until the waiter brought Mara a bowl of soup and Vale a tuna sandwich.

“I believe our lunches have been switched,” Mara said.

“Then we should question them,” Vale replied.

They exchanged bowls and sandwiches. The soup was tomato, and the sandwich contained no tuna, only a note that read, “You have been selected.”

“Selected for what?” Mara asked.

“Possibly lunch,” said Vale. “It’s a competitive field.”

The waiter returned and apologized for the mix-up. He also said he had accidentally given Vale Mara’s coat and Mara Vale’s hat.

Mara looked down at her bright yellow raincoat. Vale wore her gray wool coat with the solemn air of a man attending its funeral.

“You look like a caution sign,” he told her.

“You look like a very tired cloud,” she said.

They traded coats, but the waiter had already taken their jackets to the wrong table.

At that table, an elderly woman was wearing Vale’s green suit and insisting she was the mayor.

“I’m afraid I’m not the mayor,” Vale told her.

“Neither am I,” she said. “But this suit has the authority.”

She handed him a business card that said MAYOR, and he tucked it into his pocket.

Mara put on the hat she had been given. It was a tall chef’s toque, and everyone in the café began asking her about the specials.

“Today’s special is confusion,” she announced. “It comes with a side of regret.”

A man at the next table stood up and offered her his apron.

Mara accepted it, because the toque had made the apron seem inevitable.

Vale, meanwhile, had found a pair of sunglasses in his coat pocket and put them on.

“I’m Detective Vale,” he declared. “I have a disguise.”

“You’re still wearing your name tag,” Mara pointed out.

“That’s how they know I’m undercover.”

The elderly woman, now in Vale’s green suit, leaned over and asked if they had seen her handbag.

Vale searched the suit and found a cucumber, two receipts, and a small plastic dinosaur.

“The handbag may be hiding in plain sight,” he said.

The woman nodded. “That’s where I keep it.”

The waiter brought them the bill, but it had been printed with the wrong names.

Mara was listed as “Mr. Soup,” and Vale as “The Mayor.”

They paid anyway, dividing the total by the number of people who appeared to be in charge.

Outside, Mara discovered she had taken the mayor’s umbrella.

Vale had somehow ended up with her museum’s visitor map.

“I’ll return this,” he said. “I’ve always wanted to curate something.”

“Start with the dinosaur,” Mara said.

He placed it carefully in the map’s legend.

They walked in opposite directions, wearing the wrong clothes and carrying the wrong credentials.

At the corner, they both turned back.

“Same time tomorrow?” Mara asked.

“I can’t,” Vale said. “I have a case of soup.”

Mara nodded. “I’ll bring the evidence.”

Then the traffic light changed, and each crossed the street as someone entirely plausible.

Every Tuesday at 8:17, Martin ordered a small mushroom pizza he never finished. The delivery woman, Lena, always arrived with rain in her hair, even on clear nights. She smiled, handed him the box, and hurried back down the stairs. Martin began measuring his week by that smile. He learned her name from the receipt and practiced saying it softly in the mirror. Soon he ordered pizza on nights he wasn’t hungry. He saved the little red rubber bands from her ponytail, though he had no idea where they came from. He told himself this was devotion, not loneliness.

One Tuesday, Lena arrived wearing a silver star pinned to her coat. Martin had never seen it before, and somehow it seemed to shine through the hallway’s yellow light. “You look different tonight,” he said. Lena glanced at him as if listening to a voice far away. “So do you,” she replied. Then she left without asking for payment. Martin spent the night holding the warm box against his chest.

The following week, he waited by the door with flowers and a speech. At 8:17, the buzzer sounded. He opened the door to an empty corridor, where the air smelled of burned cheese and wet pavement. A pizza box sat on the mat, its lid slightly open. Inside, beneath the untouched mushrooms, lay Lena’s silver star. Martin picked it up, and every light in the building went out. When they flickered back on, his apartment was gone. The neighbors said the hallway had always ended at a brick wall. On Tuesdays, though, they sometimes heard a buzzer ring behind it.

Conflicting accounts of an Israeli air raid in Syria have renewed questions about the risk of a wider regional confrontation and the flow of weapons to Hezbollah.

The strike was reported in an area used by forces allied with Iran, according to accounts circulated by Syrian and regional media. Details about the target, the timing and the damage remain disputed. Syrian authorities said Israeli aircraft carried out the attack from outside Syrian airspace. They reported that air defenses responded but offered few details about the results. Israel did not immediately confirm responsibility. It generally declines to discuss individual operations in Syria.

Other reports described the target as a site linked to weapons storage or transport. Some accounts said the location was associated with shipments believed to be destined for Hezbollah in Lebanon. Those claims could not be independently verified. The discrepancy has left open whether the raid targeted a weapons convoy, an installation or another military asset. The uncertainty reflects the difficulty of assessing clandestine transfers in a conflict zone.

Hezbollah, an Iran-backed armed group based in Lebanon, has fought multiple rounds of conflict with Israel. Israeli officials have repeatedly said they will act to prevent advanced weapons from reaching the group. They have also warned against Iran establishing a stronger military presence in Syria. Tehran and its allies describe their presence in Syria as support for the Syrian government. Israel views the network of Iranian-backed forces as a direct security threat.

For years, Israel has carried out strikes in Syria against what it says are Iranian or Hezbollah-linked targets. The campaign has often been conducted without public acknowledgment. Syrian state media regularly reports attacks and claims that air defenses have intercepted missiles. Independent confirmation of those claims is frequently unavailable. The lack of detail can make it difficult to determine the scale of damage or the intended target.

The latest reports also highlight how a limited strike can carry broader consequences. An attack on a suspected weapons route could prompt retaliation by Hezbollah or another allied group. Any response could widen beyond the immediate area and draw in additional actors. Israel, in turn, could answer with further strikes. Such exchanges risk escalating even when neither side says it seeks a larger war.

The region remains particularly volatile amid overlapping conflicts and heightened military activity. Tensions along the Israel-Lebanon border have repeatedly threatened to spill into a sustained confrontation. Syria’s fragmented security landscape adds another layer of uncertainty. Iranian-backed forces, Syrian government units and other armed groups operate in areas where outside powers also maintain a presence. Misidentification or miscalculation could therefore have consequences well beyond a single target.

Analysts say weapons transfers are a persistent source of concern for Israel and a central part of its security calculations. Hezbollah has developed a substantial arsenal over time, though estimates of its size and capabilities vary. Israeli officials have voiced concern about precision-guided weapons and other advanced systems. Publicly available evidence rarely establishes the full route or intended destination of any particular shipment. That gap leaves room for competing claims after an attack.

Damascus has condemned Israeli strikes as violations of its sovereignty. Israel has argued that its operations are necessary to prevent hostile forces from entrenching themselves near its borders. Neither position resolves the immediate questions about the reported raid. Independent investigators and outside governments may seek more information about casualties, damage and the identity of the target. Access to the affected area is often limited.

Regional governments are watching for signs that the incident will trigger a response. Diplomatic channels could be used to discourage retaliation, though public statements may also harden positions. Officials have not said whether the strike has prompted new security measures. The absence of confirmed details makes it harder to gauge the likelihood of escalation. For now, the conflicting accounts have added to an already tense atmosphere.

The incident underscores the fragile balance surrounding Syria and Lebanon. Even a narrowly targeted operation can be interpreted as part of a broader contest between Israel and Iran. The parties involved may seek to avoid a direct, prolonged war while continuing actions they consider necessary for deterrence. That calculation is vulnerable to sudden changes on the ground. A response that is meant to be limited can still provoke an unintended cycle.

Until more reliable information emerges, the purpose and impact of the air raid remain uncertain. What is clear is that disputes over weapons transfers continue to shape Israel’s approach to Syria. They also keep Hezbollah and Iran at the center of regional security concerns. The next developments may depend less on the initial strike than on how each side chooses to interpret it.

The East Siberian Arctic Shelf is a broad, shallow area of the Arctic Ocean off northeastern Siberia. Much of its seafloor is underlain by permafrost, ground that has remained frozen for long periods. During past ice ages, this shelf was exposed land, so its sediments froze and accumulated organic matter. After sea levels rose, seawater covered the shelf, gradually warming its sediments. Today, researchers are investigating whether thawing subsea permafrost could release methane.

Methane is a potent greenhouse gas that traps more heat per molecule than carbon dioxide over a period of decades. It also remains in the atmosphere for a much shorter time, roughly a decade on average. Methane can form when microbes break down organic material in oxygen-poor environments. It may also be stored in icy structures called methane hydrates, though their abundance and stability in this region are uncertain.

As subsea permafrost warms and becomes more permeable, methane could move upward through sediments. Some may dissolve in seawater, while some may be consumed by microbes before reaching the ocean surface. Methane that reaches the atmosphere adds to warming, which can in turn accelerate thawing and create a reinforcing feedback. The size and speed of this feedback depend on how much methane is released and how quickly it escapes the seabed.

The East Siberian Arctic Shelf has been the focus of reports of methane seeps and elevated methane concentrations. These observations are important, but they do not by themselves establish the total amount being released or how much comes from newly thawing permafrost. Natural methane sources, ocean processes, and measurement methods all affect the interpretation. Scientists therefore combine ship surveys, seabed measurements, water sampling, and atmospheric observations.

A major uncertainty is the condition of permafrost beneath the shelf. Its depth, temperature, and ability to block gas vary across the region. Sediments also differ in their methane content and in how easily gases can pass through them. Sea ice, storms, currents, and seasonal changes can influence how methane moves from water to air.

Potential climate impacts depend on emissions over time, not just dramatic local events. A sustained, large release could add significantly to global warming, while smaller or more gradual emissions would have a more limited effect. Current evidence does not support treating a sudden, massive methane release from the shelf as inevitable. Nor does uncertainty mean the risk can be dismissed.

Understanding this system matters because Arctic warming is happening rapidly and because methane emissions can be difficult to measure in remote waters. Better long-term observations can clarify whether emissions are changing and identify the processes driving them. Climate models can then test how different release scenarios would affect future warming. The most useful conclusions will come from careful measurements, transparent uncertainty estimates, and continued research.

Sustainable roofing can reduce energy use, manage stormwater, and make buildings more resilient. The best strategy depends on a building’s structure, climate, budget, and maintenance needs. Green roofs support this approach by covering the roof with plants and a growing medium. They can absorb rainwater, provide habitat, and help limit heat gain, but require adequate structural support and drainage. Solar panels generate renewable electricity and can often be installed alongside other roofing improvements. Before installation, check the roof’s condition, orientation, shading, and capacity to support the system. Cool roofs use reflective surfaces to absorb less sunlight and reduce roof temperatures. They can help lower cooling demand, especially in hot, sunny climates. Durable, low-impact roofing materials can also reduce waste and the need for frequent replacement. Improved weatherproofing starts with well-sealed seams, flashing, penetrations, and roof edges. A continuous water barrier and properly designed drainage help prevent leaks and moisture damage. Good insulation and ventilation can further improve comfort and energy performance while protecting the roof assembly. Regular inspections and prompt repairs help sustainable roofing systems perform well over time. Before choosing an upgrade, consult qualified roofing professionals and check local codes, incentives, and climate guidance.

The paper addresses an interesting problem at the intersection of language grounding, document comprehension, and reinforcement learning. Its central idea—using written instructions or reference documents to guide agents through procedurally generated combat environments—has potential relevance to both interactive AI and embodied decision-making. The topic is timely, especially as researchers seek systems that can connect natural-language knowledge to actions under uncertainty. The paper’s strongest contribution is its framing of document comprehension as part of the control loop rather than as a separate preprocessing task. This framing could help agents adapt when objectives, constraints, or enemy behaviors vary across episodes. The procedural generation setup is also a useful way to test generalization beyond memorized maps.

However, the paper needs to make its research contribution more precise. It should clearly distinguish its method from prior work on instruction-following agents, retrieval-augmented planning, and language-conditioned reinforcement learning. The authors should explain how documents are represented, retrieved, and converted into actionable policies. It is also important to clarify whether the agent must reason over long documents, handle conflicting instructions, or identify irrelevant information. Without these details, it is difficult to assess how much of the challenge lies in comprehension versus navigation and combat.

The experimental design should provide stronger evidence that document comprehension improves performance. Useful baselines would include an agent without access to documents, one given a concise summary, and one receiving the relevant facts directly in structured form. These comparisons would help isolate the value of language processing from the value of additional task information. The paper should also report results across multiple procedural-generation settings, including combinations of layouts and combat conditions not seen during training. Generalization should be measured separately from success on familiar environment distributions. Ablation studies could test the effects of document length, retrieval quality, language-model components, and reinforcement-learning objectives.

Evaluation metrics should extend beyond episode completion. Measures of survival, resource use, completion time, instruction adherence, and robustness to misleading or incomplete information would give a fuller picture of agent behavior. The authors should report variability across random seeds and provide uncertainty estimates, since procedurally generated environments can produce substantial performance variation. Qualitative examples would also be valuable, particularly cases where the agent misinterprets a document or recovers from an unexpected encounter. The paper should discuss the computational cost of document processing and training, as this may affect the practicality of the approach. A clear account of the environment, observation space, action space, and reward design would improve reproducibility.

The paper would benefit from a more careful discussion of limitations. Combat environments may not capture the ambiguity, social context, or safety considerations found in real-world instruction-following tasks. If the system relies on a fixed set of document formats or a narrow vocabulary, that dependency should be stated explicitly. The authors should also consider whether rewards encourage exploitative behavior that achieves objectives while violating the intended instructions. Overall, the work presents a promising research direction, but its impact depends on demonstrating that comprehension contributes meaningfully beyond added information and task-specific tuning. With clearer methodological detail, stronger baselines, and broader evaluation, the paper could make a valuable contribution to language-guided decision-making.

The VCAN gene provides instructions for making versican, a large protein in the extracellular matrix—the material that supports and surrounds cells. Versican is produced in several forms, called isoforms, through alternative RNA splicing. It is especially abundant in connective tissues and the eye, including the vitreous, the gel that fills the space between the lens and retina. In the eye, versican helps organize the vitreous matrix and maintain its structure.

Wagner syndrome is a rare inherited disorder that primarily affects the vitreous and retina. It is usually caused by changes in VCAN that disrupt the gene’s RNA splicing. These changes can prevent cells from making the usual balance of versican isoforms, altering the organization of the vitreous. The condition is typically inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern, meaning one altered copy of VCAN can be sufficient to cause it.

A characteristic early feature is vitreous degeneration, in which the normally gel-like vitreous becomes abnormal and may appear thin or liquefied. The vitreous can pull on the retina as it changes, increasing the risk of retinal tears or detachment. People with Wagner syndrome may also develop cataracts, usually at a younger age than is typical. Other possible findings include reduced night vision, loss of peripheral vision, and changes in the retinal pigment layer.

Vision loss varies widely among affected people and can progress over time. Retinal detachment and other retinal complications are important causes of severe vision loss. Some people have relatively mild symptoms, while others experience substantial impairment. Wagner syndrome is distinct from Stickler syndrome, although the conditions can share features such as vitreous abnormalities and retinal complications.

Diagnosis generally involves an eye examination, review of family history, and genetic testing for a disease-causing VCAN variant. Regular assessments by an ophthalmologist, including retinal examinations, can help identify complications early. There is currently no treatment that corrects the underlying genetic change or restores normal versican production. Care focuses on monitoring vision and treating problems such as cataracts, retinal tears, or retinal detachment when they occur. Genetic counseling can help families understand inheritance and discuss testing options.

When the sky cracked open, Mara was arguing with a vending machine.
“I know you’re in there,” she told it, kicking the dented metal side.
The machine dropped a packet of crackers.
Mara looked up at the fracture spreading across the clouds.
“Finally,” she said, “a customer service department with ambition.”
The crack widened, revealing a bright white light.
The light poured down in ribbons, sweeping across the ruined city.
Everywhere it touched, the dead stood up.
They rose from sidewalks, from collapsed buildings, and from the shallow graves people had dug in a hurry.
Some were still wearing hospital gowns.
One wore a clown costume, which Mara thought was unfair to everyone involved.
The resurrected blinked at the world.
Then they began asking for directions.
Mara tucked the crackers into her coat.
She had survived the plagues, the ash storms, and the week when all the pigeons learned to speak.
She had also survived her brother’s attempt to make soup from canned peaches.
Compared with those things, the sky was only moderately alarming.
A woman in a blue robe descended on a ladder of light.
The ladder stopped several feet above the pavement.
The woman sighed and climbed down the rest of the way.
“Are you Mara Vale?” she asked.
“That depends,” Mara said.
“Are you selling something?”
“I am the angel Gabriel.”
“Then no.”
Gabriel checked a small tablet.
“Your name is on the list.”
“Which list?”
“The list for judgment.”
“Is it a bad list?”
“All lists are bad lists.”
Mara considered that.
“Fair enough.”
Gabriel held out a hand.
Mara took it.
The city disappeared.
They stood in a vast hall with no walls.
A desk stretched from one horizon to another.
Behind it sat a person with a tired face and a pair of reading glasses.
“God?” Mara asked.
The person looked up.
“Depends who’s asking.”
“Mara Vale.”
“Then yes.”
Mara glanced at the endless desk.
“Do you take appointments?”
“I used to.”
God opened a folder.
“Your life is complicated.”
“Most lives are.”
“Your file is missing several pages.”
“I assume they were important.”
“They were mostly receipts.”
God turned a page.
“Do you regret anything?”
“Not trusting the man who said the mushrooms were safe.”
“That was sensible.”
“I also regret not trusting the woman who said the mushrooms were safe.”
God paused.
“Why?”
“She had a very convincing hat.”
God made a note.
“Judgment is not a trial,” God said.
“Good, because I didn’t bring a lawyer.”
“It is an attempt to understand.”
“Then I hope you brought snacks.”
A small plate appeared beside them.
It held one cracker.
Mara looked at it.
“You’ve been watching me.”
“I watch everyone.”
“That sounds exhausting.”
“It is.”
God closed the folder.
“What do you think heaven is?”
“A clean bed, hot food, and no one asking me to save the world.”
“And hell?”
“Being asked to save the world while standing in line.”
God nodded thoughtfully.
“Those are better answers than most.”
Mara glanced beyond the desk.
Doors filled the empty distance.
Some glowed gold.
Some were dark.
Some were painted cheerful colors that looked suspiciously threatening.
“Where do they go?” she asked.
“Wherever people need to go next.”
“That’s not how the stories describe it.”
“People enjoy a simple map.”
“People also enjoy being wrong in groups.”
God smiled.
“True.”
A door opened behind them.
A crowd of the newly risen spilled through.
They were confused, frightened, and carrying their old arguments.
A man clutched a briefcase.
A little girl held a red balloon.
The clown from the street was still wearing his costume.
“Is this heaven?” the man asked.
“Not exactly,” God said.
“Is it hell?” asked the clown.
“Not exactly.”
“Then what is it?”
“Your next honest conversation.”
The crowd exchanged wary looks.
The man with the briefcase stepped forward.
“I never apologized to my daughter,” he said.
The girl with the balloon looked at him.
“Then you should.”
“I will.”
“Don’t make it a speech,” she said.
He nodded.
The clown removed his oversized red nose.
“I spent my life pretending nothing hurt,” he said.
Mara looked at the nose in his hand.
“That must have been difficult.”
“It was.”
The doors began to shift.
Gold softened into blue.
Darkness warmed into amber.
The painted doors stopped smiling.
Mara watched people move toward them in pairs.
Some went laughing.
Some went crying.
A few turned around and tried to leave.
A small gray dog trotted past the desk.
God leaned down and scratched its ears.
“Dogs get judgment too?” Mara asked.
“Dogs get biscuits.”
“Seems fair.”
God handed the dog a biscuit.
The dog accepted it with grave dignity.
Mara looked at the doors.
“So where do I go?”
“Where do you think you need to go?”
“I need somewhere quiet.”
A door appeared beside her.
It was plain wood, with a chipped handle.
Behind it, Mara heard rain.
She smelled coffee.
For a moment, she remembered her mother humming in the kitchen.
Her throat tightened.
“I thought heaven would be brighter,” she said.
“Bright isn’t the same as kind.”
“And hell?”
“Hell is often a place people make together.”
Mara looked through the door.
A figure sat at a small table, waiting.
Her brother.
He had died years before the world ended.
He looked younger than Mara remembered.
“Is he really there?” she asked.
“He is as real as your grief.”
“That’s an annoying answer.”
“It is an honest one.”
Mara gripped the handle.
“What if I don’t want to forgive him?”
“Then don’t.”
“What if he asks?”
“Then tell him the truth.”
“What if the truth is ugly?”
“Then it will still be yours.”
Mara opened the door.
Her brother looked up from the table.
“Hey, Mara,” he said.
She stood in the doorway.
“Your soup was terrible.”
“I know.”
“You put peaches in it.”
“I know.”
“It tasted like a warm mistake.”
“I know.”
She crossed the room.
He stood, uncertain whether to hug her.
Mara hugged him first.
For a while, neither of them spoke.
The rain tapped gently on the window.
Then her brother laughed.
“I’m glad you survived.”
“I had low expectations.”
“I noticed.”
She pulled away and looked at his face.
“Are we supposed to have a big conversation?”
“Probably.”
“Can we start with coffee?”
He pointed to the pot.
Mara poured herself a cup.
It was exactly the way she liked it.
She wondered whether that was heaven or merely good manners.
Her brother sat across from her.
They began with small things.
They talked about the weather, which had apparently improved.
They talked about the old apartment.
They talked about the last time he had called.
Mara told him she had been angry.
He said he knew.
She told him that knowing had not helped.
He said he understood.
It was not enough.
It was a start.
Outside, the sky continued to open.
The dead kept rising.
The living kept asking what came next.
In the great hall, God returned to the unfinished files.
Gabriel went to find more chairs.
The angel found a warehouse full of them.
Most were missing legs.
Gabriel brought them anyway.
The judgment line stretched across the horizon.
People waited with their fears, excuses, and carefully rehearsed speeches.
Some asked whether they would be punished.
Some asked whether their enemies would be punished.
Some asked whether the end of the world could be postponed until Monday.
God answered each one as patiently as possible.
The answer was usually another question.
“What do you need to understand?”
“What do you need to repair?”
“What are you ready to admit?”
The questions made people uncomfortable.
They also made the doors easier to find.
Mara stayed with her brother until the coffee ran out.
Then she opened the door again.
She returned to the hall with a warm cup in her hand.
God glanced at it.
“Is that allowed?”
“Apparently.”
“Good.”
Mara sat on the edge of the desk.
“Here’s my judgment,” she said.
“You’re not the judge.”
“Everyone keeps saying that.”
“Because it’s true.”
“Fine,” Mara said. “Here’s my review.”
God waited.
“Heaven is less organized than advertised.”
“Accurate.”
“Hell has excellent lighting.”
“Also accurate.”
“And judgment is mostly asking people to stop lying to themselves.”
“That is one way to describe it.”
“Your brochures need work.”
“We don’t have brochures.”
“Then your marketing department needs work.”
God smiled again.
Mara looked at the crowd.
A woman was confessing that she had stolen her neighbor’s generator.
The neighbor was listening with folded arms.
A boy was trying to apologize to a horse.
The horse appeared unconvinced.
At the far end, a soldier had taken off his uniform.
He stared at it as though it belonged to someone else.
Mara wondered what she would do when the hall emptied.
“Do I have to stay?” she asked.
“No.”
“Do I have to go through that door?”
“No.”
“Can I go back?”
God looked toward the broken sky.
“The world is still there.”
“That sounds like a yes with paperwork.”
“It usually does.”
Mara set down her cup.
“I’d better check on it.”
“Why?”
“Because people are bad at lining up.”
“That is also true.”
She walked toward the light.
Gabriel joined her with a stack of chairs.
“Do you need help?” Mara asked.
“I need a better chair.”
“You and everyone else.”
They reached the edge of the hall.
Beyond it, the city waited beneath a torn sky.
The sun shone through the crack, though it was nighttime.
On the street below, the living and the dead had gathered around the vending machine.
Someone had taped a handwritten sign to it.
The sign read: TAKE ONE, LEAVE ONE.
Mara smiled.
“Civilization,” she said, “is recovering.”
A resurrected man offered her a packet of crackers.
She took it.
Then she offered him half of hers.
The sky rumbled.
A voice like distant thunder asked, “Are you ready?”
Mara looked at the city, the crowd, and the vending machine.
“No,” she said.
“Good.”
The crack in the sky widened.
The light poured down.
Mara stepped into it, carrying crackers for the road.

The paper evaluates a robust reinforcement-learning approach for federated learning across datasets, comparison methods, and non-stationary settings, addressing an important challenge in practical distributed systems. Its focus on changing data or client conditions is especially relevant, since many federated-learning methods are assessed under unrealistically stable environments. The broad evaluation scope is a strength and could help clarify when adaptive decision-making offers a meaningful benefit. The comparison with multiple baselines is also valuable, provided that those baselines are tuned fairly and given comparable computational resources.

The paper would benefit from a clearer account of the reinforcement-learning formulation, including the state, action, reward, and policy-update choices. It should explain how the agent’s observations are obtained without violating client privacy or imposing excessive communication overhead. The authors should also specify how non-stationarity is introduced, how frequently conditions change, and whether the tested shifts reflect plausible real-world scenarios. Results across datasets should be reported with uncertainty estimates, such as confidence intervals over independent runs, rather than relying only on averages. Ablations would help identify whether robustness comes from the learning algorithm, the reward design, or other system components.

The paper should compare performance not only in terms of predictive accuracy, but also communication cost, convergence speed, fairness across clients, and computational overhead. It would be useful to test sensitivity to hyperparameters and to include strong non-RL adaptive baselines. The discussion should distinguish improvements that are consistent across settings from gains limited to particular datasets or shift patterns. If the method requires frequent retraining or careful reward tuning, these practical costs should be made explicit. The authors should also discuss failure cases, including conditions under which the policy adapts too slowly or becomes unstable.

Overall, the topic is timely and the evaluation agenda is promising, but the strength of the conclusions depends on greater methodological detail and stronger evidence of reproducibility. With clearer experimental protocols, statistically supported comparisons, and a fuller assessment of overhead and limitations, the paper could make a useful contribution to robust federated learning.

Soviet Plans to Use Smallpox as a Biological Weapon During a Nuclear War

Smallpox was one of the most feared infectious diseases in human history. It caused fever, severe illness, and a distinctive rash that could leave survivors scarred or blind. Before its eradication, smallpox killed roughly three out of every ten people who became infected. The disease spread mainly through close contact and contaminated materials, making outbreaks difficult to control. In 1980, the World Health Organization declared smallpox eradicated after a global vaccination campaign.

The Soviet Union maintained a large biological-weapons program during the Cold War, despite having joined the 1972 Biological Weapons Convention. That treaty prohibited the development, production, and stockpiling of biological weapons. The Soviet program was concealed behind civilian institutions and involved thousands of scientists and workers. It continued for years after the treaty was signed.

After the Soviet Union collapsed, former program officials described efforts to develop smallpox for military use. The most prominent public account came from Ken Alibek, a senior scientist who defected to the United States in 1992. He said that the Soviet program worked on producing smallpox virus in large quantities and adapting it for delivery by missile warheads. Other former Soviet scientists and officials have confirmed parts of the broader program, though details about specific plans remain difficult to verify independently.

Accounts of the program describe smallpox as one of several pathogens studied for possible use in strategic warfare. A nuclear conflict could have provided Soviet leaders with a setting in which they considered biological attacks against the United States. However, evidence does not establish that the Soviet Union had a finalized operational plan to launch smallpox against American cities during a nuclear war. Public sources also do not provide a complete, independently verified account of the program’s scale, readiness, or intended targets.

A biological attack using smallpox would have posed serious practical problems for an attacker. The virus has an incubation period, so illness would not appear immediately after exposure. Once symptoms began, infected people could spread disease to others, potentially causing outbreaks beyond the original target. Wind, weather, population movement, and public-health responses would make the spread difficult to predict or control.

Smallpox could also have endangered the country that released it. Infected individuals might travel, escape quarantine, or carry the virus across borders. A deliberate attack could therefore trigger an international epidemic with consequences that were impossible to contain. The possibility of retaliation would add further risk during a nuclear crisis.

The threat was also shaped by the world’s vaccination status. Routine smallpox vaccination ended in many countries after eradication was declared, leaving much of the population without recent protection. The United States and other governments have kept limited vaccine reserves and developed plans for responding to a suspected release. These measures are intended to support public-health response, not to suggest that an attack is imminent.

The Soviet smallpox program illustrates why biological weapons are considered uniquely dangerous. Their effects may be delayed, difficult to attribute, and capable of spreading beyond the intended battlefield. It also demonstrates the limits of arms-control agreements when secret programs are not subject to effective verification. The Biological Weapons Convention remains a central international prohibition, but it does not by itself eliminate the risk of covert activity.

Historical claims should be treated carefully. Some information comes from defectors, interviews, and later investigations rather than publicly available Soviet records. Researchers generally agree that the Soviet Union ran an extensive offensive biological-weapons program, but they do not agree on every detail of its smallpox work. Distinguishing documented facts from claims and inference helps prevent the subject from becoming exaggerated or misleading.

The broader lesson is that disease cannot be neatly confined to a military target. A smallpox attack would threaten civilians, health systems, and populations far from the point of release. International cooperation, disease surveillance, emergency preparedness, and strong biological-weapons prohibitions remain important safeguards. The history of the Soviet program is a reminder that scientific capability can be turned toward catastrophic purposes, and that preventing such use requires both public accountability and sustained global vigilance.

Creating and Saving a New Excel Workbook with VBA

VBA can create a new Excel workbook and save it to a chosen location. This is useful when you want to automate reports, templates, or recurring data-entry tasks. Before writing the macro, decide where the workbook should be saved and what its file name should be. You can create a workbook with the Workbooks.Add method. Excel adds a new workbook and usually makes it the active workbook. For example, Workbooks.Add creates a workbook using Excel’s default settings. You can also specify a template or workbook type when adding a workbook. Store the new workbook in a variable so your code can refer to it directly. Declare the variable as Workbook, then assign the result of Workbooks.Add to it. This avoids relying on whichever workbook happens to be active.

A basic macro might begin with Sub CreateAndSaveWorkbook(). Add Dim newBook As Workbook to declare the variable. Then use Set newBook = Workbooks.Add to create the workbook. Set the destination path and file name in a string variable. For instance, the path could be C:\Reports\MonthlyReport.xlsx. Ensure the destination folder already exists, because SaveAs does not create missing folders. Use newBook.SaveAs to save the workbook. Set the Filename argument to the full path and file name. For a modern Excel workbook, specify the file format as xlOpenXMLWorkbook. This format saves the file with the .xlsx extension and does not support macros. If the workbook must contain VBA code, save it as a macro-enabled workbook instead. Use the xlOpenXMLWorkbookMacroEnabled format and a .xlsm extension.

You can also use variables for the folder and file name to make the macro easier to update. Check that the folder exists before saving, or display a clear message if it does not. If a file with the same name already exists, Excel may prompt the user before replacing it. To control that behavior, adjust Application.DisplayAlerts carefully and restore its original setting afterward. SaveAs can raise an error if the path is invalid, the file is locked, or access is denied. Add error handling when the macro will be used regularly. After saving, you can confirm the result with a message box or by checking newBook.FullName. Test the macro with a temporary folder before using it for important files. These steps help create and save workbooks consistently while reducing accidental data loss.

The paper addresses an important challenge in federated learning: reducing divergence between locally trained models while respecting the limits of decentralized data sharing. Its combination of representation matching and adaptive hyperparameter tuning is promising and could offer a practical alternative to methods that rely solely on parameter averaging. The topic is timely, particularly for settings with substantial client-level data heterogeneity. The paper’s central contribution would be clearer if it stated precisely how representation matching and tuning interact, and which component is responsible for any observed gains. The authors should define model divergence carefully and distinguish parameter-space differences from representation-space differences and downstream performance disparities. The method description should provide enough detail to reproduce the matching objective, the adaptation schedule, and the hyperparameters updated during training. It should also explain how representations are aligned when clients have different model architectures or label distributions, if such settings are within scope. The experimental design should include strong, well-tuned federated baselines, including methods designed specifically for non-IID data. Comparisons should use consistent communication budgets, client participation rates, and computation where possible. Results across multiple datasets and several levels and types of data heterogeneity would make the conclusions more convincing. Ablation studies are needed to isolate the contribution of representation matching, adaptive tuning, and their combination. The paper should report variability across random seeds and use appropriate statistical tests or confidence intervals. In addition to final accuracy, useful measures include convergence speed, communication overhead, and divergence across clients. The authors should clarify how adaptive hyperparameters are selected and whether the procedure requires validation data or additional coordination. Sensitivity analyses could show whether performance depends on tuning schedules, matching weights, or client sampling. The paper would benefit from a discussion of privacy implications, since exchanged representations may reveal information even when raw data remain local. It should also address scalability and the computational cost of matching representations across many clients. If the method’s benefits are limited to particular architectures or heterogeneity regimes, those limitations should be stated explicitly. Overall, the proposed direction is valuable, but stronger methodological detail and broader, more carefully controlled experiments are needed to establish its effectiveness and practical relevance.

The paper addresses an important practical challenge in graph scattering transforms: the cost of evaluating many wavelet paths, including those that contribute little to the representation. Its proposed energy-based pruning strategy is intuitively appealing and potentially useful for scaling scattering methods to larger graphs. The work sits at the intersection of graph signal processing, representation learning, and efficient computation, giving it relevance to a broad audience. The central idea is to use estimated or observed path energy to decide which paths to retain. This could reduce computation while preserving much of the information captured by a full transform. The paper’s principal contribution is therefore both methodological and computational.

The manuscript would benefit from a clearer statement of its main novelty relative to existing approaches for path truncation, coefficient thresholding, and adaptive wavelet computation. In particular, it should distinguish pruning entire paths from discarding low-energy coefficients after those paths have already been computed. The authors should explain precisely when energy is measured, how it is estimated, and whether the estimate requires evaluating the path being considered. If energy estimates are computed from the coefficients themselves, the paper should clarify how this avoids the computational cost it aims to save. If estimates are propagated from earlier layers or derived from graph structure, the assumptions behind that procedure need to be stated and justified. A formal definition of the pruning rule would make the method easier to reproduce.

The paper should also specify whether its energy criterion is global, graph-dependent, signal-dependent, or computed separately for each input. These choices have different implications for preprocessing costs, deployment, and generalization to unseen signals. The authors should define the energy norm and explain how normalization, graph size, and signal scale affect the threshold. It is important to state whether the pruning threshold is fixed, selected by validation, or adjusted to meet a target computational budget. A sensitivity analysis over this threshold would help readers understand the tradeoff between efficiency and representation quality. The manuscript should also discuss what happens when several paths have similar energy near the cutoff.

A stronger theoretical account would improve the paper. The authors should provide conditions under which the retained paths approximate the full scattering representation, or at least establish an explicit bound on the representation error. If such a guarantee is unavailable, the paper should be candid about the heuristic nature of the rule and identify the assumptions under which it is expected to work. The relationship between discarded path energy and downstream task performance deserves particular attention. Low energy does not necessarily imply low predictive value, especially when a classifier can use a small but discriminative component. The paper should therefore separate approximation fidelity from task accuracy and avoid treating them as interchangeable.

The experimental evaluation should compare the proposed method with a full, unpruned transform and with straightforward alternatives such as fixed-depth truncation, coefficient thresholding, and random path selection at comparable budgets. Where possible, comparisons should use the same wavelets, graph data, classifier, and training procedure. The evaluation should report not only the number of retained paths but also wall-clock time, memory use, and the cost of any energy estimation or preprocessing. Timing results should include implementation details, hardware, software, and whether computations are batched or cached. It would be useful to report performance across multiple graph sizes and graph types, since a method that helps on one family of graphs may not generalize. The authors should also test several signal regimes, including cases where informative structure lies in higher-order or low-energy paths.

Ablation studies are needed to show which design choices drive the reported gains. These should include varying the energy threshold, the maximum path order, and any normalization or ranking scheme. The paper should report variability across random seeds and provide confidence intervals or suitable statistical tests where feasible. If datasets are small, the authors should describe their split strategy and guard against leakage between training and test examples. For supervised tasks, hyperparameter selection should use only training or validation data. For unsupervised or reconstruction experiments, the evaluation metric and its interpretation should be clearly defined. Reproducibility would be improved by sharing code, parameter settings, and sufficient details of the graph construction procedure.

The presentation should introduce the graph wavelet and scattering notation before relying on it in the method section. A compact algorithm or pseudocode listing would clarify the order of operations and identify which calculations are avoided by pruning. The authors should state whether the method preserves permutation equivariance or other relevant properties of the underlying transform. They should also clarify how the approach handles disconnected graphs, irregular node degrees, and graphs with very different sizes. Potential failure cases deserve discussion, particularly when energy is distributed broadly across many paths or when a low-energy path carries task-specific information. The paper should distinguish savings in arithmetic operations from reductions in measured runtime, since irregular graph operations can make these differ substantially.

Overall, the proposed direction is promising, and energy-based path pruning could make graph scattering transforms more practical. The current presentation would be more convincing with a precise pruning definition, a careful account of estimation costs, and stronger evidence that efficiency gains do not come at an unacceptable loss in representation quality. The most important revisions are to establish the method’s novelty, evaluate it against budget-matched baselines, and quantify both computational savings and approximation or task-performance effects. I recommend revision, with the final assessment depending on whether these methodological and experimental concerns can be addressed.

The Harmandir Sahib, widely known as the Golden Temple, is Sikhism’s holiest shrine. It stands in Amritsar, in the Indian state of Punjab, and welcomes visitors of every faith and background. The shrine is the spiritual center of a complex called the Darbar Sahib, set within a large sacred pool. Its history reflects Sikh devotion, community service, resilience, and the pursuit of equality.

The site’s origins date to the 16th century, when Guru Amar Das, the third Sikh Guru, encouraged the development of Amritsar as a spiritual center. His successor, Guru Ram Das, founded the city and began work on its sacred pool. Guru Arjan, the fifth Guru, completed the pool and established the Harmandir Sahib in its midst. The shrine was designed as a place where people could gather for prayer and reflection.

A distinctive feature of the complex is that the shrine sits lower than the surrounding ground. Visitors descend toward it, a design often understood as a gesture of humility. Four entrances face the cardinal directions, symbolizing openness to people from all directions and communities. The building combines architectural influences from different traditions, while expressing a distinctly Sikh vision.

The shrine’s lower level is largely of marble, and its upper portions are covered with gilded copper plates. This golden exterior is reflected in the pool, creating one of the site’s most recognizable views. The sanctum is connected to the surrounding complex by a causeway known as the Guru’s Bridge. The causeway leads visitors across the water to the central shrine.

The pool is called the Amrit Sarovar, meaning “pool of nectar.” It is central to the complex’s name and spiritual atmosphere. Many Sikhs consider bathing in its water an act of devotion and purification, though the practice is voluntary. The pool is surrounded by a marble walkway where visitors can sit, pray, or walk quietly.

Guru Arjan placed the Adi Granth, the early compilation of Sikh scripture, in the shrine in 1604. The collection included the hymns of Sikh Gurus as well as writings by saints from diverse backgrounds. Its installation established the Harmandir Sahib as a center for scripture, worship, and communal singing. Today, the Guru Granth Sahib is treated by Sikhs as the eternal Guru.

The shrine has endured repeated damage and rebuilding during periods of political conflict. In the 18th century, it was attacked and damaged several times. Sikh leaders and communities rebuilt it, making restoration a powerful expression of devotion and collective resolve. Maharaja Ranjit Singh, who ruled much of Punjab in the early 19th century, supported renovations and the gilding that gave the shrine its familiar appearance.

The Harmandir Sahib also bears witness to painful events in modern history. In 1984, during Operation Blue Star, Indian military forces entered the complex amid conflict involving armed separatists. The fighting caused deaths and extensive damage, including damage to the Akal Takht, an important seat of Sikh authority nearby. The episode remains deeply traumatic and politically contested, and it is remembered in different ways by Sikhs and others.

The shrine’s spiritual significance rests above all on Sikh teachings and worship. Sikhs gather there to listen to the Guru Granth Sahib and sing its hymns, known as kirtan. The music is accompanied by traditional instruments and continues throughout the day and night. The hymns emphasize devotion to one God, honest living, compassion, humility, and service to others.

The Harmandir Sahib is also closely connected to the Sikh principle of equality. Its open entrances represent welcome without distinction of caste, religion, gender, or social status. In practice, visitors are expected to treat one another with respect and share the space considerately. The shrine is not a museum alone; it is a living place of worship and community.

Visitors follow several customs in the complex. Everyone removes their shoes before entering and places them in designated areas. Visitors cover their heads with a scarf, handkerchief, or other suitable cloth. Head coverings are available near the entrances for those who need them.

Before entering the main complex, visitors wash their feet in a shallow water channel. People are asked to dress modestly and avoid behavior that disrupts prayer. Photography rules can vary by area, so visitors should follow posted guidance and the instructions of staff. Quiet conversation and respectful conduct help preserve the devotional atmosphere.

The langar, or community kitchen, is one of the shrine’s most celebrated customs. Volunteers prepare and serve free meals to visitors, regardless of background or ability to pay. People sit together on the floor in rows, sharing a simple meal as equals. The kitchen operates through donations and voluntary service, known as seva.

Seva is a central Sikh practice, and the Harmandir Sahib offers many ways to take part. Volunteers may help prepare food, wash dishes, clean the complex, or assist visitors. Such work is not meant to bring status or reward. It expresses humility and care for the community.

The complex includes the Akal Takht, founded by Guru Hargobind, the sixth Guru, in the early 17th century. It represents temporal authority and the responsibility to address public and communal matters. Together, the Akal Takht and Harmandir Sahib reflect dimensions of Sikh life that are often described as spiritual and temporal. Their relationship is an important part of the complex’s significance.

The shrine attracts millions of pilgrims and visitors each year. Major Sikh festivals, including Vaisakhi and the anniversaries of the Gurus, bring especially large gatherings. The complex is also illuminated during celebrations, while scripture, music, and prayer remain central. Visitors who are not Sikh are welcome to observe and learn respectfully.

The Harmandir Sahib’s importance cannot be explained by its gold-covered architecture alone. It is a place shaped by scripture, collective memory, worship, and service. Its history includes both periods of flourishing and episodes of violence and loss. For Sikhs around the world, it remains a powerful symbol of faith, equality, and belonging.

Newport’s plan to create a Welsh-medium school on the site of Duffryn High School has been rejected, leaving the school’s promised redevelopment uncertain. The proposal was part of a wider education programme intended to expand Welsh-language provision in the city. Its rejection has raised questions about what will happen to plans to modernise Duffryn High, although Newport City Council has not yet set out a replacement scheme. The drought had cracked the fields around Elias’s farm into a map of empty rivers. His wheat stood no higher than his boots, pale and brittle beneath the sun. The bank had given him until Friday to pay his debt. On Thursday, while digging a trench for the last surviving well, his shovel struck something hard. He knelt and scraped away the dirt with his fingers. Beneath the soil lay an iron box, swollen with rust. Elias dragged it into the shade and pried at the lid with a fence post. It opened with a groan. Inside were stacks of gold coins, each stamped with the face of a king long dead. Elias stared until the coins blurred. Then he laughed, a sound he had not heard from himself in months. He filled a flour sack and hurried toward town. The road was crowded with people carrying furniture, livestock, and children toward the railway. At the general store, he set one shining coin on the counter. The clerk glanced at it and shook his head. “We don’t take old crowns,” he said. Elias offered two coins for a sack of seed. The clerk pointed to a handwritten sign: SEED FOR TRADE ONLY. Elias tried the blacksmith next. The smith examined the gold, then pushed it back across his bench. “My furnace needs coal, not history.” By noon, Elias had visited every shop on Main Street. Nobody wanted the coins. The bakery had no flour, the butcher had no meat, and the pharmacy accepted payment only in lamp oil. Prices had changed overnight, the mayor told him. The country’s paper money had collapsed, and the old gold standard had vanished with it. Gold was now just metal, too soft for tools and too strange to spend. Elias returned to his farm with the sack heavier than before. His neighbors were gathered beside the dry well, arguing over a barrel of clean water. He opened the sack and poured the coins onto the earth. Their glitter drew every eye. For a moment, the crowd fell silent. Then a child asked whether the coins could be melted into a cooking pot. Elias looked toward his ruined field. He remembered the buried box, the king on each coin, and the fortune that had made him feel rich for a single hour. He traded the coins to a tinsmith for a narrow strip of metal. The tinsmith hammered it into a small blade for Elias’s plow. The blade cut through the stubborn ground at last. Together, the neighbors dug a channel toward a spring beyond the ridge. They worked for days, sharing tools and what little food remained. When water finally reached the fields, no one asked what it was worth. Elias planted beans beside the channel, one seed at a time. The gold stayed buried beneath the barn, waiting for an economy that might never return.

The bookstore stood between a pawnshop and a bakery, its windows glowing like lanterns on rainy evenings. Above the door, gold letters promised: “A Story for Every Life.” Mara had worked there since she was nineteen. She loved the smell of old paper and the way customers grew quiet among the shelves. The owner, Mr. Vale, claimed the store was a refuge from the world. He also owned a small company that sold enchanted bookmarks. Each bookmark could erase one memory when placed between a book’s pages. The memories did not vanish entirely. They were lifted from the holder and stored in a silver cabinet beneath the shop. Vale said the process helped people heal. He charged enough to make healing available only to the wealthy. Mara disliked the business, but she needed the wages. Her younger brother, Tomas, needed medicine that insurance would not cover. So she helped wrap bookmarks in velvet and smile at customers. One afternoon, a woman named Lila entered with a trembling hand. She asked for a bookmark that would erase the memory of her son’s accident. Vale welcomed her into his office. He spoke gently and offered a discount. Mara watched Lila leave, looking lighter but strangely uncertain. That night, Mara heard a child crying beneath the floorboards. She followed the sound to the cellar. The silver cabinet shone in the dark. Inside it, tiny scenes flickered like trapped fireflies. Mara saw Lila’s son laughing beside a red bicycle. She saw a birthday cake, a scraped knee, and a hospital room. The cabinet held every memory the bookmarks had taken. Vale appeared behind her and closed the cellar door. He explained that the memories powered the shop’s protective enchantments. They kept books from burning, thieves from entering, and profits from falling. “People choose to forget,” he said. “We simply make their choices useful.” Mara asked whether the memories could be returned. Vale’s smile thinned. He said that returning them would ruin the enchantment. He also reminded her that Tomas’s treatment depended on her job. For several days, Mara tried to ignore the cabinet. But each time a customer bought a bookmark, she heard the cellar whisper. Some memories were joyful, and some were painful. All of them belonged to people who had trusted the store. Then Tomas arrived after closing, pale and exhausted. He had learned where his sister worked and what she sold. He told her he would rather face his illness than have her carry someone else’s pain. His words made Mara feel both ashamed and brave. That night, she stole Vale’s key and opened the cabinet. The trapped memories surged out in a glittering storm. They raced through the bookstore, spilling into the streets. People woke with forgotten moments in their minds. Lila remembered her son’s laughter, and the grief came with it. She also remembered how he had held her hand at the hospital. Others recovered old humiliations, betrayals, and fears. Some cursed Mara for bringing pain back. Others thanked her for returning parts of themselves. Vale ran downstairs and tried to seal the cabinet. The enchantment cracked beneath his hands. Every book in the shop flew open at once. The pages filled with scenes taken from their readers. Vale’s own memories poured out last. Mara saw him as a boy, watching his mother sell their books to pay rent. She saw the day he decided never to be powerless again. The sight did not excuse what he had done. It did make Mara understand the fear that had shaped him. When the cabinet shattered, the shop’s golden sign went dark. Vale fell to his knees among the scattered pages. He asked Mara to help him rebuild the business. She said she would help return every memory, but not restore the company. By morning, the city had heard what happened. Inspectors arrived, and the enchanted bookmarks were banned. Vale faced charges for selling stolen memories as a service. Mara kept working in the bookstore, though its shelves were ordinary now. Customers came to read, not to erase themselves. Some brought back books they had once abandoned. Lila began visiting every week, carrying a photograph of her son. She still grieved, but she no longer mistook forgetting for healing. Tomas’s treatment remained uncertain, and the bills did not disappear. Mara took extra shifts at the bakery and learned to ask for help. She and Vale never became friends, but he spent his days returning what he could. Some memories came back blurred, like dreams after waking. Others returned sharp enough to hurt. The bookstore survived by selling stories honestly, one page at a time. Mara learned that pain could be shared without being stolen. She learned that kindness without consent could become another kind of greed. And whenever the evening lamps lit the shop windows, she remembered that no one should have to pay to remain whole.

The paper addresses an important challenge in federated learning: client heterogeneity can make a single shared training configuration ineffective and lead to poorly aligned local representations. Its combination of adaptive local hyperparameter tuning and representation alignment is potentially valuable, particularly for settings with non-identically distributed client data. The motivation is clear, and the proposed approach appears to target both optimization and representation mismatch rather than treating them as separate problems. However, the paper should explain more precisely how local hyperparameters are selected and updated, including what information clients may share with the server. This detail is essential for assessing communication overhead, privacy implications, and reproducibility. The authors should also clarify how representation alignment is defined, which layers or features are aligned, and how the method handles clients whose label spaces or model architectures differ. The relationship between the two components deserves further analysis: it is not yet clear whether adaptive tuning improves alignment, alignment stabilizes local tuning, or the components provide independent gains. The experimental evaluation should include strong and recent federated-learning baselines, as well as comparisons against each proposed component in isolation. Ablation studies should vary the tuning strategy, alignment objective, and frequency of adaptation to show which design choices matter. Results should be reported across multiple datasets, model architectures, and degrees of client heterogeneity, with repeated runs and measures of variability. In addition to average accuracy, the paper should report per-client performance or dispersion to show whether improvements benefit weaker clients rather than only the aggregate. Communication cost, computation time, and convergence behavior are also important, since adaptive methods may impose substantial overhead. The authors should test sensitivity to key choices such as learning-rate ranges, alignment strength, and the number of local training steps. A discussion of privacy is needed, especially if the alignment procedure exchanges representations, gradients, or client-specific statistics. The paper would be stronger with a clear account of failure cases and conditions under which adaptation or alignment offers little benefit. The theoretical discussion, if included, should state its assumptions and connect them directly to the algorithm and observed results. Overall, the topic is timely and the approach has promise, but the evidence and methodological details should be strengthened before its practical contribution can be judged confidently. My recommendation is revision, with particular emphasis on reproducibility, comprehensive comparisons, and a more careful accounting of efficiency and privacy.
