Mara met Elias in the summer she turned twenty-two, when the city was too hot for sleep and everyone seemed to be leaving for somewhere better.

He was a careful listener, the kind who remembered how she took her coffee and which songs she skipped.

For a while, she mistook being understood for being saved.

They loved each other tenderly, then badly, then not at all.

Mara left first, carrying one suitcase and a fierce belief that loneliness was easier than disappointment.

Elias did not try to stop her.

He only asked her to send word if she ever needed help.

She laughed at that, though not unkindly.

Years passed, and Mara became skilled at beginning again.

She found new apartments, new jobs, and new reasons to distrust anyone who offered to stay.

But trouble followed her from room to room.

A landlord kept her deposit.

A manager dismissed her after she missed too many mornings.

A man she trusted borrowed money and vanished.

When her mother died, Mara stopped answering calls.

She slept through afternoons and spent her nights walking beneath streetlights.

The friends who remained tried to reach her, then grew tired of knocking.

Elias, meanwhile, built a quiet life across town.

He married, raised a daughter, and worked as a school librarian.

He never spoke of Mara unless someone asked.

Even then, he spoke gently.

Once, he heard she had lost her apartment and left a grocery card with the woman who ran the neighborhood pantry.

He did not sign it.

Another time, he learned she was sleeping in her car and called a shelter to ask about a vacancy.

He gave them no name.

When Mara found a warm bed there, she assumed it was luck.

She had learned to accept luck without asking where it came from.

By the time she was fifty-eight, her hands shook when she was tired.

She lived in a small room above a bakery and kept the rent paid by cleaning offices before dawn.

Her life was narrow, but it had edges she could hold.

She had a kettle, a calendar, and a neighbor who saved her the crossword.

Then, one rainy Tuesday, the bakery owner told her that Elias had come in asking for her.

Mara felt the old years rise in her like water.

She nearly said no.

Instead, she asked where he was.

“He’s at the clinic,” the owner said. “He’s not well.”

Mara took the bus across town with her coat buttoned wrong.

At the clinic, Elias sat beside a window, thinner than she remembered and still wearing his old, patient expression.

His daughter had gone to buy tea.

For a moment, neither of them spoke.

Then Elias smiled.

“You found your way here,” he said.

“I’m not sure I found anything,” Mara replied.

He told her he was dying, though he said it as if reporting the weather.

Mara stared at his hands, folded neatly on his lap.

“Why did you keep helping me?” she asked.

Elias looked out at the rain.

“Because you needed help,” he said.

“That’s all?”

“That’s enough.”

Mara wanted to be angry, but there was nowhere for the anger to land.

She remembered the shelter bed, the grocery card, and the winters she had survived without knowing why.

“You could have told me,” she said.

“I thought you’d come when you were ready.”

She gave a small, broken laugh.

“I wasn’t ready for a long time.”

“I know.”

His answer held no accusation, only the truth they had both carried.

Mara reached for his hand.

His fingers were cool, but they closed around hers.

“I made a mess of so much,” she said.

“You made it through so much,” he replied.

She lowered her head, and for the first time in years, she let herself cry where someone could see.

Elias sat with her until his daughter returned.

Before Mara left, he asked her to promise one thing.

“Keep the small life you’ve built,” he said. “It counts.”

She promised.

He died three weeks later, with his daughter beside him.

At the funeral, Mara stood near the back and listened to people describe his kindness.

They spoke of books he had found for children, meals he had delivered, and rides he had offered without asking questions.

Mara understood then that his kindness had never been a secret message meant only for her.

It was simply how he moved through the world.

After the service, his daughter gave Mara a small envelope.

Inside was a list of the things Mara had once told him she wanted: a room with a window, work she could keep, and enough quiet to sleep.

Beside each wish, Elias had written a date.

The dates marked the years she had found those things for herself.

At the bottom, he had added, You did this.

Mara folded the note and carried it home.

The next morning, she rose before dawn, made tea, and opened the window.

Rain tapped the sill, soft as a hand asking to come in.

She let the room fill with fresh air.

Then she wrote her rent date on the calendar and called her neighbor about the crossword.

Nothing in her life had become perfect.

But the floor beneath her felt steady.

And when she thought of Elias, she no longer wondered whether he had saved her.

She knew he had simply kept a light on long enough for her to see her own way.

This paper surveys and organizes regularization methods for deep learning, with particular attention to how different strategies can be combined. The topic is timely and valuable, since practitioners face a broad and often confusing choice of techniques. The proposed taxonomy could help readers understand the assumptions, mechanisms, and intended effects of methods such as weight penalties, data augmentation, dropout, normalization, and early stopping. The discussion of combinations is especially useful, because regularizers may reinforce one another, have overlapping effects, or interfere during training. To strengthen the paper, the authors should state clearly how methods are selected for inclusion and how the taxonomy differs from existing surveys. The categories should also be defined consistently, since some methods can reasonably belong to more than one group. A comparative table summarizing each method’s mechanism, computational cost, typical use case, and limitations would improve the paper’s practical value. The treatment of combined methods should distinguish evidence from controlled experiments from informal recommendations or commonly used recipes. The authors should address how effectiveness varies with architecture, dataset size, optimization procedure, and task, rather than implying universal benefits. It would also be helpful to discuss interactions with modern practices such as large-scale pretraining, weight decay variants, and automated hyperparameter tuning. The paper should note that stronger regularization does not always improve generalization and may cause underfitting or increased training complexity. Overall, this is a useful and potentially impactful survey, and clearer inclusion criteria, more systematic comparisons, and a nuanced analysis of combinations would make it substantially stronger.

The paper investigates whether natural-language instructions can help an agent learn rules and pursue goals in a visual game environment. It combines language-conditioned reinforcement learning with visual state observations and action selection. The topic is timely, since many interactive settings require agents to follow rules stated outside the environment itself. The central question is relevant to both grounded language understanding and general-purpose decision-making.

A key strength is the paper’s focus on connecting textual rules to behavior rather than evaluating language understanding in isolation. This makes the proposed task more representative of practical interaction. The work also has the potential to clarify whether language can improve learning efficiency when the environment provides sparse or delayed feedback. If the method supports changing goals or rules without retraining, that would be a particularly useful contribution.

The paper would benefit from a more precise description of its task and assumptions. It should specify what information is contained in each instruction, whether instructions can be ambiguous, and how the agent receives feedback about rule violations. The visual observation setup and action space also need to be clearly defined. In particular, the authors should explain how the system represents game state and links visual features to language-conditioned decisions.

The experimental design should include strong and relevant baselines. These might include a vision-only reinforcement-learning agent, an agent given structured rule labels, and a language-conditioned agent trained without rule changes. Comparisons with simpler instruction-processing methods would help establish whether the proposed architecture is necessary. The paper should also report results across multiple random seeds, with uncertainty estimates and appropriate statistical tests.

It is important to separate the benefit of language guidance from the benefit of additional training data or model capacity. Ablations should examine the roles of the language encoder, visual encoder, reward design, and any memory or planning components. Results should also test whether the agent follows instructions that differ from those seen during training. Counterfactual or minimally varied instructions could reveal whether the model understands the rule or merely matches familiar phrases.

The evaluation should distinguish successful task completion from genuine rule comprehension. An agent may achieve high reward through shortcuts that do not reflect the stated constraints. The authors should include tests in which ignoring a rule still yields short-term progress but causes later failure. They should also measure rule violations directly, rather than relying only on total return. Qualitative examples of successful and failed behavior would make the results easier to interpret.

Generalization deserves further attention. It would be useful to evaluate novel combinations of familiar rules, paraphrased instructions, and changes in visual appearance. The paper should clarify whether performance transfers to new levels or game configurations. If the method depends on a fixed game or a narrow instruction vocabulary, the claims should be scoped accordingly. Robustness to misleading, incomplete, or conflicting instructions is also relevant, even if these cases are left for future work.

The paper should discuss computational cost and sample efficiency in enough detail to assess practical value. Training time, environment interactions, and inference cost are useful measures alongside final performance. It should also explain how reward signals are obtained and whether any manual annotation is required. These details are essential for reproducing the work and comparing it fairly with prior approaches.

Overall, the paper addresses a meaningful problem and presents a promising direction for language-guided interactive learning. Its strongest potential contribution is a unified evaluation of instruction following, visual grounding, and goal-directed action. However, the strength of the conclusions depends on clearer task specifications and more comprehensive controls. I recommend strengthening the baseline suite, adding targeted tests of rule understanding, and reporting uncertainty and failure cases. With these revisions, the work could offer a more convincing account of when language improves reinforcement learning in visual environments.

How shrinking social housing and rising inequality are driving homelessness in the UK

Homelessness in the UK is not simply the result of individual choices or personal crises. It is also shaped by the availability of affordable homes, the security of people’s incomes, and the support offered by public services. Social housing has historically provided homes at rents linked to local incomes. It includes council housing and homes provided by housing associations. For many people, it offers a more secure and affordable alternative to renting privately. But the supply of social housing has struggled to keep pace with need. In England, the number of council homes fell sharply after the introduction of the Right to Buy in the 1980s. Right to Buy allowed many council tenants to purchase their homes at a discount. The policy helped some households become homeowners, but many homes sold were not replaced with new social homes. Over time, this reduced the stock available to people on waiting lists. Housing associations have built homes, but not enough to fully offset the losses and growing demand. Social housing waiting lists remain long in many parts of the country. The details and scale of housing pressures differ across England, Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland. However, the broad challenge of providing enough affordable, secure homes is shared across the UK. When social housing is scarce, people with low incomes have fewer options. Some remain in overcrowded or unsuitable homes while waiting for a placement. Others are pushed into the private rented sector, where rents may take up a large share of their income. The private rented sector can provide useful flexibility and housing, but it does not always offer the affordability or long-term security that vulnerable households need. A household may be forced to move when a tenancy ends, the landlord sells the property, or the rent rises beyond what the household can afford. These changes can cause homelessness even when a person has been working and paying rent. Homelessness includes more than sleeping on the street. It can mean staying in temporary accommodation, living in a hostel, sleeping on a friend’s sofa, or being placed in an unsuitable home. Some people are hidden from official statistics because they do not approach a council or support service. This makes the full scale of homelessness difficult to measure. Rising inequality helps explain why housing insecurity affects some groups more than others. Inequality refers to differences in income, wealth, and access to opportunities. People on low or unstable incomes are more exposed to sudden rent increases and unexpected bills. Those with savings or family support may be better able to manage a financial shock. People without those resources can be pushed into arrears much more quickly. Insecure work, low pay, and periods without employment can make it hard to meet housing costs consistently. Benefit rules and delays can also leave households struggling to cover rent and other essentials. Housing costs have risen faster than incomes for many renters, particularly in areas where homes are in high demand. When rent absorbs most of a household’s budget, there is less money for food, heating, transport, and childcare. A small crisis, such as illness or a broken household appliance, can then become a housing crisis. Eviction is one route into homelessness, but it is not the only one. Family breakdown, domestic abuse, mental illness, addiction, and leaving prison or care can also contribute. These experiences often interact with poverty and a shortage of affordable housing. For example, a person fleeing domestic abuse may need a safe home quickly but may have little money and no alternative place to stay. A young person leaving care may face adulthood without the family network that helps many people find a temporary place to live. People who have been homeless can also face barriers to work, education, healthcare, and stable relationships. This can make it harder to find a home and remain there. Homelessness is therefore both a consequence of inequality and a cause of further disadvantage. Local councils have legal duties to help some people who are homeless or at risk of becoming homeless. The exact rules differ among the UK’s nations. Councils may provide advice, temporary accommodation, or help to secure a longer-term home. But local authorities often face high demand, limited housing options, and pressure on their budgets. When suitable social homes are unavailable, councils may have to use temporary accommodation for longer. Temporary accommodation can prevent people from sleeping outside, but it may be crowded, costly, or far from schools, jobs, and support networks. Children living in temporary accommodation may find it difficult to sleep, study, or maintain friendships. Long stays can affect adults’ health and make everyday life uncertain. Rough sleeping is the most visible form of homelessness, but it represents only part of the problem. People sleeping in cars, shelters, or other temporary places may also lack a stable home. Official counts provide useful information, but they do not capture every person’s experience. Understanding the causes of homelessness requires looking beyond street homelessness and examining housing affordability and security. Shrinking social housing matters because it removes a lasting source of lower-cost homes. Rising inequality matters because it leaves more households unable to compete for scarce housing or absorb financial shocks. Together, these forces increase the risk that a short-term difficulty will become long-term homelessness. There is no single policy that can solve the problem. Building more social and genuinely affordable homes would expand the options available to households on low incomes. Replacing homes lost through sales and redevelopment would help protect the long-term supply. Stronger protections against unfair eviction and sudden rent unaffordability could reduce some routes into homelessness. Adequate income support and timely access to benefits can help people keep up with housing costs. Early advice and mediation may prevent arrears or family disputes from becoming a housing emergency. Support for mental health, domestic abuse, addiction, and life after care or prison can address other pressures that put people at risk. Prevention is often less damaging for individuals and less costly to public services than responding after someone has lost their home. Policies also need to account for local differences in wages, rents, housing supply, and support services. Governments, councils, housing providers, charities, and communities all have a role to play. Progress should be measured not only by the number of people sleeping rough, but also by access to secure and affordable homes. The central lesson is that homelessness is not inevitable. It grows when too few homes are affordable, incomes are insecure, and support arrives too late. A stronger supply of social housing can give people a stable foundation. Reducing inequality can help households withstand crises before they lose that foundation. Together, these measures can make homelessness less likely and make recovery more achievable.

Mara heard the horses before she saw them. Their hooves dragged through the mud with a sound like wet cloth tearing. She climbed onto the roof of the drowned bakery and waited. Below, the street had become a black canal. Broken windows stared from the leaning houses. In one of them, a child’s red coat hung from a nail. Mara waved to it. “You made it,” she said. The coat did not answer, but it had never been much for talking. The riders appeared at the end of the street. There were four of them, wrapped in oilskins and carrying rifles. Their horses wore scraps of carpet over their eyes. Mara counted the riders twice. She counted five the second time. The extra one rode behind them on a white horse. Nobody else could see him. “The King has returned,” Mara called. The lead rider raised his rifle. “Get down,” he shouted. “We’re looking for fuel.” Mara laughed so hard that rainwater spilled from her mouth. “You’re looking for the moon,” she said. “It’s buried under the mill.” The riders exchanged glances. The white horse stepped into the street. Its hooves made no sound. Mara slid down the bakery wall and landed knee-deep in muck. She held up both hands. “I have a map,” she said. The lead rider kept his rifle trained on her. “Then give it to us.” Mara pointed at the sky. Clouds pressed low over the ruined town. “There,” she said. “That’s where the river goes now.” The youngest rider lowered his weapon a fraction. He had a strip of blue cloth tied around his wrist. Mara recognized it from somewhere, though the memory had no edges. “You’re one of the drowned,” she told him. “You’re all drowned.” “We’re alive,” he said. “For now,” said the white rider. The others stiffened. The lead rider swore and glanced behind him. There was only a muddy street, a dead lamppost, and Mara. “Who are you talking to?” he asked. “The King,” she said. “He says you’ve stolen his horse.” The lead rider looked down at his mount. It was shaking, its nostrils flared white with foam. “We took it from a stable,” he said. “There are no stables left.” “There are always stables,” Mara replied. “They sink, but they remember.” The lead rider ordered the others to spread out. Their boots sucked at the mud. Mara saw the blue-cloth boy watching her. For a moment, he looked like her brother, who had vanished beneath the flood years ago. She reached toward him. “Tomas?” she whispered. He flinched. The rifles rose again. “Don’t move,” the lead rider warned. Mara stopped. Behind the riders, the street began to ripple. Something enormous shifted below the mud. The horses screamed and reared. The lead rider fired once into the ground. A bubble burst near his boot, releasing a smell of smoke and roses. Mara shut her eyes. She knew that smell. It belonged to summer, before the waters came. When she opened them, the white horse stood beside her. The King leaned down and offered a hand. “Time to go,” he said. Mara took it. The riders watched her sink without a splash. In the morning, they found four horses and no tracks. By noon, the mud had swallowed the road again. Somewhere underneath, Mara was laughing. Somewhere above, the blue-cloth boy kept searching for his brother.

Music Technology Is Changing How We Create and Listen

Music technology is making it easier for more people to create, share, and enjoy music. Tools once limited to professional studios are now available on phones and computers. This shift is often called the democratization of music production. It means that cost, location, and access to equipment are less likely to prevent someone from making music.

Digital audio workstations, or DAWs, are central to this change. A DAW lets musicians record, edit, arrange, and mix sounds in one application. Many offer free or low-cost versions for beginners. Built-in instruments and effects can help users make music even without a collection of physical gear.

Artificial intelligence is also entering music production. Some tools can suggest chords, generate rhythms, separate vocals from instruments, or help clean up recordings. These features may speed up routine tasks and give creators new ideas. They are best used as assistance, while human choices guide the music’s direction and meaning.

Affordable recording equipment has improved, too. A basic microphone, headphones, and an audio interface can produce clear recordings in a quiet room. Modern software can reduce background noise and correct small performance problems. These improvements do not replace musical skill, but they can make a polished result more achievable.

Cloud platforms are changing how musicians work together. People in different cities or countries can share project files and add parts to the same song. Some services allow collaborators to record or listen together in real time. This makes it easier to exchange ideas without traveling or booking a studio.

Real-time collaboration can also strengthen creative relationships. A songwriter might work with a producer while a vocalist records from home. Participants can discuss changes as they happen and compare different versions quickly. Clear communication remains important, especially when collaborators have different workflows or schedules.

Online music communities offer another route to collaboration. Musicians can find session players, producers, and songwriters through forums and specialized platforms. They can also share drafts and receive feedback from listeners around the world. Constructive feedback can help creators notice strengths and areas to improve.

Emerging tools are improving sound quality at several stages. High-quality digital recording preserves detailed performances, while modern mixing software offers precise control over levels and tone. Audio restoration tools can reduce clicks, hiss, and other unwanted sounds. Careful mastering can help a track sound consistent across different playback systems.

Listening technology is evolving alongside production. Streaming services provide access to vast music libraries on phones, computers, and connected speakers. High-resolution audio options can preserve more detail than heavily compressed formats, though the difference depends on the recording, equipment, and listener. Spatial audio formats can create a sense of sound surrounding the listener.

Personalized recommendations can help listeners discover unfamiliar artists and styles. These systems analyze listening patterns to suggest music a person may enjoy. They can make vast catalogs easier to explore, but may also repeatedly promote familiar sounds. Playlists created by people, local radio, and independent music sites can offer useful alternatives.

Accessibility is another important benefit of new music technologies. Visual interfaces can help people with hearing differences work with rhythm and sound. Adaptive instruments and accessible software can make music creation possible for people with a range of physical abilities. Captions, transcripts, and descriptive controls can also make music platforms easier to use.

These changes bring challenges as well as opportunities. Creators need to consider privacy, copyright, and how their work may be used by online services. Artificial intelligence raises questions about consent, attribution, and the sources used to train creative systems. Fair payment and discoverability remain concerns for many musicians.

Technology alone does not make music meaningful. Ideas, practice, listening, and collaboration still matter. New tools can lower barriers, support experimentation, and improve technical quality. Used thoughtfully, they give more people the chance to create music and help listeners experience it in new ways.

Institutional racism—discrimination built into laws, government agencies, schools, housing, and workplaces—shaped the conditions Black Power leaders sought to change. Even after legal segregation ended, Black communities faced police violence, unequal schools, job discrimination, and limited access to housing and political power. These inequalities led leaders such as Stokely Carmichael (later known as Kwame Ture), Huey P. Newton, and Angela Davis to argue that civil rights protections alone could not ensure equality. Black Power activism emphasized community control, political self-determination, and pride in Black identity. The Black Panther Party organized community programs, including free breakfast for children and health clinics, while also monitoring police conduct. Other activists challenged racism in universities, labor movements, and public policy, connecting local struggles to wider movements for liberation. Their resistance took many forms, from protest and political organizing to education and mutual aid. State surveillance, arrests, and violence against activists revealed how institutions often defended the existing racial order. Studying this history shows how Black Power leaders responded to systemic barriers while expanding debates about justice, safety, and community power.

Alfred Kurti has been arrested in Ireland as UK authorities seek his extradition over the 2004 murder of Kalvinder Singh. Singh was killed in a case that has remained unresolved for more than two decades. Kurti is wanted by British authorities in connection with the killing, and the extradition process will determine whether he is sent to the UK to face proceedings. Irish courts will consider the request under the relevant legal procedures. Details of the arrest and the allegations against Kurti have not been independently confirmed here. Kurti is presumed innocent unless proven guilty.

Barbedienne’s bronze reproductions of Ghiberti’s biblical reliefs bring one of the Renaissance’s most celebrated works into a smaller, more portable form. They reproduce scenes from the doors made for the Florence Baptistery by the sculptor Lorenzo Ghiberti. The story of these bronzes connects Renaissance art, nineteenth-century collecting, and the rise of industrial reproduction.

Florence’s Baptistery stands near the city’s cathedral and is dedicated to Saint John the Baptist. Its bronze doors were made over several decades in the fifteenth century. Ghiberti’s first set, completed in 1424, depicts episodes from the New Testament. His later set, finished in 1452, presents scenes from the Hebrew Bible, which Christians traditionally called the Old Testament.

The later doors became famous as the “Gates of Paradise,” a name associated with Michelangelo. Their ten large panels show stories including the creation of Adam and Eve, the meeting of Abraham and Isaac, and the life of Joseph. Ghiberti arranged many figures and episodes within each panel, using differences in scale and depth to guide the viewer’s attention.

The reliefs combine careful observation with dramatic storytelling. Figures near the front project strongly from the surface, while distant buildings and landscapes are rendered in shallower relief. This gradual change in depth, known as pictorial relief, creates an impression of space on a relatively flat bronze panel. Ghiberti also used architectural settings to organize the action and suggest the world of the story.

Making the original doors required exceptional skill. Ghiberti and his workshop modeled, cast, chased, and finished the bronze, working with techniques that demanded both artistic judgment and technical expertise. The panels were integrated into massive doors whose frames and decorative details contribute to their overall design. The originals remain in Florence, where the Baptistery’s doors have been replaced by replicas for protection.

In the nineteenth century, reproductions helped make famous artworks available to a wider public. The French foundry of Ferdinand Barbedienne became one of the leading producers of high-quality bronze copies. Founded in Paris in 1838, the firm used casting methods associated with the lost-wax process and developed efficient ways to reproduce sculpture. Its works were sold to museums, collectors, and institutions across Europe and beyond.

Barbedienne’s reproductions of Ghiberti’s reliefs translated the large Florentine panels into objects suitable for display indoors. Depending on the edition and format, a reproduction might present a complete panel or a detail, and its dimensions could differ substantially from the original. Such bronzes allowed viewers to examine the figures and compositions at close range, away from the crowded setting of the Baptistery.

A cast is not simply a photograph in three dimensions. Molds and casting decisions can affect surface detail, while finishing, patination, and scale influence how a bronze is seen. Reproductions may preserve the broad contours of a relief but vary in small details or surface character. Their quality and historical significance therefore depend on the particular cast, its date, and its relationship to the original.

These objects also raise questions about authenticity. The Barbedienne bronzes are not Ghiberti’s own works, yet they are more than generic copies: they document the nineteenth-century desire to study and possess celebrated art. They show how industrial production could serve artistic education and collecting, while also transforming an artwork’s scale and setting. A museum label may identify a piece as a reproduction, replica, cast, or after Ghiberti; those terms can signal different histories and degrees of fidelity.

When looking at a Barbedienne relief, begin by tracing how the composition directs the eye. Notice which figures stand out most strongly, and which recede into the background. Look for gestures, architectural elements, and changes in depth that separate one episode from another. Then compare the bronze’s surface and scale with images or descriptions of the Florentine panels.

Barbedienne’s casts offer a useful way to study both Renaissance invention and nineteenth-century craftsmanship. They preserve the appeal of Ghiberti’s biblical storytelling while revealing how later generations circulated and reinterpreted great works of art. Through these reproductions, the Gates of Paradise became not only a monument in Florence but also a subject for close study in homes and collections around the world.

The paper offers a timely critical assessment of how deep-learning regularization methods are surveyed and organized, a topic with direct relevance to both researchers and practitioners. Its strongest contribution is the emphasis that a taxonomy should do more than list techniques: it should make explicit the principles used to group them and the assumptions behind those choices. The discussion usefully highlights the risk of treating overlapping methods as mutually exclusive categories. It also raises an important concern that distinctions based solely on implementation can obscure shared mechanisms, while distinctions based solely on intuition may be difficult to apply consistently. The paper would be stronger if it stated its assessment criteria at the outset and applied them systematically to each part of the survey under review. In particular, criteria such as mechanism, source of randomness, training-time versus inference-time effects, and dependence on architecture could help make the analysis more reproducible. The authors should clarify how they distinguish regularization from optimization, data augmentation, and architectural design, since these boundaries are often contested. A compact comparison table mapping representative methods to multiple categories would make the proposed framework easier to evaluate. The review also needs to explain how the surveyed methods and literature were selected, including the search scope and any inclusion or exclusion rules. Without this information, readers cannot judge whether the critique reflects the field broadly or a limited sample. The practical guidance is valuable in principle, but it should connect recommendations to concrete conditions such as dataset size, compute budget, model type, and deployment constraints. Where evidence is mixed, the paper should avoid presenting broad prescriptions and instead identify the settings in which a recommendation is supported. The authors could further distinguish empirical findings from conceptual arguments and note when comparisons across studies are limited by inconsistent benchmarks or tuning procedures. These changes would improve the paper’s rigor and help readers use its taxonomy without mistaking it for a definitive or universally applicable classification. Overall, the work has a useful critical premise, but clearer criteria, a more transparent review method, and more conditional practical advice are needed before its conclusions can be considered robust.

Mara Venn had once believed a poem could change the weather inside a person.

At twenty-two, she wrote one about her father’s hands and read it aloud in a basement café.

A woman in a red scarf cried afterward.

Mara carried that moment like a medal for years.

Then came the prizes, the interviews, and the invitations to rooms where the water had names.

Her poems grew shorter as the introductions grew longer.

At a gala, a critic praised her “radical tenderness” while mispronouncing her surname.

A publisher called her work difficult in a tone that meant valuable.

Mara smiled for the photograph and wondered if anyone had read the poems.

The newest collection had won the Bellweather Prize, the grandest honor in the country.

Its title appeared on banners outside bookstores.

Inside, copies sat untouched beneath a display of candles and glass pears.

One afternoon, Mara slipped into a reading at a neighborhood library.

The audience was mostly children, restless and bright-eyed.

A boy asked whether poets made things up because they were lonely.

Mara said sometimes they made things up because the truth was too small.

The boy considered this, then asked if poems had to mean something.

Before she could answer, a girl in the front row said hers was about a dragon who hated soup.

The room laughed, and the girl looked pleased.

Afterward, the librarian asked Mara to sign a copy of her prize-winning book.

Mara wrote her name and felt the old, hollow satisfaction arrive right on time.

That evening, she walked to the river and found an envelope in her coat pocket.

It contained a poem she had written on the train, folded into quarters.

The poem was clumsy, full of rain and bad comparisons.

She read it under a streetlamp and almost threw it away.

Then she noticed a man on the opposite bank, staring at the water.

He was crying quietly, though she could not tell why.

Mara wondered whether her poem could reach him, or whether the thought itself was vanity.

A barge groaned past, breaking the river’s reflection into pieces.

The man wiped his face and turned toward the road.

She never learned if he had seen her.

The next morning, a magazine asked her to explain the meaning of her work.

Mara drafted three elegant answers and deleted them all.

She wrote, “I don’t know what a poem is worth before someone reads it.”

The editor called that unhelpful.

A week later, Mara returned to the library with a new poem.

She read about a dragon who hated soup, though she had never met one.

The children listened, argued about the ending, and demanded a sequel.

Mara left with soup stains on her sleeve and no photograph to prove it.

At home, she found the Bellweather medal in a drawer.

Its gold surface had dulled where her thumb had rubbed it.

She set it beside the draft of the dragon poem.

One object said the world had approved of her.

The other said nothing at all.

She began to suspect that neither object could tell her what mattered.

Perhaps acclaim was only a crowd’s way of keeping score.

Perhaps merit was the name people gave to what they already knew how to admire.

And perhaps meaning was not a jewel hidden inside a poem, waiting for the right reader.

It might be a door, opened by accident, in a house no one had planned to enter.

Mara picked up her pen and wrote the dragon’s next adventure.

This time, she gave it a bowl of soup.

A Scottish civil court has awarded damages to a woman who sued two former footballers over an alleged rape. The case was heard in the Court of Session in Edinburgh, where civil claims are decided on the balance of probabilities. The woman said she was sexually assaulted by the men after a night out. The court found the former players liable and ordered them to pay compensation. The award was made in a civil case, which is separate from a criminal prosecution. Civil proceedings do not require proof beyond reasonable doubt, the standard used in criminal trials. The ruling does not itself amount to a criminal conviction. The woman’s legal team said the decision recognised the harm she had suffered. The defendants disputed the allegations, according to reports of the proceedings. The court’s written judgment is expected to set out its reasoning and the amount awarded. The case adds to wider debate in Scotland about how sexual-assault claims are pursued and resolved.

Life experiences and outside influences can change a person’s beliefs and attitudes over time. People often begin with ideas shaped by their families, communities, and early education. As they grow older, they meet others whose lives and opinions are different from their own. These encounters can make them question what they once accepted without thinking. For example, volunteering may help someone become more compassionate toward people facing hardship. Reading books or learning about history can also reveal new perspectives. However, change does not happen to everyone in the same way. Some people hold firmly to their original beliefs, while others revise them after reflection or important events. Changing one’s mind does not necessarily mean being weak; it can show a willingness to learn. In the end, life experiences and influences can reshape a person’s outlook, helping them better understand themselves and the world.

During a UK election campaign, rules known as “purdah” are often used to protect the fairness of the contest. The term is widely understood, but official guidance more often refers to the pre-election period of sensitivity. These rules apply to government departments and public bodies, not to political parties’ campaigning as such. Ministers remain in office and may carry out necessary government business, but should avoid announcements or decisions that could influence voters or give a party an unfair advantage. Major policy launches, publicity campaigns and other attention-grabbing announcements are therefore usually postponed. Public spending is not automatically frozen, but new commitments—especially those that are politically contentious or could affect the election—are generally avoided unless they are urgent or necessary. Essential services and routine administration continue, and public bodies must still meet their legal duties. Civil servants must remain politically impartial and may not use government resources, official information or their public roles to support a party or candidate. Staff involved in campaigning or sensitive policy work may face extra limits on public statements and contact with ministers or candidates. The exact restrictions depend on the circumstances, and official guidance helps departments decide what can proceed. These safeguards aim to keep government functioning while ensuring public resources and official influence are not used unfairly during an election.

Maya had been talking about Starfall Knights for three weeks. She described its duels, its ridiculous villain, and the soundtrack that made every episode feel like a thunderstorm. Her friend Leo listened politely, then said he wasn’t going to watch it. “It’s too hyped,” he explained. “When everyone says something is perfect, it usually isn’t.” Maya frowned, though she tried to hide it behind her mug. She thought Leo was being stubborn just to be different. He thought Maya was treating a cartoon like a life-changing event. At lunch, they argued over whether a popular show deserved a fair chance. Maya said a single episode couldn’t hurt. Leo said he didn’t want homework disguised as entertainment. Their friend Nia suggested they settle it with a deal. Leo would watch the first episode, and Maya would stop explaining it beforehand. If he hated it, she would never bring it up again. If he liked it, he would admit the hype might have a point. That evening, they met at Maya’s apartment with popcorn and no expectations. Leo sat with his arms folded as the opening music began. “I’m only here because I value friendship,” he said. “Naturally,” Maya replied, pressing play. The first scene showed a knight falling out of the sky and landing in a bakery cart. Leo laughed despite himself. Maya noticed but didn’t comment. By the time the episode ended, Leo had leaned forward without realizing it. The final scene revealed that the silly knight had been hiding a terrible secret. Leo stared at the screen as the credits rolled. “Well?” Maya asked, carefully casual. He reached for another handful of popcorn. “The animation was good,” he said. “And the villain’s voice was excellent.” Maya grinned. “So you’ll watch the next one?” Leo sighed, already searching for it on the screen. “I’ll give it one more episode,” he said. Maya let him have the last word, because she knew he’d be back next week.

The paper provides a timely review of regularization methods in deep learning and their relationship to generalization. Its broad scope is valuable, given the rapid growth and sometimes inconsistent use of the term “regularization.” The proposed taxonomy could help readers compare methods that are often discussed in separate literatures. In particular, grouping approaches by where and how they act—on parameters, activations, data, optimization, or model structure—offers a useful organizing principle. The review also has the potential to connect practical techniques, such as weight decay and dropout, with broader theoretical questions about generalization.

A major strength is the topic’s relevance to both researchers and practitioners. A clear comparison of methods could help readers understand why techniques that appear similar may have different effects. The paper would be stronger if it stated explicit criteria for including and categorizing methods. Some approaches, such as data augmentation and early stopping, can serve several purposes beyond regularization, so the taxonomy should acknowledge such overlap. It should also distinguish regularization as an explicit training objective from implicit biases introduced by architectures, optimizers, and training procedures. Without these distinctions, the categories may appear more definitive than the evidence supports.

The discussion of generalization should carefully separate empirical performance from theoretical guarantees. Claims about why a method improves generalization should be tied to the assumptions and settings of the cited studies. Results may vary with model size, data distribution, compute budget, and training regime, and the review should make these dependencies clear. A comparative table summarizing each method’s mechanism, typical use, evidence, and limitations would improve accessibility. Including negative or mixed findings would also guard against presenting regularization as uniformly beneficial. The review should discuss interactions among methods, since combinations can be complementary, redundant, or detrimental.

The paper would benefit from a transparent literature-search and selection process, especially if it presents itself as comprehensive. It should clarify how recent developments are covered and how foundational work is balanced against newer studies. Consistent terminology and precise definitions would make the taxonomy easier to apply. The organization should guide readers from core concepts to method families and then to evidence about generalization. A concise section on evaluation practices could address data leakage, benchmark selection, and differences in reporting. The authors might also identify open questions, including how regularization behaves in large-scale foundation models and under distribution shift.

Overall, this is a promising and useful review topic with the potential to become a valuable reference. Its contribution will depend on whether the taxonomy is operational, the evidence is critically synthesized, and theoretical claims are appropriately qualified. I recommend revision to strengthen the methodology, clarify category boundaries, and deepen the comparative analysis. With these improvements, the paper could offer a balanced account of how regularization methods influence generalization and where important uncertainties remain.

Mara began wearing the gray mask after the magistrate’s men beat her brother in the street. They had called it an arrest, though they left him bleeding beneath a lamp. The city called what she did afterward justice. She broke into the magistrate’s cellar and freed the prisoners chained there. She left the guards tied together, alive, with their own keys within reach. For a while, she believed that distinction mattered.

Then she found the man who had ordered the beating. He was hiding in a boardinghouse, far from the magistrate’s reach. Mara cornered him in a narrow room while rain tapped at the shutters. He recognized her eyes above the mask. “You’re no better,” he said. She told him he was right. Then she struck him.

The first blow was meant to make him confess. The second was meant to make him hurt. By the third, he was begging, and Mara had stopped listening. She felt a strange warmth rise through her fear. It was not courage, she understood. It was pleasure. When she finally left, she carried his confession and the memory of his pleading.

The confession brought down the magistrate. The prisoners went free, and the city praised the masked woman in whispers. Mara tried to be glad. Instead, she kept remembering how easily her anger had become appetite. She told herself she would never do it again. Then another name reached her: a factory owner who locked children inside overnight.

She found him in his office, counting coins by candlelight. He looked smaller than she expected. That should have made the work easier. Instead, it made her hesitate. He raised his hands and began to explain. Mara thought of the children sleeping behind a barred door. She thought, too, of the warmth she had felt in the boardinghouse.

She lowered her fist. “You’re coming with me,” she said. The owner laughed and lunged for the bell cord. Mara caught his wrist and twisted until he cried out. The old pleasure flickered, bright as a match. She let go before it could catch. Then she dragged him into the street, where the children and their parents were waiting.

They took him to the watch, with the evidence Mara had gathered. As the doors closed behind him, the crowd called her a hero. Mara heard only the echo of his cry. She walked home with her hands open at her sides. In the morning, she would decide whether the mask still belonged to her. Tonight, she would not pretend the choice was easy.

Growing vegetables in the Northeast: seasonal planning, soil preparation, crop selection, and weather protection

The Northeast has a varied climate, with cold winters, changeable springs, warm summers, and fall frosts. Growing seasons differ across the region, so use your local frost dates as a starting point rather than relying on a single regional calendar. Your county extension service or nearby weather station can help identify typical last spring and first fall frosts. Keep a garden notebook to record planting dates, weather, harvests, and varieties that perform well.

Plan the garden around the length of your growing season and the space available. Choose a sunny site that receives at least six hours of direct sunlight each day. Place taller crops where they will not shade shorter ones, and leave paths wide enough to tend plants without compacting the soil. Rotate crop families to different beds each year to help reduce pests and diseases. Avoid planting related crops, such as tomatoes and peppers, in the same spot year after year.

Start spring with cool-season vegetables that tolerate chilly weather. Peas, spinach, lettuce, radishes, kale, and many root crops can be sown as soon as the soil is workable. Soil that is wet and sticky should not be dug or walked on, since compaction can make it harder for roots to grow. Use a soil thermometer or local planting guidance to check conditions for seeds that need warmer soil. Sow small amounts of quick-growing crops every week or two for a steadier harvest.

Warm-season crops need more heat and should be planted after the danger of frost has passed. Tomatoes, peppers, cucumbers, beans, squash, and corn are common choices. In much of the Northeast, gardeners start tomatoes and peppers indoors several weeks before transplanting them outside. Harden seedlings by gradually exposing them to outdoor conditions over about a week. Transplant on a cloudy day or in the evening, and water thoroughly afterward.

Prepare soil by testing it before adding amendments. A soil test can show whether the pH and nutrient levels suit the vegetables you plan to grow. Many vegetables do well in slightly acidic soil, but recommendations vary by crop and location. Add compost to improve soil structure and support water retention, while following test results for lime or fertilizer. Avoid adding fresh manure close to planting time, because it can damage plants or introduce pathogens.

Raised beds can be useful where soil drains poorly or is difficult to work. Fill them with a suitable soil-and-compost blend, and avoid making them so wide that you must step into them to reach the center. Mulch around established plants to limit weeds and reduce moisture loss. Water deeply when needed, aiming at the soil rather than the leaves. Rain gauges or simple soil checks can help prevent both drought stress and overwatering.

Northeastern weather can shift quickly, so keep protective materials ready. Row covers, cloches, and cold frames can shield young plants from light frosts and chilly winds. Remove or open covers when temperatures rise, especially if plants need access to pollinators. A layer of mulch can protect roots from temperature swings, but wait until the soil has warmed before applying it to heat-loving crops. Secure covers well so gusty winds do not damage plants.

Late summer is a good time to plan fall plantings. Fast-growing greens, radishes, and some root vegetables can mature before the first hard frost if sown early enough. Check the days to maturity on seed packets and allow extra time as daylight and temperatures decline. Many cool-season crops taste sweeter after light frosts, though severe freezes can still harm them. Harvest tender crops before a damaging freeze, and use season extenders where appropriate.

Choose varieties suited to your location, available space, and preferred harvest time. Disease-resistant varieties can be especially helpful in humid summers. Watch plants regularly for pests, leaf spots, and signs of stress, and respond early with appropriate methods. Keep weeds under control because they compete for water, light, and nutrients. With careful seasonal planning, healthy soil, suitable crops, and simple weather protection, a Northeast vegetable garden can produce from early spring into fall.

Mara woke beneath a sky full of unfamiliar stars. She had been in a hospital bed, surrounded by beeping machines, when the world suddenly went quiet. Now she stood barefoot on a silver road that stretched between constellations. Her hospital gown fluttered in a wind she couldn’t feel. At the road’s edge, a glowing figure waited with its back to her. “Am I dreaming?” Mara called. The figure turned, revealing her own face. “Not exactly,” it said. Mara glanced down and saw a thin golden cord trailing from her chest. It vanished into the darkness below. “That leads back to your body,” said the other Mara. “Then take me there,” she replied. The figure shook its head. “You have to choose to return.” A distant bell rang, and the stars trembled. Mara followed the cord toward a dark opening in the sky. As she walked, she heard voices rising from far below. One was her sister, crying beside the hospital bed. Another voice was the steady rhythm of a heart monitor. Then came a third sound: footsteps. Mara quickened her pace. The opening widened, showing a hospital room bathed in green light. She saw herself lying motionless beneath a white sheet. The cord connected her chest to that still body. A nurse leaned over the bed, checking the monitors. Mara’s sister held her hand and whispered, “Please wake up.” Mara reached for the opening. The other Mara caught her wrist. “Something has already woken,” it said. In the bed, Mara’s eyes snapped open. Her sister gasped with relief. But the body sat up too quickly, its movements stiff and strange. The nurse shouted for help. The body looked around the room, smiling at nothing. Mara tugged desperately at the cord. “That’s me,” she cried. “That’s my body!” The other Mara’s face grew pale. “It knows where you are now.” The body turned toward the dark window. In its reflection, Mara saw no face at all, only a starless hollow. It climbed from the bed and pulled the heart monitor leads free. Alarms shrieked through the room. Mara’s sister backed away, calling for the nurses. The body tilted its head, listening to the noise. Then it pressed one hand against the glass. A crack spread through the window, though the pane remained unbroken. Up in the silver sky, the same crack appeared beneath Mara’s feet. “It’s pulling you in,” said the other Mara. The cord tightened around her chest. Mara grabbed it with both hands. Down below, the body smiled again. She thought of her sister’s warm fingers around hers. She remembered the life she had not finished living. “I choose to return,” Mara shouted. The stars folded inward, and the silver road vanished. Mara fell through the dark with the cord blazing around her. She struck her body like a wave breaking on shore. In the hospital room, her eyes opened. Her sister sobbed and clutched her hand. The monitors settled into a steady rhythm. The body on the floor lay still, its smile gone. Mara could not explain what had happened. She only stared at the window. In its reflection, for one brief moment, a second Mara stood behind her.

Amazon has selected four pilots for full-series orders, expanding its original drama and comedy lineup. The decisions bring a mix of genres and stories to the streaming service as it builds out its scripted programming. The new series grew out of pilots Amazon made available to viewers as part of its audience-feedback process. Those responses, alongside the company’s own assessments, helped guide which projects moved forward. The orders include dramas as well as comedies, though Amazon has not announced premiere dates. The paper addresses an important question: how neural network weights and gradients evolve during early training, and whether weak supervision changes those dynamics. Its empirical focus could offer useful insight into optimization and the practical value of noisy or incomplete labels. A key strength is the potential to connect parameter-level behavior with measurable training outcomes rather than relying only on final accuracy. The paper would be stronger if it clearly defined “early training” and explained how weights, gradients, and weak supervision were measured. It should also provide enough detail about datasets, architectures, initialization, optimizers, and supervision sources to make the experiments reproducible. Comparisons with fully supervised and unsupervised baselines would help isolate the effect of weak supervision. The analysis should report variability across random seeds and test whether its findings hold across different model and dataset choices. Claims about why particular weight or gradient patterns arise should be distinguished from observations, unless supported by targeted experiments. Overall, the topic is promising, but the conclusions should be calibrated to the scope of the experiments. With clearer methodology and stronger robustness checks, the paper could make a valuable empirical contribution.

The rain came down on the tower where I once ruled the world. Below, the city celebrated the death of its greatest hero. I watched from a room stripped of its gold and banners. Yesterday, the people had feared my name. Today, they cheered my fall.

The hero had come to stop my final machine, a device meant to bend every broadcast on Earth to my command. My henchman, Vex, was supposed to guard the control room. He was loyal, if not especially careful. When the hero burst through the door, Vex panicked. He pulled the wrong lever, and a steel beam dropped from the ceiling. The hero never stood up again.

For one quiet moment, the machine hummed and the world held its breath. Then the alarms began. My screens filled with sirens, soldiers, and reporters asking who had done it. Vex stared at his hands. I stared at the fallen hero.

I had imagined defeating him a thousand times. In those fantasies, I stood over him and delivered a speech. I never imagined the victory would feel like a locked door. The hero had been the reason my empire existed. Every plan I made bent toward his next appearance. Every fortress was built to withstand his fists. Without him, the world no longer needed me.

The governments united before sunrise. My generals took their ships and vanished. My financiers froze my accounts. Even the guards who had served me for years laid down their weapons. They called me a monster, though none had ever called me that while I was winning.

Vex came to my room near dawn. He was ready for me to punish him. Instead, I asked whether he had slept. He shook his head. Neither had I.

We sat together as the tower emptied around us. Outside, the city rang with bells for the hero. I could have blamed Vex, but the machine had been mine, and the empire had been mine too. So I gave him my last order: leave, and never let anyone build a throne from fear again.

Then I walked down the tower stairs, past the empty offices and shattered glass. At the entrance, I paused beneath the rain. For the first time in years, no one was waiting for me to give a command. I stepped into the crowd without a mask. No one recognized me.

For seven centuries, Elias had watched empires rise, crumble, and become footnotes. He had loved, lost, and learned that even grief eventually grew dull around the edges. So when the bakery on his street posted a help-wanted sign, he applied out of boredom. The owner handed him an apron and showed him how to knead dough. Elias had seen kings crowned with less ceremony. On his first morning, he burned a tray of rolls and apologized to each one. The baker laughed, then taught him to judge the oven by its warmth against his cheek. Soon Elias learned the names of regular customers and how much cinnamon Mrs. Alvarez liked in her buns. He began arriving early to hear the neighborhood wake: shutters opening, bicycles rattling, a baby protesting the cold. None of it was grand, and that was its charm. Every loaf demanded attention, and every customer arrived with a small, particular hunger. One rainy afternoon, a boy came in with coins short of the price of a sandwich. Elias quietly added the missing amount and watched the boy’s face brighten. The moment did not change history, but it changed the shape of Elias’s day. Years passed, and his hands grew skilled at scoring each loaf with a clean, swift line. He still outlived everyone he knew, but now he knew what to do with the mornings. Each dawn, he opened the bakery door and welcomed whatever ordinary work was waiting.

Childhood Food Insecurity in Washington, D.C.

Food insecurity means a household does not always have reliable access to enough nutritious food. In Washington, D.C., children may experience food insecurity even in a city with substantial wealth and public resources. High housing and living costs can leave families with less money for groceries. Low wages, unstable work schedules, and sudden expenses can make it difficult to plan meals. Families facing these pressures may have to choose between food, rent, utilities, transportation, or medicine.

The effects can reach well beyond hunger. Children who do not get enough nutritious food may have difficulty concentrating, learning, and participating in school. Food insecurity can also affect physical health, growth, and emotional well-being. Families may cope by skipping meals, buying less food, or relying on inexpensive options that are not as nutritious. These choices reflect constrained resources, not a lack of care or effort.

School meals help many children get dependable food during the school year. Summer can disrupt that routine when school cafeterias close. Programs such as the federal Summer Food Service Program, also called SUN Meals, and the Summer Electronic Benefits Transfer program, known as SUN Bucks, are designed to help fill the gap. SUN Meals provide free meals at eligible community locations, while SUN Bucks provide grocery benefits to eligible school-age children. Program availability and eligibility can vary, so families should check current local guidance.

Even when support exists, getting it can be challenging. Meal sites may be far from home, difficult to reach by bus, or open at inconvenient times. Caregivers may be unable to travel during work hours, and children may not be able to visit alone. Some families do not know where meals are served or whether they qualify for benefits. Information can be difficult to find, particularly when it is not available in a family’s preferred language.

Other barriers include paperwork, confusing enrollment steps, and uncertainty about what documents are needed. Families may worry that asking for help will bring stigma or affect other benefits, even when those concerns are unfounded. Some children have dietary, cultural, or medical needs that available meals may not accommodate. Summer meal sites may also be limited in number or capacity, especially in neighborhoods where families face greater need.

Communities can reduce these barriers by making programs easier to find and use. Clear, multilingual information should be shared through schools, libraries, clinics, community organizations, and trusted local leaders. Offering meals at convenient locations and hours, including places children already visit, can improve access. Transportation support, welcoming staff, and meals that respect cultural and dietary needs also matter. Schools and agencies can help eligible families enroll in SUN Bucks and explain how to use the benefits.

Residents can check current meal locations and eligibility rules through official District and federal program resources. Families can also ask a school, community center, or local food-support organization for help. Food assistance is a practical support that helps children learn, grow, and stay healthy. Ensuring that every child can access nutritious food throughout the year is a shared community responsibility.

The paper presents a timely approach to learning Nash equilibria with neural networks, a challenging problem with potential applications across economics and multi-agent systems. Its key contribution would be clearer if the authors specified the game classes and equilibrium concepts covered, and compared performance against established solvers and learning baselines. The evaluation should also report exploitability, convergence behavior, and sensitivity to random seeds and hyperparameters, since low training loss alone does not establish equilibrium quality. Overall, the topic is promising, but the paper’s claims should be supported by rigorous benchmarks and a more explicit discussion of limitations such as scalability and equilibrium selection.

In Hanoi, a restaurant is serving more than meals. It is also helping young people build a path out of poverty through training in hospitality.

The restaurant is KOTO, short for “Know One, Teach One,” a social enterprise founded by Australian-Vietnamese entrepreneur Jimmy Pham. Its mission is to give disadvantaged young people practical skills, work experience and support for a more secure future.

Pham established KOTO after meeting street children while working in Vietnam in the 1990s. He saw that many had little access to education or reliable employment, and began looking for a way to help them gain skills that employers would value.

The result was a hospitality training program linked to a working restaurant. Students learn while serving customers, turning the dining room and kitchen into classrooms.

The program is designed for young people facing hardship, including those from low-income families or with limited educational opportunities. Participants receive vocational instruction alongside support intended to help them stay in training and plan for life after graduation.

Hospitality provides a practical route into employment in a country where tourism and dining businesses create demand for trained workers. Students can learn cooking, food preparation, customer service and restaurant operations.

At KOTO, those lessons are put to use in a real workplace. Trainees gain experience with the pace and expectations of a professional restaurant, rather than studying skills only in a classroom.

The model connects education directly to opportunity. Graduates can pursue jobs in restaurants, hotels and other parts of the service industry, where experience and reliability can matter as much as formal qualifications.

For many students, the benefits extend beyond technical training. A stable routine, mentorship and confidence can help them navigate challenges that might otherwise make education difficult to complete.

Pham’s approach is built around a simple idea: people who receive support can pass it on. The name “Know One, Teach One” reflects that principle, encouraging skills and opportunity to spread from one person to another.

The restaurant also gives diners a chance to support the program through an ordinary meal. Their business helps sustain a setting in which students can practice their craft and interact with customers.

KOTO’s work takes place against a wider challenge in Vietnam: ensuring that young people from disadvantaged backgrounds can access training that leads to decent work. A certificate alone may not be enough if students lack experience, professional contacts or confidence.

By combining instruction with a functioning restaurant, the program aims to address several of those barriers at once. It gives trainees a structured place to learn, practice and prepare for employment.

The approach also depends on individual support. Students entering training may have faced disrupted schooling, financial insecurity or difficult family circumstances, so completing a course can require more than learning recipes or service standards.

For Pham, the restaurant is therefore both a business and a social project. Its success is measured not only by the food it serves, but also by whether young people leave with skills they can use to earn a living.

That combination has helped make KOTO a visible example of social enterprise in Vietnam. It shows how a business can generate revenue while addressing a need that conventional education and employment systems may not fully meet.

The model is not a substitute for broader efforts to reduce poverty or expand access to education. But it offers a focused intervention: train young people for a sector with jobs, then give them experience in that sector.

For trainees, the first shift can mark a significant change. Instead of being defined by hardship, they are learning a trade and taking responsibility in a professional environment.

Their progress is also visible to customers, who can see the training in action. A meal becomes part of a larger story about work, education and the possibility of a different future.

KOTO’s central promise is straightforward. With the right skills, guidance and opportunity, disadvantaged young people can move toward stable employment and greater independence.

Pham’s restaurant continues to put that promise into practice, one student and one service at a time.

Approaches to Differentiating Instruction for Gifted and Talented Students at BMMS

At BMMS, differentiated instruction helps gifted and talented students stay engaged, deepen their learning, and reach their potential. Differentiation means adjusting instruction to students’ readiness, interests, and learning needs while maintaining high expectations. Teachers can use pre-assessments to find out what students already know before beginning a unit. Students who demonstrate mastery may move on to advanced tasks instead of repeating familiar work. Curriculum compacting allows teachers to reduce practice on skills a student has already mastered and use that time for deeper study. Flexible grouping lets students work with classmates who have similar needs or different strengths, depending on the activity. Groups should change as learning goals and student progress change. Open-ended questions and complex problems encourage students to explain their reasoning and consider multiple solutions. Independent investigations can help students explore topics that interest them while practicing research and critical-thinking skills. Project-based learning gives students opportunities to apply knowledge to authentic challenges. Teachers can offer choices in how students demonstrate learning, such as through a presentation, written analysis, model, or performance. Clear rubrics help ensure that challenging options are assessed fairly and consistently. Enrichment activities should extend core learning rather than simply add more of the same work. Collaboration with families, specialists, and students can help teachers set appropriate goals and monitor progress. By combining meaningful challenge with support and choice, BMMS can help gifted and talented students grow academically and personally.

By noon, Martin had a headache large enough to have its own weather. He woke on a bench beside the river with one shoe missing and a paper crown stuck to his coat. The last thing he remembered was a toast to his own promotion. The promotion, he now recalled, had gone to someone named Elise. He stood, swayed, and followed the road uphill in search of coffee.

The road led past a row of shuttered warehouses. At the end of it stood a concrete building with no windows and no sign. A steel door hung half open. Martin considered turning back, but the sun hurt, and the building promised shade. Inside, the air smelled of wet stone and hot wires. A red light blinked above a corridor marked AUTHORIZED PERSONNEL ONLY.

“Probably a power station,” Martin muttered. His voice came back to him from somewhere below. He found a stairwell descending into the earth. Each step made his skull throb in time with a distant mechanical pulse. At the bottom, a narrow hall opened into a control room. Dust covered the desks, except for a clean circle around a brass dial.

The dial stood waist-high on a black pedestal. Its numbers ran from zero to thirteen, though the final mark had been scratched away. A glass panel above it showed a dark chamber on the other side of the wall. In the center of that chamber was a metal hatch. Something on the far side of the hatch tapped once.

Martin stared at the dial. A yellow note was pinned to the pedestal: DO NOT TURN PAST NINE. Beneath it, in smaller writing, someone had added: IF IT SPEAKS, DO NOT ANSWER. The headache made the warning seem unnecessarily dramatic. He leaned closer to inspect the brass.

A voice crackled from a speaker overhead. “Operator, report.” Martin jumped and struck his elbow on the pedestal. The voice repeated the question, slower this time. He looked for a microphone and found only a button labeled RESPONSE. He pressed it.

“Sorry,” he said. “I’m not the operator.” The room fell silent. Then the tapping began again, three times in quick succession. A green lamp lit above the dial, and the needle shifted from zero to one by itself.

Martin backed away. The speaker hissed. “You have been expected,” it said. The words sounded less like a machine than a person trying not to cry. Martin reached for the door, but the corridor beyond had filled with a pale fog. His missing shoe sat in the middle of it, neatly placed upright.

He turned back to the control panel. The dial’s needle rested on two now. A series of labels had appeared on the glass: PRESSURE, TEMPERATURE, and SEAL. The last label was crossed out. A second note, folded beneath the first, read: THE DIAL DOES NOT OPEN THE DOOR. IT OPENS THE IDEA OF A DOOR.

Martin laughed once, then wished he hadn’t. In the dark chamber, the metal hatch began to bend outward. The speaker clicked on. “Please,” said the voice. “It is cold in here.” Martin seized the dial, meaning to turn it back to zero. Its surface was warm and faintly pulsing beneath his palm. The needle slid to three.

A low note filled the room. The lights dimmed. Something behind the hatch dragged a heavy object across the floor. Martin tried to pull his hand away, but his fingers had locked around the brass rim. A second voice spoke from the chamber, calm and unmistakably his own. “Martin,” it said. “You left your coat upstairs.”

He had not told the machine his name. He yanked harder, and the needle skipped to four. The hatch bowed outward another inch. A long black fingernail slipped through the seam. Martin hit the emergency stop with his free hand. It shattered under his palm, and the dial spun to five.

The corridor fog surged into the control room. It smelled of rain on a grave. The speaker began counting backward from ten. Martin’s hand finally loosened, leaving a red ring around his fingers. He grabbed a chair and smashed the glass panel.

The chamber went dark. For one breath, the building was still. Then the hatch opened inward, and the thing behind it laughed in Martin’s voice. He ran up the stairs, clutching his throbbing head. The fog followed, whispering his name from every corner.

Outside, the sun had set. His missing shoe was back on his foot. Across the road, the warehouse doors stood wide open. Martin kept walking, though the laughter followed him all the way to town. At the first café, he ordered coffee and asked the woman behind the counter what day it was. She stared at him, pale and trembling.

“Thursday,” she said. “You came in here yesterday.” Martin looked down at the paper crown still pinned to his coat. A brass dial had been drawn on its inside, its needle pointing past thirteen. Somewhere beneath the street, a metal hatch tapped once.
