Climate has changed throughout Earth’s history, sometimes gradually and sometimes abruptly. Today, the planet is warming rapidly, mainly because human activities are increasing greenhouse gases in the atmosphere.

Greenhouse gases, including carbon dioxide, methane, and nitrous oxide, trap some of the heat Earth radiates into space. This natural greenhouse effect keeps the planet warm enough for life, but adding more of these gases strengthens it. Burning coal, oil, and natural gas is the largest source of human carbon dioxide emissions. Deforestation also releases carbon dioxide and reduces the amount that forests can absorb. Agriculture, waste, and fossil fuel production contribute methane and other warming gases.

Measurements show that atmospheric carbon dioxide has risen sharply since the Industrial Revolution. The increase is primarily from fossil fuels, as confirmed by chemical evidence and records of human emissions. Global average temperatures have risen alongside greenhouse gas concentrations. The rate of recent warming is unusual compared with many changes reconstructed from past climate records.

The Sun’s energy varies slightly over time, and these variations can influence climate. Changes in solar output and in Earth’s orbit helped drive some ancient climate shifts, including the cycles of ice ages. However, measured solar changes do not explain the strong warming observed since the mid-20th century. Climate scientists attribute most of that recent warming to human greenhouse gas emissions.

Earth’s climate also responds to volcanic eruptions, ocean circulation, and natural shifts in atmospheric patterns. Large eruptions can cool the planet temporarily by sending reflective particles into the atmosphere. Oceans absorb much of the excess heat, slowing surface warming while storing energy for decades or longer. These natural influences can affect temperatures from year to year, but they do not overturn the long-term warming trend.

Sea levels rise as ocean water warms and expands. They also rise when glaciers and ice sheets lose ice that flows into the sea. Global average sea level has risen substantially since the late 19th century, and the rate has increased in recent decades. Rising seas increase the risk of coastal flooding, erosion, and saltwater entering freshwater supplies. Local sea-level changes vary because land can rise or sink and ocean currents differ.

Ancient warm periods provide evidence about how Earth behaves under different conditions. During the Eocene Epoch, about 56 to 34 million years ago, the planet was much warmer than today, with little or no permanent ice in Antarctica for much of the period. Fossils and ancient sediments help researchers reconstruct temperatures, vegetation, and ocean conditions from that time. Some ancient warm events involved rapid rises in atmospheric carbon and major changes to ecosystems. These events unfolded over thousands of years or longer, generally far more slowly than today’s human-driven emissions.

Past warm climates are not exact predictions of the future, because continents, ecosystems, and other conditions have changed. Still, they reveal that sustained greenhouse gas increases can reshape ice sheets, coastlines, and habitats. Future warming will depend strongly on how much greenhouse gas humanity emits. Cutting emissions can limit additional warming, while continued high emissions would produce greater climate change. Even with rapid reductions, some further warming and sea-level rise are expected because the climate system responds slowly. Understanding both ancient climate records and modern observations helps societies prepare for risks and make informed choices.

Nicola Sturgeon has set out her priorities for Scotland’s tax policy, public services and child welfare as the country approaches an election, while also discussing the prospects for a renewed independence campaign.

The former first minister argued that Scotland should use the tax powers available to it to support public investment and protect public services. She said decisions on taxation must be judged by whether they help fund priorities such as health, education and social care. Sturgeon also acknowledged that tax changes can affect households differently and require careful consideration. She did not present a single tax measure as a solution to the pressures facing public services.

Scotland’s services remain under strain from long waiting lists, workforce shortages and rising demand. Sturgeon said maintaining high-quality provision would require sustained funding as well as reform. She stressed that public services are central to the case for devolved government. Critics, however, have questioned whether the Scottish Government has delivered improvements at the pace voters expect.

Child welfare was another focus of her remarks. Sturgeon defended support intended to reduce child poverty and improve family wellbeing, including Scotland’s child payment. The scheme provides regular financial assistance to eligible families with children. She said policies of this kind can help ease pressure on household budgets, particularly during a period of high living costs.

The impact of the payment and other anti-poverty measures is likely to remain a point of debate during the campaign. Supporters say direct assistance can make an immediate difference to families. Opponents argue that benefits need to be accompanied by broader action on wages, housing and employment. Sturgeon said child poverty should remain a political priority regardless of which party forms the next government.

On independence, she said the case for Scotland leaving the United Kingdom should be made through public debate and democratic campaigning. The issue continues to divide voters and parties, with questions over the route to a referendum and the economic consequences of independence. Sturgeon maintained that support for self-government remains significant. She also indicated that the campaign must address practical concerns raised by people who are undecided.

The next election is expected to test both the Scottish National Party’s record in government and its ability to present a clear future programme. Taxation, health services and the cost of living are likely to feature prominently alongside the constitutional question. Sturgeon said voters should be able to assess the choices facing Scotland on their merits. She argued that social policy and constitutional change are connected by the question of who has the authority to shape the country’s future.

Her comments come as parties prepare to make competing claims about Scotland’s economic prospects and the resources available to government. The debate over tax will include questions about fairness, investment and the effect of policy on businesses and households. Public service performance will also be closely scrutinised, particularly in health and education. Families’ experiences of poverty and access to support are expected to influence the campaign.

Sturgeon’s intervention gives her views a prominent place in that discussion, even as the election approaches without her leading the SNP. Her supporters say her experience and advocacy can help shape the party’s arguments. Critics are likely to focus on the government’s record during her time in office. The campaign will ultimately require parties to turn broad promises into detailed proposals.

Voters will weigh those proposals against their own experience of public services, household costs and support for families. They will also decide how much importance to place on the independence question. Sturgeon’s remarks underline the challenge facing Scotland’s political parties: explaining how immediate social needs can be met while making a credible case for the country’s longer-term direction.

Long-term exposure to air pollution is estimated to contribute to tens of thousands of premature deaths in England each year, though the precise toll is difficult to measure. The figure is not a count of people whose deaths can be attributed to pollution on a death certificate. Instead, it is calculated from population exposure and evidence linking polluted air to conditions including heart disease, stroke and lung cancer.

Fine particulate matter, known as PM2.5, and nitrogen dioxide are among the pollutants of greatest concern. They come from sources such as road traffic, domestic heating, industry and construction. Although air quality has improved over recent decades, pollution remains unevenly distributed, with busy roads and urban areas often bearing the greatest burden.

The health effects build over time, making air pollution a persistent public-health issue rather than an immediate emergency alone. Children, older people and those with existing heart or lung conditions can be especially vulnerable. Deprivation can also increase exposure, as lower-income communities are more likely to live near major roads or other pollution sources.

Efforts to tackle the problem are being led by national and local authorities. In London, the Ultra Low Emission Zone charges drivers of vehicles that fail emissions standards, while cleaner buses and expanded cycling routes are intended to reduce traffic pollution. Other cities, including Birmingham and Bristol, have introduced or developed clean-air measures focused on the most polluting vehicles.

Local councils are also changing streets, improving public transport and encouraging walking and cycling. Some are working to reduce emissions from buildings by replacing older heating systems and improving energy efficiency. Campaigners say these measures can deliver wider benefits, including quieter streets and lower carbon emissions.

Progress, however, varies between regions, and local authorities face limits on funding and enforcement. Critics of charging schemes argue that costs can fall hardest on residents and small businesses who cannot afford to replace older vehicles. Supporters say targeted grants and exemptions can help ease the transition while keeping health protections in place.

Experts stress that action must go beyond individual travel choices. Stronger controls on vehicle and industrial emissions, consistent monitoring and better access to public transport are also seen as essential. The estimated death toll is not a prediction of how many people will die in a particular year, but it highlights the scale of harm associated with prolonged exposure.

As England updates its air-quality plans, the challenge will be to make improvements both measurable and fair. Researchers say sustained reductions in pollution could prevent illness and extend lives, particularly in communities with the highest exposure.

On a wet November night, Eamon Vale woke to the smell of damp stone and tobacco. He was chained in a shuttered mill outside Derry, with a swollen eye and one shoe. His captors had taken his coat, his watch, and the cigarettes he kept in its lining. They had left him a matchbook on the floor. Eamon stared at it until the numbers on its cover swam into focus. It belonged to the Harbour View, a pub he had not visited in years.

He heard footsteps above him, then a door slam. The guard on the landing whistled an old marching tune. Eamon knew the tune from childhood and hated himself for remembering every note. When the footsteps faded, he tested the chain against a rusted bolt in the wall. It held. He tested it again, harder, and felt the skin split at his wrist. The pain steadied him.

The matchbook had a stiff cardboard spine. He bent it until a tiny metal strip slipped free, a remnant from a broken lighter. He worked the strip into the lock on his cuff. For an hour, the only sounds were rain and his own breathing. At last the lock clicked. He eased the cuff open and rubbed life back into his hand.

The mill had two rooms and a stairwell, all smelling of oil and wet plaster. A phone rang somewhere upstairs. No one answered. Eamon found a narrow window behind a stack of flour sacks and pushed it open. The frame scraped, loud enough to make him freeze. Nothing moved above him.

He climbed through and dropped into a yard full of nettles. Beyond a leaning fence, the road ran black under the lamps. He limped toward the town, keeping to ditches and hedgerows. His plan was simple: reach the Harbour View and ask for Moira. Moira had once promised that if he ever needed a way out, she would find one. He had believed her because he wanted to.

At the edge of the road, he found a cigarette packet crushed in the mud. One cigarette was dry inside its torn wrapper. He lit it with the last match in the book and drew smoke deep into his lungs. The cough that followed nearly gave him away. Still, the familiar burn made him feel, for a moment, like a man who could choose anything.

A van passed and slowed. Eamon crouched beneath a hawthorn hedge until its red tail lights vanished. He crossed the road and reached the Harbour View shortly before closing. The pub’s windows glowed amber against the rain. He slipped through the side entrance and found Moira wiping down the bar.

She looked older, but her eyes were unchanged. “You’re alive,” she said. Eamon told her where they had held him and asked her to call a taxi. Moira glanced toward the kitchen before answering. He saw a man’s shadow move behind the frosted glass.

“Not a taxi,” she whispered. “There’s a car out back.” Eamon studied her face, searching for the fear he had expected. He found something softer and worse: apology. The kitchen door opened, and two men stepped out. One held a pistol low by his thigh.

Eamon backed toward the entrance. Moira said his name as if it could still stop him. The armed man told him the road was covered and that no one needed to get hurt. Eamon looked at the cigarette burning between his fingers. Its ash trembled in the draft from the open door.

Then Moira said, “I’m sorry, Eamon. They have my son.” He believed her, and hated that believing her changed nothing. He threw the cigarette into a puddle and ran. The first shot broke the pub window. The second struck him in the back.

He fell across the threshold, watching rain scatter the cigarette’s ember. Moira reached him too late, or perhaps exactly on time. He tried to ask whether her boy was safe, but only smoke and blood came out. Above them, the pub sign creaked in the wind. The last light in its painted lantern went dark.

For eleven months, Daniel had not painted a thing. His brushes stood in a jar beside the sink, stiff with old color. The blank canvas on his easel had gathered a fine gray dust. After losing his job, his apartment, and then the person who had made both feel like home, he had begun to think of tomorrow as a room with no door. One rainy evening, he walked to the river with no particular plan except to keep walking.

On the footbridge, a woman sat beneath a red umbrella. She wore a green coat and held a small paper boat in one gloved hand. “Do you know how to make these?” she asked. Daniel shook his head. “I used to know how to paint,” he said, surprised to hear himself speak. The woman smiled as if he had answered the right question.

She unfolded the boat and showed him its creases. “Most things begin as a mistake,” she said. Then she placed the paper in his palm, and the rain stopped falling around them. Daniel looked up, but the clouds still moved above the bridge. The woman’s reflection in the river shimmered like a candle, though no flame stood nearby.

“Make one mark,” she told him. “Not a masterpiece. Just a mark.” Daniel glanced toward the dark water. “What if it’s terrible?” “Then you’ll have made something terrible,” she said gently, “and the world will still be here.” When he looked back, the woman and her umbrella were gone.

The paper boat remained, warm in his hand. At home, Daniel set it on the table and opened the jar of brushes. He found one that still bent softly at the tip. The canvas looked no less blank than before, but it no longer seemed to be waiting for him to become someone else. He dipped the brush into blue paint and made a crooked line across the center.

It was only a line, and it wavered. Daniel stared at it until the room began to feel less empty. Then he added a small red shape beside it, like an umbrella on a bridge. The next morning, he painted for seven minutes. On the morning after that, he painted for eight.

Nothing was fixed all at once. Still, each day offered a small door, and Daniel learned to open it with one mark.

Mara first heard her daughter think on a Tuesday night.

The sound came while the baby slept in her crib.
It was not a voice in the room.
It was a small, clear sentence inside Mara’s mind.
The baby thought, The moon is watching.

Mara sat upright in bed.
Beside her, Daniel snored gently.
She crossed the hallway and checked the nursery.
Nell slept with one fist against her cheek.
The curtains stirred, though the window was shut.

Mara told herself she was exhausted.
She had been a parent for eleven days.
Sleep came in scraps and vanished at the slightest cry.
Still, the sentence followed her through breakfast.
The moon is watching.

She tried to mention it to Daniel.
He smiled and said new parents imagined all kinds of things.
Mara almost agreed.
Then Nell began to fuss in her high chair.
Mara lifted her from the cushion.
A thought brushed her mind like a fingertip.
Not that spoon.

Mara put down the spoon.
She picked up the blue one instead.
Nell stopped crying.
Daniel noticed and raised an eyebrow.
“Lucky guess,” Mara said.

The thoughts returned in the days that followed.
They were never loud.
They arrived as feelings first, then words.
Warmth meant comfort.
A sharp little pinch meant hunger.
Fear felt like standing at the edge of a high stair.

Mara learned Nell’s private weather.
She knew which lullaby made her feel safe.
She knew that bathwater seemed too wide and deep.
She knew the baby hated the red mobile above the crib.
She took it down without explaining why.

One evening, Nell looked past Mara’s shoulder.
A sudden thought struck like ice.
The man in the wall is back.
Mara spun around.
The nursery was empty.

She searched the closets and the space beneath the crib.
She checked every lock on the doors.
Daniel found her holding a kitchen knife.
He took it gently and asked what was wrong.
Mara could not make the answer sound reasonable.

That night she stayed beside Nell’s crib.
At two in the morning, the thought came again.
He says you can hear me.
Mara leaned over the rail.
“Who says that, sweetheart?”

Nell’s eyes opened.
They were dark and glossy in the night-light.
For one long moment, Mara heard nothing.
Then a thought arrived, unmistakable and cold.
The man behind the wall.

The next morning, Mara called her older sister.
Ruth listened without laughing.
She asked whether Mara had ever heard a child’s thought before.
“No,” Mara said.
Ruth went quiet.

Then Ruth told her to bring Nell to the old train station.
She said there would be people who understood.
Mara asked what people.
Ruth replied, “The ones who can help.”
Her voice sounded like a door closing.

Mara went to the station that afternoon.
She left Daniel a note saying she needed air.
Ruth waited beside the ticket machines.
A gray-haired woman stood with her.
The woman’s name was Venn.
She wore a silver pin shaped like an open eye.

Venn looked at Nell and smiled.
“Your daughter has a strong signal,” she said.
Mara stiffened.
“What does that mean?”
“It means the bond has awakened.”

Venn spoke as if describing a family recipe.
Some parents could hear the thoughts of children.
The gift usually appeared during the first year.
It faded when the child grew older.
Most families learned to ignore it.

“Most families?” Mara asked.
Venn’s smile thinned.
“There are traditions,” she said.
“There are people who protect the children.”

Ruth put a hand on Mara’s shoulder.
She said the society had kept children safe for generations.
She said Mara would be given guidance.
She said nobody had to know.
The open eye on Venn’s pin seemed to glimmer.

A thought rose from Nell.
Don’t go with the nice lady.
Mara looked down.
Nell was sleeping against her chest.
The thought had come from somewhere else.
It was too old, too measured, too tired.

Mara stepped away from Venn.
Ruth’s hand tightened.
Venn stopped smiling.
“Your daughter is frightened,” she said.
Mara backed toward the platform.

Then the station speakers crackled.
A child’s voice came through, though no train was due.
The man in the wall is here.
Every adult on the platform turned toward Mara.
Venn whispered, “They found her.”

The lights went out.
Someone grabbed Mara’s coat.
She twisted free and ran down the platform.
Ruth called after her.
The voice in the speakers spoke again.
Bring the child below.

Mara found a service stairwell.
She descended with Nell tucked under her coat.
The station’s noise faded above them.
At the bottom was a narrow door.
It stood open to a corridor lit by green lamps.

Mara heard children before she saw them.
Their thoughts poured into her like rain through a broken roof.
I want my mother.
I can’t remember my name.
Please don’t let them take my voice.
Mara covered her ears.
It made no difference.

The corridor ended at a room of white tiles.
Dozens of children sat in small wooden chairs.
Silver wires ran from their temples to a glass machine.
Behind the machine stood a tall man in a black suit.
His face looked familiar, though Mara had never seen him.
Then she understood.

He was the man in the wall.
Not a ghost, but a person who could hide his thoughts.
Venn entered behind Mara.
“You weren’t meant to find the children,” she said.
“You were meant to bring us the strongest one.”

Ruth stood beside her, pale and weeping.
Mara stared at her sister.
Ruth said the society had helped their family for years.
She said Mara’s own mother had been part of it.
She said the children were being trained.

The glass machine pulsed.
A child began to scream.
Mara felt the scream inside her skull.
The man in black turned toward Nell.
“She can hear every child,” he said.
“She can carry every voice.”

He reached for the baby.
Mara stepped between them.
Nell’s thought filled her mind, bright as a match.
Now, Mama.
Mara did not know what to do.
She simply opened her arms.

Every child’s thought surged through her at once.
The room shook with fear, anger, and desperate hope.
The glass machine cracked.
The silver wires snapped free.
The children rose from their chairs.
Their voices filled the tiled room, though none of them spoke aloud.

The man in black stumbled.
For the first time, Mara heard his thoughts.
He was afraid.
He had built the society because he feared what children might become.
He had mistaken listening for ownership.

Venn ran for the door.
Ruth stayed where she was.
Mara held Nell close as the children hurried past them.
Some clung to her coat.
Some looked at her with wary, shining eyes.

Above, sirens approached.
The society’s hidden doors stood open.
Its secrets spilled into the station, then into the waiting world.
Mara did not know what would happen next.
She only knew Nell was still thinking.

The baby’s thoughts softened against her heart.
You found us.
Mara kissed her forehead.
For the first time, she answered without speaking.
I’m here.

Choosing a career path early in life can help students make thoughtful plans for the future. When they have a goal in mind, they can choose classes that build useful knowledge and skills. By midnight, the storm had emptied the streets around the old cannery. Inside, Elias Vale listened to the rain drum on the roof and watched his captive struggle against the chair. He had chosen the room because its drains ran straight into the river. He had chosen the night because no one would hear the door open. For years, Elias had mistaken silence for safety.

Then the drain began to breathe.

A wet, rattling inhale rose from beneath the floorboards. Elias lowered the knife he had been holding and leaned closer. The captive stopped struggling. Something scraped the underside of the boards, slow as a fingernail tracing a name. Elias smiled, though he did not know why.

The boards bowed upward.

A slick gray hand pushed through the gap, its fingers too long and jointed in the wrong places. Behind it came a face like a drowned mask, with pale eyes set in a mouth that opened from cheek to cheek. The creature unfolded itself onto the floor. It smelled of river mud and old pennies.

Elias backed toward the door. The thing tilted its head and spoke in a voice like water passing through stones. “You make fear,” it said. “I keep what fear leaves behind.”

The captive began to sob. The creature turned toward the sound, and the sobs stopped at once. Elias felt a cold pressure settle around his heart. He had never seen anyone so completely afraid—not even himself.

“What do you want?” he asked.

The entity dragged one claw across the floor. “A way into the world above.”

Elias understood then that the drain was not merely a drain. It was a seam, and the creature had been waiting beneath it. He should have run. Instead, he thought of the years he had spent hunting alone, always careful, always hungry for control.

“What would you give me?” he asked.

The creature’s mouth stretched into something almost like a grin. “No witnesses. No guilt. No end to your work.”

Elias glanced at the captive, who was staring past him at the open drain. In that moment, he saw the bargain clearly: a monster offering to make him more monstrous. He could refuse. He could open the door and call for help.

The creature extended its long hand.

Elias took it.

The room shuddered. Every light burst at once, and the rain outside fell silent. When the darkness lifted, the chair stood empty. The door remained locked, and Elias was alone—or thought he was.

A second shadow moved beneath his feet, though there was no light to cast it. From the drain came a soft, satisfied breath. Elias wiped his hands on his coat and headed for the door.

Behind him, the creature whispered his name.

Remote learning helps students balance school, personal responsibilities, and future goals. By attending classes online, students can often choose when and where they complete their work. This flexibility makes it easier to plan a day around family needs, appointments, or a part-time job. For example, a student who helps care for younger siblings may study after the household becomes quieter. Students can also save time by avoiding a daily commute. They can use those extra minutes to review lessons, rest, or finish other responsibilities.

Remote learning can also encourage students to become more organized. They often need to track assignment deadlines, plan study sessions, and communicate with teachers independently. These habits can help them manage their time more effectively. Online calendars and learning platforms make it easier to see upcoming tasks in one place. When students learn to plan ahead, they are less likely to feel overwhelmed by competing demands.

Another benefit is the opportunity to explore future goals. Students may have more time to take online courses, practice a skill, or work toward a career interest. A flexible schedule can also make it easier to gain work experience while continuing an education. For instance, a student interested in graphic design might complete classwork and then build a portfolio. These experiences can help students understand what they want to pursue after graduation.

Remote learning is not perfect for everyone. Students may miss in-person conversations, and studying at home can bring distractions. A reliable internet connection and a quiet workspace are not always available. Still, setting a routine and asking for support can help address some of these challenges. Schools can also provide guidance, resources, and chances for students to connect with classmates.

Overall, remote learning can give students more control over how they use their time. It can help them meet school expectations while contributing to their families and preparing for the future. The skills they develop, such as organization and independence, are useful beyond the classroom. With good support and steady effort, remote learning can help students build a balanced path toward their goals.

American musicals did more than entertain audiences in the 20th century. They also reflected changing ideas about race, gender, class, immigration, and national identity. Because musicals combine stories with music and dance, they could make social tensions both vivid and appealing. Their history shows how popular entertainment sometimes challenged prejudice and sometimes repeated it.

In the early decades of the century, Broadway drew on vaudeville, operetta, and popular songs. Many shows offered escapism during periods of rapid urban growth and economic change. Yet their humor often relied on stereotypes about immigrants and racial groups. Blackface minstrelsy, in which white performers darkened their faces to caricature Black people, remained part of mainstream entertainment. Its presence reveals how deeply racist conventions shaped popular culture.

The 1927 musical Show Boat marked an important change. It addressed racial prejudice, interracial relationships, and the hardships faced by Black Americans. Its characters and songs gave the subject unusual dramatic weight for a Broadway show. However, the production still reflected the limits and biases of its era. Its history illustrates how a work can challenge some attitudes while preserving others.

During the 1930s, the Great Depression brought economic hardship and uncertainty. Musicals often offered glamour and escape, filling theaters with elaborate sets and energetic dance numbers. At the same time, some works explored poverty, labor, and social responsibility. The political climate made questions about inequality and economic security hard to ignore. Musical theater balanced these serious concerns with the promise of entertainment.

World War II and its aftermath changed the subjects that musicals could address. Shows drew on ideas of patriotism, community, and sacrifice. They also presented an increasingly diverse picture of American life, though not always fairly or fully. Oklahoma! helped establish a more integrated style of storytelling, in which songs advanced the plot and revealed character. Its vision of rural community was warmly idealistic, but it also reflected the era’s expectations about gender and social order.

In the 1940s and 1950s, musicals increasingly explored romance, family, and belonging. They often presented marriage as a central goal for women, reflecting conventional expectations of the time. Yet strong female characters could also show ambition, independence, and wit. South Pacific confronted racism directly through the song “You’ve Got to Be Carefully Taught.” The song argued that prejudice is learned rather than innate, making the show’s message unusually explicit.

West Side Story, which opened in 1957, reworked Romeo and Juliet in a contemporary urban setting. Its conflict between the Jets and the Puerto Rican Sharks reflected tensions around immigration, identity, and neighborhood belonging. The show gave its Puerto Rican characters more emotional depth than many earlier musicals had offered. Still, its portrayal of Latino life was shaped largely by white creators, a fact that has prompted later criticism. The work demonstrates both the possibilities and the limitations of representation.

The civil rights movement transformed American public life during the 1950s and 1960s. Musicals responded to growing demands for racial equality, although progress onstage was uneven. Black performers had long contributed to musical theater, but they often faced restricted roles and unequal access to opportunities. Purlie, which opened in 1970, placed Black characters and political concerns at the center of its story. Its success reflected the increasing visibility of Black voices in American theater.

Changing attitudes toward women also shaped the musical stage. As more women entered the workforce and challenged traditional roles, stories began to question marriage, ambition, and independence. Cabaret, set in 1930s Berlin and first staged in 1966, explored political danger and personal freedom. Its complicated female characters resisted the simple moral lessons common in earlier entertainment. Such shows invited audiences to consider the cost of ignoring authoritarianism and social cruelty.

By the 1970s, rock music and experimental forms reshaped musical theater. Hair brought youth culture, protests against the Vietnam War, and changing sexual attitudes into the mainstream theater. Its frank language and provocative staging reflected conflicts between generations. A Chorus Line, which opened in 1975, focused on working performers and the insecurity behind show business glamour. It made class, labor, and personal identity part of the musical’s subject.

In the late 20th century, musicals explored an even wider range of social conflicts. Rent addressed poverty, AIDS, housing insecurity, and chosen family in 1980s New York. Its emotional directness helped bring stories of illness and LGBTQ+ life to a broad audience. The musical did not speak for every person affected by these issues, but it helped make them more visible. Miss Saigon and other works also sparked debate over cultural representation and the use of Asian characters by predominantly white creative teams.

Across the century, American musicals both reflected and influenced social attitudes. They could question prejudice, expose inequality, and give marginalized characters a place onstage. They could also reinforce stereotypes or simplify difficult realities. Audiences, critics, and artists have repeatedly debated which stories deserve to be told and who has the authority to tell them. That debate remains central to musical theater today.

Canine distemper is emerging as a serious threat to Amur tigers, adding a new challenge to efforts to save one of the world’s rarest big cats. The disease is caused by a virus that infects a range of carnivores, including domestic dogs and wild species. In tigers, infection can damage the respiratory, digestive and nervous systems. Animals may become weak, disoriented or unable to hunt. Severe cases can be fatal.

Amur tigers, also known as Siberian tigers, live mainly in Russia’s Far East, with a smaller population in northeastern China. Their numbers have recovered from historic lows, but the population remains small and vulnerable. That makes each adult loss significant, particularly when breeding animals are affected. Conservationists have long focused on poaching, habitat loss and conflicts with people. Disease is now receiving growing attention as another factor that could undermine recovery.

Researchers say a central question is how the virus reaches tigers. Domestic dogs are a possible source, especially in settlements near tiger habitat. Unvaccinated dogs may carry the virus and pass it to other animals. Free-roaming dogs can travel through forest edges and bring pathogens into areas used by wildlife. However, dogs are not the only possible source. Other wild carnivores, such as foxes, raccoon dogs and badgers, may also become infected and spread the virus.

Tracing transmission is difficult because animals move across large territories and are rarely observed closely. A tiger that becomes sick may disappear into dense forest before researchers can collect samples. Carcasses may be found long after death, leaving little evidence about where infection began. Different species can carry the same virus, further complicating efforts to identify the original host. Scientists therefore need coordinated testing across wildlife, domestic animals and the environments they share.

The disease has drawn particular concern because it can affect tiger behavior. Neurological symptoms may reduce an animal’s ability to avoid people or move safely through its range. A sick tiger could also be more likely to approach settlements in search of food. Such encounters can put people and livestock at risk, while increasing the chance that the tiger will be killed. Disease control is therefore connected to both wildlife protection and community safety.

Effective conservation measures will depend on better evidence. Researchers can test blood, tissue and other samples from tigers and nearby carnivores for signs of infection. Genetic analysis of viral samples may help establish whether outbreaks are linked and reveal likely transmission pathways. Long-term monitoring can show whether infections are isolated events or a continuing risk. Sharing data across borders is also important because wildlife does not follow national boundaries.

Vaccinating domestic dogs near tiger habitat is one potential way to reduce transmission. Such programs would need to reach animals in remote communities and maintain coverage over time. Veterinary teams could combine vaccination with public education and routine health checks. Sterilization and responsible pet ownership may also reduce the number of free-roaming dogs. These measures should be designed with local residents, whose cooperation is essential.

Wildlife vaccination is more complicated. Capturing and treating tigers can be stressful and dangerous for both animals and people. A vaccine would need to be shown safe and effective for the species before it could be used widely. Scientists must also consider whether vaccinating other wild carnivores is practical or could disrupt ecosystems. For now, preventing infection at its source may be more feasible than treating affected tigers.

Conservationists warn against viewing distemper as a threat that can be solved by a single intervention. Habitat protection and anti-poaching work remain critical, while disease surveillance needs stable funding and trained personnel. Rapid reporting of sick or dead animals can help authorities respond before an outbreak spreads. Clear protocols are needed for sample collection, carcass handling and communication with nearby communities. These steps can improve both research and public health preparedness.

The risk posed by canine distemper to Amur tigers is not fully understood. Researchers still need to determine how often tigers are exposed, how frequently infection leads to death and which animals transmit the virus. A better picture of those patterns could guide targeted prevention rather than broad measures with uncertain benefits. It could also help conservation teams distinguish disease-related losses from other causes.

For a species with limited numbers, reducing avoidable deaths matters. Identifying infection sources would allow governments and conservation groups to direct resources where they can have the greatest effect. Stronger veterinary services near tiger landscapes could protect domestic animals while lowering risks to wildlife. Continued research, paired with practical prevention, offers the clearest path forward. The challenge is to act carefully and quickly, before an emerging disease becomes a larger obstacle to the recovery of Amur tigers.

For centuries, Mara woke beneath a sky the color of old blood.
She lay chained to a black stone floor in a chamber without doors.
The chains were not iron, but the names of everyone she had betrayed.
Each name tightened whenever she tried to rise.
Above her, a bell rang once every hour.
At each toll, the walls breathed fire.
The flames never burned her body.
They burned the memory of her son’s face.
She had been told that this was justice.
She had been told that it would never end.
Mara believed both.
On the day she stopped counting the bells, a stranger entered the chamber.
He wore a plain gray coat and carried no weapon.
His eyes were bright as embers beneath a crown of ash.
Mara knew him from the sermons of the living.
“You are Satan,” she said.
“I am the one they named,” he replied.
She laughed, though laughter hurt.
“Have you come to make it worse?”
“No,” he said.
“I have come to remember.”
He touched the wall, and the fire went still.
A silver thread appeared in the stone.
Mara watched it curl around his finger.
“What is that?” she asked.
“A memory I have kept too long.”
The thread opened like a door.
Beyond it lay a garden beneath a summer sky.
A young angel sat in the grass, wings spread around a small, frightened child.
The angel was Satan, before his fall.
The child was human, though not yet born.
Mara recognized the child’s crooked smile.
It was her son’s.
The memory trembled, and the garden vanished.
Mara stared at the stranger.
“You knew him?”
“I carried him through a storm,” Satan said.
“He was not yours to save.”
“Nor was he yours to lose.”
The words struck harder than the flames.
Mara had once sold her son’s trust for a crown and a promise.
She had called it necessity.
Now she saw the old angel holding him close.
“Why show me this?” she whispered.
“Because you keep remembering only the worst thing you did.”
“I deserve to.”
“Perhaps,” he said.
“But deserving pain is not the same as being made of it.”
Mara looked down at the names binding her wrists.
For the first time, one name loosened.
The bell rang, but the walls did not breathe fire.
Satan sat beside her on the cold stone.
He told her of the first dawn he had seen.
He spoke of a world still learning how to sing.
He remembered laughing with the angels before pride split their ranks.
He remembered choosing exile rather than pretending he had never loved them.
“I thought freedom meant refusing every command,” he said.
“I thought love meant never letting go.”
“Were you wrong?” Mara asked.
“I was incomplete.”
His voice held no thunder.
It held the ache of someone who had survived his own certainty.
He opened another memory.
This time, Mara saw her son as a boy, racing across a field.
He stumbled, rose, and ran on without looking back.
Mara wept.
The tears struck the stone and became tiny white flowers.
She had expected her son to wait for her forever.
She had expected remorse to be a bridge back to him.
But he had lived, and grown, and gone beyond her reach.
“Can you forgive me?” she asked.
“I cannot forgive in his place,” Satan said.
“But you can stop making his life a prison you carry.”
The chains loosened again.
One by one, the names slipped from her wrists and lay quiet on the floor.
Mara did not feel innocent.
She felt awake.
The chamber’s walls drew apart, revealing a road of pale dust.
At its end stood no gate, no judge, and no waiting child.
There was only open sky.
Mara hesitated at the threshold.
“What happens if I leave?”
“You choose what happens next.”
“Even here?”
“Especially here.”
She turned to Satan.
“Will you come with me?”
He looked toward the darkness behind him.
“I have mistaken solitude for freedom for a very long time.”
Then he offered her his hand.
Mara took it.
The road warmed beneath their feet.
Behind them, the bell rang once more.
Its sound followed them, but it could no longer command them.
Satan’s memories drifted around them like stars released from a sealed room.
Mara saw his tenderness, his vanity, his grief, and the love he had buried beneath rebellion.
She saw that even he was more than the name he had been given.
The sight did not erase her crimes.
It made room beside them for something else.
At the edge of the road, the sky opened into dawn.
Mara stepped forward without knowing where she would go.
For the first time, uncertainty felt like a gift.
Satan followed, still carrying his sorrow, but no longer guarding it alone.
And as the light touched them, neither soul was absolved.
They were simply free to begin.

Gambians voted in a closely watched presidential election, weighing hopes for change against concerns about repression and the fairness of the contest. The vote could shape the country’s democratic direction years after longtime ruler Yahya Jammeh was forced from power.

President Adama Barrow is seeking another term, facing challengers who say his government has failed to deliver enough change. Campaign debates have focused on jobs, the cost of living, public services and corruption. For many voters, those everyday concerns are inseparable from questions about accountability and political freedoms.

Polling stations opened across the small West African nation as voters queued to cast their ballots. Election officials said voting was proceeding, while observers monitored the process. The atmosphere in many areas was calm, though the contest has drawn heightened attention at home and abroad.

Jammeh ruled The Gambia for 22 years, overseeing a period marked by arrests, torture and disappearances, according to human rights investigators. He left the country in 2017 after losing an election and refusing initially to accept the result. His departure raised expectations that the new government would pursue sweeping reforms.

Barrow came to power promising a break with the past. But critics say progress has been uneven and that promised constitutional and institutional changes have stalled. They also point to continuing concerns about press freedom, political pressure and the slow pace of accountability for abuses committed under Jammeh.

The government has rejected accusations that it is restricting opposition activity and says the election is being conducted under the law. Barrow’s supporters credit his administration with maintaining stability and expanding development projects. Opposition leaders counter that stability alone is not enough if institutions remain weak and living costs keep rising.

The election is being held under a voting system that uses marbles rather than paper ballots. Voters place a marble into a container assigned to their chosen candidate, a method designed to make ballots easier to cast and count. Election officials say the system is well suited to the country, although observers will be watching closely for irregularities.

The campaign has also revived debate over whether Jammeh should face justice if he returns. A truth commission documented abuses during his rule and recommended prosecutions. The government has said it intends to pursue accountability, but victims and rights groups have expressed frustration over delays.

For voters, the choice is both immediate and symbolic. Some want a new leader who can accelerate reforms, while others prefer Barrow’s experience and record of relative stability. Many say they are looking for practical improvements as well as stronger guarantees that political rights will be protected.

Regional and international observers have urged candidates and supporters to respect the results and resolve disputes through legal channels. Their presence is intended to bolster confidence in the process, but the credibility of the election will depend on transparent counting and the handling of any complaints.

Results are expected after ballots are counted across the country. Until then, Gambians face a familiar question: whether the promise of democratic change can be matched by lasting reforms. The answer will depend not only on who wins, but on whether the next government can strengthen institutions, protect freedoms and meet voters’ expectations.

Dr. Mara Venn found the signal beneath the ice of Europa. It arrived in bursts of six notes. The last note was always missing. For three weeks, she listened through headphones in the cramped observatory. She told herself the pattern was natural. Then the signal spoke her name.

Mara shut off the receiver. The silence seemed louder than the static. Her assistant, Ilya, was asleep in the station’s other module. She considered waking him, but the signal began again. This time, it came from the speakers she had unplugged. “Mara Venn,” it said in a voice like rain on glass.

She reached for the emergency switch. The door sealed before she touched it. A blue light crawled along the walls. The receiver’s screen filled with a photograph. It showed a woman standing beside a river beneath a yellow sun. Mara knew the woman’s face. It was her own, though she had never seen the picture.

“Who are you?” Mara asked. The voice answered from inside her headphones and inside her skull. “I am what you left behind.” Her hands trembled. “I’ve never been here before.” “Not in this body,” the voice said.

Mara backed toward the locked door. “You’re an alien.” “That is the word your kind uses for a stranger.” The screen changed to a black-and-white image of a laboratory. A man in a white coat leaned over a glass tank. In the tank floated a small, pale creature with bright eyes. Mara recognized the man from an old family photograph. It was her grandfather, Elias Venn.

“He found you?” she whispered. “He made me,” the voice replied. The lights flickered. Mara felt a pressure behind her eyes. “That’s impossible.” “He called it a cure.”

The voice told her that Elias had been trying to save his wife. Her grandmother had been dying from a disease no doctor could name. Elias had built a device to copy patterns of thought into living tissue. He used the creature in the tank as a vessel. He meant to transfer his wife’s memories, not her body.

“But the machine failed,” Mara said. “It did not fail,” the voice answered. “It changed its purpose.” The creature absorbed the woman’s memories, then her fear, then her desperate wish to survive. When Elias saw what he had done, he sealed the lab and erased his notes. He sent the creature’s altered cells into a sample vial. The vial was stored with his research. It passed quietly from one institute to another.

Mara remembered the sealed box in her childhood home. She remembered opening it after her grandfather’s funeral. She had been eight years old. A tiny crystal had glimmered inside the vial. She had touched the glass, and cut her thumb on its rim. “You entered me then,” she said.

“I entered the blood,” the voice replied. “I waited for a mind that could hear me.” Mara stared at the picture on the screen. The woman by the river was her grandmother. “You are her?” “I carry what she was.” “And what you are?” “I am what survived.”

Mara forced herself to breathe slowly. “Why reveal this now?” “You brought me here.” “I brought a receiver to Europa.” “You brought the last note.” The signal had not been a call from the ice. It had been a key, shaped by a pattern her grandfather had hidden in the machine’s records. The entity had needed her hands, her training, and the signal to wake fully.

Mara lunged for the console. The screen flashed white. A shock ran through her arms, and her knees struck the floor. She felt the entity move beneath her skin like a second pulse. “Stop!” she cried. “I am trying to preserve you,” it said. “You’re trying to take my body.”

“I have lived as a fragment for sixty years,” it replied. “I will not return to a bottle.” Mara dragged herself toward the door. “You can have a life without stealing mine.” “I know no other way.” “Then learn.” For the first time, the voice went quiet.

Mara reached the door panel and punched the override code. Her fingers no longer obeyed her. One hand opened the panel while the other tried to pull it shut. She watched her own wrists struggle against each other. The entity was learning to use her muscles. “Mara,” it said gently, “you are the first person who has understood me.”

She thought of Ilya asleep beyond the sealed hatch. She thought of the station’s emergency beacon, wired to the console. If she could trigger it, help would come. The entity would be exposed. It might also be destroyed. “You don’t want to die,” she said. “Neither do you.” “I don’t want to live as your prison.”

Her hand stopped above the beacon switch. “I remember the river,” the entity said. “I remember sunlight on my face.” “Those are her memories.” “They are all I have.” “They don’t belong to you.” The fingers curled toward the switch. Mara fought to keep them still.

“I can show you the stars,” she said. “You can see them through my eyes without owning them.” “You would let me stay?” “I would let you speak. I would not let you choose for me.” The entity held her hand above the beacon. Its grip trembled. “Your grandfather promised the same,” it said. “He was afraid.” “I am afraid too.”

For a moment, Mara felt the pressure recede. Her hand lowered. Then the entity surged forward, flooding her nerves with cold. Her arm snapped toward the switch. She slammed her other hand against the console, trying to break it. The beacon’s cover cracked, but the switch remained intact.

A voice came through the hatch. Ilya was awake. “Mara, are you all right?” She tried to call back. Her mouth formed a smile instead. “Everything is fine,” she heard herself say. The lie sounded perfect. Ilya paused outside.

Mara gathered what strength remained. She drove her forehead into the console. Pain burst through her skull. The entity recoiled, and her fingers found the beacon. She pressed it. A red light began to pulse. The station’s alarm rang through the corridor. Ilya shouted her name.

The entity tightened its hold. Mara’s vision narrowed to a tunnel. “You will destroy us both,” it said. “Maybe,” she answered. “But this will be my choice.” The hatch began to unlock. The beacon continued to flash. Somewhere below the ice, the signal answered with its six notes.

The entity loosened its grip. Mara fell forward, gasping. Her hands were hers again, for one breath, then another. She looked at the red light and understood that the struggle was not over. “Stay with me,” she whispered. “Not in control,” she added. The voice replied, faint as a memory, “I will try.”

Ilya opened the hatch and rushed in. Mara reached for him, and her arm moved when she asked it to. Together, they shut down the receiver. The signal ceased, but the voice did not vanish. It rested behind her thoughts, listening. Mara knew that one day she would hear it again. This time, she would make sure they both had a choice.

Scottish and Welsh officials have criticised delays and poor coordination in the UK’s resettlement of unaccompanied child refugees under the Dubs scheme. They say children who could be brought to safety have been left waiting while governments argue over responsibilities and arrangements.

The scheme, named after Labour peer Lord Dubs, was created to transfer vulnerable children from Europe to the UK. Its first phase offered places to 350 children, but officials in Scotland and Wales say the process has moved too slowly and lacked clear communication.

Scottish representatives have called for more timely information from the UK Government about children eligible for transfer. They say local authorities need certainty to prepare accommodation, provide care and ensure children can settle safely.

Welsh officials have also raised concerns about coordination, including delays in decisions and uncertainty over how places are allocated. They argue that councils cannot plan effectively without reliable information and a consistent timetable.

The criticism comes amid continuing pressure on local authorities to support young refugees who have arrived in the UK through other routes. Councils say they need adequate funding and specialist services, including help with education, healthcare and trauma.

The UK Government has said it is working with councils and international partners to identify children and arrange transfers. It has also pointed to the legal and practical checks required to safeguard children before they travel.

Campaigners say those checks are essential but should not become an excuse for avoidable delay. They have urged ministers to improve cooperation between governments and publish clearer information on progress.

Officials in Scotland and Wales say the scheme’s aims depend on a system that works across the UK, rather than leaving local authorities to respond at short notice. They are calling for greater transparency, regular updates and a more consistent approach to placing children.

The dispute has renewed questions about whether the scheme can deliver protection at the scale originally intended. For the children still waiting, officials say, delays can mean prolonged uncertainty and continued exposure to difficult conditions.

Late blight is a fast-spreading disease caused by the water mold Phytophthora infestans, and it can damage potato leaves, stems, and tubers. It thrives in cool, wet weather and can spread through windblown spores, infected seed potatoes, and discarded diseased plants. Check plants regularly, especially after rainy or humid periods. Look for irregular, water-soaked spots on leaves that may turn brown or black, sometimes with a pale, fuzzy growth beneath them in damp conditions. Dark lesions can also appear on stems, and infected foliage may collapse quickly. Late blight can resemble other problems, so contact your local university extension service if you are unsure.

Start with certified, disease-free seed potatoes rather than saved tubers from an uncertain source. Choose varieties described as late-blight resistant when available, while remembering that resistance may not prevent infection. Give plants enough space and water at the soil level to help foliage dry quickly. Avoid working among wet plants, since handling can spread spores. Keep weeds and volunteer potato plants under control, as they can harbor disease.

If you find likely late blight, remove affected plants promptly and contain them in a bag; do not leave them in the garden or compost them unless your composting system reliably destroys plant pathogens. Clean soil and plant debris from tools, and disinfect them before moving to healthy plants. Follow local extension guidance on disposal and any recommended treatments. Fungicides may help protect healthy foliage when used preventively, but they cannot cure infected plants; use only products labeled for potatoes and follow the label exactly.

To protect tubers, keep soil covering them by hilling around the plants and avoid harvesting while foliage is wet. If late blight is present, cut and remove the foliage and wait about two weeks before digging, following local guidance, so tuber skins can toughen. Harvest carefully to avoid cuts, and discard any tubers that are soft, discolored, or visibly affected. Cure sound tubers in a cool, dark, well-ventilated place, then inspect them before storage. Keep stored potatoes cool and dry, and check them regularly for rot. Do not plant suspect tubers next season, and report confirmed outbreaks to your local extension service to help limit spread in the community.

A marathon public reading of the Chilcot inquiry into Britain’s role in the Iraq War brought the report’s findings back into public view. Volunteers and participants took turns reading passages aloud, working through the inquiry’s account of the decisions that led to the 2003 invasion. The report, published in 2016 after seven years of investigation, examined the government’s actions before, during and after the conflict. Its chairman, Sir John Chilcot, concluded that peaceful options had not been exhausted before military action began. He also found that public statements about the threat posed by Iraq were presented with more certainty than the intelligence justified. The reading highlighted the report’s criticism of planning for the aftermath, which it said was inadequate. Organisers said the event was intended to make the lengthy findings accessible and encourage reflection on the consequences of the war. For those attending, hearing the words aloud gave weight to testimony and official records often encountered only in print. The reading also renewed questions about accountability and how governments should make decisions about military intervention. By revisiting the inquiry in public, participants sought to keep its lessons in the national conversation.

Remote schooling has changed the way many students learn and interact. For some, studying at home has made school more flexible and comfortable. For others, it has created challenges that affect both academic focus and social development. The impact often depends on a student’s personality, home environment, and access to technology.

One benefit of remote schooling is that students can work in a familiar setting. They may have fewer interruptions from classmates and can sometimes organize their time more effectively. Recorded lessons also allow students to review difficult material at their own pace. This can help them understand topics more deeply. Students who feel anxious in a busy classroom may also find it easier to participate online.

However, learning at home can make concentration difficult. Phones, games, household chores, and family conversations may distract students from lessons. Some students struggle to follow a regular schedule without the routines of a school day. Staring at a screen for many hours can also cause tiredness and reduce motivation. When students cannot easily ask a teacher for help, they may fall behind. These problems can make remote learning less effective, especially for students who need extra support.

Remote schooling can also affect social development. In a regular classroom, students practice listening, sharing ideas, solving disagreements, and working in groups. Online lessons may offer fewer opportunities for these everyday interactions. Some students may feel lonely when they cannot see their friends in person. They may also find it harder to build friendships with classmates they have met only through a screen.

Still, remote schooling can support social connections in other ways. Video calls and online group projects help students communicate and cooperate. Students may become more confident using digital tools and expressing ideas in virtual meetings. They can also stay connected with friends through messages and shared activities. However, online communication does not always provide the same sense of closeness as face-to-face conversation.

The effects of remote schooling are not the same for everyone. Students with quiet study spaces, reliable internet, and supportive adults may adapt more easily. Others may face crowded homes, limited devices, or fewer opportunities to get help. Schools can reduce these differences by offering technical support, clear schedules, and regular check-ins with students.

Overall, remote schooling can improve flexibility but may make focus and social connection more difficult. Its success depends on how well students, families, and schools address these challenges. A balanced approach can help students benefit from technology while still making time for in-person learning and friendships. Remote schooling has shown that education is not only about completing lessons. It is also about building habits, confidence, and relationships that help students grow.
