Mara found the first clue inside a file marked “Floodplain Repairs.” It was a list of towns that had never flooded, paired with casualty estimates. She brought it to her brother, Tomas, who worked in military archives. He read the numbers twice, then locked the door. “These are recruitment figures,” he whispered. “For what?” Mara asked.

Tomas showed her a second file: troop transports that vanished from public records after leaving ordinary bases. Their destinations were coordinates beyond every map. Some had returned, carrying soldiers who looked years older. Others had not returned at all. The files called the whole operation the Lantern Program. Its stated purpose was to “preserve planetary obscurity.”

Mara thought it was a joke until the lights flickered. A message appeared on Tomas’s screen, though neither of them had touched the keyboard. It said: THEY HAVE FOUND OUR TRAIL. Then the building shook, and distant alarms began to howl. Tomas grabbed the files and led her down the service stairs. Outside, the city’s billboards flashed emergency warnings about a border clash that had started that morning.

They watched people hurry toward shelters while jets crossed the clouds. “They made this happen,” Mara said. Tomas nodded. “A crisis keeps armies busy, borders closed, and satellites pointed where they want them.” He told her the secret war was fought far beyond the Moon. Human soldiers were sent there to defend a network of hidden outposts. The conflicts on Earth supplied recruits and buried their departures in confusion.

At the river, an unmarked shuttle waited beneath the bridge. Tomas said he had arranged a place for her aboard. Mara stared at the crowded shelters, at people who believed the danger was only across a border. “If we leave,” she said, “they’ll keep doing this.” She uploaded the files to every public network she could reach.

For one bright moment, the truth spread across the city screens. Then the messages began disappearing, replaced by official denials and urgent calls for calm. A new broadcast interrupted them. It showed a star field, and a vast shadow moving between the stars. Tomas looked up, afraid. The shadow turned toward Earth.

The shuttle’s hatch opened. Mara stepped inside, carrying the last copy of the files. “If they’re coming,” she said, “people deserve to know why.” Tomas followed her aboard. As the engines lifted them from the river, the city below went dark. Above it, the stars seemed suddenly much closer.

The drop capsule shook so hard that Mara’s teeth clicked together. Around her, the other five marines sat strapped into their crash couches, trying not to look afraid. Sergeant Vale checked each harness by hand, though the green lights said they were secure. “First rule,” he said. “When the hatch opens, breathe before you move.” Nobody laughed. Far below, Vesper City glowed beneath a veil of smoke. Its towers had once been silver, but now their windows were dark and their streets belonged to the occupying army. The invasion fleet waited beyond the moon, silent and hidden. Their squad’s job was to mark a landing corridor and disable the city’s eastern defense relay. If they failed, the main force would descend into a storm of missiles. Mara pressed her thumb against the scratched nameplate on her rifle. Her brother had carved it during training, back when combat was a story told over ration tins. The capsule’s pilot spoke through the ceiling speaker. “Thirty seconds to atmospheric entry.” The hull groaned as the planet grabbed them. A strip of orange light crawled along the viewport. Then came the first burst of enemy fire. The capsule lurched sideways, and one of the marines cried out. Vale’s voice cut through the alarms. “Eyes on me. We land, we move, we stay together.” Mara fixed her gaze on his helmet. She had repeated those words a hundred times in drills. They sounded different with the city rushing up beneath them. The capsule struck a rooftop and bounced. Metal screamed across concrete. Something burst overhead, spraying sparks through the cabin. The harnesses snapped tight against their chests. For one terrible second, Mara could hear only her own breathing. Then the capsule settled. Vale released his straps and drew his pistol. “Breathe,” he reminded them. The hatch blew outward with a thunderclap. Cold air and dust swept into the cabin. Red beams crossed the rooftop beyond the opening. An enemy patrol was already moving toward them. Vale tossed a smoke canister through the hatch. Gray clouds swallowed the rooftop. “Out, out, out!” he shouted. Mara hit the ground hard and rolled behind a ventilation block. The others followed, boots scraping on broken stone. Their squad’s radio crackled with static. A shape appeared through the smoke, rifle raised. Mara fired before she could think. The figure dropped behind a rooftop vent. Her hands shook so badly that she nearly lost her grip. Vale crouched beside her. “Good shot,” he said, though neither of them knew whether it was true. The squad crossed the roof in pairs, moving toward the stairwell. Far below, sirens wailed through the streets. They descended into a building that smelled of wet plaster and burned wires. On the second landing, they found a wall painted with a child’s blue sun. Mara slowed, staring at it. Sergeant Vale touched her shoulder and urged her on. The enemy had turned the lower floors into a supply post. Crates lined the corridor, stamped with the seal of the occupation. A guard stood at the far end, speaking into a radio. Tavi, the squad’s quietest marine, slipped around the side and cut the corridor lights. In the darkness, the guard’s voice stopped. Vale signaled them forward. They reached the service door without another shot. Outside, the city opened around them in narrow streets and towering shadows. A tram lay overturned in the plaza. Its windows were starred with bullet holes. A handful of civilians watched from a basement entrance. One raised a finger to her lips and pointed toward an alley. Vale nodded thanks. Mara wondered how long the woman had been waiting for someone to help. They could not stop, but Vale left a sealed water pouch by the door. The squad crossed the alley under the cover of a passing storm. Rain hammered the rooftops and blurred the enemy searchlights. Ahead stood the relay station, a squat concrete building beneath a lattice of antennas. The invasion fleet would need its signal to know the corridor was safe. Their approach route passed through a market square. Canvas awnings snapped in the wind. A row of ceramic birds hung above a shuttered shop. The sight made Mara think of her mother’s kitchen and the chipped cup she had promised to repair. A patrol rounded the corner before they reached the square. Vale pulled the squad behind a toppled delivery cart. The enemy soldiers wore gray armor and carried long-barreled rifles. One of them was limping. Another held a paper bag over his head against the rain. They looked tired rather than monstrous. Mara found that more unsettling. Vale waited until the patrol passed, then led them across the square. At the relay station’s rear wall, Tavi attached a cutting charge. The blast opened a gap just wide enough for one marine at a time. Mara went in third. The station’s control room hummed with a low electric vibration. A technician sat frozen beside the main console, hands raised. Vale kept his pistol lowered. “We’re not here for you,” he said. The technician glanced at the darkened screens. “If you destroy the relay, they’ll shell the river wards,” he whispered. Vale’s expression tightened. The invasion plan had assumed the relay controlled only the defenses. Mara looked at the map glowing on the console. A red grid covered the river district, where the civilians had been told to shelter. “Can you change the signal?” she asked. The technician stared at her. “I can send a false corridor.” Outside, boots clattered down the station stairs. Vale made his choice quickly. He ordered two marines to hold the entrance while Tavi helped the technician. Mara crouched beside the console, watching the signal bars rise one by one. The technician’s hands trembled over the keys. “Which corridor?” he asked. Mara traced a route across the empty industrial quarter. It would delay the invasion, but it would keep the river wards clear. Vale looked at her, then gave a single nod. The technician entered the new coordinates. The relay’s antennas shifted with a mechanical groan. A burst of light flashed across the console. On the screen, the fleet’s acknowledgment appeared. The main invasion would land three kilometers west of its original target. Then the station doors buckled inward. Vale and the others fired from behind the server racks. Mara heard rounds crack against the control-room walls. Tavi pulled the technician away from the console. The new signal had gone through, but the relay’s backup power was climbing. “It will correct itself in two minutes,” the technician said. Mara saw a coolant valve beneath the console. She grabbed a wrench from the floor. Vale shouted her name as another blast shook the room. Mara twisted the valve until the metal squealed. Cold vapor burst across the floor. The backup lights flickered and died. In the sudden dark, the enemy fire stopped. Vale called the squad together by touch and voice. They left through a maintenance hatch at the back of the station. Rain swallowed them as they emerged into a narrow canal walk. Overhead, the clouds brightened with distant engines. The invasion fleet had begun its descent. A transport passed between the towers, its running lights dimmed. More followed, silent shapes lowering toward the safe corridor. Mara watched them for only a moment. The city still held enemy soldiers, and the squad’s path back was unknown. Sergeant Vale checked their head count. Six helmets answered his call. He looked at each of them, then at the glowing horizon. “That was the easy part,” he said. This time, someone laughed. Mara’s hands had stopped shaking. She could still hear the city breathing around them: sirens, rain, distant engines, and somewhere, a child crying. She tightened her grip on her rifle and followed the squad into the dark.

Oral hygiene is the daily care of your teeth, gums, and mouth. It helps prevent dental problems and supports your overall health and well-being. A clean, healthy mouth can also make eating, speaking, and smiling more comfortable.

Plaque is a sticky film of bacteria that forms on teeth throughout the day. If it is not removed, it can contribute to tooth decay and gum disease. Brushing twice a day with fluoride toothpaste helps clear plaque and strengthen tooth enamel. Use a soft-bristled toothbrush and brush gently for about two minutes each time. Replace your toothbrush or brush head every three to four months, or sooner if the bristles become worn.

Flossing once a day cleans between teeth and under the gumline, where a toothbrush may not reach. If traditional floss is difficult to use, floss picks or an interdental brush may be helpful. Cleaning your tongue can also reduce bacteria and help keep your breath fresh. After brushing, spit out the toothpaste rather than rinsing immediately, so fluoride remains on your teeth longer.

Good food and drink choices are another part of oral care. Frequent sugary snacks and drinks give cavity-causing bacteria more fuel. Water is a good choice for staying hydrated and washing away food particles. A balanced diet with nutritious foods supports healthy teeth and gums.

Regular dental checkups help identify problems early, when they may be easier to treat. A dental professional can remove hardened plaque, check for cavities, and offer advice suited to your needs. Visit sooner if you have tooth pain, bleeding gums, persistent bad breath, or another concern. Do not ignore symptoms, since untreated dental problems can worsen.

Oral health is connected to overall health, although it is only one part of well-being. Gum disease involves inflammation and infection in the tissues that support the teeth. Some health conditions and medicines can affect the mouth, and oral symptoms may signal that you need professional care. Tell your dentist about your medical conditions and medications.

Healthy teeth and gums also support your appearance. Regular care can help prevent visible decay, gum irritation, and persistent bad breath. A comfortable, confident smile can make social interactions more enjoyable. Avoid tobacco, which can stain teeth, harm gum health, and increase the risk of oral disease.

Building a consistent routine is more effective than occasional intensive cleaning. Brush morning and night, floss daily, choose water often, and keep up with dental visits. Children benefit from gentle help and supervision as they learn to brush and floss well. With these simple habits, you can protect your smile and support your health throughout life.

Captain Comet was halfway through a battle with the villainous Dr. Static when the streetlights went dark.
A bolt from the doctor’s machine had struck the power station, and chaos spread across the city.
Dr. Static laughed and launched a cloud of crackling sparks.
Captain Comet raised his shield, ready to charge.
Then he spotted a postal van trapped beneath a fallen sign.
Beside it, a delivery worker clutched a sack of letters and packages.
A food truck had stopped nearby, its driver trying to get meals to the hospital.
“Hold on,” Captain Comet called to the doctor.
“You can’t just pause a battle!” Dr. Static shouted.
“I can when essential services are in danger,” the hero replied.
He flew to the van and lifted the sign away.
The postal worker hurried to check the mail.
One package held medicine for a child across town.
Another carried documents needed at the courthouse.
Captain Comet cleared a path through the rubble.
He guided the food truck toward the hospital.
Dr. Static tried to block the road with a wall of metal.
The hero turned and pointed to a notice on the city’s emergency board.
It listed protected mail routes and food deliveries.
“Those rules keep people safe,” Captain Comet said.
“They don’t stop me,” Dr. Static growled.
He fired a blast at the truck.
Captain Comet intercepted it with his shield.
The food arrived at the hospital, where hungry patients and staff cheered.
The postal worker delivered the medicine in time.
With the road clear, Captain Comet returned to the battle.
He redirected Dr. Static’s sparks into the empty sky.
The villain’s machine sputtered and fell silent.
Captain Comet helped the city restore its lights.
That evening, the last letters and food baskets reached their destinations.
And the city remembered that protecting everyday services was heroic, too.

Mara met her guardian angel in the checkout line, between the energy drinks and the frosted doughnuts. “You’re late,” she said, dropping both into her basket. “I was hoping the cigarettes would make it a party.”

The angel, who introduced himself as Felix, wore a rumpled gray suit and the expression of someone who’d read the same bad decision a thousand times. “I’m not here to judge,” he said. “I’m here to prevent your heart from filing a formal complaint.”

Mara snorted and paid. On the walk home, she cracked open an energy drink and took a long swallow. Felix hovered beside her, invisible to everyone else, and sighed so heavily a nearby pigeon changed direction.

“Water exists,” he said. “It’s free, and it doesn’t taste like a battery with ambition.”

“Water is boring,” Mara replied. “So is living forever.”

“Good news,” Felix said. “I’m only responsible for helping you reach Tuesday.”

At home, Mara sank onto the couch and scrolled through her phone until midnight. Felix pointed at the dark window, where her reflection looked more exhausted than the one in the morning. “That’s your body asking for sleep,” he said.

“It can text me like everyone else,” Mara answered, and queued another video.

Felix flicked a tiny halo-shaped lamp on and off. Mara finally groaned, set the phone down, and went to bed—mostly to stop the blinking.

The next morning, she ignored the oatmeal Felix had arranged on the counter and grabbed a doughnut. “One healthy choice,” she declared, “doesn’t make me a saint.”

“No,” Felix said. “But it might make you less likely to mistake your desk for a pillow.”

At work, Mara’s hands trembled as she reached for her third coffee. Felix nudged a glass of water toward her. She glared at him, then drank it to prove she could.

By lunchtime, her headache had eased. “Coincidence,” she said, taking the stairs instead of the elevator. Halfway up, she stopped to catch her breath.

Felix appeared beside her, wearing a sash that read MINIMUM EFFORT, MAXIMUM DRAMA. “I’m proud,” he said. “Try not to let it go to your head.”

That evening, Mara bought vegetables, though she insisted it was only because the supermarket had put them on sale. She cooked them with rice, ate two servings, and admitted they were “not entirely offensive.”

Felix raised his hands as if receiving a miracle. “Careful,” he said. “At this rate, you’ll be feeling better by Thursday.”

Mara rolled her eyes, but she filled a bottle with water before bed and left her phone across the room. “Don’t get used to this,” she warned him.

“Relax,” Felix said, settling onto the windowsill. “I’m a guardian angel, not a motivational poster.”

The next morning, Mara woke before her alarm and stretched. She still wanted a doughnut, still disliked stairs, and still thought water could use better branding.

But she drank a glass anyway. Felix smiled. “Look at you,” he said. “Making one good choice without turning it into a personality.”

Mara grabbed her jacket and headed outside for a walk. “Don’t make a big deal of it,” she called over her shoulder.

“Wouldn’t dream of it,” Felix replied, following at a respectful, sarcastic distance.

Truthfulness is one of the most important qualities in building trust and strong relationships. It means being honest about what we think, feel, and do. When people tell the truth, others can rely on their words. This reliability creates a sense of safety and respect. Without truthfulness, relationships can become uncertain and stressful.

Trust grows when people are honest with one another over time. For example, a friend who admits to making a mistake shows that they value the friendship more than avoiding blame. The other person may feel disappointed at first, but honesty gives them a chance to understand what happened. In contrast, a lie can cause greater hurt when it is discovered. It can also make people question other things they have been told.

Truthfulness is important in families, friendships, and schools. Family members need honesty to solve problems and understand one another. Friends need it to share their feelings and support each other. Students and teachers also benefit when everyone is truthful about their work and responsibilities. In all these relationships, honest communication helps prevent misunderstandings.

Being truthful does not mean speaking without care. We should express the truth kindly and choose the right time for difficult conversations. Honesty should not be used as an excuse to insult or embarrass someone. A thoughtful person can be both sincere and respectful. This balance makes it easier for others to listen.

Sometimes telling the truth takes courage, especially when we fear consequences. Still, admitting a mistake can help us learn and make things right. If we hide the truth, a small problem may grow into a bigger one. Taking responsibility also shows maturity. It can restore trust, even if rebuilding it takes time.

Truthfulness must be practiced consistently to become a habit. People are more likely to trust someone whose actions match their words. Once trust has been damaged, it may take patience and effort to repair it. Honest conversations and dependable behavior can help rebuild a relationship. Both people may need to be willing to listen and move forward.

In conclusion, truthfulness is a foundation for lasting relationships. It encourages respect, understanding, and confidence between people. Although honesty can sometimes be difficult, it is better than allowing lies to create distance. By telling the truth with kindness and taking responsibility for our actions, we can build stronger connections. Truthfulness helps people feel valued and gives relationships the chance to grow.

The UK government has promised to protect its science budget in real terms, but researchers say the commitment may not be enough to sustain the country’s research ambitions. They are also concerned that new restrictions on development aid could limit work with poorer countries.

The funding pledge means the budget should keep pace with inflation, rather than lose purchasing power. It offers some reassurance to universities, research institutes and businesses planning projects over several years. But a flat real-terms budget does not necessarily cover rising demand or the costs of maintaining laboratories and equipment.

Researchers say the government has yet to explain clearly how the money will be distributed. They want details on funding for basic research, applied science and the organisations that support collaboration. Without that clarity, institutions may struggle to plan hiring and long-term projects.

The debate comes as the UK seeks to strengthen productivity, attract investment and compete in fields such as artificial intelligence, clean energy and biotechnology. Scientists argue that those aims depend on a stable pipeline of research, from early-stage discovery to commercial application. They warn that cuts or uncertainty at any point can weaken the whole system.

Universities have also faced rising costs and pressure on their finances. Research grants do not always cover the full cost of the work they support, leaving institutions to make up the difference. A protected headline budget, critics say, may therefore feel like a reduction on the ground.

The government’s approach to development aid has raised a separate concern. Rules requiring aid spending to meet official development objectives can restrict which research projects qualify. Scientists say this could make it harder to support international partnerships addressing shared challenges, including infectious disease and climate change.

Some researchers fear that projects involving lower-income countries could lose funding if their benefits are not judged to accrue primarily to those countries. They argue that research partnerships often produce benefits across borders, while also building local expertise and research capacity. Clear guidance, they say, is needed to prevent useful collaborations from being excluded.

Supporters of tighter rules say public aid budgets must be spent in line with their stated purpose and deliver measurable benefits. They also point to the pressure on government finances and competing demands for public money. The challenge for ministers is to maintain accountability without narrowing the scope for valuable joint research.

Research organisations are calling for a funding plan that gives them confidence beyond the immediate budget period. They want transparent criteria, predictable grant schedules and support for international collaboration. Many also say the government should assess the real costs of research when setting budgets.

Ministers have presented science as central to the UK’s future economic growth and public wellbeing. Researchers broadly welcome the protection in real terms, but say it is only a starting point. Whether it proves sufficient will depend on the details of spending decisions and how aid restrictions are applied.

For scientists, the concern is not simply the total amount announced. It is whether funding reaches the people and institutions doing the work, and whether programmes can continue long enough to deliver results. The government’s next decisions will show how far its commitment matches its ambitions.

Before making an important decision, many people ask others for guidance. They may turn to family members, friends, teachers, or experts. Seeking advice from several people can be helpful because each person may offer a different point of view. One person might focus on practical concerns, while another considers the emotional effects. Hearing these perspectives can help us notice details we had overlooked. It can also reveal choices we did not know were available. Different opinions may help us compare the advantages and disadvantages of each option. In this way, advice from multiple people can make a decision more thoughtful and informed. It can also give us confidence that we have considered the matter carefully. However, seeking guidance from many people can create challenges. Their opinions may conflict, leaving us unsure about what to do. Some advisers may have limited knowledge of the situation. Others might let their personal experiences or preferences influence their advice. It can be difficult to tell which guidance is most relevant to our needs. Asking too many people may also delay a decision, especially when time is limited. We may begin to depend on others and lose trust in our own judgment. To avoid these problems, we should choose advisers who understand the issue and care about our well-being. We should listen carefully, ask questions, and consider why each person holds a particular opinion. At the same time, we must remember that advice is not a command. Ultimately, we are responsible for weighing the information and choosing a path that fits our values and circumstances. Seeking guidance from several people is most beneficial when we remain open-minded but make the final decision for ourselves.

He came home hungry enough to hear the refrigerator whisper his name. He shut the door and surveyed the kitchen. Tonight, he wanted something warm, filling, and willing to cooperate. He rolled up his sleeves. The cutting board waited on the counter, smooth and eager. He selected a firm zucchini. It had the right shape and a little shine. He gave it a thorough rinse. Then he laid it down and reached for his knife. The first cut was clean. He worked slowly, savoring the rhythm. Soon, neat green rounds covered the board. He pushed them aside and chose an onion. Its papery coat came off in one satisfying peel. He split it in half. The layers opened up before him. His eyes watered, but he refused to stop. He chopped until the onion was fine and ready. A red pepper joined the lineup. He held it steady and worked around its core. The seeds spilled out like tiny secrets. He sliced the pepper into bright strips. His stomach rumbled, impatient for the next step. He pulled a pot from the cupboard. It was deeper than it looked. He set it on the stove and turned up the heat. A generous splash of olive oil went in first. The oil shimmered as it warmed. He added the onion. It sizzled at once, delighted to be there. He stirred it with a wooden spoon. The kitchen filled with a sweet, savory scent. He leaned close, pleased by the response. The pepper went in next. It softened among the onions. He added the zucchini rounds. They settled into the pot, snug and comfortable. A pinch of salt loosened them up. Black pepper gave the mixture a little bite. He reached for garlic. Two cloves were enough to make things interesting. He crushed them under the flat of his knife. Their skins slipped away with almost no effort. He minced the cloves finely. Then he tipped them into the pot. The aroma grew bold and unmistakable. He stirred until everything was coated. A can of chickpeas waited nearby. He drained them and gave them a rinse. They were firm, pale, and ready to join the party. He poured them into the pot. The mixture welcomed them without hesitation. He added crushed tomatoes, rich and red. They spread through the vegetables in a slow, glossy wave. A splash of broth loosened the whole affair. He stirred it until it came together. The pot began to bubble gently. He lowered the heat and put on the lid. Now it needed time alone. He set a timer and cleaned the knife. The kitchen grew quiet except for the simmer. He checked the pot once. The sauce had thickened, and everything looked relaxed. He stirred in a handful of spinach. The leaves wilted into the warmth. A squeeze of lemon sharpened the flavors. He tasted a spoonful and nodded. It needed a little more salt. He added just enough. Then he reached for the pasta. He measured a generous portion into a second pot. The water boiled hard beneath it. He lowered the pasta in carefully. It slipped beneath the surface. He stirred so nothing would stick together. The timer rang before he was ready. He tested one piece with a bite. It was tender but still had some backbone. He drained it, saving a cup of the starchy water. He tipped the pasta into the vegetable sauce. A splash of water helped everything cling. He turned the whole mixture over with his spoon. The pasta took on the sauce beautifully. He grated a little cheese over the top. It melted into the warm dish. He carried the pot to the table. The meal looked hearty and inviting. He filled a bowl, then paused to admire his work. Finally, he took the first bite. The flavors met exactly as he had hoped. He leaned back and let out a satisfied sigh. His hunger had been handled with care. He went back for seconds.

At 2:13 a.m., Mara heard three knocks on her apartment door.
She knew the rhythm from the message taped to her windshield: three knocks meant the visitor was not a neighbor.
She took the small pistol from her bedside drawer and crept to the peephole.
A man in a charcoal coat stood in the hallway, holding a black umbrella though the night was clear.
“Open up, Mara,” he said.
His voice was calm, which frightened her more than a shout would have.
She unlocked the door but kept the chain fastened.
The man glanced at the chain, then at her trembling hand.
“I’m supposed to kill you,” he said.
Mara stared at him.
“That’s a very direct way to start a conversation.”
“It saves time.”
She shut the door, slid the chain free, and opened it wider.
The assassin stepped inside and placed his umbrella carefully by the mat.
He was younger than she expected, with tired eyes and a scar that vanished beneath his collar.
“Sit down,” she said, pointing toward the kitchen.
He blinked.
“You’re giving me instructions?”
“You came into my home.”
He sat at the table, shoulders squared, hands folded like a student waiting for a test.
Mara put the kettle on.
“I have a gun,” she reminded him.
“I noticed.”
“And you’re still sitting there.”
“I’ve had a difficult week.”
She set two mugs on the table.
The assassin looked at the tea bag in front of him as if it might be a trap.
“Why did they hire you?” Mara asked.
“Because I’m good at my job.”
“That’s not a reason.”
He looked down at his hands.
“My brother says I’m impossible to talk to.”
Mara lowered herself into the chair across from him.
“Do you want to talk about that?”
The man let out a humorless laugh.
“I came here to end your life, and you’re asking about my feelings.”
“Both things can be true.”
For a while, the only sound was the kettle ticking as it cooled.
Then he told her about his brother, the missed calls, and the apology he had rehearsed for three years.
Mara listened without interrupting.
When he finished, she said, “You don’t have to earn your way back into someone’s life by becoming a better weapon.”
His face tightened, but his eyes grew wet.
He pushed the untouched tea away and stood.
“I can’t do this tonight.”
Mara nodded toward the door.
“Then don’t.”
At the threshold, he turned and asked if she thought his brother would answer.
“I think you’ll never know until you call.”
The assassin took out his phone, stared at the screen, and dialed.
As it rang, Mara kept her pistol on the table and poured herself another cup of tea.

Computing through 2047: plausible predictions

Predicting technology more than twenty years ahead is uncertain, so the future described here is a set of possibilities, not a promise. Progress will depend not only on scientific discoveries but also on economics, regulation, energy, security, and public choices. Even so, several developments already underway offer clues about how computing may evolve.

Computing technology

By 2047, many devices may combine conventional processors with specialized chips for artificial intelligence, graphics, security, and scientific work. These chips could perform more tasks locally, reducing the need to send every request to a distant data center. More efficient processors will matter because the demand for computing is likely to grow faster than the supply of cheap energy. Researchers may also make wider use of new materials and chip designs, though silicon is likely to remain important. Quantum computers could solve selected problems that are exceptionally difficult for conventional machines, but they are unlikely to replace everyday computers. Their practical value will depend on whether engineers can reduce errors and build systems large enough for useful applications. Neuromorphic computers, designed to imitate some features of brains, may offer efficient ways to process certain kinds of information. Photonic systems, which use light to move or process data, could help with some high-speed computing tasks. Most large advances will probably come from combining different technologies rather than finding one universal replacement for today’s computers.

Artificial intelligence may become a routine feature of operating systems, workplace tools, and public services. Assistants could handle multi-step tasks, such as planning a trip, comparing options, and completing a booking after receiving permission. They may also interpret images, speech, text, and sensor data together. As these systems become more capable, people will need clear ways to check their work and understand when they are uncertain. Human experts will remain essential in areas where mistakes carry serious consequences. Personal data and model behavior will be governed by stronger privacy, safety, and accountability rules in many regions. Some organizations may run AI models on their own equipment to protect sensitive information or reduce reliance on outside services.

Interfaces

Screens will still be useful in 2047, but they may no longer be the main way people interact with computers. Voice interfaces could become more natural and work reliably across languages and noisy environments. Cameras and other sensors may let devices respond to gestures, posture, and surroundings. Wearable displays, including lightweight glasses, could place directions, captions, or instructions within a person’s field of view. These displays may become useful only if they are comfortable, affordable, and respectful of people nearby. Haptic technology could convey alerts or guidance through touch, especially when looking at a screen is inconvenient. Brain-computer interfaces may help some people control devices or communicate, particularly when movement or speech is limited. For most users, however, such systems are likely to remain specialized unless they become safe, practical, and clearly beneficial.

Interfaces may adapt to a person’s needs, changing language, text size, or level of detail. The same task could move smoothly between a phone, a car, a home device, and a workplace system. To make this possible, designers will need to prevent accidental actions and make it easy to regain control. Accessible design will be increasingly important as populations age and people use technology in different ways. Good interfaces will not simply add more features; they will help people understand what a system is doing. People should be able to pause, correct, or refuse automated assistance.

Networking

Networks are likely to combine fiber, mobile connections, satellites, and local wireless links. Faster mobile networks may support demanding services, but dependable coverage will matter more than peak speed in many situations. Satellites could extend connectivity to remote areas, ships, and aircraft, although cost, congestion, and orbital debris are serious challenges. Future networks may route data through nearby devices or local servers to reduce delay. This will be valuable for applications such as industrial control, remote assistance, and interactive entertainment. Not every task requires instant communication, however, and many systems will continue to work well with ordinary delays.

Devices may increasingly communicate directly with one another, from medical sensors to traffic signals. Such networks will need reliable identity checks, secure software updates, and clear limits on what data they collect. Encryption will remain essential, while future cryptography will need to withstand advances in computing, including possible large-scale quantum machines. Network operators may use AI to detect faults and respond to attacks, but automated defenses will also need human oversight. Connectivity could become more resilient through backup links and systems that continue operating during outages. Bridging the digital divide will require affordable access, useful local services, and digital skills, not just new infrastructure.

Ubiquitous applications

Computing may become less visible as it is built into buildings, vehicles, appliances, clothing, and public spaces. Smart homes could coordinate heating, lighting, security, and energy storage to improve comfort and reduce waste. In cities, connected systems might help manage traffic, water, public transport, and electricity. These services will work best when they are dependable and designed around public needs rather than data collection alone. Hospitals may use connected monitoring and decision-support tools to identify health problems earlier. Wearable sensors could help people track health trends, but medical decisions will still require qualified professionals. In education, adaptive software may provide practice suited to a learner’s progress, while teachers guide discussion, motivation, and critical thinking. In workplaces, digital assistants and robots may take over repetitive or hazardous tasks and help workers analyze complex information.

Agriculture may use sensors, autonomous machinery, and forecasting tools to manage water and crops more precisely. Transport systems could coordinate vehicles and infrastructure, but fully autonomous travel will face technical, legal, and social challenges. Digital models of machines, buildings, or even parts of cities may help test changes before they are made in the physical world. These models will be useful only when their data is accurate and their assumptions are understood. Entertainment may blend physical and virtual experiences, allowing people to collaborate in shared digital spaces. Such spaces will raise questions about identity, moderation, privacy, and ownership.

The benefits of ubiquitous computing will come with risks. Constant sensing can expose intimate details about people’s habits and health. Poorly secured devices can become entry points for criminals or disrupt essential services. Automated decisions may reproduce unfairness if their data or design reflects existing inequalities. Devices that depend on cloud services may fail when networks are unavailable or companies discontinue support. Electronic waste and the energy demands of data centers will make repair, reuse, and efficient design increasingly important. Governments and communities will need to decide which systems should be optional, who controls the data, and how people can challenge harmful decisions.

By 2047, computing may feel less like using a collection of separate gadgets and more like working with a connected environment. The most successful technologies will likely be those that are useful, secure, accessible, and easy to understand. Some predictions will prove wrong, and unexpected discoveries may reshape the field. The central question is not only what computers will be able to do, but how people choose to use them.

Schools should keep a traditional academic calendar rather than operate year-round. A long summer break gives students time to rest after months of classes. Rest is important because learning requires focus and energy. Students can return in the fall feeling refreshed and ready to study. Summer also gives families time to travel, visit relatives, and make memories together. Many students use the break to attend camps, take lessons, or explore personal interests. Older students may work summer jobs and gain useful experience. These opportunities can help them learn skills that are difficult to practice in a classroom. A traditional calendar also matches the schedules of many parents and caregivers. Families can plan vacations and child care around a familiar break. Schools, too, often use summer for repairs, cleaning, and classroom preparation. These tasks can be harder to complete when students attend classes throughout the year. Supporters of year-round school make some good points. They argue that shorter breaks may help students remember what they learned. They also say that spreading vacations across the year could reduce stress. In some schools, year-round schedules can make better use of crowded buildings. However, these benefits do not mean that every school should abandon summer vacation. Students can review important skills during the summer without attending school all year. Libraries, community centers, and online programs can provide enjoyable learning opportunities. Teachers can also assign reasonable reading or practice activities. These options help prevent learning loss while preserving a real break. Year-round schedules may also create difficulties for families with children in different schools. Parents might struggle to arrange child care during frequent breaks. Families who depend on summer programs or seasonal work could face additional challenges. Teachers need time away from school as well, so shorter breaks may not solve every problem. Each community should consider its needs before changing its calendar. Still, the traditional calendar is a practical choice for many schools. It balances learning with rest, family time, and activities outside the classroom. Schools should improve summer learning rather than remove the summer break. For these reasons, a traditional academic calendar is the better option.

At noon, the sky opened like a door.

Mara was building a tower of blocks when the sunlight turned blue. Her mother dropped a spoon in the kitchen. Her father came running from the cellar, still holding a jar of peaches. Outside, every bird rose at once and flew toward the horizon.

Then the stars appeared, though it was daytime. They hung low and bright, arranged in a circle around the sun. The circle began to turn.

The house trembled. A crack of white light split the clouds without making a sound. Windows burst inward, and the blocks scattered across the floor.

Her father pulled Mara beneath the kitchen table. Her mother wrapped both arms around them. The air smelled of rain and something like burnt sugar.

For one strange moment, gravity vanished. Chairs drifted past the ceiling. The peaches floated from the jar, shining like little moons.

Mara laughed because she thought it was a game. Her parents did not laugh.

The turning stars drew together. Far away, the mountains folded inward, as if a giant hand had pressed them flat. The sea climbed the sky in a shining wall.

Her father lifted Mara and ran for the cellar. Her mother followed, carrying the small red blanket Mara slept with. At the cellar door, the light reached them.

It was not hot or cold. It filled every shadow and made her parents look suddenly far away.

Her mother kissed Mara’s forehead. Her father whispered, “Remember the garden.” Then the world rang like a glass struck by a spoon.

When the ringing stopped, Mara was alone beneath the stairs. The red blanket covered her, and dust lay thick as snow. She called for her parents until her voice broke.

No one answered.

After a long time, she climbed outside. The house had lost its roof, and the familiar road ended at a field of black glass. Above it, the stars were gone.

Mara found the garden crushed beneath fallen beams. One sunflower still stood, bent but alive. She held it carefully, afraid the petals might vanish.

Night came, though the sun had never returned. Mara wrapped herself in the blanket and sat beside the sunflower. In the darkness, a tiny star blinked beneath the earth.

She listened, and from somewhere below, the ground gave a soft, answering ring.

Hanoi, the capital of Vietnam, has a history spanning more than a thousand years. In 1010, Emperor Ly Thai To established his capital here and named it Thang Long, meaning “Ascending Dragon.” The city later became known as Hanoi, or “Between the Rivers,” reflecting its setting in the Red River Delta. Over the centuries, Hanoi grew through dynasties, French colonial rule, and the development of modern Vietnam. Its Old Quarter preserves a lively street pattern shaped by centuries of trade and skilled craftsmanship. Nearby, the Temple of Literature, founded in 1070, honors Confucius and Vietnam’s scholarly traditions. The Imperial Citadel of Thang Long, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, reveals layers of royal history beneath the modern city. Hoan Kiem Lake is a central landmark, associated with the legend of a magical sword returned to a golden turtle. West Lake, Hanoi’s largest lake, offers a quieter setting beside historic pagodas such as Tran Quoc. The One Pillar Pagoda, built in the eleventh century, is famed for its distinctive structure rising above a pond. Hanoi’s cultural life is also expressed through water puppetry, traditional music, festivals, and its celebrated food. Craft villages around the city have long specialized in products such as ceramics, silk, paper, and carved wood. Bat Trang is especially renowned for its pottery, while Van Phuc is known for silk weaving. Together, Hanoi’s historic sites, waterways, and living crafts make it a distinctive center of Vietnamese heritage.

Warren Earl Burger was the fifteenth chief justice of the United States. He led the Supreme Court from 1969 to 1986, a period of significant political and social change. Born on September 17, 1907, Burger grew up in Saint Paul, Minnesota. His parents were of German and Swiss ancestry, and his father worked as a railroad cargo inspector. Burger attended the University of Minnesota and later studied law at what is now Mitchell Hamline School of Law. He earned his law degree in 1931 while working to help pay for his education. After graduating, he practiced law in Minnesota and became active in Republican politics. In 1953, President Dwight D. Eisenhower appointed him assistant attorney general in charge of the Justice Department’s Civil Division. In that role, Burger argued cases for the federal government before the Supreme Court. Eisenhower appointed him to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit in 1956. Burger served there for thirteen years and became known as a capable, conservative judge. In 1969, Eisenhower’s successor, President Richard Nixon, nominated Burger to become chief justice. The Senate confirmed him, and he took office on June 23. Burger replaced Earl Warren, whose court had issued influential decisions on civil rights and individual liberties. Observers expected Burger to move the Court in a more conservative direction. The Court did become more receptive to some limits on government regulation and criminal defendants’ rights. However, its decisions did not follow a simple or consistent political pattern. Burger’s leadership style differed from Warren’s. He was known for managing the Court’s workload and encouraging careful discussion among the justices. He generally sought consensus but could be formal and reserved in his dealings with colleagues. The chief justice presides over the Court’s private conferences and assigns opinions when voting with the majority. Burger used these responsibilities to influence how the Court considered cases and expressed its decisions. He also faced the challenge of leading a Court with strong disagreements among its members. One of the most consequential cases decided under Burger was Roe v. Wade in 1973. The Court recognized a constitutional right to abortion, though Burger joined the majority without writing a separate opinion. The decision shaped American law and politics for decades. In United States v. Nixon in 1974, the Court unanimously rejected President Nixon’s claim of absolute executive privilege. Burger wrote the opinion, which required Nixon to turn over recordings sought in a criminal investigation. The ruling affirmed that the president is subject to the rule of law. Nixon resigned shortly afterward. In Furman v. Georgia in 1972, the Court struck down existing death-penalty laws as inconsistently applied. Burger dissented, warning that the ruling went too far and could undermine the death penalty itself. Four years later, in Gregg v. Georgia, he wrote the majority opinion upholding revised capital-punishment laws. He argued that states could impose the death penalty under procedures designed to guide sentencing and reduce arbitrary outcomes. In Milliken v. Bradley in 1974, the Court limited a federal desegregation remedy to Detroit and nearby suburbs. Burger wrote the majority opinion, requiring evidence of violations across district lines before imposing a cross-district remedy. Critics said the ruling made it harder to address segregation between city and suburban schools. Burger also participated in decisions that expanded some rights. In Wisconsin v. Yoder in 1972, the Court supported Amish parents who objected to compulsory schooling beyond eighth grade on religious grounds. Burger wrote the opinion, concluding that Wisconsin’s requirement substantially burdened the family’s religious practices. The case illustrates that the Court’s rulings could protect individual liberty even under a conservative chief justice. Burger believed that the American justice system needed practical improvements. He was particularly concerned about crowded courts, slow proceedings, and unequal access to legal help. He supported better training for judges and lawyers and encouraged the use of modern court administration. In 1971, he helped establish the National Center for State Courts. The organization assists state courts with research, training, and management practices. Burger also advocated for alternative ways to resolve disputes, including mediation and arbitration. He argued that not every conflict needed to be decided through a lengthy trial. In 1976, he helped launch the National Institute for Trial Advocacy. The institute trains lawyers in courtroom skills through practical exercises. Burger also promoted public understanding of the courts and the legal system. He often spoke about the importance of civic education and respect for the rule of law. In 1981, President Ronald Reagan appointed him chair of the commission that planned the celebration of the U.S. Constitution’s bicentennial. Burger became an energetic advocate for the Constitution’s history and meaning. In 1986, he retired from the Supreme Court and was succeeded as chief justice by William Rehnquist. After retiring, Burger continued public service and legal education work. He served as chancellor of the College of William & Mary and remained involved in constitutional commemorations. Burger died on June 25, 1995, in Washington, D.C. His legacy includes both important constitutional decisions and efforts to improve how courts operate. His Court issued rulings that shaped presidential power, abortion rights, capital punishment, religious liberty, and school desegregation. The Burger Court also upheld some protections established during the Warren Court while narrowing others. Historians continue to debate how much Burger personally influenced the Court’s broader direction. His administrative reforms, however, helped make court management and legal training lasting parts of national justice-system discussions. Studying Burger’s life shows how a chief justice can shape the law through opinions and guide the courts through leadership.

The death of Chinese Nobel Peace Prize laureate Liu Xiaobo has drawn international condemnation and renewed calls for authorities to free his widow, Liu Xia, from years of restrictions.

Liu, 61, died Thursday in a hospital in the northeastern city of Shenyang, where he was being treated for late-stage liver cancer while serving an 11-year prison sentence.

Chinese officials said he received medical care, but his transfer from prison to hospital came only after his cancer was advanced.

Liu was convicted in 2009 of “inciting subversion of state power” after helping draft Charter 08, a petition calling for political reform and stronger protections for human rights.

He was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 2010 while in prison, a decision that Beijing denounced and sought to prevent him from receiving.

His death has intensified scrutiny of China’s treatment of political dissidents and the circumstances surrounding his medical care.

The United States, Germany, France and other governments expressed sorrow and urged Beijing to allow Liu Xia to leave China.

The United Nations human rights chief called for her release and said she should be able to live without surveillance or intimidation.

Liu Xia, a poet and artist, has been under tight restrictions since her husband was awarded the Nobel Prize.

Although she has not been formally charged with a crime, she has been largely confined to her Beijing home, with limited access to friends and communications.

Rights groups say authorities have used isolation and surveillance to punish her for her husband’s activism.

Her brother, Liu Hui, has also faced legal pressure, raising concerns among supporters about the family’s safety.

The couple had no children, and Liu Xia was among the few people permitted to visit him during his imprisonment.

In recent months, supporters and foreign officials had called for Liu to receive treatment abroad, arguing that his condition required specialized care.

Chinese authorities said he was too ill to travel and that foreign medical experts had been involved in his treatment.

The government’s account has not satisfied critics, who say Liu should have been granted greater freedom and access to care earlier.

The Chinese Foreign Ministry rejected what it called foreign interference and defended the handling of Liu’s case.

State media offered limited coverage of his death, while online discussion was quickly curtailed.

References to Liu and his Nobel Prize were blocked or restricted on some Chinese social media platforms.

Outside China, activists gathered at diplomatic missions and held vigils in his memory.

Many described Liu as a peaceful advocate who sought gradual democratic change rather than confrontation.

His writings and public statements repeatedly called for an end to one-party rule and respect for fundamental rights.

Charter 08, signed by hundreds of Chinese citizens, became a landmark document in the country’s contemporary pro-democracy movement.

Liu’s imprisonment drew sustained criticism from international rights organizations, which had long demanded his release.

His death has renewed questions about the risks faced by those who challenge the ruling Communist Party.

Advocates say Liu Xia’s continued confinement would compound the suffering of a family already marked by years of separation.

They are urging Beijing to let her travel abroad, reunite with friends and choose where to live.

Governments have also called for China to disclose more information about Liu’s final days and the medical decisions made on his behalf.

For many supporters, his death is both a personal tragedy and a reminder of the limits placed on dissent in China.

The calls for Liu Xia’s freedom are likely to continue, as international attention turns to her safety and future.

Seeking guidance from multiple sources can help people make wiser decisions. No single person knows everything, so hearing different perspectives can reveal options we might have missed. For example, a student choosing a career could talk with teachers, family members, and professionals in the field. Each person may offer useful advice based on different experiences. Comparing these viewpoints helps the student understand both the opportunities and challenges involved. Multiple sources can also help us check whether information is accurate. If several reliable people agree, we may feel more confident in our understanding. If they disagree, we can investigate further instead of accepting the first answer we hear. This process encourages critical thinking and careful judgment. It can also help us recognize our own assumptions and biases. However, seeking advice from many people does not mean following every suggestion. Some guidance may be outdated, mistaken, or unsuitable for our situation. We should consider each source’s knowledge, experience, and possible bias. Then we can weigh the advice alongside our own goals and values. Asking questions and comparing evidence helps us make a thoughtful choice. In the end, guidance from multiple sources gives us a broader view and greater confidence. It helps us learn from others while taking responsibility for our own decisions.

Adding seventh chords and rhythmic groove gives the 12-bar blues its characteristic tension and swing. The standard progression uses three main chords, built on the first, fourth, and fifth scale degrees. These are commonly called the I, IV, and V chords. In the key of A, they are A, D, and E.

A basic 12-bar pattern usually assigns four bars to the I chord, two bars to the IV chord, and two more to the I chord. The V chord often fills the ninth bar, followed by the IV chord in the tenth. The final two bars return to the I chord, though the V chord may appear in the last bar to lead back to the beginning.

To add a blues sound, change each major triad into a dominant seventh chord. A dominant seventh chord contains a root, major third, perfect fifth, and minor seventh. In A, this gives A7, D7, and E7. The minor seventh adds a gentle dissonance that suits the blues.

These seventh chords are not just decoration; they create movement between the harmony and the melody. The seventh in each chord can feel as though it wants to resolve downward. Blues melodies often play with this tension rather than resolving it immediately. Try singing or playing a blues phrase over A7, D7, and E7 to hear how the notes interact.

A common variation changes the second bar from I7 to IV7. In A, the opening becomes A7 for one bar, then D7 for one bar, before returning to A7. This early chord change makes the progression feel more active. Another variation uses the V7 chord in bar twelve, creating a turnaround that points back to bar one.

Rhythm gives the progression its groove. Start by counting four even beats in each bar: “one, two, three, four.” Then emphasize beats two and four, which often creates a relaxed, danceable backbeat. Keep the pulse steady even when the chords change.

One classic blues accompaniment uses a shuffle feel. Instead of playing three evenly spaced subdivisions, lengthen the first and shorten the second, creating a long-short pattern. Count it as “trip-a-let, trip-a-let,” while playing the first and third parts of each triplet. Use this pattern consistently, but avoid making it so rigid that the music feels mechanical.

A guitarist can play a shuffle by alternating between the root and a nearby higher note. For example, on A7, alternate A with notes such as C-sharp and E in a repeating figure. A pianist can use a left-hand bass pattern while the right hand plays clipped chord accents. Bassists can outline the chord tones, especially the root, third, fifth, and seventh.

Dynamics and articulation also shape the groove. Play short, controlled chords rather than letting every note ring for the full bar. Vary the strength of your accents, and leave small spaces for the vocal or lead instrument. A slight delay behind the beat can sound relaxed, while playing ahead of it can create urgency.

Practice slowly with a metronome, first playing one chord per bar and then adding the full 12-bar form. Say the bar numbers aloud so you can feel where the IV and V chords arrive. Once the changes feel secure, try a shuffle pattern and add a turnaround. Listen to recordings of different blues styles, since the groove can range from a light swing to a heavy, straight pulse.

Rain sheeted down the café windows, turning the street into a gray blur. My friend Theo and I had been trapped inside for nearly an hour. The coffee was lukewarm, the chairs were stiff, and even the radio sounded tired. Theo sighed and watched a woman reading by the window. “I’m going to say something charming,” he announced. I looked up from my tea. “You’re going to say something,” I corrected. He stood, smoothed his damp hair, and crossed the room. The woman glanced up as he approached. Theo leaned one elbow on her table with what he clearly believed was effortless confidence. “Reading anything good?” he asked. “A mystery,” she said, smiling politely. “I love mysteries,” Theo replied. “Especially the ones where I know the ending.” She raised an eyebrow. “And what’s the ending?” “We get coffee together,” he said. For one perfect second, the café went quiet. Then Theo’s elbow slipped on the table’s polished edge. His arm shot sideways, knocking his own cup into his lap. He sprang back with a yelp and grabbed a napkin. The napkin stuck to his wet trousers. “I meant to do that,” he said, trying to recover. The woman pressed her lips together, fighting a smile. Theo nodded toward her book. “So, who did it?” “The gardener,” she said. “That’s usually the case,” he replied. “Though sometimes it’s the coffee.” He looked down at the spreading stain on his trousers. That was when I snorted. Theo turned to glare at me, which only made the napkin flutter like a tiny white flag. The woman laughed, and then I did too, loud enough to startle the barista. Theo attempted to sit down, missed the chair, and caught himself on its back. A fresh burst of laughter escaped me. Soon the woman was laughing, the barista was laughing, and even a man by the door was grinning. Theo bowed as if he had planned the whole performance. “I’m glad I could brighten your rainy day,” he said. The woman closed her book and offered him her spare napkin. “You certainly made it memorable,” she replied. Theo took it, blushing beneath his crooked smile. Outside, the rain kept falling, but the café no longer felt dreary.

An optimistic mindset can help people face challenges and keep moving toward their goals. It means expecting that effort can lead to progress, even when success is not guaranteed. Optimistic people do not ignore problems; they look for ways to solve them. This attitude can help them stay focused when distractions or difficulties appear.

For example, a student who receives a low test score can feel discouraged or decide to learn from mistakes. With optimism, the student may review the questions, ask for help, and prepare more carefully next time. Believing that improvement is possible makes it easier to keep working. Small steps can then lead to stronger skills and better results.

Optimism also encourages people to work hard over time. Goals often require patience, and progress may be slow. When people believe their actions matter, they are more willing to practice and try again. They can treat setbacks as temporary rather than as proof that they should give up. This helps them build resilience and confidence.

However, optimism works best when it is paired with realistic plans and steady effort. Simply wishing for success is not enough. People need to set clear goals, manage their time, and adjust their approach when necessary. An optimistic mindset can give them the motivation to do these things.

In life, people will face uncertainty and disappointment. A hopeful outlook can help them respond with courage instead of fear. By staying focused, working hard, and learning from setbacks, they can make meaningful progress. Optimism does not guarantee that every goal will be reached, but it can help people keep trying and discover what they are capable of.

A council’s proposal to boycott Israeli goods has prompted a heated debate over political protest, discrimination and antisemitism. Supporters say the measure would use the council’s purchasing power to oppose Israeli government policies and show solidarity with Palestinians. They argue that boycotts are a legitimate form of nonviolent pressure and do not target Jewish people. Critics say singling out Israel risks applying a double standard and could create a hostile climate for Jewish residents. Some have also questioned whether the proposal would exclude suppliers because of their national origin, potentially raising legal concerns. The council has not yet adopted the measure, and its precise scope remains under discussion. A draft reportedly focuses on procurement decisions, though questions remain about how goods linked to Israel would be identified. Opponents have urged councillors to reject the plan or seek legal advice before proceeding. Supporters say the wording can be carefully framed to distinguish criticism of a state from prejudice against a people. Local Jewish groups and Palestinian advocates have called for their concerns to be heard in the debate. The dispute reflects a wider argument over how public bodies should respond to international conflicts. It also highlights the difficulty of separating political advocacy from conduct that communities may experience as discriminatory. Councillors are expected to consider the proposal at an upcoming meeting, where they may amend it or postpone a decision.

Mara woke on the bathroom floor with the taste of copper in her mouth and no memory of how she’d arrived there. The tiles beneath her cheek were cold, and the mirror showed a woman she almost recognized. She pushed herself upright, then froze. Perched on the sink was a figure shaped like a parrot, though its feathers looked like scraps of stained glass. One black eye blinked at her. “You’re late,” it said in a voice like her own. Mara gripped the sink. “Late for what?” The figure tipped its head toward the bathtub, where the shower curtain stirred though the window was shut. “For remembering.” She looked into the mirror again and saw the tub behind her, full of dark water. When she turned, the tub was empty. The parrot figure ruffled its bright wings. “You promised not to let the house forget you.” “I don’t live here,” Mara whispered, but the words felt borrowed. The creature clicked its beak, and every light in the bathroom went out. In the darkness, Mara heard her own voice from behind the curtain, softly asking to be let out. She reached for the curtain, shaking. The parrot landed on her shoulder, warm and heavy. “Choose carefully,” it murmured, “which one of you gets to leave.” Then the mirror lit up, and two Maras stared back.

Graduating from high school in three years may sound like a smart way to save time and money. However, finishing early can create challenges that students do not always expect. High school is not only a place to earn credits; it is also a time to grow and prepare for adult life. Students who rush through their classes may have less time to explore subjects they enjoy. They might also miss chances to take advanced courses, join clubs, play sports, or develop leadership skills. These activities can help students discover their strengths and interests. Leaving early may also mean spending less time with friends and trusted teachers. Strong relationships at school can provide support during an important stage of life. In addition, some students may feel pressured to choose a career or college path before they are ready. A shorter schedule can make it harder to balance demanding classes with work, family responsibilities, and rest. Students who skip important lessons may enter college or a job without all the knowledge they need. They may also feel less mature than classmates who graduate at the usual age. Early graduation can be especially difficult for students who have not yet decided what they want to do next. Although it may work well for some, it should not be treated as the best choice for everyone. Schools should help students consider both the benefits and the possible costs before making a decision. In many cases, taking the full four years can give students more time to learn, grow, and prepare for the future.

Solar-powered roads use photovoltaic panels to turn sunlight into electricity. The panels may be built into road surfaces, sidewalks, parking lots, or nearby roadside structures. In theory, a large road network could collect substantial energy because it covers a wide area and is exposed to daylight. The electricity could power streetlights, signs, and nearby buildings, or be sent to the grid. Some designs include sensors and illuminated markings that can warn drivers about hazards or changing conditions. These features could improve safety, but they must remain visible, reliable, and durable in rain, snow, and heavy traffic. Road surfaces face demanding conditions, so solar panels need strong protection and regular maintenance. They can also be costly, and their output may be lower than that of conventional solar panels installed at an ideal angle. Solar roads could support electric vehicles by supplying renewable power to charging stations along highways. In the future, some systems might charge vehicles wirelessly while they travel, though this technology is still developing. Their overall environmental benefit depends on manufacturing, repairs, energy production, and how long the panels last. Solar-powered roads are promising, but careful testing is needed to determine where they are practical and worthwhile.

Science and technology news helps us understand how research is changing the world.
It spans subjects as varied as climate change, biology, space exploration, and emerging technologies.
These fields are connected by a shared goal: to explain how systems work and how people can respond to change.
Good science reporting distinguishes measured evidence from speculation.
It also explains what researchers know, what remains uncertain, and why the findings matter.

Climate change is a long-term shift in Earth’s climate, including changes in average temperature and weather patterns.
Human activities, especially burning coal, oil, and gas, are the main cause of recent global warming.
These activities release greenhouse gases that trap heat in the atmosphere.
Measurements from thermometers, satellites, oceans, and ice all contribute to the evidence.
The planet has warmed substantially since the late nineteenth century.
The pace and impacts of warming vary across regions.
Heat waves, heavy rainfall, drought, and wildfire-conducive conditions are changing in many places.
No single weather event is caused by climate change alone, but warming can alter its likelihood or intensity.
Scientists use climate models to explore possible futures under different emissions pathways.
A model is a tool for understanding patterns, not a precise forecast of every local event.
Reducing greenhouse gas emissions can limit future warming.
Clean electricity, efficient buildings, and low-emission transport are among the available approaches.
Adaptation measures help communities prepare for impacts that are already occurring or expected.
Examples include heat plans, flood protections, and more resilient water systems.
Climate news should explain both the evidence and the choices involved in responding.

Future technologies may reshape how people work, travel, communicate, and produce energy.
Artificial intelligence can recognize patterns and generate content, but its abilities and limitations depend on the task.
AI systems can make errors, reflect biased data, or produce confident statements that are not true.
Human review is important when automated decisions affect health, safety, or rights.
Robotics combines sensors, software, and mechanical design to carry out physical tasks.
Robots are used in factories, hospitals, farms, and places too dangerous for people to enter.
Advances in batteries could help store renewable electricity and power vehicles.
Researchers are also investigating new materials and manufacturing methods.
Some technologies move quickly from laboratory experiments to useful products.
Others face barriers such as cost, safety, energy use, or limited performance.
A promising early result does not guarantee a practical technology.
News coverage is more useful when it describes these obstacles as well as potential benefits.

Biology studies living organisms, from tiny microbes to entire ecosystems.
Genetics examines how biological information is stored and passed between generations.
Modern tools can read DNA faster and more cheaply than earlier methods.
Gene-editing techniques can alter selected sections of genetic material.
Their possible medical uses include studying disease and developing treatments.
Gene editing also raises questions about safety, access, consent, and effects across generations.
Vaccines train the immune system to recognize a disease-causing organism or one of its components.
Clinical trials test whether a treatment is safe and effective in people.
A result in a small trial may not apply to everyone.
Researchers often need larger studies and long-term monitoring.
Microbes influence human health, agriculture, and the global environment.
Some bacteria cause disease, while many others support digestion and ecosystem processes.
Biodiversity describes the variety of life, including differences within and between species.
Habitat loss, pollution, invasive species, and climate change can threaten biodiversity.
Conservation research helps identify ways to protect species and restore ecosystems.

Space science explores objects and processes beyond Earth’s atmosphere.
Telescopes collect light and other signals to study stars, galaxies, and distant planets.
Spacecraft can visit nearby worlds, measure their surfaces, and return data to Earth.
Mars missions investigate the planet’s history and whether it once had conditions suitable for life.
Finding evidence of past water is not the same as finding evidence of past life.
Scientists also study icy moons that may contain oceans beneath their surfaces.
Exoplanets are planets orbiting stars beyond our solar system.
Astronomers can estimate some properties of exoplanets by observing how they affect their host stars.
A planet’s location in a potentially habitable zone does not prove that it supports life.
The Moon is a focus of renewed exploration and could help test technologies for longer missions.
Space observations also support Earth science, communications, and navigation.
Satellites can monitor sea ice, vegetation, clouds, and changing land conditions.
Space research often depends on international cooperation and careful mission planning.

Planetary hazards are events that can threaten people and infrastructure.
Asteroids and comets sometimes pass near Earth, though most pose no danger.
Astronomers track many near-Earth objects and refine their orbits as observations improve.
A close approach does not automatically mean an impact is likely.
Impact monitoring compares an object’s path with Earth’s position over time.
A major impact would be rare but could have severe consequences.
Researchers are testing whether spacecraft can change the path of a potentially hazardous asteroid.
The DART mission demonstrated that a spacecraft collision can alter a small asteroid moon’s orbit.
Solar storms are another space hazard.
They can disrupt radio communications, navigation signals, and some power systems.
Forecasters monitor the Sun and Earth’s magnetic environment to give warning when possible.
Volcanoes, earthquakes, and tsunamis are planetary hazards rooted in Earth’s natural processes.
Scientists cannot reliably predict the exact time and place of most earthquakes.
Monitoring, building standards, evacuation plans, and public education can reduce harm.
Understanding hazards does not eliminate risk, but it can improve preparation.

Across all these subjects, reliable news depends on clear evidence and careful explanations.
Readers can check whether a report identifies its sources and distinguishes facts from interpretation.
They can also ask whether a claim has been tested by independent researchers.
Scientific knowledge changes as new measurements and better methods become available.
That change is a strength of science, not a sign that evidence is meaningless.
Curiosity, skepticism, and attention to context help everyone make sense of a rapidly changing world.
