Summer assignments should give students the chance to choose and design their own projects. A little freedom can make learning more interesting. Instead of completing the same worksheet as everyone else, students can explore a question they genuinely care about. One student might study how plants grow, while another might create a short story or build a simple model. These projects can connect school subjects to everyday life. When students care about their topics, they are more likely to stay curious and put in effort. Choosing a project also helps students practice making decisions. They must consider what they want to learn and how they can show it. This process can build confidence and independence. Designing a project requires planning, research, and problem-solving. Those skills are useful in school and beyond. Students may also discover talents they did not know they had. A creative project can make summer learning feel less like a chore. However, students should not have unlimited freedom without guidance. Some projects may be too difficult, expensive, or time-consuming. Others might not connect clearly to the skills the assignment is meant to teach. Teachers can prevent these problems by offering a few project options or setting clear guidelines. For example, students could choose a topic but include research, writing, and a final presentation. Teachers should also provide examples so students understand what a successful project looks like. Families may have different amounts of time, money, and supplies, so projects should be possible to complete with basic materials. Students should not be graded on how expensive or polished their projects appear. Instead, teachers can assess effort, learning, and how well students explain their ideas. Check-ins during the summer can help students stay on track and ask questions. A flexible deadline can also make the assignment more manageable. Some students may prefer a traditional task, so offering choices can help everyone find a suitable approach. Choice does not mean that learning goals disappear. It means students can reach those goals in ways that match their interests and strengths. When students help shape their assignments, they take greater responsibility for their learning. Summer projects can then be both educational and enjoyable. For these reasons, students should be allowed to choose and design their own summer projects, with clear expectations and teacher support.

Schools should encourage students to take part in extracurricular activities, but they should not make participation mandatory for everyone. Clubs, sports, music groups, and volunteer programs can help students discover interests beyond the classroom. They also give students opportunities to build friendships with people who share similar goals. By working with a team, students can practice communication, cooperation, and leadership. These experiences may help them feel more connected to their school.

However, not every student has the same schedule or circumstances. Some students need to care for younger siblings or work after school to help their families. Others may have health conditions, transportation problems, or responsibilities that make regular participation difficult. Requiring every student to join an activity could add stress to an already demanding school day. Students who are forced to participate may also lose interest in activities they might otherwise enjoy.

Schools should recognize that students develop in different ways. Some may prefer sports or performing arts, while others may pursue hobbies or personal projects outside school. Academic study, family responsibilities, and rest can also be important uses of a student’s time. A single rule may not account for these different needs. Instead, schools could offer a wide range of activities at different times and provide support such as late buses or low-cost supplies.

Teachers and counselors can introduce students to extracurricular options and explain their benefits. They can also help students find activities that fit their interests and schedules. Schools might encourage participation through awards, events, or opportunities to try a club without a long-term commitment. Students should be invited to take part rather than pressured to do so. This approach respects their choices while making school activities accessible.

Extracurricular involvement can enrich a student’s education, but it is most valuable when students choose it willingly. Making it mandatory may create unfair burdens and reduce the enjoyment these activities are meant to provide. Schools should promote participation and remove barriers, while allowing students to decide how they spend their time.

California’s renewable-energy boom is reshaping the state’s power grid, producing abundant electricity at some hours and exposing new challenges at others. On sunny spring afternoons, solar farms and rooftop panels can generate more power than consumers need. The oversupply has pushed wholesale electricity prices below zero at times, meaning some generators effectively pay to keep producing. The trend reflects a rapid shift in a state that has set ambitious goals for clean energy and carbon reduction. It also highlights a basic mismatch between when renewable power is most plentiful and when electricity demand peaks.

Solar generation typically surges around midday, while household and commercial demand often rises in the evening. As the sun sets, solar output drops quickly even as people turn on lights, appliances and cooling systems. Grid operators must then replace the falling supply with other resources, including batteries, hydropower, natural gas and electricity imported from neighboring states. Managing that transition has become one of the most pressing tasks for California’s energy planners. The challenge is commonly known as the “duck curve,” a graph showing a steep decline in net demand during daylight hours followed by a sharp evening ramp.

Negative prices are not, by themselves, evidence that the grid is failing. They can signal that electricity supply is temporarily exceeding demand, or that transmission constraints prevent power from reaching consumers who could use it. Some generators are able to reduce output, but others face technical or financial reasons to keep operating. Solar plants may also receive payments under contracts that do not track hourly market prices. When excess energy cannot be absorbed, operators may curtail renewable generation, ordering facilities to reduce output.

California has expanded battery storage to shift some midday electricity into the evening. Batteries can charge when power is abundant and discharge when demand rises, helping reduce reliance on fossil-fuel plants during peak hours. State officials say storage capacity has grown rapidly, but it still must be paired with enough transmission, generation and flexible demand to serve the system through changing conditions. Batteries also have limits: they store energy for a finite period and must be recharged. Longer-duration storage remains a key need, particularly during extended periods of cloudy weather or high demand.

The surplus has prompted broader debate over how to use clean electricity that would otherwise be curtailed. Proposals include encouraging electric-vehicle charging and water heating during midday, expanding industrial demand, and producing hydrogen with renewable power. Better coordination across the western United States could also help move surplus electricity to regions where demand is higher. But new transmission lines can take years to plan and build, and neighboring states may experience similar supply patterns.

The economics of the transition are complicated. Low or negative wholesale prices can reduce revenues for generators and affect investment decisions, even as consumers may not see those prices directly on their bills. Retail electricity rates also include costs for transmission, distribution, wildfire mitigation and other programs. Policymakers are weighing how to maintain reliable service while ensuring that the costs and benefits of the transition are shared fairly. They must also consider how to protect customers from price spikes when renewable output falls or demand rises unexpectedly.

Grid operators have several tools to balance supply and demand, including forecasting, reserve generation and programs that encourage customers to shift usage. Forecasting solar output and electricity demand has improved, but sudden weather changes can still complicate planning. Heat waves are especially demanding because they increase air-conditioning use across the state and can strain equipment. Wildfires and extreme weather can also threaten transmission infrastructure. A reliable grid must therefore be prepared for both periods of excess power and periods of scarcity.

California’s experience is being watched by other states and countries pursuing rapid renewable-energy growth. The state has shown that large amounts of solar and wind can be integrated into a modern electricity system, but doing so requires changes beyond building generation. Storage, transmission, flexible consumption and market rules all play a role. The pace of those changes will help determine how much clean power can be used rather than wasted.

For now, California’s midday surplus is both a sign of progress and a warning about the work ahead. Cheap electricity can benefit the grid if it can be stored, moved or consumed at the right time. Without those options, generators may be curtailed while evening demand still depends on more expensive resources. Officials and utilities are searching for ways to align supply with demand throughout the day. The success of that effort will shape the cost, reliability and climate impact of California’s power system.

Exploring Venus is worthwhile, even though its extreme heat, crushing pressure, and toxic atmosphere make it one of the most dangerous places in the solar system. The planet’s surface is hot enough to melt lead, and its dense atmosphere presses down with a force similar to being deep underwater on Earth. Venus’s clouds also contain corrosive sulfuric acid, making direct exploration especially difficult. These conditions mean that spacecraft sent to the surface can survive for only a short time. However, the challenges do not outweigh the scientific value of studying the planet.

Venus is similar to Earth in size and may once have had oceans, so learning how it changed could help us understand our own planet’s future. Scientists can investigate why Venus became so hot and whether a powerful greenhouse effect transformed its climate. This knowledge may improve predictions about climate change on Earth. Studying Venus can also reveal how rocky planets form and evolve under different conditions. Its unusual atmosphere and volcanic landscape may hold clues about geological activity. Even the possibility of active volcanoes makes Venus an exciting place to investigate.

Exploration does not have to depend on people visiting the surface. Orbiters can map the planet, while specially designed probes can collect measurements before the heat and pressure destroy them. New materials and technology may allow future landers to operate for longer periods. Researchers can also study Venus from above its harshest conditions, including in its upper atmosphere. Although missions are expensive and technically difficult, careful planning can make them valuable. Each mission can build on what scientists have learned from earlier ones. In the end, Venus is worth exploring because its dangers are also part of what makes it scientifically important. By studying this extreme world, we can better understand Earth and the many kinds of planets in the universe.

Authorities in Honduras are investigating a deadly fire at a prison as families wait for officials to identify the victims. The blaze broke out inside the facility, prompting an emergency response and leaving numerous people dead or injured. Officials have not yet released a final toll, and identification efforts are taking longer than relatives had hoped. The delay reflects the difficulty of examining badly damaged remains and confirming identities through forensic tests.

Investigators are working to establish how the fire started and whether safety procedures were followed. Authorities have said they are gathering evidence and interviewing people who were at the prison. The cause has not been confirmed, and officials have urged the public to avoid circulating unverified accounts.

The fire has renewed scrutiny of Honduras’s overcrowded prison system. Human rights groups and other critics have long warned that crowded facilities, inadequate infrastructure and limited staffing can make emergencies harder to contain. Overcrowding can also complicate evacuations and access to medical care, though investigators have not said it caused this blaze.

Families have gathered to seek information, while some have called for clearer communication from authorities. Officials are expected to provide further updates as forensic work continues. The tragedy has added pressure on the government to explain what happened and how similar incidents might be prevented. For now, relatives face uncertainty as investigators work to identify the dead and determine responsibility.

When Mara left Daniel, she took only a suitcase and the blue teacup her mother had given her. She left the rest because every object in their house seemed to remember his hands.

For six months, she slept with the lights on in a small apartment above a bakery. She changed her phone number twice and walked home by different streets. Still, whenever a car slowed beside her, her breath stopped.

Daniel sent no messages. That frightened her more than his shouting ever had.

Then, on a rainy Thursday, a bouquet arrived at her office. Tucked between the white lilies was a note: You can’t hide forever.

Mara showed it to the police, who promised to check the building cameras. They asked if she wanted to stay with a friend. She said no, though she could not explain why.

That evening, she found the lock on her apartment door scratched. Nothing was missing, and the rooms were undisturbed. On the kitchen table sat the blue teacup, though she had left it at work.

She called the police again. While waiting, she stood in the hallway, unable to make herself enter.

A shadow moved behind the frosted glass of the stairwell door. Mara ran downstairs and out into the rain.

Daniel stepped from beneath the bakery’s awning. He looked older, his hair soaked flat against his forehead. In one hand he held a small box.

“You always did run from a conversation,” he said.

Mara backed toward the street. “Stay away from me.”

He smiled, the same patient smile he used to wear before he broke things. “I came to give you something.”

The box lay on the pavement between them. A tiny music box, scratched and familiar, played the lullaby Mara’s father used to hum.

Daniel had stolen it from her childhood home years ago. She stared at it, unable to move.

“I thought you’d want it back,” he said. “I thought you’d remember who took care of you.”

Behind him, a bus hissed at the curb. A dozen people watched through its windows, but Mara saw only Daniel.

His hand lifted—not quickly, not even toward her. He reached for the box.

Mara flinched so violently that her shoulder struck the brick wall. The box toppled, and its tune faltered.

Daniel’s smile vanished. For a moment, he looked almost surprised.

“There,” he whispered. “That’s what I wanted to see.”

The words opened a door in her mind. The flowers, the scratched lock, the cup moved from one place to another: none of it had been meant to hurt her body.

He had wanted proof that he could still reach inside her and make her afraid.

The police car turned the corner, its lights staining the wet street blue. Daniel stepped back, lifting both hands as if he were the injured one.

Mara saw the old script waiting for her: his calm voice, her trembling silence, everyone wondering what she had done to provoke him.

Then she took one step toward the watching passengers. “That man has been stalking me,” she called. Her voice shook, but it carried.

The bus driver opened the doors. A woman hurried down the steps and stood beside Mara. Daniel glanced at the crowd, and for the first time, he had no room to make himself look harmless.

The officers approached him. He dropped his hands and began to speak, but no one turned away from Mara.

She picked up the music box only after he was in the car. Its little song had stopped.

That night, she slept with the lights on. She still woke at every sound.

But when dawn came, she turned the lamps off herself.

At 2:13 every morning, Len arrived at the office with a mop and a thermos of coffee.
The building stood downtown, all black glass and bright, cheerful lettering: VANTAGE FUTURES.
Len had worked there for eleven years, long enough to stop asking what the company did.
His job was to clean up after it.

The first perk was the elevator.
It never went down.
Every night, Len rode it to the basement and came out on a different floor of the building.
Management called this “spatial flexibility” and deducted nothing from his pay.

The second perk was the vending machine.
It stocked ordinary chips, stale cookies, and small silver pills labeled TOMORROW.
Len had tried one once.
For the next day, he knew the winning lottery numbers, the name of his eventual dentist, and exactly how the cafeteria soup would taste.
He still couldn’t remember where he’d left his lunch.

On his route, he passed the executive conference room.
The carpet there was always damp, though no one spilled anything.
After meetings, the chairs sometimes faced the wall.
Len turned them around and found little handprints on the backs.

He was used to the alarms.
One warned of fire, one of flooding, and one of a “minor timeline discrepancy.”
The last one rang most often.
When it did, Len waited in the supply closet until the clocks agreed again.

The company’s health plan covered one resurrection per employee.
Len had never needed it, but the form required a beneficiary.
He’d written “whoever finds me.”
The plan administrator had returned it with a note: “Please be specific.”

That night, the alarm for a minor timeline discrepancy rang at 2:47.
Len was mopping outside the chief executive’s office when the door opened.
A younger version of himself stepped out, wearing a janitor’s uniform and carrying the same old mop.
The younger Len looked exhausted.
“You’re still here?” he asked.
Len shrugged.
“Apparently.”

Behind them, the office lights flickered.
A red message appeared on every screen: PLEASE EVACUATE THIS VERSION OF THE BUILDING.
The younger Len pointed toward the stairwell.
Len pointed toward the elevator.
They both knew better.

The elevator doors slid open.
Inside was a sunny beach, a blue sky, and a woman in a Vantage badge holding two coffees.
She smiled at Len as if she’d been expecting him.
“Your wellness retreat is ready,” she said.
Len looked at his mop, then at the dark corridor behind him.
“Does it have a bathroom?” he asked.
“It has three,” she said.
“None are in the same reality.”

Len stepped inside.
The younger janitor followed, muttering that this was probably against policy.
The doors closed just as the office began to fold in on itself.
For the first time in eleven years, Len left a mess behind.
The company sent him a bonus for initiative before the beach disappeared.
It arrived by email, addressed to “Whoever Finds Me.”

ADHD: Research, Treatment, Development, Education, and Behavior

Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, or ADHD, is a neurodevelopmental condition that can affect attention, activity levels, and impulse control. It often begins in childhood, though symptoms may continue into adolescence and adulthood. ADHD is not simply a lack of effort, poor discipline, or too much energy. Its effects vary widely from person to person, and people with ADHD also have individual strengths and interests.

Clinicians generally describe three presentations: predominantly inattentive, predominantly hyperactive-impulsive, and combined. Inattention may involve difficulty sustaining focus, organizing tasks, remembering instructions, or completing work. Hyperactivity can appear as frequent movement, restlessness, or excessive talking. Impulsivity may involve interrupting, acting quickly without considering consequences, or finding it hard to wait. Symptoms must be persistent, occur in more than one setting, and interfere with daily functioning for a diagnosis to be considered.

Research points to differences in brain development and functioning, including systems involved in attention, motivation, planning, and self-regulation. ADHD has a strong genetic component, although no single gene explains most cases. Researchers continue to study how genes interact with experiences and environmental conditions. Brain imaging can help investigate ADHD at a population level, but it cannot diagnose the condition in an individual. Diagnosis is based on a careful clinical assessment, not a single test.

Developmental factors can influence how ADHD appears over time. Premature birth and some prenatal exposures are associated with increased likelihood, but they do not determine whether a child will develop ADHD. Sleep difficulties, learning differences, anxiety, and other health conditions may occur alongside ADHD or affect similar behaviors. These factors should be assessed rather than assumed to be the cause of a person’s symptoms. A comprehensive evaluation considers developmental history, reports from multiple settings, and possible alternative explanations.

There is no single treatment that works best for everyone. Evidence-based care may include medication, behavioral interventions, educational supports, and guidance for families. Stimulant medications help many people by improving attention and impulse control, while non-stimulant options may be appropriate for others. A qualified health professional should discuss potential benefits, side effects, and monitoring with the person or family. Medication choices and doses require individualized medical supervision.

Behavioral parent training can help caregivers use clear expectations, positive reinforcement, and consistent routines. For children, behavioral approaches may strengthen skills such as planning, emotional regulation, and task completion. Cognitive behavioral therapy can help some adolescents and adults manage challenges, particularly when anxiety, low mood, or negative thinking is also present. Coaching may support practical skills, but it should not be presented as a cure. Regular follow-up allows treatment plans to change as needs develop.

At school, ADHD may affect listening, remembering instructions, organizing materials, starting assignments, or finishing work on time. A student may know the material but struggle to show that knowledge consistently. Restlessness or blurting out can also affect classroom participation and peer relationships. These behaviors should be understood as possible signs of difficulty with self-regulation, not automatically as deliberate defiance. At the same time, support can include clear and appropriate boundaries.

Helpful classroom strategies include breaking larger tasks into smaller steps and giving instructions in concise, written and spoken forms. Seating that reduces distractions, planned movement breaks, and predictable routines may also help. Schools can consider individualized accommodations, such as extra time or organizational support, according to the student’s needs and local rules. Collaboration among students, families, educators, and health professionals makes it easier to identify what works. Supports should be reviewed regularly rather than applied as a fixed formula.

ADHD can influence behavior beyond school, including household routines, friendships, and everyday decision-making. Difficulty waiting or regulating emotions can lead to conflict, while repeated struggles may affect confidence. Positive relationships, practical support, and recognition of effort can help protect well-being. Many people with ADHD also show creativity, enthusiasm, curiosity, or the ability to focus deeply on subjects that interest them. These strengths do not erase challenges, but they are an important part of a balanced understanding.

Research continues to improve understanding of how ADHD develops and which supports are most effective for different people. Findings should be interpreted carefully, because studies may vary in size, methods, and participants. No child or adult should be judged by a diagnosis alone. With accurate assessment and appropriate support, people with ADHD can learn, build relationships, and pursue their goals. Anyone concerned about persistent attention, activity, or impulse-control difficulties should seek advice from a qualified health professional.

Scotland’s Parliament has welcomed community members to mark the opening of its latest session, celebrating people whose service and achievements have made a lasting difference in local areas.

The event brought together representatives from across the country, including volunteers, campaigners, charity workers and people recognised for their contributions to community life. Their stories reflected the range of work that helps neighbourhoods thrive, from supporting vulnerable residents to preserving local traditions.

The opening ceremony offered an opportunity to place those contributions at the centre of a national occasion. Members of the public joined parliamentarians and invited guests at the Scottish Parliament in Edinburgh.

Among those recognised were people who have given years of their time to local causes. Others were honoured for stepping forward in response to particular challenges, often working quietly behind the scenes.

Community service can take many forms, and the guests represented a wide range of backgrounds and experiences. Some have helped build stronger support networks for families, while others have worked to improve access to education, sport or the arts.

Several attendees have played a role in tackling loneliness and isolation. Through clubs, outreach projects and informal support, they have helped people feel more connected to their communities.

Others have campaigned for changes to local services or raised awareness of issues affecting residents. Their work has helped bring concerns to the attention of decision-makers.

The ceremony also recognised achievements that have inspired people beyond the communities where they began. Local initiatives can provide practical solutions and encourage others to take action.

For many guests, the invitation was a chance to meet people whose work shares similar aims. It also offered a rare opportunity to see their efforts acknowledged in the setting of the national parliament.

The opening of a parliamentary session is traditionally a moment to look ahead to the work of the legislature. This year’s celebration also highlighted the contribution made by people outside political institutions.

Their efforts often depend on cooperation between volunteers, public services and local organisations. The relationships built through that work can be essential when communities face difficult circumstances.

Organisers said the event was intended to recognise both individual commitment and collective action. The achievements honoured were rooted in local knowledge and sustained relationships.

For some guests, service has grown from personal experience. They have used what they have learned to support others facing similar circumstances.

Others have become involved because they saw a need that was not being met. In many cases, their first steps were small, but their work has developed into a lasting community resource.

The gathering included people from urban neighbourhoods, rural towns and island communities. Their experiences demonstrated how local needs differ across Scotland, while also revealing common concerns.

A number of those attending have supported young people through mentoring, training and recreational activities. Such programmes can help build confidence and create new opportunities.

Community groups also play an important role in responding to poverty and hardship. Volunteers help provide advice, practical assistance and a welcoming place for people seeking support.

The event recognised cultural work as well, including efforts to protect languages, heritage and local creative life. These projects help connect generations and strengthen a sense of belonging.

For those honoured, public recognition was not the reason they began their work. Many described their involvement as a natural response to the needs of people around them.

Yet acknowledgement can bring wider attention to causes that receive little coverage. It can also encourage others to volunteer or contribute their skills.

The ceremony took place at a time when many organisations are managing rising demand and limited resources. The work of volunteers and community leaders remains an important part of local support.

Their contribution does not replace the responsibilities of public bodies, but it can help ensure that services respond to the realities of people’s lives. Community members often understand local challenges first-hand.

The event also underscored the value of listening to people with direct experience. Their perspectives can help shape decisions that affect neighbourhoods and services.

Guests welcomed the chance to share their work with representatives from other parts of Scotland. Some said that exchanging ideas could lead to new partnerships.

The opening celebration provided a public platform for stories that might otherwise remain local. It showed how individual acts of care can have a broader impact.

In recognising these achievements, the Parliament drew attention to the people who contribute to civic life without seeking office. Their work is often steady, practical and rooted in relationships.

The ceremony did not present community service as a single achievement or moment. For many, it is an ongoing commitment that changes as local needs evolve.

Those recognised have helped create safer, more welcoming and more connected places. Their impact can be seen in the people they support and the organisations they sustain.

The event’s message was clear: Scotland’s communities are strengthened by people willing to give their time, knowledge and compassion. Their work deserves to be visible as well as valued.

As the new parliamentary session begins, the stories shared at the opening offered a reminder of the role people play in shaping the country beyond Holyrood. Local action remains an essential part of Scotland’s public life.

At dusk, Mara reached the hill above the sea, where the road finally disappeared. Her boots were split, and every step seemed to borrow strength from tomorrow. Behind her lay seven years of dust, rain, and borrowed beds. Ahead, the water held no promise she could read.

She sat beside a crooked milepost and opened the small cloth pouch at her neck. Inside was a brass button from the coat of Elias, who had begun the journey beside her. He had died in a winter pass, but his last words had stayed warm in her memory. “We’re walking toward the same dawn,” he had said.

For years, Mara had thought he meant a place. She had crossed borders, rivers, and fields of burned wheat, searching for the town he named. Now she wondered if the dawn had been the walking itself. Every stranger who shared bread had become part of its light.

A shepherd had given her shelter when she was feverish. A child had guided her through a flooded lane. She had carried an old woman’s letters three hundred miles, though the woman never learned whether they arrived. Their lives had touched, briefly, and changed the shape of her road.

The sea breathed against the cliffs below. Somewhere beyond it, perhaps, waited the town from Elias’s story. Perhaps it had never existed outside his hope. Mara was too tired to decide.

She pressed the button into her palm and felt its worn edge. Devotion, she thought, was not always reaching the person one loved. Sometimes it was keeping faith with what they had asked of the world. Sometimes it was simply continuing, even when the ending had gone dark.

A lantern appeared on the shore, then another. Someone was watching for boats, or waiting for someone who had not yet come home. Mara rose slowly and began down the hill. The road did not tell her where it ended, but for the first time, she did not need it to.

The Bonobo Conservation Initiative (BCI) works to protect bonobos and their forest home in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Bonobos live only in this country, south of the Congo River, and are threatened by habitat loss, hunting, and instability. Protecting them requires more than setting aside land: it also means working with the people who live there.

BCI’s approach puts local communities at the center of conservation. Communities help shape plans for protecting forests and wildlife, rather than simply being told what rules to follow. This can build trust and make conservation more relevant to daily needs. It also recognizes that residents hold valuable knowledge about local ecosystems.

A key part of BCI’s work is supporting community-managed forest protection. Local people can help monitor forests, identify important wildlife areas, and report threats such as illegal hunting or logging. Their involvement can strengthen stewardship and help conservation efforts endure. These activities are most effective when they respect community rights and traditions.

Sustainable change also depends on livelihoods. When families have practical ways to meet their needs without relying on activities that damage forests, conservation goals become more achievable. BCI has supported community initiatives that connect forest protection with education, health, food security, and economic opportunity. The specific needs and priorities of each community shape what is useful.

Education can help people understand the ecological importance of bonobos and the benefits of healthy forests. Community discussions can also make space for local perspectives and shared decision-making. When young people take part, they can carry conservation knowledge into the future. Lasting progress is more likely when communities see both a voice and a meaningful stake in the work.

The bonobo is an important seed disperser, helping forests regenerate by spreading seeds through the landscape. Healthy forests also store carbon, protect soils, and support many other species. Their benefits reach beyond wildlife, contributing to the well-being of people who depend on forest resources. Conserving bonobos therefore supports a broader living system.

Community-centered conservation is not a quick fix. It requires long-term relationships, reliable resources, and careful attention to local concerns. It must also adapt as conditions change and measure progress in ways that include both ecological and social outcomes. No single organization can achieve these goals alone.

BCI’s model offers a useful lesson: conservation is stronger when it is built with people, not imposed on them. Respectful partnerships can help align wildlife protection with community priorities. In the Congo, that approach can support a future in which bonobos, forests, and local communities thrive together.

Syphilis is an infection caused by Treponema pallidum subsp. pallidum, a spiral-shaped bacterium that spreads mainly through sexual contact and from a pregnant person to a fetus. Related subspecies cause yaws and bejel, diseases that are usually transmitted through nonsexual contact. These treponemes are so genetically similar that distinguishing them can require detailed DNA analysis.

The genetic diversity of T. pallidum is relatively low compared with that of many bacterial pathogens. Its genome is small, and the bacterium appears to exchange genetic material with other strains less often than many microbes do. Even so, differences in DNA sequence provide clues about how strains are related and how they spread.

Researchers classify syphilis-causing strains into major genetic lineages, often described as Nichols-like and SS14-like. Both lineages have been found in multiple regions, and neither is confined to a single country. Within them, smaller genetic groups have emerged, changed in frequency, or spread across borders.

The evolutionary history of syphilis has long been debated. One question is whether syphilis originated in the Americas and reached Europe after transatlantic contact, or whether related infections were already present in Europe. Historical records are incomplete, and skeletal evidence can be difficult to interpret because different diseases may leave similar marks on bones.

Genomic research adds another source of evidence, but it has not settled every historical question. Scientists have recovered treponemal DNA from some archaeological remains, allowing comparisons with modern and ancient strains. The available ancient genomes are still few, and DNA preservation varies greatly by site and climate.

Modern global infections reveal continuing changes in the bacterium’s population. Genome sequencing has identified closely related strains in different countries, consistent with international movement and transmission networks. At the same time, local strain patterns can vary, reflecting differences in travel, sexual networks, and public health conditions.

A major concern is antibiotic resistance. Penicillin remains the recommended treatment for syphilis, and confirmed resistance to it has not been established. However, genetic changes associated with resistance to macrolide antibiotics such as azithromycin have become widespread in many regions, limiting the usefulness of those drugs.

Genetic surveillance can help track these changes and identify emerging clusters. It can also reveal whether a rise in cases involves a newly spreading lineage or an increase in transmission by strains already present. Such findings are most useful when combined with clinical, epidemiological, and social data.

Studying genetic diversity matters for diagnosis, treatment, and prevention. It may help researchers understand why some infections recur and how strains move between populations. So far, the bacterium’s limited genetic variation has made vaccine development challenging, since researchers must identify targets that remain stable and provoke protective immunity.

No single genome can explain the history of syphilis or the experiences of people affected by it. Better coverage of regions and communities that are underrepresented in research is essential for a balanced global picture. Continued sequencing, careful historical analysis, and respectful public health work can together clarify how this ancient pathogen evolves and spreads today.

A UK review of freedom of information law has found limited support for restricting the public’s right to access official records, easing campaigners’ fears of a rollback in transparency.

The review examined how the Freedom of Information Act works and whether changes are needed. It considered concerns raised by public bodies about the cost and burden of responding to requests. It also heard from campaigners, journalists and other users of the law.

Its findings suggest there is little appetite for sweeping new restrictions. That is likely to reassure advocates who feared the review could lead to a narrower right to information. The report does not, however, rule out changes to how the system operates.

Freedom of information requests allow people to seek records held by public authorities. The law applies to bodies including government departments, councils, police forces and many public services. Authorities must respond within set deadlines, subject to exemptions.

Those exemptions cover matters such as national security, personal data and some commercially sensitive information. Disputes can be taken to the Information Commissioner’s Office, which oversees the system. The commissioner can require public bodies to disclose information in certain cases.

Critics of the law have argued that handling requests can divert staff from other work. Some officials have also said that requests may be excessively broad or repeated. The review considered these concerns alongside the public interest in scrutiny.

Campaigners had warned that proposals to limit requests could make it harder to investigate government decisions. They said any weakening of the law would disproportionately affect people without other routes to obtain information. Journalists and researchers also rely on disclosure rules to examine public policy and spending.

The review’s conclusions indicate that such arguments have weighed against broad restrictions. It found limited support for measures that would substantially reduce access. The outcome is not a guarantee that the law will remain unchanged.

Officials may still consider practical adjustments to improve the handling of requests. Any proposals would need to be assessed against the right to transparency, the review indicates. The government has not yet set out a final response.

The findings come amid continuing debate over the balance between openness and administrative workload. Public bodies face a steady flow of requests, while users say disclosure can reveal information that would otherwise remain inaccessible. The review did not settle that debate.

Instead, it offers a measure of reassurance that the basic right is not facing an immediate, widely supported curtailment. Campaigners are likely to watch closely for any follow-up proposals. They have urged ministers to preserve the law’s central protections.

A spokesperson for the review said its work had considered evidence from across the system. The conclusions reflect a range of views rather than a single consensus, the spokesperson said. Public authorities have also been encouraged to improve how they publish information proactively.

Making records available without a formal request could reduce pressure on both officials and applicants. It may also help people find routine information more quickly. But campaigners say proactive publication cannot replace the ability to request specific documents.

The review’s findings will now inform discussions about the future of the legislation. Any changes could require further consultation and parliamentary scrutiny. For now, the prospect of major new barriers to disclosure appears less likely than campaigners had feared.

The “Face on Mars” is a landform in the Cydonia region that looked like a human face in early spacecraft photographs. Its appearance led some people to wonder whether an ancient civilization had built a monument there. Later, clearer images from other spacecraft showed that the feature is a natural mesa, shaped by geological processes. Shadows and the low resolution of the first photographs made its surface appear more face-like than it really is. Scientists have found no evidence that the formation was made by aliens or humans. The Cydonia face is a reminder that better evidence can change how we understand an intriguing image.

On the last night in the city, Mara answered a phone that no longer had a line. She sat alone in the emergency hotline room, beneath a ceiling light that flickered like a tired star. Outside, the streets shone with rain and the reflections of open doors. Every door stood open because everyone had left in a hurry. The radio said the gates of Heaven had appeared above the old stadium. By dawn, nearly every person on Earth had climbed the silver steps. Some took their families, some took strangers, and some went alone. Mara had stayed behind because the hotline was still ringing. She believed someone might need help on the way up.

The first call came from a boy who asked whether Heaven had dogs. Mara told him she hoped so. He laughed, and the sound made the empty room seem almost crowded. Then the line went quiet. She waited for the next call, listening to the rain tap the windows. At midnight, a woman whispered that she had reached the gates but could not find her husband. Mara asked for his name and searched the last entries in the city directory. The woman stopped speaking before Mara could read it aloud.

After that, nobody called. Mara walked through the building, checking each room as though the people might return from a break. In the cafeteria, a cup of tea had cooled beside a half-eaten sandwich. A jacket hung over the back of a chair. In the lobby, a little paper star lay beneath the desk. She picked it up and carried it outside.

The stadium was dark now, and the silver steps had vanished. Above it, the sky looked ordinary, broad and indifferent. Mara crossed the empty field and sat where the first step had been. She thought of all the voices she had answered, and all the questions she had never known how to solve. Then she turned back toward the city, where a thousand small lights still burned in unattended homes. The hotline phone began ringing behind her. Mara ran all the way back, afraid the caller might hang up. “This is Mara,” she said, breathless. On the other end, someone asked if anyone was still there. “Yes,” Mara said, and for the first time that night, she meant it for herself too.

Mara watched Link’s latest treasure-hunting video for the third time, though she hated every second of it. He was shouting beside a cracked stone pillar, waving a silver rupee at the camera. “Another ancient relic, found by yours truly!” he crowed. The pillar behind him was carved with warnings in a language older than the kingdom. Link had cropped them out of the frame.

Mara slammed her tablet shut. “He treats every ruin like a toy chest,” she muttered. Outside her window, the afternoon sky had turned the color of bruised iron. A low tremor shivered through the floorboards. Her neighbor’s chickens went silent.

She opened the tablet again and sent Link a message: Stop digging at the northern shrine. The markings are a warning. His reply arrived before she could set the tablet down. “Great tip! Any chance you know where the hidden vault is?”

Mara grabbed her coat and ran toward the shrine. She found Link there, adjusting his camera while a dark crack spread across the stone floor. “I told you to stop,” she shouted. He grinned at the lens. “And this is why we love live discoveries.”

Then the shrine groaned. A green light pulsed beneath the crack, and a shape pressed upward from the darkness. Link’s grin vanished. Mara recognized the symbols on the pillar at last: not a map, but a seal. “Put the rupee back,” she said.

He dropped it into the hollow. For a moment, nothing happened. Then the crack widened, and a long black hand curled around its edge. Link reached for his sword, but the thing dragged itself into the room. Mara snatched the camera from its stand and threw it against the wall.

The lens shattered. Link stared at it, stunned. “You can replace a camera,” Mara said, “not a kingdom.” Together they shoved the stone door closed while the creature shrieked behind them. Outside, the tremors stopped.

Link lowered his sword. “Maybe I should make a video about the warning signs,” he said. Mara gave him a tired look. “Try making one without shouting.” For once, he nodded.

The Electoral College is an important part of how the United States chooses its president. Although some people argue that the winner should be determined by the national popular vote, the current system has several advantages. It reflects the country’s federal structure, in which states share power with the national government. Each state receives electoral votes based on its representation in Congress, so both its population and its status as a state are considered. This gives smaller states a voice in presidential elections. Without the Electoral College, candidates might focus almost entirely on the largest cities and most populous regions. The system encourages campaigns to build support across different parts of the country. Candidates often need to appeal to voters in states with different economies, cultures, and political priorities. This can help produce a president with broad geographic support. The Electoral College can also make election results easier to organize and verify. States administer their own elections, using established procedures for counting votes and resolving disputes. If a close result occurs, the recount or legal process can be limited to the states where the outcome is uncertain. A nationwide popular vote could make a very small margin across the whole country more difficult to recount consistently. The Electoral College also provides a clear, predictable method for transferring presidential power. Its rules are established in the Constitution and have been used throughout the nation’s history. Supporters argue that replacing it would require a major change to a system that has generally allowed peaceful transitions between administrations. The system may also encourage candidates to form coalitions among voters from different states. Instead of winning only a few highly populated areas by large margins, a candidate must earn enough support in a range of states. Critics point out that this goal is imperfect because campaigns often concentrate on competitive “swing states.” Still, the existence of battleground states can bring national attention to voters whose concerns might otherwise receive less notice. The Electoral College does not guarantee that every state receives equal campaign attention, but neither would a popular vote necessarily ensure that candidates visit every community. Keeping the system also respects the balance between state and national authority that shaped the Constitution. Reform may be worth discussing, but changes should be considered carefully because they could affect election administration and political representation. The Electoral College has limitations, yet its federalist design, stable procedures, and encouragement of broad state-based support are strong reasons to retain it.

Motorola’s Moto X arrives as more than a new smartphone: it is a test of whether a handset can stand out through personal design and closer ties between hardware and software. The device, introduced by Motorola Mobility under Google’s ownership, puts customization at the center of its pitch. Buyers can choose from a range of colors and finishes, with options for the front, back, accents and engraved details. The choices are intended to make each phone feel more individual than a standard black or white model. Motorola is also emphasizing features designed to make the phone respond quickly to everyday needs. These include voice commands that can be activated without first touching the screen, along with a camera launched by twisting the wrist. The company is betting that such conveniences will matter as much as processor specifications in a crowded market. The Moto X also carries a notable manufacturing message. Motorola says the phone is assembled in the United States, at a facility in Texas. That makes it one of the few high-profile smartphones assembled domestically at the time of its launch. The claim offers a contrast with an industry in which much production takes place in Asia. It may appeal to customers who value US manufacturing and give Motorola a distinctive marketing point. But domestic assembly does not mean every component is made in the United States. The supply chain remains international, and the cost and scale of US production will be closely watched. Customization creates its own logistical challenge, too. A phone built to order requires more coordination than a limited set of mass-produced configurations. Motorola must deliver those choices without making the buying process confusing or slowing fulfillment. The launch also matters because Motorola now sits inside Google. Google bought the company in 2012, describing the deal as a way to strengthen its Android business and gain access to Motorola’s patents. The Moto X is the clearest sign yet that the company intends to let Motorola develop its own hardware identity. That effort raises questions about Google’s relationship with Samsung, Android’s dominant handset maker. Samsung has become a powerful force in the smartphone market, using its scale, marketing budget and broad product range to make Android a global leader. Google benefits from Samsung’s success because Samsung helps expand Android’s reach. At the same time, Google may worry that one manufacturer could gain too much influence over the platform. Samsung has developed its own software services and features, giving its phones a distinct identity beyond stock Android. A stronger Motorola could provide Google with a model for how closely hardware and Android can be integrated. It could also give Google leverage in conversations with Samsung and other manufacturers. Yet the strategy carries risks. If Motorola receives special access to Android features, competing manufacturers could see Google as a rival rather than a neutral platform provider. That could encourage them to invest more heavily in alternative software or services. Google must therefore balance its ownership of Motorola with the need to keep Android partners confident. The Moto X does not appear to challenge Samsung on scale alone. Instead, it aims to compete through design, practical features, customization and a prominent manufacturing story. Its commercial performance will show whether those advantages can persuade buyers in a market dominated by familiar brands. The phone will also test whether consumers are willing to wait for a personalized device rather than choose an off-the-shelf model. For Google, the launch is both a product debut and a strategic signal. Motorola has room to experiment, but its success must not come at the expense of the partnerships that built Android. The balance between a stronger in-house hardware business and a healthy manufacturer ecosystem will shape Google’s next moves.

At midnight, the prison speakers crackled awake. “One of you will leave tomorrow,” said the director. “The rest will remain.” Mara sat up on her bunk, rubbing grit from her eyes. Across the room, Elias gave a tired, humorless laugh. They had been awake for four days already. The experiment was simple, the director had explained: stay conscious, follow instructions, and outlast everyone else. No one had asked what happened to the losers.

At first, the prisoners competed to stay alert. They paced the room, slapped their cheeks, and told stories that grew stranger with every hour. Mara and Elias had been friends before the experiment, back when friendship still seemed useful. Now they watched each other for signs of weakness. On the fifth night, Elias began speaking to someone who wasn’t there. Mara tried to ignore him. Then the lights turned red, and the speaker ordered them to choose one prisoner for removal.

A guard unlocked the door and pointed at Elias. “Take him,” the director said. Mara could have stayed silent. Instead, she stepped between Elias and the guard. “You promised one of us freedom,” she said. “Not that we’d choose who dies.” The guard hesitated, and the speaker clicked off.

For the first time, the room was quiet. Mara looked at the other prisoners and saw fear giving way to anger. Together, they refused to name anyone. The guards came in, but the prisoners linked arms and would not move. Somewhere beyond the door, an alarm began to ring. Elias leaned heavily against Mara, still awake, barely. When the locks finally opened, they walked out together into the gray morning.

The director waited beyond the corridor, holding a single release form. “Only one,” he said. Mara tore it in half. Behind her, the other prisoners stepped into the light. None of them had slept, and none of them were free yet. But for the first time, they had chosen what to do together.

A Florida robotics camp is helping middle school students discover how technology can shape their futures. The program introduces campers to robotics through hands-on activities and team challenges. Students learn that robots are not just science-fiction characters. They are useful machines found in workplaces across the state.

At camp, students may build simple robots from kits and everyday materials. They connect motors, sensors, and controllers to make their designs move and respond. Instructors guide them through the process, but students do much of the experimenting themselves. When a robot does not work as planned, campers investigate the problem and try again.

These activities teach important skills. Students practice problem-solving, creativity, communication, and teamwork. They also explore basic ideas from science, technology, engineering, and mathematics, often called STEM. For example, they might measure distances, compare materials, or use code to guide a robot through an obstacle course.

Robotics can also introduce students to technology careers. Engineers design machines and systems, while software developers write the instructions that make them work. Technicians assemble, test, and maintain equipment. Other professionals specialize in areas such as automation, electronics, product design, and computer science.

The camp also highlights manufacturing opportunities in Florida. Manufacturing is the process of making products, from food and medical equipment to aircraft parts and electronics. Many modern factories use robots and automated tools to complete tasks with precision. People are still essential: they plan production, operate equipment, solve technical problems, and check product quality.

Students may be surprised to learn that manufacturing jobs involve more than working on an assembly line. Some roles require technical training, while others call for college degrees or specialized certifications. Career paths can begin with a high school program, continue through a technical college, or lead to a university. Learning about different routes helps students see that there is no single way to enter the field.

A robotics camp gives students a chance to explore these possibilities before choosing a career. They can ask questions, meet mentors, and see how classroom subjects connect to real work. A math lesson about measurement may help a robot move accurately. A coding activity may demonstrate how software controls a machine.

The experience can also help students understand the value of persistence. Building a robot often involves testing, adjusting, and trying again. Campers learn that mistakes can provide useful information. They gain confidence as they turn an idea into a working project.

Programs like this can make technology feel more welcoming and accessible. Students with different interests and backgrounds can contribute to a team. One camper might enjoy designing the robot’s frame, while another prefers writing code or presenting the group’s solution. These different strengths are all important in technology and manufacturing.

Florida’s industries need people who can adapt as tools and processes change. Early exposure to robotics can encourage students to keep learning about engineering, computing, and skilled trades. It can also help them recognize local opportunities in their communities. By connecting hands-on learning with real careers, a robotics camp can inspire middle school students to imagine themselves as future makers, technicians, engineers, and innovators.

Seeking guidance is valuable whenever we face a problem, have a question, or want to learn a new skill. No one knows everything, and asking for help is a natural part of learning. A teacher, family member, coach, or experienced friend may offer useful knowledge and encouragement. Their advice can help us understand a challenge from a different point of view. This can make a confusing problem seem easier to handle.

Guidance is especially helpful when we feel stuck. Instead of guessing or giving up, we can explain what we have tried and ask what to do next. A helpful person may point out a mistake we have missed. They can also show us smaller steps that make a difficult task more manageable. By following those steps, we often gain confidence as well as a solution.

Asking questions also helps us learn more deeply. When we are curious about something, a clear answer can lead to even more interesting questions. We can check that we understand by listening carefully and asking for examples. It is important to choose trustworthy sources, because not all advice is accurate. Thinking about what we hear helps us decide whether it fits our situation.

Guidance is also important when we are developing new skills. Someone with experience can demonstrate a technique and explain how to practice it safely and effectively. We may improve faster by learning from their successes and mistakes. Feedback helps us notice what we are doing well and what we should work on next. With regular practice, we can gradually become more independent.

Seeking help does not mean that we are incapable. It shows that we are willing to learn and take responsibility for improving. At the same time, we should make our own choices and try to understand the reasons behind the advice we receive. We can thank people for their help and, when possible, offer guidance to others in return. In this way, learning becomes a shared effort.

The ability to ask for guidance is useful at school, at work, and in everyday life. It can save time, prevent avoidable mistakes, and help us face challenges with courage. Most importantly, it reminds us that growth does not happen alone. By seeking guidance and putting what we learn into practice, we become better problem-solvers and more capable learners.

The United States is widening some economic and travel opportunities involving Cuba, even as its decades-old trade embargo remains in force. Recent policy measures have opened limited avenues for U.S. businesses, travelers and Cuban entrepreneurs to engage across the Florida Straits. Authorized travel includes family visits, educational programs, professional exchanges and other activities permitted under U.S. regulations; ordinary tourism remains prohibited. U.S. rules also allow certain financial transactions and support for Cuba’s private sector, including independent businesses and entrepreneurs. The changes are intended to help ordinary Cubans and strengthen ties between families and communities. They do not end the broader restrictions on trade, investment and financial dealings with the Cuban government. Most U.S. exports to Cuba still require authorization, although food, medicine and some other goods may be eligible under specific provisions. The policy shift comes amid Cuba’s severe economic difficulties, including shortages, inflation and limited access to foreign currency. Supporters say expanded engagement can create jobs and give independent businesses more room to grow. Critics argue that new economic links may still benefit state institutions or weaken pressure for political change. The Cuban government has called for the embargo to be lifted, describing it as a major obstacle to the country’s development. U.S. officials, meanwhile, continue to frame their approach as support for the Cuban people while maintaining restrictions on the government. For travelers and companies, the practical opportunities will depend on detailed licensing rules and compliance requirements. The result is a cautious expansion of contact, rather than a normalization of trade or a full reopening of tourism.

Rights advocates have also raised concerns about prolonged pretrial detention and the use of broad national-security accusations against media workers. Egypt’s government has said its measures are intended to protect national security and combat misinformation. Critics argue that such policies can discourage reporting and narrow the range of views available to the public. Media organizations urged authorities to end arbitrary detention and allow journalists to work without intimidation. They also called for the release of journalists held without credible evidence of criminal conduct. The appeal emphasized that a free press is essential for public accountability and informed debate. It urged Egypt to bring its laws and practices into line with international standards on freedom of expression. The groups said independent journalists should have access to information and be able to report without censorship or retaliation. They encouraged international partners to raise the issue in discussions with Egyptian officials. No immediate response to the appeal was reported from the Egyptian government. The media leaders said they would continue to monitor the cases and press for concrete steps to protect journalists.

Comparing Family Cultures Through Interviews and Reflective Analysis

Families pass on beliefs, customs, stories, and everyday habits that shape how people understand the world. Comparing family cultures can help us notice both the diversity of human experience and the values people may share. An interview is one useful way to learn about these traditions directly from family members.

Before beginning, decide what you want to understand. You might explore celebrations, food, language, family roles, communication, or the meaning of home. Choose a focus that is broad enough to invite stories but clear enough to guide the conversation.

Ask open-ended questions that encourage detailed answers. For example, you could ask, “Which family tradition is especially meaningful to you?” or “How have family customs changed over time?” Follow-up questions such as “Can you tell me more?” can reveal details you might otherwise miss. Avoid questions that imply there is a single correct way to live.

Invite participants to share only what they feel comfortable discussing. Explain how you will use their responses, and ask permission before recording or quoting them. Some topics may be private, sensitive, or difficult, so respect a person’s decision not to answer.

During the interview, listen carefully rather than planning your next question. Notice specific examples, repeated ideas, and changes across generations. Take accurate notes, and distinguish a participant’s exact words from your own interpretation.

When comparing interviews, look for similarities and differences without ranking them. One family may emphasize shared meals, while another may place greater importance on individual routines. These patterns reflect particular histories and circumstances, not fixed rules about an entire culture.

Be careful not to treat one person’s account as representative of everyone with a similar background. Family cultures are diverse, and individuals may interpret the same tradition differently. Differences within a family can be just as informative as differences between families.

Reflective analysis means examining both the interviews and your own perspective. Ask yourself what surprised you, what assumptions you brought to the conversation, and how those assumptions changed. Consider how your own family experiences influence what you notice or value.

A useful comparison connects observations to context. For example, a family’s celebration practices may be shaped by migration, religion, work schedules, or available resources. Avoid guessing at causes; instead, ask participants how they understand the influences on their traditions.

Organize your findings around themes rather than presenting a list of disconnected facts. You might compare how families mark important life events or teach children about responsibility. Support each observation with interview examples, while protecting participants’ privacy.

Use respectful and precise language in your writing. Describe what a person said or did instead of making broad claims about a group. If you include quotations, preserve their meaning and explain them fairly.

Finally, consider what the comparison teaches you about culture. Traditions can provide belonging, continuity, and comfort, while also changing as families respond to new circumstances. Thoughtful interviews and reflection help us learn with curiosity, humility, and respect.

European chafer beetles can damage lawns at two stages of their life cycle: as root-feeding grubs and as adult beetles. The grubs are creamy white, C-shaped larvae with brown heads and six legs, and they typically feed on grass roots in late summer and fall. To check for them, cut and lift a small square of turf where damage is visible, then examine the soil and roots. European chafer grubs often curl into a C shape when disturbed, but correct identification may require comparing them with other lawn grubs or asking a local extension service.

Early signs include irregular patches of yellowing, thinning, or dying grass that pull up easily because the roots have been eaten. Damage often becomes more noticeable in late summer and fall, and affected areas may be torn up by skunks, raccoons, or birds searching for grubs. Adult beetles are tan to reddish-brown, about one centimeter long, and often gather around lights in early summer. Their presence alone does not confirm that your lawn has a damaging grub population.

Count grubs in several small turf samples rather than relying on a single spot. The number that warrants action varies with lawn conditions and local guidance, so contact your regional extension service for a threshold. Healthy, well-rooted turf can tolerate some grubs, and treatment is not always necessary. Water lawns deeply but less often, mow at an appropriate height, and avoid excessive nitrogen fertilizer to encourage resilient grass.

If you reseed or repair damaged areas, choose grass suited to your climate and keep the soil moist while seedlings establish. Beneficial nematodes may help control young grubs when applied at the right time, usually in late summer, but they need moist soil and careful adherence to product directions. Insecticides should be a last resort and used only when the infestation is confirmed and local recommendations support treatment. Follow the label exactly, protect people and pets, and avoid applying products where they could reach drains or waterways. Because timing and approved products vary by region, consult a local lawn-care professional or extension service before treating.
