The ship stopped answering on a Tuesday.

Mara checked the clock twice, as if the day might change its mind.

“Control, this is Vesper,” she said. “Do you read?”

Only the ventilation fans replied, turning somewhere behind the walls.

She waited through the prescribed ten seconds and tried again.

The silence made the bridge feel larger.

Vesper had been built for six people, though only Mara and the pilot, Ennis, had made the last leg.

Ennis was supposed to be in the engine bay, listening for a bearing that had begun to sing.

Mara called him on the internal channel.

“Ennis, status?”

There was no answer.

She unbuckled and crossed the bridge, holding the handrails as the ship drifted through the dark.

At the engine bay, she found the hatch sealed.

The status panel showed a pressure warning, then blinked out.

She knocked with the flat of her hand.

“Ennis?”

Something knocked back, once.

Mara stood perfectly still.

She opened the emergency override and pulled the hatch wide.

The engine bay was empty.

A wrench floated near the ceiling, turning slowly.

She returned to the bridge and told herself Ennis had gone to the storage compartment.

The storage compartment was empty too.

She checked the bunks, the galley, the waste locker, and the narrow service crawlspace.

The ship held no one but her.

In the log, she recorded Ennis as missing.

Then she listened to the recording and heard herself whispering his name.

That night, she slept in the pilot’s chair with the lights on.

In the morning, the lights were off.

She blamed a failing circuit and reset the breaker.

The stars beyond the window did not move.

The navigation screen showed their course as a thin green line, ending in a blank field.

Mara tapped the display.

It changed to a photograph of Earth.

For a moment, she thought the planet looked close enough to touch.

Then the image broke into squares and vanished.

She called mission control.

She called the relay station.

She called her brother, whose number she knew by heart.

Each time, the ship answered with a hush of static.

She began leaving messages anyway.

“Day thirty-one,” she said. “Systems are holding.”

She did not know if it was day thirty-one.

The clock had frozen at 04:12.

She marked each meal on the wall beside the galley.

When she ran out of room, she drew another line beneath the first.

Her food tasted like paper, but she ate because the checklist said to eat.

She kept the checklist beside her bed.

Soon the steps began to seem unnecessary.

Soon she stopped checking whether she had completed them.

The ship developed a low, uneven shudder.

Mara felt it through the soles of her boots.

She went to the engine bay and watched the pressure warning glow red.

A voice came through the speakers.

“Hold course, Mara.”

She froze.

The voice sounded like Ennis, though Ennis had never spoken so gently.

She asked where he was.

The speakers clicked and went silent.

For the rest of the shift, she sat beneath them, waiting for another word.

When none came, she recorded the message in her log.

She wrote that Ennis had contacted her.

The next day, she read the entry and crossed it out.

Then she wrote it again, with more detail.

She described his voice, his pauses, and the way he used to clear his throat before speaking.

The ship shuddered harder.

A warning light flickered above the hatch.

Mara imagined Ennis on the other side, trying to get in.

She imagined him trapped in the walls, crawling through the ducts.

She took a screwdriver and opened the nearest vent.

Dust drifted out, slow as snow.

Behind it was only darkness and a bundle of cables.

She apologized to Ennis for leaving him there.

The lights dimmed.

Mara returned to the bridge and found the Earth photograph on the screen again.

This time, the planet was closer.

Clouds spiraled over its bright curve.

She pressed her palm to the display.

“I’m coming home,” she said.

The navigation line still ended in blank space.

She unbuckled the controls and pulled the course lever toward Earth.

The lever would not move.

She pulled harder until her hands shook.

Something clicked beneath the console.

The ship’s shudder stopped.

For a long moment, every fan and relay fell quiet.

Mara smiled at the silence, certain that the ship had heard her.

Then the speakers crackled.

“Hold course, Mara.”

She leaned toward them, eager to answer.

But this time the voice was hers.

By the time the robbers entered the bank, Martin Vale had already decided he didn’t care what happened to him.

He had come to close his account, not because he needed the money, but because the bank kept sending cheerful letters he never read.

At forty-two, he had become good at letting days pass without leaving a mark.

The lobby smelled of floor polish and damp coats.

A child was whining near the water fountain.

Martin watched the second hand on the clock move and wished it would stop asking him to notice.

Then the doors burst open.

Three masked people rushed inside, shouting for everyone to get down.

The child screamed.

Martin lowered himself to the marble floor, slowly, almost politely.

A robber kicked the security guard’s chair aside and pointed a pistol at the ceiling.

The crack of the shot made the lights tremble.

Martin felt nothing at first.

He had spent years imagining that fear would arrive like a storm, dramatic and unmistakable.

Instead, it came as a tiny, practical thought: I don’t want to die here.

The thought surprised him so much that he lifted his head.

A woman beside him was shaking, one hand pressed to her mouth.

Martin recognized her from the bus, where she always carried a paper bag of oranges.

He reached for her hand.

She grabbed his fingers hard enough to hurt.

The robbers ordered the tellers to open the drawers.

One of them, the youngest, kept glancing toward the lobby windows.

His gun wavered whenever someone cried.

Martin understood, with sudden clarity, that the boy was terrified too.

Then the child by the fountain began coughing.

The mother tried to pull him close, but the boy couldn’t catch his breath.

The nearest robber turned toward them and shouted for silence.

Martin felt the woman’s grip tighten around his hand.

For once, he did not want to disappear.

He pushed himself to his knees and said the child had asthma.

The robber swung the gun toward him.

Martin’s heart slammed against his ribs, furious and alive.

He pointed to the mother’s purse and told her where the inhaler was.

She found it, but her hands were shaking too badly to use it.

Martin crawled across the floor, every inch feeling longer than the years behind him.

The robber told him to stop.

Martin kept going.

The boy’s face had gone pale, his mouth opening around empty breaths.

Martin reached the inhaler and passed it to the mother.

She pressed it to the boy’s lips.

After a few terrible seconds, the child coughed, then drew in air.

The robber lowered his gun a fraction.

Sirens began to wail beyond the bank’s thick glass doors.

The youngest robber looked at Martin as if seeing him for the first time.

“Why did you do that?” he asked.

Martin had no answer that made sense.

He only knew he had been afraid of losing the small, ordinary future he had never bothered to imagine.

The doors opened again, this time under the hands of the police.

The robbers dropped their weapons.

The woman with the oranges was still holding Martin’s hand.

Outside, the afternoon light fell across the pavement, bright and almost rude.

Martin walked to the hospital with the mother and her son.

He stayed until the boy was breathing easily and the mother had stopped crying.

Then he called the bank and asked them not to close his account.

On the way home, he bought oranges, though he didn’t know what to do with so many.

For the first time in years, tomorrow felt less like an obligation than a place he might reach.

Mara kept her anger in a blue glass jar beneath her bed. It had no lid, but nothing ever escaped. She had learned to be quiet when her father’s footsteps crossed the hall. She had learned to smile when grown-ups asked if everything was all right. At school, she became the girl who lent pencils and never complained. At home, she became a shadow with careful hands. Years later, she still apologized when someone bumped into her. She apologized to empty rooms, too.

The jar grew heavier each winter. Some nights, Mara heard it knocking against the floorboards. She told herself it was only the pipes. Then one night, she opened an old storybook she had loved as a child. Its pages smelled of dust and rain. A silver forest waited inside, lit by moons that floated between the trees. A fox with antlers stood beside a black river. “You’re late,” it said.

Mara followed it into the book. The forest had no locked doors and no footsteps to fear. On a hill, a castle rose from the clouds, its windows bright as candles. The fox led her to a throne room where a little girl sat beneath a crown of thorns. Mara recognized her own scuffed shoes. “What do you want?” the queen asked. “I want him to know what he did,” Mara said. The words startled her with their sharpness. The castle walls trembled.

The fox placed a wooden sword in her hand. Mara imagined striking the walls, the throne, the whole bright kingdom. Instead, she lowered the blade. “I want to stop carrying him,” she said. At once, the crown cracked. A red wind swept through the room, lifting every dust-covered curtain. The little queen stood up. Together, they walked out of the castle. Behind them, the jar shattered, and its anger rose like a flock of birds.

Mara woke with the book open on her chest. Morning leaned pale against the curtains. Her room was ordinary, and the jar was still beneath her bed. But its blue glass was clear, and it felt light when she lifted it. She called her sister and told her the truth she had swallowed for years. Then she found a counselor and began, slowly, to name what had happened. The anger did not vanish. It became a signal, not a prison. And whenever Mara needed courage, she opened the book and listened for the fox.

Canada’s Rejection of the Nuclear Weapons Ban Treaty and Its Proposed Fissile Material Agreement

Canada has not joined the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons, often called the nuclear weapons ban treaty. The treaty was adopted at the United Nations in 2017 and entered into force in 2021. It prohibits its parties from developing, testing, producing, acquiring, possessing, stockpiling, using, or threatening to use nuclear weapons. It also bars assistance with those activities and establishes processes for victims and environmental remediation. Canada is not a party, so these treaty obligations do not bind it.

Canada’s position reflects its membership in NATO, a military alliance that describes nuclear deterrence as part of its security policy. Canadian governments have argued that disarmament should proceed through steps that include nuclear-armed states and that are consistent with the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty, or NPT. The NPT, which entered into force in 1970, aims to prevent the spread of nuclear weapons, promote peaceful nuclear cooperation, and pursue disarmament. Canada has supported the NPT and other arms-control efforts while declining to endorse the ban treaty.

Canadian officials have said the ban treaty could divide countries that share the goal of disarmament. They have also questioned whether it would directly change the policies of nuclear-armed states, none of which joined it. Supporters of the treaty respond that it establishes a clear humanitarian norm against nuclear weapons. They emphasize the catastrophic effects of nuclear detonations and the difficulty of providing adequate emergency relief. The disagreement is therefore partly about strategy: whether to prohibit the weapons immediately or to focus on measures negotiated with states that possess them.

Canada has promoted a different arms-control initiative: a proposed treaty banning the production of fissile material for nuclear weapons. Fissile materials, such as highly enriched uranium and separated plutonium, can sustain the chain reactions used in nuclear weapons. The proposal is commonly called a Fissile Material Cut-off Treaty, or FMCT. It is intended to stop the production of such material for use in new nuclear weapons. It would not, by itself, eliminate existing nuclear arsenals or necessarily require the destruction of existing stocks.

Canada has supported negotiations on this proposal in international forums, especially the Conference on Disarmament in Geneva. That forum operates by consensus, meaning that a single member can block agreement on a program of work. Disagreement over the treaty’s scope, verification, and treatment of existing stocks has helped prevent negotiations from beginning. Some countries favor a ban on future production only, while others seek rules covering existing fissile material as well. Verification is another difficult issue because inspections must detect prohibited production without exposing sensitive military or commercial information.

The proposed agreement is different from the nuclear weapons ban treaty in both scope and approach. The ban treaty seeks to prohibit a wide range of activities involving nuclear weapons for its parties. An FMCT would focus more narrowly on the production of materials for weapons, and its practical effect would depend on its terms and participation. Canada presents the fissile-material proposal as a step toward limiting the ability to expand nuclear arsenals. Critics argue that a production ban alone may leave current stockpiles and existing weapons untouched.

These two positions illustrate Canada’s preferred path in nuclear diplomacy. It supports gradual, negotiated arms control while remaining within NATO’s nuclear-deterrence framework. That approach has drawn criticism from campaigners, who say refusing the ban treaty weakens a growing humanitarian standard. Canada’s governments, in turn, have maintained that agreements involving nuclear-armed states are more likely to affect their conduct. Whether an FMCT can gain broad support remains uncertain. Understanding the debate requires distinguishing between a treaty that stigmatizes and prohibits nuclear weapons for its members and a proposed agreement aimed at limiting the production of key weapon materials.

The Electoral College has shaped American presidential elections for more than two centuries. Under this system, each state receives electoral votes based mainly on its representation in Congress. In most states, the candidate who wins the popular vote receives all of that state’s electoral votes. A candidate must win a majority of electoral votes to become president. This means that the nationwide popular-vote winner can lose the election. That outcome has happened several times in American history. The possibility of such a result raises an important question about fairness and representation. The United States should abolish the Electoral College and elect its president by popular vote. A direct popular vote would make every citizen’s vote count equally, encourage candidates to campaign across the country, and strengthen confidence in democracy.

The strongest argument for abolishing the Electoral College is that it gives citizens unequal influence. In a national popular vote, each vote would count toward the same total. A voter in California would have the same formal influence as a voter in Wyoming. Today, the practical value of a vote can depend on the state where it is cast. Because most states award electoral votes on a winner-take-all basis, votes for the losing candidate often do not affect the final result in that state. This can leave millions of voters feeling that their choices do not matter. A direct election would reduce that problem. It would also make the outcome easier to understand: the candidate who receives the most votes nationwide would win.

The current system also shapes how candidates campaign. Presidential campaigns often focus heavily on a small number of competitive states. Candidates may visit those states repeatedly while giving less attention to states considered safely won or safely lost. As a result, voters in battleground states can receive more campaign visits and political advertising than voters elsewhere. A popular-vote election would give candidates a reason to seek votes in every state. They might spend time in large cities, rural communities, and regions that are usually overlooked. They would still choose where to campaign based on political strategy, but their goal would be to gain votes nationwide rather than win particular states. This could make national concerns more important in campaigns.

A popular vote could also improve the legitimacy of presidential elections. When the electoral-vote winner loses the nationwide popular vote, some citizens question whether the system has treated voters fairly. Even when the result follows the law, the gap can weaken public trust. A direct election would make the connection between voters’ choices and the presidency more straightforward. It could also encourage candidates to seek broad support instead of concentrating on a narrow set of states. Support across the country would not guarantee that every group receives attention, but it would make every additional vote potentially useful. This principle fits the democratic idea that political power ultimately comes from the people.

However, supporters of the Electoral College argue that it protects smaller states. They point out that every state receives electoral votes based on its congressional representation, including two votes corresponding to its senators. Because small states have a minimum of three electoral votes, each voter there may have more influence relative to the state’s population than a voter in a large state. Supporters also say that the system encourages candidates to build coalitions across different regions. They worry that a popular-vote election would lead candidates to concentrate on densely populated cities and ignore rural areas. These concerns deserve serious consideration. Any change should aim to preserve attention to all communities, not only the largest population centers.

Still, the Electoral College does not reliably protect small states or rural voters. Candidates mainly focus on competitive states, which can be large or small, rather than on every state equally. Many small states are safely aligned with one political party and receive little campaign attention. Meanwhile, large states with close contests can attract substantial attention. Under a popular vote, candidates would have an incentive to seek votes wherever they can gain them, including in rural areas and smaller states. A vote in a small town would add to a candidate’s national total just as a vote in a large city would. Campaigns might use different strategies, but no state’s voters would be excluded from the count.

Another concern is that a nationwide election could lead to recounts or disputes over close results. A very close national vote could require recounts in many places, creating logistical challenges. The Electoral College can limit the result to a small number of decisive states, although that can also make recounts in those states especially contentious. A direct election would need clear national standards for counting ballots and handling recounts. States currently use different election rules, so Congress and state governments would need to coordinate carefully. These challenges are real, but they are not reasons to accept unequal influence as permanent. They are practical problems that could be addressed through well-designed laws.

Changing the system would also require a constitutional amendment, which is difficult to pass. The amendment process demands broad agreement among members of Congress and the states. That difficulty reflects the importance of changing the rules for choosing a president. It also means that reform would require careful debate and public support. Some people favor a different approach, such as keeping electoral votes but awarding them proportionally. That option could reduce the winner-take-all effect, although it would not ensure that the national popular-vote winner becomes president. If the goal is equal treatment of votes, a direct election is the clearest solution.

Abolishing the Electoral College would not solve every problem in American politics. Money, misinformation, low voter participation, and political division would still affect elections. A popular vote could even lead to disputes about national ballot rules if those rules were unclear. For this reason, reform should include measures such as consistent standards for ballot access, counting, and recounts. The country should also make voting accessible and protect the security of election systems. These steps would help ensure that a direct election is both fair and trustworthy. A change in how votes are counted must be matched by strong protections for voters.

The Electoral College was created in a different period of American history, when communication and travel were slower and the country faced political concerns unlike many of those today. Its defenders believe it balances the interests of states and regions. Yet its modern winner-take-all rules can leave many voters without meaningful influence and can allow a candidate to become president without winning the most votes nationally. A popular-vote system would make the basic rule simple and consistent: the candidate with the most votes wins. It would encourage candidates to seek support wherever voters live. Most importantly, it would treat each citizen’s vote as part of one national decision.

The United States should therefore abolish the Electoral College and choose its president by popular vote. The change would make elections more equal, more transparent, and more responsive to the people. Concerns about small states, recounts, and election administration should be addressed through careful planning rather than used to dismiss reform. A democracy is strongest when citizens can see that their votes matter on equal terms. No voter should have more influence simply because of the state in which they live. The presidency should go to the candidate chosen by the greatest number of Americans.

The ship Meridian lost its engines on the edge of the dark.
For three days, its crew watched the stars slide past without moving.
They had been bound for Nysa, the last unclaimed world in human space.
Now Nysa was only a pale dot on the navigation screen.
Every other habitable planet already carried cities, farms, or memorials.
There was nowhere left to divert.
Captain Imani Vale called the crew into the mess hall.
The air there smelled of coffee and hot wiring.
She told them the truth.
The reactor could power life support for six months.
The distress beacon had reached every settled system.
No rescue ship could arrive in less than a year.
No one asked what that meant.
They had all done the arithmetic.
Meridian carried 312 colonists in cryogenic sleep.
It also carried 48 awake crew members.
The colonists were families, scientists, and children.
They had sold everything they owned to join the voyage.
Their destination had promised fresh soil and a future.
Engineer Sato said the reactor might be restarted.
He needed the ship’s spare power cells.
Those cells were also the only way to thaw the colonists safely.
Without them, the sleepers would remain cold until the ship failed.
Or they could be awakened now, and share the dwindling air.
The crew fell silent.
Dr. Nwosu said the sleepers had trusted them.
She reminded everyone that the crew had signed the same promise.
Pilot Rhee said promises did not make oxygen.
Then a message arrived from Earth.
It was a recording, delayed by years.
The sender was the colony office.
Nysa had been claimed after Meridian departed.
A mining consortium had sealed the landing zone.
The planet’s new rulers offered no welcome.
The crew listened twice.
The first time, they felt betrayed.
The second time, they heard the frightened voice of a clerk.
Earth had not sent them into a trap on purpose.
The map had simply changed faster than the law.
Sato found another option in the maintenance logs.
The ship’s old survey probe could be refitted as a tug.
It had enough fuel to reach a moon beyond Nysa.
The moon was airless and bitterly cold.
But beneath its ice lay an ocean.
The probe could carry only twelve people.
It could not tow the colony ship.
The captain asked the crew to vote.
First, they voted on whether to wake the colonists.
The vote was tied.
Then Nwosu proposed a compromise.
Wake a small medical team and the oldest colonists first.
They could help repair the ship and choose what came next.
Rhee objected that choosing favorites would haunt them forever.
A young technician named Lio asked whether sleeping people could consent.
No one had an answer.
The captain looked through the glass wall at the cryogenic bay.
Rows of faces rested beneath frost.
Some wore the same hopeful smile.
Some were only infants when the voyage began.
Imani remembered her mother’s last message from Earth.
It said that a future was not a place.
It was something people made together.
She ordered the first thaw.
The crew chose the medical team by lottery.
They added one child, a girl named Mara, because she was already waking.
The process took eleven hours.
When Mara opened her eyes, she asked if they had arrived.
The captain told her they had not.
Mara listened without crying.
Then she asked how many people were still asleep.
“Three hundred and eleven,” Nwosu said.
Mara stared at the frost on the glass.
“We can’t leave them,” she said.
The medical team learned the situation before breakfast.
They argued, calculated, and cursed the ship’s builders.
One of them found a damaged coolant line.
It could be sealed with metal from the survey probe.
The probe would never fly afterward.
But the repair would preserve enough power to revive everyone.
The moon would remain unreachable.
The crew would have to seek shelter in orbit around Nysa.
The consortium might turn them away.
They might even seize the ship.
The captain asked the newly awakened colonists to decide with them.
They listened to the risks.
A farmer spoke of growing food in a sealed cargo bay.
A teacher offered to teach the children if they were imprisoned.
A quiet old man said he had lived through hunger before.
He would rather face it awake than be carried past another chance.
The vote was nearly unanimous.
One crew member voted against the plan.
She feared they were trading a certain death for a slower one.
Imani thanked her for saying so.
Then she gave the order.
The probe was stripped down to its frame.
Its engines became a patch for Meridian’s failing heart.
For the first time in days, the ship’s lights steadied.
The sleepers began to wake in waves.
Confusion spread through the corridors.
So did fear, anger, and the sound of people calling names.
The crew told them the truth, one cabin at a time.
No one pretended that the choice had been easy.
When Meridian reached Nysa, the consortium’s ships formed a wall.
The captain transmitted the names of every passenger.
She asked for shelter, not ownership.
For a long time, the planet did not answer.
Then a small vessel broke from the wall.
Its pilot was a woman born on Nysa after Meridian had left Earth.
She said her city had room for the children.
She said there was no room for a new colony.
The crew accepted the terms.
They would come down as guests, not founders.
The first landing was rough.
The children stepped onto soil that belonged to someone else.
Mara knelt and pressed both hands into the dirt.
Above her, Meridian circled the planet with its lights burning.
There was still no unclaimed world waiting for humanity.
But there were hands to help, and room to share.
For that day, it was enough.

Mara was certain the lighthouse had gone dark because her brother wanted her to fail.
For three nights, she watched the beam stop at the same stretch of sea.
On the fourth, she climbed the tower and found him asleep beside the lamp, his hands blistered from repairs.
“You knew,” she said, though she had not known what she meant.
He woke and told her the lens had cracked weeks ago.
Beyond the glass, a fishing boat had struck the reef where the beam should have warned it away.
Mara had believed the light was a promise, and that promises were kept by people who cared.
Her brother had believed he could mend the crack alone.
Neither belief had survived the wreck.
At dawn, the survivors came ashore, carrying a boy who would never see again.
Mara wanted to blame the sea, the lens, or her brother, but each answer felt too small.
So she sat beside him and held the cold, broken glass between them.
For years, she would remember how clearly she had seen his betrayal.
For years, she would also remember that seeing clearly was not the same as knowing.

Cleveland Fire Brigade is changing how it responds to fire alarms at commercial premises in a bid to reduce unnecessary call-outs. Under the revised approach, crews will no longer automatically attend every alarm activation at businesses. Instead, the brigade will assess the information available and may ask site staff to investigate whether there is a sign of fire. Emergency services will still be called immediately if flames, smoke or another clear danger is reported. The change is intended to free up firefighters and appliances for incidents where they are urgently needed. False alarms can be triggered by equipment faults, cooking fumes or accidental damage to alarm systems. The brigade is encouraging businesses to maintain their systems and ensure staff understand the updated procedure. It has not said that genuine fires will receive a reduced response. Commercial premises should follow the brigade’s guidance and call 999 whenever they suspect an actual fire.

Every morning, Milo ran the length of the city before the clocks finished chiming six.
He could outrun trains, storms, and even the rumors that chased him.
But his speed came from an odd source: the less money he had, the faster he became.
The city’s poorest boy had once crossed the river in a heartbeat.
Each unpaid bill seemed to put another spark in his heels.
Milo hated the bargain, but he hated being helpless more.
He used his gift to deliver medicine, stop robberies, and rescue cats from rooftops.
His rival, Victor Vane, understood the rule better than anyone.
Victor was rich, patient, and cruel enough to study Milo’s empty pockets.
For years he tried to ruin Milo with cash.
He offered him jobs, gifts, and envelopes stuffed with bills.
Milo refused every one.
The moment money touched his hands, his speed faded.
Then, one rainy Thursday, Victor bought a lottery ticket on a whim.
He forgot about it until a television host announced his numbers.
Victor had won the city’s largest jackpot.
He laughed so loudly that his servants thought he had gone mad.
At first he planned to buy a fleet of armored cars.
Then he remembered Milo’s weakness.
Victor sent a messenger to Milo’s cramped apartment with a certified check.
It was enough to pay Milo’s rent, debts, and groceries for years.
Milo tore the check in half.
Victor had expected that.
He had already paid the city to settle every bill in Milo’s name.
By sunset, Milo’s landlord had handed him a receipt marked PAID.
His speed sank like a stone.
The next morning, Victor staged a robbery at the central bank.
He knew Milo would still come, even if he could barely jog.
Milo arrived late, breathless, and furious.
Victor stood outside the bank beneath a golden umbrella.
“Your poverty made you powerful,” he said.
“Now you can finally live comfortably.”
A siren wailed inside the building.
Milo saw a guard trapped beneath a fallen marble column.
He tried to sprint, but his feet only stumbled forward.
Victor watched, smiling, as the seconds passed.
Then Milo noticed the lottery check Victor had dropped beside the curb.
It had been soaked by rain, and the ink was running.
The bank’s alarm startled a delivery driver, who swerved toward it.
Milo shoved the driver clear, taking the impact on his shoulder.
The check fluttered into a storm drain.
Victor’s smile vanished.
He could buy Milo comfort, but he could not buy obedience.
Milo’s rent was paid, yet his pockets were empty again.
His speed returned in a bright rush.
He crossed the lobby before the column could shift.
He pulled the guard free and carried every hostage to safety.
Victor tried to escape in a limousine.
Milo caught it at the next intersection and lifted the door off its hinges.
He left Victor for the police and kept only the wet scraps of the ticket.
Later, Milo used the scraps to light a small cooking fire.
He still had a roof, thanks to Victor’s payment, and a city that needed him.
But he knew comfort could be another kind of chain.
So he gave away the money Victor had sent to families who needed it more.
The next morning, Milo ran faster than ever, not because he was poor, but because he chose where his strength would go.

Online education has changed how students learn and access academic opportunities. Instead of relying only on lessons in a classroom, learners can explore subjects through digital courses, videos, and interactive resources. This flexibility can encourage students to take greater responsibility for their education. They can choose when to study, set personal goals, and organize their schedules. These choices help build skills such as time management and self-discipline. Online learning also gives students more control over their pace. They can pause a lesson, review difficult ideas, or move ahead when they feel ready. This makes it easier to recognize personal strengths and areas that need more attention. Many online courses include quizzes and feedback that help students track their progress. However, independent learning does not mean learning alone. Students can ask questions in discussion forums, work with classmates, and meet instructors through video calls. These tools allow them to seek support while remaining active in their own learning. Online education can also broaden academic opportunities. Students may take courses from universities or teachers located far from their homes. They can explore subjects that their local schools do not offer, such as coding, astronomy, or a new language. Recorded lessons and flexible schedules can make education more accessible to students with jobs, family responsibilities, or health challenges. Digital courses may also cost less than traditional programs, although access to reliable devices and internet remains important. To succeed, students need to plan carefully and avoid distractions. Schools and families can help by providing guidance, technology, and encouragement. When used thoughtfully, online education helps students become confident, independent learners. It also opens doors to knowledge and academic paths that might otherwise be out of reach.

Adaptive educational technology can help students who need homework support by adjusting activities to their skill level and pace. It can offer hints, extra practice, and immediate feedback, making difficult subjects easier to understand. Students may also feel more confident when they can work independently and revisit lessons as needed. However, relying too much on technology can reduce opportunities to ask teachers or classmates for help. Some programs may give confusing or inaccurate feedback, and access to reliable devices and internet is not equal for every student. Overall, adaptive technology works best as a helpful supplement to caring teachers and families, not as a replacement for them.

Northern Ireland’s tourism growth has fallen short of official targets, as visitor numbers from overseas and the Republic of Ireland shift, according to recent figures. The changing pattern has raised questions about whether the region can sustain momentum in key international markets. Tourism operators say rising costs and changing travel habits are influencing demand, while domestic visitors remain an important part of the sector. Overseas arrivals are particularly valuable because they tend to stay longer and spend more, making any slowdown a concern for businesses. Visitors from the Republic of Ireland have also fluctuated, reflecting competition from other destinations and wider economic pressures. Industry representatives are calling for continued investment in promotion, transport links and visitor attractions. They say clear, comparable data is needed to understand which markets are growing and where support is most needed. Tourism officials have said they will continue working with businesses to attract visitors and close the gap between current performance and targets.

Mara learned to keep her hands steady when the newsroom windows rattled from distant blasts. Each morning, she slipped past the warning signs and into the factory district, where workers whispered about a chemical leak their bosses denied. She never told her editor how often armed guards followed her home. The workers had begged her to keep their names out of the story, afraid they would lose their jobs—or worse. So Mara hid their notes in a tin beneath her floorboards and wrote every detail from memory. At night, she woke certain she could still smell the bitter fumes. Her mother noticed the trembling in her cup and asked her to quit. “If I leave, they’ll say nothing happened,” Mara replied. She published the investigation under her own name, with every source protected. By dawn, the factory gates were locked, and an official inspection was underway. The workers sent no thank-you, only a message: We’re safe for now. Mara read it twice, then sat alone in the dark. Relief came first, followed by anger at how close she had come to disappearing. In the morning, she returned to the newsroom, carrying the fear with her but no longer carrying it alone.

Seeking diverse opinions is valuable when making decisions and solving problems. Each person sees the world through different experiences and knowledge. By listening to several perspectives, we can understand an issue more fully. A solution that seems obvious to one person may have drawbacks that others notice. Different opinions can reveal these hidden risks before they cause trouble.

For example, a school planning a new lunch program could ask students, teachers, and cafeteria staff for ideas. Students might focus on taste and price, while staff might point out what is practical to prepare. Teachers could consider how lunch arrangements affect learning and schedules. Together, these views could lead to a plan that works better for everyone. Without discussion, important needs might be overlooked.

Seeking diverse opinions can also encourage creativity. When people share different ideas, they may combine them into a stronger solution. A challenge that feels difficult to one person may be easier to solve as a group. Respectful disagreement can help people test their assumptions and improve their reasoning. It teaches us that changing our minds is not a weakness.

However, gathering opinions does not mean accepting every suggestion. Some ideas may be based on incorrect information, and others may not be practical. We should listen carefully, ask questions, and consider evidence before making a choice. It is also important to invite quieter people to speak, since valuable ideas are not always shared first. A fair decision-making process gives everyone a chance to contribute.

In the end, diverse opinions help us make wiser and more thoughtful decisions. They broaden our understanding, uncover possible problems, and inspire new solutions. Listening to others does not remove our responsibility to decide, but it helps us decide with greater care. Whether in school, at work, or in our communities, we can benefit from considering perspectives beyond our own. By staying curious and respectful, we become better problem-solvers and more understanding people.

Subject: Proposed Tariff Changes to Strengthen Dollar Valuation and Limit Financial Exposure

Dear colleagues,

We are reviewing proposed tariff changes intended to support the dollar and limit financial exposure. The proposal would adjust selected import duties in response to market and economic conditions. Its goal is to encourage demand for domestic goods while reducing vulnerabilities linked to trade imbalances. A stronger dollar may help lower the cost of imported inputs and ease inflationary pressure. However, currency movements are affected by many factors beyond tariff policy. We should therefore avoid presenting the changes as a guaranteed way to influence the dollar’s value.

The proposal also aims to reduce exposure to sudden shifts in trade flows and foreign exchange markets. Any adjustments should be targeted, proportionate, and based on reliable economic analysis. We need to assess how higher duties could affect businesses that rely on imported materials. Potential price increases for consumers should be considered as well. Retaliatory measures from trading partners could create additional risks for exporters. Clear criteria for applying or revising tariffs would help businesses plan with greater confidence.

Before implementation, we recommend reviewing the expected effects across industries and income groups. The analysis should include possible effects on inflation, employment, investment, and government revenue. We should also identify options to limit unintended consequences for essential goods and supply chains. Regular monitoring would allow policymakers to respond if conditions change. Any tariff changes should be coordinated with broader monetary, fiscal, and trade policies. This approach can help ensure that the measures support economic stability rather than create avoidable uncertainty.

Please share your feedback on the proposal and any concerns your teams have identified. We will incorporate input into the next round of analysis. Thank you for your attention and continued collaboration.

Best regards,
[Your Name]

Sister Elian had learned to walk softly through the abbey.
The brothers punished noise as if it were a sin.
They punished laughter, too.
Most of all, they punished questions.
Elian had asked why the poor were turned away from the gates.
For that, the prior had locked her in the cellar.
For asking again, he had ordered the others to beat her.
They left her among the broken jars, bleeding and cold.
Above her, the abbey bells rang for evening prayers.
Elian tried to pray, but anger crowded out every word.
Then she heard a whisper beneath the stones.
It spoke her name.
She thought it was the fever.
The whisper came again, this time from inside her own chest.
“Rise,” it said.
A blue flame appeared in her palm.
It did not burn her.
When she touched the cellar door, its iron hinges melted.
Elian climbed the stairs into the chapel.
The brothers were kneeling before the altar.
The prior looked up and saw the light around her.
He called her a demon.
Elian lifted one hand.
Every candle in the chapel went black.
In the darkness, the brothers began to cry out.
She could see them clearly, each wrapped in a pale thread of light.
The threads trembled whenever they lied.
The prior’s thread was thick and black.
Elian remembered every blow he had dealt.
She remembered the hunger he had imposed.
She remembered the girls he had sent away into the winter.
The blue flame brightened.
The prior fell to his knees.
“Do to me what I did to you,” he begged.
Elian wanted to make him suffer.
She wanted him to feel each moment of her pain.
She could almost taste the power waiting in her hands.
Then the whisper spoke again.
“Choose what you become.”
Elian lowered her hand.
She did not forgive him.
She would not pretend the harm had vanished.
Instead, she turned toward the locked doors of the infirmary.
With a gesture, she broke their chains.
The women inside stumbled into the chapel.
Some carried bruises.
Some carried children.
All of them stared at Elian’s shining hands.
She told them the gates were open.
The brothers tried to flee.
The blue fire followed them, not as a blade but as a lantern.
It exposed the hidden rooms beneath the abbey.
It revealed stolen grain and secret letters.
It showed the townspeople who arrived what had been done in their name.
The prior was taken before the bishop and the village court.
The others were made to answer for their crimes.
Elian watched from the chapel steps as the abbey’s bells rang.
This time, no one ordered the poor away.
Weeks passed.
The broken doors were repaired, but left unlocked.
The women chose their own paths.
Some stayed to tend the sick.
Others left for the road.
Elian remained, though she no longer wore the abbey’s veil.
At night, the blue flame flickered in her palm.
It offered her power enough to punish any enemy.
She learned to use it instead to find the lost and light dark rooms.
Still, when she heard a cruel voice, anger rose in her.
She did not call that anger evil.
She only refused to let it choose for her.
And beneath the old stones, the whisper fell silent.

Andy Coulson is facing a perjury investigation over evidence he gave at the 2010 trial of former Scottish politician Tommy Sheridan. The inquiry concerns testimony Coulson provided while he was editor of the News of the World. Sheridan, a former Scottish Socialist Party leader, was convicted of perjury after denying under oath that he had visited a sex club and had affairs. He was sentenced to three years in prison, though his conviction was later quashed.

Coulson told the trial that he had not known the newspaper was paying a private investigator to gather information about Sheridan. Prosecutors alleged that the paper’s reporting had helped expose Sheridan’s private life and that his denials in court were false. Coulson’s evidence became significant because he had led the newspaper during the period when the investigation into Sheridan was conducted.

The renewed scrutiny follows developments in the long-running legal dispute surrounding Sheridan’s conviction. Scottish authorities are examining whether Coulson’s statements under oath were knowingly untrue. A perjury investigation is a preliminary inquiry and does not mean that charges have been brought. Any prosecution would require evidence that the witness deliberately lied about a matter relevant to the trial.

Coulson has previously denied wrongdoing in relation to the allegations. He was editor of the News of the World from 2003 to 2007 and later served as director of communications for then-Prime Minister David Cameron. He resigned from that role in 2011 amid the phone-hacking scandal involving the newspaper.

The Sheridan case has remained contentious in Scotland, in part because of questions about the evidence presented at his trial. In 2010, a jury found Sheridan guilty after a lengthy prosecution. The conviction was overturned by the Scottish Criminal Cases Review Commission, which referred the case back to the appeal court. In 2012, the High Court of Justiciary quashed the conviction, concluding that the trial process had been compromised by serious failures.

Sheridan has consistently maintained that he was wrongly convicted. His case has also drawn attention to the methods used by newspapers and private investigators in pursuing stories about public figures. The latest inquiry could revisit evidence gathered during the original proceedings and the roles played by those involved.

Authorities have not announced whether Coulson will be charged. The investigation’s outcome may depend on the availability of new evidence and the legal threshold for proving perjury. Coulson remains entitled to the presumption of innocence.

Virtual schooling has become an important part of education, offering students a way to learn from home. Although it provides flexibility and convenient access to lessons, it also raises concerns about academic, technological, and social effects. These concerns matter because students need more than access to assignments to succeed.

Academically, some students find it difficult to stay focused during online classes. Home can be full of distractions, such as television, chores, or family conversations. Without regular face-to-face contact, students may hesitate to ask questions or may not receive help quickly. Teachers can also find it harder to tell whether students understand the material. As a result, some learners may fall behind even when they complete their assignments. At the same time, virtual schooling can help students who need flexible schedules or more time to review lessons.

Technology creates another set of challenges. Not every family has a reliable internet connection or a suitable device for each child. When a computer breaks or a video call freezes, students can miss important instruction. Long hours in front of screens may also cause eye strain, fatigue, and difficulty concentrating. Schools and families need to provide technical support and encourage healthy breaks.

Social development is also affected by learning remotely. Students may have fewer chances to make friends, work in groups, and practice communication skills. Being apart from classmates can lead to loneliness, especially for students who depend on school for daily social interaction. Online discussions can connect students, but they may not fully replace conversations and activities in person. Virtual schooling can also make it harder for teachers to notice when a student is struggling emotionally.

Overall, virtual schooling has both useful benefits and serious drawbacks. Its success depends on students receiving academic guidance, dependable technology, and opportunities to connect with others. By addressing these needs, schools can make online learning more effective and supportive for every student.

Breastfeeding: Benefits, Child Development, and Equitable Support

Breastfeeding is one way to nourish an infant, and its benefits can extend to both the baby and the person who gives birth. Human milk provides nutrients suited to an infant’s changing needs. It also contains antibodies and other immune components that help protect against some infections. Breastfeeding is associated with lower rates of certain illnesses, including gastrointestinal and respiratory infections. It may also reduce the risk of sudden infant death syndrome, although safe-sleep practices remain essential. For mothers, breastfeeding is associated with a lower risk of breast and ovarian cancers and may support recovery after childbirth. These are population-level findings, not guarantees for any individual family. Families can make feeding decisions based on health, circumstances, and personal preferences.

Research on child development has examined possible links between breastfeeding and cognitive, language, and social outcomes. Some studies find that children who were breastfed have higher average scores on certain cognitive tests. However, an association does not prove that breastfeeding itself caused the difference. Families who breastfeed may also differ in income, education, health, and access to resources that influence development. Researchers try to account for these factors, but it is difficult to remove all potential sources of bias. Sibling comparisons and other study designs can help address some differences, yet they also have limitations. Overall, evidence suggests that breastfeeding may contribute to healthy development, but its effects are complex and should not be overstated. A child’s development depends on many influences, including genetics, responsive caregiving, nutrition, health, and a safe, supportive environment.

Breastfeeding is not possible or preferred for every family. Some parents face medical conditions, medication concerns, pain, low milk supply, or difficulty with infant latch. Others may choose formula, combination feeding, or another approach for personal or practical reasons. These choices should be respected, and families deserve accurate, nonjudgmental information about safe feeding. A healthy child can thrive through different feeding arrangements when their needs are met. Support should never become pressure or a measure of a parent’s worth.

For those who choose to breastfeed, the conditions around them can make a major difference. Skilled lactation care can help with positioning, milk transfer, pain, and concerns about supply. Hospitals and birth centers can support early feeding while respecting medical needs and parental choice. Follow-up care after discharge is important because challenges often arise at home. Partners and family members can help by sharing household tasks, offering encouragement, and protecting time for feeding and rest. Employers can provide paid leave, flexible schedules, private spaces that are not bathrooms, and time to express milk. Child-care settings can safely store and serve expressed milk and welcome breastfeeding families. Public spaces should allow people to feed their babies without stigma or unnecessary barriers.

Access to this support is not equal. Black, Indigenous, and other communities of color have faced discrimination and unequal access to health care, paid leave, and lactation services. Historical policies and workplace conditions have also disrupted breastfeeding traditions and family support networks. Low-wage workers may have less control over schedules and fewer private spaces for expressing milk. Rural families may live far from lactation specialists, while families with disabilities may encounter inaccessible services. Language barriers and culturally insensitive care can make support harder to use. These are structural challenges, not failures of individual mothers.

Equitable support means listening to families and removing practical barriers. Health services should offer culturally respectful, evidence-based guidance and connect families to affordable lactation care. Policies should protect time and space for milk expression and expand access to paid family leave. Programs should be designed with input from the communities they serve. Support must include those who breastfeed, those who combination feed, and those who do not breastfeed. It should also recognize that mothers and other parents may need different kinds of help. The goal is not to promote one feeding choice at all costs. The goal is to ensure that every family can make an informed choice and receive compassionate care. When communities support parents without judgment, infants and caregivers alike have a better chance to be healthy and well.

At 10:17, Mara escaped the office and carried her chipped mug down to the café on the corner. The morning had been a parade of urgent emails, though none seemed to matter by lunchtime. Her manager had praised her “flexibility” while adding another project to her queue. Mara ordered a small coffee and found the last empty table by the window. Outside, a delivery cyclist coasted through the drizzle, one hand lifted from the handlebars. She watched him until the traffic swallowed him. The café smelled of cinnamon and wet coats, and for a moment no one asked her to be productive. She wrapped both hands around the cup. The warmth reminded her of a winter morning at her grandmother’s kitchen table, where time moved at the speed of a kettle. Her phone buzzed against the wood. She turned it face down. A barista laughed behind the counter, and the sound rose freely, without a meeting invite attached. Mara took a slow sip and let the bitter taste settle. She imagined leaving the office for good, walking until the streets ran out. Then she pictured rent, groceries, and the half-finished report waiting on her desk. The fantasy folded itself away. Her break had lasted nine minutes. She stood, dropped a coin in the tip jar, and stepped back into the rain. By the time she reached her desk, the inbox was already waiting.

On September 27–28, 2015, a total lunar eclipse coincided with a supermoon, creating a striking sky event visible from eastern Canada. A lunar eclipse happens when Earth passes between the Sun and the Moon, casting its shadow across the lunar surface. During totality, Earth’s shadow covered the Moon completely, and the Moon appeared reddish rather than disappearing. This color comes from sunlight filtered and bent through Earth’s atmosphere, which scatters much of the blue light and lets more red light reach the Moon. The eclipse unfolded overnight, with viewing times varying across eastern Canada’s time zones. Because the Moon was near perigee—the closest point to Earth in its orbit—it appeared slightly larger and brighter than an average full moon. “Supermoon” is an informal term, and the apparent size difference is subtle to the unaided eye. Unlike a solar eclipse, a lunar eclipse is safe to watch without special eye protection. Clear skies offered observers a chance to see both the Moon’s changing color and the slow progress of Earth’s shadow.

Machines can now recognize some emotions by analyzing facial expressions. Cameras and computer programs look for patterns such as a smile, a frown, or raised eyebrows. These tools can be useful in situations where people need quick feedback. For example, a computer might help researchers study how people respond to an advertisement. However, facial expressions do not always reveal exactly what someone feels. A person may smile because they are nervous, polite, or trying to hide sadness. The same expression can also mean different things in different cultures. Lighting, camera quality, and a person’s face can affect how accurately a machine reads an expression. Machines may also make mistakes because they rely on patterns learned from examples. If those examples do not represent different ages, backgrounds, and abilities, the results may be unfair. Another problem is that emotions are more complicated than a small set of labels such as happy or angry. People often feel several emotions at once, and their faces may not show them clearly. For these reasons, machines can sometimes identify clues about emotions, but they cannot know for certain what a person feels. Their judgments should not be treated as facts or used alone for important decisions. Overall, machines can assist people in studying facial expressions, but human understanding and context are still essential.

Support may include guidance from trained health professionals, peer groups and clear information during pregnancy and after birth.

The effort reflects persistent differences in breastfeeding rates between communities. Mothers facing poverty, poor housing, limited access to services or other pressures can encounter greater barriers to feeding. Officials say support should be welcoming, culturally sensitive and available in local communities, rather than relying on mothers to seek help alone.

Evidence-based advice can also help families address common challenges, including difficulties with positioning, pain or concerns about milk supply. Health workers are encouraged to provide consistent information and refer parents to specialist or peer support when needed. Campaigners say partners and wider family members should be included, since their encouragement can influence a mother’s experience.

Improving access must go hand in hand with respecting informed choices, including a parent’s decision to use formula or combine feeding methods. Scotland’s approach aims to ensure every family receives non-judgmental support and accurate information. Progress will depend on sustained investment, monitoring outcomes and tailoring services to the needs of different communities.

The courthouse clock struck four as the jury filed into the room. Rain tapped against the tall windows. On the table lay a photograph of a broken shop window. Beside it, the judge’s instructions sat in a neat stack. The defendant, Lena Ortiz, had been accused of stealing a gold watch from the shop. No one had found the watch in her home or among her things. The case rested mostly on one witness, Mr. Bell, who said he had seen her leave the shop. He had first told police the person wore a dark coat. At trial, he described a red scarf. He had also placed the sighting at dusk, then later at midnight. “People forget details,” said Martin, the foreman. “But they don’t usually change the hour by six hours,” replied Jo. One juror pointed to Lena’s old conviction for shoplifting. “She’s done it before,” he said. “That doesn’t prove she did this,” Jo answered. The room went quiet. The jurors had heard how the prosecutor displayed the old conviction. They had also heard the judge warn them not to treat it as proof of guilt. Outside, a bus hissed along the wet street. Inside, the jurors turned back to the testimony. A neighbor had seen someone running from the shop. She could not identify the person. The shopkeeper had found the window broken the next morning. He could not say when the watch disappeared. Mr. Bell had admitted that he wore glasses but had not been wearing them that night. “I still think she looks like the sort of person who would do it,” the first juror muttered. Jo looked at him steadily. “That’s exactly what we’re not supposed to decide.” The foreman read the judge’s words aloud: a verdict must rest on evidence, not fear, rumor, or dislike. They reviewed each fact once more. The broken window proved there had been a crime. It did not prove Lena had entered the shop. The shifting story weakened the only clear identification. Her past could not fill the gaps in the present case. Martin asked whether anyone could say, without guessing, that she was guilty. No one raised a hand. The first juror stared at the photograph, then lowered his eyes. “I don’t know,” he said. “And I suppose that matters.” The foreman called the bailiff. When the judge asked for the verdict, Martin stood. “Not guilty,” he said. Lena closed her eyes for a moment as the words settled over the courtroom. The rain kept falling, but the question that had followed her into court was finally allowed to remain unanswered.

France’s Labor Unions Face a Changing Economy—and a Test of Public Support

PARIS — France’s labor unions remain a powerful force in national politics, but their influence is being tested by economic change, shifting public attitudes and debate over how workers should be represented. The country has a long tradition of street demonstrations, strikes and collective bargaining. Yet the ability of unions to mobilize large protests does not always translate into broad agreement with their demands.

French unions are numerous and often divided, with competing organizations representing workers across public and private sectors. Membership is relatively low compared with many European countries, but unions retain influence through workplace elections, sector-wide agreements and a prominent role in public debate. Their ability to call coordinated strikes can give them leverage far beyond their membership numbers.

That leverage was evident during protests over pension changes and other government reforms. Demonstrations have drawn large crowds, while transport stoppages and disruptions to schools, energy supplies and public services have raised the stakes for both policymakers and the public. Such actions can focus attention on workers’ concerns, but they can also test the patience of people who depend on those services.

Public opinion toward labor protests is therefore mixed. Many people support the right to strike and see demonstrations as a necessary way to defend hard-won protections. Others may sympathize with workers’ aims while opposing prolonged disruption, particularly when strikes affect commuters, families or small businesses. Views can shift according to the issue, the scale of disruption and whether a proposed reform is seen as fair.

The divide poses a strategic challenge for unions. A protest can demonstrate strength, but maintaining public support often requires explaining how a workplace dispute affects people beyond the picket line. Union leaders must also decide when to negotiate, when to escalate and how to keep members engaged through a long campaign.

The economic landscape makes those choices harder. France, like other advanced economies, is contending with automation, digital platforms, climate-related changes and pressure on traditional industries. Temporary contracts, subcontracting and remote work have altered how many people earn a living. Workers in these arrangements may be difficult to organize through structures built around large, stable workplaces.

At the same time, established sectors continue to face restructuring. Factories, transport networks and public services are adapting to new technologies, budget constraints and changing demand. These shifts can create fear of job losses or deteriorating conditions, while also producing new roles that require different skills. Unions are expected to defend workers during transitions without blocking every change that employers or governments consider necessary.

That balance has become central to debates over worker representation. Unions argue that collective bargaining gives employees a voice over pay, hours, safety and job security. They also say that representation can help make economic transitions more equitable by securing retraining, redeployment and compensation. Employers and reform-minded policymakers, however, often argue that labor rules must be more flexible to support investment and hiring.

The difficulty lies in defining flexibility without weakening protections. Critics of existing arrangements say complex rules can make it harder for firms to adapt or create permanent jobs. Union officials counter that flexibility too often means transferring risk from companies to workers, particularly those with limited bargaining power. The dispute is not only about regulation, but about who should bear the costs of economic change.

France’s system adds another complication. Agreements negotiated by representative unions can apply across a sector, extending their effects beyond union members. This gives unions a significant institutional role despite low membership. It also means that questions about how unions earn public trust and demonstrate representativeness remain important.

Reform proposals have sought to change workplace rules and encourage negotiation closer to the company level. Supporters say local bargaining can better reflect the needs of individual workplaces. Opponents worry that employees in smaller or less organized firms may be pressured into accepting weaker terms. The debate reflects a broader tension between uniform protections and arrangements tailored to different businesses.

Unions themselves are also adapting. Some have tried to reach workers in newer industries and less secure jobs, where traditional organizing methods may not work. Others are seeking to broaden their campaigns beyond wages, emphasizing health, working conditions, gender equality and the right to disconnect. Their success will depend partly on whether workers see unions as relevant to problems they face today.

The state of public opinion will matter as reform debates continue. Governments need to build support for changes that may affect pensions, employment protections or public services. Unions, in turn, need to show that opposition is grounded in more than defense of existing arrangements. Both face a public that may want economic modernization while resisting changes perceived as unfair or imposed without adequate consultation.

France’s experience also highlights the limits of measuring labor power by protest size alone. A large demonstration can influence the political agenda, but lasting change often depends on negotiation, workplace organization and public credibility. Conversely, a reform that passes despite protests may still leave unresolved grievances that return later in another form.

For workers, the central question is whether existing institutions can give them a meaningful voice as jobs and industries change. For unions, it is whether they can represent a wider range of workers while retaining the ability to mobilize. For governments and employers, it is whether reform can deliver economic adaptability without deepening insecurity.

The answers are unlikely to come from a single law or protest movement. France’s unions will continue to wield influence, but that influence will depend on how effectively they respond to a less predictable labor market and a divided public. The challenge is to make worker representation resilient enough for economic change—and credible enough to bring the public along.

Many young carers in England are providing regular help to relatives without being recognised by schools, health services or local authorities, campaigners say. As a result, some miss out on support that could ease the pressure on them and their families.

A young carer is generally someone under 18 who helps care for a family member because of illness, disability, mental health difficulties or substance misuse. Their responsibilities can range from cooking and cleaning to managing medication, translating at appointments or providing emotional support. Some also supervise siblings or take on tasks normally carried out by adults.

The scale of the issue is difficult to establish because many children are never identified. Estimates vary, and experts warn that official figures may not capture the full number of young people with caring responsibilities. Some families do not describe a child’s role as caring, while others may be reluctant to seek help because of stigma or concerns about outside involvement.

Young people can also keep their responsibilities private to avoid standing out among classmates. Teachers may see tiredness, lateness or falling grades without knowing what is happening at home. Health professionals may focus on the person receiving care and overlook the effect on children in the household.

The consequences can be significant. Caring duties may leave young people with less time for homework, sleep, friendships and activities. Some report anxiety, isolation and exhaustion, although experiences differ and many also describe close relationships with the people they support.

Support is available through local authorities, schools and voluntary organisations, but access can vary by area. Under the Children and Families Act 2014, local authorities in England have a duty to assess the support needs of young carers where it appears they may need help. Campaigners say that duty does not always translate into timely, consistent assistance.

A young carer’s assessment can consider the child’s wishes, education and wellbeing, as well as whether caring is appropriate for their age. Support might include help at school, access to a young carers’ group, or services for the adult receiving care. Families may also need practical assistance to reduce the amount of responsibility placed on a child.

Charities are calling for better identification, clearer referral routes and stronger links between schools, social care and health services. They say staff need training to recognise caring responsibilities and speak with children sensitively. Regular checks can help ensure that support continues as a family’s circumstances change.

Campaigners stress that identifying a young carer should not mean automatically separating them from their family or dismissing the value they find in helping. The aim, they say, is to make sure caring is safe, manageable and does not prevent a child from learning and developing. For many young people, being asked privately and without judgement could be the first step towards getting help.

A volcano is an opening in Earth’s crust where molten rock, gases, and other materials can reach the surface. Below many volcanoes, magma collects in pockets or reservoirs within the crust. Magma is molten rock underground; once it erupts, it is called lava. A volcanic system also includes the pathways that magma follows toward the surface, often called conduits or vents.

The summit may contain a crater, a bowl-shaped hollow formed by eruptions or collapse. Some volcanoes have a much larger depression called a caldera. Calderas form when a major eruption empties much of a magma reservoir and the ground above it sinks. A volcano’s flanks are its sides, where lava and fragmental material can build up in layers.

Eruptions begin when rising magma and expanding gases create enough pressure to overcome the surrounding rock. Magma’s viscosity, or resistance to flow, strongly affects how an eruption unfolds. Hot magma with little silica is generally fluid, allowing gases to escape more easily and often producing relatively gentle lava flows. Cooler, silica-rich magma is more viscous, so it can trap gases and build pressure.

When pressure is released, an eruption may produce lava, volcanic ash, gas, or mixtures of these materials. Ash consists of tiny fragments of volcanic rock and glass, not the soft residue left by ordinary fires. Explosive eruptions can send ash columns high into the atmosphere. They may also generate pyroclastic flows, fast-moving currents of hot gas, ash, and rock that are extremely dangerous.

Lava flows can cover the land and destroy buildings, but they usually move more slowly than pyroclastic flows. Some eruptions release gases such as water vapor, carbon dioxide, and sulfur dioxide. Volcanic activity can continue for days or years, with quiet intervals between episodes. Scientists monitor earthquakes, ground deformation, gas emissions, and heat to assess changes in volcanic activity, though exact eruption timing is difficult to predict.

Volcanoes build several distinctive landforms. A shield volcano is broad and gently sloped, formed by repeated flows of fluid lava that spread over large areas. A composite volcano, also called a stratovolcano, is steeper and often built from alternating layers of lava and fragmental deposits. These volcanoes can produce both flowing lava and explosive eruptions.

A cinder cone is a smaller, steep-sided hill made mainly of loose fragments, such as cinders and ash, that fall around a vent. It often forms during a relatively brief eruptive episode. A lava dome develops when very viscous lava piles up near a vent instead of flowing far. Domes may grow gradually, but their unstable sides can collapse and trigger hazardous flows.

Some landforms form when lava travels through existing terrain. A lava plateau develops when fluid lava repeatedly spreads across broad areas, creating thick, extensive layers. A lava tube forms when the surface of a flow cools and hardens while molten lava continues moving beneath it. After the lava drains away, the tube may remain as a cave.

Volcanic craters and calderas are depressions rather than volcanic hills. They may later fill with water, creating crater lakes. Repeated eruptions can also build islands, while erosion and the movement of tectonic plates reshape volcanic landscapes over time. Together, a volcano’s structure, magma, and eruption history determine the landforms it creates and the hazards it may pose.

Summer offers a chance to choose a topic that feels meaningful to them. One student might build a small garden, while another might create a podcast or learn to code. Because students choose their projects, they are more likely to feel curious and motivated. That motivation can encourage them to spend more time learning and to keep going when a task becomes difficult. Projects also help students connect classroom ideas to real life. For example, planning a garden can involve science, measurement, budgeting, and writing. A project gives students a clear goal and lets them see the results of their effort. Along the way, they can practice important skills such as problem-solving, research, creativity, and time management. They also learn to make decisions and take responsibility for their work. If they make a mistake, they can adjust their plans and try again. This makes learning feel like an active process rather than simply memorizing facts. Students can share their projects with family, friends, or classmates and learn from their feedback. Teachers and parents can support them by asking questions and helping them find useful resources without taking over. The projects do not need to be expensive or complicated; even a simple project can teach valuable lessons. Overall, student-chosen summer projects help young people learn with purpose, build confidence, and enjoy discovering new things.

Distracted driving is one of the most dangerous choices a person can make on the road. Even a brief glance at a phone can take a driver’s attention away from traffic. At highway speed, a car can travel a long distance in just a few seconds. During that time, a driver might miss a stoplight, a pedestrian, or a vehicle braking ahead. Texting is especially risky because it takes a driver’s eyes, hands, and mind off driving. Phone calls and navigation apps can also cause distraction, even when they seem harmless. A crash caused by distraction can lead to serious injuries or loss of life. It can also affect families and communities long after the collision. Drivers should make safety their first responsibility whenever they get behind the wheel. Before starting a trip, they can set their route and music while the car is parked. They should silence notifications or turn on a driving mode to avoid the temptation to check messages. If a call or message is urgent, the driver should pull over somewhere safe before responding. Passengers can help by handling navigation or answering calls when appropriate. New drivers should learn that no message is worth risking someone’s safety. Adults can set a good example by keeping their phones out of reach while driving. Laws against handheld phone use help, but personal responsibility matters just as much. Choosing to focus on the road protects the driver, passengers, and everyone nearby. Responsible phone use behind the wheel begins with one simple rule: put the phone away and drive attentively.
