Banks expand the money supply mainly by creating deposits when they make loans. When a bank approves a loan, it typically records a loan asset and credits the borrower’s account with a matching deposit. The borrower can then spend that deposit, transferring it to another person or business. The payment usually moves deposits between banks rather than removing money from the banking system. As a result, lending can increase the amount of bank money available to the public.

This process does not mean banks can lend without limits. A bank must manage its funding, capital, liquidity, and risks, and it must meet applicable regulations. It also needs to settle payments with other banks, often using central-bank reserves. Reserves are balances that banks hold at the central bank; they are not the same as the deposits households and firms use for everyday payments. In many modern systems, banks make lending decisions based on creditworthiness and profitability, while ensuring they can meet resulting payments and regulatory requirements.

When a bank loan is repaid, the principal payment generally reduces both the borrower’s deposit and the bank’s loan asset. In this sense, repayment destroys some bank-created money. Interest payments are income to the bank and do not work in exactly the same way as principal repayment. Deposits can also change for other reasons, including government transactions, central-bank operations, and flows between banks and non-bank institutions.

A larger money supply can contribute to rising prices, but it does not mechanically cause inflation in a fixed proportion. The effect depends on how much new spending occurs, how quickly money circulates, and whether businesses can increase production to meet demand. If spending grows faster than the economy’s capacity to supply goods and services, prices may rise. If new lending finances productive investment that expands capacity, the inflationary effect may be smaller over time. Inflation is also affected by factors such as energy costs, supply disruptions, expectations, and fiscal policy.

Central banks influence lending and spending through several channels. They set or guide short-term interest rates, which affect the cost of borrowing and the return on saving. They may also provide liquidity to banks and influence financial conditions through asset purchases or other operations. Higher rates tend to discourage some borrowing and spending, though the effects occur with delays and vary across households and firms. Central banks generally cannot dictate the exact amount of lending or deposits created by commercial banks.

Different theories and institutional arrangements describe the relationship between reserves, lending, and money. The textbook money-multiplier model presents banks as receiving reserves and lending a fraction of them, with successive deposits expanding by a predictable multiple. This model can be useful for introducing the idea that banking connects reserves and deposits, but it is a poor description of how lending is usually initiated in modern economies. Banks do not simply lend out reserves to households; reserves are used mainly for settlement between banks and with the central bank.

Under a fractional-reserve system, banks hold only a fraction of their deposit liabilities as reserves or other liquid assets. Such systems can support substantial lending, but lending is constrained by capital rules, liquidity needs, funding conditions, regulation, and borrower demand. A narrow-reserve or full-reserve proposal would require banks to back certain transaction deposits fully with safe reserves or equivalent assets. Supporters argue this could reduce the risk of bank runs and limit private creation of transaction money. Critics question how credit would be supplied, how the system would adapt to changing demand for money, and whether similar risks would reappear elsewhere.

Theories of money also differ in what they emphasize. The quantity theory links the money supply, the speed at which money is spent, the overall price level, and real output; in a simplified form, it suggests that sustained money growth beyond output growth can lead to inflation if money’s velocity is stable. In practice, velocity changes, and the relationship is not constant. Endogenous-money theories stress that bank lending and deposit creation respond to economic activity, credit demand, and central-bank policy rather than being determined by a fixed reserve stock. Monetarist approaches emphasize controlling money growth as a way to stabilize prices, while many current central banks focus directly on inflation targets and interest rates.

These perspectives are not necessarily complete opposites. They highlight different parts of a complex system in which banks, borrowers, central banks, governments, and markets interact. The key distinction is between money creation through bank lending and the forces that determine whether that money leads to stronger production, higher asset prices, or consumer-price inflation. Understanding that distinction helps explain why credit conditions can shape economic activity without making price changes automatic or predictable.

Maintaining a minimum academic average helps student athletes succeed both in school and in sports. It reminds them that education is an important part of being a student athlete. Sports can take up many hours, but schoolwork still needs attention. A minimum average gives students a clear goal to work toward. Meeting that goal encourages them to attend classes and complete assignments on time. It can also help them develop better study habits. When students plan their week, they learn to balance practices, games, and homework. These time-management skills are useful in many parts of life.

Academic standards also encourage student athletes to ask for help when they need it. They may visit a teacher, join a study group, or use tutoring services. Learning to seek support is a valuable skill, not a weakness. Keeping up with schoolwork can also reduce stress before tests and deadlines. Good grades may open doors to college programs, scholarships, and other opportunities. Not every athlete will play professionally, so education provides important options for the future. Even athletes who continue in sports need knowledge and skills to make informed decisions.

A minimum academic average can also teach responsibility. Student athletes learn that their choices have consequences and that effort matters. They must show commitment in the classroom as well as on the field or court. This balance can build discipline and confidence. After sports, many of the same habits will help them succeed at work, in college, and in their communities. Employers and teachers value people who are dependable and willing to learn. Sports careers may end, but the ability to set goals and work toward them remains useful. Maintaining a minimum academic average is therefore more than a rule. It helps student athletes become stronger students, better teammates, and more prepared adults.

When the city of Veyr fell, its bells rang for three days beneath the ash.
The marked people had ruled from its glass towers, each born with a silver line across the palm.
They claimed the lines made them wiser, and the unmarked believed them.
Then the river changed course and swallowed the towers.
In the years that followed, villages rose along the dry banks.
People shared tools, stories, and decisions, unsure how to live without masters.
Some still feared the silver-marked, though few remained.
One autumn night, a stranger arrived at the settlement of Lowbridge.
She wore no shoes and carried a brass compass that pointed toward no north.
Her name, she said, was Ilyan.
The village healer noticed a pale line crossing Ilyan’s palm.
It was not silver, but a deep blue that seemed to move beneath the skin.
The elders sent for the ruler, Lord Sere, who had survived the city’s fall.
He came at dawn with six guards and a smile as thin as wire.
Sere had gathered the scattered marked into a new fortress beyond the salt flats.
He told the villagers that Ilyan belonged to him.
The compass spun in her hand, then stopped, pointing straight at Sere.
At its tip, the air shimmered like heat above a road.
A voice rose from the brass: “The last seal is broken.”
Sere’s smile vanished.
Ilyan remembered nothing of the city, yet she knew the voice.
It had spoken in her dreams since childhood, calling her by another name.
The villagers stood behind her, frightened but unwilling to step aside.
Sere ordered his guards to seize her.
Before they could move, the blue mark blazed across her palm.
Every silver line in the square went dark.
Sere fell to his knees, suddenly no different from anyone else.
His guards lowered their weapons, and the villagers lowered theirs too.
Ilyan understood that her gift could erase the old order, but it could also erase the people shaped by it.
She turned the compass away from Sere.
“Let the marks fade by choice,” she said, “not by command.”
The brass needle settled at last, pointing east toward an open road.
And for the first time, the people of Veyr’s broken world chose where to go together.

At dawn on June 21, thousands of people gathered across India to mark International Day of Yoga, turning public parks, school grounds and historic sites into open-air exercise studios. The annual event, promoted by the Indian government, paired a message about personal health with a wider display of national identity. In Delhi, officials and participants took part in a mass yoga session as cameras recorded the carefully choreographed gathering. Similar events were held in cities and villages nationwide, with government offices, schools and community groups encouraged to organize classes.

The day’s central pitch was practical: regular movement and breathing exercises, organizers said, can support fitness and help people manage stress. Participants followed routines of postures, stretches and controlled breathing, often led by instructors on stages or through loudspeakers. Many described the session as a chance to build healthy habits and connect with neighbors. For some, the event was also a celebration of a practice they regard as part of India’s cultural heritage.

International Yoga Day was established by the United Nations in 2014, following a proposal by Prime Minister Narendra Modi. The first observance took place in 2015. Modi and other Indian leaders have since presented yoga as a contribution from India to global well-being, and the annual events have become a prominent feature of the country’s public calendar. Government agencies promote yoga in schools, workplaces and public spaces, while Indian missions abroad organize sessions for international audiences.

That visibility has also made the day politically charged. Supporters say the events promote preventive health and share a valuable tradition with the world. Critics argue that official celebrations can blur the line between public health campaigns and political messaging. They question the use of state resources for large-scale displays and say participation should remain voluntary, particularly in schools and government workplaces.

Religious and cultural sensitivities add another layer to the debate. Yoga developed over centuries in South Asia, with roots in diverse philosophical and religious traditions, including Hindu thought. Modern yoga, especially as practiced internationally, often emphasizes physical postures and breathing while setting aside much of that background. Some Hindu organizations see the global popularity of yoga as recognition of its origins; some minority groups worry that official promotion can imply a religious expectation in a secular, plural society.

The controversy is not simply about whether yoga is religious. Scholars and practitioners describe a complex history in which ideas and techniques changed across time, communities and institutions. The Sanskrit word “yoga” has referred to different paths and disciplines, not just the posture-based routines common in contemporary classes. In the 19th and 20th centuries, Indian reformers and teachers adapted and presented yoga in new ways, while international audiences helped shape its modern forms.

That history has prompted disagreement over how the practice should be described and who has authority to define it. Some scholars caution against treating today’s popular exercise routines as an unchanged ancient system. Others stress that modern adaptations do not erase yoga’s South Asian roots. The global fitness industry has expanded the practice while also raising questions about commercialization, cultural appropriation and the visibility of Indian teachers and traditions.

Organizers of the national event generally emphasize inclusivity, describing yoga as a discipline open to people of any faith or background. The standard sequence used at many public gatherings is designed to be accessible, though participants are advised to work within their abilities. Health professionals note that yoga can improve flexibility and balance for many people, but it is not a substitute for medical care and can cause injury if movements are forced or poorly supervised. They recommend qualified instruction, especially for people with health conditions.

The event’s scale can make the message difficult to separate from its symbolism. Matching clothing, synchronized movements and prominent political appearances create striking images of unity. For supporters, those images demonstrate collective participation in a health initiative. For critics, they can resemble a state-sponsored performance of cultural belonging.

Organizers have sought to carry the observance beyond a single morning. Local programs include classes, demonstrations and discussions about physical and mental health. Some schools introduce students to basic postures, while community centers offer sessions for older people and beginners. The quality and accessibility of these programs vary, depending on local resources and trained instructors.

The government’s promotion has also helped make yoga a recognizable part of India’s international profile. Indian diplomats and cultural institutions stage events overseas, often in parks or public squares. Participants abroad include yoga practitioners, Indian diaspora communities and people encountering the practice for the first time. The gatherings present yoga as both a global wellness activity and a tradition associated with India.

For many participants, the political arguments remain distant from the experience of stretching on a mat. They attend for exercise, relaxation or companionship, and some say the routine helps them establish structure in their day. Others avoid the official events because they feel the public presentation is too closely tied to a political or religious identity. Their differing responses reflect the diversity of views within India itself.

The annual celebration therefore carries several messages at once. It promotes fitness, showcases government priorities and asserts a connection between yoga and Indian cultural history. It also exposes unresolved questions about secularism, national identity and the way traditions change when they travel. None of those questions can be settled by a mass exercise session alone.

As participants rolled up their mats and the crowds dispersed, the event left behind a familiar debate alongside its health message. Yoga is practiced in many forms, from demanding athletic classes to contemplative disciplines, and its meaning varies among those who teach and use it. India’s International Yoga Day brings these versions into public view, where wellness goals meet political tensions and contested accounts of the past.

SP Energy Networks has delayed a public consultation on its proposed Scotland–Cumbria power line, citing changing conditions across the energy sector. The company had planned to seek views on the project, which would carry electricity between south-west Scotland and north-west England. It has not yet announced a new date for the consultation.

The proposed link is intended to strengthen the electricity network and help move power from renewable sources to homes and businesses. Its development comes as the UK’s energy system adapts to growing renewable generation, changing patterns of demand and new investment priorities. Those shifts have prompted the company to review aspects of its plans, SP Energy Networks said.

The delay means communities along the proposed route will have to wait longer for details and an opportunity to comment. The consultation is expected to explain the project’s rationale, outline potential route options and invite feedback from residents, landowners and local organisations. Such responses can inform the project’s design before decisions are made on a preferred route.

The company has not indicated that the project has been cancelled. Nor has it provided a revised timetable for the next stage of development. Further information is expected once its review is complete.

The proposal forms part of wider efforts to upgrade electricity infrastructure as the UK aims to expand low-carbon power. New transmission capacity can help connect renewable projects to the grid, but major lines often raise concerns about landscape impacts, construction and effects on land use. Local authorities and community groups are likely to seek clarity on those issues when consultation begins.

SP Energy Networks said it would provide an update when it is ready to restart engagement. Until then, affected communities will have limited information about how the delay may affect the project’s schedule.

Exploring Venus is challenging because its thick, scorching atmosphere and crushing pressure can destroy spacecraft in a short time. Yet missions such as NASA’s Magellan and upcoming probes can reveal how the planet’s volcanoes, clouds, and climate work, helping us understand Earth and other worlds. The journey takes months, but careful planning and new technology may allow scientists to study Venus more closely and discover whether its past was very different from its harsh present.

The soldiers arrived at dusk, muddy and quiet, with a white flag tied to their tallest spear. Their captain, Mara Venn, asked the villagers for shelter, promising they would leave no trouble behind. The village had heard such promises before, but winter had already taken the roof from the mill. So they gave the squad the old storehouse and watched them closely.

By morning, the soldiers were mending the bridge that had kept the village from market for weeks. They hauled stones, set beams, and worked until their hands bled. Mara traded her own coat for a sack of flour at the baker’s door. The youngest soldier, Pell, spent an afternoon teaching children to knot fishing nets. Even the village dogs stopped barking at them.

For nine days, the squad stayed. They helped the healer gather herbs and stood guard when wolves came down from the hills. At supper, they listened to stories of lost harvests and laughed at the right moments. Mara spoke little about the army, but she remembered every name. Soon, the villagers began leaving warm bread outside the storehouse.

On the tenth night, a shadow crossed the moon. The dragon descended beyond the fields, its scales dark as a burned forest. It did not roar; it only opened one golden eye and waited. The soldiers formed a line between the creature and the village.

Mara asked the villagers to gather in the square. She told them the army had sent her squad to bargain for a border pass. The dragon would keep raiders from the valley, she said, if the village supplied it with a tribute each year. The tribute was not grain or gold.

“It wants one child,” Mara said, her voice breaking. The soldiers had known this from the start, and their kindness had been meant to make the village accept the bargain. The villagers turned on them, not with stones, but with a silence heavier than any shout. Pell stepped forward and laid his sword at the captain’s feet.

Mara looked at the dragon and said the bargain was over. The beast’s eye narrowed, and smoke curled between its teeth. Then the villagers stood shoulder to shoulder behind the soldiers. The dragon studied them for a long moment before spreading its wings.

It left without taking a soul, but its shadow lingered over the valley for years. The squad stayed, not as protectors, but as people who had to earn forgiveness. And every spring, when the bridge was mended, the villagers made them help.

In 2010, the Deepwater Horizon oil rig exploded in the Gulf of Mexico, killing 11 workers and releasing millions of barrels of oil. The spill spread across the sea and reached wetlands, beaches, and other coastal habitats. As part of the response, the U.S. Coast Guard and other agencies used controlled burns to remove oil from the water’s surface. These operations are often called in-situ burning because the oil is burned where it is found.

Crews gathered floating oil into thick patches, often using fire-resistant booms, then ignited it under controlled conditions. Burning could remove large amounts of oil quickly, reducing the time it remained on the water. It was especially useful when oil was too far offshore or too widespread to collect efficiently. The method also reduced the volume of oily waste that would otherwise need to be transported and treated.

But burning oil does not make its pollution disappear. It produces smoke containing fine particles and gases, including compounds that can harm human health and the environment. Smoke exposure may irritate the eyes and lungs, and people with asthma or other breathing conditions can be especially vulnerable. Responders therefore monitored air quality and considered wind direction, nearby communities, and worker safety.

Burning also leaves behind residue, some of which can sink or wash ashore. That residue may expose marine organisms and coastal habitats to concentrated pollutants. The heat and flames can injure or kill animals at the surface, although crews tried to limit the risk by checking burn areas for wildlife. Burning is generally most effective on fresh, thick oil; weathered or thinly spread oil is harder to ignite and sustain.

The decision to burn involves weighing these risks against the harms of leaving oil in the water or using other cleanup methods. Researchers studied the smoke, residue, and effects on wildlife to improve future response plans. The Gulf response showed that controlled burning can be a useful tool, but it is not a complete solution. Its use requires careful monitoring, protective measures, and clear communication with nearby communities.

FARC’s long insurgency reshaped Colombia’s politics, rural life and security for more than half a century. The Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia, known by its Spanish acronym FARC, began in 1964 as a Marxist guerrilla movement. Its founders came largely from communist-aligned peasant self-defense groups formed amid land disputes and political violence. Those disputes were rooted in profound rural inequality and the period of civil conflict known as La Violencia. The group’s early stronghold was the southern department of Tolima, before it expanded into other parts of the country.

FARC’s ideology combined Marxism-Leninism with a call for agrarian reform and a more equal distribution of wealth and land. It portrayed itself as a force for rural communities neglected by the state. The government and many Colombians, however, viewed it as an armed organization that used violence to pursue political goals. Over time, FARC’s revolutionary program became difficult to separate from its involvement in kidnapping, extortion and the drug economy.

The group was organized as a hierarchical force, with a central leadership body known as the Secretariat. Its congresses set broad policy, while regional blocs and fronts operated across different areas. At its peak, FARC had tens of thousands of fighters and a network of supporters and informants. Commanders exercised substantial authority over local units, although conditions and practices varied across fronts.

FARC built influence in remote regions where government services and security forces were limited. It taxed economic activity, imposed rules and sometimes acted as a local authority. The group also carried out ambushes, bombings and attacks on military and police targets. Civilians were repeatedly caught in the fighting, displaced from their homes or subjected to coercion by armed actors.

Kidnapping became one of FARC’s most notorious tactics, used to raise money and exert political pressure. The group also relied on extortion, often demanding payments from businesses, landowners and local producers. As coca cultivation and cocaine trafficking expanded, FARC collected taxes from growers and drug-processing operations in areas it controlled. Investigators and officials have also accused some fronts of participating more directly in the drug trade. FARC denied that drug trafficking defined the movement, but its links to the illicit economy became a central feature of the conflict.

The conflict involved far more than FARC and the state. Colombia’s security forces fought the guerrillas, while right-wing paramilitary organizations emerged and committed widespread abuses against civilians. These groups often claimed to defend communities from insurgents, but also carried out massacres, forced displacement and targeted killings. Other guerrilla groups, including the National Liberation Army, operated alongside FARC at times and competed with it in some areas. The result was a shifting conflict with multiple armed actors and millions of victims.

Government offensives, particularly from the early 2000s, inflicted heavy losses on FARC. A strengthened military, U.S.-backed security assistance and intelligence operations pushed the group out of some strongholds. High-profile commanders were killed or captured, and desertions increased. The deaths of Secretariat members Raúl Reyes and Manuel Marulanda, in 2008, marked major setbacks for the organization. Still, FARC retained the ability to operate in remote areas and continued to recruit and fight.

Peace efforts had repeatedly failed before negotiations produced a breakthrough. In 2012, the government of President Juan Manuel Santos and FARC began formal talks in Havana. The final accord, signed in 2016, addressed land reform, political participation, illicit drugs, victims’ rights and the group’s transition to civilian life. Colombia’s voters narrowly rejected an initial version in a referendum, prompting revisions. A revised agreement was signed and approved by Congress.

Under the accord, most FARC fighters disarmed under international monitoring, and the organization became a legal political party. The deal also created a transitional justice system to investigate serious crimes and offered reintegration programs for former combatants. Implementation has been uneven. Former fighters have faced threats and killings, while disputes over land, rural development and security have persisted.

FARC’s armed strength fell sharply after the agreement, but the organization did not disappear entirely. Dissident groups rejected the accord or later returned to arms, and they operate under different names and leadership structures. These factions are not a single unified force, even when they claim the FARC legacy. Some are involved in coca production, trafficking, extortion and battles for territorial control. Their presence has complicated efforts to establish peace in areas once dominated by the guerrillas.

The decline of the original FARC resulted from military pressure, internal losses and a negotiated decision to disarm. Its transformation into a political party ended its role as a national insurgent army, but did not resolve Colombia’s deeper conflicts. Rural inequality, illicit economies and weak state presence continue to create openings for armed groups. The peace accord remains a landmark, yet its success depends on protecting former combatants and civilians and delivering security and opportunity to neglected regions.

International Women’s Day is observed around the world on March 8 each year. It celebrates women’s achievements and draws attention to the continuing pursuit of gender equality. The day has roots in labor movements and campaigns for women’s rights in the early twentieth century. Its history reflects demands for fair working conditions, political representation, and social change.

In the late 1800s and early 1900s, rapid industrialization brought many women into factories and other paid work. Women workers often faced low wages, long hours, unsafe conditions, and limited legal protections. At the same time, women organized for the right to vote and for greater influence in public life. Their activism grew alongside broader labor and socialist movements.

A key early event took place in New York City on February 28, 1909. The Socialist Party of America organized a National Woman’s Day to honor women workers and support women’s suffrage. The event followed a period of labor organizing and protests by garment workers. It helped inspire activists to consider an international day of action.

In 1910, the Second International Socialist Women’s Conference met in Copenhagen, Denmark. German activist Clara Zetkin proposed an annual day to promote women’s rights and suffrage across countries. Delegates from 17 countries supported the idea. They did not set a specific date at the conference.

The first International Women’s Day events took place in several European countries on March 19, 1911. More than a million people attended meetings and demonstrations in Austria, Denmark, Germany, and Switzerland. They called for women’s voting rights, access to public office, and equal opportunities at work. The events also highlighted the need to protect women workers.

March 8 became closely associated with the observance after women in Petrograd, then part of the Russian Empire, took to the streets in 1917. They protested food shortages, war, and the hardship facing working families. Their demonstrations helped spark the Russian Revolution of February 1917, according to the calendar then used in Russia. The corresponding date in the Gregorian calendar was March 8.

After the Russian Revolution, March 8 gained wider importance in socialist and communist movements. The Soviet Union recognized the day as an official holiday in 1965. In 1975, during International Women’s Year, the United Nations began celebrating International Women’s Day on March 8. The UN General Assembly later invited member states to observe the day in a resolution adopted in 1977.

Today, International Women’s Day is marked in countries across the globe. Governments, community groups, schools, unions, businesses, and advocacy organizations may hold events. Activities include rallies, public talks, exhibitions, performances, educational programs, and online campaigns. The style of observance varies according to local histories and needs.

For many people, the day is both a celebration and a call to action. It recognizes achievements in fields such as science, politics, education, culture, and community leadership. It also brings attention to issues including unequal pay, discrimination, violence, unpaid care work, and barriers to education and healthcare. These challenges affect women differently depending on factors such as race, class, disability, age, and migration status.

International Women’s Day is not simply a day for honoring individual success. Its history is rooted in collective organizing and demands for lasting change. Observances often encourage people to learn about women’s contributions and consider what remains to be done. The day can also support local campaigns and organizations working toward equality.

Each year, the United Nations and other groups may highlight particular themes. These themes can focus attention on topics such as women’s leadership, economic opportunity, or access to technology. There is no single format that every country must follow. The meaning of the day is shaped by the communities that observe it.

International Women’s Day offers an opportunity to connect past struggles with present-day efforts. The early activists who called for voting rights and safer workplaces helped shape a global tradition of advocacy. Their work reminds us that progress has often depended on people organizing together. March 8 continues to invite reflection, recognition, and action toward a more equal world.

Using Haskell to Sum Even Fibonacci Numbers Below Four Million

This page explains how to use Haskell to solve a classic number-sequence problem efficiently. The task is to add every even Fibonacci number that is strictly less than four million. The Fibonacci sequence begins with 1 and 2 in this version of the problem. Each later term is the sum of the two previous terms. The sequence therefore starts 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, and 21. Among these values, only 2, 8, 34, and the other even terms should be included. The number four million is a limit, not a value to add. Since four million is not itself a Fibonacci number, using “less than” still matters for making the condition clear.

A direct approach would generate every Fibonacci number and test whether it is even. That approach is easy to understand and is already fast enough for this limit. However, the sequence has a useful pattern that lets us skip all odd terms. Every third Fibonacci number is even. For example, the terms at positions 2, 5, and 8 are 2, 8, and 34 when counting the first term as position 1. This happens because the parity pattern repeats as odd, even, odd. The sum of two consecutive terms follows the same parity rules as ordinary addition. Two odd numbers sum to an even number, while an even number added to an odd number produces an odd number. These rules cause the repeating pattern.

The even terms themselves form a recurrence that is simpler than the full sequence. If an even Fibonacci term is E, the next even term is 4E plus the previous even term. Starting from 2 and 8, this gives 34, then 144, then 610. For instance, 34 is 4 times 8 plus 2. This recurrence generates only values that need to be summed. It avoids producing and checking the intervening odd values. The number of generated terms is small, so the program uses little time and memory.

Here is a complete Haskell program:

main :: IO ()
main = print (sumEvenFibsBelow 4000000)

sumEvenFibsBelow :: Integer -> Integer
sumEvenFibsBelow limit = go 2 8 0
  where
    go current next total
      | current >= limit = total
      | otherwise = go next (4 * next + current) (total + current)

The function takes a limit and returns the sum of even Fibonacci terms below it. Its helper function, go, keeps track of the current even term, the next even term, and the running total. The initial pair is 2 and 8, which are the first two even Fibonacci numbers. The initial total is zero because no terms have been added yet. At each step, the program checks whether the current term has reached the limit. If it has, the accumulated total is returned. Otherwise, the current term is added, and the recurrence produces the next term.

The comparison uses current >= limit to stop at the right time. This ensures that a term equal to the limit would not be included. That matches the phrase “below four million,” which means strictly less than four million. The type Integer is used for the terms, limit, and sum. Haskell’s Integer type supports arbitrary-precision whole numbers, so it does not overflow as fixed-width integer types can. For this particular limit, an ordinary machine-sized integer would also be sufficient. Using Integer makes the function safer to reuse with much larger limits.

The helper function is tail recursive. Its recursive call is the final operation in the otherwise branch. The next call receives all the updated state directly. This style makes the computation iterative in practice under Haskell’s optimization, without building a list of every term. The program uses constant additional memory. Its running time is proportional to the number of even Fibonacci terms below the limit. Because Fibonacci numbers grow rapidly, only a few dozen terms are needed.

The result printed by the program is 4613732. The even terms that contribute to this total are 2, 8, 34, 144, 610, 2584, 10946, 46368, 196418, 832040, and 3524578. The next even Fibonacci term is 14930352, which is above the limit. Adding the listed terms gives the stated result.

For comparison, a more direct version can generate the full sequence and filter its even terms. Haskell’s list functions make that approach concise. One possible implementation is:

sumEvenFibsBelowDirect :: Integer -> Integer
sumEvenFibsBelowDirect limit =
  sum (filter even (takeWhile (< limit) fibs))
  where
    fibs = 1 : 2 : zipWith (+) fibs (tail fibs)

The list fibs begins with 1 and 2, and zipWith adds corresponding elements from the list and its tail. Haskell evaluates list elements lazily, so takeWhile asks for terms only until the limit is reached. The filter function keeps even terms, and sum adds them together. This version is readable and expresses the problem in terms of familiar list operations. For a small limit, it is perfectly practical.

The specialized recurrence is more efficient because it never generates odd terms. It also avoids allocating list structure for the sequence. The direct version may be preferable when clarity or easy modification is more important than minimizing work. For example, it is easy to change the filter to select terms with another property. The specialized version is a good demonstration of using mathematical structure to improve an algorithm. In real code, efficiency should be balanced with maintainability and the scale of the task.

To run the program, save it in a file named Main.hs. With the Glasgow Haskell Compiler installed, use runghc Main.hs to execute it directly. The compiler should print 4613732. You can also compile the program with ghc Main.hs and run the resulting executable. Testing a few small limits can help confirm that the boundary condition behaves as intended. For a limit of 2, the result should be zero because 2 is not strictly below 2. For a limit of 3, the result should be 2. For a limit of 9, the result should be 10, from the terms 2 and 8.

The key ideas are to identify which sequence elements matter, derive a recurrence for those elements, and stop as soon as the limit is reached. Haskell supports both a compact lazy-list solution and an explicit, constant-space recursive solution. The recursive version is efficient because it tracks only two even terms and the running sum. The final answer for even Fibonacci numbers below four million is 4613732.

Military Pressure Alone Cannot Defeat Islamic State, Analysts Warn

Western governments have made significant gains against Islamic State through airstrikes, intelligence operations and support for local forces. But those successes have not eliminated the group’s ability to recruit, adapt or inspire attacks, security analysts say. A durable strategy must address the political grievances and regional conditions that have helped Islamic State take root.

The group, also known as ISIS or ISIL, lost the territorial caliphate it declared in Iraq and Syria in 2014. Its last major stronghold in Syria fell in 2019, ending its control over large, populated areas. Yet Islamic State remains an armed insurgency in both countries and has affiliates operating across parts of Africa and Asia.

Military campaigns can disrupt its command structure, restrict movement and prevent the group from holding territory. They cannot, on their own, resolve the conflicts and governance failures that create openings for extremist movements. When communities face insecurity, exclusion or arbitrary rule, Islamic State can exploit resentment and present itself as an alternative.

That political appeal does not mean the group represents the interests of the populations it targets. Islamic State has imposed brutal rule, persecuted minorities and killed civilians, including Muslims who rejected its ideology. Its ability to attract recruits has nevertheless depended partly on propaganda that frames local disputes as part of a wider struggle.

In Iraq, the group’s earlier expansion was aided by the collapse of state authority and deep mistrust between Sunni communities and a government many viewed as exclusionary. In Syria, civil war, repression and fragmented control gave Islamic State room to seize territory and build institutions. The group also benefited from weapons, money and fighters moving through unstable borders.

Those conditions have changed, but many remain unresolved. Displacement, damaged infrastructure and weak public services continue to complicate recovery in areas once controlled by the group. Thousands of people linked to Islamic State remain in camps and detention facilities in northeastern Syria, where uncertain futures and deteriorating conditions pose humanitarian and security challenges.

Western governments have often prioritized counterterrorism operations because they can produce visible, immediate results. Targeted raids and airstrikes can kill senior figures and disrupt planned attacks. But analysts warn that treating each setback as a military problem risks allowing the organization to regenerate beneath the surface.

A broader approach would require local governments to provide fair security and access to basic services. It would also mean addressing discrimination, corruption and abuses by state forces or armed groups. Without accountability, efforts to restore government authority can deepen the grievances extremists seek to exploit.

The task is difficult for outside powers. Western involvement can be portrayed by Islamic State as occupation or interference, while aid and diplomacy cannot substitute for legitimate local leadership. Strategies designed in foreign capitals may also fail if they overlook local rivalries and the differing priorities of communities.

Regional governments have a central role as well. Competition among neighboring states has helped prolong conflicts and weaken coordination against armed groups. Cooperation on border security, intelligence and the movement of illicit funds could limit Islamic State’s ability to exploit gaps between jurisdictions.

The group’s affiliates make the challenge wider than Iraq and Syria. In parts of the Sahel, the Lake Chad basin and Afghanistan, Islamic State-linked organizations operate amid conflict, weak institutions and limited state services. Their local agendas differ, so a single military model is unlikely to work everywhere.

Experts say Western policy should distinguish between preventing attacks and reducing the conditions that support recruitment. Intelligence sharing and targeted operations remain important, particularly against networks planning violence. They should be paired with sustained diplomacy, humanitarian aid and support for accountable local institutions.

Rehabilitation and reintegration programs also matter. People detained for association with Islamic State, including children, require case-by-case assessment and lawful treatment. Leaving large populations in limbo can create new risks and prolong instability.

There are no quick solutions, and political reform cannot guarantee that extremist movements will disappear. Islamic State has shown that it can adjust its tactics after losing territory, using small cells and online propaganda to remain relevant. Its continued threat is therefore not just a question of battlefield strength.

For Western governments, the challenge is to maintain pressure without mistaking pressure for a complete strategy. A lasting response must reduce the space in which the group can recruit, govern or claim to defend neglected communities. That means confronting Islamic State’s violence while also addressing the regional conflicts and political failures on which its appeal depends.

The cabin boy, Elias, was polishing a brass spyglass when Blackbeard stomped onto the deck. Beyond the bow, the sea shone silver beneath a moonless sky. “That’s the seventh sea,” the pirate growled. “And it’s full of things that’ll chew your bones and spit out your buttons.” The crew laughed, but no one looked comfortable. Elias leaned over the rail and listened to the water whisper. It sounded like someone calling his name from far below. Blackbeard snatched the spyglass from him and peered through it. “Don’t go staring too long, lad,” he said. “The sea stares back, and it’s got a rotten sense of humor.” A pale light bobbed on the horizon. The captain ordered the sails trimmed and every lantern covered. Then a bell rang beneath the waves. It rang once, twice, and a third time. The ship shuddered as something scraped along its keel. Elias saw a row of glowing eyes glide beside them. “Keep your hands aboard!” Blackbeard barked. “Unless you fancy shaking fins with the devil.” One eye rose above the water, attached to a face like a drowned sailor’s. It smiled at Elias. The boy stumbled backward, but the creature spoke in his mother’s voice. “Come home, Elias.” His knees nearly gave way. Blackbeard shoved a cutlass into his hands. “That thing ain’t your mother, you gullible little plank.” The captain’s rough words steadied Elias more than he expected. He raised the blade and shouted that the creature should leave them alone. The eyes blinked out, and the sea grew still. At dawn, the crew found a wet handprint on the deck, though no one had climbed aboard. Blackbeard studied it, then spat over the rail. “Seventh sea’s got manners worse than mine,” he muttered. Elias kept the cutlass close, and never again listened when the water called his name.

Belgium’s liberation from Nazi occupation is remembered as a moment of hope and a call to protect human rights. Allied forces entered Brussels on September 3, 1944, and Belgium’s liberation continued over the months that followed. Each year, commemorations honor those who resisted occupation and those who fought to free the country.

The remembrance also focuses on the Holocaust and the persecution of Belgium’s Jewish community. During the occupation, Nazi authorities and their collaborators deported more than 25,000 Jews from Belgium, most of them to Auschwitz-Birkenau. Many were murdered, while survivors faced the loss of family, homes, and communities. Memorial ceremonies and educational programs preserve their stories and recognize the lives that were destroyed.

Belgium also honors people who risked their lives to rescue Jews. Rescuers hid people, provided false papers, or helped them escape, often under threat of arrest and execution. Their courage shows how individual choices can challenge cruelty, even in dangerous times.

These commemorations also ask people to confront racism and antisemitism today. Remembering the past is not enough if discrimination and hate are allowed to persist. Schools, museums, and community organizations help visitors examine how prejudice can grow into exclusion and violence. By honoring victims, rescuers, and liberators, Belgium encourages people to defend dignity, equality, and solidarity in the present.

Idaho’s upland game birds live in landscapes ranging from sagebrush plains to mountain forests and wetlands. The group includes native species such as dusky grouse, ruffed grouse, and gray partridge, as well as introduced birds such as chukar, ring-necked pheasant, and California quail. Each species depends on a different mix of food, cover, and nesting habitat. Learning to recognize those needs helps explain where birds occur and how their populations change.

Chukar are especially associated with steep, rocky country in southern and central Idaho. They use hillsides with bunchgrass and shrubs, and often rely on nearby water sources. Gray partridge favor open farmland and grassland, where field edges and weedy cover provide food and shelter. Ring-necked pheasants are most common in agricultural valleys with thick grass, brush, and wetland vegetation.

California quail live mainly in warmer parts of the state, often in brushy areas near farms, streams, or residential edges. Dusky grouse occupy higher-elevation forests and mountain openings, while ruffed grouse are more closely tied to moist forests with dense understory, especially where aspen or other deciduous trees grow. These habitats can be affected by wildfire, drought, grazing, farming, and development.

Bird populations naturally rise and fall with weather, nesting success, food supplies, and habitat conditions. Severe winters or dry springs can reduce survival and reproduction, while healthy cover and favorable seasonal conditions can support stronger numbers. Because these effects vary by region and year, hunters and bird watchers should consult current Idaho Department of Fish and Game surveys and regulations rather than rely on old estimates.

Hunting opportunities differ by species and location. Chukar hunting often involves long walks on steep ground, while pheasant and partridge hunting may take place in agricultural country or managed access areas. Grouse hunters typically explore forest roads, clearings, and mountain trails, and quail hunters look for brushy cover in suitable valleys. Idaho’s seasons, legal methods, bag limits, and access rules can change, so check the current regulations before going afield.

Public lands, wildlife management areas, and private lands enrolled in access programs may offer places to hunt, but access is not guaranteed everywhere. Always obtain permission before entering private property and follow posted restrictions. Wear appropriate safety gear, identify targets carefully, and handle firearms responsibly. Whether hunting or simply observing, respecting habitat and reporting wildlife observations can help support Idaho’s upland birds for future generations.

For thirty years, Eli kept his father’s boots by the door.
They were cracked brown leather, still dusted with pale sand.
His mother had placed them there the morning Daniel vanished.
“Your father will need them when he comes home,” she had said.
At six, Eli believed her.
At sixteen, he pretended not to.
At thirty-six, he no longer knew what he believed.
Daniel had disappeared during a storm on the northern coast.
He had gone to check the lighthouse generator and never returned.
The official search lasted nine days.
They found his oilskin jacket snagged on a rock.
They found no body.
Afterward, the town learned to speak of Daniel in the past tense.
Eli’s mother never did.
She said “your father is” whenever she could.
She said “your father was” only when she was tired.
When she died, Eli found the boots still by the door.
He had come home for the funeral and expected to stay one night.
Instead, he stood in the quiet house until the dark gathered around him.
On the kitchen table lay a small brass key.
Beside it was a note in his mother’s handwriting.
“Look beneath the lighthouse floor,” it said.
Eli recognized the key from his childhood.
Daniel had worn it on a cord beneath his shirt.
The lighthouse stood at the edge of town, abandoned and salt-stained.
A rusted chain blocked its door.
Eli cut through it with a pair of bolt cutters.
Inside, the air smelled of cold stone and old rain.
He climbed the spiral stairs, carrying a flashlight.
At the top, the lantern room was empty.
Below it, a loose floorboard shifted beneath his heel.
The key opened a narrow iron hatch.
A ladder descended into darkness.
Eli almost turned back.
Then he remembered his mother waiting by the window each winter.
He climbed down.
At the bottom was a dry chamber carved into the rock.
A tin box sat on a shelf.
Inside lay a bundle of letters tied with blue thread.
The first was dated three days after Daniel disappeared.
“My dear Mara,” it began.
Eli read it standing beneath the lighthouse.
Daniel had survived the storm.
A wave had thrown him into a cleft below the cliffs.
He had crawled into an old signal tunnel and waited for help.
But the tunnel led inland, far from the search boats.
When he finally reached the road, a truck had taken him to the city.
He had been injured and delirious.
A nurse named Ada had cared for him.
By the time he remembered his name, months had passed.
He wrote that he was coming home.
The next letter was dated a year later.
Daniel had learned that Mara had moved away from the coast.
He had sent the letter to her old address.
It had returned unopened.
He kept writing.
There were letters for birthdays, winters, and ordinary Tuesdays.
In one, he described a little apartment above a bakery.
In another, he apologized for missing Eli’s first day of school.
He had seen a photograph of his son in a newspaper.
Eli was holding a paper boat, his hair blown across his face.
Daniel had carried the photograph in his wallet until it wore at the edges.
The letters never said why he had not come home.
The last one, written in careful, uneven script, explained.
A doctor had told him the injury would soon take his memory.
He feared returning only to disappear again, this time while alive.
He feared Eli would watch his father forget him.
So Daniel had stayed near the city, sending letters he could no longer trust himself to deliver.
He had asked Ada to keep them safe.
The box held a final envelope addressed to Eli.
It was dated only six months earlier.
Eli opened it with shaking hands.
“Son,” Daniel had written, “I remember the sound of your laugh, though I cannot remember the words that made it.”
He wrote that Ada had found a quiet home for him by the sea.
He wrote that some mornings he woke certain he had a family waiting.
He wrote that he hoped the letters would reach Eli one day.
At the bottom was an address.
Eli drove through the night.
The road followed the coast, bending past dark fields and sleeping villages.
He arrived at a small care home just after sunrise.
A woman named Ada met him in the garden.
She was older now, with silver hair pinned behind one ear.
She led him to a bench beneath a crooked pine.
A man sat there watching gulls cross the water.
His face was thinner than Eli remembered from photographs.
His hands rested peacefully in his lap.
“Daniel,” Ada said gently, “your son has come.”
The man turned.
His eyes were pale and uncertain.
Eli could not make himself speak.
Then Daniel looked at him and smiled.
“You’re the boy with the paper boat,” he said.
Eli felt the years inside him loosen.
He sat beside his father.
For a while, they watched the gulls.
Daniel asked if the boat had sailed far.
“It did,” Eli said.
“It made it all the way to the sea.”
Daniel nodded as if this were good news.
Eli told him about the letters.
He told him that Mara had kept the boots by the door.
At the sound of her name, Daniel closed his eyes.
“She waited,” Eli whispered.
“I know,” Daniel said.
His voice was soft, but sure.
“I wanted to come back.”
“I know.”
Daniel reached for Eli’s hand.
His fingers were cool and trembling.
Eli held them without asking for anything more.
They spoke of small things: rain, bread, the gulls.
Daniel forgot the conversation twice.
Each time, Eli began again.
There was no anger left that morning.
There was only the man beside him, breathing in the salt air.
When the sun rose higher, Daniel leaned against his shoulder.
Eli stayed until the garden filled with light.
His father’s hand rested in his.
For the first time, the silence between them felt kind.
Eli returned to the old house that evening.
He lifted the boots from their place by the door.
He carried them to the shore and set them on a dry rock.
The tide reached toward them, then drew away.
Eli left the boots there as the sky turned gold.
He did not need them to wait anymore.

The United States should replace the Electoral College with a nationwide popular vote for president. Under the current system, each state receives electoral votes based largely on its population, and a candidate usually wins by earning a majority of those votes. This arrangement can produce a president who received fewer votes nationwide than an opponent. In a democracy, the candidate chosen by the most voters should generally win. A national popular vote would make every ballot count toward the same total.

The current system also gives candidates strong reasons to focus on a small number of swing states. In safe states, voters may feel their choices do not matter because the outcome is already predictable. Meanwhile, campaign events and advertising often concentrate on battleground states. A popular vote would encourage candidates to seek support across the entire country. It could also motivate campaigns to reach voters in communities they might otherwise overlook.

Supporters of the Electoral College argue that it protects the influence of smaller states. They worry that candidates would concentrate only on large cities if the system changed. However, voters in rural areas and small states would still add to the national total. Campaigns would have a reason to seek votes wherever they could find them. The system would not guarantee equal attention everywhere, but it would make each individual vote equally valuable.

A nationwide election would require careful rules for counting votes and resolving close results. States currently manage elections differently, so national standards could help ensure fairness and consistency. Critics also worry that recounts could become complicated across the country. Clear procedures and reliable election administration could reduce that risk.

Changing the system would be a major decision, and the Constitution makes replacing the Electoral College difficult. Even so, the debate is important because election rules shape how citizens are represented. A nationwide popular vote would make the result easier to understand: the candidate with the most votes would win. It would treat voters as individuals rather than as members of particular states. For these reasons, the United States should move toward electing its president by popular vote.

The Electoral College is the system used to choose the president of the United States. Each state receives electoral votes based on its representation in Congress, and most states award all their votes to the statewide winner. Supporters argue that this system encourages participation by making state-level elections important. They also say it gives smaller states a meaningful voice in choosing the president. However, the system’s effect on voter participation and representation is mixed.

In closely contested states, campaigns often encourage people to vote because a small number of ballots could affect the outcome. This attention can increase interest and turnout in those states. Yet campaigns may spend less time and money in states considered safely won by one party. Voters there may feel that their ballots matter less, even though they still affect local and state elections. As a result, the Electoral College can focus participation unevenly across the country.

The system can also create a gap between the national popular vote and the election result. A candidate may win the presidency without receiving the most votes nationwide. This outcome can leave some voters feeling that their preferences were not represented. Winner-take-all rules add to this concern because votes for the losing candidate in a state usually do not earn that candidate any electoral votes. Thus, many voters may feel overlooked, especially if they belong to a political minority in their state.

On the other hand, the Electoral College encourages candidates to build support across multiple states rather than concentrating only on the largest cities. It also reflects the federal structure of the United States, where states have a role in national government. Still, campaign attention tends to favor competitive states, not all states equally. The system therefore does not guarantee that every community receives meaningful representation. Overall, the Electoral College can motivate participation in battleground states, but it may discourage voters elsewhere and leave many viewpoints underrepresented. A national popular vote might make each ballot count equally, though it would raise questions about how to protect the interests of smaller states. Any reform should aim to make participation feel worthwhile and representation more inclusive.

Typhoon Goni slammed into the Philippines as one of the strongest storms on record, bringing destructive winds, torrential rain and flooding. Philippine authorities reported dozens of deaths, many caused by landslides and volcanic debris flows, while hundreds of thousands of people were evacuated from high-risk areas. Homes, roads and power lines were damaged, and emergency crews worked to reach communities cut off by the storm. Goni later moved toward Taiwan, where officials issued warnings, evacuated residents from vulnerable areas and prepared shelters, though its effects there were less severe. The storm also disrupted air travel, prompting widespread flight cancellations in the Philippines and cancellations or schedule changes in Taiwan. The typhoon weakened as it moved across the region, but recovery efforts continued amid damage and ongoing risks from flooding and landslides.

James Bond arrived at the Velvet Room wearing a tuxedo and the expression of a man who had practiced smiling in a mirror.
His contact, a woman named Mara, waited beneath a chandelier shaped like a spider.
“You’re late,” she said.
“Traffic,” Bond replied.
The city outside was empty, but he had read that traffic was a reliable excuse.
Mara glanced at his shoes.
“Are you the replacement?”
“I’m the replacement with the credentials.”
He produced a small card.
It bore his name, his clearance level, and his Reddit username: u/007Actually.
Mara blinked.
“That’s supposed to impress me?”
“I have twelve thousand karma,” Bond said.
“Most of it from a post about repairing a toaster.”
“Was it a good post?”
“I included diagrams.”
Mara leaned closer, apparently curious despite herself.
Bond explained that he had reached the top of a forum about obscure spy gadgets.
He had also moderated a community devoted to identifying suspicious luggage.
“Useful,” Mara said.
“I thought so.”
A guard approached, broad-shouldered and suspicious.
Mara introduced Bond as a specialist in online reputation management.
Bond nodded with professional solemnity.
The guard asked what he knew about the organization.
“Your leader has an unusually consistent posting schedule,” Bond said.
The guard frowned.
“Online?”
“Every Tuesday at 9:14, he shares a picture of a white cat.”
Mara stiffened.
Bond wished he had stopped there.
He added that the cat’s name was probably Chairman Meow.
The guard whispered into his earpiece.
Bond tried to look casual and instead looked like a man waiting for a bus.
Mara pulled him toward a side corridor.
“How did you find that?”
“Public posts,” Bond said.
“And a forum thread about pet names.”
The corridor ended at a steel door marked STAFF ONLY.
Mara entered a code.
Bond watched her fingers, trying not to appear interested in the code.
He appeared intensely interested in the code.
Inside, screens displayed maps, bank accounts, and a video feed of the city’s power station.
The villain, Dr. Vex, stood by the largest screen.
“Who is this?” Vex demanded.
“My online specialist,” Mara said.
Bond offered a handshake.
Vex stared at it.
Bond lowered his hand and pretended he had been adjusting his cuff.
Vex asked for proof of loyalty.
Bond opened his phone and showed him a saved post praising Vex’s taste in coats.
It had three upvotes.
One was from Bond himself.
Vex smiled anyway.
He invited Bond to the control console.
Bond stepped forward, tripped over a cable, and caught the edge of the table.
The screens flashed red.
Mara shouted that the system was under attack.
Bond had accidentally unplugged the display server.
In the confusion, he copied the security codes onto a tiny drive.
Then he plugged the cable back in, which restored the villain’s screens and his own dignity, slightly.
Vex turned to congratulate him.
Bond used the moment to trigger an alarm through the control console.
Guards rushed in from both doors.
Mara grabbed the drive and followed Bond through an emergency exit.
Outside, she looked at him with reluctant admiration.
“You really are good at this,” she said.
Bond straightened his lapels.
“Thank you,” he replied, “I’m also highly ranked in a forum about lapels.”

Mara could hear the thoughts of everyone in the train station, whether she wanted to or not.
Most days, she managed by concentrating on the rhythm of her own breathing.
Then one rainy Tuesday, a stranger sat beside her and thought, I hope she doesn’t notice me noticing her.
Mara turned.
The stranger blinked, startled.
“You can hear thoughts,” he said aloud.
“So can you,” Mara replied.
They stared at each other, then laughed with the same nervous little burst.
His name was Eli, and he was a mind reader too.
For the first time in years, Mara sat beside someone whose thoughts did not spill into her mind.
Eli explained that he could choose when to listen.
Mara admitted she had never learned how.
He showed her how to focus on a single sound.
Together they listened to rain tapping the station roof.
When the train arrived, neither of them got on.
They bought coffee instead and talked until the café closed.
The next morning, Mara woke thinking about Eli.
She wondered whether he was thinking about her.
Across town, Eli was wondering exactly the same thing.
For a week, they met after work.
They discussed books, music, and the odd relief of silence.
Their hands brushed once over a sugar packet.
Mara’s cheeks warmed.
Eli’s thoughts filled with a flustered apology.
She heard it, and that made her blush harder.
“Sorry,” he said.
“Don’t be,” she answered.
“I can’t help wondering if you like me,” Eli admitted.
Mara stared into her coffee.
“I can’t help wondering if you’re wondering that,” she said.
They both laughed, but the laughter faded into a quiet pause.
Eli wanted to ask her out properly.
Mara heard the question forming before he could speak.
She wished she could make herself stop listening.
Instead, she took a breath and looked him in the eye.
“I’d like you to ask me,” she said.
Eli smiled, embarrassed and delighted.
“Would you have dinner with me on Friday?”
“Yes,” Mara said.
On Friday, they chose a small restaurant with no music and few guests.
They left their phones at home and promised not to read each other’s minds.
The promise lasted through the first course.
Then Eli accidentally caught Mara thinking that his tie was crooked.
He straightened it and grinned.
Mara caught his thought that she looked beautiful.
For a moment, she forgot how to swallow.
“Was that a thought or a compliment?” she asked.
“Both,” Eli said.
She laughed, and the embarrassment finally loosened its hold.
After dinner, they walked beneath the streetlamps.
Eli offered his hand, thinking carefully of nothing at all.
Mara took it.
Their relationship grew through ordinary days.
They learned to ask questions instead of guessing.
They practiced closing their minds when either needed privacy.
Sometimes they failed, and sometimes they apologized.
Mostly, they discovered that understanding someone did not mean knowing everything.
A year later, Eli proposed beside the station where they had first met.
He had rehearsed the words aloud and kept his thoughts quiet.
Mara said yes before he finished.
At their wedding, their friends toasted their rare gift and their patience.
Mara and Eli exchanged vows, blushing through the sweetest parts.
When the guests cheered, they shared a thought neither had to hear.
They were home.

Egyptian cinema’s long fascination with thugs is prompting fresh debate over violence, politics and religious sensitivities. The streetwise antihero has become a familiar figure in films and television, often portrayed as both a threat and a product of social hardship. Supporters say these stories reflect realities that conventional dramas have ignored. Critics counter that repeated depictions of criminal power can make brutality seem ordinary, even glamorous.

The debate has intensified as filmmakers revisit stories of neighborhood bosses, hired enforcers and men who rise through intimidation. Such characters often dominate their surroundings through a mix of physical force, personal loyalty and ties to influential figures. Their appeal, analysts say, lies partly in the fantasy of an individual who can challenge institutions that seem distant or unfair. But that fantasy can blur the line between resistance and coercion.

In many films, a thug is not simply a villain. He may be shown as loyal to family, generous to neighbors or driven by poverty and humiliation. Those details can make the character compelling, while also inviting audiences to sympathize with violence. Some viewers argue that this complexity is a strength of Egyptian storytelling. Others worry that it turns criminal behavior into a form of masculine heroism.

The discussion has also taken on a political edge. Films about powerful street figures can be read as stories about corruption, inequality and the unequal application of law. A character who defies officials may appear to embody popular anger at institutions. Yet critics say such narratives can substitute personal revenge for collective action, presenting force as the only route to justice.

Religious sensitivities add another layer. Some viewers object to scenes that depict alcohol, sexual behavior or religious language in ways they consider disrespectful. Others say that portraying flawed people is not the same as endorsing their choices. The disagreement reflects broader questions about who gets to define acceptable representation in a society with diverse moral and cultural expectations.

Filmmakers face pressure from both sides. Some want room to depict violence without being accused of promoting it, while others acknowledge a duty to consider how audiences interpret what they see. The debate is complicated by the commercial success of crime stories, which can encourage producers to repeat familiar formulas. A dramatic antihero may draw viewers, but repetition can narrow the range of stories being told.

Egyptian cinema has a long history of using crime and social conflict to examine changes in class, authority and urban life. The current argument is less about whether thugs should appear on screen than about how they are framed. Are they symptoms of a broken system, or figures whose charisma overshadows the harm they cause? The answer may vary from one film and audience to another.

For researchers and critics, the genre offers a way to discuss anxieties that are difficult to address directly. Its stories can expose social neglect and the appeal of unchecked power at the same time. Audience responses also show that viewers do not necessarily accept a film’s moral framing uncritically. Some admire the character, while others focus on the victims left in his wake.

The debate is unlikely to end soon. As Egyptian filmmakers continue to explore crime, faith and power, audiences will keep arguing over the boundary between depicting violence and celebrating it. At stake is not only the image of the thug, but also cinema’s role in reflecting society and shaping the stories people tell about justice.

Planning and Planting Corn Plots for Winter Deer Forage

A corn plot can provide standing grain and cover for deer during winter, when natural foods may be scarce. Its success depends on careful planning, suitable soil, and local growing conditions. Before choosing a site, check state and local rules for food plots, wildlife feeding, and seed treatments. In some places, planting crops to attract deer is restricted, especially where chronic wasting disease is a concern.

Choose a plot with adequate sunlight, ideally six or more hours each day. Avoid low areas that stay wet, since waterlogged soil can prevent roots from developing and delay fieldwork. A site near cover may help deer feel secure, but leave enough room for equipment to plant and maintain the crop. Consider how the plot fits into the broader habitat plan, including natural browse, shrubs, and other food sources.

Test the soil well before planting, using a laboratory or agricultural extension service. The results show soil acidity and nutrient levels, which guide lime and fertilizer choices. Corn generally grows best in fertile, well-drained soil with a pH near 6.0 to 6.5. Apply lime early enough for it to improve the soil, and follow test recommendations rather than guessing.

Choose a corn variety suited to your region, planting date, and available equipment. Some varieties mature sooner, which can be useful in areas with shorter growing seasons. Ask a local extension specialist or seed supplier about varieties that perform well under local conditions. Use clean, high-quality seed and follow the label for any seed treatments.

Plant after the danger of frost has passed and the soil has warmed enough for reliable germination. Cold, wet soil can cause poor emergence or seed damage. Follow the seed supplier’s guidance on planting depth and spacing, and use a calibrated planter when possible. Planting in organized rows makes cultivation, weed control, and harvest management easier.

Corn needs consistent moisture, especially during flowering and grain development. Rainfall may be sufficient, but dry spells can reduce the amount of grain produced. Control weeds early because they compete with young corn for water, light, and nutrients. Use mechanical or chemical control only as permitted, and follow product labels and local regulations.

Check the plot regularly for insects, disease, and animal damage. Deer may browse young plants, so a small fenced test area can help reveal how much browsing is occurring. If damage is severe, consider a temporary barrier or a different plot location. Avoid using pesticides unless necessary, and choose products and application methods that protect people, wildlife, and pollinators.

Allow some or all of the mature crop to remain standing into winter. Standing corn can provide both grain and shelter, but wind, snow, and field conditions may affect how long it lasts. A staggered planting schedule or a mix of food-plot crops can spread forage availability through the season. Do not rely on corn alone, since deer also benefit from diverse natural foods and appropriate browse.

Keep plot size realistic for your budget, equipment, and soil conditions. A smaller, well-managed plot is often more useful than a large plot with poor soil or inadequate weed control. Keep records of planting dates, varieties, soil tests, and results to improve future seasons. With thoughtful planning, a corn plot can be one part of a broader effort to support healthy deer habitat through winter.
