Andrew Puzder’s appointment as labor secretary has renewed debate over his record on worker protections and minimum wage policies. Supporters say the former fast-food executive would bring business experience to the Department of Labor. Critics argue that his views could weaken protections for workers and shift policy in favor of employers.

Puzder, who led CKE Restaurants, the parent company of Carl’s Jr. and Hardee’s, has opposed substantial increases to the federal minimum wage. He has argued that higher wage mandates can raise costs, reduce hiring, and accelerate the use of automation. Advocates for low-wage workers counter that the current federal minimum wage has failed to keep pace with living costs.

His nomination also drew scrutiny over workplace issues in the restaurant industry. Worker advocates have cited complaints and legal disputes involving wages and working conditions at some franchise locations, while emphasizing that franchise operators and corporate owners may have different responsibilities. Puzder has said he supports lawful employment practices and has defended the role of businesses in creating jobs.

The Labor Department oversees enforcement of federal wage, overtime, and workplace-safety laws. As secretary, Puzder would also influence how the department interprets regulations and allocates resources for enforcement. That authority has made the nomination consequential for workers and employers alike.

Business groups welcomed the prospect of a leader they viewed as attentive to the costs of regulation. Labor organizations warned that a shift in enforcement priorities could leave workers more vulnerable to wage theft and unsafe conditions. Economists remain divided over the effects of minimum-wage increases, with outcomes often depending on the size of the increase and local conditions.

The debate reflects a broader disagreement about how to balance higher pay and stronger protections with business costs and job growth. Puzder’s confirmation and policy decisions would determine whether his appointment brings a change in direction at the department. For now, his record has made worker protections and the minimum wage central questions in the discussion over his leadership.

Three men have been jailed for raping and sexually assaulting a woman after offering her a lift in Coventry.

The woman was travelling in the city when the men offered to take her somewhere, according to police. Instead, they drove her to an address where she was attacked.

The men were convicted following a trial at court. They were sentenced after the court heard evidence about the assault and the impact it had on the woman.

The victim has been supported by specialist officers throughout the investigation and court proceedings. Police said she showed considerable courage in reporting what happened and giving evidence.

Investigators said the case highlights the risks of accepting lifts from people who are not known to you. They urged anyone with information about sexual violence to contact police or seek support from a specialist service.

The men will serve custodial sentences for their roles in the offences. Their names, ages and the exact terms of their sentences were not provided in the information available for this report.

Police said they remained committed to investigating sexual offences and bringing perpetrators before the courts.

Mobile phones are useful tools, but using them while driving can put everyone on the road in danger. A driver who looks at a screen or answers a message takes attention away from the road. Even a brief distraction can make it harder to notice a pedestrian, a traffic light, or a vehicle stopping ahead. Because cars travel quickly, a few seconds of inattention can lead to a serious crash. For this reason, laws should prohibit drivers from using mobile phones while their vehicles are moving.

Some people believe they can safely use a phone if they are experienced drivers. However, confidence does not remove the risks of distraction. Hands-free calls can also take a driver’s attention away from traffic, even when both hands remain on the wheel. A law that clearly limits phone use can encourage drivers to focus on driving instead. It can also make the consequences of dangerous behavior clear to everyone.

Such laws can help protect passengers, pedestrians, cyclists, and other drivers. A crash caused by phone use may lead to injuries, deaths, and lasting grief for families. It can also cause financial costs, including medical bills and damage to vehicles. Preventing even some of these crashes would be a meaningful benefit.

For laws to work well, they should be easy to understand and fairly enforced. Drivers should be allowed to use a phone in an emergency when it is safe to do so, such as after pulling over. Public education can explain why the rules exist and help people build safer habits. Schools, families, and communities can remind young drivers that no message is worth risking a life.

Mobile phones can wait until a journey is over. Drivers who need to make a call or check directions should stop somewhere safe before using their devices. Prohibiting phone use while driving is a practical way to reduce distraction and encourage responsible choices. Strong laws, combined with education and enforcement, can make roads safer. By keeping their attention on the road, drivers can help prevent crashes and save lives.

Subject: California Weighs Seizing PG&E’s Transmission Network

California is considering taking control of PG&E’s transmission network as talks over a broader state takeover continue. The discussion comes as easing power shortages give officials more room to weigh long-term options for the utility’s future. Supporters say public control could improve accountability and help align the grid with the state’s energy goals. PG&E and other stakeholders may raise concerns about the cost, complexity, and potential disruption of such a move. Any decision would need to address how the network would be managed and how the transition would be funded. We’ll continue monitoring negotiations and share updates as the state clarifies its plans.

The Electoral College has shaped U.S. presidential elections for more than two centuries, but it does not always reflect the preferences of voters nationwide. Under the current system, a candidate can win the presidency without receiving the most votes across the country. This can happen because most states award all their electoral votes to the candidate who wins that state. As a result, voters in closely contested states may receive more attention than voters in states considered safely Democratic or Republican. Replacing the Electoral College with a national popular vote would make every vote count equally, no matter where a voter lives. Another option, such as ranked-choice voting, could let voters express support for more than one candidate and help ensure the winner has broad backing. Any replacement system would need clear rules for recounts, election administration, and protecting access to the ballot. Critics argue that the Electoral College gives smaller states influence and encourages candidates to build support across different regions. However, a fair national system could protect regional voices while still respecting the choices of individual voters. The United States should consider replacing the Electoral College with a system that gives every voter an equal voice in choosing the president.

Brexit could put pressure on UK tax revenues and make it harder for financial firms to serve customers across Europe, analysts and industry groups have warned. The City of London has long drawn business from the EU, supporting jobs and generating tax receipts from company profits, wages and financial transactions. Leaving the bloc has changed the rules under which British firms can operate in the single market.

Before Brexit, many UK-based banks and insurers relied on “passporting” rights to provide services across the EU. Those rights ended when the UK left the bloc, and firms now need separate authorisations or operating arrangements to serve European clients. Some have responded by moving staff, assets or legal entities to EU cities such as Dublin, Frankfurt, Paris and Amsterdam.

The scale of any resulting tax loss remains uncertain. Financial companies still employ large numbers of people in Britain and continue to pay substantial taxes, while the UK remains a major global financial centre. But a gradual shift of activity abroad could reduce future receipts from corporation tax, income tax and related sources.

The impact may be uneven across the industry. Investment banking and trading operations can be relocated more readily than some customer-facing businesses, while insurance firms may need local entities to meet regulatory requirements. Smaller firms could find the cost of maintaining operations on both sides of the Channel especially challenging.

Britain and the EU have agreed limited cooperation on financial regulation, but the UK has not received broad access equivalent to membership of the single market. The EU’s “equivalence” system grants access in specific areas and can be withdrawn, leaving firms with less certainty when planning long-term operations. Disagreements over rules and supervision could add to that uncertainty.

The government has sought to make the UK more competitive by adapting financial regulations and attracting investment. Supporters say regulatory flexibility could encourage innovation and help preserve London’s international standing. Critics warn that diverging too far from EU standards may make cross-border business more difficult rather than more attractive.

The eventual effect on public finances will depend on how firms respond and whether new industries offset any decline in financial activity. For now, the City remains a major source of employment and revenue, but its relationship with European markets has become more complicated. Companies and policymakers are watching closely to see whether the UK can retain its business while building new opportunities outside the bloc.

The fissure appeared on the Moon without warning.
One night, it was a thin black line across the Mare Serenitatis.
By morning, it had widened into a jagged scar.
The first images came from a quiet survey satellite.
Within hours, they were everywhere.
People called it a doorway.
Others said it was a weapon test, a hoax, or a warning from God.
Theories spread faster than the official reports.
Dr. Mira Venn studied the images in a windowless room at the Lunar Research Center.
She noticed the fissure’s edges were too smooth.
They looked less like broken stone than a cut made by a careful hand.
When the next satellite passed overhead, Mira found something stranger.
A pattern of lights blinked beneath the lunar surface.
The sequence repeated every eleven minutes.
She decoded it as a set of coordinates.
The coordinates pointed to a crater no mission had ever visited.
Mira requested permission to investigate.
Her director refused.
He told her the site was classified and ordered her to forget it.
That night, she copied the coordinates onto a flight plan.
Before dawn, she boarded a cargo lander with two crew members.
Their names were Jae Ortiz and Salim Okafor.
Neither asked why she had disobeyed orders.
The journey took six hours.
As they descended, the fissure glimmered beneath them like a narrow blue river.
Their lander touched down beside the hidden crater.
The ground trembled once.
A seam opened in the crater floor.
Inside was a staircase of dark metal.
Its steps descended far below the Moon’s crust.
At the bottom, they found a chamber filled with glassy pillars.
Each pillar held a faint, drifting light.
Mira recognized the lights from the satellite images.
They were not signals.
They were records.
When she touched one, the chamber filled with voices.
The voices spoke in a language her translator could not identify.
Then the pillars displayed a map of Earth.
Red lines spread across the oceans and continents.
Jae understood first.
The map showed a chain reaction already underway beneath the planet’s crust.
The lunar structure had been built to monitor it.
A final message appeared on the wall.
It showed the Moon splitting open, followed by Earth going dark.
Salim found a timer counting down in the corner of the display.
It showed four days.
Mira sent the data to Earth.
The transmission vanished halfway through.
A reply arrived instead, signed by her director.
It ordered them to destroy the chamber and say nothing.
Then the countdown accelerated.
The pillars began to crack.
Mira realized the chamber was not just a warning system.
It was holding the signal that kept the reaction dormant.
They had to open the fissure wider to restore it.
Jae and Salim braced the metal doors while Mira climbed toward the surface.
She fired the lander’s beacon into the seam.
The blue light flared across the crater.
For a moment, the Moon seemed to breathe.
The countdown stopped.
A new message reached Earth, carrying every record in the chamber.
Across the planet, hidden instruments began to answer.
The secret was no longer buried.
And humanity had only begun to understand what it had awakened.

Distracted driving is a serious danger to everyone who uses the road. It happens when drivers take their attention away from driving, even for a moment. Common distractions include texting, checking a phone, eating, and adjusting the radio. Because a vehicle can travel a long distance in just a few seconds, looking away can have severe consequences.

Drivers who are distracted may fail to notice a red light, a sudden turn, or a car slowing ahead. They may also drift into another lane or react too late to avoid a crash. Even hands-free conversations can distract drivers by taking their minds off the road. A collision can leave drivers with serious injuries, lasting emotional effects, or legal consequences.

Passengers are also at risk when the person behind the wheel is distracted. They may be injured in a crash, even if they had no role in causing it. Passengers can help by avoiding behavior that distracts the driver and by speaking up when they see unsafe choices. They should also buckle their seat belts on every trip.

Pedestrians face special risks because they have little protection in a collision. A distracted driver may not see someone crossing the street or walking near the roadside. Children, older adults, and people using mobility devices can be especially vulnerable. Drivers should put their phones away, slow down near crossings, and check carefully for people on foot.

Preventing distracted driving is a shared responsibility. Drivers should set their route and music before moving and wait until they are parked to use a phone. Passengers can encourage safe habits, while pedestrians should use crossings and stay alert. Giving the road our full attention can prevent injuries and save lives.

A regional transport group has backed plans to reopen two disused railway stations in mid-Wales, saying they could improve access to jobs, services and visitor destinations. The proposal focuses on stations that closed decades ago and would restore stops on an existing rail corridor. Supporters say the locations could serve communities currently some distance from a station. The group argues that better rail links would offer an alternative to car travel and help reduce congestion and emissions. Reopening the stations could also make it easier for people without access to a car to reach nearby towns. Local businesses may benefit from increased visitor numbers, particularly during peak tourism periods. However, the proposal would need detailed feasibility work before it could proceed. That assessment would examine expected passenger demand, construction costs and the changes required to track and signalling systems. It would also consider how new stops might affect journey times for existing passengers. Funding has not yet been confirmed, and any project would require the support of transport authorities and government. The group has called for the stations to be included in regional rail planning discussions. It says early consideration could help ensure that mid-Wales communities are not overlooked in future investment decisions. Further studies and consultation with residents are expected to be important next steps.

At 9:17 on a foggy Tuesday, two North Korean agents stepped out of a rental sedan in suburban Los Angeles.

Their names were Pak and Choi, though their disguises said otherwise.

Pak wore a gray suit and a tie covered in tiny pineapples.

Choi wore sunglasses at night and carried a briefcase handcuffed to his wrist.

They had been sent to retrieve a secret package from a royal residence.

The instructions named the place as the Crown House.

Unfortunately, the Crown House had moved three years earlier.

Their outdated map led them to a gated community called Royal Palms.

“Looks official,” Pak said.

The entrance sign featured a stone lion wearing a baseball cap.

Choi nodded. “A symbol of power.”

They drove past manicured lawns and identical stucco homes.

At the end of Royal Palm Drive stood a large house with a golden crown above its garage.

Pak pointed. “The palace.”

The crown was actually a decoration for the homeowner’s fiftieth birthday.

A woman in gardening gloves waved them toward the driveway.

She was Mrs. Alvarez, the neighborhood’s self-appointed welcome committee.

“Are you here for the royal brunch?” she asked.

“Precisely,” said Choi, who had no idea what a royal brunch was.

Mrs. Alvarez handed them name tags.

Pak’s read “Prince Porridge.”

Choi’s read “Duke of Snacks.”

They accepted these titles with grave dignity.

Inside, the house was full of folding chairs and paper streamers.

A banner announced, “Happy Birthday, Ron!”

Pak studied it carefully.

“Ron must be the king,” he whispered.

Choi spotted a table piled with muffins.

“Perhaps the package is hidden in the pastries.”

They began inspecting each muffin with a small flashlight.

A child watched them from beside the punch bowl.

“Are you magicians?” she asked.

“We are diplomats,” Pak replied.

“Can you make my dad stop singing karaoke?”

Before they could answer, a man in a crown-shaped party hat grabbed a microphone.

He began singing a power ballad with tremendous confidence and little accuracy.

Choi stiffened. “The king is performing.”

Pak reached for his briefcase.

The handcuff snagged on a chair.

The chair toppled into a tray of lemonade.

Lemonade splashed across the floor, and guests jumped back.

“Is this part of the show?” asked the child.

Pak tried to look mysterious while wiping his sleeve.

Choi opened the briefcase to find a sandwich, a phone charger, and their mission folder.

The secret package was nowhere inside.

They checked under the cake.

They checked behind the karaoke machine.

They even checked the mailbox, which contained three coupons and a gardening catalog.

At last, Mrs. Alvarez noticed the address on their mission folder.

“You’re looking for the old Crown House?” she asked.

Both agents froze.

“It’s a retirement home in Pasadena,” she said. “They have a royal-themed dining room.”

Pak and Choi exchanged a glance.

Their assignment suddenly made sense.

The package was a tiny red envelope meant for a retired chess champion named Mr. Han.

The two agents thanked Mrs. Alvarez and hurried back to the sedan.

Ron stopped singing long enough to wave them goodbye.

Choi bowed to him, just in case.

They drove toward Pasadena with the map upside down.

After two wrong turns, they arrived at the Crown House retirement residence.

A gold-painted sign stood beside the entrance.

This time, the building really did look royal.

A receptionist greeted them and asked if they were expected.

Pak presented the mission folder backward.

Choi offered the receptionist a muffin he had accidentally pocketed.

She pointed them toward the sunroom.

Mr. Han was waiting beside a chessboard.

He was small, cheerful, and wearing a sweater embroidered with crowns.

Pak delivered the red envelope with both hands.

Mr. Han opened it and read the message silently.

Then he smiled. “They finally sent my tournament score.”

The agents stared at him.

The world’s most important secret, it turned out, was that Mr. Han had won a chess match by one move.

He invited them to stay for tea.

Pak accepted.

Choi accepted too, after checking that the teapot held no hidden documents.

By sunset, both agents were losing badly at chess.

Mr. Han beat them without looking up from his tea.

On the drive home, Pak admitted the party had been more confusing than their training.

Choi said the muffins had been excellent.

Neither mentioned the karaoke.

Back in their rented apartment, they filed a report describing a successful delivery.

They left out the lemonade, the wrong house, and the name tags.

But Choi kept “Duke of Snacks” in his wallet.

And for the rest of the week, Pak called him Your Grace.

UNHCR’s Global Trends report for 2016 documented forced displacement on an unprecedented scale. By the end of that year, 65.6 million people had been driven from their homes by persecution, conflict, violence, or human rights violations. This was about 300,000 more people than in 2015 and the highest total UNHCR had recorded.

The total included 22.5 million refugees who had crossed an international border, 40.3 million people displaced within their own countries, and 2.8 million people seeking asylum. Children made up about half of the world’s refugees, highlighting the crisis’s profound effects on young people. Most refugees lived in countries neighboring the places they had fled, rather than in wealthy, distant countries.

Conflict and insecurity remained the main causes of displacement. Syria’s war had produced the largest refugee population, while Afghanistan and South Sudan were also major sources of refugees. Violence in countries such as Iraq and Yemen, as well as persecution and instability elsewhere, forced millions more to flee. In many cases, people could not return safely, and new crises continued to uproot families.

The impacts were global but unevenly shared. Turkey hosted more refugees than any other country, while developing countries hosted the majority of refugees worldwide. Large arrivals placed pressure on housing, schools, health services, and local resources, even as refugees contributed skills and labor to host communities. Displacement also separated families, interrupted education, and made it harder for people to earn a living.

UNHCR emphasized that lasting solutions included safe return when conditions allowed, integration into host communities, and resettlement in a third country. The report called for greater international cooperation and support for both displaced people and the countries receiving them. Its central message was that forced displacement in 2016 was not a temporary emergency for millions, but a prolonged global challenge.

Aerospace’s role in air travel is far from over. It has shaped how people and goods move around the world, and it will continue to influence how we travel in the decades ahead. Aerospace includes the design, construction, operation, and improvement of aircraft and related technologies. Its work connects engineers, pilots, researchers, manufacturers, regulators, and airlines.

Modern air travel depends on advances in aerodynamics, materials, engines, navigation, and communications. These technologies help aircraft fly farther while using less fuel and producing fewer emissions per passenger. Lightweight materials and efficient engine designs can reduce operating costs as well as environmental impact. Improvements to aircraft interiors and airport systems also help make journeys more comfortable and convenient.

Safety remains one of aerospace’s most important responsibilities. Aircraft are designed with multiple systems and backups so that a single failure is less likely to cause an accident. Engineers test components under demanding conditions before they are approved for use. Maintenance teams inspect aircraft regularly and repair wear or damage before it becomes a serious risk.

Pilots and air traffic controllers also rely on aerospace technology to make safe decisions. Weather radar, satellite navigation, and communication systems help crews understand changing conditions. Flight-data recorders and careful accident investigations allow experts to identify causes and prevent similar events. Safety rules and training are updated as new knowledge and technologies become available.

The future of passenger transportation may look different from today’s air travel. Researchers are developing quieter aircraft, cleaner propulsion systems, and designs that could shorten some journeys. Electric and hybrid aircraft may serve short regional routes, while sustainable aviation fuels could help reduce emissions on longer flights. These approaches face challenges, including cost, infrastructure needs, and the amount of energy required.

New digital tools may also improve how aircraft are designed and maintained. Artificial intelligence can help analyze large amounts of flight and equipment data, but human oversight remains essential. Automation may support pilots and air traffic controllers, while requiring careful testing and clear safeguards. Any new system must demonstrate that it can operate reliably in real-world conditions.

Aerospace could eventually support new kinds of passenger travel, including high-speed aircraft and, farther ahead, some forms of commercial spaceflight. These possibilities are still developing and may not become practical for everyone. Their success will depend on safety, affordability, environmental effects, and public trust. Continued research and responsible regulation will help determine which ideas are worth pursuing.

Aerospace therefore does more than build aircraft. It helps keep existing air travel safe, efficient, and connected while exploring better ways to travel in the future. Its progress depends on learning from past experience and addressing today’s environmental and operational challenges. The next chapter of passenger transportation will be shaped by how thoughtfully the aerospace community meets them.

The early response to new pension freedoms appears subdued, with demand for retirement guidance lower than some industry observers expected. The changes give people more flexibility over how they access their pension savings, but many are taking time to understand their options. Financial advisers report that uncertainty over tax, investment risk and long-term income is keeping some savers from making immediate decisions. Others may be waiting for clearer guidance or reviewing their plans before withdrawing money. The quiet start does not necessarily signal a lack of interest, experts say, as retirement choices often require careful consideration. Guidance services are expected to play an important role in helping people avoid costly mistakes. Providers are monitoring enquiries and withdrawals as more savers become familiar with the new rules. The full impact of the pension freedoms may only become clear over the coming months.

Subject: Negotiation Priorities and Proposed Revisions

Dear [Name],

Thank you for sharing the draft power purchase agreement and interconnection terms. We have completed an initial review and would like to align on several priorities before the next draft. Our goal is to preserve the project’s commercial viability while providing clear, balanced risk allocation for both parties.

First, we propose clarifying the conditions that must be satisfied before the agreement becomes effective. These should include completion of agreed diligence, receipt of required approvals, and execution of definitive interconnection documents. The long-stop date should allow reasonable extensions for delays outside either party’s control.

We also recommend revising the commercial operation date provisions. Any schedule relief should apply to delays caused by permitting, utility work, force majeure, or other events not attributable to the affected party. The parties should agree on a transparent process for documenting delays and updating milestones.

On pricing, please confirm how the contracted rate will be adjusted, if at all, over the term. Any indexation or pass-through should be tied to a clearly identified, independently verifiable measure. We would also like the agreement to specify how renewable energy credits, capacity attributes, and other environmental or market products will be allocated.

The volume and delivery provisions should account for expected resource variability and permitted outages. We propose defining the measurement point, delivery profile, and treatment of energy that cannot be delivered because of curtailment or grid constraints. The agreement should distinguish system-wide curtailment from curtailment caused by the seller’s failure to meet its obligations.

For performance remedies, we suggest that liquidated damages be proportionate to reasonably foreseeable losses and subject to an aggregate cap. The agreement should avoid duplicative recovery through damages, indemnities, and other remedies for the same event. We also propose mutual liability limitations, with customary exceptions for confidentiality breaches, willful misconduct, and payment obligations.

The termination provisions should provide a reasonable cure period before termination for a remediable breach. Any termination payment should be based on a defined, auditable calculation and should account for mitigation. We would also appreciate confirmation that neither party may terminate solely because of a change in market conditions.

For the interconnection terms, we propose greater detail on the scope, cost, and schedule of required network upgrades. The utility should provide supporting estimates and identify which costs are fixed, reimbursable, or subject to true-up. Any material scope or cost change should require prompt notice, supporting documentation, and a process for consultation.

We would also like to clarify ownership, operation, and maintenance responsibilities for interconnection facilities. The terms should specify the applicable technical standards, testing procedures, and outage coordination requirements. Please confirm how available capacity will be allocated and how curtailment will be prioritized during constraints.

Finally, we suggest adding a change-management process for revised utility requirements and a dispute-escalation procedure for technical or cost disagreements. The parties should share relevant interconnection studies and keep commercially sensitive information confidential. We are open to discussing these points in a working session and prioritizing the items that affect schedule and project economics.

Please let us know your availability next week. In the meantime, we can provide proposed drafting for the provisions that are most time-sensitive. We look forward to working toward a balanced agreement.

Best regards,
[Your Name]

On the morning of his execution, Tomas Vale was given a cup of tea.
The guard who brought it had a scar across his chin and a nervous way of looking at doors.
Tomas thanked him, though he had not spoken kindly to anyone in months.
The guard set the cup down and whispered, “Drink slowly.”
Beneath the saucer lay a folded scrap of paper.
Tomas opened it with fingers still stiff from the night’s cold.
It held only three words: “You have a choice.”
He looked up, but the guard was already gone.
For years, Tomas had written forbidden truths on scraps of paper and passed them through the city.
He had named the officials who vanished neighbors and the companies that poisoned the river.
When the authorities caught him, they called him a traitor.
At dawn, they would take him to the eastern wall and shoot him.
The scrap gave no instructions, only an address and a time.
Tomas spent the next hour imagining traps.
Then he remembered the faces of the people who had risked their lives to read his words.
He decided that fear had already taken enough from him.
At midnight, a laundry cart stopped outside his cell.
The driver wore the same scarred chin.
“Now,” the man said.
Tomas climbed into the cart beneath a stack of damp sheets.
They rolled through the service gate while the prison clock struck twelve.
At the city’s edge, the driver gave him a coat, a passport, and a small canvas bag.
The passport named him Elias Rowan, a mechanic born in a distant coastal town.
“Your old life is over,” the driver said.
Tomas stared at the name until it began to look like a stranger’s.
“What happens to you?” he asked.
The driver shrugged. “I was never here.”
He handed Tomas a train ticket and turned back toward the prison.
By sunrise, Tomas was crossing the northern hills.
At every checkpoint, he expected a hand to seize his collar.
None did.
The coast smelled of salt and engine oil.
In a village called Bellwether, he rented a room above a bakery.
The baker asked what had brought him there.
“Work,” Tomas said.
It was the first lie he had told for the sake of living.
He found a job repairing fishing boats.
His new hands learned to tighten bolts and mend nets.
His old hands kept reaching for a pen.
For weeks, he did not write.
He learned the names of the tides and the habits of gulls.
He learned that the baker’s daughter sang while sweeping.
He learned that ordinary mornings could feel like stolen treasure.
At night, though, the faces from his city returned.
He wondered whether his friends were safe and whether his words had mattered.
One evening, a parcel arrived with no return address.
Inside was a newspaper wrapped around a single sheet of paper.
The article reported that the eastern wall had seen no execution that morning.
A prison clerk, it said, had misplaced a name in the records.
Tomas read the sentence twice.
Then he unfolded the sheet.
It was a list of people who still needed help.
Beside the first name, someone had written, “If you choose.”
Tomas sat by the window until the bakery’s lamps went dark.
He could remain Elias and let the past sink beneath the waves.
He could also risk everything by answering.
In the morning, he took the train inland.
He carried no forbidden papers, only the list and a pencil.
At the first station, he bought a fresh notebook.
He wrote his borrowed name on the cover, then paused.
Beneath it, he added his own.
Tomas Vale was not the man on the execution order anymore.
But he was still the man who had spoken when silence was safer.
As the train moved toward the city, he felt fear return.
This time, he let it sit beside him.
The blank pages trembled in his hands.
He began with the first name on the list.
For the first time, starting over did not mean starting alone.

Spanish-language rock grew from the meeting of rock and roll with the languages, histories, and popular cultures of Spain and Latin America. It is not a single sound or a movement with one origin. Its many scenes have reflected local politics, social change, and musical traditions. The story begins in the 1950s, when records and films from the United States brought rock and roll to Spanish-speaking countries. Radio, touring performers, and imported instruments helped spread the new music. Young musicians began forming bands and adapting American songs for local audiences. Some early groups translated popular English-language hits into Spanish. Others wrote original songs, often combining rock rhythms with local styles. These experiments helped make rock a lasting part of youth culture.

In Mexico, early rock and roll gained wide attention in the late 1950s and early 1960s. Groups such as Los Teen Tops became known for Spanish-language versions of American hits. Their success showed that rock could connect with young listeners in their own language. Spain also developed an early rock scene, with groups such as Los Brincos drawing on British beat music and local pop. In Argentina, musicians began creating their own rock songs in Spanish during the 1960s. Artists including Los Gatos helped establish a distinctive local movement. The choice to sing in Spanish was important, because many early performers had assumed rock should be sung in English. Spanish lyrics made it easier to express local experiences and concerns. They also helped build audiences across national borders.

By the late 1960s and 1970s, rock scenes in several countries were becoming more independent. In Argentina, artists such as Almendra, Manal, and Sui Generis explored poetic lyrics and varied musical forms. Their work helped shape what became known as rock nacional. In Spain, groups such as Triana blended rock with elements of flamenco and Andalusian music. This approach, sometimes called Andalusian rock, reflected the region’s distinct cultural identity. Mexican musicians developed hard rock, blues rock, and progressive sounds, while bands such as Three Souls in My Mind became important to the country’s underground scene. Across the region, rock was not simply copied from abroad. Musicians adapted its instruments and conventions to their own cultural settings. Local slang, histories, and musical traditions increasingly shaped the songs.

Political conditions also influenced the music. In Argentina, military rule and censorship affected what musicians could perform and say publicly. Some artists used metaphor and poetic language to address repression and social unease. In Chile, the 1973 coup and subsequent dictatorship disrupted cultural life, forced some artists into exile, and made public expression dangerous. Musicians abroad helped keep Chilean rock and related music visible. In Spain, the end of Franco’s dictatorship in 1975 was followed by a period of cultural change. Madrid’s Movida movement became associated with new music, art, fashion, and nightlife. Bands such as Radio Futura and Alaska y Dinarama helped give the period a vivid pop-rock soundtrack. These different histories show that rock could offer entertainment, experimentation, and forms of social expression. Its meaning depended on the place and moment in which it was made.

During the 1980s, Spanish-language rock reached broader audiences through radio, records, and television. In Argentina, the return of democracy in 1983 helped public culture open up again. Soda Stereo emerged as one of the era’s most influential groups, combining polished production with new-wave and rock sounds. Its popularity soon extended across Latin America. In Mexico, bands such as Caifanes brought together rock, post-punk, and references to Mexican identity. In Spain, artists including Héroes del Silencio developed a powerful style that later found listeners overseas. Rock en español became a widely used label for music made in Spanish, though it covered many styles and national scenes. The term helped record companies and broadcasters promote the music across borders. At the same time, it could obscure the differences among artists and countries.

The growth of rock en español depended on more than the musicians themselves. Record labels invested in albums that could be marketed across Latin America and Spain. Radio stations played songs from neighboring countries, helping listeners discover unfamiliar scenes. Music television gave performers a new way to reach audiences, especially after MTV introduced Spanish-language programming in the 1990s. Tours and festivals brought artists into contact with fans in cities far from their home bases. These connections encouraged a shared regional audience without erasing local identities. Bands often retained distinctive accents, references, and sounds even as their records circulated internationally. Rock became one of the ways Spanish-speaking audiences imagined connections across national borders.

The 1990s brought further stylistic variety. In Mexico, Café Tacvba mixed rock with elements of traditional and popular Mexican music, while also experimenting with electronic sounds. In Argentina, musicians such as Los Fabulosos Cadillacs brought ska, reggae, and Latin rhythms into rock. In Spain, groups including Extremoduro and Platero y Tú represented harder-edged rock traditions. Colombian bands developed their own approaches, and Aterciopelados gained international attention with music that combined rock with Latin American influences and socially engaged lyrics. Across countries, artists drew on punk, metal, new wave, reggae, ska, folk, and electronic music. These combinations made Spanish-language rock difficult to define by one sound. They also reflected the diverse musical backgrounds of the musicians and their listeners.

International growth has often involved migration and diaspora communities. Spanish-speaking listeners in the United States helped create audiences for touring Latin American and Spanish acts. Cities such as Los Angeles, Miami, and New York became important meeting points for musicians and fans. Latino artists in the United States sometimes blended Spanish and English, reflecting everyday bilingual life. Digital distribution later made it easier for bands to share music beyond their local scenes. Online platforms also helped listeners find independent acts that received little radio play. Social media allowed artists to communicate directly with fans in other countries. As a result, international reach no longer depended solely on major labels or television networks.

Spanish-language rock continues to change in the twenty-first century. Established groups still tour and record, while younger artists draw on indie rock, punk, metal, hip-hop, and electronic production. Some performers sing entirely in Spanish, while others move between Spanish, English, and regional languages. Festivals and streaming playlists bring together artists from different countries and generations. These platforms can make discovery easier, although the sheer volume of music can make sustained attention harder to earn. The history of Spanish-language rock is therefore both a story of local scenes and a story of exchange. Its musicians have adapted international influences while reshaping them through their own languages and experiences. From early translated hits to experimental contemporary records, the music has made Spanish a lasting language of rock.

A historical map of the Battle of Champion Hill shows how Union and Confederate forces moved across the rolling countryside of central Mississippi on May 16, 1863. The battle was a key moment in the Union campaign to capture Vicksburg, a Confederate stronghold on the Mississippi River. The map highlights Champion Hill, wooded slopes, ravines, roads, and the Jackson Road, which shaped where troops could advance and defend. Union forces under Major General Ulysses S. Grant attacked Confederate troops led by Lieutenant General John C. Pemberton from several directions. The fighting was especially intense around the hill and the crossroads, where control of the roads affected the Confederate retreat. Terrain features such as steep ground and thick vegetation slowed movement and limited visibility, making coordination difficult. By tracing troop movements alongside the landscape, the map helps explain why the Union victory at Champion Hill brought Grant closer to isolating Vicksburg.

The court of Heaven occupied the top floor of a building with no stairs.
Mara Vale arrived by elevator, though she had been dead for six minutes.
A brass sign read: DEPARTMENT OF FINAL ACCOUNTABILITY.
Below it, someone had added: PLEASE TAKE A NUMBER.
Mara took number 8,004,119.
The ticket machine thanked her for her patience.
She had not brought any patience.
She had not brought any belief, either.
At the door, a clerk asked whether she was saved.
“I’m an atheist,” Mara said.
The clerk nodded and checked a box marked OTHER.
Inside, the courtroom was filled with clouds, filing cabinets, and nervous souls.
At the judge’s bench sat a white-bearded man who looked tired of being eternal.
“Your Honor,” said the prosecutor, “we submit the accused lived without worship.”
“Does the accused deny it?” asked the judge.
“I deny that it’s a crime,” Mara said.
The judge tapped his gavel.
It made the sound of a stapler.
Her lawyer arrived late, carrying a briefcase that was still wrapped in its shipping paper.
He introduced himself as Gabriel Finch, Heavenly Counsel, Grade Two.
“I’ve never handled an atheist before,” he whispered.
Mara stared at him.
“Then you should probably read the file.”
Gabriel opened the briefcase.
It contained a sandwich, three paper clips, and a pamphlet titled How to Win Friends in Purgatory.
The prosecutor called the first witness: a trumpet-playing angel.
The angel testified that Mara had never praised the Lord.
Gabriel stood.
“Can you prove she never praised anyone?”
The angel frowned.
“I only keep records of praise directed upward.”
“Then you can’t prove she was ungrateful.”
The judge leaned forward.
“Counsel, that is almost a point.”
Gabriel smiled with relief.
Then he asked the angel whether Mara had ever prayed.
The angel checked his notes.
“She prayed during a root canal.”
“Excellent,” Gabriel said.
“What did she pray for?”
“That the dentist would stop humming.”
The prosecutor objected that this was not a prayer.
The judge agreed, then asked the clerk to classify it.
The clerk searched three binders and found a form marked Emergency Petition, Dental.
Mara watched Gabriel look increasingly pleased with himself.
He had discovered that the rules were stranger than the charge.
The prosecutor presented a chart of Mara’s charitable acts.
It showed she had fed strangers, rescued dogs, and paid a neighbor’s rent.
“None of this was done in God’s name,” the prosecutor said.
Gabriel rose again.
“Was it done for money?”
“No.”
“Fame?”
“No.”
“Then what was the motive?”
“She said people needed help.”
The judge consulted a thick book.
“Is that motive listed?”
The clerk searched the index.
“It appears under Unapproved Explanations.”
A murmur passed through the clouds.
Gabriel’s confidence vanished.
He turned to Mara and asked if she believed in Heaven.
“No,” she said.
“Could you pretend now?”
“I’m dead. I’m not starting a new career.”
The judge struck the stapler-gavel.
The sound echoed through the filing cabinets.
“Counsel,” he said, “your client’s honesty is making this difficult.”
“That seems unfair,” Mara said.
The judge sighed.
The court recessed so the angels could consult the policy manual.
In the hallway, Gabriel admitted he had studied the wrong manual.
He had prepared for a case involving a man who claimed to be an atheist but had secretly built a shrine to a sea monster.
Mara asked whether that man had won.
“He was transferred to Marine Eternity.”
When the court reconvened, the judge announced that the evidence was inconclusive.
The prosecutor requested another century for investigation.
Gabriel objected that Mara had no appointment that far ahead.
The clerk said the calendar was full until the end of time.
Mara asked what would happen if the court simply made a decision.
Everyone looked alarmed.
The judge flipped through the policy manual.
“There is a procedure for that,” the clerk said.
It required seven signatures, three witnesses, and proof of a valid death.
Mara’s death certificate had been filed under Pending.
Gabriel suddenly stood.
“Your Honor, if the court cannot establish that my client is dead, it cannot try her for her afterlife.”
The judge considered this.
The prosecutor objected that Heaven had already received her.
The clerk said receipt did not equal acceptance.
For the first time, the judge looked hopeful.
He dismissed the case for lack of jurisdiction.
The angels stamped Mara’s papers with APPROVED, DENIED, and PLEASE RESUBMIT.
Gabriel walked her to the elevator.
“Do you think I did all right?” he asked.
“You got me acquitted by proving the office lost me.”
He smiled.
“Divine justice can be mysterious.”
“It can also be badly organized.”
The elevator doors opened onto a bright field of grass.
A sign read: WELCOME TO THE AFTERLIFE—PLEASE HAVE YOUR DOCUMENTS READY.
Mara stepped out without them.

For ten years, Mara measured her life by the weather in Daniel’s moods. A quiet breakfast meant a good day, while a sigh could turn the whole evening cold. She learned to apologize before she knew what she had done. She stopped inviting friends over because Daniel always found a reason they were “bad for her.” When she mentioned taking a class, he laughed and asked who would keep the house running. Little by little, her world shrank to the rooms they shared. Then, on a rainy Tuesday, Mara found an old sketchbook beneath the bed. Its pages held drawings of birds, windows, and a woman standing on a hill with her arms outstretched. She had drawn them before she met Daniel. The sight of that woman stirred something she had nearly forgotten. Mara called her sister, though her hands trembled as she dialed. “I think I need help leaving,” she said. Her sister answered, “I’m coming.” They made a plan in whispers, listing documents, money, and a safe place to stay. Mara packed only what she could carry without Daniel noticing. On the morning she left, he was still asleep. She stood by the door and listened to the familiar silence. For once, she did not wonder how he would feel about her choice. She walked out with her coat, her sketchbook, and the keys to her own car. The first night at her sister’s apartment, every sound seemed too loud. Mara kept waking, expecting an angry message or a demand to come home. Her sister set a mug of tea beside her and stayed close without asking questions. In the days that followed, Daniel sent apologies, then blame, then promises. Mara read each message once and gave her phone to her sister. She began speaking with a counselor who helped her name the patterns she had lived through. At first, the words felt heavy, but they also made the past clearer. Mara found a small apartment with sun on the kitchen floor. She bought a blue chair that Daniel would have called impractical. She enrolled in an evening art class and showed up with a pencil tucked behind her ear. The first drawing was awkward, but it was hers. She started seeing old friends again, one coffee at a time. Their laughter felt strange at first, then warm. Some mornings, fear still rose before she was fully awake. When it did, she reminded herself that leaving was not a single brave moment but a choice she could keep making. She placed the sketchbook on a shelf beside a bowl of keys. Weeks became months, and the apartment began to feel like a home. One spring evening, Mara walked to the hill from her old drawing. The wind tugged at her coat, and the city lights shimmered below. She opened her arms, not because she was certain of what came next, but because the space to choose belonged to her again.

Civilian careers in criminology and criminal justice help communities prevent harm, understand crime, support victims, and improve public safety. These jobs are performed by people who are not sworn police officers, correctional officers, or other law-enforcement personnel. Some roles focus on research and data, while others involve laboratories, courts, rehabilitation, or security. The best path depends on your interests, education, and preferred work environment.

Crime analysts study patterns in reported incidents to help agencies allocate resources and identify emerging problems. They may use databases, mapping software, statistics, and geographic information systems. A bachelor’s degree in criminology, criminal justice, statistics, or a related field is commonly useful. Strong analytical skills and careful handling of confidential information are important.

Criminologists examine the causes, patterns, and consequences of crime. They may work for universities, government agencies, research organizations, or nonprofit groups. Their work can inform policies on prevention, policing, courts, and rehabilitation. Graduate education is often required for research and academic positions.

Forensic science technicians analyze evidence such as fingerprints, fibers, biological samples, or controlled substances. They may work in government laboratories, medical examiner offices, or private facilities. Many positions require a degree in forensic science or a natural science such as biology or chemistry. Laboratory procedures, precise documentation, and impartial reporting are central to the job.

Digital forensics specialists recover and examine information from computers, phones, and other electronic devices. They may support investigations into fraud, cybercrime, or data breaches. Employers often look for technical training, relevant certifications, and knowledge of evidence-preservation rules. Because technology changes quickly, ongoing learning is essential.

Forensic psychologists apply psychological knowledge to questions involving law and the justice system. Their work may include assessments, research, or treatment in correctional and court-related settings. These roles generally require advanced degrees and professional licensure. The specific duties and qualifications vary by jurisdiction and employer.

Victim advocates help people understand their options and connect with services after a crime. They may provide information about court processes, safety planning, compensation programs, and counseling referrals. Employers include nonprofit organizations, prosecutors’ offices, hospitals, and government agencies. Empathy, clear communication, and respect for privacy are vital.

Probation and parole support staff help people meet supervision requirements and access services that can reduce reoffending. Civilian roles may involve case coordination, records, assessments, or program delivery. Requirements differ, and some positions require a degree in social work, psychology, or criminal justice. Patience and sound judgment are useful in work that balances accountability with support.

Court administrators and legal support professionals help keep judicial systems organized. They may manage calendars, maintain records, coordinate hearings, or assist attorneys and court users. Training in legal studies, public administration, or office management can be helpful. Accuracy and discretion matter because court documents can contain sensitive information.

Emergency management specialists prepare organizations and communities for disasters and other major incidents. They develop plans, coordinate training, and help agencies work together during emergencies. A degree in emergency management, public administration, or a related area may be relevant. Some positions also value experience in planning, logistics, or public safety.

Security careers include corporate security analysts, loss-prevention specialists, and security program coordinators. These professionals assess risks, protect facilities or information, and help organizations respond to incidents. Their work may involve policy development, investigations, training, or technology. Employers may prefer experience in security, risk management, information technology, or criminal justice.

Not every career requires the same degree or a law-enforcement background. Entry-level positions may accept an associate degree, a bachelor’s degree, specialized training, or relevant work experience. More advanced research, forensic, psychological, and leadership roles often require graduate education or professional credentials. Requirements should always be checked with specific employers and licensing authorities.

Students can build experience through internships, research projects, volunteer work, and relevant part-time jobs. Useful skills include writing, critical thinking, data literacy, communication, and teamwork. Familiarity with spreadsheets, databases, and mapping or laboratory tools can also improve job prospects. Certifications can help in some specialties, but they do not replace required degrees or licenses.

When choosing a career, consider whether you prefer direct service, analytical work, laboratory settings, or organizational security. Think about the emotional demands, schedule, public contact, and ethical responsibilities involved. Many civilian professionals handle sensitive information and must follow strict rules for privacy and evidence. Integrity, fairness, and respect for individual rights are essential across the field.

Civilian careers in criminology and criminal justice offer many ways to contribute without becoming a sworn officer. Exploring job descriptions, speaking with professionals, and reviewing education requirements can help you identify a suitable path. With focused preparation and a commitment to ethical work, you can build a career that supports safer communities and a more effective justice system.

At seventeen, Mara could make a room go quiet with a song. Her voice carried through the school auditorium, clear as rain on a roof. Teachers called her gifted, and her mother kept every recital program in a shoebox. Mara believed them, though she was never sure what they saw when they looked at her. At graduation, she won a scholarship and promised herself she would become someone worth remembering.

The first pills came after a late shift at the diner, offered by a friend who said they would help her sleep. They softened the ache in her shoulders and quieted the restless voice that asked what came next. Soon she needed them to wake, then to work, then simply to feel ordinary. She missed rehearsals, telling the choir director she had caught a cold. When the scholarship letter arrived, she left it unopened beneath a stack of laundry.

Her mother found the pills one afternoon and asked, gently, if Mara needed help. Mara laughed too loudly and said everyone was tired of worrying about her. She began borrowing money, then taking it from the jar where her mother saved for groceries. Each lie seemed small enough to forgive until they piled up between them. The songs she once knew by heart slipped away, note by note.

By twenty, Mara had stopped calling herself a musician. She stopped calling herself anything at all. In the mirror, she saw a face she recognized only from old photographs. One winter morning, she woke on a bus bench with her shoes missing and the sky turning pale above her. A stranger offered her a paper cup of coffee, and she held it with both hands to keep them from shaking.

At the clinic, a counselor asked what she wanted her life to look like. Mara stared at the floor, unable to picture a future without the next dose. Then she remembered the shoebox of programs and the girl who had sung beneath the stage lights. The memory did not rescue her, but it gave her one small direction to face. She said she wanted to hear her own voice again.

Recovery came in uneven days, with setbacks that frightened her and mornings she had to begin twice. Her mother sat beside her through the hardest appointments, never pretending that forgiveness erased what had happened. Mara learned to ask for help before shame could turn into silence. At a community center, she found an old upright piano and pressed one uncertain key. The note trembled, then settled into the room.

She did not become the girl from the photographs again. She became someone who knew how easily a promise can disappear, and how slowly it can be rebuilt. Some evenings, she sang for a handful of people who had nowhere else to be. Her voice was rougher now, but it belonged to her. When the last note faded, Mara stayed in the room and listened.

The first time Mara saw Lucan Vale cast a spell, he turned rain into glass. Each drop hung above the courtyard, bright and still, while the students gasped. Lucan smiled as if the storm had applauded for him. He was sixteen, celebrated, and already the youngest mage invited to the Crown Trials. Mara was the scholarship student who repaired cracked practice wands and borrowed books with missing pages. Her magic was modest: she could coax a candle flame sideways or warm a cup of tea. The masters called her clever, which was their polite way of calling her weak. Still, Mara noticed things other people dismissed. Lucan’s glass raindrops had all stopped at the same height. When he lowered his hand, they fell in neat rows, not all at once. She watched him practice from the archway every evening. His spells began with a tap of his left thumb against his ring. Then came a breath, a spoken word, and a turn of the wrist. The order never changed. Mara copied the gestures in a notebook, though she did not understand them. For weeks, she tried to imitate his spells and failed. Her own sparks sputtered before they could reach the target. So she began testing smaller pieces. She tapped her thumb and waited. Nothing happened. She breathed and whispered the word, and a candle leaned toward her. The turn of her wrist made it straighten again. Mara tried the steps in different orders. She discovered that the spoken word did not create the magic. It named the shape the magic was already taking. Lucan’s thumb-tap began a rhythm, and his breath fed it. His wrist turn sealed the pattern. Together, the gestures made a spell that repeated itself in perfect balance. The pattern was beautiful, but it had a weakness. If the rhythm slipped before the final turn, the magic could not settle. Mara practiced breaking rhythms with tiny, harmless distractions. She dropped a pebble during a friend’s spell and watched its flame flicker. She learned to clap offbeat without making a sound. The Crown Trials came on a clear morning, with the whole city watching. In the final contest, Mara faced Lucan across a circle of white stone. He gave her a gracious nod, already certain of victory. The judges asked them to lift a bronze bell and hold it above the arena. Lucan tapped his ring, breathed, spoke, and turned his wrist. The bell rose smoothly, glowing at its edges. Mara reached for the bell, but her magic could barely nudge it. The crowd began to murmur. Then she clapped once, softly, on the wrong beat. Lucan’s eyes narrowed, and the bell shivered in the air. Mara clapped again, this time just before his breath. His spell faltered, but he forced the word through and raised his hand higher. The bell lurched upward, dragging a strand of light behind it. Mara saw the strand pulse in time with his thumb. She stepped closer and tapped her own thumb against the stone, once, twice, then skipped the third beat. Lucan’s rhythm stumbled as his magic tried to match hers. The bell tilted, and he struggled to keep it aloft. Mara did not attack the spell; she gave it a new rhythm to follow. She tapped quickly, then slowly, then stopped. Lucan’s wrist began its final turn too soon. The glowing pattern folded in on itself. The bell dropped, and Mara caught it with both hands just above the ground. Silence swept across the arena. Lucan stared at the bell, then at her notebook tucked beneath her belt. “You found the pattern,” he said. “You left it where anyone could see,” Mara replied. The judges declared her the winner, though she barely heard them over the crowd. Later, Lucan asked her to teach him how she had done it. Mara opened her notebook and showed him the page marked with a dozen crossed-out rhythms. “Magic isn’t only what you can summon,” she said. “Sometimes it’s what you learn to notice.” And for the first time, Lucan listened before he cast.

Aluminium-backed curtains help control sunlight by reflecting some of it before it enters a room. Their reflective layer is usually attached to the side facing the window. This layer bounces a portion of incoming light back toward the glass and outdoors. As a result, less direct sunlight reaches furniture, floors, and other surfaces.

Reducing direct light can also lessen glare on screens and shiny surfaces. This may make a room more comfortable for reading, working, or watching television. The curtains do not make every room completely dark, however. The amount of light blocked depends on the fabric, its colour, and how closely the curtains fit around the window.

The reflective backing can also help limit solar heat gain. Sunlight passing through glass warms indoor surfaces, which then release heat into the room. By reflecting some sunlight away, the curtains can reduce this warming effect. They may help keep rooms cooler during sunny weather and reduce the need for air conditioning.

Their performance depends on how and when they are used. For best results, close them before strong sunlight reaches the window, and cover as much of the window as possible. Gaps at the sides or top can let light and heat through. In colder weather, opening the curtains on sunny windows can allow useful warmth in.

Aluminium-backed curtains are not a substitute for insulation or efficient windows, and they cannot prevent all heat transfer. They can also make rooms darker, so balance light control with the need for daylight. When choosing curtains, check whether the reflective side should face the glass and follow the manufacturer’s instructions.

Students should meet a minimum GPA to participate in school sports, as long as the requirement is fair and students can get support to reach it. Sports take time and effort, so students need to balance practices and games with their schoolwork. A reasonable GPA standard can encourage them to stay organized and keep up with assignments. It also reminds students that education is an important part of school life.

However, grades should not be the only measure of a student’s ability or potential. Some students face challenges outside school that can affect their grades. Others may struggle in certain subjects while still working hard and improving. Schools should consider a student’s progress and effort, not just a single number.

A minimum GPA can also help students build habits that will benefit them after graduation. Planning ahead, asking teachers for help, and managing time are useful skills in many careers. Coaches can support these habits by checking in with students and helping them find tutoring. Schools should make academic support available before removing anyone from a team.

The GPA requirement should not be so high that it excludes students who are trying their best. A fair policy might set a modest minimum and give students time to improve. If a student falls below the standard, the school could create an improvement plan instead of immediately taking away the chance to play. This approach encourages responsibility while still offering support.

School sports should promote teamwork, health, and personal growth. They can also motivate students to attend school and feel connected to their community. A carefully designed GPA rule can support both athletic and academic success. In the end, students should meet a reasonable academic standard to play, but schools must help them succeed rather than simply punish them.

On the morning of his execution, Elias Vale asked for a clean shirt.
The jailer laughed and brought him one stained with rain.
Elias put it on anyway.
He had been condemned for killing a prince, though the prince had died years before.
At noon, the gallows opened beneath his feet.
Instead of falling, Elias kept falling.
He passed through clouds of ash and a sky full of red stars.
Then he struck black stone at the bottom of the world.
A river of fire curled around him like a waiting snake.
Beyond it stood a palace with a thousand locked doors.
The guards who dragged him inside wore crowns of bone.
They took him to Prince Malrec, ruler of Hell.
Malrec was tall, pale, and smiling.
“You killed my brother,” he said.
Elias stared at the prince’s silver eyes.
He remembered a winter night, a ruined chapel, and a stranger begging for mercy.
“I killed a man who was hurting a child,” Elias replied.
Malrec laughed, and the palace shook.
His brother, the old prince, had been cruel even by Hell’s measure.
Malrec had punished Elias for the murder by bringing him here.
Now he raised a black blade.
“Your sentence is endless,” he said.
Elias had nothing left to lose.
He caught the prince’s wrist before the blade fell.
For one impossible moment, the flames went quiet.
Then Elias drove the blade into Malrec’s heart.
The prince burst into smoke, leaving his crown on the floor.
Every demon in the hall dropped to one knee.
Elias stepped back from the crown.
“I’m not your ruler,” he said.
The oldest demon lifted its head.
“The throne chooses,” it whispered.
The crown rose by itself.
Elias tried to run, but the doors slammed shut.
The crown settled on his brow, cold as a winter grave.
A thousand doors opened across the palace.
From them came the dead, the damned, and the forgotten.
They did not cheer.
They only watched him, waiting.
Elias looked at their weary faces and understood the cost of power.
Malrec had ruled through fear because he had never learned another way.
Elias ordered the chains removed from the palace gates.
The demons hesitated.
He ordered them again, and the chains fell with a crash.
Outside, the river of fire dimmed to a warm red glow.
The dead began to cross without being hunted.
Hell did not become kind in a day.
It did not become kind in a year.
But the doors stayed open.
Elias listened to every soul who came before him.
Some wanted justice, some wanted rest, and some wanted revenge.
He gave no one everything they asked for.
He gave no one nothing.
In time, the demons stopped calling him the condemned man.
They called him the Keeper of the Gates.
Elias never stopped wearing the stained shirt.
It reminded him that a sentence was not the same as a truth.
And when the crown grew heavy, he remembered the child in the chapel.

Reducing Reliance on Cars for a Better Future

Cars make it easy to travel from one place to another, but relying on them too much can create problems. Traffic congestion, pollution, and high transportation costs affect communities every day. Reducing car use does not mean that everyone must stop driving completely. Instead, it means making walking, cycling, public transit, and shared rides practical options. These changes can improve public well-being, make transportation more affordable, and protect the environment.

One important benefit is better health. When people walk or cycle for part of their journeys, they get regular physical activity. Even a short walk to a bus stop can help people move more throughout the day. Regular movement can reduce the risk of some illnesses and improve fitness. It can also support mental well-being by easing stress and helping people spend time outdoors. Streets with fewer cars may feel safer and more pleasant for people of all ages.

Reducing car use can also strengthen communities. Busy roads can separate neighborhoods and make it difficult for people to meet or visit local businesses. Quieter streets make it easier to talk with neighbors and spend time in public spaces. More trees, benches, and wider sidewalks can turn roads into places people enjoy, rather than just routes for vehicles. Children may have more opportunities to walk or cycle when streets are designed with safety in mind. Older adults and people with disabilities also benefit when sidewalks, crossings, and transit are accessible.

Transportation affordability is another major reason to rely less on cars. Owning a car can involve payments, fuel, insurance, repairs, parking, and registration fees. These costs can take a large share of a household’s income. Public transit, cycling, and walking can cost much less for many trips. A household that needs fewer cars may have more money for housing, food, education, and other needs. Affordable transportation also helps people reach jobs, schools, health care, and essential services.

However, alternatives must be reliable and convenient to serve everyone. Public transit should run frequently, connect useful destinations, and operate at hours that fit people’s schedules. Fares should be affordable, and vehicles and stations should be accessible. Safe bike lanes and well-maintained sidewalks can make active travel possible for more people. Shared rides can help people travel to places that transit does not reach. Rural communities may need different solutions, such as flexible buses or community transport services.

The environment can benefit greatly when fewer people depend on private cars. Cars burn fuel and release greenhouse gases that contribute to climate change. They also produce air pollution that can harm human health. Fewer car trips can reduce these emissions, especially when people use public transit or travel without a motor. Less traffic can also mean less noise in residential areas. If fewer parking spaces are needed, some land can be used for parks, homes, or community spaces instead.

There are practical steps governments and communities can take. Cities can improve bus and train service while building connected networks of safe bike lanes. They can design neighborhoods so that homes, shops, schools, and services are closer together. Employers can support transit passes, carpooling, and flexible work schedules. Residents can choose to walk, cycle, or take the bus when these options suit their trips. Even replacing some car journeys, rather than all of them, can make a difference.

It is important to recognize that not everyone can easily give up driving. Some people live far from transit, work unusual hours, or need a car because of a disability or caregiving responsibilities. A fair transportation system should provide choices rather than blame people for driving. Planning should include the needs of low-income households and communities that have historically faced poor access to safe transportation. Better options can make driving less necessary without taking away people’s ability to travel.

Reducing reliance on cars can lead to healthier lives, lower transportation expenses, stronger communities, and cleaner air. These benefits are most likely when alternatives are safe, affordable, accessible, and dependable. Changes may take time, but every improved bus route, safer crossing, or connected bike lane can help. A future with more transportation choices can make daily life easier for many people. By planning streets around people as well as vehicles, communities can create a healthier and more sustainable world.
