By dawn, Elias Venn had become Father Clement.

The name came from a brass plate he found in an abandoned rectory.

The collar came from a laundry line.

The black coat came from a dead priest who had been kind enough not to ask questions.

Elias had once been a locksmith, a careful man with patient hands.

Then he had opened the wrong door for the wrong client.

A week later, a banker was dead, a detective was missing, and Elias was running through rain.

The village of Saint Oran offered a church, a cellar, and no questions.

He slept beneath the altar with a pistol under his pillow.

On Sunday, he stood at the pulpit and spoke about forgiveness.

His voice surprised him by sounding almost sincere.

The villagers nodded.

They liked a priest who spoke plainly.

By Monday, they had begun bringing him their sins.

The first was a farmer named Bell.

“I stole three eggs from my neighbor,” Bell said through the confessional screen.

“Did you eat them?” Elias asked.

“Yes.”

“Then the eggs are gone, and your neighbor is still alive.”

Bell waited.

“Pay him back, or don’t,” Elias said.

“Will God forgive me?”

“God has probably heard worse.”

Bell left looking relieved.

The next visitor was a woman who confessed to wishing her husband would fall into a well.

“Is he likely to?” Elias asked.

“No.”

“Then your wish is harmless.”

“He is a miserable man.”

“Then leave him.”

“I have children.”

“Then take them with you.”

“That sounds difficult.”

“It will be.”

She made a small noise, half laugh and half sob.

Elias heard the door close.

By Wednesday, the line reached the church steps.

A boy confessed to lying about a broken window.

“Did you break it?” Elias asked.

“No.”

“Then you lied about something else.”

“I said I saw who did it.”

“Did you?”

“No.”

“Then tell the truth.”

“I’ll get in trouble.”

“You are already in trouble.”

The boy left, muttering that priests were supposed to be kinder.

Elias wished he had a pistol for the next question.

Instead, he had a wooden screen and a headache.

An old man confessed to keeping a second family in the next county.

“Does your wife know?” Elias asked.

“No.”

“Does the other woman know about your wife?”

“No.”

“Then you have made a hobby of wasting women’s time.”

The old man grunted.

“Should I tell them?”

“Yes.”

“Both of them?”

“Unless you plan to grow a second head.”

The man came back the next day and asked for advice about what to say.

Elias told him to begin with the truth and avoid the phrase “it just happened.”

The old man said he had always admired priests.

Elias said that was a poor reason to become one.

The confessions grew stranger.

A baker confessed to watering down soup.

A schoolteacher confessed to hating children.

A widow confessed to speaking kindly to her cat and cruelly to everyone else.

A fisherman confessed that he had once released a fish because it looked frightened.

Elias told him the fish had probably forgotten.

The fisherman cried anyway.

One woman confessed to stealing a spoon from a hotel in 1968.

“Do you still have it?” Elias asked.

“No.”

“Then it has escaped.”

She laughed for the first time in months.

Elias hated how much he liked that sound.

He had planned to stay three days.

The town had a train station, a cash box, and a priest who had gone south to care for his sister.

Three days became two weeks.

The police never came.

The villagers came every evening.

They confessed small failures, old grudges, and fears they had never named aloud.

Elias gave them the same counsel each time.

Stop making excuses.

Say what you mean.

Leave if you can.

Stay if you must.

Do not expect anyone to read your mind.

They called him wise.

He called himself tired.

Then a man came in wearing a gray suit and a smile like a folded knife.

“I have done something terrible,” the man said.

Elias’s fingers tightened around the edge of the screen.

“What did you do?”

“I killed a man.”

The church seemed to shrink around them.

“Who?”

“A locksmith named Elias Venn.”

For a moment, Elias heard only the rain ticking against the windows.

“Are you certain?” he asked.

“I saw the body.”

“Then you should tell the police.”

“I was hoping you might advise me.”

“Advice is free.”

The man leaned closer to the screen.

“They’re looking for you, Father.”

Elias did not answer.

“They say you murdered a banker and a detective.”

“I didn’t kill the detective.”

“But you opened the door.”

“Yes.”

“And the banker?”

“I opened that door, too.”

The man gave a quiet chuckle.

“Then perhaps you should confess.”

Elias looked at the pistol beneath the table.

He could reach it before the man could stand.

He could also hear the village outside, gathering for evening service.

“Did you kill the banker?” Elias asked.

“No.”

“Did you set up the detective?”

“Yes.”

“Then confess to the police.”

“I came to confess to God.”

“God is not a magistrate.”

The man’s smile faded.

“Are you going to absolve me?”

“No.”

“Why not?”

“Because you haven’t asked for forgiveness. You’ve asked for a witness.”

The man stood.

Elias stood, too.

For a long second, neither moved.

Then the man opened the confessional door and stepped into the aisle.

Elias came out after him, still wearing the collar.

The villagers had gathered in the nave.

They watched the gray-suited man turn toward the exit.

The old farmer Bell blocked the door.

The woman with the miserable husband stood beside him.

The boy who had lied about the window held a broom like a spear.

The man in the gray suit looked at Elias.

“You’ve made friends.”

“No,” Elias said. “I’ve made a mess.”

The villagers closed around the man.

Someone ran for the police.

The man tried to bolt, but the fisherman caught his coat.

By the time the constable arrived, Elias had removed the collar.

He placed it gently on the altar.

The constable looked at the coat, the empty holster, and Elias’s tired face.

“Are you coming quietly?”

“I’ve been coming quietly for weeks.”

They led him out beneath the church bell.

The villagers did not cheer.

They simply watched him go.

At the station, Elias confessed to opening the banker’s door.

He confessed to running.

He confessed to using a dead man’s name and a living man’s collar.

He did not confess to killing the detective, because he had not.

The police found the detective alive in a cellar two counties away.

The banker’s real murderer was the man in the gray suit.

Elias was still guilty of helping him.

At his trial, the judge asked whether he regretted what he had done.

Elias considered the question.

“Yes,” he said.

The judge asked whether he would do it again.

“No.”

The judge asked whether he believed in forgiveness.

Elias looked toward the back of the courtroom, where the villagers sat in a row.

“I believe people should stop demanding it before they’ve changed.”

He was sentenced to six years.

The villagers visited him once a month.

They brought stories, fruit, and questions they could have answered themselves.

Elias continued to give blunt advice.

He told Bell to stop counting his neighbor’s eggs.

He told the widow to be nicer to the cat.

He told the boy that courage did not require a broom.

The boy said he knew.

Elias told him that was no excuse.

On the first Sunday of spring, the village sent him a card.

It showed the church with its doors open.

Inside, someone had written, We are trying.

Elias read it twice.

Then he put it beneath his pillow, where the pistol used to be.

That night, he dreamed he was back in the confessional.

A stranger knelt on the other side of the screen.

“I have done something terrible,” the stranger whispered.

Elias woke before answering.

In the morning, he asked the guard for paper.

He wrote a letter to the village.

He told them not to wait for a priest to make them honest.

He told them not to mistake bluntness for wisdom.

He told them that a person could be wrong, frightened, and still useful.

Then he crossed out the last sentence.

It sounded too much like a blessing.

Instead, he wrote, Tell the truth before it gets expensive.

He signed his own name.

The guard laughed when he read it.

Elias did not.

But he kept the letter, and he sent it.

A week later, the village wrote back.

They said the cat was doing well.

Raising academic eligibility standards for student athletes can encourage responsibility and create stronger opportunities for their future. School athletics should support students’ education, not distract them from it. When athletes must meet clear academic expectations, they learn to balance practices, competitions, and classwork. This balance builds habits such as time management, persistence, and self-discipline. Those skills can help students long after their playing careers end.

Higher standards can also help athletes stay on track for graduation. Students who regularly attend class and complete assignments are more likely to gain the knowledge needed for college or a career. Academic expectations may motivate athletes to seek tutoring or ask teachers for help before they fall behind. Coaches can contribute by checking students’ progress and reminding them that school comes first. Families and schools can also work together to provide support.

However, eligibility rules should be fair and realistic. A student facing illness, learning challenges, or problems at home may need extra assistance rather than immediate punishment. Schools should offer tutoring, study time, and clear ways to improve grades. Standards should encourage effort while giving students a genuine chance to succeed. With the right support, students can learn from setbacks instead of feeling excluded.

Some people worry that stricter rules could keep talented athletes from playing. This concern matters, but athletic participation should not come at the cost of a student’s education. Playing time and team membership can be powerful incentives to take schoolwork seriously. Ultimately, raising academic eligibility standards can help student athletes become more responsible and prepared for life. Strong students are better positioned to pursue college, employment, and other goals after sports.

Stricter academic eligibility requirements can influence how students take part in sports and extracurricular activities. Schools often use these rules to encourage students to keep up with their schoolwork. For example, a student who earns low grades might be temporarily unable to compete on a team. This consequence may motivate some students to study harder and ask teachers for help. As a result, their grades could improve over time. However, stricter rules can also create challenges for students who are already struggling. Missing practices or activities may take away a source of encouragement and support. Sports and clubs can help students build friendships, confidence, and a sense of belonging. They can also teach teamwork, leadership, and time management. Students with learning difficulties, family responsibilities, or limited access to tutoring may be especially affected. A single low grade might keep them from activities even if they are trying their best. Schools can make eligibility rules fairer by offering tutoring and regular progress checks before suspending participation. They might also consider a student’s effort and improvement, not just final grades. Overall, academic requirements should support learning while allowing students meaningful opportunities to participate.

Mara had always believed that people got what they deserved.
She said so most often about the families who crowded the shelter on Maple Street.
From the window of her neat, warm house, she watched them line up for dinner.
She noticed their worn coats and the bags they carried.
She noticed less when they laughed.
She noticed less when they helped one another.
“They make bad choices,” she told her husband, Paul.
“They should try harder.”
Paul usually answered with a quiet nod.
Mara mistook his silence for agreement.
Their daughter, June, was twelve.
She watched her mother from the stairs.
One rainy Thursday, Mara drove downtown to deliver a box of old blankets.
The shelter director, Mrs. Alvarez, thanked her at the door.
Mara glanced at the people waiting inside.
A young man sat with his head in his hands.
A woman held a sleeping baby against her shoulder.
“Do you know why they’re here?” Mara asked.
“Many reasons,” Mrs. Alvarez replied.
Mara smiled as if the answer proved nothing.
She left before dinner was served.
That night, Paul’s truck did not come home.
At first Mara assumed he had stopped for gas.
Then she called his office.
His coworker said Paul had collapsed at the warehouse.
At the hospital, a doctor explained that Paul’s heart had failed.
They had found him unconscious beside a loading dock.
He died before Mara reached his room.
For weeks, the house seemed too large to live in.
Friends brought casseroles and stayed only long enough to offer sympathy.
The bills kept arriving anyway.
Paul had been paid by the hour.
His life insurance had lapsed when he changed jobs.
Mara learned that he had quietly borrowed against their savings.
She learned it from the bank, not from him.
The mortgage notice came on a pale blue envelope.
The heating bill came on a red one.
Mara sold Paul’s truck.
Then she sold her wedding ring.
She took a job cleaning offices at night.
June learned to make macaroni without asking for help.
Mara told herself the hardship was temporary.
Then the school called about June’s missed days.
June had been working afternoons at a grocery store.
She was tired, and she did not want her mother to worry.
Mara wanted to scold her.
Instead, she sat down beside her at the kitchen table.
For the first time, Mara understood that a bad choice could begin as a desperate one.
Still, she thought, at least they had a home.
Three months later, the landlord sold the building.
The new owner raised the rent beyond what Mara could pay.
Mara packed their belongings into borrowed boxes.
She called relatives, but each had a reason they could not help.
A friend offered a couch for two nights.
On the third night, Mara and June slept in the car.
Mara kept the doors locked and the engine running.
June pretended not to notice her mother crying.
In the morning, Mara drove to the Maple Street shelter.
She recognized the chipped green door.
Mrs. Alvarez recognized her, too.
She did not mention the blankets.
She did not ask what had happened.
She showed them a small room with two narrow beds.
Mara wanted to explain that they were not like the others.
The words rose to her mouth and stayed there.
In the dining room, a man in a work jacket offered June an orange.
He had a scar across his chin and a kind, tired smile.
Mara had seen him before.
He was the young man she once watched with his head in his hands.
His name was Leon.
He had been laid off when his factory closed.
After that, his rent had fallen behind.
His wife had taken their son to live with her sister.
Leon had been trying to find work and a place to start over.
Mara had once decided his silence meant laziness.
Now she watched him save the best part of his dinner for someone else.
The next morning, she sat with him at the shelter’s job desk.
They filled out applications together.
Mara found a part-time cleaning position at a clinic.
Leon found a warehouse shift three weeks later.
The work was not enough to solve everything.
It was enough to give them somewhere to begin.
At the shelter, Mara met people whose lives she had reduced to a sentence.
A woman had left home after years of violence.
A veteran had lost his apartment when his benefits were delayed.
A teenager had been turned out by parents who could not accept him.
A retired teacher had spent her savings on her husband’s illness.
Each story complicated the judgment Mara had carried like a shield.
She learned that people could be careless and still deserve help.
She learned that effort did not always defeat bad luck.
She learned that pride could make a hard day harder.
Most of all, she learned how easy it was to confuse an unseen struggle with a simple failure.
June began helping with dinner at the shelter.
She liked the way the children asked her to read aloud.
One evening, she saw her mother talking with a woman who had just arrived.
The woman’s hands shook as she filled out a form.
Mara took the pen gently and waited while she found the words.
June remembered the old Mara, standing in the shelter doorway and hurrying away.
She was glad that woman had not stayed the same.
Spring arrived with thin sunlight and wet sidewalks.
Mara and June moved into a small apartment above a laundromat.
The rooms smelled of soap and warm machines.
They still counted every dollar.
They still missed Paul.
But the door had a lock, and the beds were their own.
On Saturdays, Mara returned to Maple Street to serve dinner.
She did not call it charity.
She called it showing up.
One night, a man arrived late and asked if there was anything left.
Mara recognized the shape of shame in his lowered eyes.
She remembered the same look in her own reflection.
“There’s enough,” she said, and set a bowl on the table.
The man thanked her without meeting her gaze.
Mara did not ask what he had done wrong.
She asked whether he wanted tea.
Outside, rain tapped the windows.
Inside, people made room for one another.
Mara understood that a life could change without warning.
She understood that the people she had judged had been carrying weight she could not see.
Then she understood something harder.
Her own suffering had not made her wiser by itself.
Only listening had.
And listening began when she stopped deciding who deserved a place at the table.

Ensuring equitable access to digital library resources means making online collections and services usable by people with a wide range of disabilities. Libraries serve students and visitors with visual, hearing, motor, cognitive, and learning disabilities, as well as people with temporary or age-related access needs. Accessibility should be built into digital services from the start, not added only after someone reports a problem.

Web pages and library catalogs should follow recognized accessibility standards, such as the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG). Clear headings, descriptive links, consistent navigation, and readable language help people find information more easily. Text should have sufficient contrast against its background and remain usable when enlarged. Images that convey information need meaningful alternative text, while decorative images should be ignored by screen readers.

All functions should work with a keyboard, without requiring a mouse. Focus indicators should clearly show which link or control is selected. Videos should include accurate captions, and audio content should have transcripts. Documents, including scanned books and articles, should be searchable and compatible with assistive technology; optical character recognition can make image-only scans readable.

Libraries should check that e-books, research databases, and other vendor platforms are accessible before purchasing or renewing them. Accessibility statements and contact details should be easy to find, and staff should offer a clear way to report barriers. When a resource is inaccessible, staff can help locate an accessible alternative or provide materials in another format promptly.

Testing should include automated tools, manual checks, and feedback from people with disabilities. Students and visitors with disabilities should be involved in planning and evaluating services, with their privacy and consent respected. Library staff also need training to use assistive technologies and respond helpfully to access requests. Equitable access is an ongoing responsibility that improves when libraries review their resources regularly and act on what users tell them.

Subject: Requested Revisions to Draft Gas Supply Agreements for Public Service Company of Colorado and Cheyenne Light, Fuel & Power

Dear [Name],

Thank you for providing the draft gas supply agreements for Public Service Company of Colorado and Cheyenne Light, Fuel & Power. We have completed our initial review and would like to propose several revisions before the documents are finalized. Our goal is to clarify the parties’ responsibilities and ensure the agreements accurately reflect the intended commercial arrangement. The comments below apply to both agreements unless otherwise noted. Where a point is specific to one company, we have identified it separately. Please review these requests and let us know if you would like to discuss any of them. We are happy to provide proposed language for each item. We would also welcome a consolidated revised draft for review.

First, please confirm the full legal name of each buyer and use that name consistently throughout the applicable agreement. Please verify each party’s formation jurisdiction and principal business address in the introductory paragraphs. The notice provision should list current contact details for legal, operational, and billing notices. Please allow either party to update its notice information by written notice without requiring a formal amendment. We also request that notices by email be effective when receipt is acknowledged or otherwise confirmed. Notices of termination, default, or dispute should additionally be sent by a recognized overnight delivery service. Please clarify whether notice deadlines are measured in calendar days or business days. Any deadline falling on a weekend or legal holiday should extend to the next business day.

Please revise the term provision to state the initial term and the exact start and end dates. If the start date depends on satisfaction of a condition, please identify that condition and the process for confirming satisfaction. We request that any renewal be by mutual written agreement rather than automatic renewal. If automatic renewal is retained, please provide a clear notice window that gives both parties adequate time to evaluate the arrangement. The agreement should specify the required form and delivery method for a nonrenewal notice. Please also clarify whether existing purchase orders or scheduled deliveries continue after expiration. Any transition obligations should be limited to amounts and services accrued before expiration.

The quantity provisions should specify the applicable daily and monthly contract quantities for each delivery point. Please identify the source and method used to determine any forecast or nomination quantity. We request a reasonable tolerance around scheduled quantities to account for ordinary operational variation. Any take-or-pay or deficiency charge should apply only to quantities the buyer was obligated and able to take. Please exclude shortfalls caused by supplier failure, pipeline restrictions, force majeure, or other circumstances outside the buyer’s reasonable control. The agreement should describe how make-up gas is requested, scheduled, and valued. Please ensure that any make-up rights do not expire before the buyer has a reasonable opportunity to use them. If the supplier may reduce quantities, please establish an objective allocation method. That method should treat similarly situated customers consistently and provide for prompt notice of a reduction.

Please confirm the precise delivery point or points for each agreement. The documents should identify the relevant pipeline, meter, and applicable location identifier where available. Please state when title and risk of loss transfer from supplier to buyer. We request that transfer occur at the agreed delivery point after gas is delivered in accordance with the contract. The supplier should remain responsible for transportation and upstream arrangements assigned to it under the agreement. The buyer should not be responsible for costs arising from the supplier’s failure to secure those arrangements. Please clarify which party is responsible for measurement, testing, and meter data. Any correction to measured quantities should be supported by records and provided within a stated period. The parties should have reasonable access to relevant measurement information, subject to applicable security and confidentiality requirements.

Please revise the pricing section to identify the applicable index, publication, location, and pricing period. If an index is unavailable or materially changed, the parties should use a clearly stated replacement methodology. We request that any replacement methodology preserve the original economic intent as closely as reasonably possible. Please specify the treatment of applicable transportation, fuel, imbalance, and other pass-through charges. Pass-through charges should be limited to actual, documented costs attributable to the deliveries under the agreement. The supplier should provide reasonable supporting detail with each invoice. No new surcharge or fee should apply unless expressly authorized by the agreement or agreed in writing. Please state whether taxes are included in or added to the stated price. Each party should remain responsible for taxes imposed on its own income, property, or operations.

The invoicing provisions should provide a reasonable period for the buyer to review and pay undisputed amounts. We propose payment within thirty days after receipt of a complete and accurate invoice. The invoice should identify delivered quantities, applicable prices, adjustments, and supporting charges. Please permit the buyer to dispute an invoice in good faith by giving written notice with a reasonable explanation. The buyer should pay the undisputed portion while the parties work to resolve the disputed amount. No interest or late fee should accrue on a disputed amount while the dispute is being addressed in good faith. Any interest on overdue undisputed amounts should be limited to the lesser of the stated rate and the maximum lawful rate. Please provide at least twelve months for either party to submit a billing adjustment after the relevant delivery. The parties should retain supporting records for a reasonable period and provide access for verification upon reasonable notice.

Please clarify the nomination and scheduling procedures, including applicable deadlines and the system used for submissions. The agreement should account for changes to pipeline procedures and provide a practical method for communicating those changes. Each party should use commercially reasonable efforts to confirm nominations promptly. A party should not be liable for a scheduling failure caused by the other party or by a pipeline acting outside its control. The parties should coordinate in good faith to resolve operational imbalances. Any imbalance charge should be based on the applicable pipeline tariff or a clearly identified contractual method. Please avoid duplicate recovery for the same imbalance or operational event.

We request that the force majeure provision apply to both parties on a reciprocal basis. It should cover events beyond a party’s reasonable control that prevent or materially impair performance. The provision should exclude lack of funds and changes in market price from force majeure. Affected parties should provide prompt notice and use reasonable efforts to mitigate the effects. Performance should be excused only to the extent and for the duration of the actual impediment. Payment obligations for gas already delivered should not be excused. Please include a process for resuming performance when the event ends. If a force majeure event continues beyond a defined period, either party should be able to terminate the affected portion of the agreement without an early termination charge.

Please revise the default provisions to include a reasonable notice and cure period for remediable breaches. A payment default should arise only for an undisputed amount that remains unpaid after notice and the applicable cure period. Any suspension right should be limited to the affected deliveries and exercised in a manner consistent with safety and applicable law. Termination should be available only for a material breach that remains uncured after the required notice. Please make any early termination payment reciprocal and limited to documented, direct losses that are reasonably foreseeable. The agreement should prohibit recovery of speculative, punitive, or duplicative amounts. Neither party should be liable for consequential, incidental, or exemplary damages, except to the extent such damages arise from fraud, willful misconduct, or an express indemnity obligation. Please also confirm that the liability cap, if applicable, is commercially reasonable and applies consistently to both parties.

The indemnity provisions should be limited to third-party claims arising from a party’s negligence, willful misconduct, or breach of law. Each party should be responsible for the acts and omissions of its own personnel and contractors. Please exclude claims to the extent caused by the indemnified party’s negligence or misconduct. The party seeking indemnity should provide prompt notice and reasonable cooperation. The indemnifying party should control the defense, provided it may not settle a claim in a way that imposes liability or an admission on the other party without that party’s consent. Each party should maintain insurance customary for its operations and provide evidence of coverage upon reasonable request. Any additional insured requirement should be limited to the extent permitted by the applicable policy.

Please confirm that assignment requires consent that may not be unreasonably withheld, conditioned, or delayed. Either party should be permitted to assign the agreement to an affiliate or successor in connection with a merger, reorganization, or sale of substantially all relevant assets, subject to notice and assumption of obligations. The confidentiality provision should protect pricing, operational information, and other nonpublic business information. It should permit disclosure to affiliates, advisers, auditors, lenders, and regulators when reasonably necessary and subject to appropriate confidentiality protections. The provision should also allow disclosure required by law or regulatory process, with advance notice where legally permitted. Please state a reasonable survival period for confidentiality obligations, with trade secrets protected for as long as they qualify as trade secrets.

Finally, please include a provision confirming that amendments and waivers must be in writing and signed by authorized representatives. The agreement should state that it is governed by the laws of the agreed jurisdiction, without regard to conflict-of-law rules. Please identify an appropriate venue for disputes and require good-faith executive discussions before litigation, except where immediate relief is needed. Nothing in the agreement should waive any regulatory rights or obligations that cannot lawfully be waived. Please confirm that each agreement will be interpreted independently unless the parties expressly state otherwise. We would appreciate receiving revised drafts that incorporate these comments or identify any requested changes you cannot accept. Please include a redline against the current drafts and a clean copy for review. We suggest scheduling a working session after we receive the revised documents. Thank you for your attention to these revisions and for your continued cooperation. We look forward to finalizing agreements that are clear, balanced, and workable for both parties.

Sincerely,

[Your Name]
[Title]
[Organization]
[Phone]
[Email]

Leonardo da Vinci’s Studies of Flight and Flying Machines

Leonardo da Vinci was fascinated by the possibility of human flight. He lived in Italy during the Renaissance, from 1452 to 1519, when artists and inventors closely observed the natural world. Leonardo believed that understanding nature could help people create new technologies. Birds especially captured his attention because they could rise, glide, and steer through the air.

Leonardo studied birds in flight and made detailed drawings of their wings and movements. He examined how birds changed the angle of their wings and tails to control direction and balance. He also considered how wind and air currents might support a flying body. His notebooks contain sketches, observations, and ideas about these questions.

Many of Leonardo’s early designs were ornithopters, machines intended to fly by flapping their wings. Some designs placed a person inside a wooden frame, using levers, ropes, and pedals to move large wings. The pilot’s arms and legs were supposed to provide the power. Leonardo understood that the human body could not easily generate enough force to lift such a machine, but he continued exploring how its parts might work.

One famous design resembles a giant bat, with broad wings stretched across a framework. Another uses hinged wings that move through a mechanical system. These drawings show Leonardo’s skill at combining close observation with imaginative engineering. They also reveal that he had not yet solved the central challenge of powered flight: producing enough lift and thrust with the available technology.

Leonardo explored ideas beyond flapping wings. He sketched a device often called an aerial screw, sometimes described as an early concept for a helicopter. Its spiral surface was meant to push against the air as it turned. The design was inventive, but it would have required a powerful, lightweight engine that did not exist in Leonardo’s time.

He also drew a parachute: a pyramid-shaped canopy supported by a wooden frame. Leonardo proposed that a person could use it to descend safely from a height. In 2000, a parachute based on his design was tested in a jump, suggesting that the basic concept could work, although the modern test used contemporary materials and equipment.

Leonardo’s flying machines were never built as practical aircraft during his lifetime. The materials and sources of power available in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries were not sufficient for his ambitious plans. Even so, his work was not simply fantasy. He used observation, drawing, and mechanical reasoning to investigate a difficult scientific problem.

His notebooks are valuable because they show how he developed ideas as well as what he imagined. He often revised sketches, compared different mechanisms, and recorded questions for further study. His flight research reflects a broader Renaissance belief that art, science, and engineering could inform one another.

Modern aircraft do not work like most of Leonardo’s machines. Airplanes use engines and fixed wings, while helicopters rely on powered rotating blades. Yet Leonardo’s careful attention to lift, balance, movement, and the structure of wings helped make flight a subject of systematic investigation. His designs remind us that invention often begins with curiosity, observation, and a willingness to imagine what seems impossible.

The plan was called Lifeboat, though there was no boat.

The sun had begun to swell, and its storms were stripping Earth’s atmosphere one bright ribbon at a time. In a year, the oceans would boil. In two, the planet would be stone.

Humanity’s leaders gathered beneath the Antarctic ice, where the last machines still worked. They had built a seed ship capable of crossing the dark and carrying a new generation to a distant world. Its engines needed more power than any reactor could provide.

The answer was buried under the city.

A chain of fusion cores could push the ship beyond the sun’s reach, but starting them would ignite every reactor on Earth at once. The blast would destroy the planet’s remaining life. It would also give the seed ship enough speed to escape.

There was room for one person aboard.

Mara Venn was a systems engineer, not a soldier or a saint. She had a brother in Nairobi, a mother who no longer recognized her, and a daughter who had died before the storms began. She volunteered because someone had to turn the key.

The others called it a sacrifice. Mara called it arithmetic.

They spent six months preparing embryos, seeds, and libraries. The ship’s intelligence learned every language they could recover. They loaded it with tools, music, maps, and stories of people who would never see another morning.

On the final day, the command room filled with voices from around the world.

Some begged them to stop. Some cursed them. Some simply said goodbye.

Mara listened until the signal began to break apart. Then she shut it off.

She walked alone through the tunnels to the reactor chamber. Each step shook dust from the ceiling. Above her, billions of people waited beneath a red sky.

At the control panel, she hesitated.

The ship’s computer asked if she wanted to record a message for its passengers.

Mara thought of her brother’s laugh, and of her mother calling her by the wrong name. She thought of all the lives the plan would end, and all the lives it might begin.

“Tell them we were here,” she said.

The computer saved her words.

Mara pressed the key.

The planet answered with light.

Across the continents, power stations flared like stars. The ice melted in an instant, and the cities vanished beneath a white horizon. The seed ship tore free of the ground, carrying its sleeping future into the black.

Mara woke beneath a fallen beam.

The chamber was dark except for the red pulse of an emergency lamp. Her suit had sealed around a broken leg. The reactor’s final surge had hurled her into a maintenance vault built to survive the blast.

She crawled to a narrow window.

Earth was still there, but the clouds burned from within. No lights marked the night side. No voices returned through her radio.

The ship was gone.

Mara had planned for one survivor only in the abstract, a variable in a calculation. She had not imagined being the one left behind.

For three days, she rationed water and listened to the silence. On the fourth, the emergency lamp died.

She found a manual crank and coaxed a weak beam from the vault’s old battery. By its light, she wrote the names she could remember on the wall.

There were thousands.

When her hand cramped, she switched to drawing: a house, a tree, a small figure holding another figure’s hand. She did not know whether the ship would ever find a home, or whether its passengers would wake to an empty sky.

Still, she wrote beneath the names, because the words were the only thing she could send after them.

We were afraid.

We chose.

We loved.

Then Mara sat beside the window and watched the last blue fade from Earth.

Formatting a USB flash drive as NTFS prepares it to store files using the NTFS file system. NTFS supports large files, permissions, and features such as file compression. It is commonly used with Windows, though some devices and operating systems may offer limited NTFS support. Formatting erases the files on the selected drive, so copy anything important elsewhere first. Double-check the drive’s capacity and name to avoid erasing the wrong disk.

To format the drive with File Explorer, connect it to your Windows computer. Open File Explorer and select This PC. Find the USB drive in the list, then confirm it is the correct device. Right-click the drive and choose Format. In the File system menu, select NTFS. You can leave Allocation unit size at Default unless you have a specific reason to change it. Enter a name in the Volume label box if you want to identify the drive easily. Quick Format is usually suitable for a healthy drive because it finishes faster. Clear Quick Format to perform a more thorough scan, which takes longer and is not a substitute for secure data erasure. Select Start, read the warning, and confirm only if you are ready to erase the drive. When Windows reports that formatting is complete, select OK and safely eject the USB drive before unplugging it.

You can also format the drive from the command line using DiskPart. Open the Start menu, search for Command Prompt or Windows Terminal, and choose Run as administrator. Type diskpart and press Enter. Type list disk to display connected disks, then identify the USB drive by its size. Select it with select disk N, replacing N with the correct disk number. Be especially careful: choosing the wrong disk can erase another drive. Type clean to remove the selected disk’s partition information. Next, enter create partition primary, then select partition 1. Type format fs=ntfs quick to create a quick NTFS format. Optionally, assign a drive letter by entering assign, then type exit to close DiskPart. If the drive does not appear in File Explorer afterward, open Disk Management and check whether it needs a drive letter. Windows may not offer NTFS in the File Explorer formatting menu for some removable drives; DiskPart can often format them as NTFS instead. For reliable results, wait for the command to finish before disconnecting the drive.

When Titan Jack rolled into the capital, he arrived in a pickup truck with a cracked windshield and a cooler full of sandwiches. The city’s traditional superheroes watched from the courthouse roof, their capes fluttering in the wind. Jack had sold out arenas for years, and his face smiled down from billboards beside the words YOUR NATIONAL CHAMPION. “You call yourselves protectors,” he said into a microphone, “but when did any of you last wait in line at the pharmacy?” The crowd laughed, and even the silver-armored Sentinel looked uncertain. Jack wore no mask, just a star-spangled singlet and a championship belt polished bright enough to catch the sun. He said he knew what it meant to lose a job, miss a rent payment, and keep going anyway. The heroes claimed they fought dangers no ordinary person could face. Jack answered that ordinary people faced danger every day without laser vision or magic shields. Then the city sirens began to scream. A runaway experimental train thundered toward the river bridge, its brakes dead and its passengers trapped inside. The heroes leaped into action, but the Sentinel’s flight faltered beneath the train’s strange magnetic field. Jack raced after it in his pickup, honking as though traffic might politely move. At the bridge, he spotted a maintenance crane and climbed into its cab. His hands shook as he pulled the lever, but he remembered the grip that had won him a hundred matches. The crane’s hook swung down and caught the train’s rear coupling. Jack planted his boots against the cab floor and held the lever with both hands. The hook groaned, and the train slowed by inches. The heroes rallied, bracing the cars together and guiding them onto the safe track. When the last passenger stepped off, the crowd cheered louder than it had at any championship. A little girl asked Jack if he was stronger than the Sentinel. “Not stronger,” he said, handing her his sandwich. “Just used to getting back up.” The Sentinel offered him a place on the city’s hero team. Jack accepted, on the condition that they hold their meetings at the neighborhood diner. Soon the heroes were rescuing people in capes and work boots alike. And whenever someone called Jack a legend, he pointed to the crowd and said, “I’m just one of you—only with better entrance music.”

Graham Jenkins, the younger brother of actor Richard Burton, is being remembered by family and friends ahead of his funeral. Jenkins lived much of his life outside the spotlight that surrounded his famous sibling, but those who knew him say his own story deserves recognition. He was born into the close-knit Jenkins family in Wales, where Burton—born Richard Jenkins—was one of his older brothers. The family’s Welsh roots remained an important part of Burton’s identity throughout his career. While Burton became an internationally celebrated stage and screen star, Jenkins followed a more private path. That contrast did not diminish the bond between the brothers or the place Jenkins held in the family. Relatives and friends are expected to gather at his funeral to pay tribute and share memories. Their recollections are likely to focus on the relationships and everyday moments that defined his life. Jenkins’s connection to Burton may draw public attention, but those close to him remember him first as a brother, relative and friend. Burton often spoke with affection about his upbringing and the family that shaped him. The story of the Jenkins family also reflects the close ties of a community that watched one of its own rise to global fame. Jenkins’s life was not measured by celebrity, but by the people who knew and valued him. As funeral arrangements bring loved ones together, they will celebrate a life lived largely away from public view. His legacy will endure in the memories shared by those closest to him. And, through his place in the family, he remains part of the story of Richard Burton’s Welsh beginnings.

Remote learning has become a common part of education, offering students the convenience of studying from home. However, it also has drawbacks that can affect their focus, practical skills, and social development. Although online classes can be useful, they do not always provide the same learning experience as being in a classroom.

One major problem with remote learning is that students may find it difficult to concentrate. At home, they can be distracted by phones, games, household noises, or family members. Without a teacher nearby, it may be easier to stop paying attention or leave a lesson unfinished. Long hours in front of a screen can also cause tiredness and make it harder to stay engaged. Some students may keep their cameras off and participate very little. As a result, teachers may not notice when they are confused or losing focus.

Remote learning can also limit the development of practical skills. In subjects such as science, art, and technology, students often learn by using equipment and materials directly. Watching a demonstration on a screen is not always as helpful as carrying out an activity in person. Group projects can also be harder when classmates are not in the same room. Students may have fewer chances to practise teamwork, solve problems together, or receive immediate guidance. This can leave them less confident when they later need to use their skills in real situations.

Another drawback is the effect on social development. School gives students regular opportunities to talk, make friends, and learn how to cooperate. Online lessons usually provide fewer informal conversations before and after class. Some students may feel lonely or disconnected from their classmates. They might also find it more difficult to read facial expressions and body language through a screen. These experiences can make it harder to build communication skills and healthy relationships. For younger students in particular, daily interaction with others is an important part of learning how to share and resolve disagreements.

Remote learning does have advantages, and it can be valuable when students cannot attend school in person. Nevertheless, it works best when students have a quiet place to study, reliable technology, and regular support from teachers and families. Schools can also organize practical activities and opportunities for students to interact. Overall, remote learning should not completely replace classroom education. In-person learning helps students stay focused, practise important skills, and develop socially. A balanced approach can combine the flexibility of online lessons with the benefits of learning together at school.

Autonomous vehicles are designed to drive with little or no human control. They use cameras, radar, lidar, and computer software to understand the road and respond to changing conditions. Supporters argue that these systems could reduce crashes caused by human mistakes. However, adopting autonomous vehicles also raises important concerns about safety, attention, and driving skills. These concerns deserve careful attention before the technology becomes widespread.

Safety is the most immediate issue. Self-driving systems can make mistakes when road markings are unclear, sensors are blocked, or weather is poor. They may also struggle with unusual situations, such as a fallen object or a construction worker directing traffic. Human drivers can sometimes understand these unexpected events through experience and judgment. A computer system may instead interpret them incorrectly or respond too slowly. Even a small error can have serious consequences when a vehicle is moving at high speed.

It is also difficult to decide who is responsible after a crash. Responsibility might involve the vehicle owner, the manufacturer, the software developer, or another driver. Clear laws and reliable investigations will be needed to determine what happened. Companies should test their vehicles thoroughly and explain the limits of their systems. Drivers should also understand when they must take control. Without clear expectations, people may trust the technology more than they should.

Attention is another major concern. Some vehicles require a human driver to monitor the road and take over when the system cannot handle a situation. Yet people may become distracted or lose focus when they are not actively steering. They might check a phone, read, or assume the vehicle can manage every problem. Taking control suddenly can be difficult if the driver has not been watching. This gap between relying on automation and being ready to intervene could create danger.

The design of autonomous vehicles should make their abilities and limitations easy to understand. Warnings should be clear, timely, and difficult to ignore. A vehicle should not suggest that it can drive independently if a human must still supervise it. Drivers also need practical training on how to use automated features safely. Such training can help prevent overconfidence and confusion.

There is a further concern that people may lose important driving skills. If a vehicle handles steering, braking, and navigation most of the time, its owner may get less practice. Skills such as judging distance, noticing hazards, and responding quickly can weaken without use. This could make manual driving harder when automation fails or is unavailable. Drivers may also become less familiar with local roads and traffic conditions. Training and regular opportunities to practice could help preserve these abilities.

At the same time, autonomous vehicles may benefit people who cannot drive easily, including some older adults and people with disabilities. They could also make travel more convenient and reduce certain types of human error. These possible benefits should not be dismissed. Instead, they should be weighed against the risks and supported by evidence. Testing should include different roads, weather conditions, and communities, rather than only ideal situations.

Governments, companies, and the public all have roles in making adoption safer. Governments can set standards, require reporting of crashes, and enforce rules for testing and use. Companies can improve their systems and be honest about what the technology can do. Researchers can study whether automated driving actually reduces injuries over time. The public can ask questions and make informed choices about using these vehicles.

Autonomous vehicles could change transportation, but they should not be treated as perfectly safe or fully independent without proof. Safety depends on dependable technology, attentive people, and clear rules. Drivers must know when to trust automation and when to take control. They should also continue to build and maintain their driving skills. A careful approach can help society gain the benefits of autonomous vehicles while reducing the risks.

Exploring Venus may seem strange because its surface is extremely hot and its atmosphere is thick with clouds, but studying this planet could help improve life on Earth. Venus’s clouds and weather can teach scientists more about how atmospheres work and how climate changes over time. By comparing Venus with Earth, researchers may better understand the causes and effects of global warming. Spacecraft designed to survive Venus’s heat and pressure could inspire stronger materials for buildings, vehicles, and protective equipment. New sensors made to explore the planet might also help detect dangerous gases and pollution on Earth. Studying how Venus’s atmosphere traps heat could guide the development of cleaner energy and more efficient ways to use it. Venus missions also encourage advances in robotics, because machines must explore places too dangerous for people. These inventions could be useful in disaster zones, deep oceans, and other difficult environments. Space exploration can also inspire students to study science, technology, engineering, and mathematics. In this way, exploring Venus may reveal not only more about our neighboring planet but also practical ideas that help protect people and life on Earth.

Young activists in Hong Kong are forming political parties to pursue democratic reform and greater self-determination, seeking a lasting role in a political system increasingly shaped by Beijing. The new groups are trying to turn street-level energy into organized campaigns, public debate and, where possible, electoral participation.

Their efforts come amid years of political change in the territory. Hong Kong was promised a high degree of autonomy after its return to Chinese rule in 1997, under a framework that also envisaged an eventual move toward universal suffrage. Many young residents say those commitments have not produced the democratic representation they expected.

The protests of 2014 and 2019 helped bring a new generation of activists into public life. Demonstrators called for broader voting rights and greater accountability, while some also questioned the limits of Hong Kong’s autonomy. The scale of those movements showed the depth of political discontent, but did not secure the reforms protesters sought.

Since then, national security legislation and changes to election rules have sharply narrowed the space for opposition politics. Authorities say the measures are needed to protect stability and national security. Critics argue that they have weakened civil liberties and made it harder for government opponents to organize.

Against that backdrop, young organizers are experimenting with party structures. Some groups focus on local concerns, including housing, education and employment, while linking those issues to demands for political representation. Others emphasize Hong Kong identity and the right of residents to shape the city’s future.

Party formation offers activists a way to build membership, develop policy and coordinate beyond demonstrations. It can also give them a platform to reach residents who do not take part in protests. Organizers hope that sustained community work may help maintain public interest in democratic reform.

But the risks and obstacles are considerable. New parties may face scrutiny from authorities, difficulties finding venues and pressure on members to avoid statements deemed unlawful. The city’s revised electoral system also limits who can run and requires candidates to meet eligibility checks.

Several activists have left Hong Kong, while others have been arrested, prosecuted or withdrawn from public life. Their departures have reduced the pool of experienced organizers and complicated efforts to build stable institutions. Those who remain must weigh the value of visibility against the possibility of legal consequences.

The groups also face a strategic divide over what self-determination should mean. For some, it means greater local control within China’s constitutional framework. For others, it means a more fundamental change in Hong Kong’s political status, a position that carries heightened legal and political risks.

There is no guarantee that party organizing will lead to electoral success or policy change. Yet activists say that building organizations is important even when formal avenues are constrained. They argue that civic participation can preserve political ideas and connect younger residents with one another.

The authorities have repeatedly said Hong Kong’s political system must uphold national security and the principle of “patriots administering Hong Kong.” Officials also point to economic recovery and social stability as priorities. Activists counter that stability without meaningful representation leaves major grievances unresolved.

For now, the emerging parties are small and their influence uncertain. Their ability to attract members, communicate safely and respond to everyday concerns will help determine whether they can endure. Their formation nonetheless signals that some young residents are seeking new ways to pursue political change after years of protest and tightening restrictions.

School sports can be an important part of a student’s education. They help students stay active, learn new skills, and connect with others. However, some schools limit sports participation based on grades or academic performance. While students should be encouraged to do well in class, sports should be open to students of all academic levels. Inclusive eligibility policies give more students a chance to participate. They also recognize that students have different strengths and needs.

One major benefit of inclusive policies is improved physical health. Regular activity can strengthen the body, build coordination, and support overall well-being. Sports can also help students manage stress. A practice or game may give students a positive break from academic pressure. Participating can improve confidence, especially for students who have not always felt successful at school. Being part of a team can also reduce loneliness and help students build friendships.

Sports teach valuable lessons beyond the playing field. Students learn cooperation, communication, and responsibility. They practice setting goals and responding to setbacks. These skills can support their growth in school and in daily life. Teammates may also motivate one another to attend class and keep up with assignments. Coaches can encourage students and help them develop better routines. In this way, participation can support academic growth rather than compete with it.

Inclusive eligibility does not mean schools should ignore academics. Schools can provide tutoring, study periods, and regular check-ins for student athletes. Coaches and teachers can work together to notice when students need extra help. Clear expectations can encourage students to balance practice with schoolwork. If a student is struggling, support may be more helpful than removing an important source of connection and motivation.

Fair policies should also account for differences in students’ circumstances. Some students face learning challenges, family responsibilities, or limited access to academic support. A single grade requirement may not reflect their effort or potential. Schools can set reasonable academic expectations while offering support and ways to remain involved. They can also create different roles, such as team manager or assistant, for students who cannot safely participate in physical play.

Allowing students of all academic levels to take part makes school sports more welcoming. It helps students discover abilities that may not appear in the classroom. Inclusive teams can teach respect for different kinds of strengths. With guidance and support, students can pursue both athletic and academic growth. For these reasons, schools should favor inclusive eligibility policies that give every student a fair opportunity to belong and improve.

Pope Francis has spent his pontificate urging the Catholic Church to become more missionary, merciful and attentive to people on society’s margins. Yet reshaping a global institution with nearly 1.4 billion members has proved a slow and contested undertaking. His efforts have met resistance from traditionalists, frustration among reform advocates and practical limits within the Vatican itself.

Francis, elected in 2013, inherited a Church facing declining participation in parts of Europe, a clergy abuse crisis and scrutiny of its finances and governance. He has called for a “poor Church for the poor” and urged Catholics to avoid becoming inward-looking. His message has also emphasized care for migrants, the environment and people who feel excluded from church life.

Turning those priorities into lasting change is difficult because Catholic communities differ sharply across regions. In some countries, Catholics are pressing for greater roles for women and more open discussion of sexuality. In others, church leaders are focused on religious freedom, poverty, conflict or rapid growth among new congregations. A decision welcomed in one place can provoke anxiety or resistance elsewhere.

Francis has tried to give local churches more room to address their circumstances while preserving unity on core teachings. That approach has drawn criticism from those who fear it could weaken consistency. Other Catholics argue that the Vatican has moved too cautiously and left longstanding questions unresolved.

The debate has been especially visible around the role of women. Francis has appointed women to senior Vatican positions and created opportunities for them to vote in some church gatherings. He has also maintained the Church’s position against ordaining women as priests. Supporters see his appointments as meaningful progress, while advocates for broader reform say they do not alter the underlying structure of authority.

Questions about LGBTQ Catholics have likewise highlighted the tension between pastoral welcome and official doctrine. Francis has urged the Church to treat people with respect and has criticized the exclusion of gay Catholics. His comments and decisions have opened space for discussion in some communities, but have not changed the Church’s teaching on marriage. The result is a mix of hope, uncertainty and disagreement among Catholics worldwide.

The abuse crisis remains one of the most serious tests of the Church’s credibility. Francis has strengthened rules intended to hold bishops accountable and has supported measures to protect children and vulnerable adults. Survivors and advocates, however, say that implementation and transparency remain uneven. They continue to call for independent investigations, public disclosure and consequences for leaders who failed to act.

Reform of Vatican administration presents another challenge. Francis has reorganized offices, revised financial oversight and sought to make the central bureaucracy more accountable. Such changes can be slowed by entrenched practices, competing interests and the complexity of managing institutions across many countries. Financial controversies have also made it harder for the Vatican to persuade skeptics that reform is taking hold.

The Church’s future is shaped not only in Rome but in dioceses, parishes and families across the world. Catholic populations are growing in parts of Africa and Asia, while many communities in Europe and the Americas face declining attendance and fewer priests. A global strategy must respond to these different realities without treating any region as an afterthought. Francis has encouraged local listening, but disagreements over authority and doctrine continue to test that vision.

His emphasis on synodality, or shared discussion and discernment, is intended to bring lay people and clergy into wider conversation. Supporters say the process can make the Church more responsive and strengthen participation. Critics question whether consultation will lead to meaningful decisions, while some worry that it could introduce uncertainty into church teaching. The challenge is to make listening consequential without deepening divisions.

Francis also faces the limits of his own time in office. A pope can set priorities and appoint leaders, but future successors may interpret or revise his initiatives. Lasting reform depends on whether changes become part of ordinary church practice rather than remaining tied to one pontificate. That requires cooperation from bishops, priests and lay Catholics who may not share the same assumptions.

As Francis guides the Church through these disputes, he has repeatedly called for patience, dialogue and compassion. His approach has altered the tone of Catholic debate, even where policy has changed little. Whether that shift will lead to durable institutional reform remains uncertain. The answer will depend on how the Church balances unity with diversity, tradition with adaptation, and authority with accountability in the years ahead.

The United States should replace the Electoral College with a national popular vote for president. Under the current system, each state awards electoral votes based largely on its statewide result. This means a candidate can win the presidency without receiving the most votes nationwide. That outcome can make some voters feel that their ballots count less than others. A national popular vote would give every vote equal weight, regardless of where a person lives. Candidates would also have more reason to campaign across the entire country instead of focusing mainly on a few closely contested states. Critics argue that the Electoral College protects the influence of smaller states. However, a popular vote would not prevent candidates from listening to rural communities or less populous regions. Candidates would still need broad support from different kinds of voters to win. Critics also worry that a national election could lead to disputes over recounts. Clear, nationwide rules for counting ballots could help address that problem. Replacing the system would require a major legal change, so the process could be difficult. Even so, elections should reflect the choice made by the greatest number of voters. For these reasons, the United States should adopt a national popular vote for president.

Teaching Students to Read and Spell Long I Words with Silent E

The long I sound is the vowel sound heard in words such as bike, time, and smile. It is often written with the letter i followed by a consonant and a silent e at the end of the word. This spelling pattern is called i-consonant-e, or the silent-e pattern. The final e is not pronounced, but it often signals that the i says its name. Learning this pattern helps students read new words and spell familiar ones.

Begin by checking that students can hear and say the long I sound. Say a word such as bike, and ask students to listen for the vowel sound. Model how the mouth opens and the voice glides from /ah/ toward /ee/. Students do not need to describe the movement precisely, but they should be able to recognize the sound. Contrast long I with short i, as in bit. Ask students whether they hear the same vowel in bit and bite. This listening practice prepares them to connect sounds with spellings.

Next, introduce the written pattern with a simple example. Write the letters i, k, and e on the board to make bike. Point to each letter as you explain that the i represents the long I sound. The k is a consonant between the vowel and the final e. The e is silent, so it does not add a spoken sound of its own. Explain that the silent e helps the i say its name. Keep the explanation simple and repeat it as students encounter more words.

Use a comparison to make the pattern easier to see. Write kit and kite side by side. Read each word aloud and invite students to notice how adding the final e changes the vowel sound. In kit, the i has its short sound. In kite, the i has its long sound. The final e does not always work in exactly the same way in every English word, so teach this as a useful pattern rather than an unbreakable rule. Students benefit from seeing several examples and noticing what they share.

Choose clear, familiar words for early practice. Useful examples include bike, hike, like, time, dime, line, five, ride, hide, and smile. Read each word aloud, then have students say the long I sound they hear. Ask them to point out the i, the consonant, and the final e. Saying the pattern aloud can help: “The i says its name, and the e is silent.” Avoid introducing too many unfamiliar words at once. A small group of well-chosen words gives students time to understand the pattern.

Teach students a dependable way to decode unfamiliar words. First, have them look through the whole word, including its final letter. Next, ask them to identify the vowel and notice whether a consonant and silent e follow it. Then have them try the long I sound and blend the sounds together. For example, students can look at “slide,” notice the i-consonant-e pattern, and blend the sounds to read the word. If the result does not sound like a known word, encourage students to try another reasonable pronunciation or check the word in context. Decoding is a process of using clues, not simply guessing from the first letter.

Spelling practice should connect sounds to letters. Say a word such as time, and ask students to repeat it slowly. Have them identify the sounds they hear and then choose letters to represent those sounds. Explain that the final e is included even though it has no separate spoken sound. Students can tap or count the sounds in the word, then check that their spelling includes the silent e. This helps them understand why time has four letters but fewer than four spoken sounds.

Use dictation in short, manageable sets. Say one word, use it in a sentence, and repeat it before students write it. Begin with words students have already read, such as ride, pine, and five. After writing, ask students to underline the i and circle the final e. Invite them to explain how the e affects the vowel. Give feedback that identifies the pattern, not just whether the word is right or wrong. For example, you might say, “You heard the long I sound; now check whether the word needs a silent e.”

Word sorts help students compare spellings. Prepare cards with long I silent-e words and short i words, such as ride, rid, kit, kite, and pin. Ask students to sort the cards by vowel sound or spelling pattern. Have them read each word aloud as they place it. They can also sort words by their final consonant, such as bike, time, and line. Sorting encourages students to examine the letters instead of relying only on memory.

Make reading practice active and purposeful. Students can hunt for silent-e words in a short passage, on classroom labels, or in a familiar book. Ask them to record each word and mark the i-consonant-e pattern. Then have them reread the sentence containing the word to check that it makes sense. This connects word-level decoding with fluent reading and understanding. Keep the focus on accurate reading rather than speed.

Games can provide extra practice without replacing direct instruction. In a matching game, students pair a word card with a picture, such as kite or bike. In a word-building activity, they use letter tiles to change kit into kite or rid into ride. Ask them to read each word before and after making the change. A partner can say a word while the other student builds it. Brief, repeated practice is often more useful than a long activity with too many words.

Students may make predictable mistakes as they learn. Some may pronounce the final e, while others may leave it out when spelling. Some may remember the pattern but apply it to a word that does not follow it. Respond calmly by returning to the sounds and letters in the word. Compare the student’s attempt with a known example, such as rid and ride. Explain that English spelling has patterns, but also has exceptions that readers learn over time.

Pay attention to the differences among students. A learner who is unsure of letter sounds may need more practice identifying consonants and vowels before working with the full pattern. A student who can read the words but misspells them may benefit from oral sound practice and dictation. Students learning English may need clear models of how to form the long I sound and opportunities to hear it in familiar words. Use pictures, gestures, and spoken examples to support understanding. Adjust the pace so that students can respond successfully while still encountering new challenges.

Assessment can be brief and informal. Ask students to read a few practiced words and a few new words with the same pattern. Then dictate several words and note whether they include the silent e. Listen for whether students can explain the role of the final e in their own words. A quick check helps you decide whether to review, provide more practice, or introduce a related spelling pattern. Keep records of specific strengths and needs rather than labeling students as simply good or poor readers.

When students are ready, introduce longer words that include the same pattern, such as invite, sunshine, and inside. Help them locate the syllables and identify the long I spelling within each word. Do not assume that success with short words automatically means students can read longer ones. Model how to break a longer word into manageable parts, then blend those parts. Continue to review short examples so the basic pattern stays familiar.

The goal is not merely to memorize a list of words. Students should learn to notice the letters, connect them with sounds, and use the pattern when they meet an unfamiliar word. They should also understand that the silent e is a spelling clue, not a sound to pronounce. Consistent instruction, clear examples, reading, and spelling practice help make this knowledge stronger. With time, students can use the long I silent-e pattern more confidently in both reading and writing.

Renewed anti-government protests swept parts of Egypt as demonstrators accused President Mohamed Morsi of concentrating power and undermining democratic institutions. Clashes broke out between protesters and police in several locations, with reports of stone-throwing, tear gas and injuries. The unrest reflected deepening divisions over Morsi’s rule and the role of the Muslim Brotherhood, which had backed his rise to the presidency. Opposition groups said the government was using its authority to weaken critics and limit public accountability. They also objected to constitutional changes they viewed as rushed and insufficiently inclusive. Morsi’s supporters argued that the measures were needed to stabilize the country and move forward after years of political upheaval. The president and his allies rejected accusations that Egypt was returning to authoritarian rule. Protesters gathered in public squares and near government buildings, while security forces sought to contain the demonstrations. Witnesses described tense confrontations as crowds tried to push past police lines. It was not immediately clear how many people had been injured or detained. Political leaders called for calm, but rival sides continued to trade accusations over responsibility for the violence. The clashes raised concerns that Egypt’s fragile transition could be further destabilized. Analysts warned that continued polarization would make compromise on constitutional and economic issues more difficult. The protests underscored the challenge facing Morsi’s government as it sought to assert authority while answering demands for broader political participation.

William Tecumseh Sherman was a U.S. Army officer whose career included both military service and civilian work. After graduating from West Point in 1840, he served in the army during the Second Seminole War and the Mexican-American War, though he saw little combat in Mexico. He resigned his commission in 1853 and later became a banker in San Francisco, where he worked during California’s Gold Rush-era economic boom. The bank failed amid the financial panic of 1857, and Sherman returned east to pursue other work. When the Civil War began, he rejoined the army and rose quickly through its ranks. He fought at First Bull Run and later commanded Union forces in the Western Theater, including at Shiloh and Vicksburg. In 1864, Sherman led the campaign to capture Atlanta, a major Confederate rail and supply center. After taking the city, he marched his army from Atlanta to Savannah, cutting through Georgia and disrupting Confederate infrastructure. His forces seized supplies, destroyed railways, and lived partly off the land, while also confronting Confederate resistance and causing hardship for civilians. Sherman’s campaigns helped weaken the Confederacy, though historians continue to debate their military necessity and human cost.

When Milo discovered he could make pasta grow, his classmates laughed.
He could stretch one noodle until it was as long as a shoelace.
“Terrifying,” said Tessa, the school’s junior hero.
Milo laughed too, though he kept practicing in secret.
He learned that pasta expanded faster when it was warm.
He learned that different shapes grew in different ways.
And he learned that every noodle snapped eventually.
Then the notorious supervillain Dr. Dread arrived.
He blacked out the city and trapped the mayor inside the clock tower.
His machine fed on electricity, and its spinning gears threatened to crush anyone who came near.
The city’s heroes attacked, but Dread’s metal armor shrugged off every blow.
Milo spotted a narrow vent leading to the machine’s heart.
He poured a bag of dry spaghetti into the opening.
“Is dinner your plan?” Tessa shouted.
Milo touched the noodles and made them expand.
They grew through the vents, curling around gears and clogging tiny pipes.
For a moment, the machine sputtered.
Then Dr. Dread reversed the gears.
The pasta twisted, snapped, and vanished into the furnace.
Milo slumped.
But he had noticed the furnace’s heat rising through the floor.
He asked Tessa to toss him a sack of macaroni.
She did, without asking why.
Milo sent the pasta into the furnace’s cooling vents.
The warm air made the little tubes swell at astonishing speed.
They jammed the fans, sealing the vents shut.
The machine overheated, its lights flashing red.
Dr. Dread tried to escape, but his armor’s magnetic locks clamped tight.
The heroes rushed in and freed the mayor.
By sunrise, the city knew Milo as the hero who stopped Dr. Dread with macaroni.
At school, Tessa apologized for laughing.
Milo grinned and offered her a bowl.
She accepted, carefully, in case it grew.
