The duel began at midnight in the ruins of Saint Orla’s chapel.
Rain tapped the broken roof like impatient fingers.
Mara Vell stood beneath the cracked bell, wand raised.
Across from her, Lord Ashcombe swept his cloak behind him.
“You have come to challenge me,” he said.
“I have,” Mara replied.
“Then prepare to meet your doom.”
“Could you say that again?”
Ashcombe blinked.
“The doom part,” Mara said.
“It sounded a little like you were ordering soup.”
His lip curled.
“You’ll regret mocking me.”
“I already regret the shoes.”
Mara glanced at the mud around her boots.
Ashcombe lifted his wand with theatrical precision.
“En garde!”
“Is that French?”
“It’s dueling.”
“That doesn’t answer my question.”
He fired a bolt of green light.
Mara ducked.
The bolt struck a stone angel and made it sneeze sparks.
“Nice shot,” she said.
“It was a warning.”
“Was the angel warned?”
Ashcombe’s face reddened.
He launched a second spell, which spiraled off and hit the bell.
The bell rang once, loudly.
Somewhere in the graveyard, a dog barked.
Mara lowered her wand.
“Should we wait for the dog to finish?”
“I am not waiting for a dog.”
“Good, because it sounds more confident than you.”
Ashcombe charged.
His cloak snagged on a pew.
He stumbled, recovered, and pretended the move had been intentional.
“Behold,” he said, “the Ashcombe advance.”
“Does it usually involve furniture?”
“It involves fear.”
“I’m mostly feeling concern for the pew.”
He tugged free and pointed his wand again.
“Enough banter.”
“Agreed.”
They both paused.
Mara’s stomach rumbled.
Ashcombe looked down at it.
“Was that your familiar?”
“No, that was dinner asking where it went.”
For one remarkable second, they shared a smile.
Then Ashcombe scowled, apparently remembering he was evil.
“You cannot defeat me with jokes.”
“I wasn’t planning to.”
“Good.”
“Your own spellwork seems to be doing fine.”
Ashcombe’s wand crackled in his hand.
He shook it.
A blue spark popped and singed his sleeve.
“Cheap wand,” he muttered.
“Is that the one you bragged about at the academy?”
“It was a different wand.”
“You said it could split a mountain.”
“It can.”
“Does the mountain have to be very small?”
Ashcombe stepped closer.
“I once held off six duelists at the Winter Ball.”
“Were they dancing?”
“They were armed.”
“Were they also dancing?”
He opened his mouth, then shut it.
Rain dripped through the roof onto his hair.
A lock fell across his forehead.
Mara tried not to laugh.
Ashcombe pushed it back with a dignified sweep.
The lock fell forward again.
“I’m having a difficult evening,” he said.
“That’s fair.”
“I was meant to be terrifying.”
“You have the cloak for it.”
“And the voice?”
“More or less.”
“And the dramatic entrance?”
“Your entrance was excellent.”
“Thank you.”
“You were very menacing until the pew.”
“I knew that.”
The chapel settled around them with a groan.
Ashcombe’s expression changed.
Mara noticed him shifting from foot to foot.
“Are you all right?”
“I’m fine.”
“You look like you’re about to cast something.”
“I am.”
“Is it a spell?”
Ashcombe hesitated.
“It’s a bathroom break.”
Mara lowered her wand completely.
“There’s an old lavatory behind the vestry.”
“I know where it is.”
“Of course you do.”
“Don’t make this strange.”
“I wasn’t the one who announced it during a duel.”
Ashcombe started toward the vestry.
Then he turned back and raised his wand.
“Wait here.”
“Where else would I go?”
“Don’t attack me while I’m gone.”
“I’ll try to resist.”
He hurried through the doorway, cloak flapping behind him.
A moment later, something clattered inside.
“Everything okay?” Mara called.
“My belt caught on a hook.”
“Very fearsome.”
“Be quiet.”
Mara sat on the nearest pew and listened to the rain.
When Ashcombe returned, he looked relieved and a little less villainous.
“Shall we finish this?” he asked.
“Do we have to?”
He considered that.
“Probably not.”
“Good.”
They shook hands beneath the cracked bell.
It rang again, though neither had touched it.
Ashcombe jumped.
Mara laughed.
“Don’t tell anyone,” he said.
“About the duel?”
“About the bell.”
She promised, and they walked out together into the rain.

Overview of Prostate Cancer

Prostate cancer is cancer that begins in the prostate gland. The prostate is a small gland found only in people with a prostate, typically men. It sits below the bladder and in front of the rectum. The gland surrounds part of the urethra, the tube that carries urine out of the body. The prostate produces fluid that helps nourish and transport sperm. Its size and function can change with age. Prostate cancer occurs when cells in the gland grow abnormally and form a tumor. Some prostate cancers grow slowly and may never cause problems during a person’s lifetime. Others grow more quickly or spread to nearby tissues and distant parts of the body. The behavior of prostate cancer varies from person to person. A diagnosis does not automatically mean that immediate treatment is needed. Decisions about testing and treatment depend on the cancer’s features and the person’s health and preferences. This page provides general education, not individual medical advice. A health professional can help interpret personal risks and choices.

How prostate cancer develops

Most prostate cancers are adenocarcinomas. These cancers arise from glandular cells that produce prostate fluid. Less common types include small cell carcinoma and other rare tumors. Prostate cancer often develops in the outer part of the gland. A tumor may be too small to feel or see on routine tests at first. As it grows, it may affect nearby structures. Cancer cells can sometimes enter lymph vessels or blood vessels. They may then travel to lymph nodes, bones, or other organs. Spread to a distant site is called metastasis. Prostate cancer that has spread can still be treated, though it may not be curable. The speed of growth is not the same for every tumor. Some tumors remain confined to the prostate for many years. Others grow or spread more rapidly. Doctors use several findings to estimate how a cancer may behave. These findings include the PSA level, biopsy results, imaging, and the extent of disease. No single test can predict the future with complete certainty.

Symptoms

Early prostate cancer often causes no symptoms. This is one reason that screening decisions can be difficult. Urinary symptoms can occur when an enlarged prostate presses on the urethra. These symptoms can also be caused by benign prostate enlargement, infection, or other conditions. They do not, by themselves, prove that a person has cancer. Possible urinary changes include needing to urinate more often. Some people find that they need to urinate more at night. Others have difficulty starting urination. A weak or interrupted urine stream may occur. Some people feel that the bladder has not emptied completely. Urgency, or a sudden strong need to urinate, is another possible symptom. Pain or burning during urination can have many causes. Blood in the urine should be assessed by a health professional. Blood in semen can also occur for reasons other than cancer. Persistent erectile difficulties may have many possible causes as well. Painful ejaculation is sometimes reported, though it is not a typical early sign. These symptoms are common in conditions that are not cancer. A clinician can assess the cause and recommend appropriate tests.

More advanced prostate cancer can cause symptoms related to spread. Bone pain may occur, particularly in the back, hips, ribs, or pelvis. Persistent pain should be evaluated, especially if it is worsening or unexplained. Cancer affecting the spine can sometimes press on nerves or the spinal cord. New weakness, numbness, or severe back pain needs prompt medical attention. Loss of bladder or bowel control with back pain is an emergency. Advanced disease can also cause fatigue or unintended weight loss. Some people develop swelling in the legs if lymph drainage is blocked. A person with possible prostate cancer symptoms should not delay care because symptoms seem mild. At the same time, having symptoms does not mean cancer is present. Timely evaluation can help identify the cause. Emergency symptoms require urgent care rather than a routine appointment.

Risk factors

Age is one of the strongest risk factors for prostate cancer. The chance of developing it increases as people grow older. Prostate cancer is uncommon in younger adults. Many diagnoses occur after age 65. Family history can increase risk. Risk may be higher when a father, brother, or son has had prostate cancer. The risk may be greater if the relative was diagnosed at a younger age. Having several affected close relatives can also matter. A family history of breast, ovarian, pancreatic, or certain other cancers may suggest an inherited cancer risk. Inherited changes in genes such as BRCA1 or BRCA2 can raise prostate cancer risk. Changes in genes involved in DNA repair, including some mismatch repair genes, may also be relevant. Some people have inherited gene changes without knowing it. Genetic counseling can help assess whether genetic testing may be useful. A genetic test can have implications for relatives as well as the person tested.

Race and ancestry are associated with differences in prostate cancer risk and outcomes. In the United States, Black men are more likely to be diagnosed and are more likely to die from prostate cancer than White men. Differences in access to care, social conditions, and other factors contribute to these outcomes. The reasons are complex and are not fully explained by biology alone. People with African ancestry may benefit from discussing screening earlier than average-risk individuals. Guidance varies, so an individual conversation with a clinician is important. Some populations have lower reported rates, but this does not mean that any individual is free from risk. Other possible risk influences are being studied. Body weight, diet, physical activity, and environmental exposures may affect risk or outcomes, but evidence is not equally strong for all factors. No food or supplement has been proven to prevent prostate cancer. A healthy lifestyle can support overall health even when its effect on prostate cancer risk is uncertain. Avoiding tobacco and maintaining a balanced diet can benefit general well-being.

Risk factors do not determine who will develop cancer. Many people with prostate cancer have no known family history. Some people with several risk factors never develop it. People should not blame themselves for a diagnosis. A clinician can help place personal risk in context. A detailed family history can include the types of cancer relatives had and their ages at diagnosis. This information may guide screening and genetic counseling. Risk assessment should also consider age, overall health, and life expectancy. These factors affect whether screening is likely to provide benefit. Personal preferences matter too. A person may value early detection differently from another person. A shared decision can take these priorities into account.

Screening and early detection

Screening means testing people who do not have symptoms to look for signs of cancer. The main screening test for prostate cancer is a blood test that measures prostate-specific antigen, or PSA. PSA is a protein made by cells in the prostate. A higher PSA level can be associated with cancer. PSA can also rise because of benign enlargement, inflammation, infection, recent procedures, or other causes. Some prostate cancers do not cause a large PSA increase. A PSA result is therefore not a diagnosis. Screening may identify cancers that would never have caused harm. This is called overdiagnosis. Treating an overdiagnosed cancer can cause lasting side effects without improving length or quality of life. Screening can also find a cancer early enough for treatment to prevent serious illness. The balance of possible benefit and harm differs among individuals. For this reason, many professional groups recommend discussing screening rather than testing everyone automatically.

The age to begin a screening discussion depends on personal risk and the guidance being followed. People at average risk often discuss screening in middle age. People at higher risk may consider a discussion earlier. Higher-risk groups can include Black men and people with a close relative diagnosed at a young age. Those with inherited cancer-related gene changes may also need an earlier or more individualized plan. A clinician can explain how current recommendations apply to a particular person. Screening is generally less likely to help when someone has limited life expectancy or serious health problems. This is because any benefit may take many years to appear. A decision not to screen is a valid choice for some people. Choosing screening is also a valid choice after understanding its limitations. The decision can be revisited over time.

A digital rectal examination may be offered as part of an evaluation. During this examination, a clinician gently feels the prostate through the rectum. It can detect some abnormalities, but it cannot find every cancer. It is not a substitute for PSA testing or further assessment when needed. Some screening programs use PSA testing alone. Other approaches combine PSA testing with examination or risk assessment. Screening intervals can vary according to PSA levels and personal risk. A repeat test may be recommended when a result is mildly elevated. Repeating the test can help determine whether the increase persists. A clinician may suggest avoiding activities or conditions that could temporarily affect PSA before retesting. Instructions vary, so people should ask the clinician who ordered the test.

A PSA level does not have one universal cutoff that perfectly separates cancer from noncancer. Age, prostate size, prior results, and other factors may inform interpretation. Some clinicians consider how quickly PSA changes over time. The PSA density, which relates PSA to prostate size, may also be considered. These measures can help guide decisions but are not definitive. A risk calculator may combine age, PSA, family history, and other information. Such tools estimate probability rather than provide certainty. If PSA remains concerning, additional tests may be considered. These may include specialized blood or urine tests. They may help estimate the chance of clinically significant cancer. The usefulness and availability of these tests differ. A clinician can explain whether a particular test is likely to change management.

Diagnosis and staging

A prostate biopsy is usually needed to confirm prostate cancer. During a biopsy, small samples of prostate tissue are collected for examination. The procedure may be guided by ultrasound or magnetic resonance imaging. It can be performed through the rectum or through the skin between the scrotum and anus. The method depends on clinical circumstances and local practice. Biopsy can cause temporary discomfort, blood in urine or semen, or bleeding from the rectum. Infection is a possible complication. Patients should follow instructions about medicines and preparation. They should ask when to seek help after the procedure. A pathologist examines the samples for cancer cells. The report describes the type and grade of cancer.

The Gleason grading system describes how abnormal cancer cells look under a microscope. A pathologist assigns patterns to the most common and next most common cell appearances. These patterns are combined into a Gleason score. The Grade Group system is another way to describe the biopsy grade. Higher grades generally indicate cancer that is more likely to grow or spread. Grade is only one part of the overall assessment. The amount of cancer in the biopsy samples also matters. The number of samples containing cancer may be reported. The percentage of cancer in each sample may be described. Different areas of the prostate can have different grades. A second pathology review may be useful in some cases. Patients can ask for an explanation of unfamiliar terms in the report.

Imaging may help determine the extent of disease. Magnetic resonance imaging, or MRI, can show prostate anatomy and guide biopsy planning. MRI findings do not always prove cancer. Computed tomography, bone scans, or other imaging may be used when spread is suspected. A PET scan using a prostate-specific tracer may be considered in selected cases. The choice depends on PSA, biopsy grade, symptoms, and other factors. Not everyone needs every imaging test. Staging describes how far the cancer has spread. Cancer confined to the prostate is localized disease. Cancer that has grown into nearby structures is locally advanced disease. Cancer that has spread to distant sites is metastatic disease. Staging information helps guide treatment options. It can also help estimate prognosis, though it cannot predict an individual outcome exactly.

Doctors often group prostate cancer by risk. Risk categories may use PSA, Grade Group, tumor stage, and biopsy findings. A low-risk cancer is less likely to grow or spread quickly. Intermediate-risk and high-risk cancers have increasing chances of progression. Risk classifications can differ somewhat among guidelines. The category helps guide whether active surveillance or treatment is appropriate. It also helps determine whether additional treatment, such as radiation with hormone therapy, may be advised. Patients should ask which specific features place their cancer in a category. Understanding the risk group can make treatment discussions clearer.

Treatment options

Treatment depends on the cancer’s stage and risk group. It also depends on age, general health, other medical conditions, and personal goals. Some people choose active surveillance for low-risk cancer. Active surveillance is a structured plan to monitor the cancer closely. It is not the same as ignoring the cancer. Monitoring may include PSA tests, examinations, MRI, and repeat biopsies. The exact schedule varies. Treatment can begin if tests suggest that the cancer is growing or becoming more aggressive. Active surveillance can help avoid or delay treatment side effects. It requires regular follow-up and can cause anxiety for some people. Patients should ask what the monitoring plan involves and what changes would lead to treatment.

Watchful waiting is different from active surveillance. It is generally used when a person’s other health problems or limited life expectancy make curative treatment unlikely to help. Follow-up is usually less intensive. Treatment is directed at symptoms if they develop. Watchful waiting may be appropriate for some people with slow-growing cancer. The choice depends on health, cancer features, and preferences. A clinician can explain how it differs from active surveillance.

Surgery is one option for cancer confined to the prostate or selected nearby areas. The operation is called a radical prostatectomy. It removes the prostate and often some surrounding tissue. Nearby lymph nodes may also be removed in some cases. Surgery can be performed through an open incision or with minimally invasive techniques. Robotic assistance is used in many centers. The best approach depends on the case and the surgeon’s experience. Surgery may be intended to remove all visible cancer. Some people need additional treatment if cancer remains or returns. Recovery time varies. A hospital stay may be required, and a catheter is usually used temporarily. Patients should discuss expected recovery and possible complications before surgery.

Potential side effects of prostate surgery include urinary incontinence and erectile dysfunction. The degree and duration of these problems vary. Some people regain function gradually over months or longer. Nerve-sparing techniques may preserve nerves involved in erections when it is safe to do so. Nerve sparing is not possible or appropriate in every case. Pelvic floor exercises may help improve urinary control. Rehabilitation and medical treatments can support sexual function. Surgery can also affect fertility because the prostate and seminal vesicles contribute fluid to semen. People who may want biological children should discuss fertility preservation before treatment. A care team can explain sperm banking and other options. Patients should ask about the surgeon’s experience and typical outcomes.

Radiation therapy uses high-energy rays or particles to damage cancer cells. It can be used as a primary treatment for localized cancer. Radiation may also be given after surgery if there are signs that cancer remains or returns. External beam radiation is delivered from a machine outside the body. It is usually given over a series of treatments. The number and schedule of sessions vary. Techniques are planned to target the prostate while limiting exposure to nearby tissues. Brachytherapy places radioactive sources in or near the prostate. It may be used alone for selected cancers or combined with external radiation. Not every person is suited to brachytherapy. The choice depends on cancer features and prostate anatomy.

Radiation can cause urinary symptoms such as urgency or discomfort. It may also cause bowel symptoms, including loose stools or rectal irritation. Fatigue can develop during treatment. Erectile function may change gradually over time. Most side effects improve, but some can persist. Rarely, radiation can cause lasting bladder or bowel problems. The care team can offer medicines and strategies to manage symptoms. Patients should report side effects early. Treatment planning can be adjusted in some circumstances. A discussion of likely benefits and risks should occur before treatment begins.

Hormone therapy lowers the effects of testosterone on prostate cancer. Testosterone can encourage many prostate cancers to grow. Hormone therapy may be used with radiation for some higher-risk cancers. It is also a common treatment for cancer that has spread. Medicines can reduce testosterone production or block its effects. Some medicines are given by injection, while others are taken by mouth. In selected cases, surgery to remove the testicles can lower testosterone. Hormone therapy may control cancer for a long time, but cancer can eventually become resistant. This is called castration-resistant prostate cancer. Further treatments are available if that happens.

Hormone therapy can cause hot flashes, reduced sexual desire, erectile difficulties, fatigue, and loss of muscle. It may increase body fat and affect blood sugar or cholesterol. Bone thinning can occur, increasing fracture risk. Mood and memory changes are possible for some people. The effects depend on the medicine and how long it is used. Exercise, adequate nutrition, and medical monitoring can help protect health. Clinicians may assess bone density and cardiovascular risk. Patients should discuss existing heart, bone, or metabolic conditions before starting therapy. Medicines to protect bone health may be considered in some cases.

Chemotherapy uses medicines that kill or slow the growth of cancer cells. It is often considered for advanced prostate cancer, particularly when hormone therapy is no longer controlling the disease. It may also be used earlier in selected situations. Chemotherapy is delivered in cycles, with rest periods between treatments. Side effects depend on the drugs used. Common effects can include fatigue, nausea, hair loss, reduced blood cell counts, and increased infection risk. Not everyone experiences the same effects. Supportive medicines can prevent or reduce many side effects. Patients should promptly report fever or signs of infection during chemotherapy. The oncology team will explain when urgent care is needed.

Other treatments may be available for advanced disease. Targeted medicines act on specific cancer pathways or inherited gene changes. Some people with BRCA-related or other DNA repair changes may benefit from certain treatments. Immunotherapy helps the immune system recognize or attack cancer, but it is useful only for selected cancers. Radiopharmaceutical treatments deliver radiation to cancer cells or bone-related targets. Bone-directed treatments can reduce complications from cancer in the bones. Clinical trials may offer access to new approaches. Eligibility depends on the trial’s requirements. Patients can ask whether a clinical trial is appropriate at any stage of care. Participation is voluntary, and the team should explain possible benefits and risks.

Treatment for metastatic disease often aims to control cancer, extend life, reduce symptoms, and preserve quality of life. A combination of hormone therapy and other medicines may be used. Radiation can relieve pain from a specific bone lesion. Surgery is not commonly used to remove the prostate when cancer is widely metastatic, though treatment plans vary. Regular assessment helps determine whether the treatment is working. PSA may be tracked, but it is not the only measure. Symptoms, examination, and imaging may also be important. A rising PSA does not always mean immediate treatment failure. The care team can interpret results in context. Treatment may be changed if cancer grows or side effects become difficult.

Second opinions can be helpful when facing a complex decision. A second opinion does not mean that a person distrusts the first clinician. It can provide reassurance or introduce additional options. Patients can request copies of test results, imaging, and pathology reports. A multidisciplinary team may include urologists, radiation oncologists, medical oncologists, radiologists, and pathologists. Nurses, pharmacists, and other specialists also contribute to care. The right team depends on the person’s needs. Patients can ask who will coordinate communication among clinicians. Keeping a written list of medicines and questions can make appointments more useful.

Choosing among options

There may be more than one medically reasonable treatment. Each option has different trade-offs. Some treatments aim to cure localized cancer. Others focus on controlling disease and reducing symptoms. A person’s values can help guide the choice. Some people prioritize avoiding urinary side effects. Others place greater importance on preserving sexual function or limiting appointments. Concerns about cancer progression may influence decisions as well. Patients can ask how each option affects daily life. They can ask what might happen if treatment is delayed. They can ask whether treatment can be changed later. They can ask how likely a treatment is to control their particular cancer. They can also ask about the clinician’s experience with each option.

It can help to write down questions before an appointment. Bringing a trusted person may help with listening and note-taking. Patients can ask for information in plain language. They can request an interpreter if needed. They can ask for time to consider a decision unless treatment is urgently needed. A decision aid may help compare options. Reliable information should come from recognized health organizations or the care team. Online anecdotes cannot predict an individual outcome. Treatment decisions should be based on personal medical information and informed preferences. People should tell clinicians about complementary medicines and supplements. Some products can interfere with treatment or testing.

Supportive care and quality of life

Supportive care helps manage symptoms, treatment effects, and emotional or practical challenges. It can begin at diagnosis and continue throughout care. Supportive care is not limited to end-of-life care. Palliative care is a specialized form of supportive care focused on relief of suffering and quality of life. It can be provided alongside cancer treatment. A palliative care team may help with pain, fatigue, nausea, anxiety, and difficult decisions. Early support can improve communication and symptom control. Patients can ask for supportive care even while receiving treatment intended to cure cancer.

Pain management should be tailored to the cause and severity of pain. Medicines, radiation, physical therapy, and other approaches may help. Patients should describe where pain occurs and what makes it better or worse. A pain diary can be useful. Bone pain should be discussed with the care team. Sudden severe pain or new weakness needs prompt assessment. Pain medicines should be taken as directed. Patients should not stop prescribed medicines abruptly without medical advice. The team can help balance pain relief with side effects such as constipation or sleepiness.

Urinary problems can affect comfort and confidence. Pelvic floor muscle training may improve control after surgery. A continence nurse or pelvic floor therapist can teach appropriate exercises. Pads and other products can help during recovery. Persistent urinary leakage deserves medical attention, as treatments are available. Urinary urgency or nighttime urination can sometimes be treated with lifestyle changes or medicine. Blood in urine should be reported. A person should seek urgent care if they cannot urinate. Fluid intake should not be severely restricted without advice. A clinician can help identify whether symptoms come from cancer, treatment, infection, or another condition.

Sexual health is an important part of well-being. Prostate cancer and its treatments can affect erections, desire, orgasm, and ejaculation. These effects can be difficult to discuss, but clinicians are accustomed to addressing them. Treatment options may include medicines, devices, injections, counseling, or other therapies. A sexual health specialist may be helpful. Partners may also need support. Open conversations can reduce misunderstandings and isolation. Intimacy can take forms other than intercourse. Fertility concerns should be discussed before treatment. Support should respect each person’s identity, relationships, and goals.

Emotional responses can include fear, sadness, anger, uncertainty, or relief. These feelings are common and do not mean that someone is coping poorly. Anxiety may increase while waiting for test results. Counseling can help people manage distress and make decisions. Support groups can connect patients with others who understand the experience. Some people prefer individual support or online groups. Family members and caregivers may also need help. Persistent depression, panic, or thoughts of self-harm require prompt professional support. A clinician can connect patients with mental health services. Asking for help is a strength.

Fatigue can result from cancer, treatment, poor sleep, pain, stress, or other health conditions. Gentle physical activity can help some people maintain energy. Activity should be adjusted to current ability and medical advice. Short walks or light strength exercises may be a starting point. Rest breaks can be planned throughout the day. A balanced diet and adequate fluids support general health. Fatigue that is severe or sudden should be discussed with a clinician. Blood tests may identify treatable causes such as anemia. Patients should avoid pushing through symptoms that feel unsafe.

Nutrition should be individualized. A varied diet with vegetables, fruits, whole grains, and appropriate protein supports general health. No specific diet has been shown to cure prostate cancer. Extreme diets can cause harm or interfere with treatment. Patients should consult a dietitian if they have weight loss, poor appetite, or special dietary needs. Supplements can affect medicines or laboratory tests. People should tell their care team about vitamins, herbs, and nonprescription products. Maintaining bone health is especially important for those receiving hormone therapy. Weight-bearing activity, adequate calcium and vitamin D, and medical guidance may help. Supplements should be used based on individual needs rather than assumed benefit.

Exercise can support strength, mood, sleep, and cardiovascular health. People receiving treatment may need to adapt exercise to side effects. A clinician or physical therapist can recommend safe activity. Exercise is not a replacement for cancer treatment. Smoking cessation can improve overall health and may reduce risks associated with surgery or other treatment. Alcohol use should be discussed if it affects health or medicines. Managing blood pressure, cholesterol, and diabetes can also support well-being. Preventive care remains important during cancer treatment. Patients should not delay care for unrelated health problems.

Caregivers can help with transportation, appointments, meals, and emotional support. Their own health and rest matter too. Clear communication about what help is wanted can prevent strain. A social worker can help with practical needs, financial concerns, and community resources. Some cancer centers offer navigation services. Insurance and treatment costs can be difficult to understand. Patients can ask to speak with a financial counselor. Workplace protections and leave options vary by location. Keeping copies of medical records can support care coordination. A designated contact person can help share updates with family, if the patient wishes.

Follow-up and living after treatment

Follow-up care checks for recurrence, monitors side effects, and supports general health. The schedule depends on the treatment and risk group. PSA testing is commonly used after surgery or radiation. After surgery, PSA is usually expected to become very low or undetectable. After radiation, PSA often declines more gradually. The timing and meaning of PSA changes differ between treatments. A single change may not indicate recurrence. Clinicians interpret trends along with symptoms and other findings. Patients should ask what PSA pattern is expected in their situation. They should also ask how often testing is planned.

Cancer can return after treatment, but recurrence does not mean that no options remain. Further treatment may include radiation, hormone therapy, surgery in selected cases, or other medicines. The approach depends on the original treatment, PSA pattern, imaging, and general health. Earlier detection of recurrence may influence options. Not every PSA rise requires immediate treatment. Some people can be monitored before starting another therapy. The care team can explain the likely benefits and risks. Emotional support is important during follow-up, especially when test results are pending.

Long-term effects may continue after treatment ends. Urinary, bowel, sexual, hormonal, and emotional concerns deserve ongoing attention. Rehabilitation can continue beyond the initial recovery period. Patients should tell clinicians about persistent symptoms rather than assuming they must be endured. A survivorship care plan can summarize treatments and follow-up needs. It can also identify which clinician is responsible for different aspects of care. Primary care remains important. Patients should continue age-appropriate health screening and management of other conditions. A healthy lifestyle supports general health, even though it cannot guarantee that cancer will not return.

Common questions

Is prostate cancer always life-threatening? No. Many prostate cancers grow slowly and may never cause serious illness. Some are aggressive and can be life-threatening. The individual risk depends on the cancer’s features and overall health. A clinician can explain the likely behavior of a particular cancer.

Does an enlarged prostate mean cancer? No. Benign prostate enlargement is common with age and is not cancer. It can cause urinary symptoms similar to those from prostate cancer. Testing can help determine the cause. Both conditions can occur in the same person.

Can a normal PSA result rule out cancer? No. A normal or low PSA reduces the likelihood of some cancers but does not rule out every cancer. Symptoms, family history, and other findings still matter. A clinician can advise whether further assessment is appropriate.

Does every prostate cancer need treatment right away? No. Some people with low-risk disease choose active surveillance. Others need treatment because their cancer has a higher risk of growth or spread. The choice should be based on medical findings and personal preferences. Ongoing monitoring is essential when treatment is deferred.

Can prostate cancer be prevented? There is no guaranteed way to prevent it. Many risk factors, including age and inherited traits, cannot be changed. Healthy habits benefit overall health, but they cannot eliminate the risk. Screening and informed care may help identify disease earlier in some people.

When should someone seek medical advice? A person should arrange an appointment for persistent urinary changes, blood in urine or semen, or unexplained pain. A person with a strong family history or inherited risk should discuss screening with a clinician. Sudden inability to urinate needs urgent care. Severe back pain with weakness, numbness, or loss of bladder or bowel control is an emergency.

Key points

Prostate cancer ranges from slow-growing disease to aggressive cancer. Early disease often has no symptoms. Urinary symptoms are common and often have noncancer causes. Age, family history, ancestry, and inherited gene changes can influence risk. PSA screening can find some cancers early, but it can also lead to false alarms and overdiagnosis. Screening decisions should consider individual risk, health, and preferences. Biopsy confirms the diagnosis, while grade and stage help guide care. Options can include active surveillance, surgery, radiation, hormone therapy, chemotherapy, targeted treatment, and other approaches. Supportive care can improve comfort and quality of life at every stage. Patients should ask questions, discuss their goals, and seek care for concerning symptoms.

Opposition is growing to government plans that would require every school in England to become an academy by 2020.

The proposal would end the role of local authorities in directly running schools, transferring responsibility to academy trusts or other approved providers. Ministers say the change is needed to raise standards and give schools greater independence. But teachers, councils and parent groups warn that the timetable is unrealistic and the policy risks removing local accountability.

Under the plans, schools that are not already academies would need to join a trust, either individually or as part of a group. Academies are publicly funded but operate outside local authority control. They have greater freedom over matters including the curriculum, staff pay and the length of the school day.

The government argues that academy status can help schools improve through stronger leadership and collaboration. Supporters also say trusts can share expertise and direct resources where they are most needed. Ministers have presented the 2020 target as part of a broader effort to tackle uneven performance across the country.

Critics say, however, that academy status is not a guarantee of better results. They point to schools that have improved without converting, as well as academy trusts that have struggled. They argue that the quality of leadership and support matters more than a school’s legal structure.

Teacher unions have questioned whether there are enough effective academy trusts to take responsibility for every school. They warn that rapid expansion could stretch the strongest providers and leave weaker schools with limited options. Some also fear that schools may be pushed into arrangements that do not suit their needs.

Local authorities have raised concerns about their diminishing ability to coordinate services. Councils currently help plan school places, support vulnerable pupils and respond when schools face problems. They say losing direct oversight could make it harder to address issues across an area, particularly where several schools are under pressure.

Parents and campaigners have also called for clearer safeguards. They want guarantees that decisions about admissions, exclusions and school closures will remain transparent and open to challenge. Some have raised concerns about the financial oversight of trusts and how public money is spent.

Ministers say academy trusts are subject to inspection and financial rules, and that schools will not be left without support. They have indicated that local authorities will continue to have responsibilities in areas such as safeguarding and special educational needs. The government has not, however, persuaded all critics that these arrangements will provide adequate accountability.

The proposed deadline has become a particular focus of opposition. Critics say converting thousands of schools within a few years would require major administrative work and could divert attention from teaching. They also question whether the government has set out a detailed transition plan for schools that are unwilling or unable to join a suitable trust.

The debate has intensified as education leaders seek more information about how the policy would be implemented. Some headteachers say they are open to academy status but want the choice of a partner trust to reflect local circumstances. Others argue that compulsory conversion risks damaging relationships between schools and their communities.

The government faces pressure to explain how it will measure the policy’s success. Campaigners say progress should be judged by pupil outcomes, support for disadvantaged children and the stability of school provision, rather than by the number of conversions alone. They are also calling for a clear process to address failures within academy trusts.

For now, the academy plan remains a central part of the government’s education agenda, but resistance is mounting. The coming months are likely to bring further debate over whether the 2020 deadline can be met, and whether compulsory conversion is the right route to improving England’s schools.

Subject: CAEM’s 2002 Outlook for Energy Competition, Market Restructuring, and Regulatory Policy

Dear colleagues,

I am writing to summarize CAEM’s outlook for energy competition, market restructuring, and regulatory policy in 2002.
The year is likely to be shaped by the interaction of market design, investment needs, and public expectations.
Energy markets are no longer defined only by questions of supply and demand.
They are also defined by the rules that determine who may compete and how essential infrastructure is operated.
CAEM views 2002 as a year in which those rules will receive close attention.
The experience of recent market changes has made clear that restructuring is neither automatic nor uniform.
Different jurisdictions are moving at different speeds.
Their approaches reflect distinct legal frameworks, resource mixes, and consumer priorities.
The central challenge is to encourage competition while preserving reliability.
That challenge will influence policy debates throughout the year.
It will also affect business planning across the energy sector.
We expect policymakers to focus on whether existing market arrangements are delivering meaningful benefits.
Those benefits include efficient prices, reliable service, and a wider range of choices.
They also include incentives for investment and innovation.
Competition can help achieve these outcomes when markets are designed carefully.
Poorly designed rules can instead create uncertainty and weaken confidence.
For that reason, CAEM believes that market structure deserves continued scrutiny.
Restructuring should be assessed by its results rather than by its label.
A competitive market is not simply a market with more participants.
It requires fair access to essential networks.
It also requires transparent information and consistent rules.
Participants need confidence that decisions will be made impartially.
Consumers need confidence that their interests will not be overlooked.
Regulators need the authority and expertise to oversee changing markets.
In 2002, those requirements will remain central to the policy discussion.
One important question is how quickly competition should expand.
Some markets may be ready for broader retail choice.
Others may need additional preparation before opening to competition.
The timing of reform should reflect local conditions.
It should not be driven solely by a desire to meet an arbitrary timetable.
A measured transition can reduce disruption.
It can also give market participants time to develop effective systems.
At the same time, delays should not become a substitute for progress.
Policymakers will need to explain both the pace and the purpose of reform.
CAEM expects debate over the proper division of responsibilities among market participants.
Generators, utilities, transmission owners, retailers, and regulators all have distinct roles.
Clear responsibilities can reduce conflicts and improve accountability.
Unclear responsibilities can make it difficult to identify the source of problems.
They can also complicate the response to service interruptions or market stress.
Rules should therefore specify obligations in practical terms.
Those rules should be consistent with the structure of each market.
They should also be adaptable as technology and business models evolve.
Market restructuring will require more than changes to statutes or regulations.
It will require functioning institutions and dependable procedures.
It will require accurate metering, billing, and settlement systems.
It will require mechanisms for resolving disputes promptly.
It will require coordination among regional and local authorities.
It will also require communication with customers.
Customers should understand what choices are available to them.
They should be able to compare offers on a clear and consistent basis.
They should know how to obtain assistance when problems arise.
Effective consumer education can support competition.
It can also prevent confusion during a transition.
CAEM expects consumer protection to remain an important part of regulatory policy.
Competition does not eliminate the need for safeguards.
Some customers may have limited options or limited capacity to assess complex offers.
Regulators may need to ensure that essential service remains accessible.
They may also need to address unfair marketing and misleading claims.
Protection should be targeted and practical.
It should not unnecessarily prevent new products or services from reaching the market.
The aim should be to protect consumers while preserving room for innovation.
Pricing is another area likely to draw considerable attention.
Prices communicate information about costs and scarcity.
They can encourage efficient use and timely investment.
But price signals are useful only when market rules support fair and credible outcomes.
Abrupt price movements may raise questions about market performance.
They may also create concern among customers and policymakers.
Regulators will need to distinguish between legitimate changes in market conditions and evidence of dysfunction.
That assessment requires reliable data.
It also requires a careful understanding of how markets operate.
CAEM supports transparent reporting that enables informed oversight.
Transparency should improve accountability without disclosing information that could undermine legitimate competition.
Market monitoring is likely to become more important in 2002.
Monitoring can help identify unusual conduct and emerging operational risks.
It can also provide a factual basis for adjustments to market rules.
Effective monitoring depends on independence and expertise.
It should focus on behavior and outcomes rather than assumptions.
Regulators should be able to respond proportionately when problems are identified.
A predictable enforcement approach can strengthen confidence.
An inconsistent approach can create uncertainty for both established firms and new entrants.
The design of wholesale markets will remain a key concern.
Wholesale arrangements influence the costs faced by retailers and utilities.
They also affect investment decisions and operational choices.
Rules should reward reliable performance.
They should support efficient dispatch and the responsible use of available resources.
They should not create avoidable barriers to participation.
Where possible, market mechanisms should be understandable and verifiable.
Complexity may be unavoidable in some settings.
Even then, the purpose and effects of particular rules should be explained.
CAEM expects capacity and resource adequacy to feature prominently in policy discussions.
Reliable service depends on sufficient resources being available when needed.
Markets must provide credible incentives for maintaining and developing those resources.
Those incentives should reflect both short-term operating needs and longer-term planning.
They should also account for uncertainty in demand and supply.
A sound approach will consider a range of possible conditions.
It will avoid relying on a single forecast as if it were certain.
The growing importance of electricity networks will also shape the outlook.
Transmission constraints can limit competition between regions.
They can also affect reliability and the cost of service.
Network planning should be coordinated with generation and demand expectations.
Investment decisions should be based on transparent criteria.
Access arrangements should be fair to eligible market participants.
Responsibility for planning, construction, and operation should be clearly assigned.
The development of regional markets may offer important advantages.
Broader markets can increase the number of available suppliers.
They can improve the use of diverse resources across connected areas.
They can also make coordination more efficient.
However, regional integration presents practical challenges.
Participants must align operating practices and commercial rules.
Authorities must coordinate across jurisdictional boundaries.
Disagreements over costs and benefits must be addressed openly.
CAEM believes regional cooperation should be pursued with clear objectives.
It should be supported by workable governance arrangements.
It should preserve appropriate oversight and accountability.
Investment will be a major test of market confidence in 2002.
Investors need a stable framework for evaluating long-term commitments.
They also need confidence that rules will not change without good reason.
Regulatory certainty does not mean that policy can never evolve.
It means that changes should be justified, transparent, and implemented predictably.
Frequent or unexplained changes can increase risk.
Higher risk may raise the cost of capital.
That, in turn, can affect the affordability and reliability of energy service.
Policymakers should therefore consider the investment effects of regulatory decisions.
They should also consider the consequences of failing to invest.
The relationship between competition and utility regulation will continue to develop.
Some activities may be exposed to competition.
Other activities may retain the characteristics of regulated services.
Regulators will need to identify where competition is workable.
They will also need to decide how regulated and competitive functions should interact.
Accounting separation and clear rules may help address potential conflicts.
Access terms should be applied consistently.
Cross-subsidies should be visible and appropriately controlled.
These measures can support a fairer environment for new entrants.
They can also help regulators determine whether customers are receiving the expected benefits.
Environmental policy will remain connected to energy market decisions.
Energy choices affect emissions, land use, and resource development.
Market rules can influence the relative attractiveness of different resources.
Regulatory frameworks should make relevant obligations clear.
They should avoid inconsistent requirements that create needless confusion.
Environmental goals and competition can be pursued together.
That requires planning that considers costs, reliability, and environmental effects.
It also requires transparent processes for evaluating trade-offs.
Technological change may add new dimensions to competition.
Advances in generation, storage, metering, and communications can alter how energy is produced and delivered.
They may create new services for customers.
They may also change the role of traditional providers.
Regulation should not assume that current business models will remain unchanged.
At the same time, innovation should meet appropriate safety and reliability standards.
Rules should be sufficiently flexible to accommodate useful developments.
They should not give one category of provider an unwarranted advantage.
CAEM expects policymakers to continue examining the role of demand-side resources.
Efficiency and demand response can help manage costs and system pressures.
They may also provide alternatives to some forms of new supply.
Their contribution should be measured consistently.
Programs should be designed so that customers can participate without unnecessary barriers.
Compensation should reflect verifiable benefits.
Reliable measurement will be important to maintaining confidence in these programs.
The relationship between federal, state, and local policy will also matter.
Energy markets often cross jurisdictional boundaries.
Regulatory responsibilities may therefore overlap.
Coordination can reduce inconsistent requirements.
It can also help authorities share information and expertise.
Such coordination should respect the legal responsibilities of each body.
Clear communication can prevent conflicting signals to the market.
CAEM encourages practical cooperation among agencies and market institutions.
The quality of regulatory process will influence the quality of policy outcomes.
Open consultation can identify implementation problems before rules take effect.
Stakeholders should have a meaningful opportunity to provide evidence.
Regulators should explain how they have considered that evidence.
Decisions should identify their objectives and expected effects.
Where uncertainty remains, agencies can explain how outcomes will be reviewed.
Review provisions can help determine whether a policy is working as intended.
They can also provide a basis for timely correction.
A disciplined process can build confidence even when stakeholders disagree.
CAEM’s outlook is not that every market will follow the same path in 2002.
Local circumstances will continue to shape the appropriate choices.
Some jurisdictions will emphasize market opening.
Others will focus on strengthening oversight or improving infrastructure.
Many will pursue several objectives at once.
The important point is to connect policy choices to measurable outcomes.
Those outcomes should include reliability, affordability, fairness, and efficient investment.
They should also include meaningful opportunities for competition where competition can work.
Policymakers should be cautious about promising immediate savings.
The effects of restructuring can take time to emerge.
Some costs may rise during a transition.
Other costs may be difficult to attribute to a single policy.
Credible evaluation will require appropriate baseline information.
It will also require attention to both short-term and long-term effects.
Clear reporting can help distinguish performance from expectation.
CAEM believes that confidence will be one of the sector’s most valuable resources.
Confidence depends on rules that are understandable and consistently applied.
It depends on institutions that can act independently and competently.
It depends on accurate information and credible market oversight.
It also depends on a genuine commitment to reliable service.
When confidence is weak, investment and participation may suffer.
When confidence is strong, markets are better positioned to adapt.
The outlook for 2002 is therefore one of continued change and close examination.
Competition will expand in some areas and encounter limits in others.
Restructuring will advance, but its form will vary by jurisdiction.
Regulatory policy will need to balance flexibility with accountability.
Reliability will remain a core obligation.
Consumer interests will remain a central concern.
Investment will depend on durable and credible policy frameworks.
CAEM will continue to follow these developments closely.
We will encourage informed discussion of market performance and regulatory choices.
We will support practical approaches that promote fair competition.
We will also emphasize the importance of dependable infrastructure and transparent oversight.
Our objective is not reform for its own sake.
It is an energy sector that serves customers effectively and adapts to changing needs.
The policy decisions made in 2002 can help establish that foundation.
They should be guided by evidence, clear objectives, and open engagement.
We welcome continued discussion with colleagues across the industry.
We also welcome perspectives from regulators, customers, and other stakeholders.
A constructive exchange can help identify shared priorities.
It can also clarify where legitimate differences remain.
We look forward to working together through the year.
Please let us know if you would like to discuss any of these issues in greater detail.
Thank you for your continued attention and participation.
Sincerely,
[Name]
[Title]
CAEM

Scott Walker ended his presidential campaign Monday, withdrawing from the crowded Republican primary after months of declining support. The Wisconsin governor announced his decision at a news conference in Madison. He said he was stepping aside to help clear the way for a more focused debate among Republican candidates. “I encourage other candidates to consider doing the same,” Walker said, urging the party to concentrate on defeating the Democratic nominee.

Walker entered the race with high expectations. His victories in Wisconsin, including a 2012 recall election, had made him a prominent figure among conservatives. Early polls also placed him near the top of the Republican field. But his standing fell sharply as the campaign went on.

The Republican contest featured an unusually large group of candidates, competing for attention, donors and support. Walker struggled to distinguish himself in debates and to maintain momentum in a race increasingly shaped by better-funded rivals. His campaign also faced questions about its strategy and ability to build on its early promise.

The decision marks a sudden end to a campaign that had once been viewed as a serious bid for the nomination. Walker said he would return to Wisconsin and continue his work as governor. He did not endorse another candidate.

His departure is likely to reshape the Republican race, though it remains unclear where his supporters will go. Several candidates are competing for voters who favor conservative policies and experience in state government. Campaigns are expected to move quickly to attract Walker’s donors and supporters.

Walker’s exit also underscores how quickly fortunes can change in a primary campaign. A strong start did not translate into lasting support as the field grew more competitive. The remaining candidates now face pressure to make their case to voters before the first nominating contests.
