Sleep and Thinking in Later Life

Sleep is essential for attention, memory, reasoning, and emotional well-being. During sleep, the brain processes information and supports learning and memory. Sleep also helps regulate mood and the body’s daily rhythms.

The amount of sleep a person needs varies, but most adults do best with about seven to nine hours in each 24-hour period. Some older adults sleep a little less at night or wake more often, yet they still need enough total rest to feel alert and function well. Individual needs differ, so changes in sleep should be considered alongside a person’s health, routine, and daytime functioning.

Too little sleep can make it harder to concentrate, remember new information, make decisions, and respond quickly. A person may become more irritable or feel less motivated. These effects can increase the chance of mistakes and falls, especially when someone is already unwell or taking medicines that cause drowsiness. Repeatedly poor sleep may also worsen existing difficulties with thinking and mood.

Longer sleep is not always better. Spending much more time asleep than usual, or feeling sleepy despite adequate time in bed, can be a sign of poor-quality sleep, illness, medication effects, or another concern. Sleep duration alone does not explain cognitive performance; sleep quality, health, activity, and individual circumstances matter too. New or persistent changes in sleep or thinking deserve attention rather than assumptions about aging.

In long-term care, staff and families can help by learning each resident’s usual sleep pattern and preferences. A calm, predictable bedtime routine can support rest. Keeping a regular schedule for waking and going to bed helps maintain the body’s internal clock. Daytime exposure to natural light and suitable physical activity can also promote nighttime sleep.

A comfortable sleep environment matters. Where possible, reduce noise and bright light at night, keep the room at a comfortable temperature, and make sure bedding and clothing are comfortable. Staff should respond promptly to pain, toileting needs, hunger, thirst, or anxiety that may interrupt sleep. Residents should have opportunities to use the bathroom safely before bed and should not be restricted from fluids without clinical guidance.

Long daytime naps can make it harder to sleep at night, although brief naps may help some residents feel refreshed. Encourage daytime engagement and avoid unnecessary overnight interruptions when it is safe to do so. Care teams should coordinate care to reduce disturbances while still meeting medical and safety needs. Caffeine late in the day and nicotine can interfere with sleep for some people.

Medication can affect sleepiness, alertness, and thinking. Residents and caregivers should not stop or change medicines without a clinician’s advice. A clinician can review medicines and look for causes such as pain, depression, sleep apnea, restless legs, infection, or other health problems. Snoring with pauses in breathing, frequent waking, or severe daytime sleepiness should be discussed with a healthcare professional.

Sleep needs are personal, and care should respect each resident’s choices, culture, and medical needs. Keeping a simple record of bedtime, waking, naps, and daytime alertness may help identify patterns. Avoid using sedatives as a routine solution unless a qualified clinician recommends them and monitors their effects. A consistent, supportive approach can improve comfort, protect cognitive function, and promote quality of life in long-term care.

During World War II, many people found ways to help beyond the battlefield. One young man joined a wartime livestock voyage that carried animals overseas to people in need. His work was demanding, but it also led him on remarkable adventures.

Before each journey, the crew prepared the animals for the long trip. They made sure there was enough feed and water and that the pens were safe. The young man helped care for the livestock every day. He cleaned their stalls, checked on them, and tried to keep them calm.

The sea could be rough, and storms sometimes made the ship roll from side to side. Caring for animals in such conditions took patience and courage. The crew also had to work together to keep everyone safe. When the ship reached port, the livestock were unloaded and sent to communities affected by the war.

For those communities, the animals could provide food, milk, or help with farming. The voyage therefore carried more than livestock: it carried hope and practical support. The young man saw how much people appreciated the help. He learned that service could take many forms, even far from the front lines.

His journeys introduced him to unfamiliar places and people. They also taught him responsibility, teamwork, and compassion. Although the work was tiring and sometimes dangerous, he understood why it mattered. His wartime voyages showed how courage and kindness could make a difference during difficult times.

The traveler woke beneath a sky the color of a dead monitor, clutching a map that changed whenever he blinked. A sign pointed toward Home, but its arrow looped back to a roadside motel called Internet Explorer. Inside, the clerk handed him a dial-up modem and said the phone line was the only road out.

He plugged it in, and the modem screamed for what felt like a century. At last, a portal opened onto a Windows 95 desktop, where every folder was named “New Folder.” He clicked one, and a paperclip appeared to ask what he was trying to do.

“Escape,” he said, but the paperclip offered to format his journey instead. A blue screen swallowed the room, then spat him onto a dusty highway beneath a Windows XP hill. Each mile brought a popup warning that his free trial of life had expired.

He tried to close them, but every X opened two more. In a chat room, strangers typed “A/S/L?” and vanished before he could answer. His map loaded one pixel at a time, always showing him standing at the same motel.

A browser toolbar sprouted across his arms, each button leading to another abandoned website. He found a download labeled “Way Home,” but it stalled at ninety-nine percent. While he waited, the sun set, rose, and set again behind a progress bar.

Then the modem began its terrible song, and the motel clerk returned with a fresh password. The traveler entered it, only to discover that it had expired in 1998. He wept, and the paperclip popped up to suggest a cheerful font.

At last he shut his eyes and imagined a quiet road with no loading icon. When he opened them, the desktop had restarted. The sign still pointed toward Home, and its arrow still looped back.

Using a mobile phone behind the wheel is one of the most dangerous habits a driver can develop. Many people believe they can safely glance at a screen while driving, but even a brief distraction can have serious consequences. A car can travel a long distance in just a few seconds. During that time, a distracted driver may miss a traffic light, a pedestrian, or a sudden change in the road.

Phones can distract drivers in several ways. Reading a message takes their eyes off the road. Typing or searching for a contact takes their hands off the wheel. Even a hands-free call can take attention away from driving. When drivers focus on a conversation, they may react more slowly to hazards.

The danger affects more than the person using the phone. Passengers, other drivers, cyclists, and pedestrians can all be injured in a crash. Young people may be especially at risk because they often use phones frequently and may have less driving experience. However, drivers of every age can be distracted.

Some people use phones because they want to answer quickly or avoid missing important news. In most situations, a message or call can wait until the car is safely parked. Drivers can silence notifications, put their phones out of reach, or ask a passenger to handle urgent calls. These simple choices make it easier to concentrate.

Governments and communities also have a role in preventing phone-related crashes. Clear laws and fair enforcement can discourage drivers from using handheld phones. Schools and families can teach young drivers about the risks. Public campaigns can remind everyone that no message is worth a life.

Using a mobile phone behind the wheel may seem like a small mistake, but it can change lives forever. Safe driving requires attention, patience, and responsibility. By putting our phones away, we protect ourselves and the people around us. A few minutes of waiting is a small price to pay for everyone’s safety.

Schools should require students to participate in community service because it helps them understand the needs of others. Volunteering can teach students kindness, responsibility, and teamwork. It also gives them a chance to improve their neighborhoods in practical ways. For example, students might help at food banks, clean up parks, or read with younger children. These activities can connect classroom learning to real life. Some people argue that required service takes time away from schoolwork and personal interests. This concern is important, especially for students who already have busy schedules. Schools can address it by offering flexible activities and a reasonable number of service hours. Students should also be allowed to choose projects that match their interests. Overall, community service should be a school requirement because it benefits both students and the communities they serve.

The United States should replace the Electoral College with a direct popular vote for president. The current system was created in a very different time, when communication across the country was slow and many people were excluded from voting. Today, citizens can follow campaigns and elections nationwide, so choosing a president through the national vote is both possible and fair. A direct vote would make every person’s ballot count equally, no matter where they live. It would also make the outcome easier to understand and strengthen the principle that the people choose their leaders.

One major problem with the Electoral College is that votes do not have equal influence. Most states award all their electoral votes to the candidate who wins the state, even if the margin is very small. As a result, a candidate can win by a narrow margin and receive every electoral vote from that state. Meanwhile, votes for the losing candidate do not help determine how the state’s electors are awarded. This winner-take-all approach makes millions of ballots less influential. In a direct election, each vote would contribute to the national total, regardless of a voter’s state.

The Electoral College can also produce a president who did not receive the most votes nationwide. This has happened in several U.S. elections, including those of 2000 and 2016. Such outcomes can leave voters feeling that the system did not reflect the country’s choice. A direct popular vote would ensure that the candidate with the most votes wins, eliminating this possibility. It would also make the result more intuitive to the public. In a democracy, it is reasonable to expect that the person who receives the most votes becomes the winner.

The current system also shapes how candidates campaign. Because many states are reliably Republican or Democratic, campaigns often focus most of their time and money on a small number of competitive states. Voters in states considered safe may receive little attention from candidates. A direct national election could encourage candidates to seek support across the entire country. They might visit large cities, small towns, and communities that are currently overlooked. Candidates would have a reason to persuade voters everywhere, because every additional vote could matter.

Some people argue that the Electoral College protects the interests of less populous states. They worry that candidates would focus only on large cities and densely populated areas in a national election. This concern deserves consideration, since communities have different needs and priorities. However, people in small states would still have the same individual voting power as people in large states under a direct vote. Candidates would also need support from many different communities to build a broad national coalition. Smaller states could remain important through their local concerns, even without extra influence in the presidential tally.

Another argument for keeping the Electoral College is that it encourages candidates to build support across different parts of the country. Supporters believe this helps preserve national unity. Yet the current system does not guarantee that candidates will appeal to the whole country. Instead, it can reward campaigns that concentrate heavily on a few competitive states. A direct vote could encourage candidates to reach a wider range of voters, including those who live outside battleground states. National unity is more likely when citizens believe their votes matter equally.

Changing to a direct popular vote would require careful planning. The Constitution would need to be amended, or states would need to adopt a legally sound agreement that awards their electors to the national popular vote winner. Any new system should include clear rules for recounts, vote certification, and resolving disputes. States should also improve access to secure and reliable voting. These steps would take time and cooperation, but the difficulty of reform does not mean reform is unnecessary. A fairer system is worth serious effort.

A direct popular vote would not solve every problem in American politics. Campaigns could still spread misleading claims, and candidates would still need to earn public trust. Close elections might still lead to recounts and legal challenges. However, these problems exist under the Electoral College too. The country can address them through transparent procedures and strong election protections. The basic principle should remain simple: every citizen’s vote should count equally.

The Electoral College is an old system with serious weaknesses. It gives some voters more influence than others and can separate the winner from the national popular vote. It also encourages campaigns to focus on a limited number of states. Replacing it with a direct popular vote would make presidential elections fairer and easier to understand. With careful safeguards, the United States can choose its president through a system that reflects the equal votes of its citizens.

They brought Mara to the cathedral at dusk, wrists bound in silver wire.
The city called her a rebel because she had refused to kneel.
The priests called her wicked because she had asked why their granaries were full while children starved.
Above her, painted saints watched with clean, golden eyes.
“Confess,” said the High Prelate, “and we will forgive you.”
Mara looked at the crowd beyond the iron doors.
“Forgive me for feeding them?” she asked.
A murmur rose, then died beneath the bells.
The Prelate lifted his jeweled staff and named obedience holy.
From the rafters came a laugh, low as thunder under the earth.
Every candle guttered.
Mara felt the wire loosen, though no hand had touched it.
“Do not mistake me for your saint,” she told the crowd.
“I have come to make your masters afraid.”
The doors burst open, and hungry families poured into the nave.
The guards raised their spears, but the painted saints began to weep black oil.
Mara walked past the altar, carrying no weapon but the names of the dead.
The High Prelate called her a monster.
“Perhaps,” she said, “monsters are what your prayers have made.”
Then she vanished into the storm, and the people followed her.
Behind them, the cathedral bells rang on, though no one remained to pull the ropes.

Eli had been an actor for six years and a waiter for seven. When he didn’t get a part, he blamed his face, his voice, or the director’s cousin. Tonight, he decided to blame the story itself.

He rented a black-box theater and wrote a one-man play about an actor writing a one-man play. The character, also named Eli, would complain about auditions, then turn to the audience and demand proof they were real. If the audience stayed silent, he would accuse them of being characters, too.

At rehearsal, the empty seats seemed to lean toward him. Eli took it as a good sign. He added a final trick: the actor would ask the audience to raise their hands, and the audience in the story would obey.

On opening night, twenty-three people sat beneath the work lights. Eli stepped into the spotlight and began. He told them about the waiter who wanted to be seen, and the actor who feared that being seen was all he could do.

Then he reached the final scene. “If you’re real,” he said, “raise your hands.”

No one moved.

Eli smiled, as if this were exactly what he’d expected. “You see? They’re only written to watch me.”

In the second row, a woman slowly lifted her hand. The others followed, one by one, until every arm stood raised.

Eli forgot his next line. The woman in the second row looked frightened, though he hadn’t written that. Then she said, “Please don’t make us do that again.”

The words weren’t in the script. Eli looked down at his pages, and the ink shifted beneath his eyes. A new sentence appeared: Eli asks the audience why they obeyed.

He dropped the pages. The audience lowered their hands.

“Why did you?” he asked.

“We thought you wanted us to,” the woman replied.

Eli’s skin prickled. He had written that answer, he realized—or had he written it because she had said it?

He tried an experiment. “Stand up,” he whispered.

Every person rose, including the woman, who stared at him with tears in her eyes. Eli shouted for them to sit. They sat.

At the back of the theater, a door opened onto a street that had not been there before. Beyond it, people hurried beneath a purple sky, each carrying a folded program.

Eli saw his own name printed on every cover. Beneath it, the title read: The Actor Who Saw His Audience.

He turned to the woman. “Are you real?”

She glanced at the stage, then at him. “Does it matter if you’re the one holding the pen?”

Eli looked at his hands. A pen rested between his fingers, though he had never brought one onstage.

The audience leaned forward. For the first time in his life, Eli had their complete attention.

He could write himself a standing ovation. Instead, he wrote: Eli asks the audience what they want.

The woman lowered her hand, then reached toward the page. The ink trembled as if it were listening.

“We want you to stop deciding for us,” she said.

Eli set the pen down. Around him, the theater doors opened, and the people filed out into the impossible street.

He watched until the last one vanished. Then, in the silence, someone in the empty seats began to clap.

Birth order is the position a child holds among siblings, such as oldest, middle, youngest, or only child. Many people wonder whether this position shapes intelligence, ambition, or personality. Research suggests birth order may be linked to some differences, but it does not determine who a child will become. Family relationships, parenting, culture, resources, and a child’s temperament also matter.

Some studies have found a small average advantage in IQ scores for firstborn children. One possible explanation is that older siblings may spend time teaching younger ones, which can reinforce what they have learned. Firstborns may also receive more focused attention from parents during their early years. However, these average differences are modest and do not predict an individual child’s abilities.

Other research has found little or no meaningful connection between birth order and intelligence. Results can vary depending on how studies measure intelligence and account for family size or economic circumstances. A child’s learning opportunities, health, education, and support are generally more important influences. Birth order should not be used to label a child as more or less intelligent.

Birth order may also relate to ambitions and interests, though the evidence is mixed. Firstborn children are sometimes described as responsible, organized, or achievement-oriented. These traits may develop when parents entrust older children with tasks or expect them to set an example. But many firstborns do not fit this pattern, and many younger siblings are highly ambitious.

Middle children may have experience negotiating, sharing attention, and finding a role among siblings. Some may become skilled at cooperation or compromise. Others may feel overlooked, especially if family routines leave them with less individual attention. These experiences depend on how a family works, not simply on being born in the middle.

Youngest children may benefit from watching older siblings try new activities or make mistakes. They may have more freedom as parents become more experienced, or they may receive extra help from family members. In some households, younger children are encouraged to be playful or adventurous. These are possibilities, not rules.

Only children grow up without siblings at home, but they are not necessarily lonely or socially awkward. They may have close relationships with adults and frequent opportunities for focused attention. They can also build social skills through friendships, school, and community activities. Their development varies just as much as that of children with siblings.

Birth order can influence family roles and expectations. Parents may treat their first child differently from later children because their own experience and circumstances change over time. Siblings may also compare themselves with one another or compete for attention. Such dynamics can shape confidence and behavior, but they are not fixed by birth order.

Family size and age gaps matter, too. A child with several much older siblings may have a different experience from one whose siblings are close in age. Changes such as divorce, blended families, or a sibling’s illness can also affect family roles. These details make simple birth-order predictions unreliable.

Researchers sometimes find patterns across large groups, but group averages cannot tell us exactly what will happen to one child. Labels like “the responsible oldest” or “the spoiled youngest” can become self-fulfilling if adults treat children according to them. It is more useful to notice each child’s individual strengths, needs, and interests. Encourage effort and curiosity without comparing siblings.

In short, birth order may shape some experiences, but it is only one small part of development. It does not set a child’s intelligence, ambitions, or future success. Warm relationships, fair opportunities, and support for each child’s individuality matter far more.

A man with Parkinson’s disease is urging Scotland’s Crown Office to make its guidance on assisted suicide clearer, arguing that uncertainty leaves vulnerable people and their families unsure where they stand.

The appeal comes as the Crown Office and Procurator Fiscal Service (COPFS) reviews its policy on how prosecutors decide whether to pursue cases involving someone who helps another person travel abroad to end their life.

The man, whose identity has not been provided, says people affected by progressive illness need greater clarity about what support relatives may lawfully offer.

Scotland does not have a specific offence of assisted suicide, but helping another person to take their own life may amount to a crime, depending on the circumstances.

Prosecutors assess each case individually, considering factors such as the helper’s intentions, the person’s wishes and whether pressure or exploitation was involved.

The existing guidance sets out public-interest factors that may weigh for or against prosecution.

Campaigners and people living with serious illness say, however, that the wording can be difficult to understand and does not always answer practical questions.

The Parkinson’s patient says that uncertainty can compound the fear and distress caused by a condition that affects movement, speech and independence.

He wants the rules to explain more plainly how prosecutors distinguish compassionate support from criminal assistance.

That could include clearer information about accompanying someone abroad, discussing end-of-life choices and helping with travel arrangements.

The request does not amount to a call for assisted suicide to be legalised, but for people to understand the consequences of their actions under current law.

The issue is especially sensitive because Parkinson’s affects people differently, and symptoms and needs can change over time.

Some people with the condition retain decision-making capacity, while others may experience cognitive changes as the disease progresses.

The COPFS has said its review is intended to ensure the policy remains clear and appropriate.

Any revised guidance would not change the law, but would explain how prosecutors apply it when deciding whether a case should go to court.

Supporters of reform say clearer rules could reduce anxiety for families making decisions in difficult circumstances.

Those opposed to assisted suicide warn that any change must protect people who may feel pressured because of disability, illness or dependence on others.

Disability rights groups have also called for safeguards and meaningful consultation with people living with long-term conditions.

The patient’s appeal highlights the challenge facing policymakers: recognising individual choice while guarding against coercion and abuse.

Scottish ministers have previously said changes to the law are a matter for Parliament, while prosecution decisions remain the responsibility of the COPFS.

The review is expected to attract views from legal experts, health professionals, campaigners and members of the public.

For the man, the central issue is whether people facing a life-limiting condition can get a straightforward explanation of what the law permits and what it forbids.

Lord Wigley has proposed an independent process to assess whether police forces receive enough funding to meet their operational needs. The proposal would move decisions away from relying solely on existing funding arrangements and give forces a clearer way to explain the resources they require. Lord Wigley said policing needs vary across communities, making it important to account for local pressures and responsibilities. An independent assessment could examine factors such as population, crime levels, geography and the demands placed on officers. It could also compare forces’ workloads with the staff, equipment and other resources available to them. Supporters say a transparent process would help identify gaps and make funding decisions easier to scrutinise. They argue that forces should be able to plan with greater confidence when budgets reflect the work they are expected to do. The proposal comes amid continuing debate over how police funding should be distributed and whether current systems adequately capture local needs. Any new process would need clear criteria and access to reliable information from forces and communities. It would also have to clarify how its findings would influence government funding decisions. The proposal does not, by itself, set out how much additional money forces might receive. Further discussion would be needed to determine how the independent process could be established and put into practice.

Avocado prices are climbing as tight supplies collide with rapidly growing demand in markets around the world. Shoppers are seeing higher costs at grocery stores, while restaurants and food businesses are adjusting menus to manage the added expense.

The squeeze reflects a mix of production and trade pressures rather than a single shortage. Harvests can be disrupted by drought, heat, heavy rain and other unpredictable weather, all of which affect yields and fruit quality. In some growing regions, water scarcity and rising costs for labor, fertilizer and transport are also adding to growers’ expenses.

Mexico, the world’s largest avocado producer, remains a major supplier to the United States and other markets. Changes in harvest timing, export volumes or logistics there can quickly influence prices abroad. Other producers, including Peru, Chile, Colombia and Kenya, are expanding exports, but their seasons and available volumes vary.

At the same time, global appetite for avocados has continued to grow. The fruit has become a staple in restaurants and home kitchens, valued for its versatility and association with healthy eating. Demand has risen in Europe and Asia as well as in established markets such as the United States.

That popularity has encouraged investment in new orchards, but avocado trees take several years to produce substantial crops. As a result, new planting cannot immediately offset a poor harvest or a sudden surge in demand. Growers also face long-term uncertainty over water availability and changing climate conditions.

Importers say prices can shift sharply from week to week as shipments arrive and retailers compete for limited supplies. Higher wholesale costs do not always pass directly to consumers, but prolonged shortages tend to put pressure on supermarket prices. Smaller fruit and promotional discounts may become less common during peak periods.

Restaurants are responding by raising prices, reducing portion sizes or offering alternatives to avocado-heavy dishes. Some consumers are buying less often or choosing other spreads and ingredients. For growers, however, higher market prices do not necessarily translate into greater profits when production and shipping costs are also elevated.

Analysts say the outlook will depend on upcoming harvests, weather and the pace of demand. A stronger crop could ease prices, though supply disruptions may continue to cause volatility. In the longer term, sustainable water management and investment in diverse growing regions will be important to keeping the market supplied.

For now, buyers may need to adapt to prices that remain elevated compared with recent seasons. The avocado boom has created a large global market, but it has also exposed how vulnerable that market can be to weather, logistics and shifts in consumer demand.

Building student confidence in narrative writing through classroom sharing and constructive peer feedback

Narrative writing helps students turn experiences, observations, and imagined events into meaningful stories. Yet sharing a draft can feel risky, especially when students worry that their work will be judged. Teachers can build confidence by making the classroom a supportive community where every writer’s voice matters. The goal is not to make every story perfect, but to help each student grow as a storyteller.

Begin by establishing clear expectations for how classmates respond to one another’s writing. Explain that feedback should be kind, specific, and focused on helping the writer achieve their purpose. Students can practice listening without interrupting and asking questions with genuine curiosity. These routines make sharing feel safer and more predictable.

Offer several ways for students to share their work. They might read aloud to a partner, share a short passage with a small group, or display a draft for classmates to read quietly. Allowing students to choose can reduce pressure and increase their sense of control. Students who are not ready to share publicly can begin with a trusted partner.

Model constructive feedback before students try it on their own. Read a sample story and show how to name a strength, ask a question, and offer one helpful suggestion. For example, a classmate might say, “I could picture the setting clearly,” or, “What was your character feeling at this moment?” Such comments respond to the story rather than judging the writer.

A simple feedback structure can help students know what to say. Invite them to identify one detail they enjoyed, one part they wanted to understand better, and one question for the writer. Encourage feedback that points to specific words or moments in the draft. “The description of the storm made me feel tense” is more useful than “I liked it.”

Writers should also learn that feedback is information, not an order. They can decide which suggestions fit their intentions and politely set aside others. After listening, students might explain what they plan to revise and why. This reflection helps them take ownership of their writing.

Teachers can strengthen confidence by noticing effort, risk-taking, and improvement. Praise a student for adding dialogue, trying a new point of view, or revising a confusing section. Avoid comparing students or treating one writing style as the only successful one. Stories can be funny, quiet, adventurous, realistic, or imaginative.

Sharing should happen regularly, not only when a story is finished. Brief opportunities to share a promising sentence or an early idea show that writing develops through stages. They also help students see revision as a normal part of the process. A draft is not a final performance; it is a step toward a stronger story.

To keep peer feedback balanced, set a clear focus for each session. One day, classmates might listen for vivid settings; another day, they might notice how characters respond to challenges. A narrow focus makes feedback manageable and helps writers avoid feeling overwhelmed. Teachers can use sentence starters to support students who are unsure how to respond.

When students share and respond with care, they learn that stories connect people. Writers gain fresh ideas, while listeners practice empathy and close attention. Over time, supportive feedback can help students take creative risks and trust their own choices. A classroom that celebrates progress gives every student a reason to keep writing.

After World War II, many people in Europe faced hunger, poverty, and the loss of their homes and farms. In response, aid organizations and governments arranged for livestock to be transported overseas to help rebuild communities. Ships carried animals such as cattle, sheep, and horses across long distances. These journeys were difficult because the vessels had to provide enough food, water, and space for the animals. Crews worked for many hours to feed them, clean their stalls, and check for signs of illness or injury. Rough seas and crowded conditions could make the animals frightened and uncomfortable. Transporting livestock also required careful planning, since delays could threaten their health. Despite the challenges, the animals offered more than immediate food. Cows could provide milk, while breeding animals helped families build herds and restore their livelihoods. Horses and other working animals could assist with farming and carrying supplies. Their arrival gave many communities a practical way to become more self-sufficient. The work depended on the dedication of sailors, veterinarians, organizers, and volunteers. Their efforts showed that humanitarian aid could include tools for long-term recovery, not just emergency relief. Transporting livestock overseas was demanding, but it helped bring hope and a fresh start to people rebuilding their lives after the war.

Every morning, the people of Reedbank gathered beside the river with a petition.
They asked the council to recognize their neighborhood and repair its collapsing homes.
For generations, their families had lived there, though the city maps left Reedbank blank.
They carried no weapons, only folders of signatures and cups of tea.
At first, the council promised to listen.
Then meetings were postponed, letters went unanswered, and officials stopped meeting their eyes.
A newspaper called the residents “uncooperative” after they questioned a proposed relocation.
The label traveled farther than their pleas.
Soon, landlords refused to rent to them, saying the council had warned they were troublemakers.
When winter storms flooded Reedbank, the city sent inspectors but no builders.
The residents moved their belongings to the school gym, certain the damage would be temporary.
A week later, fencing appeared around the neighborhood.
A notice declared the land unsafe and ordered everyone to leave.
The residents returned to the council steps, quieter now, but still together.
They held their petition above their heads as rain blurred the ink.
A guard told them they were trespassing.
By sunset, their homes were empty and their names were missing from the relocation list.
They slept beneath the gym’s leaky roof, while the city announced that Reedbank had been cleared peacefully.
The report called the residents’ departure voluntary.
No one asked why their signatures had been ignored.
Yet each night, they told their children the stories of the river, the houses, and the neighbors who had stood beside them.
And in the morning, they began another petition.

The Electoral College has long been part of the American system for choosing a president. Although many people support replacing it with a nationwide popular vote, there are arguments for keeping it. The system reflects the Constitution’s design of balancing national and state interests. It gives states a formal role in selecting the president rather than treating the country as one undivided electorate. This can help preserve the federal structure of the United States.

One argument for retaining the Electoral College is that it encourages candidates to build support across different regions. To win, a candidate generally needs electoral votes from several states. A national popular vote might allow a candidate to focus heavily on the largest cities and most populous areas. Under the current system, candidates often seek voters in states with different economies, cultures, and political concerns. This regional competition can encourage broader coalitions.

The Electoral College can also make election outcomes easier to determine. Because electoral votes are counted by state, recounts are usually limited to places where the result is close. A nationwide vote could require recount rules and procedures to be coordinated across all states. That process might be complicated, especially if the national margin were extremely small. Supporters argue that the existing structure gives states a familiar role in resolving election disputes.

Another defense is that the system can strengthen the legitimacy of the winner by requiring a clear electoral majority. A candidate must win enough electoral votes, not merely earn the largest share of votes in a crowded race. If no candidate receives a majority, the Constitution provides a process for choosing the president. This possibility is unusual, but it is part of the system’s framework. Advocates believe these rules offer a stable way to handle an uncertain outcome.

The Electoral College also gives smaller states a somewhat larger role than they would have under a strict popular vote. Every state receives electoral votes based on its representation in Congress, including two votes connected to its senators. As a result, less populous states receive a small boost in influence. Supporters say this reflects the principle that the United States is a union of states as well as a nation of individuals. They argue that a popular vote could leave rural and less populous regions with little attention.

Critics respond that the Electoral College can make some votes count more than others and may produce a winner who did not receive the most votes nationwide. Those are serious concerns. Still, defenders argue that the system promotes federalism, regional outreach, and predictable state-based procedures. Keeping it also avoids the difficult task of creating a new national election system. Any reform would need agreement on recounts, ballot access, and election administration across the country.

In the end, retaining the Electoral College is not the only possible position, but it has a reasoned case behind it. Its supporters value the balance it creates between states and the national electorate. They also believe it encourages candidates to seek geographically broad support. Whether these benefits outweigh the system’s drawbacks is a question Americans can continue to debate. For now, the Electoral College remains a distinctive part of the constitutional system for electing the president.

Plans have been proposed to expand the Walney offshore wind farm in the Irish Sea, potentially increasing the amount of renewable electricity generated off the UK coast. The project would add new turbines alongside the existing wind farm, subject to planning approval and environmental assessments. Supporters say the expansion could help strengthen energy security and reduce reliance on fossil fuels. It may also bring investment and jobs to coastal communities during construction and maintenance. The proposal will need to address possible effects on marine wildlife, shipping and nearby fishing activity. Further details, including the project’s final size and timeline, are expected as the planning process develops.

After Mr. Alvarez died, he awoke in a quiet room lined with windows. Through them, he saw his former students scattered across the city. One was teaching a shy child to read, using the same patient tricks he had once taught her. Another had become a doctor and was comforting a frightened patient with his gentle words. A third was building a library in the neighborhood where Mr. Alvarez had held free lessons. Their kindness had traveled farther than he could have imagined. He smiled as the windows filled with new faces, each carrying something they had learned from him. At last, he understood that a teacher’s work never truly ends.

When I was seven, I dreamed the hallway outside my bedroom had gone dark. Not ordinary dark, but a thick blackness that seemed to swallow the walls. I called for my mother, but my voice came out as a whisper. The night-light by my door flickered once and died. Then something moved at the far end of the hall. I couldn’t see it, but I heard the soft scrape of its feet. I tried to hide beneath my blanket, though I knew blankets couldn’t stop anything. The darkness crept into my room, pooling around the bed. A cold hand closed around my ankle. I kicked, but my foot met only air. The hand began to pull me toward the edge. I grabbed the bedpost with both hands. “Let go,” I shouted, but the voice sounded far away. From the darkness came a slow, uneven breathing. I saw two pale shapes where its eyes might have been. My fingers slipped against the polished wood. The thing tugged harder, dragging me across the sheets. I screamed for my mother again. This time, I heard her answer from somewhere beyond the hall. Her voice sounded warm and close, but the darkness swallowed it. I clung to the bedpost until my palms burned. The pale eyes drifted nearer. Then the floor beneath me opened like a black mouth. I woke with a gasp, tangled in my blankets. Moonlight lay across the bedroom floor, and the hallway was quiet. My mother came running and held me until the shaking stopped. For years, I blamed the nightmare on shadows and an overactive imagination. But sometimes, just before sleep, I still hear something breathing in the hall.

Inflammation around a tendon, often called tenosynovitis, occurs when the protective tissue surrounding a tendon becomes irritated or swollen. Tendons connect muscles to bones and help joints move smoothly. Repetitive movements, prolonged gripping, or sudden overuse can strain a tendon and its surrounding sheath. Other causes include injury, inflammatory conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis, and, less commonly, infection. Diabetes and some other health conditions may increase the risk of certain forms.

Symptoms can include pain or tenderness along a tendon, swelling, warmth, and difficulty moving the affected area. The pain may worsen with activity or when pressure is applied. In the hand, swelling can make a finger stiff or cause it to catch, click, or lock when bent and straightened. This condition is called trigger finger and most often affects the thumb or ring finger. A locked finger may need gentle assistance to straighten.

A clinician usually diagnoses tenosynovitis by asking about symptoms and activities and examining the affected area. They may check tenderness, swelling, range of motion, and whether a tendon catches during movement. Imaging, such as ultrasound or an X-ray, may be used when the diagnosis is unclear or another problem is suspected. If infection is possible, prompt assessment and sometimes laboratory tests are needed.

Treatment depends on the cause and severity. Resting the affected area and temporarily reducing the movement that provokes pain can help. A splint may limit motion, especially for trigger finger, while a wrapped cold pack can ease swelling. A clinician may recommend pain-relieving or anti-inflammatory medicine if it is safe for the person to use. Gentle exercises or physical therapy may help restore movement once severe pain has settled.

If trigger finger persists, a corticosteroid injection may reduce swelling around the tendon. Surgery to release the tight tendon sheath is sometimes considered when other treatments do not work or the finger remains locked. Suspected infectious tenosynovitis requires urgent medical care and may need antibiotics or surgery. Seek prompt advice for severe or worsening pain, spreading redness, fever, or sudden loss of movement.

Religious Rituals and Seasonal Observances: Meaning Across Four Traditions

Religious rituals give shape to belief through actions people can see, hear, and share. Seasonal observances connect these actions to calendars, natural cycles, and stories remembered across generations. In Christianity, Hinduism, Islam, and Judaism, practices vary widely among communities, regions, and denominations. No single description can represent every believer or local tradition. Still, studying these observances can reveal how faith helps people mark time, build community, and respond to change.

What rituals and seasons express

A ritual may involve prayer, food, music, clothing, movement, or the use of symbolic objects. Some rituals take place at home, while others gather people in a place of worship or in public spaces. Repeated actions can create continuity between generations. They can also offer comfort during birth, illness, loss, and other transitions. Seasonal observances often recall sacred events or teachings rather than simply celebrating a change in weather. In many traditions, the dates follow a lunar, solar, or lunisolar calendar. As a result, observances may fall on different dates in the civil calendar from year to year. Local climate, history, and culture also influence how people celebrate. A ritual can therefore have a shared religious meaning and a distinct local expression.

Christianity: worship and the church year

Christianity is a diverse religion centered on the life and teachings of Jesus Christ. Many Christians gather for worship on Sunday, a day associated with the resurrection of Jesus. A typical service may include readings from the Bible, prayers, hymns, a sermon, and communal responses. The Eucharist, also called Communion or the Lord’s Supper, is a central ritual in many churches. Christians understand it in different ways, but it commonly recalls Jesus’s final meal with his disciples. Some churches celebrate Communion weekly, while others do so less often. Baptism is another significant rite, marking entry into the Christian community or a public commitment of faith. Practices differ, including whether baptism is given to infants, adults, or both. Across many denominations, church rituals help connect individual believers with a wider community and with Christian history.

The Christian year includes seasons that prepare for and remember key events in Jesus’s life. Advent is a period of preparation before Christmas. It often includes prayer, scripture reading, candles, and acts of generosity. Christmas celebrates the birth of Jesus. Church services, family gatherings, music, and gift-giving are common, though customs vary greatly. In some cultures, celebrations begin on Christmas Eve or continue into January. Epiphany, observed on different dates in different churches, recalls the revelation of Jesus to the wider world. It is associated in many traditions with the visit of the Magi. Lent is a period of reflection and preparation before Easter. It lasts about forty days in many church calendars, though the way it is counted varies. Some Christians fast, give up a habit, pray more, or serve others during Lent. These practices are intended to encourage self-examination and spiritual focus, not simply to impose hardship.

Holy Week recalls the final days of Jesus’s life. It includes Palm Sunday, which remembers his entry into Jerusalem, and Maundy Thursday, which recalls the Last Supper. Good Friday commemorates his crucifixion. Easter celebrates the resurrection of Jesus and is the most important feast in many Christian traditions. Services may include joyful music, candles, flowers, and readings about the resurrection. Families may also share meals or participate in cultural customs such as egg decorating. The egg can symbolize new life, though the meaning of customs differs by place. Easter’s date is calculated using a rule connected to the spring equinox and the lunar calendar. This is why it moves within the civil calendar. For many Christians, the movement from Lent to Easter expresses a journey from reflection and sorrow toward hope.

Hinduism: devotion, festivals, and sacred time

Hinduism includes many philosophical schools, devotional paths, deities, and regional traditions. Its practices cannot be reduced to a single set of beliefs or rituals. Puja is a common form of worship performed at home or in a temple. It may include offerings such as flowers, food, water, incense, or light. A worshipper may recite prayers, sing, meditate, or make a respectful gesture before an image or symbol of a deity. The image is generally treated as a focus for devotion, not simply as decoration. Temple rituals can involve priests, musicians, and the participation of visitors. Practices differ according to family custom, region, and the deity being honored. Festivals bring these forms of devotion into public life and often combine religious meaning with local art, food, and performance.

Diwali, often called the festival of lights, is celebrated by many Hindus, though its stories and customs differ across communities. Lamps and candles may be lit to symbolize light, welcome, or the victory of good over evil. Families may clean and decorate homes, share sweets, visit relatives, and pray. In some regions, Diwali is linked with stories of Rama’s return to Ayodhya. In others, it is associated with different deities and events. The festival can also carry meanings connected with prosperity and new beginnings. Its timing follows the Hindu lunisolar calendar, so its date changes in the civil calendar. The many regional forms of Diwali show how a shared festival can hold different layers of meaning.

Holi is known for the joyful use of colored powders and water in many places. It is often associated with the arrival of spring and with stories about devotion and the triumph of good over evil. Communities may gather for music, dancing, shared food, and the play of colors. Traditions vary, and participation may differ by age, location, and personal preference. Some people also use the season to renew friendships and set aside old disputes. Navaratri, meaning “nine nights,” honors the divine feminine in many Hindu traditions. It may involve fasting, prayer, dance, music, or dramatic performances. The forms of celebration vary significantly across India and the global Hindu diaspora. Durga Puja, especially prominent in Bengal, centers on the worship of the goddess Durga and includes elaborate temporary shrines and community gatherings. These festivals make religious stories visible through public art and shared celebration.

Other observances are closely connected to family and life stages. Many Hindus mark births, marriages, and other transitions with rituals whose details vary by community. A wedding may include fire, vows, offerings, and blessings from relatives. Pilgrimage to sacred rivers, temples, or other holy places is important for many people. Bathing in a sacred river may express purification, devotion, or remembrance. Some festivals are tied to the agricultural calendar or to the monsoon season. Seasonal rhythms can therefore influence both religious practice and community life. Fasting may be undertaken on particular days or during festivals, though rules and intentions differ. For some people, it is an act of discipline or devotion. For others, the emphasis may be on prayer, service, or gathering with family. Hindu observances show how sacred time can be woven into daily routines as well as major festivals.

Islam: prayer, fasting, and the lunar year

Islam is a global religion whose followers, Muslims, live in many cultures and communities. The five daily prayers are a regular structure of worship for many Muslims. Prayer may be performed at home, at work, or in a mosque. Worshippers face toward the Kaaba in Mecca and perform a sequence of standing, bowing, and prostrating. Friday congregational prayer is especially important in many communities. It usually includes a sermon and a shared prayer. The mosque can serve as a place of worship, learning, charity, and social connection. Practices vary, and not every Muslim has the same access to or pattern of participation. Ritual prayer links daily life with remembrance of God.

The Islamic calendar is lunar, and its months begin according to the observation or calculation of the new moon. Ramadan is the ninth month and is especially significant because Muslims believe the Quran began to be revealed during this month. Many adult Muslims fast from dawn until sunset during Ramadan. The fast generally includes abstaining from food and drink, though exemptions apply in circumstances such as illness, travel, pregnancy, or other needs. Muslims who are exempt may make up fasts later or provide support to those in need, depending on their circumstances and religious guidance. The pre-dawn meal is called suhoor, and the meal that breaks the fast after sunset is called iftar. Families and communities often share iftar, and mosques may host meals. The fast is intended to cultivate self-discipline, gratitude, compassion, and awareness of God. Ramadan may also bring increased prayer, Quran reading, charity, and reflection. Because the Islamic year is shorter than the solar year, Ramadan moves through the seasons over time.

Laylat al-Qadr, often translated as the Night of Decree or Power, is observed during the last ten nights of Ramadan. Many Muslims seek it through extra prayer and reflection. The exact night is not universally fixed, though the twenty-seventh night is especially observed in some communities. Eid al-Fitr marks the end of Ramadan. It begins with a special communal prayer and often includes charitable giving, festive meals, visits, and new or special clothing. The exact customs vary across countries and families. The lunar calendar means Eid can occur in different seasons in different years. Another major observance is Eid al-Adha, which takes place during the annual pilgrimage season. It recalls the willingness of Abraham to obey God, as understood in Islamic tradition. Many Muslims who are able arrange the sacrifice of an animal or contribute to a charitable distribution of meat. The act emphasizes generosity and care for people in need. Eid al-Adha is also associated with Hajj, the pilgrimage to Mecca.

Hajj is a major pilgrimage that Muslims who are physically and financially able are expected to undertake once in their lifetime. It takes place in a set period of the Islamic calendar. Pilgrims perform a sequence of rites in and around Mecca, including circling the Kaaba and gathering at the plain of Arafat. The pilgrimage brings people from many backgrounds together in acts of worship. It can express equality, humility, and unity before God. Many Muslims who cannot attend still observe the season through prayer, learning, and Eid al-Adha celebrations. Islamic observances show how daily worship and annual festivals can work together. They also connect communities across national borders through a shared calendar and practices.

Judaism: sacred time, memory, and community

Judaism is a diverse tradition shaped by scripture, law, interpretation, and communal practice. Shabbat, the Jewish Sabbath, begins at sundown on Friday and ends after nightfall on Saturday. It commemorates the creation story and the liberation of the Israelites from slavery in Egypt. Many Jewish households welcome Shabbat with candles, blessings, and a festive meal. Synagogue services, rest, study, and time with family may also be part of the day. The specific practices differ among Jewish communities and individuals. Shabbat offers a recurring pause from ordinary work and a chance to focus on spiritual life and relationships. Its weekly rhythm gives the Jewish calendar a distinctive structure.

The Jewish calendar is lunisolar, combining lunar months with adjustments that keep festivals in their appropriate seasons. Rosh Hashanah marks the Jewish New Year. It is a time for prayer, reflection, and the sounding of the shofar, a ram’s horn. Apples dipped in honey are eaten in many communities as a wish for a sweet new year. Rosh Hashanah begins a period of reflection that leads to Yom Kippur. Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement, is considered the holiest day of the year in many Jewish traditions. It is marked by fasting, prayer, and reflection for those able to fast. The day focuses on repentance and seeking forgiveness from God and from other people. Many communities gather for extended synagogue services. Together, these days encourage people to consider their actions and repair relationships.

Sukkot follows the High Holy Days and recalls the Israelites’ journey through the wilderness. Many Jews build or use a temporary shelter called a sukkah. Meals may be eaten there, and some people spend time or sleep in it, depending on custom and circumstance. The sukkah can represent both vulnerability and trust. It also connects the festival to the harvest season. Simchat Torah celebrates the completion and renewal of the annual cycle of public Torah reading in many communities. People may sing and dance with Torah scrolls in a joyful communal gathering. These observances blend historical memory, seasonal imagery, study, and celebration. Their customs vary across Jewish communities around the world.

Passover, or Pesach, remembers the liberation of the Israelites from slavery in Egypt. It is celebrated in spring and begins with a ritual meal called the seder. During the seder, participants read from a text called the Haggadah, ask questions, tell the story of the Exodus, and eat symbolic foods. Matzah, unleavened bread, recalls the haste of the Israelites’ departure in the traditional account. Bitter herbs evoke the bitterness of slavery. The meal invites people to experience the story as something that concerns each generation. Passover customs differ among Jewish communities, including traditions regarding food and the length of the festival. Shavuot, celebrated later in the spring, is associated with the giving of the Torah at Mount Sinai. It is also linked to the harvest. Some communities study religious texts through the night, while others mark the festival through prayer and festive meals. Together, Passover and Shavuot connect liberation, covenant, learning, and seasonal renewal.

Other Jewish observances mark solemn history and public joy. Hanukkah recalls the rededication of the Temple in Jerusalem, according to Jewish tradition. It is observed for eight nights, with the lighting of a special menorah called a hanukkiah. Families may sing, share foods fried in oil, play games, and tell the story. The lights are a visible expression of the festival’s themes. Purim recalls the events described in the biblical Book of Esther. It often involves hearing the story read aloud, sharing food, giving gifts to people in need, and wearing costumes. The celebrations can be lively and humorous. Jewish communities also remember days of mourning and historical tragedy through prayer, fasting, or other practices. These observances help preserve collective memory while allowing each generation to reflect on its meaning.

Shared themes and cultural significance

Across the four traditions, ritual can connect personal devotion with communal belonging. A shared meal may express hospitality, gratitude, or remembrance. Prayer can make an ordinary day feel connected to sacred time. Fasting can encourage discipline and empathy, though its meaning and practice differ. Festivals often combine worship with food, music, dress, storytelling, and family visits. These cultural forms are not merely extras added to religion. They can be important ways that people learn, remember, and share belief. The same observance may look different in a village, a city, or a diaspora community. Migration and cultural exchange continually shape religious customs. Communities may preserve older practices while adapting them to new circumstances.

Seasonal observances also connect people to the natural world. Spring festivals may emphasize renewal, liberation, or new life. Harvest-related observances can express gratitude for food and labor. Lunar calendars remind communities that religious time may not follow the same pattern as the civil calendar. Because calendars differ, neighbors may be celebrating different sacred occasions at the same time. Learning about these differences can help people plan respectfully around fasting, holidays, and worship. It can also reduce misunderstandings about why someone is unavailable or follows a particular practice. Respectful curiosity is more helpful than assuming that all members of a religion observe in the same way. Individuals may participate fully, selectively, or not at all. Their choices can reflect belief, health, family history, or personal circumstance.

Rituals are also shaped by questions of access and inclusion. Fasting may be modified or avoided for health reasons, and religious traditions often include guidance for particular circumstances. Not everyone can travel to a pilgrimage, attend a service, or celebrate with family. Communities may respond by offering practical support and alternative forms of participation. In many traditions, charitable giving is closely linked with seasonal observances. Such giving can connect spiritual ideals to action in the wider society. Rituals may also raise questions about gender roles, authority, and changing social expectations. Different communities interpret these questions in different ways. Learning about religion therefore means listening to believers as well as reading about formal teachings.

Understanding religious observances does not require sharing the beliefs behind them. It does require recognizing that rituals can carry deep meaning for those who practice them. A calendar can tell stories about creation, revelation, liberation, sacrifice, or hope. A meal can preserve memory and make room for conversation. A period of fasting can change how people think about hunger and generosity. A festival can turn a neighborhood into a place of shared music and color. The details differ, but each tradition offers ways to mark time and sustain community. When people learn these practices accurately and respectfully, they gain insight into both religious life and human culture.

At two in the morning, Eli Mercer woke beneath the library’s marble staircase.
He was wearing one slipper, a borrowed graduation gown, and a sticky note that said HELLO, INTERNET.
His phone lay beside him, recording.
Eli had taken Ambien after a week of sleepless exams, exactly as his doctor had instructed.
He had no memory of leaving his dorm.
By breakfast, the video had reached half a million views.
In it, Eli shuffled into the library, bowed to a portrait of the college founder, and whispered, “Your Majesty, the printer is haunted.”
Someone had added dramatic music.
Someone else had added subtitles.
By noon, he was trending as the Sleepwalking Scholar.
Eli watched the clip from his bed while his roommate, Marcus, tried not to laugh.
“Please tell me that’s not me,” Eli said.
Marcus paused the video on Eli’s solemn salute.
“I can tell you it’s definitely your gown.”
Eli shut the laptop.
The internet did not shut with it.
A popular account posted a compilation of his nighttime appearances.
There he was placing oranges in the chemistry department’s coat pockets.
There he was arranging a row of campus bicycles to face the moon.
In one clip, he stood before a vending machine and said, “You know what you did.”
The comments called him a poet, a menace, and the campus’s wisest man.
Eli felt none of those things.
He felt exposed, frightened, and unsure what his body might do next.
He called his doctor and explained what had happened.
The doctor told him to stop taking the medication and to come in for an appointment.
Eli also asked Marcus to keep his phone and room key overnight.
For the first time, he slept behind a locked door with someone checking on him.
The next evening, a message arrived from a news producer.
They wanted Eli on a morning show to reenact the haunted-printer scene.
He deleted it.
Then another message appeared, this one from the library’s night custodian.
The custodian had found Eli’s notebook near the staircase.
Inside were pages of hurried drawings and one clear sentence: I AM NOT A CHARACTER.
Eli read it twice.
The following morning, he posted a brief statement asking people to stop sharing the videos.
He explained that he had been asleep, under a medication that had affected him in an unexpected way.
He asked the university to remove recordings made inside private spaces.
Some viewers apologized.
Others made jokes about his statement.
Eli muted the hashtags and went to his appointment.
Weeks later, he returned to the library during daylight.
The custodian waved from behind the desk and handed him the notebook.
Eli thanked him, then sat at a table with his phone switched off.
For once, nobody was watching him become a story.

The man woke in a ditch beneath a sky the color of old steel. Rain tapped his face. He did not know his name. He did not know why his hands were bleeding. Beyond the ditch, headlights swept across the road. Someone shouted, “He’s over there!” The man tried to stand, but pain folded him in half. He crawled through wet grass as boots pounded closer. A rifle cracked, and dirt leapt beside his cheek. He ran. The woods swallowed him in darkness. He stumbled between trees, breathing hard. Behind him, men called to one another in clipped voices. Their flashlights cut white paths through the rain. The man reached a stream and fell to his knees. His reflection trembled in the black water. A stranger stared back, pale and frightened. Then blue light flickered beneath his skin. He jerked away from the stream. The glow vanished. A branch snapped behind him. He bolted downstream, slipping on stones. Another shot rang out. He threw up an arm. A bright blue arc burst from his palm. The bullet struck the arc and flattened, spinning into the water. The man froze. The pursuers froze too. For one breath, the forest was silent. Then a voice shouted, “Alive! We need him alive!” The man ran harder. Blue sparks crawled over his fingers. He reached a narrow ravine and found a rusted footbridge swaying above it. The bridge looked ready to fall. He crossed anyway. Halfway over, the first pursuer stepped onto the planks. The man turned. Fear rushed through him, and the blue light flared. The bridge cables snapped with a sound like a giant string breaking. The pursuers dropped back to the far bank. The man landed on the other side, hard but alive. He stared at his glowing hands. Somewhere inside him, a memory stirred. A white room. A voice saying, “You can stop the reaction.” Then the image dissolved. He kept moving until the trees thinned. A small town waited below, its windows dark. He descended toward a row of shuttered shops. At the edge of the square, he found a pay phone. It had no cord. He laughed once, a sound that frightened him. A church bell rang midnight. In its vibration, he heard a second sound: a pulse beneath the ground. The blue light answered it. Across the square, a locked metal door shuddered. The man touched the door. It opened inward without a key. Inside lay a room full of monitors and maps. One screen showed the forest. Another showed him, standing in the doorway. He stepped back. A speaker crackled. “Subject Seven, please remain where you are.” The voice was calm and familiar. He recognized it from the white room. The memory returned in a rush. His name was Elias Vale. He had once been a physicist. He had helped build a device meant to store energy without limits. The device had failed. Blue light had poured through the lab. Elias had been the only one to walk out. The men outside were not ordinary soldiers. They worked for the company that had funded the experiment. They wanted the power inside him. Elias looked at the monitors and saw the armed team closing in. He could flee again, but the town lay behind him. Families slept in those dark houses. He placed both hands on the control panel. Blue radiance spread across the screens. The cameras went blind one by one. The door locks clicked open throughout the building. The soldiers rushed into the square. Elias stepped outside to meet them. Their rifles rose. He felt no fear this time. He lifted his hands, and a blue shield unfolded like a quiet dawn. The first volley struck it and fell harmlessly to the stones. “You don’t know what you are,” the speaker voice said. Elias glanced at the sleeping town. “I’m beginning to.” The blue light widened, gentle as morning. The soldiers lowered their weapons, one by one. In the east, the clouds broke. Elias watched the sunrise and waited for his memories to return.

At 11:47 p.m., Mara stood on the footbridge with her phone in one hand and a paper bag in the other. The bag contained a bottle of cheap wine, a bruised apple, and the last sandwich in her fridge. She had packed it as if leaving for a picnic, which seemed funny in a way she couldn’t explain. The river below was black and glossy, like an expensive coat worn by someone with a terrible secret. Mara had spent the evening drafting a message to her sister. Every version began with “I’m sorry” and ended with nothing useful. She deleted them all. Then she called the number on a flyer she’d found in the laundromat. The flyer said, “CALL ANYTIME. SOMEONE WILL LISTEN.” Under that, in smaller print, it said, “Grief support group, Tuesdays at seven.” Mara had no grief group to attend, but she did have grief, and it was Tuesday somewhere. The number rang once. A man answered, sounding breathless and annoyed. “If this is about the raccoon, I already told you, it’s not my raccoon.” Mara blinked at the river. “I’m sorry,” she said. “I think I dialed the wrong number.” “You’ve reached the after-hours plumbing line,” he said. “And if your sink is making that gulping noise, don’t put your hand in it.” Mara looked at the water. “I’m not calling about a sink.” “Good,” he said. “The last guy who did that lost a wedding ring and an entire afternoon.” She should have hung up. Instead, she said, “I don’t know what to do.” There was a pause. The man’s voice changed, not softer exactly, but less busy. “Is something leaking?” “Maybe.” “In the house?” “No.” “Then let’s start with what you can see.” Mara looked at the streetlamps. “A bridge.” “That’s a start,” he said. “Are you on it?” “Yes.” “Okay. Can you walk to one end?” Mara’s fingers tightened around the phone. She hadn’t expected instructions. She hadn’t expected anyone to sound so ordinary. “I could.” “Great. I’m going to stay on the line while you do.” “You don’t even know who I am.” “I’m Len,” he said. “I fix pipes and occasionally talk people through bad nights.” “That seems outside your job description.” “So does raccoon removal, but here we are.” Mara gave a short, startled laugh. It came out rusty, like a tap that hadn’t been used all winter. “Why did you answer?” “Because it’s my job.” “At midnight?” “I’m on call.” “For faucets.” “Mostly.” “And now me?” “You’re making more sense than the faucet did.” Mara put one foot toward the sidewalk. The bridge seemed longer than it had on the way out. “I don’t think you can fix this.” “I’m not a magician,” Len said. “I’m barely a plumber.” “That’s not encouraging.” “I also have a very small dog who thinks I’m a god.” “Is that relevant?” “It means I’m good at pretending I know what I’m doing.” Mara took another step. The paper bag rustled against her coat. “What’s in the bag?” Len asked. “A sandwich.” “Excellent.” “It’s not a good sandwich.” “A bad sandwich is still a sandwich.” “It’s mostly lettuce.” “Then it’s a salad with structural problems.” Mara laughed again, and this time it lasted long enough to surprise her. At the end of the bridge, a convenience store sign blinked red and blue. “There’s a shop,” she said. “Can you go inside?” Len asked. “I suppose.” “Could you buy something warm?” “Like what?” “Tea, soup, one of those tragic little hot dogs that rotate under fluorescent lights.” “You have a gift for persuasion.” “I’ve been told I could sell a clogged drain to a plumber.” Mara started down the steps. “You’re a plumber.” “Exactly.” The shop door chimed when she entered. The cashier glanced up from a crossword and then back down, apparently deciding she was not a problem worth solving. Mara bought a coffee and a packet of crackers. She sat by the window, where she could see the bridge without being on it. “I’m inside,” she told Len. “Good.” “I still don’t know what to do.” “For tonight, drink the coffee and eat something.” “And tomorrow?” “Tomorrow you call someone who knows your name.” “My sister?” “If she’s safe to call.” Mara watched a bus cross the bridge, bright with people going somewhere. “She’ll be angry.” “Possibly.” “She’ll ask why I didn’t call sooner.” “Probably.” “She’ll say the wrong thing.” “Almost certainly.” “That doesn’t sound like a reason.” “It isn’t,” Len said. “It’s just what might happen.” The coffee was bitter and hot enough to sting her tongue. She drank it anyway. “You’re not very good at pep talks.” “I fix toilets. My standards are different.” Mara looked at the phone. “I called the wrong number.” “You did.” “Maybe that’s the only reason I’m still talking.” “Then I’m glad you got the number wrong.” “That’s a ridiculous thing to say.” “I’ve built a career on ridiculous things.” The cashier turned a page in the newspaper. The coffee machine hissed like an impatient cat. Mara took the sandwich from her bag and opened it. The bread had gone a little damp. “I’m eating,” she said. “Excellent.” “It’s awful.” “That’s how you know it’s working.” She ate half, then the other half, because there was no graceful way to stop. Len stayed on the line while she finished her coffee. He didn’t ask her to promise anything grand. He asked her to tell him the color of the shop’s floor tiles. Then the number of crackers in the packet. Then whether the little dog who thought he was a god had a name. “His name is Draino,” Len said. “That’s terrible.” “He came with the name.” “You could have changed it.” “I could have changed my life, too, but the paperwork looked annoying.” Mara smiled into the coffee cup. At 12:26, her sister answered on the third ring. Mara said, “I’m not okay, and I need you to stay on the phone.” Her sister went quiet, then said, “I’m here.” Mara began to cry, loudly and without dignity, while Len listened from the other end of the accidental call. When the conversation with her sister steadied, Mara asked Len how to thank him. “Call a plumber before your pipes explode,” he said. “That’s all?” “And don’t feed Draino crackers.” “I’ll keep that in mind.” She ended the call and remained at the window until her sister arrived. The river was still black, but it no longer looked like a door. In the morning, Mara saved the wrong number under “Len—Not a Faucet.” Then she called her sister again, and this time she asked for breakfast.
