Schools should encourage students to take part in extracurricular activities, but they should not require every student to join one. Activities such as sports, music, drama, and clubs can make school life more enjoyable. They also give students a chance to discover interests beyond regular classes. By working with others, students can practice communication and teamwork. These skills are useful both in school and in future jobs. Extracurricular activities can also help students make friends. A student who feels connected to a group may feel more welcome at school. Clubs and teams can provide a healthy break from homework and tests. They may also help students build confidence by giving them chances to learn and improve. For example, performing in a play can help a shy student become more comfortable speaking in front of others. However, requiring all students to join an activity could create problems. Some students already have busy schedules with schoolwork, family responsibilities, or part-time jobs. Others may need time to rest or care for their health. A student should not have to choose between an activity and an important responsibility at home. Some activities may also cost money for equipment, uniforms, or travel. This could make a requirement unfair to families who cannot afford those expenses. In addition, students have different interests and abilities. A student who dislikes sports should not be forced to join a team just to meet a rule. Schools could instead offer many affordable activities and make them easy to access. Teachers can explain the benefits and invite students to try something new. Schools can also provide flexible choices, such as short-term clubs or activities during the school day. Students who are unsure could attend a few meetings before deciding whether to continue. This approach supports participation without taking away students’ freedom. In conclusion, extracurricular activities offer many important benefits, but joining them should be a choice. Schools should encourage students to participate while respecting their needs, interests, and responsibilities.

Preventing heart disease and stroke starts with everyday habits and supportive communities. These conditions often develop over time, but many risk factors can be reduced. Choose a variety of vegetables, fruits, whole grains, beans, nuts, and other minimally processed foods. Limit foods high in salt, added sugar, and saturated or trans fats. Cooking at home more often can make it easier to control ingredients and portion sizes. Aim for regular physical activity, such as brisk walking, cycling, dancing, or swimming. Adults generally benefit from at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity activity each week, when appropriate for their health. Start gradually if you are inactive, and ask a health professional for advice if you have concerns. Avoid tobacco, and seek support to quit if you smoke or use other tobacco products. Keep alcohol use low or avoid it; drinking less is generally better for health. Good sleep and stress-management practices can also support heart health. Regular checkups can identify high blood pressure, high cholesterol, and diabetes before symptoms appear. Follow a clinician’s advice about monitoring and treating these conditions. Take prescribed medicines as directed, and discuss side effects or cost barriers rather than stopping on your own. Learn the warning signs of a heart attack and stroke, and call emergency services immediately if they occur. Communities can make healthy choices easier by creating safe sidewalks, parks, bike routes, and recreation spaces. Schools and workplaces can offer nutritious food, opportunities to move, and practical health education. Local health services can provide screenings, affordable care, and help with quitting tobacco. Community programs should be welcoming and accessible to people of different ages, abilities, cultures, and incomes. Neighbors, families, and community groups can encourage healthy habits without blame or pressure. Faith groups and local organizations can share reliable health information and connect people with support. Policymakers can help by improving access to nutritious foods and safe places to be active. They can also support preventive care and reduce barriers to essential medicines. Small personal steps and community-wide changes work best when they reinforce each other. Together, they can lower risk and help more people live longer, healthier lives.

John Senex (c. 1678–1740) rose from a modest background to become one of eighteenth-century England’s leading mapmakers and publishers. He trained as an engraver and worked with established map publishers before setting up his own business in London. In 1702, he became a member of the Stationers’ Company, which regulated the book and print trades. Senex built his reputation by producing carefully engraved maps, atlases, globes, and geographical books. His publications served both scholars and a growing public interested in travel, trade, and world geography. He often combined information from earlier sources with reports from explorers and other mapmakers. Among his notable works was a 1719 map of North America, which reflected contemporary knowledge while also showing how much of the continent remained uncertain to Europeans. Senex also helped popularize globes for teaching and private study, making geographic knowledge more accessible. His business success depended on skilled engraving, commercial partnerships, and the expanding market for printed maps. In 1728, he was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society, recognition of his standing in scientific and publishing circles. By the time of his death, Senex had helped shape English cartography and the public’s understanding of the wider world.

Continuous symmetries and conserved quantities

A symmetry is a change to a system that leaves its essential physical behavior unchanged. For example, rotating an isolated sphere does not alter its physical properties. A continuous symmetry is one that can be varied smoothly, by arbitrarily small amounts. Turning an object through an angle is continuous, unlike switching it between two distinct states. Continuous symmetries are closely connected to conservation laws. This connection is expressed by Noether’s theorem, a central result in theoretical physics. In simple terms, Noether’s theorem says that each continuous symmetry of a system’s action leads to a conserved quantity. The action is a mathematical quantity that summarizes the system’s dynamics over time. A conserved quantity remains constant as the system evolves, provided the relevant conditions hold. This relationship helps explain why energy, momentum, and electric charge are conserved.

Time symmetry and energy

Consider a physical system whose laws do not change with time. The same experiment, performed today or tomorrow under identical conditions, follows the same rules. This invariance under shifts in time is called time-translation symmetry. Noether’s theorem associates time-translation symmetry with conservation of energy. Energy can move between forms, such as kinetic, potential, and thermal energy. Yet the total energy of an isolated system remains constant when the system’s laws are unchanged over time. For instance, a falling object loses gravitational potential energy while gaining kinetic energy. If air resistance and other exchanges are neglected, the sum stays constant. If the underlying conditions change with time, energy conservation for the system may no longer apply in the usual way. A time-dependent external force can supply energy or remove it. The broader system, including the source of that force, may still conserve energy.

Space symmetry and momentum

A different symmetry concerns where an experiment takes place. If the laws of physics are the same at every location, the system has spatial-translation symmetry. Moving an isolated experiment from one point to another does not change its fundamental behavior. Noether’s theorem connects this symmetry with conservation of linear momentum. Momentum is the product of an object’s mass and velocity in ordinary classical mechanics. In an isolated group of objects, their total momentum stays constant as they interact. A pair of skaters pushing apart illustrates this rule. They move in opposite directions, and their momenta balance so the total remains unchanged. If the surroundings exert a net external force, the momentum of the chosen system can change. Including those surroundings may restore a larger conservation account.

Rotational symmetry and angular momentum

Space also has a symmetry under rotation. If the laws are the same in every direction, the system has rotational symmetry. Noether’s theorem associates rotational symmetry with conservation of angular momentum. Angular momentum describes rotational motion and depends on factors such as mass distribution and rotation rate. A spinning figure skater can increase their spin by drawing in their arms. Their moment of inertia decreases, while their angular speed increases. In the absence of significant external torque, their angular momentum remains approximately constant. If the environment exerts a torque, angular momentum can be transferred between the system and its surroundings. Rotational symmetry is therefore a statement about the uniformity of physical laws across directions, not a claim that every object looks the same when rotated.

Internal symmetries and charge

Some symmetries do not move a system through space or time. They act on internal properties, such as the mathematical phases of fields used in particle physics. A continuous internal symmetry can lead to a conserved charge. Electric charge is one familiar example of a conserved quantity associated with a phase symmetry in the mathematical description of charged matter. In interactions, particles may transform into other particles, but the total electric charge remains the same. A proton has charge of plus one elementary charge, while an electron has charge of minus one. In processes where they are created or destroyed, the total charge before and after must balance. The symmetry provides a deeper explanation for this rule than simply observing that charge happens to stay constant. Different internal symmetries can correspond to other conserved quantities in particular theories. The details depend on the fields and interactions included in the theory.

What the connection means

Noether’s theorem does not say that every imaginable symmetry produces a familiar conserved quantity. The symmetry must apply to the system’s action, and the theorem’s precise conclusions depend on the theory’s structure. It also does not mean that a conserved quantity cannot be exchanged between parts of a system. Energy, momentum, and charge can move from one part to another while their total remains fixed. The chosen boundaries matter: a quantity may appear not to be conserved if important surroundings have been left out. In modern physics, conservation laws are also tied to the structure of spacetime and to the consistency of physical theories. Symmetries help physicists identify which quantities should remain constant before solving detailed equations. Conservation laws, in turn, help check calculations and predict possible outcomes. The link between symmetry and conservation is one reason these ideas appear throughout classical mechanics, electromagnetism, quantum theory, and particle physics. Together, they show that regularities in the laws of nature have measurable consequences.

For much of the last century, owning a car came to represent freedom and success. Yet rising fuel costs, traffic congestion, and environmental concerns have made car-centered cities harder to sustain. Many people also cannot afford the purchase, insurance, repairs, and parking that come with owning a vehicle. Shifting toward other forms of transportation can make daily travel more affordable, sustainable, and socially appealing.

Public transit is one important part of this shift. Buses and trains can move many people using less energy and road space per passenger than private cars. Reliable service, frequent schedules, and affordable fares can make transit a practical choice for work, school, and leisure. However, transit must reach more than a city’s busiest neighborhoods to serve people fairly. Safe, comfortable stations and clear information also help passengers feel welcome.

Walking and cycling offer additional benefits. These options are inexpensive, reduce pollution, and support people’s health through regular activity. Protected bike lanes, wide sidewalks, good lighting, and safe crossings can encourage more residents to use them. Cities should make these routes accessible to people of different ages and abilities. Secure bicycle parking and shared-bike programs can make cycling easier for those who do not own a bike.

Some trips still require a car, especially in rural areas or where transit is limited. Car-sharing and ride-sharing services can help people access vehicles without bearing the full cost of ownership. Electric vehicles may reduce emissions, but they do not solve traffic or the problem of taking up valuable public space. For that reason, they should complement—not replace—public transit, walking, and cycling.

Changing transportation habits requires more than asking people to make better choices. Governments must invest in dependable services and design streets around people, not only vehicles. Employers and schools can support the change with transit passes, bicycle facilities, and flexible schedules. These efforts should include low-income communities, which are often most affected by pollution and poor transportation access.

A shift away from car dependence will not happen overnight. It requires thoughtful planning, public investment, and choices that meet people’s everyday needs. When affordable and convenient alternatives are available, fewer people may feel that owning a car is essential. The result can be cleaner air, less crowded streets, healthier communities, and more welcoming public spaces.

Subject: Proposed SAP Planning and Cost-Allocation Processes for Corporate and Enron Affiliates’ Billings

Hello team,

I’d like to propose a consistent SAP process for planning and allocating costs associated with corporate and Enron affiliates’ billings. The goal is to improve accuracy, transparency, and timely reconciliation across all entities. Each corporate department and affiliate should submit its monthly cost forecast using a standard SAP template. The template should identify the service provided, receiving entity, cost center, allocation driver, and expected amount. Finance should review submissions before the start of each billing period. Any forecast changes should be documented with a brief explanation and approved by the appropriate budget owner. Once approved, forecasts should be loaded into SAP and linked to the relevant billing cycle. Actual costs should be captured against the same cost centers and service categories wherever possible. We should use agreed allocation drivers, such as headcount, usage, or transaction volume, based on the nature of each service. The chosen driver and its source data should be recorded so that allocations can be reproduced and reviewed. SAP should calculate proposed charges using the approved rates and allocation rules. Finance should compare calculated charges with forecasts and investigate material variances before invoices are issued. Each affiliate should receive a detailed billing statement showing the services, allocation basis, and amounts charged. Corporate departments should also receive reports that reconcile billed amounts to their forecasts and actual costs. Disputes should be submitted through a defined SAP workflow within an agreed review period. The responsible finance team should track each dispute through resolution and retain supporting documentation. Corrections should be processed through approved adjustments rather than informal changes to source records. We should establish clear roles for forecast owners, billing preparers, reviewers, and approvers. Access to SAP billing data should be limited according to those roles and periodically reviewed. A monthly close checklist can help ensure that all forecasts, allocations, approvals, and reconciliations are complete. I recommend piloting this process with a small group of corporate departments and affiliates before expanding it. Please share your feedback on the proposed workflow, allocation drivers, and review timelines by the end of next week. After incorporating comments, we can confirm ownership and prepare a detailed implementation plan.

Welsh public services are facing a fresh period of financial pressure, with significant spending cuts under consideration as budgets struggle to keep pace with demand. Councils and public bodies say rising costs, growing needs and limited funding are leaving little room to protect existing services. The squeeze comes as uncertainty persists over how Wales will receive money that previously came through European Union programmes. Brexit ended the UK’s access to many EU funding streams, including support for regional development and agriculture. The UK Government has promised replacement funding, but Welsh officials and local organisations have raised concerns about its scale, timing and distribution. They argue that uncertainty makes it harder to plan long-term projects and sustain jobs and services. Welsh ministers have warned that any shortfall could deepen pressures already affecting local government. Councils are contending with higher demand for social care, homelessness support and services for children. At the same time, inflation and wage costs have increased the price of delivering those services. Some authorities may have to reduce provision, delay investment or seek further savings to balance their budgets. The effects could be felt in community facilities, transport, youth services and support for vulnerable residents. Public-sector unions and campaigners say cuts risk widening inequalities, particularly in areas with fewer economic opportunities. Business groups have also called for clarity on replacement funding, warning that uncertainty can deter investment. The debate is unfolding as governments face competing demands for health, education and economic development. Welsh ministers say they will seek to protect core services while pressing for fair and predictable funding arrangements. UK ministers have maintained that Wales will receive funding comparable to what it would have obtained through EU programmes, though critics dispute whether current arrangements meet that commitment. The precise impact will depend on future budget decisions and the terms of replacement schemes. Local authorities are expected to set out their spending plans in the months ahead. Until funding is confirmed, councils and service providers may have to plan for several possible outcomes. For residents, the central concern is whether essential support can be maintained as financial pressures mount.

Disney has warned that escalating trade tensions could weigh on its business, even as its Shanghai theme park continues to draw strong crowds. The company’s caution comes amid softer sales in parts of its entertainment and consumer products operations. Executives said tariffs and other trade barriers could raise costs and disrupt supply chains, though the full impact remains uncertain. The warning highlights the difficulty of forecasting demand in a volatile global economy.

Shanghai Disney Resort has been a brighter spot, supported by visitor demand and the appeal of its attractions. Its performance contrasts with weaker sales elsewhere in Disney’s business, underscoring uneven conditions across markets. The company has not said that trade tensions are directly responsible for the sales decline. But a prolonged dispute could affect both consumer confidence and the cost of goods sold in key markets.

Disney’s broader results are also shaped by changes in streaming, film releases and consumer spending. The company is seeking to balance investment in its parks and content with pressure to improve profitability. Analysts are watching whether strong attendance in Shanghai can offset softness in other areas. They are also assessing how much of Disney’s exposure can be reduced through local sourcing and pricing decisions.

For now, Disney’s message is one of caution rather than a forecast of immediate damage. The company said uncertainty around trade policy makes it harder to plan for the coming quarters. Its contrasting sales trends show how one business can face both strong local demand and rising global risks.

The United States should replace the Electoral College with a direct popular vote for president. Under the current system, people vote for electors, who then formally choose the president. This means a candidate can win the presidency without receiving the most votes nationwide. That has happened several times in American history. In a democracy, the candidate supported by the most voters should generally win.

A direct popular vote would make every vote count equally. Under the Electoral College, votes in closely contested states often receive more attention than votes in states where one party is expected to win. Candidates may spend much of their time campaigning in a few competitive states. A national popular vote would encourage them to seek support across the entire country. It could also motivate more people to vote because their ballots would matter no matter where they live.

The Electoral College does have defenders. They argue that it protects the influence of smaller states and encourages candidates to build support in different regions. They also say that changing the system could create practical problems, such as close recounts across the country. These concerns deserve serious consideration. However, a direct vote could use clear national rules for counting ballots and resolving disputes.

Replacing the Electoral College would require a major change, likely through a constitutional amendment. This would be difficult, but the difficulty does not mean reform is unnecessary. The system was created in a very different time, before modern communication and nationwide elections. Today, citizens can learn about candidates and issues across the country. A direct popular vote would better reflect the principle that every citizen’s vote should carry equal weight. For these reasons, the United States should choose its president through the national popular vote.

Summer break gives students a chance to rest, explore, and spend time with family. It can also be a good time to learn in a more personal way. Students should create their own summer learning projects because these projects help them follow their interests, practice useful skills, and take responsibility for their learning.

A self-chosen project can begin with a simple question. A student who loves animals might ask how birds find their way during migration. Someone interested in cooking might learn how different ingredients change the taste of a dish. These questions make learning feel connected to real life. Because students choose the topic, they are often more curious and motivated to keep going.

Summer projects also encourage independence. Students can decide what they want to learn, set a goal, and plan the steps to reach it. They may need to find books, watch lessons, interview someone, or gather materials. If something does not work, they can try another approach. This teaches them that mistakes are part of learning, not a reason to quit.

Projects can build skills that are useful in school and beyond. Writing a blog, making a short film, or designing a small garden can involve research, organization, communication, and problem-solving. Students can practice managing their time without following a daily classroom schedule. They can also learn to explain their ideas clearly by sharing their work with others.

Another benefit is that projects can be adapted to different interests and resources. A student can study local plants by taking walks nearby, while another can learn a new language with books or free online tools. A project does not have to be expensive or complicated to be meaningful. Parents, teachers, and librarians can offer guidance, but students should still make important choices themselves.

Some people may worry that summer projects will feel like extra homework. That can happen if the project is too demanding or adults make every decision. Students should choose goals that are enjoyable and realistic, leaving plenty of time for rest and play. A few minutes of learning on some days can be enough to make steady progress.

At the end of summer, students can look back at what they discovered. They might have a finished model, a collection of drawings, a new recipe, or simply a better understanding of a subject. They can also feel proud that they planned and completed something on their own. The experience may even inspire a future class, hobby, or career.

Creating a summer learning project turns free time into an opportunity for discovery. It allows students to learn about subjects that matter to them while practicing independence and useful skills. Most importantly, it shows that learning does not happen only in a classroom. With curiosity and a manageable plan, students can make their summer both enjoyable and meaningful.

Schools should encourage students to take part in community service, but they should not require it. Volunteering can help students understand the needs of people in their community. It also teaches responsibility, teamwork, and compassion. For example, students might help at a food bank, clean a park, or read with younger children. These experiences can be meaningful and help students discover their interests. However, requiring service may make it feel like a punishment rather than a choice. Some students already have jobs or family responsibilities that leave them little free time. Others may have transportation or health challenges that make volunteering difficult. A strict requirement could unfairly burden these students. Schools could instead offer a wide range of service opportunities during the school day. They could also recognize students who volunteer without making participation necessary. This approach would make service accessible while respecting students’ different circumstances. When students choose to help, they are more likely to value the experience and continue serving others.

Political debate has intensified in Scotland over GP recruitment, medical training funding and mounting pressure on the health workforce. Opposition parties say staffing shortages are making it harder for patients to secure timely appointments, particularly in rural and deprived communities. The Scottish Government says it is investing in primary care and expanding the number of doctors entering training. But critics argue that recruitment promises will have limited effect unless more funding is directed towards training and retention. General practice leaders say vacancies and rising workloads are leaving existing teams stretched. They warn that some practices are struggling to meet demand as the population grows older and more people live with complex conditions. Ministers have pointed to recent increases in medical school places and postgraduate training opportunities. However, campaigners say it takes years for those measures to produce fully qualified GPs. They also argue that Scotland must compete with other parts of the UK for doctors, many of whom consider pay, workload and career prospects when choosing where to work. The debate has renewed calls for clearer workforce plans, including targets for GP numbers and transparent reporting on vacancies. Rural health representatives say recruitment incentives may be needed where practices face persistent difficulty attracting staff. Others stress that better administrative support and expanded multidisciplinary teams could ease pressure on doctors. Medical groups caution that such changes should complement, rather than replace, investment in GP training. They also warn that burnout and early retirement could worsen shortages if working conditions do not improve. The Scottish Government says it is working with health boards and professional bodies to strengthen services and make primary care a more attractive career. Opposition figures say the pace and scale of action remain inadequate. With budget decisions approaching, training funds and workforce commitments are expected to remain central points of political scrutiny. For patients, the key test will be whether the debate leads to more accessible appointments and a sustainable workforce.

The court convened beneath a black sun.

Its walls were carved with skulls, hourglasses, and pale flowers.

Morpheus, judge of the dead, struck his staff upon the floor.

“Today we hear whether Death’s image has lost its meaning,” he said.

At the plaintiff’s table sat Death, cloaked in silver.

Across from him stood Mnemosyne, mother of memory.

A crowd of gods, mortals, and ghosts filled the benches.

“Everywhere I look, I see myself,” Death began.

“On posters, costumes, games, and warning signs.”

“They paint my face on coffee cups and call it daring.”

“Children wear my grin before they know what it means.”

Mnemosyne rose, her eyes bright as dawn.

“Symbols travel because people need them,” she replied.

“A skull can warn, mock, mourn, or remind us to live.”

“Your image is not diminished merely because it is repeated.”

“Yet repetition can make a sacred thing into wallpaper,” said Death.

He lifted his hood, revealing a face as calm as snow.

“I once entered a room, and every heart understood the silence.”

“Now they laugh before I speak.”

From the gallery, Hermes called, “Laughter is not always disrespect.”

“Sometimes it is how mortals stand beside fear.”

Athena nodded. “A symbol must change, or it becomes a cage.”

“But change without care turns meaning into decoration,” Mnemosyne warned.

The judge summoned a mortal witness, a young nurse named Elian.

She carried a small pin shaped like a lantern.

“My patients see Death’s symbols every day,” she said.

“Some find comfort in them; others feel mocked.”

“The same image can soothe one person and wound another.”

Death looked at the pin.

“What does yours mean?” he asked.

“It reminds me that darkness is real,” Elian said.

“And that someone can still hold a light within it.”

For a moment, the courtroom was quiet.

Then the Fates entered, each holding a thread.

Clotho spoke first. “A culture needs symbols to name what it fears.”

Lachesis added, “It needs room to question the names it inherits.”

Atropos cut a loose thread, but did not let it fall.

“Balance is not stillness,” she said.

“It is the art of keeping opposites in honest company.”

Morpheus considered the witnesses, the gods, and the silver-cloaked figure.

Then he ruled that no image belonged to one meaning alone.

“Let Death be shown,” he said, “but not emptied of consequence.”

“Let humor share the room with grief, and spectacle with silence.”

“Let every culture tend its symbols as it tends a flame.”

The crowd departed beneath the black sun.

Death walked beside Elian, neither feared nor forgotten.

And behind them, the carved skulls seemed less like ornaments than open doors.

Cheltenham Festival is preparing for another major turnout, with organisers expecting record crowds and new rules on alcohol sales. The four-day meeting, one of Britain’s biggest racing events, draws racegoers from across the country and overseas.

The revised limits are intended to manage drinking and keep the event safe as attendance grows. Specific restrictions may vary by venue and day, so visitors are being advised to check the latest guidance before travelling. Organisers are also encouraging racegoers to plan their journeys and allow extra time for entry.

The festival is expected to bring a substantial economic boost to Cheltenham and the wider region. Hotels, restaurants, pubs and transport operators typically see a surge in business during race week. Local retailers and suppliers also benefit from the influx of visitors.

The crowds create added pressure on roads, rail services and public spaces. Transport teams and local authorities are coordinating plans to reduce congestion and help visitors move around the town. Businesses are preparing for a busy week, with many staffing up and extending opening hours.

The festival’s popularity is closely tied to its high-profile races and long-standing place in the racing calendar. Its biggest days attract large audiences, while hospitality packages and corporate events add to the demand. Organisers say careful planning will be essential to balancing the event’s economic benefits with the needs of residents.

Racegoers are being urged to drink responsibly and follow stewards’ instructions. The alcohol measures form part of broader preparations for a safe and orderly meeting. With attendance expected to be exceptionally strong, the festival is set to be both a major sporting occasion and a significant test of local capacity.

A museum’s hands-on astronomy program can help first-grade students in Delavan explore the night sky through play and discovery. During a visit, children might begin by learning that astronomy is the study of space and the objects in it. A museum educator can introduce the Sun, Moon, planets, and stars using colorful pictures and models. Students can build a simple model of the solar system, noticing that planets differ in size and distance from the Sun. With a flashlight and a ball, they can explore how sunlight creates day and night. They can also use a lamp and a small sphere to see how the Moon’s appearance changes as it moves around Earth. A pretend rocket launch can invite students to count down and imagine traveling beyond our planet. Through a telescope, children may look at the Moon or observe distant objects, depending on the weather and available equipment. They can practice describing what they see with words such as bright, round, and far away. A star map can help them find patterns in the sky, called constellations. The educator can explain that stars are huge, glowing balls of gas, even though they look like tiny points from Earth. Students might make a constellation picture by connecting star-shaped stickers on dark paper. They can ask questions, share ideas, and learn that scientists use careful observation to understand space. Simple activities also help children practice counting, comparing, and using their senses. By the end of the program, young visitors can see that the universe is full of things to explore and learn about.

Mara kept her left hand tucked inside her coat, even on warm days. The burn scars across her fingers were pale and shiny, reminders of the kitchen fire that had changed her life. She told people she was clumsy, then changed the subject before they could ask more.

When Eli first reached for her hand, Mara pulled away. He didn’t ask what was wrong or insist she show him. He simply offered his own hand, palm up, and waited.

The quiet kindness unsettled her more than curiosity would have. A week later, they sat together on the porch while rain tapped the roof. Mara took a breath and laid her scarred hand between them.

Eli looked at it, then at her. “Does it hurt?” he asked. “Sometimes,” she said. “Mostly when I think someone will see it.” He traced the air above her fingers, careful not to touch without permission.

“May I?” he asked. Mara nodded. His touch was gentle, as if her hand were not broken but precious. “You don’t have to hide from me,” he said.

For a long time, she had believed acceptance meant someone would overlook the scars. Eli showed her it could mean seeing them clearly and staying. She began leaving her hand uncovered at the market, at work, and in photographs.

The scars did not fade, and some days she still felt their old weight. But when she reached for Eli, she no longer thought of her hand as something to apologize for. It was hers, and it had carried her through. As his fingers folded around hers, Mara felt whole—not because she had become flawless, but because she had finally stopped asking perfection to make her worthy.

Primary care is often the first place people seek help for depression. Yet many practices have fewer resources for depression care than for conditions such as diabetes or high blood pressure. These illnesses often have established workflows, routine tests, and dedicated care teams. Depression care can require more time for conversation, follow-up, and coordination than a short appointment allows.

Primary care clinicians may have limited access to mental health specialists, especially in rural or underserved communities. Patients may face long waits, high costs, or difficulty finding a provider who accepts their insurance. Practices may also lack staff trained to provide counseling or track symptoms over time. Without reliable follow-up, it can be hard to tell whether treatment is helping or needs to change.

Depression can affect sleep, energy, concentration, and physical health, making it harder for patients to manage other conditions. Stigma and concerns about privacy may also keep people from discussing symptoms. Screening questionnaires can help identify possible depression, but screening alone does not ensure that a patient receives effective care. Good support includes a clear diagnosis, a treatment plan, regular check-ins, and timely adjustments when needed.

Some practices use collaborative care, in which primary care clinicians work with mental health professionals and care managers. This approach can help patients receive support without relying only on specialist appointments. Telehealth and community partnerships may also improve access, though they do not solve every barrier. Better funding, training, staffing, and coordination can help primary care practices treat depression more consistently. With appropriate resources, depression care can become a routine part of whole-person health care.

Reducing reliance on cars can make communities healthier, safer, and more affordable. Cars are useful, especially in places with limited public transportation, but using them for every trip has serious costs. When more people choose to walk, bike, carpool, or take public transportation, the benefits can reach an entire community.

One important benefit is cleaner air. Cars release pollutants that contribute to smog and can harm people’s lungs and hearts. Heavy traffic also produces greenhouse gases that contribute to climate change. Fewer car trips can reduce these emissions, particularly when trips are replaced by walking, cycling, or public transit. Cleaner air is especially valuable for children, older adults, and people with asthma. It can also make streets and outdoor spaces more pleasant to use.

Reducing car use can also make travel safer. Fewer cars on the road may mean fewer opportunities for crashes. Walking and cycling can be safer when streets have sidewalks, protected bike lanes, and slower speed limits. Public transportation can move many people in fewer vehicles, reducing traffic congestion. When fewer cars crowd the streets, drivers may have a clearer view of pedestrians and cyclists. Safer streets can encourage more people to travel without a car, creating a positive cycle.

Lower costs are another major benefit. Owning a car can involve payments, fuel, insurance, repairs, and parking fees. People who drive less may spend less on these expenses. Walking and cycling are often inexpensive ways to travel short distances. Public transportation can also cost less than driving, particularly for regular trips. Communities can save money too, since roads and parking facilities require construction and maintenance.

There are challenges to reducing reliance on cars. Some people live far from work or services, and others have disabilities or schedules that make driving necessary. For that reason, communities need reliable public transportation and safe routes for walking and cycling. Employers and schools can support carpooling and flexible travel options. Local governments can improve bus service, build protected bike lanes, and design neighborhoods where daily needs are nearby. These changes make alternatives practical rather than merely encouraging people to drive less.

Reducing reliance on cars does not mean eliminating them entirely. It means choosing a car only when it is the most suitable option. Cleaner air, safer travel, and lower costs are achievable when communities offer convenient alternatives. By making thoughtful transportation choices, individuals and local leaders can help create places that are healthier and easier to live in.

For three thousand years, Elias had searched for a reason to live forever. He asked kings, poets, and priests, but each offered an answer that faded with the century. He crossed deserts seeking silence and cities seeking wonder. At last, an old woman told him, “Meaning is what you choose to do before the moment passes.” Elias took her advice and spent the next decades helping strangers, planting trees, and learning their names. He began to suspect that the search itself had been a way to avoid choosing. Then came January 20, 2017, and the crowds gathered in Washington beneath a cold gray sky. Elias watched Donald Trump take office, and felt history turn once more without asking his permission. Around him, people cheered, wept, argued, and hurried toward whatever came next. He waited for revelation, but none arrived. Instead, a young boy dropped his mitten in the crowd, and Elias picked it up. The boy smiled, and for one small moment, eternity seemed less like a sentence. Elias finally understood that meaning was never a secret hidden at the end of history. It was the work he chose to do while history kept going.

In a video released by the group, the pair said they feared for their lives and urged officials to act quickly. The recording’s date and location could not be independently verified. The captors said they would not free the couple unless authorities released detainees they described as political prisoners. They did not provide a publicly confirmed list of names or a clear deadline. Officials said they were examining the video and working to establish the couple’s condition and whereabouts. A spokesperson condemned the abduction and called for the hostages’ immediate release. The government did not say whether it would negotiate over the prisoner demand. Relatives of the couple asked authorities to prioritize their safe return. “We just want them home,” one family member said. Security analysts warned that public statements could complicate efforts to reach the captors. Humanitarian organizations urged all sides to protect the hostages and allow independent intermediaries to communicate with them. The incident has heightened concern in the area, where residents fear further violence. For now, the couple’s fate remains uncertain as officials pursue efforts to secure their release.

Captain Juno Vale had never met a danger she couldn’t make worse. So when the alien fleet surrounded the courier ship Finch, she smiled at the viewscreen. “Good evening,” she said. “You’re about to witness a demonstration.”

Behind her, Engineer Niko Renn stared at the fleet’s hundred green warships. Their weapons glowed like eyes in the dark. “What demonstration?” he whispered.

“Still working on that,” Juno whispered back. She opened the shipwide channel and ordered the aliens to stand by. Their commander answered in a voice that rattled the speakers. “Surrender your vessel, or be destroyed.”

Juno tapped the console as if dismissing a waiter. “You misunderstand. We’re not carrying cargo. We’re carrying a starbreaker.” Niko looked up from the engine panel. A starbreaker was a weapon that did not exist.

The alien commander paused. Juno leaned toward the microphone. “It’s already armed. One more hostile move, and your entire fleet disappears.” Niko’s eyes widened. He saw what she was doing, and what she wasn’t doing: buying time.

He ducked below the console and opened the emergency hatch. The Finch’s self-destruct unit sat beneath the deck, wrapped in warning lights. “You have one minute to withdraw,” Juno announced. “I suggest you use it.”

The aliens did not move. Niko pulled the first safety lever. A red light blinked awake. Juno kept smiling. “Forty seconds,” she said.

The fleet commander’s voice sharpened. “We detect no weapon.” “Then your sensors are as disappointing as your manners,” Juno replied. Niko twisted a second lever.

The Finch shuddered. A timer began counting down in the cockpit. Juno glanced at it and immediately regretted being able to read. “Thirty seconds,” she said, louder than before. The commander ordered his ships to prepare their weapons.

Juno leaned back in her chair. “That’s a brave choice.” Niko found the escape pod release jammed. He kicked the panel, and it popped open.

“Twenty seconds,” Juno said. The aliens’ weapons brightened. “Niko, tell me you’re ready.” “I’m ready,” he said. “The pod isn’t.”

He ran to the rear compartment and struck its release with a wrench. The pod’s clamps let go with a heavy clunk. Juno continued talking, inventing technical terms with the confidence of a woman describing a meal she’d never tasted.

“Your flagship is already inside the starbreaker’s target field,” she said. The commander’s ship edged backward. Juno seized the chance. “Ten seconds.”

Niko shouted from the corridor, “Now!” Juno slammed the pod launch switch. It refused to move. She slammed it again, and the ship lurched as the countdown reached five.

The commander yelled something furious. Niko sprinted back and hit the switch with his wrench. The pod shot free. Juno followed him into the narrow capsule as the Finch began to glow from within.

The door sealed just as the timer reached zero. For a breath, there was only silence. Then the Finch blossomed into a white flare.

The blast washed across the alien fleet, bright enough to turn every ship into a black cutout. When the light faded, the Finch was gone. So were two empty cargo pods that had been tethered to its hull.

The alien ships scattered, convinced the starbreaker had fired. In the escape pod, Niko stared at Juno. “You told them we had a weapon.” Juno shrugged. “We did.”

“What was it?” “A ship that was about to explode.” Niko laughed despite himself.

Juno looked out at the retreating fleet. “Next time,” she said, “you’re doing the talking.” Niko tightened his grip on the wrench. “Next time, you’re building the escape pod.” Juno grinned.

“Deal,” she said. “But first, let’s find somewhere to land.”

Jon Downey was among the 52 people killed in the London bombings on 7 July 2005, when coordinated attacks struck the city’s transport network. His death left a lasting absence for his family, friends and community. A tribute to Jon is also a reminder that his life was much more than the circumstances in which it ended.

Those who remember him speak of a person whose relationships and everyday moments mattered deeply. He shared his life with family members who knew his character, humour and kindness at first hand. Friends and neighbours valued the time they spent with him and the place he held in their lives. Their memories keep his personality present, even as the years pass.

For the people closest to Jon, grief has meant learning to carry both sorrow and love. Birthdays, family gatherings and familiar routines can bring back the sharpness of loss. They can also offer chances to tell stories and celebrate the person he was. Each recollection helps preserve a fuller picture of Jon for those who knew him and for younger generations.

The community’s remembrance reflects that same desire to honour a life, not only mourn a death. Public acts of tribute bring private memories into a shared space. They also affirm that Jon is remembered as an individual, rather than reduced to a name among the victims of an attack. In that remembrance, his family’s loss is acknowledged alongside the strength of the bonds he built.

The 7 July bombings changed countless lives and left grief across London and beyond. The anniversary calls attention to the victims, while also renewing attention to those who continue to live with their absence. Jon’s story belongs to that wider history, but it remains uniquely his. It is carried in the people who loved him and in the community that still speaks his name.

A tribute cannot undo what happened or measure the full depth of his family’s loss. It can, however, make space for gratitude for the years they shared and for the memories that endure. Remembering Jon means holding on to the ordinary details that made him part of everyday life. It means honouring the family ties and community connections that shaped his world.

Twenty-one years after the attacks, that commitment to remembrance remains important. Jon Downey is remembered not only as a victim of terrorism, but as a son, relative, friend and neighbour. The life he shared with those around him continues in their stories, their affection and their determination not to forget.

MIPAS-B2 is a balloon-borne infrared spectrometer designed to study the composition and structure of Earth’s atmosphere. The name stands for Michelson Interferometer for Passive Atmospheric Sounding—Balloon version 2. It measures infrared radiation emitted naturally by atmospheric gases, rather than sending a signal into the atmosphere. This makes it a passive remote-sensing instrument.

MIPAS-B2 is carried high into the stratosphere by a large scientific balloon. From above much of the lower atmosphere, it observes the atmosphere along lines of sight near the horizon. This viewing geometry allows it to sample air at different altitudes over a long path. The instrument can also scan vertically to build a profile of the atmosphere.

At its core, MIPAS-B2 uses a Fourier transform spectrometer. The instrument separates incoming infrared radiation into its component wavelengths, producing a spectrum. Different molecules absorb and emit infrared radiation at characteristic wavelengths, much like fingerprints. Scientists use these spectral features to identify gases and estimate their amounts.

Measurements include ozone and gases involved in ozone chemistry, such as chlorine- and nitrogen-containing compounds. Depending on the observation and analysis, the spectra can also provide information about other trace gases and atmospheric constituents. These substances can affect ozone formation and destruction, especially in the stratosphere. Measuring them together helps researchers investigate the chemical processes that influence the ozone layer.

MIPAS-B2 can retrieve vertical profiles, which show how a gas’s concentration changes with altitude. It can also help determine atmospheric temperature and pressure profiles. Such profiles are important because chemical reactions and air movement vary throughout the atmosphere. They provide more detail than a single measurement of the total amount of a gas above a location.

Turning spectra into atmospheric profiles requires complex mathematical analysis. Researchers compare measured spectra with calculations of how radiation travels through the atmosphere. The retrieval process accounts for factors such as temperature, pressure, and overlapping spectral features. Results are checked for uncertainty and compared with measurements from other instruments when possible.

Balloon observations offer a useful middle ground between ground-based instruments and satellites. A balloon can carry sensitive equipment above much of the water vapor and other absorbing gases in the lower atmosphere. It can make detailed measurements during a focused campaign, although it does not provide continuous global coverage. Its flight path and altitude depend on balloon conditions and the mission plan.

Data from MIPAS-B2 contribute to studies of ozone depletion, atmospheric transport, and changes in stratospheric chemistry. They can also help test models used to understand and predict atmospheric behavior. By measuring several gases and physical properties in related observations, the instrument helps scientists connect chemical changes with the atmosphere’s structure. MIPAS-B2 is therefore a valuable research tool for understanding how the stratosphere works and how it may change over time.

Engineered Plants as Low-Cost Sensors for Detecting Explosives and Environmental Hazards

Plants can do more than provide food, shade, and oxygen. With careful genetic engineering, they can also act as living sensors that respond to chemicals in their surroundings. Researchers are exploring this idea as a potentially low-cost way to detect explosives and environmental hazards. Such plants would not replace laboratory testing or specialized safety equipment. Instead, they could provide an early warning that prompts people to investigate further.

A plant sensor works by linking the detection of a target chemical to a visible or measurable response. Scientists may introduce genetic instructions that cause a plant to change color, glow, or alter a detectable biological signal when it encounters a particular substance. The response depends on the sensor design and the chemical being targeted. For example, a plant might be engineered to react to compounds associated with explosives or to pollutants in soil or water.

Explosives detection is challenging because hazardous materials can be hidden, present in tiny amounts, or mixed with other substances. Some explosives release chemical traces that can move through soil, air, or water. A plant with an appropriate biological sensing system might respond to those traces near a contaminated site. This could help identify locations that deserve closer inspection, such as former military areas or suspected burial sites.

Environmental monitoring is another possible use. Plants could be designed to signal exposure to contaminants such as heavy metals, industrial chemicals, or excess nutrients. They might be placed near waterways, agricultural land, or industrial sites and checked for changes over time. Because plants interact continuously with their environment, they may provide information about exposure that a single water or soil sample could miss.

One attraction of plant sensors is their potential affordability. Plants can grow using sunlight and water, and some species can be cultivated over large areas. A visible response might also be easier to notice than a subtle change in a complex instrument reading. These features could make plant sensors useful in places where frequent laboratory testing is expensive or difficult.

However, “low-cost” does not mean effortless or automatically reliable. Plants grow at different rates and respond to factors such as temperature, light, drought, disease, and soil conditions. Those influences can mask a warning signal or create changes that resemble one. Researchers therefore need to test sensors under realistic conditions and distinguish target responses from ordinary plant stress.

Sensitivity and specificity are also important. A sensor must detect a meaningful amount of a hazard while avoiding false alarms from unrelated chemicals. Its response should be consistent across plants, locations, and seasons. Scientists may use control plants, repeated measurements, and follow-up chemical tests to interpret results. In many cases, a plant’s signal would serve as a screening tool rather than definitive proof of contamination.

Safety and responsible use matter, too. Engineered plants should be designed and managed to prevent unintended spread or crossbreeding with wild relatives. Containment, monitoring, and compliance with local regulations may be necessary, especially when plants are used outside controlled research settings. Public communication should explain what a signal means, what it does not mean, and who is responsible for confirming a suspected hazard.

Plant-based sensing is still an evolving field, and practical performance varies by design. Researchers continue to investigate which species, genetic circuits, and readout methods work best for particular targets. Future systems might combine plant responses with cameras or digital tools that record and interpret changes. Such tools could help people map warning signals over time, but they would still need validation and careful oversight.

The central idea is simple: living plants can be engineered to make invisible chemical information easier to notice. If scientists can make their responses reliable, safe, and easy to interpret, plant sensors could complement existing detection methods. Their greatest value may be in pointing investigators toward places that need attention. By combining biological sensing with conventional testing, communities could gain a useful additional way to monitor explosives-related traces and environmental hazards.

William Peter Blatty, the novelist and filmmaker best known for creating The Exorcist, has died aged 89. His death was announced in January 2017. Blatty wrote the 1971 novel, which became one of the most influential works of modern horror. It tells the story of a young girl possessed by a demon and the efforts to save her through an exorcism. The book became a worldwide bestseller and helped bring supernatural horror into the literary mainstream. Blatty adapted it for the screen in 1973, writing the screenplay for director William Friedkin. The film was a major box-office success and earned 10 Academy Award nominations, including a win for Blatty’s adapted screenplay. Its frightening scenes and themes of faith and evil made it a cultural landmark. Blatty also directed The Ninth Configuration, a 1980 psychological drama adapted from his novel. The film received a Golden Globe for best screenplay and was nominated for an Academy Award. Born in New York City in 1928, Blatty studied at Georgetown University, an experience that later informed The Exorcist’s setting. Before becoming a full-time writer, he worked in public relations and wrote comedy, including material for television. His career ranged from satire to horror, but The Exorcist remained his defining achievement. He leaves behind a body of work that helped shape generations of horror fiction and film.

Pip was the youngest duck in the pond at Central Park. As December crept in, the water turned to glass and the reeds wore collars of frost. The older ducks warned him to stay near the warm bank. But Pip had heard stories about a legendary Christmas tree lighting in Manhattan. They said the tree shone so brightly that even the stars leaned down to see it. Pip wanted to witness it for himself.

One chilly evening, he tucked his feet beneath his feathers and set off. The wind rushed between the buildings, tugging at his scarf. Snowflakes landed on his bill and melted into tiny, cold tears. Pip kept going, following the glow in the distance. At last, he reached Rockefeller Center, where a great crowd filled the plaza. People laughed and stamped their boots to keep warm. Pip squeezed between a pair of mittens and found a quiet spot by the railing.

The tree stood dark against the night, its branches heavy with ornaments. A hush fell over the crowd as a countdown began. “Three, two, one!” everyone shouted. Suddenly, thousands of lights burst to life, turning the square into a golden forest. Pip’s eyes widened, and his heart seemed to glow along with the tree. For a moment, he forgot the cold entirely. Then a kind child spotted him and wrapped a small knitted scarf around his neck.

Pip thanked the child with a happy quack. Beneath the sparkling branches, he felt braver than ever. When he waddled back to the pond, dawn was coloring the snow pink. The other ducks gathered around as he told them what he had seen. From then on, each winter, they watched the Manhattan lights from the park and remembered Pip’s shining adventure.

A woman has been jailed for manslaughter after exploiting her elderly housemate and setting fire to their home. The fire killed the housemate, whose identity has not been made public. A court heard that the woman had taken advantage of the victim’s vulnerability while they shared the property. Prosecutors said the blaze was started deliberately, though the precise motive was not detailed in court. Emergency crews were called to the home, but the victim could not be saved. The woman was arrested and later charged in connection with the death. At trial, jurors found her guilty of manslaughter. The court said her actions showed a serious disregard for the victim’s safety. She was sentenced to prison, though the length of the term was not provided in the information available. The judge acknowledged the profound loss suffered by the victim’s family and friends. The case has renewed attention on the risks faced by older people who rely on others in their homes. Authorities urged anyone concerned about an older person’s welfare to contact local support services.

Schools should allow students to carry cell phones for safety and communication with their parents. Phones can help students contact their families if they need a ride or have an emergency. They can also be useful when school plans change unexpectedly. For example, a parent can quickly let a student know that someone else will pick them up. Having a phone may also help students feel safer while traveling to and from school.

However, cell phones can distract students during class. Some students may use them to play games, send messages, or look at social media instead of learning. Phones can also be used to take pictures or videos without permission. These problems are important, but schools can address them with clear rules.

Students could be asked to keep their phones silent and put away during lessons. Teachers could allow phone use only when it supports a classroom activity or when there is an emergency. Schools should also explain the consequences for breaking the rules. Parents and students should understand that having a phone is a responsibility.

Overall, students should be allowed to carry cell phones, but their use should be limited during the school day. This approach gives students a way to communicate with their parents while protecting the learning environment. With fair rules, schools can balance safety, communication, and focus.

Exploring Venus is one of the most exciting challenges in space science. Although it is similar in size to Earth, its surface is an extremely hostile place. Temperatures are hot enough to melt lead, and the thick atmosphere creates crushing pressure. The air is mostly carbon dioxide, with clouds containing corrosive sulfuric acid. These conditions make it difficult for spacecraft to survive for long. Past landers sent by the Soviet Union lasted only a short time on the surface.

Future technology could help us study Venus more effectively. Stronger materials and advanced cooling systems might allow landers to operate for days or weeks. Balloons and robotic aircraft could explore the cooler upper atmosphere, where pressure and temperature are less extreme. Scientists could also use orbiters to map the surface and measure changes in the atmosphere. Better instruments may reveal whether Venus once had oceans or conditions that could have supported life. Comparing Venus with Earth could also explain why the two planets developed so differently.

Human missions could bring important benefits, but they would be especially difficult. Astronauts would need protection from intense heat, high pressure, toxic gases, and radiation. A human expedition might be safer in floating habitats high above the surface than in a ground base. People could repair equipment and make decisions quickly, but sending them would require enormous amounts of money and careful planning. Robotic missions are safer and less expensive, so they will probably explore Venus first.

Even with these obstacles, exploring Venus could improve life on Earth. Research on its atmosphere may help scientists understand climate change and the effects of greenhouse gases. New technologies created for Venus missions could also be useful in other areas of science and engineering. Most importantly, studying our neighboring planet would expand our knowledge of how planets change over time. Venus is a dangerous destination, but future technology may make it possible to explore its mysteries.

Milo arrived at Madame Venn’s office with a list of grievances and a damp umbrella.

“I want to curse my neighbor,” he said, “but nothing permanent.”

Madame Venn adjusted her spectacles and opened a ledger ruled into very small squares.

“Do you prefer inconvenience, embarrassment, or mild confusion?”

“Could we combine them?”

“Certainly, for an additional fee.”

Milo explained that Mr. Pottle kept borrowing his garden shears and returning them sticky.

Madame Venn asked whether the stickiness was honey, sap, or an unidentified substance.

“Probably jam,” Milo said.

She made a note, underlined it twice, and quoted him three pennies for a curse that would make Pottle’s left sock feel slightly damp.

“Would he notice?”

“Eventually.”

Milo paid, and Madame Venn measured the curse with a brass ruler before folding it into a blue envelope.

The next week, he returned, furious.

“Pottle’s sock was damp, but he blamed the washing machine.”

“That is a common misattribution,” she said, checking a chart.

“Can you make his teacup wobble whenever he tells a lie?”

“Define lie.”

“Anything he says about my begonias.”

Madame Venn consulted a dictionary, a calendar, and a tiny bell.

She charged Milo six pennies and promised the cup would wobble no more than twice per statement.

When Milo came back again, he admitted Pottle had simply switched to coffee.

“Then curse his coffee,” he pleaded.

“What quality should it possess?”

“Make it taste of regret.”

Madame Venn considered this, then explained that regret varied by person and might require a consultation.

Milo couldn’t afford it, so he settled for coffee that cooled one minute faster than expected.

A month later, he arrived grinning: Pottle had stopped borrowing the shears after deciding they were haunted.

Madame Venn entered the outcome in her ledger, noting that the curse had worked through “unintended tool anxiety.”

Milo asked if she could curse the jam on the shears to vanish.

She handed him a cloth, a bottle of soap, and an invoice for practical advice.

He paid without complaint, and left with the odd feeling that his neighbor’s sticky shears were the least troublesome thing in his life.

Pumpkins grow best in a sunny spot that gets at least six to eight hours of direct sunlight each day. Choose loose, fertile, well-drained soil with a pH of about 6.0 to 6.8. Mix in compost or well-rotted manure before planting to improve soil structure and provide nutrients. Sow seeds outdoors after the danger of frost has passed and the soil has warmed to at least 65°F (18°C). Plant seeds about 1 inch deep, or start them indoors a few weeks earlier in biodegradable pots to avoid disturbing their roots. Keep the soil consistently moist, especially while seedlings are establishing and fruits are forming, but avoid waterlogged conditions. Water at the base of the plants to help keep leaves dry and reduce the risk of disease. Pumpkins need plenty of room because their vines can spread widely. For traditional sprawling varieties, space hills about 6 to 8 feet apart, with two or three plants per hill. Compact or bush varieties can usually be planted closer together, so follow the seed packet’s spacing guidance. Mulch around plants to conserve moisture, suppress weeds, and keep developing pumpkins off damp soil. Watch for pests and signs of disease, and remove weeds carefully to avoid damaging shallow roots. Harvest pumpkins when they have reached their mature color and the rind is hard enough that a fingernail does not easily pierce it. The vine near the stem often becomes dry or corky as the fruit ripens, though this sign varies by variety. Cut each pumpkin from the vine with pruning shears, leaving a few inches of stem attached, and avoid carrying it by the stem. Cure sound pumpkins in a warm, dry, well-ventilated place for about 10 days, then store them in a cool, dry location.
