North Wales has been named one of the world’s top travel destinations for 2017, placing fourth in Lonely Planet’s annual Best in Travel list.

The guidebook publisher’s rankings highlight regions expected to appeal to travellers in the year ahead. North Wales was the only UK destination to feature among the top 10 regions.

Lonely Planet praised the area’s mix of rugged landscapes, historic sites and outdoor activities. It pointed to Snowdonia National Park, where visitors can hike mountain trails and take in views of the surrounding countryside.

The region’s coastline was another draw, with beaches and seaside towns offering a change of pace from the mountains. North Wales also has a rich industrial and cultural history, reflected in its slate heritage and network of castles.

Among the best-known landmarks is Caernarfon Castle, a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The region is also home to Conwy Castle and the walled town of Conwy, both popular with visitors.

Adventure tourism has grown in recent years, with activities including zip-lining, mountain biking and climbing. Attractions such as Zip World have helped draw visitors seeking high-adrenaline experiences.

The ranking could give North Wales a boost as it competes for international visitors. Tourism businesses may benefit from greater attention to the region’s landscapes and heritage.

Lonely Planet’s annual list is based on recommendations from its travel experts and contributors. Its Best in Travel selection includes countries, cities and regions, each chosen for factors such as traveller appeal and developments that make a destination worth visiting.

The fourth-place ranking puts North Wales in the company of destinations around the world. For local tourism leaders, the recognition offers an opportunity to encourage longer stays and promote travel beyond the region’s best-known attractions.

Hello team,

We are reviewing outage notification procedures for our critical business applications and hardware. When an outage is detected, the service owner should promptly notify the IT operations team and affected business stakeholders. Notifications should include the affected services, known impact, estimated duration, and any available workarounds. For major incidents, updates should be sent at regular intervals, even when there is no significant change. Once service is restored, a final notice should summarize the resolution and any follow-up actions. We are also developing diagnostic tools to help identify the source of outages more quickly. These tools will collect relevant system health data, flag unusual behavior, and support consistent troubleshooting across teams. Please share requirements for the applications and hardware you support, including the key alerts and diagnostics that would be most useful. We will use your feedback to define priorities, testing plans, and ownership. Thank you for helping improve our incident response and service reliability.

Facial-expression recognition technology could offer several benefits in classrooms when used carefully. It may help staff notice signs of distress, confusion, or discomfort that a student has not expressed aloud. This could allow teachers to check in sooner and connect students with appropriate support. For safety, the technology might alert staff to visible signs of pain or panic, especially when a student cannot easily ask for help. It could also help teachers understand whether lessons are engaging or need to be explained differently. For students who communicate in different ways, expression cues might provide one more source of information. However, facial expressions do not always reveal what someone is feeling, and cultural or personal differences can lead to misunderstandings. Schools should protect students’ privacy, obtain appropriate consent, and never rely on the technology alone to make important decisions. Used transparently as a limited aid, it could support communication and care while keeping human judgment at the center.

Balancing sunscreen safety concerns with effective protection for children from ultraviolet radiation

Ultraviolet radiation from the sun can damage children’s skin, even on cool or cloudy days. Repeated exposure and sunburns during childhood increase the risk of skin cancer later in life. Sun protection is therefore important, but it does not need to mean avoiding the outdoors. The goal is to reduce excessive ultraviolet exposure while allowing children to play safely outside.

Sunlight contains UVA and UVB rays. UVB rays are a major cause of sunburn, while UVA rays contribute to skin aging and can also damage skin. Both types can contribute to skin cancer. A sunscreen labeled “broad spectrum” protects against UVA and UVB.

For most children, choose a broad-spectrum sunscreen with SPF 30 or higher. SPF mainly describes protection against UVB when sunscreen is applied correctly. A higher SPF does not mean a child can stay in the sun indefinitely. No sunscreen blocks all ultraviolet radiation.

Apply sunscreen generously to dry skin about 15 minutes before going outdoors, following the product label. Cover all exposed skin, including ears, the back of the neck, hands, feet, and the part in a child’s hair. Use a lip balm with sun protection for exposed lips. Ask another adult to help with areas that are difficult to reach.

Many people apply too little sunscreen, which reduces the protection they receive. Reapply at least every two hours, and sooner after swimming, sweating, or towel drying. Water-resistant products can help during swimming, but “water-resistant” does not mean waterproof. Follow the label for how long the product remains water resistant.

For babies younger than six months, keep them out of direct sunlight as much as possible. Use shade, a stroller canopy, and lightweight clothing that covers the arms and legs. If shade and clothing cannot adequately protect a small area of skin, ask a pediatrician about using a small amount of sunscreen. Babies are more vulnerable to overheating, so do not rely on sunscreen as the main form of protection.

For older babies and children, sunscreen is one part of a broader sun-safety plan. Seek shade, especially around midday when the sun’s rays are strongest. A wide-brimmed hat can protect the face, ears, and neck. Sunglasses that block 99 to 100 percent of UVA and UVB rays help protect children’s eyes.

Choose lightweight, tightly woven clothing, or garments with an ultraviolet protection factor rating. A higher UPF indicates that less ultraviolet radiation passes through the fabric. Wet or stretched clothing may offer less protection than dry, well-fitting clothing. Encourage breaks in shaded areas and provide water to help children stay comfortable.

Some parents worry that sunscreen ingredients may be harmful. These concerns are worth discussing, but they should be weighed against the established harms of excessive ultraviolet exposure. Major health authorities recommend sunscreen as part of sun protection for children when used as directed. The FDA continues to review sunscreen ingredients, and available evidence does not establish that approved sunscreen products cause harm when used according to their labels.

In the United States, mineral sunscreens commonly use zinc oxide or titanium dioxide as active ingredients. These ingredients sit on the skin’s surface and help block or scatter ultraviolet rays. Some families prefer them because they are less likely to irritate sensitive skin. They may leave a white cast, though newer formulations can reduce this effect.

Other sunscreens use organic, sometimes called chemical, filters that absorb ultraviolet radiation. These products are considered safe and effective when used as directed, although some children may develop irritation or an allergy to an ingredient. If a product causes a rash, stop using it and seek medical advice if the reaction is severe or persistent. A small test on an area of skin can help identify irritation before wider use.

Spray sunscreens can be convenient, but they are easy to apply unevenly. Avoid spraying near a child’s face, and do not let children inhale the mist. Spray the product into an adult’s hands, then apply it to the child’s face. Use sprays outdoors and away from flames, since some products are flammable.

Sunscreen should not be used to extend time in strong sunlight. It can create a false sense of security, especially when too little is applied or reapplication is missed. Combine sunscreen with shade, protective clothing, hats, and sunglasses. Check the local UV index to plan outdoor activities when sunlight is less intense.

Teach children simple habits early. Make sunscreen part of the routine before outdoor play, school events, and sports. Let older children practice applying it while an adult checks that no areas were missed. Keep a sunscreen in a convenient place, and check its expiration date and storage instructions.

Sun protection is especially important for children with very fair skin, many moles, a history of sunburn, or a family history of skin cancer. Children taking medicines that increase sensitivity to sunlight may also need extra precautions. Ask a pediatrician or pharmacist whether a child’s medicine changes sun sensitivity. Seek medical care for a severe sunburn, blistering, fever, or signs of dehydration.

The best sunscreen is one that protects well and that a family can use consistently. Concerns about ingredients can guide product choice, but they should not lead to leaving children unprotected. Use a broad-spectrum SPF 30 or higher sunscreen on exposed skin, apply enough, and reapply as directed. Pair it with shade and protective clothing for practical, effective protection throughout childhood.

Subject: Fair Compensation for Employees Affected by Enron’s Collapse

Dear [CEO/Board Members],

I am writing to express my deep concern about reports that the CEO may receive a substantial severance package as Enron collapses. Many employees are facing sudden job losses and uncertainty about their financial futures. Some have also seen their retirement savings put at risk. In this context, a generous executive payout would be difficult to justify. It would send a painful message to workers who helped build the company. They should not bear the consequences alone while senior leaders receive special protection.

I urge the board to review any proposed severance arrangement with care. The company’s remaining resources should be used responsibly and transparently. Employees who have lost their jobs deserve clear information about their pay, benefits, and next steps. They also deserve timely payment of wages and any compensation they are owed. Where possible, the company should provide continued health coverage and practical transition support. Workers nearing retirement need particular attention and guidance. The board should also explain what protections are available for employees whose savings were affected.

This is not a request to overlook due process or established agreements. It is a call for fairness during an extraordinary crisis. Any executive compensation should be assessed against the losses experienced by employees and other stakeholders. If a severance package is approved, the reasons and terms should be disclosed. The board should consider whether funds can be redirected toward a meaningful worker-support program. Such support could include severance assistance, career counseling, and help accessing benefits. Independent oversight would help ensure that assistance reaches those who need it.

Enron’s collapse has damaged trust in the company and its leadership. A fair response cannot undo that harm, but it can show that employees are being treated with respect. I ask the board to put affected workers at the center of its decisions. Please share what steps will be taken and when employees can expect an update. A prompt, honest response would be an important first step. I hope the company will choose accountability and compassion over appearances.

Sincerely,
[Your Name]

Seeking guidance is an important part of making thoughtful decisions. People often turn to others when they face choices that feel difficult or unfamiliar. However, no two people see a situation in exactly the same way. Their perspectives are shaped by their values, knowledge, and experiences. Listening to several viewpoints can reveal possibilities that one person might overlook. For example, a family member may understand our personal needs, while a teacher can offer practical advice. Someone who has faced a similar challenge may share lessons learned from experience. Their story can help us anticipate obstacles and avoid repeating mistakes. At the same time, advice should not be followed blindly. A person’s experience may be different from our own, and what worked for them may not work for us. Comparing different opinions helps us ask better questions and think carefully about the consequences. We can then use the guidance that fits our situation while remaining responsible for our choice. In this way, varied perspectives and past experiences help people make wiser, more balanced decisions.

Paraguay’s Senate prepared to consider impeaching President Fernando Lugo on Friday, a day after deadly clashes during a land eviction intensified a political crisis. At least 17 people were killed when police and landless farmers confronted one another at a disputed property in the country’s northeast, officials said. The dead included 11 farmers and six police officers.

The violence erupted in Curuguaty, in Canindeyú department, as officers moved to remove farmers occupying land claimed by a prominent landowner. Authorities said gunfire broke out during the operation, though accounts of how the confrontation began differed. The deaths stunned the country and prompted calls for senior officials to take responsibility.

Lugo accepted the resignation of Interior Minister Carlos Filizzola and the national police chief following the clashes. He appointed new officials and announced an investigation into the violence. The president also expressed sorrow for the victims and urged Paraguayans to remain calm.

Opposition lawmakers argued that Lugo had failed to maintain public order and protect citizens. They moved to begin impeachment proceedings, accusing him of poor performance in office. The lower house approved the charge, sending the matter to the Senate, which was expected to decide whether to remove him.

Lugo, a former Catholic bishop elected in 2008, has faced persistent opposition in Congress. His supporters described the impeachment effort as politically motivated and warned that a rapid proceeding could undermine democratic norms. The president said he would respect constitutional procedures but intended to defend himself.

The land dispute reflects a longstanding divide over ownership and access to farmland in Paraguay. Many rural families live with little or no land, while large estates dominate agriculture. Activists have pressed successive governments to redistribute land and resolve contested titles.

International concern grew as the impeachment process advanced. Regional governments and organizations called for due process and a peaceful resolution. Paraguay’s political future now rested with the Senate, as the country mourned those killed in Curuguaty.

Autonomous vehicles are cars and trucks that can travel with little or no help from a human driver. Their development is becoming increasingly common as computers, cameras, and sensors improve. Although these vehicles offer important benefits, they also create risks that society must manage.

One major benefit is the possibility of reducing crashes caused by human mistakes. Drivers may become distracted, tired, or impaired, while an automated system can monitor the road continuously. Self-driving vehicles could also help people who are unable to drive because of age or disability. In addition, they may make travel more convenient by allowing passengers to work or rest during a journey. If widely adopted, coordinated autonomous cars might reduce traffic congestion and use fuel more efficiently.

However, the technology is not perfect. Sensors can struggle in heavy rain, snow, fog, or unusual road conditions. A software error or a failure to recognize a person or obstacle could cause a serious crash. Autonomous vehicles may also be vulnerable to hackers who interfere with their systems. Another concern is that driving-related jobs could decline, affecting truck drivers, taxi drivers, and delivery workers. Questions about responsibility also remain: if a self-driving car causes a crash, it may be unclear whether the manufacturer, software developer, owner, or passenger is at fault.

Despite these concerns, the development of autonomous vehicles seems difficult to avoid. Companies and governments are investing in the technology, and demand for safer and more convenient transportation is likely to continue. Rather than rejecting progress, society should set strict safety standards and require transparent testing. Governments should also create clear rules about liability, data privacy, and cybersecurity. Workers whose jobs are affected should have access to training and support.

Autonomous vehicles will not solve every transportation problem, and they should not be trusted without careful oversight. Their benefits could be substantial if the risks are taken seriously. With thoughtful laws, ongoing testing, and public input, self-driving vehicles can be developed more responsibly. Their arrival may be inevitable, but the way society manages them is still a choice.

Remote learning has become an important part of education. It allows students to attend lessons from home or another convenient location. When planned well, this approach can support academic performance, mental well-being, and family connections. It also gives students new ways to organize their time and learning. However, its benefits depend on access to technology, thoughtful teaching, and support from adults.

One academic advantage of remote learning is flexibility. Students can often review recorded lessons and learning materials at their own pace. This gives them more time to understand difficult ideas. They can pause a video, reread instructions, or repeat an example without feeling rushed. Flexible schedules may also help students complete assignments when they are most focused. In addition, online platforms make it easier to find articles, videos, and practice activities. Students can communicate with teachers through messages or virtual meetings when they need help. These options can encourage learners to take more responsibility for their progress. Remote classes may also reduce time spent traveling to school, leaving more time for studying or rest. Still, students need clear routines and goals so that flexibility does not lead to distraction or missed work.

Remote learning can also benefit students’ mental well-being. Learning at home may feel less stressful for students who find busy classrooms overwhelming. A familiar environment can help them feel comfortable and secure. Some students may be more willing to ask questions in a private online message than in front of a whole class. They may also have more control over breaks and their study space. This can help them balance schoolwork with sleep, exercise, and other healthy habits. For students dealing with illness, anxiety, or difficult circumstances, learning remotely may make education easier to continue. However, spending too much time alone can increase loneliness. Long hours in front of a screen can also cause tiredness and reduce concentration. Teachers and families can help by encouraging movement, regular breaks, and contact with classmates. Access to school counselors and other support services remains important, even when students are learning online.

Remote learning can strengthen family connections as well. Parents and caregivers may gain a clearer picture of what students are studying. They can offer encouragement, help organize a study space, and celebrate progress. Shared routines, such as checking a weekly schedule together, can create useful conversations about school. Students may also have more time at home to talk with family members or help with everyday tasks. These experiences can build trust and cooperation. At the same time, families may have busy schedules, limited devices, or little space for studying. Adults should support students without doing their work for them. Schools can help by giving families clear instructions and connecting them with technical or academic assistance.

In conclusion, remote learning can support academic success, emotional well-being, and stronger family relationships. Its flexibility can help students learn at a suitable pace and make better use of their time. A supportive home environment may also make learning feel safer and more personal. Yet remote education works best when students have reliable resources, regular interaction, and guidance from teachers and families. With these supports, learning from a distance can be a valuable part of a student’s education.

Subject: Separate Credit Support Annexes for New EPMI and Existing Power ISDA Agreements
