Reducing car use can make communities healthier, safer, and less stressful. Cars are useful, but depending on them for every trip creates problems for people and the environment. When more residents walk, bike, or use public transportation, neighborhoods can become cleaner and more pleasant places to live.

One important benefit is improved health. Walking and cycling add physical activity to daily routines, helping people stay fit and reducing the risk of some illnesses. Fewer cars also means less air pollution, which can make it easier for everyone to breathe, especially children and people with asthma. Streets with fewer vehicles can be quieter, too, supporting better sleep and a calmer atmosphere.

Alternative transportation can also make roads safer. Fewer cars usually mean fewer chances for crashes involving drivers, passengers, cyclists, and pedestrians. Communities can improve safety further by building sidewalks, protected bike lanes, and reliable crossings. When streets are designed for people as well as vehicles, children and older adults may feel more comfortable getting around.

Choosing other ways to travel can reduce stress as well. Heavy traffic and the search for parking can make driving frustrating and time-consuming. On a bus or train, passengers may be able to read, rest, or listen to music instead of concentrating on traffic. Walking or cycling can also offer a refreshing break in the day.

Of course, alternatives need to be convenient and accessible. Frequent buses, safe paths, and affordable fares help people choose options that fit their needs. Not everyone can stop driving, but many people can replace some car trips with walking, cycling, or transit. Even small changes can add up when many residents take part.

By reducing unnecessary car use, communities can improve health, safety, and quality of life. Supporting a range of transportation choices benefits both individuals and their neighbors. A community designed for people, not just cars, can be a healthier and more welcoming place for everyone.

No rain ever stayed on Elias Venn’s skin; each drop slid away as if he were made of polished glass. In town, people whispered that he had been born beneath a strange star. He avoided the river, the lake, and even the public pool, claiming he simply disliked swimming. At every meal, he drank soda, never water, and kept a bottle tucked inside his coat. One foggy night, a child fell from the dock into the river. Elias leaped in before anyone else could move, and the water parted from his body like curtains. He carried the child safely to shore, then hurried away as the crowd stared. By morning, only a fizzing bottle remained on the dock, its label beaded with dry, shining drops.

A Council of Europe report has renewed calls for accountability over the 2009 death of Russian lawyer Sergei Magnitsky, while questioning whether U.S. sanctions against Russian officials are the right response.

The report, adopted by the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe, says Russian authorities failed to investigate the circumstances of Magnitsky’s death effectively. It describes his treatment in custody as a grave violation of his rights and urges officials responsible to face justice.

Magnitsky, a lawyer and auditor, was arrested in 2008 after alleging that Russian officials had carried out a large tax fraud. He died in a Moscow detention center a year later, aged 37. Russian authorities said he died from health problems, but his supporters argued that he was denied medical care and subjected to abuse.

The assembly called on Russia to conduct a thorough, independent investigation into his death and the fraud allegations he had raised. It also urged the authorities to prosecute those implicated, regardless of their rank or position. The report said accountability should extend beyond the immediate circumstances of Magnitsky’s death.

At the same time, lawmakers expressed reservations about the approach taken by the United States. Washington’s 2012 Magnitsky Act imposed visa bans and asset freezes on Russian officials linked to human rights abuses. The report questioned the use of unilateral sanctions and raised concerns about their effectiveness and fairness.

It argued that targeted measures should be based on clear evidence and accompanied by due process. Sanctions, the report said, can affect individuals’ rights and should not replace criminal investigations. It also warned that such measures may complicate international cooperation.

The report did not dismiss the U.S. actions outright. Instead, it urged governments to pursue accountability through transparent legal procedures and coordinated international efforts. It called on European states to consider their own responsibilities in addressing the case.

The findings highlight a difficult balance between seeking justice and ensuring that responses respect the rule of law. Supporters of Magnitsky have long argued that sanctions are among the few tools available when domestic authorities fail to act. Critics, however, say sanctions can be politically selective and lack the safeguards of court proceedings.

The Council of Europe’s assembly also pressed Russia to improve conditions in detention facilities and ensure timely access to medical care. It said the case had exposed broader weaknesses in the treatment of detainees and the independence of law enforcement. Those concerns, it added, should be addressed through systemic reforms.

The report is not a court judgment, and its recommendations are not legally binding. But it places renewed international attention on a case that has strained relations between Russia and Western governments for years. Russian officials have rejected allegations that Magnitsky was deliberately mistreated.

For Magnitsky’s family and supporters, the central demand remains a credible account of how he died and who was responsible. The report says that demand has still not been met. It calls for action that delivers justice without abandoning the legal standards it seeks to uphold.

At 8:03 on Tuesday, Barlow Venn stole a parade float shaped like a giant avocado. He had never driven anything larger than a shopping cart, but he announced that the steering wheel looked “mostly decorative.” The float roared awake, though nobody had turned the key. Barlow took this as a compliment from the engine.

He aimed for the town square and immediately drove through a bakery. Croissants flew into the air like startled birds, and one landed neatly on his head. “A crown,” he declared, and accelerated. The float burst through the bakery’s back wall and entered a ballroom where the mayor was practicing a speech to a roomful of stuffed owls.

The owls applauded with their glass eyes. The mayor did not. Barlow waved at them and shouted that he was late for a meeting with gravity. At the square, the float’s avocado pit popped open, releasing a marching band that had been trapped inside since last year’s festival. They marched in reverse, playing a song nobody had composed.

The music made every traffic light turn purple. Cars stopped, taxis climbed onto sidewalks, and a delivery van began reciting poetry. Barlow steered confidently through the confusion, explaining that purple meant “go, but with imagination.” Then the fountain rose from the pavement and followed him like a loyal dog.

It barked water at his tires. Barlow congratulated it on its enthusiasm. The mayor chased after him on a unicycle, still holding his speech, while the owls flew overhead in a neat formation. At the bridge, the float’s brakes detached and rolled away, leaving a note that read, “We need space.”

Barlow waved goodbye to them and crossed the river at full speed. The float’s wheels began spinning vertically, lifting it into the air. He called this an unexpected upgrade. A flock of pigeons formed a courtroom around him and charged him with reckless optimism.

Barlow pleaded not guilty because he had not been optimistic recklessly, but professionally. The pigeons sentenced him to spend one hour inside the moon. The moon, which had been waiting above the bridge, opened a small door in its side. Barlow stepped through without hesitation.

Inside, he found a laundromat, a sleepy astronaut, and the missing brakes playing cards. He asked them to come home, but the brakes demanded better working conditions. Barlow promised them a shorter week and a complimentary hat. They accepted, and the float dropped back toward town.

It landed gently in the square, right on top of the mayor’s unicycle. The marching band played a triumphant tune, and the fountain shook water from its leaves. Barlow climbed down, bowed to the pigeons, and announced that everything had gone exactly as planned. Then the giant avocado winked, and Barlow confidently climbed back in.

Rising concerns over tougher assessments of English councils’ children’s services have prompted calls for Ofsted to reconsider how it inspects local authorities. Council leaders and children’s services professionals say recent inspection findings are becoming harder to reconcile with the pressures facing frontline teams. They argue that assessments should reflect not only outcomes for children, but also shortages of staff, limited budgets and growing demand.

Ofsted inspects how councils support children at risk, children in care and care leavers. Its judgments can influence public confidence, council planning and decisions about intervention. A poor rating can also make it harder for an authority to recruit and retain experienced social workers.

Some local government representatives believe the inspection framework places too much weight on whether services meet prescribed processes. They say this can encourage teams to prioritise documentation and compliance over direct work with children and families. Ofsted maintains that reliable records and consistent practice are important safeguards.

The debate has intensified as councils report increasing numbers of children needing support. Authorities face pressure across early help, child protection, fostering and residential care. At the same time, many are competing for social workers in a tight labour market.

Leaders have called for greater recognition of these conditions when inspectors assess performance. They say councils should not be judged in isolation from the wider system, including the availability of health, education and specialist services. Delays or gaps in those services can affect children’s experiences even when a council has taken appropriate action.

Others have warned against weakening independent scrutiny. Children’s advocates say robust inspections can expose failures that might otherwise remain hidden. They argue that clear standards are essential, particularly for children who depend on public services for their safety and stability.

The challenge, they say, is to distinguish between unavoidable system pressures and shortcomings that councils can address. Inspection teams must also consider whether leaders understand risks and are acting decisively to improve practice. A shortage of resources, critics note, cannot excuse preventable harm.

Ofsted has said its inspections are intended to focus on children’s experiences and the effectiveness of services. The watchdog has also been reviewing aspects of its inspection approach following concerns raised by social workers, councils and other organisations. Any changes are likely to be closely watched by authorities and families alike.

Calls for reform include clearer explanations of how evidence is weighed and more consistent communication between inspectors and council staff. Some professionals have also asked for stronger recognition of improvement over time, rather than an emphasis on a single inspection snapshot. They say feedback should help services make practical changes, not simply rank them.

There is also concern about the impact of inspection pressure on staff wellbeing. Social workers may face intense scrutiny while managing complex caseloads and emotionally demanding situations. Council leaders warn that a system perceived as punitive could make recruitment and retention harder.

Families and young people have a central stake in the debate. Their experiences can reveal whether services are accessible, respectful and responsive. Advocates say their views must be gathered meaningfully, rather than treated as a formal requirement.

Any revision of the standards is expected to involve difficult choices. More flexibility could help inspectors account for local circumstances, but inconsistent judgments could undermine confidence in the system. Tighter rules could improve comparability while leaving less room to recognise differences between councils.

The government, Ofsted and local authorities will need to agree what a fair assessment should measure. That includes the quality of social work, the safety of children and the availability of support before problems escalate. It also raises questions about how responsibility should be shared when services outside a council’s control are under strain.

For now, councils continue to prepare for inspections while pressing for a wider discussion about the framework. Their message is that accountability must remain firm, but should reflect the realities of delivering children’s services. The debate is ultimately about ensuring scrutiny protects children while helping local services improve.

Artificial intelligence is reshaping daily life, prompting an increasingly urgent debate over its benefits, risks and effects on society. From medical research to customer service, AI systems can process information quickly and take on tasks once handled only by people. Supporters say the technology could improve productivity, expand access to services and help solve complex problems. Critics warn that its rapid spread may deepen inequality, undermine privacy and disrupt jobs.

One area drawing particular attention is elder care. As populations age and care-worker shortages grow, some facilities are testing robots to help older adults with routine tasks. These machines can remind residents to take medication, guide them through exercises, carry supplies or connect them with family members by video. Some are designed to offer conversation or companionship, though researchers say their ability to understand human emotions remains limited.

Advocates argue that robots could ease staff workloads and give caregivers more time for personal, hands-on support. For older adults living alone, monitoring systems may also help detect falls or unusual changes in daily routines. But the technology raises questions about consent, data security and whether constant monitoring could compromise dignity. Families and care providers must also consider what happens when a system fails or misreads a person’s needs.

The debate extends well beyond care homes. AI tools are changing hiring, education, journalism and creative work, while automated systems increasingly influence decisions about loans, insurance and public services. Researchers caution that biased training data can produce unfair outcomes, particularly for groups already facing discrimination. The systems can also generate convincing false information, making it harder to distinguish reliable reporting from fabricated content.

Governments and technology companies are under pressure to establish safeguards without blocking useful innovation. Proposed measures include independent testing, clearer disclosure when people interact with AI, and stronger rules for handling personal data. Experts also emphasize the need for human oversight in high-stakes decisions, including medical care and access to essential services.

No single policy is likely to settle the argument. The impact of AI will depend on how it is designed, who controls it and whether its benefits are broadly shared. In elder care, many specialists say robots should support—not replace—human relationships. As the technology advances, societies will have to decide not only what AI can do, but what responsibilities should remain firmly in human hands.

The young artist had rehearsed the announcement all morning. “Mr. Disney,” he said, clutching a stack of sketches, “we’ve settled on the title for the new animated picture.”

Walt looked up from his desk. “Wonderful. What is it?”

The artist’s mouth went dry. He had meant to say it confidently, with a grand pause, perhaps even a flourish. Instead, he blurted, “Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs.”

Walt blinked. “That’s quite a title.”

“Yes, sir,” the artist said. “It’s about a princess named Snow White, and seven little men who—well, they’re not exactly men, but they’re grown-ups, and they’re dwarfs, and there are seven of them.”

“I see,” Walt said, trying not to smile.

The artist shuffled his sketches. “We thought about calling it The Seven Dwarfs, but then people might wonder where Snow White was.”

“Fair point.”

“Then we considered Snow White, but that sounded as if the dwarfs were only visiting.”

Walt leaned back. “And you settled on the whole thing.”

“Yes, sir. The whole thing.”

A secretary passing the doorway paused at the long title. The artist noticed and turned bright red.

“It’s a little awkward to say,” he admitted.

“Most good stories are awkward before they’re finished,” Walt replied.

The artist relaxed enough to laugh. “I’m glad you like it.”

“I didn’t say that yet,” Walt said, grinning. “Tell me the story.”

So the artist began, describing the jealous queen, the forest, and the cottage with seven tiny beds. Walt listened closely, asking questions whenever the artist stumbled.

When the tale ended, Walt tapped the title on the top sketch. “Keep it,” he said. “People will remember it.”

The artist left the office repeating the words under his breath, trying to make them sound natural. By the time the film became a hit, he could say “Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs” without blushing—though he still paused for breath before “Dwarfs.”

Mara carried the sealed case through the rain, keeping one hand on its silver latch. The company had promised a bonus if she delivered it before dawn. She had also been promised safe passage, though the streets ahead were empty. At the old rail bridge, headlights bloomed behind her. Three riders in gray coats swept in from the fog. One shouted for the case. Mara dropped her bicycle and ran. A shot cracked against the bridge’s ironwork. She slid down an embankment, struck the mud, and kept moving. The riders searched the road above, arguing about which way she had gone. Mara crawled beneath a drainage pipe and held her breath. When they finally left, she climbed out with a bleeding shoulder and the case still locked to her wrist. She limped toward a service station, where a night clerk gave her a towel and called the company. “Recovery is on the way,” dispatch said. The clerk’s relief made Mara uneasy. Ten minutes later, a black sedan rolled into the lot. Its driver wore a company badge and carried no umbrella. “You’re safe now,” he said, reaching for the case. Mara asked why he had come alone. “Because the ambush was never meant to take you,” he answered. “It was meant to make sure you opened the case somewhere private.” His hand moved toward his coat. Mara bolted for the door, but her injured leg buckled. The recovery specialist caught her before she hit the floor. He took the case, then quietly silenced her. At dawn, the company logged the delivery as complete. Outside, the rain washed Mara’s blood toward the gutter.

The first thing they gave Mara after prison was a key to a greenhouse.
It opened a narrow door in the old railway station, where sunlight warmed the glass and basil scented the air.
The program’s director, Mr. Vale, called it the Pleasure Workshop.
“People change more easily when they have something good to move toward,” he said.
Mara had expected lectures, rules, and another list of ways she had failed.
Instead, she found a potter’s wheel, a piano, a kitchen, and a wall of books.
The workshop was for people recently released from prison, and its only promise was that no one had to earn the right to enjoy being there.
At first, Mara trusted that promise about as much as she trusted locked doors.
She had spent six years stealing cars and another year learning not to flinch at footsteps behind her.
On her first morning, she chose the greenhouse because plants did not ask questions.
A volunteer named Imani showed her how to pinch basil leaves above the new growth.
“Small kindnesses help things branch,” Imani said.
Mara almost laughed at the lesson’s neatness, but she took the leaves home.
She had a job interview the next day at a repair shop.
The owner saw her record and said he would call.
He did not call.
Mara returned to the workshop angry enough to break something.
Mr. Vale handed her a lump of clay instead.
“You can ruin that,” he said, “and still make something from it.”
She pressed the clay flat, then folded it, and pressed again.
By dusk, she had made a crooked bowl with a thumbprint at its center.
The next week, the workshop organized a supper for the neighborhood.
Mara chopped onions while two other participants argued cheerfully over a soup recipe.
She liked the smell of garlic browning in oil.
She liked that people asked her to taste the broth.
She liked being trusted with a sharp knife.
When the guests arrived, a little boy dropped his bowl and began to cry.
Mara crouched beside him and offered him the crooked one.
He held it carefully, as if it were treasure.
His mother thanked her, and Mara found she wanted to hear those words again.
That desire frightened her more than any guard ever had.
Wanting something meant it could be taken away.
Still, she returned each morning.
She learned to repair a bicycle, balance a budget, and keep a promise even when nobody checked.
The repair shop owner came to supper one evening.
He saw Mara fixing a loose wheel for a neighbor’s daughter.
The next morning, he called.
The job was part-time and the pay was modest, but the shop smelled of metal, soap, and possibility.
Mara kept working at the greenhouse after her shift.
Months later, she taught a new arrival how to pinch basil leaves above the growth.
The woman watched her warily.
Mara understood.
She did not tell her that pleasure could cure anything.
She only showed her the sunlight on the leaves and offered her a pot of soil.
Together, they planted seeds.
Outside, the city kept its hard edges and its old opinions.
Inside, people practiced making useful things, sharing good food, and beginning again.
Mara’s crooked bowl sat on a shelf by the door.
It held spare keys for the people who came to work.
Now, whenever someone picked one up, Mara felt a quiet, durable joy.
It was not freedom from the past.
It was the pleasure of building a future with her own hands.

The “Face on Mars” is a landform in the Cydonia region that became famous after a Viking orbiter photographed it in 1976. In the original image, shadows and limited detail made one mesa look like a human face. Some people argued that it might be a monument built by an intelligent civilization. This idea captured the public’s imagination and inspired many stories about life on Mars. However, an unusual appearance is not proof of an artificial origin. Later spacecraft took much clearer pictures of the same feature. These images showed a rugged, uneven hill with no clear facial details. Its apparent eyes, nose, and mouth were largely the result of shadows, viewing angle, and the low resolution of the first photograph. When lighting and perspective changed, the face-like shape became much less convincing. Scientists have also found no strong evidence of carved surfaces or other signs of construction there. Natural processes can create striking shapes through erosion, impacts, and the gradual movement of rock and soil. People are especially likely to recognize familiar patterns, such as faces, in random forms. This tendency is called pareidolia. The Cydonia mesa is therefore best understood as a natural Martian landform rather than an alien-made face. Although the idea of an ancient monument is exciting, the clearest evidence comes from detailed observations. The “Face on Mars” remains a reminder that science relies on careful investigation, not appearance alone.

Richard III was reburied at Leicester Cathedral on March 26, 2015, more than five centuries after his death at the Battle of Bosworth Field. His remains had been discovered beneath a Leicester car park in 2012, prompting an archaeological investigation that confirmed his identity. The reburial ceremony brought together royal representatives, clergy, historians and members of the public. A coffin made from English oak was carried in a solemn procession through the city before being placed in a specially designed tomb. The service included prayers, music and readings reflecting on the king’s life and turbulent reign. Poet laureate Carol Ann Duffy wrote a commemorative poem, “Richard,” for the occasion. Its verses considered the passage of time and the way history remembers those who ruled. Actor Benedict Cumberbatch, who played Richard III in a BBC adaptation of Shakespeare’s play, read the poem during the service. Cumberbatch is also a distant descendant of the king, according to genealogical research tracing their family lines through a shared ancestor. The ceremony renewed public interest in Richard, whose reputation has long been shaped by Shakespeare and centuries of historical debate.

Joining the Seagoing Cowboys program offered young volunteers a chance to serve people and animals far from home. After World War II, these cowboys traveled aboard ships carrying livestock and supplies to communities in need. The trips were not easy, because the ships were crowded and the ocean could be rough. Volunteers also had to care for the animals every day. They fed them, cleaned their spaces, and watched for signs of illness. This work demanded patience, responsibility, and teamwork.

One of the greatest rewards was knowing that the animals could help families rebuild their lives. Cows provided milk, while horses and other livestock could support farming and transportation. The animals were a gift of hope as well as a practical resource. The cowboys also learned about the people they were helping and saw how communities welcomed the deliveries. Meeting people from different places helped volunteers understand the world beyond their own homes. They could see that a small act of service might make a lasting difference.

The journey also brought personal rewards. Volunteers gained confidence by taking on difficult tasks and living in unfamiliar conditions. They formed close friendships with crewmates and shared memories that could last a lifetime. Many learned to appreciate cooperation, kindness, and hard work. The program gave young people a meaningful way to contribute after a time of great suffering. Although the voyage could be tiring, its purpose made the effort worthwhile. By joining the Seagoing Cowboys, volunteers helped deliver hope to people and animals overseas while discovering how rewarding service can be.

At dusk, the bells of Bellwether rang once, warning the village to close its gates. For twelve years, the valley had been protected by a ring of silver stones. The stones had been raised after the war, when the enemy captain, Veyr, swore he would return. Everyone believed Veyr had died in the fire that ended the fighting. Everyone except Mara, who had seen his shadow on the ridge the night before.

She told the village council, but they called it a trick of fading light. The gates were barred, the shutters fastened, and the children hurried indoors. Only old Jory stayed in the square, polishing the bronze bell. He had once been a soldier, and his left hand trembled whenever thunder rolled. “If he’s alive,” Jory said, “the stones will know.”

Mara climbed the watchtower with a lantern. Across the fields, a lone figure moved beneath the black pines. He walked slowly, leaning on a crooked staff. One side of his face was hidden beneath a leather mask. The other was webbed with pale scars. When he reached the silver boundary, he stopped. Then he raised one hand and beckoned.

A cold shiver passed through the village. One by one, the silver stones dimmed. The council gathered in the square, carrying spears and old swords. Their leader, Mayor Fen, ordered everyone to stand behind the gate. Jory looked at the darkening stones and shook his head. “They were never a wall,” he said. “They were a promise.”

The figure called through the dusk. “Send out the ones who burned my home.” No one answered. His voice was rough, but it carried clearly over the fields. “I have waited twelve years to hear them confess.” The villagers looked at one another. Many had been children during the war. Some had not even been born.

Mara remembered her grandmother’s story of the last battle. The village had opened its doors to soldiers fleeing the fire. In the confusion, someone had mistaken Veyr’s family for enemy scouts. A frightened guard had given the order to shoot. Her grandmother had never said who that guard was. Now Jory stepped forward, his trembling hand resting on the old sword at his belt.

“I gave the order,” he said. The square fell silent. “I thought they were reaching for weapons. I was wrong.” Veyr’s shoulders tightened beyond the stones. Mayor Fen urged Jory to retreat. Jory refused. “You came for revenge,” he called, “but I won’t hide behind a gate again.”

Mara took the lantern and walked toward the boundary. Her mother cried out, but she kept going. The silver stones had gone completely dark. At their edge, Mara set the lantern down. “You can punish one man,” she said. “But you cannot bring your family back by hurting everyone here.” Veyr stared at her through the mask. “And what would you offer instead?”

Mara had no answer ready. She only knew that fear had kept the village safe and silent for too long. Jory laid his sword in the grass and knelt. “Let the truth be written,” he said. “Let every name be remembered.” Mayor Fen lowered her spear. Then the villagers began to set down their weapons, one by one.

Veyr looked across the crowd, searching faces for the frightened guard he had once seen in the flames. Jory met his gaze without looking away. For a long time, the only sound was the wind moving through the pines. At last, Veyr removed his mask. The scars pulled at his cheek, but beneath them was a tired, grieving man.

He crossed the boundary. The silver stones remained dark, yet nothing struck him down. No one raised a weapon. Veyr stopped before Jory, and Jory bowed his head. “I remember your daughter,” Jory whispered. “She tried to pull her brother from the fire.” Veyr’s eyes filled, and his staff slipped from his hand.

He did not forgive Jory that night. He did not ask the village to forgive him either. Instead, he sat by the cold hearth while the names of the dead were read aloud. At dawn, the silver stones began to shine again. This time, they marked no boundary between enemy and neighbor. They marked the place where the village had finally told the truth.

Five men from Nottingham have been jailed for defrauding UK investors through a bogus overseas share-selling operation. The group persuaded people to buy shares in companies that were either worthless or did not exist, according to prosecutors. Investors were contacted by telephone and offered the chance to make large profits from overseas markets. The callers used persuasive sales tactics and misleading claims to build confidence in the scheme. Victims were encouraged to invest increasing sums, but the promised returns never materialised. Instead, much of the money was diverted for the defendants’ benefit. The fraud left investors facing substantial losses. An investigation traced the operation and gathered evidence against the men. Prosecutors said the defendants had worked together to carry out the deception. All five were convicted of offences connected with the scheme. They were sentenced to prison, though details of their individual terms were not immediately available. The court heard that the operation had caused serious financial harm and distress to those targeted. Authorities urged investors to be wary of unsolicited calls promising unusually high returns. They advised people to check the credentials of firms and seek independent advice before investing.

Every morning, Mara woke to the sound of a bottle being shaken.

Hidden Valley’s loudspeakers announced the day’s approved dressing: Original Ranch.

At breakfast, she poured it over her eggs, as the rules required.

The mayor said ranch made every meal—and every citizen—more wholesome.

On the walls, posters showed smiling families beneath the slogan, “Dip Together, Stay Together.”

Mara smiled when the patrol passed her window.

Then she hid a red tomato beneath her napkin.

Tomatoes were forbidden, too vivid and too independent.

Her grandfather had once told her about a place beyond the hills where people dressed their salads however they wished.

He had called it the Open Table.

Mara kept his story folded inside her shoe.

At school, children learned the sacred proportions of buttermilk, herbs, and mayonnaise.

Anyone who asked why was sent to the Mixing Room.

There, they were stirred into obedience by cheerful songs and endless taste tests.

Mara’s brother returned from the room speaking only in slogans.

She decided she would leave before the same thing happened to her.

At midnight, she slipped past the statue of the First Bottle.

Its glass eyes followed her across the square.

The gates stood guarded by two soldiers holding giant whisks.

Mara offered them her hidden tomato.

They recoiled as if it were a live coal.

While they argued over whether it counted as a vegetable or a threat, she ran.

Beyond the gate, the road smelled of rain and wild onions.

She climbed the hill as dawn turned the sky the color of an unbranded jar.

At its summit, she found no Open Table, only a vast desert of pale dust.

For one frightening moment, she thought her grandfather had lied.

Then the wind lifted the dust, and beneath it appeared a thousand tiny green shoots.

Mara knelt and tasted one.

It was sharp, bitter, and entirely its own.

Behind her, Hidden Valley’s loudspeakers began their morning shake.

Ahead, the shoots spread toward a distant blue river.

Mara laughed, though no one had taught her when to.

She took the tomato from her pocket and planted its seeds in the open earth.

By the time the patrol reached the hill, she was already walking toward the river.

The valley called her a traitor.

The wind called her nothing at all.

That, Mara decided, was the beginning of freedom.

Schools should not require students to maintain a B average to participate in sports and extracurricular activities. Grades are important, but they are not the only measure of a student’s ability or potential. Activities such as sports, music, and clubs help students discover their interests and develop new skills. They also teach teamwork, leadership, and responsibility. For some students, being part of a team or club gives them a sense of belonging at school. Taking that opportunity away could make school less enjoyable and reduce their motivation. A strict B-average rule could also unfairly affect students who learn at different speeds or face challenges outside the classroom. Instead of excluding these students, schools should help them improve. Teachers and coaches could offer tutoring or study sessions for students who are struggling. Students might also agree to a plan that gives them time to complete assignments and raise their grades. Schools can set reasonable academic expectations without requiring every student to earn the same average. For example, students could be asked to attend classes, complete their work, and show steady effort. If a student’s grades drop, the school could check in and provide support before removing them from an activity. Participating in extracurricular activities can even improve academic habits by teaching students to manage their time. Students should understand that schoolwork comes first, but they should not have to be perfect to take part. A B-average requirement may sound like a way to encourage success, yet it could punish students without addressing the reasons they are struggling. Schools should promote both academic growth and personal development. For these reasons, students should be supported in balancing their grades with the activities they enjoy.

Mobile telecommunications have evolved through several generations of technology, each expanding how people communicate and access information. The standards behind these networks are developed through international cooperation. A central organization in this work is the Third Generation Partnership Project, usually known as 3GPP. Although its name refers to third-generation systems, 3GPP has continued to develop standards for 4G, 5G, and emerging 6G technologies. Understanding 3GPP requires looking at its history, organization, standards process, and technical achievements.

Before mobile networks became widespread, national and regional systems used different technologies. First-generation, or 1G, systems introduced analog cellular voice service in the late 1970s and 1980s. Examples included AMPS in North America, NMT in Nordic countries, and TACS in parts of Europe and Asia. These systems demonstrated the value of cellular coverage but offered limited capacity and little compatibility across borders. Their analog radio links also provided limited privacy and were not designed for data services.

Second-generation, or 2G, systems shifted mobile communications to digital radio. Digital transmission improved capacity, voice quality, and support for services such as text messaging. GSM, originally meaning Groupe Spécial Mobile and later Global System for Mobile Communications, became a major international 2G standard. It was developed through European cooperation and spread widely beyond Europe. Other 2G systems included IS-95, associated with CDMA technology, and North American variants of the IS-136 family.

The need for a common framework for third-generation mobile systems grew during the 1990s. The International Telecommunication Union coordinated a global effort called IMT-2000, which established broad requirements for 3G systems. Different regional and technical proposals were submitted to meet those requirements. In 1998, standards organizations formed 3GPP to develop specifications based on GSM and related technologies. The initial partners were ETSI in Europe, ARIB and TTC in Japan, TTA in South Korea, and T1 in the United States, later succeeded by ATIS.

A separate partnership, 3GPP2, developed standards based mainly on the CDMA2000 family. 3GPP and 3GPP2 were distinct organizations, although both contributed to the broader international 3G landscape. 3GPP focused on the evolution of GSM radio technology and its core network. Its first major system was the Universal Mobile Telecommunications System, or UMTS. UMTS commonly used Wideband Code Division Multiple Access, known as WCDMA, for its radio interface.

3GPP’s early releases established a complete mobile system rather than only a radio specification. Release 99 defined the first full UMTS architecture and included both circuit-switched services, such as traditional voice calls, and packet-switched data. The core network drew on GSM and General Packet Radio Service technology while adding support for wideband radio access. This approach allowed operators to evolve existing networks rather than replace every component at once. Later releases introduced improvements such as High-Speed Downlink Packet Access, or HSDPA, and High-Speed Uplink Packet Access, or HSUPA.

Together, HSDPA and HSUPA are often called HSPA. These improvements increased data rates and reduced delays by adapting transmission methods to radio conditions. HSPA made mobile internet more practical for browsing, email, and multimedia. Further refinements, sometimes called HSPA+, improved capacity and data performance. The 3G era therefore included a series of upgrades rather than one fixed technology.

3GPP is a partnership project, not a single standards agency or company. Its organizational partners are regional and national standards-development organizations. These partners provide administrative support and a formal route for approving specifications. They include ETSI, ATIS, the China Communications Standards Association, ARIB, TTC, TTA, and the Telecommunications Technology Committee of India, known as TSDSI. The partners help connect 3GPP work with recognized standards systems around the world.

Companies and other organizations participate as individual members through one or more organizational partners. Participants include mobile network operators, equipment vendors, chipset makers, software companies, research institutions, and government-related bodies. They contribute proposals, technical studies, and expertise. Participation is generally based on the rules of the relevant partner organization. This broad membership brings commercial, operational, and technical perspectives into the standards process.

The 3GPP organization is arranged into three Technical Specification Groups, or TSGs. These are Radio Access Networks, Services and System Aspects, and Core Network and Terminals. Each group contains Working Groups that address more focused areas. The Radio Access Networks group develops radio-system specifications and related testing requirements. The Services and System Aspects group considers architecture, services, security, and system-wide features. The Core Network and Terminals group works on core-network functions, protocols, and device-related specifications.

Work usually begins with a study item or work item agreed by the relevant group. A study item examines a topic and may identify possible technical solutions. A work item is a defined task to develop or revise specifications. Members submit contributions that are discussed in meetings and recorded in documents. Technical agreements are reached through discussion, with formal approval procedures used where required. The process is collaborative, and consensus is a central objective.

3GPP meetings are held regularly, both in person and through remote participation. Working Groups handle detailed technical discussions, while TSG plenary meetings coordinate and approve their work. The project’s organizational partners formally publish the specifications. 3GPP also makes its specifications available through its website. This arrangement allows detailed engineering work to be coordinated internationally while preserving formal standards publication through the partner organizations.

3GPP specifications are organized into numbered series. Each series covers a broad technical area, such as services, security, radio access, or core-network protocols. Individual documents are identified by a specification number and a version. Specifications often use a three-part version number that indicates the release and document revision. This structure helps implementers identify which requirements apply to a particular system version.

A 3GPP Release is a coordinated set of specifications representing a development stage. A release can introduce new technologies, add features, and refine earlier requirements. It is not necessarily a commercial product or a single network upgrade. Releases are developed over time, and their contents are stabilized according to project schedules. Operators and equipment makers may deploy selected features from a release at different times.

The distinction between a standard and a deployed network is important. 3GPP defines technical requirements and procedures, but it does not build or operate public mobile networks. Vendors implement the specifications in equipment and devices. Operators choose which supported features to deploy and how to configure them. Regulators allocate spectrum and establish licensing conditions. Real-world service therefore depends on standards, commercial decisions, spectrum, and local rules.

A specification can define required behavior without prescribing every internal implementation detail. This gives vendors room to develop different products that interoperate. Conformance testing checks whether equipment meets specified requirements. Interoperability testing examines whether equipment from different suppliers works together in relevant scenarios. Device certification programs may add further testing requirements. These activities support consistent service, but no standard can eliminate every implementation difference.

As data traffic grew, 3GPP began designing a more streamlined system for mobile broadband. Release 8 introduced Long Term Evolution, or LTE, along with the System Architecture Evolution, or SAE. LTE’s radio interface is commonly called Evolved UMTS Terrestrial Radio Access, or E-UTRA. SAE introduced an all-IP core network known as the Evolved Packet Core, or EPC. The design aimed to improve data rates, reduce latency, increase spectral efficiency, and simplify network architecture.

LTE uses Orthogonal Frequency Division Multiple Access on the downlink and Single-Carrier Frequency Division Multiple Access on the uplink. These radio techniques support flexible resource allocation across different bandwidths. LTE also uses multiple-input multiple-output, or MIMO, antenna techniques to improve capacity and coverage. The system supports packet data as its native service model. Voice service could initially be provided through circuit-switched fallback to older networks, while later systems enabled voice over LTE.

LTE Advanced, introduced through later releases, added features such as carrier aggregation and enhanced MIMO. Carrier aggregation combines multiple spectrum blocks to provide a wider effective channel. This can increase peak data rates and improve use of fragmented spectrum. LTE Advanced also expanded support for heterogeneous networks, in which large and small cells work together. These upgrades helped LTE continue developing well beyond its first commercial deployments.

3GPP standards also define how devices authenticate and protect communications. Subscriber identity modules, or SIMs, and their successors store credentials used for network access. Authentication procedures help verify a subscriber and the network. Encryption and integrity protection are applied to signaling and, depending on the technology and service, user data. Security requirements evolve as threats and system capabilities change. No security standard can guarantee perfect protection, so sound implementation and operational practices remain essential.

The move to 5G was guided by a wider range of use cases than mobile broadband alone. These included enhanced Mobile Broadband, Ultra-Reliable Low-Latency Communications, and massive Machine-Type Communications. The International Telecommunication Union defined broad 5G goals through its IMT-2020 framework. 3GPP developed the detailed system specifications that enable 5G deployments. Release 15 marked the first phase of 5G standardization.

5G New Radio, or NR, is the radio-access technology developed by 3GPP for 5G. It supports a wide range of frequencies, bandwidths, deployment types, and antenna configurations. NR can operate in low-band spectrum for broad coverage, mid-band spectrum for a balance of coverage and capacity, and millimeter-wave bands for very high capacity over shorter distances. The system uses scalable numerology, allowing radio parameters to suit different bands and services. Massive MIMO and beamforming can focus radio energy toward users and improve capacity.

5G networks can use two main architectural deployment modes. Non-Standalone mode uses LTE and the existing Evolved Packet Core alongside 5G radio access. Standalone mode connects 5G New Radio to the 5G Core. The 5G Core is designed around a service-based architecture, in which network functions interact through defined services and APIs. It supports flexible authentication, policy control, mobility management, and session management. This architecture can also support network slicing.

Network slicing allows an operator to configure logical network instances for different service requirements on shared infrastructure. A slice may be optimized for broad connectivity, low latency, or a particular enterprise use case. Slicing depends on coordinated capabilities across the radio network, core, transport, and management systems. It does not mean that each slice has entirely separate physical equipment. Its performance and isolation depend on implementation, resource allocation, and operational controls.

Release 16 expanded 5G capabilities and supported the completion of the first major phase of 5G standardization. It included enhancements for industrial communications, vehicle-related services, and unlicensed spectrum operation. Release 17 added further work on reduced-capability devices, non-terrestrial networks, and expanded IoT support. Reduced-capability 5G devices are intended for applications that need less bandwidth and complexity than smartphones. Non-terrestrial network specifications help integrate satellite and other airborne platforms with mobile systems.

Later releases continue to extend 5G features and address new requirements. Release 18 is commonly associated with the start of 5G-Advanced. Work in this area includes improvements to radio performance, energy efficiency, positioning, AI and machine learning support, and network automation. These features are developed through specific work items and are not necessarily available in every network. Commercial availability depends on equipment, devices, spectrum, and operator plans.

3GPP’s technical work covers more than radio transmission. It specifies interfaces between network components, procedures for mobility and handover, service architectures, and device behavior. It also develops protocols for emergency communications, lawful requirements, charging, and quality of service. The standards support a global ecosystem in which a device can connect to compatible networks in many countries. Roaming depends on agreements between operators and on compatible frequency bands and configurations.

The harmonized use of spectrum is another important part of global mobile development. 3GPP defines radio requirements for frequency bands, but it does not allocate spectrum. The International Telecommunication Union coordinates international spectrum matters, while national regulators make local assignments. 3GPP band specifications help devices and networks operate consistently within those allocations. A phone may support many bands, but it cannot connect to every network if the relevant bands or features are missing.

Radio standards also address coexistence and sharing. Mobile systems may operate near other services or share bands under defined conditions. Technical requirements can limit unwanted emissions and help manage interference. Dynamic spectrum sharing allows LTE and 5G NR to use the same spectrum resources in some deployments. Such methods can ease migration but may involve trade-offs in capacity and complexity.

The technical development of mobile standards is shaped by feedback from deployed networks. Operators report challenges involving coverage, congestion, mobility, and energy use. Device makers identify implementation and power constraints. Researchers propose new methods, while regulators and public organizations raise policy and safety concerns. 3GPP provides a forum for these inputs to be considered in technical terms. Decisions reflect both engineering evidence and the need for a workable global ecosystem.

A key strength of 3GPP is continuity across generations. GSM and UMTS evolved into LTE, while LTE and NR can coexist in the same broader network environment. Operators have often introduced new radio technologies while retaining parts of existing infrastructure. This reduces the cost and disruption of migration. It also means that mobile generations are not always cleanly separated in practice.

Another strength is the scale of international participation. Shared specifications support economies of scale for devices and infrastructure. They make it easier for manufacturers to serve a global market and for subscribers to roam. Common standards also support competition among suppliers. Operators can choose equipment from different vendors when products implement compatible interfaces and requirements.

The standards process nevertheless faces challenges. Different regions have different spectrum policies, market needs, and legacy systems. Reaching agreement among many participants can take time. A feature that is technically possible may be too costly or difficult to deploy widely. Some specifications include optional capabilities, so devices and networks may support different feature combinations. Careful versioning and testing help manage these differences but cannot remove them entirely.

The growing complexity of networks raises new concerns. More software-defined functions create opportunities for faster upgrades and flexible service design. They also increase the importance of software security, supply-chain resilience, and operational expertise. Cloud-based network functions may run on shared computing platforms, requiring careful attention to isolation and reliability. 3GPP specifications address many technical aspects, while deployment guidance and policy are handled by additional organizations and authorities.

Energy efficiency has become a major design objective. Radio networks consume substantial energy, and traffic continues to grow. Standards can support power-saving states, efficient signaling, and adaptive transmission. Operators also optimize sites, cooling, and network configurations. The total environmental impact depends on equipment design, electricity sources, device lifetimes, and user behavior, not standards alone.

Machine-to-machine communications have also shaped 3GPP development. Technologies such as LTE-M and Narrowband IoT were developed to support devices with low data rates and long battery life. They can serve applications such as metering, tracking, and environmental monitoring. These systems are designed for wide coverage and low device complexity. Their success depends on reliable service, affordable modules, and suitable deployment strategies.

Emergency services are an important consideration in mobile standards. Networks may support emergency calls, location information, public warning, and priority access features. Exact requirements vary by country and region. 3GPP defines technical mechanisms, while local laws determine many operational obligations. Ensuring reliable emergency service requires coordination among network operators, device makers, public agencies, and regulators.

Accessibility is another area of ongoing work. Modern mobile systems support features such as real-time text, improved audio capabilities, and emergency communication options. Device operating systems and applications also play a major role. Standards can provide common network capabilities that make accessible services possible across devices and regions. The quality of the user experience depends on the complete system, not just the radio network.

3GPP specifications are periodically updated to correct errors and clarify requirements. Change requests document proposed revisions and their technical justifications. Approved changes are incorporated into later versions of the relevant documents. This maintenance is essential because standards are living technical documents. Implementers must track the versions and releases relevant to their products.

3GPP also coordinates with other standards bodies and industry groups. The Internet Engineering Task Force develops many internet protocols used by mobile networks and applications. The Open Mobile Alliance and other organizations have addressed service and management topics. The ITU provides international frameworks and recommendations. Cooperation helps avoid conflicting specifications and clarifies where one organization’s work connects with another’s.

The difference between 3GPP and the ITU is often misunderstood. The ITU establishes international telecommunications frameworks and evaluates radio technologies for global IMT classifications. 3GPP develops detailed specifications used by manufacturers and operators. Technologies such as LTE and 5G NR have been submitted to and recognized within the ITU’s IMT processes. The organizations have related but distinct roles.

The term “5G” can refer to a family of technologies and deployment configurations rather than one uniform experience. Performance varies with spectrum, network design, device capability, traffic, and geography. A 5G icon on a phone does not guarantee a particular speed or latency. Similarly, a network may use 5G radio technology while relying on an LTE core in Non-Standalone mode. Understanding the underlying architecture gives a clearer picture than marketing labels alone.

The same caution applies to claims about future generations. Research into 6G is underway, but commercial 6G systems are not yet standardized or widely deployed. 3GPP and other organizations will be involved in future technical discussions, alongside research bodies and the ITU. Potential topics include higher frequencies, integrated sensing and communications, advanced AI, and new forms of satellite integration. These ideas remain subject to research, standardization, and practical evaluation.

3GPP’s influence extends beyond public cellular networks. Its specifications support private 4G and 5G networks used by factories, campuses, ports, and utilities. They also underpin fixed wireless access, connected vehicles, and many IoT deployments. These uses often require specific combinations of coverage, reliability, security, and device management. Standards provide common technical foundations, while deployments adapt them to local needs.

The development cycle of a mobile generation spans many years. Research and early studies precede formal work items. Specifications are then developed, approved, implemented, tested, and deployed. Real-world feedback informs later releases and revisions. As a result, the capabilities associated with a generation usually arrive incrementally.

3GPP’s technical achievements are closely tied to commercial adoption. A standard has value when devices and networks implement it at scale. Manufacturers need stable specifications to design products, and operators need predictable road maps for investment. Regulators need clear technical definitions to manage spectrum and licensing. The standards process therefore balances innovation with stability.

Looking back, 3GPP helped transform mobile service from digital voice into a platform for global broadband connectivity. Its work built on GSM and UMTS, then enabled LTE and 5G. Each generation improved capacity, speed, latency, and support for new applications. The organization’s releases provide a structured path for continuous technical development.

The history of 3GPP is also a history of cooperation. No single company or country could create a globally interoperable mobile ecosystem alone. Standards emerge from negotiation among organizations with different interests and expertise. Their success depends on technical quality, broad adoption, and ongoing maintenance. This cooperative model remains central to mobile telecommunications.

To understand a modern mobile network, it helps to separate several layers. Radio standards define how devices communicate over the air. Core-network standards manage identity, mobility, and data sessions. Service specifications describe capabilities offered to users and applications. Spectrum rules and local regulations define where and under what conditions networks may operate. Commercial deployment decisions determine which features people actually experience.

3GPP’s work continues because communication needs continue to change. New applications create demands for higher capacity, more reliable links, and lower energy use. Expanding connected devices increase the importance of security and scalable management. Satellite integration can extend coverage to remote areas. Industrial uses may demand predictable performance and local control.

The organization’s future work will need to balance ambitious capabilities with practical constraints. Spectrum is limited, infrastructure is costly, and devices must remain affordable and power-efficient. Networks must support legacy equipment while introducing new technologies. Security and privacy must keep pace with software-driven architectures. Technical standards can help address these challenges, but they cannot solve them in isolation.

The most important contribution of 3GPP is a shared technical language for mobile communications. Its specifications allow equipment from different suppliers to connect and operate according to common rules. Its release process gives the industry a way to evolve systems over time. Its international structure brings together many of the organizations that shape mobile technology. Through this work, 3GPP has become one of the central institutions in the development of global telecommunications.

A Canvey Island man has been charged with murder after a woman died from a neck injury. Police have not released further details about the circumstances of her death or the woman’s identity. The man is due to appear in court, where the charge will be considered.

At midnight, the city’s simulation drivers began obeying a signal that didn’t exist. One by one, ambulances swerved toward the same empty intersection. Mara, the world’s emergency dispatcher, watched their icons pile up on her screen. The first collision sent a shockwave through the virtual streets. Buildings flickered, and the river turned briefly into a grid of blue squares. A glitch in the driving system was copying each crash and feeding it back as a new command. Soon, every ambulance in the city was racing toward the intersection. Their collisions threatened to overload the server and erase the world they were meant to protect. Mara tried to shut down the simulation, but the controls had frozen. She spotted a maintenance vehicle parked beside the server tower and took manual control. Steering through streets that vanished behind her, she reached the intersection just ahead of the ambulance swarm. She drove the maintenance vehicle across the junction and blocked the false signal beacon. The ambulances braked in a wave, stopping inches from one another. The city steadied, and its people woke to a sunrise that was still there.

Remote Highland communities are set to benefit from ultrafast fibre broadband through a series of locally led network upgrades. Residents, community groups and local authorities are working with providers to extend connections to properties beyond the reach of conventional commercial rollouts. The projects aim to improve access to remote work, online education and digital public services, while supporting local businesses. Organisers say cooperation and community investment are helping bring faster, more reliable internet to some of Scotland’s hardest-to-reach homes.

By the time Elias Venn reached the ridge, his fingers had gone numb inside his gloves. He had spent three weeks surveying the frozen north, searching for a vein rich enough to pay his debts. His pack was light, his food nearly gone, and the letter from the bank seemed to grow heavier each day. Then he saw a figure slumped beside a drifted trail. The stranger’s coat was torn, and one hand was bare and bluish with frostbite. “Water,” the stranger whispered. Elias knelt and uncorked his canteen. The stranger’s lips moved again, asking for help reaching the old camp below. Elias glanced at the map tucked inside his coat. A narrow seam of rock marked a promising ledge nearby, one he had not yet measured. If he lost daylight, another prospector might stake the claim first. “I’ll be back,” Elias said, setting down the canteen. He pointed toward the camp and hurried uphill. The stranger watched him go without a word. At the ledge, Elias found glittering flecks caught in a split of dark stone. He chipped away a sample, then another, his pulse quickening. The seam widened beneath the snow, bright with copper and traces of silver. By noon, he had enough evidence to make the claim valuable. He wrapped the samples and started back. A storm rolled over the ridge, blotting out the trail. Elias stumbled through the whiteout, calling for the stranger. When he reached the place where he had left him, the drift was smooth and empty. He followed scattered boot marks toward the camp, but they vanished beneath new snow. At dusk, he found the stranger’s canteen frozen in the trail. Beyond it lay a single dark mitten. Elias searched until the wind drove him to shelter in a rock hollow. In the morning, he found the stranger a short distance away, still and half buried. Elias covered the body with his coat. Then he took the samples and continued down to the settlement. The claim clerk listened as Elias described the ledge and studied his measurements. “You found it before anyone else,” she said. “The claim is yours, if the survey holds.” Elias signed the papers with a hand that trembled. For a few weeks, the mine brought him money and praise. But the stranger’s face followed him into every quiet room. When investigators learned of the body, they asked why Elias had left a canteen instead of carrying the man to safety. He gave no answer that sounded like the truth. The settlement withdrew its trust, and the claim was challenged for fraud. Elias had not lied on the survey, but his silence made every measurement suspect. Before winter ended, the claim was frozen in court, and his creditors seized what little he had earned. He returned to the ridge with no pack of samples and no promise of wealth. At the spot where the stranger had fallen, Elias found a small wooden marker someone had planted. He knelt beside it until the cold seeped through his coat. The land still held its treasure, but it had taken the future he thought it would buy.

When the school announced a kindness experiment, Ms. Vale asked each student to wear a colored badge showing how many friends they had at lunch. She meant to help lonely children find one another. Milo’s badge was blue, the color for “still looking.” At first, everyone smiled and invited him to sit with them. But by Friday, the badges had become a game, and the blue ones were teased as “empty seats.” Milo began telling jokes louder, then lending out his favorite pencils, hoping someone would keep him close. At lunch, he followed a group from table to table, pretending he had forgotten something each time they moved. Ms. Vale noticed him standing alone and hurried over with a new badge, green this time. “You belong with us,” she said, trying to fix the experiment. Milo looked at the badge and asked if he could choose his own color. The next morning, he arrived wearing a paper star he had drawn himself. A girl from his class asked to sit beside him and make one too. By the end of the week, the badges were gone, but Milo kept the star in his pocket.

An inquest into the death of a 16-year-old student at a school in Cornwall is awaiting toxicology results, which could help establish the circumstances surrounding the teenager’s death. The student’s death prompted an investigation and a hearing before a coroner. The inquest has heard that further findings are needed before key questions can be addressed. Toxicology testing can identify substances in a person’s system, but no results have yet been reported. The student’s identity and other personal details have not been included in the information available. The coroner is expected to consider the test results alongside evidence from witnesses and investigators. No conclusion about the cause or circumstances of the death has been announced. The inquest is due to continue once the outstanding results are received.

Errors in voter lists disrupted voting at polling stations in Barnet, prompting complaints and calls for an investigation. Some voters said their names were missing from the register or recorded incorrectly when they arrived to cast their ballots. The problems led to delays and left some people unsure whether they would be allowed to vote.

Polling staff sought to resolve cases at the affected stations, but voters reported confusion over what steps to take. Some were directed to check their details or seek help from election officials. The disruption was particularly frustrating for people who had planned their day around voting.

Complaints were made about the accuracy of the lists and the handling of affected voters. Residents called on the authorities to establish how the errors occurred and whether they resulted from problems with registration data, printing or distribution. They also urged officials to explain what remedies were available to anyone who could not vote.

The incidents raised questions about the preparations for polling day and the reliability of the voter information supplied to stations. Election officials are expected to review reports from staff and voters before determining the scale of the problem. Any investigation could examine when the errors were identified and how quickly they were addressed.

Residents said a clear account was needed to restore confidence in the process. They also called for safeguards to prevent similar problems at future elections. Officials had not yet confirmed the full number of voters affected or announced the findings of any formal review.

Students should be allowed to use phones at school for emergencies and contacting family. A phone can help students reach their parents if they feel sick or need a safe ride home. It can also be useful during serious emergencies when quick communication matters. However, phones can distract students during lessons and make it harder to focus. To avoid this, schools should require students to keep their phones silent and put away during class. Teachers could allow phone use when a student has permission or when there is an urgent situation. Schools should also explain clear rules about when phones may be used. This approach gives students a way to contact family without letting phones interrupt learning. Overall, limited phone access can help students feel safer while keeping school focused.

Summer learning projects can help students keep their minds active while school is out. But who should design these projects: teachers or students? I believe students should have the main role, with teachers offering guidance. When students help choose what they will learn, they are more likely to feel interested and motivated. They can connect projects to hobbies, questions, or future goals. For example, a student who enjoys cooking might explore nutrition and create a recipe collection. Someone interested in animals might study a local species and share what they discover. These projects can make learning feel useful beyond the classroom. Student choice also allows young people to practice independence. They can set goals, make a plan, and decide how to present their work. These are important skills for middle and high school students. However, students should not have to design everything alone. Some may struggle to choose a topic or decide how much work is reasonable. Others may not know which resources are reliable. Teachers can help by suggesting ideas and setting clear expectations. They can also make sure projects are appropriate for different ages and abilities. A teacher might offer a list of broad themes while letting each student choose a specific question. For instance, a theme about the environment could lead to projects on recycling, wildlife, or clean energy. This approach gives students freedom without leaving them unsupported. Teachers can also provide simple guidelines, such as a timeline and a final reflection. The project should not feel like a full extra course during vacation. Students need time to rest, spend time with family, and enjoy other activities. A flexible project can fit around those plans. It can also be completed with materials students can access easily. Schools should avoid projects that depend on expensive supplies or reliable internet access. Students should have fair chances to succeed, whatever their circumstances. Teachers can consider these issues when helping students plan. In the end, the best summer projects are designed together. Students should choose topics that excite them, while teachers provide structure and support. This balance can make summer learning meaningful, manageable, and enjoyable.
