The first thing Daniel summoned was a cup of coffee.

He had been standing in the kitchen, late for work, wishing desperately for one more minute and a hot drink. A ceramic mug appeared on the counter with a soft clink, steam curling from its rim.

Daniel stared at it, then took a cautious sip.

It was exactly how he liked it.

He told himself he was overtired and hurried out the door.

That afternoon, a red umbrella appeared beside him when rain began to fall. The next morning, a key he had misplaced for weeks turned up in his coat pocket.

Soon, he started testing the strange luck.

He wished for a better desk chair, and one materialized in his office while he was at lunch. He wanted a rare book, and found it waiting on his doorstep.

Each gift arrived without warning, but Daniel learned to keep his wishes small.

Then, on a cold evening, he saw a shivering dog beside a busy road.

He wished it had a warm place to sleep.

A wooden kennel appeared in the alley behind his apartment, along with a blanket and a silver bowl. The dog followed him home, and Daniel named her June.

For a while, the power seemed kind.

Then his neighbor’s son was struck by a car.

As Daniel waited outside the hospital, he wished the boy would be safe and whole again.

A white horse appeared in the parking lot.

It reared at the sight of the sirens, broke free of its reins, and galloped between the cars. A nurse fell while trying to dodge it, and an ambulance swerved into a lamp post.

No one died, but several people were hurt.

Daniel sat on the curb and shook.

He understood then that wanting something was not the same as understanding what it would cost.

That night, he locked himself in his apartment and tried not to want anything.

June whined at the door, and Daniel wished she could tell him what to do.

The dog spoke in a voice like dry leaves.

“Stop asking the world to fix what you fear,” she said.

Daniel backed away, but June only lowered her head.

The following days were harder than he expected.

His wishes crept out whenever he was tired, angry, or lonely. A storm of roses filled his kitchen after he longed for his mother, who had died years before.

Their thorns tore his hands as he tried to clear them.

He called his sister and told her everything.

She listened without laughing, then asked what he wanted now.

Daniel looked at the injured people’s names in the news and wished he could help them heal.

Nothing happened.

He closed his eyes and tried again, this time picturing not a miracle, but a simple way to help.

The next morning, he brought groceries to the nurse who had been hurt.

He visited the boy in the hospital and read to him.

He apologized to the building manager for the damage from the roses.

The power did not vanish, and neither did his fear.

But Daniel began to pause before each desire, asking what else might arrive with it.

When he wanted comfort, he sat with June.

When he wanted answers, he called someone he trusted.

When he wished for the world to change, he started with the part he could reach.

One evening, a small green bird appeared on his windowsill.

Daniel felt the familiar surge of wonder and longing.

He did not wish to keep it.

He opened the window, and the bird flew into the night.

Making important choices can feel difficult when there are many possible paths. A person may wonder which option will lead to the happiest or most meaningful life. One useful way to find direction is to seek perspectives from people with different experiences. Listening to varied viewpoints can reveal ideas that we might not discover on our own.

Each person sees the world through the lens of their upbringing, values, and experiences. Because of this, two people can look at the same situation and notice different things. A student deciding what to study, for example, might ask teachers, family members, and professionals for advice. A teacher may emphasize curiosity and learning, while a professional may describe the demands of a particular career. Family members may offer insight into the student’s strengths and needs. Together, these perspectives can help the student make a more informed decision.

Seeking advice does not mean allowing others to choose for us. Instead, it gives us information to consider alongside our own goals and beliefs. Some advice may be useful, while other advice may not fit our circumstances. Thinking carefully about the reasons behind each viewpoint helps us decide what to accept. It also encourages us to question our assumptions and notice when we are overlooking something important.

Varied perspectives can be especially helpful when a choice affects other people. Before making a decision in a group, listening to those who will experience its effects can uncover concerns that leaders might otherwise miss. In friendships, understanding another person’s point of view can prevent a disagreement from becoming a lasting conflict. In a community, people with different backgrounds can suggest solutions that are fairer and more practical. Listening with respect does not require agreement, but it can lead to better understanding.

Of course, gathering too many opinions can sometimes make a decision more confusing. People may offer conflicting advice or speak from fear rather than experience. To manage this, we can ask thoughtful questions and consider how well each person understands the situation. We can also take time to reflect instead of reacting immediately. Then we should weigh the possible consequences and decide which choice best matches our values.

Ultimately, seeking varied perspectives helps people make choices with greater care and awareness. It broadens our understanding without taking away our responsibility to decide. When we listen openly, think critically, and trust our considered judgment, we are more likely to choose a path we can stand behind. In this way, different perspectives can guide us toward thoughtful and meaningful lives.

The first crack appeared beneath the landing gear.

Commander Vale heard it through the hull, a soft tick like a spoon tapping glass. She froze with one boot on the lunar surface and one still inside the lander.

“Did you hear that?” she asked.

Mika Chen checked his instruments.

The moon answered with another tick.

A hairline seam raced across the gray dust, vanishing over the horizon. Then the ground beneath them gave a gentle, impossible shiver.

Mission Control demanded an explanation.

Vale had none.

She and Mika followed the seam to a crater, where the surface had lifted like a lid. Beneath it, darkness gleamed with a faint blue light.

They clipped their safety lines to the lander and climbed down.

The opening widened as they descended.

At the bottom lay a smooth curve, pale as polished bone. It stretched away in every direction.

Mika brushed dust from it with his glove.

The dust came away in a sheet.

Underneath was skin.

For several seconds, neither astronaut spoke.

Then the vast surface blinked.

They scrambled backward as a huge eyelid opened beneath the shell. An iris, bright green and ringed with gold, filled the crater.

“Is that a face?” Mika whispered.

A mouth opened somewhere beyond the horizon.

The sound that followed arrived through their suit radios, though no transmission appeared on their boards.

“Hello,” said the moon.

Back on Earth, every telescope turned toward the crater.

The world watched the live feed in stunned silence.

Then someone recognized the face.

It belonged to a comedian whose reaction videos had been famous for decades.

The name was Marcus Bell, a cheerful man with a crooked smile and one eyebrow that always rose too high.

Marcus had retired long ago.

He was watching from a nursing home when the moon spoke again.

“I wondered when you’d notice,” it said.

The internet exploded.

People made memes before the astronauts had time to climb out of the crater.

Someone captioned the blinking eye: WHEN THE ALARM GOES OFF AT 3 A.M.

Another post asked whether the moon had been streaming this whole time.

Mika stared at his wrist display.

The views were climbing faster than the live feed could count them.

“Why are you wearing Marcus Bell’s face?” Vale asked.

The moon’s smile widened across the sky.

“I needed a shape humans would look at,” it replied.

Marcus, watching on a tablet, gave a small, helpless laugh.

“I knew that face was familiar,” he said.

The moon explained that it was not made of rock.

The gray crust was a shell, grown to keep its sleeping mind safe from sunlight and meteors.

Its true body filled the hollow world beneath, curled around a core of warm, golden light.

It had learned to speak by listening to Earth’s radio waves.

It had learned to smile by watching old comedy clips.

It had chosen Marcus because his face made people stop scrolling.

“Can you move?” Mika asked.

“I have been moving,” the moon said.

Tides shifted across Earth.

The astronauts felt the floor tilt beneath their boots.

Mission Control ordered them to retreat.

Vale looked at the enormous eye, which was now shining with something like worry.

“Are you going to hurt us?” she asked.

The moon’s expression changed, and the famous grin softened.

“I was hoping you could tell me what happens next.”

On Earth, Marcus sat up straighter.

“First,” he said, “you stop looking at the camera like that.”

The moon blinked.

Millions of people laughed at once.

The sound reached the lunar shell as a faint tremor.

For the first time in ages, the moon laughed too.

Its laughter rolled over the oceans and shook loose the last of the shell’s dust.

That night, people looked up and saw the giant face smiling down at them.

By morning, the moon had gained ten billion followers.

And somewhere beneath its bright, famous grin, the old world finally woke.

Benefits of Teacher-Created Summer Assignments

Summer vacation gives students a welcome break from school, but a long pause from learning can make it harder to return to familiar routines. Teacher-created summer assignments can help students prepare for the coming school year while still allowing them time to rest. These assignments are most helpful when they are purposeful, manageable, and connected to what students will learn next.

One benefit is that summer work helps students review important skills. For example, reading regularly can strengthen vocabulary and comprehension, while short math activities can keep basic concepts fresh. When students practice a little at a time, they may feel more confident when lessons resume. This review can also make it easier for teachers to begin new topics without reteaching everything from the previous year.

Summer assignments can also introduce students to upcoming subjects. A reading list, a simple research project, or a set of observation activities can spark curiosity about what lies ahead. Students may arrive with questions and ideas that make class discussions more interesting. Because teachers design the assignments, they can choose activities that match the age, needs, and curriculum of their students.

Another advantage is that these assignments encourage independence and responsibility. Students learn to plan their time, set goals, and complete work without daily reminders from a teacher. These habits are useful not only in school but also in later life. A flexible assignment can also give students choices, helping them take ownership of their learning.

Summer work may help teachers understand what students remember and where they need support. A short reflection or review task can reveal which skills are strong and which need more practice. Teachers can use this information to plan lessons that better meet the class’s needs. Students, in turn, can identify areas they want to improve before the school year begins.

However, summer assignments should not take over students’ vacations. Many students need time for family, hobbies, rest, and other responsibilities. Work that is too difficult or lengthy can create stress and make learning feel like a punishment. Teachers should therefore provide clear directions, realistic expectations, and options when possible.

Assignments should also account for differences in students’ access to books, technology, and quiet study spaces. Offering offline choices or free resources can help make the work fairer. The goal should be to support learning, not to create advantages for students with more resources.

In conclusion, teacher-created summer assignments can make the transition back to school smoother. They help students review skills, explore upcoming topics, and build independence. When assignments are engaging, fair, and limited in length, they can prepare students without taking away the joy of summer. A thoughtful summer task can help students return to class feeling curious, capable, and ready to learn.

At 9:17, Mara entered the Blue Finch café carrying a red umbrella and no raincoat. She chose a table beside the fogged window, where she could watch the street and the mirrored counter. A waiter set down black coffee she hadn’t ordered. Beneath the saucer lay a brass key, warm from someone else’s pocket. Across the room, a man in a gray scarf pretended to read the evening paper. Mara recognized the scar at his temple, though he had sworn it was gone. She touched the key once and left it where it was. The exchange was supposed to be simple: the key for the names of the people who had sold her brother. Then the café door opened, and Inspector Vale stepped inside. Vale had taught Mara how to spot a tail, how to lie without blinking, and how to survive a city that sold secrets by the hour. He also knew her brother’s name. The man in the scarf folded his paper and rose. “You’re late,” he said. Mara glanced at Vale, who was already reaching inside his coat. The waiter dropped a tray, and the crash swallowed the first gunshot. The scarfed man fell against the window, leaving a dark smear across the glass. Vale grabbed the brass key and turned toward the kitchen. Mara saw his other hand, holding a pistol aimed at her. “Your brother’s list was never for you,” he said. “It was bait.” She understood then why he had brought her here alone. She knocked the coffee into his face. Vale fired, and the cup burst against the wall behind her. Mara lunged beneath the table as the café erupted in screams and overturned chairs. She reached the back door just as Vale’s shoes scraped across the tiles. The key fit the lock, though she had no idea what it opened. Behind her, a second shot rang out, then a heavy silence. Outside, rain washed the street clean of footprints. Mara closed her fist around the key and walked toward the river. In its teeth, something tiny glinted: a strip of red thread, tied there by her brother years ago.

Offering students remote schooling options has become increasingly important. Technology has changed how people learn, work, and communicate. Schools can use these changes to give students more choices about where and how they study. Remote schooling is not the right solution for every student, but it offers many valuable advantages.

One major advantage is flexibility. Students who learn remotely may be able to arrange their study time around family responsibilities, medical appointments, or other commitments. They can often review recorded lessons when it suits them. This can be especially helpful for students who need more time to understand difficult material. They can pause, replay, or revisit a lesson instead of feeling rushed.

Remote options can also improve access to education. Students who live far from a school may have fewer travel challenges when they can join classes online. Those who are ill or recovering from an injury may keep learning without having to attend in person. Students with disabilities may benefit from tools that make lessons easier to follow, such as captions, screen readers, or adjustable text. Remote learning can also support students who travel frequently with their families.

Another advantage is that students can learn in an environment that suits their needs. Some students concentrate better in a quiet room than in a busy classroom. Others may feel more comfortable asking questions through a chat or discussion board. A choice of learning settings can reduce stress and help students participate more confidently. When students feel comfortable, they may be more willing to share their ideas.

Remote schooling can help students develop useful life skills as well. They practice managing their schedules and keeping track of assignments. They learn to communicate through digital tools and solve basic technology problems. These skills can prepare them for college and many modern workplaces. Students also learn that taking responsibility for their work is an important part of independence.

Online resources can make learning more varied. Teachers can share videos, interactive activities, articles, and simulations alongside traditional lessons. Students can explore topics at different levels and revisit resources when they need extra practice. This variety may make lessons more engaging. It can also help teachers explain ideas in ways that suit different learning styles.

Remote options may strengthen communication between students, teachers, and families. Online platforms can make assignments, announcements, and feedback easier to find. Families may have a clearer view of what students are studying and when work is due. Students can also contact teachers outside class time when they have questions. Good communication can help students get support before a small problem becomes a larger one.

Remote schooling may offer practical benefits, too. Students who do not need to travel to school can save time and money. Families may spend less on transportation and other daily expenses. Schools may also be able to serve students who cannot attend a particular building or program. These savings and conveniences can make education more accessible.

However, remote learning also has challenges. Students need reliable internet access and suitable devices, which are not available to every family. Some may find it difficult to stay focused or feel isolated from classmates. Teachers and schools must provide clear instructions, timely support, and opportunities for social connection. Remote schooling should not be treated as a simple replacement for every classroom experience.

For these reasons, schools should offer remote schooling as one option within a thoughtful education system. Students should be able to choose the setting that best supports their circumstances and learning needs. Schools must also work to provide the technology and guidance students need to succeed. When planned carefully, remote learning can make education more flexible, accessible, and inclusive. Its greatest benefit is that it gives more students a meaningful chance to learn.

Irish universities are preparing to revise how they score A-level qualifications for admissions, aiming to make it easier for students from Britain to compete for places. The changes would address concerns that the current points system does not fully reflect the range and depth of A-level study.

Under existing arrangements, applicants’ grades are converted into points and compared with the Leaving Certificate results used by most Irish students. Universities say differences between the two qualifications can make direct comparisons difficult. As a result, some British applicants have argued that their grades are not being recognised fairly.

The planned review is expected to examine how points are awarded for individual A-level subjects and combinations of qualifications. Admissions bodies may also consider whether the present system gives sufficient credit to students taking fewer, more advanced subjects. Any revised approach would need to preserve consistency across courses and institutions.

The issue has gained attention as Irish universities seek to attract a wider pool of international applicants. Britain remains an important source of students, particularly following changes to higher education arrangements after Brexit. Universities have said that clear, transparent admissions rules are essential for applicants and schools.

Representatives of the sector have stressed that no final scoring model has yet been announced. The review is likely to involve universities, admissions officials and organisations representing schools and students. Officials will also need to consider how changes affect competition for popular courses.

A revised system could be introduced in a future admissions cycle, depending on the outcome of consultations. Applicants have been advised to continue checking individual university requirements, which can vary by course. Universities say the goal is to make assessment fairer without lowering academic standards.

Every morning, Elias woke to the same alarm at 6:14. The kettle clicked, the rain began, and a red bus sighed past his window. By noon, he had watched his brother die in a car crash exactly 417 times. He had tried warnings, locked doors, stolen keys, and once even chained the car to a lamppost. Somehow, the day always found its way back to the crash. At midnight, the world blinked, and Elias woke again.

On the 418th morning, a woman in a silver coat was waiting beside his bed. “I can end this,” she said, “but you must choose what comes next.” She showed him two doors. Behind the first was tomorrow, with his brother alive and the loop broken. Behind the second was his childhood, and the chance to begin his life again from the very start. “You can forget everything,” she warned. “Or keep every memory and try to make it right.”

Elias stared at the childhood door. He could mend old wounds, avoid old mistakes, and meet the people he had lost before they were gone. But he would be a child again, helpless and uncertain, carrying years of sorrow in a small body. Through the other door, he heard his brother laughing in the kitchen. The sound was so ordinary it hurt.

“Can I see him?” Elias asked. The woman nodded, and the first door opened. His brother stood at the table, alive, asking why Elias looked so tired. Elias wanted to tell him everything, but the words caught in his throat. He had spent 417 days trying to save his brother, yet never once told him how much he loved him.

Elias reached for the first door, then stopped. “If I go back,” he said, “I’ll lose the chance to change everything else.” The woman replied, “You will lose the memory of this choice, too.” Elias took his brother’s hand through the doorway. “Then let me start here,” he said.

The silver-coated woman vanished, and the alarm rang at 6:14. Rain tapped the window, and the red bus sighed past. Elias woke with no memory of the bargain, but his brother was alive beside him, laughing over the kettle. For the first time, the day did not feel like a prison. It felt like a beginning.

The Electoral College has shaped American presidential elections since the country’s founding. Under this system, voters choose electors who formally cast the votes for president. Most states award all their electoral votes to the candidate who wins the state, even if the margin is small. As a result, a candidate can win the presidency without receiving the most votes nationwide. This has happened several times, including in 2000 and 2016. Some people believe this system should be replaced with a direct popular vote.

A popular vote system would make every person’s vote count equally toward the national result. Candidates would have a stronger reason to campaign in every state, not just a few closely contested ones. Voters in states considered safely Republican or Democratic might feel that their choices mattered more. The candidate who received the most votes across the country would become president, which many people see as the clearest form of majority rule. This could also make election results easier to understand.

However, replacing the Electoral College would have challenges. Candidates might focus mainly on large cities, where many voters live. Smaller states could worry that their concerns would receive less attention. A nationwide recount could also be complicated if the final result were extremely close. Changing the system would require a constitutional amendment, which is difficult to pass.

Even with these concerns, the current system also gives some voters more influence than others. A vote in a competitive state can attract more campaign attention than a vote in a state where the outcome is predictable. A direct popular vote would not solve every problem, but it would treat each vote equally in determining the winner. The United States should seriously consider replacing the Electoral College with a popular vote, while creating clear rules for recounts and election administration.

Every morning, I polished the brass doorknob and told it we were expecting company. The debt collectors had sent three letters, so I considered them practically family. I imagined them marching up the path in shiny shoes, carrying clipboards like shields. In my mind, they had already stolen my moon, my good silver, and the left half of Tuesday.

I prepared a welcome feast of cold toast and tap water. Then I sharpened a butter knife, because the letters said “final notice,” and I thought that sounded theatrical. I wasn’t angry, exactly; I was defending the house from an invasion that existed mostly in my curtains. When the telephone rang, I answered in my best king’s voice. A recorded message asked me to hold, so I put it on hold in the pantry.

By noon, I had built a fort from unpaid bills. I appointed the toaster captain and the kettle judge. They agreed the collectors were guilty of stealing my future, which I had misplaced somewhere near the laundry. I sentenced them to a night in the garden, where the sprinklers would interrogate their shoes. I did not actually hurt anyone; the garden was empty, and the shoes were imaginary.

Still, I waited by the window, watching every passing car. Each white van seemed to carry the repossession agents, coming to take my old television and perhaps my name. I rehearsed a speech about how the television had become a lighthouse for lost thoughts. I practiced looking calm, then furious, then calm again. The curtains applauded whenever I got the order right.

At dusk, a neighbor knocked to ask if I had received a package. I mistook his polite smile for the collectors’ secret signal and offered him a chair made of bills. He laughed, and for a moment the house felt less like a fortress. Then a car door shut somewhere down the street, and I sprang to attention. The kettle blew its whistle like a tiny alarm.

I opened the door to find nobody there, only a damp envelope on the step. It contained another reminder, not a warrant, not a squad, not even a footprint. I read it twice and tucked it beneath the toaster’s paw. Tomorrow, I decided, I would call the number printed at the bottom and ask for a payment plan. But tonight I kept watch, just in case the moon came to collect what I owed.

Highland Fossils Shed Light on Ancient Life and Australian Dinosaur Tracks

Fossil discoveries in Scotland’s Highlands are giving researchers new clues about ancient animals and how to interpret dinosaur tracks found in Australia. The remains come from rocks formed hundreds of millions of years ago, long before dinosaurs appeared. They preserve evidence of life in environments that once covered parts of the region.

Among the fossils are early marine animals and other organisms that lived in shallow seas. Their shapes and positions can reveal how they moved, fed and interacted with the seabed. Some fossils also record traces left behind as animals crawled or burrowed through sediment.

Researchers say these traces are especially useful when studying tracks from other parts of the world. In Australia, fossil footprints can be difficult to identify because they may be incomplete or altered by erosion. Comparing them with better-preserved ancient traces helps scientists distinguish animal tracks from marks made by currents or collapsing sediment.

The Highland discoveries do not mean the Scottish fossils and Australian tracks were made by the same creatures. Instead, they offer examples of how different animals can leave similar impressions under comparable conditions. That comparison can help researchers interpret what a footprint records—and what it cannot.

A track’s outline alone may not tell scientists whether an animal was walking, resting or changing direction. The depth and spacing of impressions, along with the sediment around them, provide additional evidence. Highland fossils and trace fossils give researchers a wider set of patterns to assess.

The work also highlights the importance of studying the rocks that contain fossils, not just the fossils themselves. Sediment grain size, water conditions and the speed at which layers formed can all affect how traces are preserved. These details help reconstruct the environments in which ancient animals lived.

For Australian researchers, improved interpretations of tracks could clarify how dinosaurs moved across ancient landscapes. Trackways may reveal whether animals travelled alone or in groups, and how their movement changed across different ground conditions. Such conclusions remain cautious, since footprints rarely provide a complete picture.

Scientists stress that fossil evidence is often fragmentary. A single track can support several explanations, and new discoveries may alter existing interpretations. Comparing evidence from distant regions can reduce uncertainty, but it does not eliminate it.

The Highland finds are therefore contributing to a broader effort to understand the history of life and the processes that preserve it. By linking fossil anatomy, trace marks and geological context, researchers can ask more precise questions about ancient behavior. The same methods may help make sense of track sites across Australia and elsewhere.

As fieldwork and analysis continue, scientists hope to uncover further fossils and refine their comparisons. Each discovery adds another piece to a record assembled from rocks across the globe. Together, those records offer a clearer, though still incomplete, view of ancient ecosystems and the animals that moved through them.

Jane Fonda Reflects on Abuse, Gender Inequality and Hollywood’s Changing Culture

Jane Fonda has spoken about sexual abuse, gender inequality and the changing treatment of women in Hollywood, describing progress alongside problems that persist. In interviews over the years, the actor and activist has connected her experiences to broader conversations about power and accountability. Her comments come as the film industry continues to reckon with harassment and unequal opportunities.

Fonda has discussed being sexually abused as a child, an experience she has said she did not understand at the time. She has described how shame and confusion can prevent survivors from speaking about abuse. In later life, she came to recognize that what happened was not her fault. She has also urged people to listen to survivors and take their accounts seriously.

The subject, she has said, is not limited to individual incidents. Fonda has pointed to the conditions that can allow abuse to continue, including unequal power and a culture that discourages people from challenging influential figures. For many years, she said, women in entertainment were expected to tolerate behavior that would now prompt greater scrutiny. The industry’s dependence on a small number of powerful decision-makers could make speaking out especially difficult.

Fonda has also criticized gender inequality in Hollywood, including disparities in pay, roles and access to leadership. Women, particularly older women, have often faced narrower opportunities than their male counterparts. She has argued that representation behind the camera matters as much as the stories shown on screen. More women in writing, directing and executive positions can help change which experiences are told.

The #MeToo movement brought renewed attention to sexual misconduct and workplace power across entertainment and other industries. Fonda has welcomed the greater willingness to discuss abuse, while cautioning that public attention alone does not guarantee lasting change. She has emphasized the importance of consequences, institutional safeguards and support for those who report misconduct. Changing policies, she has suggested, must be accompanied by shifts in everyday behavior.

Attitudes toward women in Hollywood have changed considerably during Fonda’s long career, but she has not described the progress as complete. More actresses now speak openly about ageism, sexism and professional barriers. Audiences, too, have become more likely to question whose perspectives are missing from major productions. Yet women continue to encounter unequal treatment and limited representation in some parts of the industry.

Fonda’s remarks draw on both her personal history and decades of public activism. She has used her platform to discuss women’s rights, social justice and the consequences of silence around abuse. Her willingness to revisit difficult experiences reflects a broader effort to make such conversations less isolating. It also underscores the difference between telling a story and addressing the systems that shaped it.

The actor’s perspective resonates as Hollywood debates how to turn awareness into measurable change. Advocates continue to call for fairer hiring, transparent pay practices and safer working environments. Fonda’s central message is that progress depends on listening to women and challenging the power imbalances that have long been treated as normal.

Students should be permitted to use mobile phones at school for communication and emergencies, but their use should be carefully controlled. Phones help students contact their parents if plans change or they need to get home safely. They can also be useful during an emergency, such as a natural disaster or a medical problem. A student who feels unwell may be able to quickly notify a family member. Phones can also help students reach emergency services when no adult is nearby. However, mobile phones can distract students from lessons. Messages, games, and social media may make it harder to concentrate. Phones can also be used to cheat on tests or take photographs without permission. These problems should not be ignored. Schools can create clear rules to prevent misuse. For example, students could be required to keep their phones silent and put away during class. Teachers might allow phone use only when it supports a learning activity. Students could also be asked to keep their phones in a safe place during exams. In an emergency, schools should let students contact their families as soon as it is safe to do so. Parents and students should understand the school’s phone policy. If a student breaks the rules, the school can respond with a fair consequence. A complete ban may prevent some distractions, but it could also make communication more difficult. Responsible phone use is a skill students need to learn. With sensible limits, mobile phones can provide safety without disrupting education. Therefore, students should be allowed to bring phones to school, while following rules that protect learning and respect others.

Mara found the wishing fountain beneath a hill of black pines. Its water glimmered like moonlight, though the sun was high. A stone beside it read, “One wish, freely given, for one wish, freely asked.”

Mara laughed at the strange wording. She had never believed in magic, but she believed in opportunity. Just then, her neighbor Eli arrived, carrying a small wooden boat. He set it by the fountain and closed his eyes.

“I wish my sister could wake up,” he whispered. His sister had been asleep for months after a fever. The fountain rippled, and a silver drop rose from its surface. Before it could fall, Mara snatched it and drank.

“I wish for every treasure I can imagine,” she cried. Gold spilled from the air around her. Coins rolled down the hill, and jeweled necklaces tangled in the grass. Mara filled her pockets until she could barely stand.

Eli stared at her in disbelief. The fountain went dark. A deep crack split the stone, and the water drained into the earth. Then the silver drop appeared inside Mara’s palm, cold and bright.

The fountain had not granted her wish, it seemed. It had only taken Eli’s wish and given Mara a chance to make her own. As the last trickle vanished, Eli sank to his knees. “You stole the only hope I had,” he said.

Mara looked at the treasure scattered around her. For the first time, it seemed less like a fortune than a pile of stones. She offered Eli the gold, but he shook his head. “I wanted my sister,” he said.

That night, Mara tried to sleep in her grand house, but every coin in her room began to whisper. They repeated Eli’s words until dawn. She gathered the treasure and hurried back to the hill.

There she found Eli sitting beside the dry basin. His wooden boat rested in his lap. Mara placed the treasure at his feet and begged the fountain to return. Nothing answered.

Then she noticed the silver drop still in her palm. It had warmed, and within it she saw a tiny image of Eli’s sister breathing softly. Mara understood at last: the fountain had not destroyed the wish. It had bound it to her stolen greed.

She pressed the drop into Eli’s hand. The ground shuddered, and clear water burst from the basin. Far away, a bell rang from Eli’s home. He ran toward it, while Mara stayed behind.

The coins around her turned to dull gray stones. She did not protest. When Eli returned, his sister was awake, and he thanked Mara with tears in his eyes. Mara walked home empty-handed, carrying one lesson she would never wish to forget.

European leaders reacted cautiously to the United Kingdom’s snap election, weighing the prospect of a stronger government against the risk of renewed political uncertainty. The vote could shape the balance of power in London just as Brexit negotiations enter a critical phase. Across the European Union, officials said they would respect the outcome while preparing for talks with whichever government emerges.

The election was called by Prime Minister Theresa May, who argued that a larger parliamentary majority would strengthen her hand in negotiations. Her decision followed months of debate over Britain’s future relationship with the EU and the terms of its departure. But the campaign has also raised questions about whether voters will endorse her approach or seek a different direction.

European Commission officials have stressed that the EU’s negotiating position remains unchanged. They say talks must address citizens’ rights, the financial settlement and the border between Northern Ireland and the Republic of Ireland before discussions turn to a future trade relationship. The bloc has also urged Britain to begin formal negotiations promptly.

In Brussels, officials have privately acknowledged that the election could make the process easier if it produces a stable government with clear authority. A decisive result, they argue, could help British ministers make difficult choices and deliver on any agreement reached. Yet a larger majority would not necessarily mean Britain would accept the EU’s terms.

Some European politicians have warned against interpreting the election as a referendum on Brexit itself. The main parties broadly accept that Britain will leave the EU, though they differ on how closely the country should remain aligned with the bloc. That leaves room for negotiations over the shape of the departure, even if the decision to leave is not reversed.

The campaign has brought renewed attention to the possibility of a “hard Brexit,” in which Britain leaves the EU single market and customs union. EU leaders have said access to the single market depends on accepting its rules, including the free movement of people. British proposals for limiting immigration could therefore complicate efforts to preserve close economic ties.

The question of Ireland is another major concern for European governments. Officials on both sides have pledged to avoid a hard border, but they have yet to explain how that goal can be reconciled with Britain’s departure from the EU’s customs arrangements. Any disruption could affect trade and the delicate political balance established by the Good Friday Agreement.

The election may also affect the timetable. EU negotiators have warned that the process is complex and that the two-year period set out in Article 50 leaves little time for delays. A change in Britain’s negotiating team or priorities could narrow the window further.

For now, European capitals are avoiding public predictions about the result. German officials have emphasized the need for a constructive partnership, while leaders in France and elsewhere have reiterated that the EU will negotiate as a united bloc. That unity is intended to prevent Britain from striking separate arrangements with individual member states.

Business groups across Europe are watching closely. Companies have warned that uncertainty over tariffs, regulation and supply chains could discourage investment on both sides of the Channel. They are pressing governments to provide clarity as early as possible.

The vote could ultimately strengthen May’s authority, weaken it or produce a parliament that makes agreement harder to secure. European officials say they are prepared for each possibility. Whatever the result, the election is unlikely to remove the central disagreements over migration, trade and the future border in Ireland.

For the EU, the immediate priority remains getting negotiations started and protecting the interests of its citizens and member states. For Britain, the campaign offers voters a chance to influence the mandate their government takes into those talks. The outcome will therefore matter not only for domestic politics but also for the tone and direction of the Brexit negotiations.

Every doorway in the multiverse began with a brass key.

Mara kept hers on a cord beneath her shirt, where its warmth reminded her she had once been ordinary.

She had left her home world at twenty, chasing a job with the Cartographers, who mapped passages between realities.

The work had made her famous.

It had also given her a desk, a title, and a small room in a city that never knew the color of her childhood sky.

For seven years, she had told herself that was enough.

Then the key began to sing.

Its thin, bright note led her to a doorway in the archive basement, one she had never seen before.

Beyond it lay the valley where she grew up.

The same green hills rolled beneath the same silver clouds.

A crooked farmhouse stood beside the river, its windows glowing at dusk.

Mara stepped through.

Her brother Tomas was on the porch, older now, with gray at his temples and a cane beside his chair.

For a moment, neither of them spoke.

Then Tomas said, “You’re late for supper.”

Mara laughed, and the sound broke into a sob.

Their mother had died three winters ago.

Her father had followed the next spring.

Tomas had kept the house, though he admitted he had nearly sold it twice.

He showed Mara the kitchen, the orchard, and the chair where their father used to mend nets.

She told him about distant planets, impossible cities, and the maps she had helped draw.

He listened with the patience of someone who had spent years hearing her stories in his head.

When night came, he asked her to stay.

Mara looked at the old room upstairs, where her childhood books still leaned in crooked rows.

She wanted to stay so badly that the wanting frightened her.

In the morning, a message waited on her wrist device.

The Cartographers had offered her a promotion: chief navigator of the outer routes.

It was the work she had dreamed of, and the life she had built by leaving.

Tomas saw her reading the message.

“You don’t have to choose today,” he said.

“But the door may not stay open,” she replied.

He nodded toward the river, where their father’s little boat still rocked at its mooring.

“Then choose what you can live with, not what you think you owe.”

Mara spent the day walking the valley.

She found the tree where she and Tomas had carved their initials, nearly swallowed by bark.

She found the old footbridge, the millstone, and the place where she had first decided the world was too small.

By sunset, the key had gone quiet.

She understood that belonging was not a house waiting untouched.

It was a thread, worn thin but still strong enough to hold.

Mara accepted the promotion, then asked the Cartographers for one change.

She would keep a route home on every map she made.

Tomas watched her return to the doorway with her pack over one shoulder.

“Come back before another seven years,” he said.

“I will,” Mara promised.

She crossed into the archive, carrying the smell of river water and supper smoke with her.

For the first time, the distance between her two lives felt like a road instead of a wound.

Mara had spent three years writing a novel about a woman who loved a man she could never quite describe. The man was based on Eli, her neighbor, whose brief smiles she collected like clues. Each evening she watched his window, then returned to her desk convinced she had discovered a fresh way to write longing. She crossed out every sentence that reminded her of another book, until even the blank spaces seemed borrowed. When Eli finally knocked to return a misdelivered letter, she forgot all her careful lines and asked him to stay. He did, for tea, and told her about the woman he planned to marry. After he left, Mara opened her manuscript and wrote the truth plainly, without searching for a new way to say it. By morning, she had finished the first page.

Online education has become an important part of learning for students of all ages. It can make education more accessible, but it works best when it responds to students’ needs. Four useful ways to improve online education are flexibility, comfort, safety, and personalized learning.

Flexibility allows students to study at times that fit their schedules. Some students have jobs, family responsibilities, or health concerns that make a fixed timetable difficult. Recorded lessons let them review challenging topics and pause when they need a break. Teachers can also offer several ways to complete assignments, such as writing a response or recording a presentation. Clear deadlines and regular reminders help students stay organized without removing that flexibility. Schools should still provide opportunities for live discussions so students can ask questions and feel connected.

Comfort is another important part of learning online. Students may feel more relaxed when they can study in a familiar, quiet space. They should be encouraged to take short breaks, use comfortable seating, and adjust their screens to avoid strain. However, not every student has a quiet room or a reliable computer at home. Schools can help by lending devices, offering internet access, and providing supervised study spaces. These supports make online learning more comfortable and fair for everyone.

Safety matters in digital classrooms just as it does in physical schools. Teachers should explain how to protect passwords and personal information. Schools can use secure platforms and limit access to class activities and student records. Clear rules against bullying and respectful communication help students feel safe sharing ideas. Students should also know how to report harmful messages or uncomfortable behavior. When adults respond promptly, students are more likely to trust the learning environment.

Personalized learning helps students progress at a suitable pace. Online tools can provide extra practice when a student is struggling and more challenging work when a topic feels easy. Teachers can use quizzes and assignments to understand what each student needs. They should also check in personally, because computer programs cannot fully understand a student’s feelings or circumstances. Giving students some choice in topics and projects can make learning more interesting. At the same time, teachers should make sure that technology does not replace helpful human support.

Online education is strongest when these four features work together. Flexible schedules, comfortable study conditions, safe platforms, and personalized support can help more students succeed. Schools, teachers, families, and students all have a role in creating this kind of learning. By listening to students and improving online programs, education can become more welcoming and effective for everyone.

Every morning, Mara woke expecting to feel her left hand.

For a few seconds, her mind supplied its familiar weight beneath the blanket. Then she looked down and remembered the silver socket at her wrist.

The converters had taken her hand first.

They called it a mercy, a way to make frightened humans fit the new world. Most people agreed before the machines touched them.

Now the converted walked the streets with smooth metal limbs and calm, bright eyes. They spoke of harmony as if they had invented it.

Mara lived beneath the ruined tram station, where the old signs still showed places nobody could reach. She had survived the first sweep by hiding in a drainage pipe.

The second sweep had left her with a missing ear and a scar that pulled her mouth sideways. She kept the scar covered with a scarf, though no one remained to judge her.

Every few days, a converted patrol passed above her shelter. Their footsteps landed in perfect unison.

Mara used to know their names.

Tomas had been a baker who burned every second loaf. Ilya had sung off-key while carrying water.

Now they called each other by assigned numbers and never laughed. Once, Mara saw Tomas pause outside the station.

She lifted her good hand through a crack in the floor. For an instant, his eyes warmed.

Then the silver light returned, and he moved on.

Mara hated the converters for changing him. She hated herself more for wishing they had changed her, too.

The socket hurt when the weather turned cold. Phantom fingers curled around objects that were not there.

At night, she dreamed she was holding a cup, and the cup slipped through her empty hand. She woke with her arm pressed against her chest.

One evening, a child found the entrance to her shelter. His face was human, but a thin seam ran from his temple to his jaw.

“Are you Mara?” he asked.

She reached for the knife at her belt. The child flinched, though he did not run.

“I was told you could help,” he said. “My mother remembers a song.”

Mara lowered the knife. “What song?”

“I don’t know,” he said. “She hums it when the lights go out.”

The child’s name was Ren, though his wrist carried a number. His mother waited in a converted clinic two streets away.

Mara followed him through alleys where weeds split the pavement. The city’s bright towers glowed above them, clean and silent.

At the clinic door, a woman sat beneath a white lamp. Her eyes shone like polished glass.

Ren took her hand. “Mother, this is Mara.”

The woman stared at Mara’s scarf, then at the metal socket. “You’re missing something,” she said.

“So are you,” Mara replied.

The woman’s mouth twitched. A tune emerged, soft and wavering.

Mara knew it at once: the baker’s lullaby, sung by Tomas when his ovens failed and the bread came out black. She joined in, badly, with her cracked voice.

Ren listened. The woman’s bright eyes dimmed, just a little.

Then her fingers began to tap the old rhythm against her knee. Mara felt her absent hand answer with a phantom beat.

For a moment, the clinic seemed less like a machine and more like a room. The woman looked at Mara and whispered, “I remember the smell of flour.”

Mara wanted to forgive her. She wanted to flee.

Instead, she sat beside her and sang until the lights went out. In the darkness, none of them looked whole.

But when Ren reached for her, Mara placed her remaining hand in his.

Mara Venn had always wanted the world to look up at her.
As a child, she climbed the tallest hill and announced that one day she would command the sky.
The grown-ups laughed, but Mara never forgot their faces.
She studied machines, weather, and every legend about the sun.
By thirty, she had built a tower of copper mirrors on the edge of the city.
At its peak sat a black glass engine she called the Night Switch.
Mara said it could dim the sun for one minute.
The mayor refused to let her test it.
Mara heard only the word no.
On the night of the winter festival, she climbed the tower alone.
Below her, thousands of lanterns drifted over the river.
She imagined every face turning toward her.
She pulled the silver lever.
The engine hummed, and the sky shivered.
The sun vanished.
At first, the crowd cheered, thinking it was an eclipse.
Then the lanterns went out.
The river froze in shining ribbons.
A cold wind rushed through the streets.
Mara waited for the sun to return.
The Night Switch clicked once and fell silent.
She yanked the lever back.
Nothing happened.
She struck the engine with a wrench.
Nothing.
She begged it, then cursed it.
The darkness stretched across the world.
By dawn, there was no dawn.
People crowded into warm houses and burned furniture for heat.
The farms withered beneath frost.
Ships stopped moving in the icebound harbor.
Mara descended from the tower and confessed what she had done.
Some shouted at her.
Others simply turned away.
An old mechanic named Iven came forward.
He had once helped Mara build the engine, before she drove him out for questioning her.
“I can try to repair it,” he said.
“But you must tell me everything.”
Mara told him how the mirrors had been aligned.
She described the glass core and the lever’s hidden lock.
She did not hide the part where she had ignored his warnings.
Iven listened without forgiving her.
Together they climbed the tower.
The Night Switch was colder than the night around it.
Its black glass was cracked in three places.
Iven said the engine was still drawing power from somewhere.
Mara traced the cables beneath the floor.
They disappeared into the mountain.
The engine had been built to borrow heat from the deep earth.
Its return valve had melted shut.
Iven could open it, but the tower would shake apart.
Mara looked through the glass at the dark city.
She saw people sharing blankets in the square.
She saw children huddled beside the last public fire.
For the first time, she did not picture them watching her.
She pictured them waiting for warmth.
Mara took the wrench and wedged it beneath the valve.
Iven warned her that the gear might snap.
She pushed anyway.
The metal groaned, and a bolt tore loose.
The tower lurched.
Mara slipped, but Iven caught her sleeve.
Together they forced the valve a fraction wider.
A red glow pulsed far below.
The Night Switch roared to life.
Its mirrors began to turn, slowly and unevenly.
A pale line appeared on the horizon.
The city held its breath.
The line widened, but the sun did not return.
The engine had only broken the first lock.
Iven said the final release had to be made from the tower’s crown.
Mara climbed the outer ladder while sparks fell around her.
At the top, she found the release wheel frozen in place.
She set her shoulder against it.
The wheel did not move.
Below, the people began to sing, faintly at first.
Mara gripped the wheel with both hands.
She turned it until her palms split.
The lock gave way with a sound like distant thunder.
Light spilled over the horizon.
The sun rose, weak and red, but it rose.
Mara fell to her knees as warmth touched her face.
The crowd cheered, though not for her alone.
In the days that followed, she helped rebuild the farms and the tower.
She kept the Night Switch dismantled and its pieces buried.
People still remembered the darkness.
Mara never again mistook being feared for being admired.

Every morning, Elias arrived at the office before the lights had fully woken. He hung his coat on the same hook and opened the same spreadsheet. Outside, buses sighed through the rain. Inside, the printer coughed, the clock clicked, and nobody asked how he was. At noon, he ate a sandwich at his desk. At five, he saved his work and watched the windows turn black. His apartment waited with its quiet rooms and one unwatered plant. He called his sister on Sundays, but lately their conversations had become careful and short. “Busy?” she asked. “Same as always,” he said. He began to feel that the days were not passing so much as closing around him. The thought of disappearing sometimes seemed like a door in a wall. It frightened him, but the darkness kept suggesting that no one would notice if he stepped through. One Thursday, the office lights flickered during a storm. For a moment, every screen went dark. Elias sat still, listening to the rain strike the glass. Then someone from the next desk said, “You okay over there?” It was a small question, almost lost beneath the weather. Still, Elias answered honestly. “No, not really.” His coworker rolled over in her chair and stayed beside him. She didn’t offer a grand solution or tell him to cheer up. She asked whether he wanted to call someone together. Elias looked at his phone, where his sister’s name waited. His hands trembled as he pressed the button. When she answered, he said, “I’m scared of where my thoughts are taking me.” She told him she was coming over, and that they would find help together. The night did not become bright all at once. His sadness did not vanish because someone had heard it. But the dark door seemed less like an instruction and more like a warning. The next morning, Elias called a doctor and asked for an appointment. He also told his manager he needed time away from work. His desk remained, his spreadsheets unchanged. Yet the routine had been interrupted by one honest sentence. In the days that followed, he met with a counselor and began making a plan for difficult moments. His sister checked in, and his coworker saved him a seat at lunch. Some mornings were still heavy. Some evenings still stretched too wide. But Elias learned to treat those hours as hours, not as a verdict on his life. He started watering the plant by the window. One pale leaf slowly lifted toward the light. It wasn’t a miracle, and it wasn’t enough by itself. It was simply something living that asked for care. For the first time in a long while, Elias stayed to see what it might do next.

Driverless cars are often presented as a convenient and exciting invention. They may help people travel more easily and reduce some kinds of human error. However, their rapid development also raises serious concerns. These drawbacks should be considered before driverless cars become common on public roads.

One major concern is the loss of jobs. Millions of people work as taxi drivers, truck drivers, delivery drivers, and bus operators. If companies replace these workers with automated vehicles, many could struggle to find new employment. Some workers may need costly training to move into other careers. The economic effects could also harm families and communities that depend on transport jobs.

Safety is another important issue. Driverless cars use cameras, sensors, and software to understand what is happening around them. These systems can fail because of bad weather, confusing road markings, or unexpected events. A car might not recognize a pedestrian or respond correctly to a damaged traffic light. Although human drivers also cause crashes, a computer error could affect many vehicles using the same technology. Even a rare accident can make the public lose confidence in driverless cars.

Legal responsibility after a crash is also uncertain. It may be difficult to decide whether the blame belongs to the passenger, the vehicle owner, the manufacturer, or the software company. Different laws in different places could make these cases even more complicated. Insurance policies may also need to change to cover new risks. Until clear rules are established, people involved in accidents may face lengthy disputes.

Driverless cars may also create concerns about privacy and security. They collect information about routes, locations, and driving habits. If this data is misused or stolen, people’s privacy could be harmed. Hackers might also try to interfere with a vehicle’s systems.

These problems do not mean that driverless cars should never be used. Instead, they show why careful testing, strong safety standards, and clear laws are necessary. Governments should also help workers prepare for changes in the transport industry. Driverless cars may bring benefits, but society should address their drawbacks before relying on them widely.

Good decisions rarely come from one person seeing the whole picture. Each of us has different experiences, knowledge, and assumptions. When people bring those differences together, they can understand a problem more fully. This is why gathering diverse, knowledgeable perspectives often leads to better decisions.

A group with varied backgrounds may notice details that others overlook. For example, a city planning team might include engineers, residents, business owners, and environmental experts. Engineers can explain how a design will work, while residents can describe how it may affect daily life. Business owners may point out economic concerns, and environmental experts can identify risks to local wildlife. By listening to all of them, the team can create a plan that is safer and more useful.

Knowledge is also important because opinions are most helpful when they are informed. A doctor, a patient, and a public health researcher may each understand different parts of a health problem. Their combined knowledge can lead to a treatment plan that is medically sound and realistic for the patient. A decision based on only one perspective might miss an important fact.

Different viewpoints also help groups challenge their assumptions. People may ask questions that others had not considered. They can point out weak evidence, possible consequences, or unfair effects. This kind of respectful disagreement can prevent costly mistakes. It encourages decision-makers to explain their reasoning and improve their ideas.

However, simply inviting many people into a discussion is not enough. Leaders must make sure everyone has a chance to speak. They should listen carefully rather than dismissing unfamiliar ideas. The group also needs reliable information and a clear way to weigh the evidence. Without these habits, discussion can become confusing or dominated by a few voices.

Gathering perspectives can take extra time, but that effort often pays off. Decisions shaped by careful discussion are more likely to address real needs. People who are included may also be more willing to support the final choice. They can see that their concerns were taken seriously, even if the group did not follow every suggestion.

In school, work, government, and everyday life, decisions affect people in different ways. Seeking informed and varied perspectives helps us recognize those differences. It does not guarantee that a decision will be perfect, but it makes blind spots less likely. The strongest choices are often made when people learn from one another. When diverse knowledge is brought together with respect, a group can make decisions that are wiser, fairer, and more effective.

The Martian Face is a hill-like feature in the Cydonia region of Mars that appeared face-shaped in some early spacecraft images. However, later observations provide strong evidence that it is a natural geological formation rather than an artificial structure. The first widely publicized image was taken by NASA’s Viking 1 orbiter in 1976, at relatively low resolution and with dramatic shadows. These conditions made ordinary surface features look more like eyes, a nose, and a mouth. Higher-resolution images taken by the Mars Global Surveyor in 1998 revealed a rugged, uneven landform instead of a carefully sculpted face. Later images from Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter showed details such as ridges, craters, and slopes consistent with erosion. The apparent facial features are not symmetrical, as one might expect from a deliberately designed monument. They also change noticeably with the Sun’s angle, because shifting shadows can create or weaken the impression of a face. Wind, impacts, and other geological processes can shape hills and cliffs into forms that resemble familiar objects. This tendency to recognize meaningful patterns in random shapes is called pareidolia. Similar face-like shapes can be found in clouds, rocks, and other natural landscapes on Earth. Scientists have not found nearby structures or other evidence suggesting that the feature was built by an intelligent civilization. The available images and geological context instead fit a natural landform shaped over a long period. The Martian Face is therefore an intriguing example of how perspective and imagination can influence what we see in space.

The first time Elias sold his soul, he was twenty-three and afraid of dying.

A fever had settled in his lungs, and every breath sounded like paper tearing.

At his bedside, a stranger in a gray coat offered him a bargain.

“Ten years of your life,” the stranger said, “for ten years more.”

Elias agreed before he could ask what happened after the ten years.

He woke the next morning, healthy and trembling.

For a while, he treated the bargain as a foolish dream.

Then, on his thirty-third birthday, the stranger returned.

Elias saw the gray coat through the bakery window and felt his birthday cake turn bitter in his mouth.

The stranger named the price for another decade.

This time Elias asked what he would find on the other side.

“Nothing I can prove,” the stranger replied.

Elias bargained anyway.

He had a daughter by then, and she was still small enough to sleep with one hand around his finger.

He told himself he was buying time for her.

Years passed, and he spent them teaching her to swim, tying her shoes, and pretending not to notice when she grew taller than him.

At forty-three, he stood alone beside her wedding carriage.

The stranger waited in the churchyard.

Elias could have refused.

He could have let the years he had already bought run out.

Instead, he traded another piece of his soul for five more years.

The stranger accepted, though he said the price had changed.

“You are not bargaining with fear now,” he said.

“What am I bargaining with?” Elias asked.

“Guilt.”

Elias knew what he meant.

When he was young, he had driven home drunk and struck a boy on a country road.

The boy had lived, but his brother had not.

Elias had never confessed.

After the bargain, he began writing letters to the dead brother’s mother.

He wrote the truth each time, then burned the page before dawn.

At forty-eight, the stranger came to his door.

Elias was tired, his hair white at the temples, his daughter’s children asleep upstairs.

He asked for another year.

The stranger tilted his head.

“What would you do with it?”

“Tell the truth,” Elias said.

“Then tell it without buying time.”

The stranger left, and Elias spent the night staring at the dark window.

By morning, he had written the letter again.

This time he carried it to the post office.

The mother replied with a single sentence: “I have waited long enough to hear it.”

Elias went to her house the following Sunday.

She was old and narrow-shouldered, but her eyes were steady.

He confessed everything, including the bargains.

She listened without forgiving him.

When he finished, she asked whether the stranger had promised him heaven.

“No,” Elias said.

“Then what did you buy?”

He searched for an answer and found only the years themselves.

The woman closed the door gently.

Elias walked home beneath a pale sky, feeling neither absolved nor condemned.

On his fiftieth birthday, the stranger appeared once more.

Elias was sitting with his daughter, who held his hand as she had when she was small.

The stranger named a final price.

Elias looked at his daughter’s face and felt the old terror rise.

Then he noticed the gray coat’s shadow stretching across the floor.

It ended before reaching him.

“Is that what waits for me?” Elias asked.

“I don’t know,” said the stranger.

For the first time, Elias believed him.

He told his daughter to stay, but not to bargain.

Then he let go of the stranger’s offer.

That night, Elias died in his sleep.

No angels appeared, and no flames opened beneath him.

There was only a quiet darkness, vast enough for fear and wonder.

He could not tell whether it was an ending or a beginning.

But he entered it without asking for more time.

Students should not need satisfactory grades to participate in school activities. Sports, clubs, and other activities can help students feel connected to school and give them a reason to keep trying. They also teach teamwork, responsibility, and time management. If students are barred from activities because of low grades, they may lose an important source of support and motivation. Instead, schools should help students improve their grades while allowing them to participate. For example, teachers could offer tutoring, study sessions, or regular check-ins. Students might also agree to make a study plan and complete missing assignments. Activities should not replace schoolwork, so students still need to meet reasonable academic expectations. However, every student deserves a chance to learn from both classroom and extracurricular experiences. With the right support, schools can encourage academic success without shutting students out.

At 3:17 a.m., Marcy woke to the sound of applause coming from her locked hallway closet. She had retired from stripping five years earlier, but applause still made her reach for a robe. Inside the closet, a brass lamp glowed beneath a heap of winter coats. When she touched it, a tiny voice whispered, “Your money is growing legs.” Marcy blinked, and a dozen crisp hundred-dollar bills marched across her dresser like nervous little soldiers. She had never seen them before. They formed a line, saluted, and vanished beneath her tax folder.

At breakfast, a stranger in a silver raincoat knocked on her door. “The money has been found,” he announced, though Marcy hadn’t told anyone it was missing. He handed her a receipt for a bank account that didn’t exist. The balance was exactly the amount she’d earned in tips during her last year onstage. Marcy called her accountant, who advised her not to touch a cent until they could trace it. Then the closet applauded again.

By noon, the bills had returned, stacked neatly beside her laptop. Marcy read about cryptocurrency, wallets, and irreversible mistakes, then read the pages again. She chose a reputable exchange and called her accountant back before moving anything. Together, they documented the strange deposit and contacted the bank. As she waited for an explanation, the brass lamp flickered. A final bill slid under the door, stamped with the words “NOT A DEDUCTION.” Marcy laughed, and for the first time in years, the applause sounded like it was meant for her.

On a Tuesday, the sky opened and God announced the End of the World would be decided by a dance-off.

Nations gathered in the ruined Olympic Stadium, each carrying its flag and a suspiciously large team of consultants.

A glowing scroll unrolled across the clouds.

The rules, God explained, were simple.

No nation could use a dance move invented after the invention of the fax machine.

Every costume had to include at least one sincere apology.

And anyone who said “the people have spoken” had to perform the worm.

The United States sent a committee to negotiate an exemption.

The committee was immediately transformed into tap shoes.

France arrived with a ballet troupe and demanded that the judges pronounce “apocalypse” correctly.

The judges were three cherubs, a retired referee, and a pigeon wearing a sash that said NEUTRAL.

Russia entered in matching uniforms and denied they were uniforms.

China brought a perfectly synchronized formation, plus a form asking whether the apocalypse could be postponed until after lunch.

The United Kingdom sent a fog machine and called it a strategy.

A tiny island nation, overlooked by every news crew, stepped onto the floor with a drum and a grin.

Their leader, a retired schoolteacher named Mara, wore a cardigan embroidered with the words “Sorry About Everything.”

God checked the scroll.

“Approved,” God said.

The contest began with a solemn waltz, which several nations mistook for a trade agreement.

Then the music switched to disco.

The United States’ former committee tapped in a circle, clacking out a surprisingly persuasive argument for democracy.

France leapt gracefully, though one dancer paused to correct the pigeon’s posture.

Russia performed a stiff march that became an accidental conga line when the leader lost his hat.

China’s formation moved so precisely that the cherubs briefly considered using it to organize heaven.

The United Kingdom’s fog machine swallowed its dancers, its judges, and most of the stadium.

Mara’s island team took the floor last.

They danced the old fishing dance, a humble shuffle passed down through generations of people who had never had time for consultants.

The pigeon bobbed its head.

The retired referee wiped away a tear.

God leaned forward.

“Now,” God said, “the final test: each nation must dance while apologizing for one thing it has done.”

The United States apologized for interrupting and accidentally invented jazz hands.

France apologized for correcting everyone and performed a flawless shrug.

Russia apologized for the hat, though no one could identify which hat.

China apologized for the paperwork and distributed copies of the apology in triplicate.

The United Kingdom apologized for the fog, then apologized for apologizing too quietly.

Mara’s team bowed and apologized for nothing, because they had spent the week helping their neighbors rebuild.

The stadium fell silent.

God consulted the scroll, then tore it in half.

“No nation wins,” God declared. “The world is spared.”

The sky closed, and the judges disappeared, leaving only the pigeon.

The United Nations invited it to chair a committee on peace.

The pigeon accepted, provided the meetings included crumbs and no speeches.

He left the hall through a kitchen door, one hand clamped to his side. Behind him, the silence was worse than the shouting had been. Rain washed the smoke from the windows, but it could not wash away what he had done. He stumbled across the service yard and tried to remember where he had parked. His keys slipped from his fingers and vanished beneath a drainpipe. He crouched to reach for them, then fell hard against the bricks. For a moment, he listened for footsteps. All he heard was water ticking from the gutter. He pushed himself upright and made it to the alley. A siren wailed somewhere beyond the warehouses. He turned away from it, though every street seemed to lead back to the hall. His coat grew heavy and warm around the wound. At the corner, a bus passed without slowing. He raised one arm, but it shook too badly to signal. A shop window showed him a pale stranger, leaving a dark trail on the pavement. He kept walking because stopping meant thinking. In a narrow doorway, he found a phone and tried to call someone. He could not remember the number. The sirens grew louder, then stopped nearby. Red light swept over the walls. He sank onto the step and watched rain blur the street. When the officers called for him to show his hands, he could not lift them. By the time they reached him, his eyes had closed, and the storm had begun to quiet.

A Chilean nun has filed a lawsuit against religious authorities, alleging that she was mistreated after being raped by a worker at her convent. The case raises questions about how church institutions respond to sexual violence and support survivors.

The woman says the assault took place while she was living in a convent in Chile. She alleges that a worker at the religious community raped her. The lawsuit accuses church authorities of failing to protect her and of treating her unfairly after she reported the attack.

Details of the alleged assault and the legal filing have not been independently verified. The nun’s claims are allegations, and no finding of liability has been reported. The identities of the people involved have not been made public.

According to the complaint, the response from religious leaders compounded the harm she had suffered. It alleges that she faced mistreatment rather than receiving appropriate care and support. The filing seeks accountability from authorities who, the nun argues, had a duty to respond responsibly.

The case is expected to examine what church officials knew, when they knew it, and what steps they took after the report. It may also address whether the convent had safeguards for residents and procedures for reporting abuse. The lawsuit does not, by itself, establish that any defendant committed wrongdoing.

Sexual abuse cases involving religious institutions have drawn scrutiny in Chile and elsewhere. Survivors and advocates have called for transparent investigations, independent reporting channels, and access to counseling. They have also urged institutions to protect complainants from retaliation or pressure.

The legal action could put renewed attention on the power imbalance between religious authorities and members of their communities. Nuns may depend on their institutions for housing, work, and social support, factors that can complicate reporting abuse. Advocates say complaints should be handled by professionals independent of the accused institution.

It was not immediately clear whether the religious authorities named in the suit had filed a response. No court ruling or timetable for the case was available. The worker accused of rape also could not be reached for comment.

The nun’s claims will now be assessed through the legal process. Any determination of responsibility will depend on evidence presented to the court. Her lawsuit, however, has already brought attention to the treatment of a survivor who says she sought help from the very institution where she lived.
