Important life decisions can shape our future in lasting ways. Choices about education, work, money, and relationships deserve careful thought. When facing a difficult decision, seeking advice can help us see the situation more clearly. A trusted person may notice details that we have overlooked. They can also share lessons from their own experiences. This does not mean that we should let others decide for us. Advice is most helpful when it supports our own thinking rather than replaces it. Listening to different viewpoints can reveal options we had not considered. It can also help us understand the possible risks and benefits of each choice. For example, a student choosing a career might speak with teachers, family members, and people working in different fields. Each person may offer useful information from a different perspective. However, not every piece of advice will suit our circumstances. Some people may have different values or priorities from ours. Therefore, we should consider who is giving the advice and why. We should compare their suggestions with our goals and beliefs. It is also wise to seek advice from more than one reliable person. This can help us avoid making a choice based on a single opinion. After listening carefully, we must take responsibility for our final decision. In the end, advice cannot guarantee that everything will go perfectly. Still, thoughtful guidance can reduce uncertainty and help us prepare for challenges. Seeking advice is a valuable habit because it combines other people’s wisdom with our own judgment.

The war began over a mango.

At least, that was the version printed on the banners outside San Juan’s City Hall. Jamaica’s radio stations said it began over a badly translated recipe. Both accounts were wrong, but by then the generals had already put on their ceremonial hats.

Puerto Rico’s army marched east carrying coquí-shaped shields and a map that seemed to have been folded upside down. Jamaica’s navy sailed north with a brass band on deck, playing so cheerfully that nobody could tell whether it was a march or an invitation.

The first battle was scheduled for noon.

At 11:58, the Puerto Rican commander discovered that his troops had packed beach umbrellas instead of ammunition. The Jamaican admiral discovered that his sailors had brought enough jerk seasoning to feed an island, but only one working compass.

They met on a small island between them, where a pelican sat on a crate marked “URGENT DIPLOMATIC SUPPLIES.” Inside were microphones, party streamers, and several suspiciously potent bottles of rum punch.

The commanders accused each other of sabotage. The pelican stole a sandwich and flew away.

By then, the troops had begun comparing uniforms. One soldier admired a Jamaican beret; another asked where he could buy a Puerto Rican flag that did not keep getting tangled in his rifle.

A sergeant produced a guitar. Someone else found a speaker. The official war anthem was replaced by a song both sides knew, though each insisted its version had the proper ending.

The commanders tried to restore discipline.

They were interrupted by a council of grandmothers, who had arrived with folding chairs and a stack of handwritten recipes. The grandmothers announced that nobody would be permitted to fight before eating.

The first plates emptied quickly. The accusations slowed. The generals sampled each other’s cooking and began revising their speeches to include compliments.

Then the rum punch appeared.

It was strong enough to persuade the Puerto Rican commander that he had always wanted to learn dancehall. It was strong enough to persuade the Jamaican admiral that salsa was simply naval training with better shoes.

Someone turned up the music. Someone else hung the flags together, which looked less like a surrender and more like a very ambitious tablecloth.

By sunset, the soldiers were dancing in circles, the officers were debating whose island had the superior beaches, and the pelican had returned with a crown made of bottle caps.

The treaty was signed on the back of a menu. It declared the mango innocent, the recipe mistranslated, and all future disputes subject to a dance-off.

The next morning, the newspapers called it a historic peace agreement. The commanders called it a strategic victory. The grandmothers called it a mess and began planning lunch.

For years afterward, both governments claimed they had won the conflict. The only people who knew the truth were the pelican, the musicians, and the soldiers who still couldn’t remember why they had been sent there.

But every summer, Puerto Rico and Jamaica held a joint festival on the little island. It featured food, music, and a strict rule against bringing suspicious punch to diplomatic meetings.

The rule lasted until noon.

The European Space Agency has awarded Astrium UK a contract to develop a next-generation microwave sounder for future weather satellites. The instrument is intended to improve observations of the atmosphere and support more accurate weather forecasts.

Microwave sounders measure naturally emitted microwave radiation from gases and particles in the atmosphere. By observing at different frequencies, they can estimate temperature and moisture at varying altitudes, including through many cloud layers that limit some other remote-sensing instruments.

Astrium UK will lead the instrument’s development under the ESA contract. The work is expected to cover detailed design, construction and testing, although the agency has not disclosed the contract’s value or a full schedule.

The sounder is intended for a future European meteorological satellite mission. Its measurements are expected to complement data from other instruments, giving forecasting services a more complete picture of atmospheric conditions.

Improved temperature and humidity profiles could help forecasters track the development of storms and monitor changes in the atmosphere. The data may also contribute to climate research, which relies on long-term, consistent observations.

Microwave instruments are particularly useful because they can collect information in conditions where visible and infrared sensors are obstructed by cloud. Their measurements nevertheless require careful calibration and sophisticated processing to produce reliable atmospheric profiles.

The development will involve meeting strict requirements for sensitivity, stability and performance in the demanding environment of space. Engineers will also have to ensure that the instrument can operate reliably over the satellite’s planned lifetime.

ESA’s decision reflects Europe’s continuing investment in advanced Earth-observation technology. The agency works with national space programmes and industry to develop missions that provide data for public services and scientific research.

Astrium UK has experience in designing and building space systems and instruments. The contract gives the company a central role in developing technology for Europe’s future meteorological observations.

The project’s progress will depend on successful design reviews and testing before the instrument is ready for integration with a spacecraft. Once the satellite is launched, its observations will be processed and distributed to meteorological organisations.

Those organisations use satellite measurements alongside weather-station reports, radar and other sources. The combined data feed into numerical models that simulate how the atmosphere will evolve.

ESA has not announced when the sounder will begin delivering operational measurements. The timeline will depend on the wider satellite programme as well as the instrument’s development and qualification.

The new contract marks an early step toward the next generation of European weather-satellite capabilities. Its eventual contribution will be assessed by how consistently it can provide precise, useful data from orbit.

Manchester is stepping up its response to incidents involving Spice, a group of potent synthetic drugs linked to serious health problems and growing pressure on public services. The substances, often sold as herbal material sprayed with synthetic cannabinoids, can have unpredictable effects that differ sharply from cannabis. Local outreach workers and emergency responders have reported encounters with people who are unresponsive, confused or highly distressed after using them. Health professionals warn that the strength and contents of individual batches can vary, making the risks difficult to predict. Reported effects include agitation, panic, hallucinations, vomiting and loss of consciousness. In severe cases, users may suffer seizures or require urgent medical treatment. The risks can be greater for people with existing health conditions or those combining Spice with other substances. Police, ambulance crews and hospital staff are among the services responding to incidents. Repeated emergencies can divert resources from other urgent calls and add pressure to already busy services. Manchester’s response involves cooperation between health services, local authorities, police and voluntary organisations. Outreach teams aim to reach people who may be reluctant or unable to seek help through conventional services. Their work can include first aid, advice on drug-related risks and referrals to treatment or housing support. Supporters say building trust is essential, particularly for people facing homelessness, trauma or mental health difficulties. They also stress that a person in medical distress should receive emergency care without delay. Public health workers are urging people not to assume that Spice is predictable or safe because it is sold as a plant-based product. They encourage users and bystanders to seek help if someone becomes unconscious, has a seizure or struggles to breathe. The scale of the problem is difficult to measure, in part because substances may be misidentified and incidents recorded in different ways. Local agencies say better information-sharing could help them direct support where it is most needed. Manchester’s challenge is to reduce immediate harm while expanding longer-term access to treatment and stable support.

Mara could stop a second, but she could never make it feel less lonely. She froze the station clock at 2:17 every night, when the last train had gone and the city seemed to hold its breath. One evening, a stranger appeared on the platform while every other person stood motionless. He was looking directly at her.

Mara let time move again. The stranger blinked, then glanced at the clock. “You stopped it,” he said. His name was Ivo, and he could rewind a minute, though he admitted he often used the gift to avoid saying the wrong thing. “Does it work?” Mara asked. “No,” he said. “I just get more chances to be afraid.”

They met at the station each night, careful not to call it a habit. Ivo rewound small mistakes: a dropped coin, a clumsy greeting, a silence that lasted too long. Mara watched him repeat each moment until it became less like living and more like rehearsing. She told him she stopped time because she hated being surprised. “Then we’re both hiding from the same thing,” he said.

The next night, Ivo didn’t come. Mara froze the station at 2:17 and waited until the stillness hurt. She could have searched the city, but that would mean choosing a direction without knowing what she’d find. At last she let the clock advance. The train lights swept across the platform, and Ivo stepped out, breathless. He had spent the evening trying to decide whether to come.

Mara almost stopped time again. Instead, she asked him to stay until the next train. Ivo looked at the clock, uncertain, and said yes. The train arrived, then left, carrying no answer about what they would become. For once, neither of them reached for the past.

Schools should encourage community service, but they should not require every student to complete it. Volunteering can teach students responsibility, empathy, and teamwork. It also gives them a chance to understand the needs of people in their community. For example, students might help at a food bank, clean up a park, or read with younger children. These experiences can be meaningful and help students discover interests they did not know they had.

However, community service is most valuable when students choose to participate willingly. A student who cares about an activity may put more thought and energy into it. If service is required, some students may focus only on finishing their hours rather than helping others. This can make volunteering feel like another school assignment. It may also reduce the sense of kindness and generosity that service is meant to build.

A requirement can also be unfair to students with busy lives. Some students have jobs, family responsibilities, or long commutes. Others may have health needs that make certain activities difficult. Finding a suitable opportunity and arranging transportation can be challenging, especially for students whose families have limited resources. Schools should consider these differences before making service mandatory.

Instead of requiring service, schools can make it easy and appealing to volunteer. They can offer a range of activities during the school day and provide information about local opportunities. Teachers can explain how service benefits both the community and the volunteers. Schools could also recognize students who participate without making recognition a condition of success.

Community service should be an opportunity, not an obligation. Students are more likely to develop lasting habits of helping when they have freedom to choose how they contribute. Schools should encourage service while respecting students’ circumstances and choices. In this way, volunteering can remain meaningful for students and the people they serve.

Ancient skull fractures are offering a stark glimpse of violence among early human ancestors—and raising questions about how they treated their dead. Researchers examining fossil remains have identified head injuries consistent with severe, potentially lethal blows. The findings suggest that interpersonal violence may have been part of life long before modern humans emerged.

The fossils come from an early hominin group that lived hundreds of thousands of years ago. By studying the shape and location of the fractures, scientists sought to distinguish injuries sustained during life from damage caused after death. Some of the breaks show signs of healing, while others appear to have occurred around the time of death.

The pattern of injuries has led researchers to consider whether at least some individuals were killed deliberately. However, skull damage alone cannot establish the motive or circumstances of a death. Accidents, conflict with other groups, and attacks by animals can sometimes leave similar marks.

The remains also raise the possibility that the dead were placed in a specific location rather than simply left where they died. Such placement could indicate an early form of intentional burial, though researchers caution that the evidence is not conclusive. Natural processes may also concentrate bones in one area.

Confirming deliberate burial is difficult because soil movement, water, and scavengers can alter a site over time. Scientists therefore compare the position of remains with sediment layers and other archaeological evidence. A clear, repeated pattern of careful placement would strengthen the case.

Together, the injuries and the arrangement of the fossils may reveal a complex social world. The ancestors could have experienced serious violence while also showing concern for their dead. Researchers say more excavation and analysis will be needed to separate these possibilities.

The findings add to a growing debate over when human ancestors began burying their dead and how widespread interpersonal violence was in early communities. They do not prove that either behavior was common. Instead, they offer clues that may help researchers understand the origins of both conflict and mortuary practices.

Tensions between the United States and Iran have risen after a series of missile tests, new sanctions, and military exercises, even as Washington says it has no immediate plan to send more troops to the region.

The developments have added to concerns that longstanding disputes could escalate into a direct confrontation. US officials have criticized Iran’s missile activity, saying it contributes to instability and threatens regional security. Tehran has defended its weapons program as a necessary deterrent and says it is not aimed at launching an attack.

Washington has also imposed additional sanctions on Iranian entities and individuals. The measures are intended to restrict funding and pressure Iran over its military activities and other policies. Iranian officials have condemned the sanctions, arguing that they unfairly target the country and undermine prospects for diplomacy.

Military exercises by the United States and its regional partners have further sharpened the atmosphere. US officials describe the drills as defensive and say they are meant to maintain readiness and reassure allies. Iran has objected to the presence and activities of foreign forces near its borders, warning that it will respond to threats.

Despite the heightened rhetoric, US officials have not announced an immediate increase in troop numbers. They have said existing forces are positioned to protect American personnel and interests, while keeping options under review. The decision suggests Washington is seeking to signal resolve without taking a step that could be interpreted as preparation for imminent conflict.

Analysts say the combination of sanctions, weapons tests, and military maneuvers raises the risk of miscalculation, particularly if either side misreads the other’s intentions. The situation also puts pressure on regional governments to balance security ties with Washington against their own concerns about escalation. Diplomatic channels remain important, but public statements from both sides have offered little sign of a near-term breakthrough.

Officials have not reported an immediate clash linked to the latest developments. Still, the rapid exchange of warnings and military signals has left the region on edge. Whether tensions ease may depend on both sides avoiding provocative actions and finding ways to resume dialogue.

Deadly clashes erupted between Philippine troops and Abu Sayyaf militants as security forces pressed efforts to capture the group’s leader, officials said. The fighting took place in a remote area of the southern Philippines, where the armed group has operated for years. Military units moved into the area following intelligence reports about the leader’s whereabouts. Gunfire broke out as troops approached suspected militant positions. Officials said soldiers and militants were killed, though the casualty toll was not immediately clear. Authorities did not release the identities of those killed while families were being notified. The military said it was verifying reports that the group’s leader may have been among the casualties. The operation involved ground forces supported by surveillance and other security assets, according to officials. Residents in nearby communities were urged to avoid the fighting and follow instructions from local authorities. Some families reportedly left their homes as the clashes continued. Abu Sayyaf has been linked to kidnappings, bombings and attacks in the country’s south. Philippine forces have conducted repeated operations against the group, which has been weakened by years of military pressure and internal divisions. Officials said the latest action was intended to disrupt its remaining networks and prevent further attacks. The military said operations would continue, while emphasizing that reports from the battlefield were still being checked. The clashes underscore the continuing security challenges in the southern Philippines, despite sustained efforts to dismantle the militant group.

Although Venus is similar to Earth in size and structure, its surface is one of the most dangerous places in the solar system. It is covered by thick clouds that trap heat, creating temperatures hot enough to melt lead. Its atmosphere is mostly carbon dioxide, and the pressure at the surface is crushing. Venus also has clouds containing corrosive sulfuric acid. Despite these harsh conditions, the author supports studying the planet. One reason is that Venus can help scientists understand how Earth’s climate may change. The two planets began with many similarities, but their environments developed in very different ways. By comparing them, researchers can learn what causes a planet to become extremely hot. Studying Venus may also reveal how atmospheres form and change over time. Although spacecraft cannot easily survive on its surface, scientists can use orbiters, radar, and other technology to explore it. These tools can map the planet and gather information from safer distances. The discoveries may help scientists understand other planets beyond our solar system as well. Exploring dangerous places requires careful planning and advanced equipment. However, the risks are worthwhile when the research can answer important questions about Earth and the universe. For these reasons, Venus deserves continued scientific study, even though its conditions are far more dangerous than Earth’s.

Mara had known Eli since their first year of college, when they bonded over a shared dislike of the cafeteria’s mysterious soup. Over the years, they became each other’s first call for good news, bad dates, and flat tires. Their friendship felt as sturdy and familiar as the old blue couch in Eli’s apartment. Mara never questioned it.

Then one rainy evening, Eli showed up with her favorite tea and a stack of films she’d mentioned weeks ago. He remembered everything, she thought, smiling as she let him in. They spent the night laughing at a terrible comedy, their shoulders touching beneath one blanket. When Eli laughed, Mara found herself watching his face instead of the screen.

She told herself it was only because the joke had been especially bad. But the next morning, she caught herself wondering what it would be like to hold his hand without pretending the sidewalk was crowded. The thought startled her, so she buried it beneath errands and work.

For a few days, she noticed every small kindness: Eli saving her the last dumpling, Eli texting to make sure she got home safely, Eli listening without reaching for his phone. The gestures weren’t new, but her attention to them was. At their usual café, he leaned across the table to wipe a fleck of sugar from her cheek. Mara’s heart stumbled, and Eli’s hand paused in the air.

He looked as surprised as she felt. Neither of them made a joke to smooth it over. Instead, they walked home slowly, leaving space between their shoulders. At her door, Mara took a breath and said, “I think I might be seeing us differently.”

Eli’s smile was gentle, but uncertain. “I’ve been wondering if you were,” he said. Mara reached for his hand, and this time, neither of them blamed the crowded sidewalk.

Welsh Labour supporters are urging voters in some constituencies to back Plaid Cymru in the Assembly election, arguing that tactical votes could help limit UKIP’s influence.

The appeal reflects growing concern among parts of the Labour movement about the prospect of UKIP gaining seats and shaping the next Welsh government’s agenda. Supporters say that, where Labour has little chance of winning, a vote for Plaid could be the most effective way to prevent UKIP candidates from taking a seat.

The message is not an official Labour campaign policy. It is being promoted by individual activists and local supporters, who say voters should consider the likely outcome in their area rather than follow party loyalties automatically.

Wales elects members to its devolved legislature through a system that combines constituency contests with regional representation. That arrangement can make the regional vote especially important to parties seeking to increase their overall seat totals.

Tactical voting advocates argue that the contest in some regions is close enough for a shift in support to affect which parties win seats. They say Plaid Cymru, with an established presence across Wales, may be better placed than Labour to challenge UKIP in particular areas.

The proposal has prompted debate among Labour supporters. Some welcome cooperation with Plaid as a practical response to UKIP’s rise, while others insist that voters should support Labour regardless of local calculations.

Critics also question whether tactical voting can be predicted reliably. Election outcomes depend on turnout, the distribution of votes among several parties and the rules used to allocate regional seats.

Plaid Cymru has campaigned on Welsh self-government and policies tailored to Wales. Its supporters say a stronger showing would ensure that Welsh interests remain central to political decisions in Cardiff.

UKIP, meanwhile, has sought to convert its support into representation in the Assembly. The party has appealed to voters concerned about immigration, the European Union and the relationship between Wales and the rest of the United Kingdom.

Labour supporters urging a vote for Plaid say their priority is to prevent UKIP from gaining additional influence. They argue that even a small number of seats could give the party a louder voice in debates and negotiations.

The appeal comes amid a competitive campaign in which parties are fighting for votes across Wales. Labour has traditionally been a major force in Welsh politics, but the election is taking place against a changing political landscape.

Plaid Cymru is seeking to strengthen its position, while the Conservatives and Liberal Democrats are also competing for seats. UKIP’s prospects have added another dimension to contests that may be decided by narrow margins.

Some Labour voters may be reluctant to support a party with different constitutional aims. Plaid’s commitment to greater Welsh autonomy, and its support for independence for Wales, are likely to remain points of disagreement.

Those advocating a tactical vote say the immediate question is which candidate or party is best placed to defeat UKIP locally. They urge voters to look at constituency and regional polling, while acknowledging that such information can be uncertain.

There is no guarantee that a coordinated shift in votes would produce the intended result. If supporters misjudge the race, their choice could instead affect the balance among other parties.

The discussion highlights the challenges facing voters in an election with multiple parties and different routes to representation. It also underlines how concerns about UKIP are influencing strategy beyond the party’s direct opponents.

Whether the appeal gains traction will depend on local campaigning and voters’ willingness to set aside their usual party preference. The final balance of seats will determine how much influence UKIP and other parties can exert in the Assembly.

Ian Stewart’s defense claimed that Helen Bailey was abducted by men connected to her late husband’s business dealings, as he stood trial over her death. The allegation offered an alternative explanation for Bailey’s disappearance from her home in Royston, Hertfordshire.

Bailey, a children’s author, was reported missing in April 2016. Her body was later found in a cesspit beneath the property she shared with Stewart. Prosecutors said Stewart had killed her and concealed her body, and argued that he acted to gain access to her wealth.

Stewart denied murder and said he had no role in Bailey’s death. His defense suggested that people with links to the business affairs of Bailey’s late husband could have targeted her. The claim was presented as a possible motive for an abduction, rather than evidence identifying a specific perpetrator.

The case also drew attention to Stewart’s earlier relationship with his first wife, Diane Stewart, who died in 2010. He had previously been convicted of her murder after prosecutors argued he poisoned her. That conviction became part of the prosecution’s case against him in Bailey’s trial.

The defense’s abduction theory was challenged by the prosecution, which relied on forensic and circumstantial evidence from the couple’s home. Prosecutors said the evidence supported the conclusion that Bailey was killed at the property and that Stewart had tried to hide what happened. The jury ultimately rejected Stewart’s account and found him guilty of Bailey’s murder in 2017. He was sentenced to life imprisonment, with a minimum term of 34 years.

Prince Caelan watched the western wall disappear beneath a tide of shadow. The darkness did not burn or break stone; it simply swallowed whatever it touched. Bells rang across the capital, then fell silent one by one. Beyond the palace gates, people fled through streets already turning black. Caelan’s father had ridden out at dawn with the last of the royal guard. None had returned.

The prince clutched the silver sword his mother had given him. Its blade had once shone bright enough to light a room, but now it reflected only darkness. “We must leave,” pleaded Mara, his captain, as the palace trembled. Caelan looked toward the throne room, where the crown rested beneath a painted portrait of his ancestors. “A king should not abandon his people,” he said.

Mara took his hand, but he gently pulled away. They crossed the courtyard as shadow climbed the palace walls. At the gate, Caelan saw a little girl standing alone, too frightened to move. He ran to her and lifted her into his arms. The darkness rushed toward them, swallowing the statues behind him.

Caelan placed the girl in Mara’s arms and turned to face the coming night. He raised his useless sword, though his hands were shaking. For a moment, the darkness paused. Then it folded over him like a closing curtain. By sunrise, the kingdom was gone, but the girl carried Caelan’s name beyond its ruins.

Other people’s opinions can help us make better choices, but they should not make our choices for us. Friends, family members, teachers, and mentors may see parts of a situation that we have missed. Their experiences can offer useful warnings or possibilities. For example, a student choosing a club might ask friends what they enjoy about their activities. A teacher could suggest which club best fits the student’s interests and schedule. These different perspectives give the student more information to consider.

Listening carefully is important, even when someone’s advice is different from what we expected. We can ask questions to understand why a person feels a certain way. We can also think about whether that person’s experience applies to our own situation. Advice is helpful, but it is not always right for everyone. Each person has different goals, needs, and responsibilities.

After hearing others, we should take time to reflect. We can compare the possible choices and consider what matters most to us. It may help to think about the benefits and drawbacks of each option. We should also consider the consequences of our decision. In the end, we are the ones who will live with the results.

Making our own decision does not mean ignoring other people. It means learning from them while taking responsibility for our choice. We can be grateful for advice without following every suggestion. Different perspectives can guide us, but our values and judgment should shape the final decision.

By the time the rain began, Daniel had been in the hospital for three weeks, counting the cracks in the ceiling to keep fear away. Mara visited every afternoon, bringing coffee and stories from the life they planned to share. Then one day she didn’t come. A nurse left a newspaper on his tray, and a photograph showed Mara beside her husband, the man who had once tried to kill her. The caption said they had reunited. Daniel read it again and again, feeling the future they had promised dissolve into something cold and unreachable. That night, overwhelmed by betrayal and despair, he tried to end his life. The ward staff found him in time and stayed beside him while doctors treated his injuries. When he woke, a counselor sat nearby and reminded him that the worst moment of his life did not have to be its last. Daniel couldn’t believe that yet, but he let the counselor open the curtains, and watched the rain ease into morning.

A Norfolk homeowner is facing the loss of her clifftop bungalow after a powerful tidal surge accelerated erosion along the coast. The surge stripped away sections of the cliff, bringing the property closer to the edge. The woman, whose home overlooks the North Sea, has been told that the ground beneath it may no longer be stable. She has lived in the bungalow for years and now fears she could soon be forced to leave. Residents in the area said the sea rose rapidly during the surge, driven by strong winds and high tides. Waves battered the shoreline and carried away large amounts of sand and soil. In the days that followed, fresh cracks appeared near the cliff top. Local officials are assessing the damage and monitoring the site for further movement. They have warned that conditions could change quickly, particularly if more storms arrive. The homeowner said she was shocked by how much land had disappeared in such a short time. She is waiting for a full assessment before deciding what to do next. The bungalow’s future may depend on whether engineers consider the remaining cliff safe. Coastal erosion is a long-standing challenge in parts of Norfolk, where soft cliffs are vulnerable to waves and weather. Climate change is raising concerns about the frequency and severity of coastal flooding and storm surges. However, experts say local geology and the direction of each storm also shape the rate of erosion. The surge has renewed calls for clear information and support for people living in at-risk homes. Some residents have questioned whether existing coastal defenses can withstand increasingly severe conditions. Authorities say they must balance the cost of protection with the risks and likely benefits. In some locations, relocating homes may be safer than trying to hold the coastline in place. For the homeowner, that possibility has become painfully immediate. She said the bungalow is more than a building, but accepted that safety must come first. Officials have urged people to keep away from unstable cliff edges while inspections continue.

By six o’clock, the restaurant had dressed itself in candles and white roses. Martin, who had waited tables there for eleven years, hated both. He hated the candles for making every face look tender. He hated the roses for wilting politely in their narrow vases. Most of all, he hated the couples. They came in holding hands, brushing crumbs from each other’s sleeves, whispering as if the world had given them a private room. Martin had once believed in that sort of thing. Then his fiancée had left him for a man who owned a bakery and knew how to make a proper apology. Since then, romance had seemed like a trick performed with excellent lighting. The restaurant’s manager, Celia, found him polishing the same spoon for the third time. “Big night,” she said. Martin glanced at the reservation book. “They’re all big nights to somebody.” Celia told him table twelve had booked the full proposal package. It included a six-course meal, a violinist, a hidden photographer, and a ring delivered beneath a silver cloche. It did not include a gratuity. “The couple prepaid everything,” Celia said. “They want an elegant surprise.” Martin looked at the line marked SERVICE CHARGE: 0. “How considerate.” At seven, the couple arrived. The man wore a navy suit and a nervous smile. The woman wore a green dress that caught the candlelight whenever she moved. They thanked Martin for their chairs and apologized for being early. He disliked them at once for making courtesy look effortless. The violinist began playing beside the coat rack. Martin served oysters, then soup, then a tiny plate of something arranged like a garden. The man kept checking the pocket of his jacket. The woman kept smiling at him, unaware of the ring. Martin carried each course as if it weighed more than it did. Around them, other couples leaned together and laughed. Their happiness seemed to spread across the room like perfume. Martin began to resent the woman’s soft voice, the man’s careful attention, even the way they passed the salt. When the photographer crouched behind a fern, Martin nearly told him to stand up and be honest. The final course arrived beneath the silver cloche. Martin set it down and lifted the lid. Beneath a sugared rose sat the ring, bright as a tiny, smug moon. The man rose from his chair. His hands shook as he spoke. He said he loved her patience, her courage, and the way she sang to plants when she thought nobody could hear. Martin stared at the service charge still glowing on the reservation slip. The woman covered her mouth. The man lowered himself to one knee. Around the room, forks paused and conversations died. Martin felt the old anger climb his throat. Then the woman said yes. She said it through tears, and the man laughed as if someone had opened a window inside him. The room erupted in applause. Martin stood beside the table with the empty cloche in his hands. For one long moment, he wanted to tell them what the evening had cost him in labor and silence. Instead, he saw the woman reach down and pull the man up by both hands. She whispered something that made him laugh again. Martin remembered, against his will, the sound of his own fiancée laughing in a kitchen full of flour. The memory hurt, but it was no longer sharp enough to cut. He placed the cloche on his tray and wished them well. The man thanked him, then hurried back to the ring. No tip appeared. Martin returned to the kitchen, where Celia asked if everything had gone smoothly. “Perfectly,” he said. He still hated the candles. But on his way past table twelve, he turned one of them away from the draft.

For weeks after Daniel died, I kept setting two cups on the table. His stayed empty, gathering a thin ring of dust. I told myself it was an accident, though the word never softened what I remembered. We had argued that morning, and I let him leave without saying I loved him. When the phone rang that night, I was still rehearsing what I would say when he came home. Now every quiet room seemed to be waiting for him. I walked past the bakery where he bought cinnamon rolls and felt the sidewalk tilt beneath me. Friends called, but their kindness made me feel worse. They wanted proof that I was healing, and I had none to offer. Some mornings, getting dressed was the only thing I could manage. Other mornings, I lay still and wished the day would forget to begin. I kept hearing Daniel’s last words, though I knew memory was changing them. In my mind, he always sounded patient, even when I had been cruel. I began writing letters to him on the backs of grocery lists. I apologized for the argument, for my silence, for surviving him. The letters filled a drawer, but the guilt stayed. One rainy afternoon, I found his old scarf beneath the couch. It still smelled faintly of soap and the cedar closet. I held it to my face and let myself cry until my chest hurt. When I finally stood, the room looked no kinder, but it was still there. I washed one cup and left the other where it was. Then I opened the window and let the cold air in. The next morning, I made coffee for one and drank it slowly. I did not feel better, but I had stayed. For now, that was how I loved him: by staying long enough to meet another morning.

Phones can also help students plan their day or look up useful information. However, using phones during lessons can distract students from learning. Notifications and games may make it harder to focus and participate. Phone use can also interrupt teachers and classmates. Clear rules would help everyone understand when phones are allowed. Maya had always hated surprises, which made her friends’ plan for her seventeenth birthday especially risky. They knew she loved scary movies, so they borrowed a lightweight prop coffin from the school theater. Just before the party, Maya’s best friend, Lena, asked her to help carry a box into the garage. The lights snapped off, and the garage door slammed shut behind them. A hollow thump came from the other side of the room. Maya’s phone flashlight flickered across the floor and found the coffin lid slowly lifting. She screamed as a pale hand curled over its edge. The lid swung open, and a figure in a torn white dress sat up with a groan. Maya stumbled backward, tripped over a stack of chairs, and knocked the light switch on. The figure pulled off her ghostly mask, revealing Lena’s older brother, who was laughing so hard he could barely stand. Maya’s laughter came late, after her shaking hands finally stopped trembling. “You are all in so much trouble,” she said, trying to sound stern. Then the garage filled with the sound of clapping from the shadows. Her parents, cousins, and friends stepped forward, holding a giant cake shaped like a haunted house. The coffin had been hiding the birthday decorations, and the ghost had been guarding her favorite present: tickets to a horror movie premiere. Maya stared at the cake, then at the smiling faces around her. She hugged Lena, who whispered, “Sorry—mostly.” For the rest of the night, they told the story of the coffin, each retelling making Maya’s scream sound louder. She still hated surprises, but she admitted this one would be hard to forget.

Summer assignments should be designed by both teachers and students. Teachers know which skills students need to practice before the next school year. They can choose activities that support learning and connect to the curriculum. However, students have different interests, strengths, and goals. When students have a choice, they are more likely to feel motivated. For example, a student who enjoys drawing might create a visual project, while another might write a short story. Both students could practice important skills in ways that feel meaningful to them.

Teachers should provide clear guidelines for summer work. They can explain the assignment’s purpose, suggest useful resources, and set reasonable expectations. This helps students understand what they are supposed to learn. At the same time, students should have some freedom to decide how they complete the work. Giving students options can help them become more independent. It also teaches them to make decisions and manage their time. These are valuable skills both inside and outside the classroom.

If teachers design every detail, assignments may feel boring or unnecessary to some students. If students design everything themselves, the work might not support the learning they need. A shared approach can avoid both problems. Teachers could set a general learning goal and offer several project choices. Students could then choose an option or suggest an idea of their own. The teacher could review each idea to make sure it is practical and connected to learning. This approach gives students a voice while keeping the assignment focused.

Summer should still include time for rest, play, and family. Assignments should not take so long that students feel they never get a break. Teachers and students can work together to create activities that are useful, flexible, and enjoyable. In the end, the best summer assignments are planned with teacher guidance and student choice. This balance can make learning more engaging and help students return to school ready to succeed.

Online education has become an important part of learning for students of all ages. It offers more than lessons and assignments; it can also help students prepare for life beyond school. By working with digital tools and real-world materials, learners develop useful practical skills. They may research a topic, create a presentation, analyze information, or collaborate with classmates online. These activities help students become more confident using technology. They also teach students how to find reliable information and communicate clearly.

Online courses can help students discover what they might want to do in the future. A learner interested in science can explore virtual experiments or attend online talks by professionals. Someone curious about art, business, or computer programming can try introductory courses in those subjects. These experiences give students a chance to test their interests before choosing a career path. They can also show students what skills different careers require. As a result, students may make more thoughtful decisions about their future.

Learning online also encourages responsibility. Students often need to keep track of their schedules, assignments, and deadlines. They must remember to log in, read instructions, and ask for help when they need it. In a classroom, a teacher may provide frequent reminders, but online learners often have to take greater initiative. This helps them become more independent. It also teaches them to accept responsibility for their progress.

Strong work habits are another benefit of online education. Students learn to set goals and divide large assignments into smaller steps. They may need to work through distractions at home and stay focused on a lesson. When they make a regular study schedule, they practice consistency. Completing tasks on time builds discipline and confidence. These habits can be valuable in college, at work, and in everyday life.

Online education is not always easy. Technical problems, distractions, and limited contact with classmates can make learning challenging. However, facing these challenges can teach students patience and problem-solving. They can contact teachers, use support resources, or adjust their study routines. With guidance and effort, students can turn difficulties into opportunities to grow.

Overall, online education can prepare students for much more than exams. It helps them build practical technology and communication skills, explore career interests, and take ownership of their learning. It also encourages planning, focus, and persistence. These qualities support success in school and beyond. When students use online learning thoughtfully, it can help them become capable, responsible, and motivated individuals.

The challenge centres on the use of royal emblems and references that may be protected by law or subject to official approval. Royal insignia are not generally available for unrestricted commercial use, and some uses require consent from the relevant authorities.

It is not yet clear whether the material in question was sold, distributed, or used solely to promote the group online. The distinction could matter when assessing whether the use falls within rules governing protected symbols and marks.

Britain First has not publicly set out a detailed response to the concerns. The group has previously used patriotic imagery in its campaigns and merchandise, presenting its activities as expressions of national identity.

Legal experts say the precise design, context and purpose of each item would need to be examined. A symbol’s appearance alone may not establish a breach, while use that implies official endorsement could raise separate concerns.

The issue also highlights the difficulty of policing online content, where images can be reposted widely and quickly. Even if material is removed from a group’s own accounts, copies may remain elsewhere.

Officials responsible for royal insignia have not confirmed whether a formal complaint has been made or whether an investigation is under way. Any enforcement action would depend on the specific rules governing the symbols and the evidence available.

The controversy comes as political groups increasingly rely on branded clothing and social media imagery to attract supporters. Critics argue that invoking the monarchy can lend campaigns an appearance of national or institutional backing.

Britain First’s use of royal symbolism may therefore face both legal and reputational scrutiny. The outcome will depend on whether the relevant authorities determine that the material crossed the line from political expression into unauthorised use.

Remote learning offers many benefits for students. One of its biggest advantages is flexibility. Students can often choose when and where to complete their work. This makes it easier to balance school with family responsibilities or other activities. Learning from home also saves time because students do not have to travel to school. The extra time can be used for studying, resting, or hobbies.

Remote learning gives students access to a wide range of digital resources. They can watch recorded lessons, read online materials, and revisit explanations whenever they need to. This can help students learn at their own pace. Some students feel more comfortable asking questions through chat or email than speaking in a crowded classroom. Online classes can also help students develop useful technology skills. These skills may be valuable in college and future jobs.

Another benefit is that remote learning can connect students with teachers and courses beyond their local area. Students may be able to join classes that are not offered at their school. They can also communicate with classmates through online discussions and group projects. These activities encourage students to share ideas and work together. Remote learning can be especially helpful for students who are ill, traveling, or living far from school. It allows them to continue learning during difficult circumstances.

However, students need reliable internet access and a quiet place to study. They also need to manage their time and stay focused. With support from teachers and families, these challenges can be addressed. Remote learning is not the right choice for everyone, but it offers flexibility, resources, and new opportunities. When used well, it can help students become more independent and confident learners.

Exploring Venus is one of the most exciting challenges in space science. Often called Earth’s sister planet, Venus is similar in size and rocky composition to our home. However, its thick atmosphere and extremely hot surface make it a very different world. Studying Venus can help scientists understand how planets form and change over time.

Innovative spacecraft technology could make exploration safer and more informative. Improved heat-resistant materials may allow landers to survive on the surface for longer than earlier missions. More durable electronics could continue operating in temperatures hot enough to melt lead. Advanced balloons or aerial vehicles could explore the cooler layers of Venus’s atmosphere. These vehicles might travel for long periods while collecting information about clouds, winds, and chemicals.

New instruments could also provide a clearer picture of the planet. Radar systems can map the surface through Venus’s thick clouds, revealing mountains, plains, and possible volcanoes. Compact sensors could analyze rocks and gases, helping researchers investigate the planet’s history. Better communication systems may send more data back to Earth. Together, these technologies could answer questions that older spacecraft could not.

Venus exploration also offers benefits beyond learning about one planet. Comparing Venus with Earth may show why the two worlds developed such different climates. This knowledge could improve scientists’ understanding of climate change and the conditions that make a planet habitable. New spacecraft designs might also lead to useful advances in materials, robotics, and remote sensing.

Despite these benefits, exploring Venus remains difficult. The surface has crushing atmospheric pressure, intense heat, and corrosive chemicals in the air. Spacecraft must also travel a great distance and operate with limited power and communication. Developing equipment for these conditions can be expensive and time-consuming. A mission may fail before returning the data scientists hope to collect.

There are also challenges in planning and funding ambitious missions. Engineers must test new technologies carefully, while scientists must choose which questions are most important. International cooperation could share costs and expertise, but coordinating different teams may take time. Even so, the potential discoveries make the effort worthwhile. With creative spacecraft technology and careful planning, future missions could reveal how Venus works and what its story can teach us about Earth.

Making a decision can feel difficult, especially when the choices may affect our future. One helpful way to decide is to seek ideas and support from other people. Different people bring different experiences, values, and knowledge to a problem. Listening to these perspectives can reveal options we might not have considered. It can also help us notice risks or assumptions we overlooked. For example, a student choosing a course might ask teachers, family members, and older students for advice. Each person may offer a useful point of view. However, seeking advice does not mean letting others make the decision for us. We should compare what we hear with our own goals and values. Support from others can also make decision-making less stressful. A trusted person may help us organize our thoughts and feel more confident. They can encourage us to keep going when a choice seems challenging. Discussing a decision can improve communication and strengthen relationships, too. It is important to listen respectfully, even when opinions differ. We should also consider whether the people advising us have relevant experience and good intentions. After gathering perspectives, we can take time to reflect before choosing. In the end, combining our own judgment with thoughtful advice can lead to wiser decisions and help us learn for the future.

For many years, a strange formation on Mars has been called the “Face.” It appears in some photographs to resemble a human face looking up from the planet’s surface. This unusual image led some people to wonder whether aliens had created it. However, scientists have found strong evidence that the formation was made naturally.

The “Face” is a mesa, a raised area of land with a relatively flat top and steep sides. It lies in the Cydonia region of Mars. In 1976, NASA’s Viking 1 spacecraft took a photograph that showed shadows resembling eyes, a nose, and a mouth. The image had low resolution, and the lighting made the features look especially face-like.

Later missions took clearer pictures of the same area. These images showed that the supposed facial features were uneven and did not form a realistic face. The shape changes in appearance depending on the angle of the sunlight and the direction of the shadows. Similar patterns can occur when people recognize familiar shapes in clouds, rocks, or other random objects.

Wind, erosion, and other natural processes can gradually shape landforms on Mars. The planet’s surface has been changed by these forces over a very long time. There is no reliable evidence of structures or tools at the site that would suggest intelligent construction.

The idea of an alien-made face remains exciting to some people, and it has inspired books and discussions. Still, an intriguing possibility is not the same as a supported scientific explanation. Scientists study evidence by checking it against observations and looking for explanations that can be tested. In this case, newer photographs and geological knowledge support a natural origin.

The Mars “Face” is a good example of how our brains can find familiar images in unusual patterns. It also shows why scientists need clear evidence before drawing conclusions. Although the formation looks mysterious in certain pictures, it was almost certainly shaped by natural processes rather than aliens.

Subject: FERC Policy on ROFR Pricing After Expiration of Vintaged-Rate Agreements

Dear [Name],

I’m writing to summarize the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s approach to pricing when a right of first refusal (ROFR) applies after a vintaged-rate agreement expires. A vintaged rate is generally a negotiated rate tied to a particular project or period, rather than a rate that automatically adjusts to current costs. When the agreement ends, the parties may disagree about whether the ROFR allows the incumbent provider to retain the service at the former rate or requires a new rate. FERC’s analysis typically depends on the agreement’s language, the applicable tariff, and the circumstances surrounding the ROFR. The existence of a ROFR does not, by itself, necessarily establish that the prior rate continues indefinitely. Nor does expiration automatically mean that a replacement rate must equal the incumbent’s current cost of service. FERC may consider whether the original rate was intended to last only for the agreement’s stated term. It may also assess whether the ROFR is a right to match a competing offer, a right to continue service, or a different contractual entitlement. Those distinctions can materially affect how pricing is determined. Parties should therefore avoid assuming that a ROFR guarantees either the old rate or a particular new rate. The governing documents should be reviewed together, including any renewal, extension, and rate-adjustment provisions. If the documents leave the pricing mechanism unclear, the parties may need to negotiate or seek a determination through the appropriate FERC process. Any proposed rate must also satisfy the applicable statutory and tariff requirements. Careful drafting can reduce uncertainty by specifying the rate-setting method that applies after expiration. It is also helpful to define how competing offers, cost data, and timing will be treated. We should review the relevant agreement and tariff before reaching a conclusion about the pricing consequences in this matter.

Best,
[Your Name]

The formation on Mars known as the “Face” is a natural landform, not evidence of an artificial structure. It was first photographed by the Viking 1 spacecraft in 1976, when the image was blurry and the lighting made the hills and shadows look like a face. Later spacecraft took much sharper images from different angles. These images show an irregular, rocky surface with no clear signs of carving or construction. The apparent eyes, nose, and mouth are created by shadows and the way our brains recognize familiar patterns. This tendency to see meaningful shapes in random objects is called pareidolia. Similar face-like shapes can be seen in clouds, rocks, and other natural features on Earth. Images taken under different lighting conditions also change the appearance of the Martian formation. Scientists have found no evidence of nearby structures or artifacts that would support the idea that it was built by an intelligent civilization. The available evidence therefore shows that the “Face” is a naturally formed mesa whose appearance was exaggerated by an early, low-resolution image.

Foreign Minister Marcelo Ebrard said Mexico would respond firmly and through established diplomatic means. He also emphasized that the country would seek to protect its citizens and its sovereignty.

Media commentators echoed calls for a measured but resolute approach. Editorials described the wall order as a political gesture that risked worsening distrust between the two governments.

Some commentators urged officials to avoid retaliatory moves that could harm trade or cooperation on migration. Others said Mexico should make clear that unilateral U.S. decisions would not dictate its policies.

The dispute carries economic significance, as the United States and Mexico are closely linked through trade and supply chains. The countries also cooperate on security, migration, and regional issues.

Mexican business groups warned that heightened tensions could unsettle markets and complicate cross-border commerce. They called on both governments to separate political rhetoric from practical cooperation.

At the same time, migration advocates said a wall alone would not address the causes of migration or improve conditions for people seeking safety. They urged both countries to prioritize humane treatment and legal pathways.

The order’s announcement also prompted renewed debate in Mexico about the country’s relationship with its northern neighbor. Many voices called for unity at home, even as they differed over the best diplomatic strategy.

Government officials said they would assess the order’s details before deciding on further steps. The administration has previously maintained that Mexico would not pay for a U.S. border wall.

For now, Mexican leaders are seeking to project calm while making clear their opposition. Their challenge is to defend national dignity without closing the door to dialogue.

Personal decisions can shape our education, relationships, health, and future goals. Because these choices matter, it is useful to seek varied perspectives before deciding. Different people may notice details that we have overlooked. A trusted friend, family member, teacher, or counselor can offer a fresh point of view. Listening to people with different experiences can also help us understand how a decision might affect others. For example, someone choosing a college may benefit from hearing about costs, academic programs, campus life, and career opportunities. Considering several viewpoints can reveal options that were not obvious at first. It can also challenge assumptions that may be influencing our judgment.

However, listening to advice does not mean accepting every suggestion. People have different values, goals, and levels of knowledge. Advice that suits one person may not suit another. Some advisers may speak from limited experience, while others may have strong personal biases. It is important to consider where advice comes from and whether the person understands the situation. We should also ask what evidence supports the advice. Comparing suggestions with reliable information can help us separate useful guidance from guesswork. Taking time to reflect can prevent us from making choices simply because we feel pressured.

Careful evaluation also helps us take responsibility for our decisions. We can compare possible benefits and risks, think about our priorities, and consider the likely consequences. If advice conflicts, we can look for shared concerns or seek clarification from another reliable source. Ultimately, varied perspectives provide valuable information, but the final choice should reflect our own circumstances and values. By listening openly and evaluating advice carefully, we can make more thoughtful decisions. This approach builds confidence and helps us learn from both our successes and mistakes. Over time, it can also strengthen our ability to make independent choices.

Mara had been dead for three hundred years before anyone noticed her file was missing.

It was not, strictly speaking, missing.

It was beneath a stack of forms marked URGENT, which had been beneath a stack marked URGENT since the reign of an emperor no one remembered.

When the clerk finally found it, he stamped it DENIED.

Mara looked up from the queue. “Denied what?”

“Your appeal.”

“I never appealed.”

“Then you’re ahead of schedule.”

Hell’s bureaucracy occupied a building with no doors, only windows through which you could be told to wait.

Its corridors stretched farther whenever someone asked how long the wait would be.

Mara had arrived with a modest list of sins and a strong preference for getting things done.

The list had grown during processing.

A clerk had added “impatience with forms” after she sighed at form 8B.

Another had added “suspiciously efficient handwriting.”

By the time she reached the Appeals Department, she had been assigned a number, a supervisor, and a minor demon to monitor her posture.

The demon was kind, in the tired way of someone who had spent six centuries correcting commas.

“You can’t leave,” he whispered.

“Can’t, or aren’t allowed?”

He glanced at the ceiling, where a thousand bells rang whenever anyone asked a useful question.

Mara took that as an answer.

She waited until lunch, though Hell’s lunch breaks lasted only for employees.

Then she borrowed a red pen, a blank transfer slip, and the demon’s coat.

The coat was less a disguise than a statement of intent.

She walked past the reception desk with her chin up and her number pinned to her sleeve.

No one stopped her.

Everyone assumed someone else had approved the paperwork.

At the final checkpoint, a guard demanded her exit authorization.

Mara handed him the blank transfer slip.

He studied it, frowned, and stamped it three times.

“Keep this safe,” he said.

She ran.

Behind her, the bells began to ring, then faltered as the clerks argued over which form to file.

Mara climbed a staircase that had been labeled TEMPORARY since the beginning of time.

At the top was a small white door, unguarded and slightly open.

She stepped through and found herself beneath a blue sky.

A woman in a garden waved from beside a pear tree.

“Welcome,” she said. “Are you expected?”

Mara’s heart sank. “I don’t have the right forms.”

The woman smiled. “We don’t use forms.”

Mara waited for the catch.

There was none.

No desk appeared, no clerk emerged, and no bell rang to demand her number.

“Do I need to prove I belong here?” Mara asked.

“You’re here,” the woman said. “That’s enough for now.”

Mara sat on the grass and began to cry.

The woman sat beside her without asking her to sign anything.

For the first time in centuries, Mara had nothing to file.

It felt almost like peace.

The “Face on Mars” is a rocky mesa in the Cydonia region that looked like a face in a 1976 Viking 1 photograph. Its appearance led some people to suggest that it was an artificial monument built by aliens. However, later spacecraft images provide much clearer views of the formation. Images taken by NASA’s Mars Global Surveyor and the European Space Agency’s Mars Express show an irregular landform, not a carefully carved face. The apparent eyes, nose, and mouth in the first image are largely explained by shadows and the photograph’s low resolution. When sunlight and viewing angles change, the face-like features become much less convincing. The mesa’s shapes are consistent with natural geological processes, including erosion by wind and the breaking down of rock over time. Scientists have found no signs of tools, construction, or other nearby structures that would support the idea of a monument. Our brains also tend to recognize familiar patterns in ambiguous images, a tendency called pareidolia. The available scientific evidence therefore supports the conclusion that the Mars Face is a natural formation, not an alien creation.

Exploring Venus is important because it can teach us how planets change over time. Venus is similar to Earth in size and rocky composition, yet its surface is extremely hot and its atmosphere is thick with carbon dioxide. Studying this contrast may help scientists understand why Earth remained habitable while Venus became so hostile.

Venus also offers clues about the history of our solar system. Its mountains, plains, and volcanic features may reveal how the planet formed and whether volcanoes are still active. Scientists can study its clouds and atmosphere to learn about powerful winds, chemical reactions, and the planet’s possible past climate. Some researchers also investigate whether Venus once had liquid water, although this remains uncertain.

Exploration is difficult because Venus has crushing atmospheric pressure and temperatures hot enough to melt some metals. Its clouds contain corrosive sulfuric acid, while the dense atmosphere makes communication and observation challenging. Spacecraft sent to the surface have survived for only a short time, so engineers must build equipment that can withstand extreme conditions. Orbiters can study the planet for longer, but they cannot easily provide detailed measurements from the ground.

Despite these obstacles, new missions and improved technology may make Venus easier to investigate. Radar can map the surface through the clouds, and future probes could measure its rocks and atmosphere more precisely. Exploring Venus is scientifically valuable because it helps us understand both our planetary neighbor and Earth’s own climate. Though the challenges are great, the discoveries could change what we know about how rocky planets evolve.

The anniversary issue drew attention to how public figures and historical narratives are remembered through national symbols. The first time the adventurers came for me, I was already dead.

They kicked in the door of my observatory and shouted my name like a curse. My name is Elian Voss, and I had once been a healer. The villagers had called me kind before the fever took their children. Then they called me useless when my remedies failed. Afterward, they called me a monster when I found a way to make death wait.

I did not raise the dead to build an army. I raised my wife, Mara, because I could not bear to bury her twice. She woke frightened, but she knew my face. For seven years, we lived quietly beneath the old chapel, tending the graves and keeping the fever away. We harmed no one. We asked for no tribute. Then Baron Hadrik’s hunters found us.

They came at dawn with torches and silver chains. Mara had never learned to fight, so I stood between her and their blades. One hunter struck her with a sun-bright spear. She fell, and the borrowed breath left her. I begged them to stop. They answered by setting fire to the chapel.

I escaped with her ashes and the names of those who had taken her. The baron told the kingdom that I had slaughtered his men for sport. He offered gold to anyone brave enough to destroy me. So the brave came, one company after another, each certain the songs had chosen them.

The latest band arrived dressed in polished steel. Their leader, a young woman with a red plume, called herself the Dawn’s Hand. She demanded that I surrender the relic hidden in my tower. I told her I had no relic. She called me a liar and raised her sword.

Behind her, an archer aimed at the villagers sheltering in my cellar. That was when I understood the shape of the story they had brought with them. They had been promised glory, and I had been promised nothing but another grave.

I broke the floor beneath the archer, not his bones. I wrapped the leader’s sword in vines and took the weapon from her hand. My servants, all of them people I had once failed to save, formed a line at my side. None attacked until the adventurers did.

When the red-plumed woman saw the villagers alive, her certainty faltered. I showed her the baron’s letters, each one ordering another raid and another lie. She read them in silence. Then she lowered her empty hand and asked why I had not told the kingdom the truth.

I almost laughed. I had tried, years ago, before the first torch was lit. The baron had called my warning a threat, and the kingdom had called his word justice. So I gave the woman the letters and sent her home with her companions.

They returned at midnight, not to kill me, but to open the baron’s gates. By sunrise, his banners were down. I did not take his throne, and I did not raise his corpse. I only buried the dead he had left behind.

The songs still call me a lich, and perhaps they are right. But when the next adventurer comes seeking a monster, I will ask who sent them, and what they have been promised. Then I will give them the truth before I give them a reason to fear me.

Autonomous vehicles are no longer just an idea from science fiction. They are being tested and developed in many parts of the world. These vehicles use cameras, sensors, and computer systems to understand their surroundings. Their growing appeal comes from the promise of making everyday travel safer and easier.

One major benefit is that autonomous vehicles may reduce accidents. Human drivers can become distracted, tired, or impatient, while automated systems can monitor the road continuously. They can also react quickly to changing conditions. Although the technology is not perfect, continued improvements could help prevent many collisions.

Autonomous vehicles may also give people more freedom. Older adults and people with disabilities who cannot drive easily could travel more independently. Families might find it simpler to arrange trips for children or relatives. Passengers could use travel time to read, relax, or complete small tasks instead of concentrating on the road.

These vehicles could make commuting less stressful as well. People often feel frustrated by traffic, parking, and long drives. An autonomous car could find a route, follow traffic rules, and park with little help from its passenger. Shared self-driving vehicles might also reduce the number of cars needed in busy cities.

There are still important concerns to address. Autonomous vehicles must be tested carefully, and their computer systems need strong protection from hackers. Governments will also need clear rules about safety and responsibility. Even with these challenges, the potential benefits are appealing. If the technology develops responsibly, autonomous vehicles could make daily travel safer, more convenient, and more accessible.
