BlackBerry is bringing back the familiar feel of a physical keyboard with the BlackBerry Classic, a smartphone aimed squarely at business users. The device revives design cues from the company’s earlier handsets, including a compact screen and a row of navigation keys. Its full QWERTY keyboard is the main attraction, offering users tactile feedback for typing emails and messages.

The Classic runs BlackBerry 10, the company’s operating system for its newer phones. It includes the BlackBerry Hub, which gathers messages and notifications in one place, along with features for managing work and personal accounts. The phone also supports popular Android apps through BlackBerry’s software ecosystem, though app availability may vary.

BlackBerry is positioning the Classic as a practical tool for customers who value productivity over large displays and entertainment features. Its focus on secure communications and device management is intended to appeal to companies and government organizations. The company hopes the familiar keyboard will also attract former BlackBerry owners who have moved to touchscreen phones.

The launch comes as BlackBerry faces strong competition from Apple and Android manufacturers, whose devices dominate the smartphone market. Many businesses now support a mix of platforms, making it harder for BlackBerry to rely on its traditional corporate base. The Classic’s smaller screen and keyboard-first design may set it apart, but could limit its appeal to consumers accustomed to larger phones.

The device is part of BlackBerry’s effort to concentrate on areas where it believes it still has an advantage: security, messaging and workplace productivity. Whether those strengths are enough to win back users remains uncertain. For now, the Classic offers a clear alternative for people who prefer physical keys to typing on glass.

An inquest is to examine the mental-health monitoring and suicide-prevention measures in place before prisoner Stefano Brizzi died at Belmarsh prison. Brizzi, who was serving a life sentence, was found dead in his cell at the high-security prison in south-east London in February 2017. He had been convicted of murdering civil servant Lee Rigby’s former colleague, George Smith, in 2016. The inquest will consider the care Brizzi received while in custody and the decisions made by prison staff in the period before his death. It is expected to hear evidence about assessments of his mental health and any signs that he might harm himself. The proceedings will also examine whether his risk of suicide was identified and managed appropriately. Questions may include how often he was observed and whether relevant information was shared among staff. Belmarsh is one of the UK’s most secure prisons and holds some prisoners assessed as posing a high risk. The case is likely to draw attention to the challenges of providing mental-health care in a prison setting. Prisoners can face acute distress, while access to specialist support and consistent monitoring can be difficult to maintain. An inquest does not determine criminal or civil liability, but it can establish how someone died and identify lessons for the future. The coroner will consider evidence from prison personnel, healthcare staff and other witnesses. Findings could include recommendations aimed at reducing the risk of similar deaths.

Maritime service offers more than a career at sea; it can broaden a person’s understanding of the world. Sailors and other maritime workers may travel to ports and coastlines they have never seen before. Each new place introduces them to different landscapes, languages, customs, and ways of life. Meeting people from other cultures can challenge assumptions and encourage respect for differences. Travel also teaches practical skills, such as adapting to unfamiliar situations and communicating across language barriers.

Life at sea can offer recreation as well as work. In their free time, crew members may fish, exercise, read, or enjoy the ocean’s scenery. When ships are in port, they may explore historic sites, local markets, and natural attractions. These experiences can help people discover new interests and appreciate the beauty of the sea. Recreational activities can also strengthen friendships among crew members who rely on one another during long voyages.

Maritime service can also provide opportunities to help others. Ships may deliver food, medicine, and supplies to communities that are difficult to reach by land. During emergencies, maritime crews can support search-and-rescue missions or transport people away from danger. This work shows how important cooperation and preparation are when lives are at stake. Helping communities in need can give service members a strong sense of purpose.

Together, travel, recreation, and humanitarian aid make maritime service an experience of learning and contribution. People who serve at sea can gain confidence, broaden their perspectives, and build lasting skills. They may return home with stories of distant places and a deeper understanding of global connections. For many, the greatest reward is knowing that the sea has helped them grow while giving them chances to serve others.

The Electoral College is the system the United States uses to choose its president. Each state receives electoral votes based largely on its population, and candidates need a majority of those votes to win. One argument for keeping the system is that it gives states a role in national elections. Supporters also say it encourages candidates to build support across different regions instead of focusing only on the largest cities. In addition, the Electoral College can produce a clear result even when the popular vote is very close. However, the system has important drawbacks. A candidate can win the presidency while receiving fewer votes nationwide than their opponent. This has happened several times and can make voters feel that their ballots do not count equally. The winner-take-all rules used by most states also mean that many votes in states seen as safely Republican or Democratic receive little attention. As a result, candidates may focus heavily on a small number of competitive states. Changing to a national popular vote could make every vote count equally, but it might also create new disputes over recounts and election rules. Overall, the Electoral College offers a federal approach to choosing a president, but its unequal effects make a strong case for reform.

Backpage, the online classifieds site that once carried a large volume of adult-services ads, has faced allegations that it profited from sex trafficking and prostitution. Prosecutors and survivors have said the site’s advertising business helped facilitate commercial sex, including the exploitation of minors. Backpage has disputed claims that it knowingly enabled trafficking, arguing that it removed illegal content and operated as a publisher of third-party advertisements. The dispute raised questions about how much responsibility online platforms bear for material posted by users. In 2018, federal authorities seized Backpage and charged its former executives with crimes including facilitating prostitution and money laundering. The site’s co-founder, Michael Lacey, and other former executives faced separate criminal proceedings. In 2023, Lacey was convicted in Arizona on money-laundering charges, while jurors did not reach verdicts on several other counts. Backpage’s former chief executive, Carl Ferrer, had previously pleaded guilty to state charges related to prostitution and agreed to cooperate with authorities. Survivors have described being advertised on the site while they were minors and say the resulting cases underscored the harms of online sex trafficking. The legal battles also unfolded amid debate over Section 230, a federal law that generally shields internet platforms from liability for user-posted content. Advocates say the case demonstrates the need for stronger protections, while free-speech groups warn that broad liability could suppress lawful online speech.

South Africa’s High Court has rejected prosecutors’ bid to appeal a ruling that requires former president Jacob Zuma to face corruption charges. The decision keeps in place an earlier judgment allowing the long-running prosecution to proceed. The charges relate to a multibillion-rand arms deal struck in the late 1990s, before Zuma became president. Prosecutors allege that Zuma accepted bribes linked to the deal, allegations he denies. The case also involves French arms company Thales, which faces charges alongside him. Zuma has repeatedly sought to have the prosecution halted, arguing that the proceedings are unfair. The dispute has moved through South Africa’s courts for years, with repeated applications and appeals delaying a trial. In rejecting the latest appeal request, the High Court declined to reopen its ruling for consideration by a higher court. The decision does not determine Zuma’s guilt or innocence. It means the prosecution can continue, subject to any further legal challenges. Zuma, who served as president from 2009 to 2018, has described the case as politically motivated. Prosecutors have maintained that they are pursuing the charges through the courts.

The Welsh Government is facing scrutiny over losses incurred when it sold a group of shop properties in Pontypridd bought for a regeneration project that never went ahead.

The properties, on and around Taff Street, were acquired as part of plans to reshape the town centre and create a new retail and leisure destination. The scheme was expected to bring investment and new activity to the area. But the proposed development did not proceed, leaving the government with buildings it had purchased for a project that remained unrealised.

The properties were later sold for substantially less than the amount paid to acquire them, according to figures disclosed about the transactions. The difference has prompted questions about how the purchases were valued, why the regeneration plan failed and how the government managed the assets while they were in public ownership.

The government has said the acquisitions were intended to support the wider regeneration of Pontypridd. It has also pointed to the challenges facing town centres and development projects, including changing market conditions and the complexity of assembling sites.

Opposition politicians and local observers have called for a fuller account of the costs. They argue that taxpayers should be told how much was spent on buying and maintaining the properties, what income was received from them and how the sale price was determined.

The losses are particularly sensitive because the investment was made in the name of regeneration, a priority for communities seeking to revive high streets and attract jobs. Pontypridd, like many Welsh towns, has faced pressure from changing shopping habits, vacant premises and uncertainty over future development.

Questions have also been raised about whether the buildings could have been used temporarily while plans were reconsidered. Short-term uses, such as workspace, community facilities or pop-up shops, can help keep town-centre properties active, though they may not cover the costs of ownership.

The Welsh Government has not described the project as a completed regeneration scheme, and the sale does not in itself show that the original ambitions for the town have been abandoned. However, the gap between the purchase and sale prices has intensified concerns about the decision-making behind the investment.

Any assessment of the losses will depend on the full financial picture, including transaction costs, maintenance, rental income and the condition of the buildings. The timing of the sale and the state of the property market may also have affected the price achieved.

Local residents and businesses are likely to want clarity on what happens next. Vacant or underused shops can undermine confidence in a high street, while a credible plan for new activity could help restore it.

The episode adds to wider scrutiny of public-sector regeneration spending in Wales. Such projects often involve significant risk, but critics say that clear milestones and transparent reporting are essential when public money is used to buy property.

The government’s challenge is now to explain why the planned development did not materialise and what lessons have been learned. It must also set out how future investment in Pontypridd will deliver visible benefits rather than leave the town with another uncertain chapter in its regeneration story.

Transportation choices and urban policies shape daily life as well as the health of the environment. Cars offer convenience, privacy, and the freedom to travel on flexible schedules. They can be especially useful for people who live far from work or have mobility needs. However, heavy car use contributes to traffic congestion, air pollution, and greenhouse gas emissions. Long commutes can also take time away from family, rest, and recreation. Roads and parking lots occupy land that could otherwise support homes, parks, or businesses.

Public transportation provides another way to move around cities. Buses, trains, and trams can carry many people using less space than an equal number of cars. When public transit is reliable and affordable, it can help people reach jobs, schools, and services without owning a vehicle. It may also reduce pollution and traffic, especially when powered by clean energy. Yet crowded vehicles, limited routes, and infrequent service can make transit inconvenient. People with disabilities, young children, or late work schedules may face additional barriers.

Urban policies influence which transportation choices are practical. Cities can invest in frequent transit, safe sidewalks, protected bike lanes, and accessible stations. They can also design neighborhoods so that homes, shops, schools, and workplaces are closer together. These changes make walking, cycling, and transit easier while giving residents more options. Policies such as congestion fees or limited parking can discourage unnecessary car trips, but they should be introduced fairly. People who lack good alternatives should not be unfairly burdened.

A balanced transportation system serves different needs while reducing harm to people and the planet. Governments should listen to residents and improve transit before expecting everyone to drive less. Cleaner vehicles can help, but they do not solve congestion or the land use required for roads. By combining thoughtful urban planning with safe and dependable transportation, cities can become healthier and more accessible. The choices made today will shape the quality of urban life for generations.
